en: Commentary on the *Pramāṇavārttika*, Chapter 2: The Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition (Pramāṇasiddhi), Section 1. Section One.
The first section of the *Vārttika*, beginning with the "efficient-force of the injunction" (*vidhibhāvanā*),
is the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(1) Non-contradictory cognition is the means of valid cognition.
Homage to the Buddha.
Here begins the first chapter (the first *āhnika*);
in this commentary, the readings from the Tibetan translation are provided.
Having prostrated to the Sugata, the Protector, who is the authority for this treatise and who seeks the welfare of the world.
Out of compassion for people bewildered by fallacious reasoning, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is set forth according to the rules.

(1) Generally, speakers who possess extensive elaborations on the subject at hand are not seen at all to speak with clarity when they intend to summarize the ultimate truth, having discarded the trivial sequence [of arguments].

Therefore, in this work, my intellect—with its mind uplifted—is applied toward the consciousness of the fortunate ones whose intellects are utterly pure, so that their minds may be freed from the absence of a prolix sequence. (2)

Here, at the beginning of the treatise, the praise of the Blessed One is expressed by way of his perfection of cause and fruit and his status as an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūta*), because this constitutes the subject matter of the treatise.
For it is the Blessed One alone who is established here as the authoritative person;
therein, the "cause" consists of the perfection of intention and application, with respect to conventional means of valid cognition (*saṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*).
The intention is the desire for the welfare of the world;
the application is the teaching of the world, which constitutes the state of being a Teacher; and the fruit is the perfection of one's own and others' aims.
The perfection of one's own welfare consists in being a Sugata, based on three kinds of meaning: excellence in its essential nature, like a well-formed object;
and the sense of non-return, like a fever that has been completely cured.
The perfection of the welfare of others is like a jar completely full, in the sense of being entirely complete; "saviorhood" (*tāyitva*) arises from the rescuing of the world;
and it possesses the quality of non-parinirvāṇa for the sake of the continuity [of the lineage].
Having prostrated to the Blessed One who is thus constituted, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is set forth;

for the apprehension of the objects of knowledge (prameya) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition, and the Blessed One alone is the means of valid cognition because he possesses the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition.
That by which something is correctly cognized is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therein, he indicates the general definition of a means of valid cognition: "A means of valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge."

Knowledge is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because when it exists, the establishment of a correct apprehension (*pramiti*) occurs; it is non-contradictory (*avisamvādin*), for if there were contradiction, the opposite would be the case. Indeed, the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects and so forth acquire the status of reality only when they are characterized by knowledge that is free from contradiction.
For everyone who is engaged in the search for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does so seeking non-contradiction;
for a means of valid cognition is indeed non-contradictory, since the establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) occurs when that [means] exists.

Now, [one might object]: non-contradiction is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that cognition which serves as the means of proof; and when that nature is known, it is already known—so what is there to be examined?
Or, is it that there is no self-awareness of its own nature?
In that case, it follows that there is no means of valid cognition at all;
and this position is not tenable for you. [This concludes the section on] non-contradiction.
That is incorrect;
for the validity or the correspondence of a cognition does not consist in its own intrinsic nature alone, but rather—
Non-contradiction is the stability of purposeful action.
Indeed, this is not a means of valid cognition merely upon the apprehension of the nature of the cognition itself;
rather, it is the accomplishment of an action— such as burning or cooking— and the stability, non-deviation, or establishment of that [action].
And that causal efficiency is yet to come, not present at that time;
therefore, its connection [with the object] is not determined by the mere awareness of its own nature (*svarūpasamvedanamātra*).
Is it not the case that being connected with that [efficiency] is simply its own nature? [No,] it does not exist [at that time].
How then is it not the case that there is the ascertainment of the mere self-awareness of its own nature?
This is not so.

The cognition of a relation residing in two [terms] does not arise from the perception of a single form; rather, the awareness of a relation occurs when there is the grasping of the essential natures of both.
How, then, can that knowledge exist at the time of [the object's] engagement?
We shall explain this later.
If the first means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is for the sake of attaining purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then that attainment of purposeful action must itself be a means of valid cognition;
for there is no attainment of purposeful action through what is not a means of valid cognition. Therefore, it is a means of valid cognition.
If one were to say that the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) must therefore be sought from something else, leading to an infinite regress, this is not correct.

For if the validity of the preceding [cognition] depends on the absence of a subsequent purposeful action, then why would that [subsequent cognition] lack validity due to the absence of its own subsequent purposeful action? (4)
That in which the stability of causal efficacy is not established by another is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
but where there is the experience of causal efficacy itself from its own side,
that is all the more certainly a means of valid cognition.
Since non-contradiction (*avisamvādana*) is defined generally as the establishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*), one might object:
"Surely this kind of purposeful action, such as burning or cooking, is possible even in dreams; and in the cognition of a yellow conch and the like, [such action occurs].
However, in the case of a cognition whose object is sound, there is no purposeful action, whether intrinsic or extrinsic, because of the absence of purposeful action."
Therefore, it is argued that "a cognition which is uncontradicted is a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*);
yet this too is incorrect, because even in the case of verbal [cognition], there is the communication of the speaker's intention.
Non-contradiction;
verbal cognition has sound as its object,
but by the word "also" (api), it is indicated that this applies elsewhere as well.
The meaning is this:
every cognition would be valid simply by virtue of the mere awareness of its own nature.
Now, since it is uncontradicted cognition, why is that [validity] not present even in dreams and the like?
It is [present] by virtue of the mere nature of cognition itself.
For the occurrence of mere cognition is indeed the same in all cases, whether it arises from a dream or from other types of awareness;
however, that [mere cognition] does not accomplish the goal of human life.
If, on the other hand, [the criterion is] being an uncontradicted cognition, that too is equally the same [in all cases].
If it is argued that [the dream cognition] is sublated by the waking cognition, what indeed is this so-called "sublation"?

If it is maintained that another [cognition] makes known the absence of an object, how could a cognition that is active toward its own object make known an absence? For an absence is not produced by another cognition— whether it be dream-cognition or any other—
at that time, because it perishes of its own accord.
Nor is sublation perceived when cognition has perished due to the closing of the eyes;
for sublation— defined as the communication of non-existence— is not the removal of an object by another cognition.
Furthermore, a cognition that has engaged its own object is not capable of effecting the removal of another object;
for it is the nature of cognitions to establish their own objects through their own form,
whereas the seizing of another's object is the characteristic of a king.
1. The state of being a sublater [does not exist]. How, then, could there be the relationship between the sublated and the sublater?
Not in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, validity consists precisely in being uncontradicted;

hence, that in which there is no purposeful action (arthakriyā) is invalid, whether it is known by itself or by another that no activity arises therein. That is invalid; in reality, there is no distinction between dream and non-dream.
This so-called distinction between dream and non-dream is merely conventional usage;
likewise, it will be stated that the distinction between valid and invalid cognition is also such,
for that [distinction] does not constitute a stable causal efficacy due to the absence of immutability.
Causal efficacy is determined merely by mental cultivation, as in a dream;
yet there is no satisfaction therein.
If, however, it were uncontradicted, there would be an infinite regress.
First, there is non-sublation everywhere;
then, there is non-sublation at a later time;
and even in that case, why would there be non-sublation at a still later time?
The appearance of a sublater is possible for every cognition; however, since the absence of a sublater can also be suspected in that case, what [is gained]?
Furthermore, cognitions such as that of a yellow conch-shell are not valid cognitions at all, because there is an absence of the attainment of corresponding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
When the accomplishment of purposeful action is established through mere configuration alone, inference is indeed another means of valid cognition;
for it is thus:
That which appears as the cognition of a yellow conch and so forth is of such a nature that it is not devoid of configuration;
this is an inference because it is observed to be so in other cases, and thus it is likewise here.
Regarding the appearance (*ābhāsa*):

one for whom no deviation has ever been perceived will certainly encounter disappointment when proceeding according to his intention; however, one who is aware of the possibility of deviation acts only after due deliberation.
First, only the configuration is apprehended;
regarding that which follows, there is either doubt or error.
Therefore, the inference pertains to the configuration.
Regarding the doubt expressed as "elsewhere," these two types of cognition— both valid and invalid—
are explained by this [example] of the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel,
as we shall further explain.
Now, as for how this duality is apprehended,
we shall also explain that:
however, knowledge whose object is sound is a means of valid cognition because it communicates intention.
Verification (*saṃvādana*) is simply the communication of the nature of the intended purposeful action;
in this context, the accomplishment of the nature of the object of knowledge itself is considered the "action. Even in the case of a painting, the result is fully accomplished by mere sight.
Indeed, nowhere is a cognition of purposeful action found that is other than the awareness of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*).
For forms and the like are solely intent upon the self-awareness of their own nature; the cognition having them as its object is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding another [object].
Since the mere awareness of that [object's] own nature is common to all cognitions, there is no application of conventional means of valid cognition.
4. The accomplishment of action (*kriyāsiddhi*):

Therefore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which has as its object a future thing (*bhāvyartha*) and which ranges over other objects—effects worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) through superimposition (*adhyāropa*).
For the investigation of what is a means of valid cognition and what is not is solely for the sake of attaining another object that is a future thing.

And just as a distinct object, such as touch and so forth, does not enter into the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of color and so forth, likewise the future intrinsic nature also [does not enter] from the perspective of ultimate reality;
however, through superimposition, there is an identity with that [present nature], and by means of that, the correspondence of even another object is said to reside in the cognition.

However, where that very [entity] constitutes causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is indeed no dispute; in that case, the superimposition of unity occurs because it is the cause of that future nature, whereas in other cases, such as touch and so forth, it occurs because they depend upon that same single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Thus, there is no distinction between the two.

However, where there is no intended purposeful action—as when one obtains the purposeful action of [mistaking] a mirage from a cognition apprehending water—that is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
For this very reason, he said:
"In the case of verbal [cognition] as well, [it is valid] because it communicates the speaker's intention."
5) Investigation;
6) Just as contact and so forth have distinct objects.
7. Abandoned: (1) in the case of cognition, the desired causal efficiency is absent; (2) in the case of a mirage.
This is also the case elsewhere, such as with a painting and so forth;
likewise, there is no status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the cognition of a jar when a cloth is obtained, nor in the succession of cognitions of silver regarding mother-of-pearl,
because there is an absence of non-discrepancy with one's intention.

Everything is called a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not contradict one's intended purpose, and not merely from the production of a consciousness that is either of the same or a different class. Such is the nature even of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). However, in reality, [the definition of a valid means of cognition] consists merely in the production of a consciousness of a different class. This is the case for a subverting means of cognition.

If it is argued that the production of a cognition of a different class constitutes a sublation, then why would the cognition of a cloth not be logically considered a sublation of the cognition of a jar?
If you say "no" because some specific cognition is intended as the sublater,
then that very cognition [of "it is not"] has arrived at being distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If there were cognition of another form, it would follow [absurdly] that there is no distinction; if there were cognition of its absence, the connection "it belongs to that" would not hold.
For an absence is perceived by way of its own nature, and the nature of an absence is not perceived as being related to a jar or other such things.
For when a jar is being perceived, there can be no relation of non-existence to it,
because at that time there is an absence of its non-existence;
indeed, there is no death for Devadatta while he is still alive.
However, when [the object] is not being perceived, it is impossible to apprehend the absence [of that object] as connected with the jar;
for, as in the case of the relation of cause and effect, the cognition [of the effect] occurs only after the cause exists.

Subsequently, when its own nature is apprehended through the sequence of its perception, there occurs the grasping of the relationship between cause and effect; thus, the apprehension of the relationship arises in the form: "when this exists, that exists" (bhāve sati abhāvaḥ), and "when this is absent, that is absent" (abhāve sati bhāvaḥ).
This too is incorrect, because:
A relation with absolute non-existence is not established for anything; for that non-existence does not exist while existence is present, nor is there a reversal of this state.
Furthermore:

The nature of cause and effect is perceived without that [intrinsic nature]; however, non-existence is not perceived without existence. (18) As for the emptiness of a location, it is uniform everywhere;
therein, the distinction of prior non-existence and so forth is absolutely impossible.
19.5 But as for the distinction:

Just as the difference between objects is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too is the difference between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other types of non-existence perceived by the senses.

(20) If it is held that the cognition of that [non-existence] occurs through the means of knowledge called "non-existence" (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), then [we ask]: of which means of knowledge is there non-existence? For if [non-existence] is known through the absence of a means of knowledge, (21) why is it not [known] for every existent thing, and why not at all for one who is asleep? If a cognition that grasps non-existence is accepted as being itself non-existence, (22) [then this leads to an infinite regress].

Why is this [absence] not perceived by anyone even without the cognition of an entity? If this very [cognition] were the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that [perception], then there would be no certainty regarding absence.
(23) In reality, there is no perception of an absence that is distinct [from the entity]; the cognition "this is not here" perceives its distinctness [from the locus].
(24) How could this [cognition] arise? Not from the sense faculty without recollection; for the cognition of absence is possible through the conjunction of the sense faculty and memory. (25)

This [non-existence] is indeed directly perceived through the functioning of the sense organ according to the absence [of the object]; for if the sense organ were operating on something else, it could not be the cause of the cognition of that other thing.

(26) How can this mental cognition of non-existence be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? It is a means of valid knowledge because it is non-contradictory; it is simply another form of valid cognition.

(27) For there is no contradiction regarding a non-existence that is distinct [from the locus]. Contradiction occurs when [the object] is absent; that contradiction is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (28)
Without the notion of existence, that apprehension of the "exclusive" (kevala) would always occur; the cognition [of an object] through non-entry into another is the apprehension of the exclusive.
It is held that in the case of perception involving the apprehension of the exclusive, there is the possibility of non-correspondence (visamvāda).
Therefore, this non-apprehension [of the object] otherwise is indeed a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself;
[it occurs] when there is the direct perception of the mere absence (*kevalābhāva*).

[Objection: But how can there be a cognition of a mere absence without the cognition of a mere presence? [Response: That [cognition of a mere presence] also does not exist without a cognition of a mere absence; thus the situation is equal.

(31) Or, just as a mere absence is cognized without a positive entity (*bhāva*), so too a positive entity [is cognized without an absence]; if it were not so, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. (32) [Objection:
If you say that there is no cognition of a mere [entity] without the cognition of its absence...
It is the same [in the case of negation]: there is no cognition of absence without the cognition of the locus alone.
Or else, how can the "mere absence" exist without another absence?
For if one were to postulate an absence even in that case, there would be an infinite regress.
That very perception, which is a cognition consisting of non-apprehension dependent upon a remembered object, is the means of proving non-existence;

however, the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence occurs only in certain cases and not elsewhere due to the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—this distinction is understood. [This is] the additional portion.
Therefore, just as a waking cognition sublates a dream cognition, so too does error [sublate it] through the apprehension of the "mere" [object]; this is the logical principle.
Consequently, the claim that verbal cognition possesses validity because it communicates the speaker's intention is hereby refuted.
Furthermore, auditory cognition would be invalid because it does not accord with others.

But what is the point of the Blessed One being an authority (*pramāṇabhūta*), since all human goals are accomplished through conventional means of valid cognition (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*) alone? This is not so.

Perception operates regarding the apprehension of its own nature, while inference operates elsewhere; this [distinction] will be explained later, as well as the invalidity of another [means of knowledge]. First of all, perception does not operate with respect to the next world and so forth.
It will be demonstrated that this is because [perception] consists only in the apprehension of the thing's own nature;
however, inference does not exist without the apprehension of a relation,
and such a relation cannot be grasped by one who knows only a portion [of things].
For the apprehension of a relation cannot occur through perception, which is by nature restricted to the awareness of its own form;
if the apprehension of a relation were achieved solely through inference, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

However, perception and inference are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) merely for the sake of conventional usage, and this is only insofar as they are conducive to the proof of an omniscient being, and not otherwise.
This will be demonstrated later (1) 3 in the context of conventional usage— [the term] "additional."

Now, one might object: "Even if the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) characterized as perception and inference do not operate regarding the next world and so forth—since perception has only the thing's own nature as its object and inference depends upon the apprehension of a relation—the scripture (*śāstra*) is not like that; therefore, the desired goal is established by it alone."
"How is it that the Blessed One is established as an authoritative source (pramāṇabhūta)?
To this it is replied:
"That object which appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker's activity [is the meaning]."
In that case, the authority of the word is not based on the reality of the object;
for it will be established later that words are not authorless (apauruṣeya), but rather that they possess authorship (pauruṣeyatā).
And in that regard, the speaker's activity is the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*);
the object which is intended by the speaker and which appears in the consciousness of the listener is the meaning (*artha*).

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates precisely upon that [object], and the function of the word (*śabda*) likewise operates upon that very object; otherwise, if it were to convey what was intended in one way while presenting it in another, it would be acting without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakārī*), and thus its lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) would be all the more evident.
And that [omniscience] intended [by us] is not universal omniscience;
otherwise, there would be no mutual contradiction among the scriptures,
nor could mutually contradictory matters be put into practice.

If the goal were accomplished merely by performing [an action], then scripture would be useless as a means of valid knowledge, because the result would then follow even from performing according to one's own whims; and if that were so, there would be no dispute, and one might proceed however one desired. For indeed, there is no performance whatsoever that is fruitless for anyone anywhere. (34)
Therefore, the authority of a word resides in the object of the speaker’s activity and is not dependent upon the actual nature of the thing itself,
provided the speaker is not omniscient;
even in the case of what is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), when an object appears in the mind, one understands that object by oneself.
But when it concerns the commentator, the object of the speaker’s activity is the commentator himself;
and that meaning which appears in the intellect [of the hearer] is not the very same meaning [intended by the original author].
Otherwise, since every desired purpose would be accomplished [merely by hearing], no one would ever engage in practical application.

If it is argued that this is not so because that object is presented solely as something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), then at that time it does not exist in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*); thus, there can be no cognition of it, because in the case of the cognition of another [object], there is an absence of a relationship [to the object in question]. Consequently, there is only doubt.

Furthermore, the object that is cognized is already established; one does not act for the sake of what is already established, nor is one engaged in what has not been apprehended. Therefore, validity cannot be explained as being based on the actual nature of the object.
2. Thus, the true meaning [is as follows]:
3. The rejection of the injunction regarding the desired object. (2)
But surely, the injunction (*niyoga*) is not the meaning of the sentence, because one has the cognition "I am enjoined"; therefore, it is from the injunction itself that one is unable to desist.
The term *koyanniyoga* means that the prefix *ni-* signifies "without remainder," while the meaning of *yoga* is "junction" (*yukti*); thus,
*niyoga* is a junction that is exhaustive.
The state of being without remainder [of the injunction] is due to the absence of even the slightest non-conformity;
for an injunction (*niyoga*) is that which must necessarily be performed,
and those for whom the injunction is the authority proceed to act solely through the comprehension of that injunction.
Regarding this,
he says "the activity of the speaker," and so forth;
the meaning is as follows:

4. Commentators have declared that *niyoga*, *bhāvanā*, and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) are the injunction (*vidhi*). [However,] things such as those mounted on a machine would not be means for accomplishing a purpose by virtue of their own nature.
Therefore, whatever appears to someone in whatever way—that is the meaning of the sentence according to that appearance; this is not the true reality of the object.
And in whatever way one explains it, in that way the word does not become defective, yet the reality of the object does not abide in that manner;
and furthermore—
If cessation were caused by something appointed [as its cause], then it would follow that everything [would cease] from that;
for space, being of such a nature, would not be non-space for anyone.
37. Even if activity is one's own nature, if it is understood otherwise due to error, who will establish the distinction between error and non-error?
If, because of error, one does not engage even with words that enjoin [action],...
This being the case, the postulation of error is not contradicted even while [the action] is proceeding;
for just as this person, being mistaken, does not act out of hatred and so forth, so too another acts out of partiality toward that [object], and thus these two cases are equal.
Furthermore, it is not the case that one acts with the thought, "I am commanded."
Since there is no engagement in an action that yields no fruit,
one engages even in a fruitless command from a fierce lord out of fear of misfortune;
and this misfortune is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But here, there is no other means of valid cognition;
if the injunction were thus rendered useless, so be it— what is the fault?
For indeed, nothing that is observed can be called "impossible";
for one who acts with foresight would not be considered a prudent person if they were enjoined toward a fruitless undertaking—this is the criticism [of such a position].
But in the case of that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), however...
If it is argued that there is no fault here, since it is not logical for a non-human [Vedic] source to be purposeless;
There is no means of valid cognition here other than [the Veda] being authorless, because such [a means] is not seen elsewhere;
and if one were to act merely from an authorless injunction, then the statement "one desiring heaven" would be fruitless, as it would result in the injunction "one should sacrifice."
Since the injunction is understood from the mere statement of the injunction itself,
if one who desires a result is shown that result,
then it is the result alone that should be presented to him; what is the use of the injunction?
If it is argued that [the Veda] will proceed of its own accord due to the desire for results,
and that this objection does not apply because it is non-human (apauruṣeya) even if it lacks coherence,
then the same objection would not apply to an injunction that is fruitless; thus, a useless Veda is not tenable.
Furthermore,
if it is maintained that the injunction applies to all things— the object to be enjoined, the locus of the injunction, and the enjoiner— then the meaning of the word does not remain fixed. (38)
One should consider whose duty this so-called *niyoga* is;
for *niyoga* is certainly not perceived as independent like a cloth or other such objects.
Therefore, in this injunction (*niyama*), it must be the duty of one among the factors such as the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and others, since no other mode [of existence] is perceived.

For how could that which possesses the nature of being an object of injunction be something to be performed? If even that which is already established were to be performed, there would be no cessation of performance.
Indeed, that which is fully accomplished cannot be performed;
for "performance" in that context refers to a specific action.
Furthermore, the production of its own nature, or indeed any specific action, is entirely purposeless;
for what purposeful effect could an action have upon that which is already fully accomplished?
But to say that the production of its own nature belongs to that which is already perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) is contradictory;
for there exists no further non-perfected state in that which is already perfected,
since it is impossible for that which is not yet perfected to possess the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of a perfected entity.
For whatever is perceived as having a certain nature possesses that very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
and it cannot be perceived if it is unestablished [prior to its perception].
If you argue that it is perceived later, [we reply:]...
That is incorrect because:

"Since it is impossible for that which has already been produced to possess an unproduced nature, it cannot be perceived later as having such a nature; for perception functions by grasping the present form. (40)
Indeed, perception, which functions by grasping a present form, is not capable of observing prior and posterior forms;
therefore:
The occurrence of oneness does not exist before [perception], nor after the birth of sensory cognition. Because cognition follows the senses, it is measured as "perception" (adhyakṣa). || 41 ||
Therefore, since it is a property of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-puruṣa-dharma*), injunction (*niyoga*) cannot have the status of being the meaning of the word;

and even if it were a property of the object (*viṣaya-dharma*), because the object is not yet established and lacks its own essential nature (*svarūpa-abhāva*), how could it be possible to comprehend it from the word?

For that which does not exist, such as a hare's horn and the like, is not perceived in that manner; if it is argued that while it exists in one form as the object of practice, it does not exist in another form,
that is incorrect.

That which exists as an entity is not what is to be performed; that which does not exist at all cannot be apprehended by it either. (42) If its state of being apprehended were established without its being something to be performed, then that alone would be its own nature, and the *niyoga* (the mandate) would not be anything else.
(43) The mere state of being apprehended is common to all things; its status as a *niyoga* arises solely through its being something to be performed, and not otherwise. (44)
If only the state of being something to be performed (*anuṣṭheyatā*) appears there and nothing else, then performance would occur in that case, but not upon the mere cognition of a general [form].

(45) In the cognition of a general [form], there is no cognition of an object to be performed; thus, for those who propound it, the meaning of the sentence would not be an injunction (*niyoga*). (46) [Objection:
But surely, one perceives, "I am enjoined regarding the sacrifice and so forth."

And this very cognition of an injunction (*niyoga*) is that which arises from verbal testimony: the cognition "I am enjoined here by this [person]. In that case, the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*) is a person in ordinary speech; however, in the Veda, due to the absence of a [human] authority, it is the person who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and the sacrifice is the object (*viṣaya*). All of this is cognized.
In that regard, what kind of objection is this—"How is existence itself cognized?
For if there were nothing being cognized, who could have knowledge of its own nature? That which is experienced by way of its own nature—that is considered its cognition. (47)

And when there is no intrinsic nature (svarūpa), there can be no cognition of that intrinsic nature; since existence is defined by perception, how could that [existence] exist, or rather, how could it not exist?
Nor is a thing perceived as existing merely through cognition alone, for such [a cognition] would involve mutually contradictory meanings regarding the scriptures.
1 Nor by mere perception;
2 for it is not so there.

If it is argued that cognition arises from the Veda alone [and not from inference], this is not so, because [the Veda] is tainted by defects in its causes; for cognition cannot arise from the Veda without following worldly convention.

(50) Since sacrifices and the like are observed in the world, and since the relationship between word and meaning exists there, a cognition based on what was previously seen does not establish the actual state of things.
(51) For those whose minds are overwhelmed by the defects of lust, grief, fear, or madness, a cognition following previous [experience] does not establish what is seen or desired as it truly is. (52)

In the world, a corruption of the meaning of sentences and words is observed in some instances; is such corruption not possible in the Veda as well, following that same pattern? (53) In that case [of worldly usage], there is no fault of intention on the part of anyone, such as ignorance and so forth; yet, is it not considered a fault for someone to have a failure of comprehension even in that [Vedic] context? (54) In the world, due to a defect of intention, there is a loss of connection with the actual state of affairs.
And it is not that these [scriptures] lack validity; for is there anything in the world that is not authoritative even with respect to the Veda? (55.3) [This is the intention.]
Since a corruption of the meanings of words and sentences is observed in the world, why should such a possibility of corruption not also apply to those very same words in the Veda? (56) [Objection:

But if the Veda does not possess true meaning by its own nature, then since the objects such as sacrifices would not spontaneously arise in the world, how is it that we do not observe the performance of sacrificial acts and the like?
For this cannot be established by oneself;
therefore, because it conveys objects that are consistent with reality, the Veda is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This [criterion] is common to all scriptures (*āgama*).
For indeed, the specific intermediate divisions of the meaning of particular scriptures are not found in all scriptures; they cannot be established by an ordinary person through his own imagination.
Or rather, just as there arises a cognition in one who somehow remembers something non-verbal through a logical mark (*liṅga*), so too is the action postulated [based on the perception of usage].
This is the apprehension of usage (*vṛttyupalambha*).

Since the performance of purposeful actions such as sacrifice is common to all traditions (*āgama*), why is it that the means of its accomplishment is not the same in the Veda as well? (57) If [you argue] that it is not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): the Veda is authoritative because the learned practice its meaning, and they are learned because they practice the Veda’s meaning. (58) Furthermore:
Even those born as twice-born arise from association with other traditions; this would not be the case only if their minds did not delight in sin.

(59) From what source of pride has this distinction between the sinful and the non-sinful arisen? The state of being twice-born does not follow from being twice-born, and the state of being non-twice-born follows from being sinful.

(60) Furthermore, that which is called "twice-born-ness" cannot be known through discernment by means of birth, lineage, ritual acts, and so forth; how then can there be "refinement" among the twice-born? (61)
Indeed, the status of being a twice-born and so forth does not fall within the range of valid cognition;
for that [status] must consist either in a connection with a birth, a characteristic of lineage (*gotra*), or a preeminent capacity for ritual action.
First of all, no one is able to determine that birth by means of a specific form alone, as they can with the birth-class of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like.
Because a confusion of forms is observed, even those [beings] considered to be Śūdras and so forth are found to possess that very same form; indeed,
unlike the forms of Vāhuleya and others, the individuals belonging to Kauṇḍinya and others are not perceived as being distinct from the individuals considered to belong to a different genus.

Therefore, because it is subject to doubt due to the confusion of individuals, perception accompanied by instruction is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the authority of another's instruction concerning an object of perception; for instruction regarding worldly matters can indeed proceed otherwise [than the truth].
(62) For if the caste of Brahminhood and so forth were perceived through direct perception...
The instruction of another is not useless;
for regarding an object of direct perception, the instruction of another is not more significant—
if it were so, there would be no doubt arising from the instruction of another.
Therefore, perception requires assistance; for if perception were to establish an object even without instruction, then it would not be possible otherwise to establish the truth of that instruction.
However, when perception alone is incapable and the instruction [is likewise], then both are individually incapable, and even together they remain just as such.
If it is argued that the causal complex (sāmagrī) possesses the capacity to apprehend the universal (jāti),
this is not the case.
This entire causal complex is recognized through the observation of its effect; yet here, as in the case of a sprout and so forth, no effect whatsoever is perceived.

For the causal complex of a jar or a cloth does not produce a rice-sprout or anything else, since it is through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that water and the other factors alone are found to possess that specific nature.
And in this case, no such effect characterized by the ascertainment of a genus (*jāti*) is perceived;

for when there is a doubt regarding the truth of an instruction concerning gold and the like, that doubt is removed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but it is not so with an instruction concerning a genus, for the doubt regarding its lack of truth is not removed by direct perception at that time.
When there is a doubt regarding the unreality of the teaching on caste (*jāti*), its reality is established through perception, by way of grasping the specific nature of the caste.

For in the case of gold and the like, because of the actual existence of a particular color, the conventional usage "this is indeed gold" reaches its completion; thus, there is no harm to what is observed.
But here, however, the claim that "Brahminhood is exactly of this kind" is not a sufficient defense, as it is merely a stretching of the legs.
Because the conventional discourse regarding a transcendent world beyond is desired,
gold indeed becomes real through its consistency with that discourse, whereas Brahminhood does not;
furthermore—
When there is doubt regarding that [authorship], one must investigate the lineage, other instructions, and so forth;
there is no other means.
Furthermore, specific details such as the study [of the work] are known through investigation, not from mere instruction alone.
That too is incorrect;
for the status of being twice-born is not something to be accomplished by ritual action, nor does the status of being twice-born arise from ritual action.
Furthermore, even the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) would not exist if they were devoid of a determination of caste. (65)
For indeed, for one who is devoid of birth, the purificatory rites such as the study of the Veda do not bestow the status of being twice-born and so forth,
because otherwise it would follow that everyone would possess the status of being twice-born;
moreover—

If the universal (*jāti*) is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of the bare [object] alone, then its perception is certainly not possible even from verbal testimony (*vacana*). For direct perception, when first operating, is not capable of establishing the distinction of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) and so forth; if it does not perceive [the universal] through direct perception, then it will not perceive it through verbal testimony either, since instruction is required only after that.
For even that statement merely indicates perception;
it certainly does not produce a certainty brought about by a thorough knowledge of the person’s words.
When a person is questioned, "How did you come to know this?", he teaches only his lineage, upbringing, and so forth, as the objects of his thorough knowledge.
If it is argued that he does not speak of the perception of birth as being that very birth itself, the answer to this has already been stated:
the action constitutes the status of being twice-born, but that action is not the status of being twice-born itself.
Now, if birth were defined by lineage,
then they would indeed designate one as a "brāhmaṇa" because he is the offspring of a brāhmaṇa.

If [Brahminhood] were to follow merely from being the offspring of a Brahmin, then it would absurdly follow that everyone is a Brahmin; for no one is ever found to have been born anywhere from a non-Brahmin body.

(67) If there is a distinction of caste in the intermediate [generations], how could it be without a cause? There is no purpose served by a distinction of lineage (*gotra*) based on a difference in ritual action during the intervening period.

(68) Now, if an beginningless distinction among the lineages of the twice-born and others is asserted, then how indeed can it be known, given that no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies to it? (69)
Due to the lack of knowledge regarding that [lineage], it follows that there would be no ritual action at all; nor can the continuity of the lineage be established through inference.
(70) The non-interruption [of the lineage] is not certain for anyone who might belong to such a lineage. Otherwise, how could the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Caṇḍālas possibly come into existence?

(71) If you argue that they are indeed known by those who know them, there is no fixed rule [for this]. Furthermore, within this beginningless path of the lineage, there is no stumbling on the part of women. (72)
Thus it is known: how indeed could women ever be afflicted by desire? Since Brahminhood existed previously, the possibility of belonging to that lineage (gotra) arose.

For since that lineage was established at that time, how can this lineage be an "blind tradition" (andhaparamparā)? Or, if Brahminhood is desired through connection with a specific power (śakti-viśeṣa), [then...]
Now, no excellence of power whatsoever is seen [in you]; if it is claimed that such was heard of in former times, then this statement applies everywhere and is therefore useless.
(75) The great excellence of power belonging to those perfected ones (*pūrvasiddha*) who were yogis is sung of unanimously in all the scriptures.
(76) Therefore, it is not logical that being a twice-born (*dvijāti*) consists in the possession of a particular power.
Nor does any Vedic statement establish [qualities] such as being twice-born;
since it is a general term for the individual who possesses the state of being twice-born and so forth, it is equivalent to what has not been stated at all. (77)
For the Veda does not teach the Brāhmaṇahood of Devadatta and others, because Devadatta and the like do not exist at all times, whereas the Veda exists at all times.

If the object does not exist at the time of the Vedic instruction, how can that instruction be meaningful? If it is argued that it will be so when the object comes into existence, then how can the Veda be meaningless [now] and yet become connected with its meaning later on?
How can there be activity for that which is by nature indifferent,
being of an inactive nature? 78.2
Indeed, no distinction is perceived between the Veda’s existence and its non-existence;
and if it were of the nature of that [existence], how could it ever perceive this division between existent and non-existent objects?
3. [Regarding] existent and non-existent objects...
Therefore, this status of being a Brahmin and so forth is not perceived through direct perception, nor through instruction, nor through both, nor even from the Veda;
since it is not thus perceived, how could it be useful? What, then, should be done with it?
Consequently, "Brahminhood" is established merely as a conventional designation.

Furthermore, since even Brahmins do not derive their practical activity from the Vedas through a sequence of causal efficacy, how can there be a correspondence with worldly practice based on the Veda?
For the practical activity of some may arise even from the opposite of the Veda; thus, there is no distinction between the Veda and what is non-Vedic.
Therefore, it is not logical to engage in action based merely on an injunction derived from an unexamined Veda.
Therefore, because it does not cause [the action] to proceed, it lacks authority;
if, on the other hand, the injunction (niyoga) were a property of the person being enjoined, that would be incorrect.

Since the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*) is established in nature, the injunction (*niyoga*) itself must also be established. An injunction cannot be something to be accomplished; how could that which is already established be something to be accomplished?
Indeed, that which is established and independent of anything else cannot be accomplished in any way;
if it were so, there would be no cessation [of the process]. (79)
[The objection that] "it is useless" [is answered by saying] that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not purposeless;
for even though the mandate (*niyoga*) is a property of the instigator (*niyojaka*), it acquires its status as such only in relation to the object of the person to be impelled (*niyojya*).
No mandate whatsoever is perceived that is devoid of a person to be impelled.
Likewise, there is no state of being an injunction without an object of the injunction;
for it is thus:
For there is the cognition: "I am appointed here by him" [which is the nature of *niyoga*].
An injunction (*niyoga*), which consists of an impulsion, can never exist without an object;
likewise, even the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) understands his own state of being enjoined.
For that [injunction] would not exist within himself [if there were no such object].
And such an injunction (niyoga), being thus constituted, is indeed something to be accomplished;
for an injunction is certainly not accomplished without the performance of its own operation.
Therefore, in this case, the injunction consists in the mutual connection between the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), the injunction, and the productive urge (bhāvanā).
And since that [niyoga] does not exist at the time of comprehension,

how could there not be a lack of objective basis (*nirālambanatā*) when the meaning of the sentence is *niyoga*? Furthermore, no *niyoga* other than the meanings of the verbal roots and so forth— which are mutually dependent— is perceived.

Furthermore, the relationship between things established as cause and effect, which occur in a temporal sequence, is not within the range of appearance; for the appearance of a thing's own nature has only that which is presently existing as its object, while the appearance of another's nature is not an appearance of that [thing] itself.
Indeed, one thing does not appear in the form of another.
And likewise, in the case of that which is without an objective referent, what scope could there be for a verbal expression whose object is the exclusion of others?
For instance, [one might say]: "Perform the sacrifice and so forth."
And considering that the self's status as the performer of the sacrifice has reached the domain of cognition, it must exist at the time of that cognition;
furthermore, it is not possible to cognize something through verbal testimony that was not already apprehended prior to that testimony.

For it is only he who previously perceived another as engaged in actions such as sacrifice who understands that state of being— whether his own or that of another— and no one else; moreover, this cognition,
following its prior basis, does not transcend having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object,
nor is agency itself even previously apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since perception does not function across temporal succession (*paurvāparya*), it is nevertheless said that there is "cognition" with respect to conventional perception (*sāṃvyavahārika-pratyakṣa*); thus,
through the complete following of prior cognitions, the cognition of the self as an agent arises.
Moreover, he is not impelled by way of being an agent, but rather solely by way of being an authority;
for one does not become an agent by not acting,
whereas authority exists by virtue of fitness.
That too is incorrect;
for in no case does capacity exist without an object. And when the object is beyond the senses, how can capacity be cognized?
Indeed, one who does not know the operation directed toward the object cannot, by its own nature, apprehend the capacity as qualified by that object.

Therefore, just as in the case of agency, here too there is indeed a fault that transcends the scope of investigation; how can an injunction (*niyoga*) be accepted as the meaning of a sentence by those whose conduct is merely verbal, based on the "teacher’s fist" (*ācāryamuṣṭi*)?
[This is] because of the teacher’s instruction.

Indeed, when examined, there is no such thing as an injunction (niyoga); for, since it is impossible to conceive [it otherwise], what kind of form has been proclaimed by others as the "injunction" of a pure action? Is it merely the impulsion (preraṇā) conjoined with the action, or is it the opposite? (83)

Is it because of its predominance that the *niyoga* is held to have the nature of an effect (*kārya*), or is its status as a prompter (*prerakatā*) asserted by others on account of its predominance? (84) In the relationship between the effect and the prompting, what constitutes the state of being a *niyoga*? Is the *niyoga* the aggregate of these two, or is it something distinct from both?

(85) Furthermore, is the person (*puruṣa*)—mounted upon a machine, or desired [as an end], or existing in the form of an object of enjoyment—the *niyoga*? These are the positions formulated by others. (86)

(1) The view of those who maintain that the injunction is a pure action (*kārya*) is expressed in this verse: "Since the meaning of the suffix and the injunction are perceived as pure, and since it takes the form of an action (*kārya*), therefore this [injunction] is considered here to be a pure action. (87)

Whatever other qualification of that [injunction] is perceived, it is not logical for it to be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is [the object], like one who desires heaven.

However, since the quality of being an instigator (*prerakatva*) which is accepted here as its qualification is not denoted by the suffix, the status of the word as an injunction of action (*kāryaniyoga*) remains intact. (88–89) (2) The Theory of the Injunction of Pure Instigation (*śuddhapreraṇāniyogavāda*)

3. In the case of [the Vedic] injunction (*vidhi*), it is the impulsion (*preraṇā*) itself that is understood everywhere as the pure *niyoga*. For no one, unless impelled, perceives themselves as being enjoined.
(90) [This is the position regarding the enjoinment of an action connected with impulsion.]

When it was previously understood that "this is my task," that [cognition] would serve as the impeller for its own accomplishment; otherwise, it would not be accomplished. (91) Those who maintain that the impulsion is conjoined with the task say:
"In this world, a person is never impelled by anything other than a task. Therefore, the impulsion spoken of is the *niyoga* (injunction) conjoined with the task. (92)

(5) Those who maintain that the "task" (*kārya*) itself is the motivator through metaphorical designation say: "The task is the object of the instigation, but it is not inherently the motivator; rather, the operation of the means of knowledge is metaphorically attributed to the object of knowledge. (6) Others hold that the "injunction" (*niyoga*) is simply the relationship between the two.

For without an impulsion, no action whatsoever can be impelling; nor can an action be an impulsion. Therefore, the application (*niyoga*) is accepted as the union of the two. (94) Even according to the theory of the aggregate (*samudāya-vāda*), this is the intended meaning:
these two are perceived as mutually inseparable. Therefore, the application (*niyoga*) is the aggregate, because it consists of both the action and the impulsion. (95)

(8) Others, however, say: "The meaning of the sentence is established as being free from both [the previously mentioned] natures, since it is eternally established as the one Brahman according to the sacred tradition (āmnāya). Because it is established, it is not something to be accomplished; how then could it be an instigator? (96)
(9) Regarding the view of those who maintain that [action] is an application mounted upon a mechanical device (*yantra*):

for those who maintain that it is the desire for application, whenever there is an application, whoever desires it proceeds toward that very object, conceiving themselves as mounted upon that objective sphere. || 97 ||
(10) The doctrine of those who maintain that there is an injunction regarding the nature of the object of enjoyment is as follows:
"This is my object of enjoyment"—in this way, the nature of the object of enjoyment is perceived. And the cognition characterized by the sense of "mine" is established precisely in the enjoyer.
For that in which this conceit of ownership exists in the enjoyer, that alone is to be known as the object of enjoyment; that alone is defined as "one's own. 98–99.

That by which [an object] is understood as "this is mine" through its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpatayā*), that very thing, by virtue of its form as something yet to be realized, is designated as one's own object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). For that which is an object of enjoyment already established in its perfected form (*siddharūpa*) is not, merely by that fact, an injunction (*niyoga*); rather, it possesses the nature of an injunction here because it impels the enjoyer toward the state of being something to be accomplished.
101.2 Siddha:
[The refutation] of those who maintain that the world is produced by the appointment of a Supreme Person (puruṣa-niyoga-vādin).
3. "This task is mine; I must do this"—thus a person always thinks. The person's being qualified by the task, and the *niyoga* (the mandate) being its denotation, [are established].

When the accomplishment of the task has occurred, the person joined with that [task] is then said to be "accomplished. In this way, the person is declared to be the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). 102–103.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of every sentence, there are eight possible varieties of distinction:
Is it the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or the injunction (*niyoga*), or rather the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? Or is it devoid of both, or perhaps of the nature of both?
Is it of the nature of the operation of the word, or the operation of the person? Or is it of the nature of the operation of both, or indeed the non-operation of both? (104–105)
To this it is replied:
all of this is inconsistent,
because:
An action devoid of instigation and lacking a person to be enjoined is not called an "enjoinment" (niyoga) for anyone at all. 106

107. When it is held that the word "niyoga" has no application or function toward a purely objective action (*kārya*), by what means can its status as a *niyoga* be prevented, since it is merely a designation?

108. Furthermore, since a person is not at all perceived in relation to that objective action, how indeed could that be a *niyoga*, [any more than] the cognition of something already established or in the past?

"This is the duty of the instigator; this injunction (niyoga) is approved by the world. If it is argued that "that alone is the task," [we reply] that because it is already established, it lacks the quality of being something to be accomplished (sādhya). If it is maintained that "this injunction is designated as such by virtue of its being something to be accomplished," then that designation is merely a figurative application (upacāra) of that status to its object. Furthermore, how can that which is unestablished possess the nature of an instigator? If it is held that its status as an instigator consists in its being understood as something to be accomplished, [then we ask: what is the nature of that which is to be accomplished? It is not an action (kriyā), for an action is not something to be accomplished. Nor is it an agent (kartṛ), for an agent is one who performs an action. Nor is it an instrument (karaṇa), for an instrument is that by which an action is performed. Nor is it an object (karman), for an object is that which is acted upon. Nor is it an objective (saṃpradāna), for an objective is that toward whom an action is directed. Nor is it an ablative (apādāna), for an ablative is that from which something falls away. Nor is it a locus (adhikaraṇa), for a locus is the substratum of an action. Since it does not possess the nature of any of these six factors of action (kāraka), it cannot be an action itself. And since it is not an action, it cannot be something to be accomplished. Therefore, it is not an injunction. Thus, there is no injunction at all. Consequently, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is not an injunction. This concludes the examination of the injunction. Now follows the examination of the word-meaning (padārtha). It is said: "The meaning of a word is that which is expressed by the word when it is uttered in isolation. What is this "isolation"? It is the state of being separated from other words. What is the meaning of a word? It is that which is understood from a word when it is uttered in isolation. For example, when the word "cow" is uttered in isolation, the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns are understood. That is the meaning of the word "cow. When the word "horse" is uttered in isolation, the long neck, mane, tail, hooves, and ears are understood. That is the meaning of the word "horse. When the word "jar" is uttered in isolation, the broad base, belly, neck, and mouth are understood. That is the meaning of the word "jar. When the word "tree" is uttered in isolation, the root, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit are understood. That is the meaning of the word "tree. When the word "blue" is uttered in isolation, the blue color is understood. That is the meaning of the word "blue. When the word "lotus" is uttered in isolation, the lotus flower is understood. That is the meaning of the word "lotus. When the word "blue lotus" is uttered in isolation, the blue lotus flower is understood. That is the meaning of the compound "blue lotus. When the word "Devadatta" is uttered in isolation, Devadatta is understood. That is the meaning of the proper name "Devadatta. When the word "cooks" is uttered in isolation, the act of cooking is understood. That is the meaning of the verb "cooks. When the word "is" is uttered in isolation, existence is understood. That is the meaning of the verb "is. When the word "not" is uttered in isolation, negation is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "not. When the word "and" is uttered in isolation, conjunction is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "and. When the word "or" is uttered in isolation, disjunction is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "or. When the word "if" is uttered in isolation, conditionality is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "if. When the word "therefore" is uttered in isolation, consequence is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "therefore. When the word "but" is uttered in isolation, contrast is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "but. When the word "indeed" is uttered in isolation, emphasis is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "indeed. When the word "only" is uttered in isolation, restriction is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "only. When the word "perhaps" is uttered in isolation, possibility is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "perhaps. When the word "certainly" is uttered in isolation, certainty is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "certainly. When the word "always" is uttered in isolation, continuity is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "always. When the word "never" is uttered in isolation, non-occurrence is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "never. When the word "now" is uttered in isolation, the present time is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "now. When the word "then" is uttered in isolation, the future time is understood. That is the meaning of the particle "then. When the word "yesterday" is uttered in isolation, the past day is understood. That is the meaning of the word "yesterday. When the word "today" is uttered in isolation, the current day is understood. That is the meaning of the word "today. When the word "tomorrow" is uttered in isolation, the future day is understood. That is the meaning of the word "tomorrow. When the word "east" is uttered in isolation, the eastern direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "east. When the word "west" is uttered in isolation, the western direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "west. When the word "north" is uttered in isolation, the northern direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "north. When the word "south" is uttered in isolation, the southern direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "south. When the word "above" is uttered in isolation, the upward direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "above. When the word "below" is uttered in isolation, the downward direction is understood. That is the meaning of the word "below. When the word "near" is uttered in isolation, proximity is understood. That is the meaning of the word "near. When the word "far" is uttered in isolation, distance is understood. That is the meaning of the word "far. When the word "small" is uttered in isolation, smallness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "small. When the word "large" is uttered in isolation, largeness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "large. When the word "white" is uttered in isolation, whiteness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "white. When the word "black" is uttered in isolation, blackness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "black. When the word "red" is uttered in isolation, redness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "red. When the word "yellow" is uttered in isolation, yellowness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "yellow. When the word "green" is uttered in isolation, greenness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "green. When the word "long" is uttered in isolation, length is understood. That is the meaning of the word "long. When the word "short" is uttered in isolation, shortness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "short. When the word "heavy" is uttered in isolation, heaviness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "heavy. When the word "light" is uttered in isolation, lightness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "light. When the word "hot" is uttered in isolation, heat is understood. That is the meaning of the word "hot. When the word "cold" is uttered in isolation, coldness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "cold. When the word "sweet" is uttered in isolation, sweetness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "sweet. When the word "sour" is uttered in isolation, sourness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "sour. When the word "bitter" is uttered in isolation, bitterness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "bitter. When the word "pungent" is uttered in isolation, pungency is understood. That is the meaning of the word "pungent. When the word "astringent" is uttered in isolation, astringency is understood. That is the meaning of the word "astringent. When the word "pleasant" is uttered in isolation, pleasantness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "pleasant. When the word "unpleasant" is uttered in isolation, unpleasantness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "unpleasant. When the word "agreeable" is uttered in isolation, agreeableness is understood. That is the meaning of the word "agreeable. When the word "

How can it be maintained that a single entity possesses both the state of being unestablished (*aprasiddha*), which constitutes the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*), and the state of being established (*siddha*), which constitutes the nature of cognition (*bodha*), since these two are mutually contradictory?

(112) If it is argued that the cognition of that [entity] in the form of the probandum is what prompts action, then the nature of the injunction (*niyoga*) would belong to the cognition itself, and not to the injunction in its true sense. (113) Thus...
5. Here begins the second chapter (*dvitīyam āhnikam*).

If *niyoga* (an injunction) is the meaning of a sentence, what will be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If *niyoga* has the nature of a means of valid cognition, what then will be the object of cognition (*prameya*)? (114)

If *niyoga* is truly the operation (*vyāpāra*) intended by the person, then this operation of the person is nothing other than *bhāvanā*. But in the view that it is the operation of the sentence, it would be the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabdabhāvanā*). Others say that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote a different [kind of] *bhāvanā*, namely the *bhāvanā* consisting of the word itself (*śabdātmabhāvanā*).
But since this [verbal *bhāvanā*] has arisen from the word alone, why does the person proceed to act? If he were not impelled by the word, he would not proceed to his own operation.
If this [object] is not enjoined by the word, how can there be an impulsion toward it? If it is enjoined by the word, then the cognition would be without a real objective basis (*nirālambanatā*).
Thus, even those sentence-meanings such as "mounted on a machine" and so forth are defects of the expressed meaning (*vācyadoṣa*), because—
It is said that there is a relationship between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer by virtue of their being mounted upon a mechanism;
yet, in that case, there is no [inherent] relationship, and the person is not mounted upon the nature of the object of enjoyment.

At the time of cognition, everything lacks its own intrinsic nature because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). If that very thing were its [true] nature, then the state of being "that which is to be accomplished" would be lost. (119–120)
Thus, the injunction has been refuted.
(3) The refutation of the creative realization (bhāvanā)— the creative realization is now being examined.
For cultivation is indeed twofold: the cultivation of words and the cultivation of meaning, as it has been said:
In the *Ślokavārttika*, it is said:
"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express a different [kind of] creative intuition (*bhāvanā*), namely, that which has the word as its essence."
But here, there exists another entirely distinct [category] called "all-meaning" (sarvārtha) among them;
with respect to that, the word "agent" (kāraka) is not to be denoted. 121.2.
Now, the "productive [efficient force]" (*pratipādaka*) is the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*), which is the operation of the word;
for by means of the word, the operation of the person is brought about.
That the meaning of the verbal root [is produced] by the activity of the person, and that the result [is produced] by the meaning of the verbal root— this is incorrect;
for the operation of the word is not denotable by the word.
With respect to that [object], the word as a causal factor is not denotative,
that is, it does not convey [the meaning];
for it is thus:

When a word has been uttered, devoid of its own [inherent] operation, it is understood by people as enjoining the self. What other injunction (niyoga) could be postulated besides this mental cultivation (bhāvanā)? 122
It is incorrect to say that "śabdabhāvanā" is merely another term for "niyoga."
If the operation of the word [itself were the cause], how is it that one who has not grasped the convention does not understand [the meaning]?

For if its capacity to enjoin were inherent by its very nature, the grasping of the convention would be of no use; and if you claim that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself [is what causes understanding], [then the same objection applies].
Now, if the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is active in either instigation (*preraṇā*) or creative effort (*bhāvanā*), this is incorrect;
for:
The causal complex for grasping the convention operates toward the cognition of the object; once the object is understood, the person proceeds of their own accord.
[This is so] because the cognition [of the word] consists precisely in an instigation or a request, such as "do this."
If that [status] is not apprehended, there is no apprehension of being "enjoined" (*niyuktatva*).
And what is called "being enjoined" is the state of being occupied with a task; having reached the state of being occupied with a task, the enjoiner enjoins [the person].
Furthermore, that future state of his cannot be directly realized in its own nature;

for if its own nature were realized, everything would already be accomplished at that very moment, and thus the injunction would not be fruitful—just as the prompter in that case has a sublated cognition. The prompted person would likewise be so; for the word denotes the object of the cognition [it produces]. (124)

For just as the cognition of the instigator (prayojaka) is sublated— and thus becomes objectless— by the person being instigated (prayojya) who perceives himself as devoid of his own activity, so too is the cognition of the instigator sublated by that very same person when he perceives himself as engaged in his own activity;
if it is argued that "that cognition [of the instigator] arises from the word," this is not the case.
That word also makes known only the object of cognition,
because both [the speaker and the hearer] have the determination that "it was presented by me in this way" and "it was understood by me in this way";
or rather, "I have understood it in this way"— let his intention be such or let it not be.
"Let it be so, or let this matter not be so; for I have already acted in this way.
Therefore, he says:
"The object that appears in the intellect is the domain of the speaker's activity."
In that case, the authority of the word does not depend on the reality of the object;
rather, it concerns the sphere of the speaker's activity— that is, where a speaker exists,
[the word] shines forth in the mind, whereas where he does not exist, it does not.

Alternatively, by that very statement, it should be understood that there is a speaker therein, according to the logical principle that "whatever belongs to a certain class must have originated from something of that same class";
or else, because there is no distinction [between them], everything would be non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*).

If it is argued that this is not so because human authorship is sublated [by perception], then in this case as well, since human authorship is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), how can it be said that such authorship does not constitute a sublation?
Alternatively, that speech is indeed non-human in origin; rather, the person’s notion that "this was composed by me" is merely an illusion.
For instance,
even a work that has been utterly lost appears to someone as if it were their own, when they have developed the conceit "this was composed by me" despite having lost their memory of it.
Thus, even poets are merely imagining as poetry a work that was actually experienced in a previous birth.
Whence is this [known]? Furthermore, since everything that is non-human (apauruṣeya) likewise becomes purposeless, the state of being non-human is futile in that regard.
In that case, even in the Veda, futility would be admitted there as well; and in the assumption of another meaning, both cases would be equal.
(126) Futility is observed in both the Veda and non-Vedic texts, and the assumption of their being authorless is exactly the same for both.

If it is argued that [the assumption of] another meaning is not purposeless, then let the assumption of a true meaning there be considered merely human in origin. However, the first appearance of an unreal object arises from the Veda.
Therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "the operation of the speaker" (*vaktṛvyāpāra*) and so forth:

having set aside the primary meaning of the Veda, that object which becomes the domain of the mental operation (*buddhivyāpāra*), in that case authority belongs solely to the human intellect and is not based on the reality of the object, nor does it belong to the word itself—this is the analysis of the words.
For indeed, having set aside that first [meaning], a person [relies on] the Vedic meaning...
One should conceive of another object as purified by valid cognition; that cognition is a valid means of knowledge regarding the thoroughly purified object.

That too is merely the meaning of the Veda; thus, you have no proof for this position here. If it is argued that [the authoritativeness] arises from birth due to mastery over the Veda, why is the first [instance] not so? And if that [first instance] also has that as its meaning, how is the Veda not useless? This being the case, there is no validity in what is non-human (apauruṣeya) when doubt persists, because the primary reality of the Veda's meaning is absent; for example, [the injunction] "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā" would be purposeless.
If it is argued that it is like a deficiency in karma in that case, we say no,
because there is a lack of valid evidence.
But the postulation of another meaning, arising from human effort, is indeed human-made;
and thus it has been said:
"How could that [postulation] not belong to one who himself somehow recollects it, even if it lacks a verbal sign?"
Furthermore, everyone considers themselves enjoined by the Veda; and since the injunction, according to the preceding [analysis], consists in the form of a verbal *bhāvanā*,
if that [injunction] were the meaning of the sentence.

That being the case, in the sentence "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacet*), since the agent is not expressed [by the verbal suffix], the third case ending would apply by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā* ("the third case is used for the agent and the instrument");

however, when the agent is expressed [by the suffix], because of the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"), it does not occur, as the agent has already been denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix.
Furthermore:
If it is argued that the agent is also understood from the term "he cooks" by the force of the activity, such understanding occurring through the very implication (*ākṣepa*) of the agent— [we reply:
no.
In this way, there would be a sequential cognition: first, the understanding of the action; then, by its power, from that [action] the agent is subsequently cognized. (131)
Furthermore, no perception of succession is observed, nor do the dual and plural numbers apply, because the operation is one;
if it is argued that there will be a difference in operations due to the difference in the factors (kārakas), [we reply: no.
If it were said, "The mat is being made by Devadatta and Yajñadatta," there would be a great inconsistency;
for thus,
[the action] would be excessive, because the operation is one.
Since the action is one, it follows that the performance must be one; likewise, there is a distinction between the agents. Thus, what should be done by the wise? (132) [Objection:

But surely, because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is non-different, the singular number is used—as in "Devadatta and Yajñadatta sit down"—and yet that meaning of the verbal root is not the injunction (*niyoga*).
Since *niyoga* (the mandate) is the meaning of the suffix,
and it is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*),
being something to be accomplished by the agent; and since it varies according to the difference in agents, the expression "make the mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuruta*) is thus possible.
The meaning of the verbal root, however, is pure and does not vary according to the distinction of the factors of action (*kāraka*);
