if it were otherwise due to that connection, then this variation would belong to the meaning of the verbal root itself as well.
Even that [action], being something to be accomplished (*nirvartya*), must be differentiated precisely by its own differentiation.
However, for us,
since the determination of difference and non-difference is dependent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), all of this is consistent when the agent (*kāraka*) is denoted.
For action is intended to be expressed as distinct from both the agent and the object;
if that [action] is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) and not by the agent, then the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for the agent;
when it is denoted [by the suffix], then the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs because [the agent] is the primary meaning [of the suffix].

When there is a desire to express a distinction regarding this sense of the verbal root *bhū* (to become), as in "it is made by the Great-Souled One" (*kriyate mahātmanā*) or "the Great-Souled One does it" (*karoti mahātme*), then the agent is expressed by the third case (*kartari tṛtīyā*).

However, when there is a desire to express a distinction and the agent is denoted by the suffix *-la* (the verbal ending), one should understand that because the agent is already expressed by that very [suffix], the third case does not apply to the agent. 135–136.
But when the agent's operation is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), that very operation is *bhāvanā*;
and thus it has been said:
"Words denoting actions have the sense of *bhāva* as their meaning."
"Bhāva" is the suffix of the causative (*ṇyanta*); such being the case, this is indeed "bhāvanā," and bhāvanā is the activity of the agent (*kartṛvyāpāra*).
Impelled by the agent, he engages in his own activity;
and since the mandate (*niyoga*) is subordinate to that [activity] and is not the primary element, it is not the meaning of the sentence.
Furthermore, because the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is qualified by the mandate, when it is presented in such a manner, the agent necessarily engages in the action.
And how is it that this [person], having undertaken his own activity, does not proceed here [in this matter]?
Otherwise, his own activity would not even be enjoined; therefore, this is incorrect.
1. In the *Śavabara-bhāṣya* (?), it is said that he has abandoned [the world]; he thinks: "This is his business;
why must I necessarily [participate]? 2. He has renounced it—he considers: "This is his activity; what need have I for it?"
If this [attainment] does not exist even without a fruit, then by what means is the attainment of success achieved?
137.3 [The attainment of success].
If you think, "This activity must certainly be mine," that is incorrect;
for no one undertakes this thinking, "I must do this," without seeing a result; it is only when there is a fruit that one engages in action.
Furthermore, it has been established that [the existence of] fruitfulness is not understood;

moreover, in expressions such as "he sacrifices" (yajate) or "he cooks" (pacati), the efficient force (bhāvanā) is not perceived. Since it does not exceed the meaning of the verbal root (*yaj*), how could it constitute the sentence-meaning? (138)

If one performs the cooking and the sacrifice, and a distinction [between them] is perceived, then there would be an infinite regress, which would bring about an improper state of affairs. (139) [The phrases] "performs the sacrifice," "accomplishes its own operation," "brings about the completion of the sacrifice"—
these designations are, in some way or another, preceded by a distinction.
There is no establishment of the reality of categories from these [examples],
for expressions of difference such as "the body of a stone statue" (śilāputraka) are seen even without actual difference.
Regarding the passage beginning with "śilāputra" and ending with "dṛśyante":

just as the activity of a twice-born man is also called a "sacrifice" (yāga), so too [the action of seeing is attributed to the stone]. Furthermore, the subsequent perception is not an action [belonging to the stone] because it does not perform [the act of seeing].

Even the action of sacrificing is not distinct from the substance [of the sacrificer], for it is understood as being identical [with the agent] through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the form of "Devadatta. (140–141)

But surely, since we observe the question and answer, "What does Devadatta do? He cooks; he sacrifices," it is established that [the action] is something other [than mere "doing"], because there is doubt regarding the specific acts such as sacrificing once it has been determined that he "does" them;
and thus it has been said:
Nor is the body itself the intellect, for even when the body is established, there remains doubt regarding the specific nature of the intellect;
thus, this [position] is untenable:

"If the meanings of 'to act' and 'to sacrifice' are indeed distinct in reality, then it is difficult to maintain the sequence [of the argument], wherein one doubtful thing is used to explain another. (142)

For if "doing" (karoti) were indeed something other than sacrificial acts such as the *yajña* and so forth, then, since "doing" would be certain, how could there be a question regarding another [action] in a state of doubt?
It is only when something is uncertain that a question is appropriate.
If it is argued that the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) has a general form, while [the roots] such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) have specific forms, [we reply:
nothing whatsoever is perceived without its specific [instance]. For there is no such thing as the non-perception of that which is implied by a general term.
Indeed, it has been stated that when only the general form is perceived, there is doubt regarding the specific aspect.
If it is argued that the particular is implied by the general, then in that case the particular is already cognized; how then can there be doubt?
For there is no implication other than cognition itself.
Now, although that [object] is indeed already cognized, nevertheless, its state of being cognized does not exist as a specific form, because it is implied only in a general sense.
But surely, how can it be that the very same general property is both the impeller and the impelled?
Furthermore, there is no other general property apart from the general property itself that could be the impelled.
If that were the case, there would be an infinite regress—another [commonality] beyond that, and yet another beyond that.
Surely, doubt is indeed appropriate based on the perception of a commonality, the non-perception of the specific particulars, and the recollection of those particulars;
it is not [otherwise].

For one who maintains that non-existence is established by the means of valid cognition known as non-perception (*anupalambha*) in general, it is logical that non-existence follows from mere non-perception; otherwise, non-existence would follow only from the non-perception of something that meets the conditions for perceptibility, not from mere non-perception.
Nevertheless, since doubt arises precisely from non-perception, the claim that this [non-existence] results from the perception of a generality (*sāmānya-pratyakṣa*) is futile.

If, even when there is perception of a universal (*sāmānya*), the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) does not result in doubt regarding the universal—
because such non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perceptibility is simply impossible when there is perception of the universal—
then it follows that only the non-perception of that which has *not* reached the conditions for perceptibility (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) is the cause of doubt.
Furthermore, the term "recollection of particulars" is redundant;
for there is no doubt other than that which consists of the recollection of particulars,
since this [doubt] has the nature of a recollection that rests upon both aspects.
In places such as Kānyakubja and others, doubt arises from memory even without the prior perception of a universal;
that very [universal], such as sacrifice and so forth, being perceived without restriction, is called a "universal" through inference based on what is generally observed (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
And regarding this, it has been said:

1. [Objection: "Therefore, it acts"—this is because it establishes a mere entity that is excluded from what is not of that nature. [Reply: The logical mark (*liṅga*) is said to have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because it does not rest upon particulars (*bheda*).
The determination of a universal is merely the non-determination of particulars.
In some cases, it is cognition itself— distinct from the form of the object— that is the cause of doubt, because it is common to both existence and non-existence;
likewise, it is precisely such a non-apprehension, whether in the form of cognition or in the form of the perceived object, that is the cause of doubt.

2. [Objection: Abandoned—[it may be argued] that surely doubt, such as "Is it a post or a person?", is observed even in the absence of an experience of a common form, since only the generality of height (ūrdhvatā-sāmānya) is perceived.
If it exists, then a cognition in the form of two aspects would be perceived.

(3) Furthermore, if there were a common perception of the upper part of a shape, such that one experiences a common form [thinking], "Is this a post or not?", then doubt would not be observed; therefore, the forms of both man and post are not perceived as a commonality above that point. (4) Moreover, an entity possessing two aspects [would be required].

There is no universal distinct from its particulars here, because there is a difference in cognition; the distinction of an object follows from the distinction of the form of the cognition. (145) Now, it is indeed perceived that, setting aside the specific forms of a person or a post, there is merely a verticality at a distance; otherwise, if the experience were contained within the forms of either a person or a post, no doubt would arise regarding them. Therefore, its appearing as distinct from those [specific forms] is precisely its exclusion from them, since exclusion is characterized by this much alone.
By that experience of the conceptualization of a post or a person, (5)
That is not tenable;

for if there were a distinction from that [object] alone, why would there not be an appearance at close range? And why would there be an excessive appearance when what was appearing at a distance comes into proximity?
Therefore, if there were a distinction from that [object], [it would follow as stated].
Indeed, that which appears when situated at a distance appears all the more clearly upon being brought into proximity;
and if the universal were a distinct entity, it would appear as such [even without proximity].
How can there be a conventional usage of "unclear appearance" in another case?
Indeed, when there is the appearance of a blue object, there is no conventional usage of an unclear white appearance;
rather, it appears quite clearly.
Now, in your own position as well, what is this so-called "indistinctness"?
It is the state of having an indistinct appearance.
For an indistinct appearance is sometimes a non-appearance, and sometimes an appearance of something else.
But sometimes it is said that "it appears as that," [and thus] it is abandoned— as indistinct.
If its very manifestation is what constitutes its indistinct appearance, then how can there be indistinctness when it manifests in its own nature? Furthermore,
even if it is the manifestation of something else [that appears], how could that belong to the indistinctness of that [object] itself?

Without appearance, how could there be an entity in the act of appearing? (148) If it is argued that cognition itself is such as to appear indistinctly, then the indistinctness of the object is due to the manifestation of the nature of cognition itself.
(149) This [position] is incorrect.
When cognition itself arises without that [external] form, then the world is considered to have a practice based on indistinct appearance.
Now, if that [cognition] were the universal itself, then there would be no appearance of color and shape;
for the universal certainly does not possess color and shape, since those two [color and shape] reside in substances.
Now, if color and shape belong to the substance, then, since the universal produced from that [substance] does not appear,
it is only color and shape that manifest; and because those two are common to both a post and a person, it is logical that there should be doubt between them— yet even this is incorrect.
Since that color exists with one form, how could its configuration be perceived otherwise? Thus, the cognition is perceived as erroneous.
(151) If the color and configuration appear otherwise, that is indeed an illusion.
How is there the perception of a universal? If it is argued that it is the whole (avayavin) that appears there, and neither the universal nor the color-and-shape (varṇasaṃsthāna), [we reply:
the appearance of [the whole] as distinct from the forms of color and shape—from what does this substance (dravya) arise? What else appears apart from that? (152)
For color such as blackness and so forth appears as color-form and the like,
yet no other substance appears therein,
because no substance other than that [color-form] is perceived apart from it.
If it is argued that these two are indeed the same substance, we say no; because shape and color possess the nature of qualities.
Now, as for the substance [being] like color and shape: it is not [so],
because there is no appearance of it otherwise apart from those two.
Indeed, no substance other than distinct color and shape is perceived;
and because that which lacks distinct color and shape is sublated by a cognition produced by a different causal complex—
arising when a cognition with a distinct form occurs, such that one thinks, "This is not of such a nature"— it follows that [the former] does not exist.
If it is argued that the non-apprehension of that [object]— which consists in the apprehension of its opposite— is the subverting factor because the cognition "this is not" does not arise, we say:
no.
Even that cognition "this is not it" certainly arises;
for indeed,
there arises a cognition that sublates the [perceived] configuration by means of the [actual] color, such as "this is not that configuration."
If it is argued that there is no sublation for that which is distinct,
then for that very reason, since there is sublation of the non-distinct configuration, there will be a distinct configuration.
The apprehension of that which has the form of its opposite is non-existent,
provided that the cognition of it is of the same nature as it was prior to the sublation.
Otherwise, there would be no cognition; what else remains?
If such a configuration or substance is apprehended as non-different from color,
and if that very thing is sublated, what else remains?
Indeed, there exists no analytical distinction (yogavibhāga) by which one could establish a division such that the sublation of one [of two rules] applies while it does not apply to the other;
nevertheless, it might be argued as follows.
At that time, there is no attainment of that color, because the substance [of shape] and the substance [of color] are attained separately;
therefore, know that the substance exists after its attainment and that [the other] existed before.
Furthermore, that which is perceived through the relation of prior and posterior, and that which is not so perceived—[these are the two].
The conjunction of those two with contradictory properties is not tenable;

for every distinction must be established in this very manner, since there is no other means of establishing a distinction [for the opponent]. [Otherwise] there would be non-distinction despite the presence of contradictory properties.
If that [form] were different from that [substance] in reality, why does it not appear in perception? When could the existence of both be seen, whether in the former or in the latter?
(155) If that color and shape, or the shape from the substance, were ultimately distinct, how is it that they do not manifest in perception, whether in the former case or the latter?
Since there is no manifestation of each [part] individually, and since there is no aggregate existing apart from them, its manifestation therein is merely the power of great delusion;
furthermore, since there is no simultaneous conjunction of the two, how can there be an aggregate? Moreover, synthesis does not arise from direct perception.
In the absence of that [subject], there is no inference either; so how could there be a cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "common" (probans), because everything is established within its own self; it is exclusively particular (*viśeṣa*).
Therefore, it is not the case that "action performs [an action]"; rather, common forms such as the acts of sacrificing and so forth are the generalities (*sāmānya*) of specific instances.
Consequently, *bhāvanā* does not consist of the operation of an agent, because nothing is perceived apart from those [specific actions].
Nor does the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) exist apart from substance;

it is substance itself, appearing as a sequence of prior and posterior stages, whose distinct nature is conceptually constructed through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Although there is no actual difference, it is metaphorically treated as if differentiated; thus, it is merely a conventional usage to say that "the action is different from the substance" and "the substance is different from the action," for this is not an establishment of the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, one's own activity and the meaning of the verbal root are both understood as being yet to come at the time of the injunction (*niyoga*);

therefore, how can it be said that this cognition—which arises through the power of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), since it has those two as its support?
Now, it might be argued: [text continues]

For since perception has only the present as its object, it cannot have the future or the past as its objective support (*ālambana*); however, although verbal testimony (*śabda*) does have those as its objects, it does not possess that same [perceptual] nature.
Thus he says, "The injunction," and so forth, in the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*.
That is incorrect.

How can it be determined that "even though it is not being perceived, it exists"? For in the case of inference, there is a relationship [between the sign and the object], and it is on that basis that such a state of affairs is established.
Indeed, every cognition regarding an imperceptible object is non-erroneous precisely because of its connection with a real entity, just like inferential cognition.
For indeed, there is no necessary rule that something must exist when another exists if the two are not connected;
however, [the cognition] is without an objective basis precisely because the nature of that [object] is absent,
for it has been stated that there can be no apprehension of the nature of what does not exist.
Furthermore, there is no rule of necessary connection with that which is yet to be;
however, in inference,
the effect is understood from the cause.
Likewise, from the perspective of the ultimate [reality], neither is the causality of results for the *agnihotra* and other rites perceived,
nor is there any certainty regarding the transgression incurred by their non-performance.

[The word] *tyaktaṃ* [is explained as follows]: Understanding his own capacity without any obstruction, and realizing his status as the agent of the sacrifice, he will proceed to perform the sacrifice.
2. [The opponent's view:

Because everything is not grasped by cognition due to its being a mere mental construction (*bhāvitva*), cognition is indeed without an objective support (*nirālambanatā*).
Therefore, it proceeds by unifying the perceived object with the conceptualized object;

The object that appears in the intellect as superimposed upon it, being the domain of the speaker’s activity—that is the validity of the word; it is not based on the actual reality of the object.

1. Validity as conventional:
If, then, non-deception is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), [then...]

Furthermore, even from cognitions such as recognition—knowing "this is that very same [thing]" and so forth—one who acts upon it partakes in non-contradiction; thus, it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, a cognition of an object not previously known, which is certain and free from sublation, [is a valid means of knowledge].
A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is produced by non-defective causes and is accepted by the world.

[Objection: Since it possesses correspondence (*saṃvādakatva*), the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has as its object the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, and is therefore a means of valid cognition.
[Reply: However, this conceptual construction, arising through the power of perceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), is not a means of valid cognition.
And since the cognition of the whole [the object] arises through the capacity of the cognition of its parts,

it would follow that even that initial indeterminate perception (*ālocanājñāna*) would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it too would depend on the capacity of the contact between the eye and the object and so forth.

If one were to trace back the entire causal chain, it would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the eyes and other sense organs themselves would have to be considered the means of valid cognition.
Immediately thereafter, the consequence that conceptualization alone possesses validity was abandoned— not [so].
9. To this it is replied:
Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, conventional cognition is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because activity regarding objects to be avoided or accepted is dominated by that [recognition],
the cognition "this is that very same thing," as it arises, is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for identity, since an [as yet] unprecedented identity has not been apprehended.
Since that [object] is apprehended as being seen,

its unity with the preceding [moment], when grasped, accepts both the state of being the subject of dispute and the state of being presently existing; for if unity consisted merely in present existence, it would be a case of proving what is already established.
And because that [object] was previously grasped by a prior cognition, it is not something else;
yet, while it is in a state of flux, it is grasped by the prior cognition as if it were something new.
Thereafter, when it is again synthesized, it is perceived exactly as it is.
present tense (vartamāna)
That which has already been apprehended, or even that which was so apprehended, must be followed up [as such];

and since this is a recollection regarding an apprehension as an apprehension, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it grasps what has already been grasped, just like any other subsequent recollection.
Concordance, however, arises from the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); and such action, which is to be accomplished by a single entity,
occurs because the object arises solely through its own inherent capacity (*vastusāmarthya*).
Therefore, this [cognition] "this is that very same thing" is merely a pair of perceptions;
if oneness with the former is perceived [in the latter], that is incorrect,
because the former was not known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and thus there is no means of valid cognition (*pramā*) for their oneness.
To claim that identity with what is not perceived is perceived is sheer audacity.
(159) Therefore, this conventional identity arises from preceding conceptual constructions;
there is no validity for such a conventional cognition. (160)

Even that cognition which has an object such as a jar and so forth [arises] from the conceptualization of a collection regarding an object grasped by those cognitions of the parts, such as color and so on.
Apart from the collection, no single entity is ever perceived by anyone.
Due to the firmness of beginningless habitual tendencies (*anādivāsanā*), there is the calamity of not apprehending the [object] as it truly is.
How, then, can cognition possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) if there is no comprehension of [the object] as being prior, posterior, and so forth? 162.
T.
To this it is replied:
for that which prompts activity regarding what is to be avoided or what is to be adopted is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and in that prompting, the intellect alone is primary.
Even if the object to be produced (*bhāvyartha*) has not been apprehended, it is nonetheless a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because one acts toward it;
just as inference (*anumāna*) is a means of valid cognition despite the non-apprehension [of the object].
For it will be demonstrated that inference does not involve the acceptance of the actual nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*).

Cognition does not arise from the eyes and other sense organs alone; rather, even without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it arises through the cultivation of the intellect (*buddhi-abhyāsa*). Therefore, in regard to objects to be abandoned or adopted, the preceding cognition itself is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it initiates [the process], and not conceptual construction and the like.
However, where there is no such cultivation, there is only inference (*anumāna*); thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth do not entail an over-extension of the definition.
Furthermore, even through repeated practice,
the desire for results has been established as a form of validity in terms of conventional usage.

2— Validity as the function of distinguishing between the object and the fruit of realization: Now, validity is established by its function of distinguishing between the object and the fruit of realization,
since there is a distinction in realization based on the difference in the form of the object for the cognition.
Moreover,
validity belongs to cognition alone and not to anything else,
because:

The distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), which is the comprehension [of the object], arises from the difference in the form of the object, not from the act of instigation (*pravarttanā*). Rather, it is because it is the instrument of comprehension;
for once comprehension has occurred, one may or may not proceed to act.
Nevertheless, because it establishes the existence of the object as it truly is, it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even if it does not lead to activity regarding the object established by that means of cognition,
this is not a fault of the means of cognition.
If it is argued that [cognition] is a means of valid cognition because it brings about attainment,
we say no;
for a means of valid cognition is such by virtue of its fitness for bringing about attainment.
If that very [perception] has not occurred, how is it known?
How can there be a determination of an unerring form based on the observation of a particular form?
Because of the distinction between the object and its form, and because of the distinction between the cognition and its apprehension,
the conventional discourse regarding external objects is thereby concluded.
For, because it is non-deviant, in cognition there is only the clear self-awareness of its own nature;
and thus, how could there be any perception of external objects, other mental continua, and so forth?
This we shall explain later.
The form of this [cognition] is as if it were the form of the object; thus, "object-form cognition" (*viṣayākāraṃ jñānam*) refers to that [cognition].

The "differentiation of the object-form" (*viṣayākārabheda*) is either the differentiation of the form belonging to that [cognition] with respect to the object, or the differentiation of forms within the object itself.
*Ākāra* means the act of taking on a form; that is to say, it signifies delineation (*ullekha*),
as well as similarity to the object and orientation toward the object.

For from that distinction [of the cognition] arises the distinction in the apprehension of the intellect: namely, the awareness of blue and the awareness of its form; this constitutes the apprehension of the object. 4 T.
Because it is non-deviating,
the fruit of the means of valid cognition is either the cognition itself— just as in the case of the object— or the apprehension of its own nature.
And thus it has been said:
"The comprehension of the object of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition; and that [means] is the form of the object which constitutes the very nature of the cognition."
Therefore, knowledge alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for just as the form [of the object] is of the nature of knowledge, so too is the apprehension [of it].
Consequently, it follows that knowledge alone is the result (*phala*).

This is true according to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); there is no valid cognition other than the fruit (*phala*), nor is there a fruit beyond the valid cognition. Such is the entire relationship between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*).
This will be demonstrated further below.
Just as the eye and other [senses] are not means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too the mental aspect (*ākāra*) should not be one;
and just as the eye and other [senses], though they are causal factors (*kāraka*) for consciousness, are not means of valid cognition, so too is the mental aspect— thus he says.
1. It is abandoned— that the form is just as the agent is— because that state [of the form] exists by virtue of the very existence of that [agent].
Because when that exists— that is, when the aspect exists— this result of realization necessarily exists;
for it is certainly not the case that this result exists merely because the eye and so forth exist.
But since the existence [of the result] occurs only when the form exists, because there is no difference [between them], it possesses the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*).
And that which is the most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*);
furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the status of being the most effective means consists in the absence of any intervention.
How then is it said that "one sees form with the eye"?
It is stated thus by applying the name of the effect to the cause.
Just as it is said that "the village has been burned by thieves," so too, knowledge alone is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But how is it to be known that this very knowledge is the "attainer" (prāpaka)?
It cannot be established through direct perception;

for indeed, the direct perception of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) does not demonstrate the distinction between valid and invalid cognition, since self-reflexive awareness exists in all cognitions whatsoever.
Furthermore, at the very moment of its arising, one who proceeds with the awareness of the distinction between a conforming cognition and another would neither be deceived nor harbor doubt; thus,
validity characterized by non-sublation is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

How can that [validity], which is being established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), be self-established for those who maintain that knowledge is imperceptible? Just as the existence of knowledge is established through presumptive testimony,
the validity of that knowledge is not known by means of another [cognition] through presumptive testimony.
Validity, however, arises from itself alone,
whereas invalidity arises from a subverting cognition;
and the validity of that subverting cognition, too, arises from itself alone.
Furthermore,

while cognition arises from a cause, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic; however, that [validity] is set aside by an exception, characterized by the non-sublation [of the cognition] by a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*).
To this it is replied:
If intrinsic validity [of a cognition] arises from its own cause, then for that which has thus arisen, there can be no alteration by other subverting factors (bādhaka).
(164) Or, if the self is said to be intrinsically valid because its nature is that of knowledge, then even by a thousand subverting factors, there would be no change in it. (165)

Now, if invalidity were to arise because [the cognition] has "self" as its nature (*svarūpa*) due to the presence of defective causes, why is validity not accepted [instead] through the connection with causes possessing excellence (*guṇa*)? 166

If it is accepted that its validity arises solely from the absence of defects, why is its invalidity not likewise understood to arise from the absence of excellences? (167) Furthermore, no self other than [the nature of] being a means of valid cognition or its opposite is observed, by virtue of which its status as either valid or invalid might arise from something else. (168) 3 T.

If that [consciousness] is accepted as being of the nature of cognition, then its characteristic of being a sublater is set aside; for its state of self-awareness never departs from it, even during states such as deep sleep or the onset of death.

In states such as insentient dreaming (or deep sleep), nothing is perceived; how then can it be maintained that the self exists? Furthermore, states other than waking consciousness have gone far, even further away [from the self]. Therefore, knowledge arises as either valid or otherwise solely from its causes; its validity does not exist intrinsically.

Because of the existence of a similar form, there is no certainty regarding its true nature. Since the absence of sublation for everything is initially [uncertain], that [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*). Subsequent sublation, however, is doubtful;
its certainty comes from another source, whether through perception or inference, for there is no other means of knowledge.
2. Non-subsequent sublation (paścādabādha).
If that cognition of correspondence applies to another object, how can the validity of the preceding [cognition] be perceived when it has already passed? Furthermore,
since even the cognition of the means of proof is itself an object of doubt, how can it possess the status of a means of proof when its validity has not been established?

If it is argued that [self-awareness] is a means of valid cognition because its nature is awakening (*bodha*), then it follows that everything would be a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, even the awakening to an uncontradicted object is not established at the outset. 176.
Now, having known the efficacy [of the object], one who knows the validity of that object [thinks]: "How can there be a cognition of that means of valid cognition which was previously unestablished?

(177) If the means of valid cognition were already established, then the knower of its connection would grasp that cognition as a means of valid cognition by virtue of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). (178)

If it is held that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that alone wherein purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs, then [we reply]: purposeful actions and the like are observed even from a view that is not valid cognition. (179) Therefore, if that [purposeful action] does not arise from that [view], how can it be accepted as arising from another? Since it is sometimes not obtained from one, it is likewise observed in the other.

(180) If it is maintained that what is valid cognition is that from which there is no doubt regarding attainment, then [we ask]: how can the cessation of doubt arise from a cognition of an identical form? (181)

Through repeated practice, a distinct form subsequently becomes manifest; from that, there arises an inseparable connection with the attainment [of the object]. Thus, this is a case of mutual dependence.

(182) If it is argued that, when things have been perceived, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) occurs through recollection—which arises by the power of consciousness—precisely upon seeing those [things], then in that case, inference would be based on perception, and perception would be based on inference. (183) Because of this very mutual dependence, neither of the two can be established. (184)
For perception, which discerns intrinsic nature, object, and aspect, is not capable of bending even a blade of grass; [it is] itself incapable. (In verse form: *svayaṃ samartham*)

By that [perception], no connection between the prior and posterior [moments] is grasped. A conjunction (*saṅgati*) is called a "union" (*yoga*) because it pervades different places and times. (185) If perception were capable of grasping the pervasion across different places and times regarding everything, then it would follow that it must perceive all objects at once.
(186) Therefore, their coexistence is not established through such pervasion; rather, let there be inference for all cases based on its occasional occurrence. (187)
Now, let it be understood that this [object] exists in such a form; yet, even by means of the senses, there can be no apprehension of what resides in another place and so forth.

And if the place and other factors are not apprehended, how can their pervasion [by the object] be apprehended? If that [pervasion] is not apprehended, there can be no inference; this is an extreme rashness.

Because of the necessity of invoking further inferences, an infinite regress would ensue, and through the requirement of each subsequent one, there would be a failure to comprehend the subject at hand.
Therefore, intrinsic validity is established as the general rule; it is set aside by the two [conditions]: the presence of a sublater and the cognition of a defect in the cause.
(191) Because it is non-discrepant, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If no sublater is found, it is clearly a means of valid cognition; for otherwise, it would be a sublater. (192)
This is appropriate;
it is stated here in the *Ślokavārttika*:
The certainty of validity does not arise merely from the absence of sublation; for how could there be an absence of sublation prior [to action], when sublation occurs at the time of attainment?
Let it be known through a means of valid cognition that upon attainment, that stability of purposeful efficacy is reached;
and that [stability] is subsequently discerned from the cognition that is self-aware of its own nature.

But first, in that case, the operation of inference occurs with respect to an existent entity; therefore, that very same infinite regress would arise. How, then, could there be any comprehension of its status as a means of valid cognition?
No means of cognition other than perception and inference is accepted.
To this, it is replied: [195–196]
The cognition of its own nature occurs through itself.
Validity is established by worldly practice;
for the cognition of its own nature occurs through itself, not that of another nature.

For "direct going" (*sākṣād gati*) is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*) and direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of one's own nature, not of the nature of another; and the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) consists in the non-deviation from the object to be attained,
for there can be no apprehension of a relation when the object to be attained is not apprehended.

And that which is not so determined cannot be established as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the attachment to the form present before one is common to all cognitions; nor is there any apprehension of a connection with a future form.
Nor can there be an apprehension of the relationship with a prior form by means of a cognition of a future causal efficiency (since,
due to its nature as self-cognition of its own form, there is no apprehension of the relationship in each instance individually); nor is a collective occurrence possible,
because the apprehension of the means and the causal efficiency occurs sequentially.

However, the recollection that arises at a subsequent time, proceeding according to the original experience, conceptualizes the two [the object and the cognition] as being unrelated; yet, because it abandons the actual experience, it is itself corrupted by that [error]. Therefore, no comprehension of a relation [between them] occurs from it.

Consequently, since that relation is not grasped, how could there be comprehension later on through inference based on similarity to what was seen? Thus, this is not a means for the comprehension of validity; rather, the apprehension of the intrinsic nature [of the cognition] occurs through itself (*svataḥ*), but not its validity.
Now, if validity were the very nature [of the cognition] itself— since it is not distinct from that which is expressed by the abstract suffix—
that is incorrect.

Validity is of the nature of cognition because it is excluded from what is other [than cognition]; however, it is said to be concomitant with the form of the object to be reached (*prāpya*). When there is the apprehension of the mere nature [of cognition], that [validity] is not apprehended.
For validity is not merely the nature of cognition itself, since its establishment as such depends upon its connection with the form of the object to be reached.

And it has already been established that there is no apprehension of that [object]; therefore, since there is neither engagement nor withdrawal, there is merely the self-awareness of one's own nature, and thus there can be no entry into any philosophical system (darśana).
Consequently, discerning people should not engage in anything, nor should they withdraw from anything.
How, then, is validity established as being excluded from invalidity?
It has been demonstrated that validity is established by means of worldly convention; this is merely conventional validity.
Furthermore, when conventional worldly discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*) is subjected to critical investigation, it simply falls apart.
If satisfaction is found with this much, then nothing at all needs to be done; liberation from saṃsāra would indeed follow, because of the absolute non-existence of that [saṃsāra].
Alternatively, if saṃsāra is established by way of worldly convention...
That being the case, the distinction between valid cognition and its opposite certainly exists; therefore, no effort need be made to establish the nature of valid cognition.
[Objection: How then is it so?

Furthermore, by one who establishes conventional validity (*sāṃvyavahārika-prāmāṇya*), it is effectively stated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is only one form of perception, namely self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). This is what is meant. Furthermore... [it] becomes so.

For instance, if the status of being a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya) attains establishment through perception or through inference, then the sphere of conventional practice (vyavahāra) is rendered useless.

If one desires its establishment without doubt— whether through perception or through inference— then since the establishment of the status of being a means of valid cognition is perfectly clear, for what purpose is it said to be [established] by way of conventional practice?

Therefore, by relying on an inference established merely through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and depending upon a relationship that is well-known, one engages in the apprehension of the means for [obtaining] tangible objects and so forth, [thinking], "This is the means for accomplishing this purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*). Subsequently, even without inferential habituation (*abhyāsānumāna*), activity occurs from mere intuition (*pratibhāsa*) alone; thus, even perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is instigative. For this reason, it is said: "Validity is [established] by way of conventional usage."
But surely, by means of vision, only color-form (*rūpa*) is perceived, not the tangible; likewise, only that which is present is perceived, not that which is future or to be reached;

and likewise, only what is visible to oneself is perceived, not what is visible to another. How, then, can there be valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the perception of one thing and the attainment of another?
It has been stated here that the comprehension of the essential nature [of a means of knowledge] occurs through itself;

furthermore, its status as a valid means of knowledge is established on the basis of conventional usage. Due to the non-difference of place and other factors, the unity of the substance is designated. (199)
This has been stated:
"Validity [is established] by means of conventional practice.

Therefore, relying on the unity of the whole as established by conventional practice, the designation of "validity" occurs through the determination that "whatever was seen is precisely what was attained."
And that determination of oneness arises from the non-difference of place, time, and so forth;
even that non-difference [of place, etc. results precisely from the production of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which possesses that capacity.
Likewise, even for things past and future, there is the conceit of oneness due to their belonging to the same single continuum and because they perform the same purposeful action.
Now, since it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),

is validity (*prāmāṇya*) that which makes known purposeful action, or is it that which produces it? It cannot be the former, for if it were productive [of the action], then the means of valid cognition would instead be an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Now, if it is argued that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it makes [the object] known, that too is incorrect;

for that which makes [the object] known does not [establish] its purpose, since there remains doubt regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Since causal efficiency occurs only occasionally, how could that [efficiency] possess the status of being a cognizer? (200)
Even in the absence of the knowledge of the means (*sādhana*), purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is observed;
how then could that [knowledge] be the cause of purposeful action? For if it occurs even without it, how could it be the cause of the effect?

Nor is it an indicator, because even when an object is perceived, its purposeful activity (arthakriyā) may sometimes be absent; yet that cognition cannot be invalid, as it would then be devoid of an object.
Therefore, in the absence of both being a producer (kārakatva) and an indicator (jñāpakatva), how could it be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that brings about purposeful activity?
To this it is replied:

Even if there is doubt regarding the goal (*upeya*), the means (*upāya*) is not for that reason not a valid cognition (*pramā*). Since the means is certain, why should it not be a valid cognition by virtue of that very fact?
Indeed, there is no desire to avoid doubt concerning the goal.
Since activity occurs everywhere merely through the ascertainment of the means,
it follows that once the means are ascertained, authoritative persons should act like farmers and the like; however,
that is incorrect.
For:

"Since every person engages in activity or desists from it out of a desire for the goal to be attained, how can that [cognition] be a means of valid knowledge if there is doubt regarding that goal? (202)

Regarding that for which a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought, since there is doubt concerning the object to be attained (*upeya*), what kind of verbal expression is this, namely, "it is a means of valid cognition"? Indeed, it is the object that must be made known by the means of valid cognition, not the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) that must be performed.
For how can causal efficacy—which occurs subsequently from a particular collection of conditions (*sāmagrīviśeṣa*)—be made known?
That too is incorrect;
for if that very thing for whose sake this undertaking was begun remains unaccomplished, how can a reason whose connection with the probandum is unestablished be called a prover? (203)
2. T [reads] *avayavimātraṃ ekam atra*; "yan-lag-cam" (the whole) is an erroneous reading in place of "yan-lag-cam" (the parts). 3. T [reads] *tatsāmarthyajananasāmagryāḥ*.

4. That which is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is accepted as such because it leads to the attainment of an object. 5. It is held to be a means of valid cognition by virtue of its being a practice [that leads to the goal]. 6. It is that which brings about the attainment of the object.

The discerning person, intent on investigating the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), thinks: "May I attain the accomplishment of my desired object through this valid means. It cannot be otherwise;
for if it were otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere affliction.

Furthermore, if an object is revealed but does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), how is it any different from the non-existent hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia? There is no distinction between them.

1. [Objection: Suppose that at some time an effective action (*arthakriyā*) occurs with respect to hair and so forth, but not with respect to [hair seen by] one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) and the like;
[if that is so,] how then does one who desires that object proceed toward it?
Indeed, one who acts out of doubt does not act by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for a valid cognition is that which produces certainty and does not produce doubt;
provided, however, that there is certainty regarding that which performs a purposeful action.
If there is certainty regarding causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), how can there be such certainty?

Alternatively, if that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has demonstrated the entity that accomplishes the purpose, yet the causal efficacy does not occur due to some deficiency; [how can there be certainty?]
This is not a defect of the means of valid cognition; therefore, it is not [a fault] in that case.
That too is incorrect:

if the non-indicative nature of a means of knowledge (*māna*) is not seen as a fault, and no other fault exists for it, then everything would be valid cognition (*pramā*). That by which something is cognized—that is, by which the desired object is determined—is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And since that which does not cause cognition lacks the power of determination, it is not a means of valid knowledge;

therefore, one understands otherwise, because there is the comprehension of a determined nature of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Knowledge is the means of valid knowledge by virtue of its identity with or its arising from that [object]. (205)

Indeed, that cognition of causal efficiency, because it consists of causal efficiency itself, leads to the accomplishment of that efficiency; and regarding that causal efficiency, that very cognition of the means is [the cause],
whereas the preceding cognition of the means is so only if that object has been ascertained as being stable.
For the prior nature necessarily brings about that which is to arise at the time of its attainment; therefore,
the subsequent nature is in reality nothing other than the very nature of the prior one,
and thus even there, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*).
4. There is no designation [of them] as "the universal is other than the particular."
Alternatively, that effect which is necessarily bound to arise is indeed the cause itself, because it is pervaded by it;
and that which is distinct from it and acts as its pervader is also the cause itself, since without it the effect would not exist.
How could that which has not yet arisen be a cause?
How could it be produced? The same fault applies;

For if the cognition is produced by the object, then the object is the cause and the cognition is the effect. And since the cause and the effect are distinct, how can there be no distinction between the means of valid cognition and its fruit? Furthermore, if the cognition is produced by the object, then the cognition would be a modification of the object, and thus the cognition would be non-conscious, just like the object. Moreover, if the cognition is produced by the object, then even a false cognition would be produced by the object, and thus a false cognition would also be a means of valid cognition. Therefore, the cognition itself is the means of valid cognition, and the object is the fruit. [The opponent replies: "In that case, let the cognition be the means of valid cognition, and let the object be the fruit. But since the cognition is dependent upon the object, it is said to be 'produced by it. Thus, the means of valid cognition and its fruit are distinct. [The author replies: "That too is not correct. For if the cognition is produced by the object, then the object is the cause and the cognition is the effect. And since the cause and the effect are distinct, how can there be no distinction between the means of valid cognition and its fruit? Furthermore, if the cognition is produced by the object, then the cognition would be a modification of the object, and thus the cognition would be non-conscious, just like the object. Moreover, if the cognition is produced by the object, then even a false cognition would be produced by the object, and thus a false cognition would also be a means of valid cognition
This is not tenable, because:

"Now, let that relationship which constitutes the object of valid cognition be established through positive concomitance preceded by negative concomitance; but how can there be the possibility of a relationship for that which is eternal and lacks negative concomitance? (227)
Indeed, it cannot be understood that something which is eternal and non-distinct from [the object] is of any use anywhere;
if it is argued that its utility arises from being perceived by that [consciousness], then this very point has been challenged: "How is it by that?"

Since that [seer] exists, it is said "by him" because he is of such a nature; but how can that same [seer] be the seer of space and so forth? Because there is no indication of an object for that [space], that very one is the seer, not space and so forth.
This very point has been challenged: "Or rather, how is it seen?"
Explanation is speech; therefore, how can this very [speech] be that [object]? Moreover, if there were no distinction [between them], causality could not be understood.
(228) How can an object that is past or future appear? If it is consciousness as "past," how can it be past? (229)
Furthermore, how could there not be a reflection of the past and so forth? For such an appearance is possible when a mirror exists.

It has been stated previously that the appearance of an eternal entity cannot be an effect; [if you say it is not], why would the apprehension of objects not also apply to space and the like? (230–231) 4 T purā.

What is said to be the meaning of that word "seeing all objects"? If it is not understood as being invariably preceded by that [act of seeing], then [the word] "seeing all objects" would apply to everything, and the word would be a denoter of everything. Furthermore, a restriction based on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is not possible for something eternal. Those intentions are distinct, and likewise, the acts of seeing are distinct; how can there be a unity for the seer, and how is he a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for you?

If that very [cognition] were the apprehender of the intended object of perception, how could there be the apprehension of both that intended object and its other from a single [source]? (235) In this way, why is the unity of perception and inference not asserted? If their unity is also accepted in terms of ultimate reality, (236) then there is no difference between them, whether they occur sequentially or simultaneously. It is through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that their nature as a single entity is perceived precisely in a sequential manner. (237)
If an object is not perceived as one by that [perceiver] and another, how can it truly be one? If it is not true, then such speech is in vain.
(238) Furthermore, if that [Self] is understood by the knower himself in every way, by what means is it understood to be thus? It is merely a matter of words.

(239) It has already been established previously that there is nothing other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, this Lord is neither ultimately real nor is he a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). (240)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
although cognition is impermanent due to the impermanence of its objects, the knower is permanent;
and it is not logical to say that because one thing is impermanent, another must also be so.
Because knowledge arising in a sequence cannot originate from that which is eternal, due to the incompatibility of production from an eternal object of knowledge.
Since production from what is eternal is impossible, it has been established that what is eternal and all-pervasive— like space— is not the cause of anything;
and if [the cause] were to produce [an effect] by means of that very same nature, it would produce it at all times, because there is no distinction [in its nature].
And if there is a distinction, then impermanence is intended; therefore,
even if there is no distinction, if it is argued that the sequence of the effect arises from the presence or absence of auxiliary causes, [we reply:]...
Because dependence is still required;
if it is only the auxiliary factors that possess positive and negative concomitance, then they alone are the cause, and not that [entity].
It is also not logical to claim that even for that [subsequent state], there is causality with respect to the former;

for since there is no distinction between the states of "depending" and "not depending," whether it depends on its own or through another, the status of being a dependent is not perceived— unless, at best, this is understood merely from the statement itself.
For this very reason, he says:
"Because dependence is impossible."
For that which is eternal is always of a single form; it cannot be assisted by that which is depended upon, since there can be no assistance rendered to it.
Therefore, it would not be dependent on that [assistance].
If this is so, then valid cognition must be non-eternal, and not dependent upon means such as generosity and the like.

Because yoga arises from preceding causes of its own kind through dispassion and mastery (*vairāgyaiśvarya*), it never occurs as something that, having been otherwise, subsequently arises differently.
To this it is replied:
"In some way, because it is not something to be benefited, its impermanence is unproven. (9)
Even if God were impermanent, there would be no validity [to his cognition];
why is it that he is not a means of valid cognition?
Because he cannot be assisted in any way;

for since one who is assisted or harmed by someone in some manner would have the experience of passion and so forth, and the possibility of the realization of the antidotes to passion and so forth, there would be the teaching of those [antidotes].
Because teaching arises from affection for sentient beings and compassion, that [teaching] becomes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the world,
not merely from the existence of its own intrinsic nature; nor is this [teaching] a mere linguistic convention.
For one who is not unbroken does not become wise;
nor indeed is one who is not free from suffering [wise].
Now, regarding his lack of establishment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-asiddhi*), there is the complete thorough knowledge of it.
This is untenable:
if there is no experience of passion and so forth, how can there be an awareness of the specific characteristics of the manifold world of saṃsāra?
If there is experience, then this [subject] is itself a transmigrating being; how, then, can it possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)?

It is not merely through the realization of passion and so forth that there is the teaching of the antidote to the proliferation of passion and so forth; rather, the very union with passion and so forth is omniscience, indestructibility, and the possession of incomparable power—thus, that alone is the valid authority (pramāṇa). [Objection: That too is the root proliferation of saṃsāra;
[Response: that also is incorrect.
The teaching of the antidotes to passion and the like would be purposeless if unchanging sovereignty were possible even while one is possessed by passion and the like.

(241) Now, if this is the actual state of things—that sovereignty cannot arise when there is possession by passion and the like, and therefore the teaching of their antidotes [is given]—then, because of the absence of such cultivation, dispassion and so forth would be impossible. From what source, then, could that sovereignty and the rest be established as being accidental? (242)

For it is not known that what arises from the cultivation of antidotes such as dispassion can arise otherwise; moreover, he does not possess such power of granting boons that he would bestow sovereignty upon a petitioner even when devoid of ritual practice. (243)
Now, if that capacity does not exist at all, how could it have another [capacity] to be capable of conferring favor? Thus, in that case, the lack of validity is established.
This is also the meaning:

even in the case of what is impermanent, there is no lack of validity; for "invalidity" (*apramāṇatā*) is the state (*bhāva*) of being non-valid (*apramāṇa*), which means "that in which there is no valid cognition."

There is no authoritative means of knowledge for that [existence], meaning that it cannot be established; for otherwise, it would be impossible to effect the act of favoring others through the teaching of Dharma, which functions by way of pacifying passion and the like through the process of spiritual cultivation.

That is incorrect, because by what means is it understood that there is benefit for the world when his teachings are practiced? If it were understood solely from the scripture he spoke, then there would be a circular argument:
"This is scripture because it was spoken by him, and it was spoken by him because it is scripture. Since this is a case of mutual dependence, how can either one be established?
Furthermore, from what cause has such power as that (of his) come? T.
"How is it to be understood that this is its very nature? (247) [The opponent asks:
"Surely, from what cause has such a power (*śakti*) of his come about—a power whose form consists in favoring all philosophical systems?
If it is argued that the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things, since it is precisely because of these that they become so," [the response follows:]...
For instance, to whom can it be a matter for questioning that "this is thus" and "this is not"? Fire burns, but space does not; what room is there here for questioning?
This [position] is therefore utterly untenable.
When an intrinsic nature is established through perception, others may raise an objection; in that case, this answer must be stated: "There is no inconsistency with what is perceived.
But this does not apply to that which is imperceptible, for it is as follows: [249] na tv adṛśye... (not in the perceptible).

In this context, what is the meaning of the statement that "the answer must be given by means of the intrinsic nature of things"? It means that what is established by valid means of cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a subject for questioning as to how it is so;
just as fire, perceived directly as burning what is combustible, is not to be questioned as to how it burns.
If even space were to burn by virtue of its being a real entity (*bhūtatva*),

then, on account of its specific nature (*svabhāva*), it would follow that Īśvara as well— though devoid of all causes for the qualities (*guṇa*)— is possessed of qualities; thus [the objection] is equal, yet it is not equal.

"Because fire is observed [to exist] and because the opposite is true for anything else"—this is not a valid response. Otherwise, whenever one is rendered speechless regarding the establishment of whatever one considers to be the self, that [very point] should be stated here by means of the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*).
In this way, such would be the response, and everyone would be victorious.

Therefore, it is well stated that [the argument] refuting Īśvara applies not only to the case of impermanence, but— by virtue of the word "also" (api)— to the case of permanence as well, because [in either case] there is a lack of valid means of cognition (apramāṇatā).
Is there not a means of valid cognition?
Or is it that there is none?

Having established [the existence of] activity, specific configuration, causal efficiency, and so forth—which are of the nature of effects—how can the cause remain unestablished by means of its effect?
Otherwise, there would be no inference of any other cause either; for instance:
Whatever object, having been set in motion again and again, proceeds toward the accomplishment of a desired end, that [proceeds] through the superintendence of an intelligent cause,
just like an axe and so forth in the act of splitting wood;
for indeed, axes and the like do not proceed by themselves.
Alternatively, there would have to be either constant activity or activity following a state of rest; and for such activity to occur, it must be intended by some intelligent initiator.
That which possesses specific spatial arrangement, spherical symmetry, and so forth, must be produced by something endowed with consciousness, just like a jar or similar objects.
Likewise, that which performs a purposeful action is impelled by a conscious entity, just as jars and the like;
regarding this, it is said:
"In the case of staying, activity, specific configuration, purposeful action, and so forth..."

"Either the desired [point] is established, or there is non-establishment, or else there is doubt regarding the example. (10) These factors such as "subsisting before proceeding," which are intended to be reasons based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), are not valid reasons;
for even when these are present, only that which is already desired is established, which constitutes proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).

Furthermore, a position that is not established cannot serve as a thesis, for it is precisely that which is unestablished which constitutes a thesis; indeed, it is appropriate to present a proof only for that regarding which there is dispute,
and it is accepted that everything is presided over by a conscious agent characterized as an agent (*karman*).
For this reason:
It has been abandoned—that the world's diversity is not produced by karma; rather, that [diversity] arises from volition and is mental. 1 T.
In the Abhidharmakośa 4.1,
is it not the case that [the world] is established as being produced solely by karma?
Because it is established that [the world] is presided over by the conscious Lord who is distinct from karma;
and thus he said:
"And that [arises] solely from dharma manifested by the impulsion of the Lord."

And if [the opponent argues that] there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) in the proof that [the world] is preceded by action presided over by the impulsion of Īśvara, [we reply: [this is not so,
because] Īśvara is a conscious being distinct from action.
3. From karma alone, when it has become manifest.
That [the world arises] from the volition of Īśvara— this is not so.
If karma were of the nature of volition (cetanā), then the means for producing another's volition would be useless;
for that [karma], being supposedly non-volitional, is incapable of initiating activity, since we observe that activity proceeds only after identifying an object as "this is that."

Therefore, one must either investigate for oneself or proceed based on the prompting of an investigator, as there is no other alternative; for in that case, since insentient things lack the capacity for self-investigation,
if there were no investigation by another either, it would follow that no activity could ever occur.
Therefore, the intention is that there must be another conscious impeller;
in that regard—

If that form of volition exists by itself, and if volition alone, being the very nature of action, is the cause of activity, then even upon investigation, no further investigation of it is required. || 251 ||
Thus, the example is unestablished;

for even if they were created by an intelligent agent, pots and the like were not created by Īśvara, because there would be no purpose [for him], otherwise Īśvara himself would require another Īśvara. [If one argues that he acts] for his own sake, then an infinite regress ensues.

Furthermore, even that potter and so forth who sets [the wheel] in motion is himself set in motion [by another]. If [it is argued that] God is the knower and thus not set in motion by another due to his lack of ignorance—[we reply:
"This living being is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell. (253–254)
For an ignorant being, even if possessed of volition, is incapable of discernment;
like a jar or other such objects, because he is incapable of discernment, he is impelled by another. But this does not lead to an infinite regress, because the Lord is not incapable of discernment.
This too is incorrect.

If the status of being an agent is established, then omniscience is established; and if omniscience is established, then again the status of being an agent follows. In this situation, there is a great circularity of dependence.
7. Non-establishment due to infinite regress:

For if this Supreme Lord were established as the creator of everything, then he would possess omniscience, and not otherwise. And if he possesses omniscience, he must be impelled [to act]; otherwise, there would be another impeller for him as well, and thus that same infinite regress would ensue.
Furthermore,
if he were omniscient, why would he engage ignorant people in improper conduct?
For those possessed of discernment are seen to be givers of correct instruction.
But since it produces even a person who has engaged in error,
how can it be a valid means of knowledge?
Regarding the phrase "janaṃ sadvyavahāre"— this is a corrupt reading; rather, it should be understood that he provides sound instruction, and by that, [he establishes] authority (*pramāṇa*),
while he makes the doer of unrighteousness experience an undesirable result.
Therefore, it is only the one possessing discernment who bestows the appropriate fruit;
therefore, "bestowing the fruit of valid cognition"—this is a faulty reading.

That too is incorrect, because this [Lord] indeed causes living beings to engage even in unrighteous acts; having caused them to perform what is improper, how could he then cause them to engage in what is proper? (256)
First, he impels one toward evil;
then, for the sake of turning away from that, there is dharma. What kind of foresight is this on the part of an Ishvara who acts with deliberation?
This has resulted in the situation where one says, "I shall wash it off and then discard it."
If, on the other hand, he impels one toward evil, then he is governed by that very action; such being the case, there is a loss of his status as a conscious agent (*prekṣākriyā*).

Furthermore, the same logical difficulty applies as to why he would cause that action to be performed at all. If it is argued that he does not cause unrighteousness (*adharma*) to be performed, [the same question remains].
But as for one who performs unrighteousness, he experiences its fruit;
like another [ordinary] lord,
that too is insubstantial.

Other lords, due to incapacity, do not effect the prevention of evil; however, he is held to have a mind that is entirely turned away from those who are incapable [of such prevention]. (257) Now, if it were the case that he is indeed incapable...
One should loudly declare that "everything is created by God. But since He acts for His own interest like a sinner, what then [is the point] regarding dharma and so forth?
Furthermore, would the world not experience the fruit of unrighteousness without God?

If [the Lord acts] even without [any purpose], who would conceive of Him as having causality? (259) Furthermore, if no one experiences the fruit of demerit without that [demerit], how could a discerning person engage in this which is purposeless?
(260) If His activity were for the sake of sport, how could there be action preceded by discernment? For while one is momentarily satisfied, another is deprived of his life. (261)

Furthermore, if all other treatises are [considered] authoritative because they provide instruction on what is true and what is false based on the conceptualization of a Lord, how can this [Lord] be authoritative?
