Now, if there is no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) regarding the entire meaning of the scripture, then everything was not created by Īśvara, just as in the case of other scriptures.
Or, if he performs everything only when impelled by *dharma* and *adharma*, then the production of entities cannot occur otherwise.

If that were the case, then every self would perform all actions, such as merit and demerit, solely through the impulsion of those very factors; thus, the postulation of a Lord (Īśvara) would be useless.
Merit and so forth.
If it is maintained that the self is not the creator of everything, yet [it is said] "of everything," then [everything would be the self].
3 T. Sarvaḥ.

Where would the agency of all those [individual selves] be of any use? (263) If every single self were to perform every action, what would be lost? Likewise, one could act through many, or many could act through one.
(264) Now, if it is maintained that there is some single agent of everything, then omniscience would not otherwise be possible; thus, no other has the status of an agent. (265)
The primary agent is the one who has attained supernatural powers;
for it is not merely because of omniscience that he is served by others, since [omniscience alone] is not sufficient for those seeking [liberation].
That too is incorrect:
even one who is omniscient does not become an object of service if he provides no assistance, just as molasses and cow's milk do not serve as a remedy for a fever. (267)
5. T. *lohita* (? *guḍakārakaḥ*; *guḍagomayakāraka*—this is required [to be understood].

When omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is established and his capacity is proven, he is the maker of all things (*sarvakāraka*). And from his being the maker of all things, his omniscience follows once again. (268)

If [the world] were created by one who is not omniscient, how could there be an all-knowing [creator]? Therefore, if it is argued that this is established through an analogy, then the very nature of the observer is undermined. Furthermore, the potter and others possess knowledge regarding their own work; thus, a Lord is useless.
And since the efficacy of karma is established, what role would [such a] creator have?
And consciousness.

If even a potter or the like, though possessing knowledge, is capable [of acting] only when impelled, then God too must likewise be impelled by another, since there is no distinction between them. (271) If this is accepted...
Now, if he, desiring for himself the attainment of omniscience, has become the impeller of all, by what means can this be understood? (272) [Variant: "If he, speaking thus for himself..."]

Furthermore, regarding that agent who acts after having deliberated for himself, God is not the causal agent therein; thus, the claim that "the intellect of everyone originates from God alone" lacks any basis in valid cognition.
The causality of instruction and the like belongs to the instructor, and that [instructor] originates from another; since instruction is thus beginningless, everything desired is fully established.
Therefore, since [the world] proceeds from what is already established, how could there be an impulsion by Īśvara?
Thus, there is no certainty regarding the agency of primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), and so forth.
"It has been abandoned"—
this [reasoning], namely that it is because of its being consistent with the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), is also not a valid reason.
For it is not observed that every configuration is preceded by a person,
since such a configuration is seen even through the mere presence of specific causes such as seeds,
like the configuration of trees and the like.
In that regard, as follows: ( ) 3 T.

Because trees and the like are characterized by specific configurations, their configuration is indeed associated with non-conscious causes; likewise, jars and such would be so, not being set in motion by Pradhāna or other [primordial principles].
For just as a seed produced from a tree is the cause of a tree, so too is a jar [produced] from a lump of clay, which has not been set in motion by [an external agent] such as a potter.
Furthermore, the potter and others are always considered its witness [of the form], because the body’s color and configuration arise from something else of that same kind.
(278) The potter and others are not the producers of that configuration and so forth;
for indeed, even a highly skilled conscious being is not capable of producing a tree’s configuration that is of a different genus than the seed.
Is it not the case that a potter is observed producing the shape of a lump of clay, and not [producing the clay itself],
because the lump of clay is already of such a nature?
The lump of clay possesses exactly that same color and configuration (*saṃsthāna*) [as the jar],
just as a banyan seed possesses the color and configuration of the banyan tree;
if one asks how that is so:

To this it is replied: If the nature of color and shape does not exist in the seed by virtue of its causal capacity, then how could that nature arise in the effect, given the absence of the seed as its cause? (279)
If God is its creator, why does it not arise from something other than the seed? This has already been refuted [previously]. How can God be its cause?
For at that time, the tree—which is the effect of the seed—is not present during the time of the seed;
therefore, he cannot be the cause of its form.

Nor can it be that the Lord is its cause, because it is impossible for a tree to arise from a seed of a different species; if the Lord were its cause, why would that tree-structure not also arise from a seed of a different species?
Therefore, the tree-structure exists within the tree-seed itself in the form of a potentiality (śakti) and merely manifests.
Just as the shape of a young child situated in darkness becomes manifest through a lamp,

so too does the shape emerge from a lump of clay; and for the potter, when fashioning a jar or other objects, the shape exists in him in the form of a latent power, arising solely from that very shape.
Therefore, the person— such as a potter and so forth— is merely a witness and the enjoyer; he has no activity whatsoever,
since the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which exists in the form of potentiality, proceeds in various ways through his desire for enjoyment.
And thus it is said:
"At the time of the seed's effect."
O young girl,

the primordial matter (pradhāna) acts for the sake of achieving the enjoyment of the Spirit (puruṣa), just as the performance on a theatrical stage is for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the audience.
And from this, there follows the establishment of the opposite of [the doctrine of] an intelligent cause.

Now, since there is a distinction between individual selves, there must be another self who is free from passion and the like, acting as the Lord of all; otherwise, by whom were the specific colors, forms, and so forth of transmigrating beings displayed,
for it is out of a desire for their experience that the primary matter (pradhāna) proceeds?

It has been stated here that just as the performance of a drama by an actor is for the sake of removing the spectators' desire to see [more], due to their observation of beginningless instruction, so too, why is it not accepted that the activity of the Pradhāna is likewise for the sake of the increase of the offspring of milk, even though the transmigrating persons do not know how it occurs? (282)
For the sake of the calf's birth,
since at the conclusion [of the process] one observes that it has the nature of being sought as pleasure and so forth, the entire cause must exist in the form of pleasure and so forth.
Since it is completed by that much alone, the proof of an *īśvara* is not established; and this is also illogical. 1 T.
The method of those who know reasoning is that because the lack of prior reflection is perceived in respect to objects, the insentience of their cause [is established].
(283) [Note: T reads "padārthenopalabdhitaḥ"]
It is not logical that things lacking foresight should have a cause; for what is the use of goats and the like rolling their dung into balls? 284.
2—Refutation of Primordial Matter as the Cause—the Sāṃkhyas argue: "In that case, Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) itself shall be the cause."
On this point, it is said:
If pleasure and the like possess a positive concomitance (anvaya) because they are real entities and are conscious, then why is that reality not accepted as the cause of the Puruṣas?
However, there is no real color, shape, or configuration belonging to the Pradhāna.
How is it considered that the production of effects such as color and so forth belongs to the Pradhāna?
Furthermore, even though it is accepted here that everything exists in the form of power (*śakti*), the entity whose nature consists of all powers is called *pradhāna*.

Just as there is an inference of causality for that unperceived [entity] based on its being of such a nature, so too is the effect [inferred] from another effect because it is an effect, like any other effect. (287–288)
6. Just like the inference from the state of being a cause,
indeed, a cause is never observed to be a non-cause.
Therefore, the postulation of a cause occurs precisely by following the perceived form;
thus, because individual instances possess a commonality (*anvaya*), there must be some persisting entity (*anvayin*) of that nature as their cause.
But since the cause itself is not common to anything else, how can there be another cause for that commonality?
For although there is a difference between jars, bowls, and so forth, because they share the common nature of clay, they are preceded by a single lump of clay;
however, that lump of clay is not itself preceded by another lump of clay, because it is a single unity.
Thus, for the lump of clay as well as for the clay, the staff, and so on, there is ultimately only one [underlying] persisting entity.
That too is incorrect;
for it follows that there must be another cause for beings (*sattva*) and persons (*puruṣa*).
Let it be, then, that there is some single cause alone.
As for what was said regarding its being "abandoned," that too is incorrect;

the nature of that Pradhāna as consisting of the three guṇas and so forth is not established. Since it is connected with the state of being a real entity (vastu), let some real entity be regarded as the cause. || 289 ||
Because of the positive concomitance (anvaya) that "the thing is a thing," the effect possesses the nature of a thing [derived] from the cause;
yet there is no nature of a thing other than the form of the clay and so forth.
Therefore, it follows that the cause's very nature is that of the clay and so forth.
If that were the case, it would follow that the Pradhāna consists of everything;

however, this is not so, for the effect follows the cause in its essential nature, but not in every respect. Otherwise, smoke and other effects are seen to arise from fire and other causes that are themselves of a different nature. (290)
For that which follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something is indeed its cause, but not that which possesses the same form;

and since smoke does not arise from fire in the same way that water arises from clouds and so forth— lacking such similarity of form— there would be no relationship of cause and effect [between them].
9. T. Water, etc. Now, even in that case, if there exists some cause of similar nature, let it be inferred precisely because the effect is of such a kind.
If it is argued: "Let it be inferred that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between cause and effect by way of similarity, provided that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*);
for even that which is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is made the subject of the inference (*pakṣīkaraṇa*)."
In that case, there would be no such thing as an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), for one could simply take whatever [reason] causes a deviation as the subject (*pakṣa*) itself;
therefore, because this leads to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*), this [position] is untenable.

"Abandoned"—that is, from the [opposing] position.

The body is abandoned.

Now, this following answer is stated on the grounds that the "whole" (avayavin) exists: this will be demonstrated later as being utterly untenable.
Alternatively, there is doubt regarding the example;
because of that very [doubt], there is doubt regarding the Lord (Īśvara), and thus the probans (saṃsthāna) is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since it is unestablished (asiddha).
It is the very nature [of a thing] that is apprehended as the cause capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*),

for that God does not act by remaining stationary again and again, nor is He a performer of purposeful action while being impelled by another.

If it is argued that since he is himself capable, he is not impelled by another— whereas even potters and the like, who are capable, are impelled by another— and thus it is improper [to say he is impelled], then it follows that they [the potter, etc. are simply incapable.
If that which is perceived possesses efficacy, how can there be a lack of efficacy?

If it is argued that even for that perceived thing, efficacy exists only through inference— and that the potter has no efficacy as an independent agent because his own efficacy is established by another inference— then one would have to infer another God for that [first] God, resulting in an infinite regress.
2. Furthermore, on what basis is it held that there is no shape (saṃsthāna) of atoms? If you say it is because of their very nature (tattva), then how is that nature to be cognized? || 306 ||
For the nature of atoms is not understood in such a way that their lack of configuration would follow;
rather,
it is argued that whatever is gross is preceded by an accumulation of parts, as, for example, a mass of water consisting of a collection of many drops.
And since the gross [object] extends up to the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and consists of a collection of many [parts], the existence of the atom (paramāṇu) is established.

That too is incorrect;
for how can there be any understanding that form exists beyond the octad?
What is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) that this form is an octad or otherwise?
Furthermore: if [the self] exists through inference, how can there be any cognition of anything other than that?

If atoms were visible, their number would be definitively determined. But that [object] is gross; therefore, it is not a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). The grossness of everything would depend upon that which is being inferred; yet that form which is visible is considered to be the ultimate limit. 310.
Why is its configuration—such as roundness and so forth—not perceived? If the atom is not established, how can there be the possibility of a composite whole?
(311) If atoms were established, how could there be the possibility of a composite whole? [For] how can this atom have contact with another by means of only one part?
(312) If there is contact by means of one part, then the entirety [of the atom] would be perceived. Therefore, due to the existence of such contact, it is not an atom, just like a gross object. (313)

Furthermore, it might be argued that a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) arises between two atoms as a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*), but not a contact (*saṃsparśa*)— whether by way of its entire self or by a single part;
yet even that is incorrect.
If conjunction occurs even in the absence of contact, then how is that very same [conjunction] possible? How could there be cognitions of a single, solid form within atoms?
(314) The reading *sa kuta eva sa* is appropriate; otherwise, there would be a metrical defect.
If, on the other hand, there were another whole (avayavin) [distinct from the atoms], then cognitions would have a uniform form everywhere;
furthermore, because atoms are eternal, they would be perceived as having intervals between them.
Now, the whole (avayavin) is one.
Even if atoms are indeed invisible to people like us, it is certainly not possible for them to be visible to the eyes of God.

(316) Furthermore, if He were to perceive these two [atoms] as distinct, how could there be an inherence [between them]? Under such circumstances, people would merely be under delusion, because they would be seeing things otherwise than they actually are. (317) And from what [source] does this notion arise that "the gross [object] is preceded by the conjunction of parts"?
Even if it were indeed perceived in a lump of clay and so forth, it is certainly not perceived in a sprout and so forth;
for it is thus:
It has been argued: "The seed of the banyan tree is exceedingly small, yet its effect is exceedingly massive. How could there be a conjunction of parts therein when they were previously non-existent?
For it is a settled principle that conjunction occurs only between parts that already exist.

Furthermore, since the parts of a gross object such as a stalk of grass are not perceived prior [to its formation], how could there be conjunction, and from what could a composite whole arise? Thus, everything is like a dance in the darkness. Alternatively, atoms pervading a portion of space are accumulated with the aid of perception.
That is incorrect;
for if existing things are accumulated, how could there be the emergence of something unprecedented from them? Since this arises from a cause, we have a doubt regarding all of these.
(319) Now, even if it is not seen, it is understood to exist simply because of an example; by the force of the example of a lamp, the Sāṃkhya view has been reached. (320)
Therefore, the claim that God is the creator has gone far indeed. Furthermore, manifesting agents such as lamps and the like are established as being insentient.

How can manifestation from something insentient serve as a proof for God? As for the argument that even such an agent must be presided over by a sentient being, the answer to that has already been given previously.
Therefore, let whatever arises from whatever cause arise from that very cause; it is certain that some things arise from sentience and others from other causes.

Even yellow might otherwise be white because it is a substance, like any other white thing; [if you say] "no" because of the contradiction of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then how can there be the thought "it is not here"? (324) The thought "it does not exist for me" is not at all [valid], for your non-perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramā*). If your non-perception were a means of valid cognition, then it should be understood that God does not exist. Furthermore,

it is not the case that [a mark] infers the intended cause merely by being an effect, or merely by being a configuration, or merely by being a real entity; for indeed, reasons do not function to establish what is to be proven according to human whim.

Rather, he says that whatever is perceived in a certain way from a certain cause, that very thing leads to the inference of that same cause.
3. It is established that whatever arrangement and so forth follows the presence or absence of a presiding agent is logical; therefore, that which is inferred from it is valid. || 11 ||
It is logical that from such [an arrangement] as is observed to produce persistence through the presence or absence of a controller,

or as is perceived to follow the presence or absence of a controller, precisely that same [controller] is inferred; thus it is appropriate [to infer] the [existence of an intelligent agent] from the specific arrangement and so forth.

He says: "The configuration, substantiality, or the persistence and activity—whatever kind [of effect] is perceived from whatever [kind of cause], an inference of a corresponding presiding agent for such [an effect] is logical, and not otherwise.

[This is] abandoned— [the error of] regarding as non-different, on the basis of a similarity of words, things that are established as distinct, such as their specific arrangements and so forth.
An inference is not valid in the case of fire [based on smoke], just as it is not [valid] in the case of a white substance and the like.

For if the reason were to be employed by setting aside the distinction of configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and taking up merely that which is denoted by the word "configuration"— thereby discarding the connection with a specific agent— or if it were merely "being an entity" (*vastutva*), then an inference would indeed be valid,
just as [one might infer] fire from a white substance.

In this case as well, there would be an inference based on the apprehension of a causal relationship—that the nature of smoke is inseparably connected with fire.
And thus, the Lord (*īśa*) even more certainly fails to attain proof; for one who desires gain, even the root is lost.

Therefore, when there is a difference in entities, the inference of a specific superintendence by a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhānaviśeṣa*)—which is observed in the case of a difference in entities such as jars and the like, which possess specific shapes—is not tenable on the basis of a mere similarity of words for that which lacks such difference;
the same applies to the case of God (*īśvara*). This is a definitive conclusion.

If it is argued that [the cognition] follows the positive and negative concomitance of fire because of its paleness, then [that would apply] to the distinction between the positive and negative concomitance of that [paleness].
Furthermore, it might be argued:

if we were to proceed with an inference based on "whiteness" as a property devoid of any specific qualification, then there would be sublation by perception; however, fire-contact is not perceived in all cases of whiteness, because its opposite is observed [in some instances].
But in the case of the inference for God (Īśvara), that inference would indeed be sublated.
This is not so;
for inference does not proceed on the grounds that "it is not sublated. It has been stated that its operation occurs through the observation of a relationship.
Otherwise, [one might as well infer] some modification of clay from a potter.
From the fact that jars and such things are produced by an agent, it would follow that an anthill is also a product of such an agent.
Indeed, there is no subverting evidence against the inference that an anthill is made by a potter; nor is mere non-perception itself a subverting factor.
If the potter were the creator [of the world], he would be perceived; why then is God not perceived? [Objection:
In that case, one should not even postulate the existence of unseen karma (*adṛṣṭa*).
In that case, does the entry into the knee occur simply because it is a hollow space?

If, then, this scrutiny of yours is so subtle, why do you not observe that even among mountains and other things of irregular shape, the activity of an intelligent agent is not perceived? Thus, why does their [the mountains'] action not also follow the "half-old woman" logic (*ardhajarati*)?

for what role do the specific structural forms fashioned in those mountains and such things play? It is thus.
"Is the structure of the earth produced otherwise without the employment [of effort], or is the Person not the cause therein? Because of that, there is deformity.

For instance,

[the fallacy] "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*) occurs when one argues, "Sound is an effect because it is invariably concomitant with effort," while [the opponent] counters that there are multiple types of effects produced by effort.
Just as manifestation is observed even after another effort, and thus sound is not something produced,
so too here, a configuration is observed even though it is not produced by [any further] action.
In the Nyāyasūtra 5.2,

1. [The reason] is abandoned by the proponent because it follows from the effect, even though it is used as a means of proof in a general sense.
The fault of asserting a difference based on a difference in the relata is considered *kāryasama* (balancing the effect).

For even when the proof is established through a general property such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) which is common to the probandum, whatever fault is stated regarding the object of that proof is considered *kāryasama*, having the nature of the fallacy known as *kāryasama*.
What kind of fault?
The fault of stating a distinction;
"stating" means introducing a distinction.
What is meant by "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)? Is it taken in the sense of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) or in the sense of origination (*utpatti*)?
The fault of asserting a distinction based on the difference in these related entities is *kāryasama* (balancing the effect).
In that case as well, if one points out that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Even if one argues that there is no contradiction because of the removal of obstructions through effort, this is not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*);
rather, it constitutes a valid proof even in its general form.

Since even manifestation is indeed contradictory for that which is eternal, this is therefore a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*); otherwise, the pointing out of an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason would truly be valid.
"By anyone"—this is a reading resulting from negligence;
now follows the reply to this.

If there were a difference in the effect [of sound], then its non-production through effort would follow from the possibility of causes for non-perception and the possibility of a difference in the effects of effort. This might be so regarding the existence of sound, because causes for its non-perception—such as obstruction—are possible; however, no such cause as obstruction is possible for sound.
Therefore, there is no manifestation of this [sound] immediately following effort;
for where there is manifestation immediately following effort, a cause of non-perception— namely, an obstruction— is employed,
and through the removal of that obstruction, the perception of the object occurs, which constitutes a manifestation distinct from that [non-perception].
4 T. For the difference in the nature of the effect is the state of not being caused by effort;
[its] attainment occurs immediately after effort.
Therefore, the manifestation of the characteristic of apprehension occurs;
to this it is replied:
"That [manifestation] does not belong to sound either"—how, and for what reason, is this understood?
If it is argued that even for an eternal entity, a connection with manifestation is logically possible;

or if it should be further claimed that although the word is not perceived, a cause such as an obstruction exists— as is clearly seen in the case of jars and the like— then [the word] must be produced by effort.
That too is incorrect;
for one might as well assume that there exist obstructions and the like for sound. Since sound is recognized [through] recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), it is not subject to destruction.

Just as jars and other objects previously perceived do not perish during their state of being obstructed, they are recognized again precisely through recognition once the obstruction has been removed.

Sound, too, is rightly established as being exactly like that through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Now, if it is argued that such cognition arises merely from perception by another and not from recognition itself as a direct [experience], then this is a truly great "vision of reality" (*tattvadṛṣṭi*)!
Furthermore:
Even if that [self] is recognized by another through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) or some other means, how can its eternity be established even on the basis of that other person?
Therefore, in this case, the previously stated refutation remains valid,
beginning with the words "the relation [is not established] even when proving it by way of a universal" (*sāmānyenāpi sādhane sambandhītyādi*).

6. "In the proof," and so forth; or rather, that demonstration of the non-establishment of the probandum by means of a slight difference regarding the nature of being an effect is "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*). This, moreover, is threefold according to the intention of the speaker. (334)
7. In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
this was stated by relying on the definition of the "equal effect" (*kāryasama*) as formulated by the Teacher (Dignāga).

It has been demonstrated that the definition provided by Akṣapāda is incorrect. Regarding *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative): even when there is similarity (*sādharmya*), the statement of a distinction is *vikalpasama*.
For example, when impermanence has been established for a pot based on its similarity to [the subject] as before, one says:
"Even though this similarity exists, only the pot is impermanent due to its being an effect, its being visible, and so forth, but nothing else is."
Its meaning is this:

if one argues that sound is non-eternal because it is a product, like a jar, and then asks what would happen to the jar—which is also a product—in light of its being non-eternal, [the resulting fallacy] is "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*).
For this [fallacy] is threefold according to the speaker's intention:

if the speaker intends that "the pot's state of being an effect does not exist in sound," then it is the "unestablished" (asiddha) fallacy; however, if he intends that "the state of being an effect belonging to sound does not exist among impermanent things such as pots," then it is the same.
Then there is the appearance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
If it is argued that [the reason] does not apply even if that [subject] were eternal,
then because it is unshared (*asādhāraṇatva*), it is the "equal to the uncertain" (*aniścitasama*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that here too, the proof proceeds by means of generalities such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) or "having a configuration" (*saṃsthānatva*)?

For if one were to postulate a connection with a specific [cause], it would result in nothing but the fallacy of *kāryasama* (balancing the effect), since one would then be postulating configurations such as those of a jar or a mountain.
3. But surely, [the argument] cannot be a proof by means of a general property such as being an effect (kārya) based on its having the nature of shape (saṃsthāna) and so forth?
That [argument] is untrue;
for shape and so forth are not a universal produced by intentional action, since such is observed elsewhere as well, such as in trees and the like—so it has been described.
Any proof that is offered by abandoning a specific qualification is utterly irrelevant, like the blackness of a crow in proving impermanence. (335–336)
To this, the opponent says:
"Even if the connection with action preceded by intelligence is not observed [in the case of mountains], that very [connection] shall be the probans for the manifestation of their shape."
The connection with verbal denotation, however, will consist in [the cognition] "configuration, configuration," and so forth;
therefore, because they possess non-different characteristics, the establishment of their having a single effect follows.
This is incorrect.
For,
from a property (dharma) constructed by mere conceptualization and devoid of objective reality, when that property occurs in some desired object—
whether it be of a different class [from the original]— [a cognition arises] due to the perception of a commonality of words [applied to both]. (337)
It is not logical to establish [the existence of horns] in rabbits and the like on the basis of their being "cow," as in the case of [inferring horns from] a cow.
For the connection with horns is well-established in other species as distinct from rabbits and the like;
how could that be inferred merely from the non-difference in verbal designation, such as "it is a cow"? (15)

It has been stated that even when the meaning is not different, there is no inference because of its paleness; how much more so where there is not even a meaning, but only the word itself which is identical? First of all, it is possible for a meaning to be connected with the desired probandum, yet even that is declared by those who possess subtle insight to be non-probative.
How much more so, then, the mere similarity of words, from which even the scent of a connection with the probandum has been driven far away;
for since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, where indeed do they not exist?
But if the object is established through the existence of that [intention], then everything is established for everyone.
(16) And where do these words not exist? Since they are unimpeded everywhere by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), if the object is to be proven, it is thereby established.
No one would encounter a failure in the accomplishment of their purpose;
therefore, [the opponent's position] is devoid of merit.
Therefore, the non-existence of another self is established;

by this same reasoning, the insentience of the followers of Kapila and others has been considered, as well as the sentience of that which is impermanent and so forth, [refuted] because of death and the removal of the skin. (17)

For even the non-consciousness or whatever else [is asserted] by the followers of Kapila and others, since it does not serve as the goal for that [liberation], it is merely constructed from a similarity of words; for instance: The followers of Kapila maintain that the self is pure consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), devoid of all attributes such as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). They hold that this self, being eternal and unchanging, is liberated when it is freed from the three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—which are products of the primary matter (*prakṛti*). However, this liberation is merely a state of isolation (*kaivalya*) where the self remains as pure consciousness, devoid of any object of experience. Since this state lacks any purposeful activity or attainment for the self, it is no different from the state of deep sleep or the dissolution of the universe, and thus cannot be considered the ultimate goal of human endeavor. Therefore, their doctrine is established merely through a verbal similarity to our own position, while lacking its actual substance.
Impermanence is not established for the Sāṃkhya from the perspective of the actual nature of things; for him, it is the non-manifestation of categories, not their destruction without residue.
Indeed, impermanence as the non-manifestation of that which already exists is not established for the Buddhist;
what then is it?
) The state of being destroyed without leaving a trace 1 T.
abandoned— of that which exists.
Now, is not concealment (*tirobhāva*) exactly the same as destruction or non-manifestation?
What is this concealment?
It is the state of being invisible.
If it is argued that even for things such as a rabbit’s horn, there would be the attainment of impermanence— meaning that even what exists is impermanent—
then [we reply] that this would apply to the *pradhāna* and so forth as well, insofar as they possess a perceptible nature.
If it is argued that impermanence consists in the visible object attaining the state of being invisible,
then what is this so-called "visibility"?
If it is the very nature of the object, how can there be invisibility of that which is visible?

If that [perceptibility] is abandoned, the very nature of the entity does not exist. Now, if perceptibility were something other than the entity, then how would its absence not constitute a destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*)?
Nor can there be the concealment of one thing through the absence of another.
Alternatively, since it is always equal to the primary [cause], there is no impermanence;
therefore, why is this accepted as a proof based on mere conceptualization of sound?
Likewise, because of the nature of death, [it follows] from the exclusion of the skin.
"In the case of stripping off all the skin, [the offense is complete] because of death" means that it is merely the occurrence of the term "death.
(The word "not" is an addition in manuscript T.)
Non-apprehension [of consciousness, etc. is indeed non-manifestation;
for death, according to the Buddhist view, is the cessation of consciousness and so forth. For one for whom consciousness is unestablished in trees, their cognition is likewise [unestablished]. (340)
Since there is doubt regarding the cessation of consciousness in trees, who would believe that death—which consists of the cessation of consciousness and so forth—is free from doubt?

For there is no cessation of consciousness in the absence of consciousness; likewise, there is none of vitality (*āyus*), since it is said: "Vitality is life; it is the support of heat and consciousness."
For how could one accept that death is accompanied by consciousness?
Therefore, he states that death consists of desiccation;
and that is not an absolute proof for [the presence of] consciousness, since it is observed even in mud and similar substances.
If it is argued that this too is established because the term "death" is applied [to it],
it has been stated in this regard:
"Because it is dependent upon the speaker's intention."
Now, since the intention to speak arises here from the perception of the object, this is not a fault.
(Abhidharmakośa 2.4)
[The reading] "tarūṇām" is superior.

The word for that [death] is established only when death itself is established; and the establishment of the word occurs through its connection [to that meaning]. Thus, the proof of death—characterized by the cessation of cognition and so forth—is derived from the word; and the derivation from the word depends upon the observation of such death, while the observation of such death depends upon the proof of death. This is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Now, if the relationship between word and meaning were eternal, then it would follow that speech and other such things also possess horns.

Or, if the word "cow" applied to speech and so forth is indeed different [from the word for a bovine animal], then that [word] is not at all connected to the possession of horns; for in that case, the word "death" would likewise not be distinct [from other words]. What, then, is your proof in this matter?
Therefore, because [the argument] proceeds by means of such persistence and so forth as the proof for impermanence and the like, there is no establishment of the probandum (sādhya). 6 T.
In the same way, even by means of existence, configuration, and so forth, there is no establishment of the probandum in the case of "that which has horns."
If, then, by means of conceptualizing specific distinctions, the probans becomes non-probative—
such that [the probans] like shape and so forth,
as well as other [properties] like being produced and so forth, are likewise non-probative from the perspective of the opponent— then everything would be unestablished due to such conceptualization.
For it is thus:
conceptualization.

The property of sound being a quality of space is unestablished for the opponent; thus, there is a mutual lack of establishment regarding the property of both the probandum and the example. (342) That too is incorrect, because according to scripture, the nature of being a quality of space does not at all denote anything [specific]. Furthermore, if one were to postulate a specific [quality], the very reason (*hetu*) would be abandoned. (343)
Therefore,
when the nature of the entity itself is not established, this is the logical rule; [only] when it is established is there a qualification.

It is non-obstructive even when [the property] is unestablished, just as sound has space as its locus. For although the quality of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is not established by scripture, sound is indeed well-known in its own nature as the subject (*dharmin*). Thus, because the property (*dharma*) is unestablished, even if one imagines a specific qualification, the reason (*hetu*) is neither unestablished in relation to the subject nor inconclusive due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).

For since the locus (*dharmin*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not unestablished merely because a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished; nor is the postulation of a specific qualification useful anywhere,
for there is no necessity to adopt a specific qualification in that case.
For instance:
"The universal of impermanence and being an effect is indeed useful; however, the establishment of a particular [instance] is not accepted by anyone. (344)
The state of being produced immediately after a cause and the state of being destroyed immediately thereafter do not exist as qualities possessed by both sound and a jar.
Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever in that which is devoid of any prior or posterior nature;
nor does space qualify it.
Because it is the object of that single reflective awareness,
that conceptualization is non-existent;
however, its connection with shape and so forth is indeed unestablished.
The remainder has already been stated; however, the mere word "configuration" (saṃsthāna) is simply not a proof, because—
Even if that [reason] is unestablished for the word, it is established with respect to the established entity.

Just as the proof for corporeality and so forth was stated by a Buddhist against the Aulūkya: "Atoms are impermanent because they are corporeal. This proof was stated by the Buddhist against the Vaiśeṣika;
however, in this case, the word [“corporeality”] is not established within the subject mutually accepted by both parties.

The Buddhists maintain that "form" (*mūrti*) is the term denoting the dimension of a non-pervasive substance, and that form consists in the conjunction with touch. Even if this very word [“form”] is not established regarding the subject matter mutually accepted by both parties, nevertheless, since the object intended by that word is established for both, even though the word itself is unestablished, the intended probandum (*sādhya-artha*)— the entity established for the Buddhist— is established for both.
Now, if the probandum is established just as it is when the object is non-deviant or established, then the same would apply to the word; what, then, is the difference between these two?
No.

Even when that [object] itself is subject to deviation and so forth, the means of proof should be understood as being faultless even in the word, because the establishment of a real entity proceeds from a real entity. (20)
For it is not the case that, as the probandum is established by the force of the real entity even when the word is unestablished,

so too is the probandum established by the force of the word even when the real entity is unestablished; rather, one should know that the means of proof is defective— possessing the faults of deviation, non-establishment, or contradiction— even if the word itself is non-deviant.
To begin with, it is impossible for a word to be non-deviant when the object itself is deviant; however, even granting that the word might be non-deviant,
the proof remains defective.
How can one thing be established from another thing, and not from a word?
Surely, if the word does not invariably accompany the probandum (*sādhya*), then the probandum cannot be established from the word;
yet, if the probandum is established from it, how can the word be non-deviant?
By this, he demonstrates that a word is useful for establishing the probandum (sādhya) only by way of indicating the real object (vastu), but not directly.
Therefore, even if one desires the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) of the word, it lacks the capacity to prove the probandum because it does not abandon the [actual] object.
Therefore, only reflection directed toward the object is useful; the determination of whether the thing deviates from its nature or not will occur later.

Consequently, there is no reason consisting of the form of the object itself from which the existence of God could be established; thus, it is proven that even in the case of impermanence, [the argument] lacks validity.
Sound is established as useful.
It will be explained in the same way even regarding the eternal [nature].
Furthermore, there can be no distinction between the causality and non-causality of space and so forth and that of the Lord on the grounds of their eternity;
for in whatever way that entity is a cause, in that very same way it is a non-cause.
When that [space, etc. is accepted as a cause by whom? It is not desired to be a non-cause.

Since properties such as all-pervasiveness and oneness belong to space and so forth just as they do to Īśvara, then, despite this equality, from what basis does the distinction arise that Īśvara is the cause while space and so forth are not causes?
Now, it might be argued that [the self] is spoken of in this way simply because of its connection with knowledge characterized by the desire to act;
but that too is incorrect, for the same [objection] applies there as well.
Furthermore, [the properties such as] pervasiveness, eternality, and so forth— T. 3.

It is not observed that [an effect arises] by the mere desire to act; is this a matter of chance (*kākatālīya*), or is there a cause in that way? (346) If karma and so forth were the cause, then it would be a cause;
otherwise, why is it not accepted that everything is the cause of everything? (347)
If [it is argued that] karma and so forth are the causes of manifestation,
Alternatively, just as it was without a cause prior to creation, so too during the state of creation it remains without a cause due to the absence of any distinction; therefore,
for one who is liberated from all passion and the like, neutrality alone is appropriate.
If it is argued that one cannot attain equanimity because of the predominance of worldly karma, [we reply:
no.
If this Lord is dependent on other actions, how can he truly be the Lord?
Or, if he acts through the sequence of his own grace, why is there such a distinction as the arrangement of hell-beings and so forth, making him merciless?
If it is argued that karma alone acts thus upon the world, then his powerlessness in this regard means he lacks true lordship.

If the Noble One has the power to perform what is good, why would he commit an evil deed? (349) Indifference alone is appropriate for the virtuous toward a course of action that is unwholesome; for the virtuous, applying salt to a wound is not a noble act.
(350) Or, if this [course of action] is indeed of such a nature, then he reveals it and exerts himself to bring it about.
Such indeed is my nature;
it cannot be prevented by me,
and therefore people should conduct themselves therein according to what is appropriate.

Since he is not even master over himself, how could he possibly be the Lord of the world whose actions are determined by their own karma? (351) If it is argued that he is called "Lord" because he is impelled [by others], then there is a mutual dependence; in such a case, the existence of even one of them is not logically established. (352)
If the Lord possesses no power, then people would simply be the result of the law of good karma;
if the world were one that acts with independent will, then the doctrine of karma here would be praised as supreme. (353)
Furthermore, even if [the effect] were produced independently,
God might still occasionally be the cause, even though he is not known by people like us who do not perceive the truth.
In that case,

only one who perceives reality would be the knower for the sake of knowing that [reality], and there would have to be another knower of him; because of this infinite regress, there would be the consequence of multiple lords.
But for the sake of establishing that [point], by us and others...

When Caitra’s wound heals due to his connection with a weapon and medicine, why is causality not attributed to a post, which has no such connection? (23) Or, if you say that the post is not a cause because it lacks activity due to its lack of connection, [we reply:]...
Even in the case of a post, there may sometimes be activity,
yet it is not perceived by us who do not see reality; however,
if it is argued that because it is not perceived, the post therefore has no activity—
In that case,
even causal activity is not tenable without a difference in intrinsic nature.

Because that which is eternal is devoid of change, its causal capacity is difficult to establish. (24) Whether by way of the eternity of a continuous stream or otherwise, how could the activity of God—even as an effect—be logically possible without a difference in his intrinsic nature?
The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "of God too" (*īśvarasyāpi*) is intended to be construed with the preceding clause.

Just as there is a distinction produced by a potter and others, so too might there be one produced by Īśvara; yet, since that which is eternal is devoid of change, the attribution of causal capacity is difficult to maintain. (355)

Because [the effect] always pervades its locus and there is no absence [of it when the causes are present], if one were to postulate something other than those [causes] for which [the effect] necessarily exists, there would be an infinite regress of causes due to their being required as causes for that [other thing]. (25)
In the case of potters and others, when their activity is present, the desired result indeed occurs;

nevertheless, to postulate another [agent] there would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthiti) among all the causes of a single effect, with no finality. Indeed, once one has entered into a postulation that lacks any supporting evidence, there is no further contradiction [in continuing such a practice].
Alternatively, if that very [entity] which was previously unstable now remains stable due to causes, then even so, that same thing would be the cause; thus, any further action would be futile.
(2) "Not new" (*anabhinava*) refers to one who is not a newlywed bride (*badhū*).
If it is argued that just as the earth is an ever-abiding cause for the sprout and so forth, so too is Īśvara,
and no beginning of the earth and other elements is perceived— here is the rebuttal:

The earth and other elements are the cause for the production of a sprout through a transformation of their own nature (*svabhāvapariṇāma*), because a specific quality [in the sprout] is observed when they have been cultivated. For it is indeed observed that the growth of barley and other crops follows a sequence of modifications produced by specific activities such as the operation of the plow; thus, there is the conceptualization of the earth and other elements as causes. (26)
Furthermore, regarding the objection and its refutation:

if it is argued that just as the collection of object and sense-faculty is the cause of cognition even without a specific [quality], so too is this [the case here]—then we reply: not so, for even in that instance there is indeed a specific [quality]. || 27 ||

If those [causes] that are individually powerless lack a specific excellence in their continuum, they would likewise lack efficacy even when combined; therefore, a proven excellence [of the causes] must exist.
For the causality of the eye and other [senses] is determined by the specific nature of the effect.

For cognition is the effect; it is restricted to the apprehension of form, possesses the aspect of form, and has the nature of awareness. Since these [causes] function through mutual exclusion, a distinction is possible. Therefore, the eye and the other [senses] are the causes of this cognition as an effect;

for individually they are incapable, and within the aggregate of the aspects of cognition, there is no quality of awareness in the eye, no restriction to the apprehension of form in the visible object, and no otherness in the mental attention.
Because it is not seen in this way in each individual case; [T. adds:
not.
1T. Why? Because it is not seen.
Now, it might be argued that just as when the eye is opened, although various forms appear one after another, there is no difference in the eye at those times.

Just as there is the arising of successive states of visual consciousness while form remains constant, so too, even though Īśvara is eternally established in a state of uniformity, there is the production of successive states; thus, he is not a non-cause.
To this it has been said: [if one were to grant] that space and so forth are also causes, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
2. The *Īśvaraniṣedhavārttika* (is completed).
The fifth chapter (*pañcamāhnika*) begins.

Due to a specific quality of the eye, and also due to a specific quality of the form, there exists a distinctiveness in consciousness; therefore, form and the other [objects] possess the status of being causes.

(356) Because of a specific quality of form—characterized by such features as a vividly manifesting appearance—a consciousness associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth arises. (357) 5. Causality resides in the collection of causes.

Therefore, those things which are individually incapable but whose quality is conceived as being present when combined possess causality; this does not apply to [the cause] such as Īśvara, because there is no difference [in his case].
Likewise, due to specific conditions such as the closing of the eyes, there occurs a specific change such as lack of clarity in vision.
Being bound to that [effect], one attributes the state of being an effect to its cause;
however, there is no such reason for postulating Īśvara as the cause. Therefore...

If those [atoms] are individually incapable and there is no excellence in their continuum (*santāna*), then in the absence of such excellence in the continuum, they would lack capacity even when combined; how could that very same nature—which is the opposite of being a cause—become the cause? What is the answer to this?
As for the postulation of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth as causes, the reason has already been stated, and thus there is no fault.

1. Because he possesses knowledge, the Blessed One is an authority (*pramāṇa*).
If, then, there is no cause for the thorough knowledge of God— neither a communicator nor a creator— then such a cause would not exist elsewhere either;
for validity consists in the knowledge of an imperceptible object and the means of achieving that [knowledge].
Some declare that because [an omniscient being] does not exist, there is no practice [of the path].
As for one who was previously not omniscient but becomes omniscient—
what is the cause for his thorough knowledge of objects beyond the reach of the senses?
Indeed, no such cause has been observed from which the knowledge of everything arises through practice;
furthermore, mantras, tantras, and so forth generally arise from all [possible] commitments (samaya),
nor is there any reason for certain determination therein.
There is partial agreement with all [other] statements,
yet it is not possible for sense-perception to directly perceive supersensible objects, because sensory cognition is observed to have only proximate objects as its domain.

If the arising of omniscience occurred despite there being no distinction between sensory objects—such that contact with the tasting of impure substances and the like were unavoidable—then everyone would be omniscient, since there is no difference in their sensory objects.

(358) Furthermore, contact with the tasting of impure substances and the like would be impossible to prevent. Moreover, if the senses function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārī*), how can one be called "all-knowing"? (359)

Even its mental consciousness does not follow from the sense faculties; indeed, no one perceives mental cognition as being independent [of them]. (360) Its clarity arises from habituation, yet it would not have all things as its object; even if it were dependent on the senses, the consequence would be that it is non-erroneous. (361)
But when [an object] is established through inference, not every entity is apprehended. Therefore, since cultivation does not have everything as its object, how could one be omniscient?

(362) Through the repeated study of treatises and the like, one may indeed come to understand those very treatises and so forth; but from what source will the knowledge of everything in its entirety ever arise? (363)
Consciousness is that which knows everything; if it does not know its objects, how can it be such? Even if it were to know those objects, it would indeed be the omniscient one.
(364) Furthermore, the claim that "the teaching was composed by one who is free from passion and likewise free from conceptual construction" is merely borrowed ornamentation.
(365) Who, even over the course of many eons, could individually and sequentially understand each thing—past, present, and future, beginningless and endless—in its entirety? (366)
Who indeed does not possess some partial knowledge? For there is not even a single true fact that does not exist within a person of many kalpas.
One who is seen to possess excellence knows only a certain limited portion based on that much [study], but is not at all a knower of objects beyond the senses. (367–368)

Furthermore, it is not logically possible for one who knows the truth of only a single part to be omniscient; this would be a mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*) that would cause further confusion. [Objection: If there were simultaneous knowledge of everything, how could there be beginningless saṃsāra? That in which knowledge reaches its completion is what is called the "beginning" in this context. To this, it is replied: 369–370. Furthermore, it is not logically possible for one who knows the truth of only a single part to be omniscient; this would be a mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*) that would cause further confusion. If there were simultaneous knowledge of everything, how could there be beginningless saṃsāra? That in which knowledge reaches its completion is what is called the "beginning" in this context. The translation above reflects the content as presented.)
It is not maintained that another person knows everything as a means of valid cognition;
rather, he is not a deceiver and is capable of accomplishing what is desired.
What is the reason for this?

A person possessing knowledge is sought out for the sake of practicing what has been taught by him, by those who suspect deception in the instruction given by one who lacks knowledge. Indeed, it is not that some other [mundane] goal is desired to be accomplished, for which the knowledge of the teacher is sought elsewhere. (31)
Even if that [object] is ascertained, there remains the possibility of being deceived regarding what was intended;
furthermore, if one were to maintain that knowledge of it indeed exists even in that case,
such ascertainment would not apply to everything, because knowledge is impossible in all cases.

Therefore, that very thing must be known by him if it is known; thus, when those who are ignorant suspect deception on the part of one who teaches what they themselves do not know, this person is indeed an authority regarding his knowledge of that specific object, and his knowledge of other matters should likewise be presumed.
For he who knows the primary goal of man and who knows all the principles purified by valid cognition is alone the authority; by that much alone is he to be worshipped.
As for everything else, it is entirely the same for all those worthy of worship.
And for whom is that [teaching] possible,
by whom it was taught,
yet who do not understand what is seen through valid means of knowledge and which is the primary goal of man?

If it is argued: "Only these [ordinary people] know this, so that is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because the possibility of non-comprehension exists there; how, then, can there be instruction?"
[They] say that [the Buddha's teaching] is like the instruction of nihilism due to beginningless tradition.
Because he knows what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the Blessed One is a valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, if there is no complete knowledge [of all things], then because doubt arises regarding everything, it is possible that another person might also lack complete knowledge;
therefore, one who does not conceive of universal knowledge, how could they conceive of complete knowledge even in this case?
As for the teaching, however, it is due to traditional instruction.
That is incorrect:

regarding an object that lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a tradition of instruction is clear; however, regarding an object established by a means of valid cognition, such a tradition of instruction is impossible.
For in cases such as [the soul's] eternity, where no means of valid cognition is possible, there is no recourse other than a tradition of instruction.
If an object is determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be any suspicion of ignorance regarding it?
Or, even if such suspicion were to arise, activity toward that object would necessarily occur because of the certainty provided by the *pramāṇa*.
Alternatively, if there is no certainty even regarding what has been seen by a *pramāṇa*, then [certainty] must lie in direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).

Thus it follows that even though he has seen what is to be seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such a subtle scrutiny has arisen that he is suspected [of error] among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthya*); what then will his discourse be like? (372) For the Blessed Tathāgata, there is discourse regarding what has been seen through valid cognition.
In that regard, for one who harbors doubt even here, what need is there to mention those sacred sites where there is no following of thorough knowledge?
Therefore, because he speaks of matters established by valid cognition, the Blessed One is indeed the authority (*pramāṇa*).

Because he declares matters perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the man who knows the path to heaven and liberation is a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even if he lacks complete knowledge of other things, that [status] may still belong to him.
Therefore, let his knowledge regarding what is to be practiced be investigated.
Of what use to us is his knowledge of the number of insects?
(32) For it is only the denial of his being a knower of Dharma that is here refuted; who can prevent another from denying everything else? (374)
Now, if it is argued that the Tathāgata is considered omniscient because his knowledge of a single portion is verified, then by the same logic,
others would also be [considered omniscient] based on the verification of such statements as "fire is the antidote to cold," leading to an infinite regress;
and this is not the case.
Because practice is impossible due to mutual contradiction;
[and] because of lack of thorough knowledge.
That too is untrue;

for he who makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means for that abandonment and adoption, is accepted as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*), but not one who makes everything known. (33)

Since he is not the knower of every single object that does not have human purpose as its characteristic, he does not thereby become the knower of everything; for it is impossible for anyone not to know at least a fraction of what pertains to human purpose.

In this regard, the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted consists in the truths of suffering and cessation, while the reality of the means consists in the truths of origin and the path, which are the causes of those very two—suffering and cessation.

Therefore, he who is the knower of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—characterized by the four noble truths—and who is the communicator of that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is himself a valid authority;
this applies as much to the path to heaven as it does to anything else that can be determined through valid cognition.
Furthermore, nothing in the words of the Sugata is impossible that might merely amaze women and *śūdras*.
Therefore, only that which perceives the purpose of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because no other [means] is possible.
Having abandoned [the distinction between] what is to be discarded and what is to be accepted, let him look far beyond that, whether he perceives the desired reality or not.
"If one who sees from afar is the authority, then let us worship vultures!
For it is not the case that merely because someone possesses the power of distant vision, they can be presumed to possess knowledge of everything.

If this were so, then vultures and the like would also possess such knowledge; thus, by accepting them through worship—along with pigs and others who have keen hearing—one has utterly abandoned the path of all right reasoning."
3. Because of his compassion, the Blessed One is an authority.
(1) The proof of [the Buddha's] other births:
Now, is it the case that knowledge of all objects is impossible and entirely useless, such that only knowledge of the primary goals of human existence is sought by him?
This is not so:
that one should know everything and be the knower of all is not denied; rather, we maintain contentment with the thought that it is impossible for us to know [it all]. (375)

Indeed, the omniscient one does not know another omniscient one due to the absence of a means [to do so]; for the notion that "he knows everything" arises from knowing his objects of knowledge. Knowledge of even a single part of those [objects] arises only for one who already knows them. (376)

Even trees and the like, which possess knowledge common to women and śūdras, are known by another only through that very knowledge; there is no means [of knowing] whether they themselves have cognized it or not. As for those great ones who have attained far-reaching vision, the possibility of their being omniscient is preceded by the thorough knowledge of a single portion; even for them, the possibility of such reality is dependent upon another.
Now, one might ask: "From what does the proof of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possessing both characteristics arise, and what is its reason? To this he says:
"The proof [of that] arises from the practice of compassion. From what does the proof of that validity arise? It arises because that cognition depends upon the body.
And that compassion arises from the practice of compassion; because the intellect depends upon the body,
and because that compassion depends upon the body which is the support of the intellect, it— compassion, when accompanied by practice— reaches the highest state of excellence.
Even if there were compassion, how could its validity [as a means of knowledge] possibly arise?

For it is possible that the desire for another to be separated from suffering and from the causes of suffering is compassion; and one who possesses that [compassion] consequently develops the intent to acquire the means for that [separation]. (377)
For it will be demonstrated later that one who possesses the desire for the separation of others from suffering necessarily seeks the means [to achieve it];
alternatively, compassion is the means (*sādhana*),
for one who possesses compassion is never devoid of the intent to benefit others.
Therefore, through the teaching for the sake of others, the Compassionate One acts with skillful means as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*);
and that very skillful means is the proof of his own validity.
From what does that very compassion, characterized by the desire to protect all beings, arise? He says:
from the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇābhyāsāt*).
For compassion, through the practice of [contemplating] suffering, extends even toward those who are indifferent or hostile;
therefore, since the protection of all beings is not possible without omniscience, the practice of its means is undertaken.
Now, one might object: the intellect of the wise rests upon the body, and compassion is likewise nothing but intellect.
Furthermore, since that [practice] is dependent upon the body,
its cultivation remains unaccomplished due to the body's reduction to ashes;
for if the possibility of another birth exists, then through the accumulation of practice over many births, the attainment of the desired goal occurs.
For instance:

"The intellect (mati) is either identical with the body, an effect of the body, or a quality of the body; since these three views are held here, the possibility of cultivation (abhyāsa) does not exist.
Thus he said: [378]
If it is argued that practice is unestablished because cognition depends upon a body, we say no, because the dependence on a body has been refuted. (35)
Because the dependence of a solitary body, devoid of the intellect associated with its prior continuum, is denied, a solitary body—
whether as an effect, a quality, or otherwise— cannot indeed function as a substratum [thus,
the intellect does not depend upon the body].
Is it not the case that intellect is perceived as dependent on the body and as an effect of the body, since we observe it to rely upon the bodies of the mother and father?
For indeed, its form, conduct, mental acuity, and so forth, which follow the lineage of the mother and father, reside in the great elements of the produced body, just like paintings and the like.
The forms produced by the work of a painter, which are dependent upon a wall and follow from the consciousness of the painter’s form,

do not therefore remain existing apart from the wall, nor do they migrate to another wall, nor do they come from another wall— just like the form produced by the ripening of a mango fruit and the like.
Or rather, smoke does not come from another fire,
nor does it go to another fire;
however, the power of intoxication, which resides in the liquor, arises as something unprecedented through contact with the flavors of astringent substances and the like.
Just as [a substance] being dissolved does not depend on another liquid,
so too are the specific states of sensory consciousness;
and thus it has been said:
Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles;
earth and the others alone are the principles, and the principles themselves are earth and the others,
not space and so forth, nor momentariness and so forth.
Likewise, the principles (tattvas) themselves are neither mere consciousness nor entirely empty,
because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for such [an extreme].
The designation "object," "sense-faculty," and "body" applies to their collection.
The body and so forth are merely an immeasurable collection of specific transformations (*pariṇativiśeṣa*) of the great elements (*mahābhūta*);
consciousness arises from those bodies, sense-faculties, and objects,
just as intoxicating power arises from yeast and other ingredients.
Therefore, consciousness does not come from the next world and possess reconnection (*pratisandhi*), just like the power of intoxication;
and "like the power of intoxication" is an illustration that includes [the examples] "like a painting" and "like smoke."
Indeed, these have not been observed as wandering [mental factors];
[the reading] "śes" in place of "śes" (jñāna) is a scribal error.
Smoke does not arise from another fire, nor does it produce another fire.
The object of conventional discourse:
2. Consciousness [does not arise] from those—namely, from the body, the sense organs, and the intellect.
That is incorrect;

for apart from form and the other [sensory objects], how could there be the perception of the elements? Therefore, the determination of their number as five—namely, form, sound, odor, taste, and touch—is the five great elements—is illogical.
The designation "earth" and so forth applies to that collection because earth and the others are not perceived apart from it; furthermore,
since taste is indeed something tangible, there is a fourfold dimensionality.
Nevertheless, it is not logical [to say] "earth and so forth," for [in that case] "form and so forth" would be the denotatum;
since momentariness and other properties will be established later as the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no rejection of them.

Furthermore, if everything that is perceived were simply "the perceivable," it would follow that all things are one; however, if there is a distinction in their modes, it follows that they are infinite. (380)

Therefore, let that which is apprehended by the five bases be designated as fivefold; its internal subdivisions do not contradict its state as five. (381) As for what was said: "If there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding universal emptiness, then there is no emptiness; if there is emptiness, then the means of valid cognition does not exist"—these two [positions] are contradictory.
(382) The nature of universal emptiness and the kind of means of valid cognition that applies to it will be demonstrated later; what is the use of such haste here? (383)
(k) Refutation of the Doctrine of Consciousness as an Element of Matter:

Now, it may be argued that since the sense faculties and so forth follow the positive and negative concomitance of the bodies of the mother and father, and because they are of the same nature as the great elements of the body, they are necessarily dependent upon that body and cannot be perceived otherwise than as such;
therefore, how can the doctrine asserting the existence of a future world be more tenable?
4. But is it not the case that even this is untrue?
For:

Abandoned— because the birth of the vital breaths, the exhalations, the senses, and the intellect occurs from the body alone, and not from the body by itself independently of its own kind, when assuming a new birth. (36)
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument]:
for vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, due to specific intrinsic natures such as fickleness and the like, are not logically independent of their own genus;
furthermore, fickleness and the like follow from the habituation of the self, not from the habituation of the mother and father.

Otherwise, the nature of mother and father would not exist due to contact with non-existent things and so forth; therefore, an entity does not arise from the mere bodies of the parents alone, independent of their own species.
However, if desire and other factors previously existed within the nature of the mother and father, [then the offspring arises].
In that case, it would follow that the bodies of the mother, father, and so forth are also causes; this is not tenable.
It is not tenable.
॰śarīrānvaya:
Now, if it is admitted that the assumption of birth occurs entirely without regard for the next world;
In that case, if the assumption of taking birth were accepted, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
and the entire relationship between cause and effect would collapse;
and that [collapse] must be determined through the analysis of inference.

If all [phenomena], such as inhalation and exhalation, were preceded by practice, how indeed could they exist without their own practice, being thus without support? For this is the nature of an effect: that it does not come into being otherwise than by abandoning its cause;
otherwise, it would not be produced by that [cause].
Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the relationship of produced and producer is established;
therefore, the eyes and other sense organs are preceded by eyes and other organs of the same kind.
Now, [one might object]:...
Smoke arises from another instance of smoke and not from smoke alone in every respect; likewise, how does a lotus-root arise even from a śālka-plant, or from cow dung? (385) Thus...
A painting produced by a painter appears [realistic] even among birds; yet, that distinction which arises from practice will also occur through other means. || 386 ||
That too is incorrect;
for just as smoke is recognized as such from smoke, it is not known as such from anything else.
However, that specific quality which arises from practice remains the same at the beginning of birth and thereafter. (387)
That very same excellence which arises from the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is seen here to exist in such a manner even in the absence of practice in this life;
yet its connection with past practice is not sublated, because that past practice cannot be perceived at that time even in another case.
Just as [the fact that a cognition] has come from another village establishes its being preceded by practice,
so too it establishes that it is not preceded by a non-worldly (supernatural) practice; for there is an invariable concomitance between cause and effect,
since even that which has an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*) is still an effect of that [cause].
It also establishes that [the action] is preceded by practice in another location,
because there is an invariable concomitance between cause and effect,
and even that which has an unseen cause (adṛṣṭa) is an effect of that [practice].
Just like the thorough knowledge preceded by practice in another land, there occurs here this story of Tauta:
it is said that a certain Tauta was asked by another, "Tell me the origin."
"How can there be a dwelling for a bull with long horns whose mother [is barren]?
He replied: "These buffaloes are not born from the womb of a mother; rather, they are merely purchased for their price from those who have come to the market."
"Excessive"— this materialist doctrine (*lokāyatamata*) is indeed of such a nature within the belly,
or else:

Regarding the phrase "because of the over-extension [of the argument]": if consciousness arises as an effect from those very same great elements (*mahābhūta*) without having come from another birth, [then one might ask] why does it not arise in all living beings?

If you reply that it is because of the existence of a specific transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*), then the same objection applies: why is that specific transformation not present [in all cases]? Thus, the inquiry remains equal.

Furthermore, it is also untenable to claim that there exists some beginningless transformation or a specific succession that is not perceived, on account of which some living beings [possess this] and others do not. 2 T.
If this mutual distinction being observed is seen as a distinction of transformation, then what is this conceptualization?
That which is perceptible yet unseen is not the object of our conventional discourse regarding existence. || 390 ||

If that specific transformation were [directly] perceivable, it would be apprehended; however, if it is postulated solely on the basis of observing the effect, then in that case, only the observed repetition (*abhyāsa*) should be postulated, because of the principle of parsimony regarding the postulation of the unobserved (*adṛṣṭakalpanā-gaurava*). Therefore, it has been well said:
The vital breaths and so forth are preceded by entities of their own kind;
[that is,] they are preceded by those of a similar class.

Let it be that the existence of causes is established from their effects; but how can there be inference regarding those belonging to previous births and those belonging to future births? To this he says: "That which is observed possesses the capacity for reconnection."

What was it that he possessed previously which no longer exists later, such that there would be no continuity?
