For the reconnection of each preceding state with the following is established through inference, the inference of inferences, and so forth. But surely, restlessness and the like arise from the absence of restlessness due to the practice of that [restlessness], characterized by lack of movement and dullness.
But since that [existence] arises from the mere great elements (*mahābhūta*) alone, even when one state of smoke arises from another state of smoke, there is no continuous succession at all times;
therefore, just like smoke, there is also cessation. Thus, there is neither infinity for living beings nor the fault of the manifestation of previously non-existent sentient beings.
(That too does not exist.
Therefore, even from that [argument], the proof of previous births is not established;
consequently, the beginningless continuity of birth is not proven.
For, in the absence of beginninglessness, even though one smoke may arise from another smoke like [the sequence of] smoke and so forth, there is no constant, invariable connection at all times.
Through the practice of slow activity, there is also slowness among living beings; therefore, preceded by that [slowness], they fall into the beginningless wheel of existence.
(391) Indeed, these types of states, such as slowness and so forth, do not belong to living beings by their very nature.
Rather, it is established that [the traits] arise from the practice of their own kind:

just as fickleness and so forth result from the practice of those very traits, so too does dullness and so forth result from the practice of indolence (*kausīdya*). Thus, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is proven;

for through the practice of sleep and so forth, the eyes and other faculties become sluggish, and consequently, one who has awakened from sleep possesses fickle eyes and so forth, being joined with another such as himself.

Therefore, even at birth and so forth, just as in the case of waking from sleep, there is the engagement of the eyes and other organs due to the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) that have become manifest;
how can the eye belonging to one body be joined to another body,
and how can a power residing in one substance be transferred elsewhere?

Even at the very first birth, through the power of mantras, tantras, and so forth, the potencies of poison reside in molasses and other substances; likewise, through the power of karma, the potencies of seeing other bodies [exist]. (392)

Just as a body within a dream undergoes changes in the waking state through fear, leaping, and running, so too does it do so in other births. (393) Now, it is all the more excellent that this [body] is devoid of reality; for if even what is unreal can cause transformation, what need is there to mention that which is real? (394)
This [distinction] between truth and untruth is merely conventional; when the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is directly realized, such things as "truth" and so forth are untenable.

(395) Therefore, regarding that which was previously perceived as possessing the power of synthesis, what was there that was additional and is later absent? Because of the absence of that, it is subsequently without connection. For while it is true that an effect is absent when the cause is deficient, it is a contradiction to say that an effect does not arise when the cause is complete in all its parts.
Is there not indeed a contradiction here? Indeed, this very contradiction is the absence of the relation between cause and effect.

Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that this very thing is not an effect even when the cause remains identical in all its states? In that case, the effect would be independent; but if that were so, it would not be an effect at all.
For an effect is dependent upon its cause, and that capable cause produces it by necessity."
Even so, if [the cause] were non-existent, the effect could not come to be.
Now, as for the claim that "because it does not exist when that [cause] is absent, it is the effect," how is it known that it does not exist when that is absent?
Indeed, how is it even known that "it necessarily exists when that [cause] is present"?
Because it is delimited by its true nature (*tattva*), the fact that [the effect] does not arise in its absence is also delimited at all times; since the reason for this is the same in both cases,
one must accept it exactly as it is observed.
Both [alternatives] are observed:
that it necessarily occurs when that [cause] exists, and that it occurs even without completeness; therefore, both must be accepted.
If it is argued that, because it is not thus observed, there is no relationship of cause and effect— [the answer is:
because it is not observed in this way [in other cases].

There is no observation of either negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). How, then, can there be an observation of this causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)? If there is no observation by way of pervasion, then the causal relationship is not established; in that case, it has already been stated that there is no observation of anything other than positive and negative concomitance.
The understanding of the intrinsic nature occurs through itself;
[this applies] to some [entity] distinct from both.

There is no world beyond, nor this world, nor any obstruction to the world beyond, nor doubt, nor the transformation of the great elements; all such things are merely representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Nevertheless, according to conventional usage, it is said that there is even a "world beyond."
3. If you are satisfied by the proof of the next world through non-duality, then you are liberated in every respect. If worldly convention persists, then let the next world also be considered. 398
If a misconception must occur, this kind of misconception is better, because it is conducive to tranquility, heaven, and other such goals;
for a misconception regarding passion and the like brings about only the loss of all desired states, such as being a virtuous person, and so forth. To explain:

All distinctions such as the eye and so forth, or passion and so forth, depend upon the power of beginningless latencies (*vāsanā*) and do not differ from mere representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Consequently, even for one who is devoid of eyes and so forth in this life, there is again the possession of unimpaired eyes and so forth in another birth; thus, this very same process continues through a succession of births, and the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is established.
And as long as there is no perception of its pacification, so long does its infinity persist;

even in the case of the reality [of things], since the eye and other faculties have external objects as their domain, this intrinsic nature is beginningless; thus, saṃsāra is without beginning or end.
Indeed, [it is] for the benefit [of others].
(Intellect does not arise from the great elements.
But surely, specific qualities of the great elements, such as solidity and so forth, are indeed perceived?
Therefore, because of that specific quality, there is no over-extension [of the definition] even though [the elements] arise from the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Thus, it is said here that the specific qualities such as solidity and so forth alone constitute the essence of the seed, and from that alone arises the birth of living beings; otherwise, the very relationship of cause and effect would not exist.
Moreover, there is no part of the earth or other elements where creatures born from moisture and so forth do not arise; therefore, everything possesses the nature of a seed. (38)
Indeed, the classification of living beings does not arise from a distinction based on qualities such as solidity, because living beings are observed everywhere;
for even moisture-born and other types of living beings are certainly not seen to be without such distinctions. Therefore, the classification is not caused by solidity and the like.
If it were argued that karma alone, characterized by volition, remains as the ultimate residue,
and that a class of living beings consisting of wood and so forth is perceived, then everything of the same genus would consequently be composed of such living beings.
Whatever water is established by its own nature, all of that would consist of living beings possessing that same form;
from what cause, then, would there be the diversity of color and shape among living beings?
hardness°
7. Having been defiled, for instance, there are others with red heads, yellow bodies, and so forth.
Living beings such as aquatic creatures are observed; from what source could that specific form arise?
Is the diversity of lotuses and other plants seen to arise from seeds of their own kind, or is it sometimes observed to be non-restricted?
The differentiation of living beings is not restricted by the seed alone; there are karmas present here that act as the determinants.
Furthermore, if the eyes and other [senses] were to arise independently of their own respective species,
then just as there would be transformation for one, it would likewise occur for everyone without distinction. (39) Moreover, (the following applies).

The sense faculties, which depend upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), perform their own respective functions; however, it is not the case that the mental consciousness alone depends upon them.

Thus, [the author] shows by means of the words "each individually" and so forth that the arising of the sense faculties is from the mental consciousness itself, and not from earth, water, and the other elements.
Saṃgrahaḥ (The Summary)—[this is] additional in T.
Even when each of the sense faculties is impaired, [the mind persists], and so forth; or rather, mental consciousness does not arise from that body which is of the nature of an aggregate [of parts],
whereas inhalation, exhalation, and so on, are by nature merely transformations of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arising solely from the seeds of the mother and father.
And it is the mental consciousness that transmigrates, not the sense faculties and so forth, because:
"Cutting off, reconnecting, detachment, decline, death, and rebirth—these eight occur only in the mental consciousness; death and rebirth occur within equanimity. (Thus it has been said.
Therefore, the mind possesses the nature of transmigrating existence, not that of being dependent upon the primary elements.
For,
even when each [of the sense organs] is impaired, there is no impairment of the sense faculties for the mind's cognition.
There is impairment when this [mind] is broken, and its breaking is observed.

For when the mental consciousness (*manomati*) is broken by fear, grief, joy, anger, and so forth, one observes disturbances in the eyes and other faculties; thus, the eyes and other faculties are dependent upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, since they are likewise dependent upon it at the beginning of birth, the existence of another life is established.
Furthermore, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not dependent upon the body in this way,
because it depends on the aggregate of the five sense-faculties, which are themselves the products of mental consciousness.
Now, even if the eyes and so forth are indeed the products of mental consciousness...
But why is it that [the jar] arises from that very [fire]?
For an object such as a jar, while undergoing a transformation of fire, does not arise from fire alone. To this, it is replied:

A jar or similar object is perceived in one way [before], and therefore it is not that very same thing once it has changed; however, the sense organ is not perceived in such a different manner, because it is observed as characterized by its specific features, such as being a temple and so forth,
rather than merely as something whose modification is caused by fire like a jar.
Consequently, a jar or similar object cannot serve as an example.
Furthermore, even if mental consciousness is observed to be the support [of perception] at this time, how could it be the same at other times?
This [argument] is incorrect.
Although smoke is seen from fire, and that [fire] exists at other times as well, perception is not a means of valid cognition for anyone in this matter. Therefore...

Just as the understanding that fire preceded smoke is reached through its recognition [as such], so too is the understanding that the mind is subject to transformation occurring at birth and so forth. At birth, the eyes and other organs are recognized as being subject to transformations corresponding to a mind characterized by fickleness and the like; it is therefore logical to understand them to be exactly as they were.
Just as the production of smoke from fire is observed once in a certain place, it is recognized in another location as being likewise preceded by fire.
[The opponent argues: It is like the cognition that "it does not exist elsewhere";

therefore, even when there is a deficiency of the sense organs such as the son and so forth, mental modification (mānasavikriyā) still exists. Thus, the mind is established as being dependent on that [soul], and no restrictive rule applies to either of the two [the soul or the mind]. 405

If it is argued that there is no rule that the mind does not undergo modification when there is a modification in the son, the eyes, and so forth— since there is an absence of such a restriction— the son, the eyes, and so forth cannot be the substratum;
for that very absence of restriction is observed in both cases,
such that the mind does not undergo modification even when there is a modification in the self, the eyes, and so forth.
If [it is argued that] "for someone" [the mind is the support], then those [senses] would not be the support either; thus, the senses would lack the status of being supports.

In that case, mental consciousness (manovijñāna) would be the support for the senses, but the senses would not be the support for the mind, which results in the consequence that the mind is without a support.
Furthermore, there must be some support for all six consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and the rest.
The sense-faculty arises from the cognition of the mind, and from that, mental consciousness (manomati) exists;
therefore, even there, it would likewise exist, and thus the state of existence remains beginningless and endless.
(406) If mental consciousness were also not subject to transformation due to the transformation of the sense-faculty, then...

When the eyes and other organs are destroyed, mental dejection and the like are observed in various instances; since [such qualities] are not found to reside therein, it is inferred that they are not unwholesome here [in the self].
This is not so;
for there is no rule that everything must necessarily have some substratum.
If, however, you persist, then this is also said:

Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of the intellect, being itself dependent upon the intellect alone, is the cause of the sense-faculties; hence, the sense-faculties arise from the intellect. (41)

Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of cognition (*buddhi*)—designated as the cause of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), characterized by volition, and termed action—is itself dependent upon the eye and other faculties. To this he replies:
"And that [support] depends only upon cognition, not upon the faculties."
For the sense faculties are not its basis;
because it is stated that "volition is action" or "having willed, there is vocal action," and this volition consists of the nature of thinking, "I shall do this" and "I shall do that."
And that [memory] occurs by depending solely on the intellect (*buddhi*) which consists of prior recollection, not by depending on the body;
furthermore, it belongs only to some sense-faculties as their own support, not to all, because the sense-faculties do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
For the production of the body and sense-faculties occurs through karma accompanied by craving for a body.
Because of the application of delight therein— since delight arises toward objects once they have been obtained—
it follows that the intellect [is derived] from the senses, but the intellect is not [identical] to the senses; such is the conclusion.
Therefore, since the mind alone is the cause, it is by means of the mind that the succession of previous births is projected;
[this] prior [state] consists of the nature of recollection.

[Objection: If, then, the basis (*āśraya*) belongs to the mental cognition (*manomatih*) which consists of the conceptual construction of a self in the form of "I," then what is the cause for the continuity (*saṃpratyaya*) from the present life to a future life? Or how is it that the mind is said to be dependent upon the body? To this, he says:

In whatever manner that [mental consciousness] was projective [of rebirth] previously, let it be the same even later; for it is supported by those cognitions, it is said that the mind is dependent on the body. (42) In whatever manner the grasping at a self was the projector of the beginningless continuum of births for those transmigrating beings, such was their mental cognition.
Let such [a state] be implied even later;
it cannot be otherwise.
Thus, that very same assumption of birth occurs even subsequently.
For whatever possesses a nature not distinct from the nature of performing a certain action necessarily performs that action;
for example, another fire, though conjoined with fuel and so forth, possesses a nature not distinct from the nature of producing smoke.
Otherwise, there would be no relation of cause and effect, nor any worldly convention, and the world would be motionless.
The Accomplishment of Consciousness for those fallen into the flood of saṃsāra (kha).
Now, as for the statement that the mind also depends upon the body— the Blessed One having taught that body and mind are mutually dependent—
the resolution here is that the Blessed One spoke of the mind’s dependence on the body because it is assisted by the body-consciousnesses.
But the body is not its direct support, as the eyes and so forth are for the visual consciousness and the rest;
therefore, the mind characterized by the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) does not depend on the sense organs such as the eyes, nor does it depend on the body.
It is logical that it depends solely upon a preceding mind of the same kind.
Because it exists even in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and because its possibility is established therein;
[the objection] "it is not additional" is incorrect.

Therefore, let it be that there is no cognition of the characteristic of intrinsic nature without the senses; nevertheless, there is no absence of the next world, because of the existence of mutual dependence.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Even though cognition does not exist without the sense-faculties, nor do those [faculties] exist without it, nevertheless they are mutual causes; therefore, they are mutually caused. (43)
For just as your own admission is that the intellect (*buddhi*), consisting of the sense-faculties, does not exist without a body because it is so observed,
so too must you admit that those sense-faculties do not exist without the mind-intellect (*manobuddhi*),
since the observation upon which the admission is based is the same in both cases.
If that were the case, it would follow that the two continua are mutually causal because they benefit one another;
and since two things that are mutually causal arise from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which itself arises from another causal complex,
it should be understood that from that causal complex, the preceding and succeeding body and mind are likewise mutually causal, just as in the intermediate state.

And if the body alone were the basis for mental cognition, then that cognition arising from the body would have to arise either sequentially or non-sequentially, since there is no other possible mode. 2 T.

In that case, there is no gradual succession for mental cognitions; for a successive entity cannot arise from what is non-successive, nor can it arise from that which lacks a specific cause of dependence.
The cognition arising from the body also indicates its own sequence.
For this mental cognition is sequential;
otherwise, if it were to grasp its own form as "I," there would be the grasping of its entire nature—past, present, and future—and thus the undesirable consequence of grasping all of one's births.
Now, if the states are not apprehended, there can be no cognition of their pervasion by what precedes and follows;
and if the states are not apprehended, how could there be a cognition of the substratum of those states?
Because when the pervaded is not cognized, the pervader is likewise not cognized.
(408) For if the pervasive state is not cognized due to the non-cognition of the pervaded, how could it be understood as being a pervader?
For even if it is not perceived in that form, it does not thereby become otherwise; indeed,
it is perception alone that establishes identity or difference,
provided its pervasiveness is not unperceived.
In that case, it follows that it is perceived by means of another form;
therefore, it has no persistence over time, and thus there is no temporal succession for the other perception.
Consequently, perception occurs sequentially.
Therefore, there is no existence of that which possesses succession through non-succession.
For if [there were such], it would follow that what is past and what is future [would exist simultaneously].
Now, if the cause indeed possesses a certain sequence, must the effect not likewise possess that very same [sequence]? Why is this not so?
For the effect is certainly not non-different from the cause, since we observe it to have distinct characteristics as well.
To this it is replied:
If the effect were to exist simultaneously [with its causes], then everything would exist at that very moment; otherwise, it does not exist at all, because it has already reached completion. (409)
For in this way, that [cause] would produce its effect only if it were perceived at the time of the effect; for if it is not being perceived then, it cannot be its cause.
If it is argued that there is perception [of it], then because of its oneness, there would be perception until the point of destruction; thus, it would have to be destroyed at that very moment.
For in this way, his lack of desire would be destroyed by that [desire], and consequently, no other effect could arise from it; or, even if it were to arise, it would not be its effect.
If that which is perceived sequentially were the cause of that which possesses sequence, then in that case, it would not be non-sequential;
for indeed, that which is perceived as blue cannot be non-blue.
Alternatively, ( ) 1 T.
Thus, the effect would not exist if it were not stated that the effect arises from the cause as something possessing that very nature;
for the relationship of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
*svapara* (in place of *raṅ-bshin*, it is a scribal error for *svabhāva*) is a faulty reading.
Even though the effect is distinct in character from its cause, it is nonetheless an effect,
because the defining characteristic of the relationship between cause and effect consists in the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
however, that in which positive and negative concomitance do not exist is neither an effect nor a cause.
And that which does not arise even when the cause is present in such a state lacks conformity to its cause;
this is what constitutes the nature of cause and effect.
*tyaktaḥ*—"It is not the case that it does not arise through that state; rather, since it necessarily exists when that state is present, what is the use of this [objection]?"
5. But surely, if that [cause] is absent, the effect does not arise; therefore, when that [cause] is present, the effect necessarily exists as well.
If it does not exist even when that [cause] exists, how can it be said to be non-existent when that is absent?
"Its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that"—how could this be so? (411)
If that [effect], though capable, does not arise even when the cause is present, then that would not be its cause at all;
how, then, is it understood that its non-arising is necessitated by the absence of that [cause]?
Just as it does not arise by itself while the cause remains in that very state, so too it will not arise by itself even in the absence of that cause, because of its independence;
for if it were not dependent on another, it would necessarily arise whenever the capacity of the cause is present.
For it is logical that the non-existence (*abhāva*) of entities might indeed occur by itself; however, since existence (*bhāva*) is dependent upon other factors, how could it not arise from a cause?
[Objection: Since non-existence is causeless, it is reasonable that it occurs by itself;
but since existence is dependent on causes, it is not reasonable to say that it does not occur when a capable cause is present.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the absence of the effect is logical precisely because [the effect] is independent, such that it does not occur even when the cause exists? [Response:

If that were so, then the principle "its absence follows from its absence" would not mean that the absence is caused by the absence of the cause; how then could the effect arise from that [cause] on its own? It simply would not exist.
And that which does not exist by itself cannot be restricted by it; therefore,
even though it exists in such a way as not to exist by itself,
it is not the body.

But when [an effect] exists only when its cause exists, then even if it ceases by its own nature, because there is the production of successive moments, the cessation of the continuum occurs precisely through the absence of that [cause]. Therefore, since [the effect] is dependent upon its cause, an ordered entity does not arise from that which is non-sequential.
That which is to be ceased by something [itself]—
even if [that cause] is non-sequential— produces a sequential effect by depending upon a sequential auxiliary cause.
That too does not exist;
there is no dependence for that which is without a qualifier or to which no distinction can be imparted, because it has no dependence for the sake of attaining a distinction,
nor does it possess any distinction.

Or, if there is a specific distinction— that is, if one accepts a specific distinction other than impermanence— then since the effect arises from that very distinction while depending upon it, it cannot be said that this distinction belongs to the eternal [cause]. If this is argued, [the answer is] no.
Regarding the term "particularity" (*viśeṣa*): it means either the state of being a particularizer or the state of producing a cognition of a particularity.
It does not mean the state of being a particularizer, because that [particularity] itself lacks differentiation.

If it is argued that "from the particular [comes] the particular," that is simply the same as impermanence; in the case of a distinction [between them], the aforementioned logical consequence (prasaṅga) applies.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that [the universal] is the cause of the cognition of the particular, that too is untenable.

If there were no particularity (*viśeṣa*), no cognition of particularity could arise. If that were so, this [cognition] would be nothing but an error, and thus all effort [to establish it] would be in vain. For it is only when there is a perception of particularity that it is understood to be eternal;
and if there is error regarding its particularity, how can there be valid cognition (*pramā*) of its eternity?
414.1 If there is no perception of distinction, how could there be dependence?
Because there is indifference toward it, no distinction whatsoever exists.
If there is the possibility of a specific distinction, it is logical that there is dependence upon that [distinction] in that case; for this reason, there is the worldly convention of "dependence.
Therefore, it is correct that there is no dependence on that which lacks a specific distinction.
Since cognition arises from the body in a sequence, it makes known the sequence of the body;
otherwise, the reason for its sequence would be clearly that which produced it.
That mental cognition proceeds from each preceding experience.
That too [is established] from the very beginning; thus, there would be no infinite regress.
Therefore, if that [body] also arises from another,
and the body— depending on each preceding cognition— produces cognition sequentially,
then it follows that there must be a specific distinction in the body.
Consequently, it follows that for the body accompanied by cognition, each preceding body of that very same nature is the cause;
such being the case:
Since each preceding moment must be the cause of every subsequent moment that arises anew at every instant, let it be observed that the cause is always indeed perceived.

For that very body which was previously perceived as the auxiliary to cognition for another person is itself always the cause, even during birth and death, just as it is in the intermediate state; thus it is established.
Otherwise, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) would not be apprehended, no cause whatsoever would be a cause for anything, as there would be no other means [of establishing it].

Therefore, that which was seen once as such [a cause] from that [effect] is the same at other times as well; in this very way, this relationship of cause and effect is established. Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated previously that the relationship of cause and effect is not denied by those engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*); thus, we shall desist.
4. Regarding cause and effect:

Indeed, just as in the intermediate state the body is perceived as being preceded by a body accompanied by consciousness, so too the body at birth and other times is preceded by a body accompanied by consciousness. Thus, from the consciousness of a previous life comes the consciousness of this life, and from this life's consciousness comes the consciousness of a future life; in this way, the existence of the next world is established.
Likewise, from another reason, there is also the opposite; thus, the establishment of the opponent's position is as follows. 5 T.
Precisely because of the consciousness of one who is born— [the reading "antaraḥ" or "anyaḥ" in place of "can" appears to be a scribal error]—
this consciousness exists even from that which pertains to this life.
Whatever consciousness is that of death does not continue into another birth, because it is a mental state, just like the experience of death in one who is free from defilements. (420)

That death-consciousness which does not link to another mind—such as the mind at death of one free from passion—is not considered a death-consciousness capable of effecting rebirth in another life, because it is the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Thus, there is no linking;
otherwise, this [death-consciousness] would simply not be a cause, due to the obstruction [of the necessary conditions] in the reverse case.
"In that case, the opposite [of the reason] would also not be a reason because of this same [lack of] connection.
This is not the same;
for that which is contradictory with something else establishes the absence of that thing.
Whatever is connected with something possesses its nature;
and there is no contradiction between the mind at death and the linking of rebirth, because:
What contradiction is there in the final consciousness connecting with another consciousness?
Likewise, why is it considered that the Arhat’s consciousness does not connect?

For what contradiction exists when the non-existence of the final consciousness is to be proven by its failure to connect with another consciousness—either in relation to that [connection] itself or regarding its object—by which its absence would be established?
What contradiction [is there]? None at all—
neither that characterized by non-coexistence nor that characterized by mutual exclusion.
Because no reversal of rebirth-linking is observed upon the arrival of the mind at death,
for that very reason, its persistence by avoiding that [death] is not observed;
this is because rebirth-linking in another life is invisible.
Therefore, the state of being a mind at death is not incompatible with reconnection, since neither form of incompatibility is observed;
thus, [the state of being a mind at death] does not prove the absence of reconnection,
whereas the state of being an effect is indeed incompatible with the absence of reconnection.
Therefore, because it is capable of proving the absence of that [other], its establishment through the recognition of the contrary is achieved;
and it will be demonstrated that two [reasons] which do not err with respect to mutually contradictory objects cannot exist in one and the same place.
3. It is abandoned—it is established; what contradiction is there in its absence?
The sixth chapter (*Ṣaṣṭhāhnika*) begins here.
Furthermore, the state of being an effect is unestablished due to the absence of reconnection (*pratisandhāna*).
But surely, there is indeed here a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion; how then can there be an absence of contradiction?
For it is said:
"For the Arhat, there is no reconnection of consciousness at the moment of death; his liberation of the mind is like the extinguishing of a lamp. (421)

For just as the extinction of a lamp [is perceived], so too is the death-consciousness of a person recognized as an Arhat; since it is established that the death-consciousness exists by way of excluding that [extinction], the contradiction is well-known through such cognition. Thus, the absence of contradiction is not established.
If it is argued that because contradiction is well-known, the absence of contradiction is not unknown,
that too is incoherent;
for from what source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do you maintain that the mind of the Arhat is non-conceptual?
You possess no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this, since your very effort is directed toward refuting it;
for if an Arhat is indeed accepted,
then his non-reconnection [to saṃsāra] is due to his separation from the afflictions (*kleśa*), and not otherwise.

And since that dissociation from afflictions does not exist for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), how could there be non-relinking? Even though [the mind at death] is a mind of death, it is not the case that being a mind of death is incompatible with relinking; for it is accepted that dissociation from afflictions is what is incompatible with relinking, and that [incompatibility] has not been accepted [in the case of ordinary persons].
The state of being mind (cittatva) as well.
But is it not the case that the contradiction is understood from the very tenet itself?
No,
for the tenet is set forth specifically to demonstrate the contradiction in the case of the Arhat’s mind at the moment of death.
For the established doctrine does not prescribe a remedy for every contradiction;
where has the rejoining of a mind been accomplished by means of a [different] mind once that mind has perished?
Because it is accepted that there is no reconnection [of rebirth] when one is not dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*), it was said:

"Now, if the establishment of reconnection is not found through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, because there is no such means of valid cognition regarding it, the possibility of contradiction exists. (423) That too is incorrect.
If the tenet is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is simply not a valid authority;
how, then, could the desired goal be established from it? Why would one follow a tenet whose object is not established by valid cognition?
If that [conclusion] is due to a deficiency in the reason (*hetu*), why was that very point not stated here?

(47) If the tenet (*siddhānta*) is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then no contradiction is established by it; for [in that case], is this [tenet] followed or adhered to by means of the reconnection of the mind at death?
Indeed, even that which is being followed as a means of valid cognition does not thereby become a means of valid cognition;
for if it were a means of valid cognition, it would follow that it is a means of valid cognition in all cases—thus, the contrary [of your position] is established.
If you argue that it is a means of valid cognition in some instances and not a means of valid cognition in others, [we reply:]...
It is not [the case that the reason is unestablished], because desire is common to both the proponent and the opponent; furthermore,
the reason "because of the deficiency of the cause" establishes contradiction, not the established tenet.
If that non-connection [of the effect] is due to a deficiency in the cause, then why was that very deficiency not mentioned? Why was it not stated as the reason?
Why instead was the reason "being the mind at the moment of death" put forward as an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason?
Alternatively, if that [reason] is due to a deficiency of the reason—
meaning if there is a deficiency of the reason characterized by the body and so forth at the time of death— then what further has been said here regarding its being a reason?
This too is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
The former [reason] was inconclusive,
whereas this one is unestablished (asiddha),
because that very deficiency of the reason (hetuvaikalya) does not exist here.
Alternatively, why is it not stated here that "no" [is used] in the sense of "not"? For it is said that *amā*, *na*, and *nā* are words expressing negation.
What has not been raised? What has not been refuted? It has been refuted; it has been shattered—this is the meaning.
Incompleteness itself is unestablished, because the preceding mind, being unimpaired, serves as the cause.
And how this is so has been demonstrated [in the first and second chapters].
All this,
then, is cause and fruit.
Regarding "and the fruit" (*daṅ 'bras-bu'i*), the reading "without *daṅ*" (*daṅ-bral-ba'i*) in its place is a scribal error. 4.
It arises solely for the sake of the body;
however, it might be argued that...
This reason, characterized by a deficiency in the homogeneity of the cause, is not unestablished; for indeed,

whether it be the body endowed with sense-faculties or that which is devoid of sense-faculties— characterized by hair, nails, the tips of the fingers, and so forth— it is the basis of mental consciousness.
For it arises from the body itself—whether from that characterized as the heart or from elsewhere—yet that is incorrect;
for the body has two possible modes of being: either with sense-faculties or without sense-faculties, each of which would be a cause [of cognition] in its own way, or otherwise.

First of all, it is not with the sense-faculties; for if it were, it would follow that [the object] is apprehended just as its cognition is, and thus mental cognition would not arise from the sense-faculties.
The knowledge of the mind is not [identical] even to that which has been attained, because of the difference in the capacity for the production of knowledge. (48) 6 T.

There is no coexistence [of the two] due to a difference in capacity, nor because of insentience, nor for any other reason, since there is no difference in their causal nature; rather, transformation occurs through the medium of the object, as in the case of the sense organs, or like color and taste. (49)
To begin with, the body together with its sense faculties (*sendriya-kāya*) is not the basis (*āśraya*) for each [sense faculty] individually;
rather, it is "with sense faculties" (*sendriya*) because it exists by means of the powers of the sense faculties,
since there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power (*śakti-śaktimatoḥ abhedāt*), and thus it is simply the form of the sense faculties themselves.

And therefore, the position that mental consciousness arises from each of the sense faculties individually is as follows: he says that mental cognition does not arise from the sense faculty [as a whole], nor does it arise from the sense faculties individually.
For, like that [consciousness] and like sensory cognition, there would result the apprehension of each object individually;

for the mind necessarily follows the visual faculty, and the mind following another faculty would have a different nature. Otherwise, if its cause does not possess that nature, from where would that nature of it arise? It would thus be without a cause.
Objection: Is it not observed that even a single cause possesses a nature that produces both effects of that same nature and those of a different nature,
just as fire has the nature of producing smoke?

Furthermore, there is a distinction in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*): when the complex of visible forms is present, the eye produces visual consciousness, whereas in the absence of visible forms, it produces mental consciousness;
the same should be stated for the ear and the other sense organs.
That is incorrect;

for it is accepted that [cognition] is produced by the sense-faculty (akṣaja) by depending on the operation of the sense-faculty. Since there is no such operation [of the sense-faculty] in that case, how could it be produced by the sense-faculty?
For it would follow that it is grasped like a mental cognition (dhīvat). || 424 ||
This is the meaning:

for sensory cognition (akṣabuddhi), following after the operation of that [sense organ], is designated as "the grasper of the object" (prāhikā); this would likewise be the case if the same were true for mental cognition (manobuddhi).
That [cognition] too would be apprehending [the object] like that [prior cognition], by following its operation;
otherwise, how could it be designated as such?
Furthermore, neither the following of its operation nor the cognition of it as being produced from that is perceived; thus, [your position] is contradictory.

Furthermore, even when an object is not present, visual consciousness arises in the form of perceiving an object situated before one—just like the perception of a mass of hair by one afflicted with ophthalmia.
However, mental consciousness arises even for one whose eyes are closed; how, then, could there be sensory activity in that case?
And since there is no alteration [of the mental consciousness] when there is an alteration [of the sense organ], how can it be said to be born from the senses?

In this context, "because of the attainment of apprehension like that cognition" means "because of the attainment of a cognizing consciousness that undergoes modification through the modification of that [object].
Apprehension is indeed cognition itself.
Now, if there were no modification [of the cognition] due to the modification of that [object], then it would not be "born from that."
The refutation that [the effect] does not arise even from a collection is this very same one;
he states another refutation: "because of the difference in the capacity for producing cognition."
With respect to the production of knowledge, a capacity that is indeed distinct, separate, and independent of anything else is observed,
rather than one that is mutually dependent.
Otherwise, since it would not exist even when the collection [of causes] is absent—just as a sprout does not arise when there is a deficiency in the earth and other factors—it would not occur;
yet mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does occur even for those deficient in the eye and other [faculties]. Therefore, the mind is not dependent upon that collection.
By the word "also" (*api*), the previous reason is conjoined.
Because it is insentient, it does not arise from anything else either, since it lacks sense faculties.
Now, what is the meaning of "because it is insentient"?
If it means "due to the absence of sensory consciousness," [then...]
That is indeed accepted.
But how is this [the case]: if it does not arise from that as sense-perception (*indriyajñāna*), why does it not arise as mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

Now, if it is argued that because of the absence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), that very [body] is being considered as insentient, then the reason is merely a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). To this it is replied: When hair, nails, and so forth are not seen to be conscious, how can it be established that mental cognition arises from them? (425)

For just as contact and the other [factors] are perceived through their respective consciousnesses by virtue of volition, hair, nails, and so forth are not perceived in that way by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If they were bound to it, then in its absence there would be no mental consciousness; and upon its impairment, the mental consciousness would be impaired. If the body were not the support, then how could there be co-existence?
Thus it is said: because there is no distinction in the cause designated as "action," which effects a rule for simultaneous existence, its capacity is established accordingly,
like the sense organs or like color and taste.

Even though the eye-faculties (*akṣa*) and the yakṣas (or the faculties themselves) are not mutually dependent in terms of form and taste, there is a rule of co-existence for a certain period of time.
Indeed, the relation of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is not the sole cause for their co-existence;
rather, the eyes and other [faculties] are the supports of visual consciousness and the rest because they undergo transformation in accordance with the transformation of those [consciousnesses].

Likewise, [the claim] that there is no modification such as separation and so forth due to a modification of the body— meaning that the modification characterized by rigidity and so on does not exist— is the [alleged] relationship of substratum and superstratum;
that too is incorrect,
because the modification occurs through the medium of the object which is to be grasped.

For one who cannot endure suffering, when physical injuries such as blows from weapons are perceived through that contemplation and mental attention, they become the cause of mental affliction; it is not the physical body that is the basis of the pain,
for even an external object can be a cause of transformation.
Nor does it have the status of a substratum, for even in its absence, suffering arises through mere mental imputation;

therefore, both an internal and an external superimposed form are perceived. Through the mind, there is a transformation [of the object] by means of that [perception], and that is the transformation of the mental [consciousness]. (426)
And since there is no identity between the basis and the object,
the body is not the basis for that [defiled mind]; therefore,
the defiled mind does not depend upon the body.
And that which is its substratum will be explained later:
the object of the mind is merely the superimposition of a prior and a posterior [moment], and nothing else exists; thus, it has no objective support as its substratum.
Moreover:
The mere fact that something is not a benefactor is not the reason for its cessation; rather, it is a specific kind of causality that brings about the cessation of the effect.
What is this specific cause whose nature is to bring about cessation?
He explains it as follows:

That whose existence is always beneficial to something because it is constantly associated with it is the cause; therefore, it is said [in the sūtra], "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "due to the arising" (*utpādāt*).
For that cause is the producer of that whose existence is beneficial [to it]. (50)
"Always, because of its connection to that"—
here, "connection" (anubandha) means continuous following (anuvartana).
That whose existence is always helpful because it follows [the object] constantly,
and that which possesses the capacity to be helpful at some time— even in its absence, a specific benefit may occasionally arise from something else—
does not follow [the object] eternally; therefore, even by the cessation of the former, there is no cessation of the latter.
Furthermore, the existence of the body is not a constant benefactor, for even when there is a prior modification of the mind alone, a modification is sometimes observed;

therefore, even in the absence of the body, because a modification produced by a mental modification occurs at times, it is conceivable that the continuum of consciousness persists through its support.
Nor is the body established as a cause by virtue of being a constant benefactor.

For instance, the body would have to be understood by someone as the cause [of cognition] either by itself, by another, or by a cognition that has already arisen, or else in some other way; such are the possible conceptualizations. First of all, a cognition that has not yet arisen does not know: "I shall be," "I am," or "I was."

But when a feeling has arisen, for one who apprehends its own nature as "I" or something else, how can there even be the comprehension of that [feeling] itself, let alone the comprehension of another— that "this has arisen from that"?
Indeed, one thing does not perceive another while taking it as its object;
therefore, since that same conceptualization applies even to the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, how could there be a cognition of their being caused by the eye and so forth?
Not at all.
Because the possibility of understanding their positive and negative concomitance exists;
for indeed, a person, while merely opening his eyes, perceives that the perception of form has arisen immediately thereafter. (429)

Birth and so forth, being oriented toward the body, are not understood as the cause [of knowledge]; for they merely awaken the state of being a knower when there was previously an absence of knowledge. (430) If its perception is by means of another [cognition], then how can there be an understanding of its prior absence? For the non-perception of that which is invisible does not establish non-existence.

(431) Even for one who is asleep, there is awakening despite the non-perception of prior knowledge; yet, in that case, there is no actual understanding of the prior absence of dream-consciousness. (432)
Now, if one were to think that there exists a self-cognition [of the mind] because cognition existed previously, [we reply:
it does not exist at all in the state of deep sleep, because of the absence of memory.
The claim that because memory is observed upon waking regarding the experience of a dream, that [dream] was therefore non-existent—that is incorrect;
for what is it that is remembered? Is it something that did not exist, or is it something that existed but was forgotten? Indeed, nothing at all done while awake is ever remembered in a dream.
Indeed, no one perceives that the experience of a dream is distinct from waking consciousness;
nevertheless, it is understood as such precisely because of that [waking state], once awakening has occurred.
Even upon its awakening, it is not perceived; how can this be?
Therefore, since consciousness does not arise because the body is always providing assistance, there is no logical conclusion that consciousness ceases when the body departs.
This concludes the refutation of the doctrine that the elements constitute the self (*bhūtātmavāda*).
Now, the lotus-root (śālūka) arises from cow dung,
and yet cow dung does not assist its existence by being constantly connected with it; nevertheless, in the absence of cow dung, the lotus-root simply does not come into being at all.
That too is something trivial,
because:
Just as the initial production from cow dung is of a certain nature, so too is it when that [dung] is absent; however, such a reversal is never observed in the case of cognition.
For just as a lotus-root (*śālūka*) is seen to be produced from cow dung in a certain way, is it ever perceived to be exactly like that at another time?
But mental consciousness is of the same nature both initially and subsequently; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [in the argument].

(ii) The explanation of the formula "when this exists, that comes to be": Now, one might object that the Blessed One has stated only this definition of a cause—"when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises"—and has not further investigated another [definition] that follows [the cause] at all times.

Furthermore, it has been established that the Blessed One alone is the ultimate authority regarding the causal relationship in the absolute sense, because he perceives the pervasion through positive and negative concomitance; yet,
if there is no object possessing possible efficacy that is not described by the Blessed One,
how can this be so?
This is not a fault;
for that very reason which we have stated— namely, because it is always beneficial— the locative case (*saptamī*) is used,
and for that very reason the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also expressed as "from arising" (*utpādāt*).
The phrase "when this exists, that comes to be" expresses constant concomitance; the word "existing" (satī) is used in the locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
Otherwise, if it were to come into being even in the absence of that [cause], its existence would not be caused by that.

The fifth case is used for the ablative (*apādāna*); and since "the source (*prabhava*) of the agent of birth" is the definition of the ablative, this "source" is indeed the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Pāṇini 1.4.30
Alternatively, we explain it otherwise:
even if consciousness is preceded by consciousness, let it nevertheless be understood that the consciousness of a previous birth follows from the consciousness of birth and so forth,
because the latter is its effect.
But how is future birth-consciousness inferred?
If it is argued that there is an inference of an effect from the observation of a capable cause,
then it follows that the definition of a cause would entail a different [additional] cause.

Now, it might be argued that because there is doubt regarding the effect, the inference of capacity is not useless even when the future world (the next life) is uncertain; for the effort of engaging in dharma and so forth becomes fruitful only through the inference of a future world based on the inference of capacity. To this, it is replied:
Since the consciousness of a future birth is itself the cause, it is also that very effect.
That which always assists [a phenomenon] by being constantly associated with it is its cause.

For that which always assists an entity because it is invariably concomitant with it is its pervader (*vyāpaka*) by virtue of its pervasiveness; and when there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
the cause is the effect itself as a reason for an object other than itself— whatever makes another object known is necessarily a pervader.

Otherwise, due to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*), there would be a lack of probative force (*agamakatā*). If it is asked: "How can that which does not exist without another be the cause of that [other], and how can a cause be the effect?"
Not [is it the case],
because that is an effect;
for it is thus.

The transformations of consciousness and other such factors are established by their arising and so forth; they are perceived as being modifications of that [consciousness], and this is what is called "being an effect.
This would not even be a transformation at all if it were not brought about by an emergence; rather, the common worldly convention is that "this transformation is produced by that."
If it is argued that by this much alone the state of being an effect will exist elsewhere as well, [we reply: how can that be a cause?
Surely it is because of non-deviation from it.
But surely, that which is beneficial is the cause; and how can that which is yet to be (bhāvya) and non-existent be beneficial?
In that case, a past cause would not be established;
that too is incorrect,
because it does not provide assistance.
Since it exists at the time of its arising, what is this "time of arising"?
If it is prior to the effect, how can it be a benefactor to that which is non-existent?
For this very reason, it is called "causation of the non-existent" because its cause does not exist;
what is the meaning of "causation of the non-existent"?
It is the existence of that [effect] occurring immediately after [the cause].

This immediacy (ānantarya) is the same with respect to both; just as it is with respect to what has already come to be, so too is it with respect to what is yet to be. Furthermore, immediacy alone is not the foundation for reality.
Even that which is separated [in time] can be a cause;
for instance, the consciousness of one who has been in deep sleep arises upon awakening from a prior cognition, even though it is separated by an interval of time—this is certain. (436)
Indeed, the body is not the cause for the persistence of prior mental formations (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), because that is not observed;
for even with such a body, [the mind] arises otherwise or differently in accordance with previous cognition.
Therefore, the basis for the relationship of cause and effect is the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), which exists even when that [body] is absent. (437)
Whatever indeed follows the positive and negative concomitance of something is alone its cause; any other distinction is useless.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the definition of the causal relation is: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises."

Nor is it merely positive and negative concomitance that is expressed here, since the prior existence is indicated by the locative case and the subsequent existence by the ablative; furthermore, the subsequent existence is also demonstrated by the nominative. (438)

It is not merely the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that has been demonstrated here, because the sequence of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāpara-bhāva*) has been very clearly shown; therefore,
even that [objection] is untrue.

Therefore, it is said "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "from origination" (*utpādāt*); indeed, it is not by means of the locative case (*saptamī*) that a prior existence is indicated, nor by the ablative case (*pañcamī*),
since the latter indicates merely the state of being a cause (*nimittatvamātra*).
The meaning is that "this [effect] has that as its cause";
and the meaning is that when something does not exist, another thing which also does not exist, that very [latter] thing, being present, has that [former] as its cause.
Now, one might ask: how can that which is yet to be (bhāvī) be designated by the term "existent" (sat)?
Because that [past] does not exist, such a designation is untenable;
likewise, there is no arising of what has not arisen.
Now, how can even the past possess existence, by virtue of which it is designated as "existent"?
And how can there be the arising of that which has perished?
If it is argued that it existed [previously], then this will be the case for another as well.

What is the distinction between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)? Alternatively, since the locative case [in the formula] "this being present, that comes to be" is used according to the rule "the locative denotes the characterization by the existence of something," the word "being present" (*satī*) indicates merely the state of being a cause.

However, at that time, existence is not characterized by its absence, nor is existence characterized by existence; yet, even through what is yet to be, existence is indeed characterized, as is the common worldly expression: "the omen of death has been manifested."
If death were not to exist, there would be no such thing as "untimely death" (*ariṣṭa*);
nor would there be the temporal division [expressed by] "from birth" (*utpādāt*),
for case-endings (*vibhaktayaḥ*) do not establish specific points in time, since their capacity lies solely in the indication of the status of a participant in an action (*kārakatva*).
If it is asked how that which is non-existent can possess the status of an agent (*kāraka*), [we reply:
how is it that there is the relationship of agent and object in such expressions as "the sprout is born" (*aṅkuro jāyate*) or "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*)?
If it were the agent by virtue of being established as a Buddha, there would be no devouring of it here by crows.
(iii) Explanation of the cause:
Now, that whose perception is preceded by the perception of something else is the cause.
That too is incorrect:

if that which is perceived first were the cause of something, then a seed situated inside a storehouse would not be the cause for the arising of a sprout. Or, if it is argued that what is meant is that "that which is of the same class as it is perceived first," [then the following applies].
How can that which is unperceived be a cause?
For when one thing is perceived, another thing does not thereby become perceived; it would merely be a figurative designation.
Therefore, existence is indicated by apprehension;
and thus that very same object is the causal state of existence in the sense of "this being present."
And that [definition] amounts precisely to being the object of non-deviation;
however, if it were merely "that which is perceived first," then everything preceding [an effect] would result in being its cause.
Therefore, when there is the state of being the object of non-deviation, that alone constitutes causality.
Now, as for the claim that "the prior absence [of the cause] while being the object of an invariable relation" is the definition [of causality], that too is trivial;

for if the status of cause and effect were established merely by the fact of one thing's existence following the other's existence, then what contradiction would there be? In that case, what would be the purpose of the prior-posterior sequence? Indeed, what utility does the prior-posterior sequence have [in this view]? It is not as if something useless is required.
Moreover, it might be argued:
"If the cause is accepted as being prior, then there will be the taking up [of the material] by those who desire it; and if it is posterior, there will be inference based on its capacity.
For a cause that is prior can indeed be taken up even by one who desires the effect.
Therefore, the prior existence of the cause is asserted; for example, the appropriation of the present world here, which exists prior to it, as a means for establishing the future world beyond.

That too is not tenable; for it certainly possesses the status of a cause as well. It is not that the status of being a cause does not exist for what precedes [the effect], but rather it is said that its status as an effect occurs in relation to its non-deviation from what is yet to be.
And that which is the material cause (upādāna) when there is causality will likewise exist when there is effectuality.
For what distinction is there in the case of the material cause (*upādāna*) merely by virtue of its non-deviation? Why is this much not sufficient?
As for what was said—that inference [of the effect] proceeds from the efficient cause alone—what is the role of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) therein?
That is incorrect;
for who would transfer wealth already in their hand to their feet? Or who would endure having something cut with an axe when it can be cut with a fingernail?
For who indeed would place what is in their hand under their feet?

Or rather, one might expect that what is to be cut by a nail could be cut by an axe; for if the capacity to produce an effect were the primary indicator [of causality], then, in the case of a direct [cause], there would be a sequence. If causality were something to be established through effort, then its status as an indicator would be useless.
Therefore, it is correct to say that even a future thing can be a cause, provided there is no deviation [from the effect].

Thus far it has been stated by way of the meaning that modification does not proceed from the body; now it is further stated, even assuming— as a concession— that it does not proceed by way of being a substratum, as is the case with the eyes and other sense organs.

Or perhaps it may sometimes be a benefactor to the continuum of consciousness, just as fire and other elements are to jars and the like; yet, by that much alone, there is no cessation [of the continuum]. Even if the body occasionally acts as a support and thus provides benefit, the continuum of consciousness does not cease upon the cessation of the body merely because of that.

The mere fact that something is not a benefactor does not necessarily mean it is a cause for the cessation of the beneficiary. For instance, when fire or other such agents cease, there is no necessary cessation of a jar or similar object that has already received a specific benefit from them. Alternatively, even when gold attains a specific characteristic such as fluidity, there is no cessation of the fire upon the cessation of that [fluidity];
indeed, even if that specific quality characterized by fluidity were to cease, the gold remains exactly as it was.
For one for whom the mind is the cause of the mental state, there is a cessation [of that state] due to its deficiency even when the body remains in that same condition;
this has been stated as a refutation against the view that the body alone is the cause.
Furthermore, another [refutation] is now stated.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the mind does not cease while the body remains, because [the mind] exists when that [body] exists and because it is subject to its control; therefore, the prāṇa and apāna are not that [mind]. (52) In the absence of the body, as in the state of ashes, let there be cessation due to the absence of causes.
It remains as it truly is within the body; there is no possibility of its cessation,
for it persists even otherwise, following through all states.
Furthermore, the claim that its activity consists in inhalation and exhalation, and that it ceases from that because of their deficiency,
is also untenable.
If it is argued that "the inhalation and exhalation arise from the mind alone, but the mind does not arise from them," this is not a valid refutation.
Why?
Because [the mind] exists even in the absence of those [breaths].
Since those two exist when the mind exists, there is no reversal [of the causal relationship];
furthermore, because they are subject to its control, the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna) are not the cause of that [mind].
If the vital breaths were the cause of the mind, then they would not be subject to it; however, their subjection to the mind is indeed observed.
If, moreover, it were produced from something else, then its production would arise from that alone, and the mind would be entirely ineffective;
for one thing dependent on another cannot be controlled by yet another,
since both are dependent upon their own respective causes— the mind would merely be a discerning agent.
If the mind, acting as a co-operative cause, were to produce those two [prāṇa and apāna], then the mind would also be the cause of those two; thus, they would not arise from them.
Or, if prāṇa and apāna have arisen from some other primary source, they are nevertheless regulated by the mind, just as a servant is controlled by his master.
That is incorrect;

for the arising of a servant is seen from something other than those two [the master and the house], but not so for those two [inhalation and exhalation]. There is no arising of those two from anything else apart from the mind.
Indeed, inhalation and exhalation are never seen to exist like a servant without the mind.
Therefore, it is not from any other cause; thus, the mind alone is the cause, and not those two [prāṇa and apāna].
Yet, one might argue that because prāṇa and apāna exist even during the state of sleep, these two cannot have the mind as their cause.
For it is not the case that the very existence of such a state there demonstrates its lack of any other cause;
for how could there be impelling or drawing of the wind without effort?
(53) There would follow a decrease or increase [of consciousness] from the decrease or increase of those two;
for if consciousness were the effect of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, then the impelling and drawing [of the breaths] would occur without effort,
but this is not so, because those two consist of impelling and drawing.

Now, if it is argued that the impelling and drawing [of the breath] alone depend upon the mind, and not its essential nature, nor its nature from any other cause—and thus [the breath] comes from the mind, and from that [mind] come the impelling and drawing—that too is incorrect. For if that wind exists even in a dead person, why does consciousness not cease? If it is argued that consciousness has no cause, then it follows that the body must be the cause of it. (445)
If the wind were stable and not the cause of consciousness, the non-cessation of the mind would necessarily follow; even if it were the cause, the wind remains stable even in a dead person.

And since the out-breath (prāṇa) and in-breath (apāna) are of the nature of effects, there would be no cessation of the mind due to their absence; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of its non-cessation.
Furthermore, from the decrease and increase of the out-breath and in-breath, a decrease and increase of the mind would necessarily follow.

Because it is an effect, when the cause necessarily diminishes or increases, there must be a diminution or augmentation of the effect; otherwise, that would not be its cause. This same logical consequence applies equally to those two [the body and the mind], yet it is not the same, because in the case of the mind's cause, one factor is the sustaining support while another is held to be the actual cause. (54)
Or, even if inhalation and exhalation were the cause of the mind, there would still be the undesirable consequence that the mind would not cease while it remains in the body;
for those two, inhalation and exhalation, would also not cease, since they too are effects of the body, and thus their non-cessation follows as well.
It might be argued that because that [object] does not cease, the mind also does not cease;
however, this same consequence would apply even if the mind were the cause of the mind.
And there would be the consequence of non-cessation as long as the mind persists; nor is there cessation of a preceding mind upon the attainment of that [subsequent] state. To this it is replied:
it is not the same regarding the cause of the mind.
Furthermore, another cause for the persistence [of the continuum] is accepted;
that other cause is designated as "karma accompanied by craving for the body.
For a mind does not arise from the mere existence of a preceding mind alone.

Because that [mind] is also the cause of another [state of mind]— designated as the seed of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth— there is the arising of a mind there [in the womb] upon the awakening of that [seed] by the previous mind, or elsewhere, due to the diversity of the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and their awakeners;
just as, for example, the vision of dreams in their manifold forms does not occur from the mere existence of an established connection [between waking and dreaming].

For even when there is an equal meeting with perfected beings (*siddha*), a particular dream-vision occurs only at certain times, because of the diversity of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Indeed, cessation [of suffering] occurs due to the diversity of the awakening of latent impressions; it does not occur if the body alone were the cause, for such a thing is not observed. Why is this so? Because the mind’s latent impressions cannot otherwise be accounted for. Like the cognition of a dream, everything is caused by the awakening of latent impressions. (447)

If the mere accomplishment of the body were the sole cause, then the perception of dreams would necessarily be identical for everyone at all times; however, since it is observed that some perceive certain things while others do not, it is logical to conclude that this is produced by the connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because these impressions possess manifold forms.
Therefore, the entire mind—whether in that body or elsewhere—is subject to the disturbances caused by the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it cannot be conceived otherwise.
Its arising occurs through the power of latent impressions;
thus, by attaining its origin through the force of latent impressions, it is indeed unreal, like a dream.
That too is untrue;

for even in the absence of the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), worldly experiences such as sexual intercourse and the like are not unreal, because they accomplish their own purposes—since those things which perform real causal functions cannot be characterized by unreality.

Indeed, worldly activities such as sexual intercourse, when supported by the power of latent impressions, proceed toward the performance of their intended causal functions; how could they have their nature subverted by a connection with unreality?

Alternatively, even worldly activities such as sexual intercourse, though following from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), are not unreal because they involve real women and so forth; likewise, activities such as birth and so on are also [not unreal].
It is the same for them, as their basis consists of the embrace of another real body in that state; thus, there is no unreality.
For instance:
Having taken up another body produced from semen and blood, birth proceeds; even though this occurs through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
how can there be a transition to another body without being perceived, as in the case of transitioning between the various bodily states of childhood, youth, and old age?
Because its unity is established through having a single material cause (*upādāna*), such a transmigration into another body simply does not occur.
That [body] is indeed a body whose material cause is a single instance of semen and blood; therefore, there is no transition into another body.
However, the bodies of animals and other beings are produced from different semen and blood, and thus constitute distinct bodies.

Furthermore, since no such transference is observed in such cases, how can it be possible that there is no exclusion (*vyatirekitā*) despite the difference in bodies? It is maintained that the distinctness of the essence (*tattva*) is what effects the cessation [of identity].
For it cannot be said that the body of a youth and so forth is not one and the same as the body of an infant and so forth.
In that regard, "transference" (saṃcāra) is indeed observed;
its occurrence as something concomitant with that [object] is what constitutes transference there.
And since such an occurrence arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no contradiction.
If it is argued that the transition into another body of a different nature has never been observed,
[we reply] that this too is inconclusive because of the observation of the transition into a dream-body; for if that [dream-body] is unreal, then there is no actual transition at all.
Because that which is being perceived cannot be unreal;
for just as it lacks reality, so too does its superimposition upon that [object].
What is this so-called "unreality"?
If it is defined as being sublated by the waking cognition, then at the time that cognition occurs, it is not sublated.

If it is argued that it is improper to say "it is sublated at another time" because it is not perceived even while one is awake, then by that same logic, the waking cognition is also not perceived by that [subsequent cognition]; thus, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator remains the same.
Now, if [the self] is not perceived upon awakening, how can there be a distinction between waking and non-waking?
Since the cognition "I am awakened" arises, one might ask: since the cognition "I am awakened" occurs even in a dream, how is it distinguished from that?

Therefore, when there is an equal perception, it is not logical that there be non-existence or unreality. Alternatively, if unreality is characterized by weakness—such as non-duration due to the weakness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or uncommon perception—then where there is firmness of latent impressions, there is the opposite; thus, the movement [of consciousness] possesses reality.
And in the case of a common perception, it is thus:

because of the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no arising of unreality for another. For the wise, reality belongs to the waking state by virtue of the mere firmness of latent impressions;
that in which there is firmness of latent impressions is the waking cognition.
It is both real and commonly perceived;
however, it exists by its own nature, and therefore its transition is established.
Yet, due to a lack of firmness, it is quickly dissolved.
And where the instruction of a deity appears in the dreams of both dreamers, how can there be unreality? If, on the contrary, it is indeed real, then it follows that not all dream-objects are unreal;
such being the case—

Because the transmigration [of consciousness] is well-established and because of the conceptualization of its specific characteristics, this is clearly a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) consisting of an equalizing alternative (*vikalpasama*).
Alternatively, since proficiency— the fruit of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)— is observed at birth and so forth, it is understood that there is a transmigration immediately after death.
When the arising of a mind whose nature is the non-grasping of a body is observed among embodied beings at birth and other such times, why is the arrival from another body not likewise accepted?

(453) To begin with, this nature of the mind—consisting of the non-grasping of a body and so forth—which occurs at birth and at other times, and which exists in varying degrees for all living beings as the fruit of the gradations of prior practice, does not come to be without a mind conditioned by the practice of non-grasping a body in a previous existence.
Therefore, by the very power of that [prior conditioning], let it be understood that there is a transition from another body into this present body.
Otherwise, there would be no occurrence of inference; if perception does not exist during the transition [of the object], how then could there be cognition through inference?
This too is not a fault, because:
"The object of inference is not perceived; what fault is there in this? For it is certainly accepted that the object of perception and the object of inference are distinct.
(454) Indeed, it is precisely intended that perception and inference operate by mutually excluding each other's objects.
How is that very same fault [avoided]?
Furthermore, if perception does not function with respect to what belongs to that same class, how can there be inference?
And yet, that too is not a fault.
