Since activity proceeding from intense habituation is observed in the body— or elsewhere— apart from direct perception, why is there not an inference from that very fact? (455)
This is what is being said:
How can there be inference regarding that which belongs to such a class without direct perception, given that inference is preceded by direct perception?
To this, the following is the resolution.
Even if that movement is not indeed perceived through direct perception, the fruit corresponding to such movement is certainly observed,
just like the movement between villages.
For example, one who has come from another village or another region is observed taking pleasure in utensils and the like that belong to the same class as those he previously enjoyed.
Even if another person of such a kind coming from another village is not perceived, nevertheless, his arrival from such a place is indeed perceived through inference.

In this way, let the arrival from the world [of the gods] also be inferred solely from the excellence of the instruments and so forth; for the operation of inference is no different from the operation of perception regarding one who has come from another village.
If it is argued that when fire is inferred from smoke, the operation of perception does not apply to the fire as possessing specific qualities but only to fire in general,
then here too, the operation applies to [the object] as it moves through space and so forth; thus, the two cases are equal.
Furthermore, it might be argued that movement to another place and so forth is observed by means of that very same body without abandoning the body;

and just as the movement of the dream-body is unreal, so too here at birth and so forth, the non-abandonment of the body and the unreality [of the transition] might occur— this, however, is inconsistent.

For in this way, the transition to another body and the abandonment [of the present one] would constitute the attainment of truth; if that were so, then truth would establish the existence of the next world.
And just as there is a total cessation [of the self] during a dream upon the perception of a dream, [so too would it be otherwise].
Likewise, if [the soul] were to exist both before and after death, what would have been accomplished?
Just as movement to another country occurs without the body, if movement to another birth were likewise possible, then a contradictory proof would have resulted;

for just as movement in a dream is seen to be connected with a real body, so too would movement to the next world be [unreal], and thus the next world and the previous world would be unreal—this is precisely what the nihilists (nāstika) desire.

Furthermore, just as for one who does not see dreams during the state of sleep, there is either a total cessation of consciousness or a state of unmanifest consciousness, so too if the next world were like that, what would be gained by the proponents of the next world? The nihilists' view would not be destroyed; what would have been accomplished by those who assert the existence of the next world?
To this it is replied:
by that very same body, movement [to another place] is contradicted by perception; the abandonment of the previous body and the appearance of another [body] are likewise seen.
All experience in a dream arises from true cognition, and since true cognition arises from a dream, what contradiction can there be? (458–459)
Every instance of interruption is perceived as being accompanied by awakening; even the interruption [caused] by death is accompanied by the awakening to reality.
(460) This has been stated:

since this consciousness, which is perceived in this body as the fruit of the practice of consciousness associated with a previous body, does not occur without the relinquishing of the body, how can there be a relinquishing of the body?

If it is argued that the abandonment of a previous body is perceived at the very moment this present body is apprehended—such that the perception of the abandonment of the previous body occurs simultaneously with the apprehension of this body—and thus, since the previous body is not established, how can the abandonment of the previous body be established? We reply: no; for attachment to a body is preceded by attachment to a [prior] body. When that [attachment] is established, its preceding body is likewise established for us. (461)
The existence of a previous body is established precisely from the fact that it was the means for producing a superior pleasure in the past;
yet, that very same body is not perceived now,
nor does its non-perception at that time imply that it did not exist then either.
Consequently, the claim that there is no abandonment of the previous body is contradicted by direct perception;
furthermore, as for what was said—
that just as the arrival from a dream and so forth occurs despite being unreal, so too [the arrival] from the next world occurs despite being unreal— [that is also refuted].
And likewise, just as there is movement from here into the dream-body despite its unreality, so too in the other world; thus, the unreality of the other world is established.
This [argument] is also false, for the unreality of dreams is indeed associated with reality.
And we shall explain that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is of such a nature because it is the cause for the cognition of a being;
or alternatively—
Every cognition does not remain distinct from a dream;
we shall state this later, for that indeed is the relevant context. Indeed, it will be explained that there is no distinction whatsoever between a dream-cognition and any other [cognition].

Therefore, it is established that there is a transition even into the body of the next world, just as there is in a dream-body; hence, for one who has come from elsewhere, although there may indeed be specific qualities such as being with or without a physical body due to the particular strength of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the destruction of the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is certainly not observed. Thus, since the continuum of living beings is uninterrupted, the existence of the next world is established.
As for death and so forth, because the latent impressions that characterize persistence are diverse, there is no consequence of non-cessation; for such a mind does not exist when [the body] remains.
In that case, the Cārvāka might still have a defense, since such a body does not exist;
therefore, he says:
"If the body, when impaired by defects, is not the cause [of cognition], just like a wick and so forth."
If the fault were rectified upon death, there would be a reawakening.
For the body, being disordered by faults such as wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and so forth, certainly becomes exactly as the mind that arose from it was;
therefore, in the absence of such a body, there would follow the consequence of non-cessation [of rebirth].
This is not so;
for if it were thus, then when one has died and the humors have become balanced, the body would be restored to life through the attainment of health.

Because of the statement that "their equilibrium is health, while decrease and increase are its opposites," how then is the equalization of the *doṣas* known? It is known from the observation of disorders such as fever and the like.
For defects that do not produce modifications cannot bring about death,
as this would entail the consequence of death occurring at all times;
otherwise, the body could not be the cause [of consciousness], because that consciousness does not conform to the presence or absence of its modifications.
For in this way, the body is understood to be the cause [of death], provided there is a subsequent revival;

for if the mind were the cause, there would be no turning back of the consciousness. Indeed, when the mind is impaired, there is no returning even to one's own home. But when the body is the cause, [the process] ceases upon its impairment. Since the body is exactly such [a thing], how could it not be the cause of the mind? (463–464)

For if the body were the cause [of death], it would follow that only such a body becomes the cause at that time and not another; this is not logical. Why is there this distinction—that one person dies when there is such a defect [in the body] while another does not? However, if the mind is the cause, then the defect or non-defect of the mind is the cause of death or otherwise; thus, the distinction is not untenable. Furthermore, for some there is death even when the defects have subsided, while for others there is life even when the defects are corrupted; this [distinction] would not be established [if the body alone were the cause]. (465)
Indeed, an effect cannot arise from an improper cause;
therefore, consciousness is not the effect of the body, for if it were the effect of the body, there would be the undesirable consequence of its resuscitation.
Now, one might object that even when the cause of a defect has ceased, the defect produced by it does not necessarily cease.
Indeed, even when the fire has ceased, no transformation produced by the fire is ever seen to have ceased in the wood;
therefore—

If it is argued that [the transformation] does not cease because, even when the fire has ceased, the transformation of the wood does not cease, we say no, because of the application of medical treatment. Just as the transformation of the wood does not cease even when the burning has ceased, so too the transformation caused by the defects [of death] will not cease.
Consequently, there is no possibility of their being revived again;
thus it was said:
"Because medical treatment is administered."

For if the disorders were reversible, medical treatment would achieve its fruitfulness by reversing them. Now, it may be argued that even a disorder caused by the humors (*doṣa*) is indeed reversed— even before the disorder of death occurs— but the disorder of death itself will not be reversed.
Therefore, the objection that "defects are either reversible or irreversible modifications" is not a fault;
nor is this a valid reply, because there is no production of any modification whatsoever anywhere that results in non-recurrence.

Just as fire [is removed] from wood and gold through some reversal [of conditions], so too the first [transformation] is not removable; however, a transformation that has been produced can be restored, like the hardness in gold. (57–58)
This is its meaning:
in some cases, something initiates a modification that is irreversible, such as fire in wood;

in other cases, it does so through the opposite process, such as that very same [fire] in gold; but never does one [cause] produce both [effects] in the same place, nor does it act without producing a modification.
In this case, the modification produced by another modifying agent— the wind— is likewise irreparable;
for even the mere blackening of wood caused by fire is irreversible even by one who approaches it, whereas in the case of gold, once the fire has ceased, it returns to its original state.
From that, since even a minor modification caused by the *doṣas* is subject to cessation, it follows that there would be a cessation even of the great modification characterized by death;
consequently, the undesirable consequence of reviving would arise.
For instance, even a modification characterized by the suspension of consciousness caused by sleep ceases when the sleep is gone.

Now, if it is argued that there is simply no cessation [of consciousness] therein, that is replied to as follows: For that which is of the nature of non-experience is not accepted as experience. Even so, if its existence were [required], then let there be experience even for one who is dead. (466)

For there is no distinction between one who is dead and one who is asleep in the absence of consciousness; as for respiration and so forth, all of that has already been considered [as being possible] even in that state. (467) There is no difference between sleep and death other than the absence of consciousness;
therefore, just as a sleeper awakens, it would follow that even a dead person could be revived by means of blows, the application of medicine, and the like.
Now, it is not that there is an absence of consciousness for one who is fast asleep while it exists for one who is dead; rather, this is the distinction [between them],
because the lack of consciousness is common to both states.
Now, if it is said that even in the absence of cognition, that [object] exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*),
then let this "potentiality" be defined:
if cognition itself is the potentiality, then since cognition alone exists, how can there be non-cognition?
To say that "it both exists and does not exist" is a contradiction.

If, on the other hand, the power [to produce consciousness] is distinct from the cognition itself, then that power is simply the body; consequently, as long as the power that generates consciousness resides in the body, there can be no cessation of it. Furthermore, if the body that produced the cognition perishes and another body that does not produce it arises, then consciousness would not persist.
If it is asked: what is this "non-productivity"? Is it the absence of cognition?
If that [consciousness] exists even for one who is asleep,
then there would be no perception even for one who is asleep; and if, upon waking, there are [sensations] such as relief and so forth, then the body is not non-productive [of consciousness].
If that were so, then since consciousness would arise during the state of sleep, one would remain non-asleep even while sleeping.
Furthermore, if consciousness arises from the breaths and other factors aided by the transformation of sleep,
what indeed is this thing called "sleep"?
If it is argued that there is an absence of cognition,
then since that [absence] exists even for one who is dead, cognition would arise again upon its transformation.
If, on the other hand, one were to say that cognition does not arise from the body alone due to the lack of a companion because of the absence of breath;
Even in states such as fainting, there is no inhalation and so forth; thus, there would be no consciousness.
Therefore, it has already been explained that inhalation and so on are not the cause of consciousness, nor is consciousness the cause of inhalation and so on.
Furthermore:

Upon the departure from sleep, cognitions of that same kind arise due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior knowledge; therefore, the body is not the cause [of such cognitions], nor are [the senses such as] the eyes and so forth.
For when the production of the body is identical [in two cases], it is observed that the cognitions correspond precisely to the prior latent impressions;
hence, the body is not the cause.
Now, if it is argued that production [of the body] occurs from the body with the assistance of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), that is incorrect;
for if a latent impression were to be an auxiliary cause, then it would have to be present, which is difficult to maintain.
Indeed, that which is non-existent cannot be an auxiliary cause for that which is existent.
Furthermore, in the state of awakening, there is no existence of the previous mind as there is of the body;
nor is a non-existent [mind] a cooperative cause, because of the absence of cooperation,
for there can be no coexistence between that which exists and that which does not.
Therefore, it is the preceding mind alone that is the cause there, not the body.
[Objection: But how then are blows and the like the awakeners? [Reply: This is not a valid answer.
lam = mārgaḥ? —lan (the answer).
Awakening does not necessarily arise solely from a blow; awakening is also observed even in the absence of a blow.
For awakening does not arise from a blow alone, since it occurs through self-awakening as well.
[Objection: Surely, following awakening, a conceptual construction arises in connection with objects previously perceived?
Then, how can there be a state of cooperation between the visual perception and the preceding consciousness?
This too is not tenable,
because:

Even in this case, no fixed rule is observed regarding the awakening of proximity; for when one has fallen asleep having projected [an object] through the force of intention (*tātparya*), the awakening of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs in accordance with that very thing. (471) Whatever was projected through the force of intention at the time of falling asleep, the awakening of his latent impressions corresponds precisely to that.
But when awakening occurs, that which is perceived is seen to be closely connected to it;
and for one who possesses such habitual practice, the awakening is of that very same nature and not otherwise,
and this awakening consists precisely in internal tactile sensations, cognitions, and so forth.
And just as for whomsoever there is practice, the experience of pleasure resulting from that action is exactly in accordance with it; for instance:

The mental formations of the body, such as fear and courage, as well as the grasping of weapons and so forth, arise for living beings in the form of awakening, which consists of the experience of pleasure.

For those dwelling in the cultivation of the thought of fear, awakening takes the very form of experiencing the pleasure of flight and the like; otherwise, however, there is only the state of suffering.
For those of a fierce nature who delight in harming others and commit injuries against others, there is the experience of pleasure in the form of grasping weapons and the like;
therefore, neither the body nor the vital breaths (*āśvāsa*) are the cause of consciousness.
The preceding consciousness alone is the cause. If that [preceding consciousness] were produced from the body, then the consequence would be its non-cessation, and thus that same fault remains.
In that case, there would certainly be no continuity with the preceding consciousness;
furthermore, if it is not a cause due to being impaired by defects,
it would become a cause again once those defects are absent.

If it initiates a transformation that does not recur, then even a slight transformation produced by it cannot be reversed. Whether it be weakness and so forth characterized by the occurrence of dull cognition, or characterized by a state such as fainting where consciousness is interrupted—
for one who initiates a non-recurrent transformation, even the slightest [transformation] is irreversible.
However, that modification which is reversible by means of its cause is subject to reversion; as in the case of the hardness of gold,
for the hardness of gold, even though it has vanished, returns once the cause of the modification has been removed.
Likewise, even the great transformation consisting of the cessation of consciousness, characterized by death, would be reversed, and thus one would return to life.
naḥ śastrā°
Regarding other consciousnesses:

Is it not the case that there is no fault because of this dual nature—namely, that some transformations can be reversed through the application of medical treatment, while others, due to the presence of incurable diseases, cannot be reversed?
He states the rebuttal:

"Because the one who can effect a cure is difficult to find, some cases are declared incurable; or [they are so declared] due to the exhaustion of the lifespan. But when there is merely a [physical] disorder (*doṣa*), there is no incurability. (56)

For "curability" refers to the removal of disorders caused by the *doṣas* through the presence of an efficacious medicine and a physician; it is declared "incurable" only because of their absence, but not according to the doctrine that consciousness arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Thus, the impossibility of recovery is due solely to the difficulty of finding a healer, which results in the non-removal of the disorder. Furthermore, if there were no cause for recovery, then even upon its cessation, [the treatment] would be useless.
Therefore, if the disorder were actually removed, the consequence would necessarily be a return to life.
"Is it not the case that for the opponent as well, there is indeed the state of being unprovable?
To this, the answer is: 'But for me, it is logical that it is unprovable'; thus he says:"
Due to the exhaustion of the life-span, a disease becomes incurable; for it is observed that while one person dies from such a disease, another does not— thus,
the life-span is merely an indicative factor.
Or, due to the exhaustion of karma,
for a disease born of karma— such as vitiligo—
is incurable because of the existence of such karma.
Therefore, he states that the predominance of karma alone is the cause of recovery:
"But when there is only the affliction caused by the transformation of the humors, there is no incurability of the disease;
therefore..."

If, upon death, the cause of the transformation has ceased—either through the removal of poison and the like, or even by cutting off the bite—then he does not breathe again; how much less so otherwise? (60)

For it is established that when there is a removal of poison and the like from a dead person by means of mantras and so forth, or when there is a removal of the site of the bite itself, or through the amputation of that limb,
or when the cause of the transformation such as fever and the like ceases, then the consequence is the restoration of life.
Moreover,
there is no cessation [of an effect] upon the cessation of a non-appropriating cause,
and the body is not an appropriating cause.
And if it were to exist, it would not undergo transformation because of its lack of change; therefore—

It is not possible to effect a transformation of the derived [effect] without a transformation of the material cause, just as it is not possible for jars and the like to exist without a transformation of the clay. For indeed,
without a transformation of the body as the material cause, a transformation of consciousness as the derived effect would be impossible.
Without a modification of the clay, no modification such as a bowl or the like is perceived;
this indeed is the characteristic of a material cause (*upādāna*), namely that its own modification occurs only through the modification of that [cause].
Even among many causes, only a specific one is the material cause of something, not merely any cause whatsoever.

Even though the body is a cause [of the mind], it is not the case that a modification [of the mind] occurs solely through a modification of that [body]; for even when the body is unmodified, there is a modification of the mind through fear, grief, and so forth, occurring merely through a prior modification of the mind itself, and when that [prior state] is modified, a modification necessarily follows.

[Objection: But does not a modification of the sprout occur even when there is a modification of the water? [Reply: No, because that [water] is not its material cause (*upādāna*); for that which is the cause of the continuum is what constitutes the material cause.
The seed is the cause of the continuum, not water, because water is merely the cause of a particular state [of the seed];
the continuum does not arise from water,
as water is common to barley and other plants.
The cessation of the rice-continuum does not follow from the cessation of water, because even in the absence of water, the continuum of the rice is not necessarily terminated;

rather, its state as a sprout and so forth arises from the water, and upon the cessation of that [water], it ceases. Therefore, water is merely the efficient cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of this [state]. Furthermore, the successive transformations of the sprout and so forth arise from water and other factors only by way of the transformation of the rice seed.
Therefore, since consciousness undergoes modification even when the body does not, the body is not its material cause;
that very point he states:
For that substance which is modified without having been previously transformed— such as a clay object— is not logically its material cause, just as a cow is not the material cause of a gavaya. (62)

And since consciousness undergoes modification without the body undergoing modification, the body is not its material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, the cessation of the body does not entail the cessation of consciousness. [Objection:
Just as in the case of a cow and a gavaya, it is because of a modification of that [body] that there is a modification [of consciousness].

[Response: Let the gavaya be somehow a cause of a particular state of the cow; yet, upon the cessation of that [cause], let that very particular state cease, but let there be no cessation of the continuum (*santāna*).

Granted that there is no relationship of producer and produced between the cow and the gavaya, and thus no relation of that which is to be removed and that which removes; but what does this have to do with the body and the mind?

For it is not the case that the qualities or defects of one thing cause the qualities or defects of another when there is no relationship of producer and produced; furthermore, they would not necessarily coexist, as in the case of water in a stream of rice and so forth.
To this, it is replied:

The coexistence of the mind and the body is due to their mutual assistance in the production of effects from those causes, like the melting of copper by fire. For no other [inherent] relationship is established here; thus, even for the mind and the body, there is no relation of material cause and its effect (*anupādānopādeyabhāva*), as in the case of a cow and a gavaya, but rather merely some form of mutual assistance.

The transformation of the mind does not necessarily occur solely through the transformation of the body; therefore, because the body is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the mind, the cessation of the mind does not follow even upon the cessation of the body.

The entity that is the cause of the body’s state is not its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). For when the producer of a state ceases, let that very state cease. But that which is the cause of the continuum (*santāna*) is the material cause; upon its cessation, there would be the cessation of this continuum.

When the fire ceases, the liquidity of the copper ceases as well; for that duration, the mind remains together with the body. (476) Because they act as mutual auxiliaries, like fire and the liquidity of copper, the effect of those two causes does not persist once the mind has departed, just as gold [does not remain liquid]. (477) Just as gold, having liquidity as its material cause, exists together with fire as its auxiliary, so too the mind, being restricted to the body, arises from the mind which has the body as its auxiliary.

Even for the sake of the body, such as the *kalala* stage and so forth, the body exists only as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) for the mind; therefore, their coexistence occurs at the moment the effect is produced.
This is what is meant.

2. Because copper [and its properties] act as mutual auxiliaries, when a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is impossible, it is not illogical for even two auxiliary factors to occupy the same locus. 3.
[This occurs] because of the possibility of a single causal complex.

Because the mind acts as a cooperative condition for the body—designated as the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth—and because the body likewise acts as a cooperative condition for the mind, they coexist in the production of their effects, characterized as body and mind, like fire and the fluidity of copper.
However, when the body has ceased, the mind may exist either distinguished by another body or as a bodiless state; thus, it does not cease, being like the continuum of gold.
Furthermore, it might be argued that just as the specific transformation of the rice-continuum from water and other conditions does not cease when the water ceases,
whereas the continuum of fire and so forth— whose material cause has been impaired— does indeed cease.
Likewise, if the mind, being impaired by something, lacks the capacity to serve as the cause for a continuum, then there would be no cessation of the continuum.
Furthermore, just as a lotus root (*śālūka*) arises from cow dung which is of a different species, so too does its initial production arise from the body alone.
To this, it is replied:

4. And that [objection] regarding water is like the destruction of fire and so forth upon the appropriation of rice and other grains; however, consciousness as an appropriation is not destroyed by anything. 479.
The first arising of consciousness from a body is not observed, nor does its cessation occur without the destruction of its appropriation. 480.

Just as there is no destruction of the material cause (*upādāna*) of rice in the case of fire and so forth, so too there is no destruction of the material cause of consciousness; for consciousness itself is the material cause of consciousness, and its burning or similar destruction is not possible.
If it is argued that there is an impairment of torpor (*middha*) and so forth, we say no;
for torpor and the like are merely causes of temporary impairment.
Cognition that depends upon prior mental impressions arises even from a remote object; for it, there is no interruption [of the stream] due to sleep.
Indeed, sleep is not capable of destroying the cognition which is its material cause.
Because arising is observed even from a consciousness that has been interrupted, there is no established distinction between death, sleep, and [ordinary] interruption.

(482) If it were the case that [the stream] were actually interrupted at some point, that would be incorrect; for how could there be an observation of interruption without waking? How could such a conception—that it [the stream] exists either by itself or through another—possibly arise? (483)

To begin with, the interruption of cognition is not perceived by itself; for the interruption of a non-cognition is perceived by means of a cognition, whereas the interruption of a cognition is not perceived by anything, such as the absence of cognition. If this is your argument:
The non-existence of knowledge is unestablished; how could it establish [the non-existence of] anything?
If it were established, that very establishment would be knowledge itself—so how could there be an interruption of knowledge?
For if there were an interruption, it would always remain unknown; thus, the non-existence of the next world would be that very same thing, which is difficult to refute. (484)
That too is incorrect, because awakening is observed to depend upon prior mental impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). A mere cessation of consciousness is not observed;
for at birth and at awakening, consciousness is observed precisely as accompanied by prior mental impressions. Thus, there is no observation of a disjunction between the two ends [of existence].
Furthermore, the interruption of another's consciousness by someone else is simply not perceived,
because the conditions for perception are not met;
nor does an interruption occur through the possibility of laxity resulting from the state of being free from passion.

It is generally accepted that freedom from desire for one's own interests is what constitutes dispassion (*virāga*). However, it is not tenable to claim that one who is free from desire for the welfare of others is without fault; for indeed, that very lack of compassion is his fault.
Indeed, faultlessness is not attained through a lack of desire for the welfare of others;
rather, that which is called a "lack of mercy" is precisely his defect.
Alternatively, there is no fault, as some indeed maintain that the cessation [of consciousness] occurs upon the departure of passion;
therefore, consciousness does not cease through the destruction of the gift,
because the body has not been taken up [as its material cause].
Because it is impossible to destroy the mind due to its state of being free from passion.
It might be argued:
even if consciousness does not cease through the cessation of its material cause (*upādāna*), its cessation through the cessation of its support (*āśraya*) remains unprevented;
and since the body is perceived to be that support, then—just as when a wall or similar object is removed—the mind would cease. Thus, the existence of another world (*paraloka*) is not established.

Even that [consciousness] is not observed to have movement like a painting and the like; therefore, upon the destruction of its substratum, there would be the destruction of the entity that is the consciousness, such as a painting.
For paintings and the like are perceived as not having come from another substratum onto the cloth and so forth;

however, consciousness—at birth and in the state of awakening—is accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) associated with the bodies of other lives, and is accompanied by the movement through the body at the end of a dream. Thus, it does not have a fixed substratum like a painting.
For if there were a fixed substratum, then [the cognition] would perish upon the destruction of that substratum;
moreover, since there is no such thing as a substratum— whether it be the body or anything else— how could there be destruction upon its destruction?
In jars and so forth;
3. T. [End of section].
However, conditioned phenomena such as paintings and the like are not distinct from their substrates, such as walls;
therefore, they perish solely through their own destruction, not through the destruction of their support.
If it is argued that even if there is no non-distinction, the relationship of support and supported will exist between body and mind when they are distinct,
this is not so;
for that which is neither existent nor non-existent cannot be a support, as a support is the cause of stability.
If it is non-existent, it has no substratum, because [a substratum] is not distinct from that which abides.
Even if it were distinct, it would be the cause of that; what, then, would that have done for the entity?
To begin with, there is no substratum for that which is non-existent.
For the horn of a donkey has no substratum whatsoever; rather, one merely seeks its production from a non-existent cause.
Therefore, for that which is non-existent, only a cause is possible, not a substratum.
Furthermore, there can be no substratum for that which is existent, because it is already devoid of all dependence.
Furthermore, the claim that the substratum exists as a cause for the persistence of what already exists is also untenable; because persistence is not distinct from the persisting entity,
if one were to effect its persistence, one would simply be effecting that very entity itself.
Furthermore, there is no production of that which already exists, because it is illogical for what has already arisen to arise again;
nor is there anything unproduced within that which has arisen, since it is for the sake of producing that [unproduced portion] that the basis [is required].
Regarding the arising of any phenomenon, a cause such as a substratum is said to exist for its production; however,
stability is not distinct from its own nature, because even when it falls, its own nature still exists in the absence of stability.
If, however, stability were non-different [from the entity], then that [entity] would be non-different from stability,
and thus stability would exist at all times.

It might be argued that, while its own nature remains, [the effect] must be distinct [from its cause] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties that are being excluded; however, that is incorrect.
For if there were indeed a distinction, then that [cause] would simply be the cause of its arising or the cause of its persistence, but it would not be its substratum (ādhāra).
If it is argued that [the cause] is the support (*ādhāra*) of the entity (*bhāva*), we say no, because it performs no function with respect to the entity.

If it is argued that it is a support because it effects the persistence (*sthiti*) of the entity, then does this persistence exist as something already produced for that which is to be supported, or otherwise?
If it is argued that, because an entity does not exist prior to its arising,

the effect produced from that cause must arise as something distinct from it— since there is no relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*) between them— then what is the meaning of the phrase "inhering in that" (*tatsamaveta*)?
In that case, regarding "of duration," if there is another duration even for duration, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that [duration] exists as something distinct yet is not perceived as distinct because of its relation through inherence (*samavāya*), [we reply: no.
Granted that there is inherence (samavāya), nevertheless, let each thing be perceived by its own specific form; otherwise, how could it be perceived?
If you say it is through conjunction (saṃsarga), [that is not so].
What is this so-called "conjunction" (saṃsarga)?
If it were conjunction in its entirety, there would be no distinction [from identity];
if it were conjunction by way of a single part, what difference would there be between conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya)?
If it is argued that [the definition of inherence is] "being established as conjoined or non-conjoined," then it would follow that the parts of a tree and so forth are also inherences;
if it is argued that [the definition] includes the condition "provided there is the basis for the cognition 'here [in this]," [then...]
It is not merely conjunction [that is the cause], because that would lead to an absurdity;
for there is the cognition "a horn on the head."

Now, "inseparable inherence" (*ayutasiddhi*) is defined as the state of being inherent in the very constituent parts that constitute its own substrate; the opposite of this is "separate inherence" (*yutasiddhi*).
Even so, there can be no inherence because of the cognition of difference, nor can there be a connection with constituent parts for an entity that is partless.
If there were a conjunction with a part, it would follow that difference is perceived;
however, the claim that difference consists in being "connected" versus "unconnected" is not tenable,
because connection is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And since there is no inference in the absence of perception, there is no cognition of positive concomitance (anvaya).
Therefore, it is established that from a particular auxiliary cause, only a specifically qualified entity arises;
there is no such thing as "stability" (sthiti).
And thus, the relationship of locus and located is precisely a specific kind of causal relationship;
furthermore, since the body is not the material cause [of the self], there is no cessation [of the self] upon its cessation.
Moreover, if the body were the locus [of the self] because it provides stability, then as long as that locus remains stable, there would be no destruction of the self.
There would follow the consequence of non-destruction if that [destruction] is considered to depend on a cause of destruction;
if the same consequence applies there as well, then what is the use of a cause for stability? (65)

For as long as there is a sustainer, destruction is not possible—[meaning] destruction is without cause. Yet, it might be argued: "Even if there is no destruction while the sustainer exists, provided that there is no cause for destruction, then because destruction arises from the presence of a cause for destruction, there is no contingency of [spontaneous] destruction. To this he says:
"If you say that destruction comes from a cause for destruction..."
The same consequence does not apply there either;
for even in that case of destruction, the consequence is exactly the same— it is not as if destruction were something distinct from the entity itself.
And if it were distinct [from the entity], what would that cause have done to the entity?
For when a destruction distinct [from the entity] is produced, the entity is not said to be destroyed;
therefore, the cause of destruction does nothing at all.
Therefore, since it perishes by itself due to its lack of destruction, what is the use of a cause for its persistence?
A cause for persistence is ineffective;
or else, if destruction occurs from a cause of destruction, [then the same applies].
As long as there is no cause for destruction, the thing remains by itself; so what is the use of a cause for its persistence?

If its staying is due to the non-arrival of a cause for destruction, then that [non-destruction] is simply the inherent nature of the thing. Since this [nature] is not sublated, what is the use of a cause for its persistence? (66)
Destruction would occur even without a sustainer and without a destroyer; however,
when there is a sustainer who acts as a destroyer, it perishes,
and not without a cause of destruction.

Therefore, because it establishes [the object] prior to that which causes its destruction, the "establisher" (sthāpaka) is not redundant. But if this were so, would it not follow that destruction is causeless? No; rather, the entity itself arises from its own causes as being of such a nature, for destruction is an inherent property of things.
If an entity exists, it cannot be altered by anyone from its intrinsic nature; thus, what is the use of a cause for its persistence?
Or else, it perishes even without a cause for its persistence.
If there is a cause for stability, there must be an obstruction to destruction;
but surely that obstruction to destruction is itself distinct from destruction.
Consequently, since nothing happens to the destruction [itself], it would simply perish; how then could there be stability?
Now, if that which is perishable at every moment becomes otherwise due to the stabilizer (*sthāpaka*), then its destruction would likewise be causeless; thus, it is simply a momentary destruction,
and since it arises as something different from the stabilizer, the stabilizer is indeed the cause [of that change], and not a true stabilizer.

Alternatively, if there is no destruction because of the proof that establishes the locus [of the entity], then since non-destruction has thus arisen, this [non-destruction] is uncontradicted; so what further need is there for a cause of stability?

Now, if it were the case that non-destruction occurs only at the very time the sustainer exists, then since a different destruction would arise at every moment, what would cause the stability of one sustainer after another?
If it is argued that this is produced by its own causes, then the same would apply to the object being sustained; so what is the use of a sustainer?
Now, if there is a distinction such that for some things stability is provided by a sustainer (*sthāpaka*) and for others it occurs by itself,
then why is it not accepted that consciousness (*vijñāna*) also has stability by itself?
Or perhaps it might be argued:
A region of ground is seen as a reservoir of water, yet that [reservoir] is not actually perceived; therefore, even by that [perception], conceptual construction is sublated.
Consequently, because neither the existent nor the non-existent can serve as a basis, this verbal formulation is futile, as it is contradicted by what is observed.
Regarding this, it is also said:
"The support for water and so forth."
If it is argued that [the body] is the substratum for water and so forth, this is equally applicable here as well.
For since entities perish at every moment, the continuum of entities arises in such a way that it possesses a cause; otherwise, the notion of a "substratum" would be untenable. (67–68)

An entity such as water may indeed be a support because it prevents movement; however, what need is there for supports for qualities (*guṇa*), universals (*sāmānya*), and motions (*karman*), which are themselves devoid of motion?

Even in the case of water and the like, the absence of a support on the part of the ground and so forth is entirely logical, whether one maintains the position that they exist or do not exist; thus, the example cited is unobserved.
But surely, since the state of being a locus (*ādhārabhāva*) is observed, how can it be unobserved?
It is simply that you have a misconception regarding what is unobserved as being observed.
The logical principle is this: that which is the locus with respect to an action is so called because it supports the agent and the object.
It is called a "support" (ādhāra) because of its supporting; however, that which is falling cannot be supported by that which is also falling.
Furthermore, for that which possesses support, there is no perception of falling;
because falling and non-falling are mutually contradictory, if it is argued that there was falling first and non-falling later—

In that case, there is no persistence of that which falls, because oneness is not apprehended through perception; a single persisting entity is not perceived as pervading both the state of falling and its opposite.
And how can that which is non-pervasive be a persisting entity? For it is only when one perceives "it persists even now" that the persisting entity is grasped in such a manner.
If it is argued that [the object] is apprehended as pervasive through a sequence,
then one must consider what the meaning of "sequence" is;
for the designation of "sequence" applies only to existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, existence and non-existence belong either to the object (*grāhya*) or to the subject (*grāhaka*). If the object is conjoined with existence and non-existence, there would be unity [of the subject];
yet if the subject is sequential, the object must likewise be so. Thus, there is no unity for that which abides in the state of being an object.
Consequently, sequence belongs only to the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), wherein one thing is grasped as past, another is being grasped, and another is a future grasping.
How could there be perceptibility of sequence such that its apprehension would allow one to speak of a relationship between locus and located?
Consequently, the meaning of the phrase "neither of the existent nor the non-existent from a substratum" is precisely this.

Since the relationship of container and contained is not actually perceived, this notion of a relationship between container and contained is merely a conceptual construction. If that is so, then how can there even be a conceptual construction of container and contained without such perception?
It follows, therefore, that it must be a construction based on error.

For certain entities that perish moment by moment and arise in successive locations, their arising in a location proximate to their material cause (*upādāna*) is produced by the conjunction with a substratum;
therefore, because they arise in such a manner, the ground and so forth are the locus (*āśraya*), since they function as the cause.
The very reason is said to be the substratum of its distinguished state, by superimposing identity upon the preceding and succeeding moments through the cause of conceptual construction.

For when there is the superimposition of identity, one does not perceive arising, yet one imputes a cause to what preceded; thus, through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), this is a false conceptual construction. Consequently, because it proceeds from preceding and preceding predispositions, its existence as a beginningless continuum establishes the next world—this is the conclusion that follows.
For instance:
All mental conceptualization arises from prior causes; it exists without an objective basis, like the conceptualization of water in a mirage.
The conceptualization of identity between what precedes and what follows does not involve an objective basis, because such identity is non-existent.
That [effect] will arise from many causes alone because its being an effect of those [many causes] is not observed; therefore,
that [position] is incorrect.
For the conceptualization of water in a mirage is not based solely on that [present appearance], since it arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of having previously seen water;

nor was oneness perceived previously, so the conceptualization of oneness in another birth is preceded by the grasping of oneness in a prior birth, and that too is likewise [preceded by such grasping]. Thus, there is a mutual dependence of beginningless conceptualization, which establishes the beginningless continuum of living beings. In this way, the cognition associated with the apprehension of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, being an endless continuum, does not even from another perspective undergo interruption; thus, saṃsāra is without beginning or end.
Furthermore,
while water and other substances may have a substratum because they possess motion,
what need is there for substrata for qualities, universals, and actions, which are devoid of motion?

For it is logical that a substratum is the cause of obstruction to the movement of things such as water; however, what need have substrata for qualities, universals, and motions, which are devoid of motion and inactive?

Furthermore, consciousness—whether it be a universal, a quality, or an action—is in every respect inactive; thus, it has no requirement for a substratum. Consequently, there is no destruction of the mind, which is the thing supported, through the destruction of its substratum.
Its co-existence alone is what remains;
and as to how that co-existence occurs, it has already been explained.
Now, just as a quality is inherent even in the absence of motion, so too is the mind inherently present.
And if it is argued that a quality which has come into inherence cannot remain without an inherent cause, and that its destruction follows upon the destruction of that cause,
we say no.

The relationship of substrate and superstrate does not exist without the prevention of [independent] movement, nor does inherence exist without the relationship of substrate and superstrate; for it is stated that "inherence is the basis for the notion 'here' among things that are separately established and stand in the relation of substrate and superstrate.
This very point is expressed by:
"By this, both inherence and the inherent cause..."
The fixed status of universals (*jāti*) and so forth has been refuted because they lack a substratum.
Even if a universal were inherent (*samaveta*), it would not exist without an individual (*vyakti*) serving as its locus.
If it is argued that because a universal is eternal, it does not cease to exist even in the absence of a locus—
Since the mind, too, is dependent upon other causes, the same [argument applies];

and because there is no relationship of locus and located, by this very rejection of the relationship of locus and located, inherence (*samavāya*) is rejected, as is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
If that [substratum] is the cause, then it is not a relationship of locus and located;
if it is not the cause, then there is no status as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Furthermore, if the fixed location of universals and so forth is asserted even without causality, [it would follow that everything is everywhere].
That too has been refuted;
or rather, even if it were inherent (*samaveta*), the fact that it is restricted to that very [locus]—that is, its being established exclusively therein—has been refuted.
For a universal (*jāti*), although it rests upon individuals (*vyakti*), is not established exclusively therein, because it persists in other individuals as well.

Even if consciousness is thus dependent [on the body], it will continue to follow into another body even in the absence of the current body; therefore, there is no failure to establish the existence of the next world (*paraloka*).

Even in the absence of a single body, such a material cause for cognition (*buddhy-upādāna*) is not contradictory, just as a persisting cognition exists even when transitioning between different individual instances.
Therefore, there is no relationship of locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva) apart from the relationship of cause and effect.
If destruction occurs through another factor, what would be the use of a cause for its duration?
It would be destroyed even without others; causes for duration are not capable [of preventing it]. || 71 ||
Whatever exists is dependent upon a basis for its stability, and in the arising of everything, there too is dependence upon a basis;
therefore, no entity whatsoever ever undergoes destruction. If its nature were inherently perishable, what other [cause] could be its stabilizer?
"If its own nature is not perishable, what other [agent] could be its establisher?
(73)—these are the summary verses.
Now, one might object: is it not observed that the relationship between locus and located exists even without the relationship of support and supported, as in the case of a lamp and its light?

For light does not possess the property of falling, and the lamp exists as its support; upon the cessation of that [lamp], there is the cessation of the light. Furthermore, that light does not migrate to another lamp or to anything else.

Just as the light of a lamp perishes when the lamp is destroyed, even though it has reached another location, so too consciousness dependent on the body will cease upon the dissolution of the body, even though it has reached its objects.
Furthermore, that reaching of the objects is not [real] in the ultimate sense; rather, in that mental consciousness, there is seen only the mere appearance of their form.
To this it is replied:

because the lamp and its light undergo transformation together, they stand in the relationship of substratum and dependent; however, this is not the case for the body and the mind, but rather for intellect (*buddhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.
For instance:
Through the differentiation of the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), even the decrease and increase of wisdom and other qualities occur without the decrease and increase of the body.
This [phenomenon] is not found among things that depend [on a substrate], such as the light of a lamp.
There might be a distinction for this [intellect] even from that [body], but not when it is unassisted by the mind.
Since specific cognitions such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth evolve as they become distinguished by the force of specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*),
even in the absence of a specific bodily impression, the preceding intellect alone is the substratum of the subsequent intellect, and not the body.
Therefore, the example of the lamp's light is not applicable;
for is not the lamp's light also indeed altered by snakes and other such things?
It is not the case that this alteration, characterized by a dim shadow, belongs to the lamp itself.
Therefore, just as the light of a lamp varies according to its distance,
there is no alteration of the body at the time of a difference in mental activity;
yet, surely, a distinction is indeed observed even due to the particularity of the body.
Therefore, regarding the state of being the material cause or the state of being the substratum of the body,
he says:
Even in that case, the body’s state of being affected by changes occurs solely through the medium of the mind’s assistance;
and where there is a specific excellence of wisdom resulting from elixirs and the like during the nourishment of the body,

it is because, upon the arising of a body characterized by pleasant touch and form, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of things as they truly are are awakened in an undisturbed mind, whereby a certain person attains a particular excellence of wisdom in a certain respect.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that everyone everywhere possesses equal wisdom; just as when hunger is relieved by food, the distress caused by disease does not arise, so too, upon its cessation, only the explanation practiced according to one's habituation proceeds for this person. (490)

Because of the similarity [of the elixir] to an alchemical potion (*rasāyana*) and because of satiety, there may not even be a recollection of the study as it was practiced, nor of all the commentaries and so forth, due to the absence of mental substance (*asattva*).
(491) Therefore, whatever scripture was indeed practiced in a previous birth, his awakening of wisdom (*prajñā-prabodha*) occurs only in that very scripture; such is the conclusion.

(492) But for one who possesses the practice of all [sciences], through the excellence of their wisdom, they would otherwise become an omniscient knower by means of the application of the elixir. (493)

Apart from perception and recollection, there is no other cognition anywhere; even the distinctions such as wisdom (*prajñā*), intelligence (*medhā*), and so forth, arise solely from the awakening of memory.

(494) Wisdom is recollection of things as they truly are; its opposite is lack of wisdom (*dauḥprajña*). Intelligence, too, is simply a form of memory; it is merely the specific distinction therein that is being demonstrated.

(495) When an object that has been completely forgotten arises in exactly that same way through the force of a prior latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, one who possesses this is celebrated as "wise" (*prājña*). (496)
He who attains correct understanding through the very pursuit of recollection is called wise, due to his excellence in the practice of wisdom.
Thus ( ).
Wisdom (*medhā*) and memory (*smṛti*) are said to belong to those things perceived individually;
however, when there is a joining together of these [perceptions], that very same [faculty] becomes specifically *prajñā* (discernment).

(498) Furthermore, no such thing as "joining" is ever observed to occur without prior practice. Therefore, by means of an object belonging to that same class, a previous habituation is inferred. (499)
Now, is it not the case that passion (*rāga*) too is merely a particular state of the intellect (*buddhi*), and that there is no difference between it and the intellect?
For if there were a difference, it would follow that wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other qualities would also be distinct from it.
Furthermore, passion and the rest result in the nourishment and decay of the body.

From this it follows that cognition (*buddhi*) also [arises] from the body; otherwise, there would be no conformity to it. This is not so, because the increase of passion and so forth arises sometimes from nourishment and the like, and sometimes from pleasure and pain.

However, the notion of passion and so forth that arises from the proximity of internal objects such as the equilibrium of the elements (dhātu-sāmya) and the like is not present at all times, but only occasionally— specifically when there is the manifestation of improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manaskāra) born of habituation.
On the other hand, for one who possesses the cultivation of the meditation on the foul (aśubha-bhāvanā), that very passion is, conversely, diminished.

As for the increase of passion and so forth arising from pleasure and pain— wherein passion underlies pleasant feeling and hatred underlies painful feeling— it may be asked: "If that same prior awakening of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) occurs in one who is happy, how does hatred arise in one who is suffering?"

Since everything is unbearable for one who is suffering, it might be thought that there is no rule against the arising of aversion, which consists in the desire to abandon that [suffering]. However, even when the mind is afflicted by pain, compassion alone arises in one who possesses analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), due to their inference of [the suffering of others] from their own experience of suffering.

Passion also certainly arises from those very two—pleasure and pain—which are of the nature of cognition, when there is a cause for its remedy; thus, just as the body arises from them, so too does cognition arise, which contradicts your original premise.
This is not so.
Happiness arises solely through the medium of the object, due to the proximity of the internal state characterized by the equilibrium of the *dhātus*, and not through the medium of the substratum;
it is not the body, acting as the substratum, that produces pleasure and pain,
but rather the object itself.
Furthermore, since the body is the locus for both [the sense organ and the object] by virtue of the object being a cause of pleasure and so forth,
and because this applies equally to both external and internal objects, it would follow that the external object also has the body as its locus; however, this is not accepted.

For just as even an internal specific object, such as the equilibrium of the humors (*dhātu-sāmya*), is not apprehended by one who sees what is pleasant and so forth, at that time pleasure and pain have only that [internal state] as their basis;
the external object is not the basis, nor does [pleasure or pain] cease through the cessation of that [object],
just as pleasure arises with respect to an internal object.
Just as there is a movement toward external objects after abandoning that [previous state], so too is there a cognition regarding another body, such as in the next world and so forth.
When the arising of cognition occurs.

By this, cases such as the loss of memory resulting from a derangement of the humors (sannipāta) and so forth are explained; it is the internal cognition itself that undergoes modification based on specific internal objects.
Even in those cases, when elixirs (rasāyana) and the like are present as internal objects, the cognition of pleasure and so forth arises.
Consequently, there are lapses of memory and so forth,
but not the physical transformation of the body caused by the derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*); rather,
from that which serves as the basis, consciousness arises even when the eye and other faculties are not being perceived as objects.

And there is no modification [of cognition] through a modification of that [body], as there is in the case of one whose body has been altered by elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like; for if [the body] were the cause [of cognition] while remaining unperceived despite such bodily transformation, it would follow that it must be the cause of everything.

However, the status of the eyes and other organs as the substratum [of cognition] is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and because their modifications bring about modifications [in cognition].
It is not so for the body,
because even in its absence, pleasure and other states occur when external objects are present; indeed,
the loss of memory will occur even upon seeing external forms such as those of rākṣasas and the like.
He demonstrates this very point:
"In certain cases, when there is an excellence in the continuum of things such as the blood of a tiger, delusion and the like arise from merely hearing or seeing them. (78)
From merely hearing the word "tiger," delusion or some other state of mind arises in someone;
likewise, from the sight of blood [fear arises].
Yet that [blood] is not the substratum [of the cognition], nor does the cessation of the cognition follow from the cessation of that [blood].

Thus, because of the presence and arising of an internal object as a support (*ālambana*), there occurs the state of loss of mindfulness and so forth during the moment of their conjunction; therefore, cognition does not have the body as its substratum.
The body is merely the support for pleasure and other sensations, and consequently, those [sensations] do not cease simply by the cessation of that [body].

Because it exists even when the object of perception changes, the mind necessarily follows its own own conditioning; therefore, the mind is dependent upon that [conditioning] and is thus supported by the mind itself. || 76 ||
The mind necessarily follows the conditioning of the mind alone, not that of the body,
because the body is observed to be the support [of the mind];
for the mind of one whose attention is elsewhere does not arise in another location— thus, the mind is supported by the mind itself.
For it is thus:

due to the strength of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), distraction is averted; when distraction is stronger, the mental impression becomes turned away [from its effect]. (500) When the mental impression is exceedingly strong, then even in the presence of distraction there is no agitation of the mind; but when the state of distraction is stronger, then even though the mental impression exists, it does not produce the corresponding cognition that is its own proper effect.
Therefore, consciousness is necessarily preceded by a prior consciousness; thus, it is logical that when the [prior] consciousness ceases, the [subsequent] consciousness ceases.
But surely, sensory consciousness arises from the sense-faculties, and from that too arises mental consciousness?
Therefore, since mental consciousness arises from the body itself through a continuous succession, how can the body be said to be without a substratum?
For even in a successive causal chain, fire is not a non-cause of smoke produced from other smoke;
nor is that smoke not produced from successive fires, for it is not something unprecedented.

In this way, consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well, when arising from the body, would be subject to annihilation like smoke; however, this is not so, because it has been established that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists even without sensory cognition due to beginningless latent predispositions (*anādivāsanā*).

Just as smoke is of a certain nature [when produced] from fire, yet that same kind [of smoke] does not arise from smoke itself; so too, through practice, the mind arises in exactly the same manner. For smoke produced from fire and smoke produced from smoke do not share the same defining characteristic.

However, regarding specific states of cognition such as wisdom and the like, their form is identical prior to and immediately after practice. This is also the case for self-grasping and other all-pervasive [afflictions]. Therefore, smoke and the like are not suitable examples.
Furthermore, the continuity of smoke lasts for a certain period of time only because of a specific fire;
however, wisdom and the like arise only from a specific prior wisdom and so forth, and their persistence is not produced by the body.
Moreover, regarding these as well:
If for someone cognition were to arise from the sense-organ alone, devoid of a preceding cognition, then the example of smoke would be possible [to prove its dependence].
(502) Even when cognition arises from a sense-organ, it does not do so independently of prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*),
because it does not arise even when the object and the sense-organ are in proximity, provided that there is a disturbance of the preceding cognition.
Therefore, sensory cognition arises from the sense faculty only when accompanied by a preceding cognition, not from it alone; yet,
although that sensory cognition has indeed arisen,
it is conventionally described as "not arisen" due to the absence of ascertainment.
1. Consciousness is non-existent therein.
If even a cognition that has arisen is measured as "non-existent" due to the absence of ascertainment, then let it be understood that for him everything is non-existent;
for if the cognition of non-existence arises from the absence of ascertainment rather than from the absence of experience, then there is no such thing as the "absence of experience" anywhere,
since the absence of ascertainment is the cause in all cases.
Now, if there exists a cause for that cognition,
then cognition is inferred from the presence of its efficient cause;
well then, since cognition is also the cause for the ascertainment [of that object], let the existence of that [ascertainment] also be inferred.
Now, why is it not accepted that consciousness itself, being impaired by that agitation, is likewise the cause [of the cognition]?
Then, since the sense faculty is unimpaired and the object is not obstructed, why does it not produce cognition? [The answer is:
because the preceding cognition lacks the quality of being a producer [of the subsequent one].
If it is asked why this is so— namely, that the sense faculty alone, when accompanied by a preceding consciousness, is the producer [of the subsequent one]—
it is because [this is established] from the sensory consciousnesses of pleasure and so forth.
This will be established later when the occasion arises;
furthermore, it will be demonstrated subsequently that the cognition of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither, being sensory in nature, arises through the force of prior habituation.
Therefore, the sense organ produces sensory cognition only in dependence upon prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, even the cognition of a sound does not have its origin in the sense-faculty;
thus it is established that the entire mind is necessarily preceded by [a prior] mind.
Furthermore:
[is] of Janaka 1 T.
Today,

no sensory cognition has arisen through the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), because it possesses the nature of sensory cognition, just like the cognition of a dream. (504) If the sense organ were the cause, then in the absence of a sense organ, there would be no cognition possessing a vivid form as if facing an object before one.
And because it occurs even in the absence of that [object], it is not its cause.

Now, if it is argued that the erroneous cognition arises from the sense-faculty itself while the non-erroneous one arises from the object, this is not so; for not all cognition is produced from the sense-faculty alone. The distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition is established by the presence or absence of the object. (505)
For the entire sense organ would possess that form even without consciousness, just like dream-consciousness.
Now, if it is argued that the distinction is that what occurs without a sense organ is erroneous while the other is otherwise,
that is incorrect.
For the assumption of that [object's] form is indeed the very nature of consciousness, and since this is perceived even in the absence of a sense organ, the organ cannot be its cause.
As for the correspondence [of the cognition], however, it arises from the existence of the object; thus, it is produced by the object alone and not by the sense organ.
Furthermore, one thing does not possess the capacity to produce the effect of another;

yet, even in a dream, the sense faculty certainly exists, and thus the vivid appearance of something present before one is produced by that very faculty—therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule]. This too is not logical.

Because [the sense organ] arises from repeated practice, it is a waking sense organ, like any other [waking sense organ]; for there is no difference among causes when their effects and intrinsic natures are not different. (506)
A specific cause is inferred from a specific effect;
however, there is no such distinction in the sense faculty between the state of dreaming and other states.

Therefore, since the sense faculty itself does not arise without a homogeneous prior habituation, it is not the case that the first cognition arises solely from the sense faculty; rather, a preceding cognition is the support for the subsequent cognition.
nādya(?
Furthermore, regarding the form of consciousness, it might be argued: "Let the mind be the support of the mind; even so, our desired conclusion is not established.

For if [the mind] were established as having a support that does not belong to another world, that would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since we accept that the mind has the minds of the mother and father as its support.
If it is argued that relying on a mind directed toward the next world is inconclusive because one also conforms to the very nature of one's mother and father,
it is said in response:
Therefore, regarding the statement "the impression belongs to him alone" and so forth,
there is no necessary conformity to the nature of the mother and father, because even when they do not undergo change, a change [in the offspring] is observed.
Furthermore, because one perceives no change even when there is change,
if there were to be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that [self], then qualities such as scholarship would also arise;
just as, due to the nature of the *vaṭa* tree and so forth, the offspring of that [tree] possesses the nature of a *vaṭa* tree.

Now, just as the father’s or mother’s capacity to instill impressions (saṃskāra) through the assistance of teachers, readers, and so forth constitutes their inherent nature, so too it might be for the offspring; but that is not the case, because such impressions sometimes do not occur even when [the parents] are present,
whereas they do occur even in the absence [of those conditions].

If it is argued that— since conformity to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a preceding consciousness residing in one's own continuum is observed, whereas conformity to another continuum is not— the conformity to the teacher’s impressions is perceived [as a case of conformity to another continuum], we say no; for that [conformity] also arises from one's own continuum through a succession,
because it occurs due to a specific inclination (*abhiruci*) of the preceding consciousness in one's own continuum, and because it is not observed elsewhere in the absence of such [an inclination].

If it is argued that [the desire] arises from a companion who shares one's inclination, let it be so; nevertheless, without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there can be no conformity to the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of another. Therefore...
This very [rule] is the restriction.
5. From the seed of the *vaṭa* tree, 6. T.

Without a future world, there could be no continuation of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). The conformity to the nature of one's father is not contradictory for one who has passed to the next world.
Regarding this conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra),
it might be as follows:
If it is argued that there is a necessary conformity only to the mental formations existing within one's own continuum,
how then is the conformity to the nature of the father explained? This is the objection to be refuted.
If it follows that everyone must conform to the nature of their father, then even in the doctrine that asserts the existence of the next world, it would follow that no one conforms to it;
but this is not the case.
Because that which has such an intrinsic nature is produced from it in the next world, just as one follows the nature of a teacher;

or else, just as many trees arise from a single tree, so too many cognitions arise from a single cognition— thus it follows that the entire world has arisen from this very [single cause] through a continuous succession.
It has been stated here that, by the same logic as the consequence of following the nature of the mother and so forth,
even for one who asserts the existence of the next world, there would then have to be a persistence of the entire previous nature;
but this is not the case.
Due to the confusion caused by someone's fall [from a high place] or the suffering of dwelling in the womb,
there is indeed the persistence of mental formations (saṃskāra) for some,
as is observed in the case of those who remember their past lives (jātismara).
But for that which has arisen previously [in another life], there is no suffering; rather, that very state is its own condition and nothing else.

If that same [self] were the generator by way of being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), then just as in the case of its own body, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of memory occurring even in another body belonging to the son.
If it is argued that non-remembrance is due to suffering, that is incorrect.
If this were so...
2. Because it has been stated [in the sūtra].

For one who has arisen right there at that very moment by way of appropriation, there is no suffering, like a poison-insect; however, for one belonging to the next world, that is suffering due to the cultivation of beginningless habituation.
Furthermore:
If it is argued that there would be the consequence of the parents experiencing suffering—

just as one who has fallen asleep and entered another body experiences pain in the dream-body, or as a tree being burned does not experience the withering of the parent tree from which it grew— then [the following response follows].
This is not like the refinement of a subsequent tree, because that does not exist in the previous tree;
however, in this case, the splendor of the dreamer was observed in the previous body.
Consequently, there would be recollection only of what was previously done; furthermore,
in the case of moisture-born beings, there could be no cognition due to the absence of a mother and so forth.

Therefore, the cognition of a self and so forth is observed even in the absence of the cognition of a mother and so forth among sentient beings born from a womb; thus, since it occurs even in the absence of that [cognition of a mother], the cognition of a mother and so forth is not its cause.
Consequently, mental consciousness and the restlessness of the body and other faculties are produced solely by a preceding cognition arising within one's own continuum.
In the case of moisture-born beings,
there is cognition.
But surely, one's own continuum is nothing other than the bodies of one's mother and so forth, since a continuity of bodies is observed;
and since consciousness, restlessness, and the like are not distinct from those [bodies],
proving such a continuity would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Its own cause 8 T.

Furthermore, if the body related to the father and others is perceived as distinct [from the self], then the same would apply to the body belonging to the next world; thus, there would be no continuity between them.

Moreover, since the father and others possess that very same nature of fickleness and so forth during the various stages such as childhood, there would be a continuity of that [nature] within their own stream.
That too is incorrect,
because one does not observe the conformity of the mind and body to the nature of the mother and so forth; if it is argued that he therefore is not his father, [we reply as follows].
It is not so, because it has been observed;
nor is its specific distinction observed without repeated practice belonging to oneself.
Therefore, it is one's own habitual practice that is inferred;

even if the mind were non-different [from the elements] and a transformation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there would still be only an inference of the great elements of the previous and future lives,
and non-difference is not logical.
Because (10 T).

Just as the impressions (*saṃskāra*) such as what has been heard by one's parents manifest in the mind at the proper time due to their non-differentiation from it, so too would that quality arise even in the body. || 80 ||

For a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) such as the virtuous and so forth, being preceded by its own self-cognized practice, remains unmanifest during the state of sleep and is manifested at the time of the waking state;
likewise, though unmanifest in the body, it is perceived as if in the mind due to their non-difference.
