Just as qualities such as leanness and the like are perceived in the body by another person, [so too is the mental impression perceived].
If that were so, why is there not likewise the perception of mental qualities such as craftsmanship and the like?
For it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily be included within [the category of] visible form (*rūpa*).
If you argue that there is no perception by another because [mental qualities] consist of a specific kind of internal tangible object (*antaḥ-spraṣṭavya-viśeṣa-rūpa*), [we reply:]...
Nor [is it] external tangibles, because even wounds and the like are not perceived;
for the rough touch of wind is not perceived by another [sense-organ] other than the one [tongue] by which the wound is perceived.
If it is argued that this is simply the power of the wound itself,
then is the object perceived differently from how it is perceived due to a particularity of the perceiver?
If that were the case, it would follow that [the cognition] is erroneous.
If it is argued that this is merely a specific kind of contact with the wound, then it would follow that the wind itself is perceived;
and in that case, the pain of the person with the wound would not occur.
Alternatively, if it is claimed that the contact of the wound being struck by the wind is perceived by that very [wind], [the same fault follows].
It is not logical that there would be no perception of another person's wound simply because it is touched by someone else; for [the following reason]: 11 T.
In the twelve [factors] beginning with hearing, there are blackness and so forth.
contained within the body 4 T.
If the form of that which is being touched in the other world is not experienced when it has been touched, then how could that very same thing be known when there is cognition of another form? (509)
Indeed, it is not logical that its form should remain unknown to one whose sense faculties are unimpaired;
for self-awareness itself [is necessary],
since non-awareness is of a different nature from that [awareness].

If suffering, pleasure, or passion and so forth were merely self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), then consciousness would be something other than the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Consequently, it would not be logical for self-cognition to stand in the relationship of container and contained with the body.
How then can one say, "I have a sensation in my foot" or "I have a sensation in my hand"?
Because that [cognition] is absent precisely at the time of the hand's modification, it is so [designated] and not otherwise;
such a designation occurs because [the cognition] is concomitant with the modification of the hand and so forth.
For instance:
1. Because self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) has that as its defining characteristic;
2. T. [Tibetan source].
Because of the existence of that consciousness.

Due to the mere nature of self-awareness, there is no state of being the support and the supported; for one who is immersed in their own essential nature, there is no conceptualization of support and so forth. Indeed, how could the conceptualization of support and supported be possible in the cognition of the mere essential nature?
Such would only occur upon the apprehension of duality.
And even in that case, when there is such realization of non-duality, it would indeed be duality itself;
yet even there, it is so.
Alternatively, if that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in such a way due to the restriction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
then that conceptual construction is not distinct from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because it terminates in its own essential nature alone;
even if it consists of great elements produced by the force of latent impressions, there is no fault.

Indeed, the grasping of rebirth occurs only for that which is produced by mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and consists of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*); it does not occur even with respect to the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Therefore, since the intellect is distinct from the body, it is not born from the mother and father;

rather, it must exist as a prior state within its own continuum. If that is so, then the birth of a living being does not arise from the mere great elements (*mahābhūta*) alone. Consequently, there is an arrival from another life into the place of the womb and so forth;
thus, proceeding to an impure location is not illogical.
For it is not fitting for a discerning person to act in such a manner;
and if the impulsion of a Lord is not admitted therein, it is said in response:
For one who possesses self-attachment, the assumption of a lowly state—being led by no other being—is due to the desire for the acquisition of pleasure and the abandonment of suffering;
and in regard to suffering, distorted cognition and craving are the causes of bondage. (81)
He for whom these two do not exist is not subject to birth.

This has been stated: if one is discerning, there is no movement toward one's own nature because it is already attained; therefore, one should not set out anywhere, such as toward a village or elsewhere. Consequently, because of primordial peace (*ādiśāntatva*), saṃsāra itself would not exist.
Now, just as going to a village or elsewhere occurs somehow through a lack of foresight, so too does the movement toward the womb and other locations;
for one who is impelled by self-attachment, even that which is inferior becomes acceptable due to cognitive distortion.
Such is the power of karma that, like one led by another being or dependent on another, he proceeds in such a manner.
Even the acceptance of a low station occurs through the desire for the attainment or avoidance of pleasure and pain, like a learned *śrotriya* entering the house of a maidservant.

Why, then, does this [agent] not have the impulsion of a Lord (*īśvara*)? Since it is possible for one who is deluded to act by himself, the postulation of a Lord is not tenable; moreover, no such impulsion by a Lord is perceived.
And as for how there is no postulation of a Lord (Īśvara), that has already been established: self-attachment (*ātmasneha*) itself is the Lord, because it is perceived as its instigator.
Now, if it is argued that just as a servant or the like is impelled by another, so too is one impelled in the next world; [we reply:]...
No,
because there is no such restriction;
it is only one who possesses craving for a self who is impelled, not everyone.
If it is argued that he too is possessed of craving and is not impelled by another who is free from passion and so forth, because he attains his state through that very act of propitiation,
then it follows as a consequence that all founders of religious systems (tīrthakaras) would be [impelled] by God.
Therefore, it is only one whose mind is perverted who proceeds toward the womb or elsewhere, even though it is suffering, by means of the perception of pleasure.

Consequently, from that perverted mind and craving, birth arises; however, for one in whom these two do not exist, he does not undergo birth, and in his case, even Īśvara is not capable of granting birth.
For even among those who maintain the existence of a Lord (Īśvara), this is not accepted:
"Is it not the case that for one whose karma is not conducive to health, the physician is ineffective;

yet for one whose karma is unimpaired and conducive to health, the physicians are likewise useless, since they cannot accomplish what is impossible nor remedy what is already accomplished? Thus it follows.
This is not a fault,
because [the definition] specifies "by means of that which is undesirable and incapable."

In some cases, the physician’s efforts are futile, and likewise, is he not powerless? If that same [powerlessness] is desired even for God, then He is not God. Indeed, it is not accepted by the proponents of God that every transmigrating being is impelled by Him, while another is not; otherwise, even the propitiation of a donor would be useful for attaining a destination.
And this [objection] applies even to all the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakara*): what then is the distinction between an *Īśvara* and a non-*Īśvara*?
Therefore, it is only ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that possess the capacity for rebirth, not an *Īśvara*.

[Regarding the intermediate state body (*antarābhavadeha*): If, then, going and coming are in relation to another birth, it follows that those two should be perceived; yet since they are not perceived, they must simply be non-existent. To this, he says:

If going and coming are not perceived, it is due to the lack of acuity of the sense faculties; it is like the failure to see the movement of thin smoke by one with weak vision. (83) Even though going and coming are not seen, nevertheless, their non-existence does not follow.
The failure to see [the intermediate state] is due to the lack of proficiency of the sense faculties, and not because of its non-existence;
for it is not the case that what is non-existent is simply not seen, as thin smoke is not within the range of vision for one with weak eyes, yet it certainly exists.
Indeed, the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not perceived because of its translucence; whether departing or entering, it is not non-existent merely because it is not observed. (512)
For the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), having arisen through the power of karma with such transparency that it is accessible only to yogins,
is not perceived like a dream-body;
yet its non-existence does not follow from that.
If it is argued that [the dream body] is a false body, we say no, because it has been established that it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*).
For this very reason,
although it is corporeal due to its subtlety, it is nevertheless incapable of certain things in certain places.
Or, like water [in a vessel], like mercury [in gold], it may be non-existent because it is not perceived;

or, like a dream-body, it may be insentient because it possesses form; yet even that which possesses form may be insentient in some respects, as water is in a jar, or as light is in crystal, or as mercury is in gold;
or else, like water or mercury in gold, it may simply not be perceived despite being present.
Moreover, the intermediate state body is indeed non-existent because it is not perceived;
for thus [it is said]:
Therefore, O Sūta,
because of the similarity to the continuity of rice, the arising of existence as an uninterrupted succession has been conceptually constructed.
In the Abhidharmakośa, 3.11:
That which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is the intermediate existence (antarābhava).
at that very place 3 10
And it is not the case here that [the cause] is thus separated by time and space from its arising;
for instance, someone perceives an uninterrupted journey toward Kanyakubja and so forth through such means as traveling to a village.
Someone situated here perceives themselves at one and the same time as being in another country in a dream; likewise, there is no difference in the case of the destination of rebirth.
Nor can it be argued that the dream is unreal, for this [rebirth] which is the subject of proof must likewise be unreal.
A complete similarity between the example and the subject is not observed;

rather, reality arises from the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, there will be truth for another birth, but not for a dream, because of the absence of such [firm] impressions in the latter, since a dream is followed by a different appearance.
If it is argued that a dream is unreal due to this, then surely it must also be considered that another birth is likewise unreal. (513)

If another appearance characterized by waking cognition were to exist, then the unreality of the dream would imply the opposite—namely, the reality—of the waking cognition; however, this is not so, because the waking cognition also possesses the characteristic of being another appearance. Indeed, there is no distinction between them in terms of their being erroneous.
If it is argued that there is a distinction [between waking and dreaming] because in a dream a jar or the like is perceived quite spontaneously, even in the absence of its [usual] cause;

Even for one who is awake, jars and other objects are perceived quite suddenly; likewise, in dreams, carts and other things are seen when the necessary causal conditions are present. Even in the waking state, mountains and such things created by a yogin come within the range of perception quite unexpectedly.

If it is argued that these [mountains] existed previously and were merely perceived [then], we reply that the specific act of wandering [or the particular circumstances] is itself the causal condition in that case.
That [dream] is unreal;

but by what means was its existence even during sleep previously refuted? If it is argued that [the dream objects are unreal] because other things are not perceived [therein], then that [non-perception] is the same in the case of mountains and so forth.
If mountains and the like existed previously, they would have been perceived somewhere by one who is awake.
Why is it not accepted that it is likewise [unreal] even by one established in the dream state?
If you argue that they do not exist because they are not perceived by another person who is awake,
then there is likewise a non-perception of those things perceived while awake by one who has entered a dream.

And just as their perception arises from the causal complex of wandering, so too, because of the possibility of another state—namely, dreaming—the notion that jars and other objects appear suddenly, and how there is the waking state, is the arising of the cognition of being awake. If this is argued:
Regarding the state of dreaming:

[Objection] But surely, even in a dream, why is there not at times the cognition of being awake? For all activities such as the opening of the eyes and so forth exist there as well; thus, the two states are equal. To explain: even in a dream, the conviction "I am awake, I am alert" is found.
If it is argued: "How then can going and so forth [occur] from that? For even that dream is unreal."
Otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to the state considered to be waking,
since the mutual non-perception of both states is equal; however,
the unreality of the dream is established by the cognition that "this is unreal."
Since the cognition of the waking state is also similar to that [dream cognition], let it be unreal;
for reality does not derive from that cognition alone,
since reality exists even by means of its defining characteristic.
Moreover, what does the cognition "unreal" take as its object?

Is it something other than the real, or is it the real itself? This negation [of reality] cannot be either, for both are extremely difficult to establish, since that very form [of the real] is perceived. (517)
Indeed, it is not logical that something which is perceived precisely as having that nature should be "other than that," nor is it the case that it is not so;
for its being other than that consists precisely in its having a nature other than that, otherwise even that [nature] would be other than that.
Nor is it the case that what is being perceived simply does not exist, for that would entail the absurd consequence that everything is likewise non-existent.

If this cognition arises [thinking], "Let it arise; its objective support (ālambana) does not exist," then because it is merely purposeless, no determination of the nature of things (padārtha-vyavasthiti) can be established on its basis.

2. [Objection: But surely there is no such thing as futility in the case of what is perceived in a dream, since this cognition regarding jars and so forth is firm and non-contradictory; how then can it be futile?

For instance, in one who has just awakened from bathing, there is an immediate appearance of not having bathed; since this is subsequently confirmed in that very same way, the cognition is non-erroneous.
This is incorrect.
For the state of passion ceases immediately upon waking from a dream, yet there is no contradiction therein because one experiences that very same thing again in a subsequent dream.

This distinction between what is a dream and what is otherwise is not established even now; for if it were established through the very fact of non-contradiction with the object to be proven, there would be a circular argument.

Furthermore, the notion that "this does not exist" is not apprehended by any other cognition; this is merely a matter of [mental] apprehension, which constitutes its unique characteristic. Such cognitions arise for those engaged in worldly discourse due to the influence of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). By what specific factor [are they distinguished]? By the absence of perception on the part of one who identifies with the waking self immediately following that [dream state].

Even the conceit of being awake arises solely through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) upon the abandonment of the fallen body; this too is merely conventional and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because the state called "waking" is likewise perceived even within a dream. Now, if there is no cognition that [the objects] of those in a dream do not exist during their waking perceptions, that itself constitutes bondage.

By their very practice, they have demonstrated the non-existence [of those things]; for there is the possibility of their unimpeded movement and so forth. Since the non-existence is already established by the very fact that movement and so forth occur without obstruction, what is the point of a primary [negation] established by another conceptual construction?
For a conceptual construction establishes the unreality of even that which is real.
Otherwise, there would be no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) characterized by mutual contradiction;

therefore, because they are instantly shattered, there is the conceit of unreality. Furthermore, because there is an absence of continuity with the waking state regarding those things seen in a dream, it does not follow that even those [dream objects] are unreal for that reason alone.
Therefore, although going and coming are not perceived by another in the case of dream-objects, they nevertheless do exist; thus, the non-perception [of such objects] is inconclusive.
Consequently, it has been established that there is neither an absence nor indeed a presence of going and coming.
(a) Refutation of the whole:
Furthermore,

if consciousness were non-different from the body, and the body were merely an aggregate of atoms, then it would follow that there must be a consciousness of every single atom. Alternatively, if it is perceived as a single, gross whole (avayavin), then [it cannot be composed of atoms].
Even so, since it resides within the atoms and arises from the contact of atoms, there is the perception of atoms; yet,
if consciousness arises from them but is not established within them,
then how can there be the understanding that "it arises from them"?
There is neither self-cognition nor cognition by another;
rather, it is only cognition by another and not self-cognition. How, then, is pleasure cognized? Because its cognition is by something else that is distinct from it. That is incorrect.
If there is cognition of that which is other, what else could there be as the cognizer? That alone is cognition where the determination "this is cognition" occurs.

(523) If it is argued that there is nothing else apart from the cognition of pleasure and so forth, and blue and so forth—which are indeed other than one another—and that the body itself is the cognizer, this is not so.

Without pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, what is even the body considered to be? For it is that which is perceived, and not the perceiver. (524) If you say that the eye and other [senses] possess such a nature [of being perceivers], why is a donkey’s horn not likewise [a perceiver]? If you say that they exist in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), how can that potentiality be such [a perceiver] when it is not apprehended?
(525) Indeed, the eye and other [senses], while not being perceived themselves, are not perceivers like a donkey’s horn.

If it is argued that the eyes and other sense organs are of the nature of power (*śakti*), and therefore not of the nature of non-existence, and that even though this power is unperceived, how can its existence be known except through its effects?
What is to be done regarding them?
For their apprehension consists of pleasure and so forth;
yet surely that too is not apprehended, because it is itself a power.
By process of elimination, they must be form and so forth;
yet these are not the effects of the power of consciousness, for if they were the effects of the eye and other [senses], it would follow that they did not exist previously.
If it is argued that their state as being perceived is the effect, [we reply:]...
It would follow that every atom would be perceived;
moreover, in the absence of any distinction, there could be no difference in state,
and if a distinction were admitted, it would follow that there must be self-awareness of it.

If it is argued that the very production accompanied by power (*śakti*) constitutes the distinction, this is not tenable; for since the inference [of the word] occurs through its accompaniment, and that doctrine [of power] is derived from inference, how can this fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) be avoided? (526)
For the specific characteristic of form and the other [sensory objects] is their state of being perceived;
if that [perceivedness] consists in being accompanied by the capacity for perception, how can there be a proof of accompaniment without a proof of the capacity?
If that is not proven, how can there be an inference of the capacity?

Therefore, consciousness is simply the self-cognition of form, pleasure, and so forth; for the cognition arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that "consciousness" and "pleasure, etc. are used as co-referents. And this coreferentiality occurs through two types: primary and secondary. There is no other [type], such as in the cases: "The man is a staff," or "The conscious one is the man. If it were secondary, it would be like: "The platforms are shouting," or "The man is a staff."

If it is argued that consciousness is indeed unestablished in this context— because, among form and the other [aggregates], it is impossible to perceive a consciousness distinct from form— and is therefore inferred by this very same example;
It is not because of the impossibility of inference;
for the Sāṃkhyas accept that the person (*puruṣa*) is conscious based on primary grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, it must be accepted that a thing is exactly as its cognition represents it.

Through the repeated practice of [perceiving] the nature of things as distinct from their own-form, there arises a state of feeling regarding form and so forth that corresponds to reality; this exists by way of the transition from one form and so forth to another. || 528 ||
Indeed, consciousness does not mix with another by means of something distinct from its objective support;
therefore, that which is mixed with pleasure and so forth mixes with form and so forth,
and that which has mixed with form and so forth mixes with the pleasure and so forth of others.

Through practice, by means of grasping the signs (liṅga) of all aspects, there arises the realization of their complete forms; how then could objects such as the pleasure of another or colors be apprehended as remaining in their original state?

That is incorrect, for when there is cognition of the essential nature itself, there is no distinction between being "detached" (taṭastha) or "non-detached. This [distinction] is merely a matter of conventional usage based on the dependence upon a substratum. || 529 ||
For regarding forms, pleasure, and so forth, there is no mode of cognition other than the self-awareness of their own essential nature;
therefore, how could there be a distinction such as "this is external" or "otherwise"?
The distinction that "this is external" or "otherwise" is merely a conventional one, based on its dependence upon the body as a support.

"Surely, there is no cognition of that form without dependence [on something else]; and from the cognition of that form, no further dependence exists. (530) "This is true; therefore, this distinction does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). However, this distinction belongs to the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*); for the conventional cannot withstand critical analysis (*vicāra*). (531)
This indeed is called conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), which, when analyzed, falls apart; otherwise, it would be ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, just as consciousness—which possesses a transition—exists in identity with form and so forth in another's body, so too does it exist in the body of another's semen and blood.

Therefore, there is no other thing called "capacity" (*śakti*) which is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), by virtue of which the substratum of consciousness could possess activity; rather, it is simply that very consciousness itself, being self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), which exists in such a manner. [Objection: If [the pillar] has merged into the nature of consciousness through identity (*tādātmya*), then why is there no movement in the pillar and so forth? For, just as with one's own body, there would follow the consequence of movement for that [pillar] as well.

[Reply: That too is incorrect; movement does not occur merely through the arising of identity. Rather, it occurs from the arising of a specific nature consisting of the cognition of touch. (Verse 532)
Indeed, when tactile consciousness arises having the nature of volitional consciousness, then movement of the body and so forth arises, and not otherwise; therefore,
consciousness would have the very nature of form and the rest, and from that,
it would follow that there is sensation in every single atom.
Why does this not also apply to you?
Since another consciousness arises with that same form,
for me as well, it is the composite whole (avayavin) in the form of consciousness that exists, and not the atoms (paramāṇu).
That too is incorrect,
because it would follow that even atoms possess that same nature [of being composite]. If you argue that atoms are indeed separate entities,
then it follows that they do not exist at all.
For instance, the body is established by way of its own nature as atoms; the body is established by way of the nature of atoms.
(533) Now, if the atoms of the body do not have consciousness as their nature, then, in that case, the atoms do not have the body as their nature.
And since they are not perceived, they do not possess the nature of objects; therefore, atoms have no existence,
and thus there remains only the whole (avayavin).
That [self] also [does not exist],
because if it were present, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything would tremble when the hand and other limbs tremble, which contradicts [the nature of the self].
Because action cannot occur in one [part] alone, there would have to be separate establishment [of parts];
otherwise, if one were covered, all would be covered, and if one were uncovered, the redness in one would be seen as the state of the non-red. (85–86)

For that which is called a "substance" (*dravya*) is indeed the form of a whole (*avayavin*), possessing action (*kriyāvat*), possessing qualities (*guṇavat*), and being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunctions and so forth;
if it has no action, then because it is the inherent cause of all [its parts], it follows that everything moves. Thus, the whole would be a variegated entity, both moving and non-moving.
It follows that the whole (avayavin) is one and the same, taking forms such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta, while simultaneously possessing states such as moving and so forth;
yet, since both unity and the state of being both moving and non-moving are observed, what is the contradiction?
What indeed is this so-called "unity"?

If there is no non-difference in appearance, then that [non-difference] must consist in having a single effect. If indeed there is one effect, then the cause must also be one; but from what [reasoning] would it follow that when a part-whole (avayavin) is obscured, the whole is entirely obscured? Since there is no difference in its conjunction [with the obscuring object], it would follow that when a part is obscured, the whole is not [necessarily] obscured, and thus everything would be visible.
If it is argued that nothing would be seen at all, or else everything would be seen, because even if there were unity, the whole would be impossible to perceive due to the obstruction by its parts—
then how can there be unity between what is seen and what is unseen?
Even in the case of conjunction with passion (*rāgayoga*), this same consequence follows:
action exists; there is no single composite [entity] because of this multiplicity, as in the previous case.
If it is argued that motion is not established because there is no distinction [between the senses] and because they are atomic, [we reply:
there is no lack of distinction because of their permanence; therefore, since they possess specific qualities, they are not atomic.
If the body were manifold, then even in that case of multiplicity, there would be the same fault as before: the consequence that self-cognition would occur for every individual atom.
If it is argued that there is no movement because there is no distinction,
this is not so;
for the very absence of distinction is not established.
Since it is perceived during the state of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), it is not non-distinct from that which is unperceived;

for this very reason, even its atomicity (*aṇutva*) does not act as an obstacle during the state of self-awareness. Thus, because it is non-distinct from the non-existent despite being existent, it is not atomic.
If you ask, "How then do you perceive a distinction even for yourself? [the answer follows].
The apprehension of an object does not occur by way of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), but rather the apprehension of the object is precisely the apprehension of the consciousness bearing its form.
If it is asked why the form [of the object] is not that of atoms, this will be explained later.
(b) There is no absence of obstruction and so forth for atoms—[the opponent objects:
"But how can there be obstruction, resistance, and so on for that which is merely an atom?
By this, the absence of obstruction and the rest is also refuted. 88
Or how [could there be] a mixture of mercury, gold, and so forth, or a heated stone and so forth?
For in that very case, there is no composite whole (*avayavin*) consisting of heterogeneous parts.
If [it is argued that] the visible [object] is perceived by the eyes and other senses which are individually incapable, how can there be such a perception?

If it is said that this occurs through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then the same logical consequence applies here as in the case of gold and the wire (which are not seen separately). If it is claimed that the conjunction itself is visible, then how can there be perception of something whose substratum is invisible?
Furthermore, the connection with taste, form, and so forth would be contradictory if [the whole] were merely figurative (upacāra).
If conjunction (saṃyoga) is accepted [as the whole], then how could there be distinct cognitions such as "a row" or "long"? (61)
5–6. Likewise, even in the case of number, conjunction, action, and so forth, their form does not appear in cognition as distinct from its own nature and from verbal expression.
It is not tenable to ask how there can be obstruction for atoms given their lack of contact,
for obstruction is never observed anywhere as being tied to a composite whole (avayavin),
such that it would not exist in atoms in the absence of that [whole]. The same applies to resistance and so forth.
Now, it is said as follows:
"Resistance and so forth also [exist]."
If cloth and other objects were merely an aggregation of atoms held together by cohesion (*dhīdhratva*), how could they provide obstruction to sunlight or water?
Without the conjunction of a composite whole (*avayavin*), how could mere atoms—whose mutual interstices would be unhindered by one another—be capable of providing such obstruction?
To this, it is replied:
How can even the conjunction of atoms, which are themselves incapable [of producing effects], be produced? And how do those conjoined atoms produce a composite whole (*avayavin*),
given that conjunction does not occur through a single part, since such parts do not exist?

If conjunction were produced as a distinct category [of entity], it would follow that [the atoms] must merge entirely, down to the size of a single atom; and if they do not produce that very conjunction,
then the same logical difficulty arises as to how those atoms with intervals between them could produce it at all.
If conjunction [is required], what is the use of a further conjunction or a composite whole?
Or rather, do [the atoms] produce both conjunction and the composite whole while remaining separated by intervals?
If that were so, why do they not also produce effects such as obscuration?
To this it is replied: how [could they produce them] while remaining unmixed?

Even without the conjunction of atoms, there exists a supreme cohesion which does not undergo any state of separation even when struck; [this is] that [which is the subject]. (535) Just as hair, mosquitoes, flies, and so forth, though situated in separate locations, produce a cognition of a single, dense form, why do they not likewise produce another effect?

If it is argued that "it is so" because there is a subverting perception (*bādhaka*) in that case, then here too the cognition of a yogi who perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriya-darśin*) would serve as the subverter, provided such a yogi exists—
just as, for example, no water flows out from a leakless vessel when it is covered on top.

Likewise, even in the case of an aggregate of atoms, or else, how could the union of mercury and gold be capable of functions such as obstruction and resistance without a whole (avayavin)? Or how could there be another effect, such as the spreading [of heat] upon a heated stone and so forth?
It arises from a specific cause characterized by a particular configuration;
furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect is inconceivable.
For instance, while form and the other [sensory objects] are individually incapable of producing consciousness, they nevertheless produce it when in a state of combination.
If it is argued that [the atoms produce motion] because of conjunction, then surely conjunction itself is also an effect; how then can they produce that very conjunction?
Moreover, conjunction is not perceptible, because there is no movement of that which has an imperceptible substratum.

If it is the established doctrine that perception arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object even when the substratum is unperceived, and if that contact is indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then—

because this [quality of sound] has conjunction as its cause— it would follow that it is not a quality, since the definition of a quality is that it is "not a cause of conjunctions or disjunctions. Thus, the definition of a quality would be abandoned.

Now, if it is argued that [the motion] is indeed perceived because it is inherent in what is conjoined [with the atom], then, in the presence of conjunction with atoms, there would be motion of the atom; thus, the postulation of a composite whole (avayavin) is futile,
or else there would be motion of all [atoms involved in] conjunctions.
If it is argued that there is no non-apprehension from a distance because there is simply no contact with the sense faculty in that case, we say:
no.
Even for gross objects there would be no motion;
furthermore, if conjunction produced by conjunction were also admitted,
the statement that [conjunction] is "not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" would be a prohibition against its being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
In that case, because inherence (*samavāya*) is not the basis for the notion "here," the cognition "here" does not necessarily arise when conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is being perceived.
Consequently, even the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) would be attained;
furthermore,
Just as in the case of a perforated cup,
if *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) were the cause of perception, then there would be perception of a substance even when [its parts] are in conjunction with atoms.

If *saṃyuktasamavāya* were also a cause of perception, then the conjunction with the product-substance (*kāryadravya*) would be useless, since the product-substance would be seen simply through the conjunction with the atoms.
Now, if a composite substance exists, the conjunction of atoms cannot be postulated;

for if the perception of jars and the like arises from the conjunction of atoms alone, then the postulation of parts is useless—this is that very same fault. Alternatively, if there is no composite substance, the postulation of the conjunction of atoms is not possible otherwise.
The same applies to the opposite case as well;
nor can there be a conjunction of atoms with the whole,
because, being in the same place and time, there is an absence of spatial separation.
Alternatively, if there were conjunction even for the perceived whole (*avayavin*), then there would also have to be conjunction for the visible [parts] even when they are not conjoined;
moreover—

Let it be seen that [the perception of color, etc.,] occurs through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); otherwise, the connection of taste, form, and so forth would not be perceived in things such as a *pānaka* (a mixed drink) when they are being observed, because "a quality does not [inhere] in a quality.
For in that case, neither the form nor the taste of the constituent parts exists [in the whole].
If it is argued that such a designation occurs figuratively (*upacārataḥ*), then a distinction in cognition (*buddhibheda*) would follow;
for the very same form or taste that belongs to the constituent parts of curd and so forth is figuratively attributed [to the whole] by virtue of inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*).
But there is no perception of a different color or taste [in the conjunction],
for whatever is the color of the conjoined things, that would also be the color of the conjunction; how then could there be a different color or taste there except through metaphorical designation?
Also of [the nature of] vision— there is a different rendering of this verse in the Tibetan language.

Now, it may be argued that those very color and taste appear as such due to their conjunction (*saṃsarga*), for extreme conjunction is indeed the cause for the apprehension of identity; thus, there is simply the cognition of a difference in taste and a difference in form.

If this were so, then there would be no other composite whole (*avayavin*) at all, since the manifestation of atoms themselves would be what constitutes the conventional usage of "gross" and so forth.
Furthermore,
if it were not the case that the grossness of atoms themselves is perceived, then there would be no such thing as "a long row," for there is no such entity as a "row" apart from its constituents.
For instance:
sthūlatādi°

Because it is not a conjunction, it is not a conjunction; for that very reason, it is not a substance. Furthermore, length does not belong to genus (*jāti*) and so forth, nor is genus and so forth accepted [as being long]. (538) Just as cognitions of "long" and so forth arise due to a particular arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*), so too is the aforementioned object [of the cognition] said to belong to the atoms.
(539) Just as in the case of a garland and the like, the state of being "long" and so forth belongs to the mere arrangement itself.
And thus, that which is the subject of dispute is intended as the object of the whole (*avayavin*); therefore, it is not the whole.
As for what was said—that the sense organs and so forth produce cognition either from conjunction or from something other than the whole—and so on.
To this it is replied:
the nature of conjunction and the like is not perceived;
for it is only the colors and other qualities of the conjoined things themselves that are perceived, and there, no further entity called "conjunction" falls within the range of perception.
If it is argued that what is apprehended by the cognition "conjoined" cannot be otherwise [than the conjunction itself], we reply:

the cognition "conjoined" is simply the perception of the conjoined things themselves; there is no other objective basis for the word "conjoined" here than those conjoined things produced in close proximity. Conjunction is not the further object of the cognition "conjoined. (540)
Just as objects situated in front [are perceived], is conjunction likewise situated?
The notion that [perception arises] from conjunction is based on the method of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka).
Regarding the conceptualization of conjunction and so forth:
indeed, no conjunction appears as something distinct from the conjoined things; it is simply that the state of two things being unjoined is not perceived.
Since those two are perceived again, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that this is merely a mental construction (*kalpanā-mātra*);
however, by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is the cognition: "Such a being indeed exists; such a being has been born."
Therefore, that very non-existence is made known through its distinctness as "conjunction";
for this very reason—

Just as in the case of qualities and so forth, or in the case of things destroyed or not yet born, there is no difference in the object of the word and cognition when they follow a conceptual construction that pursues a distinction in the entity;
it is not merely from a difference in the word and cognition that there is a difference in the referent (padārtha), but rather from a difference in the cognition characterized as perception.
For conceptual cognition, arising through the power of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), fluctuates in various ways;
therefore, it does not find a firm footing in the reality of the object.

In that regard, based on a distinction that is merely imagined (*parikalpita*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there arise cognitions such as "conjunction" and so forth. Consequently, the distinction belongs only to the imagined, not to the reality of the object.
Furthermore, the differentiation of conceptualized objects arises even from the views of other schools; thus,
there would be an infinite regress in establishing the true nature of reality through such means, and by accepting that [regress], there would be mutual contradiction.
Therefore, distinct speech and cognition arise with respect to a conceptualized object through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Of what nature is this conceptualization? It follows the differentiation of the object; that is, it is the non-difference [of the object] as excluded from what is not so.
Nor is the cognition that has ceased [to exist] a beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Exclusion from others is precisely that; with respect to the continuum, it appears as an internal distinction through differentiation itself.
Do conceptual constructions proceed without a difference in the object? They indeed proceed as distinct; this has been observed.
Just as among qualities and so forth, there is one quality and one inherence, and twenty-four qualities;

yet number does not exist therein because number depends upon substance (*dravya*), nor is there a metaphorical attribution of the number of the substratum, since even when the substrata are distinct, the universal (*sāmānya*) and so on remain only one;
and how could there be oneness and so forth in things that have perished or not yet been born?

If it is held that there is a metaphorical designation (upacāra) here [regarding the past and future], then why is that very basis upon which it depends not accepted as the cause for all entities? (64) If, due to metaphorical designation, there is such a description and cognition of oneness and so forth regarding things destroyed or unborn, then why is that very metaphorical designation not accepted as the basis for both of these in all cases?
Let the superimposition resulting from beginningless conceptualization alone be the cause;
there is no occasion for the conceptualization of a real entity.
If figurative usage does not apply everywhere, it is because the qualifier is distinct [from the qualified].
If it is asked: "How can there be a difference in meaning when [the referent] is non-different, such that one is primary? [We reply:

Even if they do not have different objects as their cause, words such as "white" and so forth are not synonyms for those associated with number and the like; for even in that case, if there were a different object, [they would be distinct]. (65–66)
There would be no distinction between a quality and a substance [merely] because of a difference in their exclusion (vyāvṛtti);
even if they do not have different referents, [the distinction holds], just as in the case of the words "non-action" (akarma) and "non-substance" (adravya). [Objection:
But surely, what is called metaphorical usage (upacāra) is based upon a primary sense; how could it occur when that primary sense is absent?
Furthermore, that which possesses distinct qualifiers is primary, as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth;
whereas when the qualifiers are non-distinct, the status is secondary.

For you, however, because there is a connection with qualifiers produced by preceding successive conceptual constructions, there is a state of being primary due to the non-distinctness of the qualifiers in some instances; thus, the possibility of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) does not arise.
That is incorrect; for how can it be said that only that which has distinct qualifiers is primary?

Even that which has non-distinct qualifiers is indeed primary when, through extreme habituation, it has attained conventional usage despite its qualifiers being differentiated by conceptual construction.
For that which has as its object a causal condition for unimpeded movement is primary, while anything else is secondary; so why is this not sufficient?
Furthermore, if that which possesses distinct qualifiers is primary, then otherwise it would be merely metaphorical.
Let all such [words] be non-primary precisely because there is no distinct qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
However, in the case of "the destroyed" or "the unborn," even the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is used figuratively; this is the distinction.

If there is no other qualifier, then the qualificand alone must be expressed in every instance, and thus there would be identity of meaning in the form of synonymy, rather than grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), for that [coreferentiality] occurs only when there are different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
That too is not to be spoken of, because:
"If the cause for the occurrence of differentiation appears in that very form, how could the state of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) be produced by the meanings of words? (542)
This grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) must belong either to two words or to two meanings;
it cannot first belong to the two words, because each word denotes its own specific meaning.
If it is argued that coreferentiality occurs through secondary indication (lakṣita-lakṣaṇā), [we reply: no.

For when there is a connection with one [word] alone, all [the meanings] are already indicated; thus, there is no need for the employment of a second word, and so it does not exist. (543) By this very [argument], the co-location (*samānādhāratā*) of objects has been refuted. Even if a relation were present, how and by what means could it be cognized? (544) If an object is cognized as non-different from another due to the power of inherence (*samavāya*), then since that cognition arises from the single [word] itself, any other word would be redundant. (545)
If it is claimed that by another [word] that very same object is made known, then according to your view as well, would it not follow that they are synonyms? (546) Or,
if only that which is related to the object "blue" is conveyed by a single sound, then upon the cognition of the inherent [quality], there is no non-cognition of the other.
547 1 T. *nīlādi* (blue, etc.)
Just as when a blue object is perceived by the eye, it is understood to be a lotus, so too from a word there is the understanding of that very same thing; thus, any other sound is useless.
(548) 2 T. tathaivā°
The meaning of a word is indeed restricted; thus, it cannot be understood by another [means]. There is no object whatsoever devoid of its specific qualities; otherwise, speech would be in vain.
(549) The blueness of sapphire, lotus, and so forth is not [the same] in isolation. Since it is perceived as such through direct perception, why should the operation of a word be otherwise?
(550) If the quality of blueness resides in the lotus, then the word "lotus" is redundant. If the quality of blueness resides elsewhere, then likewise the word "lotus" is redundant. (551)

Therefore, it is the cognitions themselves, arising in accordance with their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), that construct the linguistic conventions of difference, non-difference, and grammatical coreferentiality;
thus, there is no consequence of synonymy.
For instance:

If it is argued that even though they are not distinct entities, non-synonymous terms are observed in the case of "white" and so forth, and therefore there must be a difference in entity (arthāntaratva) even there; [we reply: no.
This being the case, there would be no distinction between a quality (guṇa) and a substance (dravya);
for indeed,
a substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
If it possesses qualities, it would have the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*);
because of the presence of gravity, there would be downward motion, as in the case of syrups and the like; thus it would possess action.

Consequently, since conjunction is also a quality, and because it possesses the characteristics of a substance, it would be a substance—thereby resulting in no distinction between quality and substance.

Therefore, the word and the cognition are distinct because they are differentiated by the distinction of the objects of expression, which is itself imagined through the distinction of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).
For example, in the cases of "non-action substance" (*akarmadravya*) and "non-substance action" (*adravyaṃ karma*), there is no difference in the actual referent;
nevertheless, the words "non-action substance" and so forth are not synonyms.
In that case, the basis is indeed the difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and not any other difference in the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

How then is there the distinction between grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in "the cow is white" (*gauḥ śuklaḥ*) and "the cow-ness is white" (*goḥ śuklatvam*)?
1. Furthermore, even that which is indicated by words denoting existence in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* appears as if it were a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

By means of words such as "number" and so forth, which denote both the attribute and its possessor, the Veda distinguishes other properties of that [object]. For one who desires to know only that [specific property], the entire [other] class of properties is not excluded; nor is it implied by anything else.
In some cases, it is said that "yoga" (connection) expresses the property (*dharma*) alone by means of a finger;

[for example], "the joined finger" (*yuktāṅgulī*) denotes the substratum (*dharmin*) because it implies all [other fingers], even though it expresses a single well-known object, its conventional status being established in that manner. (vv. 96, 100)

Just as it has been established that synonymy does not arise from a difference in the imagined denotata, so too, even when there is no difference in the denotatum, the use of the ablative case (expressing distinction) occurs due to an imagined state of distinction, as in "the body of a stone-son" (*śilāputraka*), "the head of Rāhu," or "the whiteness of a cow. Thus,
the entire referent (*padārtha*) is expressed by the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), which is associated with a single uniform conceptual reflection (*ekākāraparāmarśa*).

The term "white" (*śukla*), however, is a part of that [cow]; and while it exists in connection with another referent, its distinction (*vyatireka*) is extracted through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, in the expression "the white quality of the cow," the case ending of distinction (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is employed.

And when there is no apprehension of the form of a cow, but only whiteness is perceived, devoid of any specific related entity, one then asks, "Whose is this whiteness? At that time, having ascertained the nature of the cow based on previous observation, one points out, "It is a cow"; thus, it is identity (*tādātmya*) alone that is intended as the relation here.
As for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it arises from the initial ascertainment of the thing in its isolation.

When, however, one considers that this [thing] cannot exist in isolation—even if there is a deficiency in the perception of its specific qualities due to the dullness of the eyes—one asks, "It must be either white or some other [color]; what is this? Is it a white cow or something else?
At that time, the reply is "A cow," expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Since the question arises precisely because [the object] is included therein, it is appropriate that the answer be consistent with it; and this is the true meaning [of the matter].

Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is a determination of exclusion (*vyatireka-viniścaya*). Even due to some cause, in the absence of a specific defining characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)... [552]
"This white quality of the horse" is the response for those who are wise; because the question is non-exclusive (*vyatirekin*), the determination is "it is just so.

(553) But when, through non-exclusion, there is an inclusion of a specific distinction, and the questioner’s inquiry arises after considering the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtta*), (554) then he, knowing that state, gives a reply of exactly that same kind. There is no possibility here for the occasion of any other procedure. (555)
Regarding the opportunity for another [type of] cognition:

"Having observed the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no ascertainment of difference; nor is there inference based upon it. Thus, the non-existence of difference is maintained. (556)

When positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) have been established from time immemorial, then, because difference exists [in that context], worldly transaction proceeds in exactly that manner.

(557) This worldly transaction pervading the universe has existed in this very way from beginningless time; since the world does not engage in an investigation into the nature of reality, difference is not sublated.
(558) Therefore, there are only parts; no whole (avayavin) exists.
If, then, there is no whole (avayavin) and only taste and so forth exist, it would follow that [taste and so forth] do not belong to the jar as its "color and so forth" (rūpādayaḥ);
for it does not occur that there is a "color" of colors, nor that there is a "jar" of a jar. Anticipating this objection from the opponent, he says:
The word "jar" functions by excluding non-causes that produce the same result, without implying the specific distinctions among the potencies for color and so forth.
Therefore, the expression "color is the jar" does not have a single substratum.
Therefore, this is the distinction between [the two types of words]: those that denote a genus and those that denote a collection. (102) This distinction is of such a kind.

"Color and so forth belong to the jar"—thus, with that commonality as a subordinate factor, its various specific powers are made manifest; other denotable objects should also be understood by this same method.
(103) Without implying the various specific powers of color and so forth, the word "jar" functions by implying in them a common power for holding water.
Therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) such as "the jar is color and so forth.
For this very reason, when the intention is to express the power of a collection, this is a collective term (*samudāyaśabda*);
however, when each [constituent] has a single result, it is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), as in "forest" or "tree."
How, then, is there the designation "the color and so forth of the jar"?
The meaning is that each [color and so forth] is individually capable of producing the cognition of color and so forth, and possesses the common function of fetching water.
Or, it is just as with "a forest of trees" or "trees are the forest."
Why is it that "the jar is color and so forth" or "the jar belongs to color and so forth" does not occur?
It certainly would occur if there were no linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) from other treatises; however, since people for the most part follow such refinement, it does not occur.

But for one who possesses correct understanding, there indeed arises the conviction that "certain things, such as form and so forth, are pots capable of performing specific functions," and that "the fetching of water and so on is the specific function," or that [the pot] is established by a particular configuration.
For, while there is a specific capacity for holding water due to a specific configuration,
the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "the form is the jar" does not occur, because there is no mutual pervasion between the parts and the whole due to their distinction.
When there is the intention to express a collection, [it is] the *vastu*.
[Objection: But surely, even between "tree" and "śiṃśapā-ness," there is no relationship of mutual pervader and pervaded; how then can there be co-referentiality? [Reply:

This is not so, because the cognition of "tree" occurs separately with respect to each individual object and also with respect to a single one, whereas the cognition of "jar" does not persist with respect to each individual property such as color and so forth. (559)
Indeed, the cognition of a jar does not apply to each individual [quality] such as color and so forth, as the cognition of a tree applies to each individual [part] such as a *śiṃśapā* tree;
nor is that diversity of capacities implied by the word "jar," because the specific determination of capacity is established through the conventional usage of elders.
However, the word "tree" (vṛkṣa) also implies a specific capacity; thus, there is no fault here either.

In this case as well, the basis is either the conventional usage established by linguistic practice (vyavahāra-nirūḍhi) or a distinction in capacity (śakti-bheda); therefore, everything is well-established.
[Objection: But is there not a difference here between "a cow of twenty" (*viṃśatigavī*) and "twenty cows" (*gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ*)? No, there is no such distinction here.
Regarding the expression "twenty cows," there is no difference in the capacity [of the word];

for by the word "twenty" no other capacity is expressed here. Only the capacity for carrying, milking, and so forth is understood in this context. Here, there is the manifestation of a collection, clearly evident through its plurality.
Therefore, it is said: by this same method, other designations must also be explained;
here, what is intended is a specific kind of collection in the form of a pair of ten, and by that, the capacity for carrying or milking is not implied.
Nor does it follow that there is a specific aggregate [of atoms] by means of that [cognition]; thus everything is well-established.

Alternatively, for those whose selves are conditioned by latent impressions through beginningless linguistic usage, this beginningless linguistic usage arises from conceptual construction and words: "Anādivyavahāreṇa vāsanāsaṃskṛtātmanām | Anādirayaṃ vyavahāraḥ kalpanāśabdasambhavī || 561"
1. Therefore, since [the word] is a mental construction, no objection whatsoever is made by anyone against anything.
Even if the meaning of the word were such as this, nothing at all would be lost.
What irrationality is seen here that it should be challenged? In the case of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words in the common language (*prākṛta*), no consistency is observed.
In this regard, it is as follows:
In that case, a clear distinction between the meaning of the gender and the number is observed; and there is no inconsistency therein, provided this occurs within the Sanskrit language.
syārtha°

For according to their view, a linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) is based on a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in both Prakrit and Saṃskṛta; yet, the state of being refined or unrefined is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

(565) This is merely a formal arrangement intended for the amusement of children. Just as this [distinction] has been made into a scientific treatise (*śāstra*) by foolish practitioners in some arbitrary way, so too has it been followed by others. Since it is thus maintained only by fools, we do not know what can be said of them in this matter. (566–567)

Furthermore, talk of an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is seen even in the treatises of jesters; yet there is no conviction in that [matter], and thus this is merely a tradition of the blind (*andhaparamparā*).

(568 gh) If consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the cause [of the body], then when it arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the totality of the constituent parts (*avayava*) must be the cause for the production of consciousness.

Just as in the case of a sprout, the earth and other factors act either individually—as in the case of flames and the like toward grass to be burned—or collectively; yet even when one factor is deficient, there is no capacity in each individual part, and thus no simultaneous production of many. || 104 ||
Because multiplicity is equal [in both cases], inhalation and exhalation are not the restrictive factors;
for indeed, in a case where many [factors] operate through mutual cooperation toward an effect, that effect is not possible even in the absence of one [of them].
If the effect were to occur even in the absence of that [factor], then that [factor] would not be a cause at all.

Now, if the parts produce [the mental consciousness] while being entirely independent of one another, then even when the ears, nose, and so forth are severed, mental consciousness would still arise from them.
In that case, it follows that each possesses its own capacity, and consequently, multiple consciousnesses would arise simultaneously.
For each individual [cause] is not capable [of producing the effect], since multiple sprouts do not arise from the state of being many seeds; furthermore,
if some single part were the generator of both inhalation and exhalation, that part would have a single auxiliary cause,
and the effect does not vary according to a difference in the auxiliary causes.
Even in the absence of various individual weavers, there would be no difference in the resulting cloth and so forth;
to this it is replied that since the prāṇa and apāna breaths are also multiple, that same logical consequence follows.
Even if there were a deficiency in just one part, the production of many [effects] would not occur;
for the oneness of the inhalation and exhalation is not established in the same way as that of the body.
Or, if their oneness is indeed accepted—

Nevertheless, we say: even if [the universal] is one, because its cause—the eternal presence of that [universal]—is manifold in individual instances, it cannot be the cause of [cognition] in multiple ways.
If you argue that this is not so because there is no distinction [between the instances], we reply: no, for [the cognition] would also occur sequentially. || 105 ||

Even if [the self] were one, since there are multiple manifestations of the vital breaths (prāṇa), the downward breath (apāna), and so forth, it would follow that there are multiple minds characterized by passion and other states;
for as long as their cause is eternally present,
it is illogical to claim that what has not arisen when its cause is present is caused by that very cause.
Now, [if it is argued that] a single thing cannot be the cause of many because the relationship between cause and effect is restricted, we reply:
indeed, the restriction of the causal relation is not subject to questioning.
For from fire, smoke arises as one and the same; it does not arise in various forms because there is no difference [in its cause].
For in the case of fire, the perception of various successive instances of smoke arises from that very same nature;

however, in this case, on the other hand, various states of mind such as passion arise from that very same essential nature of the vital breaths and so forth, through the association with various subsequent awakening conditions.
Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding the awakening condition itself, because its occurrence depends upon the strength or weakness of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, if that vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the cause of that consciousness, then because it is no different from anything else, it would not be a cause even for another [consciousness]; thus, there could be no succession of multiple causes either, as it would follow that only the prior mental impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) is the cause.
Furthermore, the unity of the vital breath and so forth was stated merely as a concession, but it is not logically tenable.
For thus,
since there is no restriction [on the number of objects] even when there is only one sense-faculty (*prāṇa*), because multiple objects are perceived,
let that [perception of many] occur all at once by means of a single cognition (*buddhi*). || 106 ||
Because there is no contradiction; let it not be [the case] even in succession, since there is no distinction [in that regard].
Even at the time of a single breath, because multiple cognitions exist during a long exhalation and so forth, there is no fixed rule regarding the breath and such.
Where, then, is the rule? Precisely from that [cognition], because of its apprehension.
Each preceding act of apprehension alone is the restrictive cause for each subsequent cognition;
thus, it is a single mental consciousness that takes on the form of apprehending multiple objects in succession,
and therefore it is not said that there are multiple cognitions.
That too does not exist;

there is no other mind apart from the forms of color and so forth. There is only one all-pervading mind, comparable to a clear mirror, and it is with this that there occurs the encounter with the reflections of objects.
To this it is replied:

if the arising of the reflection of an object occurs upon reaching a consciousness that is strictly indifferent [to its objects], then, due to the absence of any gradation in proximity, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous apprehension of all objects.

If, on the other hand, this is not so because of a gradation in the intensity of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then that cultivation alone is the cause of the object's form [in consciousness], and not the inhalations, exhalations, and so forth.
But for consciousness that remains stable like a mirror, what contradiction is there such that there would be no simultaneous apprehension of objects?
If, on the other hand, it lacks the capacity [at that time], then let there be no apprehension of those objects even successively, since there is no difference [in its lack of capacity].

Furthermore, even if it were the case that there is a difference in moments due to their arising, that difference in moments certainly exists there as well; therefore, the argument that the apprehension of multiple objects occurs sequentially because of this difference in moments is not a valid answer, because:
If many momentary vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of a dissimilar nature are indeed postulated as the cause for similar states of mind,
how could they be successive without a successive cause? (108)
If its own preceding [moment] were the cause of its own genus, the first [moment] could not possibly exist; for: (109)

There is no such cause for that [simultaneity], or if there were, it would necessarily follow that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are manifold because they occupy different locations; therefore, cognitions arise simultaneously. Thus, it is already established for us that the vital breaths are many and momentary.
But for you, this is not established;
yet, if it is established through the observation of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is indeed so:
for it is not logical that a single objective entity should exist sequentially; therefore, due to the sequence of causes, there is also a sequence in the effect, and thus consciousness is sequential.

If it is argued that those very vital breaths (*prāṇas*) must indeed be sequential because they lack sequential causes, [we reply: "No," because their sequence is due to the sequence of their respective preceding causes, such as the preceding vital breaths.
For if [the vital breath] were caused by something of its own preceding class, the first [instance] could not possibly exist, because such a [preceding] vital breath did not exist before.

If one accepts the existence of another world, then birth and so forth would be the cause of the vital breath; yet, if it is argued that the vital breath of the mother and father alone is the cause, [then...]
Otherwise, it would follow that such a being must exist at all times;
and this being the case, the previously mentioned consequence follows: that even the intellect (*buddhi*) would be produced solely from one's mother and father.
It is stated [by us] while granting [the opponent's premise]:
there is a plurality of vital breaths because of their association with different locations;
for indeed, association with multiple locations establishes plurality through the imposition of contradictory properties.
Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is manifold, it would follow that multiple mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) arise simultaneously;
furthermore, there is a sequential arising of minds belonging to the same class,
for the difference in effects does not arise solely from a difference in moments.

Just as there are multiple causes of the same kind, so too is the effect; for surely, a single thing arises from many, since it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces it. This is not a valid reply.
If multiple [causes] existing at one time were the cause of a single consciousness,

then even for a single [cause], it would not occur when there is a deficiency, as in the case of slow breathing and so forth. (111) Now, if the cause [of cognition] varies according to its state, then there would likewise be a distinction in the cognition.
For that which does not differ from another due to its difference [from it] cannot be the effect of that other.

When multiple things produce a single effect, there are two possibilities: either by way of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) or otherwise. If it were produced by way of a causal complex, then in the case of fainting and so forth, or in the case of a single breath, [the effect] would not occur because of the absence of a causal complex.
For this is the nature of an effect produced from a causal complex: that it does not arise when there is deficiency, whether the causes are complete or incomplete;
for if it were to arise even in their absence, it would not be their effect.
Furthermore, if duality were to exist such that only what is proximate is the cause and not necessarily the whole,
then it must be stated that only what is proximate is the cause, and even what is non-proximate is [also] a cause.

And it is not so, because the relationship of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance; therefore, from a complete [cause], only a complete effect arises, from an incomplete [cause], an incomplete one,
and from what is non-existent, what is non-existent.

There is a rule that from something that has become otherwise, only something else that has become otherwise arises; for it certainly does not have that as its effect if it lacks distinction from it despite its distinction.
If it is argued that the very fact of its arising when that exists is the basis [for the causal relationship], we reply: no.

If the state of being an effect arises from the mere fact of occurring when that [cause] exists, rather than being understood through the fact of changing in accordance with its changes, then a change would be without a cause; likewise, everything would be causeless. (569)

If it is maintained that the mere fact of [the effect] arising when that [cause] exists constitutes the causal relationship, then a modification based on cause and effect would necessarily follow as being entirely without a cause.
Furthermore, why would that very modification not have arisen from that alone at the very first moment?
For if it were arising while that [cause] remained unmodified, it would have occurred right from the beginning.
For it has been stated that its effect cannot be something that becomes differentiated despite [the cause] being undifferentiated;
therefore, just as the differentiation would be causeless, so too would that entity be. Consequently, how can the fact that [the effect] arises from the existence of that [cause] be understood?
By this, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is refuted.
As for the claim that sequential consciousness arises from the body alone, depending upon specific successive transformations,
that is incorrect.
This sequence of transformation also cannot arise from the body alone. Since the body lacks distinction [in that regard], from where does its own distinction come?
(570) Just as there is no distinction in consciousness due to the absence of a specific transformation, so too there should be no distinction in transformation due to the absence of a specific body.
[Objection: But surely, even when that [body] lacks distinction, a specific transformation of milk and so forth is observed.
Just as [the color of cloth] changes merely through the passage of time,
so too this is not the essence of the body.

For the transformation of milk and so forth arises from milk that is identical [in nature]; likewise, the bodily transformation is distinguished as being exactly the same. When there is the presence of identical milk and so forth, and when there is the occurrence of identical heat and so forth, the resulting transformation into curd and so forth is indeed identical.

However, the similarity or dissimilarity of the body is the basis for the distinction or non-distinction between cognitions— such as those arising from corresponding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*),
and so forth; therefore, it is understood that the sequence of cognitions does not arise from a sequence in the transformation [of the body].
Therefore, it is established that a distinction is possible when there is a collective effect; otherwise, multiplicity would not exist. Yet, this is not observed.
Now, for one who holds that cognition arises from cognition alone, why does not multiple cognition arise?
To this, the reply is:

consciousness is the cause of each [subsequent cognition] one by one due to the restriction of its capacity; for when a cognition is deficient in its engagement with another object, there is no apprehension of a different object. (113)

Consciousness, in the form of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), is the cause of each [subsequent] one. This is a restriction of capacity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) conforming to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), or a specific attachment;

for a consciousness that possesses firm habitual tendencies produces only a certain [specific] consciousness—even if it is separated by an interval—by imparting a particular efficacy to the immediately preceding condition, or simply through awakening in accordance with that immediately preceding condition.
For it is thus:
[the subject] of the object.

Having attained the strengthening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs even without an immediately preceding [moment of consciousness], from a prior consciousness alone.
(572) However, for some, the emergence of a conceptual construction is observed through proximity to an immediately preceding consciousness, but not for another when there is an intervention. (573)

Indeed, it is not observed that the arising of conceptualizations— whether they consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from a preceding consciousness or of intervening occurrences— occurs through any other [cause] distinct from the object-field of their own capacity;
therefore, it is logical to establish the determination that [each] cognition arises from a single [preceding] cognition.
Or rather, the accomplishment of action arises from a single consciousness—
surely, even when multiple consciousnesses arise from the body, the restriction [of action] follows from that very same consciousness.
Just as even when multiple sensory cognitions are possible, at times only a single cognition arises with respect to a particular object due to that very specific attachment,
it is said in this regard:
"The cognition produced from the body simultaneously is restricted by its own kind."
If [consciousness] arises from another, how could there be a cessation of a capable body?
(114) If consciousness were to emerge from the body, then it would arise again and again, exactly as before, because the capacity of the body remains intact.
If indeed consciousness, by the restriction of its own power, produces only a single consciousness while the body remains exactly as it was to produce subsequent and further consciousnesses, then—
because that [first] consciousness creates an obstruction to the body’s production of further consciousnesses— no further consciousness arises from the body.

That too is incorrect, for this matter has not been made an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consciousness arises from consciousness alone, based on the certainty of the means of knowledge;
