for it is not the case that multiple consciousnesses arise from the body alone, devoid of consciousness.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction of the capacity to produce multiple cognitions arising from cognition itself;
for smoke does not obstruct the fire’s capacity to produce smoke.

Therefore, if the body produces [cognition], then even when each individual cognition arises from cognition, there is no obstruction of the body's efficacy, and thus there is the production of successive and manifold cognitions.

For causes possess no capacity for deliberation such that they would now think, "Since consciousness arises from consciousness alone, why should it produce another consciousness distinct from us? and thus fail to produce a body;
or else, even so, it might happen that the cause's power to generate its own effect is somehow obstructed by the effect itself.

If multiple cognitions were to arise from the body, then subsequently, when their obstruction is observed through cognition, a doubt might again arise in some cases [as to whether they arose from the body].

However, the occurrence of this [cognition] arises from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), which produces a partiality and attachment; thus, it acquires the status of a regulator for this incorrect cognition.

Consequently, since a cognition of that same kind arises only from a cause of that same kind—once the relationship of cause and effect is established—it follows that cognition arises from cognition alone, and not from the body.

Now, it was indeed stated that there is the possibility of cognitions arising from multiple sense-faculties, and therefore that [the object] is known by a single cognition as a single cognition; this is true as it was stated.
However, a refutation does not follow merely from what was stated, but rather from a reasoned argument.
And that is not logical,
for consciousness, being by nature unattached, does not exert itself toward the non-arising of another consciousness.
And there is no attachment without prior practice;
therefore, whatever kind of cognition one has previously practiced, attachment arises again toward that very same kind. Thus, it is solely due to prior practice that other cognitions do not arise.
But for one who...
For such a person, there is no future world, nor is there the possibility of past habituation;

and without past habituation, there can be no prevention of subsequent cognitions. (577) Therefore, since cognitions arise again and again from the body, it would follow that a multitude [of bodies] must exist whenever that body exists, yet such a multitude is not observed. (578)

Now, the very first moment of this body is the producer of consciousness; because it is of a different nature [from subsequent moments], it lacks causality [for them]. For that which is distinct from the jar—being of a different character—is not a producer of cognitions; indeed, even if something is distinct from the producer, it is not a producer.
That too is incorrect;
[it is] merely a repetition.

If the arising of cognitions occurred from the very first moment of the body, then the body would be without a support; there would be only pure consciousness alone. For the relationship of support and supported does not exist in the absence of a relationship between that which is assisted and that which assists. Such being the case, there would be the possibility of consciousness existing in isolation.
Now, [it might be argued that] consciousness, with the body as its auxiliary, produces consciousness.

In that case, there would be no mere persistence [of consciousness]; rather, since consciousness arises from consciousness alone while the body acts as a cooperative cause, our own position would be established.
Now, suppose the body were the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) at the outset.
Just as in the case of the lotus root (*śālūka*), where the substance of cow dung is followed by the arising of a lotus root from that very lotus root itself,

so too, if it were the case that even without cow dung the subsequent lotus root arises from the lotus root alone, and likewise consciousness arises from consciousness alone, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its remaining in isolation.
2. Furthermore, it is observed that even the body is a cause of the utpala.
It has been stated that [the self] is not a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) but rather a cooperative cause (*sahakāri*).
Now, if it were first a material cause and subsequently a cooperative cause, [then...]

If the body were the material cause (*upādāna*), how could it subsequently become a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*)? If you argue that this is so simply because it is observed, we do not accept such observation here.
Furthermore, it has been established that a lotus (*śālūka*) of such a nature does not arise from cow dung or from a [different] lotus, because there exists a great difference between those two.
In some cases, that very first cognition which is perceived as having arisen from the clarity of sensory perception is seen to be the means for establishing another cognition.
Therefore, cognition does not arise from the body;
yet, it might be argued: [582]
If, for you as well, the body were not the support of consciousness, then it would follow that consciousness could persist even when the body has ceased to exist;
for there can be no rule regarding their coexistence without a causal basis.
Having raised this supreme objection, the following refutation is offered:
If it is argued that when the body has ceased due to the absence of its support,

the mind might persist in isolation— provided that the cause for the persistence of the mental continuum does not fail to serve as a contributing factor (*aṅga*) toward the attainment of the functioning of its own causes. (115)
Then there will surely be the abiding of the solitary [Self]; this is the completion of the sentence.
But when the cause for the arising of another body is the fivefold basis pertaining to this world... || 116 ||
In that case, how could there be the existence of the solitary [mind]?

For the cause of the persistence of the mental continuum is the functioning of its own cause—the functioning of the body known as the *kalala* and so forth—which is the orientation toward and the acquisition of the production of a body. There is no such acquisition for the solitary cause of the body;
rather, it is the cause of the persistence of the mental continuum.
The preceding mind is designated as "karma"; when it serves as an auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), that is its state of being an auxiliary.

And its state of being an auxiliary occurs in relation to the body accompanied by craving; if it does not enter into that state of being an auxiliary, then its remaining in isolation is indeed desired.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of another body, that very same fivefold sense-base of this world serves as the cause for the production of a body for those passing away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), by way of being a formative influence (*saṃskāraka*);
thus its status as a constituent factor is observed, since no production of a body is seen after death [in the case of those remaining in the formless realm].
But because the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is absolutely invisible, [the opponent] here objects:

Non-perception, which consists in the denial of the body's being a constituent part [of the soul], is said to be non-conclusive; the same applies to the sense organs and so forth, as they are also "possessing a remainder" (śeṣavat).

Although the five sense-bases of this life are not perceived to function as auxiliary causes for the production of a body in another birth, nevertheless, this is not the case for that which is designated as "karma," because it is the cause of the mental continuum. Thus, since the non-existence of something cannot be determined by mere non-perception alone—as has already been established previously that non-perception does not constitute certainty—what room is there for doubt here?
Furthermore, it may be argued that what is stated here is not mere non-perception, but rather an inference preceded by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For example,
one faculty does not reconnect with another faculty;
for instance, Devadatta’s eye and so forth do not reconnect with Yajñadatta’s eye and so forth.
And since the sense-faculty here is connected to the body of birth, this is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
This is not so, because this [inference] is of the *śeṣavat* type; it is said that such a thing exists as it truly is, for there is no comprehension through the *śeṣavat* [method].

For the non-reconnection of the sense faculties in another birth is cognizable solely through non-perception, and from mere non-perception there is no certainty regarding exclusion from the contrary (vipakṣa).
If it is argued that because the reconnection of the sense faculties occurring in this life’s body is observed, the same reconnection is inferred for another [life] as well,
then even in that case there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), since that too belongs to this very life.
Furthermore, the claim that the sense-faculty arises between the semen and the blood— like [the distinction between] this shore and the far shore—
is also incorrect.
In this case as well, the absence of the contrary is not understood merely through non-perception;
nor does the qualification "being within the semen and blood" provide protection, whether like a qualification of place or like a qualification of the word "jar."
For thus, the capacity of the preceding sense organs is observed in their respective species, since modifications are seen; and the birth of successive [beings] is established. (118)

For it is not from the qualification of a particular individual that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is understood as residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) alone; otherwise, no one could engage in any practical activity (*vyavahāra*) anywhere, since all activity is preceded by a certainty regarding capacity. Furthermore, because practical activity concerns the universal (*sāmānya*), the relationship does not have a particular individual as its ultimate object.

And likewise, when the eyes and other faculties, which are endowed with fickleness and so forth, arise in such a state due to the cultivation of habituation, one infers that they are of that same nature elsewhere because they are seen to be of that nature;
yet, at birth and the like, no sense faculty of such a nature is observed to be the cause.
Therefore, the qualification "arising from a different birth" or "produced by the senses," or some other such qualification, would be appropriate [to exclude the self];
however, if that sense-organ were indeed one and the same, then it would not be established that a subsequent sense-organ is produced by a preceding one.
Even if this were so, nevertheless—

Since [qualities] such as fickleness are seen to be preceded by practice, and since inference of that kind is thus established, any other [inference] is useless. [The opponent claims: "It is not necessarily so;
this [inference] is not useful in every respect. [We reply: From the observation of effects of that same class, one infers that the cause is of that same nature;
and it has already been demonstrated that qualities resulting from practice exist in another body during dreams.

Furthermore, because one observes successive modifications, it is established that there is indeed a succession of births; thus, in the intermediate state, one sense organ produces another sense organ. How then could there not be the production of the sense organs of another birth? For when modification constitutes the very nature [of a thing], there is only difference and no identity, just as in the case of earth and other elements.
Furthermore, it might be argued that here there is only the designation of a single continuum (*ekasantāna-prajñapti*), and thus no absolute difference;
this is the same even regarding another birth.
Another birth, too, is included within the very same single continuum—just like one who has awakened from sleep—but due to the intervention of memory, it is perceived as if it were distant.

Now, it might be argued that the production [of cognition] does not arise from the sense-faculties alone, but rather that first there is production from the body, and subsequently from the sense-faculties due to the restriction of their capacity; to this it is replied:
if its birth were from the body, the same undesirable consequence as before would follow.
If [you argue] that the birth of another body must proceed from the mind alone, then consider this:

if the first production were from the body, would it be from a body with sense-faculties or one without? If it were produced from a body with sense-faculties, then it must be produced from the sense-faculties themselves; and if the very first [body] is produced from sense-faculties, the existence of the other world is established.
If [the sense organs] were produced from what is not a sense organ, then hair, the tips of the nails, and so forth would be produced from a dead body;
furthermore, if there were multiplicity [of organs], it would follow that multiple sense organs are produced,
and thus it would follow that they are not limited in number.
Likewise, how could there be the cessation of a body that is still capable?

Furthermore, if the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are merely specific transformations of the body, then the same consequence of their indestructibility would follow, as well as the consequence that the sense-faculties arise from the body, and so forth. If it is argued that because of the absence of consciousness (*citta*), the sense-faculties do not arise in a dead body—
If, then, there is arising from the mind,

and the birth of another body and of the mind belonging to that other life proceeds from that very same mind, what is the point of this insistence on postulating the prior sense-faculties as the cause?
Therefore, the body is not the cause of consciousness; thus, because the body—the cause—is incomplete, rebirth in another life is impossible, and there is no reconnection [of the continuum]. He says:
"Therefore, due to the incompleteness of the cause, there is no reconnection for all final moments of consciousness.
By this, he considers such a proof to be *śeṣavat* (inference from the remainder).
This is the conclusion:
for the cause is the mind, conditioned by karma accompanied by craving, which is not disconnected from other births;
and there is no deficiency in that [cause].

If, however, the body were the cause, then due to its deficiency— the deficiency of the cause— there would be no reconnection; but since this is not the case, there is no deficiency of the cause, and thus the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Only this remains: "because it is the mind at the moment of death.
And that [reason] is *śeṣavat* (inference by elimination), because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is demonstrated merely through non-perception.
As for what was also said:
"The mind of this life does not link up with another mind,
because it functions within a different body, like the mind of Devadatta."

That too is incorrect, because the existence [of the object] prior to the activity [of cognition] has already been refuted, and because the substratum [of that activity] has been negated. If the meaning of the proof is that consciousness, in a single moment, takes as its objective support (ālambana) another [moment] which is present therein and is not the producer of a cognition belonging to a different activity, then the relationship of locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is negated, and consciousness would be situated in no place.

Furthermore, the body being taken as an object is not the support (*āśraya*) of consciousness, because it is the object of cognitions such as pleasure by virtue of being a specific internal tactile sensation;
and since one's own body, as an object,
generates a consciousness that takes another's body as its object, this constitutes an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.
Nor is there a difference in being another body, because [the series] is designated as a single continuum;
yet, in the ultimate sense, there is indeed a distinction even within the body of a single lifetime due to the specific differences of stages such as childhood and so forth.
Therefore, the benefit to the continuum comes from the body, but the arising of the mind is from the mind alone, just like the continuum of a rice plant.

Therefore, since the continuity of consciousness persists without beginning or end, and because the establishment of the stream of birth and death is possible through the perfection of practice, all qualities resulting from practice find their scope; thus, whether it be omniscience or any other quality, it is possible.
[Note: This concludes the *Paralokasiddhivārttika* (Treatise on the Proof of the Other World) in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*.]
(c) The cultivation of compassion:
But surely, let there be cultivation; how, however, does it reach the ultimate limit of excellence?
[Because] one observes only a slight degree of distinction.
In this regard,
the answer is:
even though there is excellence through practice, it is like jumping or the heating of water.
If it is argued that there must be no transgression of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [we reply: if that [nature] has been produced, it would require further effort;
moreover, if it were to have an unstable basis, the excellence (*viśeṣa*) would never increase, and its intrinsic nature would not be of such a kind. (121–122)

If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says: "Because the means of proof lack the capacity to bring about further distinctions in those whose powers have already been exhausted, and because that which is eternal cannot abide without a substratum. (123)

Indeed, a particular excellence (*viśeṣa*) does not necessarily partake in a fixed increase; for instance, the particularity of jumping or the heating of water does not [increase] merely by its own existence. Nevertheless, because it requires further effort, even a jump that has been performed does not—though obtained through prior effort—become independent of subsequent effort; rather, it generally requires further effort. On the other hand, the heating of water has a stable substratum.
Furthermore, it would require further effort,
for even when in contact with fire, it does not remain so,
since its excellence is unstable.

Furthermore, established excellence is pervaded by dependence on further effort and by having an unstable basis; since these two are absent and their opposites are present in the mental qualities such as compassion (*kṛpā*), they do not possess established excellence. Moreover, that which depends on further effort is not an inherent nature (*svabhāva*);
however, this reason—characterized by the qualification—is one that possesses a stable basis and is an inherent nature.
That excellence is not fixed, as in the case of a Vedic scholar or a Kāpālika ascetic;
however, for one who depends upon effort,
since that distinction is not inherent in its nature, it is produced even when [the cause] has increased.
One would not need to exert further effort, for any other effort would merely produce a specific difference (viśeṣa).
Indeed, that which depends upon further effort, even if it attains great increase,
still does not possess the nature of being inherent (svabhāva).

Indeed, it is not logical for an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to depend on the proximity of causes, because such a thing is described as flowing by its own inherent force; therefore, even when there is growth, there is no ultimate increase in it,
just like jumping or the heating of water.
But mental qualities such as compassion and others are not like external qualities; thus he says:
"In the mind, qualities such as compassion, born of repeated practice, proceed spontaneously, just as [heat] proceeds in wood, mercury, gold, and so forth, from fire and the like. (125)

For just as a specific quality produced in wood by fire—characterized by internal burning and so forth—is self-sustaining once it no longer requires effort, and likewise a quality produced in mercury characterized by flowing and digesting, or in gold produced by smelting and heating;

in the same way, when compassion and other qualities are repeatedly cultivated in the mind, they become non-receding due to the specific excellence induced by that repeated practice. At that time, once a specific excellence of compassion has been established such that one no longer requires effort, another [quality] follows from that, possessing a power not previously employed, which produces ever-increasing excellence until it reaches the ultimate limit.
1) T. dahanāhito
[Objection: But surely jumping also depends upon effort, and compassion and the like depend on that [effort] as well; so why is one [the latter] spontaneous while the other is not? [Reply:

It has been stated here that what is not spontaneous is not independent of effort, such as the heating of water and the like; however, compassion and the like, like the specific qualities produced by fire in wood, are spontaneous.
Therefore, from those [causes], the nature that has arisen produces a quality;
each subsequent effort brings about a further distinction.
And because they proceed from the growth of preceding seeds of a similar kind, [the result is superior].
Regarding those cognitions such as compassion and the like, how could their stability arise from the practice of [mere] truths?
Compassion and the rest possess a fixed excellence that arises solely from preceding cognitions of the same genus; they do not depend on the proximity of objects or other such conditions.
For instance:
1. T. *vyava॰rṣitā*—This reading [is incorrect]:
the arousal of compassion and the other [virtues] does not occur even through recollection or hearing; nor are compassion and the others dependent upon a return favor or the like. (585)

For those whose mental continuums have been cultivated by that [compassion], even when fresh and constant harms are occurring, their compassion and other virtues do not undergo slackening; therefore, at the time of the great festival of the meeting with practice, how could there be any contraction or dullness? Furthermore, this very practice of leaping is indeed present as the cause for limitless increase.
Therefore, that [leaping] is also obtained as a natural property for him, and there is no such reversal; thus he says:
"And leaping does not result from leaping alone, because its causes—strength and effort—possess established capacities; therefore, leaping has a fixed nature. (128)

For it is not the case that from compassion and so forth alone—just as compassion and so forth arise from their own similar antecedents—leaping arises solely from leaping; rather, even one who has practiced leaping is unable to leap when strength and effort have vanished.
Since strength possesses a fixed nature due to the capacity of its own causes, and effort likewise, leaping resulting from them is also of a fixed nature and not otherwise.
Furthermore, it might be argued that jumping occurs only through practice regarding the object of jumping;
otherwise, since strength exists even prior [to practice], there would be the undesirable consequence of jumping at all times.

Now, if it is argued that strength did not exist previously because it is produced only through practice, then even though jumping is of the same genus [as repeated jumping], jumping would not be unlimited; the same consequence would apply to compassion and the like as well. To this, it is replied:

At first, due to the body's impaired state, one should gradually overcome the [need for] jumping by means of effort; once the impairment has been removed, one remains established in one's own strength. (129) It is not through practice that strength is gained, but rather, strength is always present; it is merely rendered incapable of jumping when it is obstructed by phlegm and other humors.
Therefore, due to the practice of fasting (laṅghana), once the deficiency of these two [the digestive fire and the body] has been removed,
that very same prior strength returns to him spontaneously through diet and other factors; for this reason, fasting should be administered later, not earlier.
Furthermore, even though strength results from the use of rejuvenative elixirs (*rasāyana*), it is determined by the specific power of those elixirs; thus,
even when the practice of fasting (*laṅghana*) is equal, there is no equality in the fasting between a human and a young *garuḍa*.
For instance,

in the case of the encounter between the practice of leaping of Garuḍa and that of a deer, even though their leaping is equal in terms of practice, there is no equality in the actual extent of the leap. Therefore, even in the case of practice, leaping depends solely upon the strength born of one's [maternal] origin, and not merely upon the practice itself.

But as for compassion and the other [virtues], they indeed do not depend on anything else; for is it not said that "from practice comes strength, and from strength comes leaping"? Thus, that very state of being preceded by practice is not [exclusive] to compassion and the rest alone.
There is no fault in this, for even the loss of strength occurs through excessive practice.
If, then, compassion and the like depend solely upon their own homogeneous seeds, then, due to beginninglessness, they would possess that very nature eternally;
yet it is understood that they do not arise from their own seeds alone.
To this it is replied:
Compassion arises from its own seed; provided it is not obstructed by opposing factors arising from their own seeds, it reaches the state of being the very nature of the mind. (130)

Although compassion arises from its own seed and time is beginningless, it does not yet constitute a state of naturalization (*sātmībhāva*) because it is obstructed by hatred and other afflictions that likewise arise from their own seeds.

If, however, continuity is attained, then it becomes a state of naturalization; even though there is a stable basis, the nature of compassion is established only through great effort in warding off opposing factors such as hatred.
This must necessarily be accepted:
for indeed, each preceding instance of practice is the root of the subsequent refinement of mental qualities such as compassion, dispassion, and awakening. (131)
For the prior practice of compassion and the other [virtues] serves as the cause for the subsequent mental quality to arise with greater proficiency;
for once a quality has arisen, its proficiency must be produced solely through practice from its own seed, since its arising is already present. Therefore...
Because of a lack of enthusiasm for one's own welfare, while being full of longing for the welfare of others.
The nature of compassion arises from practice, just as loathing, dispassion, and passion do;
for practice performed with no other activity indeed produces the nature of compassion,
just as it produces loathing, dispassion, and passion.
For just as compassion becomes internalized when it is not obstructed by its opposites,
such that nothing at all appears as something to be grasped because of its presence,
so too should dispassion be viewed in relation to passion.
4. The Blessed One is an authority because he is the Teacher.

(1) Regarding the explanation of his being the Teacher: one who is compassionate, desiring to dispel the suffering of others, applies himself to the means for the sake of eliminating that suffering; thus he says:
2. One whose excellence of compassion for oneself and others has been perfected, being impelled by an inability to endure the suffering of others... || 132
The compassionate person applies themselves to the means for the sake of eliminating suffering; for in one who possesses compassion, effort toward the elimination of their own suffering is possible,
since without the destruction of one's own suffering, there is an incapacity to dispel the suffering of others.
Thereafter, one applies oneself to the direct realization of the cessation of one's own suffering and to the direct realization of all phenomena;
for it is indeed difficult to explain that which is to be attained and its cause when they are beyond one's perception. (133)
Indeed, for one who lacks the direct realization of the causes and fruits of heaven and liberation, it is difficult to explain them to others,
for such a person lacks the capacity therein;
even though the teaching of the Four Noble Truths is possible for one who has ascertained those truths through inference.

Nevertheless, it is not possible at all to describe the occurrences in world-systems such as the Avīci hell, because [such descriptions] cannot occur at all times— specifically during moments when one is striving for one's own self-interest— and because they would only occur when there is the possibility of rebirth in hells and the like, which is restricted to the ripening of specific karma.
Therefore, everything must indeed be directly realized;
and the means for that direct realization is investigation,
which he [the author] states as follows:
Reflecting through both reasoning and scripture, one examines the cause of suffering and its impermanent nature and so forth by means of the specific characteristics of suffering itself.
(134) Reasoning (*yukti*) is inference (*anumāna*).
And where inference has no scope, there is scripture (*āgama*), which is the cause for the cognition of objects beyond the senses;
or rather,
scripture is that which first brings about awakening.
Therefore, reasoning proceeds as that which has the result of communicating the meaning; for the determination of the meaning does not arise from scripture alone,
since [scripture] functions merely from the speaker's intention.
Because there is no obstruction to the object,
all of this occurs for one who is oriented toward investigation, and not otherwise; therefore, first comes the investigation, and then, upon subsequent encounter, the perception of that object.
In the form of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), it is not merely a matter of issuing a command;
for regarding an object that is authoritative, a discerning speaker is neither one who merely issues a command nor one who is deluded.
Therefore, the sequence is as follows: having stabilized that object through reasoning, for one who meditates upon it, there occurs direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).

In this regard, first of all, one examines the cause of suffering itself; for the purpose of removing suffering by means of removing its cause, and once the cause of suffering has been identified, one must further examine its nature—such as its impermanence—in order to determine its suitability for removal. For if its suitability for removal were not established, there would be no enthusiasm whatsoever for its removal.
For indeed, if things were either causeless or caused by an eternal [cause], no effort would be fruitful for their cessation;
because of this...

Now, if that which is causeless possesses permanence, how could there be the destruction of that which has a permanent cause? Without encountering a deficiency of causes, how could an entity cease to exist?

(587) For one whose existence is produced by a cause, that [existence] would not occur in the absence of that cause. If it were an entity even in the absence of that [cause], from what would its non-existence arise? (588)

An entity that has an impermanent cause ceases when its cause is absent; for that which has a permanent cause, non-existence does not occur, and thus it does not cease due to a lack of cause. Therefore, by means of qualifiers such as impermanence and so forth, one examines the impermanence of that cause of suffering.
Since one perceives that there is no cessation as long as the cause remains in that state, one examines its opposite for the sake of abandoning that cause.
That opposite is also established through the understanding of the nature of the cause. (135)

If some eternal cause of suffering, such as Īśvara and so forth, were to exist, then because that cause would never be deficient, one might conclude that the cessation of suffering is impossible; consequently,
no wise person would exert themselves toward its removal.
For no one engages in what is impossible,
nor does one who engages in it suffer frustration;
rather, one examines the opposite of that which is the cause of the desired result.
For the purpose of abandoning the reason,
even for you there is no cessation without contact with the counter-position (vipakṣa),
nor is there an absence of the reason in the absence of the counter-position.
If it is argued that cessation occurs precisely because of the absence of causes, [we reply] that the view of others— that cessation occurs solely through the exhaustion of karma—
is not [correct].

Since it will be demonstrated that action—both prior and subsequent—arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no fault in [the claim] that there is no exhaustion of action, and that ignorance is the cause of action as well as of suffering.
[Objection: But surely the cause of suffering is not of a fixed nature, since it takes many forms such as separation from the beloved and so forth?
Therefore, it is impossible to turn back from this;
regarding this, it is said:
"Affection directed toward the conditioned (*saṃskāra*) is produced by the grasping of 'self' and 'what belongs to self'. (136)
The vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-darśana*) is the cause that opposes it and its sublater.

Attachment (*sneha*), produced by the clinging to "self" and "mine," is the cause of suffering; and when attachment ceases, there is no suffering even when that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is being destroyed.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is no mental suffering when what belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*) is being destroyed due to the cessation of affection, how can there be no physical suffering in the case of the self (*ātman*)? To this it is replied:

For one who suffers through the suffering of others, there is no arising of happiness for their own self. Indeed, it is through the cessation of attachment to one's own [self] that the clinging to "what belongs to oneself" is removed. (590)
Indeed, those whose self-love is set aside by love for their children do not experience even physical pain arising from contact with weapons and the like; furthermore,
affection for one's own [body] is the cause of the suffering of the view of a real self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and therefore [the realization of] selflessness—
The view of a self and what belongs to a self is sublated because it is contradictory;
for a dharma that contradicts its form is indeed its sublater.

Just as moisture, heat, and so forth belong to the wind, so too, when selflessness has become one's own nature, there is the cessation of the impermanent view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the opposite of that [selflessness]. From that, upon the cessation of the grasping for "I" and "mine," there is the cessation of all physical and mental suffering.
1. [Objection: Since there is heat in the wind and oiliness and so forth in the body, how could there be an absence of the suffering of death and so on during the cutting and burning of the body?
This is not so;
for there is nothing other than the separation from the body at the time of death. And the arising of another body is "birth"—what suffering is there in this?

When one is separated from one body and joined with another, and when there is recollection of the former and latter states due to the sharpness of memory produced by habituation, then—just as in the case of abandoning and taking up the states of childhood and old age, or like the taking up and discarding of clothing—what pain can there be for that [person]?
And there can be no cause for delight in whatever one practices without an attachment that pursues pleasure;

furthermore, in the practice of equanimity, neither pleasure nor pain exists when absolute indifference toward the body and its objects of enjoyment is possible. Even when harm is done, there is no suffering for one who has turned away from the view of a self. (592)
Regarding this, he said:
"By practicing it many times, in many ways, and over a long period of time, its virtues and faults become manifest. (137)

When all causes of agitation, such as passion and the like, have been removed through the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), and the expansion of awakening has occurred, there is the illumination of the various merits and defects of practicing diverse and successive means;
this is just as the merits and defects of many kinds of treatises are illuminated when one is engaged in the study of those treatises.
Indeed, the illumination of merits and defects is the very acuity of the intellect.
Due to the clarity of his intellect and because of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he abandons [defects].
This is the distinction of the Great Sage from those such as the Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍga), who act for the sake of others:

that when there is a discernment of virtues and defects brought about by a sharp awakening, he then perceives the entire collection of defects—even though they are momentary—as residing within the midst of the qualities he has experienced.
Therefore, he exerts himself to eliminate even defects of speech and the like; thus, his latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are abandoned.
This alone is the distinction of the Blessed Sugata from the Pratyekabuddhas, Noble Śrāvakas, and other teachers.
Alternatively, even if there were the abandonment of suffering, it would not entail omniscience; otherwise, every person free from passion (*vītarāga*) would be an all-knowing one.
To this it is replied:
"In many ways, by many means," and so forth;
for indeed, the elaboration of means is manifold.
And through the practice of that, after a long time, there is the illumination of all the virtues and defects pertaining to saṃsāra,
existing as subtle, gross, and intermediate.

When there is the presence of proficiency in mindfulness, just as there is recollection of previous births, so too, by following that [mindfulness], there is again the full realization of all that [was previously experienced]. (593) 3 T.
yadā

Just as one who has come from another village is recognized by those knowledgeable of it as such because he exhibits the persistence of its impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too is one who has come from another birth [recognized]. Indeed,

just as a person coming from another village is known by those who perceive specific traits produced by contact with that place to have come from there— and thus the other village is understood through its role as a qualifying attribute— exactly in the same way, there is an inference of another birth by virtue of its being the cause of the impressions produced therein.

Even though an object is imperceptible because it occurs in another birth, why should giving and other such acts not be inferred by this means? And from that follows the cognition of the necessity between action and its fruit:
"By this action, there was a meeting of this person with this place in the past, due to the meeting with one whose nature was of such a form. (595–596)

When there is a thorough knowledge of the relationship between all actions and their fruits, and when the path to heaven and liberation is known as it truly is— consisting in the complete knowledge of specific natures (which involves the perception of the connection between the distinct natures of all causes and their effects, and the determination of the intermediate natures within the conjunction of place and so forth with their respective effects)— the teaching is considered complete merely through such knowledge of the human goal.
Furthermore, the entire world does not arise from one another except by way of cause and effect.

Therefore, through the continuous cultivation of the relationship between cause and effect in its many forms, the knowledge of the entire world becomes faultless; from that, omniscience [is attained].
Now, if this knowledge is through inference, how can he be one who sees directly? And yet, the Blessed One is held to be a direct perceiver—that too is quite insignificant.

Inference regarding all aspects does not differ from perception; even the conjunction with a sense organ does not produce any further distinction [in that regard]. Indeed, that which is the cognition of the intrinsic nature of an object in all its aspects is itself perception, for the meaning of "pratyakṣa" (perception) is direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Is it not the case that "pratyakṣa" means that which occurs in relation to a sense organ (*akṣa*)?
This is not the definition of direct perception; rather, it is the immediate cognition of an existing object.
Furthermore, non-perception is merely an indicator;
moreover,
if there is no direct perception even when there is contact with the sense organ, how can that be considered perception?
If it is argued that "it is not truly a sense-faculty (*akṣa*) because it is impaired," it is replied:
If it is considered a non-faculty (*anakṣa*) because it is not a cause for direct perception, then let it be determined to be a faculty (*akṣa*) because it is a cause for direct perception. (599)
For it is not logical that the status of being an *akṣa* (sense organ) follows merely from having a specific configuration and so forth,
because that would entail the status of being an *akṣa* even for something impaired;
however, if the status of being an *akṣa* consists in being the cause of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), then there is no contradiction in the mind (*manas*) also being such.
Furthermore, the clear perception of forms arises solely from the proficiency of the mind; for when the mind is distracted, how could there be clarity in the cognition of the senses?
Indeed, it is through the application of mental concentration that sensory cognition itself becomes direct perception.
Therefore, being produced by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is not at all the cause [of its being perception];
consequently, inference (*anumāna*) as well, when it proceeds toward the direct realization of all aspects, is indeed nothing but direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[Objection: But how can that which operates upon objects beyond the senses, such as the past and so forth, be direct perception?
This too is not tenable:
if direct perception exists, how can this [object] be indirect? If that which is directly perceived were indirect, then nothing would be non-indirect.
(601) Or, if indirectness consists in the absence of the operation of the sense organs—
How can that very operation of the sense organ be understood without direct perception?
If it were understood through direct perception, then the operation of the sense organ would also exist in all forms of inference,
since the occurrence of inference is present everywhere.
The operation of the eyes and other [senses] is also understood through inference;
moreover, when there is an inference of all aspects (sarvākārānumāna) regarding what was previously perceived, then the operation of one's own eyes and so forth is also cognized. (602)

In some cases [the object] is yet to be, and in some cases it has already occurred; it is understood through inference. When an object that has just arisen or one yet to come into being is inferred, is it not the case that there is an operation of the sense organ toward that future object as perceived by inference? Thus, in that instance, there is indeed an engagement of the senses.
When it exists, it exists as such;
and since that [object] is indeed present, being apprehended through inference in all its aspects, how can there be an absence of the operation of the sense faculties?
And how can that which is yet to be or has already been said to exist?
This is not so.

The very act of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is said to be the existence of this entity. In all cases, the existence of an entity is understood through direct perception. (604) Even in the case of an object currently intended [to be perceived], such as a pillar, its existence is understood solely through direct perception and not from anything else. [Objection: But is it not the case that even for fire and the like which are not directly perceived, existence is understood through inference?

Even in that case, it is precisely such a thing [as has been perceived] that is inferred— whether it is being directly perceived now or will be perceived later— since inference would otherwise not function;
for inference, which follows upon perception, infers only that which is perceptible.
Because otherwise it would be impossible:
if, however, nothing has seen, sees, or will see [it], then it is like the horn of a donkey— non-existent,
being a mere lack of any description of causal capacity, and thus utterly indefinable.
Is it not the case that existence consists in connection with the present time, rather than direct perception?
And thus, you maintain that yogis possess direct perception of past and future objects;
however, if they were to perceive only the state of being present, they would not be perceivers of the past and so forth.
Then others have asked: "If he is equal to all people, how can he possess the status of a Teacher (śāstṛ) or the state of a yogin? To this it is replied:
"There is no comprehension of time by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); only that which possesses form and so forth is comprehended through perception and inference. (605)
Even by means of a cognition that transcends direct perception, a function [of time] is apprehended;
for by direct perception, only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth is apprehended, not its connection with time,
since perception conforms solely to the appearance of those [objects].
For perception does not perceive anything without grasping the form present before it; otherwise, everyone would be an all-seeing seer.
Furthermore, time is not perceived as having a form present before it in the manner of a pillar or other such objects.
Nor is there inference without perception;
furthermore, if it is argued that the object of inference is what is grasped by cognitions such as "quick" or "slow," that too is not correct.
In cases such as "for a long time" and so forth, time does not reside in front of the cognitions. It is not accepted that a cognition is perceptual in the absence of such a form [of an object];
for in instances like "it was done long ago," it is only the jar or similar object that appears, and no other time is present therein.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
if only jars and the like appear as possessing the nature of being effects,
then what is the meaning of "long duration" and so forth?
To this it is replied:
the completion (*samāpti*) of the parts of a jar and so forth occurs through a slow sequence; the meaning of "long duration" (*cirārtha*) is due to the absence of causes when time is lacking.
(607) That which is the gradual accomplishment of the parts of a jar and so forth through a slow sequence is the meaning of "completion" as long duration.
Is it not the case that, in the absence of time, neither that very slowness nor its progression is logical?
No,
for those are established merely by the non-presence of the means [of cognition].
And the non-proximity of the means of accomplishment is due to the absence of a cause for proximity;
the absence of that cause for proximity, in turn, is due to the absence of its own cause. Thus, this sequence of causes is beginningless; therefore, there is no such thing as "time."

Now, if slowness or speed occurs to actions due to the power of time, one should consider: what is to be done there? Time is the initiator of actions; what then is the fruit of the operation of causes? If it is argued that time is not capable [to act] without a cause, [we reply: 608. Whether slowness or swiftness proceeds from the power of time or from the cause of actions, let it be considered: what is to be done in that case? Time is the impeller of actions; what is the result here of the activity of causes? If you say that time is not efficacious without a cause, [we respond:]...
In that case, the production of effects occurs solely through the presence or absence of causes; time, however, is not efficacious.
But if it were the case that causes lack efficacy in the absence of time, then the causal status of time would be logical.
Nor is it non-existence [that constitutes time], because time is pervasive and eternal;

if it is argued that its production arises from a cause dependent on the conjunction of successive moments of time, then from what other cause does that very conjunction of successive moments of time itself arise?
If it is argued that the sequence of effects arises from that very [time],
and that time is indeed the sequence itself, we say no.
Since the state of being conjoined or unconjoined constitutes succession (*krama*),
and that [succession] is nothing other than the nature of the objects themselves, there is no separate entity called "time" (*kāla*).
Alternatively, time is simply the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies.
[It is] not [the case],
because there is no movement apart from the essential nature of the sun and so forth,
and that essential nature is indeed accessible through direct perception.
The state of having been seen is the past; the state of being seen is the present; and the state of being about to be seen is the future—such is the determination of time.
How then is this cognition of distinction—"time belongs to this entity"—possible?
Just as the cognition of distinction "this is the body of the Son of the Mountain (Śiva)," so too is the distinctness of time established through valid cognition.
And so the world says:
"What time were you born? What is your well-being? This speech is appropriate when asking about the specific nature of that [person].
Therefore, the reality of the matter is that the past and the future are not perceived at present.
In this way, the vision of the past and so forth by yogins results in the conclusion that it is a vision of what is not being seen.
In that case, if it is said that they see what is not being seen by themselves, then it follows that a woman is both a mother and a barren woman.
Therefore, what is the meaning of "he sees the past and so forth"?
He sees that which is not being seen by another; since it exists as something being seen, it is indeed present to that extent, and thus there is no fault.
Its status as past and so forth is relative to others.
Therefore, only that which has been directly perceived exists; there is no operation of the senses regarding the past, because that [past object] does not exist by virtue of being directly perceived.

Furthermore, when its direct perception occurs through connection with that [past] time, its existence is not difficult to establish even though it is non-existent at the present moment. (612) Even if there is no connection with the present time, [it still exists].
The relation to the presentness of that very time is indeed directly perceived;
therefore, because it grasps a present object, the cognition of the past and so forth certainly possesses perceptuality insofar as it determines all aspects [of the object].
How then can it be said to be "past"?
Because the seer is perceived as being connected with the present time,

or because it is perceived by others as being connected with that same time, and because it is designated as "past" by a yogi who has arisen from meditative absorption; therefore, [the self is eternal].

If it is asked, "How can that which is past be seen by the yogin even today?", this is not so; for it is understood that the state of being in the present time belongs to the seer himself. How could a different time be a qualifier of another [the seer]? (613)
For how could that which is the time of the agent belong to another object of cognition?
Indeed, the whiteness of a horse is not attributed to a cow;
if it were perceived at that [same] time, how could it have a different time?
Because it is perceived as having another time; for instance:
"Whatever has the cognition of a certain form, whether at that very time or at another time, that object possesses that very form; its agenthood, however, does not belong to the time. (614)
For time, being perceived as a qualifier of another time belonging to the object of the agent, how can it conform to the agent’s having a different time?
For the agent later comes to possess a different time; however, he perceives his own [object] as connected to that other time—how then could it be established otherwise? Furthermore:
At that time, the very temporality of the agent is also perceived; subsequently, another time is perceived as belonging to that agent, and it has been stated that because of this,
"that" is perceived through its temporality, and thus its existence [is established].
However, my [claim] that "I have now understood that" is merely a conventional usage based on memory and not a matter of ultimate reality,
because direct perception does not function [in that regard].
Therefore, that which is cognized in all its aspects is indeed direct perception itself.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"If that [cognition] were direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could there be non-apprehension by another?
For if one has seen a future son as being currently experienced, how can there be non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatā*) when he is not apprehended by that [other person]?"
Now, [the claim] that the practitioner's realization is not like that of one who possesses a son is also incorrect;
for just as he was seen as conjoined with the body and so forth at that time, so too there is no sublation of that [realization].
However, the connection with that specific time was not seen by him; thus, even if it is so perceived, there is no fault.
For he saw him as his son in relation to a future body and so forth belonging to that time, and even if it is perceived in that way, it is not contradicted.
Even then, if there is no cognition [of it], then there is sublation,
such as [the heat of] summer and so forth.

2. [Objection: Now, if that which was not previously perceived is seen by him today, then it must likewise be seen by another, whether a yogi or anyone else; why then is there no perception of it by others? Thus, its non-perception [by others] constitutes a refutation.
That too is without substance:

if one thing is seen from afar by one person, why is it not likewise seen by another? Even when horses and such exist, they are not seen by everyone. (616) Where the capacity of one exists, that same capacity does not belong to another; because they are invisible to those who are not yogis, the established rule is that [the object] is "future. (617)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
even if it is seen by this [cognition], since it is perceived in its own essential nature at that time, how could it be future?

Since existence is [defined by] apprehension, non-existence is the absence of apprehension; even when there is apprehension, if there is no existence, then existence does not belong to anything at all.
(618) It is not the case that whatever is not apprehended is simply non-existent, for that would lead to an over-extension;
rather, when something is apprehended at a particular time, it is only then existent at that time.
That too is incorrect, for no time whatsoever is observed apart from entities; summer and the like are merely certain entities that serve as objects.
Indeed, no time at all is perceived apart from specific objects.

Since cold and so forth, as well as specific movements of the sun, constitute the seasons such as summer, and since these are perceived, they must be strictly present; how then can there be pastness or futurity?
How is the distinction between the past and so forth understood regarding summer and the other seasons?
If it is not perceived by others, then there is no distinction between the two.
Even if there is non-perception at that time, nevertheless there is non-existence; yet, regarding what is currently non-existent, how is one to distinguish whether it is past or future?
To this, it is said:
Therefore, let it be understood that the inference which is now occurring is exactly as it previously occurred; for perception also apprehends that object to be precisely the same. || 621 ||
Just as that inference cognizes [an object] by way of its being past, future, and so forth, so too does the perception produced by that inference;
for that perception produced by inference does not cognize it otherwise.
Therefore, let it be understood that an object exists exactly as it is cognized.

[Objection: Surely, for perception to be produced by inference, it must occur through a gradual process of comprehension; and thus, since the comprehension of the beginningless and endless continuum of things would never reach completion, how can there be omniscience? [Reply:
This is not so, because through extreme habituation, one knows those objects instantaneously, just as embodied beings perceive fire immediately from smoke. (622)
For those whose mental continuum is joined with repeated practice, the cognition of fire from smoke does not depend on a sequence;
therefore, since the cognition is not sequential, there is no fault.
But how can there be a completion of the comprehension of a beginningless entity through a non-sequential process? Or, if there were such completion, how could it be beginningless?
This is not the case.

Even if the Veda were beginningless, how could cognitions arise from it? For there is no end to cognitions in that which is beginningless. (623) If the Veda is both beginningless and endless, how can there be cognition from it? And if, due to its being beginningless and endless, there is no completion [of the process], then nothing at all would need to be done.

For if there were no cognition other than from the Veda— either in the past or in the future— then the Veda would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) [since it could not be distinguished] from what is other than the Veda.
Surely, for now, there is the cognition:
"This Veda is my injunction-giver"; whether this cognition exists at other times or not is irrelevant.
Nevertheless, because it is an instigator, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is designated as such by virtue of being an instigator.
This is not the case;
for if this object did not exist at another time, how could it exist now?
If there were a doubt that the Veda was not for this purpose at another time,
then even now it would not be a means of valid cognition, just as before;
or else, if it were exactly the same even previously.
Since there is no finality— because after that there is something further, and beyond that yet more—
it follows that when doubt arises at one point, there will be no confidence in what follows; thus, it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, if the universal were perceived all at once beforehand, then this would be an inference; consequently, even in the perception of all aspects [of an object], perceptuality would remain unestablished.
Therefore, there is no perception even by direct experience of that which is beginningless and endless;
and for that reason...
When one's own continuum is delimited, that which is associated with it is perceived; and when that which is associated with it is perceived, because the other is also perceived,
the cognition of infinite objects is thus not difficult to accomplish.

Therefore, through the cultivation of the distinction between the infinite varieties of cause and effect, there arises the manifestation of all distinct effects; and by the power of that, there also arises the manifestation of the distinctness of the causes.
This cultivation of the means (*upāya*) is the means for the complete discernment of everything;
hence, one who possesses compassion must necessarily apply themselves to these means.
It has already been established that even through thorough knowledge of the Vedas, they are not the means for the mere attainment of heaven and liberation; for indeed,
if it were the case that the desired complete knowledge of all things and the abandonment of passion could be achieved through the practice of those means—

Nevertheless, due to the impairment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one might even teach otherwise during the state of non-concentration; however, the occurrence of hunger and the like acts as an obstacle to the welfare of others, and thus there is no distinction between this [non-Buddhist] teacher and the Veda.
This is not so.

Because the Veda lacks a foundation, it possesses no ultimate authority; it has no connection with its meaning, and even its linguistic usage is rootless. Indeed, if the Veda were beginningless, there could be no initial apprehension of its connection with meaning; therefore, the ritualists' practice is entirely without basis, resulting in nothing more than a "blind tradition."

Even the appearance of an object within conceptual construction occurs through the power of linguistic convention, yet the attainment of the actual object does not follow from that alone, as has been demonstrated by the observation of other cases;
however, since this [convention] is rooted in inference,
there is no fault even regarding the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*).
Moreover,

due to the sharpness of his awakening and because of the cause of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this great sage is distinguished from those such as the Pratyekabuddhas who act for the sake of others;
for one whose awakening is keen, the entire collection of qualities and defects, even the most subtle, appears clearly.
Even that which is desired by one who is devoted to the welfare of sentient beings, if it causes suffering, he overcomes it through practice;
for even hunger and other such afflictions occur only for those who possess contrary mental cultivation, and not otherwise.
To illustrate this:
For one who seeks the welfare and benefit of sentient beings, even the slightest fault becomes an obstacle;

yet, when there is a connection with former support through the recollection of past lives (*jātismaratva*), then, by virtue of being a deity or similar state, hunger, wretchedness, and the like are impossible. (627)
Furthermore, by the practice of eating three times, one attains the same result as eating twice; and for one who eats twice, it is the same as eating once. Therefore, hunger is entirely non-existent.
That will become the self of that person.
But if this were merely the actual state of things and not something accomplished through practice, then—
All virtues and faults of embodied beings are rooted in practice (*abhyāsa*). That practice is dependent upon the self, and it is best when directed toward virtues alone.
(629) For this very reason, through the attainment of proficiency in practice, the Blessed One, the Sugata, is distinguished from the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
Now, has not the Teacher indeed indicated the teaching as the means for the pacification of suffering?
And so it has been said:
"The state of being a Teacher arises from the instruction of the world; how, then, could there be the practice of the means [thereto]?"
This is true;
however, he says that the teaching is nothing other than the means [to liberation] (upāya).
The practice of skillful means—
this very practice of skillful means— is considered the teaching because it has that as its purpose.
Since these two exist first at the time of accomplishment, this pair is called the cause.
Indeed, the primary teaching is not what is intended; rather, it is the practice of the means [to that end].
How so? Because of its being for that purpose; for a word denoting one thing may refer to another when it exists for the sake of that other.
Just as a pillar intended for Indra is designated by the word "Indra," so too its status as such [is established] because of the presence of that purpose;
through the practice of skillful means and the sharpness of the intellect, the teaching is brought to completion.
How is this known? To that he says:
"These two have been stated as the reason."
In that regard, the cause is the perfection of intention and application;
intention is the desire for the welfare of the world, and application is the state of being a Teacher through instructing the world—
why is it said that this is the cause?
For it is not the first liberation alone that is the primary cause of being a Sugata;
therefore, it should be understood that the practice of skillful means (*upāya*) itself is the teaching and nothing else.
Thus, through the practice of skillful means, one becomes a Sugata, a Blessed One (*bhagavān*).
(5) Because he is a Sugata, the Blessed One is an authority.
But what is this state of being a Sugata? He says:
"The state of being a Sugata consists in the abandonment of the cause, which possesses three qualities, due to the absence of dependence. (140)
The view of selflessness, or its logical reasoning, is praised as the remedy for suffering.
Affection, which is produced by the grasping at "self" and "mine," has the sphere of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as its object; it is the cause [of suffering].
The abandonment of that cause is praised for three reasons: because it is excellent, because there is no returning [to cyclic existence], and because it is an abandonment without remainder.
Abandonment is the non-existence of the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
because that non-existence lacks any basis for suffering, it is praiseworthy,
whereas for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthya*), who grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, there can be no abandonment of suffering.
Because it is conjoined with suffering due to its cause,
for when there is grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, suffering undoubtedly exists;
the abandonment of that very [grasping] is [the goal].
How is it that the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision occurs precisely through the vision of selflessness, and not merely through vision or through reasoning?
Yukti is practice, which is cultivation (bhāvanā) directed toward the mass of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;
alternatively, yukti is yoga,
the non-dual state of mutual integration.
Or even from the perspective of non-dual vision,
whether through the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) or through the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*),
by seeing selflessness in every respect, there is no taking recourse in suffering.
Thus, first there is the quality of excellence;
second is the quality of non-return.
To the question "What is this non-return?", he says:
When "return" (punarāvṛtti) is mentioned, it refers to the arising of birth and defects;
through the abandonment of the seed of the vision of the Self, there is no further coming,
meaning the cessation of the occurrence of birth and of defects, which constitutes non-return.
The state free from defects, due to the absence of passion and so forth,
as well as non-rearising and the absence of birth,
is the journey to the city of liberation.
When the defects are absent, one is said to have returned from birth;
and those defects do not arise again because the seed of the view of a self has been uprooted through the absence of such a view.
Furthermore, birth is not possible in the absence of afflictions; therefore, there is no returning again,
for it will be demonstrated later that birth arises from afflictions and karma.
And since there is no perception of a self, how could there be afflictions? To this he says:
attachment toward a benefactor arises from the recollection of having been helped by them;
aversion arises from the recollection of harm; and delusion is the perception of a self and so forth.
630 1 T. Self, etc. (ātman-ādi)
Attachment and aversion toward one who benefits or harms the self do not exist because of the absence of a self;
however, the view of a self is delusion, and that is directly dispelled by the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
In the Advaita philosophy, however, the cessation of attachment occurs all the more easily because of the absence of objects.

If it is argued that the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is the result that brings about cessation because it is the opposite of the vision of the self (*ātmadarśana*), [we reply] that this mutual opposition is equal in both cases.

Therefore, since the vision of selflessness is the very thing that turns back the vision of a self, there is no returning from that state; nor is there even a partial cessation [of the vision of self], for there is no other remainder that could lead to a return. To this, it is said:
Because that [realization] is essentially distinct from those [defilements], there is no deficiency whatsoever in body, speech, or intellect, nor any lack of proficiency in explaining the path;
this is because his vision of selflessness is truly real. (142)
And because it is the opposite,
and because the vision of a self is the opposite of that, the real is the remover of the unreal; through this opposition, there is merely a state of opposition.
Furthermore, there can be no vision of a self that is of a divided nature,
because in ultimate reality there is an absence of a self, as the self is non-existent.
In that case, what then is the "remainder"?
It is said here that it is something other [than liberation], because of the absence of repeated return.
Is it not the case that defects of body, speech, and mind are produced by the afflictions (*kleśa*)? In the absence of afflictions, how could they possibly arise?
Nor can there be liberation without the afflictions, for [defects] would persist through the mere association with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as in the case of the "Vṛṣalī" curse.
If there is an incapacity for the various etymological explanations of the path,
then from what cause would there be the loss of that remainder?
For one who has not fallen away from selflessness, there is no other cause for falling away.

Furthermore, the abandonment of faults does not occur as long as there is cognition, because speech is preceded by vitarka and vicāra; thus, it follows that even an omniscient being would be entirely subject to error.
To this, he replies:
"The complete abandonment [of faults] results from practice; thus, there is the total destruction of defects such as speech and so forth.
Some say: "No, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful and non-invariable.
For practice indeed produces sharpness of intellect; therefore, it has been stated that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are eliminated thereby."

Nor is [the probans] established by mere assertion, because there is doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka)— characterized by the absence of the heterologue (vipakṣa)— due to the statement of the proof for passion and so forth; therefore, since its negative concomitance is doubtful, it is non-probative,
or else [it is non-probative] when the thesis (sādhya) is a conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Due to extreme habituation, even in the absence of discursive thought (*vitarka*), speech proceeds by its own momentum (*āvedha*);
for it has been said: [speech indeed continues to function].

For one who has eliminated all conceptual constructions regarding the outflows (*āsrava*), there is no distinction from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor does a word function solely because of an indistinct appearance.
(631) Since words are applied even to a pillar and such things perceived through direct perception—as in "this is a pillar"—otherwise they would not be applied at all.
(632) Furthermore, an indistinct appearance of cognition is not observed here; thus, the application of words elsewhere is likewise not precluded. (633)
Therefore, it is established that even in his speech he is not possessed of faults.

Now, one might object: "Since there is no destruction of faults from any other source, how can there be an absence of faults? For it is not observed that there is a cause for the destruction of faults."
It is not that there is no cause for the absence of the destruction of defects;
rather, it is said here: how indeed could the unseen (adṛṣṭa) be postulated?
1. Or it does not exist at all;
2. T. [End of section]
Or one might imagine that the defects are incurable because they are eternal, due to the absence of a means,
or because of a lack of knowledge regarding the means. || 144 ||
Indeed, these conceptual constructions do not enter [into the mind] in any arbitrary manner; rather,
because they arise through a sequence of steps consisting of the investigation of their underlying causes,
if these defects were eternal, they would remain inexhaustible even with effort.
For it cannot be brought to destruction even by a hundred efforts,
since there is no means for its destruction nor is any found;
nevertheless, it is inexhaustible.
And these three [faults] do not exist either,
because the contradictory cause, being possessed of a cause, is destroyed through the repeated practice of its opposite.
By means of the knowledge of the nature of the cause, that knowledge [of the result] is also established;
for since that which possesses a cause lacks prior existence, it cannot be eternal.
When there is cultivation of the cause, there is then its exhaustion; thus, it is not the case that there is no means.
Because it is the means for the exhaustion of faults that are the opposite of the cause, there is no lack of thorough knowledge regarding that [cause];
for through the knowledge of the nature of the cause— which consists in the forms of "self" and "mine"— there arises the knowledge of its opposite, which is the antidote.

For whatever is the opposite of something is its counteragent; for example, oil is external to wind because of its oily and hot nature, or due to specific qualities such as power, in contrast to that which is cold and dry.
Even though external objects are not refuted, the vision of selflessness is indeed contrary to the vision of a self; thus, there is no disagreement [on this point].
Because he is compassionate, the Blessed One is a valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Although the Blessed One has attained the state of a Sugata, how can he be an authority for others based merely on the perfection of his own welfare?
For one is an authority by means of revealing the non-erroneous object,
not by being erroneous.
Nor is it by way of non-manifestation;
this [protection] of the Blessed One exists because he is a protector through the power of compassion and the application of skillful means.
To what [fault] does he [the Buddha] succumb? He says:
"The Tathāgata teaches the path as he has seen it; because his teaching is never in vain, he does not speak falsehood.
This is due to his compassion, his dedication to the welfare of others, and his commitment to all his undertakings. (146)
For it is not seen by anyone in the Vedas that such a thing is impossible;
and for one whose Sugata-hood is rooted in mere appearance, there is nothing whatsoever to be desired.
Therefore, because it would be fruitless, he does not speak untruth; because of his compassion, his practice of skillful means was performed solely for the sake of others,
and thus there is no reason for him to utter what is false.

Therefore, because there is no cause [for error] and no purpose [to deceive], there is no false statement; and due to the application of compassion, the force of [logical] implication, and the excellence resulting from practice, there is no failure to speak [the truth].
Consequently, the Sugata is a *tāyin* (protector); this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since it is impossible not to reveal the path to liberation that one has personally realized, one might object: "Is it not the case that *tāya* (the state of being a protector) consists simply in teaching the path one has seen? If so, then by that much alone, would not all founders of religious systems (*tīrthakara*) be authoritative?"
Now, the teaching of the path by them is merely the proclamation of a path they themselves have seen; that [path] does not exist, because it is a non-path.
If this is so, how can there be confidence in this case as well?
It has been stated here that [the path] is seen through the vision of selflessness or even through reasoning;
however, for them (the opponents), there is neither the vision of selflessness nor the reasoning.
They are not authoritative,
nor is there any personal realization on their part, because their teaching is mutually contradictory.
One would speak falsely by the force of an implication (*ākṣepabala*).
(I) The Blessed One, however, is the illuminator of the Four Truths for those [beings].
Therefore, either that [teaching] or the illumination of the Four Truths is the authority (pramāṇa).
Or rather, the illumination of the Four Truths is *tāya*, and nothing else.

Even though there is an exposition of emptiness at the end of those [other systems], nevertheless, because of the existence of a self (*ātman*), that is simply not the path; thus, the vision of the Four Noble Truths alone is "protection" (*tāya*). Therefore, since this unique quality of expressing the true meaning belongs only to the Blessed One, he alone is the Protector (*tāyin*) due to the presence of truth.
Even though this path is devoid of logical reasoning, it is a cause for tranquility, like the purification of a mother; therefore, no other path has been specified.
What are those Noble Truths?
They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Agitation arises even from this name,
as in the case of saying "urinary tract" rather than "genitals"; however,
that is not the case here.
Nevertheless, 5. T.
Quiescence (the four noble truths):
(a) the truth of suffering.

(a) The conditioned aggregates are suffering; the transmigrating aggregates are suffering because one observes the intensification of passion and so forth through habituation, not by chance, nor from a causeless origin, since that would contradict the nature of birth. (148)
Now, it might be argued that passion (*rāga*) is indeed pleasure itself, because it is a cause of pleasure by virtue of being a limb for embracing a desired woman;
likewise, hatred (*dveṣa*) is also pleasure, as it is the cause of the pleasure derived from the elimination of an enemy;
and delusion (*moha*), characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), is pleasure itself, since it is the cause of the pleasure of pride and arrogance born of the conceit "I am."
Since even the body and so forth, which serve as the substrata for attachment, aversion, and the like, are likewise [empty], there is no such thing as suffering.
Even that suffering such as hunger and so on is itself the cause of great pleasure, such as satiety;
therefore, there is no such thing as the Truth of Suffering, and thus the Blessed One’s teaching is entirely futile and he is not a protector.
This is not correct, because of those [reasons].
