The aggregates themselves are great suffering; yet, due to the exhaustion from wandering upon the path of saṃsāra and through association with it, they are impaired in their capacity for happiness. Ignorance views them otherwise. (634) 2 T.
Regarding the statement that passion and the like are causes of pleasure for those whose happiness is destroyed by exhaustion,
it is said in response to that:
Attachment and pleasure have practice as their cause and follow immediately upon it; they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature, because they conform to the presence or absence of practice.
(635) For if attachment and the like were to arise by chance or were eternal, [they would not depend on practice].

Or rather, that [pleasure] is improper when it arises solely from habituation, because proficiency and so forth are observed to result from that very habituation; therefore, it is merely an unreal conceptualization,
and thus the abandonment of habituation alone is superior.
Therefore, like the practice of children's play, there is no ultimate happiness,
nor is there happiness characterized by mental delight.
Through practice, or by the cessation of the phenomena of saṃsāra, the practice of reality alone is better; for why?
Even pleasure is desired only through practice, whereas equanimity alone is superior.

And this being the case, all of this appears as happiness only to one who is tormented by suffering; therefore, it is better that there be no arising of the affliction of passion and so forth, rather than the actual existence of passion and so forth, such as the embracing of a woman.
Or rather, mere conceptual construction is better.

Having brought about the cessation of a wound, no person of sound intellect desires it again for the sake of the relief from its pain; but one who lacks intelligence acts otherwise when that is the case.
(636) If the intellect delights in reality (*tattva*), it is not subject to transformation; consequently, unafflicted happiness proceeds eternally.
(637) If there were delight in unreality (*atattva*), how could there be happiness in cessation? But when there is no departure from reality, even happiness does not cease. (638)
Therefore, whatever pleasure exists in saṃsāra, all of that is in reality nothing but suffering;
for just as the causes of pleasure are observed to be the sufferings of passion and so forth, so too should it be understood that pleasure itself is a cause of suffering. (639)
Just as the suffering of hunger and so forth is the cause of the pleasure of satiety, so too pleasure is the cause of extreme suffering upon its departure;
therefore, because it is a cause of suffering, pleasure is not truly pleasure.
This being the case, this [point] is established.

The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering, while the intensity of passion and so forth arises from habituation; since it arises from habituation, it is therefore caused by a preceding cause of a similar nature. Thus, the state of being in saṃsāra is established. Now, [the opponent objects: "Passion does not arise from habituation, but rather occurs somehow or other from some other cause; therefore, these things such as pleasure and so forth are indeed ultimate realities."

Therefore, it is not the case that the aggregates (*skandhas*) of one in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*) are suffering, just as pleasure and so forth [are not ultimately real] due to habituation; likewise, suffering and so forth are also not [ultimately real]. Thus, the claim that "the aggregates of one in cyclic existence are nothing but pleasure" is not at all tenable from the perspective of the correct method (*naya*). Consequently, birth is not logical for something that lacks a cause, such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like do not have other causes, because they possess intensity through habituation;
nor does anyone habituate to suffering such that suffering would become something produced by habituation.
Rather, [it is as follows:]

When pleasure and the like, through habituation, consist of an active process of accumulation, then in the absence of that [pleasure], suffering arises; however, there is no such thing as the habituation to suffering anywhere.
Indeed, no one ever practices with the thought, "May I have suffering," for everyone acts solely out of a desire for happiness.
Therefore, pleasure is to be achieved through effort, whereas suffering arises by its very nature from the absence of that [pleasure], and not conversely;
thus, even suffering is produced solely through the habitual practice of pleasure. Consequently, it is pleasure alone that must be eliminated.
But from the perspective of ultimate truth,
even suffering does not exist at all;
that [notion of suffering] arises solely from the cultivation of fear toward it.
Therefore, from the cultivation of fear toward that [object], suffering arises;
and because of the absence of that [fear], there arises within that very suffering—or even in what is not suffering—the notion of pleasure, though not in an ultimate sense.
Consequently, pleasure brought about by such cultivation is nothing other than a cause of suffering.
If that [self] did not exist, there would be no suffering at all for one who is attached to a son; for when a son dies, suffering arises,
and when that same son is born, there is happiness.
In the ultimate sense, there is no eternal happiness for anyone; rather, for those in cyclic existence, even that which is sought after results only in suffering. (641)
The attainment of happiness by repeatedly binding oneself to suffering does not possess logical justification; for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
(642) Now, if all happiness is exactly like this and no other exists, how can the alleviation of suffering in states such as hell be considered [happiness]?
(643) Is there no arising of happiness even from the suffering of hell? For even amidst one great suffering, there is happiness when another suffering is present. (644)

Alternatively, suffering here is characterized by the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); pleasure, being its opposite, is likewise characterized by a self and so forth.
This [notion] does not exist even from the perspective of ultimate reality, but rather arises from habituation, through which the self and so forth are established in various ways.
And attachment and the other [afflictions] are rooted in that;

therefore, they arise from that very habituation and not otherwise, because there is no cause for the ultimate reality. Furthermore, if even habituation were not a cause, it would follow that there is no causality at all, and it is illogical that something could be produced from what lacks a cause.
(b) Refutation of the claim that passion and the like arise from the humors such as wind:
Now, it might be argued that passion and the like are not born of habituation, but rather are born of the humors such as wind.
For it is thus: delusion belongs to one of a wind-nature, hatred to one of a bile-nature, and passion to one of a phlegm-nature.
Just as the primary faults exist, so too do the derivative faults such as envy and the like, which arise from wind (*vāta*) and so forth;
and since wind and the others exist in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because they arise from those causes, attachment (*rāga*) and the other afflictions must also be ultimately real.
That, too, is incorrect.
Because of deviation, it is not a property of wind and so forth due to the confusion of primary elements (*prakṛti*).
If you say there is no fault [in this], then why is another property of that [wind] not observed?
For whatever is the cause of something does not deviate from it.
If great delusion and the other [afflictions] were properties of the wind and so forth, like smoke is of fire, then they would not deviate from them;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, the opposite is the case;
or rather, for one of a windy temperament (*vātaprakṛti*), there exists another temperament that gives rise to passion (*rāga*) and another that gives rise to hatred (*dveṣa*).
Therefore, because there is a natural mixture of passion and hatred, there is no deviation [from the rule];
that too is incorrect.

If that [effect] has no other property (dharma) besides it, how can there be the occurrence of a cause? If its effect does not exist, from where could there be the cognition of the existence of the cause?
If that very [cause] is the effect, how could there be another effect? If you say "from that very [cause]," then why is that other [effect] not identical to it by virtue of its existence?
If that effect were to arise from something else, then this very same fallacy of deviation would occur.

Therefore, if there were no non-deviation from the properties of wind and so forth, then even if one were to postulate a different material cause, the effect itself would have to be postulated [as arising from that].
Since an unobserved effect is not postulated, another primary nature (prakṛti) should likewise not be postulated;

for just as a cause is inferred from its effect, so too an effect may be inferred from a cause whose capacity is unimpeded. Alternatively, there is no such thing as a cause whose general causal capacity is unimpeded.
Even if an effect were to arise despite the absence of its cause,
let that [cause] not be considered its cause at all;
moreover—

If, having abandoned a perceived cause, one postulates an unperceived one, then phlegm could not be the cause of passion; rather, something else would have to be postulated. (647) Furthermore, it might be argued that whatever is actually observed is itself the cause of passion and so forth.
[Objection: But surely passion and the like are seen everywhere; why then is not everything a cause? [Reply: If you say, "It is exactly so, for it is seen to be thus," this is incorrect, because:
It is not the case that all phenomena [cause] equal passion in everyone, because that would lead to an absurd consequence;
if you argue there is no fault because it is like form and so forth, then the same objection applies there as well.
If you say that specific karmas have sovereignty over those [phenomena], then what role do the karmas play?

Since passion and the other [afflictions] must belong to every living being by virtue of their being universal properties (*sarvadharmatva*), then whoever is subject to phlegm and so forth would necessarily be the locus of passion and the rest; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence that everyone would possess equal passion and so forth.
To this, he says:

If it is maintained that passion and the like are inherent in all constitutions (*prakṛti*), then since there is no constitution that lacks the capacity [for them], how could there be an inequality of their effects?

For when passion and the like are held to arise from every constitution, then even though there may be an increase or decrease in phlegm (*kapha*) and other humors, the cause of passion and so forth remains the same; thus, it is impossible to prevent the equality of passion and the rest.
Now, even if [the mind] possesses the nature of all [factors], because there exists another specific distinction, it does not follow that there is "equal passion" (*samarāgatā*).
If that were the case, then the universal cause would not be qualified by those distinctions, and thus it would not be a universal property (*sarvadharma*).
Alternatively, since passion and the other [afflictions] have as their cause the entire complex of humors such as phlegm (*kapha*) and so forth, they are universal properties.
That they do not possess equal passion and so forth due to specific internal transformations of those very [elements] is also trivial,
because:
Just as it has been correctly demonstrated that whatever specific transformation is perceived is itself subject to deviation (vyabhicāritva):

for when a particular transformation resulting from a certain cause is observed to be the cause of passion (rāga) and so forth, yet that very same [transformation] becomes the cause of hatred (dveṣa) and so forth, there is a deviation; at that time, even if the causality of every specific factor is asserted in the demonstration of all phenomena, it remains fallacious.
The reason— that "from that specific transformation, there is indeed the state of having equal passion and so forth for all specific instances of passion and so forth"— is untenable,
because that [transformation] itself is the cause of all specific instances of passion and so forth.
Because the object is the same, that pervasive contact is the cause [of the distinction];
for even an external specific effect, when inferred as a specific transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*), is indeed observed to be the cause for the non-confusion of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
That too is incorrect because:
"Smoke that has never been seen in connection with fire would not have fire as its cause; rather, some specific property of the location itself would be the cause of the smoke. (650)

If smoke exists in the region of fire and there is no distinction from anything else, then, being devoid of such a distinction, smoke could not possibly occur elsewhere. (651) If, despite its never being observed [elsewhere], a distinction is postulated based merely on the observation of the effect,
then the specific relationship between cause and effect would collapse everywhere.
Now, if no specific conceptualization is made there,
because the observed fire is sublated by conceptualization,
then in this case as well, let the observed repetition be conceptually constructed.
Indeed, the postulation of a specific transformation is not logical;
for surely it is accepted that visible forms and so forth have the primary elements as their cause.
If you argue that they are distinguished by a specific state of those elements, this objection applies to you alone, not to us.
Because karma is the specific cause of predominance, otherwise, since they too would be included within the subject class (*pakṣa*),
there would be no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) on account of them.
Furthermore, because there is no distinction among defects even when there is a distinction [in the objects], [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*);
for not all [defects] arise from every [cause], nor does one modification [arise] from another modification.
Moreover, while the cause persists, the disappearance of the effect is not logical.
Just as in the case of heat and so forth, even a transformation arising from passion and the like is produced by pleasure and the like.

As it has been stated: "Even when other causes are present, the observation of another effect occurs because of the presence of a specific [cause]; therefore, there is also the postulation of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*).
To this, it is replied:

Granted that there may be another cause for the distinction; even so, when there is an excellence of the effect, how can the excellence of the effect resulting from the excellence of the cause be prevented?
If it is argued that this is because there is no other such distinction in that case either, [we reply:]...

If that is the case, then that specific quality (*viśeṣa*) would not be a cause; from where, then, could there be the apprehension of cause and effect? Furthermore, it is not logical for something perceptible to have an unperceived specific quality.
Therefore:

If the apprehension of its being an effect arises from the apprehension of a specific quality due to that [object], then if no such specific quality exists, how can there be an apprehension of it being an effect and so forth?

(652) But is it not the case that the reason "due to a specific quality" is unestablished (*asiddha*), since when bile is aggravated, there is an increase in aversion in one afflicted by the pain thereof? No, there is no lack of establishment.
If it is argued that hatred does not arise even in one who is by nature weak in hatred because of the pain caused by the excess of all [humors] such as phlegm (kapha),
this is equally applicable to the case of an excess of bile (pitta); therefore, it should not be said.
Now, as for the claim that they are produced by everything, that too is not tenable, because it has already been stated that "they are not produced by everything.
— O Omniscient One,
furthermore, even if there is indeed no other distinction,
nevertheless, let there be no loss of the effect caused by that distinction; from where could such a loss arise?
For when there is an increase in the cause, an increase in the effect is indeed logical, not a decrease; otherwise,
it would not possess the status of being a cause, as has been stated in the case of heat and so forth, which increase when bile and other humors increase.
[Objection: But surely, an increase in passion is indeed observed when substances that cause an increase [of phlegm] are consumed, because of the presence of phlegm;
[Response: This is not so, because it is only hatred that arises from the affliction of disease.
For passion and the like arise from pleasure and so forth, not from phlegm and the like;
and pleasure is experienced by someone in some way through the awakening of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, it is logical that passion and the other afflictions do not arise from the [physical] humors.
2 — Saturday,
the 13th. The day before yesterday.
Thus,
even if passion does not arise when phlegm is in excess,
nevertheless, that [excess] is not a cause [of passion], because its capacity is obstructed by the suffering born of physical imbalance.
Nor is it the case that what does not produce [an effect] due to another obstruction is not a cause,
for that would entail the absurd consequence that everything is non-causal.
To this it is replied:

if it is argued that passion does not arise due to the suffering born of inequality, then by what would it arise? [It arises] from equality; from that comes the increase of intoxication, and from that, love. (153)

If it is argued that passion exists in one person even when there is an unevenness of defects, while it does not exist in another despite the same degree of perceived beauty; and that intoxication (mada) may flow from the depletion of blood in some, yet not in others who are devoted to many women; and that such passion might not be intense in one woman alone, even though her limbs, form, and other qualities are identical—[then we reply: naikatrāpyatirāgo 'sti rakteṣvapi hi bhāviṣu | tathāpi madanākrānto na kaścid vītarāgavat || 155 || Even among those who are passionate, there is no excessive passion for just one object, even if she is destined to be loved. Nevertheless, no one is so overwhelmed by desire as to become like one who is free from passion. na caikatraiva sarveṣāṃ rāgaḥ samupajāyate | yenaikasyām atiprītir anyāsu viratiḥ punaḥ || 156 || Nor does passion arise in all people for only one single object, such that there would be extreme attachment to one woman and a total cessation of interest in others. na caikasyāṃ ratirnityaṃ yena syād anyanihnavaḥ | dṛṣṭā hy ekatra saṃtoṣād anyatrāpi pravartanam || 157 || Furthermore, attachment to one woman is not constant, whereby there would be a suppression of interest in others; for it is observed that through satisfaction with one, one may still proceed toward another. na caikasyāṃ sthirasneho yena syād anyavarjanam | dṛśyante hi sthiraprītayo 'nyāsv api striyo narāḥ || 158 || Nor is affection fixed upon one woman, which would necessitate the avoidance of others; It would not apply to all [people], because it is not indeterminate, nor would it be unrestricted.
(155) Even one who perceives no virtues might become a partaker [of merit], for that perception of virtue would exist even in him;
if he were to perceive all virtues, it would be so because there is no distinction in the cause. (156)

In whatever state one is considered to possess passion (*rāga*), one would likewise not be subject to hatred (*dveṣa*), because the nature of those two is identical; furthermore, no such restrictive rule is observed here.

If, due to the equilibrium of phlegm (*kapha*) and the other humors, there occurs an absence of conflicting diseases and consequently an increase of *mada*—which has another name, semen (*śukra*)—then that [increase] partakes of the designation "passion" (*smara-rāga*).

This being the case, there would be the fallacy of irregularity: one who is passionate and devoted exclusively to sexual intercourse with women would not experience passion born from the wounds of lovemaking due to the depletion of semen, because semen is common to all women; thus, passion would not be restricted to a single woman. Consequently, because of the equal presence of semen, there would be no intensity of passion toward any one woman.
1. From that, passion arises;
thus, the woman is also the cause of the object.
The distinction or lack thereof regarding the specific qualities of form and so forth is such that even form and the rest are indeed causes;
for instance, those whose minds are rendered helpless by the noose of excellence in form abandon their own wives and [desire] other women. (653)
"Perhaps, due to some auxiliary cause, intoxication (*mada*) alone does not produce passion (*rāga*) in certain cases; therefore, there is no restriction [that it must always do so].
(654) "Therefore, because of the presence of intensity as an auxiliary factor in one case, and its absence in another, there is no fault.
This also is not correct, because:
Because deviation is observed everywhere, there is no causal status at all for form and so forth, since passion occurs even toward that which is devoid of form.

(655) If it is argued that this is due to the existence of a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then form is not the cause; for form is possible even toward that which is devoid of metaphorical designation.
(656) Furthermore, passion and its metaphorical designation are not logically the cause of passion, because passion is observed in some cases toward that which is devoid of both. (657)
Not every cause [produces] all [results], because that would entail the consequence of equal passion for all;
if, on the other hand, it is maintained that the cause is indeed indeterminate, that too is untenable.
Nor is it logical that [desire] is therefore undetermined;

for desire, which is fixed upon one [object], would not be the motivator for one who is longing to perceive form when an unattractive woman unexpectedly appears before him while he is already afflicted by desire.
Furthermore:
If intoxication were the cause of passion, then passion would arise even in one who perceives no virtues;
if, on the other hand, the perception of virtues is also a necessary factor,
then it follows that everyone who perceives virtues would be subject to passion.
Since everything exists as the cause of qualities,
if there is no apprehension of qualities merely because of the existence of qualities themselves,
then from what does the apprehension of qualities arise?
If the apprehension of qualities occurs without an object due to beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*), it follows that passion and the like arise solely from habituation;
furthermore, for one who remains in a state where passion exists, hatred would not exist in that same state,
because passion and hatred are of a contrary nature due to their inequality.
Nor does that [result] occur for one established in a nature contrary to it;
yet if it does not occur at all, that too is untenable,
for no such restriction is observed here.
Alternatively, if that nature belongs to both, then it follows that there must be equality between the two; if you say it is exactly so, [we reply: no.
This is not so, because no such restriction is observed;
for here, there is no observation of a restriction regarding simultaneity.
Now, as for the claim that just as for one whose constitution is dominated by bile (pitta), sweating and so forth occur only occasionally and not at all times,
so too it is with passion (rāga) and the rest— that is incorrect.
Sweat is produced from contact with heat; in the absence of that [heat], it would not exist.

But for passion and the like, there is no cause other than form and so forth. When those [objects] are present, passion and the like do not fail to exist due to the completeness of their causes. If, however, there were a reversal of this rule through the arrival of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by internal assistance, then in that case, the latent impression alone would be the cause of passion and the like.
Since there is also no cultivation of the syllable *u* for passion (*rāga*),
it might still be argued that even for one [who holds this view], passion and so forth arise from a distinction in their latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
To the question of how this fault does not apply even to him, he says:
"For one whose [defilements] such as passion and so forth have their activity restricted by the distinctions of the latencies of their own kind, these faults do not follow. (158)

For when attachment and the like arise through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then, according to the restriction of latent impressions—that is, whichever latent impression associated with a previous birth belongs to a particular person in a particular place—it awakens for that person in that very place, somehow, at some time, and due to some cause. Thus, since there is no dependence on [external] forms and so forth regarding forms and so forth, there is no room for the aforementioned fault.
(c) Refutation of the view that attachment and the like are properties of the elements (*bhūta*).
Lest it be thought that passion and the like, though not having the nature of wind and so forth, might nonetheless have the nature of the primary elements (*bhūta*), he says:
"By this, the status of being a property of the primary elements is refuted, as well as [their status] as a support.
(156) Because of this refutation, whiteness and the like do not depend upon earth and the other elements.

He who says that these are the properties of the elements— earth and so forth— namely, that passion arises from an excess of earth and water, hatred from fire and air, and delusion from water and air;
That too is refuted because it is inconclusive in all cases;
and so it has been said:
The state in which one is considered to possess passion (*rāgin*), and so forth,

as well as the relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), has been refuted by such statements as "because neither the existent nor the non-existent can have a substratum" (*anāśrayāt sadasatoḥ*).
Now, one might object: "Just as whiteness and other qualities depend upon the great elements, so too do passion and the rest.
To this he says: "Whiteness and the like do not depend upon earth and the other elements."
If they were dependent upon earth and the other elements,
then the admission that form and so forth are distinct from the elements would contradict the admission that there are only the elements;
for in the case of the admission of mere elements, there can be no relationship of support and supported.
If cognition were dependent upon the primary elements (*bhūta*), then there would be the consequence of a multiplicity of realities;
for if there is no distinction [between them], the elements themselves would be a single unity due to their non-distinction from cognition.
Now, if one accepts that form and so forth arise based upon the primary elements, does this not contradict the refutation of a substratum?
The meaning of "derived" (upādāya) is not the sense of a substratum, but rather the sense of a cause.
Thus it is said: "The word 'derived' has the sense of a cause, and [the suffix] -ka has the sense of its own substratum. (160)
Because they exist inseparably, it is incorrect [to say] that the basis is otherwise;
for the meaning of "derived" (upādāya) is not the sense of a "basis," but rather the sense of a "cause. For it is thus:
The simultaneity of the cause with its effect is not perceived; for between two things existing at the same time, there can be no determination of their relationship as cause and effect.
Therefore, let there be the relation of container and contained, or let there be the relation of locus and located, or even the relation of cause and effect, between two things that are simultaneous.
Nevertheless, because they exist inseparably from their own substratum, it is so:
for if the restriction of form and the rest is by way of the relationship between substratum and that which rests upon it, then let it be understood that these [qualities] exist inseparably. (661)

If there were a relationship of container and contained between those two, then in the absence of the contained, the container would either perish or, if it did not perish, it would no longer be a container—just as it was not previously. Consequently, it follows that passion and the like must exist inseparably [from the elements].
Furthermore, this is stated according to the opponent's own admission, for there is no such thing as the "form of the great elements" apart from form and the other [sensory objects].

Furthermore, there is no inseparable existence of passion and the rest in anything at any time, because they exist [only occasionally], like the power of intoxication and so forth; if there were separation, it would not be a real entity.
Power is not a different thing from the entity; otherwise, the substratum would perish when the supported [power] perishes in its support.
If [the whole] remains undiminished while [a part] departs, then it is identical to that [part], for there is no distinction;
yet this is not so, because earth and consciousness are perceived as having distinct appearances.
The power of intoxication resides in a substance such as wine or liquor and exists inseparably from it.
Because [the effect] exists while the substance persists and because it arises after [the substance has undergone change],
for instance,
when a substance possessing astringent and sweet qualities comes into being, a prior latent power indeed manifests.
Furthermore, it departs again,
inseparable from the [mental] expression.

Nor is it the case that this [consciousness] exists without being supported by a form, because it is perceived as such [as having a form]. In that case, passion and the like would also be supported by the body alone.

That too is incorrect, because power is not a separate entity; for power is not something distinct from the element (bhūta), and the designation "the power of the substance" is merely a figurative expression based on the relationship between the thing designated and its designator, just as in the case of expressions such as "the body of a stone statue."
And how this is so will be demonstrated.

Now, if fire and the like possess no other power (śakti), then what is it that is obstructed by mantras, tantras, and so forth? It cannot be the person, for [the obstruction] occurs elsewhere than in the burning.
But if the power itself is negated, then its non-obstruction follows; thus, there would be burning elsewhere.
That is incorrect;
for if even *śakti* (potency) is denied, how can this distinction be established? Indeed, it cannot be maintained that "it does not exist in some cases, but exists in others.

[Objection: But surely, if there are many potencies, why should this distinction be impossible? [Response: It is not that the specific potency for burning is absent; rather, other [distinct] potencies are not being precluded.
Alternatively, if the combustibility itself is made something else, then it would not burn; yet it burns by means of something else, because its power is unimpeded.
This is not correct: from where have so many powers of that entity come?
2. They have arrived;
what indeed should be done by them such that there would be a need for them? 666

An entity does not depend [on anything else] for its existence; rather, those effects arise from the cause itself in that manner. If those potencies (*śakti*) did not exist, the various effects would not occur in their distinct divisions. (667) Indeed, the diversity of effects is not possible through a multiplicity of potencies, provided that fire and other such things are observed to be divided according to their specific functions, such as burning and so forth. (668) If that were the case, it would be impossible for fire and the like to have a single uniform nature; or, if such a thing were possible, then everything would always be combustible, or conversely, nothing at all would ever be combustible. (669)
Furthermore, the simultaneous existence and non-existence of a single entity are never found anywhere;
yet even that [objection] need not be avoided, because:
That too must be refuted:
just as this [cause] possesses various powers from a single cause alone, why is it not accepted that there are also various effects? Why is something unseen (adṛṣṭa) postulated? || 670 ||

And because a diversity of effects is observed, one might postulate a diversity of powers [in fire]. However, let those very things [the specific conditions] be what exist here; this is simply its restriction by nature (*svabhāvaniyama*).

(671) Such a thing is produced from its own causes such that, when conjoined with mantras and the like, it becomes capable of performing an effect through differentiation. Thus, [postulating] powers is redundant.
(672) Fire is a burner of everything, yet by virtue of its cause, it is deceptive [in its effects]; for that same fire, when conjoined with a mantra, becomes capable of burning for someone. (673)

The combustible object does not burn by means of that very form [of itself] by which it is combustible; it burns by means of another [form], because that [other form] arises from its own cause. (674) Thus, through the negation of [inherent] power (*śakti*), the relationship between substratum and dependent (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is impossible. Therefore, that observed example is not a proof for the matter at hand.
(675) Consequently, it is the entity itself that perishes.
But that which is dependent does not remain when it departs from its substrate while the substrate remains intact;
even so, one might argue that in this case too, it would be exactly the same for the primary elements (*bhūta*) and consciousness (*cetanā*).
To this, the following is the refutation:
Because of the distinction between the elements (*bhūta*) and consciousness (*cetana*), it is certainly not the case that consciousnesses are non-different from the elements like their potencies are;
if one asks why this is so:
Because one perceives distinct appearances,
a difference in appearance everywhere establishes a difference in the real entity; indeed,
no other means for establishing difference is observed.
The distinction of appearances.
2. If, for some [object], there is an appearance of non-difference even though it is perceivable by different sense organs and by different cognizers;
In that case, how can it be so? For it is the cognition itself, appearing in a specific form, that is the differentiator, not a difference in the cause of the cognition.
If, on the other hand, there is a difference in the cognition due to a difference in its cause, then that very difference in cognition is the differentiator; any further [cause] would be superfluous.

And in that regard, there is a distinct manifestation: for consciousness, it is the internal experience in the form of pleasure and so forth; for the object, it is not in the form of heat and so forth, but as something to be grasped.
Or rather, pleasure and the like are indeed of the nature of specific internal tangible objects; therefore, they consist of internal experience.
Sradva, Drowala, and so forth.
For whatever entity exists in a particular state is experienced exactly as it is, according to distinctions such as being distant or near, just like the perception of trees and other objects.
Indeed, an internal specific tangible object does not appear as distant;
therefore, because it resides within one part of the body, it is not experienced in the same way as an external tree.
This is not logical.
If that [atom] were indeed tangible, by what means would its perception occur? [If it were partless, there could be no contact with a single part of the self.]
If [cognition] were perceived by something else, it would follow that there is a difference in cognition;
this is the external reading: "bhinnajñānam. 778.6.
Now, if its self-cognition is not of the nature of the great elements, why is that form of self-cognition not likewise manifested by another? (779)
7. By means of one person [communicating] to another person—this is the external recension (bahiḥpāṭha).
likewise not so.
If [you argue that sensation arises] from the reality located within the abdomen, then there should be internal touch;
for it follows that one would experience sensation from the touch of internal organs,
and even the touch of an external embrace is of the nature of pleasure.
Furthermore, it would follow that one person could have a tactile cognition of another person; for when two people touch each other externally, let there be sensation in both,
whether as "another's form" or "another," but not as "one's own form"— how then can there be another?
10. Otherness [of the object] constitutes "externality"—that is, being outside (bahiḥ).
If that very same nature of the self, being touched by others outside the row— that is, from another continuum— becomes happy,
then it follows that the other person would likewise have that same cognition.
If it is argued that there is a realization of all aspects of the other [object],
then if this object were one, how could there not be a realization of all its aspects? On the other hand, if it is manifold, it must be divided according to each atom (*paramāṇu*).
If that were the case, then just as there is a perception of pleasure, so too would there be a perception of pain by someone within the differentiation of the atoms of pleasure;
yet not even a trace of another's pleasure exists,
and since there is perception only of those things experienced by oneself, a woman and a man would have identical experiences.
In the case of the perception of all [atoms], there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving multiple atoms;
[if] there were a multiplicity of pleasures, to whom [would they belong]?
13. There is no atom [as a substance] because there is no mutual contact [of parts], due to the absence of division.
For there is no association apart from those [elements], or if such association did exist, the cognition of their distinction would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that non-apprehension of distinction arises from conjunction (*saṃsarga*), then there is no apprehension of their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) either; for they appear as distinct from other entities through the differentiation of consciousness.
If, on the other hand, the whole (*avayavin*) were one and the same, then others would likewise perceive it as such.
Now, if another [opponent] is unable to accept this in its entirety, then the form [of the object] is not cognized;
this is merely an error, and even this error consists solely of a specific internal tangible form.

If one tangible object is perceived by one [sense] and another by another, and if pleasure and so forth were likewise perceived by another [sense], then there would be a single cognition [of them together]. If that were the case, [pleasure and so forth] would be distinct from [the tangible object].
Therefore,
from the connection of connections— that is, from the cognition of the distinct appearance of the external world and consciousness as separate entities.
Through the practice of contradictory properties, there exists a difference in intrinsic nature.

If it is maintained that the state of being pleasant belongs to that which is touched by another who is in a particular state of mind (*dharmāvastha*), then why does that state belong to the object itself as it is being touched? (682) If you say that "desirability" (*kāntatva*) is not the cause [of its being pleasant], then what is this "desirability" thought to be? One thing is desirable to someone due to their own fortune (*svabhāgadheya*), while another is desirable to someone else for a different reason. (683)
Karma alone, by virtue of its desirability, stands within the path of worldly usage under the term "fortune" (bhāgya).
Furthermore, no specific benefit is observed here in this present life.
Thus, even though there is no difference [between the two states], the path of distinction regarding consciousness is established; what is the use of further prolixity here concerning the next world?
Or, if its beauty arises from being produced by an instrument, it would be perceived by another as well, provided that it is not merely consciousness itself.
Now, it is postulated that [cognition] is contained within the body of the perceiver. But how can that which is perceived as being outside [the body] be contained within the body?

(687) Furthermore, because the manifestation of form is not apprehended by another, cognition—which is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—must be distinct from the primary elements (*bhūta*).
(688) Whether in a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) or otherwise, it is not perceived by another.
Therefore, that is indeed self-cognizing knowledge;
there would be a distinction [of it] from the elements.
If it is argued that [the self] is not perceived as being inside another's body, then it would follow that one's own body is also unperceived;
furthermore, if it were merely inside the body, how could there be movement? This is like the conceptualization of another object situated in darkness. (689)
One perceives the body without conceptual construction, and consciousness without the body; therefore, the rule of simultaneous perception does not prove their identity.
Alternatively, it might be argued: "Let it be that they are distinct;
nevertheless, the body alone is the cause of that [consciousness]. Therefore, pleasure and so forth do not arise in dependence upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and thus they are ultimately real."
Since the body also arises from semen and other such factors, there is no world beyond;
for [existence] is exhausted through the mere succession of this world alone, and thus there would be no state of transmigration. To this he says:
"And as long as the body undergoes transformation, the mind would remain of a similar nature. (163)
To what extent can conceptual construction (vikalpa) be dependent upon an external object, as form and other [sensory objects] are?
For when the body is the cause and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of passion and so forth, then the mind would necessarily be of an identical form prior to any modification of the body,
because the cause, the intrinsic nature, and the basis are identical.
Otherwise, the relationship of substratum and superstratum, as well as the relationship of cause and effect, would be untenable due to a failure to conform to positive and negative concomitance;
for the color and other qualities residing in the body do not remain dissimilar when the body itself is uniform.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the specific nature [of the cognition] is designated through the successive encounter with various objects,
that too is not tenable;
for what dependence on an object does mental consciousness or pleasure and so forth possess?
It has been stated that [the world] arises merely from the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā),
because there is no modification of the body and so forth.
7. Because it does not conform to positive and negative concomitance, when [the cognition] arises independent of the body, it is the cause that awakens the latent impression (vāsanā). 164
"Knowledge might belong to someone, about something, at some time; therefore, [the world] is not nothing. Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣāntara.
9. [Regarding] a certain alternative reading: for if the body were the cause, the aforementioned fault would indeed persist;

however, when it is instead accepted that the cognition of someone—namely, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—arises like a birth, depending not on the body as its cause, but on some cause that awakens the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, for that reason, there may be some degree of knowledge even when the body is unmodified; however, this is not due to the body being the cause [of knowledge].
Thus, knowledge arises from knowledge alone, and not from the body; such is the nature of transmigratory existence.
The fault follows because [it] does not depend on the body.
kāyam anapekṣya.
12. He also states another reason for the state of being in saṃsāra with respect to the aggregates (skandha).
And because consciousness does not take up [the seeds of] further consciousness, it is established that even the appearance of form [is devoid of self].
Even the manifestation of form.
If it is claimed that every object is connected to the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*),
then what person other than this beast of a Sāṃkhya would venture to speak with shamelessness,
saying, "There exist a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass," when such a thing has never been seen before? (166)
That form which is seen as having arisen was not seen previously.
Even if the cause were dispersed in a hundred ways, how could that [form] exist?

For, due to the deficiency or non-deficiency of the cognition, one necessarily observes the deficiency or otherwise of the subsequent cognition, because it invariably follows the modification of that [cause].
It is established that there is a future world because consciousness does not arise from a body devoid of the appropriation of consciousness,
and because it would otherwise follow that passion and the other afflictions would arise simultaneously.
It is not born;
furthermore, even if it were the case that consciousness arises solely from consciousness, nevertheless, the existence of a future world would not be established.
Because every entity possesses the capacity for cognition,
and because such a capacity that has not yet initiated its effect is not the "other world" (paraloka)—

how is it that this Sāṃkhya doctrine is accepted by you, who pride yourselves on being the crest-jewels of all logicians? Only a Sāṃkhya beast, shameless and taking refuge solely in scripture, would endeavor to speak in such a manner.

But one who possesses a sense of shame does not speak thus; for a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass has never been seen before, nor is it within the scope of another's speech, because of its very nature.
2. But this is not the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
Indeed, the form of curds and the like that was previously perceived cannot be seen [again] once it has been utterly scattered; how then can there be a cause for it?
(691) If you say, "It exists in another form," do not shout such nonsense! For if it exists as a form other than consciousness, how could it be known? (692)

[The opponent] says: "If it is maintained that [the self] arises from the appropriation of the consciousnesses of the mother and so forth, then its excellence as a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) would necessarily follow in every respect. (693)

Furthermore, if it is claimed that the impression (saṃskāra) of the father and others [is transferred] to the son, then there would be no universal persistence of an impression in every immediate [successor].
T.
From that consciousness, [arises] a consciousness belonging to its own continuum; thus, the next world is established.
Furthermore, if there were no prior existence [in a previous life], the consequence would follow that passion and other afflictions arise without restriction.

(168) If there were no world beyond, then there would be the appearance of beings who did not previously exist; in that case, there would be no regularity regarding passion and the rest—someone might even be devoid of passion.

But when there is arrival from another birth, then craving alone is considered the cause of a living being's birth; therefore, one who is free from passion does not take birth, because in the absence of passion and the like, there is no birth. (6) Continuously—externally.
If everyone possesses passion and so forth because they do not transcend the nature of the primary elements (*bhūtātmatā*),

and if that nature of the primary elements were the cause of passion and so forth, and it does not depart from them— then, due to the absence of any deficiency in the cause, there would be no deficiency in passion and so forth;
if this is the case, for this very reason...
If everything were of the nature of the elements, everyone would have the same degree of passion; this would not be the case if it were due to a specific excellence of the elements.
For if there were no mutual distinction among beings, then everyone would possess an identical passion;
yet such a distinction does exist, and therefore not everyone possesses an identical passion.
If this is so, [then...]
And it is not the case that there is no such distinction among living beings, even though their status as sentient creatures is undifferentiated, for this distinction exists based upon its support.
Because those [elements] exist through the decrease or increase of that [passion], one should cause them to diminish; for external elements are the generators of passion.
170.10 T. bhūtāni rāgajanakāni-bahiḥ.

9. Because of the existence of passion and so forth—regarding what was stated previously by the opponent that there is no restriction regarding passion and so forth: indeed, the aggregate of earth and so forth is free from passion;
however, could any living being ever be free from passion? No.
If the objection is that "just as living beings do not become non-living, so too passionlessness does not [become non-passion]," then, if that were the case,
just as livingness is not distinguished [among individuals], so too would passionateness not be; thus, everyone would be equally passionate, just like their state of being alive.
If some living being were one way and another were different— such that one were passionate while the other were not—

and yet the state of being a living being (*prāṇitā*) remained identical while passion and the rest were distinct, then, because the distinction arises from a specific excellence of the elements (*bhūtātiśaya*), there would likewise be an absolute diminution even in the absence of decrease and excellence; thus, one would become free from passion (*vītarāga*).
1. Like that which possesses diminution and like that which possesses excellence— externally, it may be that although the cause is characterized by such increase and decrease,
nevertheless, the uniformity of the cause of passion and so forth is not diminished.

To this it is replied: If, despite the difference [between individuals], there is no destruction of the common nature that serves as the cause for passion and so forth, then passion would be identical everywhere, because its cause possesses that same common nature. (171)
For if that similarity which exists due to causes such as passion does not diminish,
then the cause of passion is indeed its generality;
and for the sake of the effect of passion being produced by a general cause, there is a similarity in the nature of the cause.
It is logical that the effect also possesses a similar purpose;
however, if the effect were dissimilar despite the similarity of the cause— due to its association with degrees of intensity—
then it would not truly be the effect of that cause at all.
Because there is no conformity with its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),

therefore, wherever there is a gradation (*tāratamya*), even absolute non-existence would not deviate from it— either due to the presence of a gradation in diminution or due to its equality, like qualities such as whiteness. What is the reason?

For there is nowhere any gradation in the cognition of "cow" arising from objects of the same nature—whether in the case of earth and so forth, or here in the case of being a living creature and so on.
Indeed, the cognition of "cow" arises from that which possesses an identical essence. (172)
Now, if there is no distinction regarding the state of being alive among living beings, then there would likewise be no one who distinguishes between their passion and other mental states.

Furthermore, this [nature] does not possess degrees of intensity through the exclusion of that form or by any other means—such as "cow," "more cow-like," or "most cow-like"—according to the Lokāyata perspective; nor is there [such gradation] regarding earth and so forth, such as "living being," "more living being," or "most living being. Therefore, from an identical cause, there is identity, whereas in the case of diminution, there is absolute cessation.

If it is argued: "The exclusion of that form (tad-rūpa-vyāvṛtti) occurs even from other things that possess a common nature; furthermore, this cognition of 'cow'—as in 'cow,' 'better cow,' or 'best cow'—does not involve a gradation [of the universal itself]. Or, with respect to the Lokāyata view, one might say 'living being,' 'better living being,' or 'best living being' regarding earth and so forth. Likewise, although there is a gradation in heat, fire is never non-hot; the same applies here. [Response: No, because there is no denial of the difference between fire and its heat. (Verse 173)

There is indeed a gradation of heat in fire, yet it is not impossible for heat to exist in its entirety; nevertheless, it is not the case that passion and the like are entirely impossible [to exist in their totality] in the same way. This is because passion and the like are not distinct from the body, whereas here there is no difference between fire and heat, since fire is designated by the very term "heat. If heat were absent, that which is called fire would not exist at all.
But it is not the case that, in the absence of passion and so forth, that which is real ceases to exist; however,
if another substratum (dharmin) consisting of a collection of elements is postulated and heat is imagined as its property (dharma),
then at the stage of intense heat, that heat would indeed be annihilated.

Now, if it is postulated that the flame is the substratum (dharmin) and heat is its property (dharma), and that this [property] is not interrupted even when there is a gradation [of intensity], such a rebuttal by the opponent is also untenable.
3. Because of the designation as fire.
In that case, during the state of the undesirable consequence, the very earth and so forth would undergo the destruction of their cause due to that heat.
Through the power of mantras, tantras, and so forth, it might be that a jewel exists without the heat of its flame; yet that it is seen without heat is not logical. (695)
1. Fire is not [established] by means of the flame itself, nor does it possess the nature of a substratum (dharmin) with respect to heat, because of its non-separation [from it].

For that which has the color and shape of a flame cannot possibly possess heat; therefore, it is not logical for it to be the subject (*dharmin*) [of the argument]. Consequently, this is not a valid example:
a flame does not exist without heat, nor does heat exist without a flame.

Therefore, it is not logically consistent for that [heat] to be the property-bearer (dharmin), nor does the relationship of property and property-bearer (dharmadharmin) exist between a flame and its heat when they are not absolutely inseparable;
thus, the reason is qualified.
The qualities of another existing entity, which experience degrees of intensity, are sometimes obstructed when that [entity] undergoes differentiation, just like white and other colors.
(174) Those qualities belonging to another which exist while experiencing degrees of intensity are not subject to obstruction anywhere.
Just as in the case of jars and the like, there are qualities such as whiteness;
for indeed, apart from the form of whiteness and so forth, what other cloth or similar object exists,
such that there could be the destruction of the whiteness and other qualities belonging to that other existing thing?
This is true; nevertheless, jars and the like are of the nature of tangible objects and not of the nature of specific colors,
because a cloth exists even in the absence of those [tangible objects].
Therefore, the meaning of "of another" is as follows:

for that which continues by way of a continuum, those things which possess the nature of cessation and the nature of arising—even though they possess the nature of absolute cessation—are like white [cloths] and so forth; such is the sense of the sentence.
Not those [objects] such as cloth, etc. (T. 3).
Cloth and so forth;
5. T. [End]
The specific color of the cloth.
of the cloth.

Alternatively, if it is argued that although there is a variation in the arising and passing away of heat while firelessness persists, it is not so in the case of passion and the like because they are subject to total destruction, and therefore their power is not destroyed— this is not correct, because power is not a separate entity from its object.
It is not merely passion and the like that constitute power (*śakti*),
since even power is observed to be subject to occasional cessation;
for this very reason, he says:
7. There is no fixed rule regarding the arising and passing away of heat, as in the case of form and so forth, because they are inseparable from the primary elements.
If it were identical to them, then it would follow that passion and the rest must arise simultaneously [with the elements] (175).

Indeed, passion and the rest do not arise from the elements as inseparable entities like color, taste, and so forth; for the elements exist even in the absence of passion and the rest, whereas color and the rest do not exist in the absence of the elements.
Now, if you argue that the same applies there as well...
That too is incorrect,
because it would entail that passion and the other afflictions arise simultaneously with the body; thus, they would not be distinct from the primary elements.
Even the manifestation of form does not exist; nor is there a constant coexistence of passion and the like with the body;

and for one who asserts that the great elements alone exist, form and the other aggregates cannot be distinct from the elements, as that would entail the consequence of a multiplicity of ultimate principles.
Therefore, arising together is inseparable because it has the object as its cause.
9. Non-difference from those [objects]—externally (T).
Furthermore, according to your view, because power (*śakti*) is distinct [from its substrate], and because power itself is not [identical to] the seed and so forth— such as oil—
there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that reality (*tattva*) is manifold. — [Thus says] Bāhaḥ.

12. The Cārvāka says: Whosoever has a misconception regarding this world, he desires another misconception regarding the next world—if it is argued that [the object] might sometimes be non-existent due to the absence of external objects, that is not so.
Furthermore, because they are objects of conceptual construction, objects are not restrictive;
nor is there a restriction of passion and so forth due to the absence of a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).
Alternatively, there would be the arising of all cognitions at all times, since their causes are present.
Indeed, attachment and the other [afflictions] do not belong to that same mental continuum as their objects,
because they are experienced to arise even in the absence of those objects;
furthermore, a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) is not accepted [for them].
Consequently, because of their absence, there would never be a non-arising of passion and the other afflictions;
therefore, the body would either invariably coexist with each individual affliction such as passion,
or else all afflictions such as passion would invariably coexist with the body.
If it is argued that for all [beings], due to the proximity of the body,
there is a specific transformation of the body itself by which there is no coexistence with passion and the like—
should this be so?
connected with conformity 2 T.

Since there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*), how could it undergo such a transformation by which it becomes that [effect]? If you say it arises from "some cause or other," then it would occur at all times.

If you say this is not so because it is not observed [to happen always], then nothing at all would have a cause. Smoke might arise even from non-fire; why would it not be possible for it to arise from everything?

For it could indeed be said that there is some transformation of that [cause]; yet even for an entity that lacks a cause, there would be a restriction of place and so forth. (699) It can also be said that no such restriction is observed there; if one were to embrace whatever is merely seen in every respect, (700) then non-duality itself would be perceived here, and worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would collapse. If it is postulated because worldly transaction cannot be abandoned, (701) [then...]

Otherwise, how could this conventional usage regarding the next world and so forth exist? For just as every conventional usage is carried out by means of inference, so too must it be in the case of the next world and such. How then can its reality be denied?
Nor is there a distinction based on being an object of cognition, nor is there a difference in the form of blue and so forth.

Another objects, setting aside the [previous] view: "Externally, [an object] is not established by perception as having a prior-posterior sequence; therefore, all distinction is established through inference, just like worldly practice. 704.
Therefore, no one is capable of living by abandoning inference;
hence, this has been answered.
Therefore,

those fools who, having set aside the perceived object, postulate another unperceived one, abandon the very lump [of reality] and vainly destroy their own hand. Discernment regarding what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted does not arise from the functioning of the senses.

5. There is no discernment of the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Why? Because [the object] is not "to be abandoned" merely by virtue of being perceived; or because its state of being "to be adopted" precludes its being "to be abandoned. (707)

The determination of what is to be adopted (*upādeya*) follows from the opposite of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). For those who seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), purposeful action is always the criterion for adoption.

(708) That [purposeful action] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, for those desiring to engage in activity, there is no cognition of the state of being adoptable through direct perception.

(709) Direct perception does not know a future purposeful action, nor does it know that which is unperceived. Furthermore, since the negation of "being abandonable" is itself an abandonment, how could there be [an absence of] desire for the abandonable? (710)
Regarding the cessation of what is to be abandoned (*heyākṣādatyaya*):

the realization that "this object does not exist here" is not [attained] through direct perception (*akṣata*). For when two things are both perceived directly, there is no comprehension of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. || 711 ||

In this case as well, the previous logical argument applies by way of reversal: if everything were perceived through direct perception due to extreme habituation, then there could be no habituation regarding what is not perceived; thus, there would be a mutual dependence. As long as there is no direct perception, there is no habituation, and consequently, there is no state of being perceived. (712–713)
As long as there is no familiarity, there is no arising of direct perception through practice.
If mere direct perception were the means of valid cognition in this case, then there would be no discrimination between what is to be abandoned and its opposite;
rather, it would be a mere awareness of the thing's own nature, and from that, the consequence of non-duality (advaita) would follow.
Relying upon inference, there is the classification of what is to be abandoned and so forth; this is established for conventional practice, and thus no further ultimate reality is sought.
(715) Now, if one relies upon non-duality to deny the existence of the next world, let that [denial] also be carried out; it does not stop at this much alone.
(716) In that case, even this world would not exist, and consequently, there would be no such thing as nihilism; for when the mind withdraws from everything, that is precisely what is logical. (717)
Now, this very regard for things in this world is nothing but delusion. Desiring the destruction even of this, who would seek another form of delusion?

(718) From where does this delusion arise? If it is beginningless and endless, then that is simply what is known as the "other world"; what else is being said in vain? (719) Or if this [delusion] is indeed causeless, then let everything be causeless. That being the case, you have merely repeated in vain what was already stated by the nihilist. (720)

If this [reason] that has been stated is not useful anywhere, what is the point of seeking it? Or, if it has some purpose, let its status as a reason reside in that very [purpose]. (721) Furthermore, if opponents raise an objection in this manner: "What is the point of establishing this [reason], if it is not a reason for anything? (722)

Since this [world] is produced solely by ignorance (*avidyā*), whose fault is it? If ignorance is not eradicated, then the teachings of others are in vain; yet if ignorance is eradicated, the teachings of others are useless. Or, if [the world] has ignorance as its cause, there must be a beginningless course of ignorance.

This being so, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is established beyond dispute. Ignorance is nothing other than conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that too arises from a preceding conceptual construction.
This beginningless continuity of conceptual construction shines forth;
therefore, pleasure and the like are brought about solely by the maturation of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and do not exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
Consequently, in the ultimate sense, everything is indeed suffering.
(d) The truth of suffering has four aspects: therein, suffering is impermanent because it is occasionally perceived, and it is the basis of defects.
Suffering exists because it is subject to causes; it is neither the self nor presided over by one.
There is no presiding agent without a cause, and how could that which is eternal be a producer? (177)
The reason—according to an alternative reading—is that therefore many things do not arise from a single cause at different times.
The Truth of Suffering has four aspects: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Therefore, it is impermanent because it is perceived only at certain times;
for that which is eternal is not impermanent by virtue of being perceived eternally,
nor is it logical for that which is eternal and always perceived to be perceived only occasionally.
Because there is a contradiction between the perceivable and other natures due to their existing through mutual exclusion,
and because it is established that "it" is [defined] precisely by its perceivability;
yet, it is not possible to perceive everything at all times, since that which is perceived sequentially cannot be eternal, nor can sequence exist within unity.
Because that which possesses succession does not appear as a unity, perception does not operate;
and in the absence of that [perception], inference is also absent.
Since inference is preceded by direct perception, if it were not preceded by direct perception, there would be the consequence of a blind tradition;
therefore, the aggregates of cyclic existence are impermanent.
Furthermore, passion and the other defects are suffering because they provide a basis for further faults, because they are subject to causal power, and because they are constrained by causes.
According to the principle that "all that is dependent on another is suffering," and because of the word "and" [in the verse], it should be understood that [suffering] arises solely from dependence;
it is neither of the nature of a self nor presided over by a non-self.
Since that which lacks a purpose cannot be a presiding agent,
there must necessarily be a presiding agent who possesses a purpose, because purpose is the cause of causality.
And if the aggregates were identical with the self, they would be eternal; yet that which is eternal cannot be a producer, because the existence of a non-producer cannot be apprehended,
and moreover, cognition— which is manifold and occurs at different times— cannot arise from a single [cause] due to its eternity.
Nor is it perceived as having the self as its presiding controller; rather, what is perceived is the form of the aggregates and the aggregates of mental formations.
3 T. mātrani° 4 T.
Nor is it apprehended by means of a self.
Since that [body] is impermanent,
how could causes that are themselves unguided proceed toward their own effects?
Therefore, a guiding agent is inferred.
It is not [the case that it arises] merely from the presiding influence of impermanent volition, because [the process] is completed [by that];
and since volition is beginningless, therefore...
From the non-arising of the effect, even when other causes are present, there would be an inference of another cause; this is not possible in the case of eternal things. (176)
If other causes, even when combined, are incapable of producing an effect, then there must exist yet another cause whose absence prevents the effect from arising;
however, this is not the case,
because [the production of the effect] is established solely through the specific capacity of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Furthermore, there is never an absence of those that are eternal and all-pervading, such that their non-existence could be perceived through the absence [of effects]. If it were the case that [an effect] arises through mere positive concomitance (anvaya) alone, then everything—including space and the like—would become a controller, since even in their presence the causes proceed toward their own effects; for they too are identical in being eternal and all-pervading. If this is argued:
That very [self] is not established as being all-pervading and eternal;
because of its absence, it is conceptually constructed.

Even that which is non-pervasive and eternal would possess causality everywhere; for a cause is not seen to be a cause only through proximity, but is observed to be a cause even when far away. Even sound and the like, though located in a distant place, bring about their own effects. Therefore, by mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*), everything would be a cause.
(kha) The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)

(a) The fourfold nature of origination establishes that this suffering has a cause, because it occurs only occasionally; for that which is causeless and independent of anything else must either exist eternally or not exist at all. (180)

2. Because it does not depend on external factors, the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) is also fourfold: by way of cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), and condition (*pratyaya*).
Among these, "cause" is [defined] by the exclusion of non-cause and by the exclusion of a single [sole] cause.

"Non-origin" (*aprabhava*) refers to the condition (*pratyaya*), which is called "origin" (*prabhava*) because suffering arises from it; this is stated in order to exclude the notion of inefficacy and to emphasize its predominance, thereby establishing that there exists a cause for suffering therein.
For it is not observed that anything occasional is joined with another cause; for a thing that lacks a cause must either exist eternally or else not exist at all.
Indeed, as the absence of causes increases, so does its permanence, as in the case of the hair-visions of one suffering from ophthalmia, which occur even without an external object.

The eternally existent nature of the *dharmadhātu*, which is accessible through self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and characterized by its non-occasional occurrence, is seen to be without cause.
[Objection: In this regard, a challenge is raised concerning the son of a barren woman and similar things, which are eternal due to the absence of any causal essence.
"Just as there is no cause for sharpness and so forth in thorns and the like,

so too this [world] would be without a cause," say some proponents of the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetukavādin*); they maintain that the form of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is not produced by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

It is precisely the particularities themselves that are produced through their association with specific places, times, and conditions; in this regard, the causelessness of particularities is observed,
for when ironworkers and others fashion things such as arrows, needles, spears, or cushions, they do not produce the nature of iron and so forth, but rather produce sharpness itself.
Furthermore, the earth-nature (pṛthivītva) and so forth of iron and other substances is not produced by others,
because it is their very nature as iron and so on that is brought about;
moreover, even in the absence of blacksmiths and the like, the sharpness of thorns and such exists, even when they themselves are absent.
This is not merely the state of having indeterminate causes or being causeless;
likewise, other specific factors that produce the diversity of the world would also be causeless—
what contradiction is there in this?
That too is incorrect;
for this very [point] is... [incomplete].

"That in the existence of which there is the birth of something, or in the modification of which there is its modification—that they call its cause; and that [cause] exists even for those [atoms]. This is the intended meaning here.
If only the particulars (*viśeṣa*) are produced, they cannot be without a cause;
for indeed, the curvature and sharpness of the thorns of the *badarī* tree do not exist apart from the *badarī* thorn itself.
Since they conform to its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they are its effects, and thus they are not without a cause.

If it is argued that [the world] is likewise produced by a blacksmith, and thus there is no deviation [from the rule], that too is not correct; because we observe purposeful action, there must be an intelligent cause. In this way, God's status as creator is established, and consequently, there is no state of being without a cause.

Because of that very same illustration provided by the jujube thorns and so forth, there is no assumption of a specific distinction [between them]; if not, then let that distinction be based on a cause. (732) If no distinction whatsoever is perceived between the jujube seed and other things such as ironworkers, then no distinction exists at all.
(733) For a distinction is not apprehended by mere observation alone; if it were, that very thing would result in non-duality, and that very thing would be without a cause. (734)
Therefore, those specific qualities [of the object] must have a cause; for the status of being a "specific quality" cannot be established for that which is devoid of a cause.

(735) Therefore, whether it be the distinctions or the existence of external objects, everything must be caused; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. Indeed, if something arises only when another exists, then that other is its cause. [If you argue that] visual perception has touch as its cause, this leads to an absurdity; for if touch were absent, [visual perception] would lack its own nature. Thus, that [argument] is false.

Because they depend on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), visible form (*rūpa*) and tactile sensation (*sparśa*) are inseparable from one another; therefore, in the absence of that [complex], there is no perception [of form].
For in that case, without tactile sensation, visible form itself does not exist;
however, if visible form were to exist, there would necessarily be perception.
Nor is causality established by such a negative concomitance (vyatireka) alone; rather, having demonstrated the positive form [of the relationship],
one must demonstrate that [the effect] is absent when touch is absent, whether through perception or otherwise.
Because contact is the cause of visible form, it possesses the status of a causal condition (*nimittatā*) with respect to vision.

(183) Since they exist simultaneously and are never dissociated from one another, the primary elements (*bhūta*) that constitute contact are the cause of the visible forms derived from them (*upādāyarūpa*). Therefore, even though contact is not the direct cause, it is indeed a cause of vision through a mediated succession; thus, the reason does not occur in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and there is no deviation.
In this way, the absence of a cause has first been refuted; thus, the single aspect "by way of a cause" is established.
"Origination" (samudaya) refers to the second aspect;
by the negation of [theories of] eternal [causes], there is no possibility of [origination] from God or the like.
Even if suffering were to have a cause, since it would not arise from such [eternal causes], the determination of the aspect of origination occurs through the negation of a single, eternal cause.
If the cause were a single, eternal entity, it would follow from its independence that it could not admit any specific modification, for that which is eternal cannot have qualities added to it;
furthermore, the refutation of such eternal principles as *pradhāna* and the like has already been established.

If it is asked, "Why is this so?"—because of incapacity; since there is a deficiency in the power for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity, there is no state of being a sovereign.
That third aspect belongs to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone.
He says this very thing:
"Therefore, the grasping for the desire for existence is not a [valid] reason, because it is produced by men's hope for attaining a particular place. (184)
No other cause, whether karma or anything else, possesses such power;
indeed, neither the body of karma nor ignorance is the "source" (prabhava),
which is synonymous with the "efficient cause."
Because birth is absent in the absence of craving, and because it is observed that birth originates from craving—
which is designated by the term "appropriation" (parigraha) or "clinging" (āgraha)— this appropriation, brought about by the craving for acquisition, constitutes this coming together with birth.
Therefore, its origin is craving; indeed, the desire for existence in the form of a longing for future birth—
and not merely a longing for a specific location and so forth— is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
For it was said by the Blessed One:
