"In that regard, what is the noble truth of the origin? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there."
Namely: craving for existence, craving for non-existence, and craving for form.
This is not a contradiction, because:
In the *Dīrghāgama*,
it is stated that there is the occurrence of pleasure and pain for one who desires what is acquired and what is unacquired.
Furthermore, since you maintain that living beings possess the desire for sensual existence (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) and the desire for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*):

this craving for places, requisites, and so forth is the desire for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*). It is the craving for becoming, accompanied by delight and passion, which finds gratification here and there; all of this is indeed the craving for sensual pleasure (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*).
That craving for places and so forth is the craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), and that is the desire for existence (*bhava-icchā*).
That which takes the form of a prayer for heaven is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*);
that which is the desire for separation from suffering is craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction at all in the teaching on the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

There is no contradiction with the scriptures, because self-attachment is the cause that operates everywhere for one who perceives happiness in what is not happiness; therefore, craving is the basis of existence. (186)

Based on the support of the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-grasping), the series of moments of consciousness (*cittamālā*) is superimposed as a unity. The attachment toward that [series] which operates everywhere—toward places, requisites, and so forth—is the cause, because it functions for one who is afflicted by a cognitive distortion (*cittaviparyaya*) regarding what is ultimately not happiness as being happiness and the like. Therefore, it is the basis for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
For one who has not seen [the truth], there is no connection to such functioning anywhere; otherwise, through the application of compassion, it is not a cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
For this very reason, because craving is merely a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) with respect to the process of setting [the body] in motion,
it possesses the status of a condition (*pratyaya*) alone and not that of a material cause (*upādāna*); in that case, the mind itself is the material cause.

Its condition (*pratyaya*) is sometimes thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) and sometimes compassion (*karuṇā*); by this it is stated that [the body] arises through these conditions. Now, even though it is a condition, thirst is not the [sole] condition; rather, it is the body. Therefore, one who is attached to the body is not free from passion (*vītarāga*).
The teachers declare this very point: "Because one who is dispassionate is not seen to be born, and because passion is not seen in one who is bodiless, passion arises from the body. (187)
2. Regarding birth:

Just as the birth of one who is free from passion is not observed, passion is therefore the cause of birth; for this very reason, the body is logically the cause of passion and the like, since passion is not observed in one who is bodiless.
To this it is replied: birth occurs even without passion;
however, its becoming an object of delight is brought about by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Thus, because it is merely a cause for a specific distinction, it is said to have "craving alone as its condition."

Thus, if the body as well were merely a condition (*pratyaya*), and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) alone were the substantial cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of passion and the rest, then it would be shown that what is accepted [by us] is indeed subsumed [within that]. However, [the opponent] says: "The object (*nimitta*) is accepted [as a cause], but the substantial cause is rejected.
Yet, by seeking this argument, he contradicts his own position. (188)
The body, too, by following improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) of passion, is regarded as its cause;
at times it becomes a cause for the awakening of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), just like an object.
This reasoning, moreover, establishes that the body is also a cause of passion.

Therefore, because they are mutual causes, birth arises from such an beginningless complex of conditions; thus, the establishment of successive births has been discussed by the brilliant [author] following the deliberations of the Cārvākas. But surely, it is only a substance possessing qualities that is asserted;
therefore, these two [birth and qualities] cannot be mutual causes.
3. If it is argued that there is coexistence with birth because passion is seen in those who are born, [it is not so]. || 189 ||

Although it was previously established that [ignorance] is a cause for the arising of similar types, ignorance was not mentioned; rather, craving alone is [the cause], because it impels the continuum toward existence. (190b) Craving and karma are the origin of birth.
For if passion and the like coexist with birth, and thus passion and the like are not the cause of the body, then the body is also not the cause of passion and the like;
yet they cannot be without a cause.
Therefore, it is established that passion and the like are produced by causes of their own kind—this is the intended conclusion.
But is it not the case that craving alone is not the sole cause?
Since ignorance, craving, and karma are all three causes,
how can the definition of the truth of origination be "craving itself which finds delight here and there"?
This is not so; even though it is a cause, it is not the immediate cause,
for craving alone is the immediate cause because it impels the continuum in saṃsāra.
For even when delusion (moha) and karma exist, there is no impeller [of action] in the absence of craving (tṛṣṇā);
nor does even one who is mistaken engage in activity without craving for union.
Therefore, he said:
Because of its immediacy, even karma does not exist when that [dispassion] is present, since it is impossible;
and because of this, one who is free from craving abandons even acquired karma such as kingship and the like.
Is it not the case that the intellect follows karma? Thus, renunciation is itself a specific kind of karma by which one disregards what has been brought forth.

Furthermore, if it is argued that rebirth is impossible for liberated souls, we reply that even for them, liberation consists precisely in the exhaustion of karma; otherwise, it would be non-existent.
To this it is replied:
If the exhaustion of karma for one who is free from craving occurs, then it is only logical to say that craving is the primary cause in this matter.
(737) But if craving exists, there can be no exhaustion of this karma.
For one who possesses craving, there will indeed arise further and further karma.
Thus, the Noble Truth characterized by origination has been explained in its four aspects;
now, he explains the Truth of Cessation in its four aspects, stating that the cessation of that suffering is possible.
(ga) The Truth of Cessation:
(a) If there were no transmigrating being, liberation would be established [as permanent]; however, that [liberation] would not be ultimate, because obstacles to the cause and so forth are possible.

"There would be no liberation because of being subject to saṃsāra; [this is] not accepted [by us], nor is it established. (191) Regarding the four aspects—cessation (*nirodha*), peace (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and escape (*niḥsaraṇa*)—the state of cessation is indeed asserted against one who claims that cessation itself does not exist, for others maintain that even for those who are liberated, the arising of passion and so forth occurs.
By negating that [notion], there is the aspect of "peace" (*śāntata*);
furthermore, by negating the possibility of liberation being something other than this, there is the aspect of "excellence" (*praṇītata*);
and having rejected the idea that even one who is liberated might become liberated again, there is the fourth aspect, "escape" (*niḥsaraṇata*).
That first aspect is not absolute, nor is it non-absolute; it ceases,
yet because of the state of saṃsāra, there is no fault of liberation being impossible.
Because it is accepted [as a goal]:
for there is no liberation for anyone;
indeed, for one who is bound, there is no liberation.
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature, there is no bondage even for one who is liberated,
since his intrinsic nature is eternally liberated; rather,
while the mere continuum of mind remains impure, a purified subsequent portion arises from it through a particularity of causal conditions.
Setting that aside, transmigratoriness is unestablished for one who is completely pure;

nor does any transmigrator exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, because moments do not transmigrate and because the continuum does not exist ultimately. Therefore, the reason "because of being a transmigrator" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Nor does a liberator exist for whom there is liberation;
that is the ultimate aspect.
not in T. 3 T. not in T.
In that regard, an objection may be raised by another: "If the bound one is not the liberated one, then bondage belongs to one and liberation to another;
hunger would belong to one and satisfaction to another."

One person experiences the suffering of medical treatment, another is free from disease, yet another is beset by afflictions, while another experiences the bliss of heaven; one is devoted to the study of the scriptures, and another has mastered them. In that case, for what reason would a discerning person apply themselves to such efforts?
In this regard, the meditative concentration is as follows:
because as long as there is no loss of affection for oneself, one will suffer distress. (162)

Having placed [the world] in such suffering, one does not remain at ease; therefore, effort must be exerted for the sake of abandoning false superimposition, even though there is no liberator. (193b) The continued existence of liberated ones in saṃsāra—
Regarding those who have not yet abandoned passion in their current state, [the action] may be performed out of compassion or by means of karma;
this is the intended meaning here.
If, first of all, this is said with reference to those who perceive reality (tattvadarśin), [then it is as follows].
In that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established,
for they do not engage in any activity nor exert effort anywhere,
according to the statement: "The very dharmas themselves are to be abandoned."

Now, for people such as ourselves at that time, because of the conceit of its unity, it is that very same [self] which is bound and that very same one who attains liberation; thus, these two belong to a single locus. For conventional usage does not proceed merely by the fact that no entity exists in the ultimate sense, since conventional usage depends upon cognition.
For instance,
from the perspective of ultimate reality, the snake is not the object to be avoided; rather, [it is the appearance].
The object of liberation by means of that [wisdom] is the snake; there exists a real entity. 4 T. vastvastī°
Now, even if there were oneness conventionally, nevertheless, let there be conventional discourse;
however, since ultimate oneness is absent, how could there be ultimate discourse?
Therefore, its oneness exists conventionally; that conventional usage is also merely conventional. It does not exist in reality; thus, even the conventional usage regarding oneness is non-ultimate.
Indeed, even with effort, there is nowhere anything other than the thing's own nature; since the relation of cause and effect [is not distinct from it], there is no room for objection.
"What is this cleverness that asks, 'Why should this effect arise from this [cause]?'? For a discerning person, there is never any engagement or withdrawal [from action] in such a manner.

This is because the perception of a temporal sequence (paurvāparya) is not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and furthermore, since a thing lasts for only a single moment, engagement is impossible anywhere.
Therefore, there is no effort at all, and consequently, no delusion regarding anything. (741–742)
Even granting [the opponent's position], it is said:
"It is a state," and so forth;
for if [the distinction] did not indeed operate within ultimate cognition, then there would be no activity among those free from passion that possesses the division of prior and subsequent. (743)
Even when there is no cognition of one's own activity, one proceeds out of compassion, just as a king who seeks the welfare of his subjects exerts effort for the sake of his own lineage.
svasantāna°

The activity of one for whom the primary focus is the vow arises from that very vow through the power of karma; who, then, could be questioned in this matter? (745) Therefore, effort must be made to abandon such false superimposition;
otherwise, there can be no cessation of the experience of suffering for the deluded person.
If, then, persistence were due to karma, there would be a connection to another birth because there is also karma for future births;
furthermore, if karma were ineffective, there would be no persistence for one who is free from passion.
To this, it is replied:
Because it is desired that what has been projected does not cease, [the karma] is sufficient;
for those who have transcended the thirst for existence, no further karma can be projected.
That which has been projected cannot be brought to an end without effort.
And the effort of one who is free from passion is thwarted by equanimity; it does not abide anywhere for him.
Precisely because of this absence of abiding, there is no acquisition of another birth.
Therefore, because of the absence of a co-operative cause characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
this very birth is produced by a previous craving and not another;
indeed, this is what is called compassion (*dayā*), which exists toward a sentient being who is to be protected from suffering, and nowhere else.

There is no such thing as a sentient being, nor is there any perception of a sentient being; therefore, compassion does not arise from those who have abandoned the view of a self, whereas it does arise from those who have not abandoned the view of a self.
This is the resolution.
The arising of the nature of things, which carries forward previous impressions and is not in contradiction with the knowledge of suffering, does not conform to the existence of sentient beings.
For when all that is indeed suffering is directly realized as being endowed with the three types of suffering, [the mind no longer follows after the notion of a self].
Then, craving characterized by origination departs from him; for one whose origination has been abandoned, there are no longer passion and the other afflictions.
Thus, there is equality and non-opposition with the entire assembly of sentient beings.

Therefore, for the great ones, the arising [of compassion] from seeing the suffering of beings is based on the objective reality (*vastu*) and so forth; it does not arise in that state out of a desire to grasp at sentient beings (*sattva-graha*). Rather, the intention (*āśaya*) to cause those beings who have become thus to abandon their grasping is compassion (*dayā*), and that [compassion] belongs only to one who has abandoned the view of a self (*ātma-darśana*).
For how could one who has not abandoned the view of a self strive for its abandonment in others? Is there not a difference between attachment and compassion?
This is the difference.
Attachment arises from the superimposition of another self onto that which consists of those phenomena;
whereas the emergence of compassion occurs through the mere contact with the continuum of suffering.
There is a great difference between compassion and attachment.
This is due to the difference in causes and the difference in objects; for instance,
attachment proceeds by superimposing a future continuum of existence upon oneself, thereby becoming subject to the binding of an attachment to future pleasure.
When an object that is not of a certain nature is perceived as being of that nature, one whose mind is permeated by the fourfold misconceptions becomes impassioned; it is not so for anyone else.
Compassion, however, arises solely from the direct perception of the continuum of suffering, in order to bring about the disappearance of false conceit.
1. Since there is a distinction of causes and a distinction of objects, how could it be otherwise than through the intention: "I shall effect the removal of this person's suffering"?
To this, the response is as follows:

If activity were for one's own sake, such a consequence would indeed follow; however, for those whose activity is solely for the sake of others, no perception of an agent is observed. The example of the king has already been shown, and thus this is not inconsistent. Alternatively, activity proceeds from a superior mental impression (saṃskāra) deposited by each preceding moment.
He does not perceive a continuum, nor does anything proceed; it does not remain because of the absence of light—it is merely your delusion.
(748) Thus, this is the distinction between compassion (*dayā*) and passion (*rāga*); enough with excessive detail.
[Objection: But surely compassion should not exist, since it arises from those who do not see reality and are characterized by passion?

However, aversion would take the form of seeing impurity and so forth; yet liberation does not come from the cultivation of the unattractive because of the absence of turning away [from existence], but rather from seeing impermanence and so forth,
for that [aversion] exists only when there is a self.

One might feel anger thinking, "He is independent and inflicts suffering upon others. However, when he acts under the control of causes and functions merely by his own nature, it is impossible to inflict harm upon him, because at the very time of the injury, he himself is absent; thus, the adoption of anger is in vain.
Furthermore, delusion (*moha*) is the root of all faults, and that [delusion] exists only through the grasping at a self (*sattvagraha*). (197)
Therefore, there is no hatred toward the primary cause; thus, the absence of hatred is considered compassion.
If one were to see oneself being harmed, anger would arise;
yet, there is no such thing as a self.
Rather, even in the absence of a sentient being, the mere apprehension of a sentient being alone is the cause of anger; and without the apprehension of a sentient being, there is no hatred.
As for delusion, it does not exist [in this context], because delusion itself is the absence of the perception of a sentient being.
Therefore, compassion, which is free from all defects, is not a defect.
Now, if one who is free from passion remains while still possessing a body, then he would not be liberated, because his mind would still be in existence.
However, this is not a fault, since his mind is devoid of defects.
Furthermore, what is liberation? It is the non-relinking [to a new birth] upon the exhaustion of prior formative forces (saṃskāra).
Those whose formative forces have not lost their power remain as those who are free from affliction (anagha).
For how could one who exists with a mind opposed to the reconnection of another birth be unliberated?
Moreover, there is no reconnection because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced in that birth have been exhausted;

however, those who do not possess the desire for the exhaustion of latent impressions in order to prevent reconnection remain indeed in a state where their impressions are undestroyed and free from affliction.
As long as conditioned existence continues, because compassion is weak, there is no great effort required for its maintenance; however,
those for whom great compassion exists remain [in saṃsāra] even while dependent on others.
Because of the exhaustion of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and the dullness of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is no effort toward remaining [in the world];
thus they do not remain forever.
However, due to the possession of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), their very nature is to remain.
Because no basis for attachment exists there,
there is the departure from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
if that were due to the power of the Path, then non-existence would occur at the very beginning, on the Path of Stream-entry itself.
Because of the departure from the view of a self-identity;
for, through the abandonment of the view of a self-identity, doubt, and the clinging to rules and rituals, one becomes a stream-enterer.
Therefore, first [is] ethical discipline (śīla).
And it has been stated that delusion is the root of the defects, and that it consists in the grasping of sentient beings; therefore,
any other path would be futile.
To this it is replied:

through the disappearance of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), there would be non-existence from the very beginning. If [this occurs] on the path, it is because innate [ignorance] has not been abandoned; or, if it were abandoned, how could existence remain?

Indeed, the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not entail the absence of the abandonment of that which is innate simply because of the abandonment of that which is produced by effort;
for that path consists merely in the vision of the truths.

Through vision (*darśana*), there is the abandonment of the grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*) which is produced by mental construction (*abhisaṃskārika*), because it is not a root affliction (*amūlakleśa*).
For that view of self (*ātmadarśana*) is instructional (*aupadeśika*), and its perversion is abandoned by mere vision alone.

However, because the innate view of a real body (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is deeply rooted due to beginningless habituation, its abandonment occurs only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as an antidote; therefore, [the innate is not abandoned] by the abandonment of the innate [view].
However, in the view of one for whom there is no loss even of the innate [nature], in that view, how could existence arise even upon its loss?
For, in the case of one of sharp intelligence, the path of seeing itself possesses all capacities; thus, for him, that very path is the nature of the entire path.
Now, if the innate perception of a sentient being has the form of a self, then in the absence of a self, that cognition must arise solely from mental construction (*abhisaṃskāra*) and not otherwise;
for when the actual object that produces it is absent, at most only instruction can serve as the cause.
Regarding this, it is said:
for one who craves, thinking "May I be happy" or "May I not suffer," that very cognition of "I" is itself the innate perception of a self.
For no one feels affection for the self without perceiving it as "I.
Nor does one who desires happiness rush toward [objects] without love for the self.

By the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the cognition "I" arises; this is an innate perception of a self (*sattvadarśana*) that takes the form, "May I be happy," or "May I not become otherwise."
Because that [ignorance] has not been abandoned,
one does not see "I am non-existent," and thus one feels affection for the self; yet one who sees [the truth] does not feel such affection,
nor does one who desires happiness engage in striving without that affection for the self.
But for one whose innate perception of a self-existent being (*sattva*) persists, and whose attachment to the self continues to function, how could there be an absence of rebirth?

Therefore, it is certain that because of this innate perception of a being, there can be no end to *saṃsāra* on the very first path; rather, [the end of *saṃsāra*] necessarily follows only from the abandonment of the perception of a being.
By this, the aspect of "peaceful" has been explained;
[it arises] from the abandonment of that.
Now, if there is a self, there is bondage for that very self, and therefore liberation; thus, that liberation is brought about for the sake of a particular satisfaction of the self.
But if there is no self, whose satisfaction could there be?
As for the established distinction between bondage and liberation—
if that were merely an illusion, it would be defective, and thus it would not be liberation.
The solution here is as follows:
bondage is the state of being a cause for the arising of suffering; how could that belong to something eternal?
Liberation is the state of not being a cause for the arising of suffering; how could that belong to something eternal?
If the self were eternal and likewise all-pervading, then, due to the absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it would not be capable of producing suffering for itself,
just like space. Furthermore,
if it were both independent and capable, why would it produce suffering for itself?
Indeed, it is not fitting for a discerning person to employ a ritual instrument for their own destruction;
yet, if that [person] were deluded and unaware of themselves, how could their non-existence follow from the non-perception of a self?
Or, if that [self] were indeed its very nature, then it would never be otherwise.

That liberation will not come to pass; furthermore, even for one who knows [the truth], no purpose is served by that [liberation], nor is suffering produced through dharma. Nevertheless, for that which is eternal and all-pervading, there can be no causality for the production of suffering in anyone.
If that [suffering] were at that time of the nature of suffering,
then it would not be logical for there to be a suffering of suffering;
and if it possesses that nature, there can be no alteration of it.
Consequently, there would be no liberation;
and if it possessed a different nature, it would not be eternal, and thus the self could not exist.
Furthermore, if suffering or happiness were distinct from it, then the self would neither be happy nor suffer.
For one person does not become happy through the happiness of another;
if you argue that this is due to inherence (*samavāya*), then surely inherence itself is likewise something distinct.
If they were non-different, that same fault would apply;
and if they possessed the nature of pleasure, pain, and so forth, there would be impermanence due to their having mutually distinct natures.
Alternatively, if this [self] were changeless from the perspective of ultimate reality, then the perception of being happy and so on would be nothing but an illusion.
That too is incorrect: (2) or else, even for one who knows [the truth], suffering arises from the self's own dharma and adharma;
(3) or the self would be of the nature of suffering, or suffering would be produced as something either distinct or non-distinct from it.

If it is argued that this [error] is not distinct [from the self], he says: "If there were a distinction from the self externally, the self would not be known due to the error. For the self is indeed [not known].
If there is cognition of its own nature, how can there be error in self-awareness?
If happiness were present even in liberation, then liberation would not be supreme;
for that [happiness] belongs to one who possesses delusion. Therefore, the self is not the possessor of liberation.
For one for whom moments arise in succession, this liberation is proclaimed as being devoid of error and irrationality in its actual meaning.
(751) If it is argued that bondage and liberation would then result in having different substrates, we reply: their state of having a single substrate is not denied at the conventional level.
(752) What purpose would there be in a bond for one who is already liberated? If you say, "It was mine previously," even so, what use is that [past state]? (753)
One should act with prior deliberation before reaching a certainty regarding unity. If it is argued that this is improper, we certainly accept that very point.
Furthermore, it has been stated again that this application is for the sake of another; the excellence of this liberation is indeed its opposite [compared to others].
Moreover, it might be argued: the self is not eternal because of the faults previously mentioned, nor is it non-eternal because that would entail the consequence of acting without prior deliberation.

Therefore, it is not tenable to say that [the self] is indescribable in terms of being either eternal or non-eternal; for that which is indescribable as non-eternal cannot be the cause of anything. (204)
Furthermore, how could bondage and liberation not exist even for that which is inexpressible?
If it is said to be "inexpressible" by virtue of impermanence, then it lacks impermanence; that which lacks impermanence cannot be a cause.
It has been determined elsewhere that causality is pervaded by impermanence; therefore, due to the absence of the pervader, its status as a cause is also impossible.
But for that which lacks even permanence,
there is absolute non-existence; (now,) because bondage and liberation must have a single substratum, impermanence [is required].
The thesis that "there is no permanence because of being a cause" is untenable.

1. Furthermore, an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is free from both permanence and impermanence is not perceived, because everything is perceived precisely as being characterized by exclusion and inclusion. (756) Moreover, it might be argued: let there be a dual nature [of things], if it cannot be otherwise.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the wise declare that which is eternal to be that intrinsic nature which does not perish. (205)
Therefore, having abandoned this shameful view, let that which is eternal be described;
for it is a contradiction to say something is both perishable and eternal,
since that which does not perish is eternal.
It will be established that destruction, non-existence, and non-apprehension have the same meaning,
as do non-destruction and permanence with apprehension;
therefore, there is identity between the permanent and the impermanent, meaning between the apprehendable and the unapprehendable.

And how can there be oneness between that which is perceived and that which is not perceived? The established rule is that whatever is cognized as one is indeed one. If that which is unperceived were to be perceived, that would be an act of extreme audacity—[the claim] that the eternal and the non-eternal are one and the same.
In that case, it would follow that what is apprehended and what is not apprehended are one;
and thus, being perceived as connected, they cannot be understood as one in any other way.

If it is argued that what is unperceived cannot be perceived— just as a rabbit's horn, being unperceived by anyone, cannot be determined to be one with something perceived because one of the two is unperceived—
then here too, when something is unperceived, there must necessarily be non-perception [of its identity].
That which is perceived as a unity does not have its perception itself destroyed, nor is it produced anew.

If, however, the perception of another thing is non-perception, then there is no perception in the form of the perception of another; rather, the very non-perception of that [object] is the perception of its opposite form.
If that were so, it would follow that its non-existence is due to that very other form; and that is incorrect, because:
2. Therefore, non-apprehension itself is not apprehension.

3. Since that form which is superimposed as being one [with it], from that very form there follows the absence of its own momentariness; and this is contradictory, for [momentariness] would result in being other than the self—[as if it were] external.
How could one who asserts difference claim non-difference? Since for him there is no such thing as difference, impermanence is not established.

(758) If there were impermanence, there would be non-apprehension; if there is apprehension, there is no impermanence. Furthermore, if there were non-difference, there would be apprehension; and if there is apprehension, there is permanence.
(759) It is not apprehended by some form, but otherwise it is apprehended. How can it be maintained that "that which is not cognized by a certain form belongs to this [entity]"? (760)

If its cognition occurs as being prior, then it must have been so at that very time; how then can there be oneness with its present form? (761) If it is one because it is not separated from both prior and posterior forms, then why is it not considered separate when separation is actually perceived?
(762) If its separation occurs sequentially, then separation would likewise be sequential; for this very reason, it possesses a dual nature due to both non-separation and separation. (763)
Just as its nature is non-sequential, so too must its manifestation be; and for a nature that is non-sequential, there can be no connection with sequential existence.
(764) If its prior and posterior forms are not perceived, its pervasiveness cannot be established; yet if its pervasiveness occurs through sequence, then that very [nature] lacks pervasiveness.
(765) For it is not possible for that single entity to be both seen and unseen; at one and the same time, its being seen and its being unseen is a logical impossibility. (766)
If there is no difference in time, the whole [object] is not seen as anything inconsistent; since it is one, how could there be a difference in time for it all at once?

(767) Furthermore, if it were perceived again and again, there would be a grasping of what has already been grasped. For that which is to be grasped as "already grasped" must indeed be something being remembered.

(768) Since memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a sequential grasping is impossible. Nor is that form unperceived, such that its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) would be established. (769)

If present existence were not apprehended by the prior cognition, then—since there would be no difference [between the two cognitions]—how could this division of it be supported by valid means of knowledge?

(770) If present existence were not apprehended by the prior cognition, its state of having been seen would not exist; thus, it would always be in the present. If there were a sequence of before and after, by what could that be perceived? (771)

If the cognition of the distinction between those two arises from the preceding and the subsequent cognitions, from where does the distinction between those two [cognitions] itself come? If it is due to their being self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*), then there would be no cognition of duality [between them].

Nor can there be a cognition of that which is non-existent—namely, the subsequent and the preceding—if that [duality] is intended to be a single cognition by virtue of its being directly perceived (*sākṣātkṛtatayā*).

If there were identity [between the past object and its cognition], how could it have "priority" (pūrvatva) by virtue of being directly perceived? For that which is being directly perceived possesses neither priority nor even the state of having been cultivated (bhāvitā).
(774) If there were no priority, how could there be a cognition [of it] as prior? There is no such cognition of it at all; and since it is not a direct perception, it is not a recollection either.
(775) If you say, "This is a recollection of that," how can it be said to be "of that" when this recollection is observed to occur even without that [object]? (776)

If it is argued that [the object] is grasped because of the causal relationship, the apprehension would not occur merely by that much; for the state of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatā*) belongs to the object as its direct cause, and not through the reverse.

(777) Furthermore, memory does not arise directly from the object, because it is mediated by consciousness (*saṃvit*). That [memory] is not a complete perception, nor is it capable of grasping the prior state [of the object].
(778) Consequently, the prior state is certainly not established by means of memory. What is called "prior" is simply the direct perception of what has passed. (779)

When there is a manifestation (*bhāva*) through direct perception, the establishment of its state as "existent" (*bhāvitva*) occurs. Now, that which is endowed with arising, passing away, and persistence is accepted as being real (*sat*). [Objection: These very things would lack existence because they are never separated from these states. When there is passing away (*vyaya*), how can its existence be perceived?
If it was previously perceived as existent, how can there be its passing away at that time? Even if there is persistence (*dhrauvya*), if there is no cognition of it, how can existence be perceived?

Since everything is established through cognition alone, how could it otherwise exist? Therefore, an entity that is both permanent and impermanent is never possible anywhere. (g) The truth of the path has four aspects;
the path has been explained, and through its cultivation, the basis is transformed.
(206) If [you argue] that even when it has become habitual, the defects still exist, [we reply] no, because of the lack of omnipresence, just as in the case of the path.
The path has already been explained; through its cultivation, the basis—whether the mental continuum or the storehouse consciousness—becomes completely purified.

When selflessness, which is the reversal of the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, becomes habitual, there is a separation from all defects, namely, the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Now, one might object: "Just as there is the presence of virtues when there is the presence of faults, so too there is the presence of faults even when there is the presence of virtues; thus, there would be no escape from saṃsāra.
This is not so, because faults are suppressed by the arising of virtues.
Why does the reverse not occur?
Because the qualities possess the nature of real entities.
If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows:
The apprehension of an object is the property (*dharma*) of consciousness; it is apprehended as it truly exists.

It is its generator, and it exists by way of its own nature. Furthermore, consciousness is the path that impels living beings; its property is the apprehension of the object, which constitutes its essential form (*svarūpa*).
By which that consciousness comes to be;
for consciousness does not exist in the absence of perception,
since there is no such thing as non-perceiving entities.
And just as it exists, so is it apprehended as the producer;
for an object of consciousness is a cause capable of imparting its own form [to that consciousness].
The manifestation of that intrinsic nature is a property of consciousness;
likewise, the object is perceived in that very way.

Therefore, he says that the object—consisting of the impermanent, non-self, and so forth—is nothing other than consciousness itself as the grasper of such [an object], for its nature is not otherwise.

1. A phenomenon (dharma) is to be understood as being excluded [from its own nature]—the reading "outside the row" (bahiḥpaṅkti-pāṭhaḥ) is the natural state of this [exclusion], though it may falter due to another cause. 208.
In the case of exclusion, it is unstable and dependent upon a condition, like the cognition of a snake [in a rope].
Whatever dharma has the nature of apprehending selflessness and so forth is its *prakṛti* (intrinsic nature).

When that [nature] falters due to the power of adventitious conditions, it is a lapse from its rootless [state]; and because it depends upon conditions for its reversal from that lapse, it is therefore not firm, being rootless—just like the cognition of a snake [mistakenly perceived in a rope].
Now, one might object: while similarity, distance, and so forth are the causes for the cognition of a snake regarding a rope, what is the cause for eternal cognition?
For perception does not apply to [the proof of] eternality.
Nor is there any doubt that inference is devoid of authority;
thus, it will be established that momentariness is perceived through direct perception.
Therefore, how can there be a grasp of permanence? To this he replies:

even while perceiving that impermanence, one of dull intellect does not ascertain it, because he is either deceived by the suspicion that its existence persists at all times due to the perception of its presence, or deceived by the production of a similar subsequent [moment], until the certainty of those who perceive the final moment.
2. Unstable; 3. The final moment.
This is what is meant.
When there is first a perception of the nature of an object and then a subsequent non-perception, one indeed perceives impermanence;
for we define impermanence as the state of not remaining in that same condition.
However, even when it is no longer perceived, the doubt of one with dull intellect does not depart.
Consequently, one suspects its existence; thus, there is a "suspicion of its existence" as to whether it remains even now as it did before,
and this arises from seeing it again or from obtaining its causal efficacy.
Being undeceived, why would he not determine this?
For it is only when one is deceived that one might determine [something] due to the non-attainment of that [object], as in the case of a jar;

but when the existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is perceived, what occasion is there for a practical agent (*vyavahārin*) to distinguish an error? However, the investigator of reality (*tattvacintaka*), through the distinction of appearances, certainly does determine it.
The practical agent, however, seeking purposeful action,
is satisfied upon its attainment and does not investigate further, as his aim has been fulfilled.

Or, one is deceived by the production of a subsequent [moment] similar [to the preceding]. For when there is a cognition that "this is that very same thing" regarding what is similar, the intention is merely that it is not the [actual] entity itself; because fire, which arises from a collection of causes such as various successive blades of grass, becomes the object of the determination of oneness, yet in that case fuel alone is the material cause (*upādāna*), not fire. Indeed, fire does not arise from fire alone, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its non-production at the beginning.
Either fire arises from the striking of stones because there was no fire previously,
or rather, fire is produced from that very [striking] itself;
in this way, all entities arise from a preceding member of the same class.
Nor is there a cause of the same class [for the arising],
because it arises solely through the sovereign power of karma;
therefore, with respect to this, there is an alternative view.
And regarding that, the determination is as follows: it was previously stated according to the view of the proponents of karma (*karmavādin*), whereas it is stated according to another view later on.
(Tibetan: *chags-'pi-bum*) 4.
5. Like a mirage and a peacock’s tail;
6. In that causal efficiency, there is merely non-deception;
7. Indeed, fire does not arise from fire alone.
Alternatively, it should be explained as "deceived by the suspicion that it is not that [nature]";
for when its nature is [established], no suspicion whatsoever exists, because its existence is perceived at all times.
For if its existence were [known] through non-perception, doubt would arise;
but when there is non-perception in the interim, what is the situation here?
In this case too, one is deceived by the production of a similar [moment], just as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again.
If it is argued that oneness is established through the recognition of a dead person, we say no, because recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
as it cannot be classified as either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
And this will be demonstrated later; therefore, due to the internal affliction of ignorance (*avidyopaplava*), the impurities are adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Therefore it is said:
"This mind is luminous by nature";
because [the text] uses the term "adventitious stains" for that which is devoid of permanence, the stains are adventitious.
Since the superimposition of what is non-existent is rootless and consists merely of a hollow seal,
permanence does not appear anywhere in an ultimate sense;
therefore, because they are devoid of investigation, the defilements are adventitious.

Where could there be a capacity later for those things that were previously incapable of it, given that they remain entirely incapable even at the time of hearing and reflection? For they are not able to sprout at all, like fire upon the earth, even though it is moist. (210)
Even regarding a thing that is capable [of being abandoned], the capacity for the arising of a sublater lies within [the latent impression];
the capacity for the arising of a sublater is the refinement of the latent impression (*vāsanā-saṃskāra*). [Objection:
But surely, even without a cause, there is indeed the abandonment of things such as weak faith, because of one’s state of being an Arhat.
How, then, is there the non-arising of defects?
Even if a defect should arise, nevertheless, because the capacity for an internal sublater has arisen, the impurity, though capable of arising, is not able to grow excessively.
Just as fire produced on flowing ground does not take root,
so too there is no arising of defects in one who abides in a state of natural harmony (sātmya).
For it is thus:
But in the case of identity,

there can be no sublation by contrary [cognitions], even with effort, because the nature of reality— which is free from affliction— entails a partiality toward that [reality] on the part of the intellect. (211)
For an intrinsic nature cannot be overturned by one who lacks effort;

and effort proceeds toward virtues in one who perceives faults, and toward faults in one who perceives virtues; yet this is not the case for one whose perception of selflessness has become second nature.
Seeing virtues in faults,
or seeing faults in virtues,
or not seeing virtues at all.

Because the vision of selflessness is free from affliction, [it is like] a wealthy man who is separated from a thief; therefore, the true nature is the actual self and is indeed free from affliction. How could its abandonment be possible for one possessed of consciousness? (784)

And partiality of the mind does not arise toward faults; therefore, no effort whatsoever is directed toward those faults. Even if a fault were to arise in one capable of thoroughly investigating the nature of all things, that person—like a traveler who has encountered a true object and feels a sense of urgency (*samvega*)—abides in a state of equanimity and exerts effort only toward the Path due to partiality for its virtues, but does not take delight in faults.

But surely, even though desire and hatred possess contrary forms, there is not the sublation of only one; for it is observed that desire, once sublated by hatred, becomes a sublater [of that hatred] again,
and likewise hatred [sublates desire].
Likewise, it might be argued that the same applies to the views of selflessness and self;
however, this is not so, because of the [following] view of selflessness and self.

Because attachment and aversion share a single source in the grasping at a self, and because they stand in a relationship of cause and effect, there is no mutual exclusion between them despite their differences;
for both have the grasping at a self as their cause, and as long as that grasping at a self persists, not even one of the two can be utterly eradicated.
Even if there were mutual opposition [between the two], there would still be a lack of simultaneity;
furthermore,
even from the perspective of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), for that which is intended as the cause in relation to something else—
When afflicted by the cause of suffering, he necessarily desires the means for happiness, whether that be this [cause] or another;

therefore, there is a relationship of cause and effect between these two. Consequently, when the means for happiness is favored, he necessarily experiences its impairment and thus becomes possessed of aversion.
Therefore, because of this causal relationship, there is no sublation [of passion and aversion] even though they are distinct;
for this very reason, since they are not opposed to delusion, there is no absolute suppression of the defects through [the practice of] loving-kindness and so forth. || 213 ||
And all the impurities have that as their root; and that [root] is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Although loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to hatred, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is the antidote to passion (*rāga*), compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the antidote to envy (*īrṣyā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote to everything.
Nevertheless, there is no absolute suppression of defects because of the non-opposition [of the self] to delusion (*moha*).
[Objection: Even while delusion exists, all defects are abandoned due to the absence of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*); [Response:
this is not correct.
That very delusion is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), for afflicted delusion is precisely the view of a self-identity.

However, the ignorance of Arhats is not afflicted; therefore, it does not belong to them. Even in the case of delusion, those with improper mental continuums are those who possess the debased view of a self-identity. (886)

Because it is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*), because it is perceived as a mental factor (*caitta*), and because it is conjoined with false perception (*mithyopalabdhi*), ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established; anything else would be illogical.

[Objection: But if ignorance is of the nature of non-apprehension (*asaṃprakhyāna*), whereas the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of the nature of apprehension (*pratipatti*), how can the view of a self-identity itself be ignorance? [Response: There is no fault, because...
Even if ignorance were of the nature of non-apprehension (asaṃprakhyāna), it would still be a reality; for what remains when the substrata (upadhīnām) have been destroyed?
Indeed, non-apprehension exists primarily in the nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) and in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
If, on the other hand, it does not have afflictions as its cause,
then it would not have the characteristic of ignorance; for self-view alone is that which has afflictions as its cause, and thus ignorance would be nothing other than that.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is another dharma opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*), such as untruth and the like; knowledge consists of the view of selflessness (*nairātmya-dṛṣṭi*), while ignorance is the view of a self (*ātma-darśana*) which is its opposite. (788) Ignorance is not simply the absence of knowledge, because that absence exists even in *nirvāṇa*;
nor is a non-entity a cause.
It is not something other than that, because it would follow that form and the other aggregates are themselves ignorance;
therefore, ignorance is a factor opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*), like non-virtue (*adharma*) or falsehood (*anṛta*),
and that is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

For instance, dharma is characterized by the benefit of others; non-dharma (*adharma*) is not merely the absence of that [benefit], nor is it merely something other than it, but rather harm (*upaghāta*), which is the opposite of benefit. Likewise, falsehood (*anṛta*) is not merely the absence of communicating the actual state of affairs, but rather the communication of what is not true—that is, untruthful speech.
This being the case, when one who perceives non-existence through delusion regarding the reality of existence asserts "it exists," then there would be no falsity;
and when one who perceives existence regarding what is non-existent [asserts it], then it would be false.
This is not so;
words have as their objects that which is conceptually constructed. A statement is true only if it accords with how a thing is determined in reality; otherwise, the statement is false.
For words indeed have as their objects things as they are apprehended through conceptual determination.
The principle is that truth consists precisely in acting in accordance with one's resolve; otherwise, it is untruth.
For Bodhisattvas, however, deceiving sentient beings even through delusion is the supreme transgression;
for this very reason, they apply themselves with diligence toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, since ignorance is none other than the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because no other [view] serves as the antidote to knowledge (*vidyā*),
and because it is perceived as being a mental factor (*caitta*),
ignorance is simply a false perception (*mithyopalabdhi*).

They are called "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they are conjoined through equality of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance; and it has been stated in various sūtras that ignorance (*avidyā*) is precisely the practice of a distorted aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*).

In this regard, what is the removal of ignorance? It is the realization of phenomena as they truly are, free from superimposition. Likewise, whatever worldly conventional designations there may be, they all arise from the clinging to a self;
they do not arise from the cessation of clinging to a self.
Surely, attachment to a self is a view,
and that is associated with ignorance;
therefore, it should be understood that ignorance itself is expressed by way of the door of the view.
Because it is invariably concomitant [with ignorance], one might argue that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is itself ignorance;
however, this too is not correct.
The body is also a basis for the non-manifestation of form and so forth, as well as for the arising of ignorance.
Also because of the demonstration of relinquishment:

when ignorance is to be indicated as a member [of dependent origination], the revelation of its own nature is appropriate; however, an indication of something other than that would not demonstrate skill.

(790) There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here for [proving] ignorance in this way; rather, the means of valid cognition for the opposite case has been demonstrated exactly as it is. (791)
There is no evidence here that ignorance (avidyā) alone is indicated by way of the [six] views;
rather, the evidence presented here demonstrates that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) itself is ignorance, the root cause of all faults. [Objection:
But is not the view of a self-identity merely a portion of that which arises from delusion (moha)?
But delusion (*moha*), which is accompanied by all afflictions and characterized by non-clarity—or otherwise—how could it be called the "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
For a specific term cannot have the meaning of a general term.

Likewise, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were simply a view, then in the expression "ignorance associated with views," the meaning of "associated" would not hold; for a thing cannot be associated with itself.
In response to this objection, the resolution is:
[They] arise from a portion of delusion.
The contradiction that exists here must be explained;
and through that contradiction, the contradiction of the view of emptiness with all [other] faults is established.
For the object associated with the conceptualization of difference is [determined] by way of the relationship between the universal and the particular.

Just as when one says "a forest endowed with *palāśa* trees," it is in fact the very nature of the *palāśa* itself that is being expressed; so too, by means of this specific designation, its nature—which is the primary cause of ignorance—is indicated.
Since the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is ignorance, all afflictions (*kleśa*) whatsoever are rooted therein.
Because the vision of selflessness cuts off the root [of the afflictions], and because they are cut off through that severance of the root—
since the vision of selflessness is the antidote to all afflictions and does not depart from the yogin— the afflictions do not arise again;
therefore, cessation is described as having the aspect of deliverance (*niḥsaraṇa*).
It is not inexhaustible because it is a property of living beings, just like form and so forth, since its non-existence is unestablished.

Furthermore, even when there is a connection with its opposite, there is no recurrence of the fault once its adversary has arisen, just as there is no recurrence of hardness [once it has been removed]. || 216–217 ||
"Because it is of the nature of the self and thus non-perishable, and because [the argument] is inconclusive, like ashes"—these are the intermediate verses.
Now, one might object: "Is not liberation indeed attained even through the cultivation of the notion of the Self?"
In that case, what is the use of the vision of selflessness?
To this, scripture replies:
"The Self."
[text to be translated] ...
The argument beginning with "it should be considered," and so forth,
is also incorrect, because:
Verily, my dear, the Self is to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon— Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6.
Whoever perceives a self develops a constant attachment toward it, thinking "I am this.
From attachment, one craves for pleasures; craving solidifies one's faults. For one who views a self is inevitably bound to that self by a constant attachment.
And because of affection, one possesses craving for those pleasures;
for wherever there is affection, there is intense thirst for that pleasure, as in the case of the pleasure derived from a son and so forth.

But has it not been stated that attachment to the self arises from the perception of a self? Does attachment to wood arise from the perception of wood, or attachment to a woman from the perception of a woman?
Therefore, the claim that "he who perceives a self feels attachment toward it" is incorrect.

This is not the case: that one who has affection for another does not have it for oneself. Why? Because affection is indeed observed toward oneself; there is no dispute about this. That there could be affection for another without affection for oneself is utterly impossible. (792)
If affection did not arise merely from the perception of a self, then affection would not exist for anyone at all, because of the absence of any other cause; furthermore,
since one does not perceive wood as being useful to oneself, there is no affection for it.
And how could one who has affection for what is useful to oneself not have affection for oneself?
Alternatively, due to a particularity of their nature, they may have no affection for themselves at all,
yet they possess affection for others because of their great-souled compassion.
That is incorrect;

for if what is called "great magnanimity" consists merely in benefiting others, then such a state—being devoid of prior deliberation—is improper. By sacrificing oneself to make it a means of benefiting others, one would manifest within oneself a great lack of prior deliberation regarding one's own interest.

Now, if the performance of the welfare of others were itself happiness, then being deluded by attachment to that state of happiness, how could one be liberated? For such a person would even engage in the physical contact of a courtesan’s limbs. (794)
If you argue that this is a conventional practice of the untruthful, it is not so; for there is no lack of truth in that which is established in its own nature.
Just as one desires the bliss of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), so too does one desire the bliss of union with a courtesan's body;
indeed, there is no difference between that bliss and any other.
If it is argued that [the Buddha] would likewise be unreal, it is not so, because there is no distinction [in his nature].

If it is argued that this is not logical because he goes to the hells and other realms, it is not so; for, due to the excellence of his great power (*mahānubhāvatā*), he voluntarily accepts going to the hells for the sake of others.
The greatness of his majesty is such that, through such practice, there is no improper conduct and another cause of happiness arises; therefore,
it is better that proper conduct has been adopted,
for there is no lack of distinction [between the two].

Likewise, one who possesses craving for the self would, under its influence, equate faults with virtues; then, concealing the faults and perceiving qualities, becoming intensely desirous, one grasps at the means to achieve that [self], thinking "this is mine. || 219 ||

Therefore, as long as there is attachment to a self, so long as that self exists in saṃsāra as a reality in the ultimate sense, whatever benefit there is therein is also ultimately real; consequently,
one should understand that he alone who provides such ultimate benefit is truly virtuous.
Then, perceiving qualities therein, one grasps at means [of attainment] thinking "this is mine";
thus, due to the adherence to a self, there is cyclic existence (saṃsāra),
and so one even longs for the touch of a sow in a pit as a means to happiness.
Therefore, when there is a self, there arises the notion of "other"; from the division of self and other, attachment and aversion arise.
Bound to these two, all defects are produced.
For the distinction between self and other gives rise to attachment and aversion;
consequently, there arise defects such as envy and avarice, which are bound up with that attachment and aversion.
Furthermore, it might be argued:

Affection exists only for the self, not for what belongs to the self; therefore, due to the absence of affection for what belongs to the self, there is an absence of the worldly practice regarding non-existent things.
To this it is replied: one who necessarily feels affection for the self does not become dispassionate toward that which belongs to it. (221)
Furthermore, there is no cause for the removal of affection toward a faultless self;
for affection directed toward the self does not depart without the presence of a fault,
and one who possesses affection for the self cannot be devoid of affection for what belongs to the self.

Therefore, one who possesses affection for the self and what belongs to the self, by obscuring all defects, remains engaged everywhere; thus, his connection with saṃsāra is indeed uninterrupted, because affection for the self and what belongs to the self is the cause of saṃsāra, and because that which is joined with affection is flawed. Consequently, there should be no affection for what belongs to the self.
(Cultivation of the Path)—
If one does not show affection even toward that which is corrupted by other defects, how much less so toward that in which affection itself is the corruption?
To this he says:
If it is argued that affection is inherently defective, what follows from that? Is it its abandonment?
Abandonment of this [affection] is not possible when its object is unblemished;
for affection does not cease because of a defect in something else—it is logical [only] if there is a defect in the object itself.

However, it is not logical that there should be an absence of affection toward an object that is not defective and is a cause of pleasure, since it possesses positive qualities; for if you argue that affection itself is the defect, [that would be inconsistent].
If it is argued, "Let it be; what will happen? [We shall simply] abandon affection because it is evil," this is not so.
Since there can be no abandonment of affection without [recognizing] the defects of sense-objects,
therefore the abandonment of desire, aversion, and so forth, which are bound up with perceived qualities and defects, [must occur]. (223)
The non-perception of those two [occurs] with respect to the object; however, that sequence does not apply to external things.
The non-perception of those two...
For desire and aversion arise from the perception of qualities and defects; it is a logical principle that they do not arise in the absence of such perception.
Furthermore, a quality is that which is a means to one's own happiness, and a defect is that which is a means to suffering.
If that [cessation] exists,
then there is no abandonment of desire and aversion;
yet, it might be argued as follows:
Even an external object, though possessed of excellent qualities, may be abandoned;

that too is not difficult, for an external object is dependent upon external causes. But how can the successive [afflictions] arising through the power of the vision of self and attachment ever be abandoned?

For it is because the object possesses the quality of being an object of affection (*sneha*) and is thus an object of appropriation (*upādāna*) that there occurs the abandonment of affection for it and its non-appropriation;
whereas for affection itself, there is no appropriation because it lacks the status of a quality, but rather [its persistence] is due to the quality of the object.
Therefore, since the causes—the qualities of the object—exist, how could affection not arise?
For affection does not arise from the quality of affection itself, but rather from the perception of the qualities of the object.
When that cause is unimpaired, by whom can the effect be prevented?
—Thus is the summary.
Furthermore, what fault has been observed in affection? It is the basis of suffering. (225)
Nevertheless, detachment does not arise here [toward external objects] because one perceives them as "one's own," just as it does not arise toward oneself,
due to the power of perceiving the object of affection.
For the self is first the locus of suffering;
when the self exists, attachment subsequently becomes the cause of suffering.
But in the absence of a self, for whom would there be suffering?
Therefore, since both are causes of suffering, there is no detachment from either, nor even from one of them.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the self’s status as a cause of suffering is contingent upon external conditions (*paropādhika*), and thus the fault does not reside within the self itself;
rather, the self becomes a cause of suffering when assisted by self-attachment (*ātmasneha*), merit and demerit (*dharmādharmma*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). To this, [the author] replies:
If the self is not the cause of suffering without them, then they too must be of that same nature [faultless].
In this way, even suffering would be faultless; consequently, there would be no detachment toward either.

Indeed, no one ever feels detachment toward what is faultless. Furthermore, the arising of self-attachment does not occur without a self as its locus. Therefore, since they are the causes of suffering, they too—like the self—are not faultless.
Therefore, detachment does not arise from this [contemplation of suffering] alone;
if it were to arise from the cultivation of suffering, it would be like the abandonment of a limb bitten by a snake.
In this case, there is renunciation through the loss of the notion of "mine," but not in the opposite case.

When the sense organs and so forth have been grasped as the basis for enjoyment, by what could the notion of "sentient being" be prevented? How, then, could there be detachment toward them? Is it not the case that affection is the cause of pleasure?
Because its opposite is possible through the cause, there is indeed no dispassion toward one who causes harm, for that would be affection.
Regarding this self-perception,
it is said here: even when something is a cause of suffering, the disappearance of affection for it is not observed in that which is the object of the notion "this is mine."

If it is argued that detachment consists in the abandonment of the notion of "mine," and that this is simply the abandonment of the notion of "mine" itself [regarding the body and so forth], we reply:
no, for there is no disappearance of the notion of "mine" in anyone with respect to the body and other things perceived as the locus of experience.
For instance, one forms the notion of "mine" toward those [objects], thinking, "May I be a god," "May I be a nāga," or "May I possess such a distinguished body and so forth.
How, then, can one who possesses such a notion be dispassionate?
To explain further:
2. The formation of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmasaṃskāra*) is indeed directly perceived by everyone in the case of hair and so forth [falling] from the body. || 226 ||
When those things [such as hair] are fallen away, that intellect arises as one characterized by aversion; whereas when they are elsewhere, it arises as characterized by longing.
For when hair and so forth are objects of enjoyment, then there arises a sense of "mine" born of longing;
but when the reverse occurs, then there is detachment, whose nature is the departure of longing, and not otherwise—this is the distinction.
3. Manoratha: "She is just so"—that is the fault;
furthermore, what indeed remains for those such as Vaiśeṣika and others?
For in that case, the cognition of [the self] as its own [nature] is produced by a relation such as inherence (samavāya).
That relation remains exactly as it was even when pleasure and so forth are perceived; for the relation of inherence with pleasure and so forth is not lost.
Conjunction with the body;
inherence in what is conjoined [with the body] with respect to color and so forth; inherence in what is inherent [in what is conjoined] with respect to the nature of color (*rūpatva*) and so forth;
conjunction with the auditory organ; and conjunction with that which is conjoined [with the auditory organ] by means of the eye and so forth.
Thus, the connection with the self does not depart;
therefore, even upon seeing their faults, affection for them is not lost.
Now, suppose one were not to accept a relationship such as inherence (*samavāya*).
To this, the rebuttal is as follows: even in the absence of inherence and so forth, there exists everywhere a state of being beneficial.
For affection is everywhere produced by benefit.
Therefore, from where could dispassion and the like arise?
Now, if another were to object:
"If one's own cognition [of it] occurs, as in the case of a finger, through the experience of pain or benefit,"
For that is not exclusively suffering in every respect, as it is for the most part like poisoned food;
just as that is suffering, so too is pleasure like poisoned food.
For poisoned food is not exclusively suffering,
since the possibility of pleasure also exists;
likewise, even the body of a pig in a pit, though characterized by suffering, is indeed pleasure.
Therefore, the sense faculties and so forth cannot, under any circumstances, be objects for renunciation. [Objection:
But surely such suffering, being mixed with pleasure, is indeed nothing but suffering.
[Reply: If that is the case, then it follows that pleasure associated with happiness is indeed nothing but pleasure.
Furthermore, due to attachment to a superior pleasure, there would be aversion toward that which is contrary to it; one might renounce some pleasure out of a thirst for a superior pleasure. (233)
But regarding selflessness, one proceeds according to what is obtained out of attachment to a self;
when nothing is obtained, as was seen with the intoxicated woman, there is desire even for animals.
(234) If a distinguished happiness were to be obtained, detachment would arise otherwise.

If it is argued that for one who lacks discernment (*avivekin*), there is no thirst for distinguished pleasure precisely because of the absence of discernment, and therefore discernment will arise [spontaneously],
then discernment itself would be the cause of suffering; thus, discernment itself would be dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Now, if it is argued that detachment must necessarily arise from the power of causes alone, then in that case, detachment would also be unavoidable for one who has realized selflessness; thus, liberation does not come from the view of a self.

Furthermore, the cultivation of a self is impossible, because such a self as you describe—the substratum of pleasure and so forth—does not exist; since there is no cultivation of such a thing, how could such a self possibly exist otherwise? (795)
For this self is the common substratum of cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth; even when it is meditated upon, it would remain exactly as it is.
However, if it were made free from defects by relying on human effort, [it would be transformed].
That is incorrect;
for charcoal being rubbed never attains whiteness. One's own inherent nature cannot be removed by anyone.
(796) Furthermore, one who is corrupt is not capable of removing his own corruption. How could the corrupt become non-corrupt? He does not ever become someone else. (797)
For this very reason, he says [regarding the faults in the doctrine of a self]:
"How can one for whom the self is dear desire its destruction?"

The self is not defiled by passion and the like; therefore, in its conjunction with them, it remains distinct in itself. Just as when there is a conjunction with a staff, the state of being a staff does not truly belong to the person holding the staff. (798) If passion and the like were unknown [to the self], the occurrence of passionlessness and so forth would be impossible. If passion were simply the cognition [of passion], then one would be a "possessor of women" (strīmān) merely by cognizing a woman. (799) His state of being passionate arises from a connection [with passion], and not from the cognition of passion and the like. For if it were through the cognition of passion and the like, then a yogi would become passionate due to the passion of others. (800)

If there is a difference [between them], what distinction is there between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)? If it is argued that their difference is not perceived, then from where is their difference supposed to be known? (801) If it is claimed that the nature of the self (*ātman*) is distinct [from cognition], how can the self be self-knowing?
For it has been established that there is no error regarding the awareness of one's own nature. (802)

Now, if this non-cognition were to be cognized like the form of a jar, then because it would be an object of cognition (*grāhya*), that [cognition] would be its subject (*grāhaka*); but this is not so, and thus it possesses no status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
For when tastes and the like are objects of enjoyment, no status as an enjoyer is perceived [in them].

The enjoyer would have to be something entirely different from that [pleasure], and in this way there would be an infinite regress. (804) If it is argued that enjoyment is inherent in that [soul] and for that reason it is called the "enjoyer," [we reply: enjoyment is nothing other than experience, and that [experience] resides in the object of enjoyment as well. (805) The worldly understanding is of this nature: "I have cognition" or "this is mine. Therefore, the relationship of the supported and the support exists in both cases. (806)
Now, when this [self] is being inferred, it is designated as the "experiencer. But where direct perception is impossible, there inference cannot stand; such is the settled rule.
(807) Furthermore, it is taught that this [self] is accessible only to yogins. Because of its extreme subtlety, its perception is not possible for people like us.
(808) For now, it is simply not possible for us to perceive it. As for those who have reached that state [of yoga], we do not know what will happen. (809)
If the determination of things is made by setting aside the state of the yogi, then for us, there is neither the non-existence nor the cognition of that [yogi].
Therefore, the self is of the nature of self-cognition alone and is quiescent; otherwise, its non-existence would follow.
And if it, which has the nature of cognizing pleasure and so forth, were otherwise, its very destruction would occur. Furthermore, how could one who holds the self dear desire its destruction?

And if [the self] were not [distinct from the states], then one must admit that the self is suffering when there is suffering; for if the state of suffering were destroyed, the self itself would be destroyed. || 811 ||
If it is your view that its states are perishable while the state-possessor is not,
[we reply that] no state is perceived apart from the nature of that [entity].
2. It is not a persisting entity; nevertheless, it might be argued that its nature as consciousness does not perish at all.
If it is argued that there is only the destruction of pleasure and so forth, this is not so;
for due to the difference between pleasure and the rest, a difference in consciousness itself would follow, since consciousness is never perceived apart from pleasure and the rest. (813)
When [consciousness] is divided by its own nature, it is not perceived as undivided; just as, in that very division, non-difference is not perceived.

(814) If the difference between consciousness and the "consciousness-of-consciousness" is distinguished through cognition, then for that very reason, even the self of another would become one's own self.

(815) The claim that "there is no consciousness of that [other]" is also extremely difficult to maintain; for if there were a state of non-consciousness, everything else would be devoid of self-nature. (816)

If that [self] were perceived as distinct [from its states], then oneness would never exist anywhere. Consequently, there would be no oneness between the prior and subsequent [moments], and thus [the self] would be subject to destruction.
And so, how could one who holds the self dear desire its destruction? For if it were immutable and eternal, one must accept that it remains established in that very state.

If it is argued that this does not excessively follow [as a consequence] here due to the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), then why is that very recognition not accepted when such a form [of the object] is possible?
(819) Since the object is impossible, recognition—which arises solely from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—would be the cause for the persistence of things.
(820) But surely, if there is immutability and permanence, there would be no successive cognition; nevertheless, let its permanence be established according to your own view. (821)
Or, if there is simultaneous perception, this [notion of] oneness may be accepted; but if there is non-simultaneous perception, then since the difference is clear, [the object] must be perishable.
Even if, indeed, there is no successive perception due to its being immutably eternal, nevertheless its eternity consists precisely in its being unchanging;
likewise, because there is an absence of sequence in the perception.
Therefore, if its perception occurs sequentially, it follows that there is necessarily a destruction of its perception as it ceases;
and thus, when there is a desire for sequential perception, there is necessarily a desire for its destruction.
Consequently, [the following applies].
*nityatā* (permanence); 4. *de-khol-bu-ñid-du* (in the state of being fixed).
