If one holds the self dear, how could one desire its destruction?
If you ask how one could desire its non-perception, [the answer is: weakness is better than death.
If he is to be beloved, let his life be preferable to a soft glance that obstructs one's life;
for what indeed can be done by him through mere unseenness?
Thus, a further sight of him must be sought.
And this being the case, if [the entity] occurs sequentially, that very [sequential occurrence] constitutes its destruction;
thus, this is another fault for the proponent of the self (ātmavādin).
Alternatively, because of the perception of an identical form, the identity of the prior and subsequent [moments] is logical.
But when a different form is perceived, difference itself is clear; and that being so, there is indeed the destruction of the prior [state].
And thus, how could one who holds the self dear desire its destruction? [This is] not a vision of death.
Alternatively, the Self, being of the nature of consciousness, is one and the same for all; yet it assumes differentiation due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
just as there is the appearance of differentiation— such as "the space within a jar" and "the space within a cloth"— despite the oneness of space.
Therefore, the distinction between selves is indeed created by ignorance alone.

If this is so, then for one who is liberated, since there is an absence of delusion, if he were to exist as another self, that [liberated] self would not exist; rather, he alone would be the one [universal] self, and his state would be the same as the state of worldly existence. (823)

If, just as the space within a jar does not exist when the jar is absent, so too the living being (*prāṇin*) did not exist in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), then it would follow that upon the disappearance of the space within the jar, the space becomes one with another; consequently,

just as there is no division of space, there would be no division of the self either, and thus the distinction between self and other would not exist, whereby the self— defined by its nature as "I" through the exclusion of "the other"— would indeed be destroyed.

For one who has attained the state of space, there is no activity, enjoyment, or the like; thus, he is no different from space. Therefore, if the self is dear to him, how could he desire its destruction?
If it is argued that this [destruction] follows by the force of reality itself, [we reply: no.
In that case, it follows that there is simply selflessness (*nairātmya*).
What is this so-called "pervasiveness" (*vyāpitā*) of that which consists of mere self-awareness? Pervasiveness is primarily said to exist when [an entity] occupies multiple locations;
permanence is designated when [an entity] extends across multiple times. Since there is neither pervasiveness nor permanence, how can a self (*ātman*) be established?

If, on the other hand, he were established in the form of another jar or such object, then he would all the more be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*), since he would likewise be established in the form of Devadatta and others. Therefore, if he were liberated, he would simply be non-existent like space;
and thus there would be no purpose whatsoever for such beings in liberation. Oh, what great lack of foresight this is on the part of the yogins!
Now, [if it is argued that] in ultimate reality the self is not the substratum of action, enjoyment, and so forth—this is the truth.
"Due to the power of ignorance alone, there arise in that [Self] such things as affection and so forth.
To this, the following refutation is stated: "[The Self is] the substratum of all qualities, experiences, and worldly transactions, once these have ceased. (235)

How could one desire love? For the nature of love is not such as that; it transcends all worldly dealings and depends upon the cotton-wool of the perception of the Self, being of the very nature of space. Therefore, whoever has love for someone does not desire that person to be like that [Self];
such is not the nature of love itself.
Or, if it were to manifest a lack of foresight,
one might argue: "It would be better to seek saṃsāra itself, because the pleasures of saṃsāra do not produce satisfaction."
It is said:
"The self is like a stone, a piece of wood, or a scale."

Even in nirvāṇa there is no happiness capable of producing complete satisfaction; for all happiness is happiness precisely because it is something to be longed for. Indeed, there is no such thing as happiness that is not to be desired;
therefore, even for one who is established in the full abundance of all happiness, there still exists a desire for a further excellence of happiness beyond that.
Since he seeks that very same pleasure again and again, his mind is not free from longing; and this so-called "longing" is another name for craving.
This is a great suffering for the great, and therefore all pleasure is indeed productive of dissatisfaction.

Consequently, no one at all is happy or has attained final nirvana; because, by turns, he possesses a longing for every kind of happiness, and having seen [the world] or through non-appropriation, he accumulates karma for the sake of happiness— thus, he must remain within saṃsāra itself.
Thus it is not [merely] a prayer; surely dispassion (*vairāgya*) is indeed observed. It is not as if it is not observed.

For he, being weary of that very [world] because of the exertion involved in seeking its means, regards it as nothing but suffering; thus, turning toward happiness and desiring another way, he directs himself toward dispassion (*vairāgya*), but not because he is devoid of affection for the Self.
Therefore, he says:

In every way, the grasping at a self firmly establishes affection for the self; that very state remains established as the seed of affection for what belongs to the self. This is the ultimate truth in this matter.

As long as there is grasping at a self, so long will one not be freed from attachment to the self; consequently, attachment to what belongs to the self [also persists] because it relies upon that benefit.

[Objection: But surely this person, having abandoned the very grasping at a self in order to avoid faults, will proceed [to liberation]; therefore, how can there be attachment to what belongs to the self and so forth?
It is said:
if he indeed has no grasping at a self, for what purpose would there be the removal of faults?
For one who lacks desire does not engage in doing anything at all.
If it were otherwise, he would not desire that [being] to be one who possesses suffering; yet he does not have a grasping for a self in that regard—these two [positions] are mutually contradictory.

If, in his desire to accomplish the welfare of others, he desires that [being] to be happy, then let it be brought about by another; however, if there is a preference [for it], there is once again the grasping for a self.

829. 1. Let it be done; how so? Even though the self (*ātman*) is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because a specific moment is possible, altruism (*parārtha*) is indeed possible. Therefore, the grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*) is in vain. 830.
If that action is performed by him alone through the power of his great majesty for the sake of others, what kind of "great majesty" can there be for one who possesses false pride? Therefore,
for one who does not truly desire a self that suffers, it is precisely that [notion] which constitutes his grasping at a self, as well as the arising of grasping at what belongs to a self.
Now, if one who desires long-term happiness is not possessed by the grasping for "mine," how could there be a desire for that [happiness] if it has not been seen as long-term happiness?

(833) If you say, "It might happen sometime," then even if there were no engagement [in practice], it might not happen at some point; for the "moonlight of the monkey" has already vanished. (834) Will this person not become a Brahmin when he reaches the state of fitness? Since [the two] would thus involve mutual dependence, how could there be any activity in that regard? (835)
Therefore,
even with effort, one who possesses [right] conduct, by relying on even a slight portion of virtue, brings about detachment from what belongs to the self and conceals those defects.

If it is argued that one who possesses the grasping of a self (*ātmagraha*)—relying on some slight trace of a quality that benefits the self and becoming attached to it—will certainly obstruct detachment (*vairāgya*) regarding what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), even while perceiving its faults, saying "it is not so," we say no; for the perception of faults is itself obstructed by that perception of qualities.
Therefore, one who is not detached from the self is likewise not detached from what belongs to the self.
If there were detachment even from the self, then there would be no one at all who is currently becoming detached. (238)
Insofar as he abandons the self, the cultivation of suffering would be futile;
for one is unable to abandon the self,
since it is not that very [self] which is perceived by it.

For instance, renunciation does not exist in the same way that passion exists, nor does it exist in the same way that it is absent; therefore, there is no total abandonment of the self. Consequently, one who is merely free from passion is always happy through that renunciation.
To this, it is replied:

That very non-abiding in pleasures is passion (*rāga*), characterized by grasping. And it has been analyzed previously that "where there is that [non-abiding], there is passion. (836) Furthermore, if there were dispassion (*virāga*) in a self, to whom would that dispassion belong?
For at present, there exists no one who becomes dispassionate.
For one thing is detached from another;
if that very thing were by nature undetached, it would not become detached.
To this, it is said:
If the self does not exist within the self, how could it become detached? It is not detached in the way that it exists, nor is it detached in the way that it does not exist.

(837) For there is no alteration of that [self], nor is there the persistence of another; thus, whether by way of its entire nature or a single part, it is in every respect impossible. (838) A single entity has no parts, and there is no non-difference from what has parts. That which has parts must be something else; if that were so, there would be an infinite regress. (839)

If it were somehow non-different [from the self], even so there would be an infinite regress, because there would be no end to the successive conceptualizations therein. Therefore, the self itself must be abandoned by him; for as long as he does not abandon the self in one way or another, the cultivation of suffering is useless, since it is impossible to achieve detachment.
Alternatively,

if there were detachment even toward the self, then that which is currently detached would no longer exist; since he abandons whatever [object] it encounters, the self is therefore non-existent, and thus the cultivation of the notion of renunciation is a futile suffering.
Indeed, because it does not abandon the purpose of cultivating [the perception of] suffering,
it is truly incapable of being the cause for detachment from this, just as it is not the cause for detachment from oneself.
Therefore, one is not liberated by such dispassion;
for this reason as well, the meditation on suffering is useless.
Even by means of the cultivation of suffering, he would only manifest suffering. Even though that [suffering] was previously perceived directly, if one still does not possess detachment,
then it would be appropriate for the cultivation of suffering to lead to detachment.
When that [insight] is attained, it does not lead to dispassion;
for the cultivation of suffering is indeed only a cause for the direct realization of suffering,
and not otherwise for dispassion.

One might think that the continuum of suffering would become dispassionate through cultivation, but this is not so because it was [already] so previously; therefore, that suffering is indeed directly perceived,
since a certainty preceded by direct perception is possible.
Otherwise, one would not seek to abandon cyclic existence;
for suffering that has not been directly realized does not afflict,
and yet there is no dispassion [without such realization].
Therefore, the cultivation of suffering is futile;

for the suffering of separation from loved ones and so forth is directly perceived by the entire world. If one is not already dispassionate toward it, how could dispassion arise through the cultivation of suffering?
Indeed, when the cultivation of suffering occurs as a recollection and synthesis of all suffering, it manifests a vast accumulation of suffering.
If it is argued that one becomes dispassionate because of that, [we reply:
from that agitation there might indeed be dispassion,
but this is not the case.
For just as a mass of suffering, when recollected, would cause one to become dispassionate, so too would a mass of pleasure; therefore, this person would become full of passion.
Just as dispassion arises from contemplating a continuum of suffering, so too would passion arise from its opposite; thus, how could there be liberation?

[Objection: "But surely, because one is terrified of the bliss of tranquility, one remains thirsty for the pleasures of cyclic existence. [Reply: That too is incorrect, because for one who is settled in the view of a self, tranquility is not a cause for agitation. Is the dwelling in a cemetery a cause of agitation for a crow? (843)
A crow does not find such delight in a lotus grove as it finds in association with a place situated in impurity. [Objection:
Is it not the case that detachment is indeed observed toward an object of pleasure due to the perception of its defects?
How then is it that one is not dispassionate even upon seeing faults through the cultivation of the nature of suffering?
It is not so, because:
"Even if the mind is momentarily shaken by a fault in one instance... (240)
Even in that case, there is no detachment at all, just as a lover is not detached from another woman;
for although there may be a momentary detachment toward a person who has committed some offense, even so, this is not detachment in every respect.
Indeed, a lover is not detached from one woman, yet he remains undetached from another woman, and in that regard, it is merely by turns.
For it is thus:
one is detached merely by being in a state opposed to passion, whereas an ordinary person remains undetached even when in a state not opposed to it;
therefore, such a person is detached only through the suppression of the power of passion, but not in every respect.
Furthermore, because attachment is seen therein,
it was said for this very reason: "O monks, that which has been abandoned by noble wisdom is truly abandoned."
Therefore,
that attachment which arises as a single state through the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is the seed for the successive emergence of all attachments.

For one who possesses the distinction between what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be accepted (*upādeya*), there is desire and aversion, but not for everyone [equally]. Since everything is neither always to be abandoned nor always to be accepted, desire and aversion—acting as seeds for one another—arise for such a person alternately; how then could this be consistent with the notion of a self (*ātman*)?

Furthermore, for one who perceives selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward everything; since the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has been abandoned, how could passion and the like arise in one who is established in the uprooting of all attachment?

Moreover, such [passion] might occur regarding an object that possesses the nature of being disagreeable (*virūpa*), but not otherwise; and for one who perceives a self, no object is ever disagreeable.
To begin with, his self is not defective;
furthermore, the affection toward it is not defective because its object is faultless;
and the means of apprehension are likewise free from defect.
If this entire world is merely this much, where now could he become dispassionate?
How can one who asserts a self be liberated?
Affection has an object free from fault, and its means of accomplishment are likewise free from fault. Since this entire world is exactly thus, how could one now become dispassionate toward it?—
this is the summary.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "If there is faultiness in that [object], then that same [faultiness] is equal in its own self as well.
In that case, being unattached to that [self], how could he now become detached from its faults?
But surely the defects of objects are also observed, as are those of the body and so forth;

indeed, what is the defectiveness of those things that are causes of pleasure? Is it not the case that they are causes of suffering? Surely everything is a cause of pleasure at one time and a cause of suffering at another.
But surely that [attachment] is equally present in the self as well;
if one is not detached from that very self,
where could one find detachment?
If you argue that the self cannot be abandoned, then there would likewise be no detachment from what belongs to the self; furthermore,
the claim that only what belongs to the self can be abandoned because its defects can be discarded is also false.
Whenever a particular fault arises, it should be abandoned at that time and not all at once,

just as faults are abandoned. If it is argued that just as faults are impermanent, their abandonment is also impermanent— resulting in great suffering later when the cause of happiness has been relinquished and is no longer present— therefore, it is more appropriate to abandon them from the very root.
If that were so, then even when suffering exists, since great happiness follows immediately thereafter, one should embrace suffering as well;
therefore, there is no dispassion whatsoever for one who perceives a self.
Furthermore:
The perception of defects should counteract the affection born from seeing virtues; however,
this is not the case regarding the senses and so forth, since such [affection] is observed even in children and others.

Affection for the senses and so forth does not arise from perceiving their qualities, but rather from the perception of them as "one's own" (*ātmīya*). This is because affection exists even toward that which possesses defects, provided it is regarded as one's own; conversely, affection is absent elsewhere—even toward that which possesses qualities—when it is not one's own, or when it has passed away and so on. For instance, affection persists for the senses and other things even when they are recognized as defective, as long as they are embraced as "mine"; yet it is absent toward others, even if they possess qualities. Furthermore, affection occurs even in children, cattle, and the like, who have not yet discerned qualities or defects.
Moreover, since affection does not cease upon seeing faults because it has already ceased for what is past and will likewise not arise for what is future,
in that case, the very notion of "mine" will simply not occur due to the perception of faults.
And because of that state, affection [arises];
yet this is of no consequence, since the perception of "mine" produced by the perception of qualities is removed through the perception of faults.

For that very reason, the perception of virtues is not deprived of its status as the cause for the notion of "mine" either; therefore, that notion also does not arise from the non-perception of virtues.
Furthermore, because attachment sometimes occurs even toward that which possesses faults due to the presence of one's own prosperity,
and because it does not occur even toward that which possesses virtues when such prosperity has passed away or for other reasons,
the attribution of excellent qualities is indeed observed there [in attachment] on account of affection.
Therefore, how can an injunction that does not subvert its own cause subvert that [affection]? For even affection might be lost through the perception of defects;
yet, to the extent that such affection exists, that very perception of defects is dispelled by the application of the attribution of excellent qualities.
If it is argued that neutrality of mind consists in seeing faults and not attributing virtues [to others], we say no;
for through affection, that very state of neutrality cannot be attained. Unless one is constrained by another form of attachment toward a different object, that neutrality is not otherwise possible.
And so, that very injury of his is transformed when it is thus; for whatever kind of food was eaten by the mother, such is it even for the ḍākinī.
He is not liberated from that [suffering] even by a ḍākinī; for one who perceives a self, liberation does not come through the cultivation of suffering or through the abandonment of affection.
On this point, the Sāṃkhyas say:

The cultivation of the contemplation of suffering is not possible for those who perceive a self; rather, liberation comes from the thorough knowledge of the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
For it is said:

"In the ultimate sense, this person has the nature of pure consciousness; having failed to recognize the otherness of primordial nature, he has resorted to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) through delusion. (846)
The claim that the soul is not liberated because it does not grasp through discrimination its own nature as consisting of pleasure and so forth,
and that liberation occurs only upon the arising of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) from that [discrimination],
is also incorrect.
Because,
through the desire for what is higher and lower, and through the notion of destruction and origination,
these people perceive the self as something distinct from the senses and other faculties. || 248 ||

Therefore, even through the view of oneness, one who feels affection for the self [feels it] toward those things internal to perception; by their very nature, he is attached to them. Indeed, the very observation of decline and prosperity is the observation of difference, for difference exists through the states of presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The self is a persisting entity, whereas pleasure and the like are not persisting;
therefore, because of the superposition of contradictory properties, there is a difference between them.
Now, the transmigrating being does not even reflect upon this very point.
Thus, only the expression of truth is [possible],
because a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) based on discrimination (*viveka*) is impossible;
for one who desires pleasure certainly does not pay heed to its abandonment.
No discerning person who desires anything would seek union with a self devoid of pleasure and the like;
if it is argued that there was no prior transmigratory existence because one perceives identity with the *pradhāna* within oneself even before the association with the desirer,
that is incorrect.
How could there be the delusion of oneness for one who is conscious yet sleeping? Whence would there be a longing for objects, from which follows attachment to saṃsāra?
(847) For there is no entry of the *pradhāna* there; whence then could there be oneness? Indeed, it has already been established that there is no delusion regarding the Self itself.

(848) If [the Sāṃkhya] says that it is seen as an object, then there would be no apprehension of non-difference. Furthermore, since the intellect (*buddhi*) is absent, such seeing is not tenable in the Sāṃkhya system. (849)
And desire for an object that has been seen motivates men; how, then, could there be the existence of memory prior to the occurrence of creation? (850)
If it is argued that desire and memory arise from the very functioning of *prakṛti*, and that its functioning arises from desire, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

(851) If it is argued that these [desires] come from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then how could pleasure and so forth belong to this [Self], since even the latent impression of *pradhāna* must precede any modification?

(852) Therefore, if *prakṛti* is held to be the nature of that which consists of self-awareness, it cannot be made otherwise; thus, this [Self] would always be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). (853)
[Objection: Surely, since aversion is indeed observed to arise from the experience of suffering, how could it be otherwise? To this, he says:
"But that aversion toward present suffering which is of such a kind is merely hatred. (250)
It is not dispassion; for even then there is attachment in him, because he seeks another state,
since aversion, being a source of suffering, remains established only to that extent.
When that [state] has ceased, he returns once more to his own original nature.

Even though agitated by the experience of suffering, the yogi who possesses dispassion does not [react with aversion], for through his affection for the Self, he perceives the Self and what belongs to the Self as being contrary [to suffering]. Indeed, at that time, he is merely one who feels aversion toward impure objects and the like, based on the mere cognition of them as such.

But for one who perceives the self and possesses ultimate dispassion (*vairāgya*), there is certainly no liberation from affection; rather, because of the longing for a different state, hatred will always persist. In that regard, however, this [notion of] dispassion does not exist [in such a person].

As long as that suffering exists, so long does hatred proceed. But once the cause—suffering—is ceased, whence can there be hatred? (854) If suffering continues to recur, let this [state] be auspicious liberation (*mukti*). For one who is perpetually overwhelmed by hatred for suffering, the state [he occupies] is always a downward course. (855)
But surely, how can there be liberation without agitation?
For no sentient being who is not agitated by *saṃsāra* seeks liberation; nor does a person become agitated unless they are overwhelmed by suffering.
This is incorrect.
And for that very reason,
indifference toward everything— arising from the abandonment of rejection and acceptance— is called detachment for those who are like the *vāsī* (axe) and *candana* (sandalwood). //252//
O Vāsīcaṇḍana!

For it is by seeing the mere nature of phenomena (*dharmatāmātra*) that the mind attains freedom from possessiveness (*mamatā*). Indeed, through the abandonment of improper mental application (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), there arises for yogins the state of being endowed with detachment (*vairāgya-yogitā*) according to our school, and not otherwise. How then was the cultivation of suffering (*duḥkha-bhāvanā*) taught by the Blessed One?
The response here is:
"equality of mind."
Having attained that very state,
because one is free from attachment and aversion, [one remains equanimous].
Having understood the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the meditation on suffering was taught.
That [suffering] arises for us through conditions; it is the basis for the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-dṛṣṭi*).
Logic, however, is for the sake of the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*); the remaining meditations have that same purpose.
By that very [means], he taught suffering from impermanence, and likewise selflessness from suffering.
3. Selflessness.
Indeed, the cultivation of suffering was not taught with reference merely to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*);

for if the bliss of detachment were destroyed by that alone in those possessed of passion, they would abandon their partiality, and thus it was taught so that there might arise fitness for the cultivation of the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāraduḥkha*).
And that suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) is, in the ultimate sense, nothing other than emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, liberation comes from the vision of emptiness alone;
all other meditations have that as their sole purpose.
For this very reason, the teaching of the Blessed One culminates in the realization of selflessness.
When he said, "O monks, is form permanent or impermanent?"—
"Impermanent, Venerable Sir."

"Venerable sir, that which is impermanent is suffering; is it pleasant or is it suffering? That which is impermanent is suffering and subject to change; one should regard it thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'"
"No indeed, Venerable Sir. By this, it is stated that the very vision of non-self through the relationship of cause and effect is the means to liberation;
furthermore, he who perceives a self is not one who has become dispassionate.
In the Dīrghāgama or the Madhyamāgama it is said:
"One who is not dispassionate, who possesses craving, and who relies upon all undertakings—such a person is unliberated from afflictions and karma, and is called a transmigrator. (255)

For when the seed of the view of self is established, the view of "mine" remains unimpaired as a cause of saṃsāra; consequently, one who is not detached from self and what belongs to self will necessarily possess craving. Thereafter, being dependent upon the undertaking of all actions and remaining unliberated from afflictions and karma, such a person will surely continue to wander in saṃsāra—how, then, could there even be the scent of liberation for them?

Furthermore, it might be argued: "In ultimate reality, that which belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) does not exist at all; therefore, how could affection arise? For affection, by its very nature, must have an object; it cannot be without an object."
That too is incorrect;
for one who does not desire even that which belongs to a self, there exists no enjoyer of it either.
At that time, even a self does not exist, for its defining characteristics are indeed action and enjoyment.
If it is argued that one's own self as it is being perceived cannot be established as non-existent because everything is bound by ignorance (*avidyā*),
we say no; for ignorance does not exist apart from the self.

Ignorance is not other than the person, because of the statement, "The person alone is all this. Therefore, since it has ignorance as its very nature, its state of delusion would never depart; for a delusion that is identical with one's own nature does not depart from it, as that would entail the disappearance of the person itself. 1 T.
This [position] has been rejected in the Upaniṣad;
furthermore, when that which belongs to the self (the self's own nature) does not exist, neither activity nor experience exists, because the self consists essentially of activity and experience.
If it is argued that even this [self] is not accepted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
then what support is there for the self’s being for the sake of another?
If it is argued that this is because it is determined by cognition (*saṃvedana*), then it follows that everything would be cognized.

It is not logical to claim that [the world] is unreal due to habituation, like a dream and so forth; for if that were so, the self (ātman) would likewise lack ultimate reality. If, on the other hand, there is non-duality, then it must be a variegated non-duality (citrādvaita).

There is no such thing as a self (*ātman*), because permanence is not apprehended by perception—which grasps only the present intrinsic nature—since the two perceptions of the prior and subsequent [moments] cannot exist simultaneously; thus, the notion that the self is permanent in either case is not accepted even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the correct understanding.
Furthermore, there is no synthesis [of moments] because memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
and since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is absent, inference (*anumāna*) is also absent. Therefore, the desired goal is not accomplished through the vision of a self (*ātman*).
2. There is no cognition of a permanent self by means of each [moment] individually;
therefore, it has as its seed a homogeneous series that is beginningless. || 257 ||
O you who desire liberation, uproot the sprouts of the views of sentient beings.
"O you who desire liberation, uproot the view of a self-existent being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) by means of the very sword [of wisdom]!
Liberation comes only from the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*); there is no other valid path. This is the conclusion: [liberation does not come] through scripture alone."
Surely, the existence of the self is known from scripture, and its liberation exists; moreover,
that liberation consists of absolute bliss and is never non-existent,
whereas worldly pleasure is subject to interruption— thus, one finds no satisfaction in the latter.
And since that [knowledge] arises from the procedure of initiation and so forth, the entire preceding objection is indeed not to be raised;
for it has been said:
"The words of those who, through the vision of the sages (ārṣa), perceive entities beyond the reach of the senses, are not sublated by inference. (857)
Or [the claim] that "speech is not of human origin"— that too is untenable for those who do not perceive any basis for such a nature of scripture. (258)
One who speaks merely on the basis of having attained liberation does not produce satisfaction;
while this statement is true, the speech of those who do not perceive supersensuous objects is sublated by inference,
for that very fact— that the speech is produced by such [liberation]— is not understood.
Because this [system] is common to all scriptures,
it does not follow that all scriptures are authoritative,
nor is the performance of their respective purposes possible.
It has been stated that the claim of non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is not tenable—[for] initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of no avail.
[Objection: But surely, the state of seeds and so forth being incapable of sprouting is observed to result from contact with the procedure of initiation.
That too is incorrect;
a procedure perfected by means such as seeds and the like is not capable of preventing the birth of persons,
because it would follow that liberation could result even from oil massages, fire-burns, and so forth.
Now, if the efficacy of an oil massage is only of such a limited measure, then it is the same even in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*); likewise,
since the self (*ātman*) is formless, there can be no increase or decrease in the weight of one's sins.
Previously, due to the lightness [of the body] before the Guru, the removal of sin was not performed later. Let there be no heaviness for him; since sin is formless, it is not heavy.
Even if there were lightness of the body prior to the Guru for one who has been initiated...
The removal of sin does not occur by that much alone;
for lightness, being perceived as the opposite of heaviness, leads only to the inference of the absence of weight, not the absence of sin,
since sin lacks the quality of weight.
If it is argued that "this teacher is indeed [defined] by his sin," from what [source is this known]? If it is argued that it is "from scripture," then it has been said here:
moreover—

There is no liberation from even such a small amount of evil without its destruction; moreover, it is not established that there is power elsewhere [in mere existence] by virtue of its capacity. (858) Where indeed is the vision of deities and so forth not found? If liberation were to exist everywhere, what would be the distinction [between them]?
(859) Now, in your own position, if the severance of craving indeed results from the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*), one must still consider how liberation itself occurs.
Even that is not as it truly is; for [it occurs] under the influence of false cognition and the volition of thirst arising therefrom. (261)
There is no movement toward a location, and thus birth arises as something whose [prior] state has been severed;
for the causal capacity for that birth resides solely in those two [parents], because it exists only in them.
(262) Since:
Those conscious beings themselves perform karma, which is the cause of birth;
indeed, the attainment of place and so forth is observed solely through the power of craving (tṛṣṇā).
Surely karma is also a cause of birth; therefore, how can there be the state of being caused by that [craving] alone?
That too is incorrect;
for those very two conscious entities themselves constitute the action which was preceded by consciousness and characterized by consciousness.
Due to actions such as giving and their subsequent mental impressions, there arise in a future life a volition and a misconception along with the craving produced by it;
these alone are the direct karma, because birth occurs immediately following them.

But because it is the cause of that [birth], karma is only metaphorically so; it is not directly, by its own nature, the complete cause of birth. Even for one who has been initiated, that [karma] exists, and thus there is no liberation. Or rather, it might be argued:
"The substratum is the cause of both movement and cognition, and these [causes] arise from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). (263)
Because the unseen (adṛṣṭa) perishes, there is no [resultant] movement; its latent impression (saṃskāra) is not volition (cetanā).

The wholesome is of ten kinds, and the unwholesome is likewise of ten kinds; it does not have the characteristic of volition, and that [unseen merit/demerit] is destroyed by means of rituals such as initiation (dīkṣā).
That too is incorrect, because the object is not established;
moreover, [the capacity] arises from the production of the instrument, following the presence and absence [of the cause]. (264)
They have been seen in the Buddha, but not in anyone else; do they not exist?
[They do] indeed exist right now.
The instruments, such as the eyes and so forth, follow the positive and negative concomitance of the intellect; being directed by the intellect, they arise in succession.
Therefore, why does [the object] not arise?
If it is argued that there is no capacity for arising because of impairment caused by initiation (*dīkṣā*), then [this being the case]:
Retention, propulsion, agitation, and cessation are dependent upon consciousness;

they would not exist if that [consciousness] were incapable. For if the qualities of the self, such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, were rendered powerless by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and thus lacked the capacity for rebirth immediately following that initiation— || 265 ||

Then, immediately after initiation, the intellect being impaired, these [functions] would not occur: retention, acting according to one's own will, withdrawal from sense objects, impelling toward what is desired, agitation, instability, obstruction, and destruction.

Now, as for the claim that there is a lack of capacity immediately after death because causes depend upon a specific transformation [of the body], that too is incorrect. There is no such distinction as "there is no capacity now for the non-arising of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, whereas there would be after death. (860)

If even now some slight capacity were perceived, then through the attainment of excellence, there might be something further; however, when no progression whatsoever that partakes of gradation is observed, then the conceptualization of liberation is entirely groundless. Furthermore, because of the existence of the intellect, passion and the other afflictions possess a nature identical to it.
Furthermore, the claim that the phenomena of saṃsāra cease immediately after death simply because consciousness (buddhi) no longer exists is incorrect;
for how can it be said that consciousness itself does not exist in another birth?

If it is argued that [liberation occurs] after death, then the entire procedure of initiation would be useless; for since the mind ceases to exist at death, there would be no liberation. Alternatively, if [liberation occurs] while the mind still exists, then [the soul] would not be joined with impurities. (266)

If those stains, such as passion (*rāga*), were incapable of functioning within the intellect (*buddhi*) even while one is alive, they would be ineffective; for these stains, though existing, are not the causes of the intellect's absence. Thus, the non-existence of the intellect does not follow from their presence.

Alternatively, if passion and the other stains, being impaired by initiation (*dīkṣā*), are no longer capable, then they would not serve as the causes for the reconnection (*pratisandhi*) of the intellect in one who is living.
If it is argued that liberation occurs immediately after initiation,
that is not so.
Due to the excessive nourishment of the opposing side and its own side, faults arising from the continuity of their own seeds remain unprevented even in one who has been initiated.
For faults indeed arise from their own seeds; why is this so?
Due to the decrease and increase of the counteragent, which is the realization of selflessness,
and due to the decrease of one's own position, namely improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*),
such defects remain unavoidable even for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*).
In this life and in another, how can he be liberated?
If the self is eternal, there is no rebirth;
but if there is the vision of selflessness, whose liberation would it be?
For when the self, which is afflicted by the impurities of passion and so forth, becomes pure through some means, it is then liberated;
for liberation is indeed the cessation of bondage,
and that which is bondage under the view of selflessness is truly bondage.
He is not liberated simply by virtue of being eternal, because the perception of a self still persists;

that too is incorrect. For one who has no purity, there is no other [state]; fire is neither *nirvāṇa* nor a purifier (*pāvaka*). Nevertheless, the designation "fire is *nirvāṇa*" remains established. (861)
In that regard, in our position, it is merely a matter of verbal expression that does not hold together,
and that has been resolved by means of an illustrative example; however, in the doctrine of the self (ātmavāda), the very meaning itself does not hold together.
However, it does not hold up by mere verbal artifice,
nor is there anything [to be proven], because the primary reality is not undermined; furthermore, there is no illustrative example here from which [it could be inferred].
Because that which is eternal is independent, sequential origination is contradicted.
[If] there were action and non-action in what is of a similar nature, then there would indeed be a difference in the state of the self; for in such a case, liberation of the self [would occur].

Furthermore, since it has been determined in another section that while something exists in an impure state, purification is possible, the various states cannot be effects produced in succession; for if [the cause] were independent, it would follow that all the states would arise simultaneously.
Moreover:
Action is contradicted because the states of action and non-action are identical; furthermore, there would be identity between cause and effect if they were distinct from one another.
In that case, there would be a loss of the status of agent and enjoyer, and causal efficacy would not be established.
If there were identity, it would follow that the cause and the fruit are one,

because they are contained within a single self, just like that self itself; if there were difference between those two, the cause and the fruit, then he [the self] would be neither the agent nor the enjoyer.
Due to the absence of a connection with the instruments and experiences [of others],
as in the case of another self, there is no connection even from the perspective of experience;
otherwise, like another self, the yogi would become both agent and enjoyer by directly perceiving the instruments and experiences of other selves.

Now, [if it is argued that] the relation is indeed inherence (samavāya), that is not so, precisely because inherence does not exist; nor is inherence the cause of the cognition of unity even for yogins. Furthermore, if it is argued that he becomes the agent and the enjoyer by virtue of the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) between cause and effect, that too is untenable.
Furthermore, efficacy is not established;
it has been demonstrated that there is no efficacy in what is eternal.
[Now follows] the connection with memory regarding selflessness (*nairātmya*).
In that case, even in the absence of a self (*nairātmya*), memory, experience, and so forth would not be established;
therefore, the consequence that memory, experience, and so forth would belong to another does not constitute a refutation. (270)
Because of the absence of memory; for the arising of memory occurs only when something has been experienced by someone, yet there is no recollection by anyone since the rememberer is absent.
Furthermore, there is no experience because the experiencer is absent; rather, it is simply memory [that arises].

That very same [principle] applies to the rememberer and the object of remembrance; likewise, it should be stated regarding experience (*bhoga*): pleasure alone is the object of experience (*bhogya*), while experience itself is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Furthermore, that remembrance arises from its cause, which is direct experience (*anubhava*).
Now, why does it not arise from another experience—specifically one considered to belong to another—and why would there not be an experience of another's karma?

If it is argued that [the fault does not apply] because of the necessity of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), why does this same fault not apply even to the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*)? [The opponent replies: "Because of the difference of the self (*ātmano bhedāt*). [The author asks: "Whence comes that very difference?

Just as memory cannot arise from another despite there being no distinction in the self, so too, despite there being no distinction in the mind (*manas*), the emergence of recollection cannot come from another. (862)
This distinction among mental states may indeed arise from a difference in their causes; but how could this division of distinction exist for the self, which is without cause? (863) [Objection:

But if there were no single self, how could there be the connection to unity in such thoughts as "I see" and "I remember"? [Response: This same fault applies equally to the self; there is no reason for joy here [in your position]. (864)
If it is argued that the self knows both memory and perception as having a single locus by means of perception itself, we reply:

it has already been established that there is no perceptual cognition of things as being prior and posterior; therefore, since perception is impossible in this case, inference does not operate there either. (865)

If the self truly knows itself as having a prior form, then the existence of that prior consciousness would be present at this time. (866) Consequently, how could there be the possibility of its being known as "prior"? For when something is currently being experienced, its prior existence is not perceived.

(867) [Objection: Its priority is established solely through memory. [Reply: Memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: If its reality is established solely through memory, why is it not accepted in other cases as well? (868)
Therefore, even in the doctrine of a self (*ātman*), unity does not exist in reality; rather, because those two [the self and the body] exist simultaneously, they are mistakenly conceived as one.
(869) In what is merely conceived as a unity, conventional usage proceeds through differentiation; and this usage of "one" is observed due to their performing a single function.
(870) This is clearly the power of beginningless habitual practice of ignorance (*avidyā*); there is no self, yet the Veda alone thus brings about the grasping of a self. (871)
How, then, can the process of saṃsāra proceed without a self?

Since the view of a real body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) cannot exist without a self, even memory—which is incapable of grasping either unity or permanence/impermanence due to the absence of a prior and subsequent form—is rendered impossible; therefore, saṃsāra itself would simply not exist.

It has been stated here that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as "saṃsāra," because of the teaching that the movement of intrinsic nature is by its own nature [non-existent];
nevertheless, from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), this is so.
For instance,
with respect to the four truths, one becomes intensely thirsty by superimposing sixteen unreal aspects, such as "it is stable," "it is happiness," and "I am."
(iii) Right view is the view of selflessness; it opposes the aspect of the reality of a self which is contrary to that very [selflessness]. (272a) Liberation results from the exhaustion of craving.
Right view, when well-cultivated, destroys craving along with its attendants.
Indeed, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is merely the superimposition of what is unreal; it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, the sixteen aspects [of the four truths] are unreal; for one who possesses thirst due to the superimposition of those [aspects], there arises the conceit of the transmigration of karma. Otherwise, the occurrence of cyclic existence would be impossible.

Furthermore, there is no conceit whatsoever that is distinct from the cognition of "self" and "other. Therefore, even in the absence of such cognition, there arises the conceit of the oneness of the self; yet, when things are of such a nature, for one who possesses the reflection that "there is nothing here" through the possibility of proper mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), there occurs—by virtue of stability and cultivation—the purity of selflessness. This is the object of direct realization, characterized by the complete cessation of all ignorance, and is synonymous with *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, for those who perceive reality, liberation results from the cessation of craving;
[this is] the supreme and subordinate realization.
[Objection: But if karma and the body persist, how can there be liberation?
[Response: This is not so, because even while karma and the body persist, their further arising does not occur due to the absence of the three causes. (273)
Just as there is no arising of a sprout without a seed due to the absence of one, so too,
if it is the case that liberation occurs upon the destruction of either karma or the body, then liberation indeed follows from the exhaustion of karma, as they say:
"Liberation results from the destruction of karma."
This is not the case,
because,
since an opposing side is impossible, there can be no destruction of karma and the body. (274)
Furthermore, because craving persists and [suffering] arises again due to its impossibility [to be abandoned],
effort toward the destruction of karma for the sake of destroying both [karma and craving] is futile.
(275) For one whose karma is not destroyed, there is no liberation.
For there is no other counteragent to the body produced by karma than the cessation of craving; thus,
the scriptural authorities concerning initiation and the like have been explained, and it is not the case that scripture is not a valid means of knowledge.
One who is not bound by craving does not perform karma;
for from that [craving], passion, hatred, and the like arise without effort.
And when both are exhausted, it is better that craving alone has been turned back.
If it is argued that karma must also be exhausted, [we reply] no, because— as has been stated— the counteragent is impossible. 2 T.
The portion of the verse beginning with "for the sake of the destruction of the two" has been established here.
Furthermore, because a variety of fruits is observed, a diversity of potencies in karmas is inferred; therefore, [the destruction] does not result from a single form of ascetic affliction. (276)

When karma possesses the capacity to yield manifold fruits and is present within the self, how can there be its exhaustion merely through the experience of a single type of fruit? Furthermore, since the fruit characterized by the affliction of suffering is of a single form, its exhaustion from that alone is not logical;
for this reason:
1. The accomplishment of manifold fruits.
The result is a gradual exhaustion; how could that [result] produced by it be small? It cannot be of a different kind, for by whatever karma a fruit of that same kind is to be produced.
Through the experience of even a small portion of its fruit, only that fruit born of that specific karma is exhausted; by the experience of that fruit,
there is no depletion of fruits of a different nature.
Moreover, by the power of austerity, through the mixing or the destruction of powers,
it might be exhausted through some affliction;
yet, if the power of austerity exists, then the entire fruit is diminished without affliction, even by a mere fraction— such as the plucking out of a single hair.
To that also it is said:
"Then [it is] indeed entirely."
If, by merely plucking out a single hair,
one desires something other than affliction, then that austerity is indeed affliction itself.

If it is argued that there is no confusion of powers and so forth because that [tapas] is the fruit of karma, then if that austerity is the result of affliction (kleśa), the destruction of karma follows from that very affliction; what then is the use of the five-fold heat and other such hardships?
Let all karma be exhausted by that alone.
Indeed, it is not the case that when something is performed by one person, another person's capacity is understood [thereby];
nor is affliction itself austerity, because it is the fruit of karma;
and yet austerity is not merely the fruit of karma.
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even animals and the like who endure cold and heat would be ascetics;
furthermore, this is not the fruit of karma because it proceeds from desire,
whereas the fruit of karma belongs even to one who is devoid of such desire.
That too is incorrect;
at that time, it was his ascetic practice.
Through the five bones and so forth, the attainment of a kingdom and the like may occur by one's own wish; is this not the fruit of karma?
There is indeed such karma, and the intellect follows that karma.
(872) Moreover, if that were not the fruit of karma, how then could it be said by you that "karma is exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit"?
Therefore, this [intellect] is simply the fruit of karma.
Consequently, there would be the destruction of only the sin, not of the karma such as kingship;
therefore, even kingship and the like must necessarily be experienced.
Alternatively, if kingship and so forth are renounced precisely because of being free from desire for them, [then that is another matter].
Since the suffering of the hells and so forth must necessarily be experienced when it falls upon one by force,
therefore affliction itself is desired;
if that is so, then the suffering of the hell-beings must also be experienced.
Now, if it is argued that because those two are painful, they are removed precisely as suffering through such acts as the plucking out of hair in the hells and so forth— that too is incorrect.
For this too is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Now, because those two are suffering, they are eliminated by the mere fact of being suffering itself.

Because it involves the plucking out of hair from those in the hells and other realms, and because it is painful, it is not a cause for the exhaustion of karmas, like the suffering of cattle. If you argue that this [reason] is inconclusive, why is it not so in your own statement as well? 873
Moreover,
just as the absence of the pleasures of sovereignty does not hinder one who is free from desire,
so too, through practice, that hellish suffering does not hinder him.

Through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), all things in the world—such as suffering, pleasure, and so forth—are [transcended]; therefore, for one established in liberation, there is no suffering, pleasure, or the like. (875) Furthermore, it might be argued: "There exists an action (*karman*) that leads to the exhaustion of action; this is precisely your own admission. Thus, your position is contradicted by your own admission (*abhyupagama-bādhā*).
That is incorrect, because even for the purpose of destroying a fault that is about to arise, there are remedies that are opposed to that fault. (278)
They would be capable of that very action; how then could there be a loss of what has been done?
1. T. tajje
Indeed, there is no loss of a deed performed; for there is no such thing as the destruction of what has been done.
If so, how is the exhaustion of karma explained? To this it is replied:
Karma is of such a nature that it yields its fruit when another set of causal conditions (*sāmagryantara*) arises, provided there is no presence of something contradictory to that karma. (876) 2 T.
*sāmagryantara-sambhave*
Furthermore, that which is necessarily capable of yielding a fruit must inevitably bestow that fruit;
for that purpose, there is no need for ascetic exertion,
since it arrives by its own inherent power.

Upon the complete destruction of passion and the like, however, there is only the destruction of the future fruit that is the effect of passion, but not of karma already performed that is necessarily to be experienced.
If it is argued that just as there is the re-emergence of karmas when craving persists, so too there is the arising of craving again when karma persists— that is incorrect, because:

Faults do not cause one to act wickedly, nor does the absence of faults; [it is rather] through false conceptualization that desire arises even for pleasure. When craving exists, one performs action for the sake of its fruit, or otherwise; for if craving were absent, one would do nothing at all.

Now, if it is argued that because virtuous karma is capable of bestowing happiness, one who desires happiness must necessarily [perform it], then that is not so; for in ultimate reality, there is no such thing as happiness even within saṃsāra, but rather it is merely a false conceptual construction (mithyāvikalpa). Without that false conceptual construction, from where could desire arise, or for whom would that happiness exist?

Therefore, liberation occurs only through the complete destruction of ignorance characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and not otherwise; thus, the illumination of the Four Noble Truths is itself "protection" (*tāya*).
And because he protects, his status as a Sugata is established—from that which is characterized by the instruction on the Four Truths, which constitutes the effect.
Because he protects [beings], he is the means for the stable knowledge of all particularities regarding reality;
because the root *gam* has the sense of "understanding," he is superior to those both outside the fold and to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Indeed, it is through this protection that the Blessed One is recognized as the Sugata.
And that state of being a Sugata is the knowledge of all specific qualities, stable in reality,
which is the knowledge of reality.
Exalted knowledge, stable knowledge,
and non-returning knowledge.
For that which is stable— the knowledge of all particulars without exception and the knowledge of all aspects— does not return again.
For here, the root *gam* has the sense of "awakening" (*bodha*) as its object, meaning "complete knowledge";
that this exists in the Blessed One is known precisely from his being a protector (*tāyin*).
Indeed, it is not from inference alone that [the Buddha's] status as a protector (*tāyitva*) is established;
for such a status as a protector is not possible for others.
If it were established through inference, then that status would belong to others as well.
Now, if the response to inference is that "this has come down through a lineage," then that being the case,
it would also apply to other [means of knowledge] as well.
It is known as "Sugata" (4 T).
Now, [it is] that which has come down through successive tradition.
There might be a distinction such that inference occurs in some cases and not in others; however,
even for a single person, there is no such distinction once the instruction of the Blessed One has been received.
From this, it is known that the Blessed One possesses the vision of all aspects of all things;
for without the vision of all aspects of all things,
this [cognition]— such as "all things are momentary"— would not be possible, since uncertainty would arise regarding that very aspect which has not been seen.
Now, if it were to be as it is for us, then it would also be so for him;
yet that cannot be for us without his instruction.
Therefore, this certainty belongs to one who has seen [the truth] directly and who receives instruction from another, and not to anyone else.
And there is no instruction without certainty,
nor is there even the absence of instruction.
Now, if it is argued that this [error] can occur even through delusion,
that is incorrect,
because:
If [the object] were eternal, there would be delusion due to the occurrence of a similar subsequent [moment];
but if it were momentary, what could be the cause of delusion by which such [delusion] might arise?
Even with a body, [delusion] does not occur at all.
Because there is an absence of perception of both [aspects] and because it relies upon both parts,
this instruction proceeds from certainty alone;
and that certainty does not exist for us without direct realization, since inference is impossible without our [traditional] instruction.
Nor was this spoken by the Blessed One out of doubt,
for that would entail the possibility of both [types of knowledge] being taught;

therefore, because the Blessed One, the Sugata, possesses the yoga of stable and complete knowledge of reality, it is for that very reason that the Blessed One surpasses both the outsiders and those in training and beyond training.
From that [compassion] comes the attainment of Sugataship;
from that, the accomplishment of the knowledge for the sake of others; from that, his teaching; and from that, compassion.
From that [teaching] comes the state of being devoted to the welfare of others, because one who has accomplished their own goal does not cease [from activity].
It is true that the Blessed One possesses the state of a Sugata; however, for what reason is this so? This is the response.
But from what [source] is that cause, known as "Teacher-hood," inferred— the accomplishment of knowledge for the sake of others—
since otherwise the state of being a Sugata would be impossible?
Even more than that, compassion is not otherwise [possible] without the accomplishment of knowledge for the sake of others;
indeed, what is achieved by this mere state of being a Sugata? It is not so, because he is an authority [only] on this account.

Its validity does not arise from mere cognition, but from its being an instruction; it possesses validity at all times, for otherwise that [instruction] would not be a valid means of knowledge for us. (878) 3 T. Deng-la
Regarding this, it is said:
"Therefore, because one who has attained the goal does not cease [from activity], there is dependence upon the welfare of others;
for through compassion, in the application of knowledge for the sake of others, one always acts solely for the sake of others."
Furthermore, he does not enter final nirvana out of compassion, as was stated previously.
(7) Because he is consistent in his teaching, the Blessed One is a valid authority;
out of compassion, he teaches what is beneficial, and through his knowledge, he reveals reality along with its means of attainment.
Since he is diligent in speaking that [truth], he possesses the status of a valid authority.
For it is possible for one who is compassionate to speak of the highest good; moreover, through knowledge, he speaks of what is attained as being non-erroneous.

That knowledge, along with its means, and those means, along with their application—he is capable of explaining all this because he possesses these four causes. Therefore, by this [statement], he establishes his status as an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*).
In these cases—beginning and end, cause and effect, and so forth—the relationship is that of cause and fruit;
therefore, it is definitively stated that the Blessed One possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason, the Blessed One is praised by virtue of this very quality.
He states that by means of the characteristic of being an authoritative source (*pramāṇabhūtatva*): "The praise for the suchness of the teaching [is derived] from that very teaching. (284)
Because it is not excluded even in the case of inference for the sake of establishing the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*),
or because its application is seen in various ways— such as "whatever has the nature of arising is all characterized by cessation"—
why is there such praise of the teaching, characterized by its validity regarding the state of things being thus?
In order that the establishment of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may occur through his instruction,
perception (*pratyakṣa*) was taught by the Blessed One himself:
"A person endowed with the cognition of blue cognizes blue."
But it is not the case that "it is blue alone"; thus, even inference has not been excluded.
Therefore, let it be inference itself that is excluded, rather than verbal testimony and the like.
"All the doctrines of others are empty; I alone am the speaker of reality," or alternatively, there is the demonstration of the formal application characterized as inference for the sake of others,
as he said:
"Whatever has the nature of arising is of the nature of cessation; all that is such"—this very point he states:
"The basis of inference is the logical mark (liṅga), characterized by inseparable connection (avinābhāva). (286)
That [pervasion] was stated by the Blessed One as the reason for demonstrating the pervasion with the probandum;
for a reason that is clearly pervaded by the probandum is indeed the indicator,
and that pervasion has been demonstrated by the Blessed One in many ways.
"Whatever is of the nature of arising, all that is of the nature of cessation"—
since this inference was also spoken by the Blessed One, the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) is indeed originated by the Blessed One;
and because that [reality] belongs to the Blessed One as his authority, the Blessed One's supreme quality is precisely this means of valid cognition, which has been described previously.

Because the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, taught the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) as being endowed with both [aspects], there is nothing beyond this; therefore, the means of valid cognition exists only through the Tathāgata, and from him alone all success is achieved. (879) Thus ends the first chapter, "The Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition" (*Pramāṇasiddhipariccheda*), in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*.

Removed marker: sect; 1. The Number of Means of Valid Cognition (pramāṇasaṃkhyā). 1. Disagreement regarding the number:
Having thus stated the general definition, he now states the specific definitions.
Direct perception and inference are the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Among these, they are means of valid cognition because they are non-deceptive; and non-deceptiveness arises from their production from an object and from their non-deviation from that object.
Now, how is that very non-deviation regarding the object to be understood?
Furthermore, validity arises from being perception or inference,
and not from anything else.
The meaning is "because it consists of sound and so forth.
Now, one might ask: how can it be said that there is no necessary connection between sound and its object?
It is because the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consist of two types of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Validity [of a cognition] consists in its non-deviation from the object of knowledge;
yet there can be no non-deviation from an object of knowledge in the absence of an object of knowledge,
and for us, there is no object of knowledge other than that which is established by perception and inference.
As it has been said:
"There is no means of valid cognition other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa); perception has the particular as its object."
We shall demonstrate that inference has the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as its object; this very point is established by the statement:
"The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is twofold because the objects of cognition (meyadvaividhya) are twofold, due to [their] capacity and incapacity."

2. Pride is of two kinds due to the twofold nature of its objects, based on their capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); [for example], hair-nets and the like are not real objects because they are resolved upon as non-objects.

It will be demonstrated that valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be understood as being of only two kinds— namely, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)— because otherwise the apprehension of the object of cognition (*meyapratipatti*) would be impossible; thus, the nature of being perceived or inferred is established through its various modes.
Because it does not exist in any other way, there is no further means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) beyond that.
4. For it is not accepted that there is any other way to understand the non-erroneous nature of an object of cognition than through its being either directly perceived or inferable.
Since there exists no mode of apprehension other than that which consists of the universal and the particular,

and since a single object possesses a twofold nature due to the twofold nature of its modes of apprehension, the distinction in apprehension constitutes the distinction in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that very thing is the distinction of objects.
[Objection: But surely the distinction of objects is the distinction of cognitions;
for when one thing is distinct, another does not thereby become distinct.
This is true:
there is no difference in the horse, yet there is a distinct differentiation from the cow and other animals.
Because there is no connection [between them], the distinctness of form is not thus asserted for knowledge and the object of knowledge;
for the establishment of the constant cognition of entities is dependent upon knowledge.
That very object is known through another cognition when it is inferred as being a different object. (3.6) It is cognized.
When it is perceived as being directly capable of producing cognition,

then, because it is characterized by its own form, it is a particular (svalakṣaṇa); but when it is perceived through that very [particular] as being capable [of producing cognition] by way of a succession,
then, because it is characterized by a general form, it is a universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
By way of successive tradition, incapacity is simply capacity through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and not merely the absence of capacity.

However, that which is perceived by one with an eye disease (*taimirika*) or perceived through verbal testimony is not the actual reality of the object, because it is not cognized as being capable either directly or through succession;

for there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the object, and this lack of resolute conviction is brought about by the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the twofold nature of the objects of cognition [is established] from their being similar or dissimilar, and from their being within or outside the scope of the word; for when other causes are present, the presence or absence of cognition [occurs] accordingly. (2)
That which is perceived in some way through a similar form is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa); otherwise, it is the particular characteristic (viśeṣalakṣaṇa).

If it were perceived otherwise, would not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) standing right before one be perceived in a form similar to a cow and so forth? Is that then a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is perceived by comparison (*upamāna*) in the form "this is a gavaya"?
This is not so;

that from which consciousness arises by means of a form exactly similar [to itself] would be a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), whereas here there is the cognition of its own specific nature (svarūpa).
If it is argued that "that which is perceived by means of a similar form is the universal (*sāmānya*), and here, while there is the apprehension of particulars,
a similar form is nevertheless perceived," we say no.
If it is asked: "Since this [object] is not perceived as distinct from that form, how can there be the determination (adhyavasāya) that 'this is similar'?"—[we reply:
indeed, even in the case of such a determination, there is no separate perception of similarity.
And in the absence of separate dependent existence, that itself is non-dual cognition. Indeed,

similarity cannot be cognized as something distinct from the object through the cognition "this is similar," for there is no cognition of an object other than the mental representation of the established object.
Therefore, since there is no cognition of an object here, the cognition of similarity is indeed without an objective basis (*anālambana*).

However, in the case of inferential cognition, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the superimposition of a perceived form; if similarity were thus [defined], then even the object of words and so forth would be called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) here—this is the response.
"There is no object because of the conviction that it is a non-object"—
in this way, it should be understood in other cases as well:
the object of a word is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not its object.
Now, if the object of a word is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), then the word itself must also be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its object is a universal.
This is not so;
for that which is a universal is the domain of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
It is not said that the universal alone is the object of a word.
For it is not maintained that the universal is not the object of a word;
rather, that which is the actual domain of a word is the supreme universal.
The universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed the object of the word;

however, the intended meaning is that whatever is the object of a word is not necessarily a universal, nor is it necessarily the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather that the particular is simply not its object.
Therefore, this fault does not apply;

consequently, even that which has sound as its object is a certain non-entity in the form of a universal (sāmānya), and likewise, even that which is not an object is a certain non-entity in the form of a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

Furthermore, that in which the existence of cognition occurs even when other causes—such as the object and others like the conventional agreement (*samaya*) or attention (*ābhoga*)—are present, is the universal (*sāmānya*);
whereas that in which the existence of cognition does not occur even when other causes such as the eye and so forth are present, is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding this point as well, it should be stated as before.

Alternatively, that in the presence of which the cognition exists when other causes are present is the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic); that in the presence of which the cognition does not exist when other causes are present is the *sāmānyalakṣaṇa* (universal characteristic), because it is impossible to characterize what is unperceived by way of its own nature, and thus it is remote (*parokṣa*). Furthermore, that universal characteristic, when characterized by way of its own nature therein, is the *svalakṣaṇa*; otherwise, it is the remote *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*.
Now, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this distinction between objects characterized as perceptible and imperceptible apprehended—
is it by perception, by inference, or by another means of valid cognition?
If duality of the object of knowledge is apprehended by another means of valid cognition...
The reason would indeed be contradictory, because a third [type of valid cognition] is also possible.

Alternatively, if it were established by two means of valid cognition, there would be mutual dependence; and even with three or more means of valid cognition, another object would have to be established.
2. In establishing another object of cognition, there would be the establishment of three or more means of valid cognition; thus, what is intended is not established.
For the differentiation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) establishes the differentiation of the object of cognition (meyabheda).

How could there be the establishment of the imperceptible (parokṣa) through inference? There is no perception regarding the imperceptible; or, if it were operative [there], inference would be useless. (10–11)
And how could there be remoteness (*parokṣatā*) when perception is operating? Only through the cessation of perception would there be remoteness with respect to the object.
In that case, perception has not operated; therefore, that [object] is cognized by means of that [perception].
This is an unprecedented mode of expression: seeing without the use of the eye.
(Or: seeing with the sense-organ.)
Therefore, an object of perception is cognized by perception;
however, regarding that which is beyond the senses, there is no means of valid cognition— how, then, can there be a determination of its twofold nature?
Regarding the twofold nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*):

therefore, the proof [based] on the twofold nature of the objects of cognition is unestablished; how could it be contradictory? Even if the twofold nature of the objects of cognition were indeed granted, there must nevertheless be a corresponding number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For, in the absence of a proven necessary connection (*pratibandha*), every logical reason (*hetu*) remains uncertain.
Furthermore, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not based on the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For since "being a means of valid cognition" is a universal (*sāmānya*), how could it be established by perception? If that [universal] is unestablished, how could the connection be determined by the senses through it? (15–16)

Thus, there is a non-establishment of the two objects of cognition; but if they were established by another [means], there would be contradiction, and due to the relation being unestablished, the reason would indeed be inconclusive.
To this, it is replied:
The twofold nature of objects is established by direct perception itself;
