for the cognition of similarity and dissimilarity is a property of cognition alone, and that is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
Nor is cognition associated with error regarding its own nature.

In that case, if there were a suspicion of error, there would be no linguistic convention at all, or rather, it would be the cause for its non-occurrence, because of the speech of the proponent, the opponent, and the arbiter; for indeed,
in the absence of cognition, whose speech could proceed toward what?
Speech that lacks a basis never occurs anywhere.
(18) If there were a difference in the cognition of entities, there would likewise be a difference in other things;
how much more so, then, in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which has that very [cognition] as its nature? (19)
Let there be a distinction in cognition itself; how could there be a distinction in the means of knowledge?
For indeed, the status of being a valid means of knowledge was previously established through its general definition.
Now, this specific application of that distinction is what remains to be proven.
Thus, for one who would say that this direct perception is conceptual, namely, "this is fire"— 21.
Its own nature is established as unimpaired; its status as a cause for an object [is known] through similarity with what preceded.

Otherwise, one seeking an object would not proceed toward the attainment of that object if it were not apprehended. Validity, characterized by engagement and withdrawal based on worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is indeed well-established through the very definition of generality in the first chapter itself.

Now, what has been established is merely the conventional usage of distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*). In that regard, this perception is indeed one and the same, namely conceptual (*savikalpaka*), for one who says, "This is fire; it performs the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*," [the response would be] that there are two [types of cognition], because of the difference in the mode of apprehension (*pratītyākāra*) when there is a difference in apprehension. Furthermore, even external objects are not perceived as possessing distinctness;
how much less so is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which [establishes] that very form as being real?

In this regard, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), which has a luminous form, is established through direct perception itself, because it is directly realized; for that [perception] is immediate due to having an object that is not remote. However, the similarity with a previous causal efficiency, being perceived as having an identical form, is an object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is remote.
4. On the Generality of the Means of Valid Cognition (pramāṇa-sāmānya):
Now, only direct perception (pratyakṣa) is the motivator [of action], and not anything else; for even though another internal mind (manas) exists, it is not a means of valid cognition.
For it would follow that the body, the ground, and so forth would also possess the same measure as that [object], as long as they exist together with it; to this,
it is replied:
5. That [cause], although it arises from a different condition, is established as being either useful or otherwise by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
And it is not only perception that prompts action in the absence of that [object].
Now, if it is argued that perception alone, through extreme habituation, is seen to prompt action in the absence of that object— and that inference, which takes the form of grasping similarity,
does not— this too is incorrect.
If it is argued that "pure perceptual cognition is not observed to be the initial motivator [for action]— lest what was previously [non-motivating] later become so"—
this is merely a story told by a fool.
6. Regarding idle talk: if the entry into that region at first causes disease, [then it is unfavorable].
"I shall not enter first; let her enter afterwards.
For that which occurs first must be the initial activity; how then could there be a subsequent activity?
This very fact—that it does not exist without the preceding—is what constitutes the "subsequent-ness" of the subsequent.
Therefore, even a cognition other than perception is indeed impelling, since otherwise activity would be impossible;
furthermore,

Even that occurrence of smoke and the like which is other than perception, and which occurs in relation to fire and so forth— whenever it is observed even in the absence of the object to be proven— that too is fruitless. (25)

Just as, due to extreme habituation, there is activity based on perception alone even without a mediated cognition (*parokṣapratīti*), so too is there activity toward fire and the like from smoke even without a perceptual cognition; thus, that [inference] is also a perceptual motivator (*pravartakam adhyakṣam*). Or, it might be argued:
2. Inference does not establish its own object without perception.
Therefore, direct perception alone—not inference—would be the motivator here, even without that [prior] practice;
for its establishment occurs even in the absence of that [inference], thus it is established as a means of valid cognition through direct perception. (26–27)
To this it is replied:
It has been stated here that perception does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without repeated practice;
therefore, let it be understood that inference alone is the primary [means] in this case. (28)
If it is useless at one time, it must be useless at other times as well; there is no other means of proof.
Why is there a desire for inference among living beings when it has not been practiced?
How can anyone have a desire for that which is devoid of utility? It is illogical to claim that an object of desire is not useful. (29–30)
Now, if it is argued that inference is sought for the sake of prompting the activity of perception,
even perception does not extend its operation so far as to reach the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, it is established that both perception and inference possess validity only within their own respective domains.
In the same way, the cognition of the world is not authoritative.
Then, at that time, it is indeed not a means of valid cognition,
because there is no distinction [from what is not a means of valid cognition].
For even though the act of instigating is the same, if someone is an instigator, what now distinguishes between the state of being an instigator and its opposite? (32)
And there is no validity other than that of being an instigator; therefore, validity belongs equally to both perception and its opposite, or else it belongs to neither at all.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even in that case, it is perception— having as its object the effect (kārya) or the logical mark (liṅga) and so forth— that prompts action, whereas non-perception merely exists by virtue of its presence and has no functional role in prompting action.
That too is incorrect.
Thus, because [the object] exists dependently, no one concludes that perception alone is the motivator therein;
nor does perception possess any further motivating power than mere existence,
since everything is employed for a purpose solely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
According to our established tenet that this is merely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) there is no agency whatsoever for anything anywhere;
agency is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*), not ultimate.
This will be demonstrated later.
Moreover,
the meaning of this is that conventional reality alone possesses activity.

In that case as well, perception itself is the means of establishing the next world; what loss do we suffer if the inferential cognition is sublated? (33) If inferential cognition regarding fire and so forth were not a valid means of knowledge...

Let it be so; by that very cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), which functions without overstepping the nature of perception, there is the objectification of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and of the mark itself, such as the next world and so forth. Thus, there is no loss for us.

For if inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the next world and so forth would remain unestablished; let there be no nihilism, but rather its lack of validity is what we refute. (34)

Fearing that if inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then its objects—such as the next world and so forth—would remain unestablished, leading to the charge of nihilism (*nāstikatā*), we refute the rejection of inference; we do not do so for any other motive.
If that object of inference, such as the next world, is apprehended by perception even though it is not currently perceptible, then what need have we for establishing the validity of inference?

If that goal which is sought through great exertion is accomplished without effort, who else would have any further desire for it? What discerning person, having found a goal achievable without effort, would resort to another method that is a vessel for the occurrence of exertion?
If the object to be proven by inference is established by perception alone, what need have we for inference? Furthermore,
if the desired object were to be established even regarding that which is beyond the senses through perception, [what would be the point?]
It would follow that everyone could achieve everything, and everyone would become a knower of all objects.

If it is argued that this is not so because there is no connection [between the reason and the object], then in that case, inference itself would not exist; for even by those who advocate for inference, it is not accepted that there can be a cognition other than one based on a connection.

Therefore, that which is perceived through a similar form is precisely the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as established by the perception of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); by this, the object of the reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*) has been demonstrated.

Indeed, the fact that an object is the domain of a word is not itself cognizable through verbal cognition; rather, that very verbal cognition establishes the status of its own appearing object as being the domain [of the word].
By this, the demonstration of the object for the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is shown.
For instance, the determination of an object as being similar to a cow by means of comparison (upamāna) has already been explained by the preceding word "similar" (sadṛśa). || 37 ||
Its own nature is understood from direct perception alone, whereas its similarity is the object of verbal cognition.
For instance: [38] Thus it is said:

"The statement 'this is similar to that' and 'that is similar to this' have one and the same meaning; furthermore, the conventional usage of 'imitating that' depends upon two [objects], yet it is not possible to cognize those two through perception. Therefore, the nature of similarity is cognized solely as the object of verbal cognition by means of a logical reason (*hetu*), because the form of this [object] is seen there [in the other] as well."
Since the proof concerns merely the conventional usage of similarity,
whereas the two forms that serve as the basis for such a cognition are apprehended by the preceding and succeeding perceptions themselves,
therefore the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words.
And by the apprehension of sound, conceptual construction itself is perceived; that is to say, it is the object of conceptual construction.
It is observed that where there is an absence of cognition despite the presence of other causes, this constitutes the introduction of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*);
that for which there is no existence of cognition is non-existent.
In this regard, knowledge operating in one place makes it known that it has not operated elsewhere, because its form is restricted;
for it does not perceive itself as operating everywhere.
Therefore, for the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), the understanding of the dual nature [of objects] arises from perception itself, since there is no other way to account for such cognition.

And all this—such as similarity, dissimilarity, and so forth—is the object of both perceptual and non-perceptual cognitions; furthermore, it is known through the capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), which will be demonstrated later.
In the *Buddhau*,
it says:
"Now, there is no suffering for others."
In this regard, that which is said—
that there is no perception of what is beyond the senses—
is incorrect.
Wherein "I" am not, that [object] is devoid of me; the notion of "I" exists only with respect to that which is directly perceived as distinct from me.
The determination that objects are beyond perception is of this magnitude alone:

the self knows itself as being directly perceived through its nature as consciousness; and it is precisely through the cognition of its own necessity that the non-perceptibility of other things is understood.
The cognition of another's imperceptibility is the apprehension of that which is imperceptible;
even when [the object] is perceived through direct perception, there is the state of being perceived as imperceptible.
In that case, there is indeed a direct perception of the object by means of the [other] object;
for when the object is not known through direct perception, how could there be cognition of an imperceptible object?
Indeed, it is through the knowledge of that [object] that its property and its intrinsic nature are apprehended.
If an imperceptible object were known through direct perception, its property (*dharma*) would be cognized, because that property has that [object] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
for it is impossible for something that does not have that as its intrinsic nature to be its property, just like any other distinct entity (*padārthāntara*).
If it is argued that it is its property due to a relationship with it;

In that case, there would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that which is [otherwise considered] remote; for, by means of a perception that cognizes an object connected with what is remote, the remote object itself would necessarily be cognized. Consequently, it follows that even the object intended to be remote is actually non-remote, and thus there would be no occasion for the application of inference (*anumāna*).
It is not the case that only what is apprehended by perception is the object of inference; to this, it is replied: 1 T.
I am not perceived by direct perception externally.
What, then, is that object which possesses the property connected to it?

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) functions as perception regarding [the cognition] itself, while another sense-cognition functions regarding its object (*dharmī*). For the apprehension of a relation depends upon the apprehension of both [relata],
and those two cannot be cognized by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the property (*dharma*) of the imperceptible object is cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
whereas the imperceptible subject (*dharmin*) is cognized by another perception, namely sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*);
from this, the apprehension of the relationship [between them] occurs.
Therefore, even when the state of being beyond perception is cognized through direct perception, the object itself is cognized by means of inference; thus, there is the introduction of inference.
Furthermore, [as stated in] T. 3.

A property (*dharma*) that exists in the form of a positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpa*) remains inseparable from the substratum (*dharmī*). It is not logical for there to be a cognition [of it] without the apprehension of the entity; however, this is not the case through the opposite [i.e., by apprehending the entity first].
(44) For a property in the form of a positive affirmation is inseparable from the entity and is grasped by the same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its substrate (*sadharmī*).
Parokṣatva (remoteness), however, is simply the absence of cognition by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
this does not depend upon the apprehension of a subject (*dharmī*).
Now, if direct perception does not operate with respect to the remote, how can there be the operation of inference?

This is of no consequence, because the remoteness of that object is not established by inference; rather, its proof occurs when it possesses perceptibility, as in the case of an object whose form has been seen. (45)

For it is not the case that actual remoteness (*parokṣatā*) is established by inference such that the operation of perception would be required there; rather, it has already been stated that its remoteness is established precisely through the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). However, once remoteness is established as proven by perception, it is then by means of inference that the object's capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), in the form of fire and so forth, is established. And since perception has already operated there previously, there is no contradiction in the subsequent operation of inference.
Furthermore,
4. it has the very characteristics of fire and so forth.

Because inference lacks the capacity to apprehend that very form [of the object], its status as a means of cognizing what is beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*) is established precisely by that [lack of capacity]. For the capacity of inference to operate upon the actual nature of that [object] is indeed "irrelevant" (*aprakṛtā*),
and it is only at that time that such [a capacity] belongs to it.
Therefore, direct perception is not required there beforehand,
nor is there anyone who seeks an object through its being beyond perception such that they would require the operation of direct perception;
yet that [perception] occurs even with respect to what is undesired.
By this, the establishment of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is also determined; [this concludes] the section on the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapravṛtti*).

For its validity is established only when an imperceptible object is established; for it is precisely through the establishment of that imperceptible object that the connection [of the cognition] with it is proven.

(47) Validity is said to be merely the state of being connected to a real object; since validity consists in a connection with a well-established object, there is no need for an inferential mark (*liṅga*). (48)
Regarding the connection of things themselves, the remainder has already been explained previously under the section on conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth; therefore, it is not stated here.

[Objection: But surely the twofoldness of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is the cause, while the twofoldness of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the effect; how then can the effect be established from the cause? To this it is replied:
Since an effect arises from a cause when the collection of conditions is present,
how could it be illogical for the establishment of the effect to proceed from that cause?
(49) Although there is the principle that causes do not necessarily possess their effects, nevertheless, in this context, the establishment of the effect indeed proceeds from the cause.

We maintain that the two means of valid cognition are not established at all times merely from the existence of two objects of cognition, but rather from the possibility of their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*);
and we shall demonstrate the possibility of these causal complexes later on.

Furthermore, the establishment of the two types of objects of cognition necessarily establishes the two means of valid cognition; for that alone is the means of valid cognition by which its establishment— characterized as ascertainment— is achieved,
and it has been demonstrated that the establishment of both cannot occur from a single means.

When this [argument] is intended for the purpose of excluding three or more means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the exclusion of other means of valid cognition is established through the absence of their pervader (*vyāpaka*), because there is no further object [to be cognized].
For there is no means of valid cognition devoid of an object of cognition (*prameya*);
in the absence of an object of cognition—whether its own nature (*svarūpa*) or the nature of another (*pararūpa*)—cognition itself does not exist, so what could be a means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that the self exists, then since it too lacks objects of cognition in either its own or another's form, its non-existence alone follows; thus, there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, a single object is that entity which is cognized in its own nature.
In that case, however, it is established as "other" because there is no distinction [between them].
2. An investigation into the two truths:
That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real;
the other is said to be conventionally real. These are declared to be the particular and universal characteristics. 3.
—this is an intermediate verse.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "If nothing whatsoever is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), how can the capacity for causal efficiency be the defining characteristic of ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*)? For instance:"
By whom and by what means is the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsamarthatva) cognized?
For in that manner, the cognition of either the means of knowledge or the object of knowledge is not possible.
2. Of knowledge and the object of knowledge, neither is eternal nor is it impermanent.
Neither the object of cognition nor the cognition itself is perceived—either by direct perception or by inference—to possess causal efficacy;
for it is thus:
For that which is to be known, its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) or its efficacy (*arthakāritva*) is not perceived;

a permanent entity possesses no capacity because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished, and an impermanent entity possesses no capacity because its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unestablished. (51)
Causal capacity is observed to be pervaded by positive and negative concomitance. When both of these are not established, how can capacity be asserted? (52) Capacity is thus cognized.

If it is argued: "Surely there can be no such thing as the capacity (sāmarthya) of that which is eternal, all-pervading, and devoid of activity toward any effect; yet, let it not be [that it lacks capacity], for it will become non-pervasive [in its activity]; and let it not be [that it lacks duration], for it will become enduring for another time."
That is incorrect;
since it is not perceived, how can there be pervasion of space, and how can there be eternality?
Just as it lacks all-pervasiveness, so too does it lack eternality. (53)
Since even an impermanent entity is momentary, how could there be action? [How could there be] an effect? 5 T. kāryaṃ.

For a momentary entity, its existence is established as mere being. Now, if it is said that its capacity consists in this: "immediately after this, another [entity arises]," then since another [entity] also follows immediately after that, that [capacity] would belong to that too.

For all momentary entities, their very priority consists in depending on everything; if it is argued that "even in the absence of that [prior cause], that [effect] exists," how could this be so for a momentary entity? (54–56)
Indeed, it is not possible for a momentary effect to come into being again even in the absence of that [cause],
because it exists only at that very time and is non-existent at any other time whatsoever.
Now, if the continuum (*santāna*) is both the effect and the cause, then this fault does not arise;
for the continuum exists as something distinct from those [moments].
Or, if that causal relationship belongs to the entity itself, then because the moments lack capacity, there follows the consequence of their non-existence.
If it is argued that since the cause-and-effect relation belongs to those related to them, that causal relationship also belongs to the moments themselves— that is not so.
Since there is no relation other than the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for two distinct entities,
the continuum (*santāna*) would follow immediately after every moment; consequently, everything would become a continuum,
and the same faults previously mentioned regarding its permanence or momentariness would apply.
And it says:
"The reading 'that causal relationship' (sa kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ) does not occur here."
And regarding that, the previously mentioned fault applies;
for if the continuum were other than that [moment] and possessed causal efficacy, it would simply be that very same thing existing.
Because moments would lack causal capacity, the postulation of their existence would be futile.

(57) If it is argued that causal capacity is attributed to them because they possess capacity through their connection with [the effect], then, due to the absence of primary capacity, that capacity is merely a borrowed ornament.

(58) The relationship of cause and effect must belong either to the continuum or to something other than it; for if that were the case, the entire three worlds would indeed consist of nothing but moments. (59)

And by virtue of the continuum (saṃtāna), there is existence; from that, the performance of an effect [occurs]. That same fault regarding both positions—eternality and its opposite—would apply to you.
(60) If there were a transition to another continuum, there would indeed be an infinite regress (anavasthiti). If the continuum itself were an effect, it could not be an effect if it were momentary.
(61) Because here too, another continuum would be the cause of its being an effect, the notion of "being an effect" is thus seized by the tiger of infinite regress. (62)
Furthermore, if the existence of the reason were established by an effect other than cognition, then that effect too would lack existence without the arising of another effect;

consequently, because of this infinite regress, existence would not belong even to the original [reason]. However, through the effect of cognition, the uncontradicted existence of everything is thereby established.
In this case as well, how could there be a destruction of the connection with the object of knowledge by means of the effect of knowledge?
[It cannot be,] because of its connection with that [object].
The relationship of cause and effect between cognition and the objects of cognition is perceived because both appear as existing in front [of the observer].
However, it will not be stated that cognition is an effect of anything else.
It is not by that very same perception, because it has not yet occurred prior [to the object];
nor is there a cognition of the cause through that known object, because they lack simultaneity.
If it is argued that it has come into existence because it was previously non-existent, and that even prior to that it was non-existent; then [the same question applies].

Therefore, [the cognition] would be purposeless regarding activity; however, if it were not so, then how could there be a lack of finality, since the understanding of "being an effect" (kāryatā) would have already occurred previously? || 67 ||
If the relation of effect and cause were to exist only between two things that are simultaneous,

then it would likewise apply to a pillar and a jar seen together at the same time, since there is no distinction [between them]. Otherwise, even in the case under discussion, [the causal relationship] cannot be established.
By refuting the over-extension [of the definition] to a pillar and a pot,
[the author establishes that] it is the established tenet (siddhānta) that when one thing undergoes change, the other does not possess the status of being its effect.
In that case, this very point applies equally to knowledge and the object of knowledge as well;
he clarifies this meaning with the words "kevala" and so forth.

If it were not produced there [in the threads], then the very nature of being a thread would not be established; thus, if even a solitary jar were not seen [to be so produced], its status as an effect would not exist. Likewise, for cognition as well, there would be no occurrence of perception without that [causal process].
For that cognition is indeed different from this; therefore, there is no deviation.
It is not indeed something else.
Is this pillar not also something else [to us], given the arising of recognition?
In that case, there would indeed be permanence; yet recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For the form of one and the same thing is not perceived as both prior and posterior.

Because neither of the two cognitions—the prior and the posterior—individually grasps [the object], memory does not function with respect to both; nor does it possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since there is no mutual mixing of the prior and posterior cognitions. (72–73)
Furthermore, the recollection that arises from that [perception] does not perceive unity;
even if the self were indeed one, how could it perceive by means of that [recollection]?
Even that [self] understands the object through means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
For knowledge does not attain the status of a valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇya*) merely by being dependent upon a self.

Even without dependence on a self, there is validity because of non-contradiction; for the status of a means of cognition belongs to that which, having been previously perceived, is subsequently attained.
Without one who possesses the fruit of knowledge, this entity is not understood as impermanent by oneself.
1. Even if the self exists as something eternal, there is no validity whatsoever for any [cognition] of it. (77)

In that case, validity belongs only to perception and inference; nor is a nature consisting of prior and posterior states observed in the self or in anything else. (78) Whether by the self or by another, there is no possibility of permanence for it. Therefore, the state of being an effect is not perceived in either cognition or the object. (79)
The knower of the self knows the self and that which is to be known by it; as cause and effect, they exist as objects of direct perception in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior.

(80) Now, if the cause is known from the effect through inference, one then recognizes the state of being an effect, thinking, "From this [cause], this knowledge has arisen. (81) Yet, even for that inference, there would be no cognition if the [cause] were not previously known through direct perception.
That there is an occurrence of two entities has already been established previously.

If perception regarding an object were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) due to its prior non-existence, then inference could not be a valid means of knowledge either; for even in that case, there would have to be an inference [establishing it] beforehand, leading to an infinite regress.
Let alone the object of cognition such as "being an effect" and so forth—for whomsoever that [inference] might exist, they lack any cognition of it.
"Because of the absence of a root, it does not proceed further"—this is established. This property (dharma) is established for a subject (dharmin), yet this [subject] is not tenable.

When there is the state of having an object (sālambanatā) for cognition, the thing (vastu) is established; however, when the thing itself is not established, then what could have the relation of cause and effect?
If it is asked, "How is the state of having an object unestablished? [the answer follows].
It is said that in this world, only the actual cause is the object of perception, not merely what is seen. 3 T.
But by means of mere appearance, even the cognition of one with cataracts attains that [object] through mere appearance.

(85) Whatever object is the cause of something, that thing does not exist without that cause; the stability of cognitions such as those of the eye is not attained without an objective support (*ālambana*). (86)
Even without an object, visual and other sensations are observed to arise bearing the dual forms of the sun and the moon;
therefore, since it arises even in the absence of an objective cause, it is logical that consciousness is not the effect of an objective cause due to such deviation.
For this relationship of cause and effect is precisely the relationship of pervader and pervaded that exists when there is mutual distinction.

If an effect were to exist without a cause, it would not be the effect of that [cause], nor would it be a cause; therefore, because everything would be without a basis, no entity whatsoever would be established—how then could there be a causal relationship?
Furthermore, if it were argued that the basis is not as a cause but rather as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), that too is incorrect.
For, nowhere else is there any "objectivity" apart from blue and the like; and the state of being blue and so forth appears even in erroneous cognition. (87)
Regarding the phrase "of one whose nature is generosity"—this is the marginal note of the owner of this manuscript.
Is not the clarity of appearance here seen as being nothing other than error? Therefore, there is nothing that can be grasped which exceeds [the nature of] error.
(88) Now, it might be argued that all cognition is indeed erroneous.
This is not so,
because that which appears to a deluded mind possesses no causal efficiency whatsoever; therefore, it is an error with respect to an unreal object, while its opposite is the case elsewhere.
To this it is replied:

Is causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of the nature of the object itself, or is it distinct from it? Since all of that—whether it be the cognition of it or the object itself—is non-existent [for you], [the following applies]:
If that causal efficiency were a different entity, then because of its absence, the object would not exist; for if the effect is non-existent, the cause also does not exist. (90–91)
If that which is intended as an effect capable of causal efficiency does not exist, then its cause would likewise be non-existent; how could this be?
For one thing is not non-existent simply because another is non-existent, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Even if it were the case that in the absence of an effect, the causal capacity itself does not exist—
But its own nature is not non-existent; furthermore,
if cognition is the causal efficiency,
there too there are two possible courses.
Whether it be that [first] cognition or another [subsequent] cognition,
if that very same cognition arises again and performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*),
then even in the case of an error, it certainly arises again and again; for an erroneous cognition is not necessarily restricted to a single moment.
Now, as for consciousness of touch and so forth,
that too is non-existent.
The capacity of the absence of the effect is precisely this—
that is the reading, with the additional phrase "tad etat."

If indeed there is the arising of another [cognition], let that very [object] be the object while it exists; but how can there be the existence of one thing in the cognition of another? (92) Even in the case of self-cognition, there is no confidence; what then can be said regarding the cognition of another? Even if that [other] were cognized, why would its unreality not be suspected?
(93) How does the cognition of touch differ from the cognition of sight? If there is satisfaction with the object in that case, from where indeed does that satisfaction arise? (94)

Just as there is indeed a lack of an external object (*nirālambanatā*) in visual consciousness, so it is also in tactile consciousness; for there is no difference between the two insofar as both are sensory cognitions, and the possibility of impairment by cataracts and the like is equal in both, since the same [kind of] perception is observed in both cases.
Furthermore, if it is argued that [the tactile experience] arises from the sensation of heat due to the affliction of fever, or from contentment and so forth—
But even in the season of snow, why is there no satisfaction despite the experience of heat caused by the affliction of fever?
Furthermore, if satisfaction is based on the authority of experience, what is its purpose? If experience is not authoritative, what is the purpose of satisfaction? (95)

If consciousness is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the establishment of the object follows from that very source; what will further satisfaction accomplish? That which is not established by consciousness cannot be established even by hundreds of satisfactions. For how could that [satisfaction] be the means of proof? Indeed, satisfaction other than consciousness serves no purpose as a means of proof.
Now, if it is a means of proof, how can there be the establishment of one thing by another?
If it is through a relationship, by what is that relationship established?
If it is argued that [the object is established] through satisfaction, then even there the establishment of a connection must be required, resulting in an infinite regress;
if it is argued that the object is established from consciousness itself, then the object is established from that very source, making "satisfaction" redundant;
and in that case, the same fault remains.
If the establishment of an object depends upon cognition, why does it not follow from a previous cognition?
By this, the conviction regarding the object is also refuted;
for instance:
Adhimukti regarding an object is not something other than cognition that establishes that object;
if adhimukti were simply cognition, then cognition would establish all objects.
By this, longing, memory, desire, aversion, and so forth are also explained.
Furthermore,
it is a mere trifle to say that desire and so forth arise from cognition, but cognition does not arise from them;
yet, it might be argued as follows:
Let it be that all cognitions possess an object; this causes us no harm whatsoever.
If it is asked, "How then is the distinction between valid and invalid cognition established? [the answer follows].

Mīmāṃsā: In that very context, the establishment of what is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and what is not, based on whether something is worldly (*laukika*) or non-worldly (*alaukika*), is the distinction. How is that [distinction] known? Through the encounter with what is subverting (*bādhaka*) and what is other than it. (98) By what is the status of being worldly or non-worldly established for the subverting and its opposite? Because of the existence of the subverting and its opposite, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. (99)
If [you claim] it is uncommon, supramundane, or otherwise, then this is something trivial;

for there is no cognition of those two, since they are neither perceived nor inferable. Indeed, cognition occurs through perception, and that [perception] resides elsewhere than in the object to be cognized. (100)
Whether this [cognition] belongs to me or to another— perception has no scope here.
If it is argued that there is cognition through inference,
how can inference arise in the absence of the apprehension of a [logical] relation?

Indeed, there is no inference from one's own perception based on the observation of actions such as horripilation [which would prove the existence of the specific object]. For fire is not established here by the sight of its effect, smoke; because inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object and does not perceive particulars (*bheda*).

If it is argued that in that case there is unity [of the object] despite the difference in the smoke, then why is there not unity even in the case of horripilation? Furthermore, this adherence to unity is nothing other than a cognition; it is not something distinct from consciousness.
If it is argued that they are one because of the conventional usage— "wherever my eye was directed, there it [the other's] was directed as well"—
then this is equally applicable to the hair and so forth perceived by those with ophthalmia;
for in that case too, the two afflicted individuals have an identical adherence to the same object.
Furthermore,
if it is argued that just as there is cognition by someone of what is perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*),
so too there is cognition by everyone of other things, then there is no proof for this in the case of pillars and the like.

If it is argued that there is no fault in the case of a person with cataracts (taimirika), because although they do not perceive the pillar due to their impaired sense faculty, there is still no error;
[we reply: how, then, is it known that the sense faculty is impaired?
If it is argued that this is because there is no cognition of a real object,
then this is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): falsity exists if there is impairment, and impairment exists if there is falsity.
Therefore, nothing is perceived beyond that.

In the case of a jar and so forth, according to the Vijñānavāda, why is it that from a certain cognition of blue, etc., there does not arise a cognition of red, etc.? For what reason? Precisely because of that... thus, in that regard, [the object is established] as external by virtue of its being common to all.

Even if there is awareness due to the impairment of the sense faculties, one might object that [the self] is not perceived; however, this is not the case at all. For even by means of non-perception—specifically, through the perception whose nature is the discernment of the form of what is perceived by another—one negates the state of being perceived by another.
Likewise, because that [object] is an object of another's perception, it is not negated;
how then is the form perceived by another apprehended by him?
If it is argued that while that form is indeed apprehended, the state of being apprehended by another is not apprehended—
Is it that something other than that form is being perceived, or is it that very form itself? If it is that very form, how can there be non-perception?

If it has the nature of another, how can it be apprehended by that other? It is the state of being apprehended that is apprehended by the other, not the object itself; so how is that object apprehended by the other?
For that whose state of being apprehended is what is apprehended is itself unapprehended.

And thus, that object has not been apprehended by anyone; for it is precisely through being apprehended by this or that [perceiver] that its mutual exclusion from others is apprehended by both self and other. Consequently, there is no such thing as a "common" object of apprehension, nor is there any object apart from the state of being apprehended. It is merely a cognition consisting of nothing more than the form of the apprehension within self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
There is no such thing as an external object for which existence, characterized by causal efficiency, is asserted.
Because that [external object] is not its object,
if it is argued that the ultimate reality characterized by causal efficiency is established through the mutual relationship of cause and effect among cognitions themselves,
that too is incorrect.

4. For the Yogācāra: in that very state of being mere self-cognition, how can there be inference based on perception? Furthermore, even if there were a causal relationship between two cognitions, how could it be apprehended? 104
In perception, there is direct knowledge, whereas it is not so through inference;
for [inference] does not consist of two cognitions, since by that very same [cognition] one's own nature alone is known. When there is cognition of the cause, there is no cognition of the effect. 105
How can its status as a cause be apprehended through the cognition of the effect? Even at the time of the effect, that [cause] does not exist; how then can its status as an effect be apprehended?
(106) If it is claimed that the thorough knowledge of the cause is obtained through inference, then since it was not known from inference previously, how is it known now?
(107) If it was previously known through direct perception and is now known through inference, then that [prior] knowledge no longer exists; how can there be cognition by means of inference? (108)

If it is argued that there is no inference regarding [the object's] being "prior" because it is known through perception, then its being "prior" is merely an addition to that [perception]; if it were established by inference, it would be non-existent. (109) Indeed, so-called "priority" does not exist at all, because it is sublated by perception. Therefore, there is no cognition whatsoever of a prior form.

(110) This [so-called prior form] is merely a memory and is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), because it is self-cognized. And perception is merely self-awareness, because it is self-cognized. (111)

Therefore, because it is occupied with another task, there is no awareness of that [object] by it; consequently, the establishment of causal capacity does not exist between the cognition and the object known.
Furthermore, this relation of cause and effect does not exist whether [the object] is existent or non-existent; for there is no cause whatsoever for a non-existent thing, such as a horse's horn.
The wise one maintains that because of its absolute non-existence, there can be no cause for it; however, the claim that it is a "prior non-existent effect" is also an untenable answer.

How can there be a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) if it exists? And how can it be conceived if it does not exist? For there is no prior non-existence of a non-existent thing, such as a donkey’s horn. (114–115)

If it is argued that there is prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) regarding the perception of a rabbit’s horn, this would involve mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya): as long as there is no state of prior non-existence, so long there is no existence of the object;
and as long as there is no relation with its prior non-existence, so long there is no arising.

As long as there is no arising, so long does the reality of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) not exist. If it is argued that the cause's being devoid of its effect is what constitutes prior non-existence, that too is incorrect; for why would that emptiness not belong to something else that is not the cause? Consequently, through that [connection], the effect would belong to that [other thing] as well. (117)
For if the status of being an effect were due to its connection with antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*),

then that antecedent non-existence would be a distinct category of entity devoid of the effect; and even if it were something other than what is considered the cause, it would still possess the nature of antecedent non-existence.
And if there were such a connection, then that which has come into being as an effect would also possess the status of being the cause;
if it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between them, the answer to this has already been stated.
Nor is that which is called prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) graspable by means of valid cognition such as perception;
for only the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of the cause and effect is grasped,
and if it is argued that the very nature of the cause is what constitutes prior non-existence, [we reply:]...
The nature of the effect itself would likewise be so; if it indeed exists in relation to another effect,
why does it not also exist in relation to that which is considered its cause?
If it is argued that [the universal] exists because it is thus perceived, what conviction can there be in a mere perception of a thing that has not been apprehended as a real entity?

Therefore, since it is grasped by way of the nature of the real object itself, its existence as a separate entity is impossible; nor is there another apprehension therein of "being an effect" and so forth by means of "blue" and so forth. (118)
Indeed, no one perceives an entity as "blue" and so forth by way of its being an effect;

for an "effect-ness" distinct from the blue and so forth is not apprehended, and since perception does not operate with respect to temporal priority and posteriority, how could there be a grasping of prior non-existence and the rest?
Furthermore, it might be argued that an effect must indeed exist [prior to its production], because the operation of causes is only possible when an effect exists;
for if it were non-existent, how could there be an operation, since it would lack an object?
To this it is replied:
having seen, heard, or understood, does the cause produce the effect? Or is its nature such that it is dependent on other causes due to its insentience? It is held to be so.
1. The established tenet (siddhānta) is not subject to over-extension because it is restricted; [it applies] externally.
And if God were the cause, He would be the director of causes;
yet there is no cognition of a non-existent thing, because He is the source of perceptual consciousness.
2. The director of causes; 3. T. [The director of causes]
For in that regard, what is the proof for the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*)? Is the cause the Lord (*īśvara*),
or is it based on the Sāṃkhya doctrine that everything exists everywhere?
Thus, only that which exists is perceived; there is no such thing as a relationship between cause and effect.

Or rather, if the Lord of the worlds were to perceive only what is non-existent and then employ the causes with specific restriction, then if everything that exists were always perceived, the state of the world would be chaotic. If it is argued that this is not so because of the specific restrictions of the perceivers, that too is trivial;
for since perceivers also exist everywhere and at all times, what indeed could be called "specific restriction"?

Furthermore, for what reason would an effect arise from a non-existent cause, or how could an effect come from that which is non-existent? To claim that an effect arises from a non-existent cause is an untenable position. For what indeed is the difference between a negation through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)?
If it is argued that "it was the cause at that time," then it follows that what was a non-cause at one time becomes a cause at another; this is a well-spoken [refutation],
for such would indeed be the case.

4. Since they existed previously, those things which exist [now] have attained the status of being causes for what was non-existent; for no operation is observed on the part of either those [past causes] or these [present effects]. (123)
If [the word] is a cause by virtue of its operation (*vyāpāra*), from what would that operation arise?
If it arises from the object possessing the operation, then what is the purpose of the operation there?
If there were an operation even in that case, then that object would be mediated.
If the effect arises solely from the operation [of the cause], then the effect would arise even when [the cause] is dead;
and likewise, why would the effect not arise even when that [cause] has long since perished?
This series of operations is so long—how much of a life is this for anyone? (125–126)

If the operation [of the cause] occurs at the same time as its own nature, then the effect will come into being; however, if the effect exists at the time of the operation, it follows that they are simultaneous.

(127) If the cause does not exist at the time of the effect’s existence, then what difference is there between [a cause] that has perished long ago and one that has perished immediately before? (128) If existence [occurs] at the time of arising, then for that which arises immediately thereafter, arising is nothing other than the effect; therefore, it is simultaneous with it. (129)
After the refutation of the *syādvāda*, there follows the rejection of the two [opposing] positions. Since much remains to be said at this point, we shall desist from it.
(130) Furthermore, it might be argued that the object is first cognized through inference as being the cause of cognition.
That too is incorrect:

"How can there be a cognition of [the smoke's] being an effect of that [fire], when there is no mutual contact between what was previously perceived by direct perception and what is now cognized through inference?
Even if it is granted that the prior existence of what is cognized by inference is understood [through memory]," [it remains problematic].

By what means is it cognized that this is the cause of direct perception? For inference does not possess the cognition that "this object perceived by direct perception is the cause of direct perception," since inference certainly does not operate while the object itself is being directly perceived.
Because its object is beyond the senses,
perception does not operate with respect to an inferable object, since perception has as its object that which is present to the senses; nor is that which is being cognized itself beyond the senses.
If it is argued that what is being perceived is "indirect" (parokṣa) precisely because of its indirectness,
this is not so, for:
If it is perceived in its own form, what else could this "remoteness" (parokṣatā) be? If it is the appearance of an indistinct form, why is that not considered perception (pratyakṣa)?
For when there is cognition of two forms, both are accepted as being perceptual, just as a pillar is cognized sequentially by way of its near and far aspects.
If that object were of a dual nature, both clear and unclear,
then even when it is known through both perception and inference, it would possess only the nature of perception, just as in the case of grasping the near and far parts of a pillar. Alternatively,
if clarity and lack of clarity are merely due to adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), then the very nature of the object is simply its blueness.

If cognition were [perceived] in another form due to a difference in limiting conditions (upādhi), there would never be direct perception [of it], because its own nature (svarūpa) would not be cognized. || 134 ||

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of blue and so forth is called "perception" (pratyakṣa), then inference would also be perception, because it consists in the cognition of its own form. (135) If it is claimed that [inference] is not considered perception because of its separation from the sense organ, then why is conjunction with the sense organ not also measured by inference? (136)
For the very disjunction of the sense organ is not established,
because its own nature is known through inference;
since there is no object, there is no conjunction with the sense organ.
How can that which is being perceived be non-existent for an inference that grasps its own nature?
If it is non-existent, how can there be a grasping of the object's nature through inference?
Or perhaps the connection with the sense faculty is not inferred at all.
Inference would be useless, and there would be no engagement by means of it; for one should neither see nor touch that which is useless, and thus engagement therein would be in vain.
Indeed, it is for the sake of utility that one engages with an object once it has been inferred through inference;
and since a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which prompts engagement, it would follow that what does not prompt engagement is simply not a means of valid cognition.

Now, as for the claim that there is inference of a future connection with the sense organ, and therefore [the object] is not perceived because at that time there is no connection with the sense organ—that is incorrect;
for if one were to infer a future connection, the form would not have been cognized previously, and thus its status as a cause could not be known, rendering the inference useless. (138)

At that very moment, while it is being measured, its state of being measured is not manifested by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). That very state of being measured is what is called "presentness.
Indeed, presentness is nothing other than that; for at that time, because it appears as its own intrinsic nature, presentness is simply the manifestation of its own intrinsic nature.
If it is argued that [the object] is non-existent because it appears in the form of the past and so forth,
then how can its state as the past be apprehended through inference? For inference operates only upon what has been apprehended by perception,
and perception does not operate with respect to the state of being past.
If it is argued that its state of having passed away is not perceived when it is seen by direct perception,
but rather that "at this moment it has the nature of having passed away," then something entirely different must have arisen.
And since there is no perception (*pratyakṣa*) therein, how can there be inference (*anumāna*)?
Even as for that which will later become perceptible, its future state is not perceived; therefore, the application of inference there is the same [as in the case of the past].
Since appearing as a form is common to both of these,
and for the other [the external object] there is likewise no such cognition through direct perception, how can it be manifested by means of that [form’s] description?
No; for that cognition arises from the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and thus,
while originating based on an object and imitating its form, it may still possess a distinction from another [cognition] in some respect—
this will be explained [in verse 140].

That cognition is not produced directly from the object; rather, it arises through the meeting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Otherwise, even a cause might appear otherwise, as in the perception of two moons which results from a visual disorder (*timira*) and the like.

Therefore, the cognition that arises from the form of a past time-object is a determination of the past; because it apprehends [the object] as being of a past time, it is indeed past. It does not exist [in the present], for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being present at this time.
How, then, is its attainment [possible]? Precisely because of its existence.
How is there existence?

Since it is established by means of that visible mark (*liṅga*), knowledge also functions as an instigator toward that [object] through its medium; thus, the process of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is complete.
[Objection: But how can knowledge be an instigator if it does not apprehend the object?
Indeed, because it is non-deviant, even a solitary reason (*dharma*) would be a determiner; for it determines exactly as it is observed to determine, and not otherwise—so who is to be blamed?
Furthermore:

Cognition, through its attachment to that [object's] form, brings about [the object]; nothing else does. And therein, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object occurs necessarily by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, it is not cognized by cognition that "this exists now as having the same form as before"; rather, its present form does not exist and is simply not seen. Thus, that which is not being seen is indeed "indirect" (*parokṣa*).

Non-apprehension itself is the state of being beyond perception; if that which is called "beyond perception" (*parokṣa*) were the very nature of the object, then it would be directly perceived (*adhyakṣa*). In that case, there would be no room for inference, nor would there be any possibility of doubt.
[If the object were destroyed,] such a cognition would simply not arise; furthermore, there is no identity between the cognition and the object. Therefore, that object is not cognized. (142–143)

Therefore, since inference has the nature of grasping an object, and even the connection with the eyes and other sense organs is itself being inferred, it follows that the object which is the object of inference must be perceived directly (pratyakṣa). This is the conclusion [of the opponent].

[Response: But this is not so; because a cognition whose object is a remote (parokṣa) entity does not have the nature of grasping an object. Therefore, that which is apprehended by inference cannot function as a cause [for the production of sensory perception].
Therefore, there is no relationship of cause and effect; for this very reason, he said:
"If it is argued that everything is incapable [of acting]."
To this, it is said:
the capacity [of causal efficiency] is observed in the case of sprouts and the like arising from seeds and the like.

Thus, for instance, the worldly understanding—"I see the arising of the sprout from the seed"—is a cognition that occurs without [further] differentiation; let the perception be exactly of that nature. (144)

For that alone is truly perceived where there is the cognition "I see this"; and since such an inclination (*adhimukti*) as "this is mine" is observed to exist in the case of the causal relationship, one should not suspect otherwise because of the possibility of an uncontradicted inclination. To explain further:
I remember this object; there is no higher state than resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). For no connection with the object is perceived by the memory.
First of all, it is not by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because memory is not perceptible.
As for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it directly realizes only the very nature of the memory, not its connection with the object.
Nor does prior perception function in memory; for how could there be a cognition of a relationship?
Yet there exists the cognition, "I remember this," which is not otherwise possible.
Therefore, it is *adhimukti* (resolute conviction) alone that is the establisher in all cases, being the basis for all systematic arrangements.
To this it is replied: if that view is accepted, let it be so according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti). This is the intended meaning.

That which is mere conviction, arising from the cultivation of beginningless conventional usage, exists without the establishment of the reality of objects through valid cognition; that is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti-mātra*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) is not indeed the meaning of "that which is perceived" (*pratīta*).
For just as in some cases, such as with Devadatta, the conceit of having seen him persists even when he has not actually been seen, and that conceit ceases upon correct reflection,
so too this [conceit] does not exist in the ultimate sense.
Likewise, all worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) is exactly like this; thus, everything is merely conventional (*saṃvṛtimātraka*).
For convention is nothing more than the conceit of cognition in the absence of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For instance, the understanding of the causal relationship between cause and effect is attained through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Yet, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists for that [relationship], whether it be perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna). If the understanding of positive and negative concomitance were to come from perception and non-perception, and if that [understanding] were to come from inference, there would be a circular dependency (itaretara-saṃśraya).

Since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not apprehended by perception alone, it is said that the causal relationship is established by perception and non-perception; however,
this is inconsistent.
Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*),
concomitance (*anvaya*) is not apprehended by perception;
for perception does not function in such a manner as to grasp the idea that "when this exists, that comes to be."
Because its function consists merely in the apprehension of two [factors],

it is not the case that "this is seen immediately after this, therefore this arises from that. Rather, one should consider only these three alternatives here— "it arises from that," "it arises from that very thing," and "it arises from this as well"— since no other possibility exists.
If it were the case that "it arises from this alone and not from another," then by implication this would be the meaning;
yet even there, there is a twofold alternative: either "now" or "at another time.
If the thought is that "it arises from this alone now," [then...]
If it were the case that [the effect] arises from something else at another time,
then why would it not also arise from something else at this very moment in a different location?
Furthermore, such a relationship between cause and effect is not possible, because there would be no necessary restriction.

Nor is there a restriction that it arises *only* from this [cause], for at another time it might not arise from it at all; thus, the understanding of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) does not come about through perception.

Furthermore, regarding the position that it arises from this as well as from something else, since one would be admitting deviation (*vyabhicāra*) oneself, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not established; therefore, this position also is not tenable.
Or rather, there is nothing else here to be conceptualized;
rather, it is understood through non-perception that [the effect] does not exist in the absence of this [cause].

If that were the case, there would again be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For instance, is perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth "other," or is non-perception (*anupalambha*) "other"? If [the otherness] were not through perception, it would be a mere name and no proof at all. (148)

An entry [into the critique] would indeed occur if one conceives of it as being an inference, because inference proceeds from a necessary connection established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
If non-perception (*anupalambha*) were itself perception (*pratyakṣa*), then that very same fault already mentioned regarding perception would apply; however, if it is an inference...

If the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) were established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then there would be no grasping of positive and negative concomitance in the absence of inference;
and in the absence of that [grasping], there would be no occurrence of inference,
resulting in an infinite regress of inferences.
Furthermore, the apprehension of existence in the absence of that [object] by means of the pramāṇa of non-existence is also untenable,
because the cognition of non-existence occurs only with respect to those very space and time that are present.
Another says:
"The relation of cause and effect is accessible through reasoning (*tarka*);
the definition of *tarka* is that it is a cognition of something imperceptible arising from a connection that has not been previously perceived."
For instance, it is the occurrence [of one thing] when that [other thing] exists which is perceived, not a causal relationship characterized by necessity as in the case of fire and smoke;

nor is the causal relationship perceived through that connection of "occurrence when that exists," yet worldly people understand: "Because this arises from that, therefore this is the effect of that."

Therefore, the cognition of this as an effect arises either through reasoning (*tarka*) or through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Presumptive testimony consists in the postulation of an unperceived object, based on the thought: "If this were not its effect, then its very existence would be impossible."
That is incorrect,
because [the object] exists externally through an inference based on a future conceptual construction.

If the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is observed, let it be seen whether that cognition arises through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or through reasoning (*tarka*). (150) Therefore, no causal relation is perceived as anything other than the existence [of the entities themselves]; for the fault previously mentioned applies there, due to the non-acceptance of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
(151) For if the causal relation were to enter the domain of cognition, its cognition would have to arise either through reasoning or from some other source.
Furthermore, it is not determined by anyone, even with effort, that the entity exists in a form other than its ultimate nature;
nor is there any cognition [of certainty] that the entity must necessarily exist [at a later time],
because one perceives the existence of that entity only for that specific duration of time.
Nor is this causal relationship understood through reasoning (*tarka*) or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*),
since it is only now that [the effect] is perceived immediately following [the cause].
If it were argued that "at other times as well, this [object] exists for this very reason," then that same object would not exist in any other way;
yet that too is untenable,
provided that it is not perceived from this [source] at present.
If it is asked, "From what is there the cognition that 'even another [thing] is exactly so'?"—
then even a jar is perceived immediately after a cloth.
If it is argued that even in that case the same would occur because deviation (vyabhicāra) is observed here,
then for that very reason there would likewise be a lack of confidence (anāśvāsa) in that case as well.
If it is argued that [the self] does not exist at all because it is not perceived,
or if it is argued that this worldly convention is exactly so because of the repeated perception of those who lack long-sighted vision;

That very [entity] returns again; its capacity is the conventional mode of existence (*saṃvṛti*). For a cognition whose true nature (*tattva*) is not investigated is considered to be the conventional. (152) Now, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this is that same thing" at a later time, the status of being an effect was already perceived previously;
otherwise, there would be no recognition at all.
That is incorrect;

for where is this recognition seen to be connected with a previous perception? Whether it arises from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or from reasoning (*tarka*), this has already been refuted [previously].
Now, [if you argue] that it arises from memory...
For indeed,
from the cognition "I remember this very thing as having been seen by me," it is understood that even memory has no connection with the [original] experience. (154)
I do not remember, and memory is not a valid means of knowledge;
moreover, that which is established by memory is established only conventionally.
Anticipating this objection, he says:

"If that [conventional reality] is accepted, let it be so according to convention. In this very way, worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) remains unconfused; for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is employed within worldly transaction, since there would otherwise follow the consequence of the total collapse of worldly transaction. Its establishment occurs merely through the differentiation of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Just as in the case of the conventional behavior of dreams, it remains that the very restriction of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādivāsanā*) is the source for the cause of worldly convention; otherwise, the distinction between that which has an objective basis and that which is without an objective basis could not be established from the outset.
Furthermore, as for the one who asks: "Now, what is this conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)?"

Furthermore: If conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is a truth, what is this "convention"? If it is false, how can there be truth? For there is no commonality of truth between that which has a deceptive object and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
To say "it is both true and conventional" is a contradiction.
To this it is replied:
that which is called "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti) is the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*),
consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) arising from beginningless habitual tendencies (*anādivāsanā*).
Therefore, this is the meaning:

there is only mere appearance arising through the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as blue and so forth; for these are unreal, like appearances in a dream. Since consciousness does not exist apart from them, it is therefore not the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
And because it serves a purpose, there is no annihilation of worldly convention; thus, it is a truth, and so there is no contradiction in calling it "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Beyond that, by way of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), there is the discernment of the selflessness of all things.
For positive and negative concomitance are not observed with respect to an external object;
however, the causality of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) is recognized in the case of dream-appearances,
and by virtue of belonging to the same class, that [causality] would also apply to other cases.
Alternatively,
conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is precisely the intrinsic nature of arising and so forth, because it is not determined by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, "arising conventionally" is an arising precisely by way of its not being determined by a valid means of cognition.
Now, [the claim that] "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti) implies incapacity because it is distinct from the nature of all things, whereas "arising" (utpāda) implies capacity— this is contradictory;
that too is incorrect.

Conventionally, there is no capacity in the ultimate sense; therefore, there is indeed no arising. This is because the mere cognition of the capacity for "arising" is devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, there is indeed arising, yet there is no fault of "arising by means of arising.
For in whatever form there is arising, in that very same form there is capacity.
In what manner does origination occur?
The meaning is that it occurs conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), not ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*);
and thus "convention" (*saṃvṛtti*) is not a mere matter of naming.
Because it is stated as such [in the sense] of being not established by valid cognition;
[the other reading is] "being established by valid cognition."
Furthermore, as for the refutation regarding the simultaneity of cause and effect—
namely, that the effect arises in the second moment after the cause— that too is incorrect.
If it is argued that there is no distinction because the self-nature has long since passed away—
since that which has long since passed away was non-existent at the time of its arising, whereas that which has just passed away is the opposite— then [we reply]:
What is this time of origination?

If it is the time of becoming (*bhavana*), then since becoming is inseparable from the agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*), that very [time] is the simultaneity of the cause with its effect. Or else, [the cause] exists at the time of becoming.
If it were the case that existence occurs at the time of the causal operation— namely, the activity of the one who performs the cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—
then even that which is temporally remote would possess causality, because that [remote thing] also exists at its own time.
Furthermore, since all moments of existence exist at that time, there would be the undesirable consequence (atiprasaṅga) that they all possess causality;
if you argue that this is not so because they belong to different continua (saṃtāna), then this is the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).
If there is the state of being a cause, there is the state of belonging to a different continuum; if there is the state of belonging to a different continuum, there is the state of not being a cause.
Thus, there is a contradiction in [something] being both a cause and belonging to a different continuum.
As for what was also said:

The term "investigation" (vicāra) refers to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the purpose of comprehension free from conceptual analysis; it does not refer to conceptual consciousness (vikalpaka-vijñāna).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is for the sake of conventional worldly cognition (*lokapratīti*).
Even the purpose of illusion (*māyārtha*) is precisely this: for the sake of worldly cognition.
Since worldly cognition is charming only so long as it is not investigated (*avicāritaramaṇīya*), there is no fault.
However, the understanding of the authors of the treatises is not conventional, and thus it is not accepted [as such];
as it has been said therein:
"What is conventional truth?"
To whatever extent there is worldly convention—
even regarding the distinction between valid and invalid cognition— it is so only by way of conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Thus it is said:
Valid cognition is non-contradictory;
non-contradiction is the attainment of the object indicated by the cognition.

If "attainment" (prāpti) also means nothing other than being experienced— such that if an object has already been cognized, it is the very same thing [that is attained] later— then for what purpose would one seek attainment? Consequently, every cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Now, if it is shown that he subsequently takes another course, then let it not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of that [subsequent] attainment;
in this way, everything would be a valid means of knowledge.
A cognition that does not manifest another [object] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because [validity arises] from a cognition that manifests purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Regarding this, he says:
"The object is established by perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*) as having arisen from the cognition of the means of accomplishment (*sādhanajñāna*)."

Now, if [the validity] were due to the appearance of further cognitive efficacy (*jñānārthakriyā*), then its validity would depend on another cognition; and thus everything would be valid from every cognition. Furthermore, even when something has been demonstrated, there would still be something remaining undemonstrated.
) Then, validity [would follow] from the attainment of that;
but that too is incorrect,
because there is no evidence presented for its existence.
Thus, all this is trivial;

therefore, let it be as it may that nothing exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Even by this much, there is no impairment whatsoever to the established distinction between valid and invalid cognition according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Your position is precisely what we intend; for it is impossible to proceed by overstepping the actual nature of things (*vastutattva*).

(1) Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*): [The opponent objects,] "But if, even in the case of a universal of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmānya*), it is possible [to perform a function] by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), then there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition.
To this, he says:
