If it is argued that [the universal] exists everywhere because the cognition [of it] exists everywhere, [we reply:

no, because its positive and negative concomitance are not observed in the case of the universal-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of the cognitions of the eye, visible form, and so forth.

(Verse 5) Just as the conformity to positive and negative concomitance in the cognitions of the eye, visible form, and so forth, has as its object the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is not so for cognitions of universals, because such cognitions arise merely from the mental application (*ābhoga*) toward what was previously perceived; however,
cognitions of form and so forth do not arise solely from internal causes such as the eye and other [senses].

For instance, even if a prior existence [of the object] is not perceived in reality, nevertheless, due to the observation of its absence, there arises the cognition of its non-existence. (156) If the appearance of a mass of pillars, which occurs through the eye alone and is independent of an external object, were to arise wherever the eye is directed, then it would exist in every such place.
Like the appearance of hair and so forth to one with ophthalmia,
it does not exist; therefore, there is no prior existence of a pillar or the like in a location devoid of that [appearance].
Therefore, because they arise through the conjunction of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), cognitions such as that of a jar make known the causal capacity of things like cloth;
however, cognitions of universals (*sāmānya*) do not function in this way,
since they occur solely due to internal causes.
Whatever effect arises solely from a particular causal complex (sāmagrī) indicates within itself the capacity for the existence of something distinct from that complex.

For instance, the visual consciousness arises from the eye alone [and other factors], yet it does not arise in a horse; is it not then the case that there is indeed a negative concomitance (vyatireka)? If this is asked:

This is not correct; for instance, because the universal "cowness" (gotva) is absent, the cognition of a cow does not arise in relation to a horse. Nor is that [cognition] an awakening of a latent impression (vāsanā); thus, there is no cognition of cowness in that case.

This [cognition] "this is not a horse" functions to awaken the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of "cowness"; it is not that there is no cognition of cowness therein, because the convention "it is a cow" is understood in that very instance.

It is not due to the absence of cowness, but rather due to the non-existence of such a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, no common form (*sāmānākāratā*) is perceived there apart from the individual instances (*vyakti*), by which one could establish whether it exists or does not exist.
Therefore, the universal is merely a conceptual construct (pratyaya-mātra), pleasing only so long as it is not critically examined; it does not exist in ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ).
Now, if it is not ultimately real, how is there a mutual exclusion between "cowness" and "horseness"?
[The answer is: mutual exclusion belongs only to conceptual constructions (kalpanā) or to individual particulars (vyakti).

If it is argued that even in the absence of a real individual, a universal cognition would not occur everywhere except through the mere application of convention, then the universal would not be incapable [of producing such cognition] by way of exclusion; for the universal is pervasive, and therefore there is a universal cognition everywhere.

(Note: Below this point, "T. adhastāt—dānaśīlasya pustikā—iti likhitaṃ dṛśyate" is observed, which indicates that in manuscript T, the following is written: "The manuscript of Dānaśīla is seen to be written below.")
[If it were so,] it would follow that everything is produced, since there would be the same consequence for things such as hairs perceived by one with cataracts.

If it is argued that [the universal does not exist] because it is not perceived by others, then the universal is likewise not perceived by those who lack mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth; thus, the same fault applies there as well.
It is not tenable to say that its existence is indeed perceived; for why are hairs and other such things not also perceived by others when there is a visual impairment (timira)?
If it is argued that because the impairment obstructs [the senses], it causes the perception of what is unreal, [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "unreality"?
Is it the state of being perceived by impaired sense faculties?
And what is this "impairment"?
This mutual dependence of perceiving what is not real is a fault;
moreover—

Even a universal [is perceived] only through the arousal of a contrary latent impression (*saṃskāra*), because of the impairment of the internal cause; thus, this [argument regarding] the exclusion of the universal is the same [as ours], provided that it is by virtue of being a pervader (*vyāpaka*). If [it were otherwise], even those things accessible to knowledge affected by cataracts (*taimirajñāna*) would possess the status of a pervader.
If mosquitoes, which are perceivable by impaired sense organs, were unreal, then since their unreality is not established, the impairment [of the sense organ] itself cannot be established. (158–159)

If it is argued that there is a sublation [of the universal] because its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not established due to its unreality, this is the same for the universal; there is likewise a sublation of that which grasps it. Therefore, the universal is not capable of causal efficiency, since it lacks such capacity even in the case of mere cognition.
By this, [the claim that the universal appears] in accordance with internal factors such as the application of convention (*samaya*) and so forth, is also refuted.
The cognitions regarding the jar, its lifting, generality, number, and so forth have been explained.
The jar is a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) which is the locus of color, taste, smell, and touch;
"lifting" is an action (*kriyā*).
Number is a quality;
here, cognition has inherence as its object,
and that which is apprehended by it is inherence.

The cognitions regarding those [objects] are also dependent solely on internal causes such as the application of conventions and so forth; they do not follow the positive and negative concomitance of the objects.

For instance, no substance called "dravya" is perceived apart from color-form (rūpa) and the rest. Furthermore, the cognition of a jar does not possess positive and negative concomitance with respect to the jar's own self. (161)
Only form and the other [sensory objects] are perceived by the cognitions of the eye and so forth;

therefore, because only that much is perceived, this cognition—which is characterized by an internal cause consisting of awakened beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—arises as a single attachment, namely "this is a jar," and is experienced by people. There is no other substantial nature (*dravyasvabhāva*) such as a jar that exists apart from these when examined.
[Objection: But surely the whole (*avayavin*) is determined through both seeing and touching?
Substance is of two kinds, namely visual and tactile;
that too is incorrect because:

Whether that substance is apprehended through a difference in form or by the opposite [of that], if there is a cognition of non-difference, it is only the form [that is perceived] and not the possessor of form (rūpavat). If there were a cognition of difference, there would be a perception of a cognition possessing two aspects; however, the appearance of duality does not arise from the eye or the mind alone.
Now, if the cognition is "this is a jar" and not "this is a form," how is that not a cognition of difference?

For instance, the cognition "this is a red jar" or "a cloth" is non-erroneous; and there is no cause for the existence of objects other than their being cognized. For if there were only the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*), how could there be the thought "this is a jar"? It would not.
That too is incorrect:
the object that is both red and not-red is designated by the term "jar" and so forth, while the object that is both a jar and not a jar is denoted by the word "red.

Therefore, when difference is conceptually constructed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the designation occurs according to a distinction in meaning; however, the real entity does not exist in that way. (165–166)
This has been examined elsewhere; now,
if the composite whole does not exist and only the qualities such as color and so forth exist,
how is there the cognition that "wherever there is color, right there is touch"?
That too is merely something trivial,

because when a collection is conceptualized based on dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmāgryadhīnatvāt*), and there is a connection with a single effect, the conceptualization "where this is, there that is" [arises].
Why then does the designation "where there are elephants and so forth in an army, there are men" not occur?

Likewise, where there are *palāśa* trees and so forth, there are also *khadira* trees and so forth; yet, a "military array" (*senā*) is not something distinct from the men and others, nor is a "forest" (*vana*) something distinct from the *dhava* trees and others.

Therefore, because they depend upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and produce the same effect, they do not exist in mutual separation, and for this reason they are designated by people in such ways.
In that case, then, form and the other [sensory qualities] themselves constitute the whole (*avayavin*), since their bodies are not mutually distinct;
for there is no mutual distinction among form and the others as there is between a pillar,
a jar, and a tree, nor is the "whole" a mere designation, like a forest or the like.
Its parts are established as such through conceptual construction based on positive and negative concomitance;
for instance, in the cognition "that which I see, that very same thing I touch," their identity of location is perceived.
It is not the case that tangibility or edibility is perceived through the exclusion of the location of color;

that too is incorrect if color were non-different from taste and the other [sensory objects]. If there were no mutual difference between color and the rest, how could that very same thing be something else? (168)
For that very same thing does not become something else, as that would entail the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction in its appearance.
If it were indeed one and the same thing, its perception as distinct would arise from its being apprehended by different sense faculties:
when perceived by the visual faculty it is "color-form" (*rūpatā*), by the tactile faculty it is "tangibility" (*spṛśyatā*), and by the gustatory faculty it is "taste" (*rasatā*).
That is incorrect;
for is that single entity perceived as distinct in any other way? Or is it established on the path of cognition as indeed distinct through the difference in its objects?
First of all, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for [the claim] that it is one and the same.

A single entity is not perceived as possessing difference merely because of a difference in apprehension, for that would entail the consequence of it being an illusion. If, on the other hand, this very [perception] is called non-illusory simply because there is no other way to apprehend it and one has no choice, then why is it not postulated that "this object is exactly thus"? The reason for not making such a postulation is that there is no perception of non-difference. (170)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"If there is difference, how can there be co-location and non-separation?
That too is easily explained, because:

The location is not other than that which possesses the location, because no distinction between them is perceived. As for the appearance of that which possesses a location, it is already broken [into its constituent parts]; so how could there be a [separate] location?
(171) There is no "location" distinct from form and the other [sensory objects].

Furthermore, that [location] is also distinct from them precisely because of the appearance of their difference; otherwise, due to the consequence of an infinite regress [if one were to posit further locations], it would simply not be perceived.
If there were a difference by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then even for color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, there would indeed be a difference;
yet there is no form other than that which appears as its own intrinsic nature, and for appearance itself, there is simply a difference.
For the manifestation of form is not itself the manifestation of taste,
as that would entail the consequence of the deficiency of other sense faculties and the consequence of their non-distinction.
If it is argued that the difference [in cognition] arises from the difference in the sense faculties, that is incorrect;
for even when there is a difference in the sense faculties, what is non-different does not appear as different.
If it were perceived as such, then for that which is distinct [from its parts], it would follow that the whole is merely color and so forth; furthermore,

if the object were one way but the cognition were another due to the power of the sense-faculties, it would be nothing but an error, like the appearance of yellow in a conch shell to one with jaundice.
Furthermore, it might be argued that non-erroneousness [of cognition] arises from correspondence; however, that too is untenable.
Even in the case of agreement, there is merely a manifestation;
that [agreement] too is a mode of manifestation in such a way due solely to the difference in sense faculties.
Therefore, since that too is indeed erroneous, how can what is unestablished be proven by means of what is unestablished?

Since both the correspondence [of cognition with its object] and other appearances are produced by the sense faculties, the cognition is not necessarily bound to the presence or absence of an external object; thus, it is well argued that no such thing as an "object" exists here.
Indeed, the proof of the "whole" (avayavin) does not prove the non-existence of the object, because that [whole] is intended as a specific kind of object.
Therefore, it is not the case that a single entity appears as manifold solely through the operation of the sense faculties.
However, even though form and so forth are manifold, the single cognition [of them] depends entirely upon internal causes.

Furthermore, in the case of the cognition of "lifting," it is the successive moments of the hand and so forth, arising in different locations, that constitute the lifting; thus, this collection itself is a conceptual construction dependent solely on internal causes, and does not arise from the power of the external object.
In that case, then, the nature of action (*kriyātva*), which is manifested by preceding and succeeding moments, is the object of the cognition of "throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇa*);
it is not [the object] of a universal (*sāmānya*) manifested by an individual (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, the universal "action-ness" (*kriyātva*) is manifested by an individual action (*kriyā-vyakti*), not by an individual object-moment (*artha-kṣaṇa-vyakti*),
nor by an individual moment of the hand and so forth; nor is another individual action perceived as its substrate,
nor does a universal possess the property of being manifested by a different individual.
Now, as for the claim that there is a genus of action (*kriyārthajāti*) manifested by each successive moment beginning with the hand,
that too is incorrect,
because it lacks the property of being manifested by each individual moment.
For throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other [motions] are not manifested by a single moment, because it would follow that they would be perceived at the very first moment.
Now, if it is argued that the genus of action (*kriyājāti*) is manifested only by those [motions] which occur at non-simultaneous times—[we reply:
indeed, one does not necessarily follow the established doctrine of others merely because of the instruments [of cognition].
This indeed is our established position regarding the view:
it is incorrect [to claim] that if a genus (*jāti*) is unmanifest in each individual, it is therefore not manifested in the collection.
If it is argued that because no other alternative is possible, [the object] is manifested by even a single [instance of cognition] through repetition (*abhyāsa*),
then repetition itself is the internal cause; thus, that cognition does not depend upon the power of the object.
In this same way, the cognitions of conjunction and disjunction are also to be explained.
And so it has been said:
"Likewise, number, conjunction, action, and the rest do not appear in the intellect as distinct forms—either by their own nature or through verbal expression. (172)

But surely, if "incapacity for causal efficiency" is the definition of a universal, then even things such as [illusory] hairs would follow as being universals, since they too are incapable of causal efficiency;
that is not so,
because:
Hair and the like are not the universal, because they lack adherence to [external] objects; since they are apprehended as objects of knowledge, the fault does not apply to non-existents.
For it is the object itself, appearing in the form of a universal while having the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), that is perceived as the universal.

If that [particular] is a *svalakṣaṇa* because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*), how can it be a universal (*sāmānya*)? And if it does not perform a causal function, how can it be an object (*artha*), since being an object consists in performing a causal function?
Furthermore, these two—performing a causal function and its opposite—cannot coexist in one and the same thing.
This is not difficult to establish:

the universal is directly capable of causal efficiency through its capacity for it to be transmitted indirectly; thus it is both that which possesses such efficacy and that which is indeed incapable of it.
Since the universal is incapable of direct causal efficiency, it is in reality no object at all, despite being determined as an object through conceptual determination.

Its status as an object is metaphorical (*upacarita*), because it is indirectly the cause of an effect that is [actually] another object. How then can the universal (*sāmānya*) be the object of a word?
For there is no causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*)—even through a succession of effects—in the case of such things as "sugar on the riverbank" or "a cart."
In another language, it is not a heap of sugar (śarkarārāśi).
This is not so;
let it not be that [the word] is common to them—what loss is there for us? On the contrary, it is most excellent, because it establishes the lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) of the word.
For instance:
We maintain that the universal is the object of valid cognition;
if this word were also an object of valid cognition, it would itself be a means of valid cognition.
How then is it said that the object of a word is the universal?
It is not that the object of a word is the universal alone; rather—
The universal (*sāmānya*) alone is the object of a word, not the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*);
and it is by virtue of being the object of a word that a continuous form is obtained.
Likewise, the particular is "not an object" [of words]; thus, things such as [illusory] hairs are not particulars, because for words, the particular is that which is not an object.
In this case as well, it is not that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object;
rather,
the particular characteristic is simply not the object at all.
Furthermore, cognition whose object is hair and so forth is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); for it has been said:
"A valid means of knowledge is non-erroneous cognition" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.1).
1) Once the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) has been established, its differentiation according to the distinction of objects is demonstrated.
For even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), since it is determined as such when a generality is applicable, [it is distinguished] from that which is outside the series (*bahiḥpaṃkti*).

The distinction [between existence and non-existence] is considered to belong to the object itself, insofar as it is what is to be established. Therefore, how could there be "objectivity" (viṣayatā) for that which is not an object of a means of valid cognition?
If the universal were indeed the object, then non-existence would have the status of an object; however, because it is a void, it lacks the nature of a universal, and yet it is not a non-object.

The same resolution applies here as well: because non-existence is an object of non-apprehension, even though it is a universal (*sāmānya*), it pervades its own particulars such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); and because it pervades individual instances, it is designated as "the non-existence of a jar" or "non-existence at this time. Thus, there is no contradiction.
For even non-existence is indeed an object of cognition in some form, since it is apprehended as an object of knowledge;
the established tenet is that non-existence is simply the existence of something else, and that [existence] is established by the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Alternatively, even this [non-existence] is indeed determined by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and it is an object because it serves a purpose;
for even through non-existence there is indeed a purpose, since it serves the purpose of allowing one to proceed without hesitation.

Therefore, even in that case, there is an "adhimokṣa" (resolute conviction) regarding the object; for it is the object itself that is non-existent in its own form, and not the hair and so forth, because they are determined as being cognizable through delusion.

Now, one might object: when even the hair and such arise as being of this nature—namely, as "non-existent hair" or as "resembling real hair"—then in that case too, there certainly exists a basis for unreality corresponding to them, such as the purpose of walking without obstruction. Consequently, even those [hair-appearances] would become objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, if it were determined in that way, then it would be nothing but a universal form; such being the case, there would be no vivid appearance (*sphuṭābhatā*).
And if, by virtue of having a vivid appearance, it were considered an object, then that cognition would be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself and would not be devoid of an object;
thus, it would not be erroneous. To this, he says:

Since there is no refutation of their being likewise [illusory], and because the appearance of clarity consists in the nature of cognition itself, it is not an object; furthermore, the notion of "hair and so forth" has a universal (sāmānya) as its object, whereas the appearance of hair is devoid of an external referent.

If even things such as hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika) are determined to be unreal, then what is the meaning of "unreal"? It means that they are not perceived through the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or by another person.

Since their non-existence is determined by the absence of such perception, they are indeed objects of knowledge as non-existents; thus, there is no denial of the fact that being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyarūpa*) even for non-existence.

Furthermore, as for the claim that this [hair] is similar to other hairs and the like—that is, the conventional usage of "similarity" regarding its form—this too falls within the scope of the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); therefore, the hair and so forth are indeed objects of knowledge.
How, then, can there be a clear manifestation of the universal?
Since it is an object by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, that [universal] would then be nothing other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa), which is the object of perception.
Since it is indeed the object of the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), how can it have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*)?
Because it is made an object by another conceptual cognition through its similarity to the previous hair and so forth;
for it is thus:

Even when things such as hairs [seen by one with cataracts] are similar—being accessible to a cognition affected by timira (visual disorder)—it is because they are perceived in exactly that way, or because they are similar in form. For similarity is not the opposite of reality without following after a prior form; thus, similarity and unreality are determined solely by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And it will be demonstrated that non-conceptual [cognition] does not operate with respect to the forms of the preceding and succeeding [moments];
therefore, since the universal is imperceptible, if one asks, "To what cognition then does it belong? because it lacks [direct] objective reality?
The sensory cognition appearing as hair is devoid of an external object;
this is the intended meaning.

The distinction is as follows: with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is perception (*pratyakṣa*); with respect to the form of hair and so forth, it is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*); and [in the context of the external object], it is inferential (*anumāna*), while the sensory cognition itself is devoid of an object.
2. [Objection: Is it not the case that sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*) is itself sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), and that very same thing is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)?

Indeed, there is no consciousness born of the senses other than self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana-vijñāna*), because that self-cognizing consciousness arises by depending upon the senses. Now, if it is held that this sensory cognition is an error when the object is absent, [we reply: self-awareness, however, does not arise from the senses, since it proceeds even without them. (176)
If something does not exist even in the absence of another, surely that other is not its cause; yet,
it is not the case that self-awareness does not exist without the sense faculties—
this [objection] is also incorrect.
Every self-awareness is entirely vivid by its own nature;
for whatever appears here in its own form, in the mode of direct perception, that is vivid,
and the own-form of every cognition appears directly.
For its own nature is not itself remote, because that would entail the consequence of its own non-existence;
therefore, everything remote is indeed indistinct, whereas dream-cognition, even without the sense organs, possesses a distinct form.
Therefore, the sense faculty operates only toward an object; in the absence of such an object, that operation would be purposeless.
The cognition of [non-existent] hair is purposeless, yet there is no attainment of hair therein;
thus, it is determined to be purposeless only with respect to the object.

[Objection: But if it possesses the status of an object by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, then it follows that even a universal (*sāmānya*) is a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and there is a contradiction in its being both [a universal] and clearly manifest. [Reply:
There is no contradiction, because if it were an object by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, then [the consequence] would apply to the universal. (9)
There is no fault, because that is what is accepted: since it has the nature of the object, there is indeed a similarity [with the external thing];

furthermore, the universal possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatā*) and a perfectly clear form by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, for its clarity consists precisely in being of such a kind.
As for the object, it has an indistinct appearance because it appears as something other than that which has a distinct appearance;
however, since the cognition itself possesses that very same form, with respect to what could it be called "indistinct"?
Therefore, because its own nature is directly manifested, how can there be any lack of clarity?
This very clarity is the manifestation of [the cognition] in all its aspects;
however, since the intrinsic nature of the object is something else, if that [nature] does not manifest, there is no manifestation of clarity.
Because of its clear manifestation? [The theory of] *abhihitānvaya* is the expression of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*).
Regarding the process of apprehension (*vaidhāriṇaprakriyā*):
[the opponent asks] "How then is it a universal (*sāmānya*) when its appearance is indistinct? To this he replies:
"It is the similarity [of the cognition] with the form of the external object."
"Rūpaṇa" means the act of defining (nirūpaṇa) form;
it signifies the similarity of the object through its definition and the indistinctness of that object.
In that regard, its lack of clarity and its nature as a universal form arise from its being of an identical nature everywhere, due to its reliance on the exclusion [of others] (tadvyāvṛtti).
For indeed, there is an identical nature everywhere— in the sharp, the dull, the intense, the mild, and so forth.

Because it is apprehended as being equal, through a single determination by way of unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object; for thus is the universal accepted as the "existence" (bhāva) of those things that are similar, and the form of cognition is determined as having the nature of that individual manifestation. (177)
Since the universal form resides in all individuals such as the brindled cow and others,
it possesses the nature of a universal through conventional reality by way of its determination (*adhyavasāya*); thus, the particular form of the cognition,
the determination thereof, and the specific latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from that [object] are the basis for this, and so there is no fault.
Because it arises by depending on the exclusion of that [other],
for it arises indirectly by depending on excluded objects,
and because it functions toward excluded objects.
And since that state of being excluded is common to all [particulars], exclusion itself is the universal;
and because it is related to exclusion, even the form of the object possesses the nature of exclusion. Thus, this applies to the form of the object as well.
Now, why is it that the "aspect" (*ākāra*) is the universal?
For color and so forth are themselves the universal without distinction, being the object of inference; for when individual instances are not excluded, those very instances are called the universal.
If all individual instances were abandoned, it would follow that inference is not a valid means of knowledge;
therefore, one who necessarily accepts the validity of inference must accept that its object is the individual instance through the process of "indication by indication" (lakṣitalakṣaṇa),
rather than terminating in the mere form alone.
Because it would follow that [the cognition] lacks the capacity to induce activity, this same fault applies even when only the universal is apprehended.

Therefore, even from that form of the cognition, there is an inference of individuals; thus, for the proponents of the universal (the Buddhist Tīrthikas), the inference of the universal has as its object the individuals.
1. Because it appears as something else, unclearly, in dependence upon another.
This is not the reading here.

[Objection: But surely there is no inference of the individual even through the universal, because the universal also appears therein; thus, since there would again be no engagement [with the object], inference is useless.
Nor does this series of universals lead to an infinite regress—where from one universal there is the inference of another universal, and from that yet another universal;
therefore, even at the ultimate limit, individuals must be understood [as the basis]. Thus, individuals are the universal.
That too is incorrect, because that [universal] is a non-entity (avastu) by virtue of being denotable, and because the collection of sense organs is effective [only with respect to entities].
When names and so forth are uttered, they are invariably connected to the speaker, the hearer, and the object denoted;
[therefore], there would be no engagement with a name or the like that is unconnected to such [entities].
For it is not the case that color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] themselves, when being perceived by a cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*), constitute the universal.
For form and the other [sensory objects] would have to be perceived either individually or collectively by a cognition of the universal (*sāmānyajñāna*).

If they were perceived collectively by a cognition of the universal, then since the cognition of the universal arises from the word, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the collection of sense organs (*akṣasaṃhati*) is rendered useless for the apprehension of the specific nature of all individuals. For it is precisely for the sake of apprehending individuals that the collection of sense organs, such as the eye, is desired.
If it is argued that since that manifestation is perceived even when the eyes and other senses have ceased to function, what is the purpose of desiring the sense organs for the sake of pleasure?

If it is argued that [all factors] are perceived together, then the pleasure that arises through the dependence on the sense faculty would be otherwise; but that too is incorrect, because that [pleasure] is also perceived from the word alone.

(178) If it is argued that there is indeed perception from the word, yet no arising of pleasure occurs without the sense faculty, then even from the sound of the words "arising of pleasure," there would indeed be an arising of pleasure. (179)

If there were no cognition even in that case, there would be no arising of pleasure. If the arising of pleasure is apprehended by its own nature, why is it not so? (180) If the arising of pleasure, though being apprehended by its own nature, were not so, then what confidence could there be in cognition elsewhere as well?
For existence is nothing other than being perceived; thus, even if the aggregate of the sense organs is fruitless, it may arise through the power of karma—
let it indeed arise— but it would be perceived as being fruitless, just as [it is perceived] when the eye has perished despite the seeing of form.
And it is not the case that they are thus not manifested through words;
therefore, the universal (sāmānya) does indeed have the form of color and so forth.
If that is so, then it will have the form of name and so forth.
Because a non-existent [object] cannot be manifested by a collection of sense-faculties,
etc., it is merely that which is being manifested as non-existent.

That too is incorrect, for a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) that is dissociated [from consciousness] would either be connected with the speaker, the listener, or the object; or it would be unconnected even with the speaker. If it were connected with the object, there would be no engagement with it.

Indeed, there is no cognition of this [formation] when it conveys a name or a cause that is connected with both the speaker and the listener. Since there is no such cognition, how could there be engagement with an object?
This is not tenable, because if activity were to occur even toward what is not cognized, it would follow that activity would occur everywhere, and it would also follow that cognition is useless.
Furthermore, it might be argued:

"Due to the similarity between the cause and the object, even when one is communicated, there is activity toward the other—just as when one of a pair of twins is addressed, [the name applies] to Citrāṅgada and Citravīrya; for in that case, there is no lack of application to the other."
That too is untenable: "There, it is an error; here, it is not an error. If it were an error, it would not be a cognition of reality.
To be both an error and a cognition of reality is a mutual contradiction. (182)
If that cognition appears as name and sign, how can it be an error?
If it is an error, then it must be without an object;
if that were so, there would be no apprehension of name and sign.
Since the name and the sign do not appear in their own form,
there would be an infinite regress even in the conceptualization of that name and sign;
therefore, in the non-erroneous cognition of twins, there is simply no appearance of a name or a sign, and thus the example is unestablished.

In that case as well, since activity is initiated solely through the cognition of that [object], the objection remains: "How is there activity toward the object? Thus, the example is included within the class of things yet to be proven (*sādhyapakṣa*).

Nevertheless, even if we were to grant this for the sake of argument, it is said: "If activity toward the object occurred due to similarity [between the cognition and the object] and due to error, it would not occur at all times. (12)

And there is a confusion of place; for a cognition of such a kind does not arise from the production of knowledge in the same way [as it appears], because the cognition does not admit of being elsewhere than where it arises.
Or, if it were produced by means of external objects appearing [within it], it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*).
[This refers to] that which is distinct from consciousness; [this is so] because such distinction is not established.
(14) If this occurrence regarding external objects were caused by an error produced through similarity even when there is cognition of something else, then it would not occur at all times;
for in the case of twins, although there is cognition of one, the occurrence [of the error] does not always pertain to the other, since its occurrence is observed even in that case.

Furthermore, there can be no similarity between that which is material and that which is immaterial, because of the absence of resemblance; or, even if such resemblance were to exist, it could not be a dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*),
because it would fall within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) by virtue of having the nature of form and so forth.
Furthermore, there would be no confusion regarding location, because it is established that [the object] exists in this very place; for there is no similarity between that [place] and another place.
Moreover, even the location is not presented by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
Rather,
since that [object] is also perceived through error solely by way of its name and its characteristic (*nimitta*),
it follows that the place is not established by the name; thus, one would not act toward a specific place.

For when the mind and mental factors are presented as being without location, no one engages with form and so forth—which are associated with place and non-place—on the grounds that they engage [with them] through the determination of oneness (*ekatvādhyavasāya*).
If it is asked, "What is this so-called determination of oneness? [the answer is as follows:]
If it is argued that there is an apprehension of the name and its signifier (*nāmanimitta*) as having the form of an object (*padārtha*) which is the domain of their activity,
how can one thing be perceived as another? A jar is not perceived in the form of a cloth.

If it is argued that its form is superimposed there [upon the external object], then that which is superimposed is precisely what is apprehended; for when the external is superimposed, it is the external alone that is apprehended, and not even a trace of name or causal sign (nāmanimitta). Furthermore, activity would occur only where the superimposition takes place, and not toward the external object itself.

Now, if there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the name and the sign (*nimitta*) upon that [object], then since the name and sign are thus apprehended, how can there be activity toward the external object?
If it is asked: "In the case of the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl, how does activity occur with respect to the mother-of-pearl?"
Since the white [color] also exists there and that location is apprehended by direct perception,
there is no grasping of the location of the name-sign (*nāmanimitta*);
for if the location were grasped, it would not be non-spatial (*adeśasthatā*).
If it is argued that "that is the location of the object which serves as the support," we say no, because there is no distinction [between them].
If it is argued that the location belongs to the mother-of-pearl and not to the silver, and that the same applies elsewhere, we say no.
Because silver is non-existent, there is no location for it;

however, this does not mean that the name and its cause have no location or existence. Furthermore, while there is the superimposition of perceived silver, there is no perception of the name and its cause.
Since it is perceived only at the time of superimposition (adhyāropa), this function [of the word] toward the object is not due to superimposition;
nor is it graspable by a cognition whose movement falters, as in the case of the cognition of "fire" with respect to a boy.

If it is argued that [the cognition] does not arise due to extreme habituation, from what [source] is this [claim] "due to extreme habituation" known? It is because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For that which is perceived by a *pramāṇa* must be accepted as such, and not otherwise.
If it is argued that "otherwise, conventional usage would not be tenable; therefore, it must be postulated in this way, as there is no evidence [for any other]," we say:
no, for it will be demonstrated that conventional usage occurs otherwise as well.
If it is asked: "Even for one for whom cognition arises from a word with its own internal form alone—and thus does not touch the object—how can there be engagement with the object?
[The answer is: No;
this is the same regarding the external object as it is regarding the form within the cognition.

Since it arises from a deluded cognition, being produced through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it causes the practitioner of worldly discourse to engage [with objects] by conceiving its own nature as an object situated in a specific location; thus, there is nothing contradictory here.
For instance:

To the extent that a [cognition] causes activity by superimposing an object upon its own form, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is completed; what further need is there for another [cognition]? There are two possible conceptions regarding the idea that "one conceives of an object as the cause of a name":
either it is already apprehended or it is not yet apprehended.

If it is argued that the name-aspect (nāmanimitta) is determined as the object-form within verbal cognition, how can there be a perception of it as an object (*artha*) when it is apprehended in its own form?
For that which is apprehended in its own form cannot be said to be apprehended in the form of something else.
Indeed, that [cognition] does not possess a different form;
rather, difference consists only in the difference of form.

Therefore, the perception of the name-sign (*nāmanimitta*) as having the form of the object is not [the object itself], because that form does not belong to the object, since the object is absent therein.
Nor can it belong to the name or the sign, because that is impossible; therefore, that aspect belongs to cognition itself.
It would be better if that very aspect of cognition were perceived as the object—what is the use of this internal tumor of a name or a sign?
Since cognition possesses the form of the object because it arises from it through a causal succession, how can it be logical that the name and the sign possess the form of the object?
From what [source] is this known?
For there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for its having the form of an object;
and if the form of the object were not distinct even from the name and the causal sign (*nimitta*),
then that [name and sign] itself would be the form of the object, and thus the conjunction of the sense faculties would not be fruitless.

Furthermore, if it does not perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then the non-futility of the coordination of the sense faculties in the apprehension of that which performs a purposeful action is untenable;
for, since the performance of a purposeful action is not apprehended, it follows that there would be no engagement [with the object] at all.
It proceeds from superimposition (*adhyāropa*);
it has been stated that this superimposition is merely a form of cognition.

Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress—another name and cause for that [superimposition], and yet another for that one—which would be an irresolvable difficulty because of the resulting state of delusion even in that case.
It is not [established] on the basis of the name and the sign, because there is a lack of valid cognition;
for the determination of an object does not arise from a deluded consciousness.
If it is argued that "that very form is what determines the object," [we reply:]...
It is not [the case that there is no pervasion],
because of the absence of a negative concomitance (vyatireka);
for a negative concomitance is not established [for us] in the same way as it is for the Sautrāntika, who maintains the doctrine of names and signs (nāma-nimitta).
If it is argued that since cognition— which is intended to have names and signs as its objects— occurs through mere mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth,
and since one accepts that knowledge possesses the form of the object, it would be logical for that [knowledge] to consist solely of the form of the object;
why then is its form not clear?
It is not so, because even with a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), there arises at least a trace of the form [of the object];
for that which arises from something with a certain form does not do so in its entirety, just as a son resembles his father [only partially].
Because there is no superimposition of an object upon the substratum of cognition, it is otherwise—that is, external (bahiḥ).
In that very context, there is an alternative reading: "There is a lack of proof for the name 'external row' (bahiḥpaṅkti-nāmanimitta).
Now, [the opponent objects]: "Is it not the case that all cognition is indeed formless? In that regard, the form belonging to the object is that appearance which is blue and so forth;
therein, every form such as blue belongs to the object, not to the cognition."
Therefore, all cognition possesses an object and does not consist of its own form; how, then, could there be error?
Nor is this form [of the object] a property of the cognition itself, because it appears as something external.
This is not so;
it does not have its own form.

If it is argued that [the cognition] possesses all objects of knowledge, that is incorrect because in dreams and other states things are perceived otherwise; nor does it arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), since there is the appearance of blue and so forth.
It is not [the case that the object exists] because blue and so forth are non-obstructive, for [the object] is known by those who occupy the appropriate location.
Because one knows for oneself that which was previously unknown; by this, names and so forth have been described.
[Objection: How is there a pervasion (vyāpti) that all knowledge possesses an object?
For indeed, it is not from the mere experience of a form that does not reside in front [of the observer] that there is possession of an object.
If that were so, there would be no distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous, because everything would possess an objective referent (*sālambanatva*).
If it is argued that even though something possesses an objective referent, it is designated as "erroneous" because it fails to achieve purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), [we reply:]...

If it is asked, "In that case, why is it not accepted that the conventional designation of validity occurs even when there is no attainment of purposeful action because there is no objective support (*anālambanatva*), and what is the reality here? [the answer is:
the reality is precisely the absence of an objective support.

Since it is observed that even in dreams and the like, there is a perception of something present before one despite the absence of an external object, and since that same phenomenon is observed elsewhere as well, the objection— "Why is the opposite [the view that all cognition has an object] not tenable?"— is not a valid answer.
If it is argued that [the cognition] has an object because having an object is unestablished—
that is, because having an object is not established anywhere even in the waking state— then:
In that case, since that state does not exist elsewhere, the cognition therein would be without an object;
therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it is seen otherwise in dreams and so forth.

Alternatively, if one argues that even dream-cognition is not without an object because it has names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) as its objects, then it is not established that dream-cognition is without an object.
It is said here that [this occurs] from the mere experience of the formative factors (saṃskāra).

Dream-cognition does not have a name or a sign (*nāmanimitta*) as its objective support (*ālambana*). Since the name or sign lacks that specific form, it cannot be said that blue and so forth are the objective supports therein; this is untenable because the form [of the dream] is distinct from blue and the like.
Furthermore, that [dream-form] possesses no non-obstructiveness (*apratighatā*), unlike real blue and so forth.

And because the blue seen in a dream is the opposite of that [real object], so too in the case of a concealed place: since one sees a herd of elephants there in the cell where one is situated, and because there is no space for a herd of elephants within that cell, it is impossible to go outside even from the enclosed cell.

Furthermore, since no activity of a herd of elephants—such as the breaking of branches—is observed, nor any activity of fire—such as burning—is observed, [one might argue that] blue and other such things have arisen in that very manner as non-obstructive entities. If that were so, why does everyone not see them? [The answer is: because for one who is awake there, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for such [a perception] is absent.
If the causal complex of sleep, which consists of the causes for seeing dreams such as forms and so forth, were to reveal everything,
it would not be so; for dreams are seen in various different ways even in that very same place.
The perception of difference and alteration in a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is as follows:
for whatever impression exists during the waking state, the corresponding perception does not arise exactly as it was; thus, there is no perception of everything by everyone.

Now, if it is argued that the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is nothing other than the continuum of conditioned consciousness, and therefore the consciousness produced from that [continuum] perceives an object only when it is present, then it would follow that everything present would be perceived.
Indeed, when consciousness arises from the eye and so forth, it does not perceive anything among the present objects that is fit for perception.
Therefore, as in a dream, something must have arisen [from a latent impression], because there is a selective perception.
For a distinction would be appropriate if there were a perception of a prior form;

in that case, only one who has the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of having seen it previously would perceive it, while for another, there would be no perception due to the absence of that prior experience.
Let it then be the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*): what was seen at a previous time is perceived as belonging to the present time.
If it is argued that [it is not so] because of the absence of simultaneity, and for this very reason it is a case of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*),
to this it is replied:
Or, what is considered the erroneous manifestation (*khyāti*) of that which is erroneous? If there is a manifestation of the erroneous, it does not possess error.
(184) If there is a manifestation of that which is erroneous, its erroneous nature does not exist;
if, however, there is an erroneous nature, then it follows that everything would be perceived in that way.
If it is argued that even for them there is "misapprehension as the contrary" (*viparītakhyāti*), this is not tenable:
"If everything is contrary because cognition is erroneous, then what is the point of reference? For an error does not exist by depending upon something else that is erroneous. (185)

Indeed, it is not the case that another person is called "erroneous" in the same way only by depending on someone else who is already erroneous; rather, elsewhere [it is said]: "The so-called 'misapprehension of the contrary' (viparītākhyāti) intended [by others] has gone elsewhere; I would have fallen into mud, but I was born when this mud had already dried. (186)

Thinking, "I shall establish erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) by means of the dreamer," you instead establish erroneous cognition for those who are awake. Now, if it is an erroneous cognition, then that erroneous nature belongs to the cognition itself and not to the object; since the object is perceived in its own form, what is "erroneous cognition"?
The nature of that error is simply the form of the cognition itself;
it is not the form of one thing appearing as another, by which there would be a corresponding cognition of the other as well,
because cognitions are distinct from one another.
In that case, it is simply the cognition itself that is cognized in such a manner; thus, the dream-vision does not have an external object as its basis.

For at that time, the object does not exist at all; rather, its arising is from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). That which is non-existent is not seen; it is consciousness alone that is self-cognizing. (187)
It may be reasonable that an object situated in one place is seen in another place;
however, how can it be seen when it is non-existent at that time, having been associated with a different time?
Therefore, it is simply a cognition arising in such a manner from a previous perception that is experienced, not an actual object, because such an object is impossible.

If even at another time it is perceived as belonging to that [original] time, then erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) exists everywhere; for even in the waking state, when one perceives a pillar and so forth, there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) present. But is it not the case that the absence of a sublater is itself merely erroneous cognition?
If it is argued that there is no misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) because of the attainment of the object, [we reply:
is not the attainment of the object itself also a misapprehension?
For if the object is already present, how can there be misapprehension?
If it is argued that since the object is indeed perceived, how can there be non-attainment? [We reply: If it is because of its absence [in the cognition], then how can there be awareness of it?
If it is argued that [non-existence] is something other than the form [of existence],
then how is there no attainment?
For now, non-existence is indeed other than existence.
[The opponent asks: "How then is there the perception of that [past object]? Why does the attainment of the form belonging to that time not also belong to that same time?
[The proponent replies: "Because it is impossible."
If it is argued that "it can be seen," then indeed it is not known whose seeing it is.
Recognition provides the certainty that "this is the perception of what was previously seen";
this is not the case in a dream, because there is an absence of recognition regarding what was seen in another birth.
If it is argued that there is inference here as well because of similarity with something else that is being recognized,
[we reply] no, because this is absent in the case of cities of the Gandharvas and the like,
for indeed there is no recognition there.
In that case, everything to be recognized would have been seen previously; it is not the case that there is seeing at the present moment.
(Note: This reading "neha dṛśyate" does not appear in the manuscript T.)
By this, the loss of mindfulness is also explained;
by this very [explanation], even that which is supramundane is explained,
for it is as follows:
What is this "extraordinary" (alaukika) thing?
It is said here that it is uncommon (asādhāraṇa), in that it is not perceived by another.

That [object] is indeed cognition; because it is not cognized by another [cognition] situated in a suitable location, it is grasped as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) like the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*). Therefore, it is the object itself and not cognition;

for there is no grasping of that [object] as an object of apprehension, since it is grasped in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), for that object exists in its own nature and not as an object of apprehension.
If the object exists as something graspable, and there is no graspability other than its appearance,
then that [appearance] alone exists; thus, there is no such thing as an "object."
The status of being an object is perceived through its having the form of the apprehended; however, that [form] is not the actual object.
How can this be characterized as the perception of one thing by another? This is merely some triviality.
If it is argued that the cognition "this is an object, this is an object" arises, [we reply: so be it.
This has not been stated:
"There is no object because of the conviction that it is a non-object" (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* 2).
1) By this, names and so forth have been explained;
moreover, all cognition in which that which stands before one appears is here [regarded as] misapprehension (viparītakhyāti), and not otherwise.
Regarding this, [the opponent asks] why it is not the case here that there is no supramundane object. To this he says:
"By what means is the cognition of the eye and so forth considered to possess a desired object?"
If it is argued that [the cognition] is seen through the power of the object, then anything else would be rendered purposeless.
Furthermore,
by whom is this cognition of the eye and so forth— which consists of non-erroneous manifestation— held to be meaningful and produced by the presence of an object?
What is the reason for this?
For there is no difference in the fact that [the object] is being perceived.
If it is argued that the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the object is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [we reply:]...
For instance:
that object is first seen by another [means], and subsequently it is reached by oneself through inference;
thus, the efficacy of the object is perceived.
If this is so, then that cognition for which this causal complex does not exist has attained futility;
for in such a case there is no object, and the thought "all is well here" is merely conventional.
And this cognition is non-contradictory.

"It exists" [is said] because indeed only a cognition has arisen for me; there is no object here. "By my own power of prior cultivation, it was cultivated by me in this way," but it is not seen by me as an external thing, nor is it a memory; rather, this object is supramundane.

If it is argued that by whatever subverting factor its non-worldliness (*alaukikatva*) is perceived, by that very factor its lack of meaning (*anarthakatva*) is also perceived—and that what is perceived as worldly cannot be non-worldly there, because that would entail the fallacy of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*)—and that [the cognition] itself is likewise non-worldly; then [we reply]: [this is not so].
Not so, because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress;
rather, only its unique [specific] nature is perceived.

It is not the case that there is the thought "this is perceived by another" regarding the object itself; rather, when there is a cognition whose object is an external thing, it is indeed through inference that the state of being perceived by another is cognized.

In that case, however, there is no other person for whom the object is non-erroneous; rather, one perceives only one's own cognition, thinking, "This is my cognition, this is not an [external] object. Therefore, because there is the appearance of names and so forth, the logical conclusion is that there is no objective support (*sālambanatva*) when a relationship exists between a speaker and a listener.
If it is argued that there is no application [of the name] even when there is no connection [with the object], just as there is a connection with the object [in other cases],
then the past and the future would not be denotable, because of the destruction of that [connection].
(18) If the acceptance of a connection with the object is the basis for the name and its cause, then there would be no application [of the name] at all.
Since its destruction occurs along with the object,
there is all the more non-engagement when there is no connection;
for where there is the consequence of non-engagement due to the cognition of a mere connection with the object, there is all the more non-engagement when there is no connection.
Since past and future objects do not exist,
even if the name and the sign (nimitta) persist, there can be no engagement with the object because the mental imprint of the object is absent;
for engagement with one thing does not occur when another thing has been cognized.
The remainder, however, has already been explained at that time. 2 T.

(2) Regarding the faults in the opponent's view: if it is thought that there is no undesirable consequence [of over-extension] from a word because of the apprehension of a universal, that is not so; for either there is no apprehension of the universal alone, or even if there were such apprehension, [the fault remains]. 19.
Because it is not distinct from that [unmanifest], there would be its constant perception;
and if manifestation were for the sake of perceptibility, then since manifestation is eternal, it would be eternally perceived.
That which is capable of producing cognition in the self is indeed always capable.
Now, if [the universal] were sometimes incapable [of being grasped], it would be so always;
for if the universal were the object of verbal cognition,
that universal would be apprehended either in its isolated state or otherwise.

If only the universal (*sāmānya*) were apprehended, then even upon the disappearance of the individual (*vyakti*), the cognition [of the universal] would still occur; however, there would be no cognition of it as "past" and so forth, for the universal does not possess the nature of being past and so on.
Now, if it is argued that the universal is designated or determined as "past" and so forth due to its connection with individuals that are past and so on—[we reply:]...
That being the case, only that which is accompanied by the form of a manifest individual (vyakti) would be perceived;
however, past and other such individuals possess no form.
How, then, can there be a cognition of the nature of "pastness" and so forth through the medium of the form of a past or other individual?
For that which has not made its own form an object cannot be capable of apprehending another as having that same form;
and if it is argued that there is practical activity even when the universal alone is apprehended,
then there is yet another fault.
That [universal] is neither its universal nor its manifestor;
for apart from that [particular], it cannot be apprehended as something independent that is fit to be designated as "its" [universal] or as "its" manifestor.
For illumination, such as that of a lamp and so forth, is a manifestor because it is perceived by its own cognition;
if the universal were perceived alone even without the perception of the individual, then it would not be manifested by the individual,
and consequently, it would be perceived eternally.
A universal is perceived even in a location devoid of its individual instances,
just as [the universal] 'sound' is perceived in its location by means of the word even in the absence of that particular instance;
however, it is not grasped by the sense organ without a manifesting individual instance.

[The opponent argues: "A universal (*sāmānya*) being grasped by a sense organ is manifested by an individual (*vyakti*); for example, jars and the like do not depend upon lamps or similar objects when they are cognized through words, whereas when they are cognized by a sense organ, they do depend [upon them]. Thus, there is no fault [in our position]. This too is incorrect.
From a word, only the universal such as "jar" and so forth is cognized;

how then can that serve as an example? Because the universal has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument, for the subject itself cannot be the example, as that would entail the absurdity of there being no possible defect in an example.
Therefore, if a universal (*sāmānya*) is cognized from a word by way of its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), what is the use of its perception (*pratyakṣapratīti*)?

But [one might ask]: "If there is no apprehension through perception, how can there be cognition from a word? [The answer is: because of the absence of the apprehension of the relation (*saṃbandhagrahaṇābhāva*).
But is the form that appears from the word as the universal of one nature, or is it of a different nature?
If that form [of the universal] is indeed the same as the individual, then it would be perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as well; it would produce a cognition by means of that very form.

Or, if its form is perceived by direct perception, then being such, how could there be a cognition of it elsewhere when the convention (*saṅketa*) was established for it? It would appear in verbal cognition (*śabda-pratyaya*) by means of the very form apprehended through direct perception.
Nor does that which has such an intrinsic nature appear with the nature of something else in another cognition;
and since a universal is eternal, it appears at all times as having precisely that form.
Whether it possesses power or lacks power, that which is established by its very nature cannot be remedied because of its permanence; who is capable of exhausting it?
And that is perceived as conforming to a general cognition.
By whom was that slight trace of the form of blue and so forth produced in that [cognition]?
(23) If there were a cognition of the universal alone through the word, it ought to appear solely in the form of the universal;
what room is there for even a slight trace of the form of blue and so forth?

If it is argued that [the universal is perceived] because of the manifestation [of the individual], then since the manifestation itself is not perceived, how could it be said that [the universal is perceived] "because it is produced by the manifestation"? This is not tenable,
as it would entail the non-existence of the universal.
Since it does not appear apart from that [object], the nature of the recurring form (*anugatākāratā*) is also nothing other than the form of blue and so forth; this has been stated there.
And in that case, if there were a common form among objects, it would not be a "universal" (*sāmānya*).
If it is argued that [the universal] is perceived by both [the sense organ and the word], we say no; for then it would follow that it is perceptible by the senses.
To claim that it will be perceptible by the senses because the individual (vyakti) is perceived by the sense organ is not logical.

There would be no cognition of a universal from a word, for there is no such thing as a universal that exists in that manner; this is because there is no corresponding mental apprehension (*sampratyaya*) and because it appears as something distinct [from the individual]. Therefore, since something distinct from the individual must be conveyed, if the form of the individual were understood from the word, the sensory perception would not be fruitful and would become purposeless.
1. Therefore, if it is argued that the sense organs are not useless because they serve as the basis for perceptual cognition, [we reply: no.
How can that very cognition, being of a single form, have a manifestation as something diverse, such as sound and so forth?
Since perception consists precisely in the apprehension of the object’s own nature, if that [apprehension] exists, the sense organs are rendered useless.

If it is argued that the state of being non-ocular (avyakṣatā) is not the direct apprehension of the object as present before one, but rather its apprehension as not being directly [perceived], [we reply: no.

If it is argued that this is not so because the word is perceived otherwise, then the word would be grasped as being right in front [of the senses], and thus its status as an object of direct perception (adhyakṣatā) would not obtain.
If it is argued that there is cognition of [the object] in its entirety,

then that very same [object] is cognized from the word as well, because the convention is grasped with respect to that very thing and because [the word] serves the purpose of providing satisfaction. If this is argued:
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not arise from the mere existence of satisfaction, because there was no hearing of the words "such is your satisfaction" [at that time];

Since the application [of the word] is possible even with respect to the past in the sense that "it does not exist," it might still be the case that the word is applied only to the past and the future.
And it applies when [the object] is currently being engaged with in conventional usage, not when it is not so engaged; for if it were merely visible, the application [of the term] would be redundant.
Furthermore, past forms and so forth are neither satisfying nor visible when they are separated [from the present].
If it is argued that this constitutes the efficacy of the sense faculties, that is incorrect;
for how can that which is past and so forth be perceived by way of its own nature? Indeed, the past and so forth are not discerned as having a form other than being unperceivable. (189)
Even in the case of the eye and other senses, that which is perceived brings satisfaction only through the perception of its own unmediated nature;

and it is not the case that even a distant sound of music, when its own nature is cognized, does not produce satisfaction. If it is argued that [the sound] is indeed unmediated because it arrives via the analogy of water waves, [we reply: no.
Even this is not the core point:

since it is perceived from a distant location, how could there be any arrival [of the self]? If there were an over-extension of the principle, then even the material cause would be active. If that which is perceived from a distant place were nonetheless conjoined with the bodily substrates, [then the same would apply to the self].
Form and the other [sensory objects] would likewise [be perceived through words];

consequently, if the cognition of an object were to arise from the inference of a word or from some other conceptual construction, there would follow such consequences as touching a *caṇḍāla* or illicit sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman.
Therefore, if the object of a word were apprehended by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), it could not possess the status of being past and so forth.
Even though they are being perceived in their own form, the past and so forth exist only through cognition;
and even in the case of correspondence, existence arises from words such as "correspondence" and the like.
Now, existence is indeed perception by means of the sense faculty, not mere cognition.
For even defects such as the impairment of the sense of hearing are observed to function even in the absence of existence;
this is not the case for [objects] that are past and so forth.

If it is argued that existence is established by means of a sense-faculty (*indriya*), then why do mosquitoes and the like not exist [for you]? If it is said they do not exist because of an impairment [of the faculty], then how is that impairment known? (191) If it is argued that there is a different mode of apprehension [in their case] and thus mosquitoes and the like do not exist, then in that case, the apprehension of the thing’s own nature (*svarūpa*) is what is considered its existence. (192) Therefore, the apprehension of the own-nature itself is both existence and direct perceptibility (*pratyakṣatā*), being unmediated; thus, there is no distinction between verbal cognition and sensory cognition. Consequently, it is not logical for these positions to claim that the purpose of perception lies elsewhere; hence, they are simply futile.
For this reason as well, the universal is not a real entity; the genus is not of the nature of an individual possessing that genus, such that it would be established as depending on another.
If it were separate, it would indeed be called "dependent," for dependence is defined as being an effect. || 25 ||

Even though an effect is not dependent on anything other than its own production, it is connected to its cause through conceptual construction; for how could that which is not an effect be so connected in any way?
If it were something else, it would be unconnected to it; therefore, its lack of intrinsic nature is established.
Either the entity possessing birth (jātimat) is called "birth" (jāti), or something else is so called therein.

First of all, the universal (jāti) is not the very form of the individual entities themselves, because individuals are perceived by direct perception as being distinct from one another and having no other substratum;
for that which is perceived by a non-erroneous cognition cannot be otherwise than it appears.
Likewise, individuals such as brindled cows (*śāvaleyādayaḥ*) are perceived individually and independently;

then, subsequently, second and subsequent individuals are perceived in dependence upon each preceding one. This [alleged] similarity is just like that; and the claim that "this is that very same thing" is also untenable.

Even an effect is connected [to its cause] only through the conceptualization of a sprout and so forth, because once it has been produced from its own cause, it is independent. For as long as it is unproduced, there is only conceptualization; even at the time of production, since it arises simultaneously with that [cause], the cause—whether it has perished or not—is independent. Thus, the connection of effects with their causes is by means of conceptualization alone. How much more so in the case of the opposite? Therefore, whether it be an individual or a universal, that which is other than another individual is unconnected to it.
Therefore, the universal lacks intrinsic nature;
for even non-existence would become a universal if it were perceived as being connected [to particulars], whereas a universal is not perceived when it is unconnected.

Because the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) is the same [in both cases], there is no over-extension regarding non-existence; for those two, there is no dependence on a particular instance.
Even in the case of "hare's horn, hare's horn," a universal certainly exists in relation to its individual instances.
If it is asked why [the universal] does not belong to another individual, [we reply:
for one who maintains that there is a real universal (vastu-sāmānya), why would "cowness" not belong to a white horse and so forth?
Because there is no [necessary] dependence.
For it is not manifested by individual instances such as the white horse (*karka*) and so forth;

rather, in the case of brindled cows (*śāvaleyādi*) and the like, because there is no such requirement [for a separate manifestation], things such as a donkey's horn do not possess the nature of that universal, whereas for "cowness" (*gotva*), it exists precisely through its reliance upon those [individuals].
And since [the word] functions there, the relation characterized by dependence exists; thus, there is no fault.
Nor does that form belong to them, nor is there a relation of identity (*tādātmya*); nevertheless, it occurs in such a way through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, although formless, the universal (jāti) is manifested by words intended to introduce its specific instances through the medium of forms; for indeed,
the universal has no form of its own.

It is solely by virtue of being the substratum for forms that it is perceived as if it possessed form, characterized by arising therein through a traditional succession; and precisely because of its arising from that [substratum] and due to the determination of it as such, one proceeds toward the particulars when there is the cognition of that genus.
Therefore, even by words intended to introduce those particulars, it is that very [genus] which is manifested, and not something else distinct—this is the conclusion.

1. Let there be the appearance of form for the individual forms merely by virtue of being their substratum; but from what [source] does the determination of the unity of the universal arise with respect to the individuals?
For form is indeed seen, yet how can there be a determination of oneness regarding that which is unseen?
To this it is replied:
in that [cognition], there is either the appearance of form or the grasping of the object as its true nature.
That is an error, produced by the habitual practice of tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time.
Indeed, the superimposition of that [unreal] form does not occur merely from seeing the reality;
rather, a succession of errors also occurs, as in the conceptualization of a creator god (*īśvara*) and so forth.
If it is asked how there can be a clear perception even when the appearance is not manifest, the only recourse here too is a succession of errors;

therefore, an error arises only from another error, and that [other] from yet another—thus, the beginninglessness of error is preferable. Consequently, there is no purpose for that form to be established by perception.
Or else:
And as for that universal of objects which is characterized by the exclusion of others—
these words are based upon it, yet its form is nothing at all;
for there is no form in a universal characterized by the exclusion of others.
For words effect only an exclusion from that which is of a different class and undesired;
and this exclusion is simply the absence of occurrence [of the word] in that [class],
since no one seeks anything by means of mere non-occurrence.
It is not the case that when one says "bring the jar," the non-bringing of cloth and other things is what is being requested; rather,
