it is the non-bringing [of the jar] that is being negated by the command "bring."
Consequently, it follows that [the object] would be brought about by itself, and since that would also apply to what is impossible (*aghaṭa*), there must be a negation of it; yet,
there is no form of such a negation.
Now, it might be argued that the meaning of the word of the first injunction will be [the positive],
for in that case a negation is not possible because [the positive] has been occasioned;
but even that is not so.

In this context, it is precisely non-brought-forthness (*anānayanam*) that is relevant, and that is what is being negated. Since there is nothing else beyond indifference (*audāsīnyāt*), what other relevance could there be for it? Here, non-exertion itself is "non-brought-forthness," and that alone is what is negated by the word.
But surely, the negation of one thing is the very affirmation of another; how then can it be said that there is no form (*rūpam*) belonging to it?
To this, it is said:
If a positive injunction were established through a negation, then how could the absence of one thing be the presence of another?
In that case as well, the absence of one thing would simply be the absence of another, and not the reverse.

—When that form is excluded externally, the conceptualization of the other occurs spontaneously; in that case, there is no operation of words, for the understanding of the object occurs spontaneously.
If it is asked: "How is it that the very existence of one thing constitutes the non-existence of another?"

Since that conceptualization arises upon the apprehension of something else, there is no fault in stating this under the view of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as being of the nature of conceptualization;
for one who experiences their own cognition as distinct from that [other object] has the realization that "it does not exist."
Now, there certainly exists a cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*);
whatever objective form appears therein is indeed the universal.
Even if it does not possess the nature of an external object, that is because it appears in a different manner.
It is not logical to claim that this universal is not distinct [from the individuals], for it is said in response to this:
because it is observed in the cognition of a universal, even though the universal itself is formless.
Even an error regarding the object would be accepted as the universal, because it appears [therein];
yet, because it lacks existence in reality by way of having the form of an object, it does not possess that form.
For it is that which appears in the cognition of the universal that is accepted as the universal.

If formlessness— that is, the absence of an aspect— were established, then cognition would necessarily have to exist through something else, and thus it would be a universal (*sāmānya*), because it would be perceived through that universal form. However, even though there is an error regarding the object, just as that [object] is not seen as a universal,
so too is this very [cognition] perceived as an error.
Nor is that [universal] a universal by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*),

because it is restricted to its own form (*svākāra*) and is therefore a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, it is so called because it "floats" (*abhiplava*) over objects— that is, because it appears as the form of the object— and because it is understood as being non-existent in reality,
for this universal does not exist in objects.
Just as it is perceived as being established in that [object],
therefore, in that form— namely, by virtue of having an object— it is not material and does not possess intrinsic nature, because it cannot withstand critical examination.
Otherwise, even yellow and other colors would exist in white conch shells and the like;
therefore, the universal is not a real entity.
The universal is neither material nor endowed with intrinsic nature; furthermore, because it is inexpressible, it is not a real entity.
Indeed, even though a universal is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from its particulars, it is nonetheless not a real entity.

How can that which is inexpressible due to its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) be considered expressible through some statement? [Verse 32] For it is stated as an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that one universal is distinct from another universal, such as being "outside the row."
If a thing were not a thing, it could not be inexpressible in any way;
for when something is inexpressible in terms of identity or difference, it is necessarily devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*).
Indeed, you must admit that an entity which is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [something else] cannot possibly exist.

Now, if by the rule that "it must be expressible as something other than another universal," there exists a distinction [between the universal and the particular], then the entity must be a universal;

yet if even the manifestation of the entity were expressible as either identical to or different from [the universal], then precisely because it would be inexpressible [in those terms], it would be a non-entity.
If it is argued that "it is precisely because of that relation [to the cause] that there is inexpressibility," then—
since for distinct entities the relation is nothing other than the causal relationship—
it would follow that all effects are inexpressible in relation to their causes.
Nor can smoke be said to be inexpressible in terms of identity with or difference from fire;
for if it is argued that the universal is inexpressible [as identical or different] from the individual due to the non-difference of their location, we reply:
no such thing as "location" exists as a separate entity from the object itself.
If difference does not appear, how could there not be an absence of difference?
And if difference appears, by what means could there be non-difference?

Since there is no other mode for a real entity (vastu) than being either identical to or different from [something else], it is a non-entity (avastu) because it cannot be described as anything at all.
Nor can it be denoted as distinct from another universal,
because that other universal is also established as a real entity (*vastu*).
Furthermore, if it were denotable as distinct even from a conceptualized [universal], it would be a real entity.

If it is argued that even things such as a rabbit’s horn possess substantiality because they are mutually distinct, yet their distinction is due to a difference in their material causes (*upādāna*) and not in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), just as the cognition of the material cause—the head of a rabbit and so forth—is what is divided and not the rabbit’s horns themselves; [we reply: no.
Even here, when it is stated in this way, what contradiction is there?

Since there is a difference in the apprehension of the individual instances (*vyakti*), there too there is only a difference in cognition (*buddhi-bheda*) and not a difference in the real entity (*vastu-bheda*). Thus he says:
4. But that which is not at all expressible [as a distinct entity] is [only so designated] through the metaphorical attribution of difference based on the difference in its material cause. || 33 ||
Furthermore, if either the universal (*sāmānya*) or the individual (*vyakti*) were the denotatum of words,
then past and future objects could not be denoted; yet this is not the case,
since even with respect to past and future objects, [cognitions] are bound to universals.
The scriptural authorities are established [on this point]: how could there be a property (dharma) of both the existent and the non-existent?

If a universal were perceived even with respect to a past or future entity, then how could that universal be a property of a past or future thing which is neither existent nor non-existent? For there can be no property belonging to what is non-existent.
If it is argued that [the universal] is a property (dharma) of another individual that currently exists, then how can that which is perceived as possessing that property be considered past?
For the pastness of the universal depends upon the power of a past individual, not upon itself.

Therefore, by the rule that the universal is past because it possesses the state of having passed away, the universal is a property of what is non-existent; and whatever is a property of the non-existent does not exist, just as the nature of a rabbit’s horn or non-existence itself [do not exist].
Or, if it were existent, it could not be a property of the non-existent, such as the capacity to produce an effect in sprouts and the like.
If it is asked, "What is the contradiction?"—
it is simply the absence of a relation;
for a relation with that which is non-existent cannot be established.

If that is so, then the universal (*sāmānya*) is also perceived as non-existent, just as the individual (*vyakti*) is [perceived as non-existent] due to the absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*). But then the individual is also perceived as truly existent, because of the existence of the past and the future. If it exists, how can it be past?
If it is argued that because the act of cognition has passed away, that very cognition is indeed cognized as a "cognition" by way of its non-perceptibility;
It has been stated that there is no cognition of the essential nature [of a thing] precisely because it is not perceived;
therefore, for non-existent things such as the past and so forth, there is no property consisting of a real universal (*satsāmānya*).

If it is claimed that this [non-existence] is intended by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then what proximity does a present jar have to non-existence— which is not found in the case of a cloth and so forth— that would justify such a designation?
Thus, the reason "because it is non-existent" (*asad*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The intention [of the opponent] is this: since that [existence] is accepted as being merely figurative (*upacāra*) and not existing as a real property (*asaddharmatva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the reason "because it is not a real property" is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, regarding that which is figurative, it does not exist there in ultimate reality; thus, because the universal (*sāmānya*) lacks existence in ultimate reality within the past and the future, the reason "because it exists" is unestablished.
The resolution here consists of the following positions:
that there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of either the general property (*sāmānyadharma*) or the individual (*vyakti*) to the past and so forth.
If it is argued that there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the universal, that is incorrect;
for the metaphorical application of that universal which exists in a present jar to a past [jar] must be based either on a connection or on being perceived.
Otherwise, if there were metaphorical application (*upacāra*) in the absence of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, there can be no relation or similarity with that which is non-existent, because that would entail its existence; thus, the [alleged] existence of the past and so forth has already been refuted.
If it is argued that this is a metaphorical usage of the word, that too is incorrect,
because a word does not function in the absence of an object.
Alternatively, it follows that words function even when there is no [real] occurrence;
and since that [object] is a universal (sāmānya), it is not a real entity (vastu).
Now, if it is argued that this is a metaphorical designation (upacāra) for the individual (vyakti), then in that case too, there must be some degree of proximity (pratyāsatti).
Since metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is untenable for that which lacks proximity,
this same point must be stated even regarding the metaphorical application of the word [“existent”].

If it is argued that there is a metaphorical designation because the past and future are one and the same due to their similarity in form, such that "that very thing is the past" but causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not exist, and therefore the metaphorical designation is based on causal efficiency— then in that case, it is the universal (*sāmānya*) alone that is being cognized, and not otherwise.
If that is so, then everything exists; how then can there be "pastness" since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not exist for it?
If you say that because that [efficiency] is absent, it is past, then how can that which lacks existence be a thing?
If it is argued that because of its connection with that [past entity], the entity itself is indeed past,
then by what means is that connection apprehended?
For if that were apprehended, then even a non-entity would be apprehended.
Furthermore,
the reason "because dharmas are non-existent" is unestablished.
Even causal efficiency exists for that [past object] in the view that "everything exists. If it were non-existent, how could the non-existence of its existence be real?
(195) If it is argued that [the past and so forth exist] conventionally, while in ultimate reality everything is non-existent—[we ask: what is this conventionality?
If it is the state of being an objective support for cognition, then since the entirety of the ultimate is real, how can there be such a thing as conventional reality? (196)
For conventional reality (saṃvṛti) has as its objective support entities that lack real form, because it conceals reality;
however, when reality is revealed, there is no such thing as "conventional reality.
Furthermore, if the past and so forth were conventional reality, they would not be ultimate reality (paramārtha).

Since there is no entity apart from its forms such as the past and so forth, it would follow that there is no reality whatsoever. If the present alone were the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then the past and so on would be the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not the ultimate; thus, it is established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a non-entity, for a universal does not exist merely in the present. Therefore, everything is well-established.

Therefore, what is called "metaphorical designation" (upacāra) does not apply to a real entity that is the object of expression; rather, this very thing is metaphorical designation: the presentation of what is non-existent, and both the universal and the individual are non-existent.
The referent of words denoting past entities is as follows: for that which was previously perceived is precisely what is superimposed [upon the present].

That too is incorrect; for that [object] is not superimposed by means of the very form by which it is perceived through the example. Indeed, that object which is perceived by a certain [form] is superimposed by that same [form]. (197) Now, a cognition operating with respect to the past and so forth is perceived as being connected with that place and time.

Therefore, even when [the object] has passed away, that very same previously perceived form is superimposed upon it, just as, for example, the genus (*gotva*) previously perceived is superimposed upon a horse.

If this is so, then even when the object has not yet passed away, only the superimposition of the previous form is perceived, and not otherwise; for even by means of inference, it is impossible to perceive a universal (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, in all cases it is merely a conventional designation (*upacāra*) and not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because a universal (*sāmānya*) is characterized by being superimposed upon everything.
Now, if it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as something actually existing, and therefore it must be ultimately real (*paramārtha*),
then since it is not cognized by means of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, that universal would be a non-entity (*avastu*).

Now, even by means of perception, that form which is common to previous [instances] and appears indistinctly is perceived; likewise, it is perceived in the same way through verbal testimony and through inference. However, in that case, distinctness is perceived only of the individual (vyakti). Therefore, even if inference or verbal testimony does not operate regarding the specific aspect, they certainly do operate regarding the general aspect (sāmānya) which appears indistinctly.
That too is incorrect;

for here, in the case of a universal, there is no perception at all because it does not exist as an object of the senses. Furthermore, this will be explained later on, due to the lack of direct apprehension.
Indeed, it will be demonstrated that perception does not apply to what is common to preceding [moments].

Furthermore, even when a specific quality has perished, its commonality [to both states] continues to be perceived; how then could that which is perceived be a property of neither existence nor non-existence?
It has been stated that if it were common to both, it would possess the nature of a real entity, for how could it be a non-entity? It must indeed be a real entity.
That too is incorrect;
for a present manifestation is not perceived as being identical with a past manifestation,
and when there are multiple manifestations, what else could "commonality" mean?

Therefore, because it appears in the form of the past and so forth, the object of the word is indeed non-existent; nor is this a mere metaphorical usage, because it is the object of an unimpeded cognition.
For:
"The unswerving operation of the intellect is always present in both the primary and the metaphorical [senses]; there is even a worldly proverb regarding the lion and the boy.

(36) The unswerving operation of the intellect alone is the basis for both the primary and the metaphorical [applications]. Otherwise, the cognition would indeed be one of faltering movement in the case of the boy; therefore, "lion-ness" is figuratively attributed [to him].

In other cases, such as "the lion is indeed like that," the primary sense (*mukhya*) applies; however, here in both instances, there is no status of being an object for a non-erroneous cognition, and therefore it is not a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
If it is argued that it is a metaphorical usage because the referent is non-existent:

If it were the case that [the universal] is the object of a cognition whose referent is non-existent, then it would be established that the universal is a non-entity precisely because of its nature as such;
furthermore,
there are cases where people apply a word by convention even though its referent is non-existent.
That [term] is primary there; elsewhere it is secondary, its application being faltering due to similarity to that.

For the word "non-existence" (abhāva) is primary when applied to non-existence because its application is unfaltering; whereas when applied elsewhere—such as to a son—it is secondary because existence itself lacks utility [as a mere absence]. This is a well-known worldly convention.

Therefore, because non-existence and existence are equal [in this regard], the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity (*vastu*) with respect to the unperceived and so forth; for it is grasped through a cognition that assumes a form common to things that are not real entities.

Now, if you argue that this very "metaphorical application" (*upacaritatva*) consists in its functioning toward what is not a real entity—that is, its functioning toward something despite the absence of a common form—how can this be so?
If it is argued that this is because cognition itself exists in such a manner, [we reply]:
surely even when a cognition has perished, there is no difference in the nature of the cognition;
for even that cognition which occurs in the form "this has perished" arises with respect to something that has not [actually] perished.
If it is argued that doubt will arise,
even doubt would not occur at all if the object were to manifest;
if it is further argued that doubt arises despite the manifestation because of similarity, [we reply:]...
Now, it cannot be said that there is no similarity between two things even when they are non-different, provided they are characterized [as distinct];
for if their difference is not characterized, then there is only their true identity, not similarity.
If, on the other hand, difference is due to a difference in time—
That is incorrect.

Since there is a distinction [between cognitions] due to a difference in time, how can there ultimately be a distinction between that which is real and that which is unreal? Even if time possesses real objects, why is there no distinction between the two cognitions? Just as for you there is a difference in time between the preceding and succeeding cognitions despite their having real objects, so too it is in the case of those with unreal objects; therefore, how can there be a division between what has a real object and its opposite based on a difference in time?

Now, if it is argued that [the object] exists because of inference— since there is indeed a means of valid cognition for the past and the future through specific inferential marks (liṅga), and thus the distinction between the past and so forth [is established]—
then it is as follows:
It is incorrect to say that there is no uniformity in cognition because, by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*), one [aspect] is past, another is present, and yet another is future. 1 T.
If it is argued that [the word] has a real referent, no;
because [it is] atomic.
Even if that [cognition] were to arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*) regarding a real entity, there would be no doubt about another aspect, because all aspects would be grasped.
Therefore, in that case as well, it is logical that the aspect is not a real entity, just like the aspect of the word, since it is an object of doubt;
for doubt does not exist with respect to that which is being directly perceived.
If it is argued that there is doubt regarding another aspect, it is said in reply:
whether that other aspect is perceived therein or otherwise—if it is perceived, there is no doubt; otherwise, that moment remains doubtful. (201)
2. How else could there be doubt?
For if there were cognition of that [object], there would be no doubt precisely because of that cognition.
If it is not being perceived, it is simply non-manifest; what doubt could there be in that?
For if non-perception itself were the doubt, then everything that is non-manifest would be subject to doubt.
If you argue that the doubt exists precisely because it is unperceived due to the presence of another, shifting conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [we reply:]...
If there is cognition, how can there be movement of conceptual construction?
And what is this movement— is it of the intrinsic nature, or of the conceptual construction, or of the object of knowledge?
If there were doubt regarding the object of cognition due to the movement of the conceptual construction's own nature, then there would be no such doubt here,
because that which is not appearing does not possess movement.
Thus, there is no doubt in this case.
If it is argued that there is doubt as to whether one will see this or not— that is, doubt regarding the state of being about to see—
then the same dilemma remains unexhausted, revolving around whether that [doubt] itself appears or not.
If the state of being about to be seen has been perceived, how can there be doubt?
If it has not been perceived, what is there to doubt?
Furthermore, doubt arises from the perception of a general property, the non-perception of specific particulars, and the recollection of those particulars.

That too is incorrect, because as for that particular [object] which is not perceived, its non-perception is itself what constitutes it; there is no negation other than through the two modes of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and simple negation (*prasajya*). (202)

If the distinction is a *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation), such that "perception" means "a cognition other than perception," then since other cognitions also possess an object (*sālambana*), how can there be any doubt?
Now, if it is not known whether [the cognition] has an object or otherwise, then doubt arises;
and even in that case, the question of whether it appears as having an object or not recurs.

Now, there arises a doubt: since that [object] can exist even without a basis, and conversely, it might not, then if it is merely an appearance, how can it be said that "the object does not appear"? Consequently, how could inference have a real entity as its object?
Furthermore, the qualification "due to the perception of the universal" (*sāmānyapratyakṣāt*) would be meaningless.
Since there is doubt even regarding that which is cognized through inference,
there arises the dilemma as to whether the imperceptibility pertains to that very particularity or to something else;
if it pertains to that very thing, how can its own nature be imperceptible?
If it belongs to someone else, how can there be doubt regarding it upon seeing that [object]?
If you say, "That too was seen there," [we reply: no.
Even if it was indeed seen, let there be a memory that "it was seen"; how can there be doubt?
If you argue that there might have been times when it was not seen, then let there likewise be a memory that "it was not seen at other times"—what is the cause for this doubt?
If it is argued that there is doubt because [the object] is appropriately [perceived] in both cases,
and if it is asked how it can be seen in both ways at different times,
then let memory also be exactly like that; why, then, should there be doubt?
If it is argued that "it is not seen here now," then there is indeed doubt; however, the claim that "doubt arises from non-perception" and so forth regarding universals (*sāmānya*) is incorrect.
Therefore, since a cognition without an objective basis (*anālambana*) is possible, the occurrence of doubt is established.
Now, doubt is indeed an object appearing as such,
because there is an absence of conviction regarding it as being an actual object.
The conviction in this regard is that "this is mere cognition," and it has been stated that there is no difference between the non-worldly and self-cognition;
therefore, doubt does not arise except through the appearance [of an object], and not otherwise.

Therefore, if there were no doubt regarding the reality of the object of inference, then it would not be a real entity; however, since there is such a doubt, there must be a real entity there, and that is what is determined by inference.
If that is so, how is it that inference does not have a real entity as its object?
To this it is replied:
If there were a contact with the real entity in that [inference], how could there be instability? That cognition is indeed unstable when one imagines the mark (liṅga) to be fallacious. (203)

If it is argued that even when there is the cognition of fire, if an error arises— such as [thinking] "this is a line of gnats" due to real smoke— then the cognition of fire wavers and another [cognition] arises;
yet such wavering does not occur in the case of perceptual cognition itself,
because in that case too, the possibility of an impairment by cataracts (*timiropaghāta*) is equal.
If it is argued that there is no appearance of its own form because of its absence [in the external object], as in the case of saying "it moves" when the eyes are closed;

If it is argued that there is simply no production [of knowledge] due to the absence of a cause, and likewise that there is simply no production of inference due to the absence of its cause, namely the logical mark (liṅga);
For it is observed that even when smoke is present, [the cognition] is seen to be wavering due to the possibility of it being otherwise; thus,
if the absence of the possibility of it being otherwise were itself the cause, how could there be the occurrence of that cause?
That is incorrect;
for if it were seen [as such], there could be no possibility of conceiving it otherwise.
Therefore:
When there is movement of inference, there is no grasping of the real object from it; to say that one moves by means of a designation while actually seeing [the object] is an extreme audacity.
(204) In perception there is no movement; if there were movement, there would be no seeing.
For that object which has been seen, there is no movement.
For a thing does not become otherwise simply by being conceptualized as otherwise;
yet, even when one thinks "this is not fire" while it is being seen, the fire certainly does not move away from its state.
Indeed, the object of direct perception is not something tangible, for the eye does not perceive what is to be touched. Nor is there ever, through a sense organ, the cognition of a future form.
Regarding the statement "fire does not become food," there are these alternatives: does it mean that fire does not possess this very form;
or that it does not possess a taste accompanied by a hot touch;
or that it is not an object of future desired experience?

If this very thing does not exist, then it would follow that everything—even what is being perceived—would not exist, because that which is being perceived would be impossible to perceive; for even though it is being perceived, it would not be so.
Alternatively, if it is conceptualized that fire is a collection of color and touch, and therefore this color does not coexist with touch.
In that case, it is not apprehended by the eye; therefore, it is indeed unseen.
Consequently, from its very invisibility, its movement is established.
By this, the movement of future form is explained.
1. This is not [the case].
2. T. [is not present].
Likewise, since it is incapable of that, the illustration of "contact with the real object" is not appropriate as a conceptual construction;
therefore, inferential cognition does not contact the real object.

If there is doubt regarding another aspect even when something has been perceived, that doubt pertains to the object of inference; for what is already perceived cannot be an object of inference. (206) Non-contradiction with the appearance is equal for both perception and its other [inference]; yet the distinction between them as "perception" and so forth depends upon external objects.

(207) Therefore, the status of being a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) belongs to certain things despite their appearing [as such], as does that of inference; this distinction [between the two] applies to external objects. (208)
Alternatively, even in the case of inference, if a future object does not appear [to the cognizer], how can it possess reality? It possesses reality because it is perceived by another person;
but if that other person also does not perceive it as having a future form, how could it have reality for him?
Like the appearance of one suffering from ophthalmia, it would be entirely unreal;
even when perceived by another person, it is merely an inference—
how then can its reality be understood through that very [inference]?
That which is unestablished cannot be proven by that which is unestablished;
and since there is the possibility of a future form, inference must be restricted to that as its object,
yet at that time [the future state] does not exist— how then can inference have a real entity as its object?
If it is argued that even perception possesses authority only with respect to that [present state],
because truth exists there only through the cognition of a future form— and otherwise there would be no truth—
this is indeed so, and this will be demonstrated accordingly.

Therefore, while inferential cognition is similar [to perception] even when its object is non-existent, perceptual cognition does not arise with respect to another entity that is non-existent; thus, inference does not have a real entity as its object,
and its lack of a real entity as its object is precisely what constitutes its secondary status.
That too is incorrect,
because it has been established that all inference indeed has a real entity as its object; nor is this a secondary definition, because the opposite is observed,
as follows:

Whether [the cause] exists or does not exist, people may apply the designation "Pradhāna" and so forth to it according to its actual state, or even according to their own conceptualization; whether [the cause] is incapable or capable,
the world employs the term "Pradhāna" and so forth based on either its unfitness or its fitness for that role.
According to your view, however, because [the term] has a real entity as its object, it would possess primacy;

yet, regarding the *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, and so forth, according to your view, those terms such as *sāṅkhya* and *puruṣa* lack primacy because those [entities] are not real things. This is not the case for designation (*vyapadeśa*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Now, if the terms "Pradhāna," "Puruṣa," and so forth are secondary due to being superimposed upon [entities such as] a son and the like, then the definition of the primary and the secondary is not "having as their objects an entity and its opposite.
For that which is superimposed elsewhere does not exist there at all in that form;
therefore, this alone is the definition.

Thus, it is established that even by means of inference, a form already perceived in the example is superimposed upon the object of proof; therefore, inference has as its object that which is not a real entity.
Consequently, the kind of cognition that arises from words is seen to be the same whether [the object] has perished or has not perished.
It is exactly like that; this [argument] does not apply to the cognitions of the ear and other senses regarding existing objects.
(39) Because both cognitions grasp only the universal (*sāmānya*), the prior apprehension of that universal in its isolated state has already been refuted. (40)
For if only the universal were apprehended, the distinction between past and so forth would not be established; moreover, it has been demonstrated that the particular alone is not apprehended.
Now, if those very particulars are apprehended without distinction, then the universal is [apprehended], and thus inference has a real entity as its object.
To this it is replied: if that apprehension of non-distinction belongs only to the form of cognition and not to the inference whose object is a real entity,
then [the entity] must indeed be existent by its very nature.
That too is incorrect; for how could there be a non-distinct [universal] among things that are mutually distinct?
Or, if there were both form and the absence of form, how could that entity be one?
For it is not possible for specific forms to have an undifferentiated nature, because identity is impossible between two mutually contradictory things.
If it is argued that "a cow" is perceived through direct perception as a single entity consisting of both the inclusive and the exclusive aspects,
then what indeed is this so-called "inclusion"?
That which is perceived as a cow through its conformity with the notion "cow, cow"—
is there such a conformity?
If so, there would be an infinite regress.
If it is argued that its very nature is that [cognition], then is this [nature] perceived by itself? If it is perceived, there would have to be a cognition with two forms.

If it is argued that its form is simply the form of the individual object (*padārtha*), then because the form would follow [all instances] and the form would be one, there would be no difference between individuals; and thus, there would be no universal (*sāmānya*).
Alternatively, if that form does not exist as one, even so, there is no universal.
Now, individuals are perceived, and there is a recurring cognition in the form "cow, cow"; otherwise, how could this be?
To this it is said:
let it be explained for what purpose there is a recurring cognition; if it is merely a cognition, no recurring object is observed by means of it. (209)
If the cognition [is that] of an object possessing a recurring form, what follows?
Or, if it is argued that its recurrence is due to the object's recurrence, then let that very object be designated as such; what is the use of designating something else?
It is not that blue and so forth are described as such merely by virtue of being designated as cognition;
for blue and so forth are indeed designated in that very way. To explain:
"Blue is [known] because of the cognition of the form of blue, and not otherwise"—
this too is not the case,
for it is not even the world that designates it thus.
Furthermore, when one thinks "I see blue," one perceives precisely the difference between blue and yellow, or between pleasure and pain;
even in this case of perceiving difference, one would designate it as "this is present here" and "this is otherwise.
If you argue that this [perception] is indeed indescribable (*avyapadeśya*), [we reply:]...
Now, why is this nature of the existent not specified?
It is because it is impossible to specify; for there is nothing that can be specified in its entirety. That which gives rise to this cognition is called the "universal" (sāmānya). (210)

If it is impossible to indicate [the nature of things], how can they be communicated to another? And if another has not been made to understand, how can he be led to accept [the truth]? Surely, how then could even pleasure and the like be indicated?

Even these [pleasures] are not worthy of being communicated in their own nature, because they are directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); thus, there is no fault even in not communicating them.
If it is argued: "What is the use of communicating to you that 'you have pleasure'? But for me, the communication that 'there is pleasure through my seeing' is useful."
This is not merely a matter of conventional usage, since such [feelings] are observed even in relation to courtesans and the like;
and if one understands it through the observation of physical signs such as horripilation, then what is the point of instructing another? This is trivial.
If it is argued that because this proliferation of horripilation and so forth culminates merely in the cognition "this is pleasure" and the like,
therefore that which is the basis for the mental presentation "cloth, cloth" is the universal (*sāmānya*), we reply: no,
for in this way neither a universal established as having a recurring form, nor one distinct [from individuals], nor any other kind, has been proven.

This conventional usage is merely beginningless; thus, having come down through a succession of conventions, it concerns an indeterminate reality, and the latent impression of convention itself is its cause, just as in the case of conventions such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*).
For indeed, nothing is experienced that is both distinct and non-distinct.

Even in the case of [the universal] being produced, it is not something else, because it is not perceived as being other than the particular; nor can the position that it is both other and non-other exist without a different form [of appearance]. (211)
For instance: by one [person] it is perceived as reality, by another as its opposite; that which is reality through its opposite is not known to be anything else.

(212) Even though there is a difference in the form of a bracelet, is the gold not the same as the earring? Since there is no gold other than the bracelet, from where could it be separate? (213) If you say that "gold" is the state of being pervasive (*anvitatva*), then from where would this pervasiveness itself be distinct?
This has already been established by means of the cognition of the concomitant;
let that matter rest for now.
Furthermore, even if the universal were distinct from the individual, it still could not possess a relationship [with it].
If that [universal] were something entirely different from those two, it would belong to both of them;
thus, there would be no relation. However, as for its exclusion [from others], that is not problematic.
(42) If it were unrelated to those two and entirely different from them, then it would not be a universal, because it would be a separate category of entity.
If it is argued that a jar is not the universal of a cloth because it lacks the nature of a universal and thus is not a universal, that is incorrect.
2. Something else entirely connected to those two would indeed be the universal in its nature as a universal. But how could there even be a relation expressed as "of that"? || 214 ||
If it is argued that [the impermanence of the word] is due to its having that [impermanence] as its relation, then this is a case of circular reasoning:
how can there be impermanence in the word? [For you would have to say: because of the impermanence [of the relation], there is impermanence [in the word].
And thus, there will be no establishment of any entity whatsoever.
[Objection: But since the state of being related is unestablished, how can that very thing be a logical reason? Otherwise, everything would be established for everyone.
Furthermore, even a universal nature is not established for that which is intended as a universal.
Now, if the relation were established in this way,
there would still be a grasping of all individual instances, because the universal consists of the nature of all its relata;
and there is no other universal apart from the nature of these relata.
If it is argued that [the universal] has an identical form,
then "having an identical form" is merely a designation for the relation itself; for this identity of form depends upon the individuals, not upon its own intrinsic nature.
Since the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is established everywhere within itself,
and since it is common [to all instances] only in relation to the individuals (*vyakti*), it cannot be apprehended without the apprehension of those individuals;
this same defect applies even to the universal (*sāmānya*) as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).
This is not so, because exclusion is not defective; for even among things that are mutually distinct, exclusion from what is intended by another [concept] is not contradictory.
Furthermore, a common conventional usage is likewise not contradictory, because it arises from the performance of a single causal function by those [individuals].
For how can the state of having a common form be denied to that which has unperceived diversity?
And how could there be a cognition of sameness regarding things that are not the same?
Not so.
Precisely because of that [commonality], for there is no such thing as "commonality" other than being made the object of a cognition with a common form;
thus, the meaning of the objection, "How can there be a cognition of a common form regarding things that are not common? is as follows:
How can there be a common cognition regarding objects that are not the domain of a common cognition?
Furthermore, it is established that they are not the domain of cognition;
for even for the proponent of universals, it is unproven that those [particulars] are made the objects of a cognition of a universal.
Therefore, in this case, it is precisely this commonality that constitutes the definition of a non-entity.
If it were an effect, it would be manifold and impermanent; such is the view. Since destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere existence of a thing, there can be no permanence.

Furthermore, universals have no connection [to reality] because they are not effects and lack form (arūpatā). Indeed, a commonality of form cannot be established in any other way than as the form of an erroneous cognition. If it is argued that the nature of being a universal exists wherever two things occur together, as the case may allow—then [we reply]: [The verse continues: Since there is no difference between the two, the universal would be nothing other than the particular. And since the universal is not perceived apart from its substratum, it follows that it does not exist. (45) For there is no distinction between the two; thus, the universal would be nothing but the particular. Furthermore, since the universal is never perceived independently of its locus, it must be concluded that it does not exist. If one were to say, "It is perceived through its own power," then [the response is: "If it were perceived by its own power, it would be perceived even when the particular is not perceived. (46) If it is claimed that the universal is perceived by its own power, then it should be perceived even when the particular is not perceived. If one were to say, "It is not perceived because it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition," then [the response is: "In that case, it would follow that the universal is non-existent, just like a sky-flower. (47) If it is said that the universal is not perceived because it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition, then it follows that the universal is non-existent, just like a sky-flower. If one were to say, "It is perceived through the power of the particular," then [the response is: "If it were perceived through the power of the particular, then it would be perceived only when the particular is perceived. If one were to say, "It is perceived because it is the object of that cognition," then [the response is: "If it were the object of that cognition, it would be perceived even when the particular is not perceived. If one were to say, "It is perceived because it is the cause of the cognition of the universal," then [the response is: "If it were the cause of the cognition of the universal, it would be perceived even when the universal is not perceived. (6

If it is argued that, in this way, since the universal increases its form upon the production of successive individuals, it is indeed an effect of the individuals because it follows their presence and absence;
and if it is further argued that while multiplicity follows as a consequence just as it does for the individuals themselves, unity is established because it is recognized as being the same.
If there is a commonality even in the universal, then there must be a common form [of that commonality] as well, leading to an infinite regress.
If it is argued that no universal is perceived within a universal, then the same objection applies to the individual (vyakti) as well.
Furthermore, in the case of recognition (pratyabhijñā), the reason is inconclusive because of the universal itself.
Since recognition is observed even in respect to universals (*sāmānya*),
it follows that the universal would be admitted to be perishable; for it perishes upon the destruction of the individual (*vyakti*),
and its perishability is further established by its being a real entity (*vastutva*).

For it will be proven that destruction is necessarily concomitant with being merely an entity; furthermore, if [destruction] were unproduced, the universal would be both disconnected and devoid of form.
For substantiality consists in the grasping of a specifically determined form, and that is not possible for a pervasive universal;

indeed, it is impossible to apprehend a universal as being permeated by the entire succession of all points of time. Furthermore, perception itself is existence; in its absence, how could there be existence?

If it is argued that existence [of a universal] is due to its connection with existence (*sattā*), then there would be an infinite regress because existence itself would require a connection with existence;
furthermore, a universal has no connection with a separate existence.
Since it exists only by virtue of its own essential nature,
and since it is not perceived apart from the perception [of the individual],
the universal is therefore non-existent.
If it is asked, "Why does the existence of its own nature not belong to the horn of a donkey, and why is it not so for you as well?
the answer is: because of the absence of a cause.
If that were so, then even a universal, being non-existent, would be perceived there due to the absence of a cause for its perception; to this it has been replied: [as stated above].
Even things such as the horns of a hare are indeed perceived by one's own cognition; if you argue that they would have to be real [if perceived],
yet are not so when examined, then this applies equally to all cases.
Furthermore,
this universal appears in verbal cognition by the power of convention;
likewise, in this case, there is no real entity.
For instance, that cognition which arises from the power of the thing itself depends upon that [thing], not upon convention; this is not perceived in conceptual cognitions of universals. (45)
For a convention, when being established, is not made by depending on whatever is merely present;
and the cognition that depends upon it is indeed superimposed.
For instance:
If there were no convention [established] through the superimposition of the prior upon the subsequent, then, due to lack of pervasion, there would be no such inferential nature of linguistic usage.
If it is argued that comprehension occurs at the time of usage solely through the power of the word itself, [we reply:
if there were no superimposition of the prior and the subsequent, such comprehension would not occur.

If it is argued that a cognition of a universal is not observed to arise from a word without a convention, yet it certainly does arise from the perception of another individual instance even without a word—[we reply:

in that case as well, the very same logical mark (liṅga) is involved; the grasping of a convention is merely an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the presence of its application, and the logical mark too produces only a prior superimposition (adhyāropa), nothing more.
Likewise, castes such as the Hūṇas and castes such as the twice-born depend solely on the force of convention and do not require an underlying reality;
for if perception accompanied by convention were the means of valid cognition regarding the twice-born and other castes, [then...]
That which arises through the power of the thing-in-itself (*vastubala*) does not depend upon convention; for if it depended merely upon convention, there would be nothing but a blind tradition.
If it is argued that perception also exists as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), it is said in response:
If [the object] such as sound were apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then instruction (*upadeśa*) would be purposeless.
If it is not apprehended by direct perception, then instruction is useless.

(217) If it is already apprehended by direct perception, what is the point of instruction, since it has been grasped by that very means? On the other hand, if it is impossible to realize through direct perception, how could it be made known even by a thousand instructions?
For when something is perceived by the senses, there can be an instruction from another person such as "I have seen this";
however, regarding the status of being twice-born (*dvijātitva*), which transcends the senses, the authority of instruction is not possible—
this is precisely what he says.
Furthermore, when two things are perceived, there may be some cognition that follows their difference;
even without a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), it is based on the proximity of the objects.
(46) [This verse is missing from the manuscript of Dānaśīla.]
That which originates from the cognition of a person is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
However, it might be argued that a cognition with a recurring form (*anugatākārā buddhiḥ*) certainly arises upon seeing two objects even without a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).

Just as the cognition of a cow and so forth arises from the sight of a brindled cow (śābaleya) and the like without depending on convention regarding it, so too, Brahminhood would not be a genus (jāti), because it is not perceived in that manner.

The individual manifestation of a class such as "twice-born" is not perceived as being manifested [by a single word], just as the universal "cowness" (gotva) is; for if the external object were otherwise [i.e., if it were manifested by a single word] in the case of cowness, who would have any doubt about this? 218–219ab.
There is no doubt regarding his being a Brahmin; however, one might doubt whether he is a twice-born [Brahmin] because of his speech. (219) 4 T.
But there is doubt;

certainty regarding that [universal] does not arise from the action [of seeing], because it is produced by something else through the hearing [of the word]. The manifestation of the birth of Hūṇas and others is not established without instruction.

(220) If it is argued that the reality [of the universal] does not exist there at all, then what is your view regarding "cowness" and so forth? Just as the state of being denotable by a single word is accepted as the universal in the case of goats and the like. (221)

Is it not undesirable that even a white horse (*karka*) and the like should be denotable by the word "cow"? Furthermore, how could the state of being denotable by the word "cowness" apply there, given that there are infinite individual instances?

For even in that case [of the white horse], is there not an infinity due to the difference between individuals? Indeed, an infinity [of distinctions] based on variations such as high-pitched accents and so forth would not establish [the unity of the referent].
Is it not the case that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) establishes unity wherever it is possible?

For indeed, the distinction between [sounds] such as the high-pitched (*udātta*) and the gurgling (*gharghara*), which serves as the basis for their infinite variety even among vowels like *i*, exists in the same way for the *karka* and other [varieties of horses]; since identity is established through recognition even when distinctions such as gurglingness exist, it is the same in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. Therefore, in the word "cow" (*gośabda*), there is no "cowness" other than that which is denoted by the word itself.
Proximity of meaning, being denotable by a single word, and the production of a single synthetic cognition— these do not exist anywhere as something called a "universal" (*jāti*).
Nevertheless, it might be argued that this very denotability by a word and the production of a single synthetic cognition cannot occur without a universal.
That too is incorrect;

for proximity among the eyes and other [senses] in their respective cognitive effects is desired even without a universal (jāti), or else it is by means of a universal that [the cause] follows through its various divisions. (47)

If it is argued that proximity— characterized by the production of a single effect— is not impossible for the eye, light, and mental attention even without a [single] universal, since such cooperation among auxiliary factors is indeed possible;
and if it is further argued that even when two things are perceived, there is only their state of being auxiliaries, and thus there is no single cognition possessing a uniform form.
Since it has been demonstrated that the similarity of form in the object of cognition is not observed apart from two distinct entities,
only the production of a cognition remains as a possibility.
If it is argued that this [property] is common even to the eye and other [senses], since they too possess the capacity to produce a single cognition, then the same consequence applies:
because the brindled cow and others also produce a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*), there would be no "other" [distinct entity]. Thus, the logical difficulty is equal.
If it is argued that "only that [universal] is the real entity," then how is this distinction established— that those very [individuals] produce that cognition and no others?
In that case, why is there this same distinction regarding the universal— that it resides in the *śābaleya* cow and so forth, but not elsewhere?

In that case, there must be another commonality (*sāmānya*) that effects the differentiation; for that too, there would have to be yet another as the basis for its occurrence as a differentiator, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if you say that such a cause exists for them—by which those very individuals like the *śābaleya* cow and others are both the manifesters (*vyañjaka*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the substrata (*ādheya*) of it—then, in that case, since the production of that conceptual recognition occurs through the power of their own causes even without a universal (*jāti*), what is lost by rejecting the universal? Let this stubborn insistence on the universal be abandoned.
Furthermore, no commonality [of the sense organs] exists within the visual consciousness or others in any way whatsoever, because their form does not appear therein;
even if such a thing existed in the sense organs, the seer would appear with that very body. (48)
Because it possesses form; for universals are not perceived in isolation, and when an individual is perceived, nothing other than the form of that word is seen.
Indeed, a universal does not manifest in any way whatsoever within the eyes or other sense organs.
It is also cognized by way of its effect;
being cognized by way of its effect, it is cognized as having that single effect.
And thus, there would be a connection of those [particulars] with a single effect, but not a universal.
If it is argued that the relation (*sambandha*) is also one and the same everywhere because it is a universal (*sāmānya*), we say no; for the relation, too, does not manifest in any way whatsoever.

Immediately thereafter, there is only the perception of the effect; no other relation is perceived by him. And it has been said: "Even the effect is related [to its cause] only through conceptual construction.
Now, if it is argued that a single power belongs to all [the causes], then—
It has been established that this is not so because power is not distinct from the possessor of power;
nor does power itself appear [as a separate entity].
If it is argued: "Why is power not postulated even if unperceived, just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth?"
That is incorrect, because we admit that [the object] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), as stated in such passages as: "there is no perception [of it],
like the flower of the *ajājī* plant," and so forth.
Furthermore, a universal (*sāmānya*) is not cognizable solely through scripture or meditative concentration;
nor is there any cause for the appearance of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth other than the effect itself.
Therefore, there is no discernment here as to whether that [cause] is distinct from the state of the eyeball (*golaka*) or otherwise.
For instance:
Like the *sīra* flower (*aṃjīrapuṣpavat*).
2. Apart from the eyeball itself, there exists no other distinct sphere.
Or there are various distinctions of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and diverse differences of opinion.

For one who does not establish that external objects exist because they are non-different from their effects—how can such a person tolerate the inference of eyes and other organs as being distinct from their effects? Therefore, since this inference is in every way unstable regarding its object of knowledge (*prameya*), there is no apprehension by means of it.
If that were the case, there would be no scriptural authority for their possessing form;
for if they were to have a seer, the eyes and other [faculties] would be visible. Since it is accepted that they are beyond the reach of the senses, no other explanation exists. (225)
This very [method] applies to that which is beyond the senses, because it is accepted as having a form;
however, a universal (*sāmānya*) alone is not so, because the perception of a solitary universal is not admitted.
For if a yogi were to perceive a universal in isolation, [it would follow that it has a form].
Nor would there be a universal; rather, when a cognition of a similar form arises,
yogins perceive that "this is its cause."
The universal is not established by such means of valid cognition;

for we do not perceive the universal at all as something separate [from the individual], since the universal is manifested by the individual. There is no apprehension of it in isolation, just as there is no apprehension of color without the apprehension of light.
That too is incorrect;
for in inference, form is apprehended as being invariably concomitant with touch and so forth, even without light.
If it were not so apprehended, there would be no distinction [of form] from light at all.
It is not tenable to accept that a negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) is one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished;
for a universal (*sāmānya*), however, is never an object of perception in its own right,
and when it enters into the form of a particular (*vyakti*), it does not exist at all [as a separate entity].

If it is argued that "cow" is merely a name for something else, and because they occupy the same location there is no perception of their distinction—how then is there a distinction between color, taste, and so forth, given that they are apprehended by different sense organs?
To this we reply: in this case, however, the lack of perceived distinction arises from extreme conjunction (*atyantasamsarga*).

What is this absolute conjunction? Is it a merging of essential natures, or is it simply non-difference, since its nature is precisely that? (226) Even when there is no difference in location, why is there not a perception of difference due to the difference in form? For a so-called "location" is not perceived apart from the form itself. (227) Apart from the entity, what else could location be? If the entity is different, then the location is also certainly different; how then can there be non-difference of location?

If its difference [from another] is due to a difference in location, from what would that [location] itself have its difference? It would likewise depend on yet another location, resulting in an infinite regress. Furthermore, since it does not manifest by way of its own nature—like the horn of a donkey—it is therefore incapable of performing even the function of mere cognition.
Because of that unsuitability, it is formless; for that is the characteristic of non-entities.

Whatever intended object of apprehension does not manifest by way of its own nature, that cannot be the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because it does not provide its own form [to consciousness], unlike the eye and other [faculties]. If it is argued that it will therefore be the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):
Not even there, because of the absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Because it is capable of imparting its own form,
that which is the opposite of what was previously described is accepted as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, that which appears with its own form, whose capacity is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is the ultimately real particular characteristic, because it is characterized by its own nature.
Its own nature is its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa),
because it is that which is being characterized (lakṣyamāṇatvāt).

But how can there be the relationship of the characterized and the characteristic in terms of their own intrinsic nature? [It is not so] because the relationship of the characterized and the characteristic is conceptual.

And it will be stated [in the *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.219]: "The entire establishment of action and its factors is of this very nature"; thus, it is logical that the essential nature itself is the defining characteristic, and nothing else.
Because it is impossible, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), for one thing to be characterized by another,
a definition by means of another form is merely a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of that other form and is not a definition of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
How then can there be a "general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
This is true because it pervades the unmanifest; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that which is called "universal" (sāmānya) is merely the very nature of cognition itself.
It is spoken of in this way from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
because it functions through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the forms of multiple individuals (*vyakti*) and because it arises from them.
How, then, while being a non-entity (*avastu*), can there be a distinction between the reasons (*hetu*) based on non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), effect (*kārya*), and essential nature (*svabhāva*)?
If it is argued that perception and inference are distinct because their objects are distinct,
whereas non-perception and the others are not distinct because they lack a distinction of objects, but rather a distinction based on the logical mark (*liṅga*), [we reply as follows].
Is it not the case that the very same thing which was raised as an objection is now the very same thing offered as a solution? How can this be?
For instance, a mere difference in gender is not even logical;
yet if it were observed, it would result in a sixfold distinction.
Alternatively, it will be stated that two [types of reasons] establish a positive entity while one is a reason for negation;
how then, when the lack of being a real entity is equal, can there be a distinction between a real entity and a non-entity? To this, he provides the following resolution:
That universal is threefold, based on existence, non-existence, and both.
There is no ultimate difference [between them], because everything is a non-entity (*avastu*).

However, due to the difference in the cognition of the effect—based on existence, non-existence, and both—there is a distinction between the *svabhāvānupalabdhi* (non-perception of the essential nature) and the *kāryahetu* (effect-reason), by virtue of their producing those respective cognitions.
For instance,
conceptual construction that takes existence as its material cause arises from the reason of essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*),
whereas that which takes non-existence as its material cause arises from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) involves the apprehension of both [existence and non-existence]; thus, the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is a proof of what is distinct.
For distinction arises from existence and non-existence, and it is a distinct cause that is to be proven.

Alternatively, even though [the object] is not a real entity (*avastu*), a distinction of objects (*viṣayabheda*) is established by relying on the distinction of their material causes (*upādānabheda*), since they have existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) as their respective material causes.
Existence itself is twofold: distinct (*vyatirikta*) and non-distinct (*avyatirikta*). Thus, due to the distinction of objects, there are three types of differentiation;
therein, [there is] the non-perception of the unobservable regarding the two objects, existent and non-existent.
The distinction between the two types of apprehension has as its object the non-perception of the unobservable;
[this is] by means of the distinction of the basis of apprehension, relying upon the distinction of the basis of apprehension.
Then 3 T.
[Not in the Tibetan translation]—

If cognition were dependent upon an entity because it follows after the existence of that entity, [that is not so], because the answer has already been stated and because it is observed otherwise in the case of the past and so forth. (52)
It is not the case that cognition which has an entity as its basis arises [only] with respect to an entity;
for the state of having an entity as its object results from the grasping of the entity's own nature (*svarūpa*).

And conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, does not grasp the own nature [of the entity], because it would be fruitless for the collection of sense faculties (*akṣasaṃhati*). (2)

110) Thus it has been said; now, if it is argued that [the designation] exists only when there is an entity (*bhāva*), that is unproven, because [the designation] is observed even in the absence of an entity, as in the case of the past and so forth.

If that cognition [occurs] with respect to the universal or the particular, there is no status as an object belonging to the past and so forth; for an entity being grasped in its own nature does not relinquish its pastness, and in this regard, the world does not understand it to have the past entity as its object.

An entity does not exist as a condition that adheres to its own intrinsic nature; rather, it is merely an illusion, because [this] has already been answered previously. Furthermore, by stating "because it is observed," the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case is demonstrated; this constitutes the pointing out of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the reason (*hetu*) favored by the opponent.
If, then, there is a perception of conceptual construction even in the case of non-existence, and likewise in the case of existence, then the nature of existence would indeed be lost;
thus, it would possess the nature of both. To this he says:
"If there were a loss of the nature of existence, [it would have to be] preceded by the apprehension of existence."
This objection— that it would follow that [the object] is simply the cognition of that— is not a fault; for there is no objective support (ālambana) whatsoever therein,
because a universal (sāmānya), being imperceptible, is not an object of cognition.
For the universal is indeed imperceptible; and since it is not cognized in its own form, how could it be an object of knowledge? This is its state of being unmeasurable.
"The object of cognition is the single particular (svalakṣaṇa). For there is no such thing as a universal that is an object of cognition."
Because conceptual construction is not a means of valid cognition (*yoga*),

only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*); for the purpose of its comprehension is precisely the determination of its existence or non-existence.
Why is this so?

Because existence and non-existence are investigated based on the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, [it is established]. Regarding PV 3.54: "Because of the investigation into existence and non-existence through the accomplishment of causal efficiency."
For wise people seek existence or non-existence based on whether a thing performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*);
and it is for the sake of understanding that [function] that they search for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, the investigation of the means of valid cognition would be nothing but an act lacking foresight.
Therefore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is purposeful insofar as it is capable of apprehending the existence or non-existence of an entity that performs a causal function;
consequently, both perception and inference must have only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object,
for otherwise, they would lack the status of being valid cognitions.

If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone is made the object by both [means of knowledge], then because they share a single object, it follows that there is only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, on the other hand, even though the object is one, there is a distinction between the means of valid cognition due to a difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), then this contradicts the statement "because the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are of two kinds," which was stated by the Teacher (Dignāga), namely: "The objects of cognition are of two kinds [the particular and the universal]."

And if there were a distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on a distinction in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), then even the cognitions of the eye and so forth would be distinct by virtue of their respective complexes; thus, there would be as many means of valid cognition as there are such complexes. Or, [if you argue that] even when they have the same object...

But surely, if there were a distinction [of means of knowledge] even due to a distinction among the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then because there are infinite objects of cognition such as various blues and so forth, it would follow that there are infinite means of knowledge;
this is not so, because all [such objects] possess the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it is asked: "Why is there not a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that object alone, since there is only one object, even though the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) differ, because the state of being a cognition (*jñatva*) exists [in all of them]?"—[the answer is: because being a cognition is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*);
and this will be demonstrated later.

Therefore, it is precisely because the objects of knowledge (prameya) are of two kinds that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) are likewise twofold; otherwise, there would be an infinite number of means of knowledge.
If it is asked: "Why is it not the case that the objects of knowledge are infinite? [the answer follows].
Even though it is of that nature, it is precisely the duality of blue and so forth, because of this.

Because it is cognized through its own form and the form of another, that [cognition] has two objects of knowledge (prameya) by virtue of being blue and so forth; thus, the duality of the object of knowledge is maintained.
Although blue and other [objects] have infinite divisions due to the manifestation of their own forms, they are indeed *svalakṣaṇas* (particulars), because they are characterized by their own nature.

Is it not the case that ultimate particularity (*svalakṣaṇatva*) would cease to be such, because when that [particular] is not being cognized and another is being manifested, it is no longer a particular;
likewise, at that very same time, what is a particular for one person is otherwise for another?
Nor is there a distinction in the object of cognition (*prameya*),
because a distinction created by dependence is conceptual and thus not ultimately real;

and since a single thing possesses both forms— being its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and being other than that— there is no further distinct object of cognition (*prameyāntara*) therein from which another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) might arise.
This is incorrect,
because there is a distinction between the stages of practice.

The full sentence in Tibetan reads: "If the divisions of realization were distinct, would their own-characteristics not fail to be ultimate? ... If they were objects of cognition in the ultimate sense, there would be an infinity of objects of cognition; if the distinctions were made through dependence, the ultimate would not be a defining characteristic. (229) In Sanskrit: *yadi pratyayabhedena bhedaḥ syāt, svalakṣaṇaṃ paramārthato na syāt | paramārthaprameyatve syādanantaprameyatā | apekṣākṛtabhedatve paramārtho na lakṣaṇam || 229*
To this it is replied:
that which is the object of apprehension is indeed ultimate; since existence consists in nothing other than apprehension, the ultimate reality of entities [is established]. (230)
For entities do not appropriate existence for themselves without first attaining the state of being perceived in their own nature. [Objection:

But is it not the case that existence is made known by perception, rather than existence itself being the perception? [Response: No, because a rabbit's horn and the like, though perceived [in thought], lack existence;
whereas the opposite is true: perception is existence.
If it is argued that "that which is apprehended through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is non-existence," then what is this non-apprehension?
Is it the absence of apprehension, or the apprehension of something else, or [is it]... [such is the dilemma].
How is there cognition from this?
Cognition is not non-existence;
if existence were to be cognized by something else, there would be an infinite regress.
4. Regarding the proof:

[Objection] Surely there is no further apprehension of an apprehension external [to the object], by which an infinite regress would occur. [Response] Since cognition is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), its existence is cognized as being imperceptible.
And just as there would be non-existence [of an object] due to the non-perception of its referent, so too it would follow for cognition; this would be a most grievous error.

Now, if you argue that there is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in that case because the mirror is directly perceived, and therefore there is no absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:]...
[Objection: But surely, even presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) is nothing but cognition; therefore, one cognition is apprehended by means of another cognition.

Consequently, since there is no presumption based on another fact (*arthāpatti*) there, it follows that because of the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no cognition of presumption.

Now, if one argues that there is indeed a comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) there, then presumption would recur; but because of this infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), there is no comprehension.
[Objection: But surely comprehension is observed!
If mere perception is relied upon, what is the use of presumptive testimony?
Let it be exactly as it is perceived;
since it is perceived directly, let it remain so—what is the use of presumptive testimony or the conceptual construction of a cognition?
But surely, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arises [in this case].

If that is so, then because of the resulting infinite regress (*anavasthā*), there would indeed be no determination through cognition; how then can that be undesirable? Furthermore, whether it be "perceptibility" (*upalabhyamānatā*) or "immediacy" (*aparokṣatā*), if one were to cognize their absence, there would be an infinite regress.
Or, is the non-apprehension of the object itself the non-apprehension of apprehension?
If it is argued that, such being the case, even though non-perception is not perceived, perception nonetheless exists, and therefore that [non-perception] is itself non-existence;
then it follows that if non-perception is non-existence, perception must likewise be existence.
Now, if it is argued that the non-perception is simply the perception of something else,
that too is incorrect;
for even if one gives the name "perception of another" to it, how does that establish that the other does not exist?
If it is argued that this is because there is no perception of that [other], the answer has already been given:
that very perception of one thing is simply not directed toward another; therefore, there is no perception of that other.
Even if it has not occurred elsewhere, how can its non-existence [there] be established?
Furthermore, it is precisely the non-existence of that which meets the conditions for perception;
otherwise, it would have occurred there as well, since it too would be perceived in exactly the same way.
