Nor is its non-apprehension itself apprehended; by what means is that which has the characteristic of non-existence realized? If it is argued that this is not an infinite regress because there is the apprehension of a specifically determined form, [we reply: no.
Now, is this [inference] a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? If you say it is, then the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has already been stated.

If it is argued that the very perception of a determinate form is itself the non-perception of another, then in that case there is no such thing as "non-existence" (abhāva) other than the existence of something else; for there is no non-existence distinct from the existence of another which could be called "non-existence relative to itself" in dependence upon another.
And that [existence] is a determinate form, existing only insofar as it is being perceived.
Therefore, the apprehension of that which has not attained its defining characteristic is called "existence."
Now, if there is a specific restriction [of existence], it is the restriction of being perceived, but that itself is not the restriction.
[Objection: But how can there be a restriction regarding non-perception? [Reply: The cognition [of such a restriction] arises precisely through the grace of being perceived;
therefore, being perceived is itself existence.
Now, if "I do not perceive" is itself a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
then that non-perception follows after the very conceptual construction "I do not perceive";
and that non-perception has already been examined.
Therefore, existence is apprehension;
if the very fact of being apprehended is the true nature of an object of cognition, then that alone must be ultimate existence, and nothing else could be otherwise.

This does not become otherwise even in relation to another person; it remains exactly as it is. If it is asked: "Since it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), how can that very thing be cognized? just like blue and so forth?
If that [object] is indeed perceived in that very form even though it is beyond the senses,
yet if it is not so perceived by anyone, nor will it ever be so perceived, then that inference is useless;
for if it is not being perceived, how can it be said to exist in that way?
How can it be that even otherwise it is that very same thing?
If you say "otherwise" because of the absence of perception,
then surely its non-existence follows from the absence of perception.

But surely, non-apprehension would occur even in the case of existence; how then could there be non-existence? Surely, this should be said only when there is an absence of a means of valid cognition regarding existence.
If it is argued that inference is the means of valid cognition [for establishing non-existence], then:
Even that [consciousness] follows only the form already seen; since it occurs after the seeing, how can there be "being currently seen" prior to it?
If there is no state of being currently seen, how can there be existence?
If it is argued that [the thing exists] because it is perceived later, let its existence be only at a later time; how could it have existed previously?
Indeed, if it was non-existent previously, how is it perceived later?
If it is argued that because it is perceived as being perceived, it is perceived as one thing at one time and otherwise at another, [we reply:
even at other times it is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) in that very same form; thus, there is no existence in another way, because it is impossible to apprehend it otherwise.
And it will be demonstrated that inference is a means of valid cognition regarding future existence;
how then can there be a different object of cognition for it, since it is the very same thing that is cognized under another form?
Likewise, when another object of cognition is perceived through a form common to the example,
it is not so in the ultimate sense because that form is superimposed upon it due to a difference in cognition;
for in this way, being produced by dependence, it lacks ultimate reality.
It has already been established that truth is the commonality of non-entities; this is not being stated as something new.
Through the medium of correspondence with reality, those engaged in worldly practice—who do not perceive diversity—conventionally designate it as "the real" (*vastu*).
Therefore, with reference to that, this twofold nature of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is asserted.
Ordinary people, who do not perceive its various distinct aspects, employ the conventional expression "an object" (*vastu*);
therefore, with reference to that [conventional usage], this twofold nature of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is stated.
Alternatively, one might think that because it possesses both forms, there must exist a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of apprehending both.
That is incorrect,
because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to apprehend both forms; or, if it does so apprehend them, then these are simply two distinct means of valid cognition.
Because there is a distinction [in the object] precisely due to the difference in cognition,
or else because the characteristic is merely non-ultimate due to the difference in cognition, there is no consequence of it having both forms;
for the very nature of the entity is simply its being blue and so forth.

And that [cognition] does not possess diversity due to a difference in its objects of dependence; how then is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this it is replied: because of the absence of any ultimately real object of cognition (*prameya*).
Because difference has a conceptualized nature, it is precisely that which is non-ultimate; however, that which is to be attained as the actual nature of things is the ultimate reality.
3. Examination of Inference.
(1) If [you argue that] inference is established,
how then is there a distinction [from perception], given that it takes the ultimate reality as its object?
For if it were the direct realization of the intrinsic nature, it would simply be perception itself.
If there is no contact with that [object], how can it have that as its object?
To this it is replied: the second [type of] error is held to exist through an incorrect mental adherence (*abhiniveśa*).

Just as that object is now differentiated here due to a difference in its causes, so too this cognitive adherence does not occur; thus, it is indeed an error characterized by non-adherence to reality, because it is produced by the power of the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) generated by previously perceived objects, and because its determination lacks contact with the actual thing.
If, then, there is no contact with the real thing, how can it be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

If it is argued that [the cognition] is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*), then that very non-contradiction would not exist when there is the attainment of one thing while another has been reached; thus he says:

If there is comprehension by means of another form, it is not a valid cognition because of its erroneous nature. (55) If there is comprehension by means of another form, how can that be its [own] comprehension? That comprehension belongs only to the other form;
in that case, regarding the other, it is merely an error, and what is erroneous cannot be a valid cognition.
Response 1:
In that case, there is an error regarding the attainment of something else.

Even due to the non-contradiction of intention, the validity of an erroneous cognition is established, for a [cognitive] apprehension is seen to be otherwise; and this position has already been answered. How, moreover, is it to be understood that there is no such adherence elsewhere?
Precisely because there is no contradiction with one's intention, that [intention] exists here; thus, there is no adherence to what is not in accordance with reality.

However, ordinary people do not understand that this cognition arises from the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and that its differentiation occurs through the differentiation of appearances.
If it is asked, "Is this not merely the understanding of the commentator? How can that very intention [be established] from the observation of something else?"—
the answer is no, because conceptual constructions lack a fixed correspondence with actual entities.
This is simply the power of beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*);
therefore, one should not raise the objection, "How can one whose reality is undiscerned engage therein? For when something is actually perceived, no logical inconsistency can arise.
How can there be activity even with respect to perception?
For even there, there is no discernment of a form to be attained,
since there is only the discernment of that which is present.
On the contrary, it is perception alone that is the motivator, since one attains what is merely present;
even there, activity occurs only through the determination of identity with that [present object].
Therefore, activity in the case of a future entity is likewise [based on perception]; how then can it be viewed as not being the same?
Now, perception does not have the nature of determining unity; it is merely the means of discerning what is present.
However, the determination of unity at a subsequent time cannot occur without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
therefore, that [determination] is non-existent [as a function of perception].
Adherence to things as they truly are [is not possible], because by means of inference one grasps the essential nature [of the object] even more [firmly].
Because another conceptual construction (vikalpāntara) superimposes [identity] upon that which is present at the time of apprehension:

for just as perception— which grasps only the form and other qualities present before it— becomes an instigator of action when there is the superimposition of identity by another conceptual construction, so too inference, which grasps its own object even more closely than what is merely present,
becomes an instigator of action through the very same subsequent conceptual determination (adhyavasāya).

Now, if it is argued that inference, by its very nature, prompts action because it consists of a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), yet is not in contact with a real entity (*avastu-saṃsparśin*),
whereas perception is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it is in contact with a real entity (*vastu-saṃsparśitā*),
that too is incorrect.
Perception does not function as an instigator by the mere contact with an object;
rather, the subsequent conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of what is to be attained does not exist within perception itself.
That form in which there is contact with the object is not the form in which it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because it lacks the quality of being an instigator;
for that very form which is an instigator is what generates conceptual construction.

Regarding the production of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): now, does conceptual construction possess the quality of being an initiator (*pravarttaka*), by means of which perception (*pratyakṣa*) could be an initiator?
For that [conceptual construction] is itself not an initiator.
What kind of verbal logic is this—that [perception] is "inciting" by generating a non-inciting conceptual construction?
If the inciting conceptual construction does not grasp a real entity, how can it nevertheless cause one to act? What is your view regarding this inference? (234)

For if perception is established as the instigator [of action] by way of generating conceptual construction, then since conceptual construction is the instigator, it would follow that it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and if that were the case,
the validity of inference (*anumāna*) would remain entirely unimpeded.
If it is argued that inference lacks validity because it does not grasp a real entity and because it does not prompt action,
then how is it that conceptual construction, which arises subsequent to perception, [is valid], given that perception grasps the real entity therein?
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not arise with respect to a conceptual construction because it does not function toward it,
but rather functions within its continuum, then how can the first moment possess the nature of a continuum?
Furthermore, what occurs in one thing cannot occur in another;

if that were so, then inference, which occurs in its own nature, would also have to occur in the object. This is merely a figurative expression and does not provide an answer even from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Even perception, though occurring in one instance, is said to occur elsewhere as well; this is not distinct from metaphorical usage.

Furthermore, it is contradictory to claim that there is another perception occurring in that which belongs to that same class, for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which arises subsequent to perception, does not occur in that which belongs to that class.

In that regard, just as this [objection] applies to the operation of perception, it applies equally to inference; for perception has indeed already operated upon the object of inference— that is, on a member of that same class—
such as the fire in a kitchen hearth.
If it is argued that [the object] exists there within the domain of inference,
then everything is the same; for it is thus:
Just as perception does not operate upon the object of inference, so too why should conceptual construction—which arises subsequent to perception—not do so?
If it is argued that perception, having operated upon one individual, produces the inference [of universals], [we reply: 235. [This is not the case.]
If it does not occur with respect to another form, how can that [cognition] be a perception which produces conceptual construction? (236) However, the determination of oneness is the same for both;
in both cases, a universal is apprehended by reaching the real object. (237)
In that case, the first moment of the fire would be an object of the senses for conceptual construction;
however, it has already been explained that the apprehension of one thing does not constitute the apprehension of another.
If you maintain that there is an apprehension of the [fire] when there is an apprehension of something related to it, [then...]
In inference as well, the apprehension of a relation is everywhere the same. Even when the cause is not perceived, there is the perception of the effect in inference;

just as the perception of the object—which occurs prior to the conceptual construction—is the cause of the conceptual construction that arises subsequent to perception, and although that [prior] perception does not itself operate [at the time of the construction], its operation upon its own cause establishes the validity of the conceptual construction’s own activity.
Likewise, even though it has not operated upon the object of inference, that effect— having operated [upon its own cause]— may also establish the validity of the inference,
because the relationship between cause and effect is the same in both cases due to a specific connection.
Because the occurrence of an effect from its cause is not certain due to the possibility of counter-examples, direct perception alone would become invalid as a means of knowledge, and not inference.
2. From the [viewpoint of the] cause.
Now, if it is argued that the pointing out of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) is improper because [the object] is perceptible—
surely inconclusiveness is not pointed out in a case where perceptibility pertains only to what is present;
however, this [object] is not perceptible when it is yet to come.
It is not to be questioned that perception [is operative] even with respect to that which belongs to that same class;
for while belonging to that same class is an object of inference, it is also an object of perception.
The distinction is simply this: perception has already occurred there [in the past], whereas here it is currently operating.
In that regard, because it occurs in one individual and not in another, perception does not have a universal as its object,
since there is no identity between what is past and what is yet to come.
Furthermore, since it is not perceived directly, how is its status as having a universal as its object the same [as that of perception]?
Or else, how can the fact of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatā*) be understood with respect to a future object when it has not been seen?
If it is argued that this is because it is grasped as such elsewhere;
In that case, it would follow that in all instances, only the commonality shared with other individuals is apprehended by perception and inference, and not the particularity.
Furthermore, since the future [effect] necessarily follows from [the cause], there is no inconclusiveness;
for where there is a cause, there is necessity, and where there is an effect, there is even greater necessity.
And since it has been established that in the case of what is necessarily to be, there is only the relation of cause and effect,
therefore there is no distinction between perception and inference regarding a future object that is to be acted upon or attained.
If it is argued that perception, at least, is in contact with the real entity (*vastu*), and therefore it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while inference is not—
That too is incorrect;
for if there is no objective referent to be reached, there is no distinction between an erroneous cognition and a non-erroneous one.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in the existence or non-existence [of the object], then...
For it is impossible to ascertain whether that [cognition] has an object or not without corroboration;
yet, even in the case of perception, there is objective reality because of corroboration by another person, even in the absence of [external] corroboration.
That too is indeed accessible only through inference; thus there is no distinction.

Therefore, since it does not deviate from the intended object, it is not the case that the apprehension of the actual thing (*vastu*) is useful for [establishing] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, even perception would be non-authoritative.
3. That which is useful for grasping is explained right there.
Otherwise, movement is observed;

even an illusory movement is observed. Alternatively, "movement" (gati) means the placing of the feet; that is observed even in another way, namely, when there is a cognition [of an object] through its other form.
How, then, is there attainment?
Because an object exists, that which exists is attained;
for instance:
If it is asked how the attainment [of the object] is observed even through a tactile exploration of the capable agent, the answer is:
it is due to the power of the relationship itself.
Even if existence [of a relation] occurs only because of the presence of related entities, how can there be a cognition of the state of being related?
Furthermore, even in the case of perception, how can there be a cognition of a future state of being related?
If it is argued that "it is exactly so because it has been seen," then the same applies to both cases, and thus there is no dispute.
If it is further argued that "therefore, perception itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that case, because it generates its conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," [we reply:]...
If it is argued that for the same reason of producing an inference, why is that very preceding perception not accepted [as the cause],
[we reply] that because it has passed away;
[we answer] that even at the time of the arising of the conceptual construction, the perception is indeed already past.
For it will be demonstrated that cause and effect do not exist simultaneously;
furthermore, there is a distinction in that perception continues as a stream even at the same time as the conceptual construction,
because the subsequent moments of perception are not invalid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, if the validity of subsequent [cognitions] were otherwise, then because the future continuum would remain undetermined, the preceding ones would consequently lack validity;
for, since there would be no object to be reached,
the preceding ones alone would produce certainty, and thus the subsequent ones would become invalid.
For where there is doubt, there is no certainty; nor is there doubt where there is certainty, because it is impossible for certainty and its opposite to have the same object.

Now, if the preceding [cognitions] were indeed invalid, then one would not act at all. Therefore, one observes the validity of some [cognition], thinking, "What is gained here by acting, or what is lost? This is the same even in the case of inference regarding action.

Therefore, even that which is considered "perception" (*pratyakṣa*)—namely, cognition—is seen otherwise; it occurs entirely through the form of another object, for there is no cognition whatsoever regarding its own object of activity by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
However, in other cases, cognition occurs through both the form of the thing (*vasturūpa*) and its own nature. What, then, is the distinction between this and future objects?
How, then, is the distinction between the objects of perception and inference [established]?
[Is it that] the indistinct is superimposed upon the distinct, and the distinct upon the indistinct?
Or rather, otherwise?
This has been analyzed:

"In that very case where there is a future course of action, inference is accepted as the means of knowledge; whereas in a past occurrence, perception is the means of knowledge by virtue of its being merely present. (240)

1. By means of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*): in that very case where activity occurs even for one who is free from conceptual construction due to extreme habituation, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, conceptualization would result in being a separate means of knowledge.

If it is argued that where there is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the impelling means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that conceptual construction is not a means of valid cognition because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrahaṇāt*), this has already been examined; it was shown therein how there is no such thing as apprehending what has already been apprehended.
It is further stated:
for indeed, there is no utility in the activity of conceptual construction; if [it is asked], "What is the point of it? [the answer is: nothing.
If the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has utility in its operation, why is it not a means of valid cognition (*pramā*)?
(241) If the conceptual construction is indeed useless, how can it be desired as an aid to perception?
For surely no one has a need for an aid that is itself useless.
If it is argued that perception would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it does not function without that [inference], and that [inference] likewise does not function without it;
In that case, both would result in being invalid cognitions; or else, there would be the alternative of their being non-valid cognitions,
because they do not touch upon the actual form of the objects.
It was just stated that even perception is not a valid means of knowledge because it does not contact the form of the object to be reached;
therefore,
regarding the operation of conceptual construction through positive and negative concomitance:
If there were no causal relationship, then there would be invalidity.
If it is argued that conceptual construction has the capacity to function subsequent to perception, then because of this intervention, perception itself would be invalid. (242–243)

Now, if even that which is mediated were not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*), then in that case, the eyes and other sense organs would also possess the status of being means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) in their capacity as motivators.
If it is argued that this is not so because they are not cognitions (*ajñānatvāt*), [then we reply] that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) would [likewise] possess it.
If it is argued that [the inference] does not [apply] because its object is different,
then [it would apply] if the objects were the same;
if it is argued that it indeed does [apply], then...
It cannot be set in motion there because it is characterized by ignorance;

for perception, which apprehends the preceding moment, does not have the object of action as its domain. Therefore, due to its immediate succession, the means of valid cognition would necessarily be conceptual construction alone.

Furthermore, even if perception were to engage its object of activity merely through a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*) would still be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked:
"How can it not be a valid means of cognition if it apprehends what has already been apprehended?"
Because it is that which sets [the object] in motion, just like inference based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*);
for perception is not a valid means of knowledge by mere appearance alone.
If it is argued that perceptibility would still occur even if things were momentary— indeed, it does occur—
then inference, which grasps [things] as momentary, would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Since it apprehends what has already been apprehended,
or because it establishes conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) might likewise be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, even though both operate upon the same object of perception, there are two distinct types of valid knowledge due to the difference between clarity and lack of clarity.
Even when it functions through the form of another object, it is indeed a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory;
and just as it does not grasp the actual nature of the thing despite being non-contradictory, this has already been demonstrated.
Thus, he shows that even while possessing validity due to non-contradiction, there can still be error.

Just as for two people who run toward a jewel and a lamp-light respectively, perceiving them both with the cognition of a "jewel," there is a difference regarding purposeful action despite the similarity in their erroneous cognition;
so too is it with inference and its fallacy, even though they are both non-conformable to reality.
The status of being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established in accordance with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

In this regard, the delusion of a red lotus or a ruby regarding the luster of a gem— which possesses a specific shape produced by a keyhole but does not rely on a particular gem— and the luster of a lamp are not distinguished from one another.
Nevertheless, there is indeed a distinction for someone who has actually obtained the jewel;
likewise, it is precisely from that [distinction] that inference and its fallacy are distinguished as valid cognition and its opposite.
Even when the jewel is not seen, one who acts upon the determination that the light of a lamp is the jewel is indeed observed [to succeed].
Nor is it the case that [all cognition] is equally erroneous; for there is a distinction everywhere due to the specific nature of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
It is not the case that everything is erroneous simply because it is a cognition, nor otherwise.
Therefore, even an erroneous cognition is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*).

Due to a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), even an error that possesses a particularity and is determined through delusion becomes a basis for the arising of valid cognition when it is produced by related objects; it serves as a cause for attaining what is desired,
just like inferential knowledge which is based on the arising of perception.
For it has been established that inference is not a means of valid cognition without the arising of perception, nor is perception [a means of valid cognition] without the arising of inference;
for instance:
In that very same [verse], the outer row [states]: "That inference for which there is a basis in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
that inference which follows upon direct perception; in which validity is established through such a nature—such is all inference. This is the meaning.
It has been established that perception does not function at the outset without inference, and likewise, inference does not function without perception;
however, the distinction here is simply this: in some cases it is the former, and in others, the latter.
After inference, the sense organ is not required; after the sense organ, however, inference is required for the sake of purposeful activity.
(245) In that very context: after inference, no further sense organ needs to be relied upon, whereas after perception, inference must be relied upon as the cause for engagement.
The explanation of the third quarter (pāda) is not intended before the [explanation of the] letter *akṣa*, but rather the explanation of the fourth quarter is intended.
This fourth quarter [of the verse] is now explained:

it might be argued that inference proceeds even in the absence of perception, whereas perception does not proceed without inference; thus, due to this distinction, inference is not equal to perception.
That too is incorrect;

for perception without inference is not a means of valid cognition. Likewise, there is no such thing as linguistic convention in self-awareness; even if it were a means of valid cognition, what would [convention] be? (246)
And since the object is not established within the perception that consists of mere self-awareness, there would be nothing for difference; thus, non-duality alone remains.
Therefore, there is no proof for an object or for difference apart from direct perception.

In the end, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) depends upon inference; there is no [validity] without inference. (248) Furthermore, it might be argued that perception functions toward a distinct object only by depending upon inference.
Inference, however, occurs even without perception;
for instance, the inference of fire from smoke arises at a later time without depending upon perception.
Since that very object is obtained from that [inference] alone,
this is not the case;
for spatial qualification is not perceived by direct perception.
Furthermore, inference [arises] from the cognition of fire in a particular location. 249.3.
T.
Fire obstructed by a wall or the like cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*saṃvit*) as being in a specific location; nor can it be apprehended through inference (*anumāna*),
because while an inference might establish fire in general at some place beyond the wall, it is through direct perception that its presence in a specific location is grasped.
Nor is there the attainment of birth for fire in a non-restricted location;
furthermore, even in the case of the cognition of a gem within the luster of a gem, the fault lies solely in the failure to apprehend a restricted location,
and this is not the case for doubt or error.
The distinction [between them] lies in the fact that [the latter] does not lead to the attainment of a specific object;
nevertheless, it may be argued that a cognition of error is invalid because it causes one to act toward something else.
If it is argued that doubt sometimes prompts action even in that case, and thus it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that is incorrect.
There is no attainment of birth from such a [neutral] state;
for doubt, which relies upon both sides, is not a motivator. It is error that, through its own erroneous nature, impels embodied beings to action.
Indeed, doubt is inferior to error.
How can one whose mind is oscillating, leaning toward both sides, be a prompter [of action]? Therefore, that state of oscillation departs through perception.

Furthermore, the misconception characterized by the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem is [removed] by inference occurring subsequently; it is not removed by another inference. Thus, there is no distinction between the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem and [valid] cognition in terms of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that [cognition] is simply perception; how could it be erroneous? Likewise, since its validity is established through correspondence, what use is there for distinguishing between error and its opposite? (251)
"Valid cognition is non-erroneous knowledge"—
since this is a general definition,
what is the point of [specifying] whether that error exists or otherwise? It would be useless.
[Objection: "But surely non-contradiction can exist only when there is error, and not otherwise.
[Reply: This too is not true;
for in that very same work it says: "But surely non-contradiction also exists in inference."
And inference is not non-erroneous... [whereas] non-erroneousness consists in non-discrepancy;
regarding this, it is said here:
Is this expression a definitive conclusion, or is it an inquiry?
If it is a definitive determination (*avasāya*), then it exists even in the cognition of a gem, just as it does in the cognition of a jar.

If, on the other hand, it is an inquiry (*vicāra*), then there is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the occurrence [of such determination] even in the case of the cognition of a jar, because it is an inference regarding a future object.

The term *abhrānti* (non-erroneous) [is used] because of non-contradiction (*avisamvādāt*) across differences of time, place, and person; for there is no non-contradiction of error, since non-error itself is not established. (252)
One cannot determine that "this is an error" or "this is otherwise" without non-contradiction;
if it is argued that it is not an error because it is uncontradicted, we say no.
Because it is precisely non-contradiction that is so designated;
for when contradiction exists, everything is indeed an error.
If it is argued that even in the absence of sublation, that very [non-contradiction] constitutes sublation:
In that case, its non-sublated nature consists precisely in its non-contradiction; thus, it is established that non-delusion arises from non-contradiction alone.
Furthermore, the claim that even when there is non-contradiction, inference is indeed a delusion, is neither the view of the Mīmāṃsaka nor the view of the Lokāyata.
Since all that is erroneous is admitted to be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*),
if even an erroneous perception (*pratyakṣa*) were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what would be the distinction between perception and inference?
It will be stated [later] that the distinction lies in the difference of their appearances (*pratibhāsa*).
Even if there is error, there is a distinction in appearance, as in the case of fallacious inference and the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia.

If all cognition were indeed non-erroneous and thus a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) rather than a delusion (*vibhrama*), then what distinction could be observed between being erroneous and non-erroneous? (253)
For error is precisely the failure to touch the actual nature [of the object],

and that is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); just as inference fails to touch the form of the object to be attained, so too does perception— there is no distinction between them in this regard.

If it is argued that, therefore, even in the case of the light of a jewel, the cognition of the jewel is indeed perception— [and that] inference regarding a future object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—
then this is equally true for the other case as well, namely, perception.

If it is argued that in that case (the cognition of a pillar) there is no conceit of it being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the cognition of a jewel there certainly is, we reply:
no; for through extreme habituation, even in the cognition of a jewel there is no conceit of it being a distinct means of valid cognition—thus the two cases are equal.
Is it not the case, however, that the conceit of error exists in the cognition of a jewel in the glare [of a lamp], but not in the cognition of a pillar and so forth?
To this it is replied:

since the ultimate reality is identical [in both cases], the distinction [claimed] based on mere conceit lacks any authoritative basis; therefore, that is merely a duality of means of valid cognition. (254)

In all cases, whether perception or inference, there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, the mere fact that there is no conceit [of such a means] does not constitute a difference in the nature of the object.
Since a conceit lacking a means of valid cognition may arise in any manner whatsoever, there is no distinction between its existence and non-existence.
Therefore—
That cognition is indeed either perception or inference;
such is the determination of the reality regarding the cognition of a gem from its luster.
Now, if the actual nature of the gem is not grasped, how can it be considered perception?
As for pillars and the like, even if their future nature is not apprehended, their nature as it exists at that time is indeed apprehended;
that [objection] is incorrect,
for instance:

If the nature of the object were not apprehended, then the apprehension of both the cognition and the cognized would be exactly the same; however, in both cases, the attainment [of the object] occurs through a causal connection (pratibandha).
There is an apprehension of the difference in the form that is attained.
Whether that apprehension pertains to the object's own nature or to the nature of another, there is no distinction;
for the appearance of the jewel is exactly the same with respect to both the jewel and the luster of the jewel.
In this regard, in some cases there is an error regarding location, in some cases an error regarding the essential nature, in some cases both, and in some cases neither.

The mode [of error] is as follows: in the case of the cognition of a jewel regarding the luster of a jewel, there is error concerning the location; in the case of the jewel itself, there is error concerning the nature of the object to be attained; in the case of inference based on a universal, there is error in both respects; and in the case of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), there is neither kind of error.
Therefore, as for what was said:

"Whatever is a cognition, it must be in the form of a direct perception, just like the cognition of direct perception; whatever is a means of valid cognition, it must be non-erroneous, just like direct perception."
That is incorrect;
for even perception does not [grasp] the object in its own nature,
nor is there any perception that is non-erroneous.

Just as [cognition] is mistaken with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*) in the case of perceptual error, so too is it in the case of inference and other cognitions held to be mistaken; thus, demonstrating such mistakenness is of no use anywhere. If this is so, then how is there a distinction between the definitions of perception and inference? To this it has been said:
"Because of the difference in manifestation as either clear or otherwise"—
how does that very difference in manifestation arise? For one who perceives [the object] independently, there is the state of clear manifestation.

That which appears otherwise is indistinct, beyond the senses, and imperceptible; how can this very thing be so, such that it is said: "In whatever case the intellect follows [the object] through positive and negative concomitance by the power of the object"?
Therefore, its apprehension is independent; anything other than that is an object beyond the senses (atīndriya).
For that alone which has direct manifestation is an object not beyond the senses—the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

And there is direct manifestation [of the particular], because the cognition, assuming its form, is produced in accordance with the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) [of that object].

However, that which is determined as having the form of a previously apprehended object— appearing due to the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by a prior perception— is something else entirely, being beyond the reach of the senses; for in that case, neither the operation of the sense organ nor the mode of direct manifestation (*sākṣātkaraṇākāra*) possible through it is directly perceived.
And there is no cognition of it other than by way of its form;
that which is directly [perceived] is indeed not [otherwise] cognized,
whereas that which is indirect is so because of the absence of non-sequential connection.
In that case, it follows that an object is indeed perceived in its own form yet remains remote because of the absence of sensory activity; this, however,
is not what is intended.
If, because it has the form of a color seen previously, a cognition whose object is remote (*parokṣa*) does not perceive a real entity (*avastu*),
then since what is being cognized is not remote, how can its object be remote? (257)

If it is perceived, it is not remote (*parokṣa*); yet, if there is no contact with the real entity (*vastu*), how can it have the real entity as its object? If, on the other hand, it has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, how can it have a remote entity as its object? For in that case, the universal is indeed directly perceived (*sākṣātkṛta*), while the real entity itself is not touched; how, then, can the cognition of the universal have a remote entity as its object?
If it is argued that [the object] is apprehended through a "characterization by characterization" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*), in what form does the characterization of the particular (*viśeṣa*) occur?
If it is by means of the particular itself, then let the cognition of sound and so forth arise from that very particular; what is the use of an internal tumor of a universal (*sāmānya*)?
It has been stated that if the definition is in terms of a universal form, there is an infinite regress; and if it is in terms of a particular form, the sense organs would be rendered useless.
Now, [it may be argued that] only the universal appears.
The particular (viśeṣa) is beyond perception because it does not appear;
here too, only its own form, arrived through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), appears directly, while the object itself remains beyond perception— how, then, can it have that as its object?
In that regard, since there is no engagement with what has not been understood, how can there be engagement?
It has been established that engagement occurs everywhere only with respect to what has not yet been understood.

If it is argued that there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) because one observes the activity of Yajñadatta— even though he has not apprehended the form of Devadatta— due to his seeing what is similar [to Devadatta], we say no.
Since the cause of non-contradiction will be explained later—
that "non-contradiction arises from a [real] connection"—

if this [cognition] were an error, then, because it would arise through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it would be apprehended within the latent impression itself; how, then, could there be a determination (*adhyavasāya*) or an attainment (*prāpti*) of the object?
Nor is there any fault, because the object [is established] through its connection with that [consciousness], since it is also the cause for the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
He states that very point:
"If there were another object as the locus for that [inference] whose own nature is unperceived, and if it were related to that locus, then it might be a prover. (60)
For an object whose nature is unperceived is understood through a relation with something else;
if it were understood through anything whatsoever, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it were understood by itself, then everyone would be an omniscient seer (*sarvadarśin*), since there would be no distinction [between them].
And if that other [property] is related by means of that substratum, then how is it an indicator?
This is because it is observed in exactly this way.
In that very same [text]—there is a variant reading "from what is connected" (*sambaddhāt*).

[Objection: But surely it is memory itself that arises there from what is connected, and since that [memory] also arises from [other things such as] a relationship and so forth, that same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains.
Because there is no other way for memory to arise than from non-exertion (*anābhoga*) and so forth;
in that very context— the reading "even of grasping and so forth" refers to that [memory] which is established by means of instruction and so on, arising from experience and the like.

Because of the encounter with the substratum of that [object] as qualified by place and time, and because of the perception of the object connected to the subject (*dharmin*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), an object restricted by place and time is understood as being capable of attainment, and not through mere mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth;
for it is thus: [258]
*Ābhoga* is a mental activity intent on inquiry, such as "What was seen? What was it?

When that exists, there is recollection of an object at its very same place and time; it involves no further operation. Therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the resulting cognition is merely this much: "This is similar to that," based on the apprehension of something resembling it.
Similarity, however, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because that which is qualified by place and time is never always similar;
and since similarity belongs to multiple things, it is either this or that, and thus lacks a fixed determination. Therefore, it is not a means of knowledge.
However, when that which is similar to it performs what ought to be done, perception itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein;
otherwise, there would be no engagement based on perception at all, and thus it would not be a means of valid cognition, as has already been established and need not be stated again.
In this very same way, even the cognition arising from a relationship, being of the nature of inference, is not a means of valid cognition.
For it is thus:

that which possesses the characteristic of being an indicator is the nature of the mark (liṅga), such as the effect and so forth; since it has that as its characteristic, there is no other definition of a mark. (259)
This very thing—the state of being a *śiṃśapā* which performs a causal function, as well as smoke and so forth produced by fire—is understood through similarity either as an effect or as a cause.

In that case too, this "existence" (*sattva*) is of an impermanent nature, because it is devoid of prior and subsequent forms; nor is there any other form of impermanence belonging to anything else. Thus, the cognition of all inference is of such a kind. Furthermore, the nature of smoke is characterized by a proximate cause when it is specifically identified by some [observer], while the nature of ash and so forth has a non-proximate cause; both of these, accordingly, are indicative [of their respective causes]. For instance:
Whatever entity is perceived in a certain way at one time, it is in that same way [perceived] at another; for it is memory alone that, as appropriate, acts as the activator.
Otherwise, when the memory of what was previously seen wavers, [the object would not be recognized].
In that case, there would be an occurrence [of the cognition], but not a connection with contradiction. Perception is non-erroneous, while recollection is based upon it;
if that recollection were a valid means of knowledge, it would be in the form "I remember thus. (261–262)
Even if there is deviation in the act of seeing, it is not a valid cognition; for even if there is deviation in the seeing, that [cognition] is distinct from memory because of its being otherwise.
For instance, seeing occurs without an objective support, whereas memory is otherwise.

Since it possesses an object [of its own], it would not be a valid cognition (*pramā*) in that way. In the case of memory, it is not otherwise understood that perception is the means of valid cognition; rather, the defect belongs to perception itself, but in fact it belongs to the memory.
For even that memory arises otherwise due to similarity.

Memory arises from that very state of being through the clarity of recollection; it partakes of the object by means of its effect or its essential nature as they are characterized in reality. Otherwise, memory would be an error.
Therefore, all discrepancy whatsoever is caused solely by a lapse of memory;
thus, memory alone regarding an imperceptible object is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it concerns what was previously perceived in connection [with other evidence],
and that is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*).
Therefore, he says:
"At that time, the cognition occurs only in the form of a generality that follows the indicator;
therefore, every remote object is not apprehended in its particularity. (61)

For the cognition of that which is to be understood (gamyam) is dependent upon the indicator (gamakam); and that indicator exists in the form of a universal (sāmānya), not as a particular (viśeṣa), because it is impossible to define a particular.
If something were an indicator even in an undefined form, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of cognizing every aspect and every entire causal series.
Furthermore, that universal such as smoke is observed everywhere in relation to fire and so forth;
therefore, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), there can be no cognition of a particular (*viśeṣa*) from it.
If it is argued that there is cognition [of the particular] through the indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the particular:
No, because it is impossible to characterize a specific intermediate distinction;
[one might object: "But surely, the characterization of a specific distinction is indeed possible for something."
Not so; for it is impossible to establish an absolute distinction,
whereas the indication of a distinction therein is merely relative.
And as for the phrase "whatever its extent may be," we understand that for one who has cognition of it in all its aspects, because of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*),
that [object] is indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*).
If it is argued that the cognition of a particular arises from the perception of a particular, we say no;
for it will be demonstrated later that even in that case, the understanding is of the universal alone.
He says this very thing:

"And that cognition which, arising from a property belonging to a related object, occurs with respect to the subject itself, is inference; it is exclusively the means of establishing things that are beyond the senses. (62)

Because there is an absence of any other defining characteristic and because the defining characteristic of inference is possible, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than inference for objects that are not immediately perceived.
[Objection: But surely one means of valid cognition can have as its object the domain of another means of valid cognition; thus, there are not just two means of valid cognition.
[Response: To this, the following is the refutation.
There is no possibility of another object of cognition (prameya) other than the perceptible and the imperceptible;
therefore, because there are two objects of cognition, two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are accepted.
[Objection: But surely, it is logical that there are two objects of cognition because there are two means of valid cognition.
Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes existence, this is not the case:

that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is established by the means of valid cognition. Rather, the nature of the means of valid cognition is established through the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And since it is the very form of cognition that is self-aware, it has been stated that what is perceived as both particular and universal is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
The meaning is that because the objects are twofold, the aspects are twofold;
for when two of one's own aspects are cognized, it is not logical that there be only one,
nor even three and so forth.

Alternatively, the refutation of the number three [of means of valid cognition] follows from the observation of only two objects of cognition; since no object of cognition other than these two is possible,
it is established that there is no further means of valid cognition.
Now, because a second object of cognition (*prameya*) is possible, he will demonstrate that there is neither one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor three and so forth;
for when a second object of cognition is possible, a single means of valid cognition does not exist,
since there must also be a means of valid cognition whose object is that second object of cognition.
The establishment of a second object of cognition does not occur through the same means of valid cognition [as the first];

rather, he says that the two objects of cognition are established because the object of cognition consists of only one thing, namely the nature of both the universal and the particular, while no other exists.
॰viśeṣaviṣayarūpa॰: "If it is held that [the object] is a single form whose objects are specific [features], because it is immeasurable, then that is our view regarding what is non-existent. || 64 ||

This has indeed been seen: an object of cognition other than the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot be an object of cognition. Only the particular characteristic is the object of cognition;
it alone, because it is apprehended through both its own form and the form of others, is said to possess the characteristics of both the universal and the particular, as previously stated.
Furthermore,
there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding non-apprehensibility (*aprameyatva*), because even the absence [of a thing] is ascertained;
or else, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that ascertains that [absence] would be a second [means of knowledge].

For even non-existence, characterized as antecedent non-existence and so forth, is an object of cognition (*prameya*); how then can there be the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "the non-existent is not an object of cognition"?
And how can a reason (*hetu*) that lacks such pervasion be conclusive (*aikāntika*)? To illustrate:
If prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other [types of non-existence] were not perceived, everything would be eternal; there would be neither effect nor cause, as will be demonstrated later.
Furthermore, if there were mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), substances would become intermingled, and thus the entire world would become non-dual (*advaita*).
The ascertainment of that [object] is either a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or the second [type of cognition], because the cognition born of the senses is not [ascertainment].

Cognition is not born from the senses. (65) If [cognition] were produced by the power of the object even in the absence [of the object], then sensory cognition would arise even when there is an obstruction or other such conditions, since it would not depend on the capacity of the object. (66)
Indeed, non-existence (abhāva) is not an object of the senses,
because it is only the intrinsic nature of sound and so forth that appears therein; rather,
the statement "this is not here" refers to its form as a non-entity, which is not within the range of the senses.
Because that [object], even if spatially remote, is established as non-existent;
now, if it is argued that such ascertainment arises solely from the perception of a secluded place,
what indeed is this so-called "seclusion"?

If it is argued that when a particular location and so forth is perceived, the absence of anything else therein is established because that [perceived object] has the nature of the absence of those other things; how is this so?
How can there be the non-existence of one with respect to another?
If it is because of a lack of association with it, then from where does that lack of association arise?
If it is because of simultaneous perception,
then since there is no distinction [between them],
the perception of something other than that would itself be the perception of that.
If it is argued that its difference from that [other object] is grasped precisely because it is not cognized as that, even though it was previously cognized—
then how can there be a comprehension of non-existence when this very thing is not being cognized?
Therefore, this determination of non-existence is not born of the senses;
consequently, it is not perception.
Nevertheless, it might be argued as follows:
The claim that it is precisely perception, when it ceases, that serves as the cause for the ascertainment of non-existence is also incorrect;
for if the cessation of perception itself constitutes the ascertainment of non-existence, then that ascertainment belongs to perception alone.
Or else, that very same [non-perception] is the mark (liṅga) which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin).

If it is argued that the determination of non-existence occurs simply from the cessation of perception itself, this is contradictory; for that [cessation] does not exist, and yet there is cognition by means of it.
For perception, by virtue of its nature as direct experience, produces certainty regarding that object toward which it proceeds;
since certainty arises from what has been experienced,
how could there be certainty in the absence of experience?
For indeed, speakers say,
"I do not know whether there is something else or not"; since there is no equal cognition here, how can there be certainty from a non-cognition that is itself a cause of uncertainty?

If it is argued that the non-perception of something capable of being perceived leads to the ascertainment of its absence when the object is present, then there can be no ascertainment of the absence of such things as the next world, which are beyond the senses.

Furthermore, if non-perception is excluded from the presence of an existing thing, then—being pervaded by its opposite—it becomes a means of cognition; thus, through the connection of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), inference is established as another valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because it arises from an inferential mark (*liṅga*),
there is no statement here [to the effect] that "I have experienced this" (*nātra mamānubhava iti vacanam*).

By this, the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which are included therein, have been stated; he now states the reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*):
"And the two means of valid cognition are established for the sake of cognizing another's consciousness."
Furthermore, because of the engagement in speech and other activities, the certainty of its existence is established.
For the consciousness of another is not established through direct perception in the same way as one's own;
indeed, one does not know whether this [other] possesses consciousness or not.

Because the cognition occurs precisely through the manifestation of that [object's] form, the ascertainment of a specific [mental state] such as aversion is established by means of that specific effect;
however, let this ascertainment be established in whatever way it may, it does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is not a fault,
because we observe practical activity characterized by speech and so forth that conforms to it.
If it is argued that, in some way or another, this activity is entirely devoid of any valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*):

If it is argued that there is no abandonment because it would entail the consequence of abandoning [the means], and that there is no abandonment because there is no other alternative and thus no other way out;
The certainty that "there is an absence of any other means" is itself a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and this has been stated to be inference (*anumāna*).
This is said by way of accepting the opponent's own position.
Therefore, there is no fault, because what is accepted by the opponent finds its application only in inference for others (parārthānumāna);
for no one indeed establishes [a point] solely for themselves by means of what is accepted by another.

If it is argued: "I do not perceive any other state of existence [beyond this], and therefore I am engaged in this very [life]; likewise, let there be engagement even in the next world; and even if the next world were abandoned, one is still able to live—therefore, there is no engagement in that [next world]."
From where does this notion that "it is possible to live thus" arise?
Even for one who desires life, does he desire past life or present life?
In that regard, it cannot be the former, because the past has already passed away.
One does not seek the present, because that has already been attained;
if one seeks the future,

then life in the future occurs through this specific means and not otherwise— since this is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is indeed inference (*anumāna*).
Furthermore,
as for this conventional usage [of "existence"], is it yours alone or that of another?
If it is yours alone, then since it is unestablished for both parties, how could another have been persuaded?

If it is the case that there is likewise an absence of any means [of cognition] for another person as well, then the apprehension of another's consciousness must necessarily occur; how then can this apprehension be said to be "somehow" [or "in some way"]? Or, if even this [apprehension] occurs "somehow," then you yourself lack conviction; how then can there be an apprehension of another?
"I know it thus for myself, but I do not know how it is for another.
If you then argue that this results in silence, [and that] "it must be exactly the same for the other person as well," [we reply:]
This argument— that [it does not exist] because there is a lack of valid cognition— is trivial;
therefore, the cognition of another exists.
Therefore, inference must also be accepted by the opponent.

If it is argued that "it is a valid means of knowledge because it is non-contradictory, but since there is sometimes deviation, there is no confidence," [we reply: such a state belongs to one who has misperceived the logical mark (liṅga). "Such a state belongs to one who has misperceived the logical mark"—thus [says] M.
For non-discrepancy is the defining characteristic of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since that exists for inference, it possesses the status of a valid means of cognition.
Now, if one were to argue that [inference] is seen to be erroneous even when there is discrepancy, [we reply: that is a misconception.
For instance, the inference "he is dark-skinned because he is his son," although it is subject to the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), is nonetheless improper;
for this is not a valid inference at all, as it arises from a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) due to the absence of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*).

For being his son is not invariably concomitant with dark complexion, because they depend on different causal complexes; and if there were identity of form, there would be no dependence on different causal complexes.

Because of the possibility of specific differences in karma, nutriment, and time, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous production if [the effects] were dependent on a single causal complex;
therefore, since the true nature of the mark is not perceived, and because causality is superimposed even where it does not exist, the intention is to demonstrate deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Or rather, it may be that [the objection applies] only to the *liṅga* (the inferential mark).
If it is argued that all inference is of this very nature and there is no other specific definition [of it], and thus for whom could there be non-deviation (avyabhicāra)?
That too is incorrect,
because at some time there is the cognition of a thing as established in a certain place.
Therefore, that [effect] must necessarily have arisen from that [cause], or it must possess its nature;
for only a mark (*liṅga*) connected by a necessary relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is capable of proving [the probandum],
because it is of the same essence as the other.

And since the cognition of the probandum is non-deviant, that [cognition] must arise from it by way of a necessary connection (*niyama*), or possess its essential nature (*tattva-svabhāva*); for otherwise, the possibility of a non-deviant understanding would not exist, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, a cognition of everything does not arise from everything.
Because it is perceived as being occasional;
therefore, this cognition is necessarily produced by an object that is related [to it], and that relation is...
The connection is indeed of two kinds;
even for that which depends on the same causal complex, the connection characterized by origination from it is the indirect one,
and from that alone follows non-deviation.
For there is no possibility of an object existing without its own cause or its own nature—
whether from its own cause or from its own nature.
And whatever form is seen in those two [examples], that very same thing is the characteristic elsewhere as well.

Whatever characteristic is observed for a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*) or essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) in one case, that same characteristic applies elsewhere too; it is not absent in the case of a son or similar instances. Therefore, there is no lack of confidence in all cases.

For if a sublation were possible regarding that which possesses the [defining] characteristic, then that very characteristic would be undermined; thus, there would be a lack of confidence everywhere, and not otherwise—this is the logical principle (*nyāya*).
Furthermore, nothing whatsoever can come into existence without a cause or an absence;
if such a doubt were entertained, there would be no practical activity at all in any respect.
This discussion concerns conventional means of valid cognition (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*) and nothing else;
therefore, one who seeks worldly transactional activity must necessarily employ inference.
If it is asked, "How can there be engagement in the absence of a means? [the answer follows].
If it is argued that [the means] does not disintegrate when examined because the status of being a means is unestablished,
we say no.
Since even deliberation (*vicāra*) is of the nature of inference (*anumāna*),
this is like the very path forgotten by one who is walking;
if it is due to non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), then what is the obstructing factor (*pratibandha*)?
He demonstrates that this very [connection] is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*);
for it is thus: 2 T.

If [the object] is held to be "desired" (iṣṭa) in terms of its intrinsic nature or its own cause, then while other causes for seeing the visible exist, how could there be the existence of that [object] or of one who possesses it, when the visible itself is not being seen? (72)
Precisely because it is dependent upon that [cause], it does not arise in its absence;
otherwise, why would it not arise when something else is absent?
If that were the case, there would be an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in this way, these two are so linked that if [the effect or the pervaded] were to exist in the absence of that [cause or the pervader],
there would otherwise be no link;
therefore, wherever there is non-perception of a cause or a pervader that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), there is the absence of those two.
And since where those two [the cause and the pervader] are absent, there is no possibility of the effect and the pervaded, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is likewise non-deviant;
thus it has been established that inference exists in its threefold form, characterized by the non-perception of the effect, the essential nature, and the non-perception itself.
This is because:

And if the cognition of a universal were invalid, its disappearance would follow— as it does in the case of rebirth— unless it were perceived by the senses in turn. But that is not so, because sensory cognition is impossible when the capacity of the sense organ has not yet arisen.
If there were a cognition of non-existence, the arising of that cognition would be without a cause.
For if the cognition of a universal (sāmānya) were invalid, it would follow that there is no such thing as an imperceptible object of knowledge (*prameya*),
just as in the case of the next world (*paraloka*).

Now, it is not the case that every object beyond the reach of the senses does not exist, because some are perceived by the senses through a succession of moments; however, in the case of the afterlife (*paraloka*), there is no such successive operation of the senses. Therefore, it is precisely of that nature [the afterlife] that does not exist.
If you argue that it exists at the very moment it is perceived, then how can it be said to exist prior to that?
[We reply: It exists even prior to that, because it is perceived by another [means of knowledge].
If it is argued that the next world is not perceived by another prior to oneself, nor by oneself—
how then is it established that anything other than the next world is perceived by another?
If you say, "Because of such conventional usage," [we reply:]...
The validity of inference has already been established;
nor does it depend alternatively upon the sense-faculty or its capacity,
since those two are understood solely through inference based on the nature of the effect and the logical reason (kārya-svabhāva-hetu).
And in the absence of that [external object], the arising of cognition would have to be caused solely by the names of things;
therefore, both the capacity and the eye and other sense organs are indeed inferred through the observation of the effect and through the negative concomitance of the effect.
Nor can the operation of the senses enter into that [universal] even by way of succession;
therefore, the next world and so forth are likewise [unperceivable].
Consequently, the universal is not cognized without inference.

Because perception is non-conceptual with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since there is no grasping of the universal (*sāmānya*) without conceptualization, inference [operates] upon that [universal]. (75)
Even cognitions whose nature consists in the apprehension of a universal are effective in worldly transaction;
yet a universal is not grasped without conceptualization,
nor is perception conceptual, because it is non-investigative.
Therefore, inference has the universal as its object and is not perception;
how then is it that this [perception], which grasps color and so forth through aspects such as impermanence,
constitutes a grasping of a universal form?

And a restriction of the objects of cognition is accepted by you; yet, when there is such a restriction of objects of cognition, the impermanence of letters is not perceived, because that cognition would be possible through another means of valid cognition even without a logical mark (liṅga). || 76 ||

For "restriction" (niyama) refers to the fact that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*), which are the objects of cognition (*prameya*), are apprehended by their respective restricted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and this [cognition] is a mixed apprehension, because it occurs through the mutual mixing of the particular and universal characteristics in the form: "the color and so forth are impermanent."
Consequently, the apprehension of both forms [of the object] would entail a third means of valid cognition;
furthermore, since this occurs without a logical mark (*liṅga*), it is not inference,
and because there is a grasping of a universal (*sāmānya*), it is not perception.

Furthermore, there is no inference of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it does not occur through a logical mark (*liṅga*) without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because there is an appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Moreover, in the case of "inference based on what has been seen" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), there is no comprehension of a universal, because the connection of the logical mark with the universal is not perceived.
Thus he said:

In the case of inference based on perceived particulars (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), because the connection of the mark (*liṅga*) is not [previously] cognized, it is a distinct means of knowledge; or else, its multiplicity follows from the multiplicity of the objects to be known.
Or, as in the case of multiple means of knowledge operating upon a single object. (77)

From the perception of a particular [instance], there would either be the exclusion of the numbers one or three, or it would not; because there is no restriction on the object and because other objects of cognition are possible,
there is indeed no inferential mark (liṅga) here for the claim that "this color and so forth are impermanent."
Nor is that perception [the means], because there is a cognition of the impermanence of the universal as well;
and in the case of "perception of the particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), there is only the cognition of the particular,
since there is no apprehension of a connection between that particular mark (*liṅga*) and the universal.
Therefore, according to your view, that [cognition] is neither perception because it is not a direct apprehension, nor is it inference because its object is not a universal;
moreover—

Because there is a multiplicity of objects of cognition (*prameya*) due to the distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and both, there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the number three is not excluded.
Nor is the number one rejected, because multiple means of valid cognition can operate upon a single object;

for example, just as perception (*pratyakṣa*) operates together with inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) regarding a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), so too does perception operate regarding a universal (*sāmānya*).

As for what was stated—that the refutation of the number one follows from the observation of two types of objects of cognition—that would not be the case, because perception itself can function even with respect to universals (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, if there were a restriction regarding the object and an absence of other objects of cognition, then the refutation of the numbers three and one would occur; however, since neither of these is the case by the reasoning already stated, the intended purpose is not established.
Moreover, due to the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) and the multiplicity of objects of cognition, there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition.

[Objection: But has not the multiplicity of objects of cognition (*prameya*) already been refuted by the passage beginning with "due to capacity and incapacity" (*śaktyaśaktitaḥ*)? [Response: True; nevertheless, that very multiplicity is presented here in order to demonstrate that it is indeed observed.

Alternatively, there is no fault because the demonstration of the "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) was made by the opponent; however, the demonstration of the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) is indeed appropriate. Therefore, this also brings forth the proof of the non-establishment of the claim that "every remote object (*parokṣa-artha*) is not cognized in its particularity."

Therefore, the exclusion of the numbers three and one does not apply here; it is said in response: because of the application [of the term] to the generality of phonemes (*varṇasāmānya*), this fault does not follow. (79)
The universal property of "color-ness" (*varṇatva*) is conjoined with impermanence in the form "color and so forth are impermanent.

Therefore, the object of cognition (*prameya*) consists solely of the universal aspect and not both aspects; thus, this fault does not apply, because there is no possibility of an object of cognition other than [the universal] which is the basis [of the particular].
For this fault would indeed occur if there were a relation of universal and particular, but not when there is only the existence of the universal.
If one joins impermanence with the universal of "soundness" alone, then that would not be a property of the entity;
for when a property is perceived as joined to something, it is a property of that very thing.
And if it were joined to the universal, then that form would belong to the universal, not to the entity.
And since the universal is a real entity, its property would necessarily be a property of a non-entity;
but this is not the case, because:
It is not a non-entity, because its existence is established in that very way through proof;
[as stated in Manorathanandin’s *Vṛtti*]: "because it is established through proof."
If it is argued that there is no establishment of anything else apart from this, we say no, because that very thing is established. (80) If [the universal] were not a property of a real entity,
it would be a conceptual construction due to its being a non-entity.
If it is argued that even those [attributes] such as permanence and so forth must be real entities, and that both are of the nature of a real entity,
we say no.
Because the thing itself is established as such:
for whatever appears in conceptual construction— such as color-ness, impermanence, and so forth— that very [quality] exists even in the particular (svalakṣaṇa),
since the arising of a conceptual construction of that form occurs precisely through the experience of the particular.
If conceptual construction is not connected with the particular (svalakṣaṇa) because the particular does not appear therein, how can that very [particular] be established in such a way?
It is not so, because there is an indirect connection.
Even if there is no direct connection, there is an indirect connection; thus, that non-conceptual [cognition] possesses non-erroneousness.

But surely, if it is connected to mental impressions (*vāsanā*), how can it be connected to the real object? [The answer is: because those mental impressions are themselves connected to the real object.
To the question "How so?", he says:
