For whatever entity is as it actually is, that very thing is the cause of both the sign and the cognition; therefore, from that entity which has become such, there arises the cognition of the sign. (81)

2. It has been established that whatever property is to be proven (sādhyadharma) must be either the cause or the pervader (vyāpaka) of the probans (sādhanahetu). Therefore, for one who understands [the relationship between] effect and pervaded, the cause and the pervader are the probans.
Furthermore, if that cognition of gender which has arisen from that [cognition] is indirectly connected to the real entity, then [the objection does not hold].

Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) are indirectly connected to the real entity (*vastu*), they do not deceive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity].

(82) There is no attainment of the real entity [by the cognition], because the attainment of the real entity occurs solely through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) based on the appearance.
For one who is engaging [with an object] acts on the basis of mere appearance;

moreover, engagement is seen to arise from conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) as well. Otherwise, even from an appearance, one would not engage. One who has been initially engaged by conceptual determination becomes capable of engaging subsequently based on the appearance through the force of habituation (*abhyāsa*).
Therefore, since existence is established in the case of the activity [of the cause],
just as there is existence for that which appears, so too there is existence for its appearing cause and pervader; thus,
let there be attainment in both cases as well.
Furthermore, it has already been established that there is no attainment of anything that merely appears;
and just as existence is known from appearance, so too is it known from an appearance that is invariably connected [to an object].
Furthermore, if one holds the view that there is no object of attainment, the world would be nothing but mere appearance;
for, due to the failure to determine the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous,
there can be no discernment of error within mere appearance itself.

Therefore, it is certain that the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition regarding an imperceptible object cannot be established otherwise; for, although the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are devoid of the direct appearance of the object, they are nonetheless non-deceptive because they are indirectly connected to the real entity.
"And because those two [cognitions], though devoid of that form, determine it as having that form—
and despite not being deceived by that form— the classification of them as 'erroneous' is established.
(83) Regarding this, some say:

The cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is the cognition of smoke and so forth by virtue of its being tied to the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). For the mark is not an indicator merely by its existence, as is the case with the sense faculties, nor is it an indicator merely by appearing in the consciousness that takes it as its object;
for if it were, it would follow that one would also perceive the unperceived nature of the object and its relationship.
Therefore, the apprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*) consists in its apprehension as being necessarily connected;
and that necessary connection cannot be grasped without contact with both forms [of the relation],
since no such apprehension is observed otherwise.

In this regard, just as the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) has the mark as its object, so too the apprehension of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is likewise [an apprehension of the possessor];

for in the apprehension of the mark, the mark is perceived as the primary element, whereas in the apprehension of the possessor of the mark, the possessor of the mark is perceived as the primary element.

Therefore, as for what was said—that there is no inference of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), and that its non-erroneousness constitutes its validity regarding the subject at hand—that is an occasion for the cognition of the mark (liṅga); it is for this reason that an investigation of that [mark] has also been undertaken.

Alternatively, if that [cognition of the mark] were itself of the nature of inference, then it would be nothing other than the comprehension of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), and thus it would not have been mentioned separately.
Even though the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) has the nature of perception, it is not devoid of a real logical mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, even if it were devoid of a real object characterized by that mark (*liṅgin*), it would not be erroneous, because [the error] does not have that [non-existent thing] as its object.
For the cognition of a pillar is not erroneous simply because of the absence of a potter; thus, that [objection] is refuted.
Because the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) have the same object and because they are not themselves perceptual,
it is said in that very [text]: "Some," namely Dharmottara and others.
In that very same [work]—it was stated by that Śaṅkara, the *tīrthika* (or perhaps *naiyāyika*):
"The cognition of one possessing a mark (*liṅgin*) is here inference; and its non-discrepancy and non-erroneousness..."
4. In that very same [work]—the meaning is that what was stated there has been refuted by Śaṅkara.
5. In that very same [work]—if the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) is the cognition of the mark due to its being connected as a remainder (*avaśeṣa*).
The apprehension of the necessary connection between two common properties occurs through inference. To that same effect [it is said]:
"If it were so, there would be an infinite regress; for in that case as well, one must know the necessary connection."
In that case too, it [the linga] would be known only through another inference, and from yet another [inference] after that.
(267) Now, if the linga is perceived as a linga through direct perception, then how could it be devoid of the appearance of such [an inference]? (268)
Even when perceived by direct perception, smoke and the like are later remembered as being a logical mark (*liṅga*).
This being the case, memory is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); what is the point of establishing its non-deceptiveness?
For it is not a valid means of knowledge in that context.
If non-contradiction is established only for perception and inference as being valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
then memory (*smaraṇa*) must also be a valid means of knowledge by virtue of its indirect connection [to reality].

In that case, since that very [memory] is the cognition of the signified (*liṅgin*) and is thus inference (*anumāna*), what is the purpose of specifying the distinction between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*)?
If it is argued that this [subsequent cognition] is indeed not a valid means of knowledge because it apprehends what has already been apprehended,
then in that case, perception itself would be the means of knowledge regarding its own occurrence; and since that perception is not devoid of its own appearance, there is a contradiction.
Therefore, it is explained by way of an alternative interpretation:

the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) arising from a reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) is itself the cognition of the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), because in the ultimate sense there is no difference between the mark and the bearer of the mark;
whereas the cognition of the bearer of the mark arising from a reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) has the cause as its object.

In that case, because there is no difference [between the smoke and the fire], this is not a cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*); nor does the cognition of fire arise from this smoke due to extreme habituation. Furthermore, the cognition of smoke—which apprehends the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*)—does not arise [as a conceptual inference];
rather, it is precisely the apprehension of the smoke as it truly is that constitutes its state of being "concomitant" (*pratibaddhatā*).
The reality [of the object] is established through recognition; recognition arises from the perception of its form; that perception of its form is indeed inference;
and that perception of its form, due to extreme familiarity, becomes the cause of practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Thus, there is no infinite regress.
Therefore, the apprehension of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is the comprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

However, when there is the apprehension of the generality of smoke that is tied to fire, which arises from the perception of its form, that is indeed inference in the form of the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*); it is not designated otherwise.

Therefore, when a real entity is to be understood, the pervader (*vyāpaka*) or its own nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause for the mind [to grasp] the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and that [nature] is the cause for the cognition of that [pervader]. (84)
For the object to be proven (sādhya) is of two kinds: a positive entity and its negation.
When the object to be proven is a positive entity, that which pervades it is the probandum, because that pervader is the cause for the cognition of the pervaded.

And since that [non-perception] is either the nature or the cause of the pervaded mark (*liṅga*), and that in turn is the cause for the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), a connection (*pratibandha*) is possible through this indirect succession; thus,
he demonstrates how non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by showing how such a connection exists.
(2) Regarding the consideration of non-apprehension:

however, negation is established everywhere through non-apprehension; for those who state that proof is by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the object of negation] is established by implication from the opposite case. // 85 //
Wherever there is indeed a means of proof for a negation, in all such cases it is solely through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Where a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates to establish a real entity (*vastu*), there that very entity is established, and its negation does not occur;
therefore, the establishment of a negation occurs precisely through the opposite [of the conditions for establishing a positive entity].

For instance, not perceiving that which is capable of being perceived, they say "it exists," because non-perception itself is negation; and since it is invariably concomitant with that [object], the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) is indeed the logical connection (*pratibandha*). Now, even so-called contradiction (*virodha*) is nothing but a logical connection, whether direct or indirect; from that as well, the negation of a thing is established through perception.

Just as there is no cold touch in fire, nor any specific [sensory] effect such as the bristling of hair, because of the presence of a specific fire; how then is that established through non-perception? To this, the reply is as follows:
This is true; however, the perception of contradictory properties, whether directed toward that [object] or its cause, serves as an indication of its very lack of validity. (86)
Even a contradictory entity brings about the cognition of its absence,
not merely by virtue of the relation of contradiction;
for it is not the contradictory itself that is intended to be cognized.

If it is argued that [the probans] is intended to have the nature of non-existence (*asadrūpatā*), then the connection (*pratibandha*) must be considered in terms of non-existence itself; moreover, there is no contradiction with that [non-existence].
If it is argued that wherever this [connection] exists, there non-existence occurs—
If it is asked, "Why is this so? Because it was perceived exactly thus previously," [we reply:
at the time of grasping the contradiction, is that non-existence [grasped] through the perception of the object, or otherwise?
If there is apprehension, how can there be non-existence? Or if there is non-apprehension, then this follows: negation occurs precisely through non-apprehension.
Or if there is non-apprehension... [non-existence].
Otherwise, by the statement of the existence of one thing, how could the non-existence of another be understood?

If it is argued that this [non-existence] follows from contradiction, then by what is that [contradiction] established? If it is argued that it is because they do not coexist, then from where is that [non-coexistence] known?
If it is argued that "because there is no perception of the perceptible," that is a lack of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*).
For if, when one thing exists, another does not exist, then the negation of the other would apply to everything.
Even contradiction, characterized by the impossibility of coexistence, is not cognized without non-perception;
if contradiction is thus cognized through non-perception,
then the cognition of absence [of the contradictory] arises from the mark (liṅga) of that contradiction, and not from non-perception itself.

Now, if it is argued that previously there was a non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) which establishes contradiction, and that from following that very [non-apprehension] one attains the knowledge of the absence of even the contradictory [thing]— thus, that [non-apprehension] alone is what actually proves absence—
if this is so:

If the establishment of the probandum were to arise from that which is observed as being useful for the sake of establishing the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), how could inference be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*)?

(269) For it is through perception that the relationship upon which inference depends is established; since the establishment of the probandum arises from that very [perception], inference would not be a valid means of knowledge. (270) No.

For since the apprehension of the relationship [between the sign and the signified] occurs through perception alone, and the proof of the probandum—fire—occurs from that very same source, how can inference be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
If it is argued that perception has not operated with respect to the imperceptible fire, then [we reply]:
even regarding an imperceptible non-existence, has non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) not indeed operated?
Furthermore, that which has occurred is either a non-apprehension of something that meets the conditions for apprehensibility,
or it is a non-apprehension of something remembered that meets the conditions for apprehensibility;
yet even this [position] of his is poorly reasoned.

Since that which is being remembered is not present even in inference, perception alone is the authority there as well; inference is redundant. Therefore, this is the true nature of the matter here: for the absence of cold is established through fire by means of a prior perception [of fire], because the connection [between them] exists; thus, by the establishment of that [fire], its absence [of cold] is established.
And that non-existence is indeed non-apprehension;
therefore, it is non-apprehension itself— established through inference— that establishes the conventional usage of non-existence, just as it is established through perception, since he will state:
Therefore, this non-perception is established by one's own direct perception (Pramāṇavārttika 4.274).
In this case as well, it should be understood that [the object] is known through inference;
however, when the absence of horripilation is to be proven,
then by means of fire there is the non-perception of cold, and through that non-perception of a cause (kāraṇānupalabdhi), the absence of horripilation is established.

In that case, there is an inference of touch, which is hot by nature, through the form of fire, because it depends on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*); and since that [fire] has the absence of cold as its very nature (*śītabhāvasvabhāva*), the very perception of that [fire] through inference is itself the non-perception of cold. Therefore, because the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) operate in a single instance, there is no other distinct mark of contradiction (*virodhiliṅga*).
Therefore, it is non-apprehension itself, established through inference, that brings about the cognition of absence;
thus, this is an inference based on an inferred [middle term].
If this is so, then perception is being established by means of inference.
And because of that, there would be no validity for inference regarding a real entity, since its [alleged] object is not a real thing;
that too is merely something trivial.

If it is argued that perception is of the nature of apprehension itself, and that apprehension is called "existence," therefore inference whose object is a real entity is [based on] non-apprehension, and non-apprehension is "non-existence";
"Let it be; what is the fault?
It is the absence that is established by fire, not by non-perception"—this is a great fault.
For is it not the case that fire itself is the absence of cold, and thus that very thing is established by that very thing?

If it is argued that "the absence of cold exists only to the extent that a region is pervaded by heat; therefore, the absence of cold is not distinct from the tactile sensation of heat, and this is a *svabhāva-hetu* (essential reason)," then we certainly accept that non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) functions as a *svabhāva-hetu*.
Therefore, by this [non-perception], the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—namely, "there is no cold touch here because of fire"—are indicated.

Consequently, even though it is expressed by its own term, that [non-perception] which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing non-existence cannot be expressed at all by a word for negation (*niṣedharuta*). // 89 //

For when a contradictory entity such as fire is expressed by its own term—even though it is thus stated and established—it is that very non-apprehension, characterized by the presence of another, which establishes the absence;
since that [absence] is not established by any other means of valid cognition, the negation cannot be expressed by the existence of the contradictory.
Indeed, there is no other way for negation to occur.
By this, the statement of the effect of that which is contradictory to the object [to be negated] has been explained.
The formal application (*prayoga*) is merely different; the meaning remains the same in all cases.

(90) Regarding the effect of fire and so forth, which are contradictory to the object to be negated—cold and so forth—it is the non-perception itself, established through inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*), that brings about the realization of absence in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
For instance, fire established from smoke as its effect would prove the absence of cold by means of the aforementioned reasoning.

For the absence of cold could not be established otherwise; even there, the absence [of cold] exists only through a succession [of causes]. From smoke comes fire; from fire comes the absence of cold, which consists in the non-perception [of cold]; and from that, the conventional usage of the "absence of cold. Therefore, there exists merely the arrangement of the words of the formal argument (*prayoga*).
And that [contradiction] is [resolved] by not applying or by covering [the cause], along with its means.
Any statement regarding a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) intended as a negation is not in accordance with logic (91),
just like the negation of an omniscient being’s power and so forth; for there is no established contradiction between [such a being] and objects that transcend the senses (92).
Indeed, a statement is not in contradiction with all cognition;
nor is a contradiction established with that which is beyond the senses.
Since a statement proceeds from cognition itself, how could it prove its own absence?
If it is argued that [the capacity for speech] is incompatible with the experience of all sensations (*sarvavedana*), by what means is this incompatibility apprehended?

For if a decrease were observed to follow upon an increase in sensation, then perhaps some degree of eloquence (*vacasvitā*) might appear beautiful; however, in the case of the experience of all sensations, there is simply an absence of any eloquence whatsoever.
If it is argued that speakers who do not know everything are observed,
then why is it that the foolishness of everyone is not [likewise] observed when fools are observed as speakers?
If it is argued that the speaker’s erudition is perceived, that too will not be perceived; why?
For instance:
If the speaker and the cognition were both [merely] logical, what relationship of sublated and sublator could there be? (If the speaker were [merely] one who possesses logic...)
If it is argued that such [omniscience] is not perceived, let that very non-perception be the proof [of its absence].

For just as the word of a fool is a specific statement even in the absence of scholarship at the time of [discussing] learning, so too, if there were no contradiction even in the state of omniscience, what inconsistency would there be? Indeed, there is no statement that contradicts the excellence of all-encompassing knowledge.
If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction in the case of absolute excellence,
we say no;
for no contradiction is perceived.
The mere non-perception of such a speaker does not constitute a valid response, because non-perception functions as a means of cognition only when it pertains to a perceptible object; thus,
such a non-perception has been declared to be incapable of producing certainty.

In that regard, there is no certain determination of existence or non-existence concerning things that are absolutely beyond perception (atyantaparokṣa). For, regarding things that are absolutely beyond perception—such as an omniscient being or the state after death—one might [erroneously] conclude their non-existence based on mere non-perception;
yet this may still be the case.
When there is sensation of everything, how could speech be possible for one who is non-deluded?
For it is desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), arising from the reflection upon what precedes and follows, that impels words;
this [claim] is also not correct.
Even when there is a clear perception of all objects, it proceeds [as speech] due to the habituation of the desire to speak; how then could there be an impossibility of speech in that case?

(274) Indeed, it is not the case that the desire to speak does not arise from the repeated practice simultaneous with the vision of objects—whether limited or otherwise—that are most clearly apprehended by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Even in the absence of the desire to speak, speech occurs due to the momentum of previous impressions.

For the intention to speak is not the sole cause of words being employed in proximity, since we observe the distinct recitation of words and sentences even by one whose mind is directed elsewhere due to prior momentum,
and because we observe the commencement of various actions practiced previously.
By this, it has been answered as to how there can be a response from a present perceiver even without prior reflection on what came before:
"Actions performed by the body proceed without conceptualization merely through the presence of an enemy, and in the morning, processes that counteract that [enemy] also proceed."
275 1 T. rcom (perhaps = mātra)

And just as for one who has been suddenly awakened by an enemy through a blow or similar means, there occurs a corresponding action such as drawing a weapon and so forth due to previous habituation, so too are all actions of the Omniscient One; thus, it is not contradictory.

Therefore, the determination of the non-existence of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) arises from that which is contradictory [to it], whether that contradictory property be distinct or non-distinct from it.
The noble one applies himself.
Just as fire is [the probans] when "non-cold" is the probandum, so too existence (*sattā*) sublates "origination" (*janman*).

Because cold and hot touch are mutually distinct, their opposition is characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*); whereas for existence and origination, the opposition is characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*). Thus, there is no difference [between the two cases], for indeed, origination does not exist apart from existence, nor does opposition.
That which already exists is not born;
for what purpose would there be birth for that which is existent and free from all doubt?
Furthermore, how can there be mutual contradiction between two things that are non-distinct?
This is stated precisely because it is accepted that there is no distinction between the two;
for what indeed is this so-called "contradiction"?
It is the relationship between that which is to be removed and that which removes.
For instance,
when one thing has its causes complete, if it does not come into being while another is present, then a contradiction between those two is observed, as in the case of cold and fire. (276)
Now, if it is argued that it is improper for the non-existence of one thing to be produced by another because non-existence lacks the status of being an effect,
then if it is not produced, what contradiction could there be with another [factor] regarding that which perishes of its own accord?
Furthermore, the destruction of a moment is not produced by another,
because it is impossible for there to be both an arisen and an unarisen state simultaneously;
for that which is unarisen and non-existent, what could there be that is opposed to it, or what could its destruction be?
That which has arisen at its own time cannot be destroyed, because a moment is immutable;
yet at any other time it does not exist at all—of what, then, could there be destruction?
If it is argued that it is the destruction of the continuum (*santati*), [we reply:]...

It does not exist apart from that, because there is no such thing as a "continuum" (santati). But surely, the destruction of a continuum is precisely the obstruction of the succession of subsequent moments?
That too is incorrect:
if the cause exists, how can another [factor] be obstructive? Or if the cause does not exist, how can another be obstructive?
(277) If there is a cause for the arising of the subsequent moment, how could there be an obstruction?
Now, if it is argued that the *kiṃśuka* trees are naturally red by divine nature,
or if it is argued that the deficiency of the cause itself is produced by the opponent,
that too is incorrect.
For if there is a deficiency in what is non-existent, how can there be "redness by fate" in the *kiṃśuka* tree? And if there is a deficiency in its own form in what is existent, what will it do?
(278) If there exists therein a cause for non-deficiency, how can that [cause] be non-existent? Or, if there is no cause that produces non-deficiency, then it is deficient by its very nature. (279)

For even the deficiency of a cause occurs only when the cause of its non-deficiency is present and its capacity is absent; in that case, what could an opposing factor do? To this, the response is: the production of one cold [moment] from another cold [moment] occurs without fire as a cooperative condition; but upon encountering a cooperative condition, that which was not cold becomes the cause of heat. (280)

For the preceding cold touch, acting as a cooperative cause for the fire that is being kindled, produces a progressively weaker and weaker cold sensation until it reaches a point where it no longer generates another instance of cold touch; at that stage, because the cold touch ceases of its own accord and because there is an absence of causes for another [instance], it does not arise again. Thus, fire is designated as the "remover" of cold by way of producing a defective causal complex for the cold; since its production is rendered incomplete by that [fire], it simply does not arise from that point onward.
Its cessation is designated as having the characteristic of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*);
for causes operate toward production, not toward cessation.
Alternatively, coldness possesses an inherent nature determined by its own cause, by virtue of which, in the presence of fire, it does not produce its own subsequent moment of effect.
For the powers of entities are indeed restricted;
if it is asked how two contradictory things can coexist in one place, the answer is that such is precisely their contradiction, as otherwise it would be impossible.
Nor is there a contradiction between two moments, but rather between two continuities;
for it is observed that even while one is experiencing heat, there is still the conscious experience that "the cold has not yet departed," and likewise,
"the thick darkness has not yet departed."
If it is argued that darkness departs at that very moment when an extremely clear light arises, we say no;
for even in that case, because the capacity to produce another instance of darkness exists within the cause accompanied by that [light], it is the light itself that arises, not the darkness.
If it is argued that "it is precisely that which has perished," we say no, because it has arisen in its own essential nature.
By whatever nature it arises, by that very nature it does not perish; and by whatever nature it does not arise, likewise it does not perish.
Therefore, it is not that very thing which has perished.
[Objection: Is it not the case that non-perception itself is destruction? And since that very thing is not perceived during the state of destruction, how can there be the cognition "it is this"?
When it is perceived, it has not yet perished;
when it has perished, it is no longer perceived. It is perished precisely because it is not perceived.
If it were perceived otherwise, what would be the meaning of "destruction"?
If that which is no longer perceived is destroyed,
then the location where the jar was perceived would also have to be destroyed.
If it is argued that "that which was previously seen but is no longer perceived is destroyed," we reply:
that too was indeed previously seen;
yet, being unperceived at the very place where it was seen, it is said to be destroyed. To say that it is perceived at that same time and yet unperceived at that same time is a contradiction.
If it is argued that [the cause] is not perceived immediately after [the effect] at a later time,
then why is it not considered destroyed when it is not perceived immediately after [the effect] in another location?
T.
If it is not seen from another location, then that very thing has perished;
if it has not perished at another time, why has it not perished at another place? If there is no pervasion by another place, then surely what of another time? (282)

If it is argued that nothing at all can possibly extend across different locations, then that very thing has not perished; likewise, it cannot possibly extend across different times either—how then could it have perished?
Indeed, even if it is not perceived in another location, how can it be said to have been destroyed when it is being perceived in this location?
If it is argued: "In that case, just as with a different location, how can something perceived at another time be said to have perished,
given that it is not perceived at that other time?"— this objection applies equally to both cases.
Therefore, whatever entity is perceived in a certain way, it does not exist otherwise than that; for blue is seen as blueness and is not found to be whiteness. (283)

Therefore, it is not that very same thing which has perished, but rather another [thing] which has not arisen due to the absence of a cause; when that [other thing] is not perceived, there is merely the conceit that "it has perished. Consequently, in such a case, the determination of contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is merely conventional.
In the ultimate sense, contradiction is simply a specific state of being a cause;
contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion is likewise such that whatever produces a momentary nature is incapable of producing an eternal nature.
Therefore, just as non-arising itself is the very nature of permanence,
and likewise impermanence is [defined] by that permanence, so too are qualities such as blueness and the like [defined] in relation to one another; thus, there is no distinction between these two.
And just as impermanence is unmixed with permanence—
[meaning that there is no distinction between these two opposites in terms of their mutual contradiction from the perspective of ultimate reality]—
therefore, contradiction is simply the state of being mutually distinct by virtue of their respective causes.
And that [non-apprehension] is simply the nature of the object itself, for otherwise it would lack its own nature;

and since that apprehension of the two as distinct from each other's nature is, in relation to something else, precisely non-apprehension, the entire conventional usage regarding non-existence proceeds solely from non-apprehension.
Thus, while the formal application (*prayoga*) varies everywhere, the underlying meaning does not differ. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.90)

Thus it has been rightly stated that there is no contradiction regarding supersensible objects; therefore, neither the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) nor mere non-perception (*anupalabdimātra*) serves as a proof for non-existence.

The mere fact that something is not perceived does not mean that it does not exist; for only one whose vision encompasses the existence of all knowable things would be justified in speaking thus. Even then, that very person remains unrefuted as being omniscient, as well as [the existence of] the next world and so forth.
Since there is a lack of evidence for the claim that "it is not perceived by the All-Seeing One," and since evidence has been stated for the opposite case,
therefore—
Just as a real entity alone is considered the means of proving other entities, so too a real entity alone is the negator of entities in its own cessation.
Just as a real entity alone is the proof of an entity by virtue of an invariable connection (pratibandha), [so it is in the case of negation].

In whatever way it may be, a thing that is not related cannot establish another thing; likewise, only a real entity (vastu) can, through its own cessation, cause the cessation of another entity. For, without a necessary connection (pratibandha), the cessation of one entity does not bring about the cessation of another entity.

Just as an effect establishes its cause and a pervader [establishes] the pervaded, so too the absence of a cause establishes the absence of the effect, and the absence of a pervader establishes the absence of the pervaded;
otherwise, that very relation of necessity (*pratibandha*) would not exist.
This is the nature of the necessary relation: it consists in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and there is no other such relation.

By this, the property (dharma) such as "being either the subject or one of its similar instances" (pakṣasapakṣānyataratva), which is merely projected by conceptual construction and could occur anywhere, is refuted.
For "being either the subject or a similar instance" is not restricted to either the eternal or the non-eternal in any single case.
For a thesis is indeed made by choice, and that which is a similar instance (sapakṣa) according to that [choice] is likewise [subject to it];
thus, because it is bound solely to one's own wish, it does not lead to the cognition of a real entity.
For that which is bound to something else does not cause another thing to be understood, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor does it function in any way that would lead one to conclude its absence;
for even that [absence] has the status of being a subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of being intended as such.
Therefore, the property of being "one or the other of the similar instances" (*sapakṣānyataratva*) is not a probans.
Likewise, because it lacks a counter-example and so forth, the establishment of affirmation and negation arises from that very [logical] connection (*pratibandha*);
in that regard as well, a pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) is held to be the indicator of cessation.
If the cessation of the pervaded [probandum] itself is somehow delimited,
then surely even the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is indeed a means of cognition;
this is not so.
In that case, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no relationship between the signifier and the signified;
rather, it is simply the non-perception of that which has attained the conditions for perceptibility.
Therefore, by means of that established [non-perception], the absence of the pervaded is proven.

To claim that the non-existence of a means of valid cognition (apramāṇatā) is itself the logical mark (liṅga) for that [non-existence] is intended for those who are utterly deluded; for this [absence] is undisputed even among cowherds. This very absence is what is called "the non-perception of intrinsic nature" (svabhāvānupalambha).
This is well known even to cowherds and women;
however, the Sāṃkhya, deluded by his philosophical perspective, is being enlightened:
this conventional usage of "non-existence" elsewhere is caused solely by this much.
Otherwise, the distinction between pleasure and so forth and the selves would not be established.
If it is argued that the distinction is established solely from scripture, we say no.
Because they are both authoritative,

there would be no mutual distinction between the difference [of objects] and the treatise [that establishes it]; and that very perception of mutual distinctness is itself the non-perception of the other.
Furthermore, the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest cannot be established without perception; [it is established] through the perception of their mutual difference.
And that very non-perception in the case of absence has this much as its result: the determination of difference.
And that [non-apprehension] occurs when the cause or the essential nature (svabhāva) is considered visible though it is invisible;
thus, non-apprehension is of three kinds— of the cause, of the pervader (vyāpaka), and of the essential nature—

and it is the non-apprehension of such a cause and so forth, which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta), that is the indicator, and not that of anything else, nor otherwise.
Therefore, the inferential cognition produced by the non-perception of the effect or the essential nature is a non-erroneous indicator that establishes the probandum;
consequently, it is the real entity itself that is established as such, and not a property of a non-entity. [Objection:
But is it not the case that the application of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) to impermanence occurs in the form "sound is impermanent"?
How then [can it be said] that "from the application [of the reason], there is the apprehension of the universal of color," and so forth?
This is not so;
for it is accepted that the apprehension of impermanence and other such properties occurs through inference.
Validity belongs only here and not elsewhere, because it is considered to be the apprehension of what has already been apprehended.

For, having apprehended the phonemes and so forth through their own specific and general characteristics—namely, as being "indesignatable" (*avyapadeśya*) and "phonemic" (*varṇatva*), and as being impermanent—the mind synthesizes [this] with the thought, "the phonemes and so forth are impermanent.
As it was stated by the Teacher: [101]
In this regard, the following sequence is described by [the verse] beginning with "from the application, the commonality of color" (*Pravāraṇa* 2.79):
once impermanence has been established regarding the generality of "color-ness" (*varṇatva-sāmānya*) through inference, there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
By what means is that common substratum (sāmānyadharmī) apprehended?
If it were apprehended by inference, there would be another substratum in that case as well, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, when the cognition of the non-sign (aliṅga) occurs subsequent to perception, it must be a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara) indeed.
Because it is connected with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
the rebuttal applies in both cases;
indeed, there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*) in that instance at all.
Since both [the universal and the particular] are established through perception itself,
and because conceptual cognition apprehending a universal grasps what has already been grasped,
how could impermanence be established by perception?

Since there is no impermanence other than the absence [of permanence], that [absence] is already established prior [to the perception]; and it cannot be said to be manifold through the senses. Rather, the property to be expressed is born of conceptual construction.
Indeed, impermanence, color-ness, and so forth are not distinct from the nature of the non-existence [of their opposites]; that very nature of non-existence is such that,
because conceptual thought lacks the capacity to grasp it in its true form, it becomes a universal (sāmānya).
The operation is merely one of apprehension, and that is not a universal.

For in the conceptual construction "this is blue," there does not appear anything other than the form appearing in the direct perception as "this is blue"; rather, that very same thing is designated in such a way.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the universal is grasped by the subsequent cognition as being exactly as it was in the prior cognition—namely, that "this is blue just as that [prior object] was blue"—then it is simply the case that what was already grasped is being grasped again.
That too is incorrect,
for no other universal (sāmānya) is perceived apart from the preceding and succeeding forms;
rather, it is that very [entity] which, being designated by that [term], is called a universal.
And that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the basis for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
Now, as for the mutual difference and multiplicity of universals such as impermanence and their possessors, it is said in response to this:

That which consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be said to have multiple forms; for the distinction [of objects] arises solely from the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādivāsanā*) within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Since conceptual construction functions by superimposing distinction through the imagination of positive concomitance and negative exclusion based on the difference between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), when the substratum of a universal is not established, that universal itself is indeed not established.

If that [particular] is not established, then for the sake of establishing this very inference, an inference proceeds; for it is merely a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). And when the object of conventional usage—the universal—is established, convention is necessarily established either through co-referentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) or otherwise.

However, when a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is not established, that usage is brought into the scope of memory by demonstrating its cause—that is, by recalling the causality of what was previously forgotten as the cause of that usage.
Therefore, inference establishes only the mere conventional usage and nothing else.
The commonality [of the two] is not perceived;
or rather, there is only grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

Through recollection, the non-existence of the object is presented as a category; however, the many lines following this do not exist in the Tibetan translation. Indeed, from the inference based on the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), it is the entity itself—such as fire—that is established, not the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
That too is incorrect;

for even there, if a real entity is established by means of inference, then once it is established in all its aspects, no other means of valid cognition—such as direct perception—would operate with respect to that very thing.

If a real entity such as fire is established through inference, then when there arises a desire to know a specific internal distinction regarding that fire, such as "What kind of fire is this?", another means of valid cognition like direct perception would not function.
Since its establishment in all its aspects occurs through the very first inference, [the following are considered]: possibility, impossibility, and contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, "possibility" means that an effect arises from a capable cause.
The impossibility [of a cause] is defined as the non-arising of an effect in the absence of its cause;
furthermore, the contradiction with valid cognition (pramāṇavirodha) is exemplified by the statement "fire is cold.
In that regard, possibility (sambhava) consists in the apprehension of all aspects through direct perception (adhyakṣa).
Non-occurrence [of the reason] by means of inference and contradiction with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-virodha) [constitute the defects],
because of the operation of another means of valid cognition.
This is merely the manifestation of darkness (ignorance), because:

"How can there be the apprehension of a thing when it is both non-existent and contradictory? If such a thing were apprehended, these two [contradictory] states would result, which is illogical. (285)

If, because it is impossible to abandon a form that is non-different from that [object], and because it would contradict the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no apprehension of all aspects, then there is likewise no apprehension of the object itself. For how could there be a non-apprehension of what is non-different from that which is being apprehended?
Indeed, it is not logical that the very same thing is both apprehended and unapprehended.
Likewise, cognition too may be both apprehending that [object] and not apprehending it; thus this [distinction] is also impossible.

Furthermore: "Even if there were a cause for the apprehension of all aspects, the inferential mark (liṅga) would not [establish it] because of deviation; for while the universal is non-deviant, the particular is unestablished. (286)
For a logical mark (*liṅga*), when apprehended as common to all individual instances, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to any specific instance.
If there is no such apprehension of generality, then the capacity of the logical mark is impossible; since the reason is inconclusive, how can there be an apprehension of the real object? (287)

It is not known which specific fire is here; rather, only "fire" in general is perceived, in the form "some fire is here. This perception follows from previous observations of various fires and is merely conceptual, lacking contact with the actual object.
If there were contact with the object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could doubt regarding its particularity be possible?
But surely, how can there be attainment when there is doubt?
Even attainment is merely in accordance with doubt, since for some person, attainment occurs only occasionally.
Therefore, even in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), there is merely conventional usage and not the establishment of a real entity.
Now, it might be argued: "In the case of the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the real entity is indeed perceived;
but how can there be the attainment of what is unperceived in the case of the effect-reason?"

The attainment of an object does not always occur simply because it has been seen, for that object exists [as a reality]; however, for those seeking it, there is the cessation of that thing even when it is an error.
(288) Indeed, although there is no seeing of [non-existent things] such as hair-tufts and the like, nevertheless, for those who seek them, there is indeed the occurrence [of activity].
The determination is that where [the reason] exists, there is the presence [of the probandum], and not elsewhere; however,
in the case of an essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*) or a perceived effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), the object is not grasped,
because that very [object] would then follow everywhere, even where it is not grasped.
For an object that is yet to come into being (bhāvin) cannot be attained, nor can its own nature [be apprehended]; how then could it be grasped?
If it is argued that it is grasped precisely in its future form, [we reply: no.
Not so, because it is not perceived as such;
yet, it is nevertheless perceived in its future form.
If it is argued that even so, what is perceived as one thing could not have an origination different from that, because the perception [of the object] is the perception of the universal (*sāmānya*),
then how can there be the apprehension of the particular (*viśeṣa*) within the perception of the universal?
If it is argued that [the existence of the object] is established because [the mark] persists, [we reply:
no, for a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist as something other than the particular (*viśeṣa*).

In that case, smoke and the like, as a logical mark (*liṅga*), do not exist as something other than the object; therefore, its existence is known from that very [mark]. What, then, is the use of a universal? Without the cognition of a non-universal [particular], how could one act?
It will proceed toward activity only when there is the cognition of the *liṅga* (the mark);
for if there were cognition of something else, how could there be activity toward another?
Since the universal (*sāmānya*) is likewise something else, the same fault applies.
If the universal is not absolutely distinct [from the particular],
then these preceding lines [of the commentary] do not exist in the Tibetan translation.
If there were apprehension of the object only in its general form, that would indeed be its apprehension; such being the case, how could there be doubt regarding what has already been apprehended?
(289) If it is argued that there is apprehension in the form of the universal and not in the form of the particular, then how does one act toward the particular form?
If it is argued that even that [object] has already been grasped, then for what purpose does one act?
If it is argued that it is for the sake of attainment (*prāpti*), [we reply:]...
But surely that attainment (*prāpti*) is also just the cognition of its own nature; if that too has already arisen, for what purpose does it proceed?
If you say, "It proceeds because there is cognition in one form but not in another," [we reply:
it does not proceed in the form in which it is cognized, because that would be redundant.
And by that [means] through which one is not [able], there is no incapacity; nor is there doubt regarding what has been understood.
Nor does it apply when [the object] is not apprehended, because doubt consists in the contact with two forms;
for if one were to argue that since the general and the particular are of a single nature, it would therefore proceed even when the particular is not apprehended.
[It is] not [the case],
because it is impossible for that which has not been made an object [of cognition];
nor has it been established that there is identity between what is apprehended and what is not apprehended.
One perceives the identity of what is being approached; one does not perceive it without perceiving it.
Nevertheless, one perceives it at a later time.
It has been established that at another time, there is neither perception nor inference.
Now, if a thing is apprehended in its entirety because it is non-eternal, how can it be designated as "inferable"?
And if it is so designated by way of being a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
why does that very [apprehension] not become a definitive certainty (*niścaya*) consisting of such usage?
This is not a superior argument,
because that non-cognition occurs in some cases due to the arising of something similar.
For one who does not perceive the difference due to delusion, it is like [the perception of] the difference between illusory balls (māyāgolaka).
Indeed, it is not that the difference in the illusory balls is not perceived;
nevertheless, because they are similar, there arises the cognition "this is that very same thing," and thus no practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding their difference occurs.
Now, even if the recognition "this is that very same thing" is erroneous, the act of seeing itself is nonetheless non-erroneous; so why is there no cognition of difference?
If it is argued that the recognition, being suppressed, is effectively as good as non-cognition, we reply:
there is no such thing as suppression between two cognitions that are both self-aware of their own intrinsic natures.
Since the two exist by way of mutual exclusion, it follows that there is a mutual annihilation of the two;
for if concealment is established through mutual exclusion, then the state of mutual exclusion is equal for both. || 290 ||

Just as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being by nature the self-awareness of its own form, excludes experience because it is distinct from it, so too would experience exclude conceptual construction.
Alternatively, for one whose mind is intent upon their identity, the cognition of difference simply does not arise.
If that were so, there would be no experience at all; what, then, would be the purpose of its denial?
To this it is replied:
Because of destruction, one does not perceive the object as distinct from its prior state, and because of the determination of its permanence, one thinks of it as being indeed eternal. (291)

The previous perception of the object has already passed; therefore, at present, it is merely that which is to be engaged with in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and since that usage is eternal, how could this past perception negate it? However, at that time, there was a contrary conceptual determination (*viparītādhyavasāya*).
Therefore, it is that very [reality] which causes the world to function;
consequently, the "negation" of that [reality] is simply the absence of functioning in accordance with it, because [the two] are not perceived as distinct from one another.
Therefore, because the second and subsequent moments cannot be perceived as distinct from one another—just like a ball of illusion—the conventional expression "this is that very same thing" arises;
for even a child, observing a lamp or the like whose subsequent arising is not connected [to its predecessor], perceives it as perishing. (105)

Surely, the destruction of a lamp and so forth is indeed perceived as a distinction in the eyeball and other parts through analytical investigations; however, momentariness is not established in this same way.
That too is incorrect;
for it is designated as "non-abiding in that state," "destruction," and "impermanence."

Furthermore, it is not the case that lamps and the like remain in a state of absolute identity; rather, each successive flame of the lamp is produced by successive supplies of oil. However, due to similarity or because they arise from the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there arises the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that "this is that very same [lamp].
If it is argued that this entire mass of lamp-flames is produced by the oil all at once as a single entity, that too is not correct.
For if it were produced merely from the first convergence [of causes], then its continued existence over time would be useless, since [the cause] is already exhausted thereafter. Indeed,

the mere convergence of the initial causal complex of oil and so forth does not, in the case of a lamp or similar object that has come into being, somehow nourish the purpose of its subsequent persistence on the surface of the stand through the continued conjunction of the oil, the wick, and the flame.
If it is argued that because its nature is independent [of causes],
even once produced, it persists through a period of time— just as oil and so forth continue to exist and not otherwise— the answer is no.

Since production occurs precisely as a persistence through a period of time, nothing at all could be done by the subsequent causal complex of oil and so forth for that which does not persist through a period of time; thus it would be futile. If something else were produced, that itself would constitute impermanence.

And likewise, if this [object], once arisen, is apprehended in its entirety by the eye and other [senses], then its apprehension in its entirety means that the continued operation of the eye and other [senses] is indeed useless;
or else, it would have to be through successive perceptions or through an apprehension of its persistence over time.
That being the case, because there is a disjunction between successive acts of seeing, there would be no apprehension of duration over time by even the first [act] alone.
Furthermore, if the act of apprehension itself possessed duration, it would apprehend [the object] all at once; thus, it follows that the subsequent following of the eye would be useless.
Therefore, since the act of seeing does not apprehend even the slightest bit of the prior and posterior natures [of the object], only a mere moment appears.
Thereafter, there may also be [the use of] balls, cotton, oil, and so forth.
That very nature of the object, devoid of prior and posterior [parts], would become extended;

but that is impossible, for if it were perceived all at once despite its temporal length, then everything would be so. It is only through the continuity of perception that temporal extension is cognized. (293)
In whatever manner successive perceptions arise in a continuous series, in that very manner one understands the long duration [of time], and not otherwise;
nor is it understood that time is long through a single simultaneous perception.
Therefore, perception understands only momentariness.
If momentariness itself, as an inherent nature, is determined by perception, how can there be delusion even while it is being determined?
To this, it is said:
even though the capacity is an inherent nature of the entity, it is not seen in its result.
Delusion arises from a lack of immediate succession due to the lack of proficiency in determining [the cause].
Indeed, just as a potency (*śakti*), though delimited, is not determined by one who does not perceive its immediate effect,
the formulation of inference is for the very purpose of eliminating that [delusion].
Those of great intelligence determine all aspects [of an object] from a mere glance.
Even upon seeing an entity in its totality, one who lacks practice is deluded;
therefore, there is no certainty.

[The author] removes [this objection] by means of a non-breaking thin space (*tato vyāmohavyāvarttanāya*). Inference proceeds for those who possess causes of certainty, such as proficiency through repeated practice; however, those of great intelligence are capable here [of understanding] from the mere observation of a determination (*adhyavasāya*) alone. Therefore, when the locus is established, the universal is indeed established, provided that there is no delusion regarding it.
But where there is delusion, there inference [is required].
How, then, given the oneness of the object, can a plurality of properties be established by conceptual constructions that follow it?
For a conceptual construction following the experience of blue does not have the nature of determining yellow.
To this, the following reply is given:
Since that [object] is excluded from everything else, cognitions—based on those exclusions—operate upon the object as if they were distinct, even though the object itself is not divided. (108)
Just as they were designated, he naturally connects those manifestations with their corresponding names when no cause for error exists;
for all things born in the world possess exclusions from both similar and dissimilar classes.

From whatever [particular] they turn away, from that very [particular] they are perceived as possessing various properties (*nānā-dharma*), having taken up each respective substrate (*upādāna*) whose differentiation is constructed by the distinction of limits (*avadhi-bheda*).
If entities are excluded from everything, how is it that there is no certainty regarding all exclusions at once?
We reply: because of the presence of causes of error (*bhrānti-kāraṇa*).
Because of the forgetting of what was previously seen;
for there is no certainty of exclusion when that which was previously seen is made an object of cognition in exactly the same way. To explain:
*ldog-pa'i-mtshams-tha-dad-par* 3.
T.

For at one and the same time, there is the ascertainment [of an object] and the arising of a memory of what was experienced exactly as it was. Otherwise, there would be error; when [the experience] is firm, there is certainty, whereas when both are wavering, there is doubt.
(294) There is no absence of the ascertainment of a memory that accords with what was experienced.
This alone is the certainty: that recollection occurs in that very manner,
and because it is recollected in that same way through repeated practice, therefore for those possessing such practice, certainty arises immediately after the perception itself.
Otherwise, it is established that inference exists for the purpose of precluding recollection; another, however, says:
"Or rather, here too, destruction is established through the non-perception of a logical mark."
For all entities are connected with arising and passing away;
arising is established by direct perception and inference as a positive proof, while passing away is non-existence,
which is established by non-apprehension.
Whatever negation there may be, it is all to be established through non-apprehension;
there is no other means for establishing negation.
But surely, eternality, being of the nature of a positive entity, is perceived by the very same means of valid cognition that establishes its existence?
This is not so;
impermanence does not arise from intrinsic nature alone,
but rather—

For a thing that, having existed previously, no longer exists, is called "impermanent. That which, having come into being, does not continue to exist is impermanent, not merely by virtue of its coming into being.
And that non-existence serves as proof of non-perception elsewhere as well.

[Objection: From the perspective of mere existence (*bhāvamātra*), is it not the case that for this proponent, impermanence is simply existence—which mediates between the two extremes—and not characterized by non-existence?
And since both ends—the prior and the posterior—exist, their non-apprehension cannot be established through a middle [term]; how then is this so? To this, he says:
For whom the scripture on impermanence expresses existence delimited by both ends as being related [to those ends], by him those two [ends] are remembered as such.
Regarding those tantras of the Great-Minded Ones (*mahāmatitaṃtrāḥ*):
existence (*sattā*) alone is not impermanence, because it would follow that even the self (*ātman*) and so forth are impermanent;
rather, impermanence must be described as an existence that, without distinction, occupies the middle between both extremes for form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and the rest.
Furthermore, there is no transition to non-existence without the absence of both extremes;
and in that transition to non-existence, it is grasped through the non-perception of existence, not by any other means.
If there is non-existence both before and after, why is that itself not impermanence?

If it is argued that existence (*sattā*), which encompasses both prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), is impermanence (*anityatā*), then why is that very non-existence not accepted as impermanence? [If you say] "because of the impossibility of a sixth case-relationship," then how could that [non-existence] exist at the two extremes? (112)

If the intended meaning were that "impermanence belongs to an entity" (*bhāvasya anityatā*), then there could be no connection expressed by the genitive case and so forth; for if impermanence were non-existence (*abhāva*),

there would be no relation because there is no connection between an entity and non-existence, since a relationship characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like is impossible.
By what can the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified be prevented? If it is argued that even this [relationship] would not exist, then how could it exist in the case of the two ends?

(295) If, even in the case of the relation between qualifier and qualified, it is not accepted without a relation such as inherence (*samavāya*), then how is that connection expressed by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or the relation of qualifier and qualified established for the two ends—whether by "existence" (*sattā*) or by "being" (*bhāva*)? For in the formulation of the statement, "existence is the separator between the two ends" and "it is qualified by that," [the problem remains].
Because existence (*sattā*) and its relation are eternal, they cannot be distinguished by their two ends;

for if it were stated that "existence" or "the relation of existence," characterized as inherence (*samavāya*), is impermanent, then one would necessarily have to admit that existence and its relation are qualified by their two ends,
and this is not tenable.

Since both [existence and the entity] are admitted to be eternal, how could existence be qualified by an end? If it were subject to arising and passing away, then either that [end] would not exist in that entity, or the relation of existence with it would not exist; if it is thus not qualified by those two, then that very entity, being so qualified, is itself impermanent—what is the use of existence?

If it is argued that the genitive case would not occur because there is no distinction [between the two], then how could there be such an expression as "the existence of existence" (sattāyā astitvam)?
Furthermore, what [is the point]?
The impermanence of an entity consists in the prior non-existence and the non-existence through destruction of that entity; these two alone constitute impermanence.
Because it is distinct from them, there exists a case-ending expressing distinction (*vyatireka-vibhakti*).
Alternatively, it refers to the state of having both ends for cause and effect.
"Cause" is one extreme, and "effect" is the second.
By means of these two—cause and effect—no qualification of either existence (*sattā*) or its relation has been stated.
Furthermore, the relation between cause and effect is the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which, in the case of existence, is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).
The response here is as follows:
1. On the right side of the hole in the palm-leaf, the name of the owner of the book is seen—namely, Dānaśīla.
2. Right there it says: "Is there no existence here?"
This is not illogical.

If cause and effect were terminal [entities], then the relation between cause and effect would be characterized as "being" (bhāva), and the relation between existence (sattā) and the entity (bhāva) would be characterized as inherence (samavāya); thus, there would be no distinction between them. (113)

Because there is no connection [between the entity and its prior non-existence], he does not accept that prior non-existence of an entity; for when that [non-existence] is designated by means of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), neither those [adjuncts] nor this [prior non-existence] are established. For indeed, the prior non-existence of something is connected with its own cause.
Furthermore, a relationship between an entity and its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is not admitted;

for if such a relationship were admitted, then prior non-existence and destructive non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva) themselves would constitute impermanence, which would result in the abandonment of the original position and the adoption of an alternative thesis.
Therefore, there is indeed no relationship between an entity and its prior non-existence.

This specific designation is conditioned by antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); in the absence of that [non-existence], this effect would not exist, nor does a cause exist without an effect. Alternatively, there is no absence of the causal relation through any other manner.
Since existence (sattā) is the cause because it effects its connection with its own causes, and both that existence and that relation are eternal, what then is the effect here? 115
For a cause [is so called] by virtue of bringing about the connection with existence (*sattā*), and its own cause [is so called] by virtue of bringing about the connection with its own cause;
moreover, an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is that in which the substance inheres, for a thing generally possesses origination when it inheres in an inherent cause.
Furthermore, there is no status as an effect (*kāryatā*) in either the connection with existence or in existence itself.
Even for an entity, its status as an effect must be established through a relation with existence (*sattā*), and not otherwise;
for if its status as an effect were by its very own nature, it would not be so.
That whose non-existence would be produced is not an entity possessing prior non-existence;
because no relation is admitted [between them], this entire universe would consequently be eternal. (116) For there is no relation whatsoever between any entity and its prior non-existence.
Even if there is indeed no connection because of its non-substantiality, nevertheless, since that [connection] was previously non-existent, it will then possess the status of being an effect.
But surely, that which lacks a connection due to its non-existence is itself non-existent.
Otherwise, everything would be non-existent; consequently, it would follow that there is a relation with prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*),
yet this is not accepted.
Consequently, since the entire world is eternally attached [to its objects], how then can there be a connection with non-existence?

Therefore, even in the case of words intended to have identical referents, the cognitions—which serve as the basis for differentiation—possess distinct denotata that transcend the [apparent] object. (117)
Whether the object is distinct or non-distinct, in every case the relation is merely a mental construction.
If one asks: "If a thing is distinct from another thing, what is the relation? Is it not simply their distinctness itself?"
If it is granted that [the probans] is distinct [from the probandum], what relation could there be? Since distinctness is the same in all cases, there would be no relation at all.

If it is argued that the relation is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), then what connection could there be between two distinct things, or even what causal relationship could exist between two non-distinct things?
And if [the cause] exists as something distinct from the other [the effect], how could they be joined when they are not conjoined?
Indeed, there can be no relation for that which is non-different, because a relation resides in two things; thus, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would not exist.
But why should the relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) not exist?
It is not so,
because in that case the relation has a conceptualized object as its domain;
for it is established that since the two related terms there are conceptualized, there can be no relation characterized by identity when they are distinct.
If it is argued that this is the relation of cause and effect, what indeed is this so-called causality?
If it is said to be the state of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekitva*), [then...]
Not [is it perceived],
because it is imagined and because it is not apprehended through direct perception.
Therefore, all this is merely constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*) and is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Consequently, this use of the ablative case of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) functions by relying on some kind of relation imagined in any way whatsoever; there is no other mode.

Thus, even in the case of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, the relation of an entity is conventional (*saṃvṛti*), not ultimate; for in the ultimate sense, nothing has a relation with anything else—this is the definitive conclusion.

Therefore, because it involves the synthesis [of perceptions] regarding the generality of color, there is no separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as there is no separate object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore,
since there would be the consequence of non-termination in the case of repeated recognition— just like memory and so forth—
repeated recognition is indeed nothing other than that which is being remembered.
Objection: Since it conforms to the operation of the sense faculties and is non-contradictory, how can recognition (pratyabhijñāna) not be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)?
No,

because the operation of the sense faculty has as its object only that which is present; if it has only the present as its object, how could one act on the basis of the thought, "This is that very same thing"?
This is not so,
because a discerning person does not act on the basis of the thought, "This is that very same thing."
However, it does not function as the cause for the attainment of the desired fruit merely by being based on the operation of the sense organs and because of future correspondence;
even though it is indeed that very same [object], nevertheless, it is not the object of engagement.
For the activities of discerning persons have as their object the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Nor is that very [entity] itself to be accomplished as purposeful action; for entities, possessing powers dependent upon their own causes, bring about either that [action] or another purposeful action, not by virtue of being the locus of identity.
Furthermore, the connection with purposeful action is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is merely the recollection of what was previously perceived.
And by virtue of performing that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), that very same thing is the object of the cognition "this is that," not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

If it were apprehended previously as something already seen, then [the present cognition] would be mere recollection; however, in the case of this synthesis, it is inference, because here too there is the fitness for that purposeful action.

The conventional usage of "oneness" arises from the metaphorical attribution of non-difference; furthermore, even its non-contradiction does not have oneness as its object, because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is achieved despite plurality.
As for [acts such as] approaching those who should not be approached, these occur precisely because they are produced by that [continuum], and thus depend upon the continuum.
Therefore, perception does not have the universal as its object,
nor does inference have the particular as its object;
for is it not the case that inference based on the observation of a particular (viśeṣadṛṣṭa) recognizes that very same particular?
That too is incorrect,
because there is no recognition of specific qualities due to their difference at every moment;
nor does it have specific qualities as its object, since they are grasped through the similarity of the perception.
Indeed, when fire has been seen and is later inferred from smoke after it has receded and an obstruction has occurred,
that very same particularity is not recognized at a different time, because of the possibility of successive differences;
and since difference exists, the cognition through the superimposition of unity takes only the universal as its object.
In that case, where there is no possibility of difference in the nature of a stable entity due to the absence of modification,
how is it to be understood that there is the recognition of that very same particular?
For there is no certainty that a modification cannot occur when it is not being perceived;
moreover, if it is observed in other cases as well, then, by analogy with what is observed, the cognition would be of another individual instance rather than having a specific object,
and thus the example itself would be a non-apprehension of the universal.
Since it is already established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it serves as an illustration (*nidarśana*), what further need is there for another?

If that very same thing is the illustration because it was established by a previous perception (*pratyakṣa*), then since it has already been grasped by that prior perception, what further purpose is served by another means of knowledge—namely, inference (*anumāna*)?
In this case, inference is of no use.
If the very same prior perception is already established by its grasping of existence at the time of the inference based on the observation of particulars, what is the use of inference?
For it is held that inference operates upon that which is not the object of perception, and not upon that very [object] itself.
If it is argued that for this very reason it is "inference based on perceived particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), let it be so; however, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, if it is held that only an object existing at the same time as the perception is apprehended, and not any other, then inference directed toward a future object would indeed be a valid means of knowledge.
If this is so, there is another illustration: that which was previously perceived as the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) is later perceived through inference;
thus, it has indeed been grasped, but merely forgotten.
Therefore, he says that this is not a fault:
"No."
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the example] has been forgotten, then for that very reason it is not a valid illustration;
since that which was forgotten is remembered again in the same way through the medium of the logical mark (*liṅga*), inference is not rendered useless.
How then can that which has been forgotten serve as an example?
For a proof proceeds by means of an example; if that [example] is forgotten, how can it be an example?
If there is a recollection of this incomplete thing as an example prior to the logical mark (*liṅga*), then what else remains to be done here by the logical mark?
If you say, "That very thing is remembered again," [we reply:]...
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.
If, however, that [inference] is forgotten, then it cannot serve as an example.
