Now, if one were to suddenly apprehend fire from smoke even without an example, then the other [fire] which was forgotten would also have to be apprehended from its inferential mark (liṅga).

In that case, since it would be apprehended by the very same prior perception— which pervades all its constituent parts throughout time— how could it possess the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for one who does not perceive any distinction [between the two cognitions]?
[This occurs] by way of the cause.
If it is argued that, when there is recollection of what is undifferentiated, conventional usage occurs therein;

For instance, even when a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) has been apprehended in its entirety, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when there is such conventional usage; this is because,
in that case, the fitness for conventional usage is established precisely through similarity with another observed example.
But it is not so here, because [the object] has long since ceased to exist and no further practice arises; thus,
even the claim that "this has been seen" is not tenable, as otherwise the existence of the entity would be possible.
It is certainly not established that this is a memory of what has already been grasped, because there exists the state of being ungrasped.
For a form that terminates at its own time is grasped by perception; otherwise, it would be grasped until death, and thus death would occur at that very moment.
If it is argued that it is grasped continuously until death—

By means of a long [perception], there is the apprehension of the long; by means of a short one, the apprehension of the other. Yet, at that very moment, there is no apprehension of it up to its limit of death through direct perception. Therefore, since that which does not persist does not encompass an interval of time, how can inference proceed based on what has been apprehended as a "perception of the particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭam*)?
How is it that this very same illustration involves the apprehension of what is not common?

If it is argued that when something is seen at one time, the establishment of its existence at another time—due to its connection with that other time—is the proof of its being that very thing, then this is indeed a case of "inference from the particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*). To this it is replied:

If the establishment of existence in a different object is based on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what was seen [previously], [then it is not a case of inference from the particular]. (120)
If there is a superimposition of reality [upon what is not real], there is error; because that [superimposition] is established, [the cognition] lacks validity.
Now, if you accept that even when something else is seen, it is later proven to be "this very same thing," then that superimposition of reality upon what is other than that is necessarily an error.
For reality cannot possibly exist as something other than what was seen in its true nature;
and when [the object] is not being perceived, it is only possible to superimpose the form of what was previously seen, not to grasp the reality itself,
because that previously seen object was grasped by the previous cognition precisely as it was, unmixed with any other form.

If it is argued that although it is not perceived [by direct perception], it is nevertheless grasped by inference as being exactly that and not otherwise—this is not so, because inference follows upon a prior apprehension; inference is nothing other than mere recollection. Alternatively, if inference were of the nature of grasping a real entity...
Then, because of the identity of perception and its opposite, there would be the establishment of both by a single [means].

(121) If perception and its opposite were one and the same form, then, since it would be established by a single means of knowledge— whether perception or the other— the other would become non-authoritative, because no specific distinction whatsoever would be produced by the other.
Then, in both cases, there would be either a cognition with a clear form or one that is otherwise;
for if clarity arises from the operation of the eyes and other sense organs, then lack of clarity must likewise be dependent upon them.
This is not the case;

if this clarity of manifestation were tied to the eye and other [senses], then light would be entirely useless for the apprehension of form. If, on the other hand, clarity is produced by light, then how could inference—which occurs when light is present—be a non-clear manifestation?
If it is argued that this is because light is occasional,
then even though light exists in the ultimate sense, it is not perceived;
how, then, can there be the apprehension of an object?

If it is argued that there is no fault because one perceives the mere object devoid of light, then to claim that one perceives what is devoid of light while it is accompanied by light is sheer audacity;
if that were so, it would simply be the perception of a universal, and thus this would not be the "perception based on a particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*).
The wise know that when one [cognition] is being connected with another, it is a determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*) and not memory;
for if it were memory, it would depend upon a sign (*liṅga*), and because it does not so depend, it is not memory, as there would otherwise be an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).
Moreover, even that which depends on a tallinga is merely a synthesis (anusandhāna) of what was previously perceived.
At that time, there is no apprehension [of the object] by way of its distinct intrinsic nature; rather, it is merely memory.
For when there is a single form, nothing more is cognized by perception than by inference; thus, it is indeed memory, and not the grasping of a real entity.
If it arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*), how can it be recollection?
This is not so;

for it does not possess the nature of a logical mark according to your own view, because—due to the absence of the three features (*trairūpya*)—there is identity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*).
In our position, however, it has been established that this is indeed an inference whose object is a universal;
for that which was previously cognized is not the "grasped" (grāhya) when it is being remembered,
because it is not perceived as being currently grasped.
For inference is not something other than remembrance; rather, it is simply remembrance arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) that constitutes inference.
Therefore, that by which [the object] is cognized repeatedly is nothing but remembrance.
How, then, is there the cognition "it exists now"?
Present existence is understood solely through the power of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*);

that smoke existing in a particular location is produced by fire existing in that very same location—this is precisely how the prior relationship was grasped through the awakening of beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*).
This being the case, it is established that all inference is indeed nothing but recollection (*smaraṇa*).

Because there are two kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*), there are two kinds of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); namely, through the distinction between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
This is because there is no other mode [of cognition] apart from the distinction between direct and indirect apprehension.
4. Examination of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣacintā*):
(1) Refutation of Misconceptions Regarding the Definition of Direct Perception.
In that regard,
perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.
In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* composed by Dignāga,
conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the non-apprehension of the appearance of a thing as connected with qualifiers and so forth.
Appearance otherwise is error;
therefore, perception is free from both [of these].
Is it not the case, however, that error is understood through perception itself by virtue of seeing things otherwise?
But how can there be freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatā*)?
For inference, which is preceded by perception, does not find an occasion for its operation in the absence of the latter;
and every cognition arises precisely through the influence of words.
Therefore, how could perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) which is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) understand the non-conceptual nature of the self?

Even for one in whom an initial non-conceptualizing awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) first arises, the emergence of a conceptual cognition occurs through the convergence of the causal complex consisting of memory and other factors;
and that [cognition], by virtue of the operation of the sense organ, is indeed perception itself.
How is its non-conceptual nature established?
To this, the reply is:
perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself.
The conceptual construction (vikalpa) of all [beings] is to be personally realized within oneself and is dependent upon names.
Perception (pratyakṣa), which is free from conceptual construction, is known through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) alone.

For conceptual construction indeed generates a name, and a name also generates conceptual construction; that conceptual construction, being dependent upon names, is experienced through personal realization.

Because conceptualization is experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as something distinct from what is seen by the eye and other senses, there is indeed a difference between the cognition of conceptualization and other cognitions due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).
Furthermore, the claim that this [conceptualization] is always of the very same nature as that [non-conceptual perception] is also not the case.
For, having withdrawn all thought from every side, even when one stands with an inward self made motionless, the cognition born of direct perception still beholds form with the eye. (124)

If the eye does not function at all when devoid of the causal complex for conceptualization—such as in the state where conceptualization has been withdrawn or when another conceptualization is present—it would not be a grasper of objects. Therefore, in that state, the cognition appearing as free from conceptualization is indeed known through direct perception itself. Now, if it is argued that "there is no associated conceptualization in this [cognition]," then how can that state be one devoid of conceptualization? How could there be such a cognition at all?
Now, if there is indeed no conceptual construction (such as the relation of container and contained), then how can there be the cognition "this is non-conceptual" at that time?
For there is no linguistic convention without conceptual construction,
and one cannot be made to understand another without employing such conventions.
Otherwise, even if things were momentary, what would be the use of a "reason based on essential nature" (svabhāvahetu) that effects conventional usage?
To this it is replied:
you have again entertained some such conceptual construction.
Thus one does not know [the object] through the senses in the previously mentioned state;
nor does one know [it] thinking, "This is my conceptual construction."

Indeed, a conceptual construction does not arise for him [the proponent of non-conceptual perception] in the form, "This is non-conceptual," as it does for the other; otherwise, even for one who maintains that perception is conceptual, as long as the ascertainment "this is conceptual" has not arisen, how could there be the conventional designation of "conceptuality"?

Consequently, even for the conventional designation of conceptuality, another conceptual cognition must be sought, and for that yet another, leading to an infinite regress and thus a failure of comprehension.
Now, if it is argued that this [perception] is itself conceptual (*savikalpaka*), what need is there for another [conceptualization]?
Since even non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) has the nature of being a cognition, what is the use of a conceptualization? This applies equally to both.

Furthermore, if it is argued that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs later regarding the conceptual, such as "this is conceptual," then in that case too, one who subsequently reflects [on it] concludes that there was a succession of such conceptualizations; this linguistic usage does not occur in the state where conceptualizations have been withdrawn.
In that regard, [one might ask]: "How can there be a conventional expression such as 'I had non-conceptuality' if it was not being expressed at that time?

Furthermore, how can there be a conventional expression of 'dead' regarding one who is dead, given that [the state] did not exist at that moment? [The answer is: It is through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that there is conventional expression regarding what was non-existent then, just as there is the conventional expression "dead" regarding one who has died.

If it is argued that otherwise one could not explain how even a conceptual cognition is designated as "conceptual" because of the repeated perception of its subsequent members of the same class, we reply: here too, repeated perception during the state when conceptualization has been withdrawn is certainly not precluded.

Therefore, because of the difference in their characteristics and because they exist as mutually distinct entities, there is no identity between the conceptual and the other [non-conceptual] cognitions.

If it is argued that, due to the presence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), a conceptual cognition arises as something entirely different from the non-conceptual one, while in the absence of that [complex] the non-conceptual arises— this is inconsistent.

If the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is imagined [to be distinct], then because blue and yellow are distinct, this collection (*samudāya*) must be something else entirely, due to the conceptualization that "this has arisen.
For in that case, a different collection of blue, yellow, and so forth has arisen there, owing to the occurrence of a distinct intermediate causal complex.

Now, if it is argued that because of recognition—since the cognition "this very same blue has appeared, and not another collection"—there is no difference between them, then the conceptualization of difference is equal for both of these imagined forms.
Therefore, perception is indeed non-conceptual;
nor is this [conceptualization] the causal complex for sensory cognition being conceptual,
because the sense organ is engaged in the apprehension of the object.
Furthermore, an object perceivable by the senses cannot be associated with a word,
because the word lacks the capacity to denote it;
for linguistic convention does not apply to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If it is asked why this is so, given that the universal is not perceivable by the senses, he says:
"For a difference observed in one place is not seen elsewhere."

Therefore, there is no other universal distinct from that [particular], because there is no difference in cognition. For a particular does not persist across space and time; since a thing seen in one place is not seen again in another, or by another means of perception, it lacks existence at a different time. Indeed, an entity delimited by its own time is what is apprehended through direct perception.

If it is argued that, therefore, perception does not first apprehend the prior [moment] in the subsequent [moment], nor the subsequent in the prior, but rather recognizes them through perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by grasping "this is that very same thing," we say no.

Because recognition is not a form of direct perception, there is an absence of sensory operation therein; for the activity of the sense organs occurs toward an object situated in a suitable location, not toward that which has passed away or is yet to be; and the consciousness dependent upon them does not pertain to what exists at another time. (300)
For the pervasion of time and space is not grasped by sensory cognition;
if it were so, everyone would be a seer of all forms.
Furthermore, if the sense organs do not operate with respect to the past and the future, what contradiction is there for the cognition that depends upon them?
If the consciousness dependent upon that [eye] were to function with respect to the past and so forth, then the eye itself would also have such a function;
yet there is no function of the eye other than its own,
nor is the operation of the eye perceived in the apprehension of what precedes and follows.
If it is argued that because recollection of the past and future and inference occur [in the same way], the activity of inference is simply the activity of the sense faculties,
we shall demonstrate that this would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that inference, too, is perception.

If it is argued that, because of this, the universal— which is the commonality of particulars— is not something grasped by the senses, but rather that which is the commonality is what is grasped by the senses, that is incorrect.

Since there is no other universal distinct from that [particular] due to the non-difference of cognition, there is no persistence of individuals, nor indeed of a universal, because of its very absence.
The state of being individuals does not constitute their commonality,
nor is there a commonality of the universal; since that [commonality] is not perceived, and because it lacks existence, the possibility of a commonality being grasped by the senses is non-existent.
For a universal does not appear here,
because no other form appears; and if there were no distinction [from the individuals], it would be the individuals themselves, and they are not recurrent.
For this very reason, the universal is neither different, nor non-different, nor inexpressible;
therefore, every cognition born of the senses has particulars as its object.
It is impossible for words to function with respect to particulars. (127)

Because particulars lack positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) does not apply to them; for when that which possesses positive concomitance appears [in cognition], it is not of the nature of a universal,
nor do words function with respect to a particular, since convention cannot be established due to the absence of positive concomitance.
For a convention is sought by those engaged in worldly affairs for the purpose of facilitating communication across different places and times; otherwise, it would result in nothing but frustration.
If it is argued that it is for the sake of dharma and artha, who indeed would accept such a thing?
Therefore, the operation of a convention is not restricted to specific places and times.
Therefore, a particularity is not the object of words;
rather, that which is the object of words is precisely that which can be associated with them.
Consequently, there is no grasping of an association for that which is devoid of particularity.
Therefore, a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*) does not apprehend a particular (*viśeṣa*);
and that which is conceptual does not apprehend a particular,
because it associates the universal (*sāmānya*) with a word.
He asks "Why? and replies:
"For the relation 'this belongs to that' exists only between those two objects that appear [in cognition]; at that time, it is not within the range of the sense organ. (129)

Even when an object is perceived, the relationship characterized by the denoted and the denoter belongs only to those two things—the cognition of which arises in the consciousness that establishes the relationship—namely, "this is the denoter of this" or "this is the denoted of this. At that time, it is not within the range of the sense faculties; for why?
What is the meaning of "this is the denoted of this"? It means that "this is to be understood from this."
By what means of cognition [is it known]?
Is it by a conceptual cognition of an imperceptible object, or by a direct perception that is immediate?
If it is to be cognized by a direct perception that is immediate, [then...]
Otherwise, the collection of the sense faculties would result in futility.

If [it is argued that the relation is established] through indirectness (*parokṣatayā*), then there can be no relation with an object that is currently within the range of the sense faculties, for at that time such an object is not present before the senses.
Alternatively, even when the object resides in the denotable and the word itself, the relation is established by thinking, "this is the designator of this."
For in that case,
since the object appearing clearly is not perceived [as distinct],
it is indeed the difference in the appearance within consciousness that distinguishes between entities. (130)
For an object within the range of the sense faculties has a clear manifestation,
whereas an object that is remote has an unclear manifestation;
and even when there is a difference in manifestation, there is no identity [of the objects].

Now, if cognitions have the same single object despite a difference in their manifestation due to distance or proximity, how can there be a distinction [between them] based on that difference in manifestation?
[If you say it is] because of a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), [we reply:
even if there is a difference in causal efficiency, it is merely a difference in manifestation; a difference in distinct effects is not the defining characteristic of distinction.

For there is no distinction of the cause based on a distinction of effects unless it is produced by a distinction in appearance; yet, if you argue that a distinction in appearance certainly exists, then let the distinction arise from that alone—what is the use of a distinction of effects?
Moreover, if the distinction of the cause arises from a distinction of effects, then from what does the distinction of the effect itself arise?
If [the difference is] due to another difference in effect, there is an infinite regress;
if it is due to a difference in appearance, [then...]
Therefore, let the distinction among causes also arise from that very [appearance]; what is the use of a distinction among effects?

Furthermore, if there were a distinction [among causes] even through a distinction in their activity, it would be that same distinction in appearance which constitutes the differentiator, because only that which has a clear appearance performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

If it is argued that, therefore, the indistinct appearance of an object situated at a distance does not have a real entity as its object— since there is no contradiction [with reality], they must share a single object— then that same [lack of contradiction] exists for inference as well; even in that case, the distinction [between them] arises precisely from the difference in their appearances.
Therefore, difference arises solely from the difference in appearance.
When, with eyes wide open, one establishes a convention for such an object, then the word will have a real entity as its referent; in that case, there is a definitive determination.
Even when the object appears to the eye, that which one declares to be beyond [the senses]—
M.
[declares] "by the eye, the appearance of the object..."
That very [object] is connected with words, for it is certainly not within the range of the senses.
(131) Even though there may indeed be an appearance of sound, a jar, and so forth, to the eyes and ears, nevertheless, no connection exists merely through the appearance of their own forms.
That which one expresses by means of a case-ending denoting separation—namely, "this is the designator of that"—is precisely what is excluded.
Furthermore, the meaning of a case-ending does not appear in direct perception, because only the meaning of the nominal stem appears; rather,
the meaning of a case-ending is exclusively an object appearing within conceptual construction.
For indeed, the relation expressed by "of this" does not occur without the state of being the beneficiary and the benefactor;

therefore, since at times the word arises from the object which is the domain of cognition, and at other times the object resides within cognition arising from the word, the case-ending occurs by relying on a relation characterized as cause and effect between the cognition and its manifestation. Furthermore, mere appearance in direct perception is not the sole cause for establishing a relation.
Furthermore, because [the cognition] occurs even in the absence of that [object],
if the convention were applied to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) appearing to the eye and other senses, then only that [particular characteristic] would appear.
And it is not so,
because for one whose senses are not engaged, there is no investigation by means of mere subsequent speech.
Because of the non-apprehension [of the universal];
yet, it might be argued:
even if there is no convention regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), what contradiction is there in that very thing being the denotable object?
"And there would be the consequence of [the object] being known by itself without a previously established relation.

(132) On that very point: if the convention pertains to the word-meaning or to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how is it that there is a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) in exactly this way? If this is asked:
To this he replies with "na ca" and so forth:
therefore, sensory cognition, being indeed inexpressible, cognizes that which is unrelated and is thus non-conceptual (avikalpaka).
How then is this conceptual cognition, such as "this is a cow" or "this is a snake," perceived as having a clear manifestation?

It cannot be said that the conceptualization exists here as something separate [from its object], because no other cognizing subject is observed; nor is the object of this conceptualization imperceptible.
Because it would follow that there are two distinct appearances, one clear and the other otherwise;
and even if it were previously manifested, for one who does not conceptualize it,
there is no difference in its status as an object of apprehension at the time of conceptualization.
And how could there be a grasper who does not establish a distinction regarding the graspable?

That too is incorrect, because a distinction is perceived through its being either determined or undetermined. How can it be said that there is no distinction here? It is not the case that what is seen is untenable. (301)
If it is argued that what is being perceived cannot be the object of negation because conceptual cognition is non-existent, that is incorrect.
How is the unreality of the cognizer established? Because it is conceptual, [you argue]. Then let that same unreality be asserted even for non-conceptual cognition;
for it is not the case that something is unreal simply because it is conceptual, since otherwise it would follow that non-conceptual cognition is also unreal.
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not [perceive the object] because it is non-conceptual, this is equally true even for conceptual cognition; thus there is no distinction. Furthermore:
How can there be direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) if [the object] is unreal? For indeed, in the absence of conceptual determination (*niścaya*), it might be considered unreal;
but when there is a direct realization of a determined form, how can there be any suspicion of unreality?
If it is argued that this determination is inferential (*ānumānika*), then that is not so, because it cannot be an inference since its object is immediate (*aparokṣa*).
Since the distinction between means of valid cognition is established solely on the basis of the distinction between their objects,
and since the absence of the convergence of means of valid cognition has been demonstrated,
all of this [your argument] is incorrect.
Because the mind functions simultaneously with both conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions, or due to its rapid movement, the deluded person determines them to be one and the same. (133)
This is its meaning:

if indeed a non-conceptual [cognition] (*avikalpa*) were to consist in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of phonemes such as "g" in the word "cow" and were inclined toward the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it would be logical to say that this single cognition is a conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). However, since the apprehension of the form of the phoneme is a cognition in which the phoneme appears indistinctly—arising from the awakening of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā-bīja*) brought about by the force of previous perceptions—it is entirely different from perception, which is the cognition in which the pillar standing directly before one appears clearly; for in that case, conceptualization is impossible.
That very cognition is indeed perceptual;
how then can there be a determination of oneness?
There is none at all.
First of all, this cognition "this is a cow" does not determine the oneness of the individual cow Śābaleya and the phonemes *ga*, *a*, and so forth,
because their difference is understood through the difference in their appearance. Furthermore,
since the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the phonemes *ga* and so forth arise sequentially, they lack oneness.

Furthermore, the cognition that has the appearance of color (*varṇāvabhāsa*) is not the very same as the one that takes the brindled cow (*śāvaleyāvalambana*) as its object, because [the latter] appears even in the absence of the former; moreover,
since that appearance of color also appears when the eyes are closed,
appearing even in the absence of [the object], it is of a non-ascertaining nature.
If it is argued that "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is the "particular" (*viśeṣa*), then what is this so-called ascertainment?
If it is argued that it is the clear manifestation of form (*rūpa*), [we reply:]...
Not even before [the cognition], let alone at the time of its manifestation; for if it were to manifest as something prior, it would be nothing other than another indistinct form of that [object].

If it is argued that when one thing appears with a different form, how can there be a determination of another, since that determination is a determination [of the former] through the determination of their identity—
then how can the determination of identity be valid for two things appearing as distinct?
How, then, does the conventional usage of "oneness" proceed? It is simply because a single effect exists that,
by virtue of its being a single effect, there arises the determination of its oneness.
How then is it that there is no apprehension [of the object] sequentially?
It is simply because the objects are present simultaneously;
for at the time of the conceptualization of the phonemes, the perceptible object is not absent from its presence.

Just as for you, who hold the view that cognition is momentary, there is a determination of sequential apprehension due to the proximity of objects, so too is my apprehension; thus, there is no difference between us. [Objection:
But if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs elsewhere [than in the object], why does its expressed form (*vācyarūpa*) not appear indistinctly?
[Response: If you say that it has no other object at all, [we reply: no.
If, then, it is without an object because its object is unestablished there, then [the objection that] there would be an interruption of vision due to being separated by that [object] does not hold,
because there is no separation.
For it is not possible for there to be no temporal simultaneity nor the possibility of an intervention;
furthermore, T. 1.
Because there is no external object, it is determined that [the cognition] is therein [without an object]. (nirviṣayastatra...)
...in the case of an intervention...

If it is argued that perception becomes interrupted by the intervention of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then how could this be the case for one whose conceptualization belongs to a different class or for another person?
For one for whom even conceptual cognition is itself direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), there is no such interruption.
For that [cognition] cannot be obstructed by itself;

if it is argued that for one who maintains the existence of non-conceptual cognition, conceptualization is indeed something other than it and thus constitutes an obstruction, [we reply] provided that a conceptualization of a different genus is possible.
How could there not be the perception of another object?

For this conceptualization, which belongs to a different genus, does not possess the nature of a perceptual cognition for the other [person], because of the absence of conceptualization regarding the form being seen;
yet, there certainly is a distinction here.
However, because the non-perception existing in the interval between the two perceptions is overridden by the stronger [perceptions], it does not obtain its own functional operation;
therefore, there is an uninterrupted determination,
which is equivalent to that [perception].

For, if the position of existence is considered strong like the perception of a whirling firebrand, then that same [objection] applies elsewhere as well; or else, there would be a simultaneous hearing of the two phonemes. (135)

If the side of existence (*bhāvapakṣa*) is strong, then even in the case of a conceptualization of a similar kind, there is no interruption at all because it is the same for one who maintains that [the cognition] is non-conceptual; thus there is no fault.
And this was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position], yet an interruption is not possible.
For it is not because of rapidity that there is a cognition of non-intervention even when there is intervention;
for if it were due to rapidity, there would follow the consequence of hearing even two distinct phonemes as a single unit when they are uttered quickly, yet this does not occur.
Therefore, rapidity is not the cause for the apprehension of non-intervention here, even in the case of sequential order.
If it is argued that there is no such lightness (lāghava) in that case, and therefore there is no reason for its repeated mention here because lightness does exist here,
[we reply]: "Because of the non-simultaneity of the two minds' activities"—
this will be demonstrated later.
If it is argued that the cognition of simultaneity would not otherwise be possible, we say no;
for simultaneity itself exists.
In that case, let there be simultaneity even in the piercing of a hundred lotus petals; what is the use of postulating a sequence?
For in that instance, a sequential arrival at the locations is not apprehended by inference.
If it is asked: "Since there is no inference for that here, how can there be a conceptualization of succession? And what is the cause for the conceptualization of non-succession?
[The answer is: It is manifestation itself, which is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
No other means of proof is observed that directly manifests [the object] more clearly than this;
as for what was previously stated—
that "lightness" (lāghava) alone is the cause for the simultaneous hearing of phonemes— that does not exist.
Regarding this, it is said:
although all objects are simultaneously in contact with the sense faculties here, that cognition which appears as if unobstructed even when there is an obstruction by five [elements]— 136.

That cognition appears as if interrupted because it is mixed with momentary cognitions that have no limit; therefore, that variety [of objects] exists. Consequently, let there be simultaneous cognitions for one who holds the view that cognitions do not arise simultaneously.
But where there is a simultaneous determination of existence, there is no other cause for that determination than rapid occurrence; because of its swift operation, such a determination arises.
Regarding this, it is said:
[The opponent asks: "But surely, even when phonemes are pronounced rapidly, there is indeed lightness (*lāghava*); why then does it not occur [in that case]? [The author replies:

"In this case as well, there is a lightness even more minimal than that, wherein there is the simultaneous convergence of the five objects and the sixfold nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)."

Just as for one listening to a sweet song while tasting all the flavors from the mouths of fragrant, lovely women, there is an absence of extreme rapidity in the mind because it is interrupted by each of those five objects at once, yet there is still the appearance of simultaneous apprehension; so too it would be with respect to the phonemes.

For if, even when there is an intervention of five [moments], there is the capacity for the swift determination of [the object] as a single unit, then why should this not occur when there is an intervention by momentary cognitions whose objects are the phonemes?
Therefore, it is logical that cognitions arise simultaneously; otherwise, the contradiction would be impossible to resolve. Thus, this [conclusion] is established.
Furthermore, since simultaneous occurrence is equal [in both cases],
how can there be no difference in appearance between that which has an interval and that which is without an interval?
And when mental conceptualization is pure, there would be no apprehension of succession. (138) This is not tenable. (T. de mi rigs te = tadaṃyuktam)

[The cognition] is sometimes powerful with an interval where there is an intervention by a cognition of the same class, and sometimes without an interval, being uninterrupted by a conceptualization of a different class.

How do those two cognitions, with intervals and without intervals, come to be? If there is no distinction between appearance and mental conceptualization, then in that pure continuum, appearance would not be successive, because it occurs with extreme rapidity.
Now, if cognitions were to arise simultaneously—
How could there be a lack of apprehension even when an object is present?
To this, the reply is:
that non-apprehension occurs in some cases because the mind is attached elsewhere, even though the object is present.
This objection applies to both [theories], because of the incapacity [of one cognition] to produce another due to its being occupied elsewhere.

For when there is the possibility of being occupied elsewhere or of a deficiency [in capacity], that cognition does not become the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), even when all other conditions for the arising of consciousness are present.
The objection applies equally to both [theories]; however,
because the mind is restricted to a single object at once, let there nevertheless be the determination of simultaneous perception.
If it is argued that wherever there is no great attachment, [the cognition] necessarily occurs [simultaneously], we too say this:
where there is attachment, there is sequential apprehension; elsewhere, it is simultaneous.
However, there is no proof for the claim that sequential apprehension occurs in all cases;
nor is there any other object of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from a consciousness preceded by the mind.
[Objection: Even if sequential apprehension is possible when [simultaneous] perception is not obtained, simultaneous appearance is nonetheless possible.
This too is not true;
for that cognition does not arise through a synthesis of elements appearing in succession,
but rather there is indeed a simultaneous appearance therein.
For,

because it occurs with such rapidity, the visual perception of a whirling firebrand and the like produces the illusion of a circle that obstructs the perception of its continuity; it does not do so through the joining together of successive visual perceptions.
For it is due to the sequence of the rapidly revolving moments of the fire-brand that the eye, being thus affected, produces the cognition of a circle;

this is not a cognition of the mind [itself], owing to the strength of the objective side. If, however, even here—in the presence of the five objects—the simultaneous appearance is merely an illusion, then in all cases a simultaneous appearance must be considered illusory.
If it is argued that this is indeed accepted, we say no;
for there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its being erroneous.
For the simultaneous appearance [of cognitions] is indeed perceived through non-erroneous direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Even though it is perceived in such a manner, if it were erroneous despite the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), then this consequence would apply to all cognitions. Therefore, since there is no subverting cognition, it is established that the fivefold group of consciousnesses (*vijñānapañcaka*) is indeed simultaneous when apprehended at once.
Therefore, perception is indeed non-conceptual;
now, having set forth the opinion of others, he refutes it: some [hold that] because it arises from the sense faculties and so forth, it is non-conceptual like the cognition of an infant.
The foolish say that the cause for conceptualization is the dullness of linguistic convention (saṅketa).

Others say that perception is non-conceptual because it arises from the sense faculties, because it proceeds in the form of direct experience, and because it is not mental—just like the sensory cognition of a child.
And the sensory consciousness of a child is non-conceptual because of its incapacity to grasp linguistic conventions.

For those children who speak thus, there would be nothing but direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they lack conceptual construction (*avikalpana*) and are devoid of the means of linguistic convention (*saṅketopāya*); even later, that [conceptualization] would not exist for them.
(142) For those children who speak in this manner, there would indeed be only direct perception.
Let it be granted that everything for an infant is indeed admitted to be non-conceptual;
nevertheless, even for an infant, there certainly exists a reflection upon what precedes and follows in relation to purposeful actions.
If such reflection does not exist, then subsequently, too, there ought to be no conceptualization by means of thought.
Because there is an absence of the means for grasping conventions—
since the grasping of conventions occurs through conceptual construction, and that [conceptual construction] does not exist for the infant— then...
If it is held that the mind exists even when the linguistic convention has not yet been mastered;
M.
[notes]: *mano'vyutpa* (mind not yet mastered).
The same would apply to that which is dependent on the sense faculties; and this remaining point is as follows:

(143) if even for infants there exists a deliberative [consciousness] fallen within the range of mental activity, then, because of their grasping of conventions through that, the mind subsequently possesses conceptualization.
If this were so, then even that which arises from the sense faculties would be conceptual; and once it has become conceptual, by what could it be prevented?
Furthermore, since sensory cognition is incapable of grasping linguistic conventions for an infant, how [could such conceptualization arise]?
If it is argued that [the cognition] is so because it is produced by the sense-faculties, we say no,
because there is no necessary connection.
Moreover,
even if it were the case that the non-conceptual sensory cognition of an infant functions in this way in all instances, how is this known?
For the probative power of a reason is never observed without the establishment of a connection through a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), nor without an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, as for that [cognition] born of the sense faculties, because it grasps only what is immediately present, it is devoid of reflection upon the preceding and the succeeding; thus, it is not conceptual.
But how is its state of being devoid of reflection upon the preceding and succeeding established?
Since direct perception lacks the preceding and succeeding [moments], and that which is non-direct-perceptual is not perception.
In that case, the argument "because it is born of the sense faculties, like the cognition of a child" would be redundant;
for non-conceptuality would be established by perception itself,
since there is a specific experience of direct perception through the senses.
Otherwise, if perception were never a means of establishing non-conceptuality, how could an inference following upon it proceed? Therefore,
because they engage in mental discourse, conceptual investigation exists for the foolish.
Now, if the infant’s cognition has the mode of direct perception, and other sensory cognitions are likewise of that same nature,
then let the very same proof that applies to the infant be stated here as well.
Because of the similarity between the cognitions of the dice, he has stated [the following] regarding experience and so forth:

since direct perception is not observed in the case of an object that is remote (*parokṣa*) but is observed elsewhere, it is established in a general sense that perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) because its object is immediate (*aparokṣa*). What is the use of reasons such as "being born of the senses" (*indriyaja*)?
Furthermore, that direct realization is described by means of its non-conceptuality.
Since non-conceptuality sublates conceptuality, whatever is a direct perception is pervaded by non-conceptuality;
therefore, this is the apprehension of a pervasion by the contradictory.
Alternatively, direct perception is established by means of non-conceptuality.
Furthermore, if perceptuality is established as direct realization by virtue of being non-conceptual, then perceptuality would also belong to the cognition of a double moon and so forth; therefore,
it must be stated that [perceptuality] exists "provided there is non-erroneousness."
If it is argued that "non-conceptual" must simply mean "erroneous," then what is the point of its being non-conceptual?
It need not be so.
Because a qualifier depends upon the perspective of another,
it has been said accordingly:
"In a definition, a qualifier depends upon the perspective of another."
All cognitions are indeed non-conceptual and all are indeed non-erroneous; that they are non-conceptual and non-erroneous has been established by the Master through the method of negation.
Alternatively, it is *pratyakṣa* because it occurs in relation to the *akṣa*;
by that, direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is apprehended.

Therefore, all cognitions (*pratyaya*) that function in the form of direct realization are indeed non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). Or else, it is the *akṣa* because it reaches (*aśnute*) or pervades (*vyāpnoti*).

Furthermore, the pervasion of the object's own nature is nothing other than direct perception; therefore, all [cognitions] born of the senses are indeed free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).
Alternatively, the Teacher did not include the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition; his definition was simply "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
If that is so, how is erroneous cognition excluded?
Since every act of direct realization is perception,
even the cognition of two moons is indeed perception with respect to the duality that appears therein;
therefore, wherever something is directly realized, it is perception with respect to that.
For that [external object] is indeed an illusion,
because its conceptual nature is sublated by its being non-conceptual.
And since there is nothing else present as a direct perception apart from the form that appears, this [notion of another object] is merely a conceptual construction;
thus it has been said:
"Because they are objects of mental error, they are deviant."
Now, even regarding external objects, this conceptual cognition alone is true, for it is non-erroneous;
thus:
This is what the wise declare as having arrived through the force of the nature of things:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, they fall apart in that very same way"— as will be stated [in *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.209].
(2) Refutation of the Universal:
Furthermore,
[the cognition] of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation [arises] according to worldly convention.
Having grasped and synthesized this, one understands it as it is and not otherwise.

(145) Just as there is no connection with that which possesses [a universal] because the universal (*jāti*) and so forth cannot be determined through differentiation, so too there is no conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) here. (146)

For conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists in the synthesis [of attributes], and such synthesis cannot occur without the apprehension of each qualifier and so forth individually; just as in the cognition "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), there is no joining with that which possesses [the staff] because the genus and other qualifiers are not determined through their distinction [from the substrate]. Thus, how could sensory perception be conceptual? To explain: [The opponent argues: "But surely, even in the absence of the actual word, there is a conceptualization based on the recollection of the word, just as when one sees a firebrand wheel (*alātacakra*) or a painting. [Response: This is not so. For in those cases, there is indeed a conceptualization consisting in the synthesis of the object and its name, but this does not apply to sensory perception. Why? Because it is established that the conceptualization of the name occurs only through the recollection of the connection between the name and the object, and that recollection arises from previous experience. However, at the time of the first moment of sensory perception, there has been no prior experience of the connection between the name and the object, nor has there been any recollection of it. Therefore, since the conditions for the conceptualization of the name are absent, sensory perception is free from conceptual construction. Furthermore, the conceptualization of the object itself does not occur in sensory perception, because the object is not perceived as associated with a genus and so forth. Why? Because the genus and other qualifiers are not perceived distinctly [from the substrate]; and since they are not perceived, there can be no joining of the substrate with them. Consequently, sensory perception is devoid of conceptual construction. Moreover, if the genus were perceived, it would have to be perceived either as distinct from the individual (*vyakti*) or as non-distinct. If it were perceived as distinct, then the cognition of the genus would not be a cognition of that individual, just as the cognition of a cow is not a cognition of a horse. If, on the other hand, the genus were perceived as non-distinct from the individual, then the genus would be nothing other than the individual, and thus the cognition of the genus would not be a cognition of the genus. Therefore, the genus is not perceived. Since the genus is not perceived, the qualifiers such as the genus are not perceived. And since the qualifiers are not perceived, there is no joining of the substrate with them. Thus, sensory perception is devoid of conceptual construction. For what purpose, or by what means, could there be a synthesis (*yojanā*) of that which has an undivided appearance? And the synthesis of that which has a divided appearance is not supported by experience.

For if there is an undivided appearance, it is simply one; what need is there for synthesis therein, since synthesis depends upon two [distinct] things? On the other hand, if there are two with divided appearances, then because they appear as mutually distinct, there can be no synthesis at all; thus, synthesis is impossible.
Therefore, let there be no ultimate synthesis,
even if the qualifiers and so forth appear individually.
And this [distinction] is not possible for the universal (*jāti*), the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*), and so forth;
nor do the universal, quality (*guṇa*), or action appear as distinct from their possessors.
Therefore, if it is argued that "conjunction" (*yojanā*) is simply the appearance of things as conjoined;
If it is argued that this is so because there can be no appearance of a mixture between two distinct things, precisely because they occupy the same place and time;
Even for things existing in the same place and time, there is no [identity] because their intrinsic natures (svarūpa) are distinct;

for even in the case of things existing in different places and times, such an appearance occurs precisely because of the difference in their intrinsic natures, not because of the difference in place and time.
For if there were no difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) there, then even when there is a difference in location and so forth, there would be no appearance of difference;

yet even when there is no difference in location, a difference certainly appears to others between color and shape, as well as between wind and sunlight—thus, the appearance of difference is not lost despite the non-difference of location and so forth.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that the appearance [of identity] occurs through a state of total fusion (*ekalolībhāva*) by the power of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), then it would follow that one must assume such a state to exist everywhere.
Indeed, not every appearance of non-difference would necessarily be a proof of non-difference;
for this cognition, which consists of a synthesis, arises precisely from a qualified cognition such as "cow.
For a qualified cognition is never observed anywhere without both a qualifier and a qualified object, just like the cognition "staff-bearer."
"This is that" cannot be pointed out because it does not appear through discernment;
for even in the cognition "the man with the staff," there is no appearance of the staff through discernment.
If it is asked: "Since only the person itself appears there, why does [the cognition] not occur even before the connection with the staff? We say:
no.

Because there is an absence of distinctness by way of being the primary [attribute], and because no other distinctness exists in the person— since that is not perceived— it is the staff itself that constitutes the distinctness, just as in the case of [the expression] "the man with the staff."
If water and so forth were merely the auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) of the seed,
yet the cognition "staff and person" would still arise even when there is a manifestation of a staff, then all of this would be untenable.
If it were a mere appearance, it would not be qualified by non-cognition; however, in the case of an appearance, there could be "the staff and the man."
For just as in the appearance of a person alone there is no cognition of qualification, so it is also in the case of "the man with a staff.
Now, if it is argued that qualification consists precisely in being the object of a qualified cognition,
to this also it is replied:
A cognition would be distinguished by an intrinsic distinction, or [distinguished] by a distinction of the object of cognition; yet neither of these two [possibilities] is real.
(304) If, first of all, the distinction belongs intrinsically to the cognition, then there is no conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consisting of the joining of an object.

If it is argued that sensory cognition is not conceptual because of an internal qualification such as "pleasure" and so forth, and that this very qualification does not belong to the cognition in the absence of an object, we say:
no.

We shall demonstrate that the specific distinction [of the cognition] is established even from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). However, when the distinction resides in the object, there is the perception of both the staff and the person; how then can the cognition of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) have the person alone as its object?
That both are perceived is stated merely according to conventional usage, for it is not so in ultimate reality.
Because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) lacks an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*), if both were indeed objects, why would there not be a dual number?
This [dual usage] is merely conventional (*vyavahāra-mātra*); since it arises from the specific impressions (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*) of preceding moments, there is no fault.

Because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subordinate (*aprādhānya*), even though it is perceived, it is not intended to be expressed; thus, the singular number refers to the mere person (*puruṣa-mātra*).
If it is argued that by this reasoning [cognition] has only the person as its object, let it be so; however, this is not because of an absence of appearance.

Or rather, it might be that there is an appearance of isolation (kaivalya) characterized by space, time, and so forth; yet in that case, the qualified nature of the cognition is not unperceived. (305)

In that case as well, [the distinction] would have to be either a conjunction with another entity, an intrinsic nature, or a distinct characteristic. At that time, every opposing position is abandoned.
(306) If, first of all, "distinctness" means being accompanied by another entity—just as one is said to be "distinguished by ornaments"—[then...]
This [distinction] exists in that which appears to the cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth;
indeed, no other direction appears therein.
If, on the other hand, there were a difference in intrinsic nature (*vilakṣaṇatva*), then no such difference in intrinsic nature would be perceived between two jars situated in the east and west.
Furthermore, the unique particularity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object; thus, when that [nature] appears, there is necessarily non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*).
As for the status of being the object of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), that has already been refuted.
Therefore, this is the logical principle: if there is a synthesis (*yojanā*) upon the appearance of two [factors], then that is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Furthermore, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not merely the appearance of two [factors], but rather it is preceded by their individual perception and followed by their synthesis (*yojanā*).
[Objection: But surely universals (*jāti*) and so forth do indeed appear, since a corresponding cognition (*anvayipratyaya*) is observed.
Regarding this, it is said:

"Even though the inclusive cognition (anvayi-vijñāna) appears as the individual word-form, that which is intended by the term 'cowness' (gotva) is indeed devoid of the forms of color, shape, and phonemes. (147)

Even though it is identical, that very [object] is not perceived, because two appearances do not manifest within the range of the eye; furthermore, a distinction between cognitions is difficult to establish.
Indeed, that cognition which persists [through various instances] does not appear as a separate universal.
If it is argued that a form is perceived as following [the word], we say no, because nothing else appears apart from the manifestation of the sound itself.
If it is argued that a cognition with an identical form appears from the word, we say no;
for [the cognition] arises through recollection according to the perceived color and shape [of the object].
Nor does any other underlying continuity appear here,
because only the forms of color and shape appear; rather,
it is the mere association with names alone that persists across all things.
"This is a cow" and "this is also a cow"—thus the name is the same, as is the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Alternatively, it is only the conceptual cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) that is identical, not any external object. Or rather, that very indistinct form which arises from the word is the universal (*sāmānya*).
Because it is uniform everywhere, [it is not so];
for even that has the nature of a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
When the word "cow" is uttered, there arises the cognition of either a *śābaleya* (a spotted cow) or a *bāhuleya* (a brindled cow), and so forth; thus,
there is no cognition of a uniform form, because— as in the case of recollection following experience—
no such relation [of the word] with all [individuals] has been previously perceived by this means.
Like the word "cow" [applies] to nine meanings;
that is, like the application of the word "cow" to nine objects.

Now, since speech and so forth are restricted to specific objects, the apprehension of a convention is possible through the indication of those objects; however, if there were no restriction regarding the scope of the action and its grasping, how could there be the apprehension of a convention or the performance of it with respect to individual instances?
We shall explain this later.
Or, if that [object] itself remains the same, then there would be no seeing [of it as such] when it is within the range of the eyes;

for in a visual consciousness characterized by a clear appearance, there certainly does not arise the cognition "this is that very same thing" which has a dim appearance. If this is argued, it is not so.

Because unity is impossible for that which appears both clearly and unclearly, and because of the difference in causes— since [the cognition] is caused by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the eyes and other faculties—

therefore, there is no occurrence of two appearances within a cognition produced by the eyes and so forth. Now, if it is argued that this cognition appearing clearly and unclearly is indeed one and the same, even though there is a distinction between its forms and its causes;
In this regard, it is said:
if there were no distinction among cognitions even when there is a distinction in the causes of their appearance, then distinction would be difficult to find elsewhere as well;
for in all cases, the cognitions of perception and inference occurring at the same time would be one and the same.
But how is it that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is not perceived?
For there is no determination of universals (*jāti*) and so forth through their distinction [from the substrate],
precisely because of the existence of inherence.
This is not more reasonable,
because it is established that the relation [of inherence] is not perceived by the senses due to the perception of inherence itself;
since inherence is beyond the reach of the senses, its apprehension by the eye or other sense organs is impossible— this has been settled by you yourselves.
As for the claim that there is inherence (samavāya) because of the conventional usage "this is over those threads," this is not so; for:
These words such as "the cloth is here in the threads" and so forth are merely self-composed;

for indeed, there is no cognition of a cloth in the threads, nor of a cow in its horns and so on. Since such cognitions do not exist anywhere, how can there be an understanding of inherence (samavāya)?
For indeed, [it does not exist] in the threads.

In common worldly usage, one says "the horn of the cow" (*gavī śṛṅgam*), whereas the non-worldly usage "the cow on the horn" (*śṛṅge gauḥ*) occurs; for such cognitions as "the horn in the cow" (*gavi śṛṅgam*) arise, yet the dewlap and other [limbs] are not inherent (*samaveta*) therein.
Furthermore, that which is intended to be inherent in them is not perceived as being a substrate (*ādheya*).
Therefore, this cognition does not arise from inherence;
[this concludes] the refutation of the whole.
Moreover,
because no disjunction of the remaining parts known as "cow" is perceived,
the cognition [of "cow"] is indeed observed here even in the absence of inherence (samavāya).
Just as when one conceives of a tree as "the sun" at the time of sunset,
or when one conceives of a cow by means of its remaining parts, there arises the cognition "the horn is in the cow" because of the conceptualization of the horn as the superstratum;
for in that same way, there is no other "cow" apart from the collection of the horn and so forth, with which it could stand in a relationship of substratum and superstratum.
This is merely a conceptual construction;
yet it might be argued that the cognition "there is a cloth in these threads" certainly does occur.
This is not so;
the subsequent effect is said to be "this cloth [is made] by those threads," for it arises from the processing of the threads and can never exist simultaneously with them. (151)
For the word "thread" (tantu) refers to a specific state that precedes the cloth;
however, the specific state occurring at a time subsequent to that is the "cloth. Therefore, by means of those threads, this garment (śāṭī)—the effect existing at a later time—is designated.
But it is not simultaneous with the threads;
therefore, how could there be a relationship of substratum and superstratum?
For there is no relationship of substratum and superstratum between things that exist at different times.
Either there is only the relation of cause and effect, or else there is a lack of connection;
therefore, even the relation of locus and located is merely a specific instance of the relation of cause and effect,
since it depends upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*).
For such conventional usage occurs only between two things that share a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*)— namely, those regarded as the "container" (*kuṇḍa*) and its "contained" (*tadādheya*)—
since there is indeed no other state [of relation] than that which arises from the specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) of those two;
furthermore, even this conceptual construction does not exist in the case of threads and cloth.

Therefore, in whatever way one considers it, there is only conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) alone, and not a relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), because there is no difference [between them].
For indeed, in the state of being a cloth, the threads do not exist [as such].
Now, if there is no difference, since the threads are absent in the state of the cloth, how is it that there is this cognition "these are threads" and also "this is a cloth"?
This is not so;
for in that regard, from the perspective of ultimate reality, duality does not exist.
By superimposing the cause, or even by means of partial abstraction, one might apply the designation "thread" to the effect in order to demonstrate the basis for its verbal expression;
for the cloth is indeed the effect of the threads.
At that time, there are no threads;
rather, the cognition of "threads" arises through the superimposition of the nature of the cause, not in reality.
For it is thus: when there is a recollection of what preceded, the cognition "these are threads" occurs.
Or rather, it is by the exclusion of one [part] that [the cloth is perceived]; for when each individual thread is excluded, there is no other thing called "cloth" remaining.
It is those very threads, when aggregated like an army or a forest, that receive the designation "cloth."
If the cloth exists only conventionally,
then the relationship of support and supported is merely imagined;
if that is so, since there is no such thing as a "cloth," how does the word "cloth" function?
For words do not function without a basis;
in that regard,
the answer is either the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary or simply the perception [of the object], because there is no other connection.
The phrase "the basis for the designation 'cloth'" is an addition [to the text].
Here, the state of being beneficiary and benefactor refers to those very threads which are established in a mutual relationship of beneficiary and benefactor.

Alternatively, it is by virtue of a particular conjunction that [the threads], producing purposeful activity such as covering and so forth, come to bear the designation "cloth. Thus, their state of being mutual benefactor and beneficiary is designated as the "cloth. Furthermore, whereas the threads, in the absence of such assistance from the turban and other factors, can be easily separated from one another, the states of the cloth cannot; therefore, this non-perception of separation is the basis [for the designation]. Consequently, one should not postulate a separate entity based merely on the designation.
For designations are generally based on the conceptual construction of categories (*padārtha*), yet they frequently function otherwise. If,
then, there is no distinct basis for the designation, it would follow that the designation "cloth" could not be primary (*mukhya*).
Or, just as in the case of the designation "cow" applied to a *vāhīka*,

even though that designation is based on [qualities] such as impurity and so forth, it is a non-primary (amukhya) designation of "cow" because there is no universal "cowness" (*gotva*) distinct from those qualities;
likewise, the designation "cloth" would also have to be based on [qualities] such as the relationship between the benefactor and the benefited.
The response here is as follows:
That which is primary knowledge, unerring, and the object of the original convention; that which from the very beginning is the domain of the convention is the primary [meaning]. (153)
Because it is a non-erroneous cognition by virtue of having the primary convention as its object;
*paṭā* (cloth).

That which functions by way of the commonality (*sādharmya*) with the object that is the referent of a convention (*saṅketa*), through the superimposition of reality (*tattvādhyāropa*), is secondary (*amukhya*).
Because it is an object of a faltering cognition,
when there is an absence of a straightforward progression, there is a "stumbling" due to similarity by following after another thing to be placed [in its stead];
for that similarity does not exist without such following.
Therefore, there is no distinct object as the cause for words such as "cloth" based on a distinction between primary and secondary meanings;
rather, the proof for [the existence of] universals and so forth is through inference, as follows:
That cognition of a similar form occurs elsewhere due to a common cause, just as the cognition "one with a staff" arises from the very same staff [in different people].
For, although the men are distinct, there is a uniform cognition—"one with a staff"—caused by the common factor of the staff;
likewise, although the brindled cow and others are distinct, there is the uniform notion "cow," where the universal "cowness" (gotva) is the cause, just like the staff.
That [object] is unsurpassed;
for the establishment of a universal does not occur through inference.

Furthermore, there is no inference regarding a real entity that is differentiated by such things as genus (*jāti*), for the designation [of "cow" and so forth] applies everywhere even to conventional things like a staff.
If it is argued that the cognitions of "cow" and so forth apply to individuals such as the *śābaleya* by relying on a common conventional cause; [then the following applies].

This is merely a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because even in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), the staff is not the cause [of that cognition]; otherwise, everyone would be "staff-bearers."
Now, if it is argued that the relation exists because of [the cognition] "the related also is related," then this is understood from the very cognition itself;
in that case as well, if one were to postulate another relation, there would be an infinite regress.
Now, if the cognition "related" occurs even in the absence of a [real] relation,
then the relation itself must likewise be merely imagined; consequently, the cognition "one who possesses a staff" arises from a merely conventional cause,
and that very [conventional] relation is common to everyone.
Now, if it is argued that the conjunction of the staff is real and not merely conventional,
that too is incorrect,
because there is no conjunction apart from those [constituents].
In the case of a mere conjunction of two things, just as one says "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), so too one might say "the staff of the man" (*puruṣasya daṇḍaḥ*).

Alternatively, when only the two appear, the cognition would be that "these two are mutually conjoined," but there would be no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between them.
Now, if the staff is subordinate because it is the benefactor (*upakāraka*), then in that case, that very state of being a benefactor is the conventional cause (*nimitta*) for that [relation].

And since that [qualifier] does not appear in the direct perception, a cognition qualified by it cannot be sensory. Furthermore, it might be argued that while the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), the qualifier itself—the staff—is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*); and the same would apply to "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
If it is argued that the staff possesses ultimate reality because it is perceived through direct perception as distinct [from the person],
whereas genus and so forth do not possess such ultimate reality because they are not perceived as distinct due to their inherence [in the substrate].
From what does the non-appearance of inherence as distinct [from its relata] arise?
If it is due to another inherence, there would be an infinite regress.

Moreover, the ultimate reality of the object is indeed consistent even in that case; let its functions, such as carrying or milking, be considered ultimate. For just as a real staff is the common cause for the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*), so too are the [functions of] carrying and so forth the causes for the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*), or alternatively, the horns and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a difference between the horns and so forth [and the animal], then the same applies to the difference between the staff and so forth; how then can "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) serve as an example?
Therefore, that which is indeed distinct is perceived as non-distinct.

In some cases, another [basis] for the designation of a genus (*jāti*) such as "carrying" is observed; when it is asked, "What is the 'cowness' (*gotva*) here among these [individuals]?", the horns and so forth are pointed out.

For instance, when there is a question regarding the caste (*jāti*) of a Brāhmaṇa and others, their lineage (*gotra*), Vedic study, and so on, are pointed out, but not the caste itself; likewise, even in the case of "cowness," the carrying of loads, milking, and so forth are pointed out. Therefore, no further genus exists that is an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, there is no ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) whatsoever that is directly the object of a designation; thus, a genus is not an ultimate reality. A genus is accepted merely as the cause for a designation.
And that [designation] proceeds only from the conventional; thus, the universal (*jāti*) is useless.
Furthermore, if every designation were to proceed by relying upon an ultimately real basis (*pāramārthika-nimitta*), then there would be no independence of the word.
And it is observed that words such as "entity," "palace," and "row" function without depending on anything else.
The designation applied to the six categories, as well as the designation "palace" or "garland" applied to palaces and the like, does not depend on any other cause.
For among the categories such as substance and so forth, there is no further entity called "reality" (vastutva).
Reality is not a substance, for a substance is neither inherent in nor conjoined with qualities and the rest.
Nor will even the palace be a substance consisting of a conjunction, because there is no production of something heterogeneous;
to this, he says:
Although a house is indeed a conjunction, what then is a garland?
To this he says in that very same place: "Substance and so forth are the six [categories] to be praised..."
If there were an additional category, it would be a seventh category;
for although a house is a conjunction, why should that not constitute a series?
But it is neither a substance, nor a quality, nor an action, because of the absence [of action] in a substance's quality; for that very reason, it is not a quality.
Nor can it be action, because action depends upon a substance; nor can it be the two types of inherence (samavāya), because their specific effects are absent. [Objection:
But perhaps it will be a universal (jāti), since a universal exists even in a quality.
To this he says:

If it were a genus (*jāti*), then even a single house would be designated as "a row" (*mālā*), just like a tree. Just as even a single tree, such as a *dhava* or other species, is called a "tree" due to its connection with the genus "tree," so too a single house would be [called] a "row" because the genus serves as the basis for the designation of each individual instance.
Now, as for the specific arrangement known as a "garland," entities situated facing a single direction that exist simultaneously are designated as a "garland";
yet even that arrangement is not distinct from substance and the other categories.

If that were accepted, it would entail the consequence of a seventh category distinct [from the six]; and if it were included within those, the aforementioned fault would apply. Furthermore, if "garland" (*mālā*) were a genus (*jāti*), then...
If there is a plurality of garlands, how can that word [“garland”] apply when there is no universal (jāti) because there is no [higher-order] universal?
This portion of the verse does not apply here;
for if there were a plurality of garlands, how could that word [be used] as in "these are garlands," since a genus cannot [itself] be a genus?
For a universal is not admitted to exist within a universal;
or, if it were admitted, the designation "universal" applied there would be without a basis.
If that [designation] were based on a universal, then another universal would have to exist there as well, which would be incoherent.

For instance, a genus (jāti) is postulated among genera for the sake of conventional usage; yet even here, this convention is based upon a higher genus. That genus, too, is an object of usage by virtue of another genus. Thus, because cognition would involve an infinite series of concepts, [this theory] is not tenable.
Consequently, the application of words such as "garland" would lack a basis;
furthermore,

how could the conventional usage of terms like "large garland" occur with respect to a garland and so forth, given that the quality of largeness inheres in a substance, and a garland is not a substance?
If it is argued that this is due to metaphorical usage, that is incorrect, because:

And in the case of a garland and the like, greatness and so forth are intended as being figurative; yet because they are apprehended by a cognition that is indistinguishable from that of the primary object, they are not figurative.
(157) From what [source] does this notion arise that there is a figurative application of "greatness" to garlands and the like?

If it is argued that this [greatness] is not perceived as being metaphorical, nor can that which is not so perceived be accepted as such, because acceptance is based on perception, and because there is no existence of greatness as a distinct entity; then:
