From where does that very non-existence arise?

If non-existence is established, there is the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), and if there is the metaphorical designation, there is non-existence; thus, this is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that because a garland is not a substance (*adravyatva*), its magnitude (*mahattva*) is not a property (*dharma*) of a substance; [we reply: ...
This is not so, because the very absence of substantiality (adravyatva) is unestablished;
for there exists the definition of substance as that which possesses action, possesses quality, and is an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
If it is argued that there is no possession of activity, we say no,
because [the definition] does not apply to the aggregate as a whole.
Space and the like do not possess action anywhere; nor is there ever a collection of things such as those possessing action, nor is there any defining characteristic [of substance] anywhere.

Now, if it is argued that "greatness" itself does not exist when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, then how can one say that substance does not exist simply because the cognition [of it] occurs? From what [source] is this [conclusion] derived?
The argument that "the cognition is not primary" is also untenable,
because it is indistinguishable from what is primary;
for if even that which is indistinguishable from the primary were not primary, there would be no distinction between the primary and the non-primary at all.

Therefore, because there is no distinction, this is the logical principle: either everything is primary, or nothing is. Consequently, this procedure regarding substance and so forth, which is prescribed for one [word], does not apply to another; nor is any "garland" perceived apart from the trees and other components. This is merely a conceptual state (*pratyayamātra*), not something distinct in itself.
Therefore, in the case of a garland and the like, words such as "large" are neither metaphorical nor primary;
for they are not primary because there is an absence of any basis for applying them to a different object,
nor are they metaphorical because there is an absence of any ground for metaphorical transfer.
For just as in the expression "the forest is in bloom," the metaphorical designation of bloomingness is applied to the forest because of their co-inherence in a single object,
since the forest's state of being in bloom is present in the trees.
In the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra...
the state of having no other cause is equal [to that of the self], even in those things considered primary.
What other cause does the word *padārtha* perceive among the six categories?
The group of six.
As for what was stated— that "the primary cause is one that has no other [cause], while the other is its opposite"— that is impossible;

because even those things intended as primary referents, such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth, do not have a cause other than the staff itself, since it has just been explained that even the staff and such are merely conventional.

Furthermore, when the word *padārtha* (category) is applied, what other cause does it require among the six [categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, or with respect to its own nature which is the basis for its application? By force of logic, that very state of having no other cause would necessarily follow.
Yet, it might be argued:
It is logical that the word *padārtha* (category) is primary (*mukhya*) in its application when it functions by means of a specific cause;

however, as for the designation of "the Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth, which is based on the qualities (*guṇa*), since it functions there even in the absence of such a [primary] cause, it is necessarily secondary (*gauṇa*). Therefore, that which possesses the actual object is primary, while the other is secondary.
That too is incorrect,
because whatever is established through conventional usage in a certain way, another thing is likewise called by that same name due to its similarity to it.
The primary and the secondary [distinctions] apply even to non-existence with respect to entities, by way of metaphorical designation. 159.3 M.
Where...

When a term functions through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—either without a specific cause (*nimitta*) or otherwise—it is primary (*mukhya*). When it functions with respect to something else based on similarity to that primary sense, it is secondary (*amukhya*). This is because we observe the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term "son" even in the absence of an actual son. Thus, conventional usage alone is the basis for primacy when there is a real referent; otherwise, the opposite is observed.
Indeed, the absence of a [primary] cause is the basis for the metaphorical application when there is a shift in meaning.
As for what was further stated:

If it is argued that the word "referent" (*padārtha*) is indeed without a basis and is primary precisely in that way, then [we reply]: in that case, being prompted by a cause is not what constitutes being primary, because [the word] exists even in the absence of such a basis;
for when something exists despite the absence of another, that other is not its basis.
Since the nature of causality consists of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and since a cause is the basis [of a term],
how then can that very conventional usage (rūḍhi) exist for a word without a ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta)?
That too is incorrect,
because conventional usage follows linguistic convention, and that [convention] follows the speaker's intention.
Just as the name "Śabdāṅganā" [is applied] for the sake of conventional usage, so too is a *chandas* [meter] employed for the sake of linguistic convention.
That meaning upon which a conventional function (*saṅketavṛtti*) operates is a conventional meaning (*ruḍha-artha*); and this convention is itself based upon the speaker’s intention (*vaktur-icchā*).
For words do not function solely because a basis for application exists;
indeed, they are observed to function even without a basis for application when prompted by the speaker's intention,
as when names such as "lion" are applied to a human being.
Therefore, because desire possesses autonomy, it alone is logically the basis for engagement;
why then is a word applied by convention to that [object] without a cause (*nimitta*), and even when a cause exists, why [is it so applied]?
If it is argued that [the term is used] for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
this very conventional usage is the same even without a basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*);
for conventional usage pertains to the domain of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
If it is argued that purposeful action does not occur without a cause, and that it indeed does not occur without a cause, [we reply]:
no; for Brahmins are not capable of performing purposeful action without their caste (jāti).
No,
because there is no means of valid cognition for this;
for indeed, there is no means of valid cognition that establishes that any universal exists.

It is logical that only that much of a visible form is functional which is established as capable through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, even in the absence of an actual causal basis, a convention (*saṅketa*) may be established for the sake of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), such as the convention of the names *Gāyatrī* and so forth for the word "meter" (*chandas*), or the convention of [grammatical] "roots" (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
For there is no basis whatsoever for that [order],

since one may arbitrarily imagine *gāyatrī* and so forth as well as *prakṛti* and so forth; indeed, there is no basis for the sequence of phonemes, otherwise even one who has not grasped the convention would understand it.
If it is argued that since that which exists is indeed perceived, what then is revealed by the convention? No.
If it is argued that because that very [object] does not exist without cognition,
there can be no convention regarding what is uncognized,
and that cognition arises from convention alone;

Because of the consequence of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), as long as the object is not perceived, there is no application of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); and if linguistic convention is not applied, how can perception be possible? Furthermore, [factors] such as "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) do not possess a fixed form.
For instance, for some [words], this verbal root is possible, and the suffix *aḍāma* follows later; for others, it is impossible, as in cases such as *santi*, where there is elision (*alopita*).
Therefore, in such instances, the convention is intended solely for the purpose of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), and is not prompted by any distinct underlying cause (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, a convention does not follow from mere whim; nor does a universal (jāti) exist as the very cause [of a word], because it is subject to deviation, as seen through the observation of inconsistency. Therefore, words such as "substance" (vastu) or "palace" (prāsāda) are not based on distinct categories that possess real ontological existence. Consequently, since there exists a similarity in their designation, one need not postulate a universal.
If so, how is there a continuity of cognition and words? To this he says:
The continuity of the cognition does not arise from the continuity of the object; rather, its continuity arises from the awakening of the seeds of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Just as, even when an object is beautiful, the continuity of its beauty [is perceived] by virtue of habitual practice, so it is here. Thus:

By the very nature of things, objects are the cause of such a consciousness; even though there is a difference [between the object and its cognition], wherever that cognition occurs, it perceives them in that way. (161)

Just as cognitions arise from a cognition, so too do other cognitions; thus, when there is a conceptual synthesis of difference as non-difference, this is the persistence of the differentiation of effects, not of a single entity. (162)

For it is consciousness that leads one toward an object as it truly is, by means of which process the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) brings about the arising of a conceptual cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a single form everywhere, just like the experience of pleasure and so forth.
Indeed, for the cognitions of pleasure and so forth, there is no basis for their "pleasurability" residing in the external object;
for if that were the case, the non-arising of pain would follow as a logical consequence.
Now, if that reality also exists,
then there would be the consequence of perceiving both forms, just as one perceives both color and shape;
or, if it is argued that this is not so because of the constraint of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [the response follows].
If that were so, why is it not accepted that only what is perceived produces a corresponding cognition?
If you argue that what is perceived as having a restrictive function does not perform the act of production,
we say no.
In the case where both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restriction (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction alone is superior due to the absence of evidence [for the other];
for in the case of a restriction, there arises the possibility of relying on multiple assumptions.
For in this way,

if one were to postulate another unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) for the sake of accounting for the object's association with pleasure and so forth, there would be a mere postulation of the unseen. Therefore, it is only when difference exists that there occurs a conceptual reflection on non-difference in certain cases.
Since the accomplishment of the object follows precisely from that [specificity] by virtue of its capacity, what is the use of an internal, redundant universal (*sāmānya*)? Furthermore,
an internal causal basis for cognitions must necessarily be admitted.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving two distinct forms for the universal and its possessor; if it is argued that through inherence (*samavāya*) they become a single unified entity, we say no.

Since it would follow that inherence (*samavāya*) would also be perceived in a third form, one must therefore admit that in that case, the power of cognition itself depends upon an internal cause; likewise, cognitions are also "concomitant" (*anvayin*) precisely because they produce a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*), and so too are the universals (*jāti*).
Nor is it logical to accept another genus;
the remaining consequence has already been stated.
If it is argued that the linguistic convention of a "universal" (sāmānya) arises because of the effect [of cognition] consisting in the reflective awareness of non-difference—
that very effect of being such-and-such is the universal— it is not so.
Since there is no state of being its effect apart from its own nature,
it might still be argued that if such were the case, then because earth, water, and so forth also possess the state of being effects of the sprout, they would be perceived as one.
If it is argued that there is indeed a cognition of its being an effect, which constitutes a cognition of the universal, we say no; for it would have to be like the cognition of "cowness" itself.

Therefore, it is established that the cognition of a universal occurs because individual differences are not perceived, and not otherwise. Now, why is it not accepted that the universal itself is what is perceived there? Or rather, does there not arise here a subverting cognition to the effect that "the universal does not exist"?
Nor is there any purpose served by the exhaustion of dispute;
for if there is such exhaustion from the effort of multiple conceptualizations, then the same consequence applies to the exhaustion of dispute—
that too is incorrect.
Since a universal is accepted as being merely a confusion of conflicting claims, it follows that it is conventionally real, being the exclusive domain of non-investigative cognition. (315) 2 T.
Regarding the phrase "merely leading to a dispute" (*vivādamātrasāṃkaryamiti*):

when a universal (*sāmānya*) is examined, it does not exist because it cannot withstand analysis; thus, it follows that what is accepted [as a universal] is merely something that delights the mind during analysis.
However, a single functional efficacy (ekakāryatā) does exist among entities; therefore, the verbal designation (śruti) is fixed upon that [efficacy].

At that very time, there exists a universal (sāmānya) characterized by this single functional efficacy, which, by excluding those things that do not possess such efficacy, pertains to the *śābaleya* cow and others.
Therefore, let the verbal designation (śruti) apply to the object precisely as prompted by that cause for its application;
how then, since disjunction (viśleṣa) is formless, can there be a conceptual cognition (sāmānyabuddhi) possessing a form? To this, the following is the resolution.

The very connection of cognition with a form is necessarily the exclusion of what is other than that; and that [cognition] possesses a form due to its association with latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For that cognition arises from a succession of preceding cognitions of things as they were not.
Furthermore, in the cognition "this is a cow," there is no object of knowledge (*prameya*) other than the brindled cow and so forth.
And the determination of an object of knowledge occurs through the manifestation of the form of that object, not from a mere cognition devoid of the form of the object.

If, then, due to the power of beginningless latencies (*vāsanā*), this cognition is non-erroneous precisely because it is bound to that [external object], how can there be correspondence with a real entity (*vastu*)?
Therefore, it must not be a determination through the exclusion of its effects;
and that status of being its effect is either the very capacity of that external [object] itself, or its exclusion, or the very nature of the external object itself.
And in its continuity, it is that very same universal (jāti), not a negation of the universal;
and when that [continuity] is delimited, it is the external object itself that becomes delimited,
because there is no exclusion (vyavaccheda) of the external form.
(5) Although the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) culminates in the negation of external causal capacity,
that term is nonetheless applied to the conceptual reflections which are fixed upon that [negation].
Therefore, because it is focused on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the verbal expression is said to "perform the exclusion of others" (verse 164).
Even though a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from a word does not touch the external nature [of the object],
nevertheless, because that conceptual reflection is produced by way of the external— arising through a mediated succession— it is focused on the external, even if it does not touch the actual object.
And that reflected image, produced by an object excluded from others, appears as being itself excluded from others;
it is this exclusion, inseparable from the image, that is understood from the word, not an exclusion external to it.
Therefore, because it generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of exclusion from others, the word is said to perform "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

And because it functions toward things excluded from others, the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is said to be the object of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even though it does not touch upon anything external; for, despite the conceptual construction not contacting anything external, it functions for those engaged in worldly practice toward things excluded from others. [Objection: But if the object of apprehension for a conceptual construction is distinct from cognition (*buddhi*), how can it have the nature of cognition?
For that which appears as distinct from something else cannot be that very thing;
for the appearance of difference is indeed the definition of difference, since there is no other basis for difference,
and because the mere appearance of non-difference is not its defining characteristic.
For it is an unerring appearance of difference that constitutes the definition of difference, and not just any [appearance];
moreover,
this reflection of the object which appears in cognition seems to be distinct [from it].
Even that [cognition] derived from words does not have the object as its essence; it is an illusion consisting of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (165) [M.
*vāsanodbhavā*]
If it is argued that although that [cognition] appears as color and shape, it is nevertheless not the actual object but rather its reflection, and thus there is no contradiction— [we reply:
even though its production arises from a cause characterized by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), why is it nonetheless not a real entity?
Because it depends solely on internal causes, like the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia;
or rather, we shall explain that even though something arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it does not become a real entity in the same way as a real object.
In that case, some maintain that the very thing characterized by cognition is designated by the word "entity" (vastu), and that this alone— namely, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)—
is the real entity; yet, when that is denoted by words, what portion of the object is actually understood?
Furthermore, if that [external object] were not apprehended, the establishment of a convention (*saṅketa*) for its sake would be useless.

A convention is established with the thought, "Perhaps there might be an apprehension of even a trace of a real entity (*vastu*) from the word," and not merely for the purpose of conveying a mental reflection (*buddhipratibimbaka*).
Therefore, the establishment of a convention is purposeful, because its aim is the cognition of the real entity.
In that case, even the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) would not be the meaning of a word; consequently, the formation of a linguistic convention (saṅketa) with respect to it would be impossible,
because that exclusion of others is likewise a form of cognition (buddhyākāra).
It is not [the case that the word-exclusion applies to all],
because the exclusion by a word applies only to what is non-word.
For this reason:

It is said that a word expresses a portion of the object; in that case, it is the "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) that is called the form [of the object]. But since that [form] does not exist in the object, how can a word expressing it partake of the object? If that exclusion of others were itself the object, then upon its presentation, the exclusion of others would not be a mere portion of the object.

For when the question is asked, "Which part of the object does the word express, since 'exclusion of others' (anyāpoha) is itself only a part of the object?", the answer is "exclusion of others. Yet that exclusion does not exist as a form within the object,
because it is merely a form of the cognition.
For indeed, the cognition of an object through its meaning is not a cognition of the object itself, being like the cognition of hair and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia;
moreover,
it is maintained that the universal is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
For the effect of a word that possesses positive concomitance (anvayin) is with an object that possesses positive concomitance;
and that [word], being non-concomitant [with the external object], is produced by the habitual practice of perception due to the non-difference of the cognition. (168)

For a verbal [cognition] is observed to be concomitant (anvayin) with respect to individuals such as the brindled cow (śābaleya) and others; and that which is concomitant must have a concomitant object as its purpose,
yet that form [of the cognition] is not concomitant because there is no difference in the cognition itself.
Because it is produced through the repeated observation [of the object], it is non-continuous (ananvayin) just like cognition;
for it is not logical that an effect should possess continuity, since it varies according to the difference in its causes.
Therefore, precisely because it is non-continuous, the reflection is not apoha.
Therefore, exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is neither a real entity nor a mental image.
How, then, is there a cognition of a universal when an object is understood from a word?
For when the exclusion belonging to a real entity is cognized, it is the entity itself that is apprehended, and that is not a universal.
Now, if the real entity (*vastu*) is not cognized, how can there be an understanding of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which has the form of that entity? To this, he replies:
"Because the cognition of the exclusion of others occurs through the imposition of that [entity's] form."
This contradicts the statement that "the meaning of a word is that very [external object].

By means of the superimposition that the entity is nothing but the form of the cognition, one perceives it through the determination of its identity with that [cognition], but not in an ultimate sense.
And since that [entity] is excluded from others, the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

And that [exclusion], which is everywhere of the nature of cognition (and not superimposed upon an external object), is superimposed; therefore, it is perceived as the universal, the exclusion of others, and a portion of the real entity,
yet these cognitions produced by words are false appearances.
And the word that performs exclusion (*apoha*) follows this portion of the object;
because it is a false appearance, it does not have a real entity as its object, yet since the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is real, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding it. (170)
For a sublater does not operate with respect to the form of the thing itself;
rather, it is that which does not become excluded from others.
Therefore, the distinction between what is apprehended and what is otherwise is established through the presence or absence of a sublater by way of conventional usage, not in an ultimate sense.

Therefore, because it is uncontradicted and because the demonstration of anything else is contradicted, it is understood that exclusion (*apoha*) of the other is the meaning of a word. Consequently, words follow that meaning of exclusion of the other and function by avoiding what is undesired; thus, verbal cognition (*śruti*) effects the exclusion of the other.

Alternatively, the "exclusion of the other" is simply the conceptual reflection itself, which is determined (*adhyavasita*) as if it were external; thus there is no fault, for it does not exist in its own [external] form.
Therefore, nothing can be enjoined by a word in its own form; thus, injunction is not the meaning of a word.
[Objection: When the intrinsic nature [of the object] appears [to cognition], how does the cognition proceed toward the external object?
[Response: Because of the determination (adhyavasāya) of it as being external.

How can that which is determined as the object of conceptual determination be established as the object of linguistic convention for another? How could it be the object of mutual linguistic convention?
In that case, due to the practice of attachment and because of similarity— just as when one stumbles over a name—
the application of one thing to another is indeed an identification (*adhyavasāya*) consisting of the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the form of the other upon it.
Nor can it be superimposition, because that [cognition] is a distinct cognition; if that [distinct cognition] has apprehended the object, what superimposition could there be?
If it is argued that it is established elsewhere,
[we ask] what is it that exists there in such a manner?
There can be no superimposition because [the object] is real;

for if it does not exist, how then could there be a superimposition upon another? Moreover, that upon which it is superimposed must itself be either of the nature of cognition or of the nature of an object.

In that case, what is the meaning of "superimposition" (āropa) there? If it means that something already apprehended there is apprehended along with [the object], then at that time there is no superimposition.
Alternatively, if it means that what is non-existent is perceived as being existent, [then that is the definition].
If it is argued that the state of non-existence has been realized by one person and realized by another because no such form is perceived, we say:
no.
Since that [non-existence] is not within its range, how can it be known? For it is the non-perception of an object that has come within the range [of perception] which serves as the indicator;
if you argue that such a cognition occurs due to a defect in the sense faculties—
That is indeed the apprehension of what was previously unknown, not the apprehension of something already existing,
because that [object] exists at that very moment;
for one does not engage in practical activity without having reached [the object], since practical activity occurs only upon reaching it.

In that case, the very act of performing a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding one thing as being another is precisely the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of that other; thus it follows that superimposition is the taking of something as the object of a linguistic usage regarding another.
Therefore, the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
For this very reason, he says:
Therefore, even at the time of convention, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is connected to the word in the hearing, associated with a perceived object that results in one's own cognition.
Even while establishing a convention, the maker of the convention does not establish it by way of affirmation (vidhi).
Rather, it is precisely by way of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that,
even at the time of the convention, it is the exclusion of others alone that is connected to the word, and not the real entity;
for in the convention "this is Devadatta," it is observed that the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is being connected.
This is not correct;
for even when an object is indicated, it does not manifest as a reflection in this way. To explain:
One perceives only this:
the object of convention is intended for the sake of cognition by both [the speaker and the hearer]. This cognition is of a reflection, and not of an unmanifested reality. (316)

From the statement "this is its name," it must be understood that this applies to other things as well; therefore, a convention that is restricted by time, place, and state is intended by both parties, self and other, as a necessary rule. Consequently, it is only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that is connected with the word, not the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it might be argued that there is no apprehension of pervasion [in the form] "this has this name"; rather,
only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the reflection is apprehended as the object of the convention, in the sense that "this has this name."
This is not so,
because such a cognition arises from extreme habituation or from acting with prior deliberation;
whereas in the case of the opposite, the cognition of a reflection occurs necessarily.

Furthermore, for one who has understood the convention through worldly usage, there necessarily occurs at the time of the convention a determination in the form of a reflection; for it occurs to a discerning person: "This is the name of this [object]; from this convention, this [object] is understood. Otherwise, how could a discerning person act thus? (317)
Then, upon seeing that [object] being brought as a result of the command "bring this," one understands from the word itself: "This is its name; this too must be understood by me in this way. (318)

Alternatively, the object that was previously specified and established as having the nature of a reflection is conjoined with "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), which consists of differentiation; and the result of that reflection is precisely the demonstration of its differentiation, not the apprehension of its own intrinsic form.
If it is argued that because the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is non-existent in the object and exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is existent, that exclusion must be something other [than the intrinsic nature].
Nor [is it so] because the linguistic usage of their oneness occurs through the conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra*) of them;
moreover—
Because its form is not seen elsewhere, and because its perception depends on seeing it in some [specific] place;
[or] because its non-perception depends on [seeing it] elsewhere.
In the scripture, exclusion (apoha) is connected [to the word], but this is not tenable in the case of a real entity (vastu).

For since a word is observed to apply elsewhere—to that which is of a different class—and yet is also observed in some cases to apply to that which is of the same class, it is understood that the convention (saṅketa) consists in exclusion alone.
Why, then, should the convention not pertain to either the universal (sāmānya) or the individual (vyakti)?

If that were the case, since the convention would exist solely in a positive form, it would follow that [the object] would be perceived everywhere; consequently, even regarding a universal, there would have to be dependence on mere perception.
If it is argued that there would otherwise be no need for dependence on non-perception elsewhere for the sake of cognizing a universal accompanied by its exclusion (*savyatireka*),
then let that very exclusion of others suffice; what is the use of postulating a universal?
For it is the individual itself that is perceived as possessing the exclusion of others; what need is there for a universal?
If it is argued that the individual is not perceived [without it], we say no.
If it is argued that even when a universal is cognized independently of an individual, the individual is also cognized through "cognition by means of what has been indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*),
then are these two cognized here in succession?
It is indeed perceived that one first apprehends and takes as an object the mere universal "cowness" alone, and only afterwards the particularities such as the *śābaleya* cow;
this is not so,
for it is impossible to have a cognition of the internal distinctions among the *śābaleya* and other particulars.
If it is argued that even that [universal] is merely a universal,
and therefore there is no definition of particulars by means of a universal because it is the universal itself that is defined,
and thus there must necessarily be some specific distinction here which serves as the definition— [we reply: no.
Since the word has no operation here, it is not established whether this is so or not; there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this,
nor is even a universal perceived as having the nature of a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
Therefore, it is cognition itself [that is the referent], because it lacks any real entity;
how then is "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) the meaning of a word?
Precisely for this reason, because it functions solely toward the exclusion of what is other.
If, however, either the universal or the individual were perceived [directly], there would be no contradiction; for there is no contradiction regarding what has already been apprehended.
If a contradiction exists, how can even the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) be the meaning of the word?
For even when one thing is not seen, another distinct from it is brought forward.
There is no rule that it brings that [specific object] alone while another must be brought by it;
for this very reason, because it has the same form as verbal cognition, inference also establishes mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because of the dependence on non-occurrence elsewhere": when grasping a convention through linguistic usage, the grasper of the convention depends upon what has not been seen elsewhere, and in some cases, he depends upon what has been seen among similar instances;
therefore, he first understands the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that wherein it was not seen.

But in a case where a linguistic convention is observed, one does not know through discrimination whether that object exists or not; for the acquisition of the convention occurs in exactly that manner.
If it is argued that there is no activity on the part of the external agent in bringing this object, because an object that does not exist cannot be brought,
[the reply is: if this is the king's command, then he will certainly bring it.

But if it is argued that he, reflecting by means of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), makes existence the object of his cognition either through presumption (*arthāpatti*) or that verbal testimony (*śabda*), accompanied by presumption, is the means of valid cognition for existence;
It cannot be [the case that this is] due to implication (arthāpatti), because that is impossible; rather,
it would be like a request made by a child.
Therefore, it is brought forth when possible, but not otherwise; however, other [properties] are not brought forth at all.

Furthermore, others [hold that] since there is an expectation of the exclusion from everything heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) and an occurrence (*vṛtti*) in some positive instance (*vidheya*), the intention (*tātparya*) lies in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), whereas it does not lie in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); thus, the negative concomitance alone is conveyed primarily.
That is incorrect;

for even if one of the two— positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— is predominant, there is still no transgression of the meaning of the prescriptive word (*vidhi-śabda*),
nor can it be maintained that positive concomitance is not predominant.
It is not logical to claim that the concomitance [of the universal] is secondary because the universal is apprehended in its entirety even by the perception of a single individual;
or else, it is because of the requirement for observation in certain instances,
such as when one thinks, "This has this name," which does not necessarily apply at all times.

In the employment of a word, however, it is not that there is no difference [between the object and the exclusion]; rather, based on this [exclusion], one must engage with it [the object] thinking, "this is that.
Since there is no such engagement elsewhere, words have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their objective domain.
Now, in a case where an entity is apprehended through inference, how can that cognition have the exclusion of others as its objective domain?
In that case as well, it is indeed accepted that the object is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha);
for it is precisely because of doubt regarding the particularity that there is cognition [of it], since that which is not fire is certainly not this [object].
But it is not known what kind of fire it is;
indeed, if the universal is not determined, how can there be doubt regarding a particular fire?
[This is] because doubt arises from mere cognition.
This cognition certainly exists, yet the distinction is not known: whether fire exists or not, or what kind of fire is present here.
Is it not the case that wherever there is an effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), fire is necessarily present?
No.
Since fire is a specific kind of touch,
and there is no fixed rule regarding that [touch], how can there be a cognition of fire? For there is only the cognition of heat.
If it is argued that a universal is perceived, we say no,
because there is only a matter of degree.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a universal "heat" apart from the distinctions of degrees such as more or less,
nor is there any cognition of it;
for even cognition itself takes only the gradation as its object.

If it is argued that a single cognition does not apprehend a single object as having various forms at once—because cognitions arise sequentially, such that at one time it is thus and at another time it is otherwise—then there must be some non-existent restrictive factor.

Therefore, even in that case, only the mere cognition is real, and nothing else; thus, the referent of a word is merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and this is not tenable in the case of a real entity.
It should also be understood that the term "exclusion" (apoha) is connected to the indicative mark (liṅga) as well.

Therefore, the word is not connected to the universal (jāti) and so forth, nor to their connection, nor to the object; rather, words are applied solely to the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti). || 173 ||

[The object] is conjoined by that [cognition]; since there is no means of valid cognition for birth and so forth, they lack existence, and thus the postulation of a relation with birth and so forth is not possible. Furthermore, as for the postulation of a relation with a substance, what [relation] could there be between two things appearing in their own intrinsic natures?
If it is argued that [the object] appears as a conjunction, we say no;
for even for one who does not conceptualize, that form appears through the perception of one thing while conceptualizing another.

If it is argued that conceptual construction is possible by means of that much alone— that very [cognition] is itself the conceptual construction— we have no objection, as this is what we accept. Thus, nothing has been contradicted.

If it is argued that there is no cognition of conjunction as being "produced by the action of both," "produced by the action of one or the other," or "produced by [another] conjunction," but rather that it is cognized only in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*);
Since the nature of conjunction does not appear [in cognition],
it is simply two entities that have arisen in such a way which are the objects of appearance, not conjunction.
Furthermore, even the cognition that "those two very objects are conjoined" does not imply a conjunction distinct from them,
because there is no cognition of oneness with the former [conjunction].

For perception does not operate with respect to the relation of priority and posteriority; if it is argued that even if there is no cognition of "prior," there is nevertheless a cognition of "conjoined," we say no.

"For that which was previously unjoined shall indeed be joined again; 'I am the agent who shall perform the task by myself'—this is what is intended by that cognition. (319) In that very same [text]: "It will become separate."

If this cognition did not exist, the postulation of conjunction would be in vain; for this [object] becomes one, and thus non-conjunction would be meaningful. (320) Regarding perception, there is a rejection of the conceptualization of words:
there is no joining with words because the word is absent therein.
If it is argued that the word existed at the time of the convention,
even by that [admission], there is no connection,
because:

How could that [cognition], which consists of a synthesis of what has been seen and employs the recollection of linguistic convention as its means, exist in a visual perception that is devoid of reflection upon the preceding and the succeeding?
"This is a cow" does not mean that this very word "cow" is present; rather, the meaning is that "this is denotable by the word 'cow'."
Co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), however, arises from that relationship, as in the example "bring in the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*);
or alternatively, it is like [the expression] "this is a cow," where the word "cow" refers to that which has "cow" as its sound, through the employment of a single part [of the whole].
In that case, one might think, "This is what is denoted by the word 'cow'," and thus understand it through the word 'cow' as "this is that cow," whereby the word 'cow' is applied to it by convention;
yet how can such an object be grasped by perception, which by its very nature is devoid of any prior or subsequent reflection?
For it has been said:
"The functioning of the sense organs does not extend to what is past or future; and consciousness, which is dependent upon the sense organs, has as its range the activity of those very organs. (321)

If it were the case that even through the operation of the sense-faculties such as the eye, both the preceding and succeeding moments perceived everything—past and future—[then our position would hold];
for indeed, everything that is somehow connected with something previously apprehended is necessarily perceived. If this is argued, [we reply]:
no.
If it is argued that [the cognition] exists because there is always an absence of perception when memory is present,
then it follows that it is merely memory.
If it is argued that identity with the object being remembered is indeed perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no;
because memory (*smaraṇa*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).
Since that which is being remembered is indeed non-existent, how can there be a true cognition of identity with it?
Or, it might be argued: "This is indeed that very same thing, because it performs that same purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."

But surely, even the notion that "it has purposeful causal efficiency" is merely a recollection, as is the idea that "that is what is denoted by the word," and why should causal efficiency be produced by that very thing?
Therefore, this is merely conventional usage.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for unity.

If it is argued that unity is established as a means of valid cognition precisely because of non-contradiction in worldly practice (*vyavahārāvisamvāda*), [we reply: no; even non-contradiction pertains to unity only in relation to causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
And that [cognition] indeed exists;

it possesses the nature of an object because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), but it does not possess identity with the former. Now, this will be the proof: "This is that very same thing."

If there is no identity between the earlier and the later, who could be the synthesizer? If the synthesizer were a single entity, then the perception that grasps both the earlier and the later would be dependent upon that synthesizer.

Since there is no synthesis other than the forms of recollection and perception, [synthesis] is indeed perception; and although it is based on the self, its status as a means of valid cognition does not thereby cease.
If it is argued that its validity arises from its dependence on the senses, while its apprehension of identity arises from its dependence on the self—

If it is argued that there is no persistence of the cognition following that [object], because the operation of that object and the sense organ does not persist in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, and thus the cognition following them cannot persist;
It is not [the case], because it is impossible for it to follow that;
for in the former instance, there is no functioning without following the preceding cognition.
To claim that "following after that" means "following after what is other than that" is reckless;
for the cognition of oneness does not occur without the operation of the senses.
Therefore, the cognition of oneness is not sensory.
If it is argued that [the cognition] exists as such in the case of direct perception,
we say no, because there is no distinction in its unity.
If it is further argued that there is a distinction due to its clarity, we say no.
[Objection: Granted that oneness may be apprehended through clarity; but how can oneness be apprehended by perception through lack of clarity?
[Reply: It is true that its oneness with this [object] is not apprehended by perception; but why should its [oneness] with that [object] not be so? [Because] the principle is the same for both.
If the two [entities] are not apprehended by perception, how can their oneness be an object of perception?
If it is argued that "oneness is accessible to perception, but it is not a category of existence (*padārtha*)," then in that case, that oneness does not reside in the category of existence.
Since an independent singularity is impossible, that which possesses it (the substrate) is implied;
for "implication" is indeed inference.
Therefore, it is untenable to claim that while there is apprehension of an independent [entity] through perception, there is apprehension of it otherwise through inference.

Since inference is preceded by perception, there can be no perceptual cognition such as "this is a cow" in the absence of prior and subsequent reflection. Therefore, it is not a case of perception at all.
Even when [the object] has perished, the synthesis of the preceding and succeeding [moments] is possible; how then could this [synthesis] be a means of valid cognition?
Therefore, the means of valid cognition is the apprehension of that which is merely present.
And in that regard, there is no conceptual application; thus, perception is non-conceptual.
Furthermore:

Even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one perceives a form with the eye; in that case, the non-apprehension of its conventional designation is evident, as is the conceptual construction arising from it.
Indeed, one does not perceive a form or the like while simultaneously engaging in conceptualization, such that the sense faculty would require the assistance of memory.

For it is not the case that something which is a cooperative cause (sahakārī) possesses the capacity to produce its own effect in the absence of that [cause], just as a seed lacks the capacity to produce a sprout in the absence of earth and so forth;
nor is it the case that being a cooperative cause consists merely in producing an effect, since this applies even to memory—
[but] this too is incorrect.

(Consideration of the Unity of the Mental Image) If that [perception] were conceptual because it functions by means of a distinct conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding one thing, while there is the possibility of a contradictory superimposition (*viruddhādhyāsa*) regarding another.

If it is held that "conceptualization" consists in functioning together with a subsequent conceptual construction, then in such a state of being conceptual, one is merely proving what is already established— that recollection is indeed an auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*).

Now, if it is by means of a conceptual construction (vikalpa) that has become its very self, then it is not logical that something which does not exist when that [construction] is present should nevertheless exist when it is absent. Since there would thus be a conjunction of contradictory properties, how could it have unity? [For one might argue: "That [state] with conceptual construction is indeed different from the prior state without conceptual construction."
This being the case, your recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would be undermined and there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as has been stated;
therefore, it is logical that whatever is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) during a state where the mind is directed elsewhere at one time, another [instance] is likewise so.

If it is argued that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arises only through another conceptualization, then in that case, auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) would also become conceptual, because the ear also functions as a cooperative cause. Alternatively, if those cognitions are indeed distinct [from one another].
It is the same in other cases as well; thus there is no distinction.
Furthermore, if it is argued that even another person has such a conceptual construction regarding one in that state, that is incorrect.
If it is argued that [the object] is established through conventional usage even though it is not perceived because of its non-apprehension—
[we reply: for no conventional usage is observed in one who is free from conceptual construction.

The causal relationship between linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is established; since inference based on an effect occurs here, how could there be no apprehension of that convention?
Indeed, it is not the case that the association with words is not perceived through inference, for that too possesses validity.
Furthermore, there is no deviation by this very [reason],
because there is no deviation with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*).
Otherwise, even in the inference of fire from smoke, there would be deviation (vyabhicāra) by the subject itself,
and not [deviation] through apprehension by means of inference.

[The opponent argues: "The fire-essence is known indirectly (parokṣa) even from the conventional usage of 'touch,' because it is recognized through the cognition of touch and the resulting conventional usage of 'removing cold. That too is utterly untenable, if the non-perception of the fire being inferred is a subject of doubt."

If it is argued that the avoidance of deviation [in the inference] occurs because, at this very moment, smoke might exist without fire— since the form of smoke is perceived there through tactile cognition or by the behavior of warming—
that too is incorrect.
If that [object] is understood through inference based on perception and linguistic convention, then the non-deviation of that inference must also be established by another inference.
Since the process of inferring is the same, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in that case.

If, when there is a suspicion of deviation regarding an inference, inference itself is the means for establishing non-deviation, then since the nature of inference is the same everywhere, such a suspicion would arise in every instance.
Thus, this is proving the unestablished by means of the unestablished;
for the establishment of color by means of touch is not possible,
since touch is also present in the case of the cognition of a yellow conch-shell.

And where there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding smoke, there the conventional activities such as heating and so forth, which are preceded by fire, would be even more subject to deviation from it; thus, if there were deviation from the subject (*pakṣa*) itself in the establishment of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through inference, this would apply to all inference. Therefore, this [proposed] conception is not sound—that is incorrect.

Inference proceeds from smoke by the force of the real entity (*vastu-bala*). And since that [inference] is non-contradictory with what is perceived, it is not established as being [merely] a conceptual construction.
For the inference of fire, operating upon an object beyond the senses, is not sublated by perception, because perception does not have that [remote object] as its domain.

In the case of establishing conceptualization (*vikalpa*), however, because conceptualization is the object of self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), it is not "from afar"; thus, even its subtlety is relative to the perception by another,
whereas in its own nature, as subtlety is perceived in the perceived object, so it is in the perceiver as well— therefore, an outcaste does not fear an outcaste.
Furthermore, this very state of being non-cognition applies to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as well;
nor does inference operate upon conceptual construction, because there is an absence of such a perception, as is the case with fire and the like.

But surely, since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), how is it that the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandhagrahaṇa*) is not inference?
For the apprehension of the necessary connection itself exists otherwise [than as inference].

For instance, conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is possible for one who lacks prior habituation (*anabhyāsa*) without [the application of] investigation (*vicāra*) and so forth; however, such conventional practice does not occur with respect to reality (*tattva*). But when there is habituation, it occurs even otherwise; thus, it is not otherwise [than this]. (328) For conventional practice does not occur for one lacking habituation without prior reflection on what precedes and follows; this constitutes the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). But when habituation exists, it occurs even otherwise; it is not otherwise than this.

Therefore, even without practice, this conventional usage proceeds for living beings; in this very context of usage, there is no inference [required], because the operation of inference corresponds precisely to the grasping of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Otherwise, the grasping of the necessary connection would be useless for inference, and that necessary connection is grasped only in the state of non-practice, not elsewhere.
Therefore, there is no [need for] investigation and so forth, because of the conventional usage of inference. For this so-called "conventional usage" is observed even otherwise.
(330) Otherwise, since the behavior of lovers is seen toward a beautiful woman, one might as well infer that she possesses beauty even when she is ugly. (331)

Therefore, since the non-apprehension of the word perceived at the time of the convention is perfectly clear during the conceptualization of another [object], the conceptualization arising from that [perception] does not exist at all.
Now, if the connection with the word is not apprehended by perception, how can there be the conventional usage based on the thought, "This is the denotable object (vācya) of that word"?
Not so.
Since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is possible even through error,

and since even error is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its connection with a real entity— just as, for example, the cognitions of those perceiving a cluster of trees and so forth [are valid regarding the trees themselves].
Even there, there is no such thing as a "lump" (piṇḍatā);
nevertheless, the conventional usage of "tree" is non-contradictory.
Likewise, there is no such thing as a "conjunction" (yojana); nevertheless, the conventional usage of "conjoined" is not false.

For instance, the cognition "this is a cow" has a coreferential object; its meaning is that the word "cow" is the designator of this [object]. Therefore, this cognition is of such a nature that it is non-contradictory.
Since this application is observed in such a domain—
for instance, because the cognition of a solid mass occurs in relation to a tree and not elsewhere— there is non-contradiction due to the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
If, then, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not cognized from the word "cow," how is there the recognition "this is that" upon seeing it?
Regarding that which was previously apprehended by me as "this is that very thing," there is no such recognition in the world when the object is actually perceived,
because recognition is absent in the case of what is seen.

The recognition "this is that very same one" consists of two cognitions: the cognition "this" is of a perceptual form, while the cognition "that" is of a non-perceptual (indirect) form. Since these two cognitions are mutually distinct in their forms, they do not have a single object.
For it is the difference in appearance that constitutes a differentiator; thus, because [the object] is of a non-differentiated nature, there would be no difference.
Alternatively, difference arises from a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), not from a difference in appearance.

If it is argued that there is no causal efficiency apart from the distinction between appearances, [and therefore] [the difference in objects] arises from the distinction between appearances qualified by causal efficiency;

If an appearance is devoid of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), then that cognition is indeed objectless (*nirālambana*) and distinct from sensory perception; for, being produced solely by mental impressions (*vāsanā*), it does not grasp an entity capable of causal efficacy. Therefore, due to the absence of contact with a real entity, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two cognitions [of "this" and "that"].
Even the manifestation "this" determines a form common to everything present before one as "this-ness";
however, if it were devoid of such commonality, it would be purely indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*).
Furthermore, if sensory cognition were of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then this is another fault.
Conceptual constructions arise only where a word has been applied; therefore, they would proceed according to one's desire and would not perceive external objects.

For a word is applied to an object that is beyond the senses, and conceptual constructions are applied there as well; consequently, sensory cognition would not be a perceiver of the external, but would become devoid of an objective basis (*anālambana*), just like verbal cognition.
For a cognition operating with respect to something imperceptible cannot have that thing as its objective support, because it does not touch upon the object's own nature;
and if it were operating while touching upon the object's own nature, it would involve a clear apprehension such that it would be "this very thing," and not "that."
Or rather, all recollection would be sensory cognition, because there is no distinction [between them];
for verbal cognitions certainly do not touch upon external forms.
If, on the other hand, a word were applied to an external object, then just as a verbal cognition proceeds according to one's will, so too would a sensory cognition.

Therefore, even in the absence of an external object, a cognition that proceeds [toward an object] would be without a basis (*nirālambana*), because there is no distinction [between such a case and one with an external object]. Now, if it is argued that where there is compliance with intention (*icchānuvidhāna*), there is no compliance with an object, and thus the state of having an external object as its basis arises from compliance with an object— then, if compliance with an object were the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*) would necessarily be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) alone.
Because the nature of having the form of a word is dependent on desire, it does not follow from an external object, since it follows from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Now, even though the form of the word follows from latent impressions, nevertheless, that [form] is one and the same arising from the causal complex of the latent impression and the sense faculty; thus, it is indeed determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).
For in this way alone is there linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*); otherwise, if it were not made an object by reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), there would be no linguistic usage at all.
For it is observed that people engage in worldly transactions based on the conviction, "This is indeed a means to happiness";
yet even that [conviction] is non-existent, because:
Just as the arising of conditions from a causal complex is accepted, let conventional usage be exactly like that; for valid cognition exists only in this very context.

Since there is no non-difference [of the object] despite the difference in causes, and the causes—such as mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth—are indeed distinct, there is no conventional usage of oneness between the forms of the object as produced by verbal and sensory cognitions.

Since the conventional usage of the two conditions is established by their mere collection, and since such usage is possible even when there is a conceptualization of something else— because when another conceptualization is present, that [original object] is not made an object of cognition through its reflective awareness,

nor is conventional usage based on the mere association of words; rather, conventionality consists in the connection with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and purposeful action is what was previously experienced and will be experienced again.

It is not an object of sensory consciousness, because that would entail the absence of inference; what is the meaning of "those born of the senses would not perceive the external"? It means that those things which are external would also result in being perceived by the senses, since there is no distinction [between them].
"Even when there is such an intervention and so forth, the cognition would be produced by the sense-faculty"—
meaning that whatever cognition occurs even when there is an intervention and so forth, that too would be produced by the sense-faculty,
just like the part "that" (sa).
And this has already been established;
how then is it that the determination "this is an object" is the determiner of the object standing before one?
For in this case, there is no objectivity regarding something beyond the senses for the ascertainment; and as for the claim that "this is perception because its object is present," that is incorrect,
since we shall demonstrate that this is actually mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
And if there is no linguistic or practical activity (vyavahāra) without reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), such that what is not reflected upon is not grasped,
then:
One might perceive form as "form," but how could one perceive that cognition [of form]?
And yet, there is an experience of it; how then could that be non-conceptual?
(177) For according to the proponent of all cognitions being conceptual, one might perceive form as "form," but how could one perceive that cognition of it?

For there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) therein that thinks "this is its cognition"; yet even if there is no direct experience (*anubhava*) at all, empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) still occurs.

In that case, even though [the object] is not being experienced, as long as empirical usage persists, for you who hold the view of consciousness-only (*samvedana*), it is impossible for [the object's existence] to be established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or other means.
How much more so, then, in that which is experienced with a clear form through its non-conceptual nature?
For there is no absence of experience in that regard;
otherwise, how could the conceptualization "this is my perception of form" even be possible?
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are indeed experienced at that time,
yet there is no conceptual experience (*vikalpakānubhava*) therein such as "this is pleasure" and so forth;
therefore, the experience of cognition is strictly non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).

If there were no experience free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*), then just as with the intellect, there would have to be conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding form and so forth as well.

Now, if it is argued that this conceptual construction—“this is my perception of form”—is itself a conceptualized perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), we reply: is this conceptualized perception identical to the perception of form itself, or is it something other than the perception of form? There are these two possible courses.
In that case,
two conceptual constructions are not seen simultaneously in that very experience;
for if that very cognition of form were to cognize itself by means of conceptualizing it, then there would follow the consequence of two conceptual constructions occurring at once.
If it is argued that because succession is impossible for a single entity, that very cognition cannot consist of the successive experience of the intrinsic natures of form and so forth;
If a single cognition adopts succession, then succession itself would become non-successive;
if it is argued that it adopts even that [succession] through a sequence,
there would be an infinite regress.
Since there is an absence of one's own clinging during the state of clinging to form, how can there be oneness?
For there is no other cognition apart from clinging;
and since its cognition of difference is itself distinct, how could there be a sequence for that which is one?

If it is argued that the grasper is non-different from [the grasped], then in that case as well, there must be another grasper for the attachment to its own nature; thus, that same infinite regress occurs.
Therefore, if there were experience by that very [consciousness], there would be the consequence of two simultaneous conceptual constructions.
By this, the experience of another cognition occurring at the same time is also refuted.
Even if there were an experience of a simultaneous cognition, it would follow that two conceptualizations arise simultaneously;
consequently, there would have to be yet another conceptualization for that one as well, leading to the absurd consequence of an infinite regress of conceptualizations.

Furthermore, even if it were the case that [the cognition] is experienced by another subsequent cognition— whether through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*)—
this would not be correct.
Since memory occurs regarding what has passed, how could it arise with respect to that which was not previously apprehended?
Furthermore, the cognition of one's own cognition would have to be non-different in form from the cognition that discerned the other object. (179)
If it is argued that past cognition is not perception because perception has only a present object, and that at that time the cognition itself is indeed present— [we reply: in that case,
there would be no apprehension of the nature of the apprehension of form, nor would there be any other cognition.
Therefore, since cognition is of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpā*), whatever object is present within it appears as such, like a crystal or a mirror;
this is incorrect, for in that case, the apprehension of form would have to be of something already past.
But even if the nature of consciousness exists at that time, what use would it be?
Consequently, there would be no such apprehension as "this is my form," but rather [the thought] "it was"; yet such is not the operation of perception.
If, moreover, the apprehension of form possesses both pastness and presentness,
then it would follow that pastness also existed previously, which would be an impossibility.
For if it were always in a past state, then the present [consciousness] would never exist; and if that were so, the apprehension of form would occur at all times, which is absurd.
Furthermore, if it were always past, then because it existed even prior to that, the apprehension of form would never take place.
If presentness occurs first and pastness afterwards,
then that would not be a single cognition; for if there were oneness [of the two states], [they could not be successive].
If that were the case, both would be apprehended simultaneously; for if they were apprehended sequentially, there could not be even one [entity],
since unity and succession are contradictory.
The meaning of the sequence is that upon the abandonment of one, there is the apprehension of another;
and since this has already been established previously, it is not stated again.
Therefore, there is simply no apprehension of what is past.
Since even recollection does not occur without a prior apprehension, it follows that there would be a total absence of the cognition of the apprehension of form; furthermore,
if there were a cognition of a past experience such that one perceives "this is not an experience," then it would not be known whose experience this is.
There would be an equivalence in the cognition of another's thought, because there is no distinction in the recollection of what has passed;
how then is this understood [to be] "from the determination of another's thought"? Is it a determination by means of another's thought, or is it the determination of another's thought?
If, first of all, the determination [of an object] occurs by means of another cognition, this is precisely what is accepted by the proponent of non-self-reflexive awareness (*asvasamvedana-vādin*).
Otherwise, if there were a determination of another cognition [by yet another], that would be untenable.
Because it is impossible to discern another's cognition,
for the discernment of another's cognition occurs through inference,
and inference is not a means of discernment regarding one's own cognitions.
Therefore, how can there be equality between [the cognition of] the determination?
To this it is replied:
this is said with the intention that the past is beyond perception; for when there is direct establishment, the state of being past and beyond perception is impossible. (334)

For if that were perceived directly, then, like color and so forth, it would not be indirect (parokṣa), nor would it be past; because that which is being directly realized is necessarily present, otherwise its very status as present would not exist.
Therefore, everything that is indirect must be understood solely through inference.
And since that [cognition] is of the nature of recollection, there would be a similarity with the cognition of one's own awareness.

Now, if even the cognition of one's own self is measured by a means of knowledge other than inference, then that same similarity is established. Furthermore, if the cognition of another is perceived as being connected to another, whereas the cognition of one's own self is perceived only as being connected to oneself—[then how can there be similarity?]

For it is not logical for one thing to be perceived as something else; this [perception of another] could only occur if the apprehension were of the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). In inference and memory, however, there is a persistence of the previous apprehension. (335)
He demonstrates that very point:
"The cognition of an object that is past, lacks an example, and lacks a logical mark—by what means is it established? For in that case, there is neither perception nor inference. (180)

For there is no example for the apprehension of the past, because it is not perceived; therefore, inferential knowledge does not cognize a cognition as being related to oneself or another, since—just as in the case of [present] perception—it is not perceived. Furthermore, if it were perceived, it would not be "past," as has already been stated.

Consequently, since a logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot be an inferential indicator without the prior apprehension of a relation, it follows that [the cognition] would be restricted to the mere determination of the intellect itself;
however, in the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the distinction is indeed based on its being other than that [intellect].
Now, just as there is inference without a [previously grasped] relation, so too is the inference of the distinction [possible].
This too is not tenable:
that there was previously a perception of form here by which its cognition is observed, just as one might infer, "Fire was previously in this place because burning was seen.
And in that case, there is no such distinction as, "The fire was produced by me" or "by another. (336)

Now, if that other's cognition is inferred as being connected with another body, such that there is a distinction between "itself" and "otherwise," then this would be appropriate only if the cognition were perceived directly within one's own self;
for it is thus:
The distinction is logical insofar as that which is self-cognized is the apprehension of form (*rūpa*), while that which is other is otherwise;

however, just as for the Sautrāntika, forms and so forth— which exist only as past— are apprehended by a consciousness that arises immediately after them and manifests in their likeness, so too is the apprehension of form [for us], because it is likewise unreal.
If it were apprehended by the immediately succeeding cognition—which manifests its own nature—just as color and other objects are, then there would be no apprehension of that preceding cognition.
For color and the like do not manifest as having the nature of what preceded them; rather, having been transferred into the present cognition, they manifest precisely as being present.
The apprehension of the cognition of form is itself the apprehension of form,
but it is not so for the cognition [of that cognition], because there is no apprehension of that cognition;
however, if at that time the cognition of the cognition were also apprehended...

If that were the case, another cognition would have to be apprehended by that [first cognition], leading to an infinite regress; and if that were so, there would be no apprehension of anything at all.
Alternatively, it might be argued that the cognition of the cognition is simply not apprehended.
That being the case, it would follow that even the object of cognition which has transferred into the present moment would not be apprehended;
for only that cognition which arises immediately after [the object] would be grasped, and not the one preceding it.
If, however, it is maintained that a cognition possessing origination occurs even immediately after the preceding cognition, [then the following applies].

If that were the case, it will be explained later that there would be no perception of forms, cognitions, and so forth as being uninterrupted. Furthermore, if a single cognition arises in a continuous stream and immediately thereafter another cognition arises that grasps all the preceding cognitions,
even so, there would still be no apprehension of all those cognitions in their proper sequence.
If [the objects] appear to the cognition non-successively,

or if they appear only successively, then there would be no apprehension of unity through direct perception because of their being grasped as fragmented; thus, it would be nothing but memory— this very fault has already been stated previously.

Granted that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended by itself through non-conceptual [cognition], what contradiction is there in the apprehension of a distinct object of cognition (*grāhya*) by means of conceptual [cognition]? None at all;
however—
Just as that non-conceptual experience of consciousness regarding its own object cannot be designated by linguistic convention (*samaya*), so too must other things be non-conceptual.
Why, then, is the grasping of that very nature (*svarūpa*) graspable only by a non-conceptual cognition?
To this, too, the same reply applies:
for it is not possible for a thing’s own nature (svarūpa) to be conjoined with itself, whether by means of a word or by means of another property (dharma).
And if this is so, then even form (rūpa) and the like cannot be conjoined with something else, because conjunction is impossible for that which appears in its own nature.
For that which appears in its own form is not joined with another appearing thing,
because no joining is observed apart from the appearance of its own form;
and that which does not appear in its own form cannot be joined— this is not the ultimate truth.
Now, it is established here that the connection [of the word] is understood precisely through the manifestation of the cognition "this is a cow" (*ayaṃ gauḥ*).
Furthermore, this cognition is not of the nature of the word "cow" itself; rather, it is the object denoted by the word "cow," because of the experience of certain determination.
Moreover, for the Mīmāṃsaka, whose words have only universals as their objects, conceptual construction does not share that same referent.
In the absence of that non-conceptual [cognition], how could there be the apprehension of particulars?
For words have universals as their objects, and conceptual construction has the same object as those [words].
In the absence of a non-conceptual [cognition] denoting a universal, how could there be the apprehension of a particular? (183.2)
How so?

If conceptualization (*kalpanā*) were not identical with that [perception], then the particular (*viśeṣa*) would not be conjoined with the word; consequently, the determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*) such as "this is a cow," which grasps the particular, would not exist. For it would follow that the cognition of conjunction is one thing and the cognition grasping the particular is another.
Because there is a distinction between their natures— one being clearly manifest and the other not— and because of the distinction between their causes;
for it is thus:

The cause of the form of the universal (sāmānyākāratā) is one's own latent predisposition (svavāsanā). The manifestation of a clear form and so forth arises from the eye and other [senses], whereas the form of the word (śabdākāratā) indeed arises solely through the power of the cultivation of words experienced at the time of linguistic convention; it does not arise from the eye and other [senses].
Likewise, the form of the universal [arises] in the same way.
