For instance, even in the absence of the eye and so forth, there occurs [cognition] in a mind conditioned by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous experience;
whereas when the eye and so forth are present, it does not occur in a mind devoid of the corresponding latent impressions. Thus, there is an absence of being caused by the eye and so forth.

Now, if it is thought that there is simply no co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with objects whose appearance is dependent upon causes such as the eye in the absence of the eye and so forth—[we reply: [this is not so].
Even that [fire] is seen in whatever form is apprehended through inference, because of its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition "this is fire. Indeed,
it is not merely by virtue of such co-referentiality that there is the state of being apprehended by a cognition dependent on the same causal basis as the cognition that grasps it.
Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible even with that which is apprehended through the inference of other conditions and so forth,
and since coreferentiality is nothing other than the experience of those two forms [of cognition],
what then is the distinction between coreferential and non-coreferential [cognitions]?
For the experience of two forms is not impossible even for two objects that have distinct substrata;
this is easily understood because:

The conventional usage of identity based on the performance of a single purpose, as well as the conventional usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), would be difficult to establish through [the existence of] a universal (*jāti*). For the existence of such usage arises merely from some cause;
indeed, the conventional usage of coreferentiality and the like has come down through a beginningless succession of conventions and is simply incapable of withstanding critical examination.
For when one examines it, it simply falls apart;
thus, the cognition "this is fire" consists here of nothing but a duality.
Because it appears as having that very nature, there is no relation of co-referentiality;
this is the summary [verse] 340.

Why is it that even elsewhere, despite the appearance of two [distinct] things, there is a linguistic convention of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the restriction of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), since the restriction of linguistic convention follows from the restriction of latent predispositions?
Furthermore, the awakening of a latent predisposition is itself restricted by the performance of a single causal function;
why, then, when two cognitions appear, does there not instead arise a linguistic convention of difference?
It has been stated that this is due to the restriction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
therefore, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is not a single cognition by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Now, if there is no absolute difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), then even though they share a single referent, the apprehension of the particular is conceptual.
That is incorrect:
if the perception of a particular were [identical] to the universal due to non-difference, then either in its entirety or in some way, every cognizer would become equal to an omniscient being.

(341) If, in conceptualization, there is the appearance of the universal, then because of its non-difference from it, there would also be the appearance of the particular; and thus, there would be an appearance [of the particular] even in verbal cognition.
Since the logic is the same, it is certainly not the case that when the logic is identical there can be a lack of identity in the logic,
for that would entail the consequence of the absence of its propriety.
Now, if there is no manifestation of the qualified [object] due to the absence of causes such as the eye and so forth,
how then can it be non-different from that?
For it cannot be understood to be non-different unless it enters into identity with it.
If it is argued that [the object] exists because of its subsequent entry [into cognition],
then at that time the object itself does not exist;
for its reality consists precisely in that form [of cognition], and not in its entry into that [form].
If it were to appear as that [very same form], how could there be an understanding of penetration? If it were not to appear as that, how could there be an understanding of penetration?

(342) If it appears in the very same form in which it was previously seen, how can there be an understanding of penetration, since it would be just as it was before? If it does not appear in that form, then its reality is absent; how, then, can there be an understanding of its penetration?
Therefore, that which does not appear [as distinct] is neither one nor many;
consequently, the claim that what previously appeared as distinct subsequently undergoes integration is trivial.
For that reason, even due to the absence of such a cause, that which does not appear [as distinct] possesses multiplicity precisely through its oneness.
Therefore,
in the absence of non-conceptual [cognition], how could there be the apprehension of specific qualities? (183)
How can there be something that is both existent and free from conceptual construction? For it would have the same cause as [that which is otherwise].
In every case, there is indeed a difference among the results because of the difference in their causes.
Now, if one were to abandon the conceptual form and instead attain a specific cognition through the perception of a particularity imparted by the causes such as the eye,
then— this being the case— the determinate [cognition] would depend upon those very causes and would thus be non-conceptual.
Indeed, it is not logical for a distinction between entities to be established on the basis of valid cognition without depending on a distinction between their causes;
therefore, an effect must belong to the same class as its cause. Furthermore, there is no identity of cause between conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions;
for instance:
Just as the application of external objects [to words] does not depend on the recollection of convention,
so too visual cognition, without depending on convention, arises through the power of the object itself. (185)

For when the conceptualization whose nature is the synthesis of sensory perception and [mental] construction arises through the power of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) whose inherent natures are established by mutual exclusion, how could those two possibly possess a connection with an inherent nature that partakes in the existence of that same causal complex?
Synthesis depends solely on the recollection of conventions independent of external objects,
whereas sensory perception is dependent on external objects and independent of conventions.
In that case, there can be no nature of conceptualization because of the absence of a cause for conceptualization;
indeed, an effect does not arise without a cause.
Now, it might be argued that sensory cognition could become conceptual by virtue of the capacity of external factors such as the connection with words and universals (*śabdasāmānya*).
That too is incorrect, because:

"Whatever has a relation with something else appears together with that [thing], due to a necessary rule (niyama). Thus, this [object] has not at all entered the domain of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, does it follow here as well, according to this view, that there would be the appearance of all related things?
Now, as for that universal or other [category] which is established in a particular place, if it appears there, it must indeed appear;
otherwise, it would follow that the word itself could not be apprehended.
For sound does not exist in things such as cloth;

otherwise, even for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention, there would arise the cognition "this is cloth," yet this is not the case, since doubt is observed regarding its being denotable.
If it is argued that even when the object has been established, there is indeed certainty regarding its uniformity because the specific distinctions of the denoters have not been ascertained,
we say no.
Because it does not exist at the time of the first perception,
and because of the demonstration that "it is not different from that," etc.,
it might nevertheless be argued:

Perception such as "this is a cow" arises by depending on the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), and it is form (*rūpa*) and so forth alone that, acting as auxiliaries to the sense faculty, produce conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), not without such dependence, since the effect is produced from a causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
When a word, a universal, or another qualifier was previously apprehended and is now recollected, then the eye and other faculties, aided by that recollection, produce [the cognition];
therefore, it does not occur for those who lack both the prior apprehension of the convention and the present perception. Thus, that [position] is not well-established.

For if form, which depends on the recollection of convention, were not capable [of producing cognition] in the sensory consciousness independently, it would be like a logical mark (liṅga) only in relation to memory.
For there can be no connection with that [object] without a prior experience;
nor can there be a connection with specific words and so forth without a specific recollection;
nor can there be a specific recollection without the awakening of the seed of that specific recollection; and nor can there be such specific awakening without perception.

Therefore, upon the perception of that [object], there is the recollection of its denotative word, and upon that recollection, there is the application [of the word]. Thus, for that which is being perceived, the fact that it serves as the indicator (*liṅga*) for its own recollection means that the visible form and so forth, acting as the awakener, are themselves nothing but a logical mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, the entire cognition of application is purely inferential (*laiṅgika*).
Now, if the universal (*sāmānya*) is not itself directly perceived, how can it be cognized through a logical mark?
For similarity is said to be the commonality of parts,
and that has indeed been perceived previously;
therefore, it is remembered, because the possession of such parts is the objective basis for the conventional usage of "similarity."
The same applies to the constituent parts as well, due to the similarity of such parts,
up to the similarity of such cognitions, and because cognition also arises from such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*);
and since this reflective awareness also stems from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is no fault.

Therefore, if the association with a word, a universal, and so forth, occurs through a logical mark (*liṅga*), then that recollection is here [classified as] inference; however, if the association occurs through the operation of the sense organ, it is called perception itself.
If that were the case, it would follow that all inference is produced by the senses alone, and thus would result in being perception.
For instance,

in the case of the cognition "there is fire here in this place," why is it that the connection of fire with this place does not attain the status of being perceptible in the absence of the operation of the senses?
Furthermore, regarding the application of inference to mere fire, that too is simply perception, because it is [ultimately] non-cognition.
Even so, it can be said:
"Only the location is perceived directly; the connection, however, is through inference. Without the sensory cognition grasping the fire, there is no connection.
For indeed, the connection is properly established by inference alone, since the operation of the senses is impossible with respect to the fire [at that distance].
For it is not possible to connect that which has not been apprehended by perception; to say that what is not cognized by it is connected with what is cognized is a contradiction.
[Objection: But would there not then be no connection even by means of inference?

For, in a place where there is no recurrence of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), that which has not been apprehended cannot be applied [as a conclusion]. To claim that an object perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is apprehended by inference is sheer audacity.

Indeed, just as direct perception does not arise regarding a fire that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), so too inference does not arise regarding a place that is directly perceived; thus the logic is the same.
And if it were an object of inference, it would not be perceptible;

for the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) is not accepted [by you], and in the ultimate sense, no synthesis (*yojanā*) is possible for anyone. A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that kind arises immediately after two [perceptions]. (346)
The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon perception or inference, which consists of the cognition of association such as "this is here," is indeed nothing other than inference (i.e.,
*svārthānumāna*), since it arises from beginningless conventional usage of such a nature;
therefore, this association is designated as "inference."
How is it that inference also arises in the form of a synthesis?
There is no fault, because it is seen to be so by means of perception;
therefore, it is established that perception does not consist of synthesis.
And although this has already been established,
it might still be argued that perception indeed operates even with respect to what is imperceptible when it is being remembered.
Therefore, the claim that there is a direct perception [of the connection] is also false; for,
since that [connection] arises from its conjunction, the cognition would have to be either sensory or mnemonic.
Furthermore, it might occur even at a later time due to the possibility of distraction.
(187) If the arising of that sensory cognition is admitted to occur when there is a connection with memory— that is, when something is being remembered—
then the sensory cognition would arise from memory alone and would not depend upon the presence of the object.
If it were to depend upon the presence of the object, then that [cognition] would not arise from memory at all, because direct perception is distinct from recollection;
or else, it might occur even at a different time, since at that moment there could possibly be a distraction characterized by another conceptualization.
Consequently, that sensory cognition would likewise become a recollection of a past time.
Furthermore,
if that object were always to remain exactly as it was the cause of the initial non-conceptual cognition,
then perception would necessarily be non-conceptual.
If it is argued that [the sense organ] is the cause of both sequentially, then because there is no difference [in its nature], both would have arisen together beforehand.
If this [organ] were the cause of both, then both would have been produced simultaneously.
Alternatively, the sense organ, aided by memory, produces conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), and not otherwise.
That is incorrect;
for indeed, no assistance from the eye is perceived by memory,
nor is it the case that everyone is an assistant to everything simply because they are an assistant.
But that which is thus seen is certainly not made clear and so forth by memory; rather, it is the cognition through the eye and other senses that is made determinate in form.
That [cognition] is therefore without essence,

because if the determination were already present in that form due to non-difference, then it would also follow for what is not of that form, since it would be another cognition arising from the senses.

If the determination of form (*rūpa-niścitatva*) is nothing other than that which was previously manifested, then it is identical to the prior form; thus, there is no additional quality to the determination, because it is not distinct from non-determination.
If, however, an additional form appears therein, then that must be another cognition associated with a different form,
since there is no operation of the senses toward the qualifier or other such elements within that form.
Furthermore, the mental delineation "this is that" occurs with respect to that very object;
therefore, because it functions as a direct realization, it possesses the status of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That too is incorrect.

For this reason, conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) would become non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because it does not construct the sequence of priority and posteriority regarding the relationship with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth,
but rather directly perceives only the proximate form and other qualities. (348)
Because it is devoid of the apprehension of relations such as priority and posteriority or causal efficiency, it does not differ from another [cognition] that is non-conceptual;
for one who is not conceptualizing cannot be said to possess conceptualization.
Therefore, this [cognition], which has a clear form, is indeed distinct from that which has an indistinct form, such as the remembered qualifiers and so forth.
If that were the case, then memory would be useless even in that instance where it is the cause of the cognition of another ox.
Or, it might be argued: [text continues]
If the object of sensory cognition is a distinct, vivid form entirely different from the form being remembered,
then memory is useless in that regard;
for memory is not of service in the act of perception, since that [object] is apprehended in such a way even without memory.

Just as the recollection of a convention (*samayasmṛti*) is required for the sake of establishing a connection, so too must a distinction from what is not connected be apprehended; otherwise, what would be the purpose of that recollection?
If that [object] were delineated in its form by the eye and other faculties aided by recollection, then in the absence of that [recollection], there would be no cognition of it.
If it is argued that there is no such mental representation as "this exists," we say no;
for even in the absence of the representation "this," that form still appears.
Since there is no other distinction [produced] by that [existence], what is its utility?
If it is argued that its utility consists in instigation (*pravartana*), we shall demonstrate that instigation occurs even without it.
And it will be demonstrated that this [perception] is mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
Nevertheless, it might be argued that for one who is not habituated, there can be no initial engagement without memory; therefore, memory is postulated for that purpose.
To this it is replied:
if the difference is to be grasped as something entirely unestablished and disconnected,
what else can memory do in that case?
Since memory is postulated for the purpose of establishing a connection, if that [connection] is not established in such a manner, then memory is of no use for the comprehension of it.
However, the initial engagement [with the object] may indeed arise from another means of valid cognition, namely inference;
therefore, [memory] does not belong to conceptual construction.

The operation [of the mind] is directed toward the apprehension of its own nature, not toward [external] engagement; however, due to habituation, this [mind] continues to engage even though it is purposeless.
For entities do not come into being merely because there is a purpose, since the existence of an entity depends solely upon its cause.
Now, if there is the apprehension of a nature other than the previous one, then this is indeed another cognition in the form of mental perception,
as will be demonstrated later.
Or, it might be argued:
Only the universal is grasped by that [cognition], not the particular, since the latter has not been previously perceived;
if this is so, then the dependence upon particulars during the apprehension of the universal alone is not tenable.
If the apprehension of the universal alone were produced by the eye and other sense organs,

then, since the apprehension of difference by another [cognition] would be impossible, there would be no desire for the apprehension of difference once the universal has been apprehended; yet such a desire does indeed arise.
For instance, when there is the apprehension of a generality, one observes in the world that upon the cognition "this is a cow," the question arises "what kind of cow is it?
Therefore, visual consciousness arises dependent upon both the eye and visible form. (190)
Since recollection is of no use there,
visual cognition arises from the eye and visible form alone;
for it is thus:

The operation of the eye is directed toward mere form (rūpa) present before it; otherwise, how could there be an operation toward something else? (349) For it is not possible to conceive of what is perceived in one way as being otherwise.

Indeed, it cannot be said that the eye, while observed to operate upon mere form present before it, also operates upon sound, universals (sāmānya), and so forth, because there is a lack of valid evidence (pramāṇa).
If one were to conceive it thus, there would be an over-extension [of the definition].
Therefore, whether prior to or subsequent to the arising of memory, perception is free from conceptual construction because the object is distinct [from the memory]. (350)
For the cognition "this is fragrant" or "this is foul-smelling," which arises at a time subsequent to recollection, is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because the operation of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) pertains only to visible form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, only that which arises in dependence upon the eye and other bases with respect to an object is direct perception.
That [object] is not other than this;
therefore, the form of the universal of the word and so forth is not perceived.
Furthermore, that which is the cause for a clear manifestation is also grasped as its basis; thus, mental perception and the like are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*).
Alternatively, it has been stated that even that [mental perception] "attains" or "pervades" the object-form as if it were a sense-organ itself.
6.5. Varieties of direct perception—(1) sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*).
Now, why is it that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is said to be dependent on the object (*viṣaya*) for its arising, rather than being "per-object" (*prativiṣayam*)?
For designation by means of the object—such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth—is appropriate, but not by means of the sense faculty (*indriya*).
For perception is not [defined] merely as "that which is produced by a sense faculty."
However, all perception (*pratyakṣa*) indeed functions toward the apprehension of the essential nature of the object;
yet some perception is based on the sense organs (*akṣa*), while another is otherwise.
And that designation for it is appropriate which is based on a non-deviating cause.
But is it not the case that even the appearance of two moons and so forth, though produced by an object, is indeed an error?
Therefore, nothing that arises from an object can be entirely non-erroneous.
Indeed, that [double moon] is not even an object, because its cause is incapable of imparting a form [to the cognition].
In that case, then, that [sense-organ] is not truly a sense-organ (*akṣa*) because it is impaired; a sense-organ that is unimpaired is what is called a "pseudo-sense-organ" (*akṣābhāsa*).
Furthermore, in that case, it is like a sense-object (*viṣaya*) which is capable of producing consciousness directly.
If [the cognition] arises directly, then why is it not said to be produced by both, since its birth depends on two [factors]? || 191 ||
Since the object and the sense organ are equal in being causes [of cognition], why is there no designation by means of the object?
For those who act with foresight do not arbitrarily apply or abandon designations.
To this, it is replied:
For a designation is applied only after one has observed its indicative power;
it is not grasped [otherwise].

And that [capacity] exists in the designation "sense-organ" (akṣa), as does its property, namely, being subject to application. For, based on the distinction between being a signifier and not being a signifier, there is the adoption or rejection [of things];
and in the designation "sense-organ," there is indeed the quality of being a signifier.
If it is argued that there is deviation [of inference] due to perception based on the senses being impaired, that has already been refuted;
however, there is likewise no deviation even by way of the object, because that [impaired perception] lacks the status of being a valid object.
This is not a valid objection: if that [object] were not present, how could there be perception of anything else?
However, the nature of a sense faculty is not characterized by the presence or absence of a single object. (351)
For this very reason, he says:

"Designation by means of what is common is observed, as in 'the sound of a drum' or 'a barley sprout'; when 'barley sprout' is mentioned, there is no cognition of anything other than a barley sprout."
The cognition "the sprout is on the earth" occurs for him as well; so it is in other cases too.
Now, regarding the phrase "with respect to each object," this refers to the apprehension of the specific nature of the object.
Thus...
If [it were so], self-awareness alone would be perception, while in other cases there would be a lack of proof; now,
if it is said that [perception] consists in grasping the nature of an object as it is commonly established in the world,
then likewise—
Since "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is well-known in the world as that which exists [immediately], let this very definition suffice; what is the use of postulating another designation?

However, according to the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and others, even mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would result in being perception because it grasps its object; therefore, it too is rightly designated as "perception."
And thus it has been said:
"For the object is common [to all], because it is the cause of the mental consciousnesses belonging to other continua;
therefore, since [the sensory consciousness] is designated by means of the sense faculty, the nature of perception as being 'free from conceptual construction' can be defined."
It is not so, because of the designation by way of the object;
for indeed, it is possible to indicate [the cognition] by means of its object as well, as follows:
He says that it arises through the power of the object;
for that [cognition], being produced by the power of the object, would indeed conform to the very form of that [object].
It does not [conform to anything else].
Because it is inconclusive due to the deviation [found] in the form of a double moon,
there is no arising of an error through the power of an object.
If that were the case, its non-conceptual nature would not be established by this reasoning;

therefore, it is the sense faculty itself that is designated here as "of the object" because it is directed toward the object. For this very reason, since the sense faculty is the means of cognition, the designation is made by means of it alone.
Therefore, in this context of designation, the status of being subject to application ceases for that which has the nature of a mark (*liṅga*), because its non-pervasive nature has ceased.
Those who act with deliberation state that only application constitutes the capacity to signify.
If it is argued that this very [fact] serves as the indicative mark for the capacity to communicate,
then how is the agent’s acting with foresight understood?
True, indeed.
The fact that a statement possesses a true referent is not understood through the authority of a person;
rather, it is spoken of in this way according to worldly convention,
whereas in the ultimate sense, it is stated as being pervaded by way of its logical mark (*liṅga*).
By this, he states the cessation [of the object] through the cessation of the pervading nature.

Is it not the case that the designation "with respect to each object" (*prativiṣayam*) is an expression that indicates the well-known worldly conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), and that [this cognition],
being both prior and subsequent, has a single object as its domain for conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*)?

For this is well known in the world as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*); thus, that very thing which was seen by me is cognized through perception. Indeed, all word-meanings are accessible only through worldly convention. 352

A cognition that is uncontradicted (abādhitā) is entitled to the designation of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). And once something has been cognized by a valid means of knowledge, how could it be otherwise?
(353) This [notion] is indeed false;

for here, the direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa) itself is the object of perception, which consists in cognition. Indeed, there is no other means of knowledge distinct from inference than direct realization. (354)
Inference alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by non-perceptual operation;

therefore, if recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) functions through non-perception, it is simply inference, because perceptuality operates solely with respect to the object present before one, and thus there is no such thing as "recognition."
Therefore, direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is understood precisely from the designation of the sense organ (*indriya*) itself, and not from anything else;
by the designation of the object (*viṣaya*), there would merely be "having an object" (*saviṣayatā*),
but not the description of directness (*sākṣātkāritā*).
Furthermore, it is not established in common worldly usage that what is designated by that [conceptual term] is perception,
nor is perception a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) if it is not a direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). Since it is settled that perception is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*),
how then was this stated?
In that regard, because it is produced by multiple objects, [perception] has the universal as its object with respect to its own referent.
Indeed, non-conceptual [cognition] does not have the universal as its object, because the conceptualization of a universal is in contradiction with it.
He states this very point:

In that case, there is a universal belonging to the accumulated collection, and the sensory cognition as well as the cognition of the universal is necessarily followed by conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Indeed, when many things situated by mutually excluding their own natures are perceived in that very way, there is no cognition of a "collection" [as a distinct entity].
The collection (samudāya) must be either ultimate (pāramārthika) or imagined (kalpita).
It cannot first be ultimate, because there is no appearance of a universal (sāmānya) apart from those [individuals];
or if it is an appearance, let that other [universal] appear as something distinct from them.
Nor is that a composite whole;

for if it were such, let those very elements themselves, by virtue of their mutual dependence, bear the designation of a "composite"—what need is there for anything else? Or, if it is argued that their own form is concealed and another form appears, even that is merely a superimposition since no such entity exists in reality; how then can it not be the object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)?
And if [the atoms] have a conceptualized object as their domain, then their status as being determinate (*savikalpaka*) is unavoidable.
To this it is replied:
"Those other atoms which arise from the conjunction with another object..."
These have been described as accumulated, for they are indeed the cause for the arising of cognition.

That particularity (*viśeṣa*) of atoms does not exist without other atoms; therefore, because it is restricted to those [atoms] alone, cognition is said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. (195–196)
For atoms, being subtle or otherwise, are incapable of producing cognition because they lack the causal power for knowledge to arise from them; therefore,
cognition must be produced by all [atoms] together.
For it has been stated that knowledge produced by conceptual construction (*jñānanirmita*) has as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) determined by a single [form].
If it is asked why these [particulars], which are indeed mutually distinct, do not appear [as such], [we reply]:
surely even hairs and the like, when far away, do not come within the range of perception as being non-conjoined (*asaṃsakta*).
If, due to their lack of capacity to impart their own nature—which is determined by their respective causes—they do not appear, then who is to be blamed here?

In that case, since there would be no appearance of "existence" (*bhāvatva*) when [the object] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would follow that [the cognition] is erroneous; and even in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), if it appears in such a manner, it would possess conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), just like a conceptualization of another universal (*sāmānya*).
Then, in that state, it is the very nature of cognition itself that appears directly perceived as a single, solid, and gross form; consequently, non-conceptuality arises,
for now conceptualization is severed everywhere, since in every instance of conceptual knowledge it is only the form of cognition itself that manifests.
To this it is replied:

for those born at present, because there is an absence of subverting cognitions, their state is called non-erroneous; however, in reality, all [cognitions] regarding the objective support (*ālambana*) are delusions.
For those born at present, whose power of awakened realization has not yet arisen, this appears as "non-erroneous."
With reference to that, it was stated that [cognition] is non-erroneous;
however, in the ultimate sense, everything is indeed erroneous with respect to its objective support (ālambana).
Therefore:
Thus, it is this very non-conceptuality that is stated regarding perception; because its nature is direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), it is not associated with conceptual grasping.
For conceptual cognition is not direct realization, since it involves the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a previously apprehended object upon the [present] thing.
For direct realization itself is not called superimposition, since reality is established through its opposite; therefore,
in that case, [superimposition] would lack the status of having a universal as its object.
Because they possess the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) according to worldly consensus,

it has been said that these have specific characteristics as their objects with respect to the specific characteristics of the sense-bases (*āyatana-svalakṣaṇa*), but not with respect to the specific characteristics of substantial entities (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*).
That too is incorrect;

for this distinction was formulated by the former teachers with reference to the ultimate reality (paramārtha). Therefore, there is no contradiction in its being an object of conceptualization (sāmānya-gocara). It is the atoms themselves, when perceived in such a manner, that constitute the universal (sāmānya).
Regarding the claim that "everything is indeed non-conceptual," we reply:

that very [distinction] has already been established through valid cognition and actual experience; it was only by relying on what is commonly accepted by others that the author of the treatise taught this division. (358)

Relying on the consensus of others, such as the Mīmāṃsakas and so forth, the author of the treatise established the presentation of conceptual objects by way of recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), noting that such [conceptualization] does not exist in direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*); thus he made the distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition].
Furthermore, even though they belong to a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*), multiple [atoms] are not apprehended simultaneously.
1. Then, due to the superimposition of an object previously apprehended, it is conceptual (savikalpaka).

For if multiple atoms were apprehended simultaneously, there would be no superimposition (adhyāropa) upon an object previously apprehended; thus, it would not be conceptual (savikalpaka) by virtue of being a recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*).

However, if apprehension occurs sequentially, it is difficult to avoid [the charge of being conceptual], because a single cognition is incapable of apprehending multiple things at once, since when the mind is occupied with one thing, it cannot simultaneously operate toward another.
Or rather, a single composite substance must be admitted because it is perceived all at once;

for even when many individual things are grasped, that unity is also apprehended. [359] Is there not an appearance of simultaneous perception even in the case of sesame seeds and the like when they are separated? [197]
If atoms are not perceived simultaneously, then, because of the superimposition of what precedes, we indeed accept that it is conceptual;
but if they are seen [simultaneously], then its non-conceptual nature is established due to direct perception.
Furthermore:
If it is argued that this well-known multiplicity, situated in various suitable locations, is not perceived simultaneously by a single [perceiver] because the mind is unitary, we say:
no.
Because that which contradicts the simultaneous arising of cognitions— namely, the "mind" (*manas*)— is unestablished,
since it is well-known that "mind-ness" (*manastva*) consists merely of mental attention (*manaskāra*); furthermore, (the following applies).

The perception of simultaneous apprehension is indeed observed in the case of sesame seeds and rice grains, or a staff, a water-pot, a vessel, and earrings, which are distinct from one another; however,
the claim that this appearance of simultaneity arises due to the rapidity of the apprehension is also incorrect,
because:

The objection regarding lightness has already been answered in the case of those very [cognitions] that occur in succession: why is there no perception of non-succession? Furthermore, are all cognitions simultaneous, or are some among them appearing without succession while others appear with succession? (198)
Therefore, it follows that there would be no sequence in the apprehension of all objects.
For simultaneous apprehension is not tenable on the grounds of rapidity, since rapidity has already been refuted due to its non-existence.
How is this known?
If it is argued that "due to rapidity, there is the conceit of simultaneous apprehension, as in the case of piercing a hundred lotus petals," we say no.
Since the matter is not established by a mere example—
for what is established in one case is not necessarily so in another—

in the case of piercing a hundred leaves, however, because it is impossible for them to be pierced simultaneously while maintaining their upper-lower relationship, the sequence is established through inference.
Furthermore, such an assumption cannot avoid the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
therefore, in the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), error is not established.

Moreover, if you claim that there is a misconception of simultaneous apprehension due to parsimony (*lāghava*), why does this same [misconception] not occur in those very cases where things are perceived sequentially, even though they were previously non-existent?
If it is argued that this is because there is no [perceived] lightness [of cognition],
then why is it so even in this case?
If it is argued that it is because of the conceit of grasping [the object] all at once, [we reply:]...
Why is this so?
Because a mutual dependence arises:
as long as the erroneous nature of the single apprehension is not established, the establishment of parsimony cannot occur.
Furthermore, as long as that [momentariness] is not established, the fact of error remains unestablished.
Moreover, since all cognitions are equal in duration due to their momentariness, why is it that there is no appearance of succession in any cognition? (360)
For the manifestation of the object of cognition lasts only as long as the duration of the intellect;
therefore, the entire manifestation of the object would necessarily be non-successive.
Consequently, even the simultaneous appearance [of objects] is not caused by rapidity, because it exists in that very same way [as a single, non-successive event].
However, where there is no simultaneous manifestation due to a deficiency in causes, the opposite case is established:
if one [element] is not apprehended, the appearance of a non-conceptual [cognition] is possible; yet in the absence of conceptualization, the apprehension of a distinct object is impossible.
(361) How could there be a clear manifestation of that which was previously seen through superimposition? Because of the total absence of cultivation, it is indeed non-conceptual. (362)
For in this way, the cognition of yogins is likewise non-conceptual;
and thus there is indeed a simultaneous manifestation, because there is no grasping of a prior form.
How could a single form, such as a variegated butterfly and so forth, be seen?
If it is argued that "this variegated thing is one," then this is even more variegated than that.

(200) If, because the mind does not function in multiple places simultaneously, there is no simultaneous apprehension of many [colors], and therefore the form of a variegated butterfly is not apprehended, and thus a single composite whole (*avayavin*) is accepted— then this acceptance is even more variegated than the variegated butterfly itself.
For that which is variegated does not have a single nature, just like the form of a gem;
the designation "variegated" occurs because the essence of the entity consists of mutually interconnected natures, otherwise what would be the meaning of "variegated" here?
Therefore, just as there is unity in a certain variegated butterfly despite its possession of a collection of various forms and jewels, so too,
while there is multiplicity due to the suitability for the division of the gems, there is no such [multiplicity] for the butterfly.
Even there, since division is possible,
division is simply the appearance [of things] through mutual division;
for even when division exists, there may be unity.
That being the case, even in a collection of jewels, there is another division therein called "separation"; therefore, that which is not separated— even if variegated— is indeed one.
Because separation is possible everywhere;
for indeed, through cutting, splitting, and so forth, separation is possible in all cases. Thus, the destruction of the substance occurs in every instance. (363)
If separation, termed "disjunction," is possible—as in the case of a collection of jewels—then there is no single composite whole (*avayavin*) therein;
why then does this not also apply to variegated butterflies and the like? [Objection:

In that case, since disjunction arises through effort by means of cutting and so forth, the composite whole is destroyed, and consequently there is no disjunction [of its parts]; thus, there is no fault.
The same logical consequence applies here as well: let it be postulated that this [process] occurs even in a collection of jewels.
In that very context—the reading being "separation" (which implies the refutation of the whole)—the same point holds.

[Objection: "But even though blue and other qualities are perceived as mutually exclusive, since touch has that same single nature and because the parts are not distinct from one another, the whole (avayavin) must be one and the same. [Reply:
That too is incorrect, because:
Furthermore, the appearance of blue and other colors is identical in both cases:

in artificial variegated cloth and the like, which consist of a collection of threads of different kinds, the same differentiation of blue and so forth occurs, accompanied by an undifferentiated tactile sensation and the rest.
Therefore, how can there be this distinction that in one case there is a composite whole (*avayavin*) and in the other there is not?
In that case, if only the form of the parts is perceived,
then having set aside [the notion of] blue and so forth, you perceive another "variegated" variegation;
for if, in artificial things such as painted cloths, only the form of the parts is perceived in that way through an adherence to unity.

At that time, having abandoned the blue and other colors which exist in a state of division, there is no other "variegated" (citra) quality even in non-artificial [natural] things; the only recourse in this regard is the mental adherence to them as a single unit,
and that [adherence] exists even in artificial things without a whole (avayavin).

Consequently, since that hope has also vanished, it is not logical for the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) to possess variegated color (*citrarūpa*), because neither perception nor inference establishes such a thing; however, the pulling of one [part] while another is pulled is indeed observed in the case of magnets, iron balls, and the like.
In that case, it is established that multiple things are perceived simultaneously;
however, if you argue that there is a distinction such that blue and other colors are perceived only sequentially in artificial objects, whereas they are perceived simultaneously elsewhere,
that too is incorrect.
Of those two cognitions which are not characterized by having identical objects, forms, and times.
One [cognition] has multiple objects and is successive; why is it that the other has a single object and is non-successive?

(203) Even though the two cognitions are identical in terms of the form of the object and time, one appears as having multiple objects and is successive, while the other, establishing only a single composite object (*avayavin*) within its own range, is not successive—what is the basis for this? Indeed, when identity is observed everywhere, difference is not a subject for acceptance.
If this [distinction] between the artificial and the non-artificial, as conceived through various notions, is accepted,
then this acceptance is without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) and is merely a claim that cannot provide protection [against contradiction].
Indeed, if this division into the one and the many were established by the force of some means of valid cognition, then what fault would there be in this?
This is not tenable,
because it is through the manifold forms of cognitions themselves that entities possess their manifold nature.
If that [external object] is not a factor, by what means is this established distinction between difference [and identity] achieved?

(204) Only those cognitions which possess the appearance of both unitary and manifold forms have the authority (*prāmāṇya*) to establish such a nature; there is no other process of valid cognition (*pramākrama*).

And if those cognitions—which, though their procedure for establishing such a state has not been subverted—were to be set aside by another cognition whose validity is merely imagined on the basis of a commonality, [then the distinction would collapse].

If it were argued that "this similarity (sādharmya) is not found anywhere," then there would be no established status for existing things, and everything would become incoherent. Therefore, it is logical that those cognitions serve to establish the non-failure of other appearances and declare that the appearance is not in vain. (364) If an entity were established merely through similarity, then since such [similarity] exists everywhere, everything would be established—or else nothing at all would be established anywhere. (365)

For an inference whose invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been grasped by perception cannot be subverted by another inference that arises in the same manner, nor by another perception that possesses the status of a counter-correlator (*pratiyogin*); indeed,
one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not subverted by another means of valid cognition.

If they possess equal strength, what constitutes the sublation? And how can there be validity if there is sublation? Or, if there is no sublation, then there is an inequality of strength. Furthermore, that which is contradicted by inference cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all.
That which occurs through perception is not inference; thus the same undesirable consequence applies.
Since the appearance of an object arises in some way from a defect in its cause, it is not inference;
therefore, that [perception] alone is the sublater.
That too is incorrect;

for while it is logical that a cognition regarding an object of knowledge might be otherwise due to a defect in the cause, how could it be logical for its own nature to be otherwise even due to hundreds of defects in the cause?
(366) It is not tenable to say that the nature of a sequential appearance becomes non-sequential due to a defect in the cause.
For it is not the case that a single entity has multiple intrinsic natures, because that would entail the consequence of multiple cognitions [of it];
if it is argued that there is no appearance of a single [entity], we say no.
Because it would follow that there is an absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*); for indeed, when there is no manifestation, what is called "manifestation" cannot exist,
and it is a contradiction to claim that non-manifestation has manifestation as its intrinsic nature.
Now, [you might argue that] it is only the gradual manifestation [of the letters], and nothing else;
and that everything else is merely an illusion.
But what is this illusion?
Is it non-appearance, or is it appearance in another way? And what follows from this?
If it were non-appearance, then error would be unrestrained everywhere. If that very thing appears in such a manner, how can it be called "error"? (367)
If every appearance were an error, it would follow that even one in deep sleep or a stone would be in error.
Furthermore, if there is no appearance of sequence, then sequence itself appears unimpaired; how then could this be an error?
For the mere appearance of a pillar or such things is not itself an error.
If error is the appearance of something else, how can there be an appearance of its own nature? And if there is no appearance of its own nature, how can there be the delusion that "that exists"?
(368) If the appearance of something other than the intended object is what constitutes error, then in that case, there is no appearance of its own nature at all; how then can that cognition exist?
If a cognition could exist even without appearing, then one would have to say that all cognitions of everyone exist at all times.
If that cognition is indeed non-existent as an error,
then how can there be an error when a sequential cognition, being non-existent, appears as non-sequential because it has arisen in succession?

Now, if it is argued that this is merely an error because there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) for her, [we reply]: on the contrary, in the case of sesame seeds and the like which lack sequence, there is indeed an object of cognition for a cognition that itself lacks sequence; however, for a cognition possessing sequence, an object of cognition is impossible, because it appears otherwise [than it actually is].

If it is argued that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is indeed not sequential, and therefore [the cognition] is thus [sequential], then in that case there would be no appearance of sequence even in its own nature (*svarūpa*); consequently, there could be no connection with error (*bhrānti*).
Now, if...

If another cognition were to grasp the nature of [the preceding] cognition, then how could there be the appearance of simultaneity for that which is by its very nature sequential? (369) If a sequential cognition were grasped by another cognition,
there would be no appearance of simultaneity for objects of knowledge such as jewels, pearls, and so forth.
Because the cognition grasping that [object] arises sequentially, and because the cognition grasping that [cognition] does not operate upon the object of knowledge,
nor does sequence appear as non-sequential.

If it is argued that the appearance of that [object] is due to error, then it follows that this very [cognition] is non-erroneous; for who can prevent its grasping of the object of cognition in that way? (370) If the cognition arises as appearing in succession, then the cognition of that cognition must likewise be so;
if, however, there is simultaneous apprehension through error, then it would follow that a single [cognition] could simultaneously grasp many things.
If it is argued that there is no cognition of identity because the preceding and succeeding apprehensions lack such identity, and that identity is instead cognized by a subsequent cognition—
then how can that [subsequent cognition], which itself possesses a temporal sequence, cognize identity?

For the time of apprehension does not transcend the time of the apprehender; thus, it would be simultaneous. If that were the case, there would be the apprehension of many [objects] by a single [cognition].
If it is argued that this [cognition] is therefore an error,
even so, the appearance of multiple natures remains unrefuted;
for if the cognition of variegation is indeed one, [how can there be such a manifold appearance?]

If gems, pearls, and so forth, as well as blue and other colors—which appear with distinct forms—are nevertheless of the nature of cognition, then it would follow that all objects of cognition are likewise [of the nature of cognition].
Therefore, even in the case of error, simultaneous appearance of multiple things is not logical;
thus, whatever is experienced—whether simultaneously or otherwise—it must be accepted exactly as it is experienced.
In the same way, because it follows the sequence of investigation, otherwise there would be no established status for the object of cognition;
[one might object: "But surely, in paintings and the like, a perception of variegated form (*citra-buddhi*) is observed."

How is it that unity is not tenable in the case of gems, pearls, and so forth? It is not that there is no cognition of variety and unity therein; rather, this distinction arises from the very differentiation of the appearance within cognition itself.
Because it would contradict one's own tenets;
for since heterogeneous [atoms] do not initiate [a composite], there can be no cognition of variegation in paintings and the like.
Because it is formless, it cannot be variegated through conjunction, nor can it be the locus of figurative attribution (bhakti).
If one were to follow the [opponent's] reasoning, one's own established doctrine would be abandoned;

for since things of different classes do not originate [a single effect], a cloth or similar object produced by the conjunction of threads of different classes could not possess a variegated nature as its constituent whole.
Now, even if this cognition is erroneous, there is still simultaneous apprehension. When there is the apprehension of an unreal form, why is there not also the apprehension of a real form?
(371) For even an erroneous cognition, when it arises, does indeed arise in the apprehension of many things simultaneously;
for what distinction is there between the real and the unreal in the manifestation of something standing before one?

Now, if that form belongs to cognition itself, then how is it that this unreal thing—which is the very nature of the cognition of reality—is not [itself] real? For if they are of one essence, this distinction between the real and the unreal cannot exist; or else, there can be no unity at all. (372)
Furthermore, it might be argued that the self exists as that form because it is the object of cognition, whereas the external form consisting of yellow and so forth is unreal.

This is not its essence, nor is that its form; if it were so, this conceptualization would be logically consistent. Furthermore, it might be argued that even a single cognition can operate toward multiple objects within the nature of the self, because there is no effort required therein.

But regarding another form, there is great exertion on the part of the mind characterized by its movement and so forth; therefore, simultaneous apprehension is impossible, because apprehension cannot occur at once in contradictory locations.
If, then, the mind is not the cause of apprehension when it is moving—

If it is argued that the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon is impossible because they move at different speeds, and that there is merely an appearance of simultaneous perception due to the rapid motion [of the eye],
we say no.
Because rapidity is impossible at an extreme distance; furthermore,
what is the proof here that the eye and other sense organs function by reaching their objects?
The opponent says:

If the eye and other [senses] were to function without reaching their object, there would be no dependence on obscuration or its absence, nor any dependence on distance or its proximity, regarding perception and non-perception.
As it has been said: "The eye, the ear, and the mind do not reach their objects.
If that were so, there would be no such thing as non-perception due to the presence of an obstruction, nor perception otherwise.
For in that case [of non-contact], there is no obstacle capable of causing an obstruction;
however, if [the sense organ] functions by reaching its object, an obstruction is logically possible due to the repulsion by material substances,
and in the case of extreme distance, because of the absence of movement.
That is incorrect;
for even if it acts without reaching its object, it still requires a suitable location, just like a magnet.
Indeed, a magnet, though acting by attracting without reaching the object, is not capable of attracting every piece of iron.
Now, even there, the touch of iron certainly exists, though it is not perceived due to its subtlety, just as the touch of the rays of the eye is not perceived.
But surely this very point is being established by another [argument]; how then can that same thing be the means of proof?
Therefore,
this extremely painful fabrication being made by those who have lost [their way] serves only for the ridicule of the wise, and not for true understanding.
(374) Now, it might be argued:

It is observed that there is an attraction of what is in contact [with a magnet]; however, this is not the case even for that which is being attracted by a magnet. Furthermore, if it were held that a mantra also possesses the power of attraction, then because that which is attracted would necessarily involve contact, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle (atiprasaṅga).
If it is argued that "let it be so even there," [we reply] no,
because sound is a quality (*guṇa*).
Alternatively, if that very same property is attributed even to the object of the observation of inconclusiveness, then there could never be anything characterized by inconclusiveness; for instance,

in the case of the [faulty] inference "He is dark-skinned because he is his son," when a deviation is observed in the form of a fair-skinned son, it would follow as an absurd consequence (prasaṅga) that dark skin must also exist in that case.
As for why it is not seen,
let the cause of its non-perception be considered;
furthermore:

If the visual rays (cakṣūraśmi) go out and come into contact [with the object], why is there no perception even at an extreme distance, as in the case of the rays of a lamp when there is no obstruction? This is not a fault; for in that case, it would follow that [the eye] must grasp what is extremely close, since the rays of a lamp do not fail to function at an extreme proximity.
Therefore, another property distinct from the eyes and other sense organs must be admitted, arising from the lamp;

that alone is the cause of perception, not the contact with rays. Furthermore, if there were rays from the eyes and other organs, it would follow that perception would occur even when those rays are absent.
Now, as for the mind, its capacity is such that it possesses rapidity.
In that case, let the single apprehension itself produce [the result]; what is the use of this laborious conceptualization?
Furthermore, such a mind is not established by valid cognition;
rather, it is the mental attention (*manaskāra*)—which has the form of the preceding cognition—that performs that purposeful activity.

Since knowledge cannot arise elsewhere when there is a deficiency in the mind’s attention toward another object, the non-simultaneity of cognitions follows; and because [the mind] is thus established by another means, the mind is not understood from that logical mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, it is the cognition itself that is designated as the grasper of those causes. Like a pair of tongs, it is through cognitions that there is the perception of the grasping of objects, and not otherwise. Thus, the simultaneous grasping of multiple forms in a painting is indeed non-erroneous.
Now, in that case, the conjunction is variegated, but it is not the form of a composite whole;
since conjunction is a quality (guṇa), there is no inherence (samavāya) of color in it.

If that were the case, then because it possesses qualities, it would be a substance itself; and thus, there would be a violation of the established tenet that "like does not originate from unlike. Alternatively, if the variegated nature of conjunction is attributed through metaphorical designation, [the same fault follows].
That too is incorrect;
for just as the cognition "forest-flower" arises through inherence in a single object, so too would this [cognition of a forest] arise,
yet there is no equality between these two cases.
For a forest is that in which the quality of being in bloom—which belongs to many trees under the numerical category of plurality—is co-inherent in a single object; thus it has been said.
However, variegation (*citrātva*) is not co-inherent here in the parts where conjunction resides, as he says:
Because each individual [element] lacks variety;
for indeed, there is no variety in the thread and so forth individually, such that the conjunction inhering in them would likewise possess it.

Now, just as when "fire-ness" is perceived in a fire, the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire—brought about by the perception of common properties such as sharpness—leads one, while remembering it, to superimpose the nature of fire even upon a young boy.

Likewise, it is argued that when blue and other colors are apprehended sequentially, they are superimposed upon the color being perceived at the time of apprehending any one of them; thus arises the cognition of a variegated whole (*citrapratīti*).
This is untenable, because:
And even if they were grasped sequentially, there would be no synthesis of a variegated cognition, because multiple [colors] cannot be grasped by a single [cognition].

For in that case [of the hair-tuft], sharpness and similarity are the grounds for superimposition; but here, how could there be a superimposition of the blue and so forth that are being directly perceived?
Now, as for proximity (*pratyāsatti*),
it is logically tenable only in the case of simultaneous apprehension; however, in the case of sequential apprehension, there can be no apprehension of proximity.
If it is argued that this is because [the color] is perceived in that location,
even when perceiving that location, there is no perception of the variegation of the preceding and succeeding parts;
thus, it is not tenable to say that it arises through superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

Since this very [object] is what is to be reflected upon, how can there be a misapprehension of one thing as another— namely, that the remembered appears as if being perceived— due to the non-apprehension of their difference?
If it appears having abandoned its nature as a remembered form, then that is merely a perception; therefore, there is no synthesis.
Alternatively, if synthesis itself has the nature of perception...
If that were the case, it would follow that multiple things are apprehended by a single [cognition],
which is not accepted,
because we observe that the entire [object] is perceived through the operation of the eye.
Therefore, since these [theories] are stained by the stains of baseless conceptualization and imagined by dull-witted people, he says [in the *Citraikatvacintā*]:
"Consequently, it would have multiple objects; therefore, even though it is established as non-conceptual..."
1. Even while conceptualizing various objects as one, because he sees something other than that, [he realizes] the one object. || 208 ||

For even when one conceptualizes "this is blue" regarding a variegated appearance consisting of various forms such as blue and so forth, one certainly perceives the yellow and other colors situated at the periphery; yet, since multiple simultaneous conceptualizations are impossible,
if it is argued that one simply conceptualizes it as "variegated," we say no.
Because there is no such rule;
for it is not necessarily the case that one must conceptualize [the object] as being variegated,
since conceptualization is observed even in respect to a single [part].

And thus, the cognition that simultaneously possesses all forms such as blue and so forth is a single, variegated form; in this regard, the objection is raised: if unity is not tenable for objects that appear as variegated, [then how can it be so for cognition]?
How, then, can that very cognition be unitary while manifesting variegated forms?
This is what he establishes: just as cognition is accepted by you as possessing variegated aspects...
In that very same way, if there is also external differentiation therein, by what is it produced?
For since the diversity of cognitions consists in the variegated nature of things, why should that [differentiation] not belong to the cognition which has mounted upon them?
Therefore, this [argument] that "because of its variegated nature it must be manifold" is not inconclusive with respect to the example of the intellect (*buddhi*).
To this, it is said:
this is what the wise declare as having arisen from the power of the thing itself (*vastubalāyātam*).
In whatever manner objects are contemplated, they fall apart in that very same manner;
for it is there [in that very process] that they are analyzed.
How could there be such variety in a single [cognition]? It would not exist even in that cognition if this [variety] were pleasing to objects by itself; in that case, what role would we have?
This is the meaning.
Indeed, even though cognition is one, it is not manifold; for in that case as well, because it possesses multiple forms, it is manifold, since a real entity is characterized by its forms,
and by necessity, the entity itself [is manifold] through the multiplicity of its forms.
In that case, if there are exactly as many cognitions [as atoms], what loss is there for the proponent of the opposing view?

However, if cognitions are manifold such that there is one cognition for each atom, it would follow that there is a perception of individual atoms and a simultaneous occurrence of multiple perceptions,
because there would be no mutual non-perception [of the other atoms].
Indeed, there is no realization of multiplicity among those things that are self-cognized, because [otherwise] it would follow that another mental continuum would also appear;
this is not the case.
Because it is observed;
for indeed, there is no such thing as "inconsistency" even with respect to what is observed.
If that is so, then self-awareness [is established], because there is awareness of one another.
Because sensation is not possible without self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), and this will be demonstrated later; however,
in the case of awareness, there is indeed a purpose served by awareness of another.
Who, then, can apprehend plurality?
No one at all,
because there is no cognizer apart from that [plurality].

Therefore, neither unity nor plurality is logically tenable for cognitions. If there were unity, there would be an absence of variety; if there were plurality, it would be even more utterly non-existent.
Thus, in whatever way a thing is examined, it simply falls apart; what can we do about this?
Therefore, he says that consciousness is empty of the nature of consciousness; thus, the emptiness of all phenomena alone is logical.
Now, why does that which appears not arise simply from the conceptualization of oneness or multiplicity?
Even though it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it nonetheless appears;
there is no fault in this, for it is like the appearance of illusions, mirages, and the like, which appear despite being non-existent.
[Objection: If those too are non-existent, how can they appear?
If it is a manifestation, how can it be non-existent?

Precisely because of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), for existence is characterized by causal efficiency; the conventional usage of "existence" does not occur based on mere manifestation alone.
Since there is certainty regarding non-existence even when [an object] such as hair appears, [one might ask:
what is this "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*)? What indeed is this causal efficiency?
Is it something other than that which appears, or is it that very thing itself?
If it were other, then for that [other] as well...
If causal efficiency is admitted for an object other than that which appears, there is an infinite regress and thus no cognition [of the object];
if, on the other hand, that very [efficiency] belongs to all appearances, it follows that all things must exist; therefore, illusions and the like are not non-existent.

To this it is replied: for some [things] [difference] is indeed distinct, while for others it is the opposite; such is the established distinction of the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of entities. (377)
For it is not the case that everything which appears is necessarily capable of causal efficiency;
rather, only that which appears as having the nature of causal efficiency possesses that very nature of causal efficiency.
And since the establishment of existence occurs through the presence of the nature of causal efficiency, while non-existence occurs through its absence.
In that case, it is not the case that all appearances are non-existent, because some are connected with causal efficiency;
nor is this a reductio ad absurdum based on the opponent's own admission.
For proponents of existence accept that existence consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Indeed, apart from the appearance of that [causal efficiency],
no nature of causal efficiency other than the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth is perceived.
Whatever is desired by someone is itself the causal efficiency for that person; this [notion] is indeed unstable, for what is desired by one person is not necessarily so for another.
If it is argued that the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) consists in the cessation of suffering and the production of pleasure, we say no;
for even suffering and pleasure are not established as permanent.
And since everything arises through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
and since it is absent when cultivation is absent, its non-existence alone is established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
If this is so, then by the force of cultivation it is cognition itself that becomes such [an appearance], and not non-existence.

Non-existence is precisely the state of being produced through the power of ignorance, because that which has arisen in such a manner lacks an abiding nature; since it exists merely as an appearance that is charming only so long as it is not investigated, it is nothing but conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Therefore, there is no appearance of grossness either in objects or in cognition; since it has been refuted in the case of a single [entity], its occurrence in many is also impossible.
For indeed, among objects—whether they be atoms or composite wholes—there is no appearance of grossness.

For grossness (*sthūlatā*) is differentiated by spatial directions; and since spatial directions, by mutually excluding one another, do not occupy a single location, [grossness cannot be a real entity].
Alternatively, grossness is merely an appearance among many [atoms];
for it is in this way that many atoms of a similar kind, appearing without interruption, are designated as "gross."
This too is not tenable;
for if it is argued that although these [atoms] do not possess grossness individually, they will possess it as a collection, [we reply: many indeed they are.
A collection [of atoms] is not a single,

solid appearance that can be designated as "gross," because there is no such unity in an appearance where [atoms] are perceived as mutually distinct, since the intervening spaces between them are also perceived.
If, on the other hand, it does not appear [to you], then those [atoms] would not have appeared to you at all.
Furthermore, if upon the dissolution of the atoms a distinct composite whole (*avayavin*) arises from their conjunction,
then in that case there would be no atoms or any parts whatsoever.

If a distinct whole (*avayavin*) were produced [as something entirely new], then in that case, even the atoms (*paramāṇu*) would perish and a different whole would be produced— just as a sprout arises from a seed— and consequently, the atoms and other parts, aided by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), would initiate the whole inherent (*samaveta*) within themselves; thus, the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) would not belong to the threads and so forth, because a relation must reside in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*).
In this case, cognition would be without a support because of the non-existence of the referent of the locative case;
or, if that [object] were apprehended as being partless, it would entail the consequence of apprehending its "other side" and so forth.

Furthermore, if the far side were visible, the other side would also be visible; since that [other side] too is a whole possessing parts, it would follow that everyone would be an all-seeing observer of the far side.
Alternatively, if the far side is not seen...
Since the "other part" itself does not exist, how can it be seen by another? If you say, "It is something entirely different," then it is not a part at all.
And if it is argued that its perception as grossness occurs only successively, we say no.
Because it is impossible for two [distinct] things to occupy the same location,
and because one cannot establish that "this is that very same thing" due to their being perceived respectively as tangible and visible— if you argue that there is therefore a "whole" (avayavin);
Since there is no means of valid cognition [for such a thing],
how can there be oneness when they are apprehended as mutually excluding each other's essential natures?
This mutual distinction is produced by the act of apprehension; however, the object of apprehension is indeed one.
In that case, every distinction would dissolve, and there would be only a duality.
Nor does that [object] appear apart from those [parts]; thus, all phenomena are empty.
Furthermore, there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that whatever is seen is the very same thing that is touched.
Therefore, neither the whole (*avayavin*) nor the parts are within the scope of appearance.
Let it be simply a manifestation;
if that is so, then since this is merely a manifestation, it follows that it is either consciousness or not consciousness—
how, then, can there be the emptiness of all phenomena?
To this it is replied:
This internal discernment appears as if it were an external part; for the appearance of division in cognition, which is itself undivided, is indeed a cognitive distortion (upaplava). || 213 ||
If this cognition is also self-aware (*svasaṃvedana*), then because it terminates within its own nature, the appearance of difference is not tenable;
for in self-awareness there is no awareness of another,
and therefore there is no manifestation of difference.
If it is argued that there is a distinction [between cognitions] because they are mutually aware of one another, then in that case too,
if each were apprehended individually, there would be the fault of [each being] a separate stream of consciousness (*santānāntara*), just as in the case of other persons.

"In that way, it was delimited by me"— this is not possible in the absence of self-awareness (asvavedana). If those two cognitions were to know both themselves and the other, then duality would result in [the admission of] self-awareness for both.
For self-awareness does not enter into the awareness of another;
otherwise, if there were no self-awareness,
there would be only the awareness of the other by both of them.
If that were the case, the two would not be perceived as distinct from one another— like Devadatta and Yajñadatta—
and there would be no such realization as "this has been known by me," because the agent does not appear through self-awareness;
consequently, those two [the object and the act of knowing] would themselves be instances of self-awareness.

And likewise, just as there is no cognition of two [objects] by one who has not entered another continuum, for this very reason the self is postulated as the cognizer of the two; otherwise, this undesirable consequence would follow—thus says the opponent.
To this, it is replied:
Whether it be self-awareness or something else, because it does not transcend the logic previously stated, even that [position] is not liberated from this same critical inquiry.

(379) If it is argued: "If the Self is of the nature of awareness, then because each [awareness] is submerged within its own self, there is no awareness of another; however, what contradiction is there in the awareness of another?"
It knows the other by means of that form, or it knows [it] by means of another; these two conceptual constructions must reside in one place.
To say that it knows [the other] by its own nature is not logical, because the own-nature is established within itself.
How can that form which is established in its own nature and directed only toward itself know another? If it were directed toward another's face,
then it would not perceive its own self.
If it is argued that, unlike the perception of two distinct mental continua,
there is no cognition of duality because he who possesses it has but one face— then who is the person capable of apprehending this "duality"?
If it is argued that "it is that very same [consciousness]," then there would be a need for two further acts of facing toward it, resulting in an infinite regress; therefore,
the triad is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Therefore, one who is intent on cognizing that [feeling] must further posit another self; thus there arises a great succession of calamities.
