Consequently, since there is only a single cognition from that feeling, the appearance of difference within non-dual cognition is a delusion. Thus, cognition, not being apprehended in its own nature, is simply non-existent, and emptiness alone remains.
Since both are lost through the absence of even one of them, therefore that very emptiness of duality is the reality of that [duality] as well. 214
It might be argued:
if one [of the two] is abandoned, there will be mere cognition;
if that which appears is abandoned, then both are likewise [non-existent], or else nothing at all—this is an absolute conclusion.
If it is argued that both [alternatives] may be the case, we say no,
because the answer has already been stated.
Since it has been established that there is neither self-cognition nor cognition of another, it is logical that emptiness alone is superior;
now, he explains the meaning of emptiness according to the systems of the Mādhyamikas, the Yogācāras, and the proponents of external objects (Bāhyārthavādins).

The establishment of entities such as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness depends upon their differentiation; this fixed state of the differentiation of entities relies on that [establishment]. And when that [establishment] is a delusion, their differentiation is also a delusion. || 215 ||
O Venerable One,
the two [aspects] are distinct, appearing as separate.
"Consciousness is that which cognizes"—thus, there exists no characteristic externalized in the form of grasped object and grasping subject;
therefore, because they are empty of characteristics, [all phenomena] are revealed to be without intrinsic nature. || 216 ||

"The definition of the aggregates and so forth, in their particularity, is entirely conditioned by functional activity; and since that [activity] is not the reality itself, these [aggregates] are not distinct from it."—
These are the intermediate verses (antarashloka).
One might ask: "How should one explain the Blessed One’s teaching on external objects such as form, as well as his other teachings? To this he says:

"Just as for those whose minds are overwhelmed by ignorance, a representation arises with a false aspect in dependence upon their own respective conditions, like the appearance of hair-tufts and so forth. (218)
And that [reality] is not understood in its true nature by all other philosophical systems, because for them it is impossible without the distortions of the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, having closed their eyes like elephants (gajanimīlana) while disregarding the true meaning of reality, [they fail to see it]. || 219 ||
External reflection is extended solely through worldly understanding.
[Objection: But if, in the ultimate sense, everything is indeed empty, and the Blessed One is a seer of reality—
How then is the Blessed One’s teaching of external objects [to be understood]?
For one who perceives reality does not teach what is unreal; or, if he were to teach it, how could he be known as a perceiver of reality?
To this it is replied:
the Blessed One’s teaching of external objects is not for the purpose of establishing external objects,
but rather for the purpose of restating them.
Since the negation of the self is intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [self], how can it even be a restatement? For one who perceives emptiness, that [self] does not appear.
Since restatement is possible solely through worldly cognition,
and such a cognition in the world arises from the practice of beginningless ignorance, one might object: "If the Blessed One possesses worldly cognition, how can he be a seer of reality?"
It is not [perceived] due to a prior impulse, because the teaching would otherwise be impossible,
like the whirling of a wheel.
Therefore, for the sake of introducing the world to the teaching of manifold aspects, it is indeed contradictory [to deny this].
Thus far, having accepted that cognition is empty, the avoidance of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] has been established;
now, he avoids it by accepting its variegated nature.

Even though cognition possesses variegated appearances, it is indeed unitary because it is distinct from external variegation; for while a variegated object is divisible and manifold, the blue and other elements within cognition are indivisible.
Thus:

In a variegated cognition (*citravijñāna*), the blue and other [colors] are attributes of the cognition (*jñānopādhi*) that cannot be perceived as separate from it; for one who attempts to distinguish them falls back upon the object itself. Since the blue and other [colors] that constitute the nature of the variegated cognition cannot be perceived in isolation—because they cannot be distinguished from it—there is indeed only oneness of the cognition, even in the case of a variegated one.
If, then, even a variegated [object] were one, then the appearance of sound and so forth would also have to be one;
let it be so if it cannot be distinguished.
However, even with the ears covered, color-form and the like are still perceived.
Therefore, the claim that there is multiplicity because of the apprehension of the isolated [object] is also incorrect, for there is no differentiation of cognition.

If it is argued that, because the previous appearance has ceased at that time and no longer appears, the word remains as something non-apparent, and therefore there is a distinction [between the two states];
At that time, because [the object] is not directly perceived by cognition, one who discriminates in this way would fall upon the object itself, since the object is not being cognized.

Alternatively, the discrimination is as follows: "This which is appearing now as something solitary is different from the form of the previous cognition, because it appears simultaneously [with the cognition]."
That too is incorrect;
for direct perception does not operate with respect to [an object's] prior state, but rather,
a cognition is experienced exactly as it appears.
The self manifests.
Thus, there may indeed be the name [of the object],
but it does not follow that it appeared in experience;
for direct perception through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) does not operate upon what is beyond its reach.
Because that which is beyond perception is not self-cognized, it is argued that it is known through recollection;
however, this is not tenable.
Since memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [one might argue:

"Memory is indeed a valid cognition because it arises from experience; it does not arise from memory. There is no proof for this, as memory is absent at the time of the experience, nor does one recognize through that memory: 'I have arisen from experience.'"
Because the experience is not seen by that [cognition], or else, if there were an experience of the experience, there would be no memory; rather,
it would simply be another experience.
Therefore, there is no fault in [the claim that] a variegated [object] is a single entity whose distinctions cannot be discerned.
If it is argued that external objects likewise possess oneness because their distinctions cannot be discerned, we say:
no.
If it is argued that at that very time, because one thing is seen by another,
what is seen by another must be something entirely different— and therefore there is a clear distinction—
then [the opponent replies]: "Only that which is seen by oneself is one."
Because it appears as self-awareness, that [cognition] is indeed cognition itself; thus, there would be a single nature for the mind possessing variegated forms. (222)
For in the mind,
there is no discernment apart from the nature of cognition itself.

Therefore, the variegated cognition—consisting of the forms of the grasped, the grasper, blue, and so forth—is indeed one; thus, there is only variegated non-duality (*citrādvaita*), for it is impossible to establish that variegation as distinct from the non-variegated.
Consequently, it is established that there is only consciousness alone as non-dual, because of the absence of anything else.
If that is so, since distinction is possible through both existence and non-existence, how can there be non-duality?

For indeed, there is no difference; therefore, because of the absence [of difference], non-difference is established as distinct from it. But if non-existence is not apprehended, how can there be non-duality for that which is to be distinguished? (380)

If there is no difference, then it would be understood that "non-difference alone exists as something other than difference. This being the case, one who apprehends non-existence and existence would indeed apprehend a duality between existence and non-existence; so how could there be non-duality?
For instance:
When one negates here that "the pillar is not in the pot," the cognition of difference does not arise without the non-existence [of the pillar];
indeed, every negation is necessarily concomitant with difference, for one understands the negation therein as being characterized by distinction.
But if there were no comprehension of the negation, then because of the admission of things as they truly are, nothing at all would have been established;
furthermore, by one who seeks to establish something for another, that other must be admitted [as a real entity]. How, then, could there be non-duality? For no one establishes themselves alone.
Now, if someone were to establish [the truth] for another, then, such being the case, it would be a delusion of one's own self; how then could there be an establishment of non-duality?
Or, if that delusion were to cease, because of the arising of the form of another, there would be an absence of non-duality;
and furthermore, how could there be the comprehension of what precedes and follows? Thus, everything would be inconsistent.
To this it is replied:

This so-called "difference" is not something perceived, such that what has been set forth in this way would be tenable for one who maintains such conceptual constructions as existence and non-existence.
To begin with, this difference between the prior and the subsequent is not manifest to perception.
Since perception does not operate with respect to the prior and the posterior,
if it were prior to perception, it would have to appear at that very moment; thus, it would possess only presentness.
As in the second case, its very existence as "present" consists in its manifestation within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) characterized by immediate intuition (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Now, [one might ask: even if it does not manifest through the direct intuition of yogins, how can the past and so forth be [known]?
To this, it is replied: "It is not so."
How can there be feeling of the past and so forth?
That is non-existent;
for in this life, it is not perceived by anyone at all. As for those who have entered that state [of death], we do not know what will become of them. (383)
For where there is a negation even of that which is currently being perceived as real, what regard can there be for the future?
Here too, those who perceive a true dream certainly know the past and so forth,
because such conventional usage occurs even when they have awakened and are in a state of non-perception.
Therefore, the past is not grasped by perception, nor is the future; how, then, can there be a cognition of their difference from that [present]?
Regarding the past, it is merely memory, and that too is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Now, if it is argued that one will understand the difference [of the cause] from that [object] through inference because of the cognition of hardness and so forth,
that too is incorrect, since:
For inference is indeed useless because the connection is known through that [inference]; nor is there a cognition of the firmness of the cause by means of perception.
(384) If the apprehension of the connection between the future object and the firmness of the cause were established, then inference would be appropriate;
for those who maintain the doctrine of inference hold that "inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object based on a necessary connection."
If it is argued that inference occurs even without the apprehension of a necessary connection because it has been observed [to do so],
then an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) follows; for by the very same reason— that it has not been observed— it would simply not occur.
For it is not possible to unify that which is seen with that which is other;
if one were to offer a rebuttal on the grounds of "being seen," it must be considered whether this "being seen" occurs through inference or through perception.
If that very [inference] is being examined by means of inference, how can it be so? Or if [it is examined] by means of perception...
This is incorrect;
for inference cannot be perceived by means of direct perception, since the latter has as its object only that which is present to the senses.
Furthermore, since direct perception does not operate with respect to what is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), how can inference be accepted as having the imperceptible as its object?
For it is impossible to understand inference as being qualified by that [imperceptible] without making the imperceptible its object.
Now, if it is argued that [inference] is not apprehended as having that as its object...
That being the case, how can that inference be said to be "seen," such that the reason "because it is seen" [is valid]?
Inference is merely the self-awareness of its own nature, because it is seen as such by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
Now, if conventional usage is exactly like this, then let it be mere conventional usage; what is the use of an insistence on distinction?
If it is argued that an insistence on distinction is indeed observed:
It is indeed impossible to remove what has been seen as such;
and it is not tenable to say "it is thus," because since all delusion cannot be removed by means of what is seen, your effort in giving instruction is entirely futile.
If it is argued that [this effort] is likewise futile for you as well,
we say no;
for since there can be a misconception of having seen what was not actually seen, it is appropriate to state that things are as they truly are.
This being the case, since you possess the conceit of an adherence to difference even without an actual adherence to difference, that very [conceit] alone is logical.
For indeed, the present manifestation is partless and does not possess difference; nor is there a perception of difference in either of the preceding or succeeding cognitions individually. (385)
If it were argued that [the effect] arises from the combination [of two moments], like the action of jaggery and ginger, then there would be a single effect produced by the two acting together.
(386) But in this case, no effect whatsoever could belong to the preceding and succeeding cognitions. Therefore, the subsequent cognition is a memory, which occurs after the experience.

(387) Furthermore, if there is a difference [between them], there is no experience; and there is no memory without experience. If there were a perception of [the object] at the same time as that [memory], then non-duality would be established. (388)
For in the case of sugar-cane products and mercury, the effect produced—namely, the removal of a disease to be cured by them or the restoration of health—is performed by those two;
therefore, they receive the designation of a "composite" (*samudāya*).
However, in this case, there is no further effect produced by the preceding and succeeding cognitions, which consist merely in the apprehension of their own respective objects.
And since the cognition of those two is their very self-nature,
if there were a difference in that [cognition], what else would remain non-different such that, in relation to it, there could be a "collection"?
Their single effect is memory, which consists in the grasping of both the prior and the subsequent.

Memory, arising from experience, does not conform to the form of that [experience] as it actually occurred; nor does the experience itself grasp two [objects]. Therefore, memory also does not [grasp them].
How then [is this explained]? This is a mental conceptual construction (*smārtavikalpa*) regarding the objects of the cognitions of form and touch.
That was stated with the intention of referring to the apprehension of their difference.
And in this case, there is no such procedure here,
nor does memory function in the apprehension of an object in such a way that it would function independently;
for if both were apprehended by memory, [it would follow that]...

It has been established that those two are one and the same at the same time due to their non-discrimination; furthermore, the view might be held that memory alone is the apprehender of discrimination, and not experience—this being a conventional perception of difference. (389)
For instance, if the appearances of red and non-red were to constitute a single variegated [whole], then that which was seen by me as separate would likewise be seen again [as such].
In this way, the perception of difference does not occur otherwise; therefore, the apprehension of difference is not established anywhere in reality.
Nor can the distinction between variegated and non-variegated be determined by mere appearance alone; therefore, all of this is distinguished in accordance with what preceded it.

(392) If it is argued that the apprehension of difference arises from perception due to the proficiency gained through the practice of memory and so forth—[we reply: how could that which is not established by perception be established by practice? Even through practice, its simultaneous manifestation is what is intended. (393)
Even in that case, the production of the discernment of those [two] is held to be by means of memory alone. And thus, a distinction established upon direct experience is not proven anywhere.

(394) If, between memory and experience, there were only experience in memory, then even that multiplicity would not be distinguished from one another, because it is impossible for it to be distinguished either by itself or by another entity. (395)
That which cannot be led away by being cut apart, nor seen otherwise [than as it is],— for even when divided,
gold retains its status as the material cause of its products.
Now, if memory were also born at the same time as the perceptual cognition, it would indeed assume identity with it.
It follows that perception would necessarily be conceptual in nature; consequently, there is a loss of the subject under discussion— that perception is non-conceptual—
which is like falling into the mud while intending to land on dry ground.
This is not the case;

for when addressing the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), it is stated that memory is distinct from [the object] because everything is differentiated by the difference in its cause and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Indeed, for the proponent of difference, every instance of difference arises from a difference in cause and from a difference in intrinsic nature.

In that regard, the arising of memory occurs from mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), whereas that of sensory cognition does not; memory has an imperceptible object, while sensory perception does not. Therefore, the proponent of external objects (*Bāhyārthavādin*) is awakened by his own admission that there is a difference between these two, just as there is between a pillar and other things.
But for the proponent of non-difference (*Abhedavādin*), how can this distinction exist?
For consciousness is not perceived like its cause, because it is not grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); and inference does not operate without direct perception. (398)
Indeed, there is no perception of two objects—the preceding and the succeeding—simultaneously through direct perception;
rather, at the time of perceiving that which is considered the effect, there is only remembrance of that which is considered the cause.
When that [cause] is grasped, it is grasped solely in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), not as a cause.
Because the effect is not perceived [at the time of its production],
and at the time of perceiving the effect, that [effect] has already passed and is thus merely within the scope of memory;
yet there is no memory of what has not been experienced, nor is there an experience of causality— how then can there be memory?

Now, if it is thought that this [effect] is experienced even at the time of its production, then, since there is no experience of its prior form and because they are inseparable due to their simultaneity, there is simply non-difference; how, then, can there be a relation of cause and effect?
Or, if it is established by means of memory that "previously this was experienced alone," [the same problem remains].
Therefore, from this discrimination, there is indeed distinction:
now, what is that? Is it inference, or is it mere recollection?
If, first of all, it is inference, how can it exist without perception?
For there is no prior apprehension (*pūrvatā*) by means of perception; indeed, every perception grasps only the present.
Now, that which is apprehended by perception as restricted and unmixed with what follows is designated as "prior" in relation to the apprehension of what comes after. This is the conventional usage.

Even that [subsequent cognition], being non-existent [at the time of the first], does not cause the initial perception to function through dependence on it; therefore, "prior-ness" is not grasped by it, because it rests within itself. (399)
For how could a prior perception, grasping its own time, know itself as dependent on another?

Likewise, the subsequent perception [would not know it either]. Therefore, this sequence of prior and subsequent perceptions is not graspable by prior and subsequent perceptions; consequently, how could even memory function with respect to that?

Therefore, neither through direct perception nor through memory is dependence cognized. Consequently, how could inference proceed with respect to that which is already known? (400) Now, if it is merely a matter of memory, how can that be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? By what means could the dependence between the prior and the subsequent be cognized, whereby one would know the effect?
(401) If, by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there arises a cognition grasping identity in the form "this is that very same thing," and from that [cognition] comes the discernment...
The cognition "this is that very same [thing]" is likewise merely a pair of cognitions consisting of memory and direct experience; therefore, by what means is their identity grasped?
If it is argued that their grasping is indeed perceived:
It is not perceived through direct apprehension, but rather through the apprehension of memory; however,
why then is there no cognition of the remembered and the perceived as being like [the relationship between] a cart and its parts?
In the same way, if cognition is examined, there is no perception of identity between the forms of memory and direct perception; for if that were the case,
those two would not exist as distinct,
and thus there would be no perception of identity between the prior and the subsequent.
For it is not possible for that which is not perceived in the form of a memory to be designated as "prior";
the principle is that in direct perception there is only presentness, not prior-ness. Now, [one might argue] that their identity is established by observing their practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
This is merely a dance in the dark:

whether cognition establishes the distinction between the object and its opposite, or not—if cognition itself is unestablished, how can there be an understanding [of these]? For what indeed is this so-called "conventional usage" (vyavahāra)—is it a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or not?
If it is argued that [this] is not a means of valid cognition because it is established that it is non-probative due to being included within perception and inference,
then let it be investigated: how, in that case, can the establishment of difference [between the two] occur?

How, then, can there be linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) in the absence of difference? Is this not equally the case even when there is difference? It is not equal; for in the case of that which is different from cognition, because there exists an object to be attained, one who desires it engages [with it].
But in the case of [the object being] identical [to cognition], it would be entirely inconsistent.
To this it is replied:

Even if there is a difference [between the object and its cognition], if that [difference] is known, for what purpose would one act? Or, if it is unknown, how could one act on account of the son of a barren woman?

(403) Since the non-existence of that [difference] follows from the existence of this [cognition], why is it considered to be only this much? Since touch and so forth were previously perceived, one should have acted at the very first moment. (404)
Now, how can there be activity when the non-perception [of the object] is possible? If it is argued that there is cognition through inference, for whose sake then does one act?

(405) If it is the cognition of its generality (*sāmānya*), how does one act toward the particular (*viśeṣa*)? If the generality is non-different [from the particular], then activity would be fruitless.

(406) Whether [the generality] is different or non-different, how could one who possesses [cognition of] the different act toward that [particular]? If it is not different, since that [particular] has already been attained, for whose sake is there activity therein? (407)

If it is argued that activity is observed, is it perceived directly or otherwise? For activity is not perceived through direct perception, because [consciousness] consists in the awareness of its own object. (408) For in that case, the nature of activity as being prior and posterior is not known by the senses; nor is there inference, since that which is not perceived cannot yield knowledge of activity.
(409) The objection—"How can there be activity even in non-duality?"—is thus refuted: what connection is there between "as is Bali, so is Yakṣa"? (410)
By this, the following objection is also refuted:
"How can one engage in activity for the sake of awakening another if there is non-duality?
For this purpose—namely, the distinction between self and other—is not established.
This [notion] that "this is another" and "that is not me" arises as nothing other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*);
here, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no division.

When I am the questioner and another speaks, for both it is merely the cognition colored by their own respective mental forms (*svākāroparaktapratyaya-saṃvedanam*); there is no division, just as in the case of a dream-cognition.
And like the incoherent ravings of a madman, the proponent is now even more mad; how then can there be even the cognition of non-duality?
Indeed, this entire process proceeds as nothing but the incoherent ravings of all cognitions; here, no cognition whatsoever arises.
Rather, what is there for the opponent or anyone else to do? Whatever might be done is not observed;
and how it is not observed has already been demonstrated.

How then can there be existence without a cause? What existence here is perceived by you as arising from a cause? It has been established that there is no cognition of a causal relationship. In that case, existence must be accidental; this [existence] would never cease for anyone at any time.
Likewise,
there is either eternal existence or non-existence of a cause, because it does not depend on anything else. (Pramāṇavārttika)
This, too, is not a fault.
For has this existence ever been observed by you anywhere to cease? Moreover, [the claim that it does so] due to its occasional nature is merely the babbling of falling ignorance;
thus was that path shown against the proponent of difference.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, it will turn out that there is no such thing as a non-differentiated [object] even for the intellect; therefore, it is established that cognition alone is variegated in its manifestation. Now, if it is argued: "What contradiction is there in the form of a jar and so forth being likewise a single, variegated unity, just like the cognition itself?"
If the form of the cloth and so forth were one, there would likewise be a lack of distinction;
for if the form of the cloth and so forth were non-distinct, then it would be nothing other than the form of the intellect, because it would possess properties identical to those of the intellect.

For just as cognition is not seen by another, nor at a later time, nor even when covered up or broken into pieces, so too it would be with the external object; if that were the case, then that [object] would be nothing but cognition, being merely "I" (the self), and the external would be non-existent. Alternatively, if it were covered up, then something else entirely different would arise.
Since that which is seen as having half-measure and so forth is perceived exactly as it exists, why should there not be a single entity even in a mind with variegated forms? (413)
In this regard, the meditative concentration is as follows:
if an object arises exactly as it is perceived, then it would not arise by way of being imperceptible or perceptible to another.
(414) Thus, let it be understood that there is no arising from other causes; for what is born from the causes of consciousness is indeed consciousness itself. (415)

Indeed, an object is not perceived as something remote, nor by means of another's perception; furthermore, it does not arise from other causes such as the eye and so forth, but rather its manifestation occurs just like that of the perceiver— so how could it not be consciousness?
Now, as far as anything is perceived, all that is indeed an object;
even pleasure and the like do not have the nature of cognition, but are rather external entities— this is the opponent's view.
This too is incorrect,

because if the status of being a real entity were attributed to everything that is perceived, then the existence of cognition— which is itself not perceived— would be without any means of valid proof.
If that by which the object of apprehension is perceived is itself consciousness, then that too is non-existent; for in that case, there would be a cognition of what is to be perceived by itself.
(417) If there is no perception of the subject, how can it be said to exist? From the perception of the object being perceived, the perceiver is inferred.
(418) Or rather, [the perceiver is] the perception itself.

Otherwise, if there were no presumption (*arthāpatti*), the objection— "By whom was this perceived?"— would remain unanswered; therefore, the cognition of the existence of consciousness through presumption is untenable, because the very fact of its being perceived is itself subject to investigation.

If the cause for being perceived by another is that it is perceived by itself and by another, then by whom is that [perception by another] perceived? If you say it is perceived by yet another, then an infinite regress (anavasthā) follows.

(419) If it were perceived by itself alone, then it would follow that even the object of apprehension (grāhya) is so; let every entity be grasped as having the nature of its own cognition, just like the self. (420)

Now, the self is perceived as having the nature of its own cognition, whereas form and so forth are perceived through dependence on another, as determined by such designations as "this was perceived by me" or "this was perceived by another.

If the knower is dependent on another, how is it not the perception of another? Without another, there can be no dependence on another; if there is dependence on another, how is that not [the perception of] another? (421)

Even when something is doubtful, there is dependence on another; and by means of things that are themselves doubtful, certainty is reached. However, that which is itself uncertain cannot serve as a reason for the sake of establishing certainty. (422) Alternatively, if knowability is dependent upon a self, then it is established through the self-cognition of the self. Just like the self, all cognition would then be self-cognizing and not cognizing anything else. There is no other [object] such as "intellect" (buddhi), because the matter is exhausted by that much alone. (423)

Furthermore, it might be argued that just as there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expressions "I am the self," "I am the agent," and "I am the knower," so too there would be [coreferentiality] in such cases as "I am a wall," "I am a pot," "I am a cloth," and "I am a cart.
Likewise, just as there is [the expression] "my cognition," so too there would be [expressions] such as "my color," "my touch," and "my smell."
Even that is of little consequence;

if oneness [is established] by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), why is it not the case that "I am fair-complexioned" and so forth also possess a common substratum? Wherever there is coreferentiality...

If, in that case, there were necessarily unity, then [by its] absence there would be multiplicity; thus, in the case of multiplicity, neither the probandum nor its opposite would exist. Likewise, even in the case of "Rāhu’s head," which lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), no difference is negated, provided that the head is [recognized as] Rāhu’s through the perception of difference.
In this case as well, self-awareness exists as that which sublates the superimposition of difference;
for just as the superimposition of difference in the form "Rāhu’s head" is sublated by the perception of the opposite [of that distinction].
Likewise, let my experience—such as "the seeing of my own form"—be sublated by mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
For the awareness of one's own nature is established as being without division, unlike the awareness of blue, the body, the face, and so forth;

a thing that has arisen and been cognized does not appear as having a common locus [with its cognition]. Why, then, should there be a conceptualization of a distinction between the object of cognition and the cognition itself? (427)
How then, when ultimate difference is not perceived, can there even be a superimposition of difference?
Indeed, nothing occurs without a basis;

this conceptualization of difference is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). [One who knows positive and negative concomitance] acts from the influence of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (428)
Even apart from me, form and so forth are perceived by another;
let them remain unperceived,
or else let them exist elsewhere.
Therefore, the introduction of the conceptualization of difference arises from the constraints of place, time, and intrinsic nature;
and it has been established that, in the ultimate sense, there is no cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
This is because:

Through perception, there is the cognition of the positive concomitance itself and of its essential nature; yet, even when there is no cognition of the distinction between existence and non-existence, some maintain the conceit of cognition, as in:
"This was done by me" or "This was seen by me. (429) Even in the absence of actual cognition, there is the conceit of cognition for some.
If it is argued that there is conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding non-feeling because it has passed away and been forgotten,
then what is this so-called "forgetting"?
If it is argued that it is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of something contrary [to reality], then...
If it is argued that the exhaustion of formative forces (*saṃskārakṣaya*) is the same here as well, we say no.
Because of the non-existence of conditioning (*saṃskāra*);
for there is no destruction of a conditioned phenomenon without its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*),
and it has been established that what has already come into being cannot be brought to destruction.

And if the absence of conceptual construction (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of the superimposition of the contrary, then let the superimposition of difference and the superimposition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) be likewise; what contradiction is there in this?
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no cognition of positive and negative concomitance other than through conceit (*abhimāna*).

Since everything is merely a product of conceit (abhimāna), even when grasping [an object] through discernment (viveka), one must admit the identity between the preceding and succeeding moments; otherwise, it would be nothing but mere cognition,
and such [mere cognition] cannot be admitted.

For it is said in that very same [text]: "In that very place—there is a variant reading 'vedanasya' (of the feeling); having discarded the discerning [state], at another time the discerning is not perceived. (223)
2. One does not perceive it; for it is impossible to maintain that what is not being perceived exists.
Furthermore, it is impossible to demonstrate that there is a partless whole [distinct] from its parts when such a thing does not exist;
therefore, one who accepts an external object must accept its simultaneous apprehension. But how can a plurality be seen by a single [cognition] all at once?
For a single act of perception that has engaged with one object is not capable of engaging with another at that very same time;
this has been established insofar as multiple perceptions cannot function in this way and not otherwise.
However, in ultimate reality, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed only one.
It is impossible for one thing to be apprehended by another;
moreover,
what is called "apprehension" does not belong to anything at all, but rather consists in the arising of cognition in the form of that [object].
Nor can multiple things be the producer of a single [effect],
because what contradiction is there in many things having produced an excellence simultaneously?
1. They would exist separately if they were the cause of cognition, like the self, the sense organs, and so forth. // 224 //

For just as the sense-faculties, objects, and mental attention—or the contact between the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects—simultaneously produce a single sensory cognition, so too, if atoms were to do the same, what contradiction would there be? [Objection: But even if atoms are impermanent, what excellence (*atiśaya*) do they possess? For atoms do not become large even when their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are present.
If it is argued that they cannot be apprehended because they do not abandon their subtlety, that too is incorrect;

for in this case, there is an excellence of magnitude, not an excellence of capacity. It is due to a lack of capacity that something is considered a non-cause, whereas it is not accepted as such merely due to a lack of magnitude. (430)

If "visibility" means the production of a cognition that conforms to the specific nature of the atom, then that does not exist at all, and thus the argument proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Alternatively, if it means the mere production of consciousness...
That [appearance] certainly exists and is not contradictory, because it is observed in the case of hair and the like.
Just as hairs, even though they are not actually joined together when at a distance, appear to be in a dense mass, so too are atoms; thus there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, subtle [beings] can somehow bring this about.
If it is argued that [the atoms] are merely individual, we reply:
because individuals lack causal capacity,
it is precisely this lack of capacity that is incompatible with being a cause, not their subtlety.
O Keśavadeva, no specific quality such as grossness arises in the sense organs and so forth during the state of causal totality;
nevertheless, their status as producers arises solely from a specific capacity.
How is it, then, that this capacity is not perceived by another who is in close proximity?
If the causal factor (*aṅga*) is not perceived, how can it exist?
And if it exists equally [in both], why is there this distinction—that it produces an effect for one and not for the other?
[This is] due to the distinction in auxiliary conditions (*sahakāritā*), such as being located at a distance.
But surely, even due to being at a distance, why are those very hairs not perceived?
As for the distinction [between them], it has already been investigated that this is due to the non-inclusion of other causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

If perception were to occur simply because of causality, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the eyes and other [faculties] are also objects of perception, since they too possess causality.
Therefore it is said: "Apart from being a cause, there is no other such thing as 'being an object of apprehension' (grāhyatā).
When the cognition has a certain appearance, that [cause] is called its object of apprehension. (225)
That which has the form [of an object] by way of the generality of the sense-sphere of form does not, in ultimate reality, possess that form.
For instance, while the blue-form of consciousness arises from a collection of blue atoms,
let there not be an appearance of the form of the atoms themselves.
But if the form of the atoms does not appear, how can it be said that "this much is the blue-form of the atoms"?
There is no fault [in our position] because it cannot be otherwise;
moreover, if multiple things were not perceived simultaneously, then there would be this further fault,
as he says:
Or how is the whole to be apprehended? If it is argued that it is indeed apprehended simultaneously with its own parts, we say no.

For the cognition of a cow is not observed when the dewlap and other [characteristics] are not perceived. Even if it were accepted that the apprehension of the subordinate and the primary occurs simultaneously,
the animal with its complete parts would not be grasped all at once, nor would it be grasped as possessing its qualities and so forth.

If it is argued that because [the object] is grasped by means of only those very parts intended to be qualifiers, the whole with all its parts is not grasped— [we reply: no, for all of those are indeed qualifiers.
Because the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*),
that which is employed as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) is indeed apprehended by that very [intention].
For the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
For it is perceived by another at one time and by that very same thing as the qualified at another;
for instance:
"the horn of a cow" and "the horned cow."
A variety of cognitions is observed, such as "the cow is white," "the cow is round," or "it is not spherical";
there is no simultaneous apprehension of all qualifiers,
because it is impossible to grasp multiple qualifiers at once.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the relationship between qualifier and qualified cannot occur without conceptualization;
moreover,
this is because [the object] is not inherently distinct from other things, and because there is no differentiator such as a quality (guṇa) and so forth.
Due to non-apprehension, there would be the cognition of difference even for one who perceives another [object] immediately following it.
M.
Due to non-apprehension, there is the cognition of difference, even for one who perceives both the higher and the lower.
For indeed, a cow is neither a cow nor a non-cow by itself;
it is a cow through its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*).
Likewise, white is neither white nor non-white by itself; it is white through its connection with "whiteness," and so forth.

Furthermore, since the difference [of the substance] from its qualities and so forth would be perceived simultaneously, even upon seeing both the higher and lower [categories], there would be only a single cognition;
it would follow that the quality is grasped alone only afterwards.
Alternatively, one might argue that the cognition of difference will arise later, following the perception of the quality.

To this it is replied: if the apprehension of diversity arises from the perception of differences such as qualities and so forth, let it be so; nevertheless, there would still be a confusion of their relations. (230)

If a substance is first apprehended as a unity, then even when a qualifier is subsequently apprehended, there can be no distinction between their connection [and the object itself]; thus, the consequence of confusion (saṅkara) follows.

For in that case, since multiple qualifiers—even though they are many—would be connected to that very same single entity which was previously apprehended as one, it would follow that a single thing possesses multiple qualifiers.
If it is argued that [the universal] is not one because its conjunctions are distinct due to the difference in locations, we say no;
for since location-difference is also a qualifier, that location-difference too would belong to the very same single [entity].
Therefore, multiple things cannot be apprehended at once;
furthermore, if a qualifier were apprehended later, it would not be known to which [qualificand] it belongs.
However, in the position that the qualifier is both distinct and non-distinct, there is no distinction for anything whatsoever, and thus there is an even greater confusion of related entities.

In the Sāṃkhya system, however, because sound and the other [qualities] are manifold, the simultaneous perception of many is established; for it is impossible to perceive a configuration [of objects] all at once unless those things possessing the configuration are themselves perceived. (231)

A specific arrangement of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) constitutes a complete object such as a jar, which is composed of the three *guṇas*; therefore, upon the perception of sound and the other [sensory objects], there is either the perception of the three *guṇas* or the perception of the subtle elements,
for it is not possible to perceive that specific arrangement without perceiving those [elements].
The grasping of a fist does not occur by grasping the tip of a finger; nor is there only one internal ear,
because it is maintained that every effect is non-different from its cause.
And they maintain the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*), not the position of a new effect (*kāryapakṣa*).
Transformation is the relinquishing of one attribute while not falling away from its essential nature (*tattva*), followed by the arising of another.
In that regard, space (*ākāśa*) is the transformation of sound (*śabda*).
Air is the transformation of sound and touch;
fire is the transformation of sound, touch, and form;
water is the transformation of sound, touch, form, and taste.
Earth is the transformation of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; thus there is a multiplicity in jars and other such things.
The proof that by grasping those [qualities] one grasps the [substance] as a unity is established;
the remaining refutation is exactly as before.
Therefore, even when multiple things are apprehended simultaneously, there is no conceptualization;
it is established that perception is indeed non-conceptual.
[Objection: If perception is non-conceptual, how then can the apprehension of the subject (dharmin), its properties (dharma), and so forth, occur through perception?
If the subject (*dharmin*) is not apprehended through perception, there can be no introduction of inference;
if the subject is apprehended through inference, then that too would require another subject, leading to an infinite regress.

And since the apprehension of the subject (dharmin) involves the apprehension of it as having a nature inlaid with multiple properties, how can it be non-conceptual? To this it is replied: "The subject, which possesses multiple forms, is not grasped in its entirety by the sense faculty. The object of the sense faculty is a form that is self-cognized and inexpressible. (431)

For no substratum (*dharmin*) endowed with multiple properties such as color and so forth is apprehended even by sensory consciousness; rather, it is apprehended only by its own specific form (*svarūpa*), and that very form is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain:
The apprehension of form and so forth occurs through their mutual distinction from the eye and other [senses], because they are not perceived as having a single substratum.

Indeed, it has been established that the subject (dharmin) consisting of form and so forth is not apprehended by the sensory consciousnesses; for there is only the apprehension of form and so forth as mutually distinct, and no other substratum or anything residing therein falls within the scope of such apprehension.
Now, it might be argued that because of the cognition "that very thing which I saw, I now touch," there is understood either a single substratum or identity;
however, this is not recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), since it has been established that perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not constitute such [recognition].
Rather, such a cognition arises from the awakening of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) triggered by the cognitions of color and touch.
For it is observed that the perception of mere visible form and the perception of mere tangible object proceed as distinct perceptions within the act of feeling;
yet, no mutual contact between those two is perceived by another [perception].
If it is argued that "this [eye] sees while touching," no;
for there is an absence of the application of touch to visible form (*rūpa*).
And oneness is established in that way only if there is the cognition of their being directed toward a single object.
But surely it is observed that what was seen as white is perceived by touch as having been soiled, and it is also found clinging to the hand; how then is there not a convergence upon a single object?

This very thing, which rests upon the support of the space within the sky, is that object which is touched and that which is the range of touch. If there is no cognition of it by that [other], then inference is not a means of proof.

When there is no mutual adherence between two perceptions as the grasped and the grasper, even a thousand inferences have no power to proceed toward the determination of difference through perception.
Now, this mental cognition—"I am touching that very same thing"—is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It is not the case that only what is produced by the sense organs is a valid means of knowledge;
for even that which is produced by the sense organs is a valid means of knowledge because it does not deviate from the object, and not merely because it is produced by the sense organs.
Since it is also possible [to argue] that this is not so because [the object] is born of the mind, therefore:
"Whatever I saw," and so forth—this is the non-deviation [of perception] regarding a cognition. No one of limited vision understands this without inference.
For in that case, if someone were to question:
"How do you understand that what was previously seen is now being touched? [one must resort to inference].

If it is asked, "In that case, how is there such a cognition [of identity]?"— this is not so; for when one touches something, that which was seen at the time of seeing is not seen [at the time of touching],
so how can there be the cognition, "This very same thing is being touched"?
In this regard, the following is the answer:
since it has been defiled by that [cause], one knows this from that; thus he teaches inference.
If it is argued that "in that case, how is untouchability defiled?
Why then is touchability not perceived as 'this is white,' since touchability has the same form as both white and its opposite?"—
this is not a valid answer.
To claim that a single entity is both similar and dissimilar is a rash assertion;

for since the very same thing constitutes the similarity and dissimilarity of touch and form respectively, their identity is untenable due to the imposition of contradictory properties. Therefore, this is understood.
This is now investigated:
is it by means of a cognition of a single form, or by means of a cognition of manifold forms?
If it is being cognized by means of manifold forms, how can it be one?
Now, if that unreal form is not perceived as having a single aspect while the touch is being perceived, how can it be grasped as having a single aspect?
For that which is being perceived and that which is not being perceived cannot both be the object of apprehension, since it is impossible for something to be unperceived while being grasped;
therefore, there is no such thing as a "whole" (avayavin) distinct from color and the other qualities.
Consequently, they are cognized only by their own respective forms.
Form and the other [sensory objects] do not exist as they appear through one another’s forms;

rather, form is only self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*) and not cognized by another. Therefore, because it cannot be pointed out to another by means of words, sensory consciousness has an inexpressible object (*avācyagocara*).
If that is so, and the object of the senses is not pointed out by words, how is there the understanding: "I see this very thing which I heard"?
For how can there be such a cognition of that which has not been specified?
Indeed, it is concluded that it must be specified from that very [source]; therefore, this [objection] is untenable.

Since it has been established that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), how then can this object be considered cognized on the basis of that [recognition]? For at the time of cognition from a word, that object does not appear [to consciousness].
Doubt indeed arises from a word regarding an object; otherwise, as in the case of what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be no connection with doubt.

Now, if it is argued that the mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*) of an object’s existence or non-existence is the same from a word, and therefore doubt arises—then why does such doubt not occur even in the case of direct perception?
In that case, since it does not occur merely from the observation of a particular appearance,

by what means could the apprehension of a particular appearance even here be removed? Therefore, if there is indeed no particularity, verbal cognition cannot be a grasper of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity.
Because it would be distinct from perception,
if its own nature were being presented [again],
then that vision would be invalid as it would involve the apprehension of what has already been apprehended, and there would be an absence of an object.
Since the nature of the form is understood from the word itself,
if it were perceived through a general form, then even one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice would perceive a white object as having a yellow form.
If it is argued that even that [cognition] should be considered a valid means of knowledge because it is predominant,
we say no.
Because it is sublated, the cognition produced by the word "Bring the cow" is not itself sublated; therefore, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Here too, because it is subject to sublation: if "bring the cow" implies existence, then that [existence] might sometimes not even occur;
or, if it is not implied.
Therefore, because bringing [the object] is impossible, it is all the more non-authoritative; furthermore,
if the speaker's intention is "bring it" because it is possible, then because the injunction to bring is doubtful, it is indeed non-authoritative.
If it is argued that "only what is doubtful has been urged," then since "only what is doubtful is apprehended," every cognition involving doubt would become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
yet no object is ever apprehended by means of what is not a valid means of knowledge.
How then is there non-deviation in cases such as bringing [something] near?
There is no possibility of non-deviation,
because no one performs [the action].
For an agent does not necessarily perform what is enjoined;
moreover,
is the word considered to be a producer of action or a communicator?
Because there is an absence of non-contradiction in its status as a producer [of an effect], it lacks the nature of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For indeed, there is no conventional usage that "a producer is non-contradictory";
rather, reliability (āpti) occurs only when [the action] has been performed, based on another means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the status of being an indicator (jñāpakatva) of the essential nature [of the word] is impossible due to the existence of an action yet to come;
for an action that does not exist cannot be grasped by way of its own nature, and if it were to exist by way of its own nature, it would not be something yet to come.

If it is argued that the universal (sāmānya) is apprehended, then that universal exists even in the absence of action; therefore, one does not engage in action for the sake of apprehending the universal.
Consequently, the word is not an indicator of the sensory object.
Therefore, the object of the senses is indeed inexpressible;
how then is there the perception of the multiplicity of the subject (dharmin) and its properties (dharmas)?
To this it is replied:

For one who has turned away from everything, the cessation [of conceptualization] occurs from whatever [particular aspect]; this diversity, inferred from those various distinctions, constitutes the manifold nature of the subject (*dharmin*).
That [exclusion] is differentiated,
for the conventional usage of the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth is indeed constructed based on the differentiation of exclusions;
for instance:
Does the golden jar, appearing first of all, manifest as distinct from its color, shape, and so forth, or do those [color and shape] manifest as distinct from it? 2 T.
The ritual vessel (kalaśa) of the Dharma and so forth, characterized by color and shape.
However, it is only a single entity consisting of color and so forth that is the direct object of perception.

Those who have fallen into the river of worldly existence, while engaged in the path of conventional usage, construct distinctions by means of conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra*), relying on the exclusion of various other objects with different forms.
If there were no difference between the color and the specific configuration [of the parts], how could a blue pot be distinguished from a non-blue pot? (438)
If there were indeed no difference between color, shape, and so forth, then the exclusion of blue from a non-blue jar would not occur;
for even that which is non-blue would necessarily have to be blue by virtue of having that same [shared] nature of shape.
Since shape is not distinct from blue color,
and since blue also occurs as one with shape,
the world’s conceptualization manifests as a distinction between the two.

If it is argued that the distinction is therefore ultimately real, we say no; for it is not logical to call something "ultimately real" when it is merely figuratively attributed through conceptual construction.
Only if that very whiteness and so forth were to appear as having a nature other than its own configuration would the distinction be ultimately real.

If it is argued that because inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) is the cause for the appearance of non-difference, there is an appearance of non-difference even where there is difference—[we reply:

but surely, even in the case of inherence in a single object, there is an appearance of difference between color (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), since they are perceived by different sense organs (*bhinnendriyagrāhyatā*). If this is the objection:
If the power of inherence (*samavāya*) manifests [the related entities] as non-different, then it is impossible for them to be perceivable by different sense organs;
for if they appear as non-different due to occupying the same location, this is rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by the case of color, taste, and so forth.

Thus, it is established that while [universals] such as "cowness" are established through the conceptualization of difference from [particulars] such as "Śābaleya-ness," and [particulars] such as "Śābaleya-ness" are established through the conceptualization of difference from [individuals] such as "Khaṇḍa" and "Muṇḍa," [they appear as distinct].
In this regard, in some cases a substratum (*dharmin*) is postulated as distinct from [its] qualities such as form (*rūpa*), as in the case of a jar;

for if the jar were not a single composite whole (*avayavin*), then upon the successive perception of its color and taste, there would be no cognition of the jar. In other cases, a property (*dharma*) is postulated; for instance, if "cowness" (*gotva*) were neither non-distinct nor both distinct and non-distinct [from the individual cow].
There would be no difference among the brindled cow and others that are non-different from that [universal];
the same logic should be applied to other cases as well.
Therefore, difference must be inferred by taking recourse to the difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
But surely, even a difference known through inference is indeed real; this would be true if that inference were preceded by perception,
just as fire, when perceived through inference, is exactly as it appeared in direct perception.
If it is argued: "In that case, if the distinction between property and property-bearer ever appears [as real], what is the use of inference?", we reply:
this is the same even in the case of fire.
If it is argued that inference applies here as well because of a lapse of time and so forth, let it be so;
however, if it is claimed that there is here only constant inferability (*nityānumeyatā*),
that too is incorrect.
In a case where [the subject] is always inferable, by what means can an example be established in reality? If it is not established through another inference, this results in a blind succession.
Now, if jars and the like are the examples, they must be distinct from the jars and the like; for indeed—
The distinction between two things is established through their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as in the case of a jar and a cart; such is the case with color and shape.
However, even in that instance, there is no positive concomitance because it is not apprehended by perception.
Nor can difference therein be established through positive and negative concomitance;
how then? It is simply because difference appears simultaneously.
Now, if the variegated appearance itself were to occur without positive and negative concomitance, it would not be difference.
In that case, since there would be the consequence of non-duality (advaita) because nothing [exists] from any source whatsoever, the proof of difference is all the more untenable.

Alternatively, the cultivation of the notion of difference regarding a jar and so forth occurs through their appearing as distinct; however, that [distinction] does not exist at all in the case of shape and the like, nor is there any similarity with cloth and such things. (440)

However, since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of "cowness" and the like is not accessible through perception, its difference [from the individual] cannot be established from that which is non-concomitant.
Rather, it is those very individuals themselves that are conventionally treated as being in a state of concomitance by virtue of their connection with a single unifying cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*).
If this is so, then the universal must be something other than the particulars, being the very object of that single unifying cognition.

If it is asked, "How can there be a single unifying awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*) regarding things that are distinct, since they do not appear as distinct from the perspective of a single unifying awareness?"— to this it is replied:
There is no inconsistency regarding what is perceived, nor is there consistency regarding what is not perceived; for existence and non-existence are established through perception and non-perception.
(441) Indeed, the single unifying cognition is consistent because it is being perceived;
likewise, it must be consistent with the non-difference from that which is not being perceived. This is not a mere mental fabrication.

Nor is there a single conceptual cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*) regarding things that are distinct, because such a cognition abides solely in their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); furthermore, this single conceptual cognition is never observed in the case of actual unity,
for it arises from perception (*upalabdhi*).
And that [cognition] is successive,
yet it is not possible to have a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of each individual moment, because there is an absence of the experience of such a realization;
therefore, in all cases, a single reflective awareness must necessarily concern multiple [moments].

Therefore, if it is argued that the entire relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is merely a product of conceptual construction (*kalpanākṛta*), and that this very [relationship] should be apprehended by perception (*pratyakṣa*),
this is not the case.
Because those various forms of imagined nature belong to a mind that is free from conceptual construction.

The appearance of diversity is not the object of that which is non-diverse and occurs only occasionally. Regarding the phrase "not of the non-diverse," it is because perception (*pratyakṣa*) functions by way of direct manifestation; therefore, it is not logical for it to have the form of an object that is merely imagined.
For, due to their dependence on real entities, direct perceptions manifest only occasionally; however, conceptual constructions manifest forms that are not occasional.
Furthermore, while direct perception has a single form, conceptual construction possesses manifold forms.

Therefore, the ultimate point is that the distinction between conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises not only from the absence of mental images (*ākāra*), but also from the difference in their causes.
Now, one might object: "There do exist non-conceptual distinctions among properties such as white and so forth; these will be the objects of the sense faculties.
This objection is not valid, because:
Even though whiteness and so forth exist as objects of the senses,
they are not denoted by words because of the difference in form between [sensory] cognition and [verbal] cognition.
For whiteness is not grasped by the sense organ either as a property (*dharma*) or as a substratum (*dharmin*) belonging to anything.

Or, while there is a distinction based on configuration (*saṃsthāna*), verbal cognition grasps [the object] through a distinction such as its being a substratum (*dharmin*) and so forth, or its being indistinct and so forth; thus, the form [of the object] is indeed inexpressible for the cognitions of the sense organs.
Therefore, due to the difference in the forms of cognition, verbal cognition does not operate upon those things grasped by the senses.
Therefore, a difference in form is not logical if there is identity of object;
yet it might be argued that a difference in form will arise due to a difference in their substrata.
For instance,
one whose visual power is impaired by the coating of jaundice sees even white as yellow due to the difference in its locus; likewise,
one with cataracts sees things indistinctly.

Thus, there is no fault even in other cases for one who accepts a difference in aspect despite the identity of the object; this is not so, for even if the objects of cognitions are identical, [the distinction remains] due to their having different substrates. If that is the case...
Now, how is it that the sense-faculties, such as the ear and so forth, have distinct objects? [It is because] they are distinct from the mind. 235.3 M. cittāni°

For if the occurrence of a difference in form were due to a difference in substratum, then the determination of multiplicity would be lost, since even a single object can possess different forms; furthermore,
the difference in form for sounds and the like would likewise arise merely from the difference in their substrata, such as the ear,
and the illusory nature of appearances such as yellow would also apply to sounds and other objects.
By this, the distinction of capacities (*śaktibheda*) is also refuted— that is,
the claim that the capacity of the word itself is such that it brings about a cognition of something otherwise.
If there were apprehension otherwise than through differentiation, then its erroneous nature would not be subject to investigation;
for indeed, even an object presented otherwise by a word is seen to be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārī*).
How, then, is it logical for that [entity] to be erroneous?
For it is that very same [entity] which is indicated by words such as "the speaker's saliva" and so forth, and it performs that purposeful action.
It is not for the sake of spitting into water and so forth.

Furthermore, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is also dependent upon mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), just as the neutralization of poison and so forth are dependent upon the cultivation of [the deity] Garuḍa and others;
therefore, even when there is identity of object, there is no difference in form despite the difference in its substratum.
Moreover, that which is called "produced" is not something other than the basis [of its cognition] for the mind directed toward that object.

How could that which is based on names and is mutually [dependent] have the appearance of various forms when it is of only one nature? For while a difference in the basis might produce a difference in cognition, it cannot produce a difference in the object.
But the object, such as blue and so forth, is a single entity; it would appear in that consciousness in a single form.
For there can be no appearance of what does not exist;
and if there is an appearance, then it is not [an appearance of] that [non-existent thing].
There is no relation such that one thing appears while another appears;
nor can it be said that because it is the cause of that [appearance], it appears as that,
for if being the cause were the criterion for being an object, then it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs would also be objects.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", [the answer is:
there would be a contradiction regarding the unity of the object, because even that which is visual would be an object [of another sense].
For if there were objecthood—that is, if there were identity of referent—then even for cognitions, the subject matter under discussion would be contradicted;
for in the case of objecthood, there is no state of being a substratum.
Therefore, this is an external object.
Even if there were identity of object, if that [object] were [determined] by the multiplicity of cognitions, there would be mutual contradiction;
therefore, manifestation itself in its own form constitutes objectivity, and there is no other way.
Now, as for the rebuttal that "it is because [the word] is the locus of the sound," the cognition of the object occurs through the word in its own form;
yet that word is not the objective referent (*viṣaya*) of the cognition of the object, because it has already been cognized.
If that is so, then the object too would not be the objective referent.
Since it is perceived in its own form,
the claim that the object is the mirror obtained from that [perception] is incorrect.
What is the connection between that [object] and its attainment?
For it is attained by way of its own nature;
how then can it be said to be attained from something else?
If it is argued that [the object] exists because of subsequent activity (*pravṛtti*), then one must consider how this activity arises from cognition;
for if it is argued that the attainment of that [object] is observed from its form (*ākāra*), [we reply: no.
Since that very form is cognized from that [word],
and consequently activity occurs toward it, this attainment would be inferential rather than verbal;
and thus it follows that this is an object of inference alone, not of the word.
Consequently, the object of sensory cognition is indeed an indefinable form; in that case, it follows that it must be an object of inference.
But this is not so, because its own nature does not appear even in inference.
How, then, can there be activity toward something that does not appear?
It has been established that activity occurs only when [the object] is manifest at all times;
it does not occur when it is not manifest at all times.
Surely it proceeds with the thought, "This is perceived by me as real";
yet even so, this is not the ultimate truth.

If it is argued that even regarding what is not [actually] cognized, because of the conceit of cognition, all activity occurs, and that this very [conceit] is the ultimate reality—such that whatever there is a conceit about is itself the object—then we reply: the ultimate status of an object as being within the domain of words is denied for the object of sensory perception, but its conventional status is not; thus, there is no fault.
If that very [object] is admitted by the opponent, then what is desired here is established;
however, if that [object] is perceived in its own nature, then its status as an ultimate object would be demonstrated.
Therefore, even if it has multiple substrates, that which does not manifest by way of its own nature cannot be the object of anything.
If it is argued that it is indeed an object because its form enters into that [cognition],
then, in ultimate reality, this [form] must have entered into the cognition of the word.
It might be perceived by another [cognition] as well, provided it grasps the form clearly; for it is not possible to perceive something otherwise without having entered into it.
But surely, through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), unity is not contradicted even when there is a difference in form.

That too is not true, because the recognition of cows and other such things— which would otherwise be precluded by the observation that verbal designation and conceptual construction lack a reference to the perceived object— is seen to arise from the mental state [of the vṛtti]. (237)
It has just now been refuted that even the object of perception (*dṛśya-vastu*) is touched by either the designation (*abhidhāna*) or the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
What has been grasped is recognized;
however, there is no grasping by means of either sound or conceptual construction—
so how can there be recognition?
How, then, is the cognition "this very person who was instructed by him at that time is this one here" established?
[It is] established right now.
But surely, even when there is no actual realization, there may be the conceit of having realized;
how then is one not sublated?
One is indeed sublated for one who reflects upon it.
For a difference in cognition is indeed a sublater, and such a difference certainly exists between verbal expression and conceptual construction because their objects are remembered;
and that memory concerns what was previously grasped as well as what is being perceived now.

If, however, verbal expression and conceptual construction were merely a reflective awareness of the presently perceived object, then it has already been established by the question, "What would be the use of perception? [since they would be redundant].
Therefore, even recognition is merely a matter of conceit and is not a realization in the ultimate sense.
Rather, based on a prior perception, it is solely a conceptual construction that establishes the conventional usage of identity, but it does not grasp the ultimate reality.
Furthermore, inference from positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding the relationship between names and conceptualizations [is likewise not a realization of the ultimate].
By this, the [existence of] universals (*jāti*) and so forth in perceptible objects such as cows and the like is also refuted.
For there is no contact with a real entity through either verbal designation (*abhidhāna*) or conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
indeed, it has been established that no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of anything is apprehended in an ultimate sense, as this is merely a matter of subjective conceit (*abhimāna*).

Because one remembers exactly what was previously seen, and because when the object of perception is not being contacted [at the time of recollection], a form that persists as related to the perceived object is not grasped,
there is consequently no cognition that "there exists a universal of the perceived object."
If that is so, how then does the single conceptual construction "this is that very same cow" arise?
To this he replies:
"Even though the perceptions themselves are distinct, they produce a single conceptual construction."
It has been described as being "by its own nature" among those things reckoned as recognition (pratyabhijñāna).

Indeed, perceptions (*darśana*) arising as they do—grasping objects distinguished by their higher and lower [qualities]—do not stand within the range of a capacity to grasp what is either distinct from or non-distinct from a single form;

rather, having entered into the turbulence of the proficiency and power of awakening the seeds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to their own nature, they produce the conceptual construction of recognition because there is no other alternative.
Consequently, the conceptualization of genus and so forth is an undertaking upon a path of meaninglessness;
therefore, it is established that perception has an inexpressible object.
2. Mental Perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa).
In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*: "Mental [perception] is the self-awareness of objects, passion, and so forth; it is non-conceptual.
Mental perception, which is the awareness of the nature of objects, passion, and so forth, is direct perception because it is free from conceptual construction.
Regarding the claim that it proceeds in the form of experience:
is it not the case that only visual and other sensory consciousnesses are perceived as proceeding in the form of experience?
Indeed, it is only the sensory consciousness produced by the eye and other [faculties] that is so perceived.

Now, that mental cognition which arises from that [sensory perception] must be a grasper of what was previously experienced; for if it were to grasp what was previously experienced, the mental cognition would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*),
because what was previously experienced cannot be cognized in a manner other than through the form of memory.
If it is asked: "Since direct realization occurs through non-recollection, how can it be established that there was actually a prior experience?",
then how is this to be understood?
Recognition has already been refuted; furthermore, if it were to apprehend the unseen,
such being the case—
