If the apprehension of the unseen were possible, then even the blind and others would perceive objects;
furthermore, since the mind also possesses [the capacity to grasp] objects,
it would follow that it could apprehend all objects, as would any other [sense organ].
Furthermore, because the past perception is momentary, its existence as a blind obstruction is impossible;
or, even if it were non-momentary, the definition would have to be stated with a qualification. (241)
1. "Even if [the object] is non-momentary, the definition must include a qualification"—this is the reading in manuscript He; M.

states: "If it were non-momentary, then since all entities are indeed subject to momentary destruction, how could there be a grasping of the past, by which one would grasp that which has already been grasped?"
Now, if non-momentariness is admitted,

then because it has already been apprehended by a previous perception, the apprehension of what is already apprehended is not a valid cognition, just like memory. Or, even if it were a valid cognition despite apprehending what has already been apprehended, one would have to state a definition for mental [perception] that includes a qualification.
Furthermore,
when the action has already been accomplished, why is it desired that a sense organ or any other means should produce some further distinction for the sake of that action? (242)
For one whose own nature is determined by sensory consciousness alone, what further function could there be for another [consciousness]?
If it is argued that "that very nature is being determined," then once it has already been determined, what is the purpose of determination?
That which was previously [unconditioned] is the very same even when unconditioned; what, then, is the meaning of "conditioning," since its own nature is already manifest?
What fault is there even if it were otherwise? Indeed, in this way, that which is eternal would remain eternally limited;
so what else could it accomplish therein?

Now, it is not correct to argue that [an object] is delimited by another at this time, but not by that same [other] even now because of its permanence; for there is no capacity in another delimiting factor, since such a thing does not exist.
If it is argued that, because there is no separate delimiting factor, the eternal [sound] is not perceived by itself but will be perceived by another [means], we say:
no.
Since [the first cognition] is not a means of valid cognition (*apratyayatvāt*), how could another [cognition], while cognizing at its own time, cognize [that first cognition's] permanence?
Therefore, that very delimiting factor must exist; thus, a further apprehending subject is useless, as the realization occurs through that very form.

Furthermore, all cognitions produced by that [eternal object] would have to arise simultaneously; for it is contradictory for an entity that lacks any difference in its effects to depend on other factors [for its own production].

Indeed, if all cognition were to function at once toward an eternal object by imprinting its form upon it, why would they not be simultaneous? And if they were simultaneous, would not their status as having an eternal and unitary object be contradicted?
Even if it arises at a later time due to a difference in form or from another cause,
it must still occur through an adherence to that very [earlier] time; otherwise, its apprehension would be impossible.
Like the seeing of a true dream,
for the seeing of a true dream perceives the grasper by means of that very [consciousness] which follows it at that time;
nor is any other form of experience, consisting of sensory consciousness, perceived.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that there is perception by means of what is unperceived, because of the absence of any valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Others, however,
argue that if there were no perception by the mental faculty (*mānasa*), then there would likewise be no recollection by the mental faculty.
Nothing known here by oneself is ever remembered by another;
if it were not remembered by the mind because it was grasped by sensory cognition,
then even that which is grasped by conceptual cognition would not be remembered, due to their distinctness.
If it is argued that even for those two [the eye and the ear], there is a distinction because they are mental,
then one might as well argue that they are so because they are cognitions.

Therefore, the mental consciousness (*manas*), arising from the immediately preceding condition of the sensory consciousness, perceives an entirely different object; it is not, consequently, blind sight.
Thus, even mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is produced by the sensory consciousness acting as a cooperative cause for an object that follows immediately after its own object.
Now, if that [mental consciousness] occurs at the same time as the sensory consciousness, it would be redundant because it is already apprehended by that very sensory consciousness;
or, if it occurs after the sensory consciousness has ceased, it would be unperceived, so of what would this be the definition?
To this, it is said:

This cognition, beginning with "this," which arises from repeated practice regarding what stands before one, is considered mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) because it functions through direct manifestation (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
That is to say, it is mental perception when it proceeds toward the object situated in front in the form of direct manifestation as "this";
however, when it arises from the operation of the eye, it is indeed visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*).

The eye has no utility in the mere appearance of form; rather, its function lies in attachment due to prior habituation. Since the eye has no operation here, and because this [cognition] arises from the mind characterized by prior habituation, it is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, it might be argued:
Since that aspect is apprehended by visual consciousness and so forth alone, mental [consciousness] would be redundant; yet it is not redundant,
because there is the possibility of a superior degree of resolute belief (*adhimukti*).
Thinking "this is it," one proceeds;

therefore, because it causes one to proceed, sensory perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, however, [the subsequent conceptual cognition] would not be that which causes one to proceed.
Because it functions even when there is conceptualization of something else due to excessive habituation, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, such a mind does not recollect what was previously apprehended; rather, it arises at a subsequent time, and it is not a grasper of what has already been grasped, because the previous apprehension does not recur when [the object] is present.
In that case, would not two forms be perceived simultaneously?
Indeed, this is just two forms; how then is there the determination of oneness?
There is no fault here, as it is according to the analogy of two moons seen by a person with ophthalmia.

In that case, pleasure and the like, when arising from repeated practice and grasping the form of what is present before one, would result in being mental perceptions (*mānasapratyakṣa*); therefore, the claim that "pleasure is sensory" is lost.
This is true—it is indeed lost; yet nothing is lost by this being lost.
If it is argued that this contradicts the claim that pleasure and pain arise solely through the senses,

here too the statement of the Root Teacher (Mūlācārya) is contradicted: "Self-awareness regarding attachment, aversion, delusion, pleasure, pain, and so forth, is mental perception because it does not depend on the senses."

This is indeed a long-standing infamy for Dharmakīrti: that he [asserts] pleasure and so forth [to be the objects of sense-cognition] just as [the Sāṃkhya claims] pleasure and pain belong to the *aindriya*.

This means that by the word "pleasure" and so on, not only the causes of pleasure, such as tastes, are denoted; rather, even for one who does not conceptualize, something bitter or sweet appears to sensory cognition.
Or rather, it is called "mental" precisely because of its common property of being non-conceptual; thus, there is no contradiction.
If it is argued that mental cognition would then perceive the object differently than sensory cognition—which perceives it differently and possesses multiple forms—the answer is no.
The same consequence applies even to sensory cognition;
for sensory consciousness, too, proceeding with various forms according to its proximity [to the object], cannot be prevented.
In that very context, there is an alternative reading: "Sensory cognition is a grasper of what is not otherwise, yet possesses manifold forms."
If that is the case, then even the cognition "this" should arise from the sense faculty alone due to repeated practice,
rather than being mental, because another distinct operation is also perceived.
"This is thus" is a mental operation because it is apprehended in exactly that way;
how then could this mental cognition not also function toward something remote, such as "that"?
This [objection] is not sound.
444. "For that which exists in the absence [of the object], there is no state of direct realization; how then can its status as perception (pratyakṣatā) be determined?
[Response: The very nature of direct realization is the meaning of perception.
Why should that same [nature] sometimes take the form of direct realization and sometimes not?
If it is argued that sensory cognition, too, is sometimes erroneous and sometimes not because of the presence of another causal complex such as ophthalmia (*timira*), we reply:
here too, there certainly exists another causal complex.
Since sensory cognition is a cause that apprehends only its own object and its concomitant object, it is held that even when it perceives something else, its range of objects is restricted.

The first moment of sensory cognition, or its continuum— the subsequent series of object-moments— is that which, depending upon its own object, produces both sensory cognition and mental cognition. However, whatever arises from this causal complex [of sensory cognition] is not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*).
And for this very reason, because it has a restricted object of apprehension, there is no cognition of another object;
for why is it that [the cognition] is produced by that very [object] and not by another, such that it does not arise from another object?
This is the same even in the case of sensory consciousness:
why is it that visual consciousness is not also produced by sound?
If you argue that this is because the relationship between cause and effect is fixed, we reply: [this is not so].
In this case too, it is the same as elsewhere: there is no curse of Brahmā.
Indeed, even in the second moment, one perceives by means of sensory consciousness alone;
and so it is observed.
Nor can it be mental, because no such mental representation is possible there;
nor is it conceptual, because it consists solely of the vivid form of that which stands before one.

If, then, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which arises simultaneously with sensory consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can sensory consciousness be its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

For the object of the preceding sensory consciousness cannot be a simultaneous auxiliary cause for the mental consciousness, since cooperation between two things existing at different times is impossible.
To this, it is replied:
If it is asked: "How can an object, which exists at a time different from the time of its own cognition, be a cooperative cause for the sensory consciousness?"—it is not tenable [to say so]. (246)

Since that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity prior [to its arising] and is of no use afterward, the prior existence of all causes is not for the sake of that [effect], [but rather] for the sake of their own cognition. (247)
For an object of mental consciousness is not simultaneous with the sensory consciousness,
because it exists prior to that mental consciousness; thus,
the object is the cause, and there is no simultaneity between a cause and its effect.

For if there were simultaneity with the fruit, there would be non-existence [of the cause] prior [to the fruit]; and that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity. If it is argued that it possesses capacity later at the time of the effect, then since the effect already exists at the time of the activity, such capacity is redundant.
For if that were indeed the time of the effect, then the effect would already exist;
therefore, since all causes must exist prior to [the effect], a cause is not something that exists simultaneously with the cognition that apprehends its own result.

If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be an object of cognition, those who know the logic of the matter understand that its very status as an object consists in its capacity to impart its form to the cognition.
[Objection: But surely, being an object of cognition means appearing in its own form, not the production of a cognition possessing that form.
And since manifestation occurs simultaneously with cognition, how can causality itself be the state of being an object?
What is this so-called "manifestation"? Is it the intrinsic nature of the object or something else entirely?
If it were the intrinsic nature of the object, then it would be like blue and so forth.
Since it never departs from its own nature, there would be the consequence of it appearing at all times.
If it is argued that it does not appear because of the absence of cognition, [we reply:
surely that very thing must be produced by cognition, and since that [nature] exists even previously, how could there be no appearance before?
If you claim that knowledge is useless, this is another fault of yours alone; it is not the case that the nature of that [object] itself does not appear previously.
To say "it exists" and "it does not exist" regarding that very same thing is a contradiction.
If it is argued that [the object] is seen only when there is cognition and not otherwise, then does cognition possess the status of a causal agent (*kārakatva*) with respect to its own manifestation?
And it cannot be a causal agent, because [cognition and its manifestation] are simultaneous.
Since it is established by statements such as "of that which is non-existent," [the object] is seen at the same time [as the cognition], and not without cognition; what can we do about this?
In that case, the eye itself would possess origination at that very moment.
Therefore, the nature of the object does not exist prior to the object; it arises now, at the time of its production.
That which has arisen while something else remains perishes even while that [other] remains. Therefore, let it be something entirely different, since the characteristics of difference are possible.
For a reflection of a face occurs in the face; yet it appears as distinct from the face afterwards. Let it be so for us.

If the reflection were distinct because it occupies a different location, then that distinction between the face and its reflection would have to be established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, no proof for the distinction of the appearance is seen to arise from the object itself; therefore, on the basis of the object, the unity of the appearances of blue and so forth is established. If this is so, then...

Just as the locus of appearance [of consciousness] arises now from the eyes and other [senses], so too would it arise for blue and other [objects], because they are equal in terms of their capacity for yoga (i.e., causal efficacy).

(449) Just as the object exists prior to its appearance from the eyes and other [senses], so too would the appearance exist [prior to the object]; however, this is certainly not observed. (450) For if it were accepted that blue and other [objects] are distinct from the appearance, [then...]
It should be accepted that there is first the manifestation of the blue object and so forth, which possesses the quality of existence;

immediately thereafter, consciousness arises possessing the manifestation of the blue and so forth as its apprehender, just as one perceives the form of a father. For an effect, even when arising from multiple causes, emerges by conforming to [one of them].
Therefore, it is said that [the cognition] has grasped that form which was presented by that [object].
This is like the conventional designation: "The son takes after the father's appearance.
0 3. Self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
If the self-awareness of pleasure and so forth is indeed mental perception,
then it follows that the nature of conceptual construction itself would not be perceptible;
and if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a doctrine in which cognition is always indirect.
[This is] not [the case], because the self-cognition (*ātmasamvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
however, the mention of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating clearly perceived cognition.
Now, if it is argued: "Since conceptual construction lacks the nature of being non-conceptual, how can it possess the status of perception?
For the intrinsic nature of conceptual construction is not itself non-conceptual;
rather, its conceptualizing occurs with respect to the object."
That is incorrect, because:

"If it is conceptual with respect to the object, then it must also be conceptual with respect to its own nature; for it is not tenable that it should have any other nature in relation to its own nature. (453)
To this, it is said:

"The self of passion and the other afflictions cannot be the object of a linguistic convention, for it does not participate in anything else; therefore, their self-awareness is not associated with verbal expression. (250)

At the very moment it attains its arising, consciousness, being of the nature of pleasure and so forth, bears the state of being an object; since there is no such consciousness apart from that [object],
what occasion is there then for the application of designations such as "prior" and "posterior"?
If it is argued that there is subsequent conjunction, we say no, because at that time such [conjunction] does not exist.
For if it were experienced as having a prior form, then at that time there would be no experience of that [present] object at all;
indeed, pleasure and so forth, when experienced as having a prior form or otherwise [as something else], do not become truly experienced,
just like the experience of another's pleasure.
Therefore, when pleasure and so forth are apprehended as being present, their apprehension must be either clearly non-conceptual or,
if it is thought that mental pleasure is to be apprehended through conceptual apprehension,
that too is incorrect.
Since,
if its non-perception by memory is asserted to be due to it being mental, then there would be no experience of that pleasure because it was not perceived previously;
and if it were brought forth at that very time, there would be no conceptual construction in its direct perception.
If it is argued that [the cognition] arises at that very moment because of its association with that verbal expression, then there is no state of being expressible [by words]. (455)
If pleasure is distinct from that [object], how could there be the possibility of contact? This is not called "contact" merely because they exist at the same time.

(456) Even a mental form of color and so forth does not reside within itself; since it exists only at the moment of its arising, how can it be an object of conceptual construction? (457) But then, how is it reasonable for this [cognition] to be conceptual even with respect to an object? Because the object is not grasped by it, and thus its own nature is not conceptualized either. (458)
What you have said is indeed true:

"If there is apprehension of an object, how can there be conceptual construction (vikalpa) in this case? Or if there is no apprehension of an object, how can there be conceptual construction in this case?

(459) "Or if its status as conceptual construction is defined there by the superimposition (āropa) of an object, even then, apart from apprehension and non-apprehension, there is no other object present. (460)

If you think that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) exists when there is both apprehension (*grahaṇa*) and superimposition (*āropa*), [we reply: it is untenable for both to exist if apprehension and superimposition are identical. (461) In that case, the fault already described under one of the two positions has been stated previously. Alternatively, if there is a difference between the two, it follows that there must be two distinct cognitions:
a conceptual awareness and at that very same time, a non-conceptual one. (462)
Therefore, where there is the conceit of grasping, that is called "the apprehension of destruction. For it is precisely this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is observed in our position.

[Objection: What is this "conceit" (*abhimāna*) other than the apprehension or non-apprehension [of an object]? [Response: It is that which possesses agency (*kartṛtā*) with respect to the activity of grasping. (463–464)

If the capacity to incite action exists even toward that which is not apprehended, why does it not exist everywhere? If the capacity to incite action exists even toward that which is apprehended, why does one act [only] from some [cognitions]? In that case, all cognition would now be conceptual, since one acts from every cognition even when [the object] has not been apprehended.
And since [the object] is not grasped here [in that way], we say:

that which, despite having the form of non-perception, functions through other conceptual constructions—that alone is what is accepted by the world as "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) in this context. (467)
Where there is the inclination toward seeing, that cognition is non-conceptual; because it is a direct realization and an act of resolute conviction, it is called "perception" (pratyakṣa).
But in the ultimate sense, all consciousness is indeed non-conceptual, because for everyone, its operation regarding its own apprehended object is free from conceptualization. Furthermore: 468–469.

That cognition which arises anywhere by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and in accordance with the distinctions of prior cognitions is called "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*). That which proceeds by assuming dependence upon the true object is called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) according to the conventional usage of such knowledge. Furthermore, because pleasure and the like are non-conceptual by virtue of their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), their non-conceptual nature is accepted by everyone.
Therefore, their self-awareness is not associated with linguistic expression (*abhijalpa*). Nor is such linguistic expression here appropriate as an instrument of action (*karmakaraṇatva*).

(473) Furthermore, when a cognition in the form of an ascertainment (*adhimukti*) arises—such as "this is pleasure" and so forth—with respect to pleasure and the like, while they are appearing in a continuous stream, why is there no state of conceptualization (*savikalpakatā*)?
In this regard, it has been described that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is [conceptual] just like [the perception of] an object.
For instance,

when the cognition "this" occurs with respect to an object, a form, pleasure, and so forth, all such cases are accepted as being mental [perceptions] provided there is direct apprehension of their own nature (*svarūpa*);
for even in those instances, there is no room whatsoever for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Because that [self-awareness] is non-conceptual, it is indeed perception.
Now, as for self-awareness and mental [perception], even though both of these two factors are present together, how is it that there is no cognition of two forms, since they do not touch one another?
It certainly does occur.
However, according to the analogy of two people with ophthalmia seeing two moons, such a lack of conventional usage arises precisely because of the adherence to a single object.
[Objection: But even in that case, why does such conventional usage not occur despite self-awareness?
[Response: Because inference functions in that manner.

For in that case, when a common form and effect are observed, the perception of a second [instance] occurs through the inference of their identity, and thus there is the conventional usage of "identity.
But here, since both are perceived directly, how can there be a conventional usage of "identity"?
Moreover, there is no inference involved here.
If [cognition] is self-cognized, what is the use of inference? [Objection:
But since there is a succession of cognitions, how can both [the object and the cognition] be cognized?
[Reply: If it is argued that the person is one and that both of those are cognized by him—
Since there is no person apart from cognition,
there is no perception of both by means of those two.
Just as there is a cognition of both form and taste, so too there is a cognition of two [objects] in that case;
furthermore, it has been established that this occurs even while self-cognition exists, because the same consequence would follow even in the case of cognition by another.
Therefore, it has been established that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is manifold in form;
furthermore, this is stated while relying upon external objects and accepting the relationship of apprehended and apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*).
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), everything is merely self-awareness, and there is no differentiation of cognitions such as those produced by the sense faculties.
Since the operation of the sense faculty is also cognized simultaneously [with its object], like color-form and so forth, then,

from the perspective of conventional usage, the eyes and other faculties possess causality; likewise, there is a distinction between mental cognition and sensory cognition, even though they share the same object of awareness.
[Objection: But surely, in this case, there is no empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), and even inferential [usage] is merely empirical usage; thus there is no fault. [Reply:

In that case, since even the inferential usage regarding the self (*ātman*) and so forth would be merely empirical usage, it would follow as a consequence that these [entities] also possess existence (*sattva*).
Nor [is it the case that there is no convention],
because the conventional usage of sublation exists therein;
therefore, it is established that the self of pleasure and so forth, being of a specific nature, cannot be the object of a linguistic convention.
Since they are not knowers even of themselves, how could they possibly know the nature of another?
Some maintain that they are known by a consciousness that resides in the same substratum as the object.
(251) As for that consciousness which supposedly knows another, it does not even possess self-awareness; how much less, then, can it know pleasure and so forth which are distinct from itself?
[Objection: Surely pleasure and so forth must be self-cognized because they are objects of cognition; otherwise, there would be no cognition at all. [Reply:
No, because self-cognition is unestablished.

If it is argued that if cognition were perceived by another, it would lack self-awareness just like a jar or similar objects, and consequently, it would follow that it is perceived as being in an external location just like a jar or similar objects— [we reply]:
no.
Because feeling is [produced] by a consciousness that inheres in the same object,
jars and the like do not indeed inhere in the same object as the consciousness;
therefore, they are felt by way of being objects of apprehension and as something external.

However, some maintain that pleasure and the like, being perceived from consciousness itself without any distinction, as if having assumed the very form of consciousness, are experienced as residing within in the capacity of the subject; thus, the same consequence [of external objectivity] does not apply to them as it does to jars and the like.
For those who hold this view, entities possessing such-and-such a nature are produced by causes possessing such-and-such a nature.

Is that pleasure and so forth non-cognition, produced from a cause not distinct from cognition? (252) First of all, for you, this is certainly not established by direct perception; nor is its comprehension through inference admitted without a logical mark (liṅga).
Indeed, pleasure and so forth are not perceived as distinct from cognition. (475)
Because the co-inherence in a single object is contradictory [to the universal],
inference does not proceed without a logical mark (liṅga).
There might be a logical mark here if it were possible to demonstrate a distinction between causes.
For that which is not perceived cannot be understood without inference;
however, you should understand the difference [in effects] through the difference in causes,
for a difference in the causal complex necessarily results in a difference in the effect.
Furthermore, a difference in effects does not establish a difference in their causes,
because even from a single cause, a diversity of effects is observed— as in the case of ash and smoke;
nor is a difference in effects perceived that would establish a difference between the cognitions of pleasure and so forth.
Therefore, a difference in cause must be demonstrated; yet that does not exist.
Why? Because what is perceived as having non-different causes and a non-different nature is nevertheless designated as "different"—what is the proof for this?
Alternatively, if consciousness is distinct from pleasure and so forth, then what is the cause of pleasure and so forth for that consciousness?

The eye, visible forms, and mental attention arise, and from them pleasure and so forth are produced. Since these [pleasures] arise from the causes of consciousness, such as the eye, why is it that they are not perceived by that consciousness?
If you argue that they do not exist at all, [we reply: no.
If it is asked: "Since [the object] arises with consciousness as its cause, how can it be unperceivable? Why is it not likewise [unperceivable] even in your own position?"

Nor is it untenable that consciousness sometimes takes the form of pleasure, pain, or otherwise, because it is caused by a specific awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for, by the power of the distinctions in the awakening of these impressions, such variation occurs.

He demonstrates the very fact of having a common cause: "When the object is present, the sense organ is capable, and the respective mind is also present, the birth of pleasure and so forth is observed; that is equal for the mental [cognitions] as well. (253)
There is no enjoyment of seeing forms without the eye, nor [is there enjoyment] without a form that captivates the mind,
nor when the mind is impaired by grief and the like.
This very same causal complex [is responsible] for the arising of consciousness; therefore, a difference in the cause cannot be the indicator of a difference [in the effect].

Nor is it logical that pleasure produced from the causal complex of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, when there is contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*), should be non-conscious.
If, on the other hand, pleasure had not arisen at all then, then that which is non-existent would necessarily be non-conscious.
For that which does not exist cannot be grasped;
regarding this it is said: whether these [conditions] are absent or present, there is neither birth nor non-birth anywhere.
It is observed that pleasure and so forth, or cognition itself, arise from that [cause] and not from anything else for you.

Indeed, pleasure and so forth do not come into existence merely when the eye, visible form, light, and attention are present, such that one might postulate another cause for pleasure and so forth distinct from consciousness;
therefore, the very cause of consciousness is itself the cause of pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is the cause of pleasure and so forth— namely merit (*dharma*) and the like— and its opposite, demerit (*adharma*) and the like, do not exist;
for when the eyes and other [faculties] are present, non-arising is never observed, such that through the absence of the effect one could postulate the existence of another cause.
Now, even if one accepts that dharma and so forth are indeed causes despite the absence of a [separate] exclusion (vyatireka),
pleasure is desired and pain is undesired; in this regard, the causality of dharma and adharma is necessarily established,
and this is well-known to all proponents of philosophical systems— with the sole exception of the Cārvāka.
That too is incorrect;

for the efficacy of dharma and so forth is not established because they are non-distinct [from pleasure and so on]. Dharma and the rest have efficacy only with respect to pleasure and its like, but this does not prove the desired [point].
For dharma and the rest depend equally upon the means of achieving pleasure and so forth, and not upon pleasure and its like alone.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of pleasure and so forth occurring even without their means of production.

Furthermore, it might be argued that although the means of producing pleasure and pain— such as visible forms and the like— are present, pleasure does not arise because the internal organ's capacity has been impaired by grief and other such factors.
Therefore, it is understood that the cause is indeed the phenomenon itself and not form and so forth; thus, [the opponent's position] is illogical because:

When the causal complex consisting of grief and so forth is presented by unrighteousness (*adharma*) itself, the suffering that arises from it does not have unrighteousness as its cause. [Verse 477] Let the suffering belong to that very causal complex of grief and so forth which has been brought about by unrighteousness; let that suffering arise spontaneously.
Alternatively, let there be happiness alone from righteousness (*dharma*), while suffering arises from something other than that.
Nevertheless, on the grounds that it must produce a distinct cognition,
how is it that even when pleasure is produced as non-different from the cognition, nothing at all has been assisted by you through the property?
For your purpose lies in pleasure and the like, and even though it is non-different from the cognition, it does not become bitter [to you].
Now, as for the claim that there is a distinction [between cognitions] due to a difference in their causes—that too is incorrect;

for there certainly exists a distinction between pure consciousness (*śuddhavijñāna*) and the cognition of pleasure (*sukhajñāna*). However, an absolute distinction is not established even in this case. (478)

For a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) accompanied by specific factors (*dharma*) produces that very same effect in a distinguished manner, rather than something entirely different; for through an additional contribution, it is simply that [complex] itself which becomes specialized.
Indeed, when there is fuel together with moisture, the smoke produced is not distinct from the ashes.
For smoke does not absolutely exceed ash, since darkening and other forms of soiling are possible there as well;
therefore, it is not established that [fire] has the capacity to produce an absolute distinction from smoke and the like.
For this very reason, he says:
Furthermore, the distinctions such as pleasure and pain belong specifically to those [mental states] themselves, just as the variations of dullness and sharpness belong to cognition itself.
(255) If consciousness, pleasure, and so forth share the same cause, then let it simply be "consciousness" and nothing more; how then could there be a distinction between pleasure and the rest?
Because there is no difference in that very causal complex,
[the result does not arise] even when milk or other substances are poured [upon it], just like the causal complex of a *dhātrī* seed and so forth.

Even when there is an abundance of nourishment such as milk, the *dhātrī* plant produces an effect that is indeed distinct from the seed, yet it does so without overstepping the nature of that [seed], being instead governed by other specific conditions; why, then, does it not produce something entirely different?
It should not be stated that [the cause] produces only something distinct;
for in this way, the distinction [of the effect] is demonstrated by the distinction of its causes.
If it is established that a causal complex produces distinct effects,
and furthermore,
since dharmas such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth also possess origination from the very beginning, it follows that they too must be distinct from cognition (*buddhi*).

If it is argued that wisdom and the like arise from repeated practice and so forth rather than from merit and the like, then pleasure and the like would also arise from the repeated experience of what is desired or undesired; thus, they could not have merit and the like as their cause.
If it is claimed that the proximity of what is desired and so forth is itself due to merit and the like, [the same objection applies].
In that case, pleasure and so forth do not arise from the object (*dharma*), but rather from the unimpaired mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors;
and since that unimpaired state of mental attention and the rest is also a cause for cognition, pleasure and so forth are not produced by a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"Wisdom and the other [faculties] do not have pleasure and so forth as their causes, nor do they have dharma and so forth as their causes, because wisdom exists [independently].
Since that which is pleasure is itself caused by dharma and so forth, it is unproven that pleasure and the others possess identical causes."

That too is not well-spoken, because wisdom and the other [faculties] do not arise from the factors (dharmas) and so forth; rather, these are pleasure and the like. How can this be established by means of valid cognition for those such as yourself?
For that which is not established by valid cognition is merely the manifestation of one's own system and effort, which does not satisfy others.
If it is argued that qualities such as wisdom do not arise from anything other than the Dharma,
and are seen even in the absence of the Dharma through mere habituation, we say no.
If it is argued that, because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), that very practice cannot be complete in the absence of *dharma*— and thus lacks its constituent parts— then, by the same logic,
pleasure and the other [mental states] must also arise solely from a particularity of the continuum (*santānaviśeṣa*).

For happiness exists by its very nature in the state of being undaunted, which is the cause for overcoming all calamities; it arises solely from an excellence of the mental continuum produced by previous practice.
Happiness arises precisely from an excellence of one's own nature, as seen even in those of wicked conduct who have been driven by their former habits.

If it is argued that even though the dharma exists, [pleasure and so forth arise] from the dharma itself due to the absence of one who perceives equality, and because they are assisted by the opposite of the practice of cultivating equality—

then in that case, the dharma has no efficacy, because [pleasure and so forth] are preceded by practice, just like wisdom and the rest; therefore, pleasure and the others are indeed of the nature of cognition.

Now, an objection: pleasure and the like arise from objects and other such causes, whereas cognition arises from a formative impression (*saṃskāra*) called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), which has cognition itself as its cause; thus, there is a difference in their causes. For instance, [one thinks]: "This is that very person whom I saw before," due to the occurrence of a prior formative impression. Is such a cognition of that specific form present in pleasure and the like? (481)
Therefore, that [cause] is non-existent even in the case of pleasure and so forth;
for it has already been established that pleasure and the rest arise solely through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).

Furthermore, it might be argued that pleasure and so forth are purely mental and arise from conditioning rather than being born of the sense faculties; in that case, it follows that consciousness itself is purely mental and arises from conditioning— thus, the two cases are identical.

Now, if even sensory consciousness possesses specific qualities such as acuity due solely to a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then it follows that pleasure and the like—which are also born of the senses—possess acuity and so forth for that very same reason; thus, the case is identical.
Furthermore:
Has it not been established that everything, such as pleasure and so forth, is purely mental?
Indeed, when some object has been apprehended, proficiency is logical because of the repeated arising of cognitions regarding that very same object due to the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If pleasure and the rest are also apprehended by this cognition, then it is logical that their apprehension becomes proficient. But in the view of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what kind of mental cultivation could there be?
For if self-awareness has arisen, what kind of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) could there be therein? And if self-awareness has not arisen, what kind of cultivation could there be therein?
Since one self-awareness of pleasure arises after another, there is no application of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-yoga*).

If, however, that very same thing is perceived again and again, then it receives the designation of "repetition" (abhyāsa); yet the object remains one and the same. In that case, although there is an experience through successive cognitions conditioned by mental cultivation (bhāvanā), why indeed should pleasure not also be one?
But what, then, is the meaning of "repeatedly" (*punaḥ-punar*) with respect to a single object? Even if the object is one, repetition is produced by the recurrence of experience;
that too is incorrect.
If there is a difference in cognition from its objects, how can there be a [cognitive] transition?
If it is by virtue of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), why does this not also apply to pleasure and the like?
Indeed, pleasure is not a single [undifferentiated] entity.

How is it that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is tenable there, even when the cognitions [of the object] are distinct? For recognition pertains to the object; indeed, it arises from the perception [of that object].
Furthermore, there is no perception of a single entity through a diversity of cognitions;
and how could there be recognition within a cognition?
In ultimate reality, there is no such thing as recognition therein.
Now, having superimposed that unity upon it by means of its oneness, it is conventionally designated as "one cognition.
Here, this is investigated:
is this position being stated that cognition is self-cognizing?
Now, [if you argue that] it is cognizable by another cognition or cognizable through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), what follows from this?
If it relies upon self-cognition, how could recognition (pratyabhijñā) occur? For there can be no delusion of oneness at that very time regarding something that is perceived as distinct. (484)

For if self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is clearly established as involving the perception of difference, how could there be at that very moment an illusory superimposition (*āropavibhrama*) caused by that [perception] even when the objects are non-different?

This is the same even in the case of awareness by another cognition. However, in the case of awareness through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the postulation of a cognition conforms to the object; therefore, the cognition must also be postulated as being non-different.
If it were otherwise, it would not be logically possible—this is presumptive testimony.

The object consists of nothing but sensation, and it is produced by the conceptualization of nothing but sensation. Since a single object cannot be grasped by multiple [cognitions], let it be postulated as one.

(485) For it is not possible for multiple cognitions—occurring at successive times and determining their own respective objects—to conceive that "this is one and the same object existing across prior and subsequent times," because a single [cognition] lacks such activity and a collection [of cognitions] does not exist.
That which synthesizes [the experiences] is the self, which is one; for it is possible for that [self] to remember. Indeed, its capacity lies in remembering and also in synthesis. (486)
This is incorrect;

for under the view that the self is of the nature of consciousness, this [objection] is not seen to be logical: "How can there be a valid means of knowledge for the obscuration of that which is of a single nature?
If it is argued that there is no fault in the view that the self is both different and non-different [from consciousness], [the response follows].
By that form in which [the object] is undifferentiated, there is no recognition by that same form,
because it is differentiated by the differentiation of cognition;
for if cognition were non-differentiated, there could be no differentiation of that which is non-differentiated from it.
If the object were identical with the form by which it is perceived through cognition, then there would be no recurrence [of that perception].
Alternatively, if the self were of a non-cognitive nature, it could not be known by cognition; and since that [self] would be distinct [from cognition], how could there be a grasp of non-difference?
Therefore, the grasp of identity through the distinction of cognitions is logical; thus, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), cognition must be postulated as being one alone.

If the distinction between cognitions is apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), even so, unity is not perceived within cognition; therefore, how can there be recognition? If it is argued that recognition occurs despite the multiplicity being unobserved, then the same would apply to pleasure and other mental states as well, since their unity is possible only conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*).
Furthermore, because there is repeated experience of those very same things, a specific intensity or distinction arises for pleasure and so forth through habituation (*abhyāsa*).
Moreover, pleasure and the like arise from habituation only as having the nature of cognition (*bodha*).
[Objection: But surely, through habituation, even actions such as walking become graceful and so forth, yet they do not have the nature of cognition.

To this it is replied: From the practice of that which is of the nature of non-awareness, only non-awareness arises. Why, then, does the emergence of the nature of awareness not likewise occur from the practice of that which is of the nature of awareness, just as in the case of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth? (488)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"What is this 'cultivation of the nature of consciousness'? Is it the cultivation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), or is it the cultivation of the object grasped by the nature of consciousness?"

If self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is unestablished, then that [first] position is untenable; as for the second position, it is likewise improper because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since even when there is practice in walking while grasped by the nature of cognition, one does not perceive the nature of cognition within the walking and so forth.
To this it is replied:
whatever is practiced exactly as it truly is, that very thing is intensified accordingly. Thus, the practice of internal self-awareness results in pleasure and so forth being of the same nature.
For pleasure and the rest are indeed perceived as having the form of internal self-awareness.

Being insentient in nature, they are perceived through inherence in a single object; thus, one who has attained satisfaction by acquiring such consciousness practices that very form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Consequently, that which is of such a nature would manifest through the practice of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-prakarṣa*).
First, there would be an absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
for by the statement "of whatever kind [it may be]," etc., that too is of such a nature.
Therefore, it is established that those [cognitions] arising from the power of cultivation are of the very nature of self-awareness, just like wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth;
by this, the following [objection] is also refuted:
"Entities possessing such-and-such a form are produced from causes possessing such-and-such a form, or from causes not possessing such-and-such a form."

Is that [object] such as form (rūpa) non-cognition, since it is produced from causes not distinct from those of cognition? [The opponent replies: "That [is] pleasure (sukha) and so forth. (252) 1 M. That [is] pleasure and so forth.
2. Regarding the nature of giving and ethical discipline, these three verses have been extracted:
"When there is a meaningful object, a functional sense faculty, and a corresponding mind, the arising of pleasure and so forth is observed; it is the same for mental cognitions as well.

(253) When these [factors] are absent or present, neither the arising nor the non-arising of pleasure and so forth, or of cognition, is ever observed anywhere. Therefore, it is not from anything else. (254)
Furthermore, the distinctions such as pleasure and pain belong specifically to those [faculties] themselves, just as the states of dullness or acuity belong to that very cognition.
This is the meaning:

by way of mutual cooperation, the eye, mental attention, and the cart or other objects standing before one—all arising from a common causal complex—would either all be of the nature of consciousness or all be of the nature of non-consciousness.
For there is no distinction therein between what is primary and what is otherwise;

indeed, that collection of form and so forth has its causal capacity observed in the production of multiple effects consisting of both cognition and non-cognition, and it cannot be established otherwise.
Therefore, if it is argued that the reason is inconclusive precisely because of that [collection], we reply: no.
It is not otherwise, because the meaning of the reason is intended as follows:
just as wisdom and so forth arise from cultivation and other [causes], why then would pleasure and so forth not be self-cognizing for that same reason? (490)
For the meaning of the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that whatever is practiced in a certain way becomes exactly so;
yet, it is impossible for form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] to have internal nature as their object of practice.

As for one who holds that specific excellences such as wisdom (*prajñā*) are to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how is he to understand that they are inherent in the self (*ātmasamavāyin*)?
It is understood through presumption (*arthāpatti*) that whatever cannot be accounted for without something else must be inferred;
and since nothing can be accounted for without its inherence in a self and without its being of the nature of consciousness,
there must necessarily exist another [entity], because the state of being beyond perception has arisen regarding the object.
Therefore, how can there be a cognition of its inherence in the self and so forth?

Consequently, the resolution is that people have merely practiced the internal nature of cognition such that it appears as something internal, leading to the perception of internality in the form "this has been understood by me.

Even for those who describe another cognition as being perceptible within a [primary] cognition, they must necessarily accept this very position: that it appears as inherent in the self and consisting of the nature of awareness.
Otherwise, it would be a distinct category altogether;
however, since the status of being a grasper is well-established,
it appears in another perception as that very grasperness mounted upon it.
And that being the case, even there that object would have to appear;
but how can there be an appearance of what has perished?
Furthermore, how could cognition appearing in isolation appear as either a grasper or as an apprehended object?
If it is objected that the self and so forth are likewise [superimposed], the response would be that the superimposition arises as being inherent in the self due to beginningless time;
and this being the case, wisdom and so forth, or even pleasure and so forth, arising precisely in that way through the power of cultivation, are indeed of the nature of consciousness.
Now, even so, others do not accept that cognition and the like have the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

But [we reply]: even if there were no self-awareness, it has been established that there would be neither perceptibility nor internality. However, since cognition manifests itself as having such a nature and also manifests the object, this alone is logical.

Now, one might argue: "Even by the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), pleasure and the like arise and perish while remaining inherent in the self (*ātman*) alone; they are grasped by a cognition that is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*).
Thus, through contact with that cognition, they appear in the form of awareness, but not by virtue of having the nature of awareness itself. Why is this not postulated?
To this, it is replied: [Verse 491]
Because this [world] is established as being thus due to the absence of beginningless cultivation, a conceptual construction of a different process is not introduced by the world.
It is maintained that "this arises through the power of cultivation";
in that case, no other process is perceived as arising.
Even if one were to say, "It is thus and so," nevertheless, based on the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is the conventional usage that "this is exactly as it is seen";
what purpose, then, is served by postulating a co-inherence (*samavāya*) in a single object?
In that case, to whom does that pleasure belong if its inherence in a self is not admitted?
Well then, to whom does that self belong if its inherence elsewhere is not admitted? For how could a self be independent by virtue of its eternity, yet dependent on another?
Regarding pleasure and the like, however, the assumption of dependence on another follows from their impermanence.
For it is logical that the Self, because of its permanence, is independent and unconditioned; this is indeed correct.
But pleasure and the other qualities are impermanent; therefore, they must necessarily exist as dependent entities.

This is incorrect because: "If there were substratum-ness, there would be quality-ness; or if there were quality-ness, there would be the subsistence of the substratum. Due to this mutual dependence, neither of the two could be established. (494)
If the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) were first established, then the conceptualization that "a quality must necessarily be dependent" would arise;
however, that is not established, because its establishment depends on something else.
It has already been demonstrated that no such relationship of substratum and superstratum exists for anything whatsoever.

Although it has been stated that because of its permanence the self is independent, whereas pleasure and so forth are not because they are the opposite [of permanence], even though these are impermanent, since they arise from causes, they too are independent; thus, since there is no duty to be performed by them, how can there be dependence on another?
If they have not arisen at all, how could there be dependence on another for them?
Now, if it is argued that since [the cause] has arisen from some cause or other, how can there be any dependence on another (parāyattatā) in its production of its own effect?
If you say that its dependence on another consists in its dependence on something else for the production of the effect, we reply:
no, because its production of the effect arises from its own cause alone; thus, there is no possibility of dependence on another. Enough of this digression.
Therefore, let pleasure and the other [feelings] be independent; what is the use of postulating a self as their substratum?
Furthermore, if pleasure and the others were not self-cognizing, how could they possess the capacity to apprehend objects?
If it is argued that this will occur through a cognition that is in a relation of "co-inherence in the same object" (*ekārthasamavāyin*) with them, [we reply: no.
To this it is replied:
Are they cognized by a sensory consciousness that is inherent in the same object, or by another?
First of all, not by sensory consciousness.
Since those pleasures of cognition and so forth arise through the occurrence of a particular object,
how could that [cognition] apprehend only pleasure and the like while excluding that object? (256)

How can that very sensory cognition, which is intent upon form and so forth, apprehend pleasure and the like—since it is directed toward form and the rest by means of the eye and other faculties? For there is no such cognition as "my eye is engaged with pleasure.
If it is argued that the consciousness apprehending pleasure will function while being directed toward form itself—
Since that is the case, it has been established that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
namely, the consequence that inference (*anumāna*) would also be visual; therefore,
it is said that no other apprehending form (*grāhakākāra*) is perceived apart from the sensory cognition itself.
In that case, it follows that even conceptual construction would be grasped by the sensory consciousness at the same time;
thus, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would apply even to the object of inference. This has already been pointed out, for no other grasping aspect is perceived there.

Now, if it is argued that this conceptualization of the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*)— just as there is a conceptualization of the form of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*)— is equally applicable even to words,
then why is the form of the apprehender not likewise postulated for pleasure and so forth?
It is not [the case that it lacks objectivity] because of a lack of experience as something to be grasped;
for even when there is inherence in the same object, one cannot say that there is no objectivity simply because it is not grasped by another act of grasping.
If it is argued that this is due to the cognition occurring through a state of complete unification (*ekalolībhāva*),
then that [cognition] would be identical to that [object], whether it be pleasure or the intellect;
for since even the single [subject] is not apprehended in its own form, there would be only a consciousness in the form of pleasure alone.
If it is argued that there is an absence of pleasure even for another because of its non-perception, we say no;
for the state of being dependent on another is not perceived.
Just like the cognition of the form of a tree-cluster,
if it is argued that its being conditioned by another is established through inference— namely,
that whatever is perceived is conditioned by another, like a cluster— then [the following applies].
Nor [is it so] because of the consequence that external objects would be non-existent,
since the conditioning of latent predispositions (vāsanā) is possible.
Therefore, whatever is perceived in a certain way must be accepted exactly as it is; it should not be established otherwise through inference.
Consequently, an external object, being perceived as something to be grasped in its own form, is established as such, because establishment is necessarily bound to perception alone.
Pleasure and the like are not cognized as objects of apprehension; therefore, they are self-cognized.
Alternatively, the cognition produced merely from the conjunction of the self and the mind is the grasper of pleasure and the like, and not sensory cognition.
If that were the case, since multiple cognitions do not arise simultaneously, there would have to be a sequential apprehension [of them].
And consequently,
if there were a perception of succession, that cognition would not appear as uninterrupted.
Furthermore,
if the apprehension of succession were being set aside, the cognition of pleasure and so forth would not appear as uninterrupted;
for this very thing called "non-simultaneity" is what constitutes succession.
Furthermore, the apprehension of pleasure and so forth is observed simultaneously with the apprehension of form and so forth;
yet, to claim that they are apprehended together in that case is contradictory,
for two contradictory things cannot coexist in a single location.
If it is argued that [the perception of pleasure] is similar to that [of the lamp-flame] due to its rapidity, why is there no such cognition?

(257) If the apprehension of pleasure consists in the perception of an uninterrupted flow of a rapid occurrence, and this very perception is itself the absence of any intermediate non-apprehension, then this rapidity is equally present even when pleasure and so forth are not being apprehended; consequently, it follows that the non-apprehension of the two forms of pleasure must itself be uninterrupted.

Moreover, even the non-apprehension [of one] appears as uninterrupted, because the non-apprehension of pleasure is indeed nothing other than the apprehension of form; likewise, there is no non-apprehension of form that is distinct from the apprehension of pleasure. (496)

And thus, the meaning that "there would be an uninterrupted non-apprehension of the pleasant face" implies that "the apprehension of form and so forth is uninterrupted"; since that is certainly the case, the same should be stated even in the opposite scenario.
Therefore, is this not merely a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—namely, that there is no [such] non-apprehension?
To this it is replied:
The existence of one thing is defined as the non-existence of another; for that non-existence is conceived through its being distinguished from that [other].
Indeed, this non-existence of anything does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, but rather by virtue of its being distinguished from that [thing].

Furthermore, if it is accepted that the apprehension of form is perceived as distinct from the apprehension of pleasure, then by parsimony (*lāghavena*), the apprehension of that [form] as distinct [from pleasure] would be possible through their non-interruption; how then could there be the experience of pleasure?
For the experience of pleasure would follow that very same sequence, and thus there would be no apprehension of either of the two.
It has been well said: "Why is it not simply non-apprehension?
For even when another [object] is being perceived, there is no apprehension of that other as distinct from it;
and this very non-apprehension of it as distinct is what constitutes its own nature, because that nature does not enter into it. If this is argued:

There is no apprehension of [things] without succession when there is an apprehension that does not involve the mutual entry of their own natures, because such apprehension is possible even at the same time,
given the acceptance that parts and the whole are apprehended simultaneously.
Regarding that, as for the phrase "due to entering therein":
surely, even when there is no perception of the space between due to the grasping of many hairs from a distance, there is indeed no perception of the form of the hair itself.

In this regard, just as the perception of the intervals between hairs is sublated by the perception of the form of the hairs as being without intervals, it is not the case that the perception of the intervals sublates the perception of the hairs;
likewise here, non-perception does not sublate the perception of the interval.
To this, it is replied:

In that case, how could the apprehension of the intermediate [moments] possibly constitute a sublation? For what does not exist cannot be a sublater, nor is it desired; the world merely desires [the sublation].

If it is asked, "Why is there no apprehension of the intermediate [moments] at all?"—this is simply the nature of things (*bhāva-śakti*); why should it be questioned? Therefore, the non-arising of the apprehension of the intermediate [moments] is not a sublation.
Nor is it merely a case of sublation where a designation has simply become conventionalized in the world in some way or another;
for in that case, it would not be logical to say that the apprehension of the form of pleasure and so forth, or the non-apprehension [of it], has not arisen.
If that were the case, the apprehension of succession would be impossible.
If it is argued that there is indeed non-apprehension in that case because the subsequent apprehension has not yet arisen,
this is not so.

In the act of apprehension there is no apprehender; in the apprehender there is no further apprehender. This is likewise accepted by others; otherwise, it would be incoherent. (500) For the act of apprehension must be self-luminous by nature, whereas for the apprehender—whether conceived as a causal agent or an actor—one would have to posit another apprehender.
If the act of apprehension were not self-luminous, it would follow that no objects whatsoever could be apprehended.

If it is argued that the apprehension (*graha*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), whether it arises from the sense-faculty or from something else, then what need is there for another apprehending subject (*grāhaka*)? If this is said, this is yet another fault of that very position;
for it is not the case that an apprehension which is not luminous by itself is called "apprehension."

If it is argued that it is manifested by another, then indeed the manifestation by that other is also imperceptible, and for that [other] too there must be another; thus, in effect, the entire world would be reduced to mere meaninglessness, as will be demonstrated. Furthermore, since that which appears arises with a mutual distinction of time, how could it not be a sublater of the other? This is quite trivial.
Now, it might be argued that the apprehension of pleasure is indeed sublated at times because form (*rūpa*) and so forth are apprehended alone.

For instance, when one beholds a captivating form, there is sometimes no experience of pleasure; therefore, since the apprehension of pleasure has not arisen—just like the apprehension of other hairs—the sublation is established.
But this too is not correct.
For,
just as the perception of [illusory] hairs always sublates the perception of anything else, so too at that time the arising of pleasure and the like is not accepted by the world.
Just as the perception of hairs always sublates the perception of [other objects] in between.
In this way, the apprehension of form and so forth might also [be considered] the apprehension of pleasure and so forth;
yet, in ultimate reality, that is not the apprehension of hair, because the intrinsic nature of the hair is not perceived.
However, when there is no perception of pleasure during the mere apprehension of form and so forth, then pleasure itself has simply not arisen.
But it is not established that non-apprehension alone constitutes what has arisen.

If you argue that the conventional designation of "unproduced" follows from non-perception, then the conventional designations of "production" and so forth would now be abolished; therefore, even non-perception [would not exist].
Therefore, at the very moment that the arising of pleasure and so forth is perceived, that is precisely when pleasure and so forth arise;
even then, according to your own position, there would be no suppression by the perception of form and so forth, just as it follows [in your view] that other hairs are not perceived.

Now, one might argue that a single sensory cognition will subsequently proceed to apprehend pleasure and so forth; therefore, this fault of sequential apprehension would not arise. To this he says: "And there is no cognition of two [objects] by means of a single [cognition], because of the restriction of the sensory consciousness."
Even in the absence of pleasure and so forth, [the cognition] arises from the object, because the capacity for that [pleasure] is not established.
(258) If it were argued that sensory cognition itself is the grasper of the object, pleasure, and so forth, this is not tenable;
for it has been demonstrated that pleasure and the like are grasped by a non-sensory cognition produced solely by the conjunction of the self and the mind, as is accepted [by our opponent].
Now, even if someone were to assert this, it would still not be possible [to establish their claim].
For, since sensory cognition arises from the object alone even in the absence of pleasure and so forth, the causality of pleasure and so forth cannot be determined.
Indeed, when something does not arise in the absence of another, while other capable causes are present, that [latter] is determined to be its cause.
Nor is it the case that the sense-faculty and the mind do not arise without even the totality of form and so forth, along with pleasure and so forth.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
when blue appears in sensory cognition together with yellow, then blue would have no causal efficacy, because [the cognition] arises from the yellow even in the absence of blue.
Moreover, even in that case, it possesses that capacity;
for just as a cognition appearing as blue and yellow does not arise from yellow alone,
so too the appearance in the form of pleasure does not arise from visible form alone— the principle is the same.

This is not the same [case], because the separate efficacy of the blue [object] is observed in sensory cognition; even in the case of a collection, the establishment of capacity is not seen in this way for pleasure, or else it would have to be admitted [as such]. (502)

If the two had separate capacities, like blue and other [objects], pleasure would be perceived alone; for it is not perceived as having that [object] as its cause. Indeed, the perception [of pleasure as being caused by an object] is neither logical nor observed, nor is it accepted by anyone.
It is logical that when there is apprehension together with the object itself,
that sensory consciousness arises from form and so forth alone, which are devoid of pleasure and the like.
For prior pleasure and so forth do not exist as something distinct from consciousness like a form (rūpa), because that [pleasure] arises from that very [consciousness] simultaneously with it;
if, on the other hand, it is maintained that even things existing at the same time possess the status of co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu), that is incorrect.

Let it be that the two [cognitions] are mutually dependent by virtue of being co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*), just like the primary elements (*bhūta*); however, there is no relationship of the perceived and the perceiver (*vedya-vedaka-bhāva*).

For that which does not have the nature of self-cognition (*asvasamvedana-rūpa*), there is no mutual apprehension; nor is there mutual apprehension for that which has the nature of self-cognition (*svasamvedana-rūpa*).

(503) If apprehension is maintained on the grounds that [the cognition] is oriented toward its own cause, then even for this [cognition] existing at the same time [as the object], [apprehension would occur] through the nature of another's cognition. (504)
How could that which is directed toward pleasure be considered born of the sense-faculties? It has already been stated that there is no cognition of the operation of the senses therein.
Furthermore, if they possessed separate causal capacities, pleasure and so forth would be apprehended alone;
if it is argued that they are indeed apprehended just like blue, [we reply: 505.
No,

for it is not logical that there be a perception of pleasure and so forth without the perception of its causes, such as visible form and so forth; even if [pleasure] were being experienced, it would still be illogical.
Indeed, no seeker of pleasure whatsoever desires that pleasure at that very moment without the attainment of the charm of a woman;
yet such is not observed to be the case.
Now, as for its very capacity:
if that were so, then the second moon would also exist;
therefore he says:
If [the object] is grasped together with the object itself,
what capacity do pleasure and so forth have, such that a cognition arising from them is not admitted? (260)
For the establishment of causal capacity is not possible without positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), nor is it accepted;
indeed, for our opponents, cognition arising from the eyes and other [senses] is not even desired.
Moreover:
Without an object, form and so forth would never be perceived by the eyes and other senses through the expression of distinctions such as "woman" and so on;
nor would form and so forth be grasped as the causes of pleasure, pain, and the like, nor as being agreeable or disagreeable, nor as a woman and so forth. (261)
If it is argued that there must be some cause for the apprehension of the [object] alone,
whereas there is an apprehension of the cause when there is an apprehension of the [object] together with [it], then [the answer is] mutual—
There would likewise be a perception of blue and other [colors] as being causes, yet such is not the case;
therefore, this [position] is untenable.
And if pleasure alone could be apprehended by the eye and other [senses], then the apprehension of form and so forth would never arise;
for when an internal object is present, the intellect does not perceive external things.

If the experience of pleasure itself could not occur without the perception of external distinctions such as women and so forth, then, because the experience of pleasure is invariably concomitant with that external perception, one must admit the apprehension of the object. If this is your view, then there is this further fault: if the object is apprehended, there would be no cognition of the pleasure and other [mental states] produced from it. (262)

For at the time of perceiving an object, although pleasure may arise, there is no causal complex for its perception; because the mind— which arises from the conjunction of the sense organ, the object, and the internal organ— perceives objects such as form,
and it is not admitted that another mind exists simultaneously for the sake of the non-occurrence of simultaneous cognitions.
Therefore, pleasure and so forth produced by that [object] would not be perceived;
furthermore, if the simultaneous arising of cognitions is asserted, then there is yet another fault—thus he says:

In the Nyāyasūtra, it is stated that if two cognitions were to arise simultaneously, there would be the experience of pleasure and pain at once, because their respective objects could exist simultaneously. (263)
When there is the possibility of both desirable and undesirable objects occurring simultaneously, it is impossible to prevent the concurrent experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth; indeed,
this is clearly observed,
for instance, during the cold season, when pleasure and pain are experienced as they arise from the sensations of cold and heat.
That too is incorrect,
because the intended meaning is that [the two] would exist at all times.

Furthermore, for one whose mind is not averse to the passion for battle, who desires to make himself successful by being dependent on the acknowledgment of his master’s honors and favors, there would be the experience of suffering through contact with the treatises;
and since the arising of that [suffering] is necessary when the cause of suffering exists,
it would follow that he must experience pleasure and suffering simultaneously.
Furthermore, the claim that there is no perception of another [subtle object] due to being overwhelmed by something else is incorrect, because such overwhelming is impossible;
it is not right to say that overwhelming occurs through [the presence of] largeness and so forth.
The consequence that there would be no simultaneous cognition of an elephant and a horse is not correct,
because both are indeed perceived together.
If it is argued that because the simultaneous experience of suffering and pleasure has been established, there is experience [of both] due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a cloth,
we say no.
Since no other formative factor (*saṃskāra*) is observed apart from mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
and if their arising is indeed due to the power of cultivation, then it has already been established that for you, pleasure and the like are of the very nature of consciousness (*bodha*).
Nevertheless, it might be argued as follows:
"Knowledge regarding pleasure and so forth arises from the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), whereas pleasure and so forth are produced solely from causes such as form (*rūpa*) and the like"—
this too is a false construction, because: [506]
Scholars do not admit that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is required for a cognition that arises through the force of the object itself; if that were so, it would be inconsistent.
For if pleasure and the like are already present, they are indeed perceived even without cultivation.
For it is not the case that entities which were previously neither thought of nor experienced become objects of perception all at once;
if you argue that even in such cases there exists a latent impression (*bhāvanā*) that has been interrupted,
what is the proof for this?
Moreover,
the cultivation of cognition cannot occur without the cultivation of the form of the object,
because it is impossible to cultivate cognition in isolation.

If cognition arises through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) like [the cognition of] a rising [object], why would it depend on an object and so forth? Or, if [you argue that it arises] because of repeated practice together with an object, then in that case, even the form of the object (*arthākāra*) arises solely from the power of cultivation.

This being so, cognition is devoid of an object, just like the cognition in dreams and the like; thus, by means of the cognition of external forms, pleasure, and so forth, the proponent has actually established the non-externality of the object itself. What great skill in refuting others this opponent possesses!
Furthermore, there is the thought: "The non-occurrence of pleasure and pain simultaneously is precisely because,
even when another truth is taken as the basis, the occurrence of suffering and so forth exists within cognition."
If it is thought that there is no appropriation for that which is contradictory, and that [appropriation] is one;
then by what means could consciousness be the appropriating cause of non-consciousness? (264) M.
