The predominance of that ignorance is observed even in its opposite,
just as light is predominant for the eyes of both nocturnal and other animals. || 265 ||
It produces both the deficiency and the non-deficiency of the perception of form simultaneously.

(266) If pleasure and so forth arise in dependence upon a cognition that is preceded by its own material cause (*upādāna*), then it is not logical for a single material cause to produce two contradictory [states];
however, that very [single cause] is untenable, since the cognition of even contradictory things, such as pleasure and the like, is observed.
Now, if that which is contradictory does not become [the cause],
then how could consciousness be the appropriation (*upādāna*) of non-consciousness?
Furthermore, what is called "the state of being an appropriation" is merely the sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) of causes over their effects.
And that [simultaneity] occurs even in the case of opposites, just as the impairment and non-impairment of the eyes of Kauśika and another person both arise from the same single light;
therefore, pleasure and so forth [arise] from objects that appear as having been transferred into their own [cognition].

If pleasure and the like, being non-cognitive in nature, arise solely from their own causes and simultaneously with consciousness from the causal complex of form and so forth, then why would it not be the case for you as well that both the experiencer of pleasure and the experiencer of pain would exist simultaneously whenever desirable and undesirable objects are present? *Note: The verse fragment "vedakāḥ svātmanaścaiṣām arthebhyo janma kevalam" (267) means: "And these [pleasures, etc. are the perceivers of themselves; their birth is solely from [their own] objects. The commentary explains the logical consequence of this position.*
Nor is it the case that,

due to the absence of such an awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), only something specific occurs for someone specific at a particular time— as in the case of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding form and so forth— [but rather] there exists a cause for the awakening of latent impressions.
If it is argued that "it is the same for me as well," it is not so, because:

If [cognition] were produced by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it would follow that it is nothing other than awakening itself; for latent impressions are characterized as the cause of memory, recognition, and so forth.
Now, one might argue that even memory and the like do not consist of self-awareness, because in those cases too, only the object appears;
it is the very form of the object—consisting of color and shape—that appears therein.
Nor is the form of another cognition there the object of awareness;
therefore, every cognition is indeed beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*).
If only the object itself were the domain of the appearance therein, then its apprehension would be consistent with being directly perceived (*pratyakṣavat*). (509)
For an object appearing in its own form cannot be considered perceptual, because only the appearance of its own form constitutes perception, and there is no other definition of perception;
if that were the case, there would be no distinction between perception and memory.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because [the object] appears as "prior" and as "indirect" (parokṣa), [we reply:]...

This so-called "remoteness" has certainly not been apprehended by direct perception, and it is only when something has been apprehended by direct perception that recollection can occur. Otherwise, if the previous form had not been grasped, how could there be recollection? (510)
For it is not the case that recollection has as its object a thing previously apprehended;
rather, since it is the grasping of the very same apprehended object as being remote, the notion that "this is recollection" is incorrect.
That too is false.
Is this hiddenness (parokṣatā) the nature of the object or the nature of the cognition? If it is the nature of the object, then it should appear in direct perception (pratyakṣa).
For whatever is the nature of an object appears in direct perception, just as blueness and so forth do;
[if you argue that it does not appear there because] it appears only in memory due to a restriction of capacity (śakti-niyama), [we reply: 511.

Just as in an object consisting of both existence and non-existence, the aspect of existence is apprehended by direct perception, whereas the aspect of non-existence is the domain of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding existence through the form of another [positive entity],
so too is that partiality toward one's own side;
for it is thus:
For if non-existence were itself an existence, how could it not be apprehended by perception? If it were distinct from that [existence], how could that existence possess duality?
Since the distinction between existents is characterized by a difference in form, if there were no distinction despite the difference in form, everything would become a single uniform nature.
Now, identity does not exist between two entities due to the difference in their forms and so forth; nor does it exist between existence and non-existence,
because there is a distinction between two entities by virtue of their being non-existent [in relation to one another],
whereas for existence and non-existence, there is no further entity [that unifies them].
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.

If non-existence were non-different from existence, how could there be a perception of their difference? If it is argued that this is due to a difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then from where does the perception of their non-difference arise? (Verse 513) If the aspect of existence is apprehended by perception and the aspect of non-existence by another means of valid cognition, then since they are understood as mutually unmixed, how can there be a cognition that a single entity consists of both existence and non-existence?

If the apprehension of form occurs through visual consciousness and that of sound and so forth through another, how can there be an apprehension of the unity of the agent in the thought "I myself have apprehended both"? This cognition arises from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and not from reality; who, then, can be blamed for this?
If it is argued that the same applies here as well,

then if the cognition of the exclusion of non-existence occurs solely through the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), what is the point of postulating a separate entity? Furthermore,
even that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called "non-existence" would be produced merely by the power of latent impressions, rather than being ultimately real.

Therefore, because it is distinct from that [positive entity], the exclusion from it appears through perception itself as a distinction from non-existence. Thus, the cognition "this is not here," which occurs at a subsequent time and arises through the force of that [perception], is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended; there is no such thing as a separate means of knowledge called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

The individual linguistic usage of the world—“I have apprehended non-existence by means of the instrument of cognition known as non-apprehension”—is equivalent in meaning to the worldly usage: “That which was fit to be seen has not been perceived by me; therefore it does not exist here, and its non-existence is established.
Furthermore, we shall explain that this very non-apprehension is nothing other than perception itself.

In ultimate reality, however, that which is called "non-existence" (abhāva) is neither a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) nor an object of cognition (prameya); thus, the example is unestablished. Furthermore, even if there were a restriction of capacity within that very nature [of the cognition], just as non-existence would be a separate means of valid cognition, so too would memory (smṛti) be one.
If it is argued that memory is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when its object is not present to the senses, we say no,
because it lacks the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition.

Even if the state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) is apprehended, what purpose is accomplished? For the operation of inference (*anumāna*) occurs through the cognition of a connection with a factual substrate (*dharmin*).
It might be argued:
"When there is knowledge of the state of being beyond perception, since there is currently no occasion for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), discerning people employ inference."
Therefore, this is the purpose of knowing [an object] as being beyond the senses: that memory is authoritative.
This is not so, because:
Since the operation of inference proceeds solely from the apprehension of the relation [of concomitance] and the reliance upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*),

no one— upon the arising of an inference following the perception of an effect such as smoke— determines that the apprehension of fire is ultimately "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*) even before that point; nor is there any purpose in making such a determination.
If it is argued that at some time [the self] is indeed perceived as something distinct, even that is of no consequence;
for instance:
Is some specific factor observed as a causal agent only occasionally? Or does some object, being a causal agent, cease to be so?
For a causal agent is indeed a cause.
Furthermore, causality does not exist when there is a deviation from positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), because that is its defining characteristic.
Moreover, by means of memory, what object is indicated as being beyond the senses? It is that very object whose apprehension occurs through inference which falls within the scope of memory. (516)
For an object that exists at the time of inference is not within the scope of memory;
otherwise, it would follow by implication that inference is useless, since that [object],
being beyond the senses, would already have been apprehended through memory alone.
If it is argued that memory perceives only its state of being absent from the senses and not its existence at that time,
then for whom is that state of being absent from the senses perceived?

If it is argued that [memory] pertains to what was previously grasped, then memory would cognize only that object delimited by its own time as being remote; it would not cognize anything else. Thus, such memory would be entirely useless.
If it is argued that recollection functions by taking an object as absent from the present, and therefore memory is a valid means of knowledge because it leads to the operation of inference—
this must be examined: when one acts "having recollected," does one act toward its existence at that [past] time, or toward its existence at the present time?

If it were to exist at that time [of the original perception], it would be impossible to attain it; and one who seeks attainment would act only if they were discerning, not otherwise. (517) Since present existence is not known through memory, how can there be validity? For the object was known as being remote in the past, and that cannot be attained.

Alternatively, it is precisely through perception that there is the apprehension of hiddenness—that is, the apprehension of the temporal limit [of the object] by means of perception itself; this very same thing, in relation to a subsequent time, constitutes hiddenness.
Furthermore, the assumption of that form [of the object] belongs essentially to the recollection itself, by virtue of the power of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
If it is argued that this [object] is indeed of such a nature,
we say no;
for its status as reality is established precisely through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding its being an object.
For an object, while being cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), does not attain a definitive status as either "existent" or "non-existent";
rather, it is established as such by a subsequent mental engagement (*adhimukti*).
And that [subsequent engagement] does not exist in the form of memory (*smaraṇa*).
For instance,
that object which was previously perceived, wise people recognize as being now capable of arising once again through the power of cultivation alone;
therefore, pleasure and so forth [are established] as objects that appear as having transferred into [the cognition] itself.
The experience of these [pleasures and so forth] consists solely in their arising from objects;
just as memory, which arises from the impression of self-cognition, is a single awareness of the form of the object transferred to itself, so too are pleasure and the rest,
since they too are the experiencers of that very internal specific tangible quality which has arisen through the impression of mental cultivation.

How, then, is there a dependence on objects such as form? It is because, through that [form], there is an awakening of a corresponding latent impression (*vāsanā*), resulting in a cognition in the form of pleasure produced by contact with the tangible. A latent impression arises; its awakening occurs through the sight of that [object]. For the latent impression of the experience of the pleasure of embracing, having arisen very intensely, upon the subsequent sight of a similar form, undergoes awakening and produces an internal experience of the pleasure of touch exactly of that same kind.
He demonstrates this very point:

"For the object-nature, having become their own self, is experienced by them; therefore, there is the designation 'experience of the object,' while the objective support is merely the appearance thereof. (268)
A specific internal tangible object that has become one's own self is experienced through pleasure and so forth;
it is precisely there that the manifestation of the experience of the object occurs.
Otherwise, if there were cognition of another [object], there would be no connection [between the experience and the object] by means of that [cognition].
For it is logical that there is an experience of one's own nature, since [that] nature arises from its own cause;
how then could the experience of another's form be separated from it? (519)
For how could that which has one form be manifested by something else that has a different form? However, in the case of a lamp, there arises in the jar a luminosity of such a nature [as the lamp].
But from consciousness, which is of the nature of light, the object does not arise as light. For if it were an effect, how could its cognition occur through that knowledge?
Indeed, the logical principle is: that which is the effect of something is not cognized by means of that cause.
A bodily activity arising from a cognition of something as otherwise would be experienced by that [activity];
therefore, it is logical that only the nature of the self (ātman) should be experienced. For experience occurs through being directed toward [an object], not through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
That is incorrect:

if the state of being oriented toward [the object] arises from its own cause as its very nature, what has that to do with the object, by virtue of which it would become a cognition of that object? (522) If it is argued that its orientation toward the object [arises] from the object itself, then why is it not the case that the eye’s orientation toward it is also a cognition of that object? (523)
If it is argued that the eye is directed toward the object, how can there be cognition? For the perception of being directed toward an object would only occur when the object itself is perceived.

Indeed, if the object is not perceived in its own form, its state of being directed toward it cannot be perceived. If the object is perceived by itself, what then is the use of consciousness being directed toward it? For an object that presents itself as already established does not require [consciousness] for its utility.
If it is argued that the object cannot be perceived without that [cognition],

then let it be that the object appears only together with that [cognition] and not as something distinct from it; for to claim that the object is grasped as something other than that [cognition] is merely a borrowed ornament.

Another [opponent] asserts that pleasure and so forth are external, insentient, and objects of apprehension; for him as well, the simultaneous apprehension of both [the cognition and the object] is not logical. (269)
"By necessity" is the ellipsis of the sentence.

For there is no reason why pleasure and so forth must necessarily be perceived together with something else, such as blue and so forth, as independent objects of cognition in the manner of blue and the like.
Now, if these pleasures and so forth are of the nature of transformations of *pradhāna*, which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion—
For the process is as follows:

from Pradhāna comes Mahat; from Mahat comes Ahaṃkāra; from Ahaṃkāra come the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five sense organs, the five action organs, and the mind; and from the five subtle elements come the five gross elements—this alone constitutes the entire range of evolved effects.
Furthermore, a transformation follows the nature of its original substance,
just as a jar or other objects are transformations of clay;
regarding this, it is said:
In that very same [text]: "From the five subtle elements (tanmātras) arise the five gross elements. This is an alternative reading:

"If the stalk and so forth are not perceived simultaneously because they are non-different in form from pleasure and the rest, then what is non-different between the object and the consciousness which appear as distinct? (270)

If it is argued that pleasure and so forth are nothing other than the very forms of the primary substance whose nature consists of pleasure and so forth— on the grounds that one observes their conformity with those forms— then it is as follows: (text continues)
[Objection: Modifications of clay are seen to follow from it [the clay];
however, this is not an inconclusive [reason], for sound arises from the conjunction of a drum and a stick, yet it does not follow the form of the drum or the stick.
Even if it is maintained that air, atoms, and sound undergo the transformation into soundness (*śabdatva*),
this is nonetheless not established;
for one might as well postulate here, as in the case of the modifications of clay, a cause belonging to the same genus.

In that case, whatever is an effect is of such a nature that it arises from something heterogeneous; for example, effects such as sound and so forth arise from heterogeneous causes, and effects such as a jar and so forth likewise arise only from a heterogeneous cause, namely the potter and others.
The pervasion that "everything arises from what is of the same genus" is not established; rather,
there is proof of the opposite— that [things] arise from both what is of the same genus and what is of a different genus—
since a cause consisting of a single, unaccompanied member of its own genus is never observed anywhere.
Now, since everything is observed to be endowed with pleasure and so forth,
it has been stated here that the cause must therefore have the very nature of pleasure and so forth, just as a lump of clay is the cause of its clay products.
Since another assistant [cause] can also serve as a cause, it follows that the cause must be both similar and dissimilar [to its effect]; thus, the primary cause (*pradhāna*) is not established.
Furthermore:
Since pleasure and the like also possess the attributes of being objects of cognition (*grāhyatā*) and so forth, another object of cognition—the *pradhāna*—is established;
consequently, ultimately, there would be a cause such as "objectivity" (*grāhyatva*) and "substantiality" (*vastutva*).
Now, if that [pradhāna] too consists of pleasure and the like...

Since the nature of being a category such as "substance" (padārtha) is pervasive because it consists of pleasure and so forth, it follows that pleasure and so forth must consist of jars and so forth, because they consist of jars and so forth; thus, the nature of the jar and so forth would necessarily belong to the Pradhāna.
And if this is accepted, then its nature is indeed everything.

If the entire aggregate of transformations is perceived within the nature of the Pradhāna by that very same essential form, though mutually distinct, what indeed could constitute the relationship between cause and effect here?

If it is argued that this consists merely of manifestation and disappearance— that manifestation is the transformation and disappearance is the cause— then what is this so-called manifestation, and what is this disappearance?
Manifestation is indeed appearance; what then is this disappearance? If it is argued that manifestation is appearance and disappearance is the absence of that [appearance], then:
This individuality is the nature of being perceptible;
its absence is non-perception, which is concealment.
Now, if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has an established nature, its non-perception cannot be asserted;
however, if it is unestablished, then its very non-existence would be its arising, and thus there is no establishment of *pradhāna*.
Furthermore, if jars and other such things, though previously unperceived, remain exactly as they were, what is the use of *pradhāna*?
If it is argued that, by virtue of being conceptualized as causes, pleasure and so forth are themselves the primary [nature] of these [elements], we say no.

Furthermore, since pleasure and the other [feelings] are perceived as distinct through their different forms, and since they appear as distinct and are grasped by the mind, how could they be non-different?
Moreover...

If external objects such as blue and so forth were themselves pleasure and the like, then since there is no difference in those external objects, there would be no gradation in cognition based on the gradation of cultivation, nor would there be a gradation in pleasure and pain. (271) If pleasure and the like were indeed external forms such as blue and so forth...

In that case, there would be no possibility of specific variations such as joy or distress arising from specific variations in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), just as there are with blue and other [colors].
Indeed, it is not observed that the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth varies according to specific variations in mental cultivation.

If that were so, then everything—both internal and external—would follow the sequence of mental cultivation; thus, it would follow that the entire world is merely unreal, produced by the power of mental cultivation.
Furthermore, if pleasure and so forth were external, there would be the undesirable consequence of their appearing as external forms; if it is argued that this is an illusion, we say no.

If even cognition, which consists of pleasure and so forth, is not contradicted because no cause for error is seen and because it is not sublated, then how can this external object now be understood to consist of pleasure and so forth? (272)
This may be the intended meaning:
just as sound and the other objects have the nature of being transformations of the *pradhāna*, so too does the intellect (*buddhi*);
therefore, when the self experiences pleasure and so forth in the form of the intellect, there is necessarily an experience of that which is not external in form.

Due to the gradation in cultivation, there is a gradation in the intellect; consequently, pleasure and the other qualities also possess a gradation by virtue of having that [intellect] as their essence.
For what is called "cultivation" is that which is set in motion by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind (*manas*), and that ego-sense [manifests] as "I" within the intellect (*buddhi*).
Since the mind (*manas*) consists of volition (*saṅkalpa*), there is repeated cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that very volitional mind; from that arises the intellect (*buddhi*).
When the intellect—being dependent upon the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—attains the nature of pleasure, it manifests in that way.
If this is so, how is it understood that pleasure and the like have external forms?

Nor is the argument—that external objects such as sound and so forth are likewise transformations of the *pradhāna*—a coherent resolution. From what source has this [conclusion] arisen? [The answer is: "These [objects], such as sound, arise from the transformation of the *pradhāna*; there is no observation of their being permeated by its nature.

(525) If it were established by valid cognition that sound and the rest possess the same permeation of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth as the intellect (*buddhi*), then people living in the world would recognize that the effect is permeated by its cause, and thus know that they are produced by such a cause. However, this is not the case.
If it is argued that the determination [of the object] is made in such a way precisely because of the transformation of the primary cause (pradhāna) into the forms of pleasure and so forth,
this results in nothing but mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayaṇa);
for it is as follows:

If its being a transformation of the *pradhāna* were known, then it would possess the nature of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. From the thorough knowledge of its nature as pleasure and so forth, there would be the ascertainment of the reality of sound and the rest.
(Verse 526) If sound and the rest were transformations of the *pradhāna*, they would be conjoined with pleasure and so forth.

And if that conjunction with pleasure and so forth were ascertained, then [their] nature as a transformation of the *pradhāna* would follow; thus, if one is not established, neither of the two is established.
Furthermore, even if smoke were indeed of the nature of a transformation of fire, how could its luminosity be established?
If it is argued that this is not so because it is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*), [we reply: no.

This might be the case regarding sound and the other [objects] if sound and so forth were not of the nature of pleasure; for there could be no cognition that apprehends them, since it is impossible for two things of different classes to stand in the relation of apprehender and apprehended.

To this it is replied: If [the distinction] were due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper between two things of different classes, then the person would not be a grasper of anything at all; consequently, his status as an enjoyer would be lost. (273)

If it is argued: "The person (*puruṣa*) is not of the same genus as sound and so forth, because he does not consist of the primary nature (*pradhāna*), whereas pleasure and the like do; therefore, let it be that he is not a grasper."
For it would follow that there is no enjoyer,
whereas the Puruṣa is indeed accepted as the enjoyer.
Nor is there any state of being an enjoyer other than experience;
by this, the relationship between cause and effect has been refuted.
Why?
Since the relationship of grasped and grasper does not exist in cause and effect, that [relationship] would have to exist elsewhere as well, even where there is existence. || 254 ||
Since the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject exists precisely in the pleasure derived from cognition, words, and so forth—
because an object such as blue is the apprehended object by generating a cognition through the imparting of its own form, and not otherwise, since there would be no relationship of cause and effect—
the relationship of cause and effect is established solely through that very status of being the apprehended object.
And that state of being an object of apprehension, which bestows the status of being an effect upon a person in relation to sounds and so forth,
would likewise exist for those [sounds] in their capacity as effects; thus, it is not the case [that they are always objects], and therefore there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

Alternatively, he states that the relationship of cause and effect is refuted by this [argument] because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*): "Because the relationship of grasped and grasper exists between cognition and pleasure, which are not cause and effect;
for wherever there is a relationship of grasped and grasper, there is no relationship of cause and effect."
Just as in the case of the word "puruṣa" and pleasure,
if the causal relationship between cognition, pleasure, and so forth arises solely from the status of being the grasped and the grasper,
then that very causal relationship must be based on that [status].
This being the case, it would follow that even the self (*pums*) is an effect; this is undesirable, or else [the reason] is inconclusive for that very same reason.

Alternatively, cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are not cause and effect because they lack the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject (*grāhyagrāhakatā*); or, if such a relationship did exist, it would have to exist elsewhere as well.
Therefore, they are indeed internal; and since they are objects of cognition, how could they be insentient?
That which is not of a certain nature cannot be the cognition of that [nature].

(275) Because there is no means of valid cognition for its externality, and because it is experienced precisely as internal, an object is accepted exactly as it is cognized. Without cognition, there is no determination of the existence of entities. (527)
For that which is not the cognition of a form cannot be its perception;
nor is the perception of pleasure and so forth conformable to external form, because it would then follow that the cognition is one thing and the object another, which is not logical.
For it is not logical that there should be a cognition of blue as "of yellow";
likewise, when consciousness proceeds by way of being self-cognizing in nature, it cognizes only its own self-cognizing nature.
Indeed, pleasure and other such states, when perceived by another [subject], are not what is being cognized [by that other].

Form and the other [objects], however, are perceived by means of the eye and so forth, and thus they do not possess the nature of being self-cognized; or rather, they are not apprehended without a form. Since pleasure and the like are perceived precisely through the form of pleasure, the fact that consciousness possesses the form of pleasure is established.
It is thereby proven that the pleasure contained within that [consciousness] is of the very nature of cognition (*bodha*).
In that case, pleasure and so forth would also be external, just like jars and the like.
This is not tenable;

for although the form of a jar and so forth is of the very nature of consciousness, it arises through the influence of something else, since no operation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is perceived therein.
Because the aspect of pleasure and so forth is enhanced through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it does not depend upon external conditioning.

Now, even if they depend on cultivation, pleasure and so forth do not possess the nature of consciousness (*saṃvedana*), because they are experienced by an experience that does not have that [consciousness] as its intrinsic nature;
for even when enhanced through cultivation, pleasure and so forth do not become the nature of consciousness.
To this it is replied:

if experience, which does not possess that [pleasure's] nature, were to apprehend those mental states [such as pleasure], then—given that self-awareness exists—pleasure and the like would have the nature of consciousness; they could not [be known] by another self that lacks their own form.
Therefore, one perceives the effect as present.
Even that [cognition] does not become the effect of the person, because it would have to be an effect by virtue of having arisen with the form of that [person];
yet such is not the case, because that [cognition] does not possess the form of that [person].

For pleasure and so forth, whether they are internal to cognition or are the experience itself, possess a nature other than that [of the cognition]. Therefore, due to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), there arises the conceit of identity between the awareness and the cognition.
Apart from this awareness—which consists of the forms of perception and memory—what else could "cognition" be here? (276)
What is this cognition? What is this determination? What is this consciousness?

[Objection: Experience—surely this is said only when there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference; [for otherwise] "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) and "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) would be mere synonyms.
If it is argued that cognition consists of the non-perception of the form of the object,
while the perception of the formless is the nature of consciousness— then there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this claim that perception is formless.
If it is argued that because consciousness is not perceived, there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:
there is no valid cognition for the claim that "there is a perception of the formless"; if it is argued that because consciousness is not perceived, there is an absence of valid cognition, [we reply:
no.
Since an admission [of a premise] cannot serve as a reason—
given that even inference does not occur in the absence of perception— an admission itself is therefore not tenable.
If it is argued that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of not experiencing pleasure and so forth in the absence of another [subsequent] cognition,

then what contradiction is there in their being experienced through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? Since all practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is accomplished by that alone, another [cognition] is useless.
Furthermore, it might be argued:

"If consciousness is not admitted to exist in another [state], then in the state of liberation, how could one who is devoid of pleasure and pain be liberated? For if its own nature were abandoned, it would follow that the substratum itself is destroyed. (528)
For one's own self cannot be abandoned;

however, pleasure and the like—which are distinct [from the self] and have been made objects of the superimposition of identity—are merely words that can be abandoned, even if they are currently perceived as non-different from the self in the present state.
Even if this were desired, it is nonetheless not established, because it is not proven by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is not the case that "what is desired by me does not succeed," because an object lacks validity when its existence is merely a matter of established dogma; nor do causes conform to one's desires,
and there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever here to establish that such a cause exists for this object.

Since even at this very moment, upon the attainment of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), a reduction of the afflictions (kleśa) is observed, it is simply another cognition of that same nature which arises now; however, there is no apprehension of a difference [of essence] from the cognition of pleasure and so forth.
The same applies to the state of liberation; thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore,
by depending upon various such objects, there is the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
One [of these] is seen as manifesting, while the other remains unperceived within.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is a distinction [between them] precisely because of the difference in designation, such as "cognition," "pleasure," and "pain"? Otherwise, how could there be a difference in designation without a difference in the object?
No.
This is indeed one [reality], which we perceive as manifesting in various forms such as joy, sorrow,
and so forth; let whatever designations you wish be applied to it,
for the designation of difference is solely for the purpose of indicating the distinction between its states.
If, due to conjunction, there were no distinction [between entities], as in the case of the designations "seed," "sprout," "leaf," and "stalk"— or like a fire-ball and its fire—
then the established distinction between difference and non-difference would be destroyed in all things. (278)

[Objection: If it is argued that "this pair is conjoined" is merely postulated—even without a means of valid cognition—on the grounds that "if such a thing were seen, there would be an example"; [Response: ...

That being the case, there would be no establishment of oneness in pillars and the like, which are perceived everywhere as having a single form; and if oneness is not established, then neither is multiplicity—defined as the aggregate of those [unites]—established. Thus, the entire system of entities would collapse, because an entity cannot exist apart from being either one or many.

For thus, if sensation were unitary and undivided, that which is not so would be established as possessing division; since this [unitariness] is not proven, the proof for division is not established. (276)
Therefore, when one is not established, both are unestablished; thus, it is logical for the Sāṃkhya that there is only a single cognition, whereas from its opposite, there is multiplicity.
"If the cognitions of suffering and so forth, which have distinct appearances, were non-distinct, or if the cognitions of the Buddha,
which have a non-distinct appearance, were distinct, then upon what would distinction and non-distinction depend? (Verse 280)— this is an intermediate verse.

Furthermore, it might be argued that just as no mutual distinction is perceived among mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and volition (*cetanā*), which belong to the category of "great ground" (*mahābhūmika*) factors,
or even if a distinction is not observed, a distinction is nevertheless asserted; [so it may be here].

Likewise, why is it not accepted that cognition (*buddhi*) and awareness (*samvedana*) also constitute a single, non-differentiated experience? Furthermore, [the argument] that these are merely adjuncts to the mind (*citta*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
To this, the following is said:

Since a distinction is sometimes perceived even within a stream that is otherwise obscured by its intensity, the established distinction between the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) is proven.
The distinction between mental states is not accepted in this way, because of the statement that "mental factors are not other than the mind."
This is a response granted for the sake of argument (*abhyupagamya-parihāra*):

even if consciousness and the like, being obscured by another [feeling] that functions more intensely, are not at that time objects of intense perception, they nevertheless become objects of perception at other times; thus, consciousness and the like are indeed distinct from feeling and the rest, because they are perceived in their own specific nature at other times.
At that time, the cluster of stars was as if its power of self-illumination had been eclipsed by the multitude of suns;
yet, there is no such clear apprehension of a distinction between cognition and the object of cognition at any time,
whereas for mental states, there is sometimes the apprehension of something that has become manifest.
Is it not the case that the grasping of signs and so forth is perceived only in conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) and not in non-conceptual [cognition]?
Even there, mental factors (*caitasika*) certainly exist.

For instance, sometimes immediately after an experience there arises a conceptualization of the objective sign (*nimitta-vikalpa*), and sometimes there arises a conceptualization such as "I shall do this" and so forth; therefore,
it is established from these conceptualizations that follow upon experience that these [mental factors] are also non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).

Therefore, not even a trace of a logical argument for the distinction between these two exists; this applies neither to cognition (*buddhi*) nor to self-awareness (*samvedana*). This is the ultimate truth.
(4) Yogic perception.
The knowledge of yogis previously mentioned— consisting of meditative cultivation, with the web of conceptual construction shaken off— appears clearly to them.
The knowledge of yogis concerning the four noble truths was mentioned earlier.
From what cause does that arise? He says:
it consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), has cultivation as its cause, and through the power of cultivation it possesses a clear appearance;
precisely because it possesses a clear appearance, it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).
Therefore, since it arises through the power of an object that is directly present, it is logical that [perception] has a present object as its domain and is non-conceptual;
but how can there be non-conceptuality for that which has a past or future object, or for that which has a non-existent object, based on mere mental cultivation?
He shows that meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is likewise capable of producing a real effect, even with respect to an object that does not exist:
"For indeed, those who are afflicted by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and so forth..."
They perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.
For a cognition whose object is non-existent does not arise through the causal efficiency of an external thing;
nor is that [cognition] conceptual, because it perceives [the object] as being present before one.

And likewise, if it is argued that perception is non-conceptual because it is of the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), yet even when it is conceptual it is still non-conceptual insofar as its manifestation is clear (*spaṣṭābha*),
that is not so.
For one who is bound by conceptual construction, the appearance of a clear object is not remembered even in a dream; that [dream-cognition] is a memory and does not possess such an object.
It has been established that the very nature of conceptual construction is to have an imperceptible object.

And if that [external object] did not exist, then there would be no conceptual construction at all; for even in dreams, conceptual constructions are experienced as having the forms of objects that are beyond direct perception.
Nor are those [cognitions] clearly manifest; for if clarity were due to the power of a distortion (*viplava*), then nothing in dreams and the like would be unclear.

Yet, in dreams, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) in the form of memories of previously experienced objects are observed. Therefore, even for a conceptual construction, clarity does not arise from distortion;
consequently, only a non-conceptual cognition possesses a perfectly clear form.
On this point, the Vaibhāṣikas say:

"Is it not the case that when an object is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that there arises a clear appearance through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); for when the turbidity of ignorance is removed by cultivation, the object manifests in its own true form?"
But since it does not exist, how can there be an appearance of its own nature?
As for the knowledge of yogins regarding past and future objects, that is because the past and future do exist [for them]. To this, he says:
Even though it is unreal, the meditation on the foul, the earth-totality, and so forth, appears clearly and non-conceptually, being produced by the power of cultivation.
(285) Because the meditations on the foul and so forth involve mental attention to what is not reality, there is no actual existence of earth and the other elements in space.
Now, earth and the other elements do exist, because they are perceived through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis.
A yogi does not become such merely through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*);

rather, having grasped objects through knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*) and having established them through reasoning derived from reflection (*yukticintāmaya*), he cultivates them. Upon the completion of that cultivation, that which has an unerring object is itself a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is for this reason that yogis are so designated.
And likewise, regarding the statement that "yoga" is the path that proceeds by yoking together calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*):

although these [objects] appear to yogins in that context, nevertheless, for the sake of the task at hand, this cultivation is of a non-real nature; therefore, they appear to them precisely as having a non-real form. Consequently, if they appear to yogins as having a non-real form, how could there be existence [of those objects] on that basis?

Therefore, even for those things that appear in the cognition of a yogi, their nature is simply non-reality; for reality does not arise from mere appearance, but rather from critical investigation (*parīkṣā*).

Furthermore, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that attains its rise through mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not the cause for the realization of reality; rather, it is only that which is brought about by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is so—this is the definitive conclusion.
For it is said that what is produced by mere mental cultivation is not the ultimate reality; however, the determination of a real entity is desired from the cognition of the actual thing itself.
But [that which arises] from mere mental cultivation...

Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon results in a clear, non-conceptual cognition once the cultivation is perfected. For it is not only that which is real which is cultivated, since even other things can be the object of cultivation.

Therefore, if whatever is being meditated upon results in a clear and non-conceptual cognition at the completion of that meditation— that is indeed the fruit of the meditation; for no other kind of result is seen to arise from meditation.

In that regard, that which accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādi*)—like an object previously determined—is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) born from cultivation (*bhāvanāja*); all others are distortions (*upaplava*).

Indeed, even when produced by the power of cultivation, only that direct perception which possesses non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) regarding objects previously determined—such as the next world, the Four Noble Truths, and so forth—is [valid].
But that [cognition] which has desire and so forth as its object is indeed a distortion (*upaplava*), because it appears with such vivid clarity even though it is non-conceptual;
by this, it is established that cognitions such as those in dreams, which are non-corresponding, are not perception at all.

But surely, if it is argued that knowledge is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then it follows as a logical consequence that the direct perception of all non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*) would also be [valid];
for it cannot be said that they lack such cultivation,
as is indeed the case.

"Whatever object is common to the world might belong to someone; does such a restriction exist that does not overstep logic? (530) Therefore, why is it that for those other teachers as well, the multitudes of categories included within their own systems—which are established by perception arising from meditative cultivation—do not exist?
Consequently, one should also proceed according to their instruction."
If it is argued that [the Veda] is not [authoritative] because it is sublated by inference and other means of knowledge, we say no;
for those who perceive with the prophetic eye (*ārṣa-cakṣus*) entities that are beyond the senses and imperceptible, their word is not sublated by inference. (531)
Now, if it is not known by them that "this was seen by them," then if they see it, this statement is not contradicted; likewise,
from what [source] is it known that even the Blessed One realized the Truths and so forth?
That is incorrect;

for in the word of the Tathāgata, correspondence with valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃvāda*) is observed, whereas others are contradicted by valid cognition. Therefore, the Tathāgata is the seer [of reality].
[Objection: But surely human testimony is not a valid means of knowledge regarding objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya-artha*).

How then can there be the sublation or establishment of an object beyond the senses by that [means of knowledge], since the status of the sublated and the sublator is established only when they have the same object? And regarding that which is beyond the senses, no means of valid cognition belonging to those in the cycle of existence functions.
Even by the knowledge of a yogin, there is only the sublation of those [objects].
For indeed,

since the word of the Tathāgata is established in contradiction to them, it would reveal that their words are sublated by the cognition of the reasons [stated] therein. This same [argument] applies equally even in the case of the opposite.
That is incorrect,
because if the Veda were to speak solely of supersensuous matters, no wise person whatsoever would act on its word. (535)

For indeed, words concerning supersensuous objects exist for everyone, yet they are mutually contradictory; therefore, one should not apply oneself to them. If it is argued that, consequently, when demonstrating something to another, only those things that can be determined by others should be demonstrated, because [otherwise] it would be impossible— [The verse continues: 536. Therefore, one who intends to instruct another must demonstrate only that which is capable of being ascertained by others; otherwise, it is impossible. If this is the objection:
It must be considered how even the knowledge of a yogi could possibly exist in that regard:

"Either the Veda is established by its own nature, or the yogi is its proponent. If this is the conclusion, then what means of valid cognition (*pramā*) is there regarding the existence of such a thing? (537) Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that for those seeking [liberation], the determination of words is not to be adopted; for the cessation of suffering is not something secondary. (538)
Indeed, the removal of all suffering is certainly not something that should not be pursued;

for it is through the obsession with grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that living beings encounter suffering. When that [grasping] is removed, there arises the dissolution of all sufferings. (539)

If even among pleasures, the supreme pleasure is simply the absence of suffering, and if one remains always experiencing that which is the opposite of suffering, then what other [state] could be more logically worthy of being accepted as supreme? If it is argued that this is like the extinction of a lamp, we say no, for that lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
This...

Since knowledge cannot be severed by means of burning, cutting, or other such methods, it therefore remains undisturbed due to the non-interruption of its continuity. (542) For one who has reached that state, aversion arises through discernment; if there is aversion toward that which is loathsome, what contradiction is there? (543)
For one who perceives equanimity, what cause could there be for aversion? For him, who abides in the power of meditative concentration, nothing causes affliction.

(544) Because hunger, suffering, and the like are mastered through concentration, everything is experienced [as such]. Therefore, even the pain of weapons and other harms is entirely experienced by him as that very same thing.

(545) Everything—heroism, fortitude, and so forth—is possible through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Indeed, without steadfastness (*dhṛti*), food does not lead to the nourishment of anyone. (546)

However, for anyone who, through the practice of concentration (*dhṛti*), [attains this] even without nourishing themselves with food, there is the possibility of attaining this goal by means other than that [ordinary path].
(547) The cognition of past lives and so forth arises precisely from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*); from that comes knowledge of the fruits of karma, and from that, the perception of everything.
(548) When the relationship between cause and effect has been specifically ascertained, his knowledge of the past and future will clearly manifest. (549)
If it is argued that knowledge arises even for outsiders through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), we accept this; however, for the Protectors (*tāyin*), it possesses all aspects (*sarvākāra*).

(550) The realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth is stable and immediate for those who have cultivated it; such realization does not exist for the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthya*) because they are agitated by passion and other afflictions.
(551) The comprehension of the author of such words regarding reality is like his knowledge itself; there is no perfectly pure speech without one who possesses perfectly pure knowledge. (552)

If this proliferation of [erroneous] views arises from the recollection of one's own reasoning, then even the knowledge resulting from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) would have a real object; for there is no lack of respect [for that]. (553) Therefore, when he is free from passion (*vītarāga*), the possibility of knowing all objects exists; it is certain that everything appears to one who is in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
(554) Why does this not occur for all those who are free from passion? For they apply their effort solely toward the destruction of passion and the like. (555)

Upon the cessation of that [state], for those who still harbor the conceit of a self and have not yet achieved their goal, there is no further effort whatsoever at that time, due to their desire for the pleasure of rest.
(556) However, at another time, for those who have developed a longing for the qualities of an omniscient one, the attainment of omniscience is unimpeded through slight effort.
(557) If it is argued that this is like the extinction of a lamp, that is not possible; for how could detachment arise in a self that is already free from afflictions? (558)
If one who acts with foresight desires that [pleasure] to an excessive degree, does he not thereby incur a loss?
(559) For one free from passion, there is no pleasure born from embracing a woman; for one free from hatred, how could there be pleasure born from crushing an enemy's army?
(560) For one free from delusion, there is no pleasure born from attachment to what is "one's own. Therefore, what use would such [pleasures] be to those seeking liberation? (561)

Therefore, consider this: such things as the drinking of liquor are likewise unreal. O twice-born ones, there is no constant happiness in the drinking of liquor or similar acts. (562) There is no happiness in eating excrement for those born as elephants or boars; nor is there any happiness in the acquisition of raw meat for those who are not protectors. (563) What happiness from a master’s favor can exist for one who is not a servant? What happiness from being struck on the head can be revealed for one who is not a slave? (564)
Thus, all this that has been sought is found among those with resolute faith; even the union with the hips of one's mother and others does not occur in the land of Aparasīka.

And for one who has not reached the Avīci hell, there is never the happiness of being separated from it; therefore, all such things as falling into hell would be desired by living beings. If, however, a superior happiness is desired, then in that case, exactly what we ourselves have sought has arrived.

Now, he explains how the knowledge of everything is possible, how there can be consistency in that regard, and how, in the case of knowing everything, faults such as passion and so forth would arise from the direct perception of the minds of others—including their passions and the like:
"Because of the existence of manifold means, through the application of an extensive period of time, and by virtue of practice, his attainment of omniscience is logical. (567)
For indeed, what is there that cannot be attained through practice over incalculable aeons? Furthermore, it is accepted by us that there is no correspondence regarding the cognition of everything;
and thus it has been said:
Who, not being all-knowing, could possibly perceive you, the All-Knowing One? Homage be to you, whose vast majesty is known by yourself alone.
For one who is not omniscient cannot know the Omniscient One. (568)
"O monks, let no person judge another person—
whether it be myself or anyone else of a different kind.

For even if one were to know everything through every aspect of one's own being, the claim that one possesses passion and so forth simply by knowing the passion and so forth in the mental continuum of another is not tenable."
For instance,
when there is cognition of another's mental continuum, it is utterly impossible to say that even while perceiving his state of being free from passion, he also possesses passion;
for at the very moment he perceives another’s passion, he likewise perceives another’s freedom from passion and is himself free from passion.
If it is argued that both [the object and the cognition] exist at that very time, we say no;

for if there is an absence of experience even by a single one of them, how can passion be attributed [to the subject]? Indeed, for a neutral observer, the occurrence of passion and the like is impossible.
For instance, when a jar is perceived, it does not become part of the perceiver;
likewise, even passions (*rāga*) and so forth, when belonging to another mental continuum and being apprehended from a distance, do not produce passion in the observer.
On the other hand, if they were perceived in their entirety—such that the observer experiences them exactly as the subject themselves does—then there would be no loss of his own state of passion.
That is incorrect;
for if it were cognizable by its very nature as that [object], and passion were possible in itself, then the cognition of another's passion and so forth could not be established in any way.
Indeed, there is no cognition of another's passion and so forth without its entering into the nature of that [cognition].
If it is argued that "this very [attachment] is one's own," this too is another fault;
for it is thus:

If it were known as something standing apart [from the self], there would be no cognition of it as such; but if it were known as being of the nature of that [self], then it would follow that one is indeed subject to passion.
This is incorrect, for as follows:

The transformation of speech and body caused by the passion (rāga) and so forth residing in another does not at all belong to him; for his own latent impression (vāsanā) of passion and so forth does not exist [in him]. Indeed, it is passion arising from the power of one's own latent impressions that brings about the state of being impassioned, and not that which arises from the force of another’s impressions, since it is experienced as being present only in the perfected one (siddha). Now, if there is awareness of its own nature, why does he not experience bodily transformations such as horripilation, as well as a transformation of speech?
This is not the case;
this transformation of body and speech arises from the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). For one whose predispositions have been abandoned, neither of these two occurs.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the knowledge of another's mind arises solely from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that cultivation is indeed a formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*)?

In that case, since the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is possible, how could there be no latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)? For there is no distinction whatsoever between the cultivation and its latent predisposition;
this [objection] is not tenable, as follows:

When a specific indicative mark is characterized through its intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is an appearance of the particular; this is as in the cognition of another's mind. For in that case, it is the operation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that characterizes the specific indicative mark, and not the cultivation of the object to be known.
Or, even if it exists, because it is not connected to the self, there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding it; thus, there is no passion even when it appears.
By this, the objection regarding the experience of impure flavors and the like is also refuted.

If there were perception of this [object] by means of a sense organ, there would be a connection with impurity; however, this is not caused by another [organ] born of karma, but rather by that which arises through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because perception is produced by generating a gustatory organ through the power of mental cultivation, then there would likewise be no fault in sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman (*agamyā*) during a dream.

If it is argued that there is no fault because of its unreality, how can there be unreality when there is correspondence [with reality]? When even a mother’s dream is of such a nature, then why would the fault of approaching an unapproachable woman not be possible for you? (577)

If it is asked: "Therefore, since the ultimate [object] is non-existent, how can there be a gradual cognition of a beginningless entity?"—it is not so, because all objects are cognized simultaneously. (578) Just as the entire meaning of a treatise, when well-practiced, appears in the mind in a single moment, so too is the cognition of the infinite and beginningless [reality]. (579)

If it is argued that just as the meaning of a treatise appears in the mind in a single moment through thorough practice, so too does beginningless and endless cognition [appear] because the treatise has a finite measure;
If it is argued that although there is no appearance of [the object] as having a limited magnitude, nevertheless, through repeated practice,
that entire subject matter of the treatise appears, and thus it appears in memory— [we reply: no.

Since even that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*) appears as the meaning of the scripture, one might object: "The meaning of a scripture consists of mutually connected elements; in that case, another element also appears through some cause of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), but this is not so for things that are beginningless and endless. Therefore, how can there be an appearance of the unprecedented? To this we reply: everything is equal in this regard; for instance: [The text continues: ...the connection between words and their meanings is established by convention (*samaya*). Although the relationship between words and meanings is beginningless, it is nevertheless determined by the intention of the speaker (*vivakṣā*). Just as a single word, such as "cow," brings to mind various objects like a cow, a jar, or a cloth depending on the speaker's intention, so too does the meaning of a sentence appear according to the speaker's intention. Furthermore, because the relationship between words and meanings is beginningless, it is not possible to determine a specific sequence among them through any other means of knowledge. Therefore, the appearance of the unprecedented is indeed possible. Thus, the meaning of a sentence is understood through the power of the sentence itself, and not merely through the individual words. Consequently, the unprecedented is indeed manifested. This is the conclusion.

There exists no proximity (*pratyāsatti*) among things that is not inseparable from the relation of cause and effect; is this [proximity] not likewise present even in linguistic usage? For the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between things is what constitutes proximity in the treatises, and from that [relation] arises the manifestation of the preceding [cause];
thus, it is the same in linguistic usage as well.
For instance, this is indeed its transformation; it must have such a cause,
and that cause is the indirect generator of these many effects.
One who knows the minds of others perceives whether such prior conditions for this [person] exist or do not exist, by virtue of which there are no auxiliary causes for him.
(581) And through the knowledge of previous births and so forth, he knows everything in its entirety as it is interconnected through a continuous succession; thus, he knows even other eons.
(582) Through the knowledge of the causal relationship between one eon and the arising of another eon, he knows the reality of the entire world and its intermediate state. (583)

Thus, having set aside all [other] systems of reasoning, the knowledge of all categories of existence has been demonstrated here; may that which follows the [correct] system be easily scrutinized by others.
Thus ends the first section (folios 308) of the Tibetan translation.
(7) [Section 5: An Investigation into Fallacious Perception.

If a cognition possessing a clear aspect through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then conceptual cognition would not be a valid means of knowledge, because it lacks a clear aspect.
If it is maintained that an object has an indistinct form [in the case of doubt], and is not otherwise a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then let it be accepted that this is also the case with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*).
The nature [of the cognition] itself has a clear form, whereas the object does not;

therefore, with respect to its own nature, that [cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), while with respect to the object, it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Thus, there is recollection of the object, and with respect to its own nature, it is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
How is this so?
[Because it is said that] "it is non-erroneous with respect to its own nature, but erroneous with respect to the object.
This is because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not cognizable by anything other than itself.
However, the sublation of the cognition of another form occurs because that [form] is cognized differently by another cognition; therefore, it is an error.
For recollection of its own nature is impossible, since that [recollection] arises at that very time and because [the object] is being directly experienced.
If its own nature (svarūpa) also existed previously but does not exist now, then there could be no memory at present;
yet if memory occurs now by means of that very [nature], then it follows that even a dead cock would have to crow.
Therefore, he said:
Thus begins the second section:
even conceptual construction is admitted to exist within self-awareness, but not with respect to an external object, because that would involve conceptualization.
Because the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is free from conceptual construction and because it is not established as being remote,
its apprehension by that very [nature] entails the possibility of direct perception;
for this very reason, cognition is said to be perception (pratyakṣa).
Since conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is that cognition which apprehends a word-meaning with respect to an object,
and since the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is not a word-meaning, it follows that all [cognition] therein is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (288)
The intrinsic nature of both the conceptual and its opposite is neither the referent of a word, nor a universal, nor an object of ultimate reality;

for if that were the case, there would be no application of words and no connection with universals. Thus, a cognition that grasps the referent of a word without conceptualization [is not conceptual], whereas a cognition that possesses the application of words and the connection with universals is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Therefore, why does the unmanifest not appear clearly?
Since it is indeed clear, why is it said that it is not so?
Because it abandons that form, it is described as "unclear. Let it be understood how there can be an abandonment of one's own nature (*svarūpa*).
Indeed, it is impossible to abandon one's own nature; for it has been stated that if that were abandoned, there would be no cognition at all.
And thus, since there would be neither self-awareness nor awareness of another, there would be a total absence [of cognition];
nor, if it is argued that awareness occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), is there self-awareness.

The nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) must also be apprehended by means of direct cognition itself; if there were another presumptive testimony for this [cognition], that too would require another, leading to an infinite regress. Since the cognition of the object is already established, what is the use of presumptive testimony regarding that cognition of the object?
If it is argued that when the object is established, the cognition of the object is not yet established, then what is this "establishment" of the object?
If it is its production, then there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing all objects simultaneously.
Now, if it means "knowledge of the object," then this is the meaning:
"the cognition of the knowledge of the object from the knowledge of the object"—this is a clever way of speaking.
Or, if it means "making known by means of the object," then it is "the cognition of the knowledge of the object."
What is this "knowability" of the object?
If it is its appearing within cognition, then how can that appearance within cognition be known— whether when the cognition itself is unknown or when it is already known?

If it is argued that an object which appears is indeed perceptible, then let its establishment as perceptible be exactly so; what is the use of postulating another object? This very perception would be impossible otherwise, if perception were not cognition.

If it is argued that this [perception] occurs when the eye is active and not otherwise, and therefore cognition arising from the operation of the ear and other senses is perception— then what is this "operation of the ear and other senses"?
If it is argued that "it is knowledge," then how is that knowledge known if it is indirect?
If it is argued that "knowledge is simply the functioning of the ear and other senses," then...
The functioning of the ear and other senses is perceived; by that, [the existence of] cognition is known. But how so?
If you ask, "Otherwise, what would be the purpose of the manifestation of the ear and other senses? we reply: Do entities come into being in dependence upon your own purposes?
The existence of entities arises solely from their causes, not from a purpose. Otherwise, for you, there would be no existence at all without a purpose.
(587) Even if [the object] were not present before the ear or other senses, what does that matter to cognition?
If cognition had not arisen, the object would simply remain beyond perception.
If cognition has arisen, what has happened to the object? Even so, it would remain only indirect (*parokṣa*),
for there is no such thing as the directness (*pratyakṣatā*) of a cognition, since that would entail the consequence of [the cognition itself] being indirect.
Since it is beyond the range of perception,
if it is indeed seen,
let it be exactly as it is seen.
If it is asked, "How is that so for you as well?"—
the answer is that the "knownness" (*jñātatva*) of an object consists in the cognition having the form of that object;
and this [knownness] is accessible through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), not through another cognition possessing that same form, which would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, it is logical that self-awareness alone is the means of establishing the nature of cognition;

for if, then, even dream-cognition— which is a perception arising with clarity through the power of mental cultivation— is attained as a perception, non-contradiction is indeed present there as well, since one actually reaches the places visited in the dream.

This is not so, because that which is erroneous, conventional, conceptual, inferential, derived from inference, mnemonic, or aspirational— along with that accompanied by cataracts— is pseudo-perception. (588)
Conceptual cognition resembling direct perception is of two kinds,
and furthermore, it is of four kinds; thus he says:

There are four kinds of fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*): three types of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) arising from a disturbance of the basis (*āśrayopaplava*), and one type that is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).
This same [non-conceptual] one is twofold, and through the threefold division of the conceptual, it becomes fourfold.
Perception is free from conceptual construction; therefore, all three types of conceptualization are pseudo-perceptions (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
Among these, erroneous cognition is a pseudo-perception because it functions through the conceptualization of water and so forth regarding a mirage and the like;
it is also a pseudo-perception because, with respect to conventionally real things, it functions through the conceptualization of their form by superimposing something else.
The cognition of inference, its result, and so forth, occurs through the conceptualization of what was previously experienced; therefore, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which appears as a shimmering mass of rays is indeed direct perception itself, whereas the conceptualization of water and such is a semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
Because perception has the form of direct apprehension, even regarding conventionally real objects, perception consists merely in the grasping of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth;

however, in the case of a composite whole (*avayavin*), there is no direct apprehension of it as such, because it is merely a superimposition of previously perceived other qualities, such as touch, upon that which is intended to be its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Alternatively, since no whole (*avayavin*)— conceived through a preceding series of causal conditions (*pratyaya*)— ever appears in perception apart from [its] color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities,
inferential cognition is simply the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The fruit of that [inference] is the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), which does not occur without a prior experience;
and this inferential cognition is in some cases non-perceptual, while in others it is indeed perceptual, as in the case of the apprehension of fire from smoke when it occurs spontaneously.
If it is argued that there is no conceptualization of what was previously experienced, and how can there be comprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*) without conceptualization,
[the answer is] because it is observed to be exactly so.
Indeed, it is not reasonable for what has been seen to be otherwise;
why, then, is there an instruction on the various types of conceptualization?
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of elaborating upon examples:
Not so, because there is no difference in the characteristic;
however, if it were a mere indication of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is not so;
there is another purpose,
for it is thus:

To establish that [the cognition] is not produced by the senses, two [reasons] were stated; because of the observation of error, the statement regarding inference and so forth is for the sake of proving the two preceding ones.
[The opponent's view is: "That is indeed produced by the senses," [as seen] in the case of the cognition of water in a mirage.

For instance, in the definition "perception is cognition produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbalizable and non-erroneous," the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) was made in order to exclude the cognition of water in a mirage.

If, however, that [mirage-cognition] were indeed not produced by a sense-organ, it would have been excluded by the very first word [of the definition]; what, then, would be the purpose of including the term "non-erroneous"?

If it is argued that [the definition] is for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as that of two moons which arise without an object, we say no; for such cognitions are already excluded by the very inclusion of the phrase "contact with an object" (*arthasannikarṣa*).
By the mention of "senses," that which is not produced by the senses is excluded;
however, the claim by others that even that which has a conventionally real object (*saṃvṛtisat*) is produced by the senses is indeed a matter of dispute.
In that case, the statement regarding inference and other means of knowledge would be useless.
For its not being produced by the senses is not established by that [scripture], because the fact of inference and so forth not being produced by the senses is already established.
To this, it is replied:
1. Nyāyasūtra 1.1.1

Even though inference and the like are already established, they are included because they serve as means of proof; for in every case, there is a requirement for an established example. If it is asked: "Why is there a cause for error here such that the two preceding [means] are considered to be what is to be proven (the *sādhya*) by means of what is not yet established? [The answer follows: 589. For that which is unestablished is not proven by that which is unestablished. What is the cause of delusion here [that leads one to think otherwise]? By what [reasoning] could the two former be regarded as the *sādhya*?
He said:

Because it does not exclude [the object] through direct perception when there is conceptual construction that superimposes another object based on linguistic convention, it may at times be a cause of error. (291)
[Objection: There is no dependence on perception for the application of a convention to a whole (*avayavin*), because the mere convention is itself the cause for its establishment.
The water [perceived] as having another object is a superimposition (*samāropa*), an excessive attribution (*adhikādhyāropa*),
a conceptualization (*vikalpana*), and a recollection (*smaraṇa*); for water is indeed recollected because it was previously seen.

In that case, there is not merely superimposition (*āropa*) alone, because perception occurs with equality; or rather, "superimposition" refers to the conceptualization of water as a whole (*avayavin*),
while in both cases, both [superimposition and conceptualization] are present.

And since those superimpositions and conceptual constructions do not at any time cease for perception born of the senses—which is [by nature] non-erroneous regarding what is present—it follows that either this "non-cessation regarding the present" is the cause of error therein, or rather, that very [perception] is the cause of error by virtue of that [non-cessation].
When this cause of error exists, there is an inference by way of an example;
in that very context, there is an alternative reading: "as reality" (*sattyatayā*).
