4. Just as this conceptualization of an imperceptible object, such as memory and so forth, occurs when there is the cessation of direct perception born of the senses, so too does that [cessation] itself [occur].
5. Memory, being of the nature of recollection and dependent upon convention, does not determine an object as if it were a direct perception. || 292 ||
[The mind] determines [the object] within the middle [of its perception], just as [it does] with regard to jars and other things, without [prior] recollection of what was previously experienced.
And one who pursues [the existence of] conditions (pratyaya) falls away from direct perception (pratyakṣa).
For the conceptualization of inference and the like depends upon the apprehension of a relation (sambandha), and that very apprehension of a relation is the convention (samaya);
since the cognition of an imperceptible object arises from that relation, it does not [arise] from direct perception.
For that [recollection] would indeed occur through direct perception;

likewise, in the case of jars and the like, once color and so forth have been apprehended by some single sense organ, there subsequently arises a recollection of taste and so forth based on what preceded.
If it is argued that the recollection occurs only regarding the taste and so forth, and not regarding the whole (avayavin):

If it is argued that the whole (*avayavin*) is the object of the cognition of identity— such as "that which is white is the same as that which is rough"— because it is not perceived apart from [qualities] such as taste and so forth;
For instance, there is first of all no identity between color and touch;
therefore, if there were no whole (avayavin), there would simply be no cognition of unity.
Even if there were a whole, how could there be co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) among color, touch, and so forth?
If it is argued that there is no identity between the two because their identity consists in having a common substratum, this is merely a figurative expression.
Nor can there be an understanding here based on metaphorical usage (*upacāra*); for if it were understood metaphorically, the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) would not be established,
since co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible through metaphor even otherwise.
Because they do not exist in different locations, because they are employed for a single purpose, and because [the one] undergoes modification when the other does, they are designated as being one.
That very location which is perceived for touch is the same as that for color; therefore, there is a determination of their unity.
Whatever is the function of touch—such as the supporting of water and so forth—in that very same function, color also operates.
When touch is rendered smooth, there arises the singularity of form as well;
from that, there occur the linguistic conventions and determinations that "this is indeed one. However, if the substratum were something else entirely, [such conventions would not arise].
One must cultivate the realization of those [parts] through their distinction from form and so forth;
for that which is not perceived, yet meets the conditions for perception, is non-existent.
Now, why is there no mutual disintegration of the parts in the absence of a whole?
Even if a whole (*avayavin*) exists, why is there no disintegration of this triad? Let there also be separation for that [whole] due to the force of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

If it is argued that this is its very nature, then let this be stated from the very beginning: "This is the nature of color and the other [sensory qualities], which arises from its own causes. One should consider: how can this [nature] belong to an eternal inherence?
Even if the whole (*avayavin*) is something distinct, nevertheless, since a triad has arisen, why is there no disintegration of these three from one another?
If you say that inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause of their non-disintegration, then why does that [inherence] itself not disintegrate?
To say that its very nature is such [as not to disintegrate] is no answer.
Let that very nature belong to form and the rest; what is the use of postulating a separate entity?
It is logical that the nature of form and the rest arises from their own causes, but how can there be a nature for *samavāya*, which is itself causeless?
If it is argued that the nature of the substratum of inherence arises from its own cause such that inherence is thus [established],
then what is the use of this succession?
Those things must be produced by their own causes in such a way that inherence would effect their non-disjunction.
Since that very cause is itself the cause for its non-disruption, what is lacking here that a causal chain must be postulated?
If it is argued that "this is seen to be so," let it be so, provided it is actually seen; for it is impossible to conceptualize what is being perceived otherwise.
However, it is only forms and so forth that are perceived as mutually inseparable, and nothing beyond them; therefore, let this very nature be postulated for these [elements] alone.
Consequently, the superimposition of a "whole" (avayavin) is not a matter of direct perception.
Thus, the presentation of the example and the thing exemplified is intended to demonstrate this detailed logical argument.
For what purpose is the inclusion of the term "accompanied by obscurity" (*sataimirika*)?
Someone [objects] that even an observation accompanied by obscurity is conceptual (*savikalpaka*);

therefore, that statement is made for the sake of excluding it. Otherwise, since this too would be included under the category of "recollection" (*smārta*) and so forth, its separate mention would be purposeless.
If it is argued that whatever is non-conceptual is perception because it is free from conceptual construction, [we reply:
not everything that is free from conceptual construction is perception; rather, only that which is free from conceptual construction and is non-erroneous is perception, not everything.

If it is argued that the general rule (*utsarga*) operates only after the scope of the exception (*apavāda*) has been conceptually delineated, such that the exception does not apply where the general rule prevails;
then [we reply]: [this is not so].

The fourth [type] here is an exception; therefore, it was stated that the darkness (*timira*) therein arises solely from an impairment (*upaghāta*). The mention of "darkness" as the fourth [type] among the three kinds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an exception (*apavāda*).

"Free from conceptual construction" is the general definition of perception, while "free from optical defects" is the specific definition that establishes the status of what is merely a semblance of perception;
since a specific rule sets aside a general one,
what is the proof for this case?
Since a general cognition is sublated by a specific cognition,

when an inference based on "the remainder" (śeṣavat) proceeds against the negative instance (vipakṣa) merely because of its lack of prior observation, it does so solely on the basis of its being free from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha). (593)

For one who is excessively attached to that [universal], there is a clear sublation regarding its specific [particularity]. Therefore, the occurrence of that former [universal] is only in what is other than that [specific].
Indeed, an inference based on what is observed generally (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is not sublated by another perception or inference merely because of the non-perception of the counter-example;
therefore, it is established by perception.

The relationship of sublation and sublated between the general and the particular is the same as the relationship of sublation and sublated between the two statements that indicate their respective objects;
if that is so, why did the Teacher state the definition based on inference from general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)?
The Teacher did not intend inference as something specifically observed; however, because its meaning cannot be indicated by a single statement, he did not state it without its exception.

Why, then, was the term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) not used together with the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta)? What is the difference between accepting the "bathing of an elephant" [i.e., stating everything at once] and obtaining the meaning of "non-erroneous" through the exception of the mention of "with cataracts" (sataimira)? Alternatively, what is the distinction?
If it is argued that the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) may be understood immediately [after the mention of direct perception],
we say no,
because there is no distinction [between the two cases].
For it has been indicated by implication that for things which are not identical in meaning, immediate succession is not a cause [of contradiction],

and the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is so that one might understand that such a reason does not necessarily mean that the sublator must occur immediately after.
If it is asked, "Why not simply employ the term 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*)?"—
this is true;
for perception is direct realization (*sākṣātkārin*), and that can indeed be demonstrated by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous."

For [cognition] that does not have the aspect of direct perception is not non-erroneous, because conceptual cognition is erroneous; however, others maintain that even conceptual cognition has the aspect of direct perception and is non-erroneous.
It is with reference to those [others] that these two [points] are stated.
And so it is said in the definition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*): "With respect to the views of others, all [cognitions] are indeed non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
Alternatively:
The entire system of sublation and the sublated depends upon the perspective of the proponent. One who has not yet perceived a sublation first understands [the matter] in a general sense;
he does not know the teacher’s intention that "this specific point is intended here."
Through the observation of a sublation, one subsequently understands that even this [human cognition] possesses a specific qualification;

however, in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) speech, because it lacks a foundation in a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is no relationship of sublated and sublater. In the case of human speech, however, the error of the prior cognition is made known by a subsequent cognition that is rooted in a means of valid cognition.
But it is not from the Veda that erroneous cognition arises;

for if the Veda were a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) in that way, it would follow that everything is likewise [valid], since [the definition] "that which is uncontradicted is indeed a means of valid knowledge" would apply. If this is argued:
If it is argued that even later on, because of the possibility of a sublation,
the object becomes something else when examined through its various aspects, and that the same applies to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
No,
because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stable;
thus, the meaning of the scripture that contradicts the means of valid cognition is abandoned by the proponents of the Veda.
Otherwise, the explanation of [certain passages] as *arthavāda* (eulogistic statements) would be groundless;
therefore, the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) exists only in the case of human speech.
If it is argued that only cataracts (*taimira*) are the sublater and not jaundice (*kāmalā*) and so forth, [we reply:]...
He said: "By that [statement], it was stated that everything [perceived] is produced by an impairment;
however, 'timira' (visual disorder) is merely an illustration of an impairment, not an exclusion of other types of impairments."

For, because it is devoid of an object and because it is not a direct perception, the status of being a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is assigned, thereby negating its status as true perception.

Furthermore, that state of being devoid of an object is not lacking even by a fraction in the cognition of those whose visual power is impaired by the thick coating of jaundice; therefore, it should be understood by those who speak according to logic (*nyāyavādin*) that the inclusion of the term "with cataracts" (*sataimira*) serves as an illustration.
"Timira" (eye-disease) is an illustration indicating all types of impairment;
others, however, maintain that this mention of "being free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is merely a counter-example and not an exception. Thus he says:
Some say that even this [cognition of two moons] is mental; however, their textual authority contradicts this, as it states:
"The sense faculties are also the cause of cognitions such as the blue [color] and the double moon.
This cognition of a double moon and so forth is purely mental, like the cognition of water in a mirage.

For instance, in the case of a mirage, first a sensory cognition arises that is indeed non-erroneous; subsequently, however, due to the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the experience of water, there arises a conceptual cognition of water,
and that awakening occurs solely from the sight of the mirage.
Just as rays of light possess similarity and have such a nature,
so too here, first there is a non-erroneous cognition regarding the moon, and subsequently there is a conceptual construction in the form of two moons;
regarding this, some say:
"The single moon, situated between two fixed eyes, is perceived as if simultaneously on both sides due to the subtlety of time; thus, there is a superimposition of duality upon the two sides.
This [view] contradicts their own texts.
Although atoms are the cause of sensory cognition, because they do not appear [in that cognition], atoms are not its object, just as the sense organs are not.
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 597)
For those very atoms of the eye and other sense organs, existing both in their normal state and otherwise, are the causes for the appearance of things such as two moons or blue;
for if the appearance of two moons were purely mental, it would not be possible to speak of the sense organ as its cause.
However, even if it is mental, it is not contradictory for the sense organ to be its cause through an indirect succession.
It is argued here that the direct causality of the sense organ is contradicted by its being mental in nature within the cognition of a double moon; however,
if it is claimed that the sense organ is a cause through a mediated succession, then [this applies] to the object of sensory cognition.
When this is being investigated, what kind of scope for the mind is there here?
When it is asked, "What is the object-sphere of sensory cognition?
the opponent must state whether sensory cognition arises directly [from that object] by assuming its form, or otherwise.
First of all, it cannot be an object by virtue of having that [perceived] form, because it is impossible for atoms to possess a gross form consisting of a single mass; alternatively,
if it is argued that whatever is the cause of something— even if it does not have that form— is its object.
That too is incorrect.
Even if [the object] is a cause of a cognition with another form—just like the sense faculty—it would not be its object;

for if the Teacher intended that there is causality through a mediated succession, as expressed by the words "for those very [atoms]," then he would not have implied the status of being an object for the sense faculty in relation to the opponent.

Since the opponent has stated that if atoms were the direct cause [of cognition], they would necessarily be its objects, one must say that the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is therefore not tenable;
why then is it asked, "What is the relevance here of the mental [perception]?"
The intention here is as follows:
first, there is the appearance of atoms mutually distinct from one another; however, from conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*), they appear as a dense mass. Thus says the opponent.
The appearance of conceptual cognition as a single,
solid mass has atoms as its object through a causal succession, because atoms are its indirect cause; this is just as memory has the object as its domain.
The Teacher said:
"Because it does not appear as that [external object], its objects are not atoms, unlike the case of the sense organs."
Just as the sense organs, despite being causes through a succession of steps, are not the [direct] object, so too are atoms;
otherwise, the sense organs would indeed be the indirect cause of the cognition of two moons.
Regarding this, it has been said:

When the domain of sensory cognition is being investigated, what occasion is there here for mental [perception]? Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the determination of an object is valid if it is mental, because it would then be objectless;
likewise, it is the Master’s proper reply that "there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever in this case," rather than the objection regarding an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
That very point has been stated by the passage beginning with "the introduction to the mental [cognition]," and so forth.
Others, however, say:

when one explains that the sense organs are the cause even in a mental cognition such as the perception of two moons, then the consideration of "having an object" (*prativiṣayatva*) would apply to the mental [cognition] alone.

Furthermore, the response to the question "What kind of occasion [for inference] is this? has been established as incorrect; for if [the cognition] were sensory, would it not conform to the presence or absence of the sense organs?
If it were similar to that [dream-cognition] and possessed of modification, why is this very [nature] not denied?
(297) If, first of all, this cognition of two moons and so forth were mental, it would not conform to the presence or absence of the sense organ; therefore, [it must be sensory].
Even that which conforms to existence and non-existence is purely mental;

if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence that cognitions of pillars and the like would also be purely mental, since first the cognition has its own form and only subsequently takes on the form of the object in the mind. Furthermore, it would follow that the mind itself is the sense faculty.

If it is argued that even [the cognition] of a sense organ is merely a modification [of the self], then it follows that both [types of cognition] would be produced directly from the sense organs. If this is asserted:
If it is argued that [the cause] must also be known as modified, following this [same logic], because no further modification is observed; 134.
Even that [cognition] would be purely mental; because it is a distortion, it would be like this [other cognition], leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, this very [cognition] must be born from a sense organ, and even when there is a defect in the sense organ, it would be like the illusion of a snake and so forth.
Even when the impairment of the sense organ has ceased, the cessation [of the error] would not occur;
for at some point, it might still be apprehended by verbal expressions in another mental continuum.
Furthermore, it would depend upon the recollection of what was previously seen and would not appear with complete clarity.
If mental cognition of two moons and the like ceases even when there is no impairment of the sense organ—
since the delusion of a snake ceases upon investigation even while the sense organ remains impaired, whereas the delusion of two moons does not—
and if, moreover, the delusion of a snake characterized by its blackness and so forth also does not cease [upon investigation], [then how can it be called mental]?
For in a place of deep darkness, the delusion of a snake occurs; therein, even in the absence of an ocular disorder (*timira*), there is the appearance of blackness and so forth.
But when an ocular disorder is present, even though the eye has become otherwise, there is still the appearance of blackness and so forth.
How could that [appearance] cease even when the defect of the sense organ is removed?
Therefore, cessation is unestablished; how then could it be a means of proof?
As for what might be said—that "it would not cease even when the impairment of the sense organ has ceased"—that too is incorrect.

For even in the mind, the delusion of water is not seen to persist once the sensory disorder has ceased; this is because such a delusion occurs only when there is an awakening cognition characterized by being heated by the sun, and it does not exist in its absence.
Furthermore, the transmission of the delusion of water to another mental continuum has never been observed.

This serpent-like form does not belong to a word that has not been heated [by a defect]; nor does it depend on the recollection of what was previously seen, because its blackness and so forth exist even prior to that.
Furthermore, a vivid appearance belongs indeed even to a mental error, such as in dreams and the like.
"Therefore, it would not appear clearly"—this entire [argument] is incorrect;
for being permeated by the existence of that [cause] and undergoing modification through the modification of that [cause] certainly occurs in the effect, even through a mediated succession.
To this, it is replied:
The appearance of blackness and so forth that occurs therein is indeed sensory; the claim that properties such as non-cessation [of the appearance] belong to it is not a valid response.

For the appearance of blackness and so forth there must necessarily be produced by the senses, since it does not cease when those [sensory organs] do not undergo alteration; moreover, its vividness also exists only when it is produced by the senses, not when it is mental.

If it is argued that through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even for one scorched by the heat of the sun, there is a state of mental perception (*mānasatā*) characterized by extreme clarity, we reply:
since this [mental perception] is non-conceptual (*avikalpikā*) precisely because of its extreme clarity, it does not differ from sensory perception (*indriyajātva*).
Thus, the status of the apprehension of cataracts as an exception (*apavāda*) is not contradicted.
For the opponents intend "conceptual nature" (*savikalpakatva*) because it is mental in nature, not merely "mentalness" (*mānasatvamātra*);
thus, what is to be proven here is simply that [the cognition] is non-conceptual and unitary.

There are two kinds of fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*): conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the distortion of non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpakaviplava*). And that [latter], which is entirely erroneous and conceptual, is what is being refuted here; it is not otherwise. If it is argued, "In that case, let the error of a double moon and so forth, though perfectly clear, be mental," we say no.

Since mental states exist even in the absence of [external] objects, it is through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that a mental state attains clarity; because that [cultivation] is absent, its being produced by the sense organs cannot be prevented.
Indeed, there are only two causes for the manifestation of a clear form: the sense organ (*akṣa*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that even here there exists [an error] mediated by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*) has been abandoned; enough of this digression.
What then is the mental delusion regarding snakes and so forth, and what is the delusion regarding water and so forth, which serve as examples?

The appearance of being harmful or beneficial is indeed the very manifestation of harm and benefit; for this appearance ceases even when there is a defect in the sense organ, yet it does not cease at all for one who reflects upon it even when the impairment of the sense organ has ceased.
In this same way, other cases should also be applied accordingly.
And thus:
Whether for one who is asleep or awake, whatever cognition appears clearly is non-conceptual in both cases; otherwise, it is conceptual.
Whether by virtue of being mental or otherwise, in both cases its non-conceptual nature is established by its clarity; this has been demonstrated.
Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, its validity is refuted because of its lack of correspondence [with reality];
and for that reason, pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is said to be of two kinds.
The Teacher has shown that the nature of pseudo-perception is indeed twofold, by way of being conceptual and being erroneous.

Thus, because of the distinction made by the instrumental case (*karaṇa*), there is a separate mention of the distortion (*viplava*) characterized by *timira* (ophthalmia) due to the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Otherwise, since there would be no purpose for a separate mention, it would result in the implication of a lack of skill [on the part of the author].
How, then, was it said:
"That [cognition] is not [valid], because its object is erroneous (*vyabhicārin*) due to being a locus of delusion (*bhrānti*)"?
This is stated according to the intention of the opponent;
for one who holds the definition that "perception is that which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object," it is established that [the cognition] has the mental error as its object,
since deviation is not possible for that which arises solely from the contact of a sense-organ with its object.

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case where there is conceptualization (*vikalpana*) of something additional by means of the mind (*manas*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4)
But surely, that which arises from the sense-faculty alone even in the absence of an object is also inconstant; why then is it said to be "within the scope of mental error"?
[It is so stated] because, since that [cognition] has been refuted by the very fact of grasping an object, even though it exists, it is as good as non-existent.
And so it has been said:
"In that which arises from the sense-faculties and their objects, there is no possibility of [being] designated and so forth."

It must be understood that [perceptions] such as "the expressible" (vyapadeśya) and so forth are purely mental; for indeed, the qualifiers such as "inexpressible" (avyapadeśya) and so on do not serve to exclude [other types of cognition], but rather are intended to describe its essential nature— that [perception] arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object and is of such a kind, and not otherwise.
It is not [the case that] "having the nature of determination" [is the definition], because it would result in an over-extension;
for that which arises from the contact of sense-organ and object is not exclusively of the nature of determination, since inference also possesses the nature of determination.

Therefore, since that which is of the nature of determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is perception and nothing else, it is logical that [the definition] should consist solely in its differentiating character (*vyāvarttakatā*).

Now, if one were to argue that one part [of the definition] is differentiating while another part is merely a statement of the essential nature (*svarūpa-kathana*), then it would follow that if [cognition] arises from the contact of sense-organ and object and is of the nature of determinate judgment, it is non-erroneous (*avyabhicārin*) and also inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*);
however, this is incorrect, for it is more appropriate to state its non-erroneousness [as the defining characteristic].
For validity is thus established;
but why [is it] not [established] by having as its object that which is inexpressible? For validity exists even otherwise.
Therefore, this [attempt] to state its essential nature leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
since it would follow that even the contact of the self (*ātman*) and so forth with an existent object would be impossible.

Now, if that which is unique to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is being stated, and not the self (*ātman*) and so forth which are [also] unique, then the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) serves to differentiate [it from others] and is not intended to state its essential nature (*svarūpa*). By this, the mention of "contact with a real object" (*sat-sannikarṣa*) and so forth is refuted.
For instance,
this would either be a definition or a statement of its own nature for the purpose of enjoining another matter;
in that case, if it were a definition, one should simply say "contact with the existent" (*satsannikarṣa*).
Perception is that which apprehends real objects, or perception is that which is produced by the sense faculties and is uncontradicted;
thus, its essential nature is restated here for the purpose of demonstrating that it is not a means of knowing *dharma*.
Even so, one should simply say "produced by the sense faculties"—what is the point of this other superfluous chatter?
Furthermore,
a mere restatement is improper;
for it is as follows:

Those who profess the Vedas, as well as the Mīmāṃsakas, must exert effort in establishing external objects; for the definitions of perception held by others, such as the Buddhists, are otherwise conceived and are not conducive to the [Vedic] system. Therefore, in order to exclude them, a definition must necessarily be formulated in a different manner.
Since the hundred names are conducive to the doctrines of Vijñānavāda and Śūnyatāvāda, it is certainly appropriate to formulate a different definition in order to refute them;
for it is not possible to remove a camel by means of its horns,
so what fault could there be in formulating a definition?
If it is argued that [the object] is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is as follows: in that very same [text], "not by those who have fallen below" is the meaning.

"The definition must be established based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and from that [definition], certainty [of the object] follows. Because they are mutually dependent, not even one of these two is established here.
Since there is mutual dependence, neither one is proven; thus, if this is the case, the formulation of a definition is impossible.
Furthermore, if this were so, even a restatement (*anuvāda*) would not be appropriate for something not already established by a valid means of knowledge."

If it is argued that [the truth] is established by worldly consensus, then dharma too will simply be what is established by worldly consensus; thus, Mīmāṃsā is not the cause for the destruction of dharma.
If it is further argued that [dharma] is unestablished from the perspective of ultimate reality because we observe the subversion of dharma, [we reply: no.

If this is so, why has the Mīmāṃsā school not prevented the subversion of Dharma by means of punishment? Otherwise, after such a long period of time, there would surely be no other doctrine [remaining].
Therefore, even a restatement (anuvāda) must be made only when established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and likewise, a definition (lakṣaṇa) must be faultless.
Nor is a definition provided for these by means of the Gatisūtra, because it is a restatement of well-known meanings;

for just as the restatement is for the purpose of demonstrating that they are not causes with respect to Dharma, so too is it for the purpose of demonstrating that they are causes— thus it is the same in both cases,
as has already been shown previously.

Therefore, the definition "perception is the cognition of an object" [is established] by the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), because there is no other subject under discussion; it is understood as "only from that object which is seen by perception.
By this, the erroneous cognition of two moons and the like is excluded.
For that [consciousness] does not arise from that very [object], but rather from something else;
how then was it said by the Ācārya:
"That which appears is not [the object] itself; therefore, the pentad is indeed the support of the mind"?
In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
it is stated that visual and other sensory cognitions arise from atoms (*paramāṇu*) with their own specific forms;

if even a cognition possessing a different form were to have those atoms as its objective support (*ālambana*) simply by virtue of being its cause, then it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the atoms of the eyes and other sense organs would also be objective supports.
For whether they exist in that way or otherwise, they are the cause of cognitions appearing as two moons, blue, and so forth;
this was stated with reference to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
whereas the analysis of the debate is conducted according to worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*).
For the world indeed accepts as far as this [the existence of objects] through such conceptualizations as atoms;

it is well-known in the world as being perceptible. However, when examined, it is not logical. Therefore, the claim that [the object] is established by its own nature is clearly inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This would be inconclusive with respect to atoms. (603)

If you maintain that atoms alone are the producers [of cognition], then there is an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the eyes and other sense organs when they serve as objects (*ālambana*). Furthermore, if it is said that "they" refers to what appears [in consciousness], then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), for that which is simultaneous [with the cognition] cannot be its producer; moreover, there is an inconclusive argument with respect to things such as a double moon.
Furthermore, it is also untenable that [the whole] is the producer even at the same time [as its parts],
because the composite (samudāya) is not a real entity (avastu).
And there is inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to erroneous cognitions. Furthermore, if it were the producer of the prior existence, even then there would be unestablishedness;
for the prior existence is not grasped by that cognition. If it were grasped by another [cognition], that too would be subject to the same inquiry. (604)
If [the object] is known through inference, that [inference] must arise from perception itself; yet, if these two are mutually dependent causes, which one could possibly exist first?
There is never a simultaneity of perception and its object. Therefore, this definition is indeed unestablished from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
however, it is not contradictory when considered with respect to worldly convention (*lokapratīti*).
As for the claim that perception is the functioning of the auditory and other senses,
that too is incorrect.
Even in the case of error, the functioning of the ear and other senses certainly does exist; yet, without cognition, the functioning of the ear and so forth is not possible.
For one who desires to act seeks a means of valid cognition such as perception, and how could the unperceived functioning of the ear and other senses constitute a definition?
How could this [cognition] proceed from that which is not perceived?
If it is argued that the functioning of the auditory organ and so forth is perceived through perception, then the definition of that perception must be stated.
To this, the rebuttal is that perception has the form of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), and that it is perceived by itself;
such being the case, that very direct realization is the definition of non-erroneousness.

Furthermore, even if consciousness is erroneous, how could the functioning of the auditory faculty and so forth constitute a defining characteristic? There is no fault here, for "functioning with respect to objects" means being directed toward objects. (Arthāmimukhyatvam)
Even that exists for one who is deluded;
therefore, the definition is simply that the self-awareness of its own nature is itself the awareness of its own nature.
And that very direct realization, which has "non-conceptual" as its other name,
is therefore nothing other than the second definition [of valid cognition]; [this concludes] the investigation of the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
(1) Explanation of the fruit of the means of valid cognition:
What, then, is the fruit of this means of valid cognition?
It is the comprehension of the object of cognition.
And it has been said [in that same work]:
"For the comprehension of the object of cognition (prameya) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
In that very context, regarding that which is to be postulated:
Now, it might be argued: "If that very cognition is itself the result, then what now constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
[Is it] the contact between sense-organ and object, the initial perception (*ālocana*), and the cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*)? Some hold this view, but it is incorrect.
That alone is the means for realization, since it is from that [means] that realization arises.

Indeed, the production of knowledge is seen to come from the sense faculties and so forth; therefore, the means for realization must also be that very same thing. What is the use of this conceptualization?
For no conceptualization other than what is observed is justified by reason, as it involves the abandonment of what is actually perceived.
If it were so, an infinite regress regarding the object of cognition would be unavoidable.
This is not the case;
for everything is the means of action for every action.
For that which is an action is not the means of accomplishing it;

[if it were], then whatever action is observed to have efficacy in one instance would be assumed as the means for another instance as well. If, by employing just any means of accomplishment, all desired goals were accomplished, then the entire world would be well-situated with little effort.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, whatever action is observed from which [a result arises], that alone is the means of accomplishment there, and nothing else.

For cognition, whose nature is merely that of experience, must exist in that very form by which it is differentiated according to each respective object; otherwise, it would contradict the fact of specific objects. (303)
For that experience of what is called "cognition" is the same with respect to blue, yellow, and so forth; therefore, by its mere existence, it would establish everything,
just like the objects established as intended.
Just as it is not established, so too that which is capable of being established [is not], because there is no distinction between them;
for just as that thing is a cognizer of it, so too is it a non-cognizer of it. When it is a cognizer of it, by what reasoning is it not desired to be a non-cognizer? (609)
2 In the Nyāyabhāṣya, at that very same place: "The meaning is 'the means of valid cognition' (pramāṇāni).
This verse is analyzed by Alaṃkāradeva and Rājaputra in their *Nyāyaviniścaya* and its commentary (*Tadvivaraṇa*),
at page 244, verses 1–28.
For, while assimilating the distinction of the state of non-activity, one might understand that "this [cognition] is active here and not there";
nevertheless, does it deviate from its own nature?

If [the cognition] were the self, then even though it is of the nature of the self, if it does not know, then that object would simply not have been known by me; consequently, it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This world understands the object of enjoyment as being the very self of the person;
yet that self does not truly know it—how noble is the established order of enjoyment!

In that very same [text]: "If it is argued that the self does not cognize, for the cognition 'this is an object of enjoyment' establishes the self as having the form of a determination regarding pleasure, blue, and so forth—then in that case, that [cognition] itself is the enjoyer; what need is there for another consciousness?"

If it is argued that the form alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the Person (*puruṣa*) perceives the object as determined by the intellect— wherein the intellect consists of the determination of pleasure and so forth, or has the form of pleasure—
then what is this "intellect"?
What is determination?
Or rather, what is the person? It must be said:
the intellect is the instrument.
If it is argued that determination is the action and the person is the agent, [we reply:
the person perceives the object.

If it is argued that the determination belongs to the agent [the Self], and that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the instrument for that determination— just as the intellect is the instrument for cognition and the person (*puruṣa*) is the agent of cognition—
we do not perceive any distinction between cognition and determination. For "cognition" (*avagama*) is simply the direct realization of the form of that [object].

If it is argued that this very determination (*adhyavasāya*) is simply the cognition taking on the form of that [object], and not a direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), then even if the cognition indeed possesses that form, why is it not the case that the object itself is likewise [directly perceived] through the direct perception of that form? (611)

2. Herein, up to the end of the third chapter, the examination of the translation is based on the *Ter-gī* manuscript; from here until the conclusion of the second section, it is based on the *Nara-thaṅ* manuscript.
3. From here until the completion of the work, the text taken above was written by Vibhūticandra; however, regarding the variant readings from the *Dānaśīla* manuscript, they appear in the footnotes.

When the cognition of the form [of the object] is directly realized, the meaning itself is likewise [realized]; thus, a cognition that takes the form of an object [when the object is absent] is purposeless.

The form of the object is presented to the intellect; consequently, there would be a cognition of the object as being in a location not distant [from the self]. Since the self is all-pervading, everything would indeed be in a location not distant from it, and thus there would be no cognition of anything as being at a distance.
Furthermore, the object would not exist apart from that cognition of its form.
If it is asked: "If there is no external object, from where does that cognition with such a form arise?"
But surely it is maintained that objects possess the form of cognition itself; why then is this [claim] a reversal?

For it is not possible to perceive [an object] as if it were one's own face [reflected], since it has not been transferred [into the cognition], because the face is in an unsuitable location. Indeed, the transfer of the face into a mirror or similar medium is what is accepted.
If it is argued that this is not the case for others, and as for the mirror, how can there be a perception of it since it has not been transferred [into cognition]—
if you say that even for that [mirror], it has been transferred into the mirror of cognition,
then one must likewise accept that cognition is itself cognition and that there is no transfer into another mirror.
If it is argued that "let cognition remain unknown," then the world would be rendered purposeless since the Self is directly perceived;
and if the Self were not the object [of knowledge], let the object itself be what is cognized— what need is there for cognition here?
If it is asked how one sees without an instrument,
[the answer is that] the eyes and so forth are the instruments, while the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) serves as the means.
If that [internal organ] were also internal, there would be no purpose [for another], leading to an infinite regress; nor can that which provides no assistance be an instrument.

If the Puruṣa is manifested by them, then— since manifestation belongs to one who is not indifferent— the Puruṣa would lack the capacity for apprehension; therefore, there must exist a Self that is distinct from those [qualities].
Bṛhaṭṭīkā 5: Because [the practice] is restricted even at the time of understanding the meaning, just as it was at the time when the meaning was not understood.
If it is argued that, like a mirror, there is an assumption of its form [in consciousness] without undergoing any modification,
we say no;
rather, it is in dependence upon the mirror that a cognition assuming its form arises.
Therefore, what other modification could there be? If there were no modification, what would be the meaning of "transition," as in the case of the reflection of a face in a mirror?
There is nowhere any deluded cognition that arises;
even here, the cognition possessing the form of an object is merely deluded, for in ultimate reality there is no manifold of objects.

Since the world consists of nothing but primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa), then the world's nature as primordial matter is likewise merely an illusion, just like its nature as jars and other objects;
so too is its nature as the person.
And we shall establish this later; otherwise, it would not be according to the Sāṃkhya system. 1 Bṭi. [The] Sāṃkhyas.
2 Bṭi. Siddhāntin 3 Bṭi.
Therefore, by means of another approach, this pure experience must be realized through the Self, whereby the distinction between action and object— such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow"—
is established. Now, it was indeed stated that perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the functioning of the auditory and other senses.
This has been stated, but it is improper;
for even though a distinction exists among the causes, it does not constitute its [the effect's] own nature.
When the action is undifferentiated, there can be no regulator through differentiation for that which is undifferentiated.
For this person, who is undifferentiated in every action such as [perceiving] blue and so forth, the differentiation of the sense organs and other factors cannot be the regulator.
For that [differentiation] could only be a regulator if it were either the producer (*kāraka*) or the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [action].
It is not logical for it [the mind] to be a regulator by way of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), because it is eternal and because it would follow that it possesses form (*sākāratā*).
If it were formless (*anākāratva*), that same fault would apply, as it would follow that it perceives itself.
Now, [if it is argued that] it is a regulator because it is an indicator, how can something be an indicator regarding an object that is not yet known?
Since the knowledge of the restriction arises from the indicator, and the indicator [is known] from the knowledge of the restriction, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that light is the indicator [of objects],
no;
for if those too were to require being indicated, there would be a need for another indicator, resulting in an infinite regress.
Furthermore, light is not an indicator in all cases;
and if [an object] is indicated by light, what is the use of the eyes and other [senses]?
If it is argued that, in that case, sound and so forth serve as the light, [we reply: no.
Nevertheless, we shall explain how this [consciousness], whose nature is self-awareness, knows those things that do not abide within its own nature.
Therefore, the relationship [is that] from which its distinction of self-nature is understood; this is [the point]. 5 M.
The restriction of the object for the activity of apprehension is established; that [activity] is proven by that [restriction].
For, when the cause is its own nature, there is this restriction of that cognition: "this is the apprehension of blue," and "this is the apprehension of yellow."
That goal as well is established by the means for its attainment,
because this very restriction exists solely on account of that;
and so it has been said:
Since this [cognition] exists only through the existence of that [object],
and since this connection with the object does not arise from similarity, it follows that [the object] belongs to the cognition.

For it is by means of the object that one connects this [cognition] with it; indeed, apart from the form of the object, there is no other way whatsoever for the difference in the object to differentiate the cognition from its own internal distinctions. (306)
Therefore, the means for the apprehension of the object of cognition is its conformity to the form of that object;
otherwise, the true purpose of the operation of that means would not be established.
The connection with that object [is established] regarding the sense-faculty and so forth;
the meaning is this: the object is made known by the regulating sense-faculty and so forth, but the regulation itself is not known by it.
If it is argued that "how is certainty known? For there is knowledge of restriction regarding an object already known," this is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
For it is the cognition possessing the form of the object that establishes the object as "blue" or "yellow."
We shall demonstrate later how cognition possesses a form;
however, in other proofs, one's own purpose is not accomplished by that object through its activity.
For if the cognition’s having the form of that [object] were abandoned, how could there be the rule that "there is a cognition of it"?
If it is argued that the restriction will arise simply from direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*),
then what is this direct realization? Is it the nature of the object itself, or is it consciousness, or is it something else entirely?

If the direct realization of the object is held to be its very form, then how could cognition—which is itself direct realization—be possible for the object? (612) Alternatively, if the act of direct realization is considered to be the very nature of consciousness itself, then how can that object be said to be directly realized? For one thing cannot possess the nature of another. Even if they were distinct, this same fault would remain unavoidable. (613)

For instance, if the manifestation of an object were its own nature—such as blue and so forth—and were thus common to all, then that object would be cognized by everyone. Furthermore, it is not logical for the manifestation to belong to the object itself, because it is a property of cognition. If, on the other hand, this [manifestation] is a property of cognition whose object is the thing, then the object is said to be "cognized" by virtue of that.
Regarding the phrase "having the object as its domain," what is the meaning of "domain"?
If it is argued that it is because [cognition] has the nature of the awareness of the object,
then what is this "awareness of the object"?
If it is argued that "because cognition has the form of the object," [then] cognition itself possesses the form of the object; or else,
because the object is known, there is the cognition of the object.
If that were the case, since the eye too would be an object of cognition, it would follow that there is a perception of the eye;
if you argue that "it sees the object, not the eye," what is the meaning of "it sees the object"?
Seeing the object, it is seen by that [consciousness]; thus it is said, "it sees.
By what does it see? By its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).
If that is so, then it sees its own nature by means of the nature of self-cognition (*samvedana-rūpeṇa*).
Thus, in the manner that the object exists as the form of the object, the object possesses the nature of being cognized and cognition possesses the nature of being the cognizer;
therefore, it is precisely this possession of the object's form that establishes everything,
and no other distinct intrinsic nature connects consciousness with the object.
1 B.ṭi.
by way of the form of the object;
2 B.ṭi.
And that [cognition], being of the nature of self-awareness, is indeed identical with its own essence; therefore, there is no result that is a separate entity.
For those who maintain that the result is a separate entity, everything becomes difficult to establish.
The very form of the object within cognition is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and cognition itself, being of that same nature, is the fruit of the means of valid cognition;
apart from the experience of the form of the object, there is no other apprehension of the object.

The cognition of an object does not consist in its having the form of pleasure and so forth, because that would entail the consequence of experiencing the specific qualities of the object [simply] from the specific qualities of that [pleasure].
If it is argued that the experience of the object occurs by virtue of the object being the cause [of the pleasure],
then if the object did not possess that form, only the pleasure itself would be experienced.
If it is argued that there is the experience of pleasure with respect to the object, then why is there not an experience of yellow with respect to blue?
Since they are mutually distinct, this [argument] also results in the subversion of your own position.

If it is argued that the same applies to pleasure and blue, and thus enough of this grinding of what is already ground, [and that] its very nature is such that it is not an operation of cognition— [we reply:
3 B.ṭi.

It is not the apprehension of the form of the object that is [the cognition], but rather the apprehension of the form of pleasure; and this [cognition] bears that [form of pleasure] within itself by way of having the apprehension of the object as its essence. (308)
Although it is itself devoid of agency, it appears as if active in its own function through that [reflected] activity, because its determination occurs by virtue of that [reflection]. (309)
For, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no activity whatsoever belonging to anything;
rather, it is the very nature of entities that appears as such. Therefore, what is called "activity" by those who know reality is not activity in the ultimate sense.
Furthermore, knowledge is the self-interest of the person,
just like the cognition of pleasure; therefore, when the cognition of pleasure arises, it is the self-interest [of the person], but nothing is produced by the cognition of pleasure itself.
In this way, even the cognition of form and so forth has its own object by virtue of its very nature; it is not that the object is known by means of that cognition,
but rather that the object arises from it— thus the conventional usage is concluded.
What is the purpose of such an activity?
In that case, the cognition of the object would not be the result.
[Reply: Even as a result, the cognition of the object is simply the cognition that bears the form of the object; what contradiction is there in this?
How, then, is there the conventional usage of a distinction, such as "it cognizes an object"?
It is designated thus because it cognizes that very form of the object which it bears;
for instance, when visual consciousness, having abandoned yellow, operates upon blue and so forth, its activity appears as if characterized by the acts of abandoning and assuming.
If the cognition of blue were itself the very form of blue, then yellow would not appear; for the nature of one thing does not manifest as that of another.
Therefore, by means of reasoning, it is established that [the cognition] is distinct from that [object]; and both that operation and that presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*) are indeed nothing but this.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is only consciousness itself, appearing in various successive forms of "that" and "not-that.

In that case, there is no operation or exclusion [of external objects]; rather, the conceptualization of distinct entities and operations arises from the connection with beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and is not preceded by the manifestation of actual entities. (614)

That [conceptualization], which has as its seed the conceptualization of exclusion (vyatireka-kalpanā) and is produced by the latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by the experience of cognitions from previous births, is merely a blind tradition.
B.
Ṭīkā:
Since "distinction" (vyatireka) is an indicative mark, it also includes "difference" (bheda).
(——) Regarding the two intermediate verses:

[Objection] If that object is excluded from there because the cognition produced by it possesses its form, then it is the object itself that is excluded there, not the cognition with respect to the object; so how can there be the certainty that "cognition grasps [the object]"?
To this, the resolution is as follows:
Just as in the world, because an effect arises with a nature similar to its causes, it is said that the cause assumes the form [of the effect], even though the cause possesses activity. || 311 2 B.

[Objection: It is like this: in the world, it is said that a son who resembles his father "assumes the form of the father," even though there is no actual act of grasping [that form]. If such a designation applies to cognition as well, what contradiction is there? [Response: In that case, the assumption of its form is observed; but how can it be so here?
Here too, it is observed that in cases such as desire or grief, that assumption of an object's form arises from cognition alone and not from the object itself—this is the objection.

To this, [the reply is]: first, that assumption of an object's form is perceived as occurring; if there is the capacity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then the cause for its appearance in perception is the assumption of that form through experience.

Now, if it arises with respect to something never before seen or heard, then—since there is an absence of the capacity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) [to account for it]—it must arise from something else that possesses that form; this is the meaning of the statement. That form is the instrument (*karaṇa*);
for thus it is said:
As for the cause of that [cognition’s] form— according to an alternative reading— it is that which has arisen from latent impressions (*vāsanā*); that exists only for a single [individual],
whereas if the object were actually present there, its arising would be common to all.
Therefore, the very fact of having the form of the object is the means of proof for the initial perception,
the sensory contact, and the specific cognitions [of qualifiers].
4B. The validity of these [cognitions] called "observation" (ālocanā) is not accepted with respect to the action, because of the intervention [of another cognition]. || 310 ||

Some say that the knowledge of mere observation (*ālocanājñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); following that, the result (*phala*) consists of the ascertainment of an object qualified by its genus and other attributes;
from that comes purposeful activity (*pravartana*); from that, attainment (*prāpti*); and from that, pleasure (*sukha*).
Thus, the sequence is such that each preceding stage is the means of valid cognition and each succeeding stage is the result.
For the determination of specific objects occurs solely through the power of the form (ākāra), and not from anything else.
If the sensory perception (*ālocanavijñāna*) were not to assume a specific form, how could it be said that "this is the perception of this [object]"?

Furthermore, other cognitions such as the determinative cognition (*niścaya*) and so forth likewise acquire their designation based on reality [through their forms]. However, each preceding [cognition] is a cause only for the production of each succeeding one, and not for the determination of specific objects; for it is precisely the possession of that [specific] form which is the means of proof (*sādhana*) in that regard.

Even though all factors (kārakas) are useful with respect to an action, that which is the ultimate differentiator [of the action] is considered its most effective means (sādhakatama). For that which is most effective is indeed the instrument (karana). (Pāṇini 1.4.42)
And even when all the factors of action (kārakas) are employed, how can there be excellence (prakarṣa) in the action?
For it is not merely the accomplishment of the action itself [that constitutes excellence].
Even though [the sense organs] exist there, that alone is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the action for which there is immediate succession;
for even when the sense organs and so forth are present, if the specific form were not apprehended due to factors such as distance, [cognition would not arise].
B.
Ṭīkā:
Even in the absence of the performance of an action.
Ṭīkā:
"na pariprāpyeta" means it would not be obtained; "nopadīyeta" means it would not be taken up.
The determination of the object as having that form is the "action" (kriyā) which appears immediately after that [cognition]; thus, that very [determination] is the instrument (karaṇa).

But surely, it is merely the proximity in space (adūradeśatā) that is the means (sādhana), for even when there is proximity in space, if the sense organ is impaired, there is no determination of the object with certainty.
"In that case, the absence of impairment (*anupaghāta*) is the means of proof. This is not so either, because:
"The absence of impairment of the sense organ is [known] through the specific form of its cognition; therefore, that [impairment] is excluded from the object. (617)

Is it not the case that it follows that the very form (ākāra) itself is what is obstructed? For it is by means of that form that a certainty, which is unimpaired, serves as the cause for the determination of a specific object.
This is not correct, because:
If the restriction of form is established when there is a determination of objects, then why is the arrow maintained as a cause when it has already been established?
(618) The restriction of form is not unestablished; it establishes that which follows from the senses.
If that [restriction] is well-established, then that itself is the determination of objects.
The non-impairment of the sense organs is indeed useless;

for certainly, when an object is already established, no one can bring it about through attainment, since it is impossible to prove what is already proven. Therefore, what is required by that which merely presents what is already established?
If it is argued that even regarding the possession of that form, another determination is required for a fixed and specific establishment, we say no;
for this discussion concerns the validity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For when there is familiarity through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition; and it is from the mere form [of the object] alone that activity occurs even without a definitive ascertainment (*niścaya*).
However, when there is a requirement for ascertainment, then inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition, since activity occurs from its mere form as well.
Therefore, there is no dependence on anything other than that aspect; likewise, there is no other uncommon instrument [of cognition] therein.
B.
Ṭīkā: At the time of practice, because all [objects] are common causes for the sense-faculties, there is nothing of this kind [that is not perceived].
For even when there is a difference between those [objects], how could that which is non-different [from them] be designated as "this belongs to that"?
(313) [This is so] because it does not possess the nature of those [objects].

Indeed, since the sense organ (*akṣa*) is the cause of all objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth in a general sense, it cannot be the differentiator [of those objects]. [Objection: But surely there will be distinct sense organs for each respective object—blue, yellow, both, and so on; for the orientation toward them (*tadabhimukhatā*) is indeed different in each case. Therefore, since there is a difference in the properties (*dharma*) of the sense organs, the cognition of their difference arises precisely from that [difference in the organs]. Why then is it said that [the organ is not the differentiator] because it is the cause of everything in common?
That is incorrect.

Since it is impossible to comprehend "directness" (ābhimukhya) without a distinction in its qualifying aspect (viśeṣaṇa), even if such a distinction exists, how could this directness—being devoid of an aspect—be specified as having blue, yellow, or other objects?

For there is no comprehension of a specific directness without the comprehension of the specific [objects] such as blue; if that [comprehension of the object] exists, what is the use now of postulating a manifestation of directness?

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "even when there is a difference in that [object], for that which is non-different": even though there is a difference in that cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, how can it be said that "this is the instrument of this" with respect to the non-different sense organ?

If it is argued that the distinction [in the cognition] arises from a specific orientation (*ābhimukhya-viśeṣa*), we reply: no, because it has already been stated that it is impossible to perceive a distinction in the state of being oriented without first perceiving a distinction in the cause.
Therefore, only a specific form (ākāra) is to be sought;
if that exists, what is the use of anything else?
For surely the form belongs to the object itself and not to the cognition, since it is apprehended as being the object.
For that form is perceived as being of an insentient nature by way of color and shape,
whereas cognition is its opposite, being of the nature of awareness;
this is because it is impossible to perceive the nature of awareness apart from the form.
Since no form of cognition other than blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, is perceived,
it follows that cognition must be imperceptible; yet this is not the case, and thus [the opponent's position] is untenable.
For instance:
if that cognition is imperceptible, on what basis is it known to be a cognition?
Who is capable of defining the nature of that which is imperceptible?

If it is argued that the cognition of an object is what constitutes its perceptibility, then let there simply be the cognition of the object's perceptibility; what need is there for anything else in that regard?

But in the case of persistence, this [persistence] does not occur for one who is non-persistent; therefore, the statement "it exists by means of an object" is established without effort. By this, non-existence is also refuted;
moreover, at the time of experiencing blue and so forth, nothing is experienced apart from immediate presence (aparokṣatā).

Therefore, that [cognition] which possesses the form of blue and so forth has as its proximate cause (upadhāna) something else entirely— such as the reflection of a face in a mirror— whereas the blue object itself is merely the form; it is not the object in its own right.
Now, one might object: "In this world, both the reflection in a mirror and the face are perceived; however, here [in the case of cognition], there is no perception of an object without its form.
We shall establish this point later, so let it rest for now.
But how can the insentient nature [of the object] be established against that which shines forth by itself?
And if there were some other [cause] for the directness of the object from which this [cognition] is established as "this," then it would be a latent impression (*vāsanā*);
by the power of that impression, this form belongs to consciousness.
Nor can an object exist by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā),
because that would entail the consequence of its non-existence.

Surely that which appears [in a dream] is devoid of an external object because it arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like the forms in a dream; however, is there not some specific distinction in those latent impressions by which the form perceived in the waking state does not become devoid of an object? (622)

For it is observed that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are indeed the producers of mental forms (*ākāra*), as in dreams and the like; therefore, even this [object] which has become an object of waking perception arises from that very source, because it belongs to the same class.
But is it not the case that its being a mere form is unestablished, since it is apprehended as "this is an actual object"?
It is not [the case that there is] no deviation,
for it is indeed perceived that the form of dream-cognition is an object.
If it is argued that there is a different apprehension due to a lack of thorough investigation,
then even here, thorough investigation is not devoured by crows; rather,
it is better to postulate that the specific latent impression (*vāsanā*) taking the form of the waking state is the object.

If it is argued that even cognitions such as those in dreams are not possessed of an aspect (sākāra), because in those cases too an object is possible, we shall demonstrate the refutation of that later on. Alternatively, if the possession of the object's aspect is not directly perceived— [the opponent might say] that the object itself, such as blue and so forth,
is the "aspect of the object," and that [cognition] [appears as such] due to its proximity to the real entity.
It is perceived in such a way, like a reflection in a mirror;
for by the appearance of a face, the mirror— though itself formless— is perceived as if it were possessed of form,
or like the light of a lamp and so forth.
For the light of a lamp, though itself formless, appears as if it possesses the form of a jar and so forth when reflected in them;

yet that is untrue, because a mirror and the like are perceived even apart from the [reflected] face and other objects. However, nothing is perceived as being directly present (aparokṣatva) apart from its own form.

For directness (*aparokṣatā*) is always observed as being essentially identical with the form of blue itself, and not otherwise. Why, then, should it appear through proximity alone in such a way? What is the proof here that it appears only as such?
If you ask what the proof is for you [the opponent], it is simply the perception of non-difference (*abhedopalabdhi*).
If it is argued that this is merely an error, we say no, because there is no subverting cognition;
and if it is argued that there is the attainment of the object, [we say] no.
Since even attainment (*prāpti*) is characterized by its form (*ākāra*),
we shall demonstrate that there is no such thing as attainment apart from having that form;
for if that [object] did not possess such a form, no one could establish any specific object.

By this, the remainder is explained: furthermore, for cognitions of qualifiers, there is no difference [in their nature] even when they lack that form; or likewise, the same applies to other cognitions.
The "remainder" refers to the initial sensory contact with the object and so forth.
Even the contact with the object is not known by assuming its form;

therefore, those [factors] also lack the status of being the most effective means toward the action [of cognition], because they are separated [from it]. Furthermore, if the assumption of that form did not exist, the cognition of the qualifier itself could not be established.

If it is argued that the status of being a cognition of the qualifier and so forth does not constitute their instrumentality, then how is it to be known that "this is the qualifier" when there is a cognition of a temporal qualification?

For there is no such thing as being a qualifier apart from having its form mounted upon the qualified object; nor is there a grasping of the state of being a qualifier without the grasping of its being mounted upon that [qualified object].
And since the qualified object is already grasped when its form is apprehended, how could a further cognition of that qualified object need to be established by means of it?
For that which is being grasped at that very moment cannot simultaneously give rise to a cognition that grasps it.
If it is argued that even when there is a distinction, the qualifier appears at that very time as something to be grasped by the grasper,

then its prior apprehension would be useless; for it is not tenable to claim that the qualified object also appeared previously, precisely because that would entail the absence of [the qualifier's] status as a means of proof (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, since the cognition of the qualifier occurs with respect to the qualifier and the cognition of it occurs with respect to the qualified object, a difference in objective domain (*viṣayabheda*) results for the action and its instrument.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—[this is the objection].
B.
At the time of qualifying [an object], the qualified object is that which is to be grasped by the cognition grasping the qualified object as produced by the cognition grasping the qualifier;
nor is a delimitation of the object desired for both the action and its means.
Ṭi—at that time, at the time of apprehending the qualificand (viśeṣya), there is also a difference in the object (viṣaya). M. [End of commentary].
If they had a single purpose, the two would be redundant, and there could be no occurrence in succession.
Indeed, the application of instruments such as an axe to a *palāśa* tree does not result in a cut in a *nyagrodha* tree; if they shared a single purpose, the same consequence as before would follow.
Furthermore, the futility of two [cognitions] and the sequential occurrence of all those cognitions which have that object as their cause would be contradicted;
for if there were oneness [of the object], a sequence would be impossible.
If it is argued that there is a sequence due to a difference in repetition, we say no;
for a difference in repetition cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If that very same cognition were to recur, there would always be the impression of recurrence;

yet, among cognitions that grasp an identical nature, there can be no mutual relationship of agent and action. Even if they occur sequentially, the preceding cognition performs only the act of producing the succeeding one, not the act of apprehending it, because it is no different from the preceding one.
Furthermore, it has been established elsewhere that even the act of production is nothing other than the essential nature [of the cognition] itself.
"If the two parts of cognition were to exist simultaneously, there would be an absence of the relationship between the probandum and the probans;
rather, the establishment of the probandum and the probans occurs by virtue of their being the basis for that determination.
This is an intermediate verse (antarashloka).
Nor is sensory contact (saṃnikarṣa) the means of valid cognition, because even when [an object] is connected in its entirety, it is perceived only through certain properties;
that restriction would not exist, since there is no distinction in the connection itself. (317)
If the contact between the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its result is the apprehension of the object; that contact is either conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), or inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*).
Inherence, inherence-in-what-is-inherent, and the relation of qualifier and qualified between what is conjoined.
The sense organ’s conjunction with a jar or similar object;

its inherence in what is conjoined [with the object]—namely, with a quality inherent in the jar; and its inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined [with the object]—namely, with whiteness and so forth as a universal of quality (*guṇatva*).
The auditory organ, which is of the nature of space, has an inherence relation with sound; it has an inherence-in-the-inherent relation with soundness;
and it has a relation of being qualified by what is conjoined (saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva) with the auditory organ at a particular location due to the absence of a jar there.
In that case, if indeed its apprehension consists in a connection with something conjoined,
how could there otherwise be a cognition of fire and so forth based on a connection with smoke?

Now, if it is argued that cognition occurs through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), then in that case, there would also be cognition by the eye of touch and so forth, which likewise inhere in the same object;
for the argument regarding "occupying the same location" has already been refuted.

If it is argued that just as there is no apprehension of a continuum because it inheres in a single object, so too there is no apprehension of touch and the rest because they are not visible, then this is precisely our position.
Since they are inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), it must be considered why this is not the case;
therefore, it is not logical to claim that although [the sense organ] is connected with [the object] in its entirety, it is perceived only through certain attributes (*dharma*).

For if the atoms of the eye and other senses were to go outwards and, by moving to another location, become the cause for grasping an object through conjunction with it, then—given such a connection in its entirety—the perception of all forms would occur, and even properties such as being a wheel or a jar would appear with perfect clarity.
If it is argued that color is perceived and not merely shape,
and likewise that there is no manifestation of the remaining categories such as genus (jāti) and so forth because the sense organ lacks the capacity at a distance and the like;
If there is incapacity, let there simply be non-apprehension at all times;
if it is argued that such is the nature of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) by which such a cognition arises,
we say no.
Because shape is not distinct [from color],
for shape is not perceived as separate from color.
If it is argued that the form of "ākāra" is apprehended even apart from color,
[we reply: even in that case, since darkness is perceived as having a dark color,
and because darkness is not a non-entity, there is indeed the perception of color.
If it is argued that this too is incorrect because it is impossible for that which is being perceived to be non-existent, since there is cognition even of light by one whose eyes are closed;
Not so,
because that [cognition] is erroneous;
nor does the error of one [instance] entail error everywhere, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Because it would follow that external objects do not exist,
one must therefore state once again:
some cognition is erroneous, while some is not.
Therefore, the apprehension of shape occurs only in light, not in darkness;
and only when [the object] is near, not at a distance.

Ṭīkā: Because it would follow that external objects do not exist, this distinction [of the object] exists even though there is no difference [in the cognition]; for that [cognition] is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). 2 B.
Ṭīkā: Even though there is no difference in that [object], this distinction exists because it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is logical that there should be either the apprehension or the non-apprehension of that object in its entirety;
