If it is argued that in a dream, objects such as trees appear instantaneously in their respective places without effort, due to passion and so forth for them—well then, by whom has it been established that there is appearance "without effort"? For an effect is grasped by a cognition occurring at the time of the effect, while a cause is grasped by a cognition occurring at the time of the cause;
the sequence is: "this arises from that."
The determination that "this [occurs] after this" is also a sequence; yet in this matter, there is neither perception nor inference,
for even the notion that "this is confused" is not known by anyone.
And through the excellence of cultivation, there arises a state of non-distraction and so forth even in dreams;
likewise, in the waking state as well,
there is the observation of distraction in the case of portents and the like.
If it were due to the fault of the omen itself,
then there would be no distinction between an auspicious and an inauspicious omen.
If it is argued that even there another must perform the discrimination,
and yet another there as well, such a thing does not exist, because discrimination is itself inherently discrimination.
It is not so, because this [consciousness] consists merely in abiding in its own nature;
for that which abides in its own nature cannot have the cognition of another.

If it is argued that the mere cognition of one's own nature— which is similar to both the agitated and the unagitated, persists for a long duration, and is free from deviation— is indeed "unagitated" (anākula);
Since a long-term continuity cannot be apprehended by direct perception,
nothing remains but conceptual construction beyond that.
And by that [conceptualization], there is no comprehension of the object;
nor can there be a determination [of its validity] from that either, because that too is directly perceived in its own nature.
If it is argued that the conceptualization produced by the experience of the real entity is consistent with reality (*saṃvādī*), [we reply:]...
Because the connection [between them] is not apprehended:

when there is the experience of the object, there is no conceptual construction; when that [conceptual construction] is present, there is no experience. Thus, how could there be the apprehension of a real object here?
If it is argued that [the relationship is established] by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
this too is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because that too depends upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and thus requires another conceptual construction, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
In that case, how can the apprehension of a relation occur even through mental impressions (*vāsanā*),
since it cannot occur through them either from the perspective of ultimate reality? Thus, it has been established that this is indeed our very position.
The proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) accept the latent predisposition (vāsanā) known as the relation of cause and effect, but not the proponents of consciousness-only (vijñānavādins).
There is no fault [in our position], for it has already been established that this is mere consciousness even without being produced by a latent predisposition.

If it is argued: "But surely, the state of being permeated by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not perceived in waking consciousness, whereas in the dream state there is no perception of the dream [as real]; this is the same [in both cases]. However, for one who has awakened, it is not so in the waking state."
Even that is of little consequence,
for it has been said: "Indeed, awakening is experienced even in a dream."
Therefore, the state of waking is not distinct in its characteristics from dreaming;
since the thought "I am awake" occurs even in a dream,
how can the distinction [between the two states] be established based on the appearance of waking?

If it is argued that even that [dream-cognition] was reduced to the state of being a dream by another awakening, this [present cognition], however, has not been so reduced by anything at all; therefore,
although the establishment of objects is not exactly like that, nevertheless, because of its similarity to it, there is no ground for doubt regarding the cognition.

For smoke existing at the time of inference is not considered an inference because it is established as being preceded by fire, but rather because it possesses that defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

In the same way, this waking state also has that very nature simply because it possesses that defining characteristic. [Objection: But surely no operation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is perceived there in the waking state; how then can it be equal to a dream?
Thus he says:
even when there is an interruption in cultivation, there is indeed a manifestation perceived by the ignorant, just as it is observed in old age. || 707 ||
When death is possible as a sleep following the perception of another birth and so forth, why is it not understood that the emergence of another birth is a dream?
Just as there is sleep during the night, so too is there sleep during the night of death.

It is strange that there is a perception here day after day; why is it not the same as from waking after sleep? Is this the reason—that the perception of the former is the cause for the perception of objects? In this regard, they are indeed equal. (709) Just as what was seen on a previous day is the cause for the perception in a night-dream, so too is what was seen on each preceding day the cause for the perception in a dream on a subsequent day, even when separated by nights; thus, this is a vast succession of dreams.
If it is argued that there is also the perception of what was previously non-existent, then the same applies even to what is considered a dream; thus everything is equal.
Just as the going and coming in a dream is produced by the perception of various other things, why is the going and coming in the waking state and in dreams not accepted in the same way? (710)
If it is argued that there is an absence of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), is it not sufficient to say that for the wise, conventional usage exists precisely through this inference?
Just as the conventional usage of cause and effect is based on inference, so too is this [usage of momentariness]; thus, the case is the same.
Furthermore, if there were no conventional usage regarding momentariness, why should it not exist? Why should it not be established?
If it is argued that even this is not so,
we shall demonstrate that point later.
Now, it may be argued that it is logical that the perception of dreams arises from the impairment of sleep and thus has unreal objects.
But surely, while this [dream] is clearly manifesting, how can it be a dream?
For at its inception, the state of being a dream is not applicable;
if that very [manifestation] were the cause of that appearance, [it would contradict its nature as a dream].
There is no [determination] based on a distinction in cultivation, because a distinction in appearance is observed;
for even when the onset of sleep is the same, someone becomes a dreamer in a certain way.
If it is argued that [the waking state] is absent when that [dream-object] is absent, let it be a mere cause; nevertheless, it is not the cause of the specific appearance [of the dream].
This appearance also occurs immediately after sleep; therefore, it is equal to a dream upon waking, if you say.
If it is argued that there is no awakening apart from the appearance, because the cognition "I am awakened" constitutes awakening;
It has been stated that even in a dream, that cognition [is not produced by an external object];
therefore, there is no distinction between a dream and its opposite.

Therefore, the refutation of one who, based on a perceived distinction, asserts a difference between [waking cognitions] having an object and being without an object is that "its distinctness is unestablished"; it is not, however, a proof of the opposite— that the existence of an object is now established because waking cognitions are indistinguishable [from dreams].
Because it would follow that erroneous cognition and the like do not exist, [your position] would be contradicted by your own admission, just as in the case of waking cognitions;
furthermore,
the subverting cognition is evident through reasons such as its being a cognition.

It is not possible for that [subsequent cognition] to invalidate it in any other way. For a sublating cognition—characterized by non-apprehension, consisting in the apprehension of the opposite, and being of the nature of perception—cannot be invalidated by inference on the grounds of its being a "cognition" and so forth.
If, in the inference of fire from smoke, a perceptual occurrence regarding the opposite were to arise later, how could that inference be a valid means of knowledge?
Now, even if inference is the sublater regarding the object of the "two moons" [illusion] while it is functioning as perception, what is that perception? The same logic applies;
for in that case too, it is perception itself that possesses the power of sublation.
Because one has previously seen [the relationship] in one instance,
there would otherwise be no inference at all;
however, perception is not preceded by inference.

If, however, it were the case that inference itself would serve as the sublater even in that instance, then perception would be non-authoritative regarding the sublation by inference; and thus, due to mutual contradiction, nothing at all would be established.
Therefore, inference has perception as its basis, but perception does not have inference as its basis;
indeed, it is established that perception alone has inference as its basis.
Likewise, perception does not first function without inference; for the engagement [of perception] would occur only when the relationship has been grasped through inference. (712)

For if the apprehension of the relationship [between means and object] occurs through inference, then perception would be the initiator by means of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and from that [efficiency] inference [would derive its validity]; thus, the mutual sublation of inference by perception and perception by inference would be equal.

If this were so, there would indeed be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), and not the validity of even one of them. This has been stated: "The cognition of the nature [of the means] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)."

Validity is established through worldly convention regarding an object distinct [from the cognition] which serves as the locus of activity; and that [convention] arises from a beginningless succession of the blind; furthermore, it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and this correspondence pertains to the future.
And since there is only self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) regarding the future [object],
how can there be validity with respect to an external object?
If it is argued that inference, too, is like perception even without [direct awareness of] its own nature, [then the following applies].
In that case, it is not a matter of direct perception for him; therefore, by means of inference, the direct perception is sublated with respect to what is distinct [from it].

If it is argued: "Since that [object] is the domain of inference and is thus beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), how can direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is beyond the senses?"
If it were not apprehended by way of being an instigator, then it would simply not be an instigator at all.
For it is thus:
ṭi—[in] the future.
ṭi—of that which is to come (bhāvin).

Ṭīkā: Because the sublated and the sublator have the same object, if that [sublator] were to operate upon the very same thing that appeared in the preceding perception, for what purpose would it be necessary [since the object] has already been attained in its own nature? || 713 ||

The activity of one who seeks purposeful action would not occur [if the object were already known]; for if it is already manifest, there would be no further engagement. Even when the purposeful action has been manifested, one still engages in order to attain it.
Since there is no appearance [of the object] at the time of attainment, its occurrence must be in that which does not appear.
And if it is not sublated by that [perception] or by inference, then our desired conclusion is all the more established;
for instance:

Perception is set in motion by inference regarding an object distinct [from itself], and since that [object] is beyond the senses, it is the domain of inference; therefore, the sublation of perception occurs precisely there [by inference]. And in that case, when there is a sublation of inference by inference, it would be the inference itself that is sublated by inference.
That inference which has come down through a blind tradition is never undermined by either another inference or by perception when it contradicts it; however,
the rule is that neither perception nor an inference produced by perception can be sublated by an inference.

If it is argued that even a perception whose object is two moons is indeed sublated—either by another perception occurring subsequently that manifests a single moon, or by some other means—because it is not actually a valid perception, we reply:
why? Because it is sublated.
If it is argued that there can be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator between two things existing through mutual exclusion,
then it follows that both [of them] would stand in the relationship of the sublated and the sublator.
It is not because of being a means of attainment that one [cognition] possesses the status of a sublater; for in a given case, one may be a means of attaining what is intended while the other is not.
In that case, it follows that the sublated status of inference is actually due to its being mediated by another [cognition].
Therefore, what is the meaning of the statement that all conditions whatsoever are without objective support (*nirālambana*), like the conditions of a dream?
It means that they have their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) as their objective support;
and in that regard, there is perception (*pratyakṣa*), as well as inference (*anumāna*) produced by it, and the form of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

And that [cognition] cannot be sublated by inference or by any other means; furthermore, the proof for an external object is neither perception nor the inference generated by it, because they would be caught in a blind succession of one depending on the other. In this regard, there is this absolute rule: that only perception or inference can serve as a sublater.

Therefore, the claim that "all [cognitions] have an objective basis (*sālambana*), like waking cognitions" is not a valid counter-proof; for since dreams and the like lack a foundation in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the cognition that negates their having an objective basis is itself without an objective basis (*anālambana*).
If that is the case, how can the existence of an objective basis be established by using that as an example?
But surely, objectlessness resides in another cognition, and that is what is being established by this [present] cognition;
and since that [other cognition] is distinct from this one,
the other cognition as well must have a distinct, established object as its domain because it is a cognition— so how can it not be a counter-proof?
Granted that this [cognition] has a non-distinct object because it is preceded by perception,
what follows for the contrary cognition seized by error, such that it too is held to be so? Moreover,
that [contrary cognition] does not establish a real distinction, since it merely establishes conventional usage.
Furthermore, it corroborates an object that is distinct from its own nature;
and that corroboration is an adherence to the experience of that very [object] at that time,
such that it does not appear to me here now.
Since I myself terminate in my own form, I establish that very self as being without an object; therefore, another cognition possessing an object is not established by me, who possess an object.
(B. Ṭi:
By means of a cognition that establishes the absence of an object.)
Ṭīkā: Even now, the waking cognition, which is without an external object, does not have "I myself" as its object in the sense that it is a cognition possessing that [external] form.
Ṭīkā: The determination of the appearance of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender, which is established through inference.
Now, if it does not take that form as its object, how is it established by this [cognition]?
To this it was said: "It is known to have been taken as an object because of correspondence (*sambāda*). Because of correspondence, it is understood that it has been taken as an object.
Therefore, he says:

"It has the form of neither the cognized nor the cognizer; it appears as such due to the delusion of the forms of the distinct characteristics of the grasped and the grasper, just as it is perceived by those who are mistaken. (331)

When this arrangement has been established in such a way—just like the distinction between the cognition of hair and so forth—then the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper is not to be challenged. For, even when reaching an object such as [illusory] hair, the cognition possesses the form of a knower despite the object being non-cognizable; indeed, in that case, the cognition is not a knower of the hair and so forth, because those do not exist.

However, by those who are deluded, it is perceived as a "platform" (vedikā) that has been reached; and from this perception, it is understood that there is no attainment for those currently engaged in it— therefore, its lack of a real objective basis (anālambanatva) is perfectly clear.
By that, the absence of an object is established, because while there is the perception of a similar form, there is no perception of anything distinct; however,
since "having an object" has never been perceived anywhere, how can the proof of all things having objects follow from similarity to that?
For that which appears as a form is not apprehended by means of its [subsequent] perception; otherwise, because it would have already appeared, there would be no engagement [with it].
If it is argued that one engages again for the sake of further appearance even though it has already appeared, then, since it is appearing again, it was not [previously] appeared.
Since that [object] too would have to proceed by way of appearing, there would be an infinite regress; and for what purpose would there be further appearance?
If it is argued that [the person] acts for the sake of happiness or for the sake of grasping [an object], then they act for that purpose; however,
that [purpose] is not at all manifested [in the cognition].

Therefore, since everything is an object only when it does not appear [as such], all cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*). How, then, can there be a proof of the opposite from that? For how could one act toward something that has not been made an object by cognition? That is incorrect.

For it has been asked: "Even when [the object] has been made an object of cognition, how does activity arise? This very relationship of cause and effect is established in this manner. Because it is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it occurs immediately after that apprehension, either from the capacity of its own cause or without a cause; let it be accepted exactly as it is observed. All phenomena are devoid of activity;

or rather, since a distinct entity was not previously apprehended, and since there is no means of valid cognition for its difference [from the effect] even after it has been attained, how could there be a cognition of something distinct? By this, the causal relationship of cooperation is also refuted.

Since no distinction between preceding and succeeding moments is perceived, and since that which exists at the same time cannot be produced [by another], causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is nothing other than the thing's own nature (svarūpa). And since this [nature] exists even in dreams, it follows that cognition is identical in both states.

Therefore, the forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, characterized as distinct, are merely a cognitive distortion (viplava); thus, cognition possesses only the forms of the non-apprehended and the apprehender.
Then, following the recollection of what was previously experienced, there arises merely a conceptual construction (vikalpa) intent solely upon the awareness of its own nature;
from that, such a determination is established, but this is not the ultimate reality (paramārtha) regarding its being so.
For instance, when there is a cognition of [illusory] hairs, it is only through the recollection of the past that, immediately after such an appearance, there was an attainment.
Therefore, conceptual construction arises with the manifestation of the grasped and the grasper;
yet even that [construction], being devoid of the nature of grasped and grasper in its own essence, is established as such by another [cognition],
for it too has no establishment through itself.
By means of cognition, the externality of the object is not established; yet, if it were to exist outside of cognition, that very [externality] would not be established.

(717) If blue is cognized, how can it be called external? And if blue is not cognized, how can it be called external? (718) If it is cognized by another [cognition], then how can it be called external? If it is cognized by another, then there is an infinite regress of "by another" and "by another. (719)
How can this sensation be determined by the self through something else? It cannot be, because its status as an effect [of that self] is unestablished, since its effect is not observed. (720)
It has already been explained that the relationship of cause and effect is not established, because inference was described as having only universals (sāmānya) as its object;

thus, the very fact that "this is seen by another" is not proven. And just as the identity [of a person] is established from seeing effects such as the bristling of hair, [so too is the identity of the self established]. (721)
In that same way, the oneness of pleasure and so forth is established for that very reason. Let it be that pleasure is one thing, and its object of apprehension is another.
(722) If it is thought that pleasure and the rest are distinct because of their difference in location, then how can a difference in location be established in reality if there is oneness?

(723) Why then are the bristling of hair and so forth not [considered] other than the pleasure itself? If pleasure is distinct from the bristling of hair and so forth because of their distinctness, [then the same logic applies]. (724)

If [the two] were different, why would the object of apprehension not also be apprehended as something else? If even the bristling of hair and so forth were contained within our own consciousness, how could there be a clear appearance of mutual contact and the like? If the bristling of hair and so forth belong to this person even without our pleasure, why do the bristling of hair and so forth not also belong to him even without our object of apprehension? If it is claimed that even in that case there is a difference due to a difference in time—

What can time do to that which is indivisible by its very nature? Let there be non-difference [of the cognition]; even in that case, it would not be beyond perception. How could that single entity remain existing while devoid of consciousness?
If it persists as one and the same even now, how can it be imperceptible?
Furthermore, it must be considered how that which is established through the mutual exclusion of individual cognitions can be one;
and if its commonality appears [to you], then why is there a question such as "Was it seen by you or not? for the sake of corroboration by another means of valid cognition?
If one does not believe through direct perception, one will certainly not believe even through verbal testimony;
for that too merely indicates one's own mental representation, such as "what appears to you appears to me. Therefore, even by that means, it should be understood to be in vain;
hence, others—
There is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itarāśrayadoṣa*):
how can that which is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be understood through verbal testimony?
For in the case of an object already perceived directly, the instruction of another is not more authoritative.

Moreover, if perception is a means of valid cognition, then verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition; and if verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition, then perception is so—this is incorrect.
For two people suffering from ophthalmia do not assist one another [to see]; since they lack the capacity individually, their collective assembly likewise lacks it. (729–730)

Therefore, because it is self-cognized in dependence upon instruments such as the eye, cognition itself is the blue object and so forth; thus, the intellect—which consists of the forms of the cognized and the cognizer—is established as being of the nature of cognition precisely in that way, since it is experienced in that very manner. This is the ultimate truth.

Therefore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the result, and the determination that "this is the object" occurs in that very [self-awareness]; there is no such thing as the awareness of an external object.
Consequently, as for what was stated—that there is no example whatsoever for a cognition being the apprehender of its own nature—[that objection is refuted].

In that case, since the absence of error has been established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), how can there be the status of being "without an example"? A rabbit’s horn or the like, which is not apprehended, serves as the example. Or, if [the absence of error] is already established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is the use of an example? Therefore, if we are able to clearly exclude the apprehendable [object] within its own parts, then your thesis (*pakṣa*) would be pure, devoid of any qualification, and would consist solely in the exclusion of the apprehendable.

Furthermore, as for the opponent's claim that this position is contradicted by perception— since it has been stated by him that among the group of cognitions beginning with perception, only external objects remain as their objective supports once the apprehension of one's own parts [of the cognition] is excluded— that is incoherent.

If it is argued that because it has been established that perception lacks external objects, these waking cognitions possess a basis precisely through their own self-certainty since they are free from sublation—[we reply:
no, for their self-certainty is observed only within themselves; as for the certainty regarding an external object, that does not exist when [the object] is not manifest. (731)
There is no such thing as "ascertainment" (niścaya) apart from appearance and recollection;

first, there is no appearance of an object [if it does not appear], and in the absence of appearance, there can be no recollection, because there is no other ascertainment [than these]. Therefore, the statement that "ascertainment is an external object" is merely words and is thus futile.
For a negation is indeed appropriate regarding an object grasped by a defective cognition;
why then is the negation of a grasper that apprehends what was not previously grasped not also logical?
In the *Ślokavārttika*, on page 225, these verses are found;

however, therein, the two half-verses beginning with "agṛhītagrāhyagrāhi—" and "agṛhītasya sattvaṃ tu—" as well as the two verses beginning with "bhedena pūrvagrahaṇāt" and "viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatvam" are not present.
Furthermore, [the verse] "gṛhītamātrabādhe tu svapakṣasyāstyasiddhatā" is also absent.
"How can it be said by you that [the object] is not apprehended?
(Ślokavārttika, pāda 733). The reading is: "one's own position (*svapakṣa*) is not established either."
Furthermore, because the qualifier and the qualified cannot be apprehended as distinct, one must state that both are unestablished, or that one of the two is unestablished. (734)

3. Or there is the reading *aprasiddhobhayatvam vā*. Since difference is apprehended first and its true nature (*tattva*) is subsequently determined, difference does not exist in the ultimate sense; therefore, what contradiction could there be?

(735) The relationship of qualifier and qualified is conceptually constructed through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); in the established doctrine of the Buddhists, it does not function as a causal agent nor does it fall within the range of verbal cognition. (736)

The cognition of the qualifier and the qualified that arises through the eye and the ear— [regarding the reading "of the speaker and the listener,"] because that [cognition] lacks a real objective basis, it does not constitute a self-refuting statement for anyone. (737)
The possibility of a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified exists; therefore, why should the investigation of the meaning of the thesis not be considered sound?

(738) Furthermore, that which is called "objectlessness" (*nirālambanatā*) is not understood as any real entity whatsoever; consequently, a question regarding its exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth is simply not tenable. (739)

If it is a non-entity (*avastu*), how can you wish to awaken us to it, or how do you yourself understand it through your own intellect? Or perhaps it is established by means of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). (Ślokavārttika 226, p. 5) What kind of conceptual construction is there of that which is non-existent? In that case, a real entity (*vastu*) is being postulated with difficulty. If it is asked, "How can a desired [object] exist in the absence [of a real entity]?", it will be stated in reply: "The entity itself is also [non-existent]. (Ślokavārttika 227, p. 5)

This has been stated: the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is established as if distinct through forms imagined by the differentiation of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). This lack of an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*) is thus posited separately by means of the distinction of imagined external objects, for the purpose of making known such a nature; however, no ultimate difference is taught, because the reality of things consists in the teaching of non-difference.
If it is asked, "How can there be conceptual construction regarding a non-entity? [the answer follows].

For this very reason, what kind of conceptualization of a thing could there be otherwise? In that case, it would follow that it is a non-entity; for the activity of conceptualization does not occur in the absence [of an object], nor does that entity exist. (742)
Now, as for this term "condition" (*pratyaya*), it might refer to an object (*karman*), a state of being (*bhāva*), and so forth.
If it refers to a state of being and the like, there would be a contradiction; if it refers to an object, it would be proving what is already established.

In the *Ślokavārttika* (p. 226), it is stated that "karma" is not what is meant by "pratyaya. This [term] is of a different nature as a substratum (*dharmirūpa*), or it may be derived from the analysis of "karma" [as *pra-tyaya*], meaning "that which is made known" (*pratyāyyate*) is *pratyaya*;
or else, *pratyaya* means "cognition" (*pratīti*).
The term *pratyaya* may mean "that which causes one to understand," "that by which one is made to understand," or it may possess the nature of an action (*bhāva*),

an agent (*kartṛ*), or an instrument (*karaṇa*). All of this is untenable if *pratīti* (cognition) is the *pratyaya*, for that cognition does not exist without that which is to be cognized (*pratyāyya*).
In this way, even the agent and so forth [are established];

therefore, the notion that "the cognition is without an object" because it depends on an external object, and that "it is without a basis" because of the non-existence of that [object], involves mutual contradiction.
That is incorrect;
for if cognition (*pratīti*) is what constitutes a mental state (*pratyaya*), how can it be said that it does not exist without another [object],
since that other is not perceived within it?
And in that case, its own nature alone will be what is to be made known; what need is there for anything else?
Thus, it causes its own self to be understood when it has been set forth, and it is by means of itself that it is understood—what contradiction is there in this?
If it is argued that "action" (karma) is not understood as such by its own nature—
since blue and other objects appear in their own form rather than as something else called "action-ness"—

and that this [action-ness] would only be perceived if it were sought after by another agent through its own operation, then that very thing [the object] is the objective support (ālambana) for that other; and since that [separate action-ness] is refuted, how can this be a case of proving what is already established?
However, that very [object] is not established even when being sought; therefore, how could it exist as an object (*ālambana*) by way of being an objective support (*karman*)?
If it is obtained in its own nature at that time, then this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
[Objection: But surely, when it is being apprehended by itself, it is cognized as "I cognize blue. [Reply:
That is incorrect;

for even that cognition which is "I" is a cognition of the body, the sense organs, and the self, because it is experienced as having the same locus [as those], such as "I am one-eyed," "I am happy," or "I am fair-skinned. (744)

Indeed, we do not perceive a self other than the senses and so forth as the objective support for the notion of "I," such that it would be the self which impels them; for if it were so, it would be independent of anything else. Since their own nature arises [spontaneously], there is no other means of proof for them anywhere.
And if that from which their arising is observed were itself the impeller, then they would be mutual impellers by virtue of being mutually dependent. (745–746)

When another aggregate arises from an [initial] aggregate, conventional usage proceeds by way of the relationship between cause and effect. (747) Apart from the form of cognition itself, no other impeller is perceived; or rather, in some cases, it is the prior habituation to such a state that acts as the impeller.

(748) If another cognition arises from a cognition having the form of pleasure or a sense-faculty, then once that [cognition] has assumed the form of blue and so forth, how could there be the status of agent and object? (749)

Alternatively, if they exist simultaneously, there can be no mutual operation [between them]. Consequently, the status of being an object (*karman*) and so forth is not logically possible for existing entities.
(750) As for what was stated:
"For it is accepted that a cognition has no external support (*nirālambanatā*); since it consists of its own consciousness, it does not support anything [external]. (751)
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "pratyāyyasya" [2];
on page 227 of the *Ślokavārttika*,
that [position] is utterly non-existent.

For it is not maintained that a cognition lacks an object in the sense of being devoid of form and so forth; rather, since this [cognition] is excluded from what is non-conscious, it indeed takes its own constituent parts as its object.

Furthermore, it has been established that its lack of an external object—by virtue of its very nature as consciousness—is all the more evident when considered in terms of having no object distinct from itself.
Furthermore, as for what was further asserted— that even the two words possess the status of being the subject [of the proposition] in terms of either their agency or their instrumentality—
Because it lacks a basis, the consequence follows that there is no thesis;
this is an excellent statement, for:

Indeed, it is by those two [terms]—the word "cognition" (*pratyaya*) and the word "without an object" (*nirālambana*)—that [the absence of an object] is made known. Therefore, even for those two, their status as cognitions is established through that very lack of an object. Someone might think: "In this case, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of an external object is merely a property residing in the word itself; since it is merely consistent with reality, its status as the subject of the thesis (*pakṣatva*) is not contradicted. (754)
For the subject (*pakṣa*) is not necessarily within the range of verbal expression,
because it is the object of the means of proof (*sādhana*),
and the means of proof is non-apprehension characterized by perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, the fact that [cognition] has its own form as its object (*svākārālambanatā*) is what is to be proven; that is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
How then can there be an absence of a thesis? Furthermore, since "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is understood here from the context, how can there be occasion for a refutation by means of words?

For that which is not made an object of cognition through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is not what is conveyed by the word; rather, it is precisely that which arises from the context (*prakaraṇa*). Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of meaning from words.
Even for general terms, a specific application is observed through context, as in the case of "bring the *saindhava*," where at the time of a meal, only salt is understood.
This too has passed away with a single puff of breath, as it were,
when he said: "Of that..."
Regarding the word or the cognition:

[the suffix] *ṭi* [indicates that] knowledge is without an objective support (*nirālambana*), and without a sentence that conveys a distinct object, the agent and other grammatical factors cannot exist.

In the *Ślokavārttika*, at the verse beginning with "vākyena," the reading is "bhinnena" (by the distinct); and at the verse beginning with "bandha," the reading is "bādha" (sublation). [This] sublation occurs either in the suffix or in that which is caused by it, according to your own statement. (755) Ślokavārttika, page 227.

If it does not cause cognition, or if nothing is caused to be cognized by it, how can it be such [a means of cognition]? Or, in the absence of an object of cognition, what could the cognition have as its object, since the status of being an agent and so forth is impossible without a distinct object of cognition? Furthermore, if the cognition and its cause are sublated, how could that be avoided by one's own statement? (756)

The agent, the object, and so forth are merely imagined; they do not exist in the ultimate sense. It is said that "the self destroys itself by means of itself. (757) Furthermore, since both the cognition (*pratyaya*) and its object are devoid of external causes, there is no contradiction with one's own statement. Moreover, even if "cognition" were used here in its conventional sense, for us it is established that the apprehending entity is a cognition of another real thing. (758)
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "grāhakaṃ vastu siddhaṃ naḥ" (the apprehending object is established for us).

On page 228 of the *Ślokavārttika*, it is stated that even in its conventional sense, the word *pratyaya* (cognition) establishes a distinct entity as being independent of [mere] conceptualization (*pratīti*). Thus, it is established that *pratyaya* is indeed a separate reality.
Therefore, the fact that [cognition] has external objects as its domain is already established by worldly consensus;
for what is established by worldly consensus cannot be otherwise ordained,
as that would be non-existent.

The establishment of things does not occur through mere worldly consensus; rather, for the establishment of reality, the world acts as an investigative agent. (759) What "world" exists apart from consciousness for the sake of establishing objects? If the world were identical to consciousness, then that [world] would not have been made into an object of support. (760) If the world could discern reality without consciousness, then all these beings—stones and the like—would discern it. (761)
As for what is also said:
"If, having accepted that position, the thesis contradicts what has been accepted"—[the commentary] states:
the thesis is that cognition has an object (*sālambana*) or is without an object (*nirālambana*); having accepted that it has an object, he says...
For you, there is the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmī*) and the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); for us, however, this is not the case in such [a context].
(762) 2 B ṭi—[In the case of] that which is without an objective support (*nirālambana*).
In such a case, your [argument] is unestablished regarding the cognition of another object; for us, it is otherwise regarding the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
Likewise, even if one imagines that the self and its attributes are independent, the same would hold true.
And there is no such thing as "mere conditionality," because it cannot be defined. For instance: || 763 || Thus:

If the cognition (*pratyaya*) were made the subject (*pakṣa*) by accepting that its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is distinct [from itself], then such a property-bearer (*dharmin*) would not be established for you;
for the Buddhist does not accept such a thing.
Alternatively, if the opposite is accepted—that the means of accomplishment is non-distinct—then it remains unestablished for us, the opponents.
For we do not accept that cognition has a means of production other than the senses; likewise, the property of being a quality of the self is unestablished for the Buddhists,
independence is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsakas,
and there is no such thing as mere cognition.
Because its nature as a phenomenon (*dharmittva*) cannot be defined apart from both sides [of the dichotomy],
it has been stated in some way that "the face exists," since this has been said:
That which has become the subject of dispute is necessarily unestablished. If its establishment were already known, for whom would the proof be a proof?

(764) For that very property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) which is distinct [from the subject] and is unestablished as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), it is precisely through the non-establishment of that [qualification] that you intend to point out the non-establishment of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). That very thing, being the locus of dispute, is what must be proven by you. And since the non-establishment of the subject is indeed accepted at the time of the proof by means of that qualification, if that [qualification] itself were established, what then would be the use of a proof that presents what is already established?

It is not the case that a thesis with an unestablished qualification (asiddhaviśeṣaṇa) is necessarily defective, as in the case [of the argument] "sound is perishable" directed against a Sāṃkhya; for that [objection] is incorrect because:

Even with respect to the Sāṃkhya, the defectiveness of the thesis has been refuted; for when the object [of the reason] is established in the example, the thesis cannot have an unestablished qualification. Furthermore, if destruction is unestablished in the example, there would be a defect in the reason—either it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or contradictory (*viruddha*).
If [it is argued that] the fault is that "destruction" (*nirāma*, i.e., self-destruction) is not established in the thesis, [we reply: ...
That is incorrect;
since it is established by that very [reason],
the fact that the qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is not a fault— how could it be a fault?
Indeed, the essential nature itself is not a fault;
if there is a lack of proof in the example, then that would be a fault of the example or a fault of the reason, but it would not constitute a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
Nor would there be a non-cognition of the property (*dharma*) simply because the property-possessor (*dharmī*) is unestablished.
For it is not the case that sound fails to be established as the subject (dharmin) simply because the quality of space has not been established.
Its status as the subject is established by the mere fact of its being apprehended by the auditory organ;
otherwise, nothing could ever be a subject, because the property (dharma) proposed by the opponent would be unestablished in every instance.
Therefore, this is not a fault at all; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
For that very reason, another point stated by the opponent is also incorrect:
the description of others [of the self] as being merely of the nature of word and meaning.
3 B ṭi— in the form of a mere mountain;
4 B ṭi— even so, for you who propound a universal (sāmānyavādin) and do not accept the distinction of the Syādvāda, it would not exist.
768 Thus, by this manner of conceptualization as well, the conceptualization regarding phenomena distinct from the self has been explained.

In the *Ślokavārttika*, verses 228–229, it is stated that because [the opponent] does not admit the distinction between the denoter and other denoted objects, and because for such a proponent it is impossible even to define [the object] as being merely the form of the word-meaning— since, in the absence of the admission of universals (*sāmānya*), it would be impossible for that opponent to raise an objection once the conceptual distinctions (*vikalpana*) regarding properties (*dharma*) and so forth have been established— that [position] is incorrect.

Since the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is used without qualification to mean the mere object of a word, and since its synonym is "manifestation," this [objection] is invalid; for that which constitutes "being a cognition"— whether in the case of a cognition of two moons and so forth, or elsewhere— is already established.
That which is the object of the conceptual determination of a single form is indeed established;
however, as for its further "whatness," since it is entirely subject to investigation, it rests within the middle of the probandum as unestablished—so what is improper here?
This lack of establishment will be raised and refuted later.
First, it is said:
If here [in this argument] objectlessness is being proven in every respect, there would be a non-establishment of the qualification, and no example would exist. (769) 1 T.
In the Ślokavārttika, on pages 228–229:
"If every cognition whatsoever is to be proven as being without an objective basis (nirālambana),
what example (dṛṣṭānta) can there be for that?"
Now, even if one were to argue that the waking cognition is the example, it remains unestablished;
for the dream cognition also possesses an objective basis (*sālambana*), since it has as its object, in some way, things belonging to that time or to another time.
Alternatively, if you claim there is an absence of an object at that time, [the same response applies].

If it is argued that [the cognition] is without an objective support (nirālambana) in some manner or other, then since the cognition of taste is devoid of color-form and so forth, this would be a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
As stated in the *Ślokavārttika* on pages 229–230:
"In whatever way an object is the support (*ālambana*) for a cognition—whether at that same time or at another time—it must be accepted as its support.

Nevertheless, if [cognition] were without a support (*anālambanatva*), it would follow that even the cognition of taste would be without a support in the form of color; yet this is precisely what is desired, so [your argument] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)."
Now, if the cognition has a certain form, then the exclusion of that [external] object is impossible; for since its own form is admitted [to exist], its non-existence is contradicted.
(771) [Ślokavārttika 229–230]
For it is your own admission that the subjective aspect of cognition does not consist in having the form of an object, but rather consists solely in having the form of cognition itself; in that case,
the absence of an object of cognition for cognition would now follow, which is undesirable.

In that case, one must conceive of [the object] as having the nature of an apprehended thing by means of an objective support; yet, if there is no external objective support, then that [external thing] is non-existent.

If, even in the absence of an external objective support, there is still the grasping of it as "external," then the cognition of a pillar and so forth would not occur at all—thus, [your argument] merely proves what is already established.
In this case as well, regarding the cognition "the pot is outside," it is not the pot alone that is the objective support; rather, it is the external object itself.
However, due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pot, there arises the corresponding cognition in relation to the pot.

Now, if it is argued that [cognition] is without an objective basis (nirālambana) because it takes on the form of a pillar and so forth, then a contradiction arises, since the fact of cognition itself is directly perceived.

If it is argued that this is the same in the case of a double moon and the like, [we reply]: no, for that status of being "without an objective basis" applies there because of the sense organ's failure to reach its object; it does not apply because of the absence of the cognition of an actual object.

The claim that cognition perceives what is presented by the sense organs, such as the eye, is said to be "without an objective basis" (nirālambanā) in the case of cognitions of double moons and the like; however,
this does not mean that such a cognition has no object at all.
Previously, he had the cognition of a single moon; by means of that same sensory faculty, there is a [cognition] of two, which is thus without an objective basis (*anālambana*).
However, it is not the case that the object does not exist at all times;
rather, when the perception of a single moon occurs, its opposite [the perception of two] lacks an objective basis. This is the reason for the cognition of its being without an objective basis.
This very point is demonstrated:

"In all cases, when consciousness exists, the status of an object as apprehended or non-apprehended does not depend on the presence or absence of a conjunction between the sense-faculties and their objects.

But for you, since the sense-faculties and so forth are absent apart from the act of apprehension, there can be no reason for them to serve as objective supports; therefore, your negation [of the external world] is untenable. (775–776)
"bhavata" according to the Tibetan translation 5 T.
"Not by way of negation"— thus it says in the He manuscript:
"Cognitions are without objective support."
Thus, this mind, stained by the impurity of false conceptualization, has manifested through supreme egoism; such is the great magnitude of delusion.
For it is as follows:

If it is well-established by means of valid cognition that the word *nirālambana* (without support) has as its denotation something that takes its own part (*svāṃśa*) as its support, how can there be a refutation?

For, through the negation of a support graspable by the senses as imagined by others, this word is employed [to mean] precisely "having its own part as its support"; this is understood from the context and so forth, because otherwise there would be no comprehension of meaning from the word.
In that regard, this meaning is understood from the word in common worldly usage; how then can its definition be impossible?

Is it not the case that even for that [meaning], there is a distinction from the denoter and from other denoted objects? Thus, how can it be said that "the mere word and meaning" constitute the subject (*dharmin*)? True, you have spoken correctly, but what was spoken was improper—so what of it?
It is not only now that non-duality follows, such that there would be no distinction; rather, [the cognition] is indeed distinct from other cognitions and from itself.
In that regard, the cognition of the word "pot" is one thing, and the pot itself is another; and so forth.
Furthermore, words bring the very object previously apprehended within the scope of recollection.

In this regard, what is improper about one who informs another that those very conditions which appear as objects of cognition by way of being the objective supports for blue and so forth are actually without objective support?
If someone perceives smoke that is indeed devoid of fire, should he not be told: "The smoke that you perceive as being without fire does not exist in that manner"?
Or rather, how could there be any suspicion of fault in the speaker?
Now, he might be made to understand by means of the previously observed state of having fire; but how can it be so here?
For here too, cognition arising from a visual disorder (*taimirika-jñāna*) is established as being without an external object (*nirālambana*), since an external thing is impossible.
If it is argued that even there, the sky (*gagana*) is the objective support (*ālambana*):

If it is argued: "Just as in the case of perceiving hair [in the air], space is the object; so too, even when space is the object, there is simply something else appearing, because that which appears lacks the status of being an object; therefore, in the cognition of space, that which appears is itself the object."
In this case as well, let there be everywhere, in the cognition of hair-threads and so forth, a loss of memory due to erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*);
thus, the postulation of a primordial [creation] among worldly things—or its absence anywhere—is indeed an absolute certainty.

Since there would otherwise be no distinction between them, it might be argued that for one who has perceived the cognition of a single moon as having an objective basis (*sālambana*), the cognition of two moons is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*);
but how can this be said of the cognition of a single moon?
If it is argued that even that [reason] has been established as being sublated because it belongs to that same class,
then it has been established that sublation applies to that case as well.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that there is no object of cognition (*ālambana*) which does not appear [to consciousness],
and we shall also demonstrate that blue and other such objects possess the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*).

Just as the cognition of hair-veils and the like is not based on an object consisting of actual hair-veils, so too it follows that the cognition of the form of blue would be based on an object consisting of yellow, sweet, and so forth.

How is it that proving [the non-existence of external objects] by means of the fact that [cognition] does not have taste and so forth as its objective support results in proving what is already established for the cognition of color?

If you argue that the cognition of water does not occur without parched salt-earth heated by rays [of the sun], even though taste and so forth are absent, why then does the consciousness of color occur?
Furthermore, the cognition of water occurs even in the case of real water, even without parched salt-earth heated by rays.
If it is argued that there is a distinction in that case,
then because of their mutual distinction, it follows that both are either without an object or otherwise;
let it be granted, then, that both have an object.

If it is argued that one should not say "scorched by rays" and so forth regarding what appears, because a non-appearing object cannot function as a cause, then [we reply]: the latent impression (*vāsanā*) will be that cause; thus, our desired conclusion is established.

If it is argued, "Then let there be only that which appears; what is the use of anything else?", [we reply] no, because it would follow that there is no distinction between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); for if everything that appears were merely perception, [the object] would possess an objective support (*sālambanatva*). *Note: Ti. = Ṭīkā (Commentary).*

3 B ṭi.—If [cognition] were non-apprehending (anālambana) by virtue of not having a cause for its appearance, there would be no distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous, nor would it possess what is established by worldly consensus. "Everything is non-erroneous with respect to its own nature; with respect to the nature of another, there is error. If it is argued that it possesses an object (*sālambanatva*) because of attainment (*prāpti*), it has been proven that such attainment does not exist.
The attainment of the delusion of water in a mirage might indeed occur; however,
because of momentariness, it is seen that "it does not exist at all times" and "it is not present everywhere at all times."
1. Ṭīkā: Since it has perished, how could that which is perishable remain unperished?
Therefore, recognition (pratyabhijñā) is indeed refuted; thus, everything is consistent.
Therefore, since everything is understood through perception and inference, it has been stated that [the object of cognition] is entirely without a real objective basis (*anālambana*).
Thus, if one refutes a qualification imagined by another after having merely restated it, what fault could there possibly be in this?
By this, the following [argument] is also refuted, which he stated as follows:
"For indeed..."
Since external existence is not established, how can cognition be proven to be without an object? For this subject (pakṣa) is not known when [the existence of external objects is denied].
As it is said in the *Ślokavārttika*, verses 230–231:

"Just as the establishment of the subject (*pakṣa*) cannot occur when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unknown because it is impossible to communicate it to another, so too would it be in the case of a qualifier of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣaṇa*)."

For the meaning of a sentence is not apprehended when the meanings of its constituent words are unknown; and since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established as the meaning of a sentence, it will be demonstrated that the property to be proven (*sādhya*) consists in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*).
(Ślokavārttika 230–231, p.
783) It will be demonstrated that the sense of the possessive suffix is the thing to be proven.
This very thing is non-existent,
since for that [opponent] alone, an external object of cognition is not established in the ultimate sense,
yet is merely accepted by him.
For that very reason, [the existence of the object] is negated in order to eliminate error, since the means of proof (sādhana) is applied for this purpose; this will be demonstrated later.
But how could the non-existence of something established by a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) be the probandum (sādhya)?
If it is argued that [the contradiction] occurs by way of subverting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for if one *pramāṇa* were to subvert another *pramāṇa*, there would be a lack of confidence, leading to the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of the status of *pramāṇa*.
We shall demonstrate that what is called a "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is not possible.
If it is argued that there is a negation elsewhere of what was observed in a particular place, time, and so forth, we say no, because of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).

For that which is observed in one place, such as another country, is not postulated elsewhere; since there is no error [in the observation], the proof of its non-existence there would be futile. (784) Now, if it is argued that the postulation [of the object] elsewhere arises from some scripture or from the absence of other means of valid cognition, [we reply:
indeed, errors are not seen to be absent.

In that case, whatever error there may be regarding a certain place or object perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed sublated by that very means of valid cognition; for what incapacity can there be regarding an error itself? Indeed, it is that which is occasionally an error that is sublated.
But as for that which is absolutely [erroneous], it must be turned back;
in turning it back, there is great human effort.
Is it not the case that it is turned back by demonstrating elsewhere a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)?
As for that which is always merely an error, how is it to be removed? And since there is no sublater (bādhaka), how can it be called an error?
That too is incorrect.
Since there is no such thing as a sublater at all— for what would this sublater be? Is it the destroyer of that [cognition], or is it the one that causes the loss of the object to be apprehended?

In the absence of an object to be grasped, how can there be another [opposing] position consisting of three alternatives: [1] that the sublater is the indicator; [2] that it produces the absence of the cognition of the sublated; or [3] that it [produces the absence] of its objective support? In that case, would that [absence] be something already produced or something unproduced?
How can the non-existence of that which is unborn be established by him? Never has the destruction of a donkey’s horn been brought about by anyone.

(787) Nor is the non-existence of an entity that has already arisen established in such a manner; to say "it exists because of its cause" and "it does not exist because of a sublater" is mere recklessness.
(788) If this entity has already arisen, by whom could its non-existence be produced?
The *kiṃśuka* flowers are dyed by fate; who now dyes them?
If they are so produced from a cause, then as they are produced, so they exist; how then can there be an onset of destruction?
If that were so, it would follow that what was destroyed is the very same thing that exists—this is a great inconsistency.
Now, if it is destroyed in the same manner that it was not born, then in that case,
if that which is born in one form were to be destroyed by another, let blue and so forth be destroyed by another form such as yellow and so forth. (789)
And yet that [nature] does not belong to it; thus they alone are "colored by fate" (daivarakta).
Furthermore, it is destroyed either later or at all times by that very nature. If it were destroyed later, then it would have possessed that nature previously. (790)

How can there be the destruction later of that which was born with that very form? That which was born with that form at that very time is destroyed later. (791) If that form does not exist later, then that *kiṃśuka* tree is [as good as] dead by fate; if its destruction occurred previously, then it was so due to the cause itself.
(792) Let it be examined: what further purpose would there be for a destroyer of this?
This is the same even regarding the destruction of the object;

for just as it was not born by that [nature], there is no destruction of its form by that [destruction]; and just as it was not born by that [destruction], there is likewise no destruction of its form by that [destruction]. (793)

Because it is purposeless, because it is impossible, and because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could even the conceptualization of this object not be absent for those possessed of intelligence? (794) Furthermore, if you claim that the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) makes known the absence of an objective support (*ālambana*),
that too is incorrect.
When that entity is perceived, it is not then understood as being non-existent. (Yadā sa dṛśyate bhāvo nābhāvapratyayas tadā)
)—This additional reading appears in the Tibetan version:

"When that entity is seen, then non-existence does not exist; when the entity is not seen, its non-perception is the sublater [of existence]. Thus, when the entity is not established, there is no non-existence with its qualification; and when the qualification is not established, how can there be the power of cognition for you? (795–796)
Furthermore, a qualification established elsewhere is here treated as a mere restatement; for that [qualification] exists there as a positive entity and cannot be a qualification of a non-entity.
(797) If it is argued that "that very thing does not exist elsewhere," then what is the purpose of negating something already understood in that way?
(798) Nor can there be a negation of something understood otherwise; this has already been stated previously, so it need not be repeated again and again. (799)
When an entity is not perceived, there can be no negation of it. If its negation is performed by first qualifying it through memory, [we reply:

if one apprehends it according to how it is remembered, there is no negation whatsoever. If one apprehends it through memory as having its own intrinsic nature (svarūpa), that is not a qualification of non-existence.
Now, whatever appears in memory or in conceptual construction (vikalpa), that exists only to that extent; an external form does not exist.
If that is the case, then whatever appears as "external" elsewhere in worldly convention exists merely as such; its true reality is not perceived.
(803) The object of apprehension is mere cognition, for no external thing is perceived; indeed, there is no discernible distinction between this and cognitions such as those in dreams. (804)
Because this [cognition] arises merely from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and lacks the determination of specific distinctions, cognition is without an objective basis (*anālambana*).
How, then, is the relationship between the sublated and the sublator perceived?
Having superimposed unity upon that which is being perceived, when a subverting cognition occurs in the interim, the status of the sublator is established therein. (vv. 805–806)
If this sublater did not exist, this [object] would remain exactly as it is; therefore, since it remains uninterrupted, the sublater is considered to be without a cause.
For instance, when the persistence of every entity through another time occurs precisely within that same interval, [another nature...]
When another cognition characterized by transformation occurs,
then the preceding object of focus, being interrupted by it, ceases to be the object of determination;
therefore, that [subsequent cognition] is established as the sublater.
For if this [present cognition] were not to exist, then the object of the preceding cognition would remain uninterrupted, just as it is at other times;
therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood through a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that [the object] is indeed interrupted.
Thus, there exists both the relationship of the destroyer and the destroyed, and the relationship of the apprehended and the apprehender.
For instance,

when one has ascertained an object such as a jar that is currently out of sight, the establishment of that [object] as the objective support occurs through a cognition in which the form of that [object] arises. (808) Likewise...

Cognition is as clear as crystal; whatever object is presented to it, having assumed that particular form, it shines forth in exactly that way. (809) For instance, if cognition were not clear, then an object—established through some scripture or inference as being "present" and "existent"—would merely be in a state of flux, with no certainty as to whether it exists or does not exist therein.

When the object itself has been fully perceived, the mind—having been as if floating—reaches the shore and becomes stable; therefore, that [object] is established as the objective support (*ālambana*). For it is said: "One whose mind is engaged in reflection, with a mind that was previously floating, becomes stable regarding what was formerly seen, thinking, 'This is that which was seen. (810)

When one conceptualizes what has been seen or heard but forgotten—searching for what was seen there or what was heard in that proliferation of discourse—and brings to mind what was heard and so forth, then, as it becomes present, one establishes it as an objective support (*ālambana*) for the purpose of abandoning the state of floating [in uncertainty] by means of its stability; such is worldly convention.
If you ask, "Is this the very reality?"—is this so for this object? No, because it is not established through either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), it is a non-entity (*avastu*).
For the existence of something remote is not perceived by means of perception.

Since that [object] is absent, inference also does not exist; how then, while there is a cognition of something remote, could the existence of perception as having that [object] as its objective support be established? And only when perception possesses an objective support is it established as being connected with a real entity.

From that [perception], inference proceeds; because it arises from a mark (*liṅga*) that is connected to a real entity (*vastu*), it makes that entity known. Therefore, since inference has as its object an entity established by inference, perception must have an objective support (*sālambana*). From that, there is a connection between the entity and inference, and from that, the comprehension of the entity—thus there would be a circularity (*cakraka*) and a lack of stability. Consequently, the attainment of a real entity is impossible. For if the entity is not thus comprehended, one’s acceptance of it is merely based on faith, since the prior cognition of the form of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be impossible. (Verse 812)
In accordance with that [perception], I previously established the relationship of qualifier and qualified, simply to avoid disregarding its form.

(813) Alternatively, if you [the opponent] disregard it, how could there be the cognition of this? If, upon such investigation, it does not exist in reality, (814) then what fault is there in its non-existence, such that you should be questioned? If you argue that there is a relationship of sublated and sublator between two successive cognitions, (815) [we reply: ...

In one's own cognition, whose fault is it that one should be questioned? Is anyone ever known to question themselves? (816) From where does that person's error arise? The self is not the object of questioning. If error is already established here, what is the use of searching for its cause?
(817) When even another person is made to understand this very clearly, then he too does not say, "Why is my error such as this? (818)

For when, upon the occurrence of an error, one who possesses self-reflection subsequently sublates it by thinking "this is not silver," does anyone then direct a challenge to oneself [as follows]: "How is it that I, while silver has not been apprehended, establish its qualifier, which is non-existence? And how, while the qualifier is unestablished, could I know that remote qualifier by means of which there would be no fault in my own position?
The same applies even in the case of communicating to another.
But surely, while error is possible there because of the perception of real silver, how can there be error here when nothing at all has been perceived? We shall demonstrate this later.
Furthermore, if error were somehow apprehended in an ultimate sense, what would be the point now of the exertion in searching for the cause of that error?
If there were no cause, there would be no error at all;

this is not the case, for when a cause exists, there is no error even regarding the ultimate reality. If it is argued that error exists because it has a cause, then even so, what you desire is undermined. (819)
The very notion that "there is no cause" is itself an error;
otherwise, every cognition of yours would be an error.
Furthermore, even regarding what is not an error, one must certainly inquire: "From where does this error arise?"
If it is argued that this is because it is not so perceived,
this is equally true even in the case of error; for if error is preceded by non-error, [then the same applies].
If, for some reason, there is no such thing as non-erroneousness at all due to the absence of its cause, then why should there be error? Let it be so; however, how is it to be understood?
For error is established precisely through the opposite of non-erroneousness.
The same applies elsewhere as well: non-delusion is the opposite of delusion;
furthermore, delusion does not exist in a positive form, but rather as the opposite of non-delusion, which occurs when there is a sublater (*bādhaka*).
Therefore, from the opposite of that, there is error because of non-error.
1. The passage following this, which was located on pages 33a6–34a3 of manuscript C, has been set aside due to negligence;
that too is incorrect.
Whatever is perceived in a positive form is indeed understood as such; the certainty is that there is no external positive entity, and it is only an error in that regard.
Now, if it is not said that where there is a cause, that is an error, [then one must admit] that whatever is an error does not exist without a cause.
"In that case, then, the reason is qualified.
Why this very delusion? For delusion occurs through inversion;
it is not stated as being in a positive form"—this reading was rewritten by Vabhūticaṃdra at the end of his own manuscript.
Error occurs because of the existence of a cause for error, and not otherwise; and the determination of that cause is possible only when the nature of the error has been known.
For when a reason is qualified [by its effect], the error must first be known, and then that error itself must be known as arising from a cause; thus, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, in whatever form that error exists, let that very cognition of that form be the cause for its establishment, or let it not;
for an entity exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), not by way of the nature of its cause.
If it is asked, "From where does that own-nature come? [the answer follows].
What of this? Why should even this cognition of the nature of error not itself be an error? If it exists in the manner in which it is cognized, what fault is there?
If it is argued that the preceding [cognition] was not an error, that too is incorrect;

for there would be the cognition of silver when the perception of the mother-of-pearl has ceased. And if there were yet another [cognition] that causes the cessation of the perception of the mother-of-pearl, [the same problem would recur]. (822)
In that case, how could there be truth in that cognition which apprehends silver? Or rather, why is it not seen that both [silver and its absence] do not exist?
(823) Furthermore, if truth were perceived anywhere, then because of the existence of a firm basis (*avaṣṭambha*) in that case, there would be a reversal in the other case.

(824) For the reversal in the other case would occur through a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*); if there is no sublater at all, then that [reversal] cannot establish the truth of the opposite. (825)
Who could then establish the non-existence of error?
To this it is replied:
whether there is a cognition of error or otherwise, how can there be a determination of its non-existence?

Furthermore, if certainty is produced by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), what need is there for another means of producing certainty? (826) If it is argued that the apprehension of the opposite [of the object] constitutes the proof of its non-existence, then let there simply be self-cognition alone; consequently, there would be no cognition of an external object. (827) Therefore, the logical conclusion is that non-apprehension alone is the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and nothing else.
Since that [nature] exists here as well, how could consciousness be "possessing an object"?
From this follows the cognition of a self consisting of the cognized and the cognizer.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the refutation of the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is being established—that too is utterly untenable.

In this context, what is to be proven from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*) is precisely the absence of the sense of possession (*matvarthābhāva*). Otherwise, the proof of the lack of an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) would not be established.

(828) Since the proposition "consciousness is without an objective support" intends to prove the non-existence of the state of having an objective support (*ālambanatva*), why is it that [the opponent] projects that very [non-existence] as the thing to be proven (*sādhya*)?
For how could that which has been made the subject (pakṣa) by one's own intention be treated otherwise? Whatever is intended to be proven is precisely the subject;
yet, if it were such [as you claim], it would be impossible to prove.

That being the case, this is merely a fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) and not a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*). When proving [something] by means of its possessing non-existence (*abhāvavattva*), it is simply the sense of possession (*matvartha*); however, there is no evidence for the ultimate reality of such a possessive relation, since one relies upon an imagined relationship between a substratum and its property (*dharmidharmabhāva*).

By means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), a property that is in fact identical with its own nature (*svabhāva*) is established as if distinct and is conceptually imagined as having objective reality; although this linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) exists by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there is no harm in that. Let this convention proceed for now like the closing of an elephant's eyes; yet, upon further investigation, even this will surely fall apart.
Now, what is this "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti)?
If it is a real entity, then that very thing should be stated; why use another name for it?

Now, if nothing exists, then what is this so-called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) other than the appearance of truth? However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is not reality; when examined, it is empty, and thus it is called "conventional. Because it conceals reality, it is "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). For it is not logical to claim that the form appearing before us is non-existent merely because of that [conventionality].
Furthermore, when subjected to investigation, because it is non-existent, there is the ascertainment of its absence;
therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is called "conventional," whereas it is said to "exist conventionally" from the perspective of deluded people.
And since there is no arising of a sublation for that which is erroneous, it is called "conventional truth" (saṃvṛtisatya) because of the conceit of its reality;
therefore, this too must be said:
"If it is non-existent, what is this 'error'? If it is existent, how can there be error?"

If it is argued that an appearance of what is not real is an error, why is there not a "conventional" [reality] regarding that which is not real?
