(Ślokavārttika 231–32) If there is no truth in that which is not real, would there not be an appearance of truth? Therefore, conventional truth is also the state of being an appearance of truth. (Ślokavārttika 231–32)
The statement that it is a deceptive utterance—like that of a *tāla* bird, a crow, or a flute—is inconsistent even regarding what appears to be true;

for what deception could there possibly be in speaking of something that does not appear to be true? Therefore, when one’s own intentions are unknown to others, any talk uttered with the desire to proclaim one’s own excellence is mere idle chatter; there is no other deception whatsoever.
Let this matter rest for now; something else is stated here, which was said by another [author] in this very context.

Whether it be a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) or an absolute negation (*niṣedha*), [the argument] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the world is non-different from [the cognition] in terms of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth.
(834) There is no distinctness at all from the cognition on account of the world's being an object of knowledge,
because there is no external objective support (*ālambana*) that is separate from it.

If you argue that the proof is already established because [the object] is utterly distinct [from the cognition], then it is said to be without an objective support (*nirālambanatā*). But if [you claim they are] somehow [distinct], your initial thesis is contradicted by what you have postulated.

(835) If it is maintained that cognition is without an objective support due to the difference in forms such as the "object" and so forth, yet it is non-different from the apprehending subject, then a difference in functional capacity (*śakti*) is contradicted. (836)

If it is argued that the arising of a cognition devoid of an objective support is established, we accept this as being free from both an external object and a grasper, since it is so observed. However, you do not in any way accept its correctness;
for this cognition terminates within itself, like the cognition of water in a mirage.

If the objectlessness of cognitions such as those of a shrine (caitya) were not apprehended by the cognition arising from the proof as being their very nature, then—because of the diversity of objects and because no counter-example is refuted—the existence of having an object would be established by its very form; who could then prevent it? (839–840) If even the word "cognition" (pratyaya) is grasped as being a cognition, and its having consciousness as its object is what is being denied, then you are proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). (841)
If the capacity to produce cognition is to be negated, then the probandum is not established;
for, according to you, the employment of a means of proof is impossible without [the means] being informative.
Nor is there any denotation without a connection, and that [connection] does not exist because of the difference [between the word and its object].

And this [inference] cannot occur without a cognition that makes known the distinction residing therein (i.e., the distinction between the subject and the property). Furthermore, if the application of the proof were desired for the sake of producing that [cognition], it could not take place unless the audience has grasped the sentence with its constituent parts separately—namely, the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the proponent (*vādin*), and the opponent (*prativādin*). In that case, the thesis would be sublated by one's own prior admission.
In some places there is a difference in the reading; thus, all this [that has been said] is of little consequence, because... [Ślokavārttika, p.
It is said to be without an external object because it is not distinct from consciousness. Furthermore, blue and other such objects are not separate from cognition, as they possess its attributes;
yet, even though they share those attributes through properties such as being knowable, they remain indeed distinct because they lack the nature of cognition itself.

For even when one possesses human status, a *caṇḍāla* is not something distinct from a Brahmin; therefore, because cognition has as its objective support that which is distinct from the self, it is not "possessing an objective support" [in the sense relevant here]. By the context, this is understood to mean "devoid of the nature of cognition. Furthermore, just as knowability (*prameyatva*) is non-distinct from the object of knowledge (*prameya*), so too how could there be a difference between this [self] and cognition? Thus, how can this be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?

If it is argued that there is no difference between consciousness and that which is other than it because both are objects of cognition (*prameyatvāt*), [we reply: because of its being consciousness, that which is other than it does not exist at all; it is simply consciousness itself. (847) In the proof of the absence of an objective support (*anālambana*) based on the requirement of absolute difference, why is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)? For if there were absolute difference in the state of non-cognition (*abodhatva*), how could there be such extreme distinctness?

(848) If there is difference in any form whatsoever, there is always difference alone, because it is impossible to perceive something as both different and non-different. Therefore, for that which is different, there is indeed absolute difference. If that [object] were to have an objective support, it would necessarily have only its own part as the objective support. Consequently, how can there be the charge of "proving what is already established"?

Even if there is no difference [between the object and the cognition] because the object has the form of cognition, let there be an internal distinction; nevertheless, since the nature of awareness is not distinct from that [object], how could both [the subject and object] have an objective support (*sālambana*) when only the form of awareness exists? Furthermore, in the case of pleasure and pain, even though they are both of the nature of awareness, that [objective support] does not exist for both.

If you claim there is a distinction between the grasped and the grasper, how can there be such a distinction between two things that are non-different from awareness? And as for the distinction between white, blue, and so forth—who would deny the non-difference [of these appearances] from awareness? (vv. 849–850)

Just as this distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth exists even for those whose nature is consciousness, so too there is a distinction between the white [color] and the pleasant [feeling], yet there is no cognition of them as being distinct in the sense of being the grasped and the grasper.

Just as there is a real distinction between pleasure and pain despite their non-difference in terms of being consciousness, what contradiction is there in their being distinct by virtue of being white and pleasant?
However, the state of having the forms of the grasped and the grasper does not manifest at all.
For apart from [the objects such as] white or pleasure, no state of being a "grasper" (subject) is perceived as appearing;
therefore, the designation of "grasper" and so forth has been proposed by wicked people whose minds are corrupted by their own arbitrary fancies.
And if the arising of a cognition that is without an objective support (*nirālambana*) is being established, how is this very same position shown as distinct from the previous position? (852)
All cognition is without an object, and likewise all that has an origin [is without an object];

there is no difference between these two in their proof. How then could a property (*dharma*) not be proven? (853) This very property must be proven by a cognition arising from the means of proof; for if cognition were to possess an object, its state of being without an object would be destroyed. (854)
For when it is established that all cognition arises as being without an objective support (*nirālambana*),
then, by implication, the state of being without an objective support is established as the property of the subject (*dharmin*).
This being so, the state of having an objective support (*sālambanatā*), which is accepted only through the force of delusion, is indeed refuted.
How is the presentation of the proof futile?
For it has been established that, in the case of the word "pratyaya," the word "pratyaya" does not apply at all due to the context.

Consequently, the argument that the proof is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) because sound is not of the nature of consciousness is untenable; for it was never intended to deny the capacity of sound to produce a cognition, which would render the proof redundant.
It is not that cognition itself does not possess origination;
rather, this is the meaning of the doctrine of "without an objective basis" (*nirālambanavāda*):
if cognition, even though it arises, is without an objective basis, then what is the use of its having arisen at all?
If, on the other hand, it has an object, then it is inconclusive by virtue of that very fact;
that too is incorrect.

Since it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that is to be proven, the proof-effect (*sādhana*) merely effects an exclusion of the opponent’s position; how, then, could such a proof be futile? (855) This point—that all cognition is without objective support (*nirālambana*)—must be understood through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, how could there be the presentation of a proof? And if that were so, then by means of that very proof, the fact that even the cognition of the lack of an objective basis is itself without an objective basis would be established;
but if that [cognition] is without an objective basis, how can the establishment of the lack of an objective basis [of all things] be achieved?

The validity of inference does not derive from its correspondence with an object, nor does it possess an objective referent by virtue of having an objective referent; for how could there be correspondence when the objective referent is not perceived?
How can there be correspondence with the cognition "it does not exist" if that object is subsequently not perceived due to the non-perception of what is perceptible?
If this is so, even a cognition without an objective basis becomes the cause for the determination of reality;
therefore, the application of a means of proof is indeed a communicator of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and not a non-communicator.
Therefore, even if the meaning of a word consists in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there is indeed a relation among the word-meanings;
furthermore, the distinction between them is merely conceptual,
and a thesis (*pakṣa*) with parts certainly exists as an object for the apprehension of difference by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti*).

The apprehension of a distinction between the proponent and the opponent collapses at the very outset; and even that [apprehension], like a dream, is subsequently without objective support. When the task has thus been accomplished, what will the objection regarding "unestablished" (asiddha) and so forth achieve now?
Moreover—
Since that has already been established previously, what is the point of this objection?
It is merely a means of astonishing women and Śūdras, uttered by wicked and wretched people who are ignorant of the truth.
Furthermore, for one who lacks the realization of reality, that which is joined with illogic does not reach dissolution.

Therefore, even if one were to provisionally accept the position of the manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*) and so forth—as if closing one's eyes like an elephant—one would incur no fault by subsequently establishing its non-existence through the process of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

Now, one might object: "If I am demonstrating that I perceive only my own appearance, I am contradicted by another who perceives otherwise. To this we reply: even that [contradiction] is indeed perceived.
Therefore, how can it be established that cognition has its own self as its objective support?
That [objection] is incorrect;
for it has been demonstrated that there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the claim that "it is perceived by another."

If it is argued that for the *prāśnikas* (judges/arbiters) as well, there is no cognition of anything other than their own respective parts, and thus—because of the statement that [cognition] is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*)—there is indeed such a cognition, then from what source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does this cognition of yours arise? For the *prāśnikas*, the operation of the means of proof (*sādhana*) cannot occur without the apprehension of difference.
Alternatively, if those who do not possess the cognition of difference are not considered *prāśnikas*, then...
That is incorrect:
if those who perceive the truth in this matter do not possess the status of judges, then those who do not know the truth certainly have no qualification for being judges.
(857) Furthermore, if the status of a judge does not exist due to partiality toward one side, how could there ever be one who is free from partiality? (858)

For it is improper to understand two things that are mutually contradictory; from the cognition of each one individually, there arises a partiality toward one side or the other. (859) Consequently, when two disputants themselves are mutually contradictory, there must be other judges for their dispute, leading to an infinite regress.
(860) If the disputants themselves were to act as judges, there would be mutual dependence, because they too would certainly have partiality toward their own respective positions. (861)

Therefore, when something falls within the scope of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), its acceptance must be mandatory. As for that which was previously accepted by you, it contradicts this [position].

When the judges possess the perception of a distinction among the proponent, the opponent, and the disputants, even so, if they should reverse their view due to the words of the proponent, they must not contradict that which has come forth by the force of valid cognition.

If, for those who investigate by means of their own intellect, that [position] turns out to be perfectly pure, why would there be a reason not to accept it? Therefore, since it is already accepted previously, how can one say "by his word" in such a manner?
Indeed, even if this [subsequent position] is supported by the force of valid cognition, what is this that you say so loudly regarding the former [position], which is as weak as a fireless hearth?

In the thesis that "the cognition in which there is the conceit of reality is without an objective basis," there is a contradiction for one who does not accept that [cognition] possesses reality. (863) Furthermore,
it might be argued:

Furthermore, since the understanding of phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth is not established from the perspective of ultimate reality, the instruction of phenomena and the like to the disciple and to oneself would not be possible.
Ślokavārttika, p. 234:

"Furthermore, because of the performance of that [practice], a distinction is clearly intended by the Buddhas; since it is accepted in other sūtras, there would be a contradiction with scripture (āgama). Moreover, because it is well-known to the whole world, there would be a contradiction of the [proponent's] thesis."
And if the cognition of the complete means [of proof] is held to be false, then—
[as stated] in the sealed manuscript— the deficiency [of the argument follows].
If it is asserted that there is a total absence of all [objects] or a deficiency as one pleases,
then, if those [cognitions] possess an objective support (*sālambanatva*), the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to them.
In the three sealed treatises:

if that other [thesis] were the proposition (*pratijñā*), then the cognition of that other would be false, because it does not fall within the scope of the thesis and so forth; therefore, it cannot be considered part of the thesis and its components.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading here is "pakṣabādho 'tra te dhruvam" (the sublation of your thesis is certain here),
and "pakṣādī" does not exist [in that version].
By the consequence of that falsity, nothing prior would be established;
for at that time, there would be no distinction between the means of proof and the object to be proven.

In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "stambhādisādhanajñāna. To the extent that the very thesis itself is stated as being distinct from those [other things], to that same extent there would be no sublation of the falsity and so forth for the opponents.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is: "yāvadyāvatpratijñeyaṃ tadanyasya pratīyate" (870.7);
in the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is: "tadanyabādhanam" (8).

There is no non-erroneous contradiction, nor is there sublation by means of inference; in this manner, a counter-argument (pratisādhana) must be stated for all these positions. [Verse 871] "The cognition that has an external object as its support is a valid cognition, because it is a cognition free from sublation, just like the cognition that sublates dreams and the like. [Verse 872] If one should say that even that [cognition] is false, provided that dreams and the like are not sublated...
"In that case, you would have no example based on similarity for your proof now.
This is found in that very same printed text: "Therefore, sā..."
If it were accepted that the cognition of consciousness’s existence, its distinctness, its momentariness, and so forth, were likewise true, then [the reason] would be inconclusive (anaikāntika). 874

In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "and correctly" (*samyak ca*). If there were a false apprehension of that [object], it would follow that the thesis is sublated; and in that case, the established distinction between those bound and those liberated could not be maintained.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "abhyupapattau ca";
and consequently, the futility of the effort for liberation would follow for you.
12. This [argument] is incorrect; see Ślokavārttika, page 236, verse 236.

For if the notion of a transmigrating being were established with reference to something other [than the self], then this consideration of dharma, adharma, and so forth would be entirely inconsistent. (877) Even if it were not the ultimate reality, the pursuit of what is desired and so on is said to be like children’s play; therefore, for the sake of accomplishing one's desires, dharma is not taught [as the primary goal]. (878)

This transmigrating being certainly determines the distinction that "dharma is the means to what is desired" and "that which is other than this is not dharma," because his latent impression of duality has not yet vanished.

And when he attains liberation, he has no purpose whatsoever; for one who knows the ultimate truth does not engage in activities for the sake of achieving desired objects that are merely the domain of children's play.

Since all people proceed toward that in which they possess the cognition of reality— just as one does not fail to act out of passion with the notion that a deformed woman is beautiful— therefore, even regarding what is unreal, people proceed with the cognition of it as real. Why, then, having closed one's eyes like an elephant, should one not provide instruction on each such [object]?

By this, it has been established that practice therein is not contradictory. What contradiction could there be with those [teachings] stated in the Sūtras according to their intended meaning? (881) If there were sublation by the perception of one who does not know reality, it would be a case of proving what is already established; for no instruction is given to him regarding the lack of objective support (*anālambanatva*) of all [cognitions]. (882) Furthermore, his cognition of the entire means of proof is devoid of objective support. However, when he is awakened to reality, there is no fault even if everything [else] is absent. (883)

In that case, the non-existence of everything whose nature is an object of cognition is accepted; therefore, its proof would be without an object. If that [proof] is not established, then by that [reason], the non-erroneousness [of cognition] proves the existence of an objectless state. Since that is observed to have a similar property (*sādharmya*), how can there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntatā*) because of it?
(884–885) If this is accepted as the proposition regarding something other than that, then even for a cognition of something other than that, non-falsity is not denied. (886)
How can a fault based on that [objection] be false, given that the desired [point] is not established? There is no infinite regress in the thesis regarding that which is other than this.

(887) Where there is the conceit of existence, that is considered to be without an objective basis; even in the case of correspondence with something else, "lack of objective basis" has been defined. (888) And in this way, how can a counter-argument be demonstrated? It has been proven that the state of having a cognition free from sublation is unestablished. (889)

The cognition that sublates [the dream-cognition] and so forth has been established by the non-perception of reality; therefore, because it serves as a sublater of the inference arising from that [dream-cognition], [the opponent's reason] is unestablished (asiddha). (890) Furthermore, regarding the argument that the reason [“because it is a cognition”] establishes that cognitions free from sublation possess an objective basis, the objection that this reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to cognitions such as those of momentariness is improper.
This is because cognition is indeed momentary and devoid of external objects. (891)

Since the momentariness of consciousness and form has been established, this cognition of momentariness possesses an objective support (*sālambana*). Therefore, the position [of the opponent]—to the effect that "therefore, the state of being without an objective support is not established for anything including external objects"—is [refuted].
Cognitions do not have external objects as their supports, just like dream-cognition.

If it is argued that the specific thesis has been made inconclusive (anaikāntika) by the cognition of momentariness and so forth, we say no; for in the system of the Yogācāras, what is to be proven is precisely that [the object] is of the nature of consciousness itself. Therefore, just as the state of having an objective support is observed in the case of consciousness, so too is the state of having an objective support of that same nature [established], despite the difference [between the example and the subject].
Now, first of all, an external object is not established;
for the cognition of momentariness does not have an external object as its basis,
because it is as follows:

The cognition of momentariness and so forth is either perception or inference; it is not inference, because [inference] stands as having an object-support through something other than that [direct experience].
For those who possess knowledge, the state of having an object-support does not arise from mere non-discrepancy;
for that non-discrepancy which exists by means of inference is mediated by another cognition.
Therefore, inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it produces another cognition of that same nature,
and not merely because of the apprehension of its own internal form;
furthermore, this other cognition is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For the conceit of grasping an object occurs only upon direct realization;

and that direct realization, being the very nature of a momentary cognition consisting of knowledge, can be apprehended only through self-awareness (*samvedana*), not by means of a separate awareness distinct from its own essence. Now, if there exists a counter-argument, this very position of self-awareness is not established.

For when that [object] is being experienced and nothing else is experienced, who then can prevent the self-awareness of its own nature? (894) If it is argued that there is awareness through non-awareness, why is there not awareness of everything? If you say, "It is not seen to be so," then why is it not observed otherwise? (895) Since the argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*) is thus exhausted, one should accept things exactly as they are observed. The self is seen as the experiencer; how then is its perception [of itself] considered to exist? (896)

If this [self-awareness] is established through self-cognition, then there is nothing additional regarding blue and so forth either. If the substantiality of the self is not at all proven by that which is measured [by cognition], then why is it not accepted that the occurrence of blueness in blue and so forth also arises from cognition?
Just as the nature of the self as a substance is cognized by another consciousness (*saṃvitti*), why is it not likewise admitted for blue and so forth?
Even for blue, its nature as self-cognition will be one thing and its nature as a substance another;
thus, like the self, blue and the rest would also be of the nature of self-cognition— or else, for the Buddhist, the dual nature [of being both cognition and object] would be unestablished.
That [objection] is equally unproven for anyone;

for it is not possible for a single thing to possess two forms merely by name. The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) functions on the basis that "what is one must be of a single form. If that which is one were to have multiple forms, it would follow that everything is one. (898)

If the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*) were one and the same, why is blue and so forth not accepted as such? For in that case, both the object and the cognizer would be one within the self and the blue. (899) If [you argue they are not one] because they occupy different locations, why not because they have different forms? Indeed, a distinction based on a difference in form is well-known to all the world.
(900) For how could there be a distinction by way of spatial location if there is no difference in form?
And this being the case, there would either be a distinction of place and so forth, or else a distinction based on pervasiveness.
Therefore, without self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), cognition itself is not established; thus, every cognition is indeed without an external object (anālambana).

Even the distinction between the bound and the liberated does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; for indeed, no distinction ever appears to those who perceive with equanimity everywhere. (902) Even the effort toward liberation and so forth does not, in any case within the world, establish an ultimate state.
If the consideration of its futility is applicable there, why would it not also be applied to the horn of a hare? (903)
Just as that effort is not ultimately real, so too is the distinction between those who are bound and those who are liberated; this is the same for both cases.

Furthermore, the cognition of external existence and so forth, which arises through conceptual construction, is false; however, the discernment of "externality" and the like is not established by non-conceptual means. (904)
It is precisely through conceptualization that one establishes external, internal, and common objects, as well as the causes of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth;

however, it has been demonstrated above that by means of non-conceptual direct perception, only the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended, not the nature of another. Therefore, this [objection] is refuted:
if the cognition of the existence of knowledge and so forth arises through conceptualization...
In the Ślokavārttika, it is stated:
"Falsehood is accepted [by you], yet no cognition of this [object] is observed here through any other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
Therefore, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge, the existence of cognition and so forth is difficult to establish. (905)
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "and existence and non-existence are difficult to establish";
for it is said that the object of non-conceptual [perception] is indeed the external object itself, which is to be understood through sublation (*bādha*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Furthermore, that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is conceptual in nature, and for the Buddhist, conceptual cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, the existence of cognition and so forth would necessarily collapse due to the absence of a valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, this [position] is untenable.

For, if the validity of conceptual construction were logical only in the absence of anything else, then it would be logical that the validity of conceptual construction is not [universally] tenable; however, when neither conceptual construction nor anything else possesses the status of a valid means of cognition, [then its validity is untenable]. 906–907.

Even if it were being disintegrated at that time, one might commit an offense against everything; yet if conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is not thus [denied], by whom can it be prevented from the perspective of the conventional (*saṃvṛtyā*)?

(908) [Objection: Is it not the case that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself is the conventional? If that is the cause of conventional practice, then that [conceptual construction] itself would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it is non-contradictory with conventional practice.
[Reply: That too is incorrect.

If there were the possibility of an appearance whose form has not been discerned— an appearance arising from the attachment of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of non-erroneous misapprehension (*avisamvādi-akhyāti*)—
then, in the case of two [objects] such as gold or the like perceived by one with jaundiced eyes, what ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*) could there be in their mutual consistency?
We shall explain this further below.

Furthermore, all the false cognitions of those such as ourselves arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpanāt*); it is not difficult to find [examples of] existence and so forth, whether in proximity or at a distance.
(Ślokavārttika, page 237)
This is the presence of the Blessed One,
and from that arises the teaching of the Dharma; yet the opposite of these two— namely,
"this is existent" and "this is non-existent"— is indeed difficult to establish, because the conceptualizing mind that seeks to prove it lacks reality.
Therefore, due to the restrictive power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even that which is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality appears as if existent;
thus, partiality toward the Buddhist view is justified,
and even if cognitions are false, no sublation (*bādha*) is ever actually perceived.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, this is the rebuttal to the statement that partiality toward the Buddhist view is not tenable:
"Because the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is such, that very [impression] is the cause of sublation. How can there be awareness of error in the absence of an opponent? (913)
This has already been established previously and is not being stated again;
for if, due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), appearances of both the real and the unreal arise for you as a living being who is dependent on others,
and those two cannot be sublated, then what is the use of further dispute or of instructing opponents?
If his latent predisposition is inclined toward awakening, he will realize it by himself;
otherwise, even with a hundred words,
it will not become true for him.

"Having understood that this awakening of latent impressions occurred for me through this [instruction], so too will it occur for him; thus the other should proceed with his speech. (914) Therefore, as for what was said—that [the world] is false because cognition is sublated—why is no such sublation perceived?
If that [cognition] were to exist even without sublation, then no systematic distinction would be possible.
(Ślokavārttika, p.
237) [Note: There is an alternative reading: *bādhaḥ*, *syāt*, *vyavasthā*, *pratyayaḥ*.

When the waking cognition, which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is perceived, our dream-cognition and the like become false. In that case, what could possibly account for the difference [between them]? (916) Furthermore, there exists no other auspicious counter-correlate to the waking cognition by whose perception the cognition of pillars and the like would transition into falsity. (917)

The status of being a counter-correlate to dreams and the like is well-established by common worldly consensus, just as in the case of a subverting cognition due to its dissimilarity with the properties of that [object]. (918) That too has been refuted; for although every awakening or delusion is in fact merely the activation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), nevertheless, one must certainly employ speech in order to communicate to others.

For indeed, the activity of speech proceeds for the sake of awakening specific latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), having ascertained the desire to awaken such predispositions in others, so that they may understand: "Just as this very awakening of predispositions occurred in me in this manner, it will likewise occur for another.
Therefore, it is not purposeless.

If, therefore, cognition is false, why is no sublation perceived? [The answer is: because there is no awakening of such latent impressions (*vāsanā*). How, then, is its falsity thoroughly known? Precisely from the knowledge that it is bound by latent impressions.
For falsity is of two kinds: being non-existent in meaning and being non-concordant.
Non-concordance arises from the awakening of a contrary latent impression (*vāsanā*), while concordance arises from the awakening of a non-erroneous latent impression.
[Objection: But if there is concordance, how can there be non-existence in meaning?
Since even the aspect of non-contradiction is dependent upon latent predispositions (*vāsanā*),
there is indeed no conformity to the presence or absence of an object even in the case of a non-contradictory appearance; this very fact constitutes its lack of a real object.
Therefore, because it is similar to cognitions such as those in dreams, it does not have an unreal object.

For the unreality of dream-cognitions does not follow merely from the existence of a subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya), by virtue of whose absence the reality of waking cognitions would be established. If both are equally constrained by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can this distinction be made: "This one is consistent with experience, while the other is not"? There is no contradiction in this [distinction] within a single framework. (919)
That is incorrect;

for even when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are obstructed, why is it that the differentiation [of objects] such as blue, the occurrence of dreams and the like, and correspondence (*saṃvāda*) do not likewise exist? If something is similar in some respect, is it similar in every respect? (920)
Even though humanity is the same, how is there the distinction between being a Brāhmaṇa and being other? (Ślokavārttika, p. 238)

If [cognition] were bound to the object as it truly is, then no cognition would ever be subject to non-correspondence; likewise, even in the case of the opposite, why should this [non-correspondence] be impossible?

(922) For those who know the object, there is certainly no cognition whatsoever that is bound solely to mental impressions (*vāsanā*), since the penetration of the actual object is observed in all [cognitions].
(923) That [claim of yours] is false.

If that object exists exactly as it is perceived by one seeking it, then let there be the attainment of real objects; how then can there be a subverting cognition? (924) Because it is non-worldly, because of the conjunction of both natures, because of the loss of memory, and because of a contrary perception, its status as a subverter [of the first] exists; however, the existence of the object is not [established] in that way. Therefore, there is no connection with it by way of correspondence. (925)
Because it is not an object of cognition that can be verified by correspondence with an extra-worldly object;
or else, the existence or non-existence of that entity is seen from that [cognition] and is also sublated.

Alternatively, an unreal object being remembered appears as if it were present before the eyes while situated in another location, rather than remaining exactly where it is; therefore, there is no attainment [of the object] at that [remembered place]. This same principle should be applied to the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) as well.
This is an instance of invalid cognition (*apramāṇavṛtta*);

for one who has never previously seen a snake, the notion of a snake in a rope does not arise anywhere. Since it follows upon a prior perception, how can latent impression (*vāsanā*) not be the cause?
Indeed, without a prior observation, the cognition of a snake in a rope does not occur.
The conviction of the entire world is that this cognition arises from a prior perception and that no external object exists here;

otherwise, the entire system of cause and effect would be utterly destroyed, because nothing could be apprehended through mere appearance alone. For it has been established that in the case of mere appearance, there is only self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), which is devoid of any cause.
Therefore, the causal relation exists precisely because of that certainty;

here there is no perception of a connection with an erroneous appearance or the like. Nevertheless, it might be argued that even this is merely an erroneous appearance, and that no object exists here at all.
If the status of being a cause for prior cognition belonged to [an object] that is perceived erroneously and so forth, then other cognitions as well should be understood to be exactly like that.

(927) In another case, there is the attainment of the object; therefore, there is no such thing as "extraordinary" (alaukika) and so on. It has been established previously that in all cases, there is no attainment of the object.

(928) If you say, "It is not so, because [the object exists] due to certainty," that is not consistent. For even in the case of the extraordinary and so forth, why would that [cognition] not be [a case of] an external object? (929)

Because there is no engagement with the conviction that "this is a benefit" when it is actually a harm, this conviction of harm is not non-conclusive [with respect to the status of being a dream-cognition].

(930) The knowledge that [cognitions] are rooted in latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) constitutes their "beneficial nature"; that is not a sublation. Therefore, there is no possibility of waking cognitions having a counter-correlative [in the form of dream-cognitions]. (931) If it is argued that cognition arises from a prior perception, let that too arise from something else; all cognition is produced by the limbs of beginningless predispositions. (932)
For this very reason, this doctrine of non-referentiality (nirālambanavāda) shines forth;
for this very reason, the following [objection] is also refuted:
that "the cognition arising in yogis is sublated by its contrary."
Therefore, cognitions such as those of a pillar while awake are equal to those of dreams and the like.

(Ślokavārttika)—The reading is "equal to dreams and the like. And for all living beings who have reached that state, this sublation will occur; therefore, its status as having a counter-correlate is established. (933–934)
Ślokavārttika, p. 238:

For indeed, by the power of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of objects purified by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there arises for yogins a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that constitutes a valid means of cognition and which sublates error;
by that—
In this present life, such a state is not perceived in anyone; yet, we do not know what will become of those who have entered that state.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "yogāvasthām" (T).
The objection "in that very case" is refuted,
because the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) is already well known.
Therefore, why do we not know that this cognition will necessarily come to pass?
Hence, what is said is indeed perfectly consistent: [the following].
Furthermore, for us yogins, there will arise a subverting cognition that is either the opposite of what you have stated or contrary to what you have asserted. (936)
For it is said in the Ślokavārttika, page 238:
"yataḥ" (because).
"For those yogins whose intellect arises from the power of cultivation attained through immeasurable strength, why is their mind not overwhelmed by grief and the like?
(937) It has been established that there exists such an instance regarding the intellects of yogins.
This [verse], beginning with "īdṛktve" and ending with "grāhyantaratayāpi ca," is refuted along with a paraphrase of the *Ślokavārttika* (page 240, verses 95–98).
Not a single example exists for your [position].
Therefore, cognitions of pillars and the like would possess a counter-correlate or would be sublatable, because they are cognitions, just like the cognition of a mirage and so forth. (938–939)

940–941. It may be argued that the cognition of a mirage and the like possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratyogitva*), and that it is sublated either in its own nature or by way of having a different object of apprehension. This, however, is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*); for such a [mere] status of being a sublater does not exist. Indeed, the intention to assert "sublativeness" in this manner results in the total eradication [of the opponent's position].
To speak in this way is merely a manifestation of stupidity.
For it is not mere counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitvamātra*) that is intended, but rather counter-positiveness with respect to a sublater (*bādhaka*).
Therefore, mere counter-positiveness as a probans (*sādhana*) is irrelevant;
furthermore, being a sublater is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and its distinctness from that [sublater] is as explained previously.

Regarding the phrase "and also by subverters" (*vādhakaiś cāpi*), the two half-verses from the *Ślokavārttika* (p. 240, verse 99)—namely, "the state of being the counter-correlate of false cognition" (*mithyādhī-pratiyogitvam*)—are cited here and subsequently refuted.

Ṭīkā: That cognition which is sublated is like the cognition of a dream; yet the sublating cognition itself is a cognition, so [your argument] is inconclusive (*anekānta*) with respect to non-sublation. Furthermore, the cognition that establishes the difference from the cognitions of the Buddha and others is false. To this point as well, we have already provided our response previously. (943)
Every cognition of a Buddha and so forth has as its objective support only its own constituent parts; however, the establishment of conventional usage will be explained accordingly.

[Objection: It might be argued that for you, there would be the status of being the counter-correlate of false cognition, as in the case of dreams and the like. This was already refuted previously, and no further answer shall be stated here.
Ṭīkā: False cognition possesses the status of being a counter-correlate with respect to waking cognition;
for instance:

In the state of falsity (*mithyātva*), this relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists among all cognitions due to their varying degrees [of intensity] and so forth, arising from the varying degrees of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

(946) Just as, even though there is falsity, this relationship of the sublated and the sublator occurs for you [the opponent] in accordance with external objects without dispute, (947) so too here, because it is a manifestation of the contrary and so forth, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists through the presence or absence of the firmness of latent impressions; thus, there is no fault.

Now, is it not the case that the cognition of the Blessed Buddha has as its cause the destruction of passion and so forth through yogic power, and that this [reason] is contradictory because it subverts the very subject [of the thesis]?
For instance:

"Insofar as a particularity is intended—such as having as its cause the destruction of passion and so forth, or being based on such [causes]—there is contradiction due to the subversion of everything. (948)

In the *Ślokavārttika* (p. 240), there is a variant reading: "If the specific excellence consisting in the attainment of the cause for the destruction [of defilements] is intended, then [the reason would be inconclusive] because of the absence of all [such excellences]. This means that in the case of the cognition of the Buddha and others—which sublates cognitions such as those of pillars and the like—there are as many specific excellences as there are, such as being caused by the destruction of passion and so forth; because these are sublated, the reason would also be contradictory (*viruddha*).
For instance, it has already been established that the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) to false cognition belongs to cognitions such as those occurring in dreams.
In that case, even the knowledge of the Tathāgata would follow as being false because it possesses a counter-correlate,
just like the cognition of a pillar or other objects that sublates a dream;
to this, it is replied:

If it is argued that there is no flaw here because the reason is not invalidated by the "contradiction of the particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*), then surely the reason is not at all refuted; for that contradiction which obstructs the power of every reason is certainly not absent in its entirety.
Just as dream-cognition is established as being false because it is the counter-correlate of the cognition of pillars and the like,
so too the state of being the counter-correlate of a counter-correlate cognition is established by its being a cognition, just like dream-cognition;
and likewise, just as smoke establishes fire.
Likewise, since it now establishes even the non-existence of fire here, no reason at all would be capable of proving its probandum;
moreover,
because it is a cognition, it proves merely the status of being a counter-correlate.

It is not the case that being the counter-correlate of a specific property (*viśeṣapratiyogitva*) functions in the same way as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) proves the impermanence of sound; for if it did, one would also have to conclude that it proves the opposite of its being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).

Nor is "being a quality of space" something to be proven because it is accepted by the treatise (*śāstra*), for it will be stated that "only what is intended [by the proponent] is the thing to be proven" (*iṣṭaḥ sādhyaḥ*).
Therefore, "contradiction by a specific [property]" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) is not a refutation of the logical reason (*hetu*).
Is it not so?
There must be stated either a sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*) or a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*), as in the case of the cognition of a common person today. [Ślokavārttika, p.

240]—In the variant reading "as in the case of the sublating cognition today," the cognition of pillars and so forth is true, like the sublating cognition of today, because there is an absence of a cognition that sublates it for the common people; thus, the cognition of the pillars and so forth which is the subject of dispute is unsublated.
Because no subverting cognition arises for the great multitude regarding that object— just as there is no such cognition regarding dreams and the like—
that [cognition] is not inconsistent with reality;
for it is thus.

If it is claimed that the establishment of the probandum is accepted when it is established merely by perception that is both connected and inseparable [from the reason], then this is a valid response.

However, the cognition of dreams is not uncontradicted in the ultimate sense, because a contradictor in the form of direct perception is indeed observed; yet, even if the cognition of pillars and so forth were uncontradicted conventionally, there would be no harm whatsoever to our position.
If [the waking state] is unreal, how then can there be sublation by cognition, as in the case of dreams and so forth? For it has been previously stated that a gradation [of reality] always exists.
Furthermore, waking cognition does not sublate the vision of a dream because of its own truthfulness.
Because that [object] is not perceived as an object of knowledge, what does it have that is unreal? This has already been established:
a so-called "sublater" (bādhaka) is not a sublater by virtue of its own objective reality; rather, it is [a sublater] because of that [other's]—
And that non-apprehension, being established as having the nature of the apprehension of the opposite,
does not lose its status even when there is self-awareness of its own part.

For in this way, every other object of cognition or its own nature is the opposite of that [awakened state]; therefore, it is sublated by the waking consciousness, which persists even within its own constituent parts. 954
Now, if this [awakened cognition] is also an error, then upon what basis could that dream-cognition be sublated?
That too is incorrect;
for if the purpose of the means of proof has ceased, there would be an equality with dream-cognition. What need have we for the relationship of the sublated and the sublator in that case? (955)

Now another [objection] is stated: "The defects of the previous proof must also be considered for this one; because it is non-distinct from the probandum (*sādhyābheda*) and because it is inexpressible (*avācyatva*), the reason (*hetu*) is not established for both parties.
(Ślokavārttika, p. 249)—with the reading *sādhyābhedād avācyatvāt* as an alternative.

The conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding "awakening" (*bodhana*)—namely, that it is the act of awakening or that which is awakened by means of this [instrument]—entail the same faults as before. Furthermore, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is non-different [from the subject], the reason (*hetu*) "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) constitutes a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthekadeśa*), and thus it lacks establishment for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*).

[Objection: But surely, the specific cognition (*pratyayaviśeṣa*) is the subject (*dharmin*) and the general property (*sāmānya*) is the proof (*sādhana*); therefore, there is no [fallacy of] being a part of the meaning of the thesis.
Regarding this, he says:
"A universal and the state of being a cause do not exist as either different or non-different;
nor is anything [of these] perceived even in direct perception, since they are absolutely distinct."
In the *Ślokavārttika*, the reading is "matyakṣepī";
by virtue of its similarity [to the preceding], it will be understood as meaning "and not the exclusion of others."

In the *Ślokavārttika*, with the variant reading "sārupyānyanivṛttiśca netyetatsādhayiṣyate," [it is stated]: "Therefore, a universal as a cause is not established for either of the two. (Ślokavārttika, pp.

This is not tenable because, for us, both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the nature of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) are held to be both different and non-different. However, it will be explained later that there is no such [identity] between the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the common state [of the universal].

Precisely for that reason, through the connection with the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), a cognition is called a "cognition" by virtue of its object; this occurs through a causal chain (*pāramparya*) that is ultimately connected to the real entity (*vastu*).
What is the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya)? It is mere awareness, the consciousness of its own nature;
therefore, this [argument] is unestablished.

Ṭīkā: The opponent states what was previously mentioned—that the particularity (viśeṣa) may be with an objective support (sālambana) or without an objective support (nirālambana), and whether it is a property of the self (ātmadharma) or a property of the non-self (anātmadharma);
and that the two particulars serve as the reason (hetu) when they reside in the subject (pakṣa) and its similar instance (tattulya).
It would not [be so], because it is not subject to daily diminution and because it also lacks that nature.
Thus [it is said].

Nor can that cognition, being devoid of an object, serve as a logical reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, it has been stated that the substratum is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*) because the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not established.

Likewise, the contradiction of the reason and the absence of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*) in the example have been made known precisely through the analysis of the meaning of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). 961–962.
B.
Ṭīkā: Since all of this is already refuted [in the previous section] on the grounds that it is pervaded by having a specific objective support (*svalambanatva*),
therefore this [objection] is untenable.
Therefore, this is faultless: all cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālamba*), because they are cognitions, like the cognition of a dream.
(g) Thus, there is the refutation of external objects; for that reason, all cognitions are without an objective basis.
Therefore, because there is no cognition of another [object], self-cognition is held to be the fruit.
Self-cognition alone is the fruit;
consciousness, as it arises by itself, illuminates its own nature and not an external object.
Because it lacks the capacity to convey meaning and because the conveying of meaning is not observed [in it],
the following is said in this regard:

If the external were experienced, what fault would there be? None at all. Why then was it said that this object is experienced as external? What is the use of such subtle scrutiny? The external is indeed not experienced at all.
What is the fruit of this effort?
Let it be just as worldly convention is;
nor does the demonstration of the lack of an objective basis result in anything other than [the persistence of] convention, and there is no fruit here other than convention.

That too is indeed non-existent if conventional practice is what is to be established, regardless of how that practice occurs; what fruit, then, is there in your effort to prove the authorlessness of the Veda? For surely, that beginningless conventional practice was not created by another.
If that [non-existence] were established by the presence or absence of authorship such that it would exist through its absence,
then that very [authorship] is what must be investigated;
and if that is the case, let something else also be investigated.

Now, if [the Veda] were of human origin, it would lack authority; but this is equally true for the other [position] as well, because even if it were not of human origin, there would still be an absence of authority.
Furthermore:
When there is an absence of external grasping, then passion and the like are abandoned; for they arise through the power of mental cultivation, and in their absence, the opposite occurs.
Indeed, it has been established that the destruction of defects such as passion occurs when reality is investigated, and that this is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Therefore, that reality is now examined:
there is no experience of an external object;
for instance:

What is the meaning of the statement "the external object is experienced"? Does it mean that it is designated as "experienced" because of the existence of its entry into experience, or because of its non-entry [into consciousness]?
To this, he says:
If cognition has that form, it exists as something that enters into that form [and] is qualified by it.

This deserves the following investigation: does it [the cognition] arise from something external or otherwise? What is the meaning of the statement "cognition has that form"? Does it mean it has the form of blue and so forth?
Is this not now being investigated?
From where does it come that "the cognition has that form"?
For the sake of full understanding that "therefore the cognition has that form," that [object] must again be examined.
In that case as well, if it is seen by means of its own form, there would be an infinite regress;
if, on the other hand, it is seen without a form,
then why postulate a form for that very perception?
Now, regarding the phrase "having that form": because it has the form of determining that [object], it has the form of seeing that [object];
at that time, it is said to be "the determination of that" and "the seeing of that. What is the meaning?

Now, if both are seen, then in that case the two are seen in their own nature; consequently, there would be no mutual apprehension, or rather, no apprehension of anything at all. Thus, it has been established that the two are indeed self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
Now, if this [object] does not exist at all without the external,
then it follows that manifestness (*aparokṣatā*) cannot exist without cognition;
yet, manifestness is indeed perceived.
If that were the case, something else would have to be postulated;
yet the cognition bearing that very form is itself perceived—so what need is there for another postulation?
For:

Because that which is devoid of the adjunct of perception is not apprehended, while it is apprehended when perception is present, perception itself appears as blue; there is no external object existing in isolation.
Whatever is seen, that alone is admitted [to exist].
For indeed, it is only the blue that is apprehended as it appears; nothing else [is perceived] apart from that appearance.
Since there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than that appearance, there is no acceptance [of an external object].
Now, that which belongs to the appearance does not appear within it, because the appearance is internal while blue and the like manifest externally;
nor is there an appearance of something distinct from it, because it appears in its own nature as something immediate. For instance:

If that which is distinct [from the cognition] were always non-existent, there would be no directness (*aparokṣatā*) for the blue object. Since it is direct by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), it possesses no other directness.

(965) For in this way, the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*) is direct by its own nature, not because of the existence of another apprehender; likewise, the blue object and so forth, even though they exist at the same time as that [apprehender], are so.

And just as the form of the apprehender arises from the eye and other [senses], so too does the form that corresponds to it, because the relationship of cause and effect is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The non-existence of an object prior to or subsequent [to its perception] is not determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not operate with respect to what is prior or posterior.
Now, if it is asked how it is understood that "this [object] did not exist even previously," [the answer follows].
Or why is the form of the apprehender not postulated as being prior [to the apprehended], whether it be the cognition or the pleasure and so forth?
If you argue that this is precisely because the self is eternal,
then why is its direct perceptibility (aparokṣatā) not likewise postulated as existing even earlier?
If it is argued that this is because of contradiction, [we reply:
no, for it is not logical that immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) should remain unperceived,
whereas an object distinct from that [immediacy] could logically remain unperceived as well.
By whom has it been understood that [the object] is distinct?
For this very reason, there arises the objection of doubt, namely, "it might exist at some time.
If it is asked, "Why is its direct perceptibility not likewise [doubted]?"
Because it would follow that [the object] is directly perceived;
for there can be no such conceptualization as "it is not directly perceived by me" based on the direct perception of something else,
just as in the case of whiteness and so forth.
Although whiteness does not belong to a single object such as a jar, it certainly belongs to another substance; therefore, there is no blue or other quality apart from its manifest perceptibility.
Now, when the whiteness of an object departs, does it go elsewhere?

Nor is there even non-mediacy; for [cognition] does not go elsewhere, being other than [the object]. In that case, because it is not distinct from that [cognition], the object would also be absent due to the absence of that [cognition].
If it is argued that the non-exclusion itself is not certain, then even in the case of fire, the absence of the nature of fire would not be established when its effect is absent;
for if one were to argue that fire is absent because of the absence of that [effect], [we reply: no.
It is not so, because the non-distinction [of the object] is unestablished, since it is not perceived apart from that [cognition]; thus everything is the same.
Therefore, that which is distinct from immediate manifestation is simply non-existent.
Inference, too, does not establish [the object] as being non-distinct from direct perception;
how could it fail to establish this when it establishes it even during the state of indirectness? Therefore, the blue object certainly exists, such that I shall cognize it later.

In that case, because there is no cognition based on following the prior form, the memory follows that experience; and that experience belongs only to that which has a direct (non-conceptual) form. Furthermore, it is not the case that memory of blue and so forth takes as its object something established separately as having a direct form.
If it is asked how one should practice in this case,
[the answer is: here too, that very same [nature] is superimposed,
provided that it does not abandon its prior state of being non-manifest.

One must indeed abandon even the blue form [of the object], since it is not distinct from that [cognition]; for memory is not an inference, as there is no recollection of [the object] as divided [from the cognition]. If it is argued that [memory is an inference] because there is a comprehension of something additional, we say no, because there is no cause for the comprehension of anything additional.
If it is asked, "How is there the apprehension of that which is additional [to what is already known]?
[we reply: No, because of its non-existence;
how then could it be a means of valid cognition?

Since the pervasion is established at the very first moment— when one perceives smoke arising from fire in connection with fires in various successive locations— one's understanding occurs in this way.

Wherever this [fire] is brought, there it produces smoke; it does not produce smoke connected to one location while being in another location. Therefore, if fire exists elsewhere as well, it certainly produces smoke there too.
By that [perception], the locus of smoke is indeed apprehended as belonging to fire;
and that future smoke or fire is superimposed precisely in its own form, for it cannot be otherwise.
Consequently, from the observation of further smoke, there arises the apprehension of a greater amount of fire.
But for one who, without any prior superimposition regarding the object of fire, has an immediate comprehension upon seeing smoke—how can that be?
For even in his case, there is no comprehension without a connection based on a universal (sāmānya). To explain:
Even if there is indeed an immediate comprehension, when one is questioned—
"If there is smoke here, why is there fire?"—
the answer is simply, "Because it has been observed to be so."
He should say this:
that perception does not exist even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because of the determination [of identity] through the oneness of perception and superimposition;
nor could it be conceptualized as distinct from the perceived object and so forth, for otherwise the seeker would not act toward the object based on perception.
One should not instruct one who desires to see;
for one does not become a seeker of seeing without perceiving that which is being seen.
If it is argued that "that which exists is perceived," [we reply:]...
If the connection with perception has not been grasped, how could the mere cognition of existence be a motivator for action?
Therefore, one who desires that object acts only upon apprehending its very perceptibility, and not otherwise;
for it is never observed that one who desires blue or the like acts without first cognizing its blueness and so forth.
Therefore, neither inference nor any other conceptual cognition apprehends the state of being blue and so forth as distinct from its being perceived;
how then can inference have an imperceptible object?
It is through the superimposition of the previous perceptibility [onto the present object].
How, then, is there the cognition "there is fire" in that case?

[It arises] because the superimposition (adhyāropa) exists in that manner, just like the water previously seen in the object of a mirage. If it is argued that "that in which something is superimposed is other than the fire," [we reply: no.
If it is argued that this is indeed its nature because its own form is not apprehended;
If it is argued that "that [object] is indeed immediate," how can there be mediacy?
For mediacy consists precisely in the cognition of the thing's own nature by another; if this is the case, then that very [cognition] is immediacy—thus, the objection remains unrefuted.
The claim that "cognition by another occurs through the force of a logical connection" is merely a superimposition;
thus, the idea that cognition of another arises from such [a connection] is false.

Even if the cognition of an external, imperceptible object were logically possible, since one perceives it oneself later on, there is a superimposition of identity—thinking, "this was previously imperceptible"—and if that [identity] is what constitutes the cognition of another, then that too does not exist.
This very cognition of another was previously beyond one's perception;
therefore, that which is "beyond perception" (parokṣa) is indeed non-existent.
Therefore, since there is no apprehension of that which is devoid of the adjunct of perception, how can there be a comprehension of the exclusion (vyatireka) of the object?
If the object does not exist apart from consciousness, from what source does the distinction between the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth arise?

[The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that the appearance of hair and so forth arises from the eye and other [faculties] themselves through the power of impairment? From what, then, does this 'impairment' arise?"
If it is argued that [the appearance of blue and so forth] is due to the appearance of [a mass of] hairs and the like, then let it be postulated that it is due to the appearance of blue and so forth;

however, in that case, there would be a single form, just as with the mass of hairs, such that even though they occupy various locations, there would not be a multiplicity of blues and so forth. Is it not the case that just as the eye moves when it is spinning, so too does the blue and so forth move?
And if an external object is held to be the cause of visual consciousness, then why is blue and so forth not [likewise] the cause,
just as the eye is the cause in the apprehension of form?
Likewise, upon the apprehension of the intermediate [object], there follows the establishment of the external object from that [apprehension],
due to the specific determination of consciousness.
To this, it is said:
For someone, a particular internal latent impression (vāsanā) alone serves as the awakener;
therefore, the restriction of cognitions arises from that, and not in dependence upon external objects.
This has already been stated: an external object is not established through direct perception.
An [additional] cause is postulated because of the absence of the effect;

however, when there is an absence of the effect, it is better to postulate the eye itself rather than postulating a different entity. It is better to postulate that the perceived eye and so forth are simply distinguished by those [specific qualities].
Even that is stated only out of deference to others; it would be better to postulate a distinction in the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) itself,
rather than [accepting] the body as a cause.
If it is argued that [the body] does not exist apart from its appearance as a body, because it is non-existent except for that appearance; and [that it exists] when that appearance is present.

Nevertheless, since one cognition arises from [another] cognition alone, and the simultaneity with the appearance of the body and so forth belongs to the appearance itself, there is no causality [between them].

For instance, just as the restriction of time and so forth regarding the conceptualization of passion and the like is evident—whether through a specific awakener or even without such awakeners—[so too is the case here]. (966)
Likewise, there is the convergence of determinate appearances such as blue and so forth;
for passion and the like arise in specific places, times, and states by virtue of awakening conditions,
but there is no restriction regarding their objective referents (*ālambana*), because they deviate from them.
Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding the awakening of the cognitions appearing as "Kānyakubja," "hunchbacked woman," and so forth, depending on whether the awakener is present or otherwise;

nor is it the case that only an external object acts as the awakener, since even by means of a cognition appearing as such, another cognition may be awakened through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of its own capacity, thereby giving rise to experience according to its own power.
For there is no partiality on the part of the mental effort (*ābhoga*) toward any particular object;

even when the mental effort is equal, what is the cause for the specific restriction of certain cognitions— such as those in dreams and so forth— arising from the manifestation of a vivid form due to habituation or other factors?
If it is argued that what was perceived in another birth and so forth is the external cause of the restriction, we say no;
because everything would then be perceived, and since that [external object] is absent at that time, what could be the cause for the restriction to that specific time?

If the external object, restricted by place and so forth, were the determiner of the appearance, then in the absence of that external object in that place, from where would that restriction come? (967) If there were no external object there, then how could there be an appearance restricted to that time and place? Alternatively, if the restriction exists even without that time and so forth—on account of having previously seen the object—then what is the point now? For the restriction is possible from the previous appearance alone.
For instance:

"The conceptualization of an object is intended so that there might not be an appearance devoid of an object. If [the cognition] is restricted by the previous object itself, what has been accomplished by the appearance?
Now, it is not logical for that [appearance] to manifest here without an object. (968)
Since the appearance has already ceased previously, there is no appearance of that [object];
for it is not the case that what is non-existent appears here now. Thus, an external object is postulated.
However, if even a non-existent object, having been perceived at a previous place and time, appears here [now], [then the following applies].

Let it be that the very appearance itself possesses the prior time and so forth; what is the use of postulating an external object, since even the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) admit the existence of appearance?
If it is argued that in that case the external object itself appears there, whereas here [in our view] it is not an appearance because of its impossibility—
If it is asked, "In that case, on what basis is there 'correspondence' (saṃvāda)?"— surely,
is it not also logical that correspondence itself is established through another correspondence?
Therefore, rather than one correspondence following another correspondence, it is more logical that there is merely a succession of appearances of correspondence.
For surely, that which, having arisen, perishes, is a false cognition—such as "this is not silver.
But this pillar and so forth are firmly determined by themselves; how could they be erroneous?
That is incorrect;

because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is firm, there is no immediate destruction [of it], just as in the case of conceptual constructions such as passion which arise through the power of latent impressions.
Indeed, the conceptual construction of passion and so forth depends solely upon the power of the latent impression.
Just as that [dream-object] is devoid of external reality,
yet it does not suddenly dissolve even when one's eyes are closed,
so too the continuous narrative of the dream-explanation does not dissolve by any means whatsoever.
This is due to the firmness of the latent impression (*vāsanā*);
for instance, that very same previous reciter, rising again and again, is repeatedly explained [to him] in a dream.

Therefore, the restriction does not depend upon external objects; for instance, this dream-vision does not persist for one who is awake, just as a child’s urination occurs in such a state [without external cause]. (970)

The state of urination seen by a child during sleep persists even in the waking state; furthermore, the non-deviation from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the states of youth and so forth has already been established previously, so it need not be elaborated upon again.
Nor is there a duality of cognition (*vijñānadvairūpya*).
Therefore, there is a single [cognition] possessing two forms, which is thus experienced and remembered; the awareness of this [cognition] as having both aspects is the result.
"Possessing two forms" means it has the form of consciousness and the form of blue; it is "single" because no distinction between them is perceived.
How is it that [the cognition] has two forms through the conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra*)?
Because it is experienced and remembered in this way.
Therefore, since there is no cognition other than that which possesses both forms, it is concluded that the cognition of the object is not the result for that which possesses both forms. [Objection:
But it is perceived as the cognition of an object; how then can it be self-cognition?
To this it is replied:
When an external object—whether desirable or undesirable—is the cause of a representation because its nature has been fully established, there is likewise an experience of it;

yet, since that cause whose nature was established is absent [at the time of cognition], there is only the awareness of the experience itself. Because blue-ness and so forth belong to the experience itself, the experience occurs precisely as blue and so on; thus, this is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in the ultimate sense, not the awareness of an external object.
Even if there is an experience [of the object] as an object, it is like the self-awareness in a dream;
or rather, the cognition of the object itself is the result,
because [it is from that].
When cognition possesses an object because the object is established through a portion of the cognition itself,
then that very self-experience of the cognition is the determination of the object.
Furthermore, when one does not conceptualize another external [object], it is understood as being external only by virtue of being a portion of the cognition itself.

In that case, whatever is the experience of the cognitive form of the self, by virtue of the restriction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there arises the ascertainment "this is the object. Then, by the force of that ascertainment, it is established that the cognition of the object is the result;
at that time, whether it be consciousness itself, the cognition of the object is the result, and the apprehended form (*grāhyākāra*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
The aspect of the apprehender is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and its self-awareness is the fruit (*phala*;
alternatively, it is understood that this very [aspect] is the object).
And because that [apprehending aspect] is itself awareness, awareness itself is the fruit.
Moreover,
even for those who accept an external object, self-awareness alone is the result,
because:
If the self were of the form of the object of desire, or otherwise experienced—
whether as desired or undesired— then by that [experience] the object would be known.
For it is not possible to say that when the cognition is otherwise, the object is otherwise.

Therefore, since the determination of an object occurs solely in accordance with its cognition, and because it shares the same identity and destiny as that cognition, the awareness of an external object is in fact self-awareness itself;
it is called "awareness of an external object" only by way of metaphorical designation.
This is why:
If the self of this cognition has a desirable form, while the object is experienced otherwise— as either desirable or undesirable— then,
even if the desirable [object] is [perceived] by way of an undesirable form, the object is known through that [cognition] in a primary sense; otherwise, it is merely figurative.
Therefore, he shows that even regarding an external object, self-awareness alone is the result.
[An objection: But surely, if it exists, the awareness of the object itself is appropriate;
however, since it does not exist, self-awareness is appropriate by necessity.
That is incorrect;
for even when an external object exists, it is precisely as it is experienced.
B.
[The self] is indeed determined as having a single nature by its own essence, because of the fault of having a manifold nature. || 342
For even in the Vijñānavāda, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not accepted out of necessity; rather, it is accepted as a consequence of that very consciousness itself.
If it is accepted due to the lack of another recourse, why is the external object (*bāhyārtha*) not likewise accepted?
For:
If the external does not exist, of what could there be cognition?
If, having no other recourse, it is the nature of the [cognition] itself, why is it not considered as being just the external?
This is the understanding of similarity.
Therefore, it must be stated that only the self-cognition of its own nature is observed, and not a lack of cognition;
for if even with respect to an external object only self-cognition is observed, let that be so— but the cognition of an [external] object is not tenable, and thus it is abandoned.
