Since cognitions are indeed distinct by their own nature, it is logical that there is a perception of various forms for each individual person;

however, it is not logical that the object itself is perceived as having various forms, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the object possessing a manifold nature by its own essence.
The view of the outsiders (bāhyadarśin) is that even though it is not experienced through various modes of apprehension, the object is indeed one;
therefore, for them, the experience of a single [object] as having multiple forms is untenable.
If it is argued that the object itself consists of multiple forms:
Even if there were a distinction in the means [of cognition], there would be no experience of both;
that is, there would not be an experience of both with respect to one and the same object.
Because it is complete in its own form,
if another form were also to appear by entering into that very same [form], then there would be the realization of oneness;
or else, there would be no experience of two— this is the meaning of the object.

Alternatively, there would be no experience [of all objects] through differentiation that culminates in each individual [object], because it would follow that everything would be experienced in multiple forms;
if you say this is not so because of the obstruction of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), then indeed there is no comprehension of the object by virtue of its own nature.

If it is argued that [the non-perception of the second moon] occurs because of an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), then if the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is the obstruction, there would be no perception of the two; for in that case, the cognition of oneness would have been prevented by the very thing that is seen. Whence, then, could there be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for oneness? Like the visual impairment (*timira*), the unseen might exist;
however, this conceptualization—that there is indeed a second moon, but the perception of the one is prevented by the unseen obstruction of the perception of the second—might also apply here.
Consequently, because it is as invisible as darkness, the operation of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) cannot be determined by its effects;
for why not simply accept that consciousness is produced devoid of external objects by the unseen force itself?
Alternatively, it must be explained how the unseen force is capable of preventing the cognition of an object situated in a location where it is otherwise fit to be perceived.
"Showing a manifold entity as having a single nature—
how could that unperceived [cognition] possibly be the knower of the object?
(This is the summary verse, 345).

Moreover, it is observed that the cognition of desired and undesired objects is produced by the power of habituation (*abhyāsa*). How then can it be understood here [in the case of the afterlife] that this is achieved through something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)?
If you say that "that very thing" is the unseen, then our desired point is already established; for it is proven that everything arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

But surely it is not the object that appears as desirable or undesirable; rather, it is the mental constructions (*kalpanā*) themselves that become so in accordance with the form of the object. To this, it is replied:
If conceptual constructions, which manifest as desirable and undesirable, are not sensory cognitions— whether they are [considered] cognitions of objects or [cognitions of] meaning.
Even in that case, there is no reconnection of the mental states with what is undesirable; this is the meaning in the manuscript of M. He. (Hevajra).
4. "iṣṭam"—thus [it is said]. In the manuscript of He, it is observed that even the perception of the dice by those seized by Ariṣṭa was seen otherwise.
Therefore, this is established;
for that reason, even when the object of cognition (*prameya*) is external, it is logical that self-awareness (*svānubhava*) is the result.
"Therefore, even when the object of cognition is external"—thus it says in the manuscript *He*.
Since the determination of an object is exactly according to its nature,
therefore, even with respect to an external object, self-awareness alone is the result,
not the awareness of the object, because that [awareness of the object] is subsumed within self-awareness.
In this case as well, with respect to the result [of cognition], the very fact of having the form of the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As the Teacher said:
"But when the external object itself is the object of cognition (*prameya*), then the very fact of having the form of that object is its means of valid cognition."
For instance,
although cognition is self-cognized, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists solely in its appearing as the object, independent of its own nature;
because that object is measured by it.
For just as the form of an object appears as beautiful and so forth, and as it is apprehended, that object is perceived in that very form;
thus, the distinction between the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is metaphorically attributed according to the differentiation of forms.
Ṭi—by way of being pleasant and so forth;
Ṭi.—the portion of the text up to this point is by Dignāga.
But surely, since there is no distinction [between them], why is the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*) not also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this it is replied:
its being the appearance of the object (*arthābhāsataiva*) is what constitutes the means of valid cognition, and not its mere existence.
The nature of the grasper [is established] because it is not for the sake of another; thus it depends upon external objects. (348) [Note:
"it depends" (*apekṣate*) is the reading in the He manuscript.]
For there is no corresponding existence of external objects,
because [self-awareness] is not for the sake of another;
indeed, self-awareness does not establish anything for the sake of another.
Because it is identical everywhere except for its specific form; for in whatever way that objective essence is established within the cognition, in that very same way [it appears].
Therefore,
it is determined that "this is thus established," for it is by virtue of its aspect (ākāra) [that this is known].

If the cognition is that "the object itself, such as blue and so forth, is established in its own form," then the very form of the object is the cause for the conceptualization of the object; consequently, that [form] alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the experience of the object itself is the result (*phala*); what, then, is the use of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)?
Since this [external object] is unreal,
the conceptualization of its object is precisely in accordance with self-cognition;
he says that very thing:
) Of self-cognition. || 349 3 B.
Ṭīkā: The meaning is that "being the fruit" (*phalatvam*) means that the fruit is precisely in conformity with the cognition (*saṃvedana*).
Thus, the cognition of the object itself is what is intended, because the nature of the object (*arthātman*) is not perceived [independently].

Since that which is not being perceived is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), how indeed could there be an operation of perception with respect to an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*)? And yet, the determination of the result of perception has been introduced; therefore, because the object is not cognized as having the nature of perception itself, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the result.

Inference is not directly perceived; therefore, for the purpose of its exclusion, the object to be established is introduced into that cognition, and that [cognition] is the means of proof for it. (349) 5 M.
Therefore,
the reading "evetyadhikaḥ" (and so it is additional) is found in the manuscript; for by that [reading], she is produced, and thus its fruit is that, because she manifests through that sequence.

If that is so, then the form (ākāra) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to the external object, while the self-cognition (saṃvedana) is the result (phala) with respect to its own nature; thus, there would be a difference in objects.
That is incorrect, because:
For in whatever way that object is settled, in that very way it manifests; B.
ṭi—since that [cognition] expands in accordance with the way that object is settled.
Because the stability of an object consists in its being of that very nature, self-cognition is also considered to be cognition of the object. (350) [Note:
There is a transposition of the quarters here in manuscript S.]
In the ultimate sense, this is self-cognition alone;
however, from the perspective of conventional usage, it is the cognition of an object.
Therefore, with regard to conventional usage, the object itself is the fruit.

If only the object (*artha*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be a distinction between objects? Even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), both [subject and object] are likewise [non-dual] in their own nature; nevertheless, why is this so?
He says this very thing:
Therefore, there is no difference in the object either; (cha) as for the result being the cognition of the object—
the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) would then be the result with respect to the external object.
To the question, "Why was it not stated [as the result] with respect to the object of cognition? he says:
"Self-awareness is the result," as was stated in the investigation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because the cognition of the object is identical (*tādātmya*) with it. (351)
There is an inversion of the quarters here; however, in manuscript *sa*,
with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is also the awareness of this object.
If indeed that cognition of the object is not the nature of the cognition itself, then for the purpose of defining it, self-cognition alone must suffice.
But if the object does not appear by its own form and only the cognition appears in its own form, how can the object have the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*)?
If you argue that this is because the object is like a mirror, [we reply: no.
How is it known that it is "of such a kind," given that it has been stated that "representations (vijñapti) indeed have various forms"? To this, it is replied:

Even though an object may be the cause of a cognition that appears in such a way— whether it be of that same nature or otherwise— the object's status as a cognizable (prameyatā) is nonetheless accepted.

Although a cognition appearing as water arises even in the absence of water, it is nevertheless called "object-based" by relying on some degree of causal efficacy toward an object, since it arises in dependence upon mirages.

Now, if being an object of cognition follows solely from being a cause, then it is logical that [the object] has only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) as its cause; for that [impression] is not a non-cause,
and the capacity of the latent impression to produce an object with that specific form is observed.
And thus it has been established by you yourself:
"If, however, that assumption of the form [of the object] were not possible without an object existing as such, then the cognition of the object would be logical."
Otherwise, however,
in whatever way its object-aspect appears through reasoning, [it is as follows].
How can there be the apprehension of an object when [the cognition] is liberated [from it]? Truly, I do not know even this to be so.
When there is the assumption of that form even in the absence of a proximate object, then at that time there is no apprehension of that object whatsoever.
If it is argued that there is the apprehension of what was seen in another location,
then if that [object] does not exist even in that other location, how can there be an appearance?
If it is argued that the appearance occurs where [the object] exists, [we reply:]...
If it does not exist anywhere, what means is there [to know this]?

It is known from the very appearance itself that it must necessarily exist somewhere; for an appearance has never been seen without an object—thus, the understanding arises from this necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
If that is so, then since it has not been seen, how can it appear?
If you argue that it too was indeed seen in another birth and so forth, we say no.

Since there is no restrictive rule [to the contrary], even an unperceived appearance is indeed admitted. Thus, the meaning is this: at that time, the object exists in the place where it is produced; it appears at that time, not appearing at a time devoid of the object.

4. B.ṭi—The intended meaning of "it remains" is as follows: for even that which is unseen appears elsewhere than its actual location. If everything were to appear [everywhere], then it would follow that everyone would be an all-seeing seer.
(974) If even that which is unseen, situated in another place and so forth, were to manifest, it would follow that everyone would be an all-seeing seer.
If it is argued that [the object] does not appear except in a particular state, whereas it does appear in cases such as ophthalmia, we say:
no.
Since cataract is common to all, it would follow that everything would appear [to everyone]; furthermore, since cataract is that which obstructs vision, how can it itself be the cause of vision?
If it were the cause of perception, there would be the consequence that everything is perceived;
if you argue that it produces perception only of that which is actually seen,
then it follows that only what is already present is seen.
If it is argued that this very [non-perception] should produce the cognition of non-existence, since perception has never been observed to occur without an object;

and if it is further argued that there is no such deviation [in the rule], because perception is likewise never observed to occur without the object being situated in a location suitable for it—then [we reply]: No.
If it is argued that the meaning of both is the same, we say no, because there is an absence of actual referentiality.
If it is argued that the object is exactly as it is [described],
then everything would be exactly as it is; and if it were non-worldly (*alaukika*), then everything would be non-worldly.
For it has been established that there is no other distinction apart from perception;
if you say it is "attainment," that too is simply perception.
By this, seeing and the rest have been explained. [Commentary:

Just as the first cognition produces the seeing of the object, it requires the attainment of that [seeing]; and by the attainment of that, another attainment is required; thus there is an infinite regress. (975)

If it were maintained that for some [cognition] there is the nature of being a valid attainment (*prāpti*) by itself, then since that would be absent even for the first [cognition], the situation would be the same for all. (976) Alternatively, if the reality of the attainment is due to its being preceded by a prior form of attainment, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); thus, neither of the two [cognitions] possesses reality in that sense. (977) However, the extreme reality of a cognition arises from the purity of the object and its cause; likewise, the reality of that [subsequent] cognition arises from the purity of its own causes. (978)

Thus, by depending on a succession [of causes], an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result. That [blue] exists as the water of a mirage produced by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā). Therefore, it is entirely consistent to conceive of everything in this way: for one for whom blue and other [objects] proceed as bound by the attachment to beginningless latent impressions, no fault whatsoever is seen. 979–980.
Now, if even the obstruction caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resides within the self-nature of self-cognizing awareness (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*), how could it be obstructed from its own nature?
If it were something else, by what would it be apprehended? If it were indeed nothing other than the self-nature itself, then it would be a mere matter of names.
(981) If the obstruction were of a nature distinct from the self-nature, and that [awareness] were where it occurred, then self-cognition would consist in the apprehension of something separate.
If there is no separate existence [of the relation], then neither the related nor the relata exist; thus, the apprehension of a relation would be impossible.
That too is incorrect, because:
This connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is perceived quite easily; remembrance is perceived as being connected to a prior cognition.
As remembrance arises, it establishes its own connection to experience; it is for this reason of determination that it is so stated. [Objection:
If that is so, how can there be a perception of the connection with latent impressions by one who does not remember?
For instance, the recollection "I have seen this" occurs only when there has been a prior cognition; however, non-recollection does not communicate its own existence to anyone.
It is only while recollecting that one determines "this was seen," because otherwise it would be impossible to determine that something was seen.

But in the case of a cognition that is not accompanied by recollection, there is no apprehension of its being a consequence of a prior perception; therefore, how can it be understood as being bound by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that [perception]? Even in that case, because of the cognition "it was seen," and because it is unified with recollection, that cognition also cannot be accounted for otherwise [than through a prior perception];
thus, there is a cognition of the identity between the object being recollected and the object being perceived.
Therefore, everything is indeed bound by latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
thus, the apprehension of identity between that which is being remembered and that which is being perceived is an error.
Because there is no sublation, [one thinks]:

"I remember this very thing; my previous perception was here. And there is no sublation here, for there is an identity with that memory. Now, if the previous form is not grasped in the form of the memory...

That being the case, how could there be a cognition of difference between the preceding and the succeeding? Therefore, non-duality alone [remains]; and that being so, it is all the more so by virtue of its nature as consciousness.

Because it is impossible to establish a rule of causal relationship regarding external objects; for instance, since the external object has not yet been perceived, how could its being an effect of consciousness be established? However, since consciousness is already perceived, its being an effect of [the external object] is logical.
Thus... (985) ...so too.
Because that effect arises differently depending on circumstances such as place and time, the restriction of the causal relationship is not logically tenable. However,
in the view that [consciousness] is self-cognizing, a prior cognition arises solely from cognition itself.

If it is argued that although smoke may indeed occur without fire, it nevertheless arises from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of smoke, and thus this appearance to people is not causeless— just as the case with a gnat’s wing, a mirage, or smoke appearing as water— and that it is precisely an external object that arises through the power of latent impressions; [we reply:]

This is indeed accepted; since it is dependent on the power of external latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it would be a mere name. And that [name] is already established by the world itself—what room is there here for your personal effort (*puruṣakāra*)?
But surely, [the object] does not appear as an effect of latent impressions; how then can there be the state of being an effect of latent impressions?
For one who perceives fire from smoke that arises spontaneously, does the state of being an effect of a sublater (*bādhaka*) appear?
If it is argued that [the cognition] arises for one who reflects,
this is the same even if it is an effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), since the awakening of latent impressions from another birth and so forth is also possible.
And from that, it is like the occurrence of childhood play or dreams for a Buddha.

It is said that there is an appearance of what was seen in previous lives and so forth; the determination is that such an appearance arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (987) Consequently, the manifestation of each preceding cognition is everywhere established as being external to consciousness, as if it were an external object.

(988) For those whose minds are brought under the sway of beginningless attachment to latent impressions, this manifold appearance occurs within a single locus, just as for those experiencing a dream. (989)

Because it is an effect, every effect arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just like the work of a potter or the effects seen in a dream. (990) Whether it be *pradhāna*, the Lord (*īśvara*), karma, or whatever else is postulated, that is merely the movement of a mind deluded by attachment to latent impressions. (991) Among all *pradhānas*, it is the supreme *pradhāna*; likewise, among all lords, it is the supreme lord. Latent impression is the highest deity, the creator of the entire world. (992)
How could one who acts with foresight be the creator of a world that functions in such a discordant manner, proceeding with agitation?
(993) If one who exists in independence, who is capable and fully cognizant, were to act in a discordant way, who could be taught by whom? (994)
If he who gives instruction is himself the creator of his own future birth, yet creates that which is deformed, what consistency of speech can there be for him?

(995) If the Creator acts for the sake of disorder while intending order, then it would be better to avoid contact with filth from afar than to attempt to wash it away. (996) How can power be attributed here to one who is unable to act otherwise? Even he proceeds in such a manner solely due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (997)

Thus, these ever-swiftly flowing rivers of doctrines asserting Primordial Matter, God, or a Creator, having set forth, enter and reach exhaustion only within that very ocean whose measure is the latent impressions (*vāsanā*). 998.
"O fools, it is better that this very latent impression (*vāsanā*) be purified by a virtuous means; for from that alone comes the accomplishment of all that is desired.

"Therefore, you should not ask me how the apprehension of an object occurs. My purpose is to lead you to the ultimate realization of his intention. Furthermore, I am in no way able to justify such a view of yours. As for what is utterly ill-conceived, who is capable of justifying it? What can a farmer do with a seed that is completely rotten?"
(ja) The establishment of the means of valid cognition and its result within the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*):
Now, if there is no form of apprehended object and apprehending subject, how can there be such conventional usage?
This too is merely your own delusion.

The meaning is that even the conventional usage of "the apprehended" and so forth is not perceived as distinct, because it dissolves into the very nature of consciousness; thus, such usage is essentially identical with that [consciousness].

For in this way, although it is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, due to the distorted vision of those whose intellects have been subverted by error. (354)

Just as for those whose sense-faculties are impaired by mantras and the like, objects such as lumps of clay appear in a manner entirely different [from their true nature], even though they lack that [apparent] form; so too,
it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that the nature of cognition is undifferentiated.
And thus it has been established: however,
by those whose vision is perverted, it is grasped in the form of an object of perception and so forth, but [it is not so in reality].
Rather, it is observed that even when another is present, [the object] is seen; having thus superimposed a misconception, one engages in such conventional usage:
"This is my perception now, whereas the external object was indeed seen by the other."
Furthermore, he does not investigate this:
"How is it that what was seen by another was seen by me?
For another person does not know in this way.
That [object] is also unique to him, just like our own cognition;
if he too knows it only through the inference "it was seen by me," then there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that this is because the effect is not observed [in the absence of the cause], we say no,
for that would entail the impossibility of apprehending identity;
indeed, fire arising from smoke is not known to exist only where the kitchen hearth is located.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is distinct because smoke is distinct [from fire], then, because effects such as horripilation are also distinct, there would be another apprehended form for one person belonging to another;
furthermore—
The horripilation and other [physical reactions] arise from the internal experience [of pleasure] and not from the object;

furthermore, there is no cognition of a mutual mixing of the two perceptions [of the object and the pleasure]. Otherwise, inference would not be required, for inference does not operate when perception is present.
If it is argued that only the form (*rūpa*) itself is perceptible, whereas its being seen by another is imperceptible therein and must therefore be inferred—then we reply:
is there not even a lack of proof for the claim that "being seen by another exists therein"?
For in this very point, there is doubt.

In that case, why is the yellow form not also a subject of doubt when it is perceived as a blue form? Furthermore, how can one conclude that the nature of fire exists in what is to be perceived later simply because of that subsequent perception?
But in this case, even subsequently, there is no apprehension of being seen by another;
for surely, if the state of being seen by another is not cognized, there can be no linguistic usage at all?
No.
Since linguistic convention is established through mere similarity, on what basis can it be said that such convention does not exist without [the object's] identity?
Now, if inference operates with respect to something imperceptible, it must also operate with respect to identity; if it does not, how could it operate even with respect to similarity?
This is true; even in the case of something similar, how can there be inference?
This is merely conventional practice based solely on the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object.
In ultimate reality, however, inference has as its objective support only the thing's own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
If it is asked, "How can there be an object that is beyond perception? [we reply:
How could it be logical for cognition to have an object beyond perception? For if something appears therein, how indeed could there be any state of being beyond perception?
Even though there is no manifestation [of the object], the object is nevertheless cognized as being beyond the senses; this is the pure formulation of the statement.

(1001) If it is thought that its cognition occurs because of a subsequent correspondence, then since there is an attainment [of the object], let it be stated what exists at the time of that attainment. (1002)
But by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could its prior existence be known? For if it were perceived at that time, it would exist even in the absence of that [present] non-existence.
(1003) If there is no inference regarding a future object, how can there be any cognition of it? It is certain that in all cases, there is a cognition of a future form.
(1004) If there were a cognition of both the present and the future, then how could the future and the present be cognized as having a single nature? (1005)
Therefore, there is no cognition of [the object] through inference in the ultimate sense. If the jar is imperceptible, how could it be cognized later?
(1006) If its arising occurs at that very time, how could it be without a cause? Since it is seen [to arise], it is exactly so; who here is subject to such an objection?
(1007) Why is its prior non-existence not postulated because it is seen? It is not seen as such, and therefore it is not postulated as such. (1008)

Nevertheless, that which is directly perceived cannot be [known] through inference in that same way. By what other means could it be known that "it exists"? This is an invalid response, because: (1009) [From: *Nyāyaviniścaya* 2.34–35ab; *Tattvasaṃgraha* 1876–1877.

Even another person does not understand that [an object] is known by someone else; for even in the case of that [other person], there would be a reliance on yet another knower through inference. (1010) When it is said that "it exists" because it is known by another who is common to both, the validity of the inference lies in its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that existence. (1011) Therefore, if existence is known through perception, there would be an inference regarding it; and if existence is known through inference, there would be no apprehension of perception. (1012)
Thus, due to mutual dependence, even a single [element] is not possible; indeed, no such mutual dependence is observed anywhere else.

Therefore, since the conceptualization of the apprehended and the apprehender proceeds from the postulation of external objects based on an inference that functions through a beginningless succession of such inferences, it is established that, in ultimate reality, conceptualization of the apprehended and so forth is nothing but non-dual cognition itself.
If you ask: "From where does this realization of yours arise?"
For objects such as lumps of clay and the like, which have been aided by mantras and so forth, appear in the form of snakes and other things even though they lack that nature;
for these people, until their ignorance is dispelled, treat as visible what is invisible to others.
If, however, that which has a certain intrinsic nature were perceived by perception exactly as it is,
then perception itself would not depend upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
If it is argued that [the inference] is so because it depends [on perception], no; for the capacity [to establish the object] is seen to belong to inference itself.
If it is argued that the capacity belongs to perception alone, [we reply: no.
If it is argued that inference must not be denied its status as a valid means of knowledge, and therefore let it be simply perception itself,
then in that case, even perception would be dependent upon the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, it is not ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Moreover, there is indeed inference even in the case of the opposite; so how could there be two types of inference?
If it is argued that let there be [inference] on both sides, then...

If it is argued: "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—[we reply that] this is not [the case], because it would entail the consequence that the existence [of the self] is established as distinct for each individual person.
That very [cognition] has arrived at self-awareness because it is unique due to the non-mixture of one with the other;
therefore, although another does not apprehend it in that way, there is nevertheless a cognition of it as something common.
Now, why is it that only this [person] is not one who possesses realization?
If you say "by means of inference," then let inference also apply to the opposite case.
If it is argued that inference is non-existent due to the opposite case,
how so? Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not apprehended as a unity.
In cases of similarity, inference indeed achieves its purpose;
however, in this case, on the contrary, an action observed in accordance with non-perception necessarily infers that non-perception,
and this is something that only the opponent would admit.
Likewise, because they are not perceived by those whose minds are undisturbed and who possess [clear] vision— thus says Hē.
B.
Just as even a small object is seen from afar in deserts;
if that object is seen by another person as well,
then such is the admission of the other party as well.

Likewise, considering that approaching [an object] with the conviction "this is indeed great" and with a desire for it is common to all, one abandons inference in any other way; for such inference is perceived by everyone and is well-known to all people.
However, from the perspective of those who see reality (*tattvadarśin*), this is accepted only through the concessions of others.
Alternatively, when something is perceived exactly as it is, what occasion is there to postulate an object of such a nature?
If inference also terminates merely in its own internal form, it is indeed nothing but perception;
for even in this case, there certainly arises for the practitioner the cognition that "the external object exists, whether it is being perceived or not.
Let that [cognition] also remain submerged within itself as long as it is regarded as perception.
The understanding is that [consciousness] is submerged in its own self and there is no other object existing outside of cognition;
furthermore, even common experience arises solely through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as in a dream.
How then is the establishment of the object (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the result (*phala*) possible?
To this it is replied:
"This establishment of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the fruit exists according to how it is perceived;
[it is not] 'according to reality'—thus says He."
Even though it does not exist [as a separate entity], it is produced as the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper (grāhyagrāhakasaṃvid).

That very object which is being perceived exists there; thus, by virtue of being the object of perception, it is the "grasped," which is of the nature of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) and independent of anything else.

The grasper is established through conventional usage by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the experience of the cognition itself as having that nature— namely, as being of the form of perception and as consciousness;
this conceptual construction is an "after-perception" (*anudarśana*), which conforms to the [prior] perception.
Alternatively, even though they do not exist,

there is the grasping of the apprehended, the apprehender, and consciousness with respect to an object that lacks an existing basis; or, by means of the grasping of what is non-existent, there is the [grasping] of the apprehended and so forth in relation to common objects and the like.
The rest has already been stated by others; therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only consciousness (*samvit*), not the triad [of subject, object, and means].
Now, if it is argued that everything is merely a transformation of the Self, why is there non-existence?
For even if those transformations into diversity occur, they do not deviate from the true nature of that [Self].
Thus it is said:
"Otherwise, how could the aspects of a single entity—which appears in manifold forms—be real? For that would entail the loss of its unity. (358)
If it is one, how can it manifest as manifold?
And if it manifests as manifold, then its oneness is lost, because [of that very fact].
And because the otherness of one thing would be lost [if it were identical]; nor is there non-difference, because no form [of distinction] is perceived.
"Of one thing"—thus [it is stated] in the He manuscript.
For the cognition perceiving the non-difference of form determines non-difference;
even when there is no difference in form, the cognition perceiving it establishes non-difference—thus in the manuscript of He. (Helārāja).
If it is argued that for anything else as well, this very reality is what is called the appearance of non-difference, and that for anything else there is no otherness at all, nor is it even admitted;
In that case, since there is the appearance of a difference in form, how can non-difference be accepted?
Even if you do not admit difference, how can it be admitted when it does not appear at all?
For an admission is valid only when a non-difference in form is actually perceived.
If all those distinctions are of the nature of light, then they are all real;
however, if they are not of the nature of light, how can things that are non-luminous be non-different from light?
For if they were luminous, then like the self (*ātman*), they would all be real.
If the very nature of the Self were its state of luminosity, just as it is for the individual self, then all selves would be identical; consequently,
the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāma) would be destroyed.
Now, if multiplicity were an illusion,
it would follow that nothing exists at all; everything would become a mere void,
for even so-called illusion does not exist apart from the self.
Or rather, by designating it as "error" (*bhrānti*),
one implies that if error were non-existent, none of this would occur; thus, although there is no real distinction [between the object and its appearance],
it is established as "non-error" because it does not have the manifestation of unreality as its cause.

As long as its status as something to be sublated is not established, it possesses no erroneous nature; yet once its status as something to be sublated is known, it is understood to be nothing but an error. (1014)
Having attained a certainty based on delusion, one would act for the sake of cessation; from that, cessation [would follow]. Thus, by what means could this circular reasoning be stilled?
Therefore, whatever form by which entities are conceptualized does not exist in reality.
Because neither a single nor a manifold form exists for these [atoms].
(460) Or "a single"— thus it is in the He manuscript.
The one does not exist because it appears as many;
nor is non-cognition [perceived], since it is perceived as having the nature of cognition;
and in self-cognition, multiplicity is not apprehended.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that while [the parts] are perceived because they are included within that [whole], their being included within it is not perceived; for this has already been addressed.
Alternatively, since a single [entity] possessing variegated forms does not exist, nor indeed do multiple [entities exist], how then can there be the appearance of difference?
It has been established, and will be further established, that no difference appears;

or rather, the entire form of difference appears otherwise through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Thus, it is unreal because it can be turned away by one who cultivates [the truth] through contrary cultivation; for since there is no certainty regarding its being impossible to turn away, it is unreal.
Is this not so?

In the world, an error arises from the perception of similarity through the determination of identity in that which lacks that nature; but here, that is not so, because not even a single thing of that nature is observed in this world. (361)
To this it is replied: error does not arise from the mere observation of similarity alone;
there is also this [kind of error] which arises from a disturbance within the internal organ. (362)
By its very nature, that [consciousness] is the manifestation of what is spread out, yet it is false due to the arising of defects.
It is like the vision of those with cataracts and so forth, which does not depend on the perception of similarity and the like.

(363) Indeed, for those whose vision is obscured by cataracts, mosquitoes, flies, and the like do not arise through the power of another perception; rather, they arise solely from the cause that is the cataract itself.
[Objection: But even that which arises from cataracts does so through the power of the object itself, not through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
However, what is intended here is merely the status of being an internal cause;
for everything, the internal cause is indeed mental impression (*vāsanā*),
just as in the case of cognitions such as dreams.
That latent impression (*vāsanā*), when awakened in some way or another, is the cause for the production of a cognition corresponding to itself;
and in that regard, it is precisely the preceding [cognition]— the perception of similarity— that is initially seen, by virtue of which this error arises.
In the case of perception, how can it be said that there is perception of that [object]?
For, because of their identity, the entire [cognition] would simply be non-erroneous;
otherwise, if it were perceived differently, how could the entire [cognition] be erroneous?
Because it arises from the perception of similarity, this is not merely a succession of errors.
It has been established that there is no non-erroneous [cognition];

therefore, if one asks: "How can there be a systematic arrangement of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth within this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is a conceptual construction based on unreal habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?"
To this it is replied:
In that case, the determination of the cognition is accepted as having the form of the grasper;
because of its identity with that [cognition], self-awareness is considered to be the means of proof for it. (364)
1. Then—"Thus," it says in manuscript H: "That very thing is the goal (sādhya), that very thing is the means (sādhana), and that very thing is the accomplishment (siddhi)."
In that regard, regarding the cognition whose object is the self, just as there is the experience of passion and so forth,
this status of the object, the means of knowledge, and the result is to be applied everywhere.
For it has been established that objects and the like, arising by the power of mental cultivation, are of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Furthermore, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that consists in the experience of pleasure and so forth is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in that case, the distinction between the means of cognition, the object of cognition, and the act of cognition is indeed non-distinct, as it is said:
And in these four categories, reality is fully encompassed: namely, the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the resulting cognition.
— Vātsyāyana’s Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.1.
1.1 (Page 1) That [position] is untenable because there is only a slight difference.
If it is argued that since everything is completed in one [moment],
there is indeed non-distinction with respect to pleasure and so forth,
but there is distinction with respect to yellow and so forth;
This established state of the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the result is not to be applied everywhere;
for as it is in the case of the cognition of an object and so forth, so it is also in the case of the cognition of blue and so forth.
Whether it be "having the form of blue" or "having the form of the object," what difference is there between these two?
Since both are experienced by their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*),
therefore the experience of blue, pleasure, or the body is entirely by way of its own nature alone, and not by way of another's nature.
If everything is self-cognition by its very nature,
then surely the subjective aspect, which is identical with the cognition of blue and so forth, is like pleasure and the rest; how then can those [pleasures] serve as your example?
How is it that pleasure and the like are self-luminous by nature, like the Self?
What is this so-called "nature of luminosity"? It is the state of being immediate (aparokṣarūpatā), just as [the Self is].
In that case as well, because they consist of the nature of experience, they are capable of self-awareness;

thus, that capacity is the means of knowledge (*māna*), the self is the object of knowledge (*meya*), and self-awareness is the result (*phala*). The nature of determination within the self is what is designated as the form of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*).
And that [capacity] is declared to be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is the self-cognition [of consciousness].
(367) This reading exists in the He manuscript; however, since neither the root text nor the commentary for this verse is seen here, this point requires further consideration.
Those [objects] such as blue and so forth, being of a non-mediately perceived nature, consist of experience;
therefore, like pleasure and the like, they are capable of self-awareness.
For those [objects] such as blue and so forth are not non-mediately perceived by way of another form.
Is it not the case that the immediacy of blue and other objects arises from the power of the eyes and so forth, rather than from their own intrinsic nature alone?
For they possess immediacy by virtue of their very essence.

For it is not the case that whatever the eye reaches is necessarily perceived; although the eye may reach a seed, it does not always perceive it, since perception is possible even when there is no such reaching. To explain:
When passion and the like arise, a form appears in quite another way; for even though the eye has extended [toward the object], its own nature does not appear.
(1016) If the object is not manifested in its own nature even when the eye and other [senses] are directed toward it, how can it be immediate?
Indeed, immediacy consists precisely in the manifestation of its own nature.
Now, if this defect of the eye were due to the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then it is said:
"If, through mental cultivation, there is a transformation of the eye and so forth, then by the power of cultivation, everything—blue and the rest—would appear. (1017)

For cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which has the alternative name "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), is the cause of the appearance of [objects] such as blue that enter through the eyes and other sense-faculties;
at that time, the appearances of blue and so forth arise solely through the power of latent impressions.
Is it not the case, however, that appearing otherwise is the cause of the latent impression?

However, since the manifestation of an intrinsic nature (svarūpa) occurs without [the influence of] latent impressions (vāsanā), it is dependent on the eyes and other sense organs; yet, because all things are distinct from one another in mutual dependence, it is not known through the appearance of multiple forms what the intrinsic nature actually is. If manifestation is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because it is non-deviant, how can there be any confidence?
Therefore,
even though every appearance is produced by the cultivation or non-cultivation [of mental impressions], it is like the nature of an appearance that is other than what is intended as its own nature.
Thus, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator has already been refuted.
Therefore, even with respect to an external object, self-awareness alone is the result, while its form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But is it not improper to say that consciousness possesses a form?
For instance:

If [the eye] were as clear as a mirror, then it would follow that it perceives through the coloring of the object placed before it; yet the eye and other [senses] are not observed to do so. (1019) Whatever is present [before it], all that appears in a mirror; therefore, it would follow that there is a perception of all things, such as forms and the like.

(1020) Alternatively, if the eye were the cause of the appearance [of objects] just like a mirror, then there would be a vision of what has been transferred [into it], as in the case of a mirror and similar objects, even for that which is not coarse. (1021)

Consequently, it is not known what the form [of the eye] is like, nor what its dimension is; there is even a distortion of color, as in the case of glass, clouds, or films. (1022) Or rather, having emerged from the eyeball and not falling upon visible forms and the like, the perceivers are known in their own forms within the great elements and so forth. (1023) A distinct form arises through contact with the light of a lamp.
If self-awareness were like the contact between a lamp and its light,
then even in that case there would be an infinite regress due to the operation of something else.
If, on the other hand, it is self-awareness, then how can those rays [be perceived]?
Therefore, when the object is present, cognition arises bearing its form. If [you claim] it arises from that [object] alone, then it would follow that it possesses all forms.
(1026) If it were to bear the form of that from which its production occurs, then it would also possess the form of the eye, since it is produced from that as well. (1027) To this, it is replied:
Indeed, all consciousness indeed arises from objects.

Even if that object were the cause, how could there be a form resembling the object? For it is not the case that whatever arises from something else must necessarily possess the very form of that [cause].

For instance, although factors such as the time of eating and other conditions are causes for the birth of an offspring, it assumes the form of one of its parents and not that of any other whatsoever. (269)
For the offspring produced from both parents does not possess the identical form of either parent by its own nature, but rather that of one or the other.
Therefore, it is from the object itself that the cognition takes on the form of the object;
for instance, from a tree situated at a distance, a cognition arises having that very form. It is always observed that cognition does not take on the form of the sense organ. (1028)
Even though it is equal [to other things] in being a cause, its status as an object is held to be due to that specific aspect; in the absence of that, it would not be so.
An object is not such by virtue of being a cause in general, but rather by virtue of being the cause of a cognition bearing its own form.
If being an object were defined by causality, then the eyes and other sense organs would also be objects;
furthermore, in the case of the cognition of water in a mirage, water from another location would also have to be the object because it bears that form.

Indeed, consciousness, whether as a cognition of the nature of awareness or otherwise, is incapable of establishing an object through its form in the absence of that form, since it has been demonstrated that the states of being perceived and not being perceived are incompatible [without such a basis].
If that [object] is cognized, what is the use of another [means], since it would be redundant? If it is not cognized, then too [it is useless] because of incapacity;
for that which is not being cognized cannot be an object of cognition.
If it is argued that the very cognition of the object as it appears is its cognition of that form,
and that a separate action is not tenable— this has been established hundreds of times—
it might be asked: "But surely, in the *Sākārasiddhi*, it is stated that the aspect (*ākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the result (*phala*)."
But how is that very point established?
To this it has been said:
"Moreover..."
The nature of cognition consists in the distinction between the cognition of an object and the cognition of that [cognition].

Regarding an object such as color and so forth, the cognition thereof has the appearance of the object itself; however, the cognition of that cognition of the object has the appearance of the cognition conforming to the object and also the appearance of itself.
Otherwise, if the cognition of the object were to consist solely of the form of the object, [the subsequent cognition could not distinguish it].
Alternatively, even the cognition of an object would be no different from its own form;
for the thesis to be proven is that "the cognition regarding an object possesses the appearance of that object," and this is the subsequent reason.
The subverting proof begins with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth.
When one reflects, "What was my cognition like?", one then engages in discourse through recollection precisely as the object appeared, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, whatever is made an object by a particular conceptual determination (*adhimokṣa*) becomes exactly so; for example, a *śābaleya* cow when made an object by the conceptual determination "this is a cow."
For instance:

"Such an appearance exists in cognition; but what is the object like?"—because the object is thus abandoned, there is no determination of the object within the cognition. (1029) If one is questioned by someone, "How was that object known by you?", then one answers that there is no certainty as to whether the appearance of the object is such that the object exists therein, or not, nor whether it is of such a nature or otherwise.
Therefore, one who abandons the [external] object must accept that cognition is nothing but a manifestation.
For if the object were a single entity, how could there be certainty regarding that very same thing and uncertainty regarding that very same thing?
This is because certainty and uncertainty are mutually contradictory.

However, regarding the object (*artha*), there is no certainty within the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) that there is no internal differentiation; therefore, the meaning is that the manifestation is of such a nature only to that extent, while that which is other than it does not manifest—
thus, that very [object] is both certain and uncertain.
"Because it exists as two parts"—
this very point will be explained later; moreover:
"Even in a mind that possesses an object,
there may be the apprehension of the form of a non-object"— thus it is in the He manuscript.
When the apprehension of past objects is established, there is the self-cognition of a dual nature;
"of a dual nature"— thus it is in the He manuscript.
He who says that cognition does not appear because of the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
and that it is never remembered either, [asserting] that only the object is [remembered] in all cases;

Just as in that case [of perception], knowledge is postulated for the object through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on recollection, so too, by the impossibility of recollection, there is no unperceived knowledge, nor does it possess a form; therefore, the claim that "knowledge is twofold" is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*). Since the statement of the reason (*hetu*) occurs when there is doubt, the reason lacks a locus (*anāśraya*). Furthermore, because the connection (*pratibandha*) is grasped in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the reason functions [there]. (1030)
If it is argued that this is not the case because the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is a subject of dispute in all instances,
that is incorrect.
One might indeed suspect that wherever an object exists, it does not constitute the form of the cognition;

however, in the case of a mind devoid of an external object—such as [the appearance of] hair and the like, or the manifestation of yellow and so forth—the possession of two forms (the form of the object and the form of the cognition) is already established, as is the self-awareness thereof.
Thus, the claim that "cognition is imperceptible" is directly contradicted by perception itself.
Then, through the observation of that example, there is the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
and from that, since its appearance is of such a nature, how could a certainty—which has arrived at the reality—arise with respect to the object?
Since certainty occurs in this very same way in every cognition, the existence of the aspect (*sākāratva*) is established.
That very nature of the determination of appearance is the nature of the cognition of that [object] within the cognition of the object;
or, if at some point even there the object itself exists, then if it is not an individual, it will be a universal (*jāti*).
(Jha) Refutation of the eternality and non-eternality of the universal:

To this it is replied: Because it is differentiated by the appearance of blue and other [colors], the object is not a universal (jāti); for that [universal] does not possess those [qualities], and if it were impermanent, it would not be a universal, nor if it were eternal, how could it be a producer? (372)

A universal (*jāti*) such as "blue" and so forth is not [the cause], because it is devoid of the form of color and the like, and because, being eternal, it lacks causality; for it has been established that what is eternal cannot be a producer.
Furthermore, if it were eternal, it could not be a generator, since an eternal entity lacks the capacity to produce anything. Thus it is demonstrated.

Names and so forth were refuted previously; this is not the sequence for those things that possess real meaning, because since [names] are dependent merely upon the speaker's whim, they do not establish a real capacity for the object.
All of this has already been established previously, and thus it will not be elaborated upon here.
(2) Recollection and Reflection (ka) Memory does not have the form of the object— memory is a cognition of this kind, and its arising occurs from experience.
And how can that [consciousness], which is devoid of the form of the object, now possess it?

Since memory arises from experience, how could it—occurring in the absence of the object—possess the form of blue and so forth? Or rather, does the memory possess that form because of the object itself?
Regarding this, it is said:
"In that case, existence would not arise from the object, because of its absence at that time;
even if there were such an experience, if memory were direct from the object, then the object would have to exist in exactly that same way."
Nor is that [external object] present;

yet, since memory bearing its form arises even from an object that is spatially remote, experience would likewise occur in the same manner. This has already been demonstrated, and it is demonstrated here as well.
And that form does not belong to the object, because it is distinct from the clear form.
Furthermore, the object is apprehended as having a clear form through its experience; if that [form] were indeed the form of the object, then the object would necessarily exist in exactly that way.
If it appears as such because it is apprehended by memory,
then it follows that its clarity is due to its being apprehended by direct experience; therefore, this form does not belong to the object.
If another person were to perceive that form as distinct [from the cognition], then that object would be perceived by others as well; however,
since it is connected only to oneself, it does not appear to another.

What is the meaning of "connected to the self"? Does it mean that the effect has the self as its essence, or that the effect is of the nature of that [self]? In the latter case, it would indeed appear to another [person].
For being an effect does not lose its commonality; if it were of that nature [the nature of cognition],
then it would simply be of the nature of consciousness itself.
And if there were identity, it would be eternally connected to the self and not otherwise;
and thus, even if it were explained, one would not comprehend it.
If, however, one does comprehend it, then one would comprehend it even in the absence of that [identity].
For instance,
external form and so forth are perceived even when not mentioned by another,
whereas that which is perceived when it has been mentioned is indeed something else entirely.
In that case, since the relationship with the self is eternal, why is it not perceived when [the object] is spoken of? (376) 1.
He.
In the manuscript, the half-verse "nityam ātmani" is seen, and there is also a commentary on it;
however, it is not seen in the Tibetan translation,
and the connection is not appropriate even with each individual [term].
2. Regarding the reading "anusandhānam" (which is an additional reading), he explains what kind of synthesis it is:
its nature consists in the focused application toward a single object.
Since that [body] would be distinct, there could be no cognition of it as "this is one"; therefore, he asks: "Of which two is there the connection?"
Because the minds of the speaker and the listener are engaged in grasping different objects,
if it is argued that there is a single linguistic convention regarding them due to their similarity— which makes them appear as if they were not [different]— [that is untenable].
If the object is distinct from the self, how could it be grasped? In that case, cognition would be purposeless.

For a conventional usage based on similarity occurs only between two things that are both perceived, and not otherwise; and since there is never a perception of what is seen by another, how could there be a conventional usage of identity in that regard? (378)

For in this case, there is indeed only the appearance of mutually distinct objects; if, however, similarity were a real entity, then one would perceive "this is one" by following that [similarity]. If that is so, then:
Even when it is not stated, one should understand what resides in another by following one's own realization— namely,
that even when the other does not say,
"I have also understood it in this way."
If it is argued: "It speaks of what is true for that particular time; how then is there comprehension [of it] if it is seen to be exactly thus even in the absence of an object?"
In that case, cognition would be purposeless;

for just as a cognition might determine the appearance of another even without that other’s appearance, so too it might possess a form (*sākāra*) even without the appearance of an object. Thus, the fact that cognition possesses a form is established, whether by means of critical reflection or by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), in the case of certain cognitions such as memory and the like.
But from what does this arise for everyone? He says:
"And that cognition of experience [arises] by means of that which relies upon both parts.

By means of the cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*), which possesses a specific single form, both are connected by that cognition. The cognition of experience— which is of the nature of non-recollection and has blue and so forth as its object— is connected, inferred, and reflected upon by a second [cognition] which has that same object and is of the nature of recollection (*smaraṇa*).
By what kind of [cognition]— one that relies on both parts [of the object and its appearance]—
did [the person think], "I had a cognition with a blue appearance," and not [a cognition] as it actually is?
That [object] is determined by others solely through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); likewise, someone may follow what has been established by that [testimony],
yet no presumptive testimony arises for anyone in the world.

For the world does not understand in this way—that "I possess another cognition by which an object was seen"—because the nature of cognition itself is not established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Indeed, its nature is easily determined; it is not possible [to determine it] otherwise. (1031)
No one is able to determine through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or by any other means that cognition has any form other than the manifestation of form and so forth.
If it is argued that it is determined by its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpatā*),
then surely that very nature of consciousness itself is not known.
Indeed, there is no difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) due to a difference in the suffix (*pratyaya*), nor is there a difference in the meaning of the suffix itself;
for by what means could a difference in the meaning even be admitted? Since there is no difference in the meaning, how could an explanation of it proceed by means of that [suffix]? (1032)
Therefore, cognition is not defined as "awakening" (bodha) distinct from blue and so forth; rather,
it is simply the differentiation of attributes inherent in the very nature of that blue and so forth,
expressed as "the cognition of blue" or "the cognition having blue as its object."
Therefore, when one pursues the thought "I had a cognition having blue as its object," one is merely pursuing its objective form;
for indeed, no cognition as a subject is perceived apart from the blue. Any distinction [between them] following upon the cognition is constructed by the artisan of conceptualization. (1033)
If, then, the cognition is designated as distinct from the very nature of blue and so forth, then blue and so forth alone exist, and there is no such thing as "cognition" apart from them—
just as whiteness and so forth do not exist apart from a cloth; thus it follows that cognition itself is not ultimately real.
It is asserted that the external object is ultimately real; however, this is incorrect,
for as follows:
In some cases, the negation of something occurs by relying upon something else; that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serves as the gateway for the negation of another.
(1034) If an object is established by a means of valid cognition, then the notion that "there is no other cognition apart from that" leads to the abandonment of [the contrary] cognition.
Now, if cognition (*buddhi*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the object (*artha*) [is established] therein;
in that case, since the establishment of the object occurs through cognition, cognition cannot be abandoned by one who possesses the object.
However, for one who possesses cognition, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition is not something to be accomplished by means of the object.
Therefore, since it is possible to accept [cognition] even in the absence of an object,
one accepts cognition and thereby abandons the object distinct from it;
furthermore, the object itself is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
This being the case, the object would be nothing other than the cognition itself; yet, since an object exists even though it is not perceived, it must be abandoned because of its non-apprehension,
whereas the cognition is not like that and thus should not be abandoned.

Furthermore, it is not accepted that a substance exists apart from whiteness and the like; likewise, let it be understood that an object does not exist apart from cognition. For, just as... [1035] Just as...

Momentariness is in no way distinct from blue and the like; nevertheless, it is not shown that momentariness is non-existent. Therefore, because cognition—having the form of blue and so forth—is determined as such by another cognition, and because both parts [of the cognition] are abandoned [in that process], cognition is indeed not apprehended [as an object]. Thus, how is it not of dual aspect?
Or rather, cognition is apprehended by a second knowledge as being qualified by a single aspect.
The meaning is that it is apprehended by a single aspect;
as to what kind of single aspect, he says: "by one that apprehends both parts."
Therefore, because it pervades both parts, there is the conceptualization of those two parts;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, those two forms have indeed entered into that single form.
Therefore, those two pervasions exist; furthermore, those two forms— the nature of consciousness and the form of blue—
are as explained previously.
It should be understood that "by way of a specific single aspect" means "by way of an additional single aspect";
even if it is established as having two aspects, how can it be said here to have two aspects?
For otherwise, how could that which does not possess that form ascend into cognition? Indeed,
it would not have such a form.
If one did not experience oneself as having that form through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), how could the cognition, by virtue of possessing that form, ascend into memory?
For such an ascent is produced by the possession of that form.
How can it be said that "it ascends to that"? Because the cognition arises in exactly that same manner; for each subsequent cognition has a single form. (380)
This must necessarily be accepted;
for indeed, each subsequent [moment] becomes increasingly greater by one form at a time, and not otherwise.

For instance, by the first [cognition] blue is apprehended; by the subsequent one, the cognition of blue; by the next, the cognition of the cognition of blue; and by the one following that, it ascertains even more than that.
This could not be otherwise;
he demonstrates this very point through an illustration: its form as an object, or some other form whatsoever.
2 M. ˚ṇākākhātmā˚ 3 He.
In the book— it is explained that, in accordance with that [object], its form or some other form is indeed discerned by a second cognition through a third cognition.
(381) It is analyzed— thus, in the book.

The second cognition is discerned as having both the form of the preceding two cognitions and its own form; by the third and fourth [cognitions], that same pair is discerned with one additional form. This continues until one is able to count or remember them.
Thus, in the second moment, the cognition itself is not known in isolation.

Since that cognition is connected to the object because it is directed toward it, when there is a recollection of that [cognition], there is also a recollection of the object due to its being inseparable from it; thus, cognition cannot be remembered otherwise [than as having an object]. Therefore, it is remembered in that way.
Consequently, because it was directed toward that [object], it possesses its form; this synthesis is the perception of its having that form through error.
To this, it is replied:

If, due to the causal efficacy of the object, there is a false synthesis with the memory of the object within the recollection of the cognition, then that same [synthesis] would also occur in the case of the mental attention toward light.
(The word "error" is to be supplied as the connection.)

If cognition is the effect of the object, or if it has an operation directed toward the object, then there is necessarily a recollection of the object within the recollection of the cognition; therefore, for one whose mental continuum possesses such a hidden nature, comprehension occurs in that manner.
If this were so, then even in the case of mental attention to light, comprehension would likewise occur in that same way.

Just as consciousness has the object as its causal factor, so too it has light as its causal factor and mental attention as its causal factor; therefore, it would be perceived through the combination of both.
Indeed, there is no difference in its being a causal effect.

Now, if you argue that the combination [of factors] applies to the object because consciousness is active toward it, whereas it does not apply to mental attention because it is not active toward that, then the same applies to light as well; for consciousness does not operate upon form while excluding light.
This is incorrect;
therefore, just as it is not the case that there is an appearance of light, so too there should not be an appearance of form.
Or rather, since light is included within the object itself, it is already apprehended by the very determination of the appearance of form.
[Objection: Since light lacks the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) by virtue of its being an illuminator (*prakāśaka*), how can there be an operation [of cognition] upon it? [Response:
Even though light is an illuminator, because it falls upon form (*rūpa*), it becomes form itself; thus, it is an object.
That being the case, cognition too, because it is dependent upon form as its illuminator, would be nothing but form itself—just like light possessing an aspect.
Just as light cannot be perceived without form, so too cognition [cannot exist without its object];
for no one knows that there is such a thing as cognition in the absence of the objects to be illuminated, such as form and the rest.

Therefore, consciousness has the very form of color and so forth; however, if it were apprehended as such merely by virtue of being an effect, then all effects would likewise be grasped by their causes [as identical to them], and consequently, a jar would not be remembered as distinct from the potter and other factors. || 383 ||
Even an effect such as a jar produced by a potter and others would not be remembered apart from its own cause;
for there exists some excellence produced by the object within the cognition, by virtue of which the object is also remembered when the cognition is remembered,
and the object is grasped when the cognition is grasped.
There is neither perception nor recollection of pure cognition alone;
however, even a jar or the like is perceived in its isolation, as is a potter or the like—
this too serves to refute your own position.
For indeed,
because cognition becomes the receptacle for the connection with an object due to some excellence,
what else could that [excellence] be than similarity, given the observation of twins and the like? (384)

If that consciousness were not to possess the form of the object, then what would be the basis for this rule—that consciousness is perceived and remembered only simultaneously with the perception of the object? However, since that which is included within the object is necessarily perceived by the very perception of it, this constitutes a rule.

Therefore, consciousness is indeed the very nature of the object; its perception is inseparable from the perception of the object, and its remembrance is inseparable from the remembrance of the object.
Moreover, when one of a pair of twins is perceived, there occurs the appearance of the other, as well as the memory "this is that," and the conceit of perceiving a tree by way of its dark form;
likewise, if the first cognition, having experienced the object, were to have only the apprehending aspect, then the second would be the same.
Regarding this, he says:
"For if the first were of neither nature [of being or non-being], then the second, established as having a single form, could not be distinguished by the reflective consciousness. (385)

For by a subsequent reflective cognition (*parāmarśacetas*), a second [moment] could not be established as distinct from the first, since that second reflective cognition would also—given that it lacks both the nature of the first and its opposite—be established as having only a single form, namely, the very form of the subject (*grāhakākāra*). Consequently, how could there be a determination of distinction? Therefore, consciousness possesses only the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*).

From that very [cognition], the second intellect, characterized by the synthesis and integration of objects, subsequently takes hold of the cognition appearing before it in the form of blue and so forth. (386)

Therefore, because it possesses the form of the object, the second cognition relies upon the preceding first cognition; it embraces the synthesis of the object—thus, "embracing the synthesis of the object" (*arthasaṃkalanāśleṣa*).
Since it embraces (*āśliṣyati*) by means of the synthesis of the object, that cognition—the second one—relies [upon the first]; this is the meaning.
If, however, there were no assumption of that form [of the object], one would indeed apprehend the cognition alone;
for one certainly does apprehend it alone, as when people remember only the subject, thinking, "I do not know what it was that I saw at that time."
That too is incorrect;
because there is doubt regarding the apprehended object, there is likewise doubt regarding the apprehending subject.
Since there is apprehension in a general sense, this same principle applies equally to the apprehended object as well. (1037)
In the case of the recollection of the apprehender in a general sense, the same principle applies to the apprehended object as well;
for instance, the recollection "someone was seen by me" occurs precisely in the form of a general appearance of that which was perceived.

And if the very nature of the grāhaka (the apprehending subject) is remembered as being devoid of the activity of the grāhya (the apprehended object), then that alone is its form; it did not have another form during the presence of the grāhya.
Consequently, how could that which is being remembered—which possesses a different, non-apprehending form—subsequently become a grāhaka in that very same way?
Now, if in memory the form [of the object] is indeed situated as something to be grasped in its true nature (*tattvena*), then how could there be a memory of it alone?

Therefore, its form as mounted upon that [object] cannot be separated; thus, it is one and the same [form] appearing as the essence of color and so forth. And if cognition does not possess a dual form, then only the first [moment] would have the aspect of blue, and not the subsequent ones.

The Master [Dignāga] said that it is not the case that subsequent cognitions would have the appearances of the objects of preceding cognitions as their own objects, because those [preceding objects] are not the objects of [the subsequent cognition].
For:

Otherwise, only the very first [cognition] would be connected, because the object exists there; for a subsequent cognition is not connected with the object of a preceding one, since a subsequent cognition does not have as its object the object-domain of a preceding cognition.
(387) Indeed, a subsequent cognition does not possess the status of having the object of a preceding cognition as its own object.
And how can that which is not an object be apprehended?
For when the first [cognition] has the form of the object, then the second [cognition], having arisen from that, also possesses the form of the cognition of that object-form.
For it is thus:

when there arises the knowledge or non-knowledge of a cognition possessing the form of that object, there is a connection [of the object] by virtue of having that form, just as in the case of a distant tree and so forth as described.
Otherwise, the cognition could not be remembered.
It is remembered precisely as accompanied by its object;
since being mounted upon that [object]— characterized by being occupied with it— is its very nature,
there is therefore a recollection of it together with its object.

In the case of jars and the like, however, even their intrinsic nature alone—not necessarily accompanied by the potter and so forth—is perceived; yet the object is apprehended only when accompanied by consciousness.
Therefore, it is precisely such [an object] that is remembered.
But that [is not the case] for jars and so forth; for that too is non-existent because:
It is logical that there is a conjunction [of cognition] when two distinct things are perceived; however, there is no definition of cognition apart from the form of blue (nīlākāra).
