[If you argue it exists] by way of having the nature of pleasure and so forth, this very point is not established for you.
For it is not your established position that cognition has the nature of pleasure and so forth.
If it is argued that because pleasure and so forth are objects,
just as there is no consciousness other than pleasure and so forth, so too blue and so forth have no existence as external locations or as objects of cognition other than [the consciousness itself];
Nor is there "externality" for pleasure and so forth, because their status as objects of cognition (*prameyatva*) is admitted;
nor is it ultimately logical to speak of "external" or "internal" with respect to their self-awareness (*saṃvedana*),
for pleasure and so forth do not possess the nature of a grasper (*grāhakatā*) toward blue and other such objects.
Even in the absence of that [external object], because it appears in exactly that same way,
and because whatever occurs even without something else cannot be produced by that [other thing]— just as pleasure and so forth occur even without the apprehension of blue and so forth—
it has been established that the apprehension of blue and so forth is produced solely by a specific nature [of the cognition itself], since it occurs even in the absence of that [object].
Therefore, it is established that there can be no determination of the apprehender of blue and so forth without the immediate presence of blue and so forth; thus, a twofold aspect is proven.
Furthermore, even if the aspect of the apprehender exists as something distinct from the experienced aspect of blue and so forth, nevertheless—
By what means can the distinctness of an object from its cognition be established, given that the object being cognized is necessarily experienced simultaneously with the cognition?
For objects such as blue and the like are indeed perceived together with their cognition at one and the same time.

Since it is not perceived separately from the cognition, and there is no object other than that [cognition], how could it be that the cognition is of such a nature? It has been established that it is impossible to distinguish [them].
If it is argued that the appearance of difference occurs,
then that difference would be seen by erroneous cognitions, just as non-duality [is seen] in the moon;
for example, the perception of two moons is a perception of difference within a single moon located in one place, and so it is with respect to the self of consciousness as well.
But surely, even in the case of a single object, the perception of difference is logical because of the difference in the forms of consciousness;
however, how could this apply to its own self?
For it cannot be otherwise at that very same time.
For how could its own nature be cognized by that very [cognition] which has the form of another? This would entail the consequence of its non-apprehension;
yet this is not the case, because:

If it is impossible to cognize an intrinsic nature (svarūpa) in any other way, then it is even more impossible [to cognize] an extrinsic nature (pararūpa). Even so, it remains impossible. If it is impossible to cognize an intrinsic nature otherwise, yet it is also impossible to cognize an extrinsic nature by means of an intrinsic nature, then it follows that an extrinsic nature is just as impossible to cognize as an intrinsic nature. Therefore, this is the meaning: [The opponent argues: "If it is impossible to cognize an intrinsic nature otherwise, then it is even more impossible to cognize an extrinsic nature; thus, like the intrinsic nature, the extrinsic nature is likewise impossible. Therefore, this is the point.
If self-awareness exists, a distinction [between objects] cannot be apprehended if it were the nature [of cognition itself].
However, if consciousness were a single entity possessing variegated forms (*citrākāra*), it could be apprehended through self-awareness, as otherwise it would be impossible.

Therefore, even in the case of seeing two moons, if there were no unity, it could not be apprehended because it is impossible for either oneself or another to perceive it; this has already been established.

Therefore, the conceptual construction of a distinction between two things—based on positive and negative concomitance by means of a conceptualization occurring at a subsequent time—is not a perception;
this very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "And the distinction [is made] by deluded cognitions," and so forth.
That which is intended as a pair of moons is in fact non-dual, because it is contained within a single cognition.

In that case, one must also admit that even for blue and yellow, which are perceived simultaneously, there is a single variegated form (*citrākāra*); for this very reason, since the variegated form consisting of that cognition is also unitary therein.
However, if a distinction between them is maintained, then it must be admitted as follows:
There is no restriction of simultaneous cognition for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow;
this very fact—that they possess distinct *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation)—is the cause of their difference.
However, because the appearance of two moons lacks distinct *yogakṣema*, it is indeed a single unity.
But surely, how can there be oneness given the superimposition of contradictory properties?
For this very thing is what is called "difference," namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties; and here, contradiction is characterized by the state of mutual exclusion.
This is not so.

That contradiction exists only between permanence and its opposite; there is no contradiction between the two when they enter into a single cognition. Precisely because they enter into a single cognition, there is no contradiction between them; this very fact—that they are not dissociated—is what constitutes their nature.
And it is not contradicted by that very [cognition];
therefore, it is designated as "its single form" through conceptual construction based on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
He demonstrates that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is indeed an absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) by stating:
"There is no object whatsoever that is not cognized, nor is there the cognition of a non-object.
Nor is the object seen; there is no distinction between those two as they are being experienced.
There is a contradiction because there is neither positive nor negative concomitance; the cognition of blue is one alone, since it is never observed apart from the other,
as follows:
An object that is not cognized is never seen to be an object, nor is cognition itself [an object]. Since they are always inseparable, there is therefore an absolute cognition of the object.

One who understands difference desires difference for the sake of its distinct application; if that [difference] does not exist, then what distinction can there be between difference and non-difference?
Therefore, in this case, the opponent must establish "difference" as a mere name.
There is no harm whatsoever to another;
if there is no distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted therein, what is the use of such a differentiation?
How then is it that when one says, "Bring the blue," the bringing of the yellow is not performed?
At that time, it is precisely the non-appearance of that yellow which is not brought [to consciousness] by him; however, that blue which is inseparable from it is indeed manifested and,
being established in cognition, is liberated.
It cannot be led otherwise;

for it has been established that the conventional usage of difference, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is indeed unreal. Therefore, the object appearing at the time of cognition is unavoidable [as being distinct].

Since it is non-distinct from cognition, and because its acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are inseparable, the identity of the object with the cognition is unavoidable— it cannot be prevented— and thus cognition is established as possessing a form (*sākāra*).

In that case, then, only cognition alone would be perceived, not the object; and even when that [cognition] is perceived, there would be the awareness of two forms, such as blue and so forth; and if that too were to appear only at the time of the cognition, the object would again not be seen. Thus, because of the infinite regress resulting from the projection of further forms, an inconsistency would arise.
To this, the following is the rebuttal:
There would be an inference of a distinct cause:

for one who has perceived a cognition with a blue form, it must have some cause; thus, a cause corresponding to that [form] is inferred, but this [cause] is not directly an object of perception due to the previously mentioned fault of contradiction.
If it is asked, "How can there even be inference for that which is absolutely unperceived? he says:
"Because of the absence of sensory cognitions, even though other causes are present."

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam anumānam*) proceeds solely by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). For instance, even when the eye, light, and mental attention are present, visual consciousness in the form of a pillar does not arise with respect to what is intended to be empty of a pillar; yet elsewhere it arises instantaneously. Therefore, it is known that there must be some other entity present here.
That object which, by its absence, there is an absence elsewhere— that such object is the external object of cognition, known precisely as being devoid of the adjunct of perception;
how then can it be the object of direct perception?
Since that which possesses that form is the object of perception, there is no other way [to account for it]; thus, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), it is indeed the object.
If this is so, then the external object alone is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and not mere consciousness.

He shows that there is no middle ground here unless one asserts a restrictive rule: "If [the cause] were not stated as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), would another object be postulated as the producer of the difference in form, or is it simply some particularity of the immediately preceding condition itself? (392)
In this regard, the postulation of an object that has never been perceived is not tenable, except when such a postulation is made precisely because there is no other possible recourse.
However, when this mental image is established solely through the power of having previously perceived something, then the postulation of an external object is redundant;
furthermore, a postulation must follow what is actually observed and not otherwise.
For it is not possible to postulate what has not been perceived, since conceptual constructions are observed to follow from what is perceived; thus, it is impossible to conceive otherwise.
But surely even an external object is indeed perceived as the producer of the mental image?
Just as the state of being a cluster does not exist without a tree,
yet even there it is not the tree alone that is the producer— by whom is this seen?
No one.
If it is argued that because it has the form of ignorance,
it is seen by another person, and that for this reason it is subsequently seen by that very same person; [this is what was examined].
If it is argued that although it is seen later, its prior existence must follow from that very later perception—
if indeed it is perceived later, let it simply exist as something posterior.
For that apprehension does not operate with respect to the prior [object];
moreover, that apprehension belongs only to the form of the cognition, not to the object.
Therefore, even in that case, the certainty that "the object exists" arises only subsequently through another apprehension.
Even in that case, because the phrase "subsequently" lacks a definitive conclusion, there is simply no comprehension;

therefore, since the non-perception of an external object has already been established and its dependence on mental impressions (*vāsanā*) proven, it must be concluded that the capacity of the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) alone is the cause of restriction. This is so when one proceeds by the method of subtle analysis. However, for someone who is not thus trained, the status of an external object of knowledge is established through the inference of a difference in causes.
But surely, in the absence of external objects, how can there be the relation of cause and effect, as well as the relation of the signified and the signifier?
For indeed, without external objects, the status of being cause and effect would belong to those who know [the truth].
And because there is no fixed rule regarding them, there is neither effect nor cause.

For instance, from that which appears blue, there arises that which appears yellow, and from that [yellow], that which appears blue; thus, how can there be a mutual relationship of cause and effect between them? (1045–1046)

When a cognition appearing as yellow occurs immediately after a cognition appearing as blue, since there is no yellow apart from the appearance of yellow, the cause of that [subsequent cognition] is precisely the appearance of blue and not the [external] yellow;
nor is there any fixed rule in that regard,
for from an appearance of yellow, an appearance of blue may also arise.
If they were mutually caused, it would contradict logic;
for how could there be mutual causality between cause and effect?
However, if external objects exist, then in that case, blue itself is the cause.
The yellow appearance, however, is precisely the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
and since the immediately preceding condition is differentiated by the difference in the objective auxiliary cause (*arthasahakārin*), it does not attain unity,
whereby there would be no lack of restriction.

Alternatively, the activity of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) lies in the nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpatā*), whereas regarding the form (*ākāra*), it belongs to the blue object and so forth; since there is a restriction (*niyama*) in that regard, there is no fault. If the nature of consciousness were to arise even from something other than the nature of consciousness, or if the form of that [object] were to arise even from something other than the blue, there would be a lack of restriction (*aniyama*).

But surely, even from a white conch and the like, a yellow form is perceived, and even from something small, a large form [is perceived]; therefore, even in this case, there is indeed a lack of restriction.

This is not so, because this [objection] is inconsistent insofar as it concerns what is produced by a continuous stream of error; however, when there is a negation of non-error, there is necessarily no other alternative. (1047)
Since the perception of what is inconsistent due to delusion is simply non-authoritative, there is no deviation [from the rule] by means of it;
likewise, the production of a sprout from a seed is accepted, not the reverse.

For the Vijñānavādins, however, there is no seed or the like other than the appearance of a seed and so forth; consequently, there would be no fixed rule that from the appearance of a seed comes a sprout, and from that [sprout] comes the appearance of a seed.
Thus, worldly convention would be destroyed, and the relationship between the signified and the signifier would be utterly cast aside.
From smoke, it is established that fire exists;
and that which is imperceptible is what is to be inferred.
Now, neither external fire nor the appearance of fire is imperceptible, because both consist of the nature of cognition.
If it is argued that what is being established there is not the appearance of another, because of the possibility of deviation, but rather an inference of one's own future appearance— [we reply:
no.
Because there is no such restriction, the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda) alone is more tenable;
to this it is replied:
Even that state of causal and epistemic relations which relies upon external objects— such as the production of a sprout from a seed or the establishment of fire through smoke—
is likewise [accounted for] by cognitions that manifest in those forms and possess a fixed, regular association.
If it were to be conceptualized by relying upon cognition, what contradiction would there be?
In this case, the purpose is fulfilled by the appearance itself, not by the object; for that which does not appear is no different from the non-existent, even if it exists.
For it is thus:
apprehension is said to be existence;
for it is thus.

Even in the absence of an external object, the appearance is not faulty; however, without appearance, the external would always remain [merely] external. For it has been established that appearance occurs even without an external object;
whereas without appearance, the external is simply non-existent, because it is never perceived.

If [you argue that] "the appearance of the sprout follows from the appearance of the seed," then what contradiction is there in the relationship of cause and effect? For in that case, the appearance of the sprout would have to occur independently; indeed, if it were to appear independently—since it exists even in the absence of the appearance of the seed—it would follow that it is causeless.
For those who maintain the existence of external objects (bāhyārthavādins), however, there is no lack of a cause,
because even though it appears clearly, the seed exists;
for instance:
Even though the external object does not appear, its externality is not lost; however, for one who knows [the truth], it does not exist at all when there is no appearance.
Now, if it is argued that the appearance of another exists therein, then it is not causeless, because there would be a lack of restriction.
Nor does the arising of a dream-appearance occur from the appearance of another;
that [objection] is also the same, because:

If this [seed] does not appear as an object to anyone at all, then what proof is there for its existence, by virtue of which the sprout could have it as its cause? If it is argued that the "inexpressible" (nirupākhya), characterized by the absence of any description of causal capacity, exists because it is perceived later; ||| 1050 ||

If it is argued that the answer has already been stated—that [the cause] is known to exist by means of its effect—then only when the relationship between cause and effect is established is the existence of this [cause] understood; and only when its existence is established does the causal relationship come to be. (1051)
Therefore, due to the fault of mutual dependence, there is simply no establishment [of the object];
for surely, since this [superimposition] is observed even through the superimposition of a single meaning,
who can prevent such superimposition even in the case of cognition?

Since consciousness does not exist [ultimately], how can there be superimposition? This is the same even regarding the external; for the external also exists only through superimposition, and thus even its appearance exists indeed from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
For there is no existence other than the superimposition of an external object existing at the time of inference;
and thus, if there were something here, that superimposition would be fire as it is perceived;
likewise, if there were nothing here, there would simply be the appearance.
If it is argued that one [cognition] has an appearance while the other is the object, this is equivalent;
for even in that case, unity does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.

Or rather, even in the case of cognition, conventional usage occurs just as it does for two people with ophthalmia seeing two moons; and since this is the case elsewhere as well, there is no contradiction in the Vijñānavāda (Idealist) position either, provided that causal relations are established by relying on cognitions through the convergence of appearances determined by those forms. However, in the Bāhyārthavāda (Realist) position, a contradiction has been demonstrated due to the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, if the external object were eternal, it should be perceived only later; if it were perceived previously, then everything would have been perceived in all its aspects [at once].
If the external fire and so forth were eternal, its cognition would have occurred in a single form even earlier—why, then, would one proceed to infer it?
Now, if its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not apprehended through inference, how then can there be a cognition of its existence?
For being apprehended through another's form (*pararūpeṇa*) is equally applicable to the nature of consciousness itself.
Any further conceptual construction proceeds by unifying the perceived object with the mental construct; it is this that superimposes [the nature of the object] upon [consciousness].
If it were otherwise, then in the absence of that [continuity] superimposed by the mind, the object would subsequently arise as something interrupted;
for how could there be the existence of something interrupted without that [superimposition]?

If it is argued that, even if there is a purpose for postulating non-interruption, a latent impression (*vāsanā*) will nonetheless exist in the interval, nevertheless, there would still be an interruption of the latent impression because it lacks the nature of that [non-interruption].
Even if this were accepted regarding the object, its [the cognition's] nature would not follow; for that which is perceived cannot be understood as being identical to that which is unperceived—
it is merely a case of superimposition.
This is indeed the same for the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*) as well;

for how could a latent impression (*vāsanā*), which consists of a heterogeneous consciousness and exists in the interval, ensure that [the stream] remains uninterrupted when a heterogeneous [consciousness] arises, just as in the case of the application of lac-dye?
Just as the uninterrupted continuity of the world is accepted [to exist] by means of lac-dye,
so too there is the occurrence of a series of heterogeneous cognitions in the interval.

(1054) Precisely because it follows from that very latent impression (*vāsanā*), there will be no interruption. Likewise, in the world, the application of lac-dye is said not to produce a disconnected result, as it imparts a specific potency— inferrable from the final fruit— to the seeds, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and so forth occurring in the intervening stages.

In the same way, let it be designated or determined that even a previous cognition of fire produces its result as if uninterrupted— having merged its own causal capacity into subsequent cognitions of fire while passing through intervening cognitions of a different class—

such that it is said, "that very previous cognition of fire produces the cognition of fire, not the cognition of smoke. In this regard, just as the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) infer from a subsequent cognition of fire that "fire existed previously," [so too may one infer the existence of the prior cognition].

Thus, for the Vijñānavādins, the impression (*vāsanā*) exists; therefore, there is no difference between these two [positions]. Even from the appearance of smoke, the impression of smoke is postulated, and the causality of the impression has been established, whereas the status of an external object as a cause is not tenable.

And this has already been established: if smoke were not produced by fire, there would be no cognition of the cause from its effect; or, even if it were the cause, how could there be a certain cognition [of it]? (395)

If the appearance arises solely from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of smoke, then that [impression] itself is the smoke; that itself is the absence of the causal relationship [between fire and smoke].
For in that case, smoke would not arise from fire, because it would be bound exclusively to its own latent impression.
Now, if even the appearance of fire is a cause because it serves as the cause for the appearance of smoke by way of being conducive to the awakening of its latent impression (*vāsanā*),
then smoke too would be a cause of fire; and if that were the case, how could there be any certain cognition [of the relationship], given the possibility of deviation?
To this it is replied:
even in that case, a cognition appearing as smoke leads only to a cognition appearing as fire—due to a latent impression (vāsanā) potent enough to awaken it—and not to the actual fire itself. (396)

For cognition appearing as smoke is bound by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire; therefore, that impression is inferred. Since that impression is on the verge of being awakened, it produces the appearance of fire; thus, through the attainment of the appearance of fire, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For example, according to those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), an inferred fire either produces the appearance of fire or another actual fire, whereby the attainment of fire occurs through dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*).
In the same way, the appearance of smoke and the appearance of fire are dependent upon the latent impression.
If it is argued that the fire perceived directly and the fire not perceived are one and the same,
we say no,
because there is a lack of valid evidence for this.
It has been established that oneness exists solely through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and thus it is the impression itself that is ultimately one, not the object; furthermore,
even regarding external objects, fire is not inferred [independently].
Rather, it is only the future appearance that constitutes the object for living beings,
because there is no purpose for anyone served by fire that does not appear.
And when there is a present manifestation, let the future manifestation be that which is being inferred; what is the use of inferring fire?
If it is asked how there can be an inference regarding something that is yet to be, [the answer is] because it is observed to be exactly so.
Since it has been seen that "it is exactly thus," this [position] is not viewed as illogical. However, regarding an external object, there is neither correspondence nor the possibility of perception.
Everything is consistent when [the object] is inferred from a future manifestation;
but as for an external [object], even in the case of a dream, its existence is impossible.
For in this way, the cognition of a future object is well-ascertained through inference; however, it has been established that there is no cognition of a present object [in such a case].
Otherwise, no one would ever act with regard to a future object.

If, on the other hand, one proceeds by determining the identity between the present and the future, then that would be a cognition of the future object alone, not a cognition of the present; for it is through attainment that the reality of the cognition is inferred. (And this cognition is "excellent" [prakṛṣṭā]).
Therefore, because the present form is not attained and the future is its opposite, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has only the future as its object;
whereas the present state, though existing there, is non-existent [for that cognition].
Even perception is a valid means of knowledge only with respect to what is yet to come, as has been established;
therefore, the claim that "this object will exist in the future and does not exist at the time of cognition" is refuted.

Since it does not exist without that which is to come into being, perception arising from its conjunction is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, this [objection] is also refuted: "It is not a cause, because it is the apprehension of what is presently existing. Therefore, since perception and inference have future objects as their domain and do not follow the presence or absence of those [objects], they possess validity in the ultimate sense; indeed, everything has only its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) as its object.

From the perspective of conventional usage, [consciousness] has an object as its domain, and that object is something to be realized (*bhāvya*) which is the domain of attainment; therefore, since only that possesses causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), it alone possesses the status of being an "object" (*arthatva*), provided that conventional usage is accepted. Thus, it follows that [consciousness] has only an object as its domain.
And since that object is indeed present, why is it explained as having a future state?
To this it is replied:
This conventional usage is threefold, distinguished by those who are untrained and so forth; based upon that, all of this appears to be logical. (1057)
The linguistic usage of the unlearned has as its object perception directed toward a present thing;
that of the learned has as its object a future thing; and that of the highly learned has as its object mere appearance.

Therefore, if one were to establish—on the basis of the perspective of unlearned people—that [perception] has a real thing as its object and that this object is present, then what has already been established is being proven once again.
In the very same way, we too maintain that the consciousness appearing as smoke leads one to infer only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire;

and since that impression is perceived as being identical with a future appearance, it functions as the cause for the appearance of that [fire’s] form. Thus, it is that very future appearance which is inferred, just like the future fire in the view of those who assert external objects.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the appearance itself is the object.
Now, if even subsequently there is a mistaken appearance, there would be no desire for it;
for in the world, desire is directed toward the actual object, whereas in the case of an appearance, there is no desire for it.
For no worldly object, such as the pleasure of a dream, is desired [as a means to an end].
This is incorrect,
because:

If, having attained the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the continuity] were not subject to reconnection at the end of the day, then that would be the pleasure of a dream; what harm is there in that for you?
However, where there is such non-interruption due to a specific latent impression, that is not merely the pleasure of a dream.
For even for the Vijñānavādins, there is indeed a distinction between "dream" and "non-dream" based on a specific latent impression.
Whether it be a distinction between one who has awakened and others within a dream,
or even a particular state of dreaming itself, there will still be purposeful activity therein; what loss is this to you, who are not yet wise?

From the perspective of ultimate truth, for those who desire liberation and are adorned with the supreme jewel-ornaments of refined wisdom, all pleasure is indeed undesirable—like the play of children; thus, the attachment to engaging in activity is merely the proving of what is already established.
For it is as follows:

Those who desire liberation are endowed with forbearance; they do not seek the pleasures of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing their turning away from those [pleasures], their engagement in dharma is for the purpose of their livelihood. For those discerning individuals who have directed their gaze toward liberation and who view all the means for achieving dharma as merely like children’s play for the sake of worldly pleasure, there is an engagement in dharma to turn them away from the mockery of worldly conduct. Consequently, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely conventional, having as its object only that which appears.

If, then, the appearance of fire and so forth is restricted solely to its latent impression (*vāsanā*), and that [impression] is restricted solely to a homogeneous latent impression, then from the appearance of smoke, only that [specific] latent impression should be inferred; how could there be a comprehension of the latent impression of fire?
For indeed, latent impressions are the cause of an appearance of a specific form, having been set in motion by that very form; they do not lead to the manifestation of anything else. (Verse 1061)
The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire does not produce the appearance of smoke,
because that [appearance] is produced by the latent impression of smoke alone; therefore, what is produced by one thing cannot be made to depend upon another which is not its cause.
To this it is replied:

it is the mental continuum itself, containing the latent impressions (vāsanā) appropriate for that [cognition], which manifests the cognition appearing as smoke; therefore, smoke [is known] from fire. (397)
The entire manifold of cyclic existence arises from mind alone;
therefore, from the continuum of mind supported by latencies capable of producing the appearance of fire, there arises the appearance of fire,
and that same continuum produces the appearance of smoke through the reinforcement of another moment of mind that awakens the latency for smoke.
Then, the latent impression of smoke (*dhūmavāsanā*), assisted by the latent impression of fire (*agnivāsanā*), is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the appearance of smoke;
likewise, for the future appearance of fire, the latent impression of fire is the material cause,
while the appearance of smoke is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) because it acts as an awakener, and so too is the latent impression of smoke.

Therefore, because they depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*), the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between fire and its effect, smoke, is logical.

Now, if the status of being a signifier arises from dependence on a single causal complex, then the relationship of signified and signifier would belong only to things existing at the same time; thus, there could be no cognition of what is future, due to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This objection is not valid.

Since it has been established that everything which is yet to come possesses the quality of being cognizable, why is fire not also cognized at that very moment as something to be reached by means of smoke? For only that which is yet to be (bhāvin) is the object of valid cognition.
For if it were understood that "because there is smoke, fire exists at that very time,
but will not exist later," then it would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all;
for there is no need for that fire which exists at that specific time.
If it is argued that there is doubt regarding what is yet to come,
how can it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
[It is] a valid means of knowledge because it reveals the object.

It is not the case that the object must be shown to the cognizer by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only at a later time; for even though the object has been seen, if no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is produced by it, then it is indeed non-existent, because [existence] consists in the possibility of future causal efficiency. Thus, even that [present object] is considered a producer of causal efficiency only figuratively (*upacārāt*).

If it is argued that this is because the effect is metaphorically designated upon the cause, then even for those [entities] such as the cognition of a circle of fire (alātacakra), there is indeed accessibility through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that time;
however, they lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). If one asks, "What of it? [the answer follows].
This is equally true for the object as well;
since it performs purposeful activity by way of being an object to be realized, it too possesses causal efficacy. This is likewise true for the mental impression (*vāsanā*);
even the object, at that time, is accessible only through the mental impression alone.
If it is argued that [the object] is understood by means of something else, then the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is likewise understood by means of something else;
for even regarding the latent impression, there is no comprehension of another [entity] through conventional usage.
Therefore, the inference is identical for both the proponent of external objects and the proponent of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Therefore, it is only logical that there is cognition alone here.
(Kha) How then is the two-fold nature of consciousness with respect to an external object stated by the Teacher? It is logical only as a cognition of an object.
To this it is replied:

This consensus among the learned exists; however, the twofold nature [of cognition] is accepted by relying on external objects, and that is established through the rule of simultaneous awareness. (398)

The dual nature [of cognition] is described from the perspective of others who accept external objects; however, for the wise, it has been established that the restriction of consciousness to a single form is indeed impossible for two distinct things. Furthermore, if cognition were formless and its form were something else entirely, then the form of the apprehender would at some time be perceived separately.
If it is argued that "the very same form which is perceived in yellow, distinct from blue,
is that same blue [form] appearing as the aspect of pleasure, and that same [blue] appearing as the aspect of pain," we say no.

That very same form of the apprehender which was previously seen is also this [present] yellow and so forth. Is this cognition perception or inference? It is not perception first of all, because perception does not function regarding the relation between prior and posterior; and in the absence of that, it cannot be inference. Thus, priority and posteriority are not objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How then is it that, because perception is incapable of grasping positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is inference even regarding fire and the like elsewhere?

It is not because inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object; rather, inference intends a single [object] as the domain of a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*). For example, having superposed oneness upon those things residing in the kitchen and other locations by means of another individual instance, it is established that "this very same fire" exists.
It is not so.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is indeed only oneness;

likewise, in this case as well, that very same form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*) and that very same blue (*nīla*) exist even today as non-distinct from it. Thus, having accepted the non-difference of the continuum (*santāna*), the difference between the apprehended and the apprehender—or rather, between the nature of consciousness and the form of the blue—is established.
Therefore, there is no difference in the actual entity (*vastu*), but rather [the distinction exists] within the conventionally designated (*prajñaptisat*) continuum in a general sense.
However, with respect to the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*), which is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is indeed a rule of simultaneous apprehension;
therefore, non-difference alone is the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, if consciousness were formless (*nirākāra*), then it would always remain pure, and would not possess forms such as sharp, dull, or turbid.
Moreover, it is also otherwise; for thus,
consciousness possesses a twofold nature.

Cognition, bearing a variety of appearances—such as sharp, dull, or turbid—due to the differences among the sense faculties, is observed with respect to a single object. How can there be such a multiplicity of forms in relation to one and the same object? (399)

Since the object possesses an undifferentiated nature, the mind would have to be of a single form toward all those objects; if [the mind] were [identical] to the object, then it would lack self-awareness. (400)

If consciousness is formless (*nirākāra*), then only the object would appear as having a single form; since it appears as that [single form], and that [object] indeed has only a single form, there would be no distinction in the appearance, nor could there be a multiplicity of forms in the object. To this, [the opponent] replies: "But even if the object possesses multiple forms, how can it be that the form of cognition must also consist of only a single form?"
Therefore, the fault of having various forms remains exactly as it was;
for there is no fault,
since [the cognition] arises based on the object and imitates its form.
There may be a distinction from another [perspective] in some respect regarding that "vision"— so it is in the He manuscript.

If it were argued that there is the consequence of [the cognition] arising with that form [of the object], then that same form could arise even from something other than the object— just as the appearance of two moons arises from the power of cataracts and so forth,
or just as a son, though possessing the father's form, is distinct from the father upon whom he depends.
It relies on some distinction from something else.
For a son, while being born resembling his father, does not fail to assume even the form of his mother;
thus, it demonstrates difference precisely through the difference of the sense faculties.
Having the form of a peacock’s eye, radiant with blue and red,
and brilliant.
Those with dim vision perceive a halo from a lamp and such;
those whose visual power has been weakened by a cataract see the lamp as radiant, distinguished by various forms such as blue, and surrounded by a perimeter.
Now, if that form of the lamp were indeed real in that manner, [then...]
If that [cognition] were external in form, what would be the objection against one with clear vision?
Even one with clear vision would perceive it;
or rather, he too would simply be one with clear vision, not one whose sense faculty is impaired.
For how could one who perceives reality as it is, seeing that very thing, have his senses destroyed?
Or how [could he be so]? || 404 || 3 || How indeed?

Vision is said to be impaired because of the non-perception of real objects; however, if one were to assume that vision is impaired even when real objects are being perceived, then those who see entire pillars and other such things would have to be considered as having impaired eyesight.
For it is not the case that an impairment of the power of vision is perceived through direct perception in its own nature; therefore, it must be assumed on the basis of inference.

And just as a capacity (*śakti*) is postulated through the observation of an effect, and just as the postulation of an obstructer arises from the obstruction of an effect, so too is its effect [in this case] observation (*darśana*).

And that vision of reality—or even if it is something other than the vision of reality—is called "non-affliction" by virtue of not being impaired by conceptual construction; otherwise, if one were to see even what exists as being otherwise, then one would have impaired faculties.
Such being the case:
The eye of one who perceives supersensuous objects has clearly been purified of darkness; how then could that [eye] perceive what is visible to other senses as indistinct?
For how could one who sees even what is invisible to others perceive what is visible to others as unclear?

For it is not observed that one who sees something subtle and otherwise invisible sees that which is otherwise invisible more clearly; this is not seen to be the case, and therefore it is not logical to say "one sees what has not come into being. But surely, to say "what has not come into being is seen" is a contradiction.

If that which is being perceived were unreal, how could there be the reality of that which is real? Apart from perception, there is no other basis for determining what is real or unreal. If one establishes that what is perceived is unreal, it follows that there is nothing at all that is real, because there would be no distinction [between them].
And yet, it is impossible for what is actually perceived to be untenable.

That is incorrect; for whatever is perceived in a particular form, it must be accepted as being exactly in that form. Otherwise, how could that which is being perceived be understood in any other way? (1065) Since [cognition] is observed to follow the presence and absence of sensory modifications such as *timira* (ocular disorder), it is not logical to claim that its birth is produced by other causes [external objects], or that it is not permeated by the nature of consciousness (*saṃvedana*).
Furthermore, the very conformity to disorders such as cataracts (timira) is what is to be proven;
nevertheless, even if one accepts [the existence of] external objects, it remains a mere assertion,
for instance:

It is understood that the capacity of one thing—distinct from light, the eye, and mental attention—is the cause; therefore, nothing else is the cause, and how could that which is not a cause be an object?

(406) Since it is only the lamp itself, as distinct from the light and so forth, whose capacity is perceived—and not that of the circle [of light]—therefore, because other things lack the status of being a cause, they cannot have the status of being an object.
It has been established that what is not a cause is not an object;

however, it is not tenable to claim that something is an object simply because it appears, since even an erroneous appearance is possible. If it is asked, "How can that which appears in its own nature be an error? [the response follows].
If it is argued that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) appearing in its own form would not be an object [of cognition], because self-awareness consists in appearing elsewhere,
then how is it logical for that which appears in its own form to appear elsewhere?
For if that in which [an object] appears were itself to appear [only through another], there would be an infinite regress;

whereas if it appears to itself, then by that same logic, the appearance of another [object] is also simply the appearance of its own nature. Thus, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone [is established]; for if blue and other such objects appear to one another, they are nothing but awareness itself.

Since even blue and other [objects] reside within cognition by virtue of having the very nature of cognition, the object is that cause whose capacity is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
However, because the capacity of the eye of a peacock’s tail-feather (*mayūra-candraka*) is not determined through positive and negative concomitance,
it does not possess the status of being an object.
If it is argued that, because it is impossible to establish the existence of pillars and the like as distinct from the nature of the cognition itself,
whereas those perceived while awake are established as distinct through another subsequent cognition and through the observation of their effects such as burning,
[we reply that] here too, the perception occurs due to an identical impairment caused by a visual disorder (*timiropaplava*).
Nor does it apply to them either, because they are equal;
for it is not observed that fire perceived through delusion has the effect of burning different types of earth.
Consequently, both [the fire and the fuel] are illusory; thus,
that fire is indeed non-burning.
If it is argued that because things are perceived as such [i.e.,
as they appear], the perception of what is not so as being so is indeed an illusion, and thus,
with respect to worldly convention, it is an error;
Even the status of being an "object" (arthatva) depends solely upon worldly convention;
since everything appears as having its own nature, it is not logical to make a distinction [between them].
Therefore, the principle is that an object is nothing other than that which performs purposeful action (arthakriyā).
If it is asked, "Why is not everything an object?
[we reply: why is it not accepted that everything is indeed cognition?
And since everything exists as cognition, it is all merely self-cognition; how, then, can there be the status of being an external object?
If it is argued that [consciousness] is a perception of something absent,
no;
because there is a lack of valid proof.
If it is asked, "How is there self-awareness?
[the answer is] no,
because it is observed.
If it is argued that [the object] is seen even when being experienced by another, what is the proof for this?
And if you ask, "What is the proof for you as well? [we reply: it is the same.
If it is argued: "Is it not the case that there is simply no cognition of another? For in the absence of a manifestor, how could there be manifestation of something unmanifested, like a jar?"—we say:
No.
Because luminosity itself lacks established existence,
it is just like a lamp.
If it is asked, "How [is this] regarding the jar?", [the answer is:
because it persists in a state capable of action;
from what [source] could it be said that form exists therein?

Because touch and so forth are observed to depend on a single causal complex, and because [the object] is perceived by another, such as a night-stalker (*niśācara*), it is not actually the case [that they are distinct]; this is precisely what we intend.
Therefore, like a lamp, everything is indeed self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*).
Furthermore, even the form perceived by one with ophthalmia [would be affected];
moreover, if it had such capacity, there would be the undesirable consequence of seeing a portion of the moon— even one devoid of light— just like a section of a variegated cloth.
For if that very [atom] were the cause of cognition, why would it depend upon a lamp?
Moreover, a portion of an extended form is perceived even without another portion.
If it is argued that the cause is exactly the same, we say no;
for blue and so forth are perceived precisely as dependent upon other forms.
Thus, the causality of both is postulated because of their existence by means of the lamp alone; therefore, neither of them is the cause.
Because of the absence of the intellect (*dhī*), neither [of the two causes] exists;
even when that place is covered, [the perception] occurs due to the mere presence of the lamp. Thus, that perception does not have both as its cause.
If it is argued that it is impossible to cover it because it arises otherwise, [we reply: no.

If its arising occurs at that very moment, then it does not have the nature of non-luminosity; thus, the claim that "perception functions there [regarding itself] and therefore there is no self-awareness" is inconsistent, because perception, being simultaneous with its object, lacks any functional activity toward that object.
However, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it would follow that by its own operation of that nature, that very [form] is produced by the lamp, just like light;
or else, just as the lamp arises from its own cause endowed with its own light, so too the eye is endowed with the form manifesting before it—thus there is no fault.
If it is argued that the light is indeed distinct from the lamp:
Granted that there is a distinction [between light and its illumination], yet it follows that light is not something to be illuminated by a lamp in the same way as the lamp itself;
therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it, consciousness (vijñāna) here is non-existent as something distinct from the eye and visible form.
However, that very duality, when established by the self-awareness of its own nature, is what constitutes "cognition";

thus, another cause for such cognition must be postulated, and so it is established that cognition possesses two forms. Furthermore, if the object itself, present before one, were endowed with form and were the very thing grasped by consciousness, then the object would be grasped in its own essential nature.
It is not tenable for that [object] to be both manifest and unmanifest based on distinctions such as distance and proximity;
if it were argued that this is due to differences in illumination, then the same would apply to its being covered or uncovered—
either the perception or the non-perception would be identical.

Indeed, an object existing without transgressing the limits of the range of vision would appear by its very nature, due to the acquisition of a fixed nature through the relinquishing of other natures brought about by a succession of its own causes. How could there be a difference in its manifestation even when it is at a distance or nearby, such that the consequence of it having a manifest or non-manifest nature would arise? Yet this difference is observed; therefore, it is not the external object itself that appears through the assumption of a nature possessed of form.
For when a determinate and complete form appears, there can be no appearance of difference, because that would entail a difference in the form itself.
Indeed, the form appearing before one is the object itself, since that is the very definition of an object;
therefore, if there were a difference in that [appearance], there would necessarily be an actual difference in the object.
Furthermore, if there were a difference [between the object and its manifestation], there would be no designation of the object as "manifest" and so forth;
nor, when another object appears, is there anything else called "unmanifest," for that [object] has that very same nature, and that [nature] is indeed manifest.

If that [cognition] has that very [object] as its own nature, how could it have the nature of another? If you say it is because it is perceived as having that form, then how can there be such perception when there is a difference in form?
For if there is perception [of them] as non-different, let there be a distinction in the perception itself; but if the form of the object is non-different, how can a distinction be maintained?

Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that there is a distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest due to the distinction between near and far, or due to the distinction between the light and the seeing.

Since there is no transcendence of the conceptualization of its own form versus other [forms], even when there is a difference in illumination, if it appears by way of its own form, how could it not appear clearly? Even so, as to why this is the case, it is nothing at all;
for in the difference of illumination, that other [factor] is present therein.
But how can the object be grasped when it has an unmanifested form and so forth?
If it is argued that there is a dull perception due to the intervention of a distant location, then even for you, it would simply not be seen at all because of that very same intervention.
Moreover, if it is beneficial, then let it be seen quite clearly; how then could there be any distinction?
If you claim there is a difference because some subtle part of it is seen through dim light, [we reply: no.
For it is only the subtle part that is obstructed by distance, not the gross form;
however, the subtle part, being obstructed by distance, is simply not seen. But surely this whole (avayavin) is one and remains present in its full magnitude?
In that case, since the whole [object] is entirely perceived, how could there be an indistinct apprehension?

Alternatively, if it were not a single [entity], then the cognition "this is a subtle whole" would simply not occur; or, if it did occur, it would have to grasp the form of the atoms as being perfectly distinct.
He demonstrates this very point:

"If the external object were a single unity, how could there be a distinction between the seen and the unseen? If it were manifold, divided into atoms, how could there be a distinction between the seen and the unseen? (410)

[Objection: But surely, because even a single composite whole possesses subtle parts, when it is perceived while devoid of them, its form is indistinct; otherwise, there would be a difference in its nature. [Reply: That is not so, because:
If blue is not perceived without yellow, how can that [blue] be called indistinct? When one thing is not perceived while another is, the perception of its own nature is indeed distinct.
[Objection: But surely, if there is multiplicity, then the non-perception of one thing when another is being perceived constitutes a lack of clarity.
That too is incorrect,
because the same [objection] applies there as well:
if that which is perfectly clear in the apprehension of the object is [itself] the cognition of the object, what other form could there be for the cognition of the object?
If that [cognition] is indeed the object itself even when other things are not apprehended, how can it be indistinct?
If, on the other hand, it arises from that [object], then the object is not its [nature]; so how could there be an apprehension of the object?
If it is argued that even then, being such [an arising], it is the very form of the thing itself—
If it were of the nature of a real entity, it would be seen in that same way by another as well;
since it is not so seen, it has been demonstrated that it is merely a cognition belonging to the other person alone because of its uniqueness.
For instance:
"The cognition itself has arisen in a doubled form"—this is how people understand it;

thus, through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the cognition is designated as such because it perceives an object that appears doubled. Just as a person, due to contact with a staff, comes to bear the designation "staff," so too is the case here.
But that is incorrect.

Since my eye has been contracted [in its function] by that very meeting with the vision, let that designation be based solely on the observation of its effect. For there is no other effect of vision, nor does it persist as an effect through that [vision] itself.

Likewise, if it were [the case that] blue too would be sorrowful simply through such a conjunction, then where is this vision of mine? For it is never accepted by you. Therefore, the lack of clarity in perception is established by the consensus of all the world;
for a certainty that does not arise from all [senses] is called erroneous without cause.
For an effort that establishes unerring practical activity cannot be conceived otherwise;
therefore, a distinction in cognition is logically justified by the appearance of the object itself.
If the difference in cognition is due to a difference in the appearance [of the object] through its varying degrees of dullness or clarity, [then the distinction is established].
When one thing is distinct, how can that which is non-distinct appear as distinct?
(411) For its existence does not consist in being an effect of that [external object].
Another says:

"The difference in cognition regarding even a single object arises solely from the difference between the dullness and sharpness of external light, and not from an intrinsic difference in the nature of the cognition itself; therefore, that form does not belong to the mind.
This is untenable.
For if the appearance of an object were accompanied by its own light, then when it appears conjoined with another [light], there would be no dimness of manifestation. (1072)

If it is argued that when there is the appearance of forms of light mutually excluded from one another, it is those very two that appear in such a way, and thus there is no appearance of an indistinct form; for indeed,
when one thing possesses the manifestation of its own nature, another distinct thing does not become like it—
just as in the case of the appearance of an object screened by a cloth dyed with safflower (kusumbha)— then [we reply]:
Even in that case, because it is identical [to the other], there is no appearance of redness by way of its own nature or by way of manifestation.

If it is accepted that the very same form belongs to that [object] because it appears as such, then since the entire [form] would appear as such due to the dimness of the light, how could there be a difference in cognition?
Therefore, even when there is a difference in the light, there is no appearance of difference; and furthermore—
If you argue that the light is faint because it is obscured by dust at a distance, then why is that [obscuration] not present here as well?
Since this lack of intensity exists elsewhere too, it must be due to the thinness of the light itself;

for even in that case, obscuration by dust is possible. If the light is faint because it is covered by dust in a more distant location, then that location must also be faint in its form, since obscuration by dust is equally possible there.
Indeed, it is not that there is no dust here being stirred up by the wind,

for even though it exists, its nature as a non-obscuring cause is due to the extreme subtlety of the dust; however, in a more distant location, the absence of its falling within the intervening space is due to the abundance of that dust.
That very same logic applies to the cow-dung ash;

for there too, it is precisely the predominance of light that exists, whereas near [the fire], as there is a thinning of dust, so too is there a thinning of light— so what is the point of saying this?
And when it is very near, that light becomes clearly manifest and exceedingly distinct.

If it is argued that when there is a clear manifestation of light due to the thinness of dust in a book, then at an even closer proximity the manifestation would be extremely clear because the dust is thinnest,
since the sense organ lacks the capacity [to perceive it otherwise] in that case— then [we reply]:
It has been stated that, in every respect, total non-perception would necessarily follow;
even in that case, if another form were to arise by relying on the unseen (adṛṣṭa),
there would then be an obstruction of light due to their mutual concealment.

Relying upon an insentient object with which one has had no prior acquaintance, a different form indeed arises therein; by that [form], the light is obstructed or covered, and thus there is no perception of anything else.
This being so, everyone would perceive only that single thing and nothing else, because the light [of the other] is obstructed.

Moreover, both [the near and the far] are seen when one is close; at that time, there is no obstruction at all because [the object] is situated behind [the observer], since only a single part is visible.
Indeed, the form of one situated in a nearby place is not perceived from behind by someone standing in a distant location, as it is held to be indistinct.
If it is argued that this is an error,
then how could error possibly arise for those who perceive the true nature of things?
There is indeed a spatial delusion, just as there is the perception of the sun as being in contact with the tops of trees.
If that object were visible even though it did not exist in that place, then why would it not be consistent with perception even though it does not exist at that time?
(1073) If there were perception of what is non-existent at that time, then it would follow that for one who perceives all objects, everything [would be perceived]; yet that is not seen. (1074)

If all this is justified on the grounds that its connection [to reality] has not been observed, then for the opponent as well, everything would arise from what is merely seen. As it has been said: "When something is stated by you for the purpose of refuting the views of others, then all of this [refutation] belongs to you. (1075) When you state anything at all to refute the views of others, then all of this [refutation] belongs to you.

It may be argued that it is you yourself who are at fault, for you are capable of saying that it is precisely because the capacity [of the unseen] has not been perceived that refutation appears rather than proof;
and just as the warding off of what exists occurs through the unseen, so too does the presentation of what does not exist.

Therefore, your refutation appears to be non-existent even though it is presented as existent, and likewise your defense is not effective; thus, no one would be a valid disputant. Whatever a thing is observed to be, let it be understood exactly as it is; let it be understood that there is nothing further behind it for one whose veil of ignorance has been cleared away. (1076)

If for anyone there were an obstruction behind [the object], then because it would be covered by the obstruction situated in front, everyone would see only a single indistinct form. However, if that [obstruction] were not an obstruction, then even one situated at a great distance would simultaneously see both forms—distinct and otherwise. Thus it follows that [both] would be seen at once. To this he says: "In that case, only one would be seen; if it were not an obstruction, one would simultaneously see the distinct and indistinct forms. (414)
Now, if it should be argued that "only one [object] is perceived when the perception of another is prevented by the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," to this it is replied:
If that [is excluded] by the non-perception of one [of the two], the completion of the sentence is: "it is not seen."
That is incorrect;
for what does that "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) produce, by which benefit and harm do not exist?
Indeed, this so-called "unseen" is characterized as merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).

If it is argued that [the existence of an unseen agent] is understood through the sudden occurrence of gain or loss, rather than through direct perception—and that this [unseen agent] also accounts for the fact that things are seen indistinctly or from a distance even in the absence of any other cause for such lack of clarity—then [we reply]: [This is not so. For the sudden occurrence of gain or loss is understood [as being caused] by the intervention of visible factors, such as the proximity or remoteness of the object, and not by an unseen agent. Furthermore, the fact that things are seen indistinctly or from a distance is also produced by visible causes, such as the nature of the sensory organ or the distance of the object. Thus, there is no need to postulate an unseen agent.
This much has been said in response: that all refutation and justification would, in reality, be possible;
yet even what you have rightly stated is not understood by you because of the power of unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, consciousness, arising according to its causes by depending upon objects, assumes a variety of appearances; all other [theories] are the fallacious conclusions of those with poor intellects.
Furthermore:

(gha) There is no manifestation of that which is non-momentary, because cognition, sound, and lamps— whether as causes of perception or of anything else— are destroyed due to their being momentary in their prior states. || 417 ||
How can there be manifestation of non-existent things through cognition?
For that which does not exist cannot be perceived by way of its own nature,
nor can it possess priority in time relative to the cognition that serves as its cause.
And if [the object] exists prior [to the cognition], it does not exist at the time of the cognition due to its momentariness.

Alternatively, if it exists only when [the cognition] exists, then there is apprehension at that very time; or even if there is no state of being a cause, causality may exist simply by virtue of simultaneity.
That is incorrect;
for that which is not beneficial to cognition is another thing that provides no assistance.
If it were manifested, every object would be manifested;
nor can there be causality for that which is simultaneous, because such is not perceived;
and if there were the apprehension of the unconnected, everything would be apprehended.
If it is argued that there is a restriction [of the object] because of its cause:
[we reply] no, because the grasped and the grasper are restricted by their respective causes.
Such a grasper is restricted by the eye, such that it perceives only a specific [object].
The opponent [argues] that either the object of apprehension is apprehended by that very same [cognition],
or else both [the cognition and its object are apprehended by another cognition]; however, that is incorrect.
For this conceptual construction does not exist within cognition;
by means of this conceptual construction, there is no apprehension of a specific object.
For the causal determination of entities pertains to both their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and their causal function (*kāryakāraṇa*).
Regarding their essential nature first:
when there is a specific determination of essential nature, the very essence [of the cause] appears as such through its causality.

Consequently, it follows that the manifestation of their own forms depends solely on their respective prior causes and not on each other; thus, there is no relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject between them because they arise simultaneously.

For it is logical that those two things which depend upon a certain factor for their status as apprehended object and apprehending subject must have that very factor as their apprehended object and apprehending subject.
Nor is there any subject-object relationship other than that which consists of the cognized nature of consciousness itself;
how then could there be the cognition "I am the grasper" and "this is my object"?
It is not so.
Since no other relation is perceived, this is merely a mental construction dependent on beginningless predispositions;
thus it has been said:
"It appears as if it possesses an activity."
Therefore, because the nature [of a thing] is restricted by its own causes, there is no relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject.
If, on the other hand, the restriction by its own causes pertains to the production of an effect,
even then, if a specific effect-nature is produced by those two, how could there be a relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject?
There may indeed be a state of cooperative causality (*sahakāribhāva*), yet by that much alone there is no relationship of grasped and grasper;
therefore, the relationship of grasped and grasper does not arise from a causal basis.
Alternatively, this conceptualization does not apply to cognition either;

for when a cognition is the object of another cognition— whether that other cognition be perceptual or otherwise— how could there be simultaneity between the two cognitions, and how could there be the arising of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper from a cause?
Furthermore, it is not accepted that two [moments] exist at the same time;

nor, even if they were simultaneous, could there be simultaneity with another [moment], and yet another with still another— thus there would be no end to the succession of cognitions, and the object itself would likewise be perceived [only as a sequence].

It is not accepted [that the object exists prior to cognition], nor does that which was previously non-existent as an object later become an object, because that would entail the consequence that its nature is not apprehended;
if it is argued that the very nature of the object exists even beforehand...
If it is argued, "Let there be the consequence of [the object] being perceived even prior [to the cognition]; what is the fault?", we say no.
Furthermore, because the consequence of a [separate] grasper would follow even prior [to the cognition],

if that [cognition] arises by the power of the causal complex of the eye and so forth, then its very nature as cognition would be the form of the grasped, and not the status of being an object; even so, if it were an object, there would also have to be a form of the grasper.
Now, because the object exists previously and the grasper undergoes change,

it is not the case that the prior non-existence [of the grasper] is not apprehended; and it has been stated that if such were the case, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of every possible conceptual construction.
How, then, is it established that there is a conceptualization of objects in relation to the views of others, such as the Trāntikas?
For this very reason, he says:
Whether manifest or unmanifest, by everyone situated far or near—it is thus that a missing portion in the verse is found right there at the end of the line.
Knowledge is said to "reveal" [the object] because it consists in the manifestation of the object; even in its absence, [the effect] is produced by it. (419)

Because it appears in that form, there may be the designation that "the object appears even though it does not exist," provided that the object is established as being perceived by another person and also cognized by oneself through inference; thus, when a cognition with that form arises from that object, it is logical to say "it has been apprehended. However, in the absence of such [an object], the established position is that what has arisen is a deluded cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*).
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no inference;
for all inference proceeds preceded by perception. If perception were to depend on inference, there would be a mutual dependence.
As long as inference is not a valid means of knowledge, perception cannot become a valid means of knowledge regarding an external object;
nor, in the absence of the validity of perception, can inference arise, because it is preceded by that [perception], otherwise there would be a blind tradition.
Therefore, in ultimate reality, only the own-form of cognition is cognized, not the object.
Nevertheless, it is stated even while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]:
for not everything is established according to ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
Therefore, when an object exists prior [to cognition], that form which the consciousness arises with is the apprehended (*grāhya*).

Furthermore, another object does not produce its form [in cognition] because it provides no assistance; rather, the nature of the object arises from its own cause and is produced exactly as it is. Thus, since there is an absence of assistance by that [object], it is not the apprehended object of the cognition, because it does not generate a cognition bearing its own form.
Therefore...

How could that which is unmanifest manifest cognition by means of its own form? (420) Since the nature of the object exists as the producer of a cognition bearing its own form, yet its own essence remains unknown in its true nature, it is logical that the object is known only through the perception of the cognition bearing its form;
thus, its manifestation occurs thereby.

If it appears in its own form, however, there is no simultaneity due to the power of its own cause; for without another [cognition], that [object] has nothing [to do with it]. If it is the cognition of that [object], let it occur merely by way of its exclusion; for if non-existent things such as cognitions and so forth are not perceived in their own form at the time of cognition, then even the conceptualization of a cognition having that form would follow from the capacity [of the object] toward it.
Furthermore, as for stable objects such as diamonds and stones, how could their cognition of their own nature be untenable?
That too is a trivial point,
because:
Even objects such as diamonds and crystals would be permanent, since they do not depend on other causes;
[if so,] they would themselves produce all the cognitions of the world simultaneously. (421)
2. It is said that [the Self] is equal, not pervasive, eternal, and stable because it does not enter into the divisions of time.

And if its very nature were that [of being momentary], then it would be grasped as having reached its conclusion through the cognition that fully appropriates all its own forms; thus, being completed at the very time of a single cognition, it could not be eternal. That which is called "eternal" is not completed at that [single] time alone, nor is there any duration of time in the perception of every fraction of time.
Furthermore, if cognition were unitary, this same fault would apply: the seasons such as summer and so forth would have to exist simultaneously.
Now, one might ask: how can moments of time that occur sequentially be apprehended non-sequentially?
If, however, there is no apprehension [of it], then there is no pervasion by time for this; how, then, could it be eternal?
Therefore, if it were a single entity, it would be perceived exactly as such all at once;
or else, if it produces successive cognitions in dependence upon other causes, there is a sequence.
That too is incorrect because of its independence;

for that which has arisen from its own cause in a single form does not depend on anything else for its existence. If, however, a subsequent state of being visible were to occur later, [it would require dependence].
If the object exists only later, then there is no permanence; thus he says:
"These [faculties] arise for him sequentially through the assistance of auxiliary conditions."
They say there is a distinction at every moment; that fault here is also as before.

If those cognitions occur sequentially by way of the assistance provided by the auxiliary causes such as the eye and so forth, then, that being the case, since the cognitions occur sequentially, their perceptibility must also occur sequentially;
for perceptibility cannot exist apart from cognition, otherwise it would follow that the object is self-cognized.
Furthermore, visibility, which exists simultaneously with cognition, does not possess a prior or subsequent form, because cognition itself lacks such [temporal] existence;
therefore, just like cognition, it undergoes differentiation at every moment,
being dependent either on causes existing within its own preceding continuum or otherwise.
Consequently, as before, the same fault applies here as well.

Alternatively, if the conjunction of causes such as the eye and so forth occurs as a single, uninterrupted [process], then, because of that lack of interruption, there would be a single apprehension resulting from that non-interruption; thus, there would be permanence for things such as diamonds and stones.
This is not the case;

for in the instance of diamonds, stones, and the like, there is no perception [of sound] without an interruption. Since it is not so in every respect, by what means could this non-interruption be perceived?
Even when there is non-interruption, it has been stated that there would follow the consequence of perceiving it up to its ultimate limit.
Therefore, this is exactly the same even in the case of diamonds and the like.

Consequently, since it is illogical for non-existent things such as sound and so forth—which would have to serve as causes—to be perceived, it is established that consciousness possesses the form of the object;
this has also been demonstrated by the Master (Ācārya).
And memory occurs at a later time; for it does not arise with respect to what was not previously experienced.
Thus he said:
And since the twofold nature of memory is established, [it follows that] the reflection on self-awareness [is necessary]; cognition possesses the form of the object.
