Furthermore, it might be argued that the meaning of the text is that [cognition] has a dual nature consisting of the form of the object of cognition and the cognizer, but not the form of the object;
however, that is incorrect.
"But the two-fold nature [of cognition] arises from the distinction between the knowledge of the object and the knowledge of that [knowledge]"— this is the subject under discussion (1078).
And in that context, since it was the objective aspect (*viṣayākāratā*) that was introduced as the subject to be proven—
namely, how consciousness arises in two forms— it follows that consciousness indeed has a twofold appearance: the appearance of itself and the appearance of the object.
In this regard, there is great insistence precisely on the state of being an object (viṣayatā),
because no one disputes that consciousness is identical [to its object].
Its status as having the form of an object is unestablished; yet that too is established through conventional consensus.
[Objection: But surely there is even dispute regarding self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). [Reply: This is not so.
This is stated with the intention that it is mere awareness;
however, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is what remains to be proven, and this is indeed logical.
And so:
And its self-cognizability will be established later;
therefore, the point here is that the dispute concerns whether cognition is of a nature distinct from self-cognition.
However, there is no dispute regarding its having the form of the object, because that [nature] is not unestablished.
Moreover, that state of having the form [of the object] is established as a distinction of memory through right mindfulness;
for indeed, even if memory were formless, it would still be logically possible for it to possess distinctions.
Thus, how can there be an establishment of the object from a reason that is inconclusive?

This is not so, because what is intended here by "recollection" is that which occurs through mutual distinction; since such recollection does not exist without a clear distinction, it is stated to be the logical reason. || 1079 ||
When this [object] has not been experienced through differentiation and remains undivided from its own sensory domains,
the cognition "it is thus" and not "it is not thus" would not be differentiated.
Furthermore, no distinction whatsoever is discerned by mere experience alone.
Nor is the intellect of one who discerns [the distinction] indistinct regarding the difference, as in the case of [the vision of] two moons and so forth.
(425) If that cognition were indistinct, then, due to the influence of passion, it would not arise as something distinguished by a specifically determined, distinct blue form.
In that case, it would not be remembered with its distinction;
or, if some difference necessarily arises from a particularity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then memory itself would possess that distinction—
this is incorrect.

For a distinction [between cognitions] cannot arise from mere experience alone; rather, the basis of memory is that which is inferred through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since there is no clear difference [between the experiences].
Nor does memory become discriminative merely because the difference is unclear, as seen in the case of twins and the like.
If it is argued that even in those cases, the object is remembered because it was experienced there...
Because that [object] is invariably concomitant with it, even though it is not itself distinct, it becomes the object of memory through its distinction [from others].
Even in the case of twins, when there is a connection with a distinguishing staff or the like, a specific characteristic is indeed perceived.
Just as experience is postulated by the force of the object, so too is it [postulated] from that which is being remembered; therefore, the conventional usage "recollection of cognition" occurs.
That is incorrect;

for in the absence of the form of the object, how could there be recollection of that object? Indeed, that form of a past object is not perceived [now]. If it were present, how could it be called recollection?
If that form belongs to the recollection, does it belong to the consciousness or not?
It is logical that the recollection, arising from an experience possessing a form, takes on that same form;
for thus it is.
If memory were to arise from the object itself, it would occur everywhere without distinction; one would observe the emergence of memory even when objects are at a distance.
Alternatively, if it relies upon experience (*anubhūti*), that very [experience] is our cause, because the arising of memory is possible through experience even in the absence of the object.
This would not be the case if knowledge possessed no form (*sākāratā*).

How does memory possess that form? For even by a yogi who has transcended all attachment, when consciousness is being apprehended by the cognition of recollection, it is not apprehended as something distinct from its form.
Whatever is made an object by whatever mode of conviction, it should be understood as being exactly so;
therefore, it is logical that memory possesses a dual nature, and self-awareness is likewise [established],
as the Master [Dignāga] has stated.
And self-cognizability has been stated [as follows]:
Even by means of proving the dual nature [of cognition], self-awareness is for the most part established, because at that time the appearance which constitutes its own nature is perceived.
(426) Now, it might be argued that self-awareness is not established by everyone through the proof of the dual nature.
What is meant by "mostly"?
This is not so;
for while the establishment of duality is primary in proving the twofold nature, the self-cognizance is incidental.
Since the manifestation, which constitutes its own nature, is perceived at that time, and there is no perception other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one might object:
"Self-awareness is the grasper of the self; therefore, that very same thing must be both the grasped and the grasper."

If it is argued that there is no illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) for such a nature [of identity], by which the establishment of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator could be proven— as in the case of a lamp and so forth— then [the response follows].
Since lamps and the like do not depend on another illuminator, they do not possess the nature of being illuminated at all;
how, then, can they serve as an example based on the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator?

But when those [cognitions] are themselves objects of apprehension, then the sense organ would become their apprehender; furthermore, for both the intellect and the sense organ, self-awareness is not established.
Therefore, indeed, so-called self-awareness does not exist at all;
yet you maintain that the self is both of the nature of the apprehender and the apprehended.

That too is incorrect, because even in that case, the nature of the grasped and the grasper can be established through a distinction in their properties (*dharma*): the state of being the grasped exists by way of its substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*), while the state of being the grasper exists otherwise. (1085)

It is logical that the status of being the apprehender belongs to the self by virtue of its specific nature as a substance (*ātmatva*), whereas the status of being the apprehended belongs to it by virtue of its general nature as a substance (*dravyatva*);
however, for you, all of this is inconsistent.
Furthermore, an example cannot be established merely on the basis of what is accepted by another.
Because it lacks the status of being a means for one's own realization, this [position] is incorrect;

for, in ultimate reality, the state of grasped object and grasping subject does not exist at all. Suchness is a nature that is not dependent on another and is likewise defined by its exclusion of what is other than itself. (1086)
For that very thing in which the illuminating nature of another is not perceived is designated as "illuminating itself," because it is excluded from being illuminated by another.

And just as in the case of a lamp or similar objects appearing [to the senses], there is no illuminating of another, so it has been demonstrated; for this very reason, the lamp serves as an illustrative example.

Even when the eye is functioning, an object is not perceived in total darkness; its manifestation occurs through the proximity of a lamp. Since lamps and the like do not function in this way, they are self-illuminating. Furthermore, the sense organ is not the grasper therein, because it is manifested by its own nature.
Nor do these [mental states] such as pleasure arise from the cognition of another; for if pleasure and the like were graspable by the self, they would become external.
Through the occurrence of inherence (*samavāya*), that very thing would become self-cognition; however, it has been established that inherence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

(1090) Now, if one accepts the self-cognition of form and other [objects] that are intended as objects of apprehension, there would arise the cognition "I am form" and so forth, just as [there is] with respect to the self;
likewise, there would be [the cognition] "I am pleasure."
This is not so,

because is it not observed that there is a cognition such as "I am fair" or "I am dark"? Nevertheless, form and the other [sensory qualities] certainly possess the state of being objects of apprehension for the embodied being.
For color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] are grasped by the cognition "I," which inheres in the body;
yet, according to your own position, they are not self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*).
Now, it may be argued that one does not perceive "I am color-form," and therefore there is only the state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatā*), not the state of being self-cognized.
That too is incorrect;
for even in the absence of that [universal], the perceived object is not bound to that form. White and other colors are not established as being distinct from the nature of color (rūpatva).
If this cognition of "I" were not directed toward an apprehended object, it would not occur with respect to white and other such forms.
Nor does the notion "I am form" arise;
therefore, the notion of "I" is neither based on the state of being an object of apprehension, nor is it opposed to that state.
Rather, the notion "I am fair" occurs through metaphorical designation (upacāra) due to its connection with the self.

Since one perceives a distinction by thinking "this is my form," is it not the case that because there is no difference [between the self and the body], one does not say "I am fair," but rather says "my form is fair"? What is the basis for this?
Therefore, this notion [of "I"] is entirely without foundation;

consequently, because [the notion of] "I" is excluded [from them], it is not established that color and other [sensory objects] lack self-awareness (asvasamvedanatā). Nor is the expression "I am fair" a figurative application (upacaritavṛtti), since there is no other primary [referent] for it to be secondary to.

Furthermore, nothing distinct in form— such as my face and so forth— that could serve as the objective support for the cognition "this is mine," is found within the range of perception; it is just as in the case of [the expression] "the body of a stone statue."

The word *śilāputraka* (son of a stone) is seen to denote a stone; yet, that very same thing is again observed to be denoted by the word *śarīra* (body). (1093) Likewise, the body has become the denotation of the word *mama* (mine); however, no object other than [the body] is perceived for the word *rūpa* (form) and so forth. (1094) Even when thoroughly investigated, no objective support (*ālambana*) other than the form and so forth belonging to the body is found for the cognition "I."
Therefore, the cognition "my face" is merely a cognition of a connection with the body, arising from a specific construction of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
If that is so, then just as the notion of "I" occurs with respect to the body, its form, and so forth due to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
it would likewise occur with respect to walls and such things, such that one would have the thought, "I am the wall."
Just as the state of being in front belongs to the wall in relation to the body, so too would it belong to the body in relation to the wall;
yet this is not the case, therefore there is no self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatā*) of walls and the like.
To this it is replied:

Just as there is no sense of "I" with respect to a wall and the like even though they are self-cognizing, so too there is no sense of "I" with respect to a wall and the like even though they are self-cognizing. Or, just as a wall and the like lack a body due to the absence of attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), so too is there an absence of the sense of "I" due to a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Just as there is a mutual distinction between a wall and a body due to the power of their respective specific latencies (*vāsanā*), so too is there a distinction between the object of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and other states;
therefore, because it is impossible for it to be the object of the operation of another grasper, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatā*) exists,
and there is an illustrative example for this.
For that which has no presiding controller, there is no cognition of it as being independent;

and since there is no controller whatsoever for walls and the like in relation to consciousness, it follows that consciousness is independent, and thus the state of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is established.
However, the eye possesses the nature of a grasper, because it is not an object of grasping in the manner of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Indeed, it will be demonstrated that there is no distinction whatsoever between a producer (*kāraka*) and a manifester (*vyañjaka*);
therefore, with respect to something distinct [from the object], the absence of a manifester is simply the absence of a producer.
But it is logical that luminosity belongs to [cognition] itself, because it is perceived as such and remembered as such; this is the principle.
Moreover:

Because there is no permanent association with a wall, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) does not arise therein; rather, its connection with the body is eternal. Therefore, since the cause of the ego-sense is this eternal association, it does not occur in relation to walls and the like—this is the distinction.
Furthermore, self-cognition does not arise from the ego-sense.
Since it exists in such a state as being independent of anything else,
its perception by way of a subjective aspect is likewise untenable.

Because there is no cognition of their forms apart from the eye and other [senses], and because all those [objects] are asserted by the proponents of externalism to have the nature of being apprehended;

and because there is no perception of pleasure and so forth apart from that [consciousness], therefore, since their connection is independent [of external objects], everything is indeed self-cognized.
Indeed, nothing else is perceived apart from the body and the forms and so forth derived from the primary elements, which could serve as the grasper;
nor are pleasure and the like discerned as distinct from the body,
and even when they are discerned, they do not function as graspers because they terminate in their own nature alone.
If it is argued that even though there is no difference in the status of being an object (*grāhyatā*) for pleasure and so forth,
a difference [in cognition] would nonetheless occur because they appear as having different forms (*virūpa*) and so on due to the difference in desire and other factors— [we reply:
no, because if they appear with different forms and so on, they lack the nature of the object (*artharūpatā*).
Indeed, it is not logical for a single entity to possess mutually contradictory forms;
nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because it is relative to the perceiver, for such relativity is untenable.
For it does not become something other than that [object] in relation to another perceiver, as that would entail the consequence that the perceiver is the cause [of the object].

If you argue that its form as blue and so forth is merely manifested while already existing, then if it is manifested while already existing, how could it be sublated later through reflection? This is quite trivial.
Now, all of this that has been proposed must indeed be accepted;

however, the apprehending cognition is distinct, and it is that very [object] which is cognized through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In relation to that [cognition], there is no self-cognition (*asvasamvedana*).
Furthermore, it is argued that because of recollection, this [object] is perceived at a later time as being exactly as it was;

however, that too is incorrect, for the world does not perceive the form of the apprehended object as something distinct from the cognition itself, nor is its clarity of form established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) or through direct perception. (1100)

Indeed, people engaged in worldly activity do not perceive through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) a cognition possessing a form distinct from color, pleasure, and so forth—such that they would think, "I have a cognition.

Rather, it is merely a web of conceptual constructions (*vikalpajāla*), consisting of the nature of a cognition with specific forms, that flutters above [the mind], appearing as something distinct from the manifested form of the object (*grāhyākāra*).
Furthermore, there is the manifestation of specific forms belonging to material objects themselves, which are established by spatial and other constraints.

But it is not the case that cognition is of such a nature that its very form consists merely in the illumination of the object of knowledge; for if it were so, there would be no manifestation of a specific form as there is with color and other qualities.
That too is incorrect, for if that which has not manifested a form could still be a grasper, why then could a rabbit's horn also be a grasper? (1101)

If it is argued that those [objects] are not thus perceived because cognition itself is not perceived, [we reply: "I have a cognition"—this [statement] does not, however, reveal another self distinct from form and so forth.
It is precisely the particularity of form and so forth that enters into the illuminator; having assumed a distinction within its own nature as a property, it is designated in such a way.
For form and so forth are common to both the imperceptible and the perceptible.
However, the state of being manifest (prakāśamānatā) is a specific quality of form that is distinguished even from other forms of the same genus;
thus, due to this difference in exclusion (vyāvṛtti), there is a difference in properties (dharmabheda).
Consequently, the designation "cognition of form" and so forth functions as a process of conceptual determination (adhyavasāya).

Therefore, since no other cognition is perceived at the time of the experience or at the time of the recollection, it is established that self-awareness exists by way of the forms of color and so forth; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted:
"If the grasped object and the grasper are one, then from the perception of that one, there must necessarily be the perception of the other as well, or else it would be otherwise. (Verse 1103)
It follows that by the cognition of one, there is the cognition of another, and by the non-cognition of another, there is the non-cognition of yet another;
for indeed, the nature of form and so forth, as well as the nature of luminosity, are certainly cognized—of this there is no doubt.
As for what was also said:
They remember only the apprehender, thinking, "Someone was seen by me," because that [memory] is invalid;
for in that case, there is indeed doubt even regarding the apprehender as a specific entity.
Even when the universal is the object of apprehension, there is no doubt [of its being the Self],
for people show that it is connected with the body by saying "mine";
and even in the case of that body, its nature is simply self-luminosity and not any other kind.
This has already been stated;
nevertheless, the opponent’s intention is as follows:
"It is true that cognition is not something other than form and the rest; nevertheless, it does not possess self-awareness, because it is not apprehended by anything else. (1104)
That is incorrect,
because when cognition is restricted by a mind that does not possess the form of that [object], how can there be experience?
And she does not know her own form; thus, the experience of the wise is sublated. (427) 1 M.
B.

If that [cognition] is held to be known by a subsequent cognition— occurring at a later time— that is of a different form and consists of presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) or the like, then the preceding perception would have ceased;
for it is admitted that such a cognition is momentary and does not persist until the time of another cognition.
Therefore, when the previous experience has ceased at the time of another cognition, from where could there be an experience?
Since its own nature is not cognized and the object lacks its own nature, the entire experience would utterly perish;
for it is impossible to experience that which lacks its own nature.
Since the experience of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) is an experience in all cases,
and since there is no such nature for a prior experience that has ceased to exist, there is no experience of that prior [experience]; thus,
it is not accepted that there is an experience of the prior [experience] by a subsequent experience, nor an experience of its own nature.
It cannot be seen because it is devoid of the form of an object; or, even if it possessed the form of an object, because self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) is not admitted [in that case].
It will be demonstrated that this leads to the fallacy of infinite regress;
moreover,
the claim that cognition is experienced by another [cognition] is not tenable.
For that cognition which appears as the manifestation of an object is directed outward, whereas the cognition that grasps the intellect is always inwardly directed toward the Self. (428)

If there were another cognition that apprehends a cognition, then it would appear as something directed outward, like the cognitions of form and so forth; for one thing cannot be perceived by another as being non-external. Furthermore, cognition always appears as internal, or rather, its determination as internal is due to its being grasped as belonging to the self (*ātman*).
Even through recollection, there would be an internal grasping of the cognition;
for when one's own cognition is taken as an object by recollection, it too would not appear as something external.
If it is argued that it appears thus due to a difference in time, why is it not accepted here as well that it appears thus due to a difference in its own nature?
Nor can it be determined that what does not appear as a distinct form is something other than the apprehending subject;
therefore, since cognition is experienced as being internal, it is logical that it consists solely of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
If it is argued that such an experience occurs because [the object and the cognition] occupy the same location, [we reply: no.
Even though they occupy the same location, they are perceived solely through their difference in intrinsic nature; as for the non-distinction of their conjunction, that has already been rejected.
Therefore, the logical principle is that for one whose cognition is apprehended by another cognition, that [apprehension] must be by means of something external;
moreover,
whatever appears as the object of something, one knows that [appearance], not [the object itself].

For when there is an appearance of a particular object residing within cognition, one does not know that cognition as "having the appearance of that object" because of the non-perception of the appearance of the object which constitutes its own nature.

Indeed, if the form of the object were experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then in reality that object too would be experienced; this alone is the apprehension of the object (*arthāvagraha*).
Just as there is the apprehension of a mass-form [of a tree] and so forth, if self-awareness were absent, everything would become inconsistent.
If it is argued that "what other awareness could there be? [It is simply the cognition] because of its conformity to that form," [then we reply: 426.

If cognition arises in that form, then that alone is the perception of the object; for in the absence of the perception of that form, there would be no perception of the object. However, let it be that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is not something other [than the cognition itself], for in its absence, that [perception of the object] does not occur.

For in the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), blue would not be non-blue, and likewise cognition would not be non-cognition; if cognition were known by another, it would not be cognition. Furthermore, the nature of the object is the defining characteristic of self-awareness, and not [the state of] being self-aware [in the sense of being perceived by another].
Because it would follow that [cognition] would arise even in the absence of a self,
therefore, if cognition itself— residing in the self and possessing its form— exists even without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
then [it must be admitted that] even without self-awareness, [cognition arises] either from the mere form of the preceding object or otherwise.
Cognition is attained through mutual similarity among all [cognitions]; for if there were no self-awareness (*asvasaṃvedana*), nothing would remain but the mere possession of that form.

In that case, there would be no distinction at all between the object and the cognition; for if cognition consists merely in having that form, then the object too would possess that [nature of cognition]. Therefore, even the object—being of the nature of another object—is nothing but cognition, because it possesses the defining characteristic of cognition.
If you say, "No, because it is an object," what is this so-called "object-ness"?
If it is argued that there is no cognition,
then even if the object exists in a state of non-cognition, not even a single thing would be established;
therefore, self-awareness alone must be admitted.
If the principle is that [existence] consists solely in being an object of cognition,
or if it is the subsistence of the self through the relation of inherence or otherwise—
that too is incorrect.

Even if [the self] possesses the nature of being the locus of cognition, since effort and the like share a mutual similarity with cognition, they too would attain the status of cognition; how then could there be a distinction regarding their residing in the self?
Furthermore, it would follow that effort and the like, which are mutually similar, must also be conscious.
By what means is its existence within the self ascertained? Surely, even the nature of cognition itself is not ascertained;
how then can it be said that [it is ascertained] by another cognition?
If two cognitions reside in the self, how can there be a mutual apprehension of one by the other, given that they occupy the same location and thus lack distinction?
If, on the other hand, a distinction is perceived, then the self must also be perceived as distinct; thus, these three would be entirely separate.
For if the self is not perceived, its being situated therein cannot be perceived;
and how can a self that is not being perceived be perceived by the intellect as having the form of cognition?
Indeed, even forms and other objects, though perceived by the intellect, are not the objects [of the claim] that they are perceived as being situated within the self.
If it is argued that this is because they are not established in a self, [we reply:
surely the self is all-pervading; how then can there be a lack of establishment therein?
If it is argued that [the object] is not perceived there because of non-inherence,
then how is there non-inherence?
If it is argued that it is because of the lack of apprehension there, [then...]
In that case, cognition (*buddhi*) also is not perceived within the self (*ātman*), because there is no perception of the self apart from it.
[Objection: Surely this perception exists as an action (*kriyā*);
there must necessarily be an agent (*kartṛ*) for it, for there is no action without an agent.

If it is argued that the very things from which this [cognition] arises—namely the eye and so forth—are themselves the agent because they possess the nature of instruments, then what is the use of postulating another agent? Let these alone be the agents; for they do not lack the status of instruments in the absence of another agent. Furthermore, if the body itself is the agent, what need is there for anything else?
In that case, cognition existing within the body is perceived as manifesting inwardly;

for this very reason, the cognition of another is not perceived otherwise [than as external]. If that were so, then certain parts of the body itself would possess the nature of cognition; consequently, in the absence of self-awareness (*asvasamvedana*), cognition would be identical to color-form (*rūpa*) and other such objects.

Therefore, consciousness is attained as being mutually similar to all [objects]; thus, if cognition is of the same form as its object and cognizes it, then the exclusion of other forms must arise from that self-cognition itself.

Not every cognition of an object consists in its similarity [to that object]; rather, it is the similarity residing in the cognition, given that it is a cognition, which constitutes the cognition of the object,
and not mere cognition alone.
Nor is mere similarity [the cause of cognition],
for if it were merely the experience of a sensation, there would be only the sensation itself and not the experience of an object;
furthermore, if it were merely similarity, it would follow that objects themselves would mutually experience one another.
This is incorrect,
because at this time [the cognition] does not possess the same form as its object. (430)

If having the same form (*sarūpatā*) is the defining characteristic of cognition, then the object as well, being of the same form, would result in being cognition; to this, the answer given is that it is "intellection" (*buddhi*).
In that regard, it has already been stated that if they were to cognize one another, it would follow that even those [objects] possess the nature of intellection.

Regarding that which was stated—"consciousness would follow as a consequence, and thus even those [objects] possess the nature of cognition"—it has already been stated that in that case, how could there be a subsequent awareness of them? For there is no distinction.
Since:
Since "cognition" (samvedana) and "intellect" (buddhi) do not have different referents,
any further distinction that must be stated between them cannot be anything other than their similarity of form (sārūpya).
Now, it is observed that objects of similar form do not apprehend one another;
yet cognition (*buddhi*) is the form that apprehends.
If this were so, then the form that apprehends—cognition—would not be imperceptible.
If [it is argued that] even form and so forth would follow as being consciousness because they possess the nature of a grasper merely by virtue of similarity [to cognition], [we reply:
if it is [argued] that they are not graspers, [we ask:

surely, only when the status of being a grasper is established can one thing be determined as a non-grasper and another as its opposite; however, that [status of being a grasper] is not yet established.
Now, if the grasper is distinct from form and the other [objects],
then since it would not be self-cognizing and would possess the same nature as form and so forth, how could it be distinct from form and the rest?
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a conceptual construction.
If it is argued that the object does not exist in the manner in which it is apprehended, [we reply]:
it exists exactly as it is perceived; what is the use of anything else?
Therefore, the specific characteristic [of cognition] is simply the self-awareness of its own nature.
And this being the case, since cognition-ness (*buddhitva*) is simply that specific exclusion from objects such as form (*rūpa*), cognition-ness does not arise from similarity (*sārūpya*).

In cognition-ness, which is characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), that which is similarity is "knowing" (*vedana*); thus, cognition-ness is defined solely by knowing, not by the definition of similarity.
For what purpose, then, is similarity accepted as the criterion for validity (*prāmāṇya*)?
Similarity (*sārūpya*) is intended as the cause for the determinate cognition produced by that [object];
therefore, what is called "similarity" is merely a specific feature of the nature of cognition— which is characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—
and there is no similarity other than that.
In that case, it follows that "cognitiveness" (buddhitva) is also merely a specific kind of similarity and nothing beyond that;

this is true. Nevertheless, for the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin), similarity is necessarily bound to self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), and self-awareness does not arise from similarity alone.
Moreover:
The self-experience of that [cognition] possesses similarity; however, that similarity is not the cause of it,
for similarity is not the cause of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
If its own nature is directly apprehended without depending on another, what is the use here of similarity?

If it were to possess similarity with something else, then this [nature] would be known only when that [other thing] is known, and not otherwise; thus, one should not entertain such a conceptualization, for there is the maxim: "When the water has already flowed away, who indeed would build a dam?"
Nor should it be said, "What is the use of similarity now? because that [similarity] is the basis for the conventional distinction between action and object in the world. (431)
The nature of the cognition of an object distinct [from the cognition itself] is established by this [similarity], for otherwise it would not occur; thus,
it is maintained for the sake of the specific determination of action and object that there is a cognition of blue as an object, and not of yellow.
For those who maintain the existence of external objects, blue and so forth are not established as external through self-cognition based on the presence of similarity [with the cognition];
otherwise, there would be no establishment of the externality of blue and other objects in the world.

The designation "experienced" applied to blue and so forth arises from the error of superimposing the cognition of that form which is the very nature of self-awareness onto external blue and so forth, driven by the flow of beginningless latent impressions; it does not arise from the experience of an external object distinct from that [awareness].

(432) That which is the nature of self-awareness—the form of blue and so forth—is superimposed upon external blue and so forth through the error [of the mind] flowing with the stream of beginningless latent impressions, and thus the designation "experienced" is applied to blue and so forth.
But an external object, such as blue and so forth, is not in any way the object of experience;
rather, its experience is simply the experience consisting of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), [only] metaphorically so called, because:

Even in the case of the cognition of another, when an object of that same form is perceived as something else, the conventional usage "this has indeed been cognized by me" proceeds. For when there is a cognition of something possessing those characteristics as being other [than oneself], the worldly convention "this is known by us" occurs; for this very reason he says "in the world.
However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is only self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
If cognition possesses the form of blue and so forth, what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could establish an external object?
If cognition does not possess the form of blue and so forth, how could that [object] be its experience?
If consciousness itself, having the form of blue, is self-illuminating, by taking recourse to what means of valid cognition would an external object be known?
For there is no perception [of the object] therein, since that [perception] terminates in self-awareness alone;
nor does blue appear beyond that [awareness], because two forms of blue are not experienced.
If, on the other hand, that were the form of the object, then the awareness would have to be known by another form, or else it would remain unknown.
If that experience of his is unknown,
how can it be consistent to say that there is a cognition of it whose own nature is not known?
And if it is known...

Nevertheless, whether perceived simultaneously or otherwise, how can one cognition belong to another? Since that very form is what is communicated by these two, how could there be a mutual relationship of the cognized and the cognizer? If [the object] were imperceptible (*parokṣa*), then the designation of it as "blue" and so forth would arise from the cognition of its form; thus, one could employ the conventional expression, "by this [cognition], this [object] was known. But if both are directly perceived (*sākṣāt*), then the cognition of each is mutually dependent upon the other.
Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition [for it]; thus, rather than saying that what is not itself cognized is made known by another that is cognized, this [position] alone is better.
Indeed, the nature of cognition is not merely self-cognition, but it is logical [to hold] that it exists when there is similarity (*sārūpya*).
If it is argued that self-awareness is established because the fact of being an awareness is not proven by mere similarity of form; provided that there is self-awareness.
If this is so, let there be only the nature of self-cognition; what is the use of similarity?
If it is argued that even in the absence of similarity, cognition certainly occurs, then what is the purpose of similarity now?
If [cognition] were to occur even without similarity (*sārūpya*), it would indeed be so; however, it is said that "there is cognition because of similarity," and this is not the case.
For this reason:
when it is established that the nature of cognition does not depend on similarity [to an object], why is it brought about by an external object through its own inherent nature? (434)
Its very nature is that by which it possesses the character of consciousness;
even its other nature is [consciousness] through itself, because of its similarity [to the object].
Therefore, if that were not its nature, what connection would there be such that [the cognition] is a consciousness [of the object] on account of that similarity?
If it is argued: "Could the nature of self-awareness, having arisen, ever depart?
Therefore, its form is established as being intrinsic; what need is there for another [cognition], such that the awareness of that object would not occur?"
This too is not tenable:
even if it were to know its own form or the form of another, let it know that;
how could the object be known by it?
Thus, how is it consistent to say that "the cognition of an object" is being established?
For an object does not enter into self-cognition such that it could become cognized; therefore, there is no such thing as the "cognition of an object."
Moreover,
if cognition were based on similarity, then there would be a great calamity,
because:
For if there were identity in every respect, cognition would lapse into non-cognition;
if there were similarity in some part, everything would be the knower of everything. (435) And there is no identity in every respect, because that would entail the consequence of non-cognition.
Nor is there a cognition of everything by anything in every respect;
for identity in its entirety would only occur when all distinctions have vanished, and in that case, it would be the object itself, like one individual thing being identical to another.
How could one cognition be equal to another cognition in every respect, both in its nature as knowledge and in its excellence?
If, on the other hand, there were even a difference in some respect, then everything would be the cognition of everything, because the equality of all things in some respect would never cease.
If it is argued that there is no cognition of other things by way of complete similarity while abandoning the aspect of awakening (*bodhākāratā*),
then it would follow that all cognitions are cognized [simultaneously].
If it is argued that only that from which [a cognition] arises is what is cognized, then...
Even if it were indeed produced from that, how could it be said that it is "unperceived"?
It is perceived because of the perception of its form, not because of its production from that;
furthermore, there is no relationship of producer and produced between twin brothers.
Moreover, even when there is only a single cognition, there is still the conventional designation of "cognition" for another [object].
And if that which is produced from something and possesses similarity to it is its cognition, then,
just as the experience of blue and so forth is held to occur because of the form of blue and so forth, [so too would the cognition of the self occur].
Likewise, because it consists of the nature of experience, the experience would be identical;
[this applies] to that experience as well.

Since there is a similarity with the cognition [of blue] by virtue of its having the nature of making [the object] known, there is also a similarity with the blue [object] itself by virtue of its having the nature of blue and so forth; therefore, just as there is the cognition of blue and so forth, there must also be the cognition of the experience [itself].
Furthermore, it is postulated that just as blue and so forth exist as the conditioning factors (*upadhāyaka*), the experience must likewise exist as a conditioning factor.

That too is incorrect, because there is no conceptualization of a substrate for the appearances of hair and so forth; nor is it logical to conceptualize a substrate as something distinct [from those appearances]. (1108)
For indeed, there is no concern for the conceptualization of a pillow made of hair in the appearance of hair perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*).
If it is argued that "hair and so forth were previously seen there," then let this same method be postulated in all cases:
just as the conceptualization of blue arises from the perception of a blue form because it belongs to that class, so too would it occur even without an actual pillow.

Nor is there the possibility of postulating a "non-erroneous contradiction" (viruddhāvyabhicāritā), because there is no apprehension of an invariable relation (pratibandhagrahaṇa) [between the cognition and the object], since the object is always to be inferred; furthermore, while the prior perception is seen to be the producer [of the subsequent cognition], the perception of the object does not occur in every case, as disputes are possible everywhere; thus, regarding the fact that the immediately preceding [cognition] possesses the form of the object, what could be its instigator?
It has been demonstrated more than once that this is not so, because we observe the application of lac-dye and the like even when it is separated [from the object];
nevertheless, one might still argue as follows.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the determination "the experience has been experienced" is meaningful, [we reply: this [determination] does not always exist even with respect to an object,
just as the worldly determination "it has been experienced" is not necessarily in accordance with reality.
Therefore, because certainty— which is the cause of perception— is observed [to follow], it should be understood that this is an experience of the object and not of the experience itself;
for if it were an experience of the experience as well, such certainty would indeed arise.
To this it is replied:

A cause does not produce its effect at all times merely by being a cause; rather, having obtained auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), the cause becomes an effective agent (*kāraka*). He demonstrates this very point [in the following verse]:
This [ascertainment] does not exist even with respect to the object at all times;
for there is no ascertainment regarding the object anywhere, since it is observed to appear [only occasionally].

Alternatively, this ascertainment never exists with respect to the object at all, because the object of ascertainment is exclusively the aspect (ākāra) which consists of the nature of experience itself.
If it is argued that it is so by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), we say no, because the postulation of such a metaphorical designation is untenable.

The nature of an object is never perceived by anyone in its primary sense; in the absence of that [primary perception], how could the conceptualization of metaphorical usage arise? (1110) Therefore, the determination "this is the object" relies on the power of beginningless mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and is not produced by mere direct experience alone;
for even in a dream, there is no perception of an external object, yet the determination "this is an object" still occurs.

Therefore, since there is an absence of certainty even when there is the experience of an object, and its presence even in the absence of that [object], certainty is not absolute; how then can there be an establishment of reality,
or why would it not exist when experience— which is the basis for existence— is present?
If it is argued: "In experience, indeed, everything has its basis in experience; nevertheless, there is no certainty—how can this be?
It is not so because of the deficiency of auxiliary conditions."
In that case, it is not the case that the determination of experience is based on certainty, since [certainty] is absent even when there has been experience; therefore, this argument is trivial.
For the determination of experience occurs through the assumption of its form (tadākāratayā), and thus the experience of an entity is not sublated.
Indeed, the absence of certainty caused by the absence of other causes is not capable of establishing the absence of experience;
for it should be understood that there is simply no other cause, and not that there is an absence of experience.
Furthermore, this [cognition] which appears when something white or the like is being seen— || 438 ||
The cognition of men, which has the form of the manifestation of white and so forth, is clearly [perceived].
Is that [cognition] of the nature of something other than the manifestation of white and so forth, or is it of its own nature?
For the perception of an object is not merely the existence of the object itself; necessarily, there must be something additional to the mere object in the perception of the object.
If that [object] were external to what appears, it would likewise be of the nature of an object; how then could there be a perception of an object?
Therefore, it must exist as that which appears at the time when white and other such things are being seen.
If one conceives that this clear perception is either distinct from or identical to the manifestation of white and so forth— then, regarding that manifestation of white which you intend,
how could the white be manifested if the manifestation itself remains unmanifested in its own form?

For nothing whatsoever is manifested by that which is unmanifested; thus, that very form which has been produced as manifestation is what is known, and that alone is manifestation. Let anything else—standing in the place of the eye and so forth—be considered non-manifestation; it is not manifestation, nor is it perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from the eye and other senses, since the desired result is accomplished through the eye and the rest alone.
If it is argued that "that [cognition] alone is manifestation, and no other is," [we reply: no.
If indeed an unperceived manifestation has arisen, that very [manifestation] is the luminosity of the awareness of one's own nature.
"What is this appearance of arising (*utpattibhāsaka*) which is the manifestation of the nature of cognition?"— if this [question] is added,
then how is the object manifested by those [cognitions] that have arisen?
If it is argued that nothing else is involved in its production, [then we ask]: regarding the object, what is this relationship called "this belongs to that"?

If it is argued that "one sees the object," then surely seeing itself is not perceived; how then can one say "one sees"? And if the object possesses the status of being the direct object (karman) [of the action of seeing], [then the subject must be distinct from it].
What is this so-called "objectness" (karmatā)?
If it is something additional to the mere object that is perceived, then there must be yet another perception of that [objectness].
Consequently,
that [second] objecthood is also perceived,
and from that again another objecthood; thus, there is no liberation from infinite regress.
Therefore, cognition is the manifestation; since that [manifestation] is not manifest, the entire world remains unmanifest.

For the manifestation of an object does not consist merely in the production of a luminous form—as occurs with a lamp and the like—but rather consists in the manifestation in the form of cognition. And if that [cognition] is not itself perceived, how can the object be said to be manifested?
If it is manifested by its own nature, then it follows that everything would be manifest;
if you say this is due to its own specific distinction, then any other cognition is redundant.
If it is argued that its manifestation occurs in exactly the same way,
[we ask] by what is this manifested?
If it is said, "by another manifestation," [then we reply:]...
No,
because even if one manifestation were manifested by another manifestation, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress.
Since that [manifestation] would likewise not be perceived as another individual instance, it follows that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the prior individual instance is what is manifested;
yet, since the manifestation of that [nature] too would not be perceived by another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of further individual instances.
Therefore, when the nature itself is perceived, it is perceived precisely as being endowed with manifestation.
Otherwise, there would be no cognition that "this has been manifested"; for how could perception, by which the relationship [of the object] was previously unknown, qualify it? (441)

In the expression "the object is seen," it is understood that "seen" functions as a qualifier; yet, when the qualifier is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of the qualified object as distinguished by that qualifier.
[Objection: But in the case of "a cow," is the universal "cowness" perceived as something distinct from the very apprehension of the qualifier?
This is not so,
because the nature of "cowness" (gotva) is the exclusion of non-cows;
nor is it accepted by you that the cognition [of cowness] has the nature of being the exclusion of non-cognition.
If that were so, it would follow that the object is self-cognized;
yet you maintain that cognition is distinct [from the object],
and since that [distinct cognition] is itself not apprehended, how could it serve as the basis for the linguistic convention "it is cognized"?
How then, even for you, is there the conventional usage "it is cognized" when there is no cognition of anything distinct [from the cognition]?
For even by you, it is not admitted that both the cognition and the object are cognized as being distinct from one another;
and in this regard:

Since, when two things occupy the same location, there is no perception of the second at the time of perceiving the object, nor is there perception of the object at the time of perceiving [the cognition], how can there be a perception of their distinction?
Therefore, how could this be so? This is logically sound.
When two things are perceived in conjunction, there arises the certainty that "it has been seen.

For even the certainty that "it has been seen" is indeed a certainty regarding a conjoined state; therefore, according to your view, this [certainty] must arise from an experience of exactly that nature, and there is no other principle than yours.

But for us, the mind—driven by the wind of powerful latent impressions—falls like a pale leaf of certainty elsewhere, casting its shadow upon the tree of the object; thus, the determination of reality proceeds from certainty alone.
Therefore, there is no cognition of an object,
nor is there the production of a certainty that "this is not the object"; thus, it follows by logic that your position is untenable.

Now, if it is argued that when a cognition possessing a form is perceived by another mind, it is then designated as "seen," then its self-awareness is established through its similarity [to itself]. (443)
It might be argued:

it is not because of a cognition that has the same form as the object (*arthasarūpātmavedana*) that there is the determination (*vyavasāya*) "the object is seen"; rather, it is because of the cognition of that very [object] in its suchness by means of another cognition, just as there is the determination "he is a man with a staff" upon the apprehension of a person joined with a staff by means of a cognition of that [person] which is distinct from it.
The intention is that the apprehension of objects existing as qualifier and qualified is never observed in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
therefore, this results in a contradiction of your own position.
For it is thus:

The relationship of qualifier and qualified between two things does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; for sometimes, something is considered to be the qualified (viśeṣya) or the like in relation to another.
Indeed, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not ultimately real, since at times even that which is the qualified is perceived as the qualifier.
Therefore, it is that very cognition which exists in such a state that is perceived,
and since that cognition is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), self-awareness is established.
It is established that the cognition of this very nature [of the object] occurs through its similarity [to it];
thus, the object does not exist as such [independently].
For if cognition were not self-cognized, it would follow that only the object—standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified—is perceived.
Now, if one who cognizes the form of another does not cognize its own form, how can he know the form of another?
If he does not cognize his own form, then he cognizes only the form of another;
and since there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between them, how can there be a cognition of that [other] as qualified by it?
Now, [it may be argued that] there arises a perception of that form, but not a self-awareness of it;
however, when it is subsequently perceived by another [cognition] as having that form, it is designated as "seen.
But [we reply: if the particularity of what was not previously seen is first grasped, how can its status as a qualifier of that [object] be cognized later by another [cognition]?
If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the object] is subsequently cognized,
that is incorrect; for:

If that [object] is experienced in its own form by a subsequent cognition, let it be of that very form; however, it does not possess the quality of being qualified by the object of cognition (*meyaviśiṣṭatā*). For at the time of its own manifestation, the object of cognition is known precisely as indistinguishable from the act of seeing.

But at a subsequent time, when there is a cognition of that same form, let it be that very form itself; however, there is no cognition of it as qualified by that [previous state] through that [subsequent cognition].
Otherwise, what was previously known in one way would be cognized in another way at a later time. If this were so, it would not be understood which of these two possesses reality.
Or, moreover, it might be argued: [text fragment]
Even if the qualifier was not perceived at first, what contradiction is there in its being perceived later?
That too is incorrect, because:
If there is a perception of the qualifier and the qualified as being unconnected, then the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not perceived at all.
For it is not possible to establish the status of qualifier and qualified merely from the perception of each one in isolation;
moreover—
And it has already been established that it is called "feeling" (vedanā) because of its similarity [to the object]. || 444 || 1 M.
B.

For there is no possibility of its being experienced by another, because when merely a similarity arises through sensation, it is impossible for that other to experience it by thinking, "This is a sensation similar to that."
For it is thus:

since one has not previously seen either the object or the apprehension of similarity between two things that have been seen, how can one determine through perception its similarity to that [object]? (445)
For one who does not even accept similarity [of cognition] on the grounds that "it is knowledge" or "it is as if known," there can be no perception of both.
At that time, the discussion regarding whether the object is [identical to] cognition or distinct from it comes to an end;
for there is no perception of similarity in the case of a solitary perception, since the cognition "this is similar to that" does not occur.
Furthermore, because past and future objects and their perceptions are not cognized simultaneously, there is no such cognition [of the object through its perception];
even if one posits that [perception], it is merely the cognition itself and not the cognition of the object.
Moreover, if that [cognition] were also not self-cognizing, the fault of infinite regress has already been stated.
But for one who does not even accept similarity (*sārūpya*), the object is not cognized,

because the superimposition (*āropa*) [of the form of the object upon the cognition] is impossible; subsequently, the perception, being cognized in a form distinct from the object, cannot be that [object] by virtue of having that [object's] nature.

Since its identity [with the object] is not admitted, and since it is perceived as a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*) by its own nature, what meaning is there in asking "what is known? or "by whom? This discussion has come to an end; one must remain silent.
If it is argued that pillars and the like are indeed perceived as objects,
for nothing is impossible when it is actually seen.
This much has been answered:

if it is seen in its own form, then it is seen as such; therefore, when white or other colors are being perceived, that which appears [as a distinct object] must, if it were so, clearly not be the white color itself.
If, on the other hand, it is its own form, then it shines forth by itself.
If that [cognition] were unmanifest, the object would remain unmanifest.
(447) If its very nature (*svarūpa*) is that which is manifested, then it must manifest itself, because there is no other illuminator;
for if it does not manifest by its own nature, then while that nature remains unmanifested, the object would remain unmanifested.
If the appearing form were not manifested, the object would indeed not be said to be manifest;

for here, the object is remote (parokṣa), and this very manifestation of a clearly apprehended form constitutes the remoteness of the cognition. Therefore, it is precisely the non-manifestation of the clearly appearing form [that constitutes its remoteness].
If that were the case,
the object would be entirely indirect (*parokṣa*), just like inferential knowledge;
for even in inference, indirectness consists precisely in the indirectness of the clear appearance.
If even that inferential cognition were to manifest with an indistinct form, there would likewise be no comprehension of the object;

therefore, it is established that if there is no self-cognition, there is indeed no perception of any object whatsoever. By this, [the argument] regarding those who hold the position of self-awareness—that through the non-perception of all objects [in the absence of such awareness]—is refuted.
They too have been refuted by those who have explained [the matter] above, who maintain that cognition is imperceptible. (448) Thus [it has been] refuted.
The same reasoning applies here: if there were no awareness of its own constituent parts, cognition would not be the knower of either the object or of itself;
it would not be the knower of the object because the manifestation [of the object] would be imperceptible, nor would it be the knower of itself because [the existence of] a self is not admitted.

Furthermore, pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth arise as being self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), and these are of the very nature of awareness (*bodha*). Therefore, how can the non-perceptibility of cognition (*buddhi*)—which is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhitā*)—be an object of acceptance?
If, on the other hand, they are not of the nature of cognition, that is incorrect.

Due to differences in their basis, object, and cultivation, these cognitions— which function differently through distinctions such as pleasure, pain, and desire— are indeed nothing but cognitions. 449.2 T.
Regarding the desire for pleasure and pain (*sukha-duḥkhābhilāṣādi*):

first, as for the distinction of the basis (*āśrayabheda*), the pleasure produced by the eye and so forth is indeed mutually distinct, as are the objects such as visible forms; yet, due to repeated practice, even when the objects of the eye and so forth are the same, there arises a greater intensity and so on.
If consciousness alone— and not the object and so forth— is produced by the objective support (ālambana) and other factors,
and if the object also were to arise solely from the causal complex of consciousness, then a final farewell has been given to it;
for in that case, by admitting their imperceptibility, there would be a contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa-bādhana).
Since nothing other than that [object] and what is distinct from it is perceived as being directly present (*pratyakṣa*),
that cognition which exists when the apprehender is not perceived is itself direct perception; this is called self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), as has been stated more than once.

If it is accepted that their feeling is experienced by another consciousness, then in that case, even another person would experience that feeling, provided they know it through that other [consciousness]. (450)
For these [pleasures and so forth] existing even in the mental continuum of another are experienced by means of a different consciousness.
Consequently, even when experiencing the happiness and so forth of another,
one would become happy and so on;
for there is no distinction whatsoever between the experience of one's own happiness and that of another's when both are experienced by another [consciousness] as an object of apprehension.
If it is argued that there is "pleasantness" only in the experience of pleasure belonging to oneself, we say no;
for even that which belongs to another has the nature of being refreshing.
Fire belonging to another does not burn, nor does sandalwood belonging to another provide delight;
yet, for a wise person, sandalwood brings delight according to its own nature. What is the true essence of that which belongs to another? It is simply of the nature of burning.
O mindless one, what news is there of the arising of happiness for that which belongs to oneself? Let it be conceived in this very same way regarding the perception of another's happiness.

(1117) When that which belongs to oneself has not arisen, why is there no happiness for this [person]? If you say there is happiness because of one's own happiness, it is not so, because there is no distinction in the essential nature [of the happiness].

(1118) If you argue that there is a distance from perceiving that form [of happiness] due to its being remote, what kind of distance is there [in the case of one's own happiness]? If you say it is otherwise because of a lack of contact, then upon contact, there would be self-awareness. (1119)
For contact in its entirety is characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If there were contact with only one part, that would not be the cognition of [the object] as other.
(1120) If there were penetration into the self or the body by pleasure and so forth in their entirety, then self-awareness or the body would be attained;
for penetration occurs either through direct awareness or otherwise.
For one who knows [an object] with their entire being, self-awareness alone is attained,
because such is the very definition of awareness;
even if it were to enter into another's pleasure, it would indeed be self-awareness, for otherwise that awareness would be impossible.
Now, even if there is no penetration [of the object], the experience of pleasure does not arise from non-differentiation because differentiation is possible. What is this differentiation?
It is the cognition of pleasure produced by that [object] which has its appearance; it is not [pleasure] in any other way whatsoever.

However, in the case of the experience of another's pleasure, that [experience] does not arise directly from that other's pleasure; rather, it arises solely from a logical mark (*liṅga*). It does not arise from the object itself, because this is an inference based on the experience of another's pleasure and a perception in which the form of that [pleasure] appears. This is the distinction;
regarding this, he says:
If a cognition—either produced by that [object] or having its appearance—does not know [the object], then for anyone else who takes it as an object, these two [properties] necessarily exist.

(451) Even another person who takes another's pleasure as an object perceives its very nature; therefore, its being an appearance of that [pleasure] is established simply by the fact of its being admitted [as such].

Therefore, since the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is common to the eye and other [senses], it follows by implication that it must be produced from that very [object]; thus, there is no distinction regarding the "duality" [of the object].

Alternatively, if it were not produced from that, then that cognition appearing as such would result in being without an object (*nirviṣaya*); and the universal (*sāmānya*) would not be grasped in its absence. (Verse 452)
It is said that "it is not apprehended"; nor is there any acceptance of that entity whatsoever, for an acceptance does not rely on the force of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, this alone is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

If it is argued: "Cognition is observed to arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*), not from an object, nor as a direct manifestation of that object; therefore, since an external object characterized as a particular (*viśeṣa*) is absent, another's pleasure and so forth cannot be the object. Thus, this cognition appearing as the experience of another's pleasure does not manifest the form of an object, but rather manifests a universal (*sāmānya*), because inference has the universal as its object."
It has been established that there is no apprehension of a universal when its individual instances are not apprehended,
and because a universal is devoid of the form of the individual's letters.
If it is argued that, in that case, cognition would likewise be devoid of that form, and therefore the form of cognition would not exist [in the object],
that is incorrect.

For it is not considered impossible that cognitions should have an affinity for their objective supports; one who knows the world understands that through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the intellect takes on the form of that [object].
Therefore, he said: "Consequently, this appearance of the object is nothing other than that cognition itself. (453)
When it is established that there is direct perception of the nature of consciousness, then the perceptibility of the mental image and the self-awareness of cognition are proven,
even if one must resort to inference regarding the nature of another's happiness.
If it is argued that even when it has a different form, it is simply self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and that this too is of the very nature of another's pleasure,
we say no.
Since it is sublated by another's report through reliance on another's cognition, how can that be its true nature?
For in that case, the possibility of intervention and so forth does not exist.
If it is argued that one's own pleasure is "mediated" because it is experienced as being related to that [pleasure],
we say no.

Since there is no cognition of a relationship with another, one who says "you possess a nature unknown to another" is not a fool; rather, standing at the top of the ladder of royal edicts, he is [like] a king. Even another person, while investigating, does not determine that your consciousness exists in such a manner.
"This is my own cognition, not his cognition"—this is how it is perceived.

Furthermore, even if another person perceives that very same form, he still does not experience pleasure; for pleasure is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), not through inference (*anumāna*).
To this it is replied:
he grasps them again.
If it is argued that this [cognition] is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), from what cause does this distinction arise between two [cognitions] that are equally capable?
For it has been established that direct perception is indeed the immediate realization of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, this very distinction between two things of identical form is not tenable.

If it is argued that "the distinction arises from a distinction in their causes," then the distinction must reside in their essential nature itself; for if it is admitted that the distinction exists even without [an external] cause, then why should a distinction in the cause be accepted?
However, a distinction [between the two cognitions] must reside in their very nature;
since the nature of both is direct perception, a difference in their causes is not logical,
provided that such a difference is indeed observed.
Therefore, even a difference in essential nature must be admitted; consequently, it is not logical that there be identity of form.
Alternatively, if you argue that the distinction in the nature of cognition arises from the difference in its causes, [we reply:]

If it is argued that, although there is no difference in the nature of cognition as being of a clear form, the restriction of consciousness [to a specific object] arises from the connection with an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) or a single object and so forth— such that one would not perceive anything else at all— then the distinction between different cognitions has already been refuted. || 455 ||
Furthermore, it might be argued that even though there is no difference in form, the restriction of being perceptual or otherwise is due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa);
likewise [it is determined] by connection with the sense organs and by inherence in the same object,
for instance:
One's own happiness is inherent in one's own self, whereas that belonging to another is not so;

therefore, if the state of being happy through the experience of another's happiness were possible without a difference in mode of apprehension, there would still be a restriction characterized by perceptibility and imperceptibility.
In that case, even regarding what is manifest, it would follow that there is a restriction of both manifestation and non-manifestation;
and this being so, what is the point of postulating distinctions such as differences in objects?
It would simply mean that a thing—due to its connection with the unseen (adṛṣṭa) and so forth—would exist in one way and then otherwise, such that pleasure itself would become pain and so on.
If it is argued that, therefore, a difference [between them] is not logical because this too arises precisely from the non-perception of a difference,
then let there be self-awareness; likewise, let there also be a difference in form.

Therefore, for that very reason, another [subject] could not apprehend [the object] in any way; even in the case of a common objective referent, a difference in consciousness has already been refuted, and even the eye and other [senses] are postulated solely on the basis of their manifest distinction.
For instance:
"First there is the perception of clarity; from that follows the establishment of perceptuality. 'I have not seen this with my eyes; this was observed indistinctly.
(1123) People first apprehend perceptuality by means of their cognition of clarity itself.
For, even though the eyes and other [senses] function as causes, if one does not perceive the clarity of what appears—
thinking, "I have seen something entirely indistinct; this cognition is not perception"— there arises this uniform consensus among people.
One might say that perceptuality consists in being produced from objects and sense-faculties, and clarity [consists in] being distinct;
for indeed,
through clarity there is correct apprehension, while from the sense-faculty comes the cognition of proximity.
Because this duality does not exist, there is no attainment of duality in any way whatsoever.

Indeed, that alone which is an object of cognition by virtue of its proximity and clarity is accepted by the world as being "perceived" (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, there is no cognition of proximity without the sense faculty; therefore, due to the deficiency of that factor [the sense faculty], it would follow that [the object] is not perceived.

This is incorrect, because proximity and its opposite are not the causes for perception and non-perception respectively; otherwise, that which is seen from afar by vultures would not be perceptible. (1125)
For instance, one person may be a man of far-reaching vision, while another is otherwise.
Consequently, what [distinguishes] the perceptual and non-perceptual nature of their respective cognitions?
Or rather, it may be that the very same [object] is described as "clear" and "not distant";
for the determination of distance and proximity depends solely upon the capacity of vision.
If it is argued that whatever one is capable of seeing clearly is indeed not distant for that person,
then so be it.
If it is said that whatever is clearly perceived is "near," then its absence is "far"; the sense faculty is not the cause of this [distinction].

Therefore, between sensory consciousness and mental consciousness—which have an equally clear manifestation—there is no established distinction of being "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) and "other. This is logically consistent; thus, even in the case of experiencing another's happiness, one would become happy through direct realization.
And in the absence of direct realization, there is self-awareness precisely through its having a form;
this is the lack of affliction for those yogins who [perceive] the pleasure and so forth of another through their own direct perception.

Those who possess an experience equal [to that of another] would likewise be afflicted by it. For those Lokāyatikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and Yogins such as Kaṇāda and others, who maintain that yogis necessarily perceive the pleasure and so forth of others through direct perception, even those yogis would become possessed of passion and other afflictions.
The remaining elaboration has already been made and is not repeated here;
furthermore,
because of the absence of the contact between objects and sense-faculties, that [suffering] does not arise for them.
If it is argued that suffering does not arise [in the yogi],
then only one for whom pleasure and so forth arise upon the contact of the sense faculties with their objects deserves the designation "happy" and so on; yet,
for the yogi, there is no arising of pleasure and so forth from contact with objects such as women, and therefore he does not possess that status.
For even that pleasure and so forth of his which is produced by the sense faculties and their objects is unreal, because:
Indeed, there is no arising of suffering;
rather than the non-perception of suffering, it is the arising of the cognition of suffering.
There is no sensation of suffering that is not perceived as suffering and so forth; it is the cause of affliction or benefit.
Because it is not the cause for experiencing suffering and so forth, nor for torment or benefit.
For instance,

why does the pleasure arising from the mutual contact of the sense organs through touch not produce common physical reactions such as horripilation in both the man and the woman? In that case, it would follow that consciousness itself must be perceived as something common to both.
Therefore, happiness exists when there is self-awareness (saṃvedana),
and not otherwise;
nor would the two [the subject and the object] possess equal happiness even if there were no mere arising or contact with the eyes and so forth, in the absence of self-awareness.
If it is argued that there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that [feeling] therein, we say no;
for the function of cultivation consists merely in the arising of pleasure, and since that pleasure has already arisen, the two experiences would be identical.
If it is asked, "How is this distinction yours?", he says:
"When suffering is pain itself, manifesting by its own nature."
For one for whom pleasure is self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), that [pleasure] is his;

however, for a yogin who perceives another's pleasure and so forth merely by taking it as an object through a different awareness, that yogin does not possess passion and the like. Thus, the consequence [of the yogin being affected by passion] does not apply in this way. ||459||
Therefore, those yogins are not afflicted by that suffering and so forth.
If it is asked, "How is it that they are not afflicted in the experience of fire and the like?",
[the answer is] because of the absence of that [affliction] in yogins.
If it is asked how it is for others,
[the answer is] no, because external objects and so forth are likewise cognized as such.
However, that which pleasure and so forth produce through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not produced by anything else; thus, not everyone who knows them possesses an identical experience.
