Therefore, since for every cognition the object and the awareness are distinct, the objective support (*ālambana*) consists in the similarity to the object (*arthasārūpya*), while the self is the awareness itself, manifest by its own nature. (460)

If it is argued: "The object of cognition is that which is capable of imparting its form [to the cognition], whereas the nature of the cognition itself is self-luminous; therefore, the self-cognition of pleasure is established by the very fact of its being felt, not merely by the imposition of its form. What, then, is the difference between the two?"
Nothing exists from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for there is no distinction whatsoever between pleasure and its mental aspect.
It is only because one considers oneself to be seized by it that one determines, "I am suffering."
The yogi, however, is not like that; thus his state of happiness is not of that nature.
Therefore, consciousness is indeed self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*); otherwise, the distinction between pleasure and so forth would be impossible.
But surely, wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other [faculties] also arise from a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone?
Nor is there a distinct characteristic in them apart from the object being reflected;
and that object is not of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth,
because cultivation does not operate therein.
For in that case, the object does not possess the quality of being produced by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
therefore, there is no other wisdom (*prajñā*) distinct from the object, and thus that [wisdom] is not endowed with an aspect (*sākāra*).

[Objection: But surely wisdom and the other [faculties] do not have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their intrinsic nature; therefore, even if they lack an aspect, consciousness itself would not be aspectless.
That is incorrect.

Discernment (*prajñā*) is the investigation of reality; how could it exist even when reality is not apprehended? If it were formless (*anākārā*) even when apprehending an object, then consciousness (*vijñāna*) would likewise be so for that same reason.
If discernment is formless even when it apprehends a specific object, why is consciousness—which also apprehends an object—not likewise formless?
If it is argued that even that [inference] must be formless, this is not correct;
because what is called *prajñā* (wisdom) is the immediate manifestation of a pure object, whereas inference is not so, since it would otherwise fail to qualify as *prajñā*. (1128)
And it has already been established— and will be further demonstrated— that this [consciousness] is indeed endowed with an aspect (*sākāra*).

Furthermore, if self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) were not admitted for consciousness, then there would never be any apprehension of it, and thus there would be a total absence of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
To this he says:

Furthermore, in the absence of direct perception, the cognition [of the sense-organ] would have to be understood through an inferential mark (liṅga); and that [mark] would have to be either the sense-organ, the object, the preceding cognition, or even the mental attention (manaskāra). || 461 ||
Furthermore, because there is no direct perception,
the mind arises from conceptualization.
Furthermore,
in this causal complex, there is no other related factor besides either the sense faculty or the object, or else the mental attention.
2. [The cognition] is related [to the object], not to anything else, because no other capacity is observed there; nor does the sense-organ [function as the cause], because of its deviation. || 462 ||

In the absence of direct perception, inference operates upon an object that is beyond the senses; and that inferential mark (*liṅga*) is precisely the sense organ and so forth, up to mental attention (*manaskāra*),
because nothing else possesses the necessary relationship [to the object].
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also [does not apply], because it functions only upon seeing a related entity such that [the fact] would otherwise be inexplicable;
in that regard, the sense organ (*indriya*) is first excluded due to its fallibility.
For a logical mark (*liṅga*) must be non-fallible, and the sense organ is not so, since it is accepted as being a cause [of perception] rather than something that "would otherwise be inexplicable."
Furthermore, the capacity of that which has not yet produced its effect cannot be ascertained in such a manner;
thus, its meaning is also subject to deviation, just like the sense organ.
Likewise, the object, the intellect, and mental attention— knowledge [is derived from] these two; yet they are not established,
because the intellect itself is unestablished, for it is that which is yet to be proven and thus lacks a logical mark.
As for mental attention (*manaskāra*), it is that very same prior cognition;
and since that is not established at the time of the [initial] impulsion, how could it be established at any other time?
For this reason:

That which is not well-known cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*); for a logical mark must be something that is already established. Otherwise, if everything were a logical mark, then everything would be established by everything.
Furthermore, even if it were the case that the object is indeed manifest and established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [it would still not be established].

Otherwise, even the conventional usage that "something exists" would not occur, and the world would become blind and mute. Furthermore, an object is not manifested by the mere existence of the object; otherwise, because all objects would be manifested simultaneously, it would follow that everyone is omniscient.
Therefore, that from which the manifestation of an object arises is cognition (*buddhi*).
For this very reason he says:
"Indeed, no one perceives cognition with respect to an object that is unknown;
but when it is known, one understands it through inference."

Furthermore, in the absence of direct perception, the cognition of the intellect would have to proceed from a logical mark (liṅga); and that [mark] would have to be either the sense organ, the object, the preceding cognition, or even the mental construction (manaskāra). To this, the reply is as follows: || 1129 || [The verse continues: If it were the sense organ, then because it is not perceived, there would be no cognition of it; for how could one perceive the sense organ through inference when its own nature is not apprehended? If it were the object, then since the object is external, it would follow that the cognition of the intellect would be external. If it were the preceding cognition, then since that too is not perceived, there would again be no cognition of it. And if it were the mental construction, then because it is internal, it would follow that the cognition of the intellect would be internal. Therefore, the cognition of the intellect cannot be established by means of a logical mark. || 1130 || [The verse continues: Nor can it be established by means of verbal testimony (śabda), because there is no scripture that establishes it. Nor can it be established by means of analogy (upamāna), because there is no similarity to anything else. Nor can it be established by means of presumption (arthāpatti), because there is no other possible way for the existence of the intellect to be accounted for. Therefore, the cognition of the intellect is not established by any of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 1131 || [The verse continues: Moreover, if the intellect were eternal, then because it would be unchanging, there could be no cognition of it. If it were non-eternal, then because it would be momentary, there could be no cognition of it. Therefore, the cognition of the intellect is impossible. || 1132 || [The verse continues: Furthermore, if the intellect were a substance, then because it would be distinct from the self, there could be no cognition of it. If it were a quality, then because it would depend on a substratum, there could be no cognition of it. Therefore, the cognition of the intellect is impossible. || 1133 || [The verse continues: And if the intellect were the agent of cognition, then because it would be distinct from the object, there could be no cognition of it. If it were the object of cognition, then because it would be distinct from the agent, there could be no cognition of it. Therefore, the cognition of the intellect is impossible. || 1134 || [The verse continues: Thus, since the cognition of the intellect is not established by any means of valid cognition, it does not exist. And since it does not exist, the self, which is defined as the possessor of the intellect, also does not exist. || 1135 || [The verse continues: Therefore, the self is not a real entity, but is merely a conceptual construction (prajñapti) based upon the aggregates (skandha). Just as the "chariot" is a designation for a collection of parts, so too the "self" is a designation for the collection of the aggregates. || 1136 || [The verse continues: This has been taught by the Blessed One in the Sūtras: "Just as, depending upon the various parts, the word 'chariot' is used, so too, depending upon the aggregates, the conventional term 'being' (sattva) is used. || 1137 || [The verse continues: Therefore, one should abandon the false view of a self and cultivate the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of all phenomena. By doing so, one will attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death. || 1138 || [The verse continues: Thus ends the refutation of the self. Now, following this, the refutation of the permanent entities such as space, time, and atoms will be set forth. || 1139 || [The verse continues: Space is not a real entity, because it is not perceived by the senses. If it were a real entity, it would have to be either visible or invisible. If it were visible, it would be a material object; if it were invisible, it would be a non-material entity. || 1140 || [The verse continues: Furthermore, if space were a real entity, it would have to be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were eternal, it would be unchanging; if it were non-eternal, it would be subject to destruction. Since neither of these is possible, space is not a real entity. || 1141 || [The verse continues: Time is also not a real entity, because it is not perceived by the senses. If it were a real entity, it would have to be either a substance or a quality. If it were a substance, it would have to be composed of atoms; if it were a quality, it would have to depend on a substratum. Since neither of these is possible, time is not a real entity. || 1142 || [The verse continues: Atoms are also not real entities, because they are not perceived by the senses. If they were real entities, they would have to be either spherical or non-spherical. If they were spherical, they would have parts; if they were non-spherical, they would be like space. Since neither of these is possible, atoms are not real entities. || 1143 || [The verse continues: Therefore, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva). They arise dependently (pratītyasamutpanna) like illusions and dreams. One who understands this is liberated from all suffering. || 1144 || [The verse continues: Thus, having refuted the self and the permanent entities, the wise person should cultivate the path of wisdom, which is free from all conceptual proliferation (prapañca). By doing so, one will quickly attain the state of omniscience. || 1145 || [The verse continues: This is the teaching of the Buddha, the Great Sage, who has compassion for all beings. May all beings, by hearing this Dharma, attain the bliss of Nirvāṇa. || 1146 || [The verse continues: Thus ends the chapter on the refutation of the self and the permanent entities. May it be auspicious. || 1147 ||

If it is held that the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the object is the mark (*liṅga*), then surely that manifestation itself is the cognition, since the object is described as "manifested" by means of it; for if the manifestation has not been experienced, there can be no certainty regarding the object's state of being manifested.

Whether the individual (vyakti) is the mark (liṅga) or whether the object is the individual, in either case there is no purpose in the perception of the individual, because the perception of the individualized [object] is preceded by the perception of the individual. At one time the individual is inferred independently, and at another time it exists as a qualifier;
in every case, it must be experienced through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
If there were experience through inference, there would be an infinite regress;
and since that manifestation of the object is perceptual, cognition itself must also be perceptual.
Therefore, because the manifestation is indirect, the object itself would necessarily be indirect as well.
Therefore, it is not the inferential mark (*liṅga*) [itself];

rather, the object appearing as an objective case (*karman*)—which has the other name "the state of being apprehended" (*grāhyatā*)—is the inferential mark. For the state of being an objective case does not exist without an action (*kriyā*), and cognition (*buddhi*) is that action.
To this he says: "Then that [object] connected with the external region is perceived through direct perception.
To this it is replied:
For objecthood (*karmatā*) exists only when there is a distinction produced by action, and never otherwise;
if there were a distinction produced by action, one would infer the mere action itself.
(1130) If what is called objecthood is indeed a distinction produced by action, then let the mere action be inferred.
There is no inference from the activity of the intellect,
nor is there any other activity apart from the nature of the object itself;
for it is thus.

Action may be said to reside in the object (*karman*) or it may be said to reside in the agent (*kartṛ*), but it is not something other than these; for that which resides in the agent is not distinct from the agent, and that which resides in the object is not distinct from the object.
Therefore, vision is not something superior to, or other than, that which is being seen.
Now, if it is argued that the object alone is cognized as the apprehended (grāhya), while the cognition is [cognized] only as the apprehender (grāhaka)—
such that the experience is "the object was grasped by me through cognition"—
that too is incorrect.

In that case, the intellect would possess the status of an instrument, while the apprehension [of the object] would follow thereafter; let that alone be the supreme cognition—why is another postulated?
(113) If perception were [the cognition] from the perspective of ultimate reality, then a dual nature would be apprehended;
or else, some specific quality of the object itself is intended as its manifestation. (114)
In that case, there would be no distinction whatsoever regarding the object as something produced by action,
for an object being apprehended by cognition is not then admitted to possess origination.
For the apprehending cognition is indeed dependent upon what is established; it merely performs the act of grasping "it exists" by means of the intellect,
and that which is being grasped does not itself become qualified [by that cognition].

If it were to grasp another form, there would be error; if it were to grasp that very form, there would be the consequence of grasping both the prior and subsequent forms—just as lamps and the like do not exist at the same time as jars and other objects. The same objection applies equally to the ignorance of the manifester; the critique is identical in that case as well. (1133)

If an object is manifested by a lamp exactly as it already exists, then that lamp must also possess a nature that pervades all divisions of time; otherwise, it would be a mere illusion. Alternatively, if at the time of perception the object arises in a different manner, then—
Or, if that [external object] is accepted, the consequence of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) follows:

if this [object] arises as something entirely distinct from the nature of cognition, then self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone—being simultaneous with the cognition—is momentary; so what is the point of postulating another object?
But surely it has been established that the intellect is perceived as the grasper (*grāhaka*), while the object is perceived as the grasped (*grāhya*).
If it were the case that the object, once established as real, could change its form,
then when it arises in such a state, one who says "that very thing has arisen in such a way" would be asserting nothing other than the object's status as a graspable entity. Furthermore,
the designation "it was grasped by my cognition" establishes nothing more than the mere fact of arising in dependence [upon causes].
Thus it is said:

"All relations between things are established for people solely by virtue of specific utilities and distinctions, as well as through particular nuances of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), for the purpose of indicating specific states;
however, the reality of a thing is not established by its designation alone, since that [designation] is possible even otherwise."
For this object existed previously as well, by virtue of its own causal nature; therefore, this perception of it has now arisen regarding that very thing.
This object is not established through either direct perception or inference; thus, this worldly convention is merely a succession of conventional realities.

Moreover, if the very particularity of the object were its state of being apprehended, then that [particularity] would be either known or unknown; for only what is known can serve as a logical mark (liṅga).
If it is not determined within the cognition itself, how can it be said that "this object is known"?
If its determination as "known" is of that very same nature [as the object], then a further cognition is useless; let the specific distinction [of the object] be stated in that way.
(1136) How could that [object] be a means of knowledge if it were not determined as "known"?
(466) One who knows "the object is known" understands [it as] a cognition; one who knows simply "the object" is the knower of the object-ness of that [cognition]. (1137)

"The establishment of objects as having that same nature [as their cognition] occurs through the cognition of them in that form. When there is a cognition of a white object, what other whiteness could there be for the object besides that?"—this has already been stated.
Furthermore, if the perception were something entirely different [from the object], then there would be no determination that "it has been seen."
Regarding this, it is said:
"The unseen visions have never been seen by another seer; indeed, the unseen visions are not seen by any other seer.
(M. 1) Unseen visions have never been perceived by another observer.
If the vision [of an object] is different from the [subjective] seeing, then how could there be a determination of the seen form?

Otherwise, even when one person has seen something, another might engage in the conventional usage of "seen," thinking, "This was seen by me," just as one thinks, "It was seen by me. This would occur because the vision of a specific object arises merely from the perception of the object itself;
thus, that specific feature would necessarily be present even in the vision of another, and so it would follow that "this was seen by another."

Now, if it is argued that this very thing is not different [from what was previously seen], because one does not perceive a difference in what was seen by another, whereas one perceives a difference in what was seen by oneself, and thus there is the cognition "it is seen by me"—
that too is incorrect, because:
That particularity exists even when perceived by another; thus, there would be the cognition of one's own intellect.

(468) Even though there are many particulars, since they lack self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), they too must be perceived [by another]; consequently, there would be the cognition of both one's own and another's intellects.
Therefore, it must exist as something perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
if that [awareness] too were perceived by another awareness, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because that [second awareness] would likewise require being perceived.
Now, if that state of being seen were one and the same, then even when it is seen by another, it would be that very same thing, and its apprehension would occur through one's own cognition alone.

When the state of being seen by another is perceived by someone else due to the existence of that other person, then—even in the absence of one's own seeing—it would follow that there is an apprehension of one's own cognition because of the observation of being seen by another;
for there is no distinction in that state of being seen based on whether it is relative to oneself or another.
Now, if being seen by oneself indeed exists, then there is the apprehension of one's own cognition;
for there is no distinction between what is seen by oneself and what is seen by another,
and "being seen by oneself" is known only upon the perception of a connection with one's own act of seeing.
But if that [perception by another] is not established, how can it be said that "it was seen by oneself"?
Therefore, even when something has been seen by oneself, if there is a cognition of its having been seen by another, the realization of one's own cognition would occur.
Alternatively, if the very person who establishes the fact of its being seen is the one for whom the realization of their own cognition occurs, then there is no fault.
Indeed, there is no harm here;
yet, even if there were no harm, it would still be a harm because the reality of things is not as [you] claim.
For it is thus:
For how could it be known whether "unseen-ness" belongs to me or to another?

Indeed, in that case, no one's dependence on another can be prevented. But if there were the state of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this [dependence] would be preventable; for it is sheer audacity to claim that self-awareness is something to be experienced by another.
This very self-awareness is what is called "manifestation" when it does not fall within the scope of anything else.

Therefore, the inference of cognition does not arise from a mere property of the object independent of its own property; for the property of one's own cognition is distinct from the property of the [external] object. (469)
That which is the cause of cognition and is perceptible;
[that which is] apprehended through perception.
For, by means of something residing in the intellect, there is an inference of one's own intellect;

indeed, the demonstration of a common object or property through a common inferable [subject] must be accomplished by means of a property of the self that serves as the inferential mark for the self’s intellect.
Therefore, it must be a property of the self that brings about the inference of the self’s intellect.
There is no "one's own duty" (svadharma) other than the intellect; if one's own duty is nothing but the intellect,
and that [intellect] is not perceptible, how could it serve as a means of inference?
Now, [it might be argued that] pleasure and so forth arise from the same causal complex as cognition; therefore, cognition is inferred by means of them because they are attributes of the self.
To this, he replies:
"[If they were] born from the same causes..."
Whence could there be a distinction for that cognition, since it is non-deviant and not born from anything else?
(470) If it has been established that all pleasure and so forth produced by the causal complex of object, sense-faculty, and so on, are of the very nature of self-cognition (*samvedana*), then,
when pleasure arises with respect to a perceived object, the inference of one's own cognition from that [pleasure]— since that pleasure does not belong to another— how [could there be a distinction]?
How can the happiness of another be apprehended by oneself?
For if there were no self-awareness (*asvasamvedanatva*), how could this distinction [between self and other] exist? Indeed, even from fear and the like, horripilation certainly arises.
(1141) If pleasure and so forth were established as being self-aware, then it would be logical that those belonging to another are not perceived.
Otherwise, who could prevent its being related to another?
If you argue, "Therefore, these [thrills] belong to me alone because they produce horripilation in me," from where does this [conclusion] arise?
For another's wife does not produce pleasure when it is being experienced;

rather, that which consists of pleasure and so forth produces horripilation and the like in one with whom it is connected, or otherwise. Thus, what is the use of this [notion]? When it is established that horripilation and the like are produced by one's own pleasure, the cognition of its being "connected to oneself" follows as a matter of course.
If it is argued that [the object] produces [the cognition] upon the perception of its own relation [to it], there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore,
would the object be the inferent of cognition by following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of cognition, or by following its cause?
In that regard,
apart from the five objects such as form and so forth, and the sense faculties and their apprehension, no other effect of that [consciousness] is perceived. (471)
The sense organs and so forth arise from the same causal complex as cognition, or else cognition itself arises later;

in that case, two things would be beyond perception. Among the five objects, not even one is seen [as such], since [cognition] is born from the sight of form; otherwise, its occurrence would be impossible. (472)

It is said that both the sense organ and the perception are beyond the senses; yet among the five objects, such as form and the rest, not even one is observed to be of such a nature as to be produced from the seeing of form.
For form and the other objects do not arise from the seeing of form, because they are produced from other causes.
If they were produced from the seeing of form, then those very [objects] would not exist.

For indeed, the perception of forms of all objects whatsoever occurs; it would be distinct for every living being, and likewise the object [would be distinct] because it arises from that [perception]. (1142) Just as the perception of form differs for each individual, so too do form and the other [objects].

If all [objects] were indeed perceived by those two [the senses], then, upon the determination of their specific differences, there would follow for every living being a cognition in which they appear as manifold. (1143)

If, however, there were perception of each [object] individually, then if cognition itself were self-aware, all forms and so forth— which possess distinct natures for every living being— would be perceived by everyone, and there would be a simultaneous perception of multiple forms and so forth;
yet such is not the case.
In that case, this would first of all be a non-position [for us].

Alternatively, if form and so forth are perceived as produced solely from one's own view, then, since it is not experienced by another, its status as an object (*arthatā*) would be lost. If self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is accepted, then if it is perceived by another, it must possess a further distinction produced by that [other].

That [cognition] too would be perceived by another, and that by yet another; thus there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, it is sheer audacity to claim that a sign (*liṅga*) is something not cognized through self-awareness (*svavedana*) or through non-self-awareness (*asvasamvedana*), for indeed, that which is not cognized cannot function as a sign.
Furthermore, the claim that "intellect is cognized through inference because it lacks the characteristics of a logical mark (liṅga)" is incorrect.
Let it be granted that there is a cognition of some other object;
nevertheless, to say that what is thus not cognized is the "logical mark" is an act of extreme audacity.
"The *liṅga* is something supramundane" [is said] because one does not perceive it together with the suffix *-ta*, even though the *liṅga* exists. || 473 ||
How so? For a sign that serves as a means of cognition does not reveal what has not been perceived;
rather, it is only through fire that has already been perceived that there is inference by means of smoke and the like, which are its own products, and not otherwise.
Indeed, smoke is not observed to be an inferential indicator of fire unless that fire has first been perceived.
Therefore, if one describes that very mark (*liṅga*) prior to its establishment,
then that [mark] too must be proven by another example, leading to an infinite regress;
for inference does not reject the requirement of an example.
If that were the case, inference itself would not exist, just as with perception;
for if there were another definition for perception, that same logic would apply to its being an inference.
Consequently, that inference which establishes the example would require another example, and that one yet another, leading to what is known as the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Now, it is not established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that no one has such a cognition;

for there is no one who has the cognition, "The object itself would not be possible if there were no cognition," nor is there anyone who has the cognition, "The cognized object would not arise if there were no cognition. If you say [there is such a cognition]:
What is this so-called "cognizedness"?
If it is the state of being made an object by a cognition,
then surely, while that very cognition itself is not yet cognized, its status as being made an object by a cognition must be considered.
If it is "presence before the eyes," then how can that presence before the eyes establish cognition if it itself is not cognized?
If it is cognized, then there must be another "presence before the eyes" for that as well; thus, the charge of infinite regress has already been stated in that case.
Therefore, whether it be "presence before the eyes" or something else, since it is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for establishing the fourfold cognition,
the establishment of the object does not arise from the cognition in any way;
for if that [cognition] is not established, the object itself is likewise unestablished.
The establishment of an object depends upon the intellect; if the establishment of an object were possible without the intellect, then everyone would be an all-seeing seer.

If the intellect perceives itself as being active toward an object, then that object may be said to be cognized; otherwise, nothing would be apprehended. Or else, everything would be cognized by [the intellect] itself.
Therefore, the establishment of cognition does not arise from the object, because that would entail the previously mentioned faults;
rather, it occurs after one has perceived the cognition through direct perception and [observed] its effects, such as speech and so forth. (476)
Furthermore, there would be no inference of another's mind, because the relationship [between the mind and its object] is not perceived in oneself.

If, through direct perception, there were some cognition of the intellect and its correlate within oneself, then, upon seeing a sign (liṅga) related to that [correlate], an inference of the intellect could occur in another as well; otherwise, it would not be logical.
If you argue that the object is known by another through inference, then how is there cognition of what one has perceived oneself?
If you say it is through inference alone, then for that too there must be another example, leading to an infinite regress.

If it is argued that [the object] is cognized by perception itself, [we reply: surely perception cognizes objects such as blue and so forth; how then does it cognize their "having been seen" or even their relation to oneself? If this is asked:

In that case, being related to itself would be its "seen-ness" (dṛṣṭatva). If that is perceived within the self, then it must be established through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). If its perception were by another [cognition], there would be an infinite regress, because in that case as well, "seen-ness" would likewise be an object of perception.

Then, [one might argue that] the object is seen, the seeing is perceived, and the perception of the perception is perceived, and so forth; and when one perceives the perception, at that time the perception itself would be the object of sight rather than the state of having been seen.
Therefore, only the mere object is perceived, and not what is called "the state of having been seen"; thus, there is no basis for the emergence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Moreover,
it is not a matter of direct perception such that the object could serve as its logical mark (*liṅga*),
for memory itself is not direct perception.
Therefore, because no sign (liṅga) for an object is established in the mind or the intellect, [there is no inference]. (477)
"How is it inference?"—this is the supplementary question.
Now, if even there the object itself, such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, appears [to consciousness], then inference has been refuted; this is the answer given here.
And if that [cognition] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could an object appear?
For it is observed that while something appears, there is at most a dispute as to whether it is real or unreal. If this is argued, what indeed is this so-called "unreality"?
That which is non-deceptiveness is not [non-existence],
because there is an absence of deception regarding that nature.
If it is argued that because of the linguistic usage "unreal," that form must necessarily be unreal,
then what is this "usage"?
If it is apprehended by a means of valid cognition, how can it be unreal? And if it is apprehended precisely as unreal, [how can it be real]?
Nor is it tenable to claim that, because unreality is not perceived apart from that form,
only the intrinsic nature itself is perceived and not the performance of a function for another.
If that were the case, it would follow that [the cognition] is self-cognizing;
if, however, it is cognized by another, [then...]
Because memory clings to the perceived nature [of its object], it does not possess the form of the past; therefore, there is no cognition of that [past object].
If, on the other hand, this [memory] also takes that as its object, then it is no longer memory.
In this context, it is logical that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is perception;
for such is the linguistic convention: "This is my cognition of this object in this way.
A cognition devoid of an object of cognition is simply unreality.
Nor can it be supramundane and so forth, because such a conventional usage does not exist; moreover,
how could a cognition be illuminated for you by another cognition, whether through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or by some other means?
For cognitions are illuminators of one another; since they are not of the nature of light, how could there be that relationship of the manifested and the manifestor? How could it exist? (478)
For it is not logical that two things which are non-luminous by nature should stand in the relation of the manifested and the manifestor, either to each other or otherwise.

Indeed, it is by means of luminosity—such as the light of a lamp—that non-luminous objects like cloth are made manifest, and not otherwise. How else could there be the manifestation of an object? It occurs through the transfer of form into the luminosity.

For illumination is the manifestation of an object through its own transition [into consciousness], just as a jar or similar object is manifested when it has transitioned into the light of a lamp and so forth; and that illumination, being of that very nature, illuminates itself. 479.
If it is argued that just as the form of the jar is one thing and the light is another, so too the form of cognition is one thing and the forms of color and so forth are another—
This [position] is indeed untenable;

nevertheless, for this [consciousness], there must be an external object, just as there is for a lamp. For in the absence of a thing to be perceived, there can be no cognition of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator.

Even if it were the case that the object and the consciousness arising at another time [are distinct], nevertheless, like a lamp, it must exist as the nature of consciousness through its own self-luminosity.
Now, if it were as you suggest—that this [object] is apprehended by another cognition—then that is incorrect;
for if its perception were by a cognition distinct from itself, then consciousness too would possess externality by virtue of having that same nature. (1145)
Now, if it has no externality, why does it not possess self-awareness?
Even for that [external object], there is no illumination by means of a separate light.
Therefore, he says:
If it is accepted in this way, then cognition is established as self-cognizing within cognition;
otherwise, the object would likewise possess the same properties as the cognition.
If, when cognition is itself manifest, the [object-]cognition is manifested through its transfer into that [subjective] cognition, then cognition is self-cognizing; otherwise, it is not.

If cognition were illuminated by something other than itself, then— because the object possesses the same property [of being illuminated]— the object too would become an illuminator of the cognition by virtue of its similarity to it;
therefore, for us, cognition, being of the nature of illumination, manifests itself.
The means of proof (*sādhana*) shines forth by itself; another thing, having transferred its form (*rūpa-saṃkrānti*) into it, shines forth while being luminous.

In this very way, the relationship between the manifest and the manifester exists between the form and the cognition: namely, that one is self-luminous, while the other arises with the form of that [self-luminous one].

(ga) [Objection: Let it be that the manifestation of an object occurs in the form of consciousness; surely cognition is self-luminous, while another [object] is what is manifested, because similarity is possible—just as one is said to "grasp" the form of the father.
Regarding this, it is said:

"Even though there is similarity, another cognition is not considered to be manifested by that [first cognition], because it is self-manifesting; rather, the object is manifested in the form of that [cognition]. (482)
[The object] is that which is manifest;
for it is the manifestation of what was unmanifest, and not the manifestation of what is already manifest.
Merely by virtue of similarity,
even that which is not manifest does not become manifest in the ultimate sense; how then could an object be manifest?
The object manifests in its own form—that is, in the form of the manifestor—and is not manifested by anything else.

Furthermore, since both cognitions possess the quality of self-manifestation equally, there can be no relationship of the manifested and the manifestor between them, just as in the case of two lamps or a lamp and a jar; that is the basis [for this conclusion].
The conventional usage is extended by way of the relationship between the manifested and the manifester. (483) 2. By means of the distinction of the manifester.
It does not follow that, even though the production of similarity between two lamps is possible, there exists a mutual relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator between them.

In that case, how is it that from the causal complex of the lamp, the jar arises in that form [of being illuminated], such that it too is illuminated as self-luminous and not otherwise? Thus, such conventional usage is established through the analytical extraction based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but not in an ultimate sense; enough of this digression.
It is certain that vision does not occur by means of the object and the sense-faculty alone;

therefore, for that [vision] as well, the seeing of something else must be stated. (484) If the certainty "it has been seen" were to arise from the object and the sense-faculty alone, [then this would follow].
If it is argued that "the whole is determined as seen," or "only what is seen is determined as seen," or "only what is seen is determined as seen."
What is this that is called "seen," wherein seeing has arisen?
And what is this "seeing"?
That very point is subject to further inquiry: when the eye and so forth are directed toward an object, how is it understood that "the eye is directed"?
Even in that case, if one asks how there can be the conventional usage of "having been seen," there is an infinite regress.
Now, if certainty arises merely from the occurrence of perception,
it would not be a certainty based on having experienced [the object];
nor can there be a certainty that "it was not experienced" based on mere experience alone.
For there is no certainty that "it is white" without the experience of whiteness;
therefore, it is logical that the certainty which conforms to an experience must arise from that very experience itself— this is the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
(ka) Self-awareness of memory is established by memory itself as being the awareness of the self [of the cognition]; for if cognition were known by something else,
there would be no apprehension of long [sounds] and so forth, because many moments do not persist.
Self-awareness is established not only from the specific nature of the cognition arising from the cognition of an object, but also from memory;
for surely, it might be argued that memory establishes only the experience, not self-awareness.
If there were cognition by another [cognition], memory would indeed be logical; however, that is not the case.
If one cognition were perceived by another, there would be no apprehension of length and so forth.
Because there is no stability in the duration of the *bahumātra* [measure],
just as in the case of the continuous application of two short (*hrasva*) measures, it has been previously established that what is unstable cannot be perceived as one with what is stable;
thus, there would be no apprehension of long (*dīrgha*) or protracted (*pluta*) measures at all.

If it is argued that when each individual mora is apprehended, neither the long vowel and so forth nor the aggregate is apprehended, and that cognition occurs through the synthesis of the preceding and succeeding [moments];
Not so, because that too has an already cognized object as its domain.
[Objection: But surely the object characterized by length and so forth is indeed cognized; it is not uncognized.
However, since an object characterized as "long" and so forth is not perceived, that [designation] is understood to reside in two morae— just as in the case of two short vowels—
and no other "long" entity exists.
Now, even for one for whom cognition is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), how can there be the apprehension of length and so forth?
For the determination of the perception of length occurs only when there is the experience of a single cognition possessing that form.
Even for the proponent of non-self-cognition (*asvasaṃvedana*), there is indeed the experience of a single cognition possessing that form.
It is merely by another cognition [that this is known], for there is no distinction between these two states;

indeed, that which is to be known is known by something other [than itself], because it is an object of knowledge, like anything external to the object of knowledge. Therefore, cognition as well, being an object of knowledge, must be known by something else. (1147)
That is incorrect, because even so it would follow:
"The manifestable is manifested by something else, because it is manifestable, like the entity of a jar."
Therefore, it follows that even a lamp must now be something that is illuminated by another.
And regarding this, it has been said:
"If a preceding cognition were to be known by a subsequent cognition..."

In that case, because there is no cognition of another form of that [object] by the intellect, and because the object itself is absent at that time, there is simply no perception; thus it has been established that experience is lost for one who desires [to perceive].
Now, it might be argued that there is no instability of the atoms (mātrāḥ), and therefore there is no failure to grasp length and so forth.
(kha) Refutation of Sphoṭa:
That too is incorrect, because:
If the cognition were to appear all at once while the [syllables] remain in a non-sequential state,
then the phoneme would be non-sequential and long;
for that which remains stationary and is perceived without sequence does not become long, since the convention of "long" is established only for that which is perceived through a temporal succession.
There is indeed a sequence of the phonemes (mātrās), yet there is no cognition of "long" and so forth at the final stage;
and when that sequence is being perceived, it is not otherwise than what was apprehended by the preceding cognition.
Or else, this [cognition] is a single one which grasps both the prior and subsequent parts.
That too is incorrect; for how could that which possesses a sequence [produce] that which is without sequence? (486)
The parts of a phoneme might assist [the cognition] without being joined;
for how could the preceding and succeeding parts of a phoneme, being unconnected due to their lack of simultaneous duration, assist a single cognition?

For cognition is the grasping of an object, and since there is a difference in objects, there is also a difference in cognitions; thus, cognition is not one. How, then, could there be a perception of succession?
And so it has been said:
"Indeed not..."
And because of grasping [objects] out of sequence, cognition would not possess a sequential order, just as in the case of death. (487) [Note:
The half-verse is missing in manuscript B; there is a transposition of the half-verses in manuscript M.]
In a book,
one perceives an understanding regarding an unknown object,
but once it is known, one understands it through inference.
And just as this [cognition] is conceptualized in accordance with the knowledge of its object, so too is it conceptualized when that [object] possesses distinctions;
for thus does the world designate: "Now my cognition..."
Now, although it has arisen as a single entity whose nature is the object, it is perceived as "long" and so forth;
for that which is "long" and so on arises first as a single thing.
Furthermore, if there were only one long [sound], then the cognition of "long" would also be only one;
that too is false, because:

If some sound were to increase upward from its previous state until the end, and if this [sound] consisting of phonemes were indeed a single entity, then it would have been apprehended by the very first cognition; thus, there would be no lapse of time. Furthermore, if the initial portion were not heard, then even by the final cognition, [qualities such as] length and so forth would not be perceived.
If the cognition of "long" and so forth arises through dependence on successive parts,
then it would not be the case that there is one long [object];
for if the preceding part persists, there is also the cognition of the subsequent part.
If that were the case, there would be an increase in the sound due to the persistence of the preceding [moment] and the emergence of the succeeding one;
and in its final state, there would be the cognition "it is long."
If it is argued that "simultaneous apprehension" would not be "possessing sequence," and that sequence exists in relation to what precedes it, we say no;
for the cognitions of the prior and the posterior are distinct from one another.

Now, it is also incorrect to say that the cognition first produced remains as a single entity; for cognition has no inherent stability of its own, since it does not persist once its subsequent object has been apprehended. (488)
For a sound that has not yet accumulated does not remain for the duration of the time required for accumulation;
if it were so, there would be further accumulation, leading to the same infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Alternatively, if it remains by itself even when the object is not present, then in that case as well—
In that case, it would not perish by itself, nor would it ever perish subsequently without distinction;

for if the intellect, whose nature is the apprehension of that [object], were to persist even in the absence of the apprehension of an object, it would never perish, and thus there would be an excessive duration.
Now, if there is an absence of the apprehension of objects due to the absence of objects, then it would not be a grasper of length,
because only a portion would be apprehended. Alternatively, [if one were to argue that] a single phonetic essence (*varṇātmā*) arises simultaneously and persists for a duration of time;
That is incorrect;
this same fault applies even if the phonemes remain in a non-sequential state after having arisen all at once.
If, having arisen all at once, it remains for some duration of time, it would have to persist forever, because there is no subsequent distinction [in its nature].
Furthermore, because it would arise from a single effort, subsequent efforts would be useless;
for by the very same effort by which the first form was produced, the other parts would also be produced, since they are not distinct from it. Therefore, further effort is indeed purposeless.
This same defect attaches even to the theory of manifestation (*vyakti*):
because everything would be manifested by a single effort, a subsequent effort would be useless;
therefore, there is no grasping of the long constituent parts by a single cognition.
In that case, one must admit the apprehension of multiple cognitions; and if those [multiple cognitions] are not apprehended, then that final cognition which occurs must itself be experienced.
And that [final cognition] would not be a memory of the perception of length, for it does not grasp length;
since the parts of length are not grasped by a single cognition, the final cognition is experienced by another subsequent cognition, and that [subsequent one] does not grasp length. Therefore...
How can there be the recollection of a long duration of thought,
since there is no recollection of what has not been experienced, and the final cognition is not experienced by another subsequent cognition?
Because the preceding cognitions are intervened by others, there is no direct experience of them;
and since the final cognition is occupied with grasping the long [vowel], there would likewise be no recollection of the cognition of the long vowel and so forth.
Furthermore, it might be argued that there is a recollection of a long series of cognitions because all cognitions are remembered through the apprehension of each cognition by subsequent cognitions;
however, that too is incorrect, because:
Furthermore, when cognitions are perceived individually, the sound is heard [only] once.
Because of the hearing of that sound, there would be no appearance of continuity, and the synthesis [of parts] is refuted.
(492) Since the cognitions of the parts of the word are separated by the cognitions that grasp those [parts], there could be no perception of continuity.
If it is argued that what is interrupted cannot be cognized as uninterrupted, and that cognition occurs through a process of synthesis (*saṃghaṭana*),
to this he replies:
And the objection regarding the combination [of sounds] has been refuted elsewhere as well by the statement beginning with "the simultaneous hearing of those two colors," and so forth;
furthermore—
If there were an uninterrupted illusion even for one who hears [the sounds] as interrupted, then there would also be an uninterrupted illusion when two short vowels are pronounced. [Objection:
There is no continuous pronunciation of the two short vowels.
If there is an absence of a single cognition due to interruption,
and if that same interruption applies even to the phonemes (*mātrā*), yet there is still the conceit of non-interruption,
then that same logic would apply equally to the pronunciation of two short vowels; why, then, is it not observed?
Moreover, in this case, there is not even the cognition of a separation; rather, there is simply the separation itself, and not an illusion—this alone is the tenable position.
Furthermore:
When the perception through the eye has ceased, there is the superimposition (or mounting) of what was perceived without interruption.
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that all sensory cognitions are false.
(494) If this cognition of non-interruption were merely an error, it would have to be either produced by the senses or mental;
if it were produced by the senses, then all sensory cognitions would be false.
For indeed,
even the very last phoneme has a duration equal to a mere blink of an eye, and it comes to rest through a sequential connection with multiple atoms. (495)
"A period of ninety-one [atomic] moments is considered a very brief time, and cognition is momentary; therefore, it perceives the phonemes in succession.
Thus, with respect to phonemes, there is an uninterrupted appearance of form and so forth.
Thus, even if cognition is interrupted among the phonemes, all such cognition would have to be of an unreal object. || 497 ||
For the comprehension of all phonemes occurs gradually;
since cognition is momentary, it grasps the phonemes in a form consisting of a continuous succession of distinct moments.
Likewise, material forms and other [sensory objects] also arise sequentially.

Therefore, even in that case, if a sense organ were to produce a mistaken cognition like that of a whirling firebrand, there would be no instance of error whatsoever; if, on the other hand, the delusion is mental,
then another fault arises.
For instance,
that synthesis of entities which occurs elsewhere due to a sensory illusion—
a memory confused regarding distinctions and characteristics— is conceptual construction (vikalpaka). (498)
How can that which is associated with verbal discourse possess a clear manifestation?
For it is untrue to claim that a mental distortion becomes clear only while existing beyond clarity;
yet, cognition is held to have a clear form, such as the form of letters and so forth.
Therefore, how is it appropriate to call this a mental error?

For it has been stated that clarity is impossible for that which is associated with verbal expression, and that there is no manifestation of a clear object for that which is bound up with conceptual construction;
thus it is likewise here.
It has been analyzed that there is no application of words to objects perceivable by the senses.
Now...
If conceptual construction were to join together an object and its cognition— which are both constantly appearing— even for one who perceives them as interrupted by the senses,
then in the absence of any subverting evidence, how could it be established that they are "interrupted"? (500)
That which appears without interruption cannot be conceived as interrupted;

indeed, direct perception does not admit of such a contrary conception. Rather, it is more reasonable to conceive of the conception itself as non-existent, because it is sublated by direct perception.
Therefore, this [position] is untenable.

Now, if self-cognition does not exist, one must accept the cognition of a subsequent cognition; yet, since two cognitions cannot occur simultaneously, perception would be interrupted by that intervening subsequent cognition.
To this, he says:
If it is argued that [the non-simultaneity of cognitions] is due to the restriction of the capacities of the intellects (*buddhi*), from what is that [restriction] held to arise?
If it is because simultaneous cognitions are not observed, then this very point is what is being investigated:
for it is precisely the restriction of the capacities of the intellects that results in their non-simultaneity.
But from what is this restriction of capacity to be determined?
If it is argued that the restriction of capacity follows from the non-simultaneous observation of cognitions, then observation is interrupted; for even in that case, non-observation is possible.

Now, non-perception in that case is not a means of valid cognition; even so, how could simultaneous non-perception be a means of valid cognition? That very same non-apprehension which does not establish the absence of the arising of a discrete cognition—how could it establish simultaneity? (1149)

In this regard, it must be examined whether the simultaneous production of cognitions is due to their perception being uninterrupted, or whether, because they are not perceived simultaneously, their perception is to be conceived as interrupted.
Now, is it not the case that there is indeed no perception of cognitions simultaneously?
For even though [the objects] are eternal, a simultaneous perception of both future and past forms is not observed; rather, they are perceived only in succession.
There is also scripture for you;
for it has been said:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two minds, one preceding and one following, should arise simultaneously."
That too is incorrect;
for there would be a restriction of their capacity toward objects of the same class.
For instance, conceptual constructions are clearly perceived as occurring in a temporal sequence.
For the restriction of the capacities of cognitions is with respect to the production of cognitions of the same kind, not in a general sense.
Visual and other sensory cognitions do not produce only visual and other sensory cognitions of the same kind;
rather, if they were to produce both the grasped and the grasper forms therein, what contradiction would there be in producing something of a different kind?
(5) Refutation of Recognition:

Now, it may be argued that even conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), which has a clear manifestation, is accepted by others as a perceptual cognition called "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*); let it be so, but it is not [perceptual] in that way.

For in this way, whoever might imagine that even with respect to an object present before one's eyes, there is a perception characterized by clear manifestation and consisting of recognition— that person too has been refuted.

Furthermore, he who maintains that sense-perception is that which possesses a clear manifestation— on the grounds that sensory consciousness lacks the capacity to grasp preceding and succeeding forms, and that such grasping occurs only in conceptual construction— is also refuted;
for conceptual construction does not possess a clear manifestation, so how could it be perception?
Even if there is a clear manifestation, it does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its fallibility;
for instance, even in the case of [illusory] clusters of hair, a circle of fire, and so forth, there is a clear manifestation. (504)

Even when a difference is perceived, how could the cognition be such [i.e., non-conceptual]? Since perception is sublated in that case, by what is its non-perceptual nature not sublated by the intervening interruption?
Here too, there certainly exists a disruption characterized by the non-appearance of a prior and posterior form;
therefore, the determination of the oneness of phonemes and so forth does not arise from recognition.
Consequently, as to why [the opponent] says that [recognition] lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa):

Even when there is a difference in duration (mātrā), the identity of phonemes is recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); therefore, by what means could there be a non-perception of long vowels and the like?
This statement of his [the opponent] is merely a word, because it has been established that recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore:
Recognition is not perception born of the senses;
for it occurs without the recollection of a previous experience and the superimposition of its attributes [upon the present object].

The cognition "this is that very same [thing]" does not exist; and how could it arise from what is produced by the senses? Without a prior experience there can be no recollection, and without recollection there can be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same [thing]. For recognition consists in the grasping of the identity of what was previously experienced with what is being experienced now.
Furthermore, there can be no apprehension of a thing's prior form without recollection;

nor can an object that is the content of recollection be within the range of perception, otherwise everything previously experienced would be perceptual—so what, then, would be the use of the operation of the senses?
Moreover, it may be that something previously seen has died or perished; therefore, the operation of the senses is disregarded in such cases.
If this is so, let the operation of the sense organ occur right there; what is the use of going to that place?
[Objection: Without being in the appropriate location, the sense organ is not capable [of perceiving]. [Reply:
If that were the case, there would be no recognition here of something seen in another place.

For it is not the case that the form connected with another location is situated in a suitable location while being one and the same as that which is connected to both locations; therefore, that very [form] is the suitable location, and thus this is not a fault.
If that is so, then why is it not perceived in that way even without recollection?
If it is argued that there is no recognition because of the disappearance of that connection, then how could there be the thought "this is that very same thing" even in the case of memory?
There is no fault here, for even that which has disappeared can be remembered.
If it is argued that recognition is not a valid means of knowledge because the object related to the connection is not the same as the one possessing the connection,
then, in the absence of a connection with the previous place and time, the form would be merely the present one; thus, there is indeed a difference between the former and the latter.
Therefore, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not a [perception of] difference.
Now, one must investigate by what means that very cognition [is established];
for mere cognition is not itself a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), otherwise, what [would be required]?
He was restrained by his insistence on proving [the object's] perceptibility.

If permanence is asserted while the connection with prior time and so forth is not perceived, then all things whatsoever would be permanent; for even those things possessing an origin would be permanent, since they are perceived in their present form. If that were the case, why would there not be permanence in something produced at that very moment? Even if its "prior-ness" has not yet arisen, it nonetheless exists.
The objection—"How can that which has not arisen exist? How can that which has perished exist?"—is the same in both cases.
Furthermore, there is no difference between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
yet this is the distinction: that which has been destroyed is remembered.
Even that which has not yet come into being is perceived through inference based on possibility;
it is perceived as something "to be" (bhāvitayā), not as something "already past" (pūrvatayā).
Now, if it is perceived as "to be," the meaning is that there will be a future perception (bhāvipratyakṣa).
Therefore, it does not exist then, but will exist later; even here, it is perceived as having been real, in the sense that "it was directly perceived," and thus "it does not exist now.
[Objection: Let that be so; how then can it exist even now?
If it exists now because it is perceived now, then how could it have existed in the interim? For it is observed only at this very moment;
indeed, that which was non-existent previously is not what is apprehended now.
In that case, this is neither perception nor even inference, because its prior existence [at the time of the first observation] cannot be grasped as a relation;
if it is argued that the relation is grasped through uninterrupted observation, we say no.
If it is argued that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for uninterrupted perception—

since there is no means of valid cognition other than the recollection "I have perceived [this] uninterruptedly," and that this very [recollection] is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— then [the response follows].
If it is argued that validity need not be investigated because a means of knowledge is defined as that which is non-discrepant;
Because there is no lack of non-contradiction regarding permanence,
this non-contradiction therefore pertains only to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); and such causal efficiency is produced by an object of that kind,
not by that very same [permanent] object.
Because there is a lack of valid cognition [to prove otherwise];
for if it were otherwise, then since it would be connected to causal efficiency at all times, that causal efficiency would have been experienced at that very moment.
If you argue that this is because the causal efficiency was absent [at that time], [we reply:]...
How is it that there is no distinction between that which is connected to causal efficiency and its opposite,
such that causal efficiency is subsequently experienced only in the former?
This is not tenable, as it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Since, even in that case, another non-contradiction with purposeful action (arthakriyā) must be accepted, and yet another in that case as well, there would be no finality;
therefore, it is established that recognition is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

Therefore, because the perception of the *mātrā* is separated [from the others], there is an absence of contiguity (*nairantarya*), and thus there is no perception of long vowels and the like. Furthermore,
if it is maintained that simultaneous cognition is possible, that too is incorrect, because:

Furthermore, it is not accepted that the cognition of the object and the self-cognition [of that cognition] occur simultaneously; nor is a distinct appearance of the object and the cognition of the object observed. (507) 1 M.
The non-simultaneous arising of two cognitions is the mark of the existence of the internal organ (*manas*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.16)
16) Because of this statement:
cognition does not appear as an object, nor is a solitary object perceived as appearing;
rather, it is only an external appearance, such as blue and so forth, that is perceived by way of its own self-cognized nature.
Furthermore, it is not because they possess a single form of object that those two are unperceived,
as is the case with pleasure and its cognition.
That too is incorrect,
because:
For it is not the case that cognition appears as the object while the object is merely external;
otherwise, since they would be grasped by a single form, the consequence would be the absence of any distinction [between them].
(508) If, according to that view, pleasure and so forth, as well as the mind, possess a single form, then in that case too there would be non-difference alone.

It is not logical that difference exists without the appearance of difference, such that [difference] would be nothing more than the mere experience of pleasure and so forth; likewise, it is not logical for blue and other objects to be so.

Therefore, since there is no cognition here in this world other than that of pleasure and so forth or blue and so forth, it is logical to conclude that blue and other objects are self-cognizing (svasaṃvedana), just like pleasure and the rest.
Now, even if a cognition is not perceived here with perfectly distinct differentiation,
nevertheless it certainly exists, just as light is invariably present in relation to form and so forth.
That too is incorrect;
for instance, those two which are not perceived as distinct by means of a clearly discernible difference cannot be said to be cognized.
Now, if those two suffixes (*atha* and *athe*) are subsequently remembered, how could they be [perceived] separately?
(509) Even if there were light, if there were no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to grasp its distinction from this [object], there would be no separate perception of it at all;
for a distinction can only be considered as distinct by consciousness when its differentiation is actually perceived.
But it is not so;
therefore, there is no cognition of light as something separate from blue, whereas light is sometimes perceived alone.
Or, if by some [it were held that] form [is perceived],

then just as there is form alone, light alone, and form together with light, so too there would be consciousness alone and the object alone; thus, there would be a dual appearance, namely, the perception of the object and the perception of the consciousness itself.
Even if experiences arise sequentially, this fault regarding the multiplicity of appearances in the case of the object and the mind is difficult to remove.
Just as when simultaneous cognition is admitted, there is the unavoidable fault of the consequence that two appearances— the object and its representation— would occur together.
Likewise, even in terms of sequence,
for it is as follows:
First, there is the cognition of the object, and from that, the cognition of the absence of the object;
for a pure cognition could not be the cognition of an object.
Indeed, when the cognition of an object is itself known by another cognition, it must be known precisely in its form as the cognition of that object.

Likewise, there would be the consequence of the object appearing twice—once as the object itself and again as its cognition; otherwise, how could one cognition perceive that object? Therefore, even at a later time, there must be an appearance of the object.
And it is not so; for indeed,
the form of blue and so forth is one, and the cognition is also one.
In the perception of a blue appearance, no other perception is perceived as distinct [from it].
pṛthak
Here it is considered: is the fault only in the position of simultaneous cognition, or is it also in the position of sequential cognition?
If [the fault applies] when they are simultaneous...
Therefore, these two— the form of the blue object and the consciousness— are not perceived simultaneously;
this has been established accordingly.
Furthermore,
even then, it is not mere cognition that is subsequently perceived by memory, because [memory] perceives it precisely as being accompanied by blue.
Therefore, this is not a fault;
this is its meaning: it is not a fault.
The form such as blue is one, and the cognition is one with that blue form; however, within the cognition of the appearance of blue,
we do not perceive any other cognition distinct from the object.

Alternatively, we experience a single form such as blue and a single cognition in the form of pleasure and so forth, and no other apprehender in the experience of that pleasure and so forth, nor yet another in that [second] case; thus there would be an experience of an infinite series of forms and cognitions.
Now, he returns to the subject at hand:
"There might be an experience by means of another cognition, and in that case too, there would be memory."

If that [cognition] is seen, by what is its experience [known]? If it is by another [cognition], then who produces this continuous garland of those who possess knowledge, if one cognition is experienced by another cognition? || 513 ||
How is that to be known?
In that case as well, memory is observed;
therefore, one should know it.
If it is not by another cognition, then in that case too, memory alone would be the means of valid cognition;
and at that time, what cause would produce this continuous chain of cognitions and their respective experiences?
If the preceding cognition were that very [chain], there would be no transition to another object. (514)
If each preceding cognition were to be apprehended by each succeeding one, rather than the object such as blue, then there would be no apprehension of that object at all;
for [the cognition] would be that which has attained the status of being the apprehended, is proximate, and is the producer [of the subsequent cognition].
Without grasping the subsequent cognition, how could one grasp another?

(515) If cognition, being of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), were to grasp an object, then—just as there is a grasping of an object that is present—there would be a transition to other objects.

However, when a cognition is grasped by a subsequent cognition, then, since it has attained the status of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyalakṣaṇaprāpta*), how could the subsequent cognition fail to grasp that preceding cognition and instead grasp something such as blue?
For there is no capacity for grasping another object while setting aside what is proximate and connected to oneself;
if it is argued that the transition to another object occurs because an external object is present and acts as an obstacle,
that is incorrect.
Since that [cognition] is fixed in its own nature for the production of knowledge within itself, who indeed could obstruct it— an internal factor— by means of an external one? (516)
This verse does not appear in manuscript B:
"Even when an external object is present, it is not capable of obstructing that [cognition]; otherwise, no one would ever experience cognition while an object is in its proximity. (517)
And thus, there would be no recollection;
if it were to occur upon the absence of an obstacle, that would be false.
Since there is no state whatsoever in which an object is present [to the senses], memory—whose very root is destroyed—is also utterly destroyed; this is the brilliant doctrine. (518)

One might remember only the object itself and not that it was experienced; however, if it is argued that the experienced object, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), leads one to postulate its own experience,
that too is incorrect.
When the experience of an object itself has arisen as a continuous stream, then there is no presumption (arthāpatti) [of that experience];
and when that presumption is remembered, then there is another presumption, which results in the very same infinite regress (anavasthā).
Therefore, it is an experienced experience that is remembered, and not otherwise.
Therefore, because there is a contradiction regarding the object, there is neither experience nor recollection;
nor is there experience of an object from mere existence alone.
Even that [experience] arising from the connection with the sense organ—how is it to be known?
Because of the connection with other sense-faculties, there would be an infinite regress;
for those conceptualizations of the past and so forth, since the object is not present and there is no cause for its movement [into the present], the contemplation of the object would perish. (519)

Since there is no connection with the sense faculties regarding conceptualizations of the past and so forth, how can there be a determination of their having been experienced? Consequently, there would be no reflection upon objects; and if there were reflection, there would be an infinite regress of reflections.
Now, if even in that case the object itself were to consist in a difference of place and time, then it would necessarily always produce a contradiction; and thus,
there could be no movement at all.
Because it is precisely that which causes the impairment;
for in the case of sensory consciousness, only an object present [at that moment] acts as an obstructer.
Consequently, there might sometimes be an interruption of the continuity of the cognition and its feeling, and sometimes otherwise.
However, in the stream of thought (*cintāsantāna*), even an object that has passed away is always a cause of contradiction because it remains an object [of cognition];
thus, in that case, only the object would be known and not the cognition itself, and consequently there would be no recollection of the cognition.

Alternatively, if it were not a cause of contradiction, then the very experience of the stream of thoughts such as "thought" and "non-thought" would be the thinking of the object, and the thinking of objects would simply cease to exist.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "There exists a certain capacity by which cognition is produced within the self;
when that capacity is exhausted through gradual production [of cognitions], there would be a transition to another object."
That too is incorrect,
because [the soul's capacity] for generating cognition gradually diminishes due to the exhaustion of its power.
If there is a transition to another object, how can that very cognition of the object [be explained]?

(520) If the preceding cognition were devoid of the capacity to produce the apprehension of a subsequent cognition, then in the absence of that capacity, that cognition of the object would not be what is intended as having undergone a transition to another object.
Therefore...
When the capacity of the preceding cognition has perished;
"If the capacity of the previous cognition [remains]."
In reality, there is no transition [of cognition]; for when the power of the preceding cognition perishes, there can be no transference to the object, nor any movement toward another object.
For an intellect does not exist without a preceding intellect;
what then is the cause?
Because when cognition is impaired by attachment to another object, there is no arising of [subsequent] cognition;
(this refers to the ālayavijñāna).
For if the preceding cognition were not the cause, then even when it is impaired by attachment to another object, there would be the arising of a subsequent cognition.
For neither deficiency nor non-deficiency, neither contradiction nor its opposite, can be attributed to that which is not a cause; therefore,
since the preceding cognition is indeed the cause,
if it were incapable [of producing its effect], the subsequent cognition of the object would likewise not occur, and thus there would be an absolute absence of transition to another object.
In that case, for whom the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the generator of all evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), [how could it be established?]
It does not possess the status of being the cause of that preceding consciousness;
for precisely because the evolving consciousnesses arise from that very same storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) simultaneously,
it is therefore not their cause according to us either.

If, however, the preceding active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) were the cause, then the effect would not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [preceding consciousness], and thus the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would not possess causality.
To this it is replied:
even when various heterogeneous [effects] arise simultaneously, by means of a single, more powerful [cause]...
