Because of the deficiency caused by the mind, there is no other possibility than the ālaya;
for even for one for whom the ālayavijñāna is the cause, it arises from that very [ālaya]. || 522 ||

Even if, at some time, a single cognition of a different kind should arise, it cannot possibly originate from anything other than the *ālayavijñāna*, because its capacity has been impaired by a preceding active (*pravṛtti*) cognition that was more powerful and distracted by another object; therefore, in that case as well, that very [preceding cognition] is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). If, then, the arising and non-arising of cognitions result from that very [preceding cognition] when it is impaired, what is the use of the *ālayavijñāna*?
Let this consideration of the *ālayavijñāna* rest;
or, if it is conceptualized as the substratum for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no fault.
However, if the causality of the preceding consciousness is not accepted, then...

One should not expect the cessation of the mental state to depend on another mental state; for if it were to depend on another mental state for its cessation, then that [subsequent state] would have to be its cause, since it is illogical for something to depend on what is not its cause.
Therefore, because it does depend [on a cause], the logical conclusion is that it is indeed a cause.
Moreover,
the sequential arising of mental cognition must also be established as being dependent [on conditions].
For the cause of mental consciousness is indeed nothing other than its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
If that [subsequent cognition] were without a cause, it would arise simultaneously [with the first], because of being uncaused.
Therefore, the subsequent cognition has the preceding cognition as its very cause; thus, in the absence of the power of the preceding cognition, nothing at all would come to be.
If it is argued that, because the mind is a single entity, when it is attached to one [object], it cannot go to another—
The non-arising of another cognition is never [possible] because they arise simultaneously.
(524) If it is argued that since the mind is a single entity, when it moves toward one place it cannot move elsewhere, and thus the preceding cognition is without cause—
this too is incorrect.
For even that [simultaneous cognition] is merely consciousness preceded by the mind (*manas*), and not some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established [independently];

for its existence is established precisely by the non-arising of cognitions simultaneously. And that [non-arising] occurs simply because the previous cognition is rendered defective by its own attachment; moreover, simultaneous arising is occasionally observed, and in the case of equal activity, there would always be the arrival of others due to their equality.
But for one who holds that the non-arising of another cognition is caused by the unity of the mind, there would be non-arising at all times—both during the state of equanimity and otherwise.
For us, however, there is arising during the state of equanimity and non-arising at other times; thus, nothing is contradicted.
Surely, how can there be a sequence without the mind?

It has been established that [the sequence] arises from a deficiency in the cognitions; otherwise, for those things born from the mere conjunction of the self and the mind, their production would occur simultaneously. (525)

For in that case, there is no transition to another object from which a sequence of cognitions such as pleasure could arise, since it has been established that [these cognitions] consist solely in the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Now, if it were the case that because the mind is one, there would be only a single act of cognition, that is incorrect; for:
If action were one, there would be only one [agent]; how then could a lamp be seen by many?
(B. Action arises from one.)
Just as a single lamp produces the perception of many [objects],
so too is the mind;
this is the same [in both cases], whether by virtue of there being many perceivers or by virtue of there being many objects of perception.
Nor can the mind be the cause, because such a state [of consciousness] arises solely from the restriction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within consciousness itself;
furthermore, since the mind is eternal, it would be incapable of even sequential activity, as there would be no distinction between its earlier and later states. (526)
This body is explained as the person (pudgala),
if it is determined [to be] from the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
If it is asked from what [the cognition arises] later, it is indeed from the mind itself; however, this is precisely what we maintain:
that there is the imparting of a specific quality (*viśeṣādhāna*) to the eternal [mind].

Because of the practice of either the reality or the otherwise of some particularity, that particularity would then belong to its own nature; if it were something else, what would happen to it? Even if there were a connection with it, that [nature] would certainly not possess a single uniform form. (1152)

By this, the body and the person have been discussed. If the restriction [of rebirth] is due to *saṃskāra* (formative impressions), from what does that arise? If it is from the intellect (*buddhi*), let it be as is accepted [by us].
(527) By this, the body and the person have been discussed.

As for the one who thinks that because the body and the person are one, there is only a single action— that too has been refuted by this very [argument]; what need is there for a lamp to see many things?
Even in the case of succession, there is no capacity [in the body or person] because there is no distinction;

if, however, there is a distinction, then consciousness itself— endowed with a superior capacity— is the cause of that succession, and thus the assumption that the body and the person are the causes is futile.
If the restriction [of memory] is due to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), from where do those come later? If it is due to cognition (*buddhi*), let that be accepted;
for the mental impression is likewise established.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule;
for how could that which arises later be born from knowledge and yet be the cause of knowledge? Thus, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) belongs to cognition itself.

If this is indeed agreed upon by us—that the impression (*saṃskāra*), which has another name, "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*), is produced from cognition—then the restriction [of memory] belongs to the preceding cognition alone, because there is no evidence for anything else;
for apart from cognition, there is no such thing as a latent tendency.
Nevertheless, it might be argued:

The mere production of another cognition is not itself "graspability" (*grāhyatā*); therefore, even a preceding cognition that produces [the subsequent one] would be ungraspable, and thus there would be no transition to another object.
That is false, because:
There is no apprehensibility other than production; for production is the defining characteristic of the apprehensible,
since, in the case of an object that is apprehensible, the very production of cognition is the defining characteristic of being apprehensible.
For there is no light that is ungraspable, nor can it exist in something partless due to its subtlety and so forth. (528)
1. Regarding the phrase "in the portion of the [solar] transit"—this is not found in the manuscript designated as He; for knowledge is not produced in any way by that which is ungraspable.
For indeed, every object of apprehension is seen [as such];

however, light, because it possesses parts, is not apprehended even though it is a producer [of cognition], due to its rear side and so forth; for there is no part of consciousness that is not a constituent [of the object].
For light, being composed of parts, is thus logically subject to the loss of its capacity to be perceived; this is not the case for that which has the nature of producing [an effect],
so [your argument] is incorrect.
For,
in the case of the definition of being apprehended, there is certainly no other "production" [of the cognition];
otherwise, form and the like would not be direct benefactors of the cognition.
For even that which is to be grasped may, through a traditional succession, be helpful to the intellect by way of being ungraspable;

however, it is not so directly. Thus, the intellect is the producer precisely as that which is grasped. What other fixed rule for its existence could there be than this characteristic of being grasped? (530)
"Since that [nature] exists even in the intellect, the intellect too is established in reality"—
this is an intermediate verse;
therefore, the intellect is not something ungraspable.
Because the perception of the object to be grasped and its appropriation are the defining characteristics of the mind as the grasper;
for in consciousness, the state of being the appropriation of that [object] constitutes the mind's quality of being a grasper.

Perceptibility (*samvedanatā*) and being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatā*) are nothing other than this [nature]; there is no such thing as subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*) or the like here. Thus, there is no lack of apprehensibility.

If being an object of apprehension consists precisely in the state of being the material cause (*upādānabhāva*), and that state of being the material cause belongs only to one's own cognition—otherwise, it would follow that even another person's cognition would be perceived.

The distinction between objects is as follows: the non-apprehension of another's mind is due to its being without a basis (*anupādāna*); the non-apprehension of form is due to its being distant, subtle, or otherwise [unfavourable]; and the non-apprehension by the sensory faculty is due to the lack of a supporting consciousness (*vijñāna*) that would grasp it.
However, if even cognition (*buddhi*) were ungraspable, it too would not be graspable, just like the eye and other [faculties].
If it is argued that cognition is apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and memory [of that cognition] follows from it,
that is incorrect, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of [memory] occurring at all times, which is impossible.

When one quickly enumerates pillars, pots, and so forth, there is an excessive abundance of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, no presumption (*arthāpatti*) arises from that. For a presumption does not arise for one who enumerates quickly;
nor is presumption operative in that case, because no such operation is perceived.

Furthermore, the existence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not perceived by those engaged in worldly discourse. This [cognition] would have to arise either from the object, from the cognition of the object, or from both.

(1154) First of all, it cannot be that every cognition of an object arises from the object itself; nor can there be a cognition of the object through the cognition of the object, such that one thinks, "This is mine. (1155) Nor is the comprehension established through both together. Therefore, the establishment of self-cognition occurs solely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). (1156)
If cognition were understood solely from the object itself, then only cognition in general would be understood, not self-cognition.
But if it is argued that it is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) from the cognition of the object— surely that very cognition of the object is what is being understood?

For that very reason, how can there be presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), given the fault of mutual dependence? Since presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived object based on the fact that a perceived object cannot otherwise be accounted for, and since the perception of an object is not itself perceived, how can there be presumptive testimony?

Nor is there a perception of both [the cognition and its object] for this very reason; for the perception of one thing is not the perception of both. Therefore, cognition is indeed self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because it cannot be established otherwise.

Consequently, if it is accepted that [a cognition] is known by another subsequent cognition whose nature is perceptual, then, in the case of grasping all preceding cognitions, there would be no transition to other objects.
If sensation is the material cause of cognition, and form and so forth are its objects because they are subtle and so on,
then why is it not a fault for yogis to perceive the minds of others or forms that are subtle and so forth? This is the problem.

Since, for one of impure intellect, such is the consideration of the characteristic of the apprehended object regarding form and so forth as well as the mind, this way of the yogins is inconceivable. (530)
Indeed, how it is that yogins perceive things distant, subtle, and so forth, as well as the minds of others, is not even considered at this time;
for we have stated this definition of the "grasped" (grāhya-lakṣaṇa) with reference to those whose vision is limited to the mundane realm.
As for how the lords of yogins, whose mental continuums are completely purified, [perceive these], what is the use of such deliberation? Let this matter rest.
And just as this has been reflected upon even in brief, [one might ask]:

"If one's own cognition were perceived, would not everything be perceived? How can it be that it is not perceived? This is understood precisely from the fact that [the mind] moves toward other objects.
That too is not logical, because in that case, by virtue of its subtle nature and so forth, the object of perception would lapse into unperceivability.
What has arisen from the cognition of form and so forth that did not previously exist?
Indeed, its state of being subtle, distant, and so on was not something that did not exist before.
Even if a distinction [in the object] were impossible, if there is nevertheless a division in the apprehension, then that [division] would be without cause and thus could not possess such a division.
Therefore, when there is the grasping of one's own study, that very state of being an immediately preceding cause (anantara-hetutā) is what constitutes "immediately preceding" (anantara).

That very [cognition] is the object of the mind; therefore, there is no apprehension of an external object. (534—this is an intermediate verse) (6) The Doctrine of the Causal Complex (*hetusāmagrīvāda*).
Now, it is not correct to say that being a cause is itself being an object of apprehension. This is because entities possess multiple powers;

distinct from [the power of being a cause] is the "power of being an object of apprehension" (*grāhya-śakti*), which has ceased at the time of shifting to another object, while there is another power, namely the "power of mere production," by whose influence the subsequent cognition arises having the entity as its object.
And the multiplicity of powers in entities is determined precisely from their production of multiple effects.
Otherwise, there would be no production of multiple effects;
for even that is something trivial, since an entity does not produce multiple or single effects merely by lacking multiple or single powers.
It has been stated that this is "by nature" (*prakṛtyā*);
for this nature of entities whose birth is dependent upon causes does not deserve to be questioned as to how it is so.
For those things that attain their arising from their own causes according to specific determination, who is there to negate it?
Otherwise, how could even such a capacity exist?
Thus, there is no escape from this objection.
If you say it arises from its own cause, then let the completion [of the effect] occur through this very nature (*prakṛti*); what is the use of postulating a separate entity?

Surely the world’s understanding is that "this capacity (*śakti*) is dependent upon its own cause. This understanding exists, but it is not an understanding of a capacity that is distinct [from the cause].
If it is asked how this is so— given that [the object] is cognized merely through the superimposition of distinctions upon the dharma that constitutes its own nature—
the answer is that even in the case of a capacity (*śakti*), one observes the cognition of another capacity.
For if a thing is a cause for the production of an effect due to its possession of power, why is it not further questioned: from where does that power itself derive its power? (1157)
Therefore, power (*śakti*) is merely a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because it is established through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Now, one might object: "How can diverse entities become unified without power?
It is logical that they do so when there is a distinction of powers."
To this he says:
"If it were not from both the manifold and the single, then nothing would arise from the single; the production of an effect occurs from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). (535)
1. It has been stated that "everything is possible from a single [cause], because it occurs through two causal complexes"; therefore, that [single cause] produces many [effects]. (536)
For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, effects generally come into being; thus, some things arise from one, some from many, and some many from one.
Whatever the specific causal complex for a given thing may be, from that alone it arises—whether as a single entity or as many.
This is generally the nature of phenomenal manifestation;
for instance, from its own cause, it becomes either manifold or unitary.

By which [cause] it produces an effect, whether single or manifold— no differentiation of power (*śakti*) is of any use there; rather, even the powers themselves participate in that assistance, and thus they receive the designation "its [powers]."
For otherwise, if powers were distinct entities, they would merely appear as such;
and if they were indeed distinct entities, it would follow that they should be perceived as such.
Alternatively, there is nothing whatsoever such that a single [cause] produces multiple effects from itself alone;
how then is it said that "the manifold arises from the one"?
It is designated in that way because each individual [cause], while being subsumed within a pair of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), produces its respective effect.
When a single lamp is the producer of multiple perceptions because it is conjoined with the various immediate causal complexes (*samanantara-sāmagrī*) of many persons—
just as a single entity possesses multiple potencies, so too does it possess multiple effects— therefore, the state of having multiple effects exists even without multiple potencies.
In that case, just as a single [cause] produces multiple effects, so too a single cognition will produce both a cognition of its own object and a cognition of another object.
Therein, at one time the cognition would have the [preceding] cognition as its object, and at another time it would have the external object as its object; thus there is a transition between objects.
It cannot be argued that it must always produce both, for there is no distinction [between the two capacities].
If it is argued that [the self] indeed exists,
that is not so, because at that time—
If a subsequent cognition were to grasp the object first,
then because it would manifest both the preceding and succeeding objects within a single consciousness,
two expressions [of the object] would not be desired; for what is seen to occur in sequence would then appear as non-sequential.
*pūrva-abhilāpa*—there is a transposition of the positions of these two half-verses:
"The one [object] would appear twice, twice, due to the manifestation for both the self and the knower of the self. (538)
Regarding those two cognitions:

if both—the cognition apprehending the preceding [object] and the cognition apprehending the object such as form, which possesses an origin—were to arise, then because both the object of the preceding cognition and the subsequent object would appear, that pair of expressions perceived in succession would appear as non-successive.
For cognition does not manifest itself apart from the nature of grasping an object, since that is its very essence;
and when the grasping of an object manifests, it is the object itself that manifests. Thus, there would be a manifestation of two [successive] verbal expressions, one preceding and one following.
In that way, even a single [object] would appear as two,
because of the appearance of both the object itself and its cognition;
first, it appears by itself, and subsequently, when its cognition appears, there is thus a twofold appearance.
Now, if cognition is not apprehended immediately after the appearance of the object,
and if cognition is not apprehended either by itself or by another through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
then it must be apprehended through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) if it indeed appears.
Even then, since manifestation belongs to both the self and its cognizer, that same logical consequence remains.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) at a later time, this is not so; for at the time of the sequential grasping of various objects within that continuous stream, no one experiences an *arthāpatti*.
This is not the case.

If it is argued that comprehension occurs through implication (*sāmarthya*), then it would have to occur either always or never at other times; consequently, when there is cognition by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the object would appear a hundred times over. Alternatively, if one synthesizes one's own cognitions, then the arising of presumptive testimony occurs at a later time.

Even then, nothing was seen at that time from which an *arthāpatti* could arise, because the perception of the object had passed away by the time the *arthāpatti* was produced. [Objection: How can there be the occurrence of an *arthāpatti* from a past perception of the object?
[Response: If it is argued that the *arthāpatti* arises even at a later time from what is being remembered, [we reply: ...

If it is argued that the apprehension [of the object] occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) only in the case of recollection and not in the case of direct experience—wherein even there, there would likewise be the appearance of the word, the object, and the act of recollection—and that therefore, since what has not been experienced is not remembered, the existence of experience is established; [we reply: no.
In the occurrence of memory in the form "that was not experienced by me," the cognition "I had such-and-such an awareness" is impossible through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
For when one first applies the memory itself to the mind in the form "I remember a previous experience," [the self is already established].
In that case, there is no presumption (arthāpatti) either before or after; thus, how could memory be possible?
Even when there is a memory of an object, since both the memory and the experience would have to be inferred, it follows that the forms of the memory and the experience would appear simultaneously.
Consequently, even at the time of memory, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the clear form of the object.

If it is argued that the perception of two indistinct forms is likewise not seen [as a distinct cognition], then that too is no solution. Now, if for someone it is accepted that "there is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) because I remember, therefore it was experienced; or because there is remembrance, therefore there was experience," then in that case, the verbal formulation would simply be: "because there is experience, therefore there is experience. This is mere empty talk.
Likewise, since recollection arises from that very same source as recollection, this is a great feat of logical skill; for desire arises toward what has been experienced,
and since experience has never occurred [without an object], how could presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arise through desire?
Therefore, the cognition of a cognition by another cognition is indeed non-existent.
Furthermore,

If the final [cognition] were not experienced during the transition to another object, it would follow that there is no experience of any [cognitions], just as in the case of another person's experience.

For at the time of transitioning to another object, if the final cognition— the preceding consciousness within the continuum of cognitions— at that time of transition to another object, [were not experienced...]
In that case, all experience would be like the experience of another,
because there is an absence of "experiencedness" for an experience of what was not experienced, just as in the case of the experience of another.

Therefore, because one experiences the final [moment], there is an experience of those preceding it, up to and including the first moment. Just as in the case of another’s experience, that experience is not experienced by anyone else—and thus there is no experience by another—so too, even when one has experienced it oneself, since that very nature of the object is likewise [dependent] upon another, how can there be experience?

[Objection: Just as in the case of another’s experience, the experience of another is established because one does not experience it oneself, so too, let it be established that one’s own experience [occurs] because it is not experienced by another. [Reply: That is incorrect.
Let it be established if there is a means of valid cognition;
for just as that which has been experienced by another cannot be established as being either one's own perception or another's,
so too that which is claimed to be one's own perception does not deserve to be established as belonging either to oneself or to another.
But surely an object is cognized by its own nature; how then can it be non-perceptual?
For when one thing is not being cognized, another cannot be said to be uncognized; indeed, it is [the object itself] that is cognized.
Let it be cognized by itself; that [cognition] too is cognized by itself alone; therefore, there is indeed self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
Now, if the self is perceived as an agent,
it is not so; for there is no self apart from the body.
If the body were the agent, it could not be so,
because the body is also the object of action.

If it is argued that because self-awareness does not exist in the body and so forth, there is no dispute regarding their lack of self-awareness, yet there is indeed a dispute regarding the non-awareness of cognition;
Since self-awareness of the self is sufficient for the experience of an object, cognition is redundant;
therefore he says:
"If that which is experienced by the self is perception, it is not experienced by others."
How is that self-experience established, such that it can be asserted in this way? [Verse 540] From what source is there the experience of a self?
If it were experienced by another, how could it not be another's self?
If there is experience through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), then the establishment of self-cognition is itself certain; thus, there is no dispute on this point.
Therefore, if there were no self-cognition, it would follow that nothing at all could be experienced.
[Objection: But surely, even when something is not experienced by the eye and so forth, there occurs the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that "it was experienced by the eye and so forth."
If it is asked why self-cognition is not accepted even when there is no experience [of it],
it is replied here:
for one who desires the manifestation of manifestation, there would be the non-establishment of the cause of manifestation.
1B. Even if the manifest is not established as manifest, if this world is manifest,
then since the eyes and so forth are the causes of manifestation, even if they are unestablished, there is no lack of manifestation for the object, because it is manifested through manifestation.
Regarding the claim that "this eye is manifest" (*vyakta*): how can it be designated as "our eye" simply because it generates our cognition?
For the "ours" of that cognition arises solely from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Furthermore, if that cognition were not established as related to oneself through self-awareness, then if manifestation occurred merely by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), the entire world would become manifest—an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.
[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no over-extension [of the definition], since that in which a manifestation (*vyakti*) has arisen is itself "manifest"?

[Response: If something were manifest merely by the arising of a manifestation, then everything would be so. Furthermore, the notion "this is the manifestation of this" cannot exist without a relationship [between the two].
Therefore, everything would become manifest by its own nature alone. Alternatively, if the object is of that very nature, let it be called self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). (vv. 1161–1162)
Thus ends the second chapter, on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*.
In the *Pramāṇavārttikabhāṣya*, the third chapter is the *Pratyakṣapariccheda*.
Chapter Four is the *Parārthānumānapariccheda*.
Chapter Three is the *Parārthānumānapariccheda*.
1. Dignāga’s Definition of Inference for Others (parārthānumāna).
The result of the inclusion of the term "seen by oneself" (svadṛṣṭa).
Inference for others is stated immediately after inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).

Since inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is preceded by inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), it is therefore [defined as] "the manifestation of an object seen by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭārthaprakāśana*). "Seen by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭa*) means that which has been perceived by both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*), who are respectively the expounder and the one being addressed; this is the meaning of "seen by oneself."
If there are judges, then because they too possess authority,
the removal of disagreement is established by their very capacity;
by this [statement], one's own perceived object is made known to another.
And that form consisting of bodily and vocal intimation is the mark (liṅga) there; its own nature is the object seen by oneself.
But why is it said that "the mark has three forms"?
Since it is possible to establish all objects by means of grasping an object perceived by oneself,
it follows that inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*) is simply the illumination of the entire inferable object— which is of a hidden nature— to another person.
To this, it is replied:
Apart from the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*), there is no other means of manifestation. Since it cannot be understood by anything else, it is not manifest.
For it is said to be "manifested" only where there is a correct comprehension on the part of another;
for this very reason, the prefix *pra-* denotes excellence.
Furthermore, there is agreement with another regarding what is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If the object of inference (*anumeya*) were also established by valid cognition, then there would be no dispute at all. Rather, it is through the manifestation of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) that the understanding of the object of inference—which has become the locus of dispute—is achieved; thus, the statement [of the reason] is not purposeless. Therefore, inference arises from this, and that too is "inference" only in a figurative sense (*upacāra*).
If speech were considered "for the sake of others" (parārtha) because it produces inference, then it would also be "perceptual" (pratyakṣa) because it produces perception;
this [position] is not tenable.
Furthermore, that statement which is free from dispute is also perception for the sake of others.
Just as when there is a recollection of a previously grasped relationship, inference arises from a statement, so too does perception never arise [from a statement].

(2) The arising of inference occurs necessarily upon the recollection of a three-featured mark (*liṅga*); however, it is not the case that perception arises from a statement merely concerning an object already cognized by oneself.
(3) Perception of another does not arise from a mere statement.
Objection: Is it not observed that there arises the perception, "Look, the deer is running"? [Response]:
Even in that case, it is because inference follows immediately thereafter.
For instance, when there is an orientation toward that object, he is enjoined thus: "See this! And this has been established by implication.
"O gazelle-eyed one, turn toward me"—this is an injunctive statement.
And since turning toward [the speaker] occurs for you just as it does for me, one proceeds by recollecting that such a turning toward is the operation of causes; thus, this is indeed inference.
Thus, having observed the possibility of perception through inference, one indeed proceeds [to act].

In that case, the inference based on possibility (*sambhavānumāna*) operates upon the object of perception; it is either a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) or a reason of effect (*kāryahetu*), and it is not manifested directly from the statement alone.
For instance, by the statement "there is fire here because of smoke," [the connection] is made manifest; however, the smoke itself is manifested through direct perception. (5.3) B.

Consequently, the statement in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* that "inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the exposition of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)" would be contradicted;
this [interpretation] is not tenable.

Since all speech is for the purpose of recollection, it is therefore designated as a means of valid cognition (*pramā*) in that regard; however, when [an object] is already perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), speech is always rendered useless.
This has been said:
for to the wise, only the reason itself is to be stated.
In the same way, it should also be understood that the "mere" connection (*pratibandha*) is likewise [to be considered].
Alternatively, even in that case, one must indeed rely upon the statement of another, such as "this is smoke," for the purpose of dispelling error;
for it is thus:
"By my certain conviction, this smoke has arrived here as a means of cognition. Why, then, do you have such an error regarding it? Thus is one awakened by another.
(7) This is the meaning of the statement.

In that case, an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not being communicated to another by means of verbal expression; rather, it is inference itself that is "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*), because it is the cause [of that understanding]. This [inference] is to be understood as nothing other than smoke: "This is not otherwise than the smoke previously observed.
By implication, this is what is meant, because it possesses that defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is only the operation of inference that is made manifest by the word; the word never functions with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, due to extreme familiarity, the world perceives it otherwise, as if there were no unfolding of inference.
Therefore, speech is only capable of being accepted as a cause for inference; thus,
speech is indeed an inference based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*) because it is its cause, and not an inference based on a cause (*kāraṇānumāna*), as is the case with smoke here.
Because speech is an inference based on essential nature (svabhāvānumāna);
[or] because it is the cause of an inference based on essential nature— externally.
It should be seen that this is incorrect.
For even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), when smoke as a form is recognized as an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*),
there is still no cessation of error in the interim for the discerning person due to the absence of the essential reason;
regarding this, he says:

What contradiction could there possibly be here that would cause the "cause of the effect" (kāryahetu) to be lost? Even when there is an intervention, this [reason] does not forfeit its status as the cause of the effect. (8)
*Bahiḥ* (External). Regarding the Buddhist objection, he establishes the conclusion with the first two quarters and the second two [quarters] respectively;
by this, inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is vindicated.
If it is intended merely that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) certainly exists in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), then what is the use of demonstrating this mediation?
However, in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the effect-reason is not even possible,
because the statement of smoke and so forth functions directly as a nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

Therefore, this inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) does not exist [as a distinct category]; rather, it is based on what is possible that the status of being an inference for others is stated by the author of the treatise. Let that [status] be so; what harm is there if it is otherwise?

Alternatively, where there is no error, in that case, in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is indeed immediate; and since the same principle applies to inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the arising of inference occurs directly from the word. If it is asked: "What is the use of speech if there is no error? [the answer follows].
There is no fault in this, as it is for the purpose of demonstrating the necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
furthermore, it was stated just now that the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) occurs according to the circumstances.
Moreover:
Inference is not authoritative unless it is inseparable from speech; this much alone is intended, but not that every word is so [authoritative].

As for one who asks: "How can there be authority for perception and inference alone, when even speech is a cause of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and without speech, worldly transaction is not complete"?
1 B. Regarding this, it is said in response:
Without perception, inference, and verbal testimony, how could there be any worldly activity? Yet, what validity does that [activity] possess?
Even when one acts by recollecting an object previously perceived, why does one not act without perception and the other means of knowledge?
Is memory, then, also a valid means of knowledge?
Now, even that very statement which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is likewise not a means of valid cognition regarding its object;
however, where it is a means of valid cognition, it is so only by virtue of being a cause for inference (*anumāna*), and not otherwise.

Only this much is intended here, and not that every utterance is the cause of all inference; for an utterance is merely inference itself and does not possess independent validity as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the demonstration that [all] inference consists of utterances is of no use;
therefore, an utterance is simply the communication of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).
In that case, how is the Vedic word authoritative?
Even there, its authority arises precisely from its communicating objects that are established through perception and inference, as in the statement "there are twelve months" and so forth.

If it is argued that there is simply no means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*) elsewhere— just as in the case of human speech, where validity arises precisely because of its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*)— we say no.
Because it lacks credibility;
for indeed, no one gains conviction from mere words alone.
If the Veda were like direct perception, why would everyone not believe it?
Even from the inference of momentariness and so forth, not everyone understands [it] due to delusion; if it is argued that there is delusion even in this case, [the response is as follows].
It is by means of an inference of that same class, which serves as a basis for conviction, that [the doubt] is removed;

however, in the case of the Veda, it is not by way of its being a statement of that same class—thus these two cases are not equal. For the validity of an inference lies in its being connected with positive concomitance (anvaya), whereas in the Veda, no such concomitance is observed; this was previously investigated. || 12 ||
Alternatively,
this is the meaning:
inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is precisely speech in the form of the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics (trirūpa).
The Vedic word is not [the probans] for that [conclusion], because it lacks the three forms;
for its concomitance with truth is not observed, nor is it a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

For thus, because it lacks truth due to being non-human (apauruṣeya), there is no logical connection (*anvaya*) with its explanation; however, in the sense of existence, there is a connection, namely:
"then there are twelve months."
To this it is replied:
[it is] excluded.

The Vedic character of the passage concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites is not definitively established; its human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) might also be possible, since it could have been composed by someone. It is even conceivable that at some point this was inserted among the non-human (Vedic) texts by someone, for it is heard in certain other recensions (*śākhā*) that these were composed.
If it is argued that such conventional usage occurs when there is recollection, we say no,
because [recollection] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatvāt*).
Since this would also lead to an over-extension in other cases,
and all of this has already been established previously, it will not be elaborated upon here; let it be,
provided that the term "svadṛṣṭa" (seen by oneself) refers to the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself as possessing the three characteristics.

It should be stated that "inference for others" is the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics; what is the purpose of including the phrase "an object seen by oneself," since it does not serve another function?

For some say that because another is the one to be convinced, even if [the reason] has not been seen by oneself, it is a means of proof provided it has been seen by others; therefore, the statement "seen by oneself" is for the purpose of excluding that.
For in inference for the sake of others, there is no concern with one's own realization,
because it is the other person alone who is to be persuaded;
and if that logical mark (*liṅga*) is established for the other person, then the other person indeed realizes it.
It should not be asked, "How can the other person possess understanding without the proponent's understanding?

For even when the proponent has understanding, another does not necessarily understand it. If that [understanding] occurs without one's own cognition, let it be so; what is the use of another in this case?
One does not, at least, correctly perceive that this is the proponent's understanding here.
However, [the proponent] acts solely on the basis of his own conviction, thinking, "I have understood it exactly thus.

But as for this [opponent], whether he has understood it and made it public or otherwise—what is the use of such an investigation that results in excessive proliferation? Therefore, according to this intention, even that which is not personally realized is accepted as a logical mark (*liṅga*) when it is realized by others.
In order to refute that intention,
there is the statement "seen by oneself";
if it is thus "seen by oneself," then because it excludes what is seen by another, it results in nothing other than a synonym.
This is not [the case], because it is for the purpose of establishing what is seen by both;
thus, this is its characteristic as it truly exists.
And by that, even the misconception has been refuted;
therefore, it should be "for that very purpose," and not [the other way].
Furthermore, it is logical that the object for which this undertaking was begun is precisely what is expressed by the word.
For it is not possible to say that what is not cognized by oneself is cognized by another. Furthermore,
in inference, there is no authority for scripture.
Now, it might be argued: "Let that [object] be cognized by the other;
however, the thorough knowledge that it has been understood by the other is not useful, because the purpose of the other is fulfilled merely by one's own cognition."
How, then, can there be the presentation of that which is not known by oneself?
If it is by virtue of what is established for another, then it follows that "it is established for the other"— this is precisely what has now arrived.
Furthermore, since this [object] is not itself perceived, how can it be so? For one who perceives only what is near cannot directly perceive the cognition of another;
even inference depends upon one's own cognition.

Therefore, that which is ascertained by the other as being cognized by them is also [considered] cognized by oneself. Furthermore, if something is understood by the other through scripture (*āgama*), it is indeed cognized by oneself as well;
however, because the proponent does not accept that scripture, it is designated as "not cognized by oneself."
Therefore, even that which has been accepted by another on the basis of scripture, but not by oneself, is indeed a means of proof;
regarding this, it is said:
"In the domain of inference, [scripture] is not desired, because of the acceptance of what has been examined."
For in this case, inference does not operate; rather, it is the authority of the word [itself] that is at issue.
That scripture is either a valid means of knowledge or an invalid one.
If it is a valid means of knowledge, then its validity must be established for both parties.

Since it is not accepted by anyone that [the object] is non-authoritative in the same way as something perceived by another means of valid cognition, it is established for the opponent alone— this is the point.
Scripture is not an authoritative means of knowledge regarding the object of inference,
because it is accepted only after having been examined.
And where there is no object for perception or inference, that [scripture] is not a means of valid cognition;
for if validity were universal, what would be the use of inference, since the object would be established by the mere word? For instance:

"Pleasure and the like are insentient because they are produced or because they are impermanent, like form and so forth"—this is what is intended by the Sāṃkhya as established for the opponent, not as established for the Sāṃkhya himself. For him, neither "being produced" nor "impermanence" is established. In that case, if establishment occurs through the authority of a statement, then the Sāṃkhya's own statement must also be authoritative; thus, the insentience of intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure, and so forth would be established from that very source—what is the use of inference?

Now, if the Buddhist statement proving impermanence and so forth is [the means of proof], then by that very [statement] the sentience of cognition and the rest is established; thus, there is no establishment of the opposite through inference, and the inference is therefore entirely useless.
Alternatively, if the opposite is established because inference also possesses validity, then [inference] is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa);
for he says this because the means of proof was stated against the opponent in order to refute their scripture (āgama).
At that time, that [statement] is unestablished as a means of valid cognition; therefore, everything else is established from it.
For when one begins to prove the opposite by means of inference, at that moment that statement is indeed not a means of valid cognition, because it cannot withstand critical examination.
Because even the commitment [to that scripture] becomes lax;
for when the status of that scripture as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which was established by that very commitment—is weakened, its validity likewise becomes so.
Consequently, due to the weakening of the reason well-known to him, there is also a weakening of the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*).
If it is argued that "that which is not dependent on something else does not necessarily follow its nature, because otherwise it would follow that it is not dependent on it;
therefore, there is no proof for the reason [of being conscious], as the reason is unestablished," we say:
No.

Because if one were to see deviation in some instances, it would follow that there could be no confidence in anything at all. If, on the other hand, that portion of the statement is consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that reason must rest upon what is established for both parties.
Even if it is indeed established by valid cognition, for the Sāṃkhya—who is ignorant of the functioning of valid cognition—it remains merely "established for the other" (*paraprasiddha*).
That too is improper;

for in this way, that Sāṃkhya would merely be exposing his own private parts. Even so, what is the fault? For he has been refuted by that mark which is established for himself. One cannot conclude a lack of knowledge regarding everything simply because there is a lack of knowledge in one particular case. (15)
It is not the case that because one is unable to prove a reason, one is likewise unable to prove the probandum;
for the reason established by oneself possesses the existence of the probandum as it has been apprehended.
Thus, the proponent speaks with confidence, asserting that this [reason] is capable of being made manifest.
That too is incorrect;
for once a reason is established, it is capable of proving the probandum—what need is there for anything else? To explain:
To that extent, this [reason] is already established; but what benefit is there in its being established by me? What rule is there that says, "Every operation must be performed by me alone"?
Is it a royal decree that the reason, like the probandum, must be established by me alone?
Certainly not, for it is impossible to establish everything for everyone.

Now, it might be argued that this [definition] is improper according to the *Nyāya* because a proof (*sādhana*) is stated with the desire to produce a certainty in others that corresponds to one's own certainty;
yet even that is not correct, for as follows:
"The purpose for another here consists merely in the production of certainty, just as it does for oneself; therefore, this qualification is useless.
(17) For the other person's interest lies in certainty alone, and not in some further qualification that serves no purpose therein;
indeed, a wise person does not accept a qualification that is of no utility.
To this it is replied:

How could one who does not know another’s conviction through discernment have the thought, "He has been convinced by me"? For how can there be conviction for one who himself does not recognize, "I have not deceived him; rather, this is his own firm conviction"?
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"What does it matter if there is merely an understanding for the opponent? To that extent, the proponent's statement has fulfilled its purpose; what fault is there in this?
If that were so, then the following reply would also be valid:
"Even though you have been awakened by me through whatever rambling I have uttered, what other purpose is there here for me, based on my conviction toward you?
(19) When he says, "I have demonstrated to you by means of some elaborate display of fallacious proofs," then what answer should be given to him?
If it is argued that a refutation should be stated in that regard:
The opponent's position should not be established by means of a refutation;

rather, that proponent should then offer this reply: "What purpose do you have for my position? If [the opponent] should say, "This is non-apprehension because it lacks proof," [the proponent replies:]
In that case, one should not present a refutation to another;
rather, one should simply say, "I do not understand.
However, it must indeed be stated that the lack of understanding is accompanied by its justification, for the purpose of demonstrating this, the refutation must also be stated.
In that case,
if the opponent is to state a refutation supported by reasoning, the proponent must likewise state a proof supported by reasoning.
For the opponent must explain with supporting arguments how he lacks such an understanding of this very point as I do.

Likewise, even for one who speaks thus, the proof must be accompanied by reasoning; otherwise, the doubt might not be dispelled that "just as I lack understanding here, so too might another [lack it] at some time.

For one who acts for the sake of others does not find satisfaction without relying on what is established for the sake of others. Nor do the learned engage merely out of a desire for victory, nor are treatises composed for that purpose alone, since their aim is the entry into reality (*tattva*).

Therefore, one who has correctly apprehended [an object] thinks: "This has been apprehended by him, but this has not been apprehended. However, without his own apprehension, [stating that something is not apprehended] is merely a false statement;
it is the demonstration of a non-apprehension [that does not exist for the other].
But if the opponent does not accept it, the proponent would not be a speaker who establishes [the point]; for who would desire their own defeat?
However, even if one does not accept it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for oneself, the opponent’s state of being a speaker of falsehood is still perceived.
Now, even if one has understood it oneself, how can there be understanding that the other has also understood?

Even if the opponent indeed understands it, the adjudicators (*prāśnikāḥ*) will understand it; if he does not understand what has been understood by the adjudicators, then it is due to a deficiency in his own causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and it is not the fault of the proponent (*vādī*).
The speaker’s duty is not exhausted by merely describing milk to a blind man;
nor should anyone provide eyes to the opponent.
If, when it is stated that "the milk is white," the opponent does not believe it due to a visual impairment, that is the fault of the opponent alone—the blind man;
how can there be any fault here on the part of the proponent?
Let the statement of the proponent be considered successful once it has been understood by the judges.
Now, it might be argued:
"How is it appropriate that those who act for the sake of others, whose minds are drawn by compassion, should be subject to refutation merely because they have been accepted as judges?
For those who act for the sake of others do not desire their own mere satisfaction. (22)
However, their intended purpose is the removal of the delusion of others;

in that case, one who has girded his loins for the sake of instructing the opponent (the *prativādin*) would be satisfied merely by instructing the judges (*prāśnika*). Where is the [intended] goal, where have you landed, where is the commencement for the sake of instructing the opponent, and where is the conclusion by means of instructing the judges alone?

Furthermore, if an arbiter who is corrupted by partiality toward that side should dispute, then yet another arbiter must be sought for those disputants. If one arbiter moves on to become another arbiter while the opponent remains as an arbiter, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, whom could the proponent ever convince?
Now, even if the audience is likewise devoted to the proponent, nevertheless, because of that partiality, their status as judges is not entirely clear.
To this it is replied:

Is this one who acts for the sake of others [not] likewise [inclined] toward the unworthy? He does not overstep his capacity, nor is he one whose nature lacks compassion for those who have not acted [for the good]. (25–26)
Even one possessed of compassion is capable of, indeed, able to, accomplish the welfare of a worthy person.
For there is no contradiction of compassion when [the opponent] is incapable;
indeed, the audience does not perceive him as being devoid of compassion.
However, if the audience is partial, he is effectively the opponent himself; therefore, one must necessarily rely on another audience.
Nor is it the case that everyone contradicts one another due to a lack of purpose or because of mutual dependence;
for if even among them there were only the relationship of proponent and opponent, then all worldly transaction would be destroyed.
Since it is not observed [to occur],
the conclusion of a debate consists solely in the awakening of the judges;
furthermore, this imposition of defeat upon others through rules such as the failure to grasp [the argument] is nothing but cruelty.
Therefore, having announced one's own position to the judges and others, the power of demonstration must be brought under one's own control;
for that reason, [the proof] must be established by scripture alone, not by what is established for another.

But surely, when that scripture is accepted by the opponent as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then he himself necessarily understands it through the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) established therein;
for it is impossible to accept [the scripture] in such a way while one part of it is sublated.
Therefore, he says:

If it is established for one who possesses that scripture, then whose is it, and what is the scripture? How can that which is sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) be established as scripture?
If it is not a means of valid cognition and is not accepted by the opponent, then whose is it, and what is the scripture?

If [it is argued that] even without acceptance, the Sāṃkhya also possesses that scripture and thus it is established for both parties, then [we reply]: if it is not so because of non-acceptance, then no one at all possesses that scripture,
and thus it is not established for anyone.

This scripture is certainly not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge; it would be a fallacious scripture (*āgamābhāsa*) since its comprehension arises from a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Thus, that person is indeed deluded; therefore, that [scripture] cannot remove the delusion of another. Furthermore, if the opponent does not recognize the fallacious nature of the means of knowledge, how could he be deluded? He would not be a disputant at all.
Nor is it that he does not know;
for how could there be an acceptance of something contradictory to that very [knowledge] by him?
If he accepts something other than that, then that member of the proof (*tyāgāṅga*) lacks authority.
(5) At the very moment he accepts what is contradictory to it, he simultaneously realizes the unreality of that scripture, because the acceptance of the contradictory is inseparable from it.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the opponent] is deluded;
It has been stated that being unconvincing does not constitute delusion; since he was removed after having produced confusion, the proponent's duty is not yet accomplished.

If it is argued that "being a debater" (*vāditva*) consists in deluding others through eloquence, [this is] not so, because it would follow that even the giving of poison and the like would constitute being a debater.
Because eloquence consists in making a thoroughly pure subject matter clearly understood;
for thus, those who know reality maintain that eloquence is desired through the illumination of a subject matter that is free from error, both in its concise and detailed forms. (27)
If it is argued that one who desires victory must by any means whatsoever remove the opponent,
we say no;
for by removing him by any means whatsoever, one becomes an object of ridicule.

If, then, there is delusion of others even by means of speech concerning a perfectly pure object, how so? Because what has been stated is sufficient for the understanding of the judges; it is not as if the sun fails to illuminate because a blind man does not see it.
For it is thus:
by means of demonstration.

The fault would belong to the proponent if he fails to communicate [the meaning], provided that the opponent is capable; for if, despite the words, the opponent does not understand due to being of a different class [of intelligence] or other reasons, then what faith can there be in his status as a respondent? It is only appropriate for him to enter the school of a teacher who recites the *Mātrikās* alone.
Furthermore, it might be argued that such a presentation of proof is not intended for those who are learned,
because it is presented against an unlearned opponent; for even he would offer a refutation that is indeed irrelevant.
For indeed,
at every price, the wrapping of the packet was exactly as it had been; thus,
this story of the leather-worker has arrived.
"He has drunk wine from my alms-bowl; I, however, must drink his urine. And so it was. 2 B.
It must be so.

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya does not personally realize its own lack of consciousness because of its [alleged] eternality; therefore, for the Sāṃkhya to know itself, another means of valid cognition would be required. || 29 ||
For it is not logical to understand one's own probandum through a means of proof established only for the opponent;
therefore, this [proponent] must possess a means of proof established for himself that accomplishes that object.
If you say, "That [means of proof] certainly exists," [we reply:]...
If that is so, then [it follows] for her...
Why then has that [cognition] not been stated as the proof, from which one's own realization arises? Why has it not been called the proof?
Why then is that very proof, which is the cause for your own conviction, not put forward? What is the use of this other effort of "chewing on the sky"?
For when a reason with a perfectly clear nature is available, an arduous effort at conceptual construction is certainly not superior.
It is established for the Sāṃkhya on the basis of scripture; therefore, this is not an introduction of a means of proof that is [only] recognized by oneself.
But surely, that scripture is indeed a means of proof even for the opponent?
No.
Since it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) for another,

how can there be comprehension for oneself from what is not a means of valid cognition? If it is a means of valid cognition for that person because it is a means of valid cognition for him, why is it not so for everyone?
Since there is no admission [of such a position],
how can there be an admission of this even for the Sāṃkhya?
Because it has been examined by him,
if this were the case for the opponent as well,
then since—
Since [the opponent] does not accept it, why is that very same reasoning by which scripture is to be accepted not also the means of grasping this [reasoning] itself? 6
2. Furthermore, just as the scripture of the Sāṃkhya, when examined by reasoning, is accepted by another as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
If it is argued that this is not a valid argument even for a Buddhist because he does not accept it,
then how could he accept the argument that "because they are impermanent, they are insentient"?

It is equally necessary to accept what is established by logic even when adopting a specific treatise; and since a proof that is established for both parties is possible, why would one undertake the effort of presenting another proof?
This matter is accessible to yogis; therefore, the opponent must be convinced by whatever means of proof is available.
In the proof (sādhana).
Regarding the term *sambhavaiḥ*: in the He manuscript it says,
"Indeed, even an opponent is capable of asserting that 'this is accessible only to yogis' regarding their own thesis."
Nor can it be said that [the cognition] of one who possesses that [yoga] is not a valid means of knowledge;
for,
previously, when he was an ordinary person, those [means] by which his comprehension and perception were possible—
The means of proof are sufficient for one who possesses knowledge of the power of objects;
for there is no yogi whatsoever who exists by virtue of his own nature, because there is a lack of valid evidence,
as was previously established.
Since there is no authority even for that which is impermanent,
therefore, one who is initially an ordinary person later attains the state of a yogi through the practice of means, and not by means of [attaining] well-being.
And thus it is said:

By means of those instruments through which there is the comprehension of the methods for accomplishing that [object], and through the performance of those methods, the capacity of the senses arises; thus, perception itself—which consists in the comprehension of that object—has been described.
Alternatively, the means for achieving such comprehension has been described;
these are the instruments for that object, which serves as the means for the capacity of the sense-organ to accomplish it.

If their capacity is known, then those very things which are capable [of producing cognition] are accepted as having the objects apprehended by those yogins; what, then, is the use of putting forward a proof for something non-existent?
Just as the proof for a yogin was stated by the Buddhists, it is likewise proper for others to state it.
If it is further impossible to adopt that means of proof even by way of its occurrence in a yogi,
then silence is the only appropriate course here,
because:
And for those objects which are disconnected from [logical] concomitance and are not even within the scope of generality,
there is no consideration whatsoever of a probandum or a probans.

For whatever object can be followed by a means of proof— whether by way of generality alone or by way of a general property and its particularity— [only such an object is subject to logical analysis].
In that regard, an investigation into the probandum and the probans should be undertaken; therein, an investigation in general may first be conducted as follows:
"Is it possible for a yogi to exist for us?"
This [statement], "this object was seen by him," is also possible;
or rather, the thought "only this object is possible" occurs with specific reference.

However, regarding those things that cannot be made objects of cognition even in a general sense because they do not conform in any way whatsoever, there is no consideration whatsoever of the locus of the probandum and the probans.
Let the investigation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) rest for now;

for this object is to be understood solely through scripture (āgama). Therefore, by introducing a means of valid cognition regarding that matter, this wicked person merely reveals his own ignorance of the domain of valid cognition.
Moreover, as long as he has not attained proficiency [in that domain], he will not recognize what constitutes a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa).

Therefore, when it is understood according to that intention that "this is indeed a means of proof," yet later one realizes, "This is not a means of proof," then what fault could there be in saying, "It will not be a means of proof"?
That too is incorrect, because:
When the determination of reality and unreality depends upon the subjective intention of men,
both the valid reason (*hetu*) and its fallacy (*tadābhāsa*) are lost, because that [determination] relies solely upon the thing-in-itself (*vastu*).

For if the nature of an entity were merely a matter of human intention, then even what is a cause would be rendered a non-cause, and even what is a non-cause would be rendered a cause; thus, the distinction between a true cause and a fallacious cause would not be based on reality.
Or rather, it sets aside the intention of men;
therefore, a means of proof accepted by another [is not valid],
for from an unexamined scripture there arises only a mere cognition, not a certainty regarding the object.
Furthermore, an object is not established by mere cognition alone;
for an existing object depends upon cognition, whereas a non-existent one cannot be established by cognition.
Even for that which exists, a connection with a real entity is a fitting course; [otherwise], it would be like a course unconnected to a real entity. 10.2 M. [The reading is: *vastvasaṃśliṣṭā*.
If it is argued that only an existent thing can be the means of establishing another, and not a non-existent thing—
lest there be causelessness— and therefore knowledge exists regarding the non-existent, and from that [knowledge] its establishment follows;
If that [object] does not exist, how can there be the cognition "this is its cognition"?
If it is argued that cognition alone is the direct means of proof, we say no.
Because it would follow that [the object] is directly perceived, there is therefore no establishment [of the object] from cognition when it is non-existent;
yet, there is indeed a way of understanding even from mere cognition, such as through an object that is in some manner superimposed.
The apprehension of a superimposition that possesses a real basis occurs solely by way of that basis; however,
if this apprehension were to occur even without a real entity as its inferential mark (*liṅga*), then it would be a mere semblance of apprehension.

Because it arises from a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), there is no valid cognition of fire in what is not smoke based on the perception of smoke. A contrary superimposition (*samāropa*) is not a means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*).
Moreover:
This has been established in the section on inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*): only these three types of evidence (*liṅga*) are the means of proving an object, and nothing else;
and therefore—

The logical mark (*liṅga*)—whether it be an essential nature (*svabhāva*), an effect (*kārya*), or simply the non-perception of the perceptible—is established by way of a real connection (*vastutaḥ*). How could that be unestablished for oneself?
If the essential nature of the probandum is established in reality because it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how could it be unestablished for the Sāṃkhya himself?
The establishment of valid cognition is common to both types of means of knowledge; therefore,
if there were no means of valid cognition, it would be improper for the opponent as well to proceed on the basis of anything else.

For just as the Sāṃkhya argues, "Since the reason such as impermanence is established for you, accept it from that," so too the opponent [argues] that this is well-known to you; and precisely because the reason is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as you have understanding [of it], so too does another discerning person.
Otherwise, the Sāṃkhya himself would not be acting with deliberation.
For it is not the perception of the conscious that "I alone am clever, but the other is not so";
therefore, the employment of a proof based merely on what another accepts is not appropriate among the learned.
How then was the establishment of the probandum intended by the former teachers and by you through proofs well-known to others?
That is incorrect, because [it is based on] things imagined by others.
In a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), because of the connection between two things, the negation of one serves to negate the other.
12.3 M. Prasaṅga—He.
That is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum);
however, from it there is no ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*),
for the ascertainment of the probandum does not arise from the mere acceptance by the opponent.
What, then, is the purpose [of this]? It is for the sake of establishing the absence of one thing when the other has occurred;
for indeed, the presence of the probans (sādhana) is not possible in the absence of the probandum (sādhya).
And this is a consequential argument (*prasaṅgasādhana*):

because a single entity that subsists in many [locations] lacks any other nature distinct from its connection with one particular individual—which is restricted by specific place, time, and state—there can be no conjunction of it with another thing possessing a different place and so forth;
likewise, due to non-difference, there would be coloring of all parts even when only one part is colored, and so on.
Because there is a contradiction for that which has such an intrinsic nature [to exist] in conjunction with different locations and so forth, time is excluded.
[Objection: But even a single entity, due to its pervasiveness, may be conjoined with multiple locations and so forth; if so, what is the contradiction?
No,
because it is impossible to perceive its connection with multiple times;
for indeed, the pervasion of prior and subsequent times is not apprehended through direct perception.
Since the state of being prior and posterior is an object of conceptual construction—
wherein that which has past vision is "prior time" and that which has future vision is "subsequent time"—
there is no other time apart from the objects perceived at those times.
Now, [an objection may be raised]: "In the absence of time, how can there be the conventional usage of 'prior' and 'subsequent'?
Likewise, even if time exists, in the absence of space, how can there be the conventional usage of 'prior' and 'subsequent'?"

If it is argued that [the designation] "connected with time" alone is not the object of the conventional usage of "prior" and so forth— because such a usage would then over-apply even to the present due to the distinction of time—
it is as follows:
That which is associated with prior time and so forth receives the designation "prior" and so on; its status as prior or posterior arises from its own nature alone, not from anything else.
(30) That which exists at a prior time is "prior," and likewise, that which exists at a subsequent time is "subsequent," and so forth.
If it is asked how time itself is "prior," [the answer is that] time possesses priority and so forth by its very nature,
just as space does.
This is untrue because:
"How can eternality and omnipresence possess priority and so forth? If it is argued that this is due to their co-occurrence, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence. (31)

For since the co-existent factors such as attachment and so forth are prior [to the cognition], it follows that even space and time—which are all-pervasive—are likewise [prior]; what contradiction is there?
Indeed, nothing is ever not designated by its co-existent;
as in the expression, "The galleries are shouting."
Likewise here too, the designation "that time has passed" [is used].

In this case, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) swiftly pursues you: for the priority of co-existent things arises from their association with a prior time, while the priority and so forth of time itself arises from its dissociation from co-existent things. (32)
If neither of the two is previously established, how can there be the existence of either one? If they exist simultaneously, there would be no state of being produced by one another.
As long as time itself has no priority and so forth, there can be no such thing for simultaneous co-existents; thus, that which you intend to prove remains unestablished.
Now, if it is argued that both possess a simultaneous lack of priority and so forth—

That being the case, since there is no perception of mutual operation between two things existing at the same time, they cannot be produced by one another; rather, that nature arises from its own cause. Thus, the state of being "prior" and so forth belongs to the entities themselves, and the conceptualization of "time" is therefore useless. For instance, an object that has passed away is called "prior."
That which is future is the subsequent; that which exists is the present. [Objection: But how can this even be so, given the non-existence of time?

Even regarding the existence of time, how [it could exist] has already been explained; thus there is no further answer. Since the effect is both existent and non-existent due to the presence and absence of its cause, why postulate an unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) for the establishment of priority and posteriority?
For the states of prior, posterior, and middle [sequence] exist by virtue of a dual arrangement;
that [arrangement] exists through the presence or absence of causes;
and that cause, too, possesses presence or absence only by virtue of its own cause. Thus, the postulation of an unseen [primal matter] is not logical.
If it is maintained that time— which is without beginning or end— is the cause for the determination of forms such as "long" and "short," that too is of little consequence,
because:

How can there be cognitions of "quick" and so forth from time, which is without beginning or end? If it is maintained that time is the object of cognitions such as "long" and "quick," [then consider this:

if these cognitions apprehend the very nature of time, then let that [time] alone be apprehended as being without beginning or end and as all-pervading, since it is impossible to apprehend such a thing in any other way, such as through "length" and so on.
Whatever form is actually apprehended, that alone is logically the nature of the object; the existence of a thing is not accepted in any manner other than that which is perceived. (35–36)
37–38. Since there is a mutual distinction between forms such as "long" and "quick," this [analysis] would also apply to time; how then can it be all-pervasive and one?
Because of the distinction in the persistence of the notion, "This object is long-lasting," the various distinctions such as "long" and "not long" follow the nature of time.
For indeed, "long," "quick," and so forth, are perceived through their conformity to the nature of time.

The pervasive establishment of time is not by way of entering into the form of individual objects; for instance, whatever is perceived as concomitant with something else is necessarily connected with it— just as a brindled cow, being perceived in the form of "cowness," is connected with it— so too is the case with time.
In that case,
[it is] by means of inference.

The universal called "temporality" (*kālatva*), which would follow upon the distinctions of "slow," "quick," and so forth that conform to the nature of time, is not established; for if "temporality" were a universal, time itself would not be established,
since time is accepted as a substance (*dravya*) among the categories of existence, whereas a universal is a distinct category.
Furthermore, time is not perceived as something distinct from forms such as "long" and so forth;

rather, the designation "time" is merely a name applied by someone for the sake of brevity to those very [forms]. Nor are these [notions] such as "long" separate from action, for [the expression] "it was done long ago" enters into the form of the action itself. (40)

For since "it lasts for a long time" (*ciraṃ karoti*) is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action, in reality, terms such as "long" (*cira*) and so forth follow the very form of the action.
(2) Refutation of Action:
