Nor is even action something distinct from the categories of object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*).
For instance,
in the expression "Devadatta acts," no "acting" (kāra) is perceived by means of valid cognition as something distinct from the agent, because they are perceived as one. Indeed,
in the case of the statement "the mat-maker makes a mat," no action is apprehended through perception as something separate from the specific agent who is the maker of the mat.
Because that [difference] is absent, action is non-existent even from the perspective of inference; for it is said:

"There is no difference other than that which is being differentiated, nor is there any other recourse in the face of contradiction; it is only cognitions that are differentiated due to the difference in beginningless latent predispositions. (42)
Opposing [the opponent's position],
according to T.

Indeed, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*)— having constructed a distinction [between agent and action] and having their obsession with the true nature of things weakened by a continuum (*saṃtāna*) supported by beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)— perceive a distinction even when there is no such distinction; therefore, this determination of a distinction between actions is merely a cognitive error (*viparyāsa*).

If the action were not non-different from Devadatta, then another [person] would likewise [be non-different]; yet, because of the connection with action in another case as well, it is conceptualized that "the action is different. This has already been established previously, and it is not the case that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are accessible through perception, since they are accessible only through mental cognition produced by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The first lesson (is completed).
Now, this so-called "action" (kriyā) is not a substantial entity; therefore, it is not perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Now, even if [the action] were indeed non-existent, let there be no connection with gender and so forth;
however, if it were distinct from the word-meaning, there would be a contradiction with its being perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, "slow," "quick," and so on, are merely specific actions that are conceptually constructed (*kalpita*), not real (*tāttvika*).
"How is it so? and so forth are meaningful;

for indeed, these [words] "how," "thus," and "so" would be distinct from the referents of the objects [they denote] only if they were conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that establish a distinction. (44)

If whatever conceptual construction arises were to have that very object as its form, such that that alone—the object of conceptualization—were the ultimate entity, then what would become of entities such as these? Where could they be subsumed?
For time and so forth are neither accepted as the basis for those [entities] nor are they perceived.

If that were the case, then those very specific actions would be [the basis for such designations], and thus terms like "long" and so forth would also be [mere names for actions]; consequently, the effort expended in postulating time and the like would be futile.
Therefore, because there is no apprehension of objects existing at prior or subsequent times through perception, the all-pervading [entity] is simply not apprehended by perception.
(3) This is the refutation of the universal (*sāmānya*).
Now, if it is thought that even when the pervasion in time is not apprehended, the apprehension of the pervasion in space is not contradictory—
[we reply] no;
because even in that case, the universal and so forth are not perceived apart from their substratum.

Because it is contradictory for that which has such a nature [to exist] through connection with different locations and so forth, it does not follow that when it has entered into one place, it exists elsewhere at that same time. Since there would be no distinction [between them], universal entry would result in a single mass;
for indeed, if it has not entered into its own substratum, there can be no entry into what has already entered therein.
Likewise,
when the cognition arises that "these two are identical," then a universal (sāmānya) that is both different and non-different [from its particulars] results.
To this it is replied:

If cognitions possess an identical form, how can there be an identity of objects? For when one thing possesses identity [with another], that other thing cannot be identical with it. (45) If the object were to possess an identical form, it ought to be perceived as distinct [from the cognition]. Since it is not seen among objects, how can it be postulated in relation to those objects? (46)
What is the meaning of this statement: "A cognition with a recurring form arises through the differentiation of objects"?
For a statement whose meaning has not been critically examined does not, merely by being understood in some way or another, establish the truth of its object;
and critical examination consists in a cognition of an identical form, because there are only two possible modes for a word and its object—
either identity of essential nature or identity of the form of the object— and no other mode is possible.

If there were identity of form with the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then that [object] would be the intrinsic nature itself, and not an object possessing a common form; thus, the universal (*sāmānya*) would be the object, and that [universal] would be merely the form of the cognition. That is indeed a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), not a universal, because it is absent in other cognitions and because it does not reside in the object.
Now, as for the claim that "the object-form itself is common [to both cognitions], and thus the cognition has that form," that too is untrue,
because it would entail the appearance of two distinct forms.
If it is argued that those two forms merely appear [as such],
we say no,
because:

In one's own view, the statement is not accepted here on account of partiality; for the meaning would be established for everyone through the cognition [of it], since the resonance (dhvani) functions everywhere.
Therefore, the notion that "the cognition has an identical form" is a delusion for those of steady intellect.
Therefore, it is not a universal (*sāmānya*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because the state of having an identical form by virtue of possessing a dewlap and so forth constitutes a universal characterized as non-different from those [individuals], and that this is joined with other individuals restricted by space and time—
this is incorrect.

For even the universal (ākṛti) does not possess unity, since it is not perceived as such by direct perception; if it were unitary, then upon the cognition of one [universal], there would be the apprehension of all individuals. Because the universal is unitary, it would follow that even when a single form is grasped, there would be the consequence of grasping all objects possessing that form.
Now, it may be argued that while the form (ākṛti) is indeed perceived, the perception of the possessor of the form (ākṛtimat) is impossible because of their difference;
for it is not possible to perceive what is distinct, yet [the former] is perceived as identical [to the latter].
This too is incorrect.
For identity [is established] through that nature, but it is not called "identity" [itself]. If there were identity through a mediated succession, then non-difference itself would result.
(49) That which has that nature is the identity of one form with another form;
since that other form possesses that nature, it is of that nature; thus, there is the apprehension of that which possesses a form of that nature.

And if that which possesses the form (*ākṛtimat*)—being non-different from it—is not apprehended, then even when another form is apprehended, there would be no apprehension of that [other] thing; for non-difference is not the basis for apprehension, since that which possesses the form is not apprehended. If indeed... [the form].
Now, if it were not a different configuration because of that difference,
then likewise, because there is no difference in the configuration, the possessor of the configuration would also not be different.
Nor indeed is it [the case] that it is not so.
By this, the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya is refuted; for it is not the case that because [a universal] is destroyed in one instance, it is destroyed everywhere,
since it is not perceived in other individual instances.
For an individual entity is not non-different from another individual simply because their form is non-different, just as it is with different forms; rather,
it remains distinct due to differences such as blackness and so forth.

If it were distinct from blackness and so forth, that [universal] would not exist as a different form; for how could there be differentiation through such a difference? If you say the difference arises through association with those [qualities], why would this [association] not also apply to the universal itself? (50)
If blackness and so forth are indeed distinct from that which possesses form, how can there be a distinction [in the latter] based on the distinction [in the former]?
For one thing being distinct does not cause another thing to be distinct;
if you argue that it does cause it to be distinct by way of being its cause—then [we reply]: [this is not so].
It is not so, because of the absence of causality;
for qualities alone are not the cause of a substance, since they arise with that same unity of fate (ekayogakṣema).
Or, if it is a cause, then from that [cause] another distinct [effect] arises; for that [second effect] as well, there must be another related differentiator.
Furthermore, the cause itself cannot be the related factor;
otherwise, even fire would become the related factor of smoke.

If it is argued that this is not so because [the relationship] is not observed, then since the causality of even those things that are conjoined is also not observed, their status as causes should not be postulated.

If there is difference in the case of non-difference, then the form (ākṛti) must also be different. For that which is non-different from the different is indeed different; otherwise, difference would not exist. (51)

Blackness and the like are non-different from that which possesses form; and since that which is non-different from what is different [from the possessor of form] is itself different, there follows the distinction of the possessor of form.
But then, because it is non-different from that, the consequence is that even the form would be different;
for the form also does not differ from the possessor of form.

And thus, [the universal] would be both different and non-different from that which possesses form (ākṛtimat) and from the form itself; for if the form were indeed non-different [from the individual], there could be no connection between the form— which has become subordinate— and a quality such as blackness.
It is not correct [to say] that because qualities do not inhere in one another, their inherence must reside in the possessor of qualities; such is the established doctrine.

It is appropriate to speak of this [distinction] when there is difference, but not when there is non-difference due to lack of division; for the notion "this is here" and "this is not that" arises only where there is difference.

(52) In that case, let there be difference; let this be a child’s plaything, since you have abandoned the position of difference and resorted to another position. (53) Even in that case, upon seeing the same fault again, one must resort back to the previous [position]. (54ab)

Therefore, neither the universal nor even the configuration (*ākṛti*) constitutes the definition [of a substance]; by this, the definition of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is also refuted, because if it were a continuous entity, one would perceive all its states, leading to the absurd consequence that everyone would be omniscient.
Because those things existing in that state are not a different reality from the primary form;
or else, in some cases, the delusion is that in ultimate reality everything indeed appears, but due to error it does not appear.

That too is untenable, because is there a non-appearance of everything, or is it an error even when there is appearance? There is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this at all; it is merely a conceptual construction (kalpanā).
The existence of all things in the cause in the form of potentiality—that is the Pradhāna, the source of the emergence of all worlds.

(55) If that very [Pradhāna] exists as a pervasive universal by virtue of its eternity, then how can there be manifestation after manifestation, characterized by mutual distinctions? (56) This is contradictory here.
That which is said to be the very great form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision; but that which has reached the path of vision is as utterly void as an illusion.
For: [Verse 57] Since:

If it is argued that because that which is postulated by way of its effect is insubstantial, the cause must also be insubstantial—since the nature of the cause is necessarily of the same form as that [effect]—then this is not so;

for otherwise, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would now be abandoned. Furthermore, whatever entity is not perceived is precisely what is non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*).
Therefore, even that which is characterized as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is not a universal (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, it might be argued that although a universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived as pervading individuals separated by differences in time—
since perception does not function with respect to temporal priority and posteriority— it is indeed perceived as pervading individuals located in different places at the same time.
That too is incorrect,

because when there is no apprehension of the pervasion by individual instances existing at different times, there is no utility for a universal; for practical activity does not proceed in that manner.

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice a white goat," because there is a continuity of the genus (*jāti*)— such that one recognizes "this is that very same [kind of animal]"— those who desire its practical application accept a universal (*sāmānya*) as the object of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, for two things perceived simultaneously, there is no utility for such a designation, since both are already cognized as belonging to that same genus by following from what was previously seen.
Furthermore, even in the case of the preceding and succeeding moments, no universal distinct from the clear and non-clear forms of the prior and subsequent individuals is perceived;
likewise, even for two [individuals] existing at the same time, [no universal is seen] apart from the two clear forms.
How then does the cognition "these two are similar" arise?
This condition is the same for both that which occurs in the preceding and succeeding times;
for in that case, no identical form has been observed by direct perception.
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "the sense organ does not perceive even simultaneous individual instances of a universal.
A distinct commonality (*sāmānyākāratā*) is not perceived among simultaneous instances, as it is in the case of preceding and succeeding individuals.
This cognition is merely a cognition, because that which is being cognized is not perceived;
for a cognition does not cognize anything if it is devoid of the form of that which is being cognized. That cognition, possessing a corresponding form, arises without an external object.
Because it does not appear as that which is to be grasped, like the preceding and succeeding particulars;
whatever cognition has a uniform appearance is entirely without an external object.
In this regard, because there is no appearance of an apprehended object (*grāhya*), [the argument is as follows]:

just as a cognition intended to have as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) existing in distinct individuals at different times lacks the appearance of a universal form, so too a cognition—even one whose object is a universal existing in individuals at the same time—lacks such an appearance; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Moreover, since everything is distinct in its characteristics, how could every causal condition arise without similarity?
That too is merely some triviality.
If this cognition occurs only in certain instances, then restriction [to those instances] would require a cause; but how could there be such a movement toward a universal?
Since a restriction cannot be without a cause, it is only the cause that deserves to be postulated;
what, then, has been gained for the universal?
Alternatively, let the universal be merely the exclusion of others; there is no harm in this, and it has already been established that it is formless.
Moreover:

That projected form which is fit for mere conceptual construction arises from the awakening of the seeds of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Is it not sufficient that it consists of just that much? Why should there be no other, separate category [of existence]? (63)

Since even a genus (*jāti*) that has not investigated its true nature suffices for mere conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*), why is any further effort exerted toward something else? Furthermore, in this case:

If it is argued that the universal (*jāti*) is ultimately real for the sake of establishing dharma and adharma, by what means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) could its status as a means to dharma be measured?
For the fact that the universal is a means to dharma and so forth is not perceived through its own nature alone—even if it were established—because it is not distinguished from other universals;
nor is it useful for the production of an effect while remaining unestablished. Thus, the apprehension of a universal is entirely futile.

Alternatively, even regarding cognition, it is precisely those individuals characterized by such specific cognitions that possess the capacity to accomplish dharma and so forth; thus, that itself is the universal (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, if the universal were not eternal and all-pervading, then the cognition of a uniform form would likewise not be pervasive.

Therefore, it is understood that there is no cause whatsoever for that cognition; rather, the conceptualization of an object of cognition arises from the existence of the form of the object of cognition itself.
Furthermore, there is no experience of an object of cognition possessing an identical form [to the cognition].
And thus it has been established previously:

therefore, because it is not experienced through direct perception—even though its form is visible—it is indeed non-existent as a universal (*sāmānya*), since it is not experienced as something common to others. Thus, [it is concluded that] there is no universal.

"But surely, since a universal resides in a single individual, there is no substratum (dharmin); thus, because the substratum is unestablished for you, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā).

This is not correct, for this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), so there is no unestablished locus from that [perspective]. If it were otherwise, then even this [argument] would not hold, because both [the subject and the predicate] are accepted [by us]. (66)
If it were thus restricted to a single individual, then there would be no connection with another [individual] possessing a different location, nor could both [properties] coexist.

Now, if there were a connection with another, it would not be restricted to a single individual; this is not a case of proving what is already established, for its presence is not in one individual alone, since it pervades all individuals.
It is not maintained that the universal resides in only a single individual;
this is not a fault, for if it were common [to many], its cognition as being pervasive would remain unimpaired. Indeed, that form cannot be apprehended by another form without error. (67)
If a universal were pervasive, it would certainly be apprehended by perception as being pervasive; for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed not one that apprehends its object erroneously.
Moreover, if pervasiveness were perceived, there would necessarily be the perception of all individual instances.
Since pervasiveness is not perceived when the pervaded is apprehended,
and it is not perceived [otherwise] either, it does not exist in that form;
therefore, the universal itself does not exist, which constitutes the negation of both properties.

If this were a case of a neutral position (*sthitapakṣa*), there would be the fault of the unestablished locus (*dharmyasiddhi*); however, this [text] is merely intended to reveal mutual contradiction,
for we are not capable of accepting such a matter, as no other instance of such a kind is observed.
Furthermore, inference does not function without an example;

however, when a universal is cognized through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), it is indeed distinct from all other categories of entities, and thus no contradiction should be raised against it on the grounds of its opposition to other properties.
For it is not logical that the property of one thing should belong to another;
indeed, the properties of material objects cannot be applied to an immaterial universal.
This is not so.

Since others do not accept pervasiveness even for those final particulars (antyaviśeṣa) which are formless, let it be understood that the same lack of pervasiveness applies to the universal (sāmānya) as well. Indeed,
even those final particulars that are associated with formlessness have restricted locations and are not pervasive.
Likewise, even a universal (sāmānya) cannot transcend the state of being non-material and all-pervasive; if,
on the other hand, it is non-pervasive despite being non-material, then this distinction is certainly not caused by the nature of being material or its opposite.

If it is argued: "In that case, let the very relationship of generality and particularity be the basis for pervasiveness and its opposite; what is the fault? [We reply: Is it not the case that this is simply unestablished?
For is it not true that the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed established by you as well, since you have taken it as the subject (*dharmin*)?
This is not so, because:
"If its pervasiveness is not perceived, how can the perception of the universal be asserted? If it is perceived in its own form, then how can there be similarity [to particulars]? (69)
"The seizing is performed"— this is the completion of the sentence.
For when a universal (*sāmānya*) is apprehended in its own nature, it must be apprehended either as pervasive or otherwise;

if it were apprehended as pervasive, perception would not have such a limited scope, since its operation would extend to a universal that pervades all individual instances (*vyakti*). Now, if the individual instances are not apprehended...
If that is the case, then how can a universal, when perceived as associated with a single individual, be grasped as being all-pervasive?
If it is a qualifier of one individual, then, like that individual, it would be a particular and not a universal.
Alternatively, if by another way of speaking, its status as a qualifier of other individuals is also grasped—
That being the case, how can there be the cognition that "this is that very same universal"?
It has already been examined that the recognition "this is that very same" is not perceptual;
therefore, since its nature as a universal is unestablished, how can it serve as a proof for pervasiveness?
Therefore,

because it is formless, the proof of its omnipresence cannot be established through a universal [as a logical reason]; nor is it perceived by us anywhere through direct perception, and thus it is devoid of a universal.

If the universal (*sāmānya*) is unestablished, how can you prove its pervasion over the objects of the universal by taking the universal itself as the subject (*dharmin*)? Since no property (*dharma*) can be established therein otherwise than through such a subject,
this [argument] is not valid.
For it has been stated that this is a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana).
But this is not the primary reason:
if you accept that a universal is pervaded, it must be apprehended by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because the acceptance [of such a thing] is based upon a means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth.

Furthermore, how is it reasonable to accept that [the universal] is all-pervasive when it is perceived as being devoid of any other nature, being delimited by a specific place and time and connected to a single individual?

Moreover, since perception grasps multiple objects, it is not reasonable to accept something that is not perceived—whether that [universal] is perceived as distinct from those [individuals] or otherwise.
If it is argued that the *ākṛti* (form/structure) itself is the perceived universal, [we reply:]...
No,
because the generic form lacks pervasiveness;
for if it were perceived as pervasive, there would have to be the perception of all individual instances.

And thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the universal form (*ākṛti*) would be perceived as distinct in every individual instance across different places and times. Furthermore, if the universal were restricted to a single individual, then even the objection regarding the "unestablished locus" (*dharmyasiddhi*) in the proof of its non-pervasive nature is already avoided.
How then is this a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum)?
Since one person accepts that the universal is merely the form (*ākṛti*), while another accepts something else, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*prasanga-sādhanatā*).
(2) [This is refuted] by means of perception and its concomitants.
Alternatively, the meaning of the reductio (*prasaṅga*) is that, because [the universal] is all-pervasive, its perception would not be restricted to a single individual;
the reversal of this [leads to] the original reason (*maula-hetu*),
while the reductio itself serves solely to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for that original reason.
Others, however, maintain that "because of separation" is the original reason (*maula-hetu*);
this presentation is made in such a way to show that the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), while being led toward that [conclusion], actually culminates in the original reason itself.
And the reason "because of separation" is of the nature of a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha),
and that is indeed established even in the absence of a universal.
For when the reason is a non-entity, a subject (*dharmin*) in the form of a real thing is not admitted;
and because that [subject] is absent, even the statement "it is not" is understood as referring to it, and thus that [non-entity] is simply non-existent.

If the universal were the subject (*dharmin*), then the proof of its non-pervasion [would fail]; for when the reason (*hetu*) is a mere absence, what could be established by what, and where? If the reason consists in a mere absence of connection, then since that [absence] has no relation to anything else, how could there be a proof of the probandum (*sādhya*)? If, on the other hand, it is the absence of connection with another individual, even then it must be determined *whose* this absence is.
Therefore, there must necessarily be a universal, expressed by another and present in the intellect;

yet a reason is not capable of proving the probandum without the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Now, if the universal characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is established for the Buddhists, then that is precisely what is desired by the opponent.

Because that which is accepted by the opponent is also intended to be refuted by him; moreover, a universal characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is indeed admitted to be all-pervasive,
for instance:
Even by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is indeed a commonality;
however, a real entity (*vastu*) does not persist [as a universal], because that would entail the consequence of [the object] being engaged in activity and so forth.
Now, even though a universal does not exist, its cause—characterized by its absence—is certainly present.
That too is incorrect, because that which does not exist cannot function as a cause; if it is argued that there is indeed a connection when the probandum (sādhya) is non-existent, [we reply: no.
When there is no necessary connection, the absence of one thing cannot lead to the cognition of the absence of another; and such a connection is grasped through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Therefore, by the force of that [invariable concomitance], one merely demonstrates the absence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)— that where the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent, there is an absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—

but this is not the primary reason (*maula-hetu*). Now, even the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakatānupalabdhi*) is employed to establish the absence of an object restricted to a specific thing.
That being the case, according to the maxim "there is no *śiṃśapā* here," there must be another locus (*dharmin*) established by valid cognition; however,
if it is argued that even here a locus common to both existence and non-existence is adopted,
that too is incorrect.

If it is argued that, since there is no other entity common to both existence and non-existence, the appearance of conceptual construction itself possesses both properties and is thus the common factor,
then in that case:
When that non-apprehension of it is to be established as the non-appropriation of entities,
to claim that this is a completely different reason is merely trivial.
Therefore, there is no fundamental reason here [for the objection], because the subject (*dharmin*) as a universal is not established;
for in the position that "form and so forth are themselves the universal," this is not a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*).
Because their non-pervasiveness is perceived through direct perception,
the reason must be established for both parties, and not for the opponent alone;
this is the purpose of including the term "object" (artha).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that whatever is established for both parties is already an *artha* (object/meaning); for what purpose, then, is the term *artha* included?
This is not so, because:

Just as [the property of being] one or both is established merely through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), for these conceptual constructions are not without names, and their occurrence is restricted by association. Therefore, even though [the property] is established for both [proponent and opponent], properties such as "being either the subject or the similar instance" (*pakṣasapakṣānyataratva*) lack objective reality (*arthatva*) and are thus not valid reasons (*ahetu*); for that reason, the term "object" (*artha*) is included [in the definition of a reason] to exclude those whose nature is superimposed by verbal conceptualization.

The inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*)— which qualifies the phrase "perceived by oneself"— is for the purpose of establishing that [the reason] is not a mere mark (*aliṅga*), because the object itself is established through its own meaning; it serves to demonstrate that things whose nature is constructed merely from conceptual verbalization (*śabdakalpanāmātra*) lack probative force,
since only the actual object can function as a means of cognition.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a logical reason (hetu) characterized by being unestablished (asiddha), contradictory (viruddha), or inconclusive (anaikāntika) is precisely what fails to establish the intended object?

If this [reason] possesses the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), how can it be a non-reason? Or, if there is an absence of the three characteristics, then its exclusion follows from the very definition of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*); what, then, is the purpose of including the word "for others" (*para*)?
For inference for others is indeed the communication of the three-characterized mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).

Even in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the definition of a logical reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) necessarily results in being a three-fold character (*trairūpya*) superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); how then can there be an exclusion [of such reasons] from it?
In that case, the term "real" (*artha*) should not be included here at all.
This does not occur because the necessity of performing [the proof] is established only in the case of inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).
How is there a turning away from that? In that case, then, the mention of "that" (tad) should not be made here.
To this it is replied:
There is no fault here because of the statement, "As with one's own certainty, so it is for others," [meaning] what is done here will come to pass there.
If it is asked, "Why not do it right there?", the reply is: "Let it be done right there or here; what contradiction is there?"
And there is a purpose in this, as follows:

It has been established that for one who speaks improperly, even the statement of another is accepted as a means of proof (*sādhana*), just like one's own certainty (*svaniścaya*). This is because [the opponent] does not find even the statement "even the statement is a means of proof" in other versions of the text; furthermore, the fourteenth verse is missing from the middle.
No one should postulate a cause for their own sake that is fabricated through mere imagination; would anyone contradict their very own self regarding what they desire?

Furthermore, since the supreme effort must be directed toward the welfare of others alone, it is precisely here that a great effort must be exerted by the noble-minded; this is the meaning of the inclusion of the word "for oneself" (*svārthe*) here.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, however, a reason that is superimposed by conceptual construction is necessarily inconclusive;
for it follows the mere whim of the author of that construction or scripture.
Because the thing itself undergoes change, those [reasons] produced by it are fallacious.
"Kalpitā" is also a reading found in that very same place.
Indeed, there can be no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the object to be proven for that which is superimposed by conceptual construction,
because it proceeds solely from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
if this is so, then it is not a logical reason (*hetu*) precisely because of this lack of connection.
For this very reason, there is no implication of the necessary connection (pratibandha),
since there is no direct demonstration of that connection.
Therefore, there is no apprehension of an object [by such a reason],

for being either a dissimilar instance (pakṣa) or a similar instance (sapakṣa) is not restricted to one side in the case of the eternal and the non-eternal; since whatever is made the subject (pakṣa) shifts accordingly depending on that specific context,
and such an establishment of a real entity does not occur because, when the intention is different, another [reason] is employed as the proof.
2. Examination of the Thesis (pakṣacintā) 1.
The Statement of the Reason and the Thesis is Not a Means of Proof (1) The statement of the reason is not a means of proof.

But surely, the subject (*pakṣa*) is precisely that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), since anything other than it is a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); therefore, the property called "being either the subject or a similar instance" is excluded from its opposite (the dissimilar instance). Consequently, why is this not a valid reason (*hetu*)?

For a property restricted to the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) cannot deviate from the probandum; this is because there is no restriction whatsoever regarding the existence of the subject or the similar instances. The subject is not merely "eternality," since that [property] could also belong to something else. (76)

If this meaning is that [the probandum is established] because it is either the subject or a similar instance (*pakṣasapakṣānyataratvāt*), or because it possesses a property that is invariably concomitant with the generality of the impermanence of sound and jars, then that property is precisely characterized by being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth.
Because the non-deviating similarity is expressed by the word "either" (*anyatara*),

it is not the case that the non-deviating property— characterized as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth— is itself [the reason]; and this being so, that reason is indeed the actual object, not a conceptual construction.
Now, because it is intended to be expressed as being other than that which has been made the subject (pakṣīkṛta),
and because it is non-deviant (avyabhicārī).
That is incorrect;
for even if there is an intention to designate [the subject] as the thesis by way of its impermanence, impermanence is nonetheless not established by that alone,
because if it were intended [as the subject] by way of permanence, that [intention] would have vanished at that very moment.
If being a subject were established by way of actual impermanence, then what is already established would be proven;
therefore, an imagined property is not the means of proof,
and that [property] which is established for oneself is the means of proof.
The logical mark (liṅga) possesses exactly three forms; therefore, the communication of the three-formed logical mark is inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna).

Consequently, it is established that those who maintain that even the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana) is a means of proof (sādhana) are speaking incorrectly, because such a statement is unestablished (asiddha).
For it is the means of proof (*sādhana*) that establishes the object to be proven (*sādhya*), not the object to be proven itself;
if you argue that the statement [of the reason] is the means of proof, [we reply: no.
Because a verbal statement is not a direct means of proof,
as it lacks an invariable connection with the probandum.
There is no necessary connection between the word and its object;
therefore,
since the understanding of the object arises from the object itself, the statements of the thesis and the reason have no [inherent] power [to establish it].
Therefore, for those two, there is no establishment of proof by way of their own nature.
[Verse 15] "Sound is impermanent because it is produced"— it is the three-featured state of being produced itself that makes impermanence known,
because it does not deviate from that [impermanence].

Neither the statement of the thesis nor the statement of the reason would otherwise bring about the establishment of the probandum; for even here, there is both the statement of the reason and the statement of the thesis, namely: "Sound is eternal because it is knowable."
If it is argued that [the word] is not a reason because its object is not invariably connected to that [object],
then it follows that the cognition of the object arises from the object itself due to its invariable connection, and that the word is not a direct means of proof.
Since speech exists even in the absence of its object,
and since the statement of a reason is not a means of proof in those cases where it is not, the fact that the statement of the thesis is not a means of proof is established without even being stated.

Now, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not the means of proof (*sādhana*), because it merely communicates the object to be proven; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the reason (*hetu*) being redundant.
Now, if it is argued that a mere thesis is not a proof and therefore a reason (*hetu*) is employed, [we ask]: how is that which is not a proof a proof when conjoined with a proof?
If you say it is a proof because it is conjoined with a proof...
How could that which is useless constitute literature?
No one desires literature that is useless;
therefore, mere speech is not a means [to the goal].
Furthermore,
(2) the statement of the thesis is not a means of proof;
that statement of the thesis serves only to communicate the speaker's intention.
It is not a means of valid cognition because it gives rise to doubt; therefore, it is not a direct proof.
For that which is a cause of doubt is not itself the [valid] cause in this context, since its status as a cause of doubt arises from its lack of connection with the actual object.
Otherwise, the statement of the reason would be purposeless;
for just as the statement does not establish the probandum,
so too the meaning of the proof itself should not be understood [as establishing it], because even in that case there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them.

Or, if there were a necessary connection (pratibandha) even with respect to the probandum (sādhya), what would be the nature of that connection? [In that case,] the very [use of the word] "connection" would be meaningless.
This is true;

even for the sake of establishing [a point], speech does not actually bring about proof, because it serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only in communicating the speaker's intention; therefore, it is not a direct proof.

If it is argued that just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is implied by the statement regarding the proof (*sādhana*), so too should the means of valid cognition be implied regarding the probandum (*sādhya*),
we say no.
At that very moment, because a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists there,
the previously occurred [cognition] is indeed implied by the means of valid cognition.
The reading contained within the manuscript is not established by the statement in another language, because there is the possibility of forgetfulness in that regard;
however, in the present case, perception alone is the authority, but what is the use of a statement in this matter?
For when an object is directly perceived, the instruction of another is not more authoritative;
since a verbal statement is not a means [of proof] in itself,
the statement of the thesis is therefore a means [of proof] only indirectly, just like the statement of the actual means of proof.

This too is incorrect; for even though the statement of the reason is itself incapable, it indicates—either directly or through a succession of steps—the very thing that is to be proven, which is what was intended. (17)

Just as the statement of the proof (*sādhana*) is a proof, so too would the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) be [a proof] if it were indicative of that which is capable; however, how can the indication of what is unestablished (*asiddha*), even if established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), be a proof?
For that which is itself powerless does not become powerful by relying on another that is also powerless;
for instance:

Nothing that is falling can ever become stable by relying on something else that is falling; likewise, that which is unestablished cannot be established by that very same thing which is unestablished.

(77) Since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated as being unestablished, how could the statement of the thesis be a means of proof? However, the statement of the reason (*hetu*), although itself incapable, is a means of proof because it expresses that which is capable. Thus, [the statement of the reason] is called the "proof."
Because it expresses a means of proof that is connected to the object to be proven, speech is called a "means of proof" (*sādhana*); however, it is not a means of proof in its own right.

Therefore, what was stated—that [inference] for others (*parārthānumāna*) is also inference—is contradictory; for, from the perspective of the person being instructed, it is indeed inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
However, from the perspective of the proponent, that [objection] has been refuted because it is merely a restatement.
That [inference] is called "inference" only by way of metaphorical designation because it is the cause of inference,
not in its own right;
therefore, to claim that it is "for one's own sake" (svārtha) in relation to the opponent is merely a trivial argument.
For it is only the logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics that establishes its own object because it makes it known;
the verbal expression does not, because the object is not understood from it.
If it is argued that [the passage] is indeed an injunction because even its mere recollection is beneficial,
we say no;
for it is established as such by means of a statement that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Therefore, with respect to both [the speaker and the listener], the statement is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*);

its status as being "for the sake of another" (*parārthatā*) is from the perspective of the one who is to be informed, not from the perspective of the informer, for it provides no benefit to the latter.
However, by virtue of being the cause of inference, that [statement] is an inference only from the perspective of the one to whom it is communicated.
But surely it follows that [inference] is for the sake of another (parārtha) in view of its object, while [perception] is [for one's own sake] in view of something else;
how then can this be? Indeed, it is simply a quality that is superimposed as a defect.

For that very reason by which it is not an inference for that proponent, nor for the person being addressed, it is "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*) for the proponent; otherwise, it would also be "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*), since he himself also effects its purpose through it.
Furthermore, the purpose for the metaphorical designation has been stated.
Since there is no way for a statement to establish its object other than through this [process],
is it not the case that even in the instance of recollection, the statement is either a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not?
If it is a means of valid cognition, why would it not [apply] to the object?
If it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be recollection from it?
For this very reason, otherwise, it would be a means of valid cognition itself and not recollection.

Furthermore, that which produces recollection is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*); thus, its nature is that of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, how could it [be an indicator] with respect to an object?
Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) [between it and the object].
For if the smoke is indeed connected to fire, it produces a recollection;
likewise, if the word were also [inherently] connected, it would produce such a recollection,
and thus there would be an absence of its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For instance, whatever is a recollection exists by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); just as there is a recollection of the invisible dark essence from smoke.
[The opponent’s claim that it is] "not connected" is incorrect.
Memory is not merely [a matter of] being connected; rather, there will be both a connection and memory because of the absence of a connection— so what contradiction is there between these two?

For instance, why does recollection not arise even from mere attention toward an object already seen? Or rather, it generally arises from some object that is concomitant [with it]. (80) Now, if recollection is of a determinate nature, it must arise only from what is related, and not from anything else.
That is not correct;

for in the absence of an obstruction, there is no certainty regarding that [object], but rather it is a memory of a form ascertained from the word—thus [the reason] is unestablished (asiddha). Therefore, the relation is not established. To explain:
For one who does not consider the relationship [between word and object], doubt alone arises;
and indeed, it is observed that doubt is produced from words.
How, then, can there be certainty?
It is indeed so,
as this [person] says;
for that is determined not from the means of valid cognition alone.
Since certainty arises precisely from the investigation of previously established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not from mere verbal assertion,
certainty regarding the *pramāṇa* itself likewise arises [from that] and not from verbal assertion.

Nevertheless, it is said here that even a mere statement is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this matter, we certainly accept that [validity] is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in this regard; for even though this point is well-established, there is no harm whatsoever to our position. (81)
Therefore, with respect to the object of valid cognition, speech is not a means of valid cognition regarding that object.

Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, nothing at all is diminished by the statement "it is a means of valid cognition," nor is the means of valid cognition established merely by such a statement, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); in that regard, there is only recollection,
while the ascertainment arises precisely from self-awareness.

Does it not happen even from mere attention (*ābhoga*), as is seen in the case of recollection? If you argue that when [recollection] does not arise from attention, then the verbal testimony is authoritative (*pramāṇa*).
This is not so,
because:

Even a false recollection regarding an object is seen to arise from speech even without [prior] speech; no distinction in the speech itself is observed by way of its being true or false. (82) In that case, the perception of the object would be an inference, and it would thus be only for one's own sake (*svārtha*). Even from mental attention (*ābhoga*), false modes of recollection arise. (83)

Therefore, the determination of the nature of the previous means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs only through the thorough investigation of some inferential mark (*liṅga*); thus, verbal testimony (*vacana*) is not itself a means of valid cognition. Rather, it is inference alone that is the means of valid cognition regarding an object beyond the senses, and it is by means of that [inference] that verbal testimony [functions].

Objection: Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehended the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has now passed away, how can there be a determination of that connection? [Response:
It is indeed a memory; yet it is not [invalid], for it is a valid cognition precisely because it was produced by that [original] means of valid cognition.

And therefore, why is it not accepted that memory, having arisen from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is itself a valid cognition by way of metaphorical designation? However, that which arises from what is not a means of valid cognition is held to be non-valid.
[Objection: But surely this memory arises from a means of valid cognition; thus, in this case as well, memory alone is the basis.
Furthermore, since that recollection also attains its purity through another recollection, how can a firm certainty arise?
If this [first] recollection is firm, why is its firmness not considered false? If it is not false because the object is obtained, then that is merely the presentation of what is already established.
To this, it is replied: [Verse 85] Regarding this, it is said:
This has already been stated at the outset:
the cognition of the essential nature [of a means of knowledge] occurs intrinsically, while its validity is established through practical application.
(Pravā.
1.4) Furthermore, it is observed that practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is characterized solely by the attainment of the object, and no other [activity] is useful.

Now, if it is argued: "Surely, some memory is firm by itself; therefore, the ascertainment that 'this is a means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) arises from that [memory], and not from practical activity."
That is incorrect, because that firmness exists only through repeated practice based on attainment; firmness never arises in one place from what has been practiced elsewhere. (86)
If this conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), characterized by the attainment of an object, were not habituated, how could there be firmness regarding that which is useful for attainment?
For it would mean that what is practiced is one thing, while firmness occurs in another; thus, there would be a total cessation of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*).
Therefore, since this much is the course of those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇa*) remains unshaken, and thus there is no fault.
Therefore, it is established that speech is inference because it is a cause of inference. But is it not the case that the Teacher himself accepts the statement of the thesis,
as he says:

With the desire to produce in others a certainty that is like one's own certainty, there is the exclusion of anything else [than the three characteristics] through the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the connection (*sambandha*), and the probandum (*sādhya*).
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 3.87)
May it be [accomplished] by the mother herself.
॰vyatām.
This is not so,
because it has been stated that the expression of its incapacity is due to its having the meaning of the reason as its object.
As it was said: "But for us..."

In that context, the statement of the object of inference (*anumeya-nirdeśa*) is considered to have the logical reason (*hetu*) as its object; however, for us, that statement of the object of inference is [considered] by virtue of having the logical reason as its object, and not as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
Therefore, because its status as a direct means of proof is rejected, it is stated that the statement of that probandum (*sādhya*) lacks the capacity [to prove it].

How then is there the acceptance of the three requirements—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the statement of the connection (*sambandha*), and the statement of the probandum (*sādhyokti*)?
It does not mean that these are [three separate things]: "the property of the subject," "the connection," and "the statement of the probandum."

Rather, the statement of the probandum (sādhyokti) that is connected with the statement of the relation is the "statement of the probandum together with its relation" (*sambandhasādhyokti*), such as "whatever is produced is impermanent. This statement of the probandum is included within the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and does not take the form of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
For it is necessary that the pervasiveness of the probandum over the probans be demonstrated.
Therefore, only two members [of the syllogism] need to be shown;
for by the very connection [of the reason], the two forms [of the property in the subject and the similar instance] are implied, and thus the reason possesses its three-fold character.
Consequently, it is not necessary to show [the example] at the beginning or at the end, as in the case of "therefore sound is impermanent."
Since the probandum is established from the mere two aspects of the form itself, the statement [of the reason] is incapable; [it lacks] the property [of being present in the similar class].
If that [reason] also possesses power because it prompts the statement of a reason, then for one who desires to know due to that doubt, there would be a reliance on further arguments;
and since this would be the case even when a counter-position is accepted, there would be an infinite regress. (18–19)
(3) Faults in the definition stated by the Nyāya school.
(a) The non-statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*):
Now, it might be argued that...

If, in the absence of the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*)— being like the fall of a blind man’s staff— is considered irrelevant and does not proceed,

then because the statement of the reason does proceed [only when the thesis is stated], that [thesis] would also necessarily be a means of proof (*sādhana*). Consequently, since doubt, desire to know, the context, and the wish for comprehension would also attain the status of being means of proof, the sentence would come to have ten members.
This is what is doubted by you here;
this alone is what you wish to know; this alone has been introduced by you.
"This has been understood by me;
here, this is my desire"—
thus, arranging the beauty of the beard, one should employ a sentence consisting of ten components.

Likewise, if the proof (*sādhana*) operates even when the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is present, it follows that the counter-example would also possess the status of a proof; for [the proof] exists together with that counter-example.

Now, if it is argued that the mere ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhyaniścaya*) occurs even without the presentation of doubt and so forth, then no purpose regarding the object is served by those [elements] which are merely useful for verbal elaboration (*śabdaprapañca*); therefore, doubt and the rest should be abandoned.
Since restating that [the reason] would be of no consequence,
if this were so, even the statement of the thesis would be a mere restatement for the proponent; it would not possess any internal necessity.
O you who possess the splendor of the full moon!
May you both be well.
Because it is not subject to dispute,
the capacity [of the means] resides within the three forms [of the syllogism].
In that regard, the stabilization of mindfulness is established precisely upon those words.
First of all, in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), that object to be proven (*sādhya*) is understood from the very [reason] possessing the three characteristics;
for in inference for oneself, the object to be proven does not appear first, since the reason must be one that has already been ascertained.
If it is argued that, just as in one's own inference, there is first no mention of the probandum (sādhya) and only later the mention of its form,
then even later there is no such mention, just as in the case of inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).
It appears to another as well.
When a cognition arises from [the reason] possessing the three characteristics, what difference is there between that [cognition] and inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)?
Therefore, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) should certainly not be uttered, nor should the application (*upanaya*) be stated.
Because it is intent upon demonstrating the observed capacity,
and its capacity there is nothing other than mere existence;
and that mere existence is already understood in the case of sound simply from its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, it might be argued that scripture is the thesis and inference is the reason.
Perception is the example;
application is the analogy;
and the conclusion is intended to demonstrate the scope of the operation of all means of valid cognition.
This is incorrect;

for if it is established through inference, what is the use of other means of valid cognition here? And if it is not established through inference, what is the use of other means of valid cognition here? (88)
The second daily lesson is concluded.

If this object is understood solely through the power of the logical reason (*hetu*), what is the use of the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? What can we do in this matter? Indeed, the entire collection of causal factors (*kārakagrāma*) is not dependent upon the logical reason alone for its operation.
If you were to be subject to such an inquiry as "How does this come to be so?",
it would indeed be true that it is so;
however, a mere thesis (*pratijñā*) is certainly not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it has been established that doubt arises from it.
(kha) Refutation of *upamāna* (analogy):
Analogy is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, without analogy—in the form "and this is likewise"—there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the reason (*hetu*).

This is not so, because it is precisely the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) that is demonstrated by means of analogy; and thus, "sound is produced" is shown in this manner. (89)

For if the connection were grasped only in a general sense, how could there be the establishment of [the reason] as residing in a particular locus, such as impermanence? It is precisely because the state of being produced and so forth is established as residing in a particular locus that this very state constitutes its residence in a particular locus.

If it is argued that, by establishing [the object] through analogy as "it is thus," and by demonstrating its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharman*) as "from where does this [come]," another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely analogy (*upamāna*), would result— [we reply:
no.

Since it is included within inference, the establishment of the specific relation— “this is a *gavaya* because of its similarity to a cow”— is not something other than the domain of verbal testimony; thus, inference alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that case,
and no separate inference is accepted even by those who advocate for comparison (*upamāna*).
If it is argued that similarity is its object by virtue of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), we say no; for there exists no similarity apart from the two instances of being produced.
There is no similarity to the state of being a punisher apart from the two [entities] that possess the staff;
if there is no such similarity here, how can there be a cognition of exclusion? It would follow that one must postulate another cause for the notion "this is similar.
That is incorrect.
If the cause is postulated from the effect on the basis of a perceived connection, then by that same logic, the perception of the cause itself would have been attained.
Furthermore, if there is similarity here, why does it not appear? If you say it is because of subtlety, then how can reality be postulated when it has not been seen?

Even in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is nothing that appears apart from the nature of the entity itself; yet, the determination of that which is distinct from its own appearance is a great marvel! (93) Resemblance (*sādṛśya*), which consists of superimpositions by imagination and is accompanied by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), does not exist as a reality upon examination; thus, "that is this" (*tattvam asi*) cannot be established on that basis. (94) Furthermore, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is accomplished through the connection with real entities (*vastu*); for how could causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and purposeful objects be observed to arise from mere resemblance? (95)
If it is argued that there is a further internal distinction, why is nothing [such] observed even in that case? 2 B. ॰viṣayaḥ.
Moreover, that [object] is certainly not something other than the object of inference;
for the attainment of purposeful action does not arise from what is merely considered similar, such that similarity could be the cause of that purposeful action,
since one obtains purposeful actions such as milk even from buffaloes and the like.
Now, if it is argued that there exists an internal distinction therein,
and for that reason [the causal efficiency] of one dissimilar thing is not the same as that of another,
then [we reply]: if this is so, there is indeed an internal distinction among cows themselves as well.
Consequently, since there is no causal efficacy corresponding to that similarity, there is no correspondence;
furthermore,
it follows that because a distinct cognition arises, there must also be distinctness in the other [object].
Just so, 1. Just so.
If it is argued that there is an action by which [an object] is designated as "that" based merely on the absence of similarity,
then it follows that similarity too must exist based merely on the absence of difference.
If it is argued that similarity itself is the absence of dissimilarity, we say no; for how can a state of being (kathambhāva) be an absence?
Why, then, is it not the case that similarity is simply the absence of dissimilarity, since dissimilarity is established by both disputants?

Since the conventional usage of similarity is fully accomplished by the mere absence [of difference], the postulation of another "similarity" is useless; therefore, comparison (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This concludes the refutation of the proposition [that it is a separate means of knowledge] based on scripture (*āgama*).

Now, if it is argued that the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) is established by scripture (āgama), and thus the proposition is called "scripture," even so, what is the purpose of the proposition? For instance:
If this matter is established by scripture alone, what is the use of a thesis? If this matter is not established by scripture, what is the use of a thesis? (96)
Why is it not established by the means of valid cognition known as scripture (*āgama*)? It is not established that something is the meaning of scripture merely by a thesis (*pratijñā*).
(97) Furthermore, if through extreme habituation there is the attainment of understanding from the mere reason (*hetu*) along with the thesis, then in that case the word "thesis" is purposeful.

(98) Even then, since the five-membered [syllogism] has been practiced, why would such a statement [be used]? Even so, that [statement] is not a "thesis," because it is seen to possess the property of the five [members]. (99)
It should be applied.
Because of this, [the author] says "of the wise" and so forth.
How then was it stated: "But our presentation of the thesis is not for the sake of being a proof (*sādhana*), but rather for the sake of being the object of the meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*)"?
He says exactly this:

If it is thought that, because the operation of a reason is impossible when the object has not been stated, its capacity [to prove] arises solely from the statement of the object itself; || 21 || 5 M.

If its capacity for proof were established merely by the statement "because it is produced," then when it is said that "it is impermanent," it would not be known of what the impermanence to be proven consists;
therefore, the thesis-statement "that sound is impermanent" must be employed.
Therefore, this [subject] must now be presented either as the object of the reason or otherwise;
for in every case, if this external arrangement were not made known, the operation of the reason would be impossible, and thus the object must necessarily be made known.

If it is argued that the presentation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is necessary because the thesis (*pratijñā*) must necessarily exist prior to the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), since otherwise the means of proof would lack the status of being a means of proof—[we reply:
in the statement [of the definition], the thesis is the "subject" (*pakṣa*); thus, there is no escape from this by merely changing the name.
And this principle— that "he said 'the stake' and 'the wheel'"—
establishes its capacity through the very disclosure of the object;
this has been stated here.

There would follow the undesirable consequence that even doubt and the like would be means of proof. This statement, which is preceded by a pervasion (*vyāpti*), must either be formulated as "the object is to be demonstrated by the proposition" or otherwise; both of these [alternatives] are untenable.
It is now considered whether the object is indeed to be demonstrated by the proposition.
In a formal argument preceded by the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
when the reason (*hetu*) is indicated by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), what follows from this?
Pervasion exists even without this [logical reason]: "Sound is produced; it is of such a nature.
Regarding this, it was said: "without... (vinā).
Even when it is stated that "all things are impermanent," the cognition of their destruction follows by implication.

When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is shown through a universal application—that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is pervaded by that [impermanence], is demonstrated therein as being exactly of such a nature; thus, it is already known that sound is impermanent. Therefore, what is the use of the member of the thesis (*pratijñā*) for the purpose of indicating the subject, since the subject is established in quite another way?
Now, [an objection: how can there be the ascertainment of a contradictory reason (*viruddhahetu*) without a thesis (*pratijñā*)?
This is not a fault.

Otherwise, the opponent would understand the contradiction entirely differently. Why then make an effort toward a proposition that leads only to one's own defeat? (101) If it is asked: "If the words of the proposition are not employed, how is the opponent to know that 'this reason is contradictory'?"—to whom does this objection belong? If you say it belongs to the proponent (*vādin*), [we reply:]...
This is not correct;
rather, something auspicious has occurred. Let the opponent not know [this]. What strength must I display toward him?

If it is argued: "When the author of the treatise has stated that an inference preceded by pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be employed, the fact that this prevents the proponent from using a contradictory [reason] is a great benefit to the proponent; thus, there is no fault on the part of the author of the treatise either, for he did not compose the treatise for the purpose of slaying the proponent, but rather because assistance must be rendered to the opponent."
"What aversion is there to anything else?"— this is trivial;
for if sound is eternal because it is produced,
then whatever is produced is impermanent.

In this regard, no one who is not insane would, at that very moment, having proposed "permanence" as the thesis, demonstrate a pervasion by means of "impermanence. If, on the other hand, he were to demonstrate a pervasion by means of "permanence," then the recognition of the reason's contradictory nature would arise precisely from the reversal of that pervasion.
Furthermore, when there is the employment of a proposition (*pratijñāpada*), a contradictory statement (*viruddhābhidhāna*) is made in relation to it, as in the case:
"Sound is eternal because it is produced. At this juncture:
Now, a statement of proof (*sādhana-vākya*) that lacks the component of the proposition (*pratijñāpada*) would be like a falling thunderbolt unseen from afar, causing distress;
therefore, it must be included, since the proposition serves to announce the subject matter of the treatise (*prakaraṇārtha*).
Regarding the objection, it is said here:

If it is argued that even the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) would extend without limit— since the opponent might claim that the introduction (*prastāva*) has been made even when none exists—
then the term "proposition" is superfluous; enough of this digression.
2. The thesis is not a member of the proof.
Now, [an objection may be raised: "Without the word of the thesis, there would be a deficiency in the proof;
and thus it has been said:"
A proof is deficient if it lacks even one of its members, such as the proposition and so forth;
for only when it is established that these are indeed members of a proof does that deficiency occur. (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.12–13)
Furthermore, the status of the thesis as a member of the proof has been refuted;
if a proof were deficient by lacking a member of the proof, it would be an incomplete argument.
Furthermore, the thesis is not a member of the proof,
because even when it is not stated, there is no obstruction to the establishment of the subject (pakṣa).
The deficiency is stated as the non-mention of any one of the three forms;
for that which is unrelated is not a constituent part of it,
nor is it deficient by virtue of that.

Even if there were a deficiency consisting of something useless, it would not constitute a lack [of the thesis], because that which is useless does not possess the nature of being a constituent part (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, even in the absence of something useless, the thesis is not deficient; since this is the case, the objection that "it is the same as [the case of] what is non-existent" is untenable.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that when there is a proof of a proposition (*pratijñā*), [the statement of that proof is also the proposition], then the definition of a proposition— "the statement of what is to be proven" (*sādhyanirdeśaḥ pratijñā*)— would be over-extensive (*ativyāpin*),
because even that which is unproven (*asiddha*) may serve as a proof (*sādhana*).
The proof is stated in the Nyāyasūtra.

Even the statement of a proven reason would become a thesis for one who holds that there is no proof of a thesis other than the indication of what is to be proven; thus, by the definition of a thesis, even a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) would be a thesis, because the indication of what is to be proven—even when it does not constitute a proof—is a thesis.
Therefore...

By stating the thesis (*pratijñā*), which is the expression of the probandum (*sādhya*), he is not joined with faults; for it is precisely because the [statement] is authorized as a means of proof (*sādhana*) that there is no occasion for it to be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Indeed, a means of proof does not thereby become a non-means of proof.

Therefore, because it is a means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no application [of the definition] to that; for the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is the subject under discussion by virtue of being a means of proof,
and it lacks the character of being a statement of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Because it lacks the defining characteristic of a proposition (*pratijñā*), the statement of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) is not a proposition.
[Objection: But why is it that a proposition is the statement of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and not the statement of the proof (*sādhana*)?
It follows that a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) would also be a thesis (*pratijñā*). To this it is replied:

regarding the statement "the indication of the probandum" (*sādhyānirdeśa*), if "indication of the probandum" means an indication by way of being a probandum (*sādhyatvena nirdeśaḥ*), then a fallacious proof is not [a thesis], because it is not indicated as being a probandum.
However, that which is to be stated remains unstated;

since it is said that "the statement of the probandum" [is required], it is not known what is being stated. Now, if it is argued that the statement belongs to that which deserves the means of proof (*sādhana*), [we reply: no.
Even then, how is it defined? Since no specific mode is specified—
due to the absence of a distinction as to whether [the thesis] functions as a means of proof (*sādhana*) or as that which is to be proven (*sādhya*)—
then even a fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) would possess the status of a proposition (*pratijñā*).

And how are they designated as the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*)? It must be stated that designation by means of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), or by any other case-ending except the first (*aprathamā*), is as the means of proof; designation by the first case-ending is as the object to be proven.
Why is this so?
Because the meaning of the word "thus" (tathā) is well-established [in that sense].
If it were the case that the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) is "the statement of what is to be proven" (*sādhyānirdeśa*), then such a definition need not be formulated.
The conventional meaning of the word "proposition" (*pratijñā*) in the world is simply the statement of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
However, we shall explain later that the definition of the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is for the purpose of eliminating misconceptions.

Therefore, since the definition "the proposition is simply the statement of the probandum" is redundant, the consequence follows that even a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) would be a proposition, because it too is a statement of the probandum.
But surely, even in your own position, the statement of the probandum is indeed the thesis (*pratijñā*); so why is it not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? [Reply:
This has already been answered by the fact that it is the statement of the probandum which does not function as a means of proof (*asādhana*).
[Objection: But could it not sometimes also function as a means of proof? What, then, is the cause for the removal of this doubt?
We say that it is indeed a case of heterogeneity;
for even a statement of non-distinction can give rise to doubt when applied to things of the same class.

Otherwise, it would follow that every statement of something to be proven (sādhya) constitutes a proposition (pratijñā). First, this [opponent], who is so eager to raise objections, must be challenged: if "the pot is being made" were a statement of what is to be proven, it would result in its being a proposition.

However, because this occurs within the context of the "indicative reason" (*jñāpaka-hetu*), the statement of the probandum (*sādhya-nirdeśa*) is defined as the thesis (*pratijñā*) only when it is dependent upon that [reason].

If this is so, then it is established that the statement of the probandum which does not function as a means of proof is not a thesis; for the statement of what is already established is not a means of proof.
If you argue that this does not apply to the opponent's case either, because their statement is also a means of proof, we reply that it is not defective.
Now, how is it that the statement of the probandum (sādhya), which is inseparable from the proof (sādhana), [is not the thesis]?
Surely the opponent might also say: "The statement of the probandum, being a constituent of the proof, is the proposition (pratijñā)."
A fallacious proof, however, is not a proof because it is unestablished; and because it is not a proof, it is not a thesis, since a thesis functions as a proof.
If a fallacious proof is not a proof due to its being unestablished, then how could a thesis—whose object is itself unestablished—be a proof?
For the status of a thesis as a proof consists precisely in its being unestablished.
If it were established, it would not even have the status of indicating an object;
if this were so, then even a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) would unavoidably become a thesis (*pratijñā*).
If it is argued: "Let it be so; what fault is there in its being a proof by way of a thesis? [The response is:
There would be no fault of the reason (*hetu*) being unestablished (*asiddha*).
If it is then argued: "A thesis known as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is not a proof for a thesis that consists of the probandum (*sādhya*); therefore, it is indeed a fault."
