If it is a means of accomplishment, why is it not a means of accomplishment with respect to its own purpose? If it were a means of accomplishment [with respect to itself], it would not be so, because it is a means of accomplishment only when conjoined with an object.
And that very [word] cannot be its own means of proof;
for if it were, then the word would be a means of proof merely by its existence as a sound, since it would then follow that every denotable object is a means of proof.
However, regarding the communication of one's intention, its status as a means of valid cognition has already been stated;
it is not a proof by way of a thesis.
It is indeed a fault.
Nor is the meaning itself the proof;
for if that were so, every thesis would be capable of communicating an external object, and the establishment of the probandum would follow from that alone.
Therefore, because neither direct nor indirect proof arises from it, the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a means of proof (*sādhana*).
However, another says:
the thesis is a means of proof, because it is stated along with its fallacious counterpart (*sābhāsatvena*).
Because it is observed together with the proof of the state of having an appearance,
[this is] from the author of the *Nyāyamukha-ṭīkā*.
The proponent of the refutation says:
"There is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to perception";
the response is that this is not a fault because of the qualification by the nature of being speech (vacanātmatva).

If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the presence of a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), the response is that this is qualified by "provided it is not a refutation" (*adūṣaṇatve sati*).
All of this, however, is incorrect.

For instance, the mockery regarding the neglect and improper refutation of the statement about "having fallacies" and so forth is irrelevant; thus it has been indicated that this is not a logical principle. || 27 ||
Indeed, the probans is not a means of cognition with respect to the counter-instance merely by its non-perception there.
Nor is there no single solution; for by qualifying [the reason] in some way with a property that is contradictory to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), that [objection] is avoided.
This was stated previously:

when the objection was raised that "studying is preceded by another instance of studying" because it is subsumed by the study of the *Mahābhārata*, the solution was stated by qualifying [the reason] with "the Veda."

Furthermore, what is this distinction regarding the Veda such that it cannot be studied otherwise? If there is no such [distinction], there is indeed no rebuttal; for a qualification that is not incompatible with the contrary cannot exclude the reason from that contrary case.
Otherwise, who would not be able to say "given that there is multiplicity"?
Therefore, this introduction and refutation are invalid; the previously stated objection regarding the thesis being a means of proof remains.
And there is no avoidance of the inconclusive [reason].

3. The Purpose of Formulating the Definition of the Thesis (*pakṣa*). If, then, the thesis need not necessarily be explicitly stated, for what purpose is the definition of the thesis formulated? Since the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is understood through the power of the reason (*hetu*), does it become the thesis regardless of whether it is [explicitly] stated or not? What is the use of this investigation?
"As it is perceived, so shall it be"—
this is true;
even though the meaning is already understood, the statement of the probandum (sādhya) is provided as a definition to prevent confusion.
That [definition] possesses four characteristics; it is stated by the proponent himself in words within the context of the presentation of the thesis (rūpa-nipāta).
It consists of the inclusion of what is unestablished (asiddha), the non-probative (asādhana), the stated meaning (arthokta), and the proponent’s own admission (vādy-abhyupagama).
Indeed, there is no such thing as a "definition" (lakṣaṇa) in this book; rather, every word, even that which is beyond measure, is set forth for the sake of destroying total delusion.

Furthermore, regarding the subject matter of the opposite of what is to be proven (sādhya), even great scholars hold significant disagreements, and these, if not resolved, lead one into a path of immense and widespread calamity.
Indeed, the presence of a fault that has not been refuted does not lead to excellence;
for instance,
they say that in the argument "the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another," even though mere "otherness" is not the actual probandum, it is nevertheless treated as such.

Proponents of the authority of the treatise (*śāstra*) assert that even what is not to be proven (*asādhya*) is to be proven if it is for the sake of oneself, and that even what is already established is to be proven on the basis of the treatise. Furthermore, there is a disagreement regarding the definition "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (*sādhyānirdeśaḥ pratijñā*), which results in the undesirable consequence that even a reason (*hetu*) stated as a means of proof would become the subject (*pakṣa*). Thus, even that which the author of the treatise does not intend to be proven [is claimed by some to be so].

Even if [the opponent] does not accept it, the thesis (*sādhya*) follows from that; therefore, in order to refute it, its occurrence in its own form (*svarūpa-nipāta*) is required by means of the four words [of the definition]. It should be understood that "unestablished" (*asiddha*), "not a means of proof" (*asādhana*), "that which has been stated," and "the proponent's acceptance" (*vādibhyupagama*) are the terms [to be used].
That which is unestablished is indeed the thesis; the same applies to the others as well.
From this restriction, the exclusion of its opposite should be understood.

(In this regard, the reasoning is as follows: If that object is already established solely from the treatise, which is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why then would it be established by another means of valid cognition for the sake of another?
If it is argued that "the treatise is not a means of valid cognition for another," and therefore [another means is required] for that purpose—
If it is argued that the proof for one's own [position] is simply through acceptance, then the opponent must also be made to accept it.

Likewise, if that [object] were already established, why would it be designated as the "probandum" (sādhya)? If, however, what is expressed by the meaning [of the sentence] were not the probandum, there would be no understanding of the sentence-meaning at all; furthermore, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the meaning of a word is determined through the power of the context and the proximity of other words.
Furthermore, one who does not understand the context does not comprehend the intended meaning; what possibility is there, then, for such a person to enter the path of linguistic communication?
Thus, as it has been said: "Even a beast would grasp a meaning that is clearly articulated. What superior capacity for understanding could there be in such a case?
For this very reason, he says:

[the proponent] who speaks for the purpose of proving what is not yet established.
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by [the proponent's] intention is considered to be the probandum (*sādhya*), just like "for one's own sake.

For example, when the fact that composite objects exist for the sake of another is to be proven, "existing for one's own sake"—though not explicitly stated—is pervaded by the intention and thus constitutes the probandum. The inclusion of the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating this.
If it is asked: "How is it known that it is pervaded by intention? [the answer follows].
For desire conforms to the context because of the context itself; otherwise, there would be the consequence of lacking discernment. To illustrate:
If one thing is under discussion and something else is established,
that is not at all a fault for the proponent;
however, this would indeed be a fault for him if he were to state it of his own accord by way of mentioning something irrelevant, for in that case, he himself would have exposed his own defect.
Let that fault belong to him;
however, for the opponent as well, there would indeed be a fault if he fails to point out the actual fault,
provided that [the fault] does not exist because the meaning has been successfully demonstrated.
As it says: "In that [state],

Consequently, because this reason proves the opposite of that [intended] state, it is contradictory (*viruddha*);
for example, as this reason establishes impermanence in sound.

Likewise, one who says that [the reason] is contradictory because it also lacks the absence of impermanence qualified by sound (*śabdaviśiṣṭānityatvābhāva*) is also refuted by this statement of the intended probandum (*iṣṭasādhyavacana*); for it is not "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) as impermanent that is being established, but rather the mere quality of impermanence (*anityatāmātra*) that is being established.
If it is asked, "How is there a proof of the whole when only impermanence is being proven? [the answer is:
No, because the whole is proven in that very same way.
Because the composite whole is established together with the subject (*dharmin*),
there is no other composite whole consisting of sound and impermanence to be proven in the case of sound as the subject;
therefore, even if that [composite] is refuted, there is no fault.
If it is asked, "Why is there a fault in merely refuting impermanence, rather than a subversion of the whole? [the answer is:
because when one of two [factors] is absent, the whole is thereby refuted.
Since a collective cannot exist when there is no single remainder,
therefore the property alone is to be proven in the locus;
for it is in this very way that the collective is established.
Since the collection [of subject and predicate] is established together in a single second proof,
how then is there a distinction between the negation of the property, the subject, and their collective specificities?
It is because they are negated by means of that [second proof].
For when a collection is negated by means of a particular member, it is designated by that [member] in the ultimate sense; thus, "sound is impermanent" is precisely the negation of the collection.

If it is argued that the thesis is the refutation of the aggregate [of "sound" and "that which possesses impermanence"] as in "Sound is that which possesses the impermanence of sound," this is not so,
because such a thesis is impossible;
for when the thesis is stated as "Sound is impermanent," there is no cognition of the proof of an aggregate with respect to another locus (*dharmin*).
Therefore, since it is impossible to prove the aggregate in any other way,
the refutation of the aggregate follows precisely from the refutation of the mere subject (*dharmin*) and so forth;
such is the case for the property (*dharma*) and the rest.
But it is not so in the case of sound, because the property of being a non-eternal sound is what is being refuted;
thus, since the probandum is not intended [to be negated], there is no fault in refuting what is unintended.
"For a refutation of the whole does not contradict the property-possessor (dharmin) in the proof; rather, what is intended here as the probandum is the property alone."—
this is the summary (verse 41).
5. The Purpose of Including the Word *Svayam* (Itself):

If, then, the inclusion of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is intended to demonstrate that there is no fault even when what is not intended is excluded from the probandum (*sādhya*), then just as there is no fault when the impermanence residing in the sound itself is sublated in the subject (*dharmin*), so too there would be no fault whatsoever even when the impermanence qualified by being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is sublated.
This is true.
Nevertheless, the inclusion of the word "itself" (svayam) is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions;
for even though multiple properties may be established for a single subject within a treatise, [the proponent must state what he himself accepts].
"The object of proof (*sādhya*) must be that which is desired by oneself; thus, the scripture (*śruti*) is adopted [as an authority] of its own accord.

(42) Some maintain: "Let that which is seen in the treatise (*śāstra*) indeed be the object of proof; and if that were subverted, there would be a fault in both the reason (*hetu*) and the proposition (*pratijñā*).
For instance:
In the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, [it is stated]: "Tradition (*āgama*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*); it is called tradition because it indicates the meaning of tradition, and not otherwise. (*Nyāyavārttika*)

Otherwise, since scripture (*āgama*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*) establishes what is doubted, how could there be identity [between them]? That very meaning of scripture which is being pointed out to another is the meaning of the thesis. Therefore, scripture is the thesis; thus, when its meaning is sublated, it is a fault of the reason (*hetu*), because it sublates the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*).
Furthermore, a reason that contradicts the treatise (*śāstra*) cannot establish the probandum (*sādhya*),

and this constitutes a fault of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*). For instance, if impermanence (*anityatva*) were to be established as co-inherent in the same substrate as the quality of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), such that it would be proven by some other reason or by the treatise as being a quality of space, then such impermanence would be the meaning of the proposition.
And in the refutation of that [position] by him, there is a flaw in the thesis; for instance:
"Therefore, it is not a composite."
3. Because the probandum (*sādhya*) is thus [established]—so says He.
4. B. Distinguished: (1) momentary, without a substratum.

If it perishes immediately after a moment, its nature as a quality of space is useless; even if it perishes at a later time, its nature as a quality of space is still useless. (105) If that which consists of sound perishes after a moment due to the absence of a cause for its destruction, what is the use of its being a quality of space?
For a substratum is indeed the cause of stability.
Furthermore, that which is momentary cannot have stability even for a single moment, as it arises solely from its own causes.
On the other hand, if it were to endure for a period of time having arisen from its own causes, it would nevertheless remain by the power of those very causes; so what is the use of a substratum?

Now, if it is argued that its persistence for a period of time is due to the force of a substratum (*āśraya*), then surely it will persist simply because it is indestructible; what need is there for a substratum?

Furthermore, sound possesses no weight (*gurutva*) by which its falling might occur in the absence of a substratum. Nor does space possess the nature of supporting things; indeed, heavy objects are certainly not supported by space.
Even then, because of its weight, there is no quality of supporting space in the act of falling; light things do not fall at all—what then will the supporter do? (106)
If it were carried away by the wind, it would fall; therefore, let it be supported by that [wind]. For one for whom space is not an obstructer, there would indeed be its destruction.
That which supports]
For its very nature is such that it perishes only by depending on this [condition], as long as no destroyer exists; there is no movement toward that state other than from its own abiding.
Thus, the certainty is that its existence is without any substratum,
whether it be for a momentary duration or for a duration of another time;
even for eternal things, such dependence on a substratum does not exist, as it would be purposeless.
This is true; nevertheless, this is its innate nature, always so. 110.3 B.
Furthermore,
one might even entertain the notion that "he is not to be questioned"; however,

since this [reason] is not the locus of an impermanent entity, it establishes impermanence while simultaneously subverting its own status as a locus— thus, it constitutes a fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*).
And there is a flaw in the thesis regarding its having a substratum.
(2) "Qualities have no substratum"— to this it is replied:
because of the acceptance of the treatise itself, [the opponent's position] is refuted by the inclusion of everything.
In that case, there would be a fault even for one [of the two] if there were a discrepancy between the reason and the thesis.

If the destruction of sound were to be proven, [the reason "because it is an object of the sense of hearing"] would be contradictory because the quality of being an earth-element (bhūguṇatā) in the case of odor remains unimpaired; if you say this is not so because [odor] is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛti*), then that same [fault] applies elsewhere as well.

If it is argued that a fault arises in the proposition and the reason simply because a treatise has been accepted, and thus there is a contradiction with that treatise, then—just as in the case of contradicting the quality of being a quality of space (ākāśaguṇatva) attributed to sound—one would also encounter such a fault when subverting the contrary claim that smell is a quality of earth. For just as impermanence is the probandum (sādhya) because it is possible for it to be connected with the quality of being a quality of space as enumerated in that treatise, so too is the fact of being taught by the treatise connected with the quality of being a quality of earth as intended by the author of that treatise for another subject (dharmin) such as smell;
therefore, even when that [quality of being a quality of earth] is contradicted, the connection with that treatise remains untenable, and thus the fault of the proposition would certainly follow.

One should not say, "How [can there be fragrance], since fragrance is not under discussion," for the same applies to its being a quality of space; there is no distinction between the two cases. If, however, the subject (dharmin) here is the topic at hand, then there is a contradiction with the meaning of the treatise.
Is it not the case that even in another subject, the topic under discussion [remains relevant] because of the acceptance of the meaning of the treatise? No, it is the *prakṛti* (the original state).
If indeed the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion here is intended solely as the locus for that specific property (*dharma*),
yet by means of the treatise it is also the locus for other properties,
then the same fault applies: namely, that there would also be a connection with properties residing in other subjects mentioned within that same treatise.

Furthermore, it might be argued that since the substratum of those properties (the *dharmin*) is the subject under discussion, even another property (*dharmāntara*) is indeed included within the thesis (*sādhya-pakṣa*), because the proponent also intends it to be so;
thus he says:
Alternatively, one might say that [the property] is intended by the proponent through the means of proof consisting of the subject, its properties, and so forth.

Even the quality of being a quality of space (ākāśaguṇatva) is indeed intended by the proponent, because it possesses the status of being a property of the subject already accepted as the locus of the probandum, just like impermanence.
Likewise, regarding [the reason] "because it is a specific instance of a portion of the collection of the probandum" and so forth,
he says:
"The mere fact that it is not a specific instance of a portion of the collection of the probandum does not constitute the intended meaning of the context."
For instance, by certain arguments there may arise a desire, and that [desire] is understood through them;
thus, "this is your desire" is clearly the work of a Lord. (46)
The mere fact of being a specific instance of a portion of the probandum-collection does not incite the activity of desire;
or, if it did incite it, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the activity of desire and the application of the means would never cease.

If, on the other hand, you think it is because it is not desired as a specific instance of a portion of the probandum-collection, then in that case, "desirability" itself is the probandum and "desirability" itself is the means; thus, the very meaning of the thesis becomes the means of proof.

Therefore, desire occurs only where there is a relevant context; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, desire proceeds only toward that which is the subject of dispute, not toward the quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).
[Objection: Desire arises from context, and context is the cause of that [desire].
If it is asked, "For what reason is there the accomplishment of the effect?
How is it to be understood that an unobstructed cause leads to the cognition of the effect?"—
how is that to be known?

Since the effect of that [intention], namely speech, is observed, the understanding [of the intention] arises from the speech alone and not from the context; how then can it be said that it is understood by those [contextual factors] alone? To this, it is replied:

The capacity [to indicate] is understood from the statement; therefore, the comprehension [of that specific object] arises from it. Because desire is restricted [by context], its comprehension is said to arise from the context (*prakaraṇa*).
From the statement, there is the comprehension of mere desire, and since context is the cause of desire, it is not the indicator [of the specific object].
Therefore, once the capacity is established through the statement, it is the context itself that indicates the restriction of desire; thus, it is said, "by those very [factors]."
Moreover, even if there were no causal efficacy (*apra[karaṇa]*), you would still desire this very [conclusion]; there is no logical principle (*nyāya*) here for that.
Therefore...
When one speaks by way of verbal testimony (*vacanagata*), it is not sublated by deviation (*vyabhicāra*) up to the point of the mark of what is to be accomplished (*kāryaliṅga*).
And when a meaning that is not invariably concomitant is sublated, what harm is done to the other [meaning]?
For it is intention that indicates whether something is an effect or a cause, and the context is the cause; it does not indicate the quality of being an attribute of space.
Since that [sound] is absent there,
speech must be its effect; yet even so, this desire of yours [that sound is a quality of space] remains unproven.
One who asserts a desire that lacks a logical mark (*akāryaliṅga*) is sublated by deviation (*vyabhicāra*);

for [the property of] being a particular part of the collection of the probandum (*sādhyasamudāyaikadeśaviśeṣatva*), and so forth, is not the effect of a desire, nor is it its unimpeded causal capacity. Furthermore, when there is a sublation of the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*), the probandum would be absent due to the absence of its pervader (*vyāpaka*); thus, there would be a fault in either the probandum or the probans.

Nor is being a quality of space necessarily concomitant [with sound]; and when that which is not necessarily concomitant is sublated, what harm is done to the probandum, which is something else? [Section 3: Examination of the Invalidity of Verbal Testimony; Section 1:
Contradiction with Treatises is Weak in Inference]
Is it not the case that debate proceeds precisely by accepting a treatise?
Therefore, for one established within their own treatise, there is necessarily a fault in subverting its meaning.
No.
Because the answer has already been stated:
even if there were a reversal of the fact that odor is a quality of earth, the same fault would apply;
and it has also been said that inference does not depend upon scripture regarding its own object-domain.
By that [means], it is well-established; at that time, the scripture is not required.
(48) He observes: "He does not observe.
For inference, relying on the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) within its own domain, does not depend upon scripture.

Since it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) just like perception, whatever is seen—whether that be inference—is it all dependent upon scripture? Likewise, does even our own perception necessarily depend upon scripture? [If so,] because it would be sublated by scripture, it would be nothing but an error.

Indeed, the statement of those possessing the divine eye is not sublated by the direct perception of people such as ourselves; nor does the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia sublate the vision of others with respect to its own object of proof.
This is true,
provided that the author of these words were one possessed of divine vision;
for even if it were appropriate for such a person to speak thus regarding some being, it is not our firm conviction that he is so, as this [evidence] clearly demonstrates.
For, because their statements contradict one another, those who compose the scriptures are not understood to be omniscient anywhere;
let them not be omniscient, yet even so, you yourself do not escape [the same fault]. In that case, the contradiction with all the scriptures must indeed be avoided, and that is simply impossible.
In that case, inference would not arise at all;
if, on the other hand, one must simply avoid contradicting the treatises that are the objects of one's own scriptures,
then even that acceptance must be made after critical examination.

If it is argued that at the time of investigation inference is not a valid means of knowledge because the contradiction with the treatise has not been resolved— and that at that time there is no acceptance of the treatise at all, so what is the point of resolving it?— then,
in that case, the probandum is already perfectly established by that very fact.
If it is argued that what has been established cannot subsequently become unestablished because it contradicts the acceptance of a contrary scripture— and thus remains unestablished—
then that very point constitutes the avoidance of contradiction with all scriptures.
If it is argued that [the relationship] exists in relation to what has been accepted and not otherwise,
then why does acceptance itself not apply everywhere?
If it is argued that [acceptance] is indeed subject to critical examination, [then the same applies to the relationship].
In that case, the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be the investigation, and that [treatise] would be sublated by it; this is like raising a weapon to strike at one’s own body.
Therefore, because it contradicts the means of valid cognition, the treatise itself is not relied upon at that time, and consequently, it cannot be a sublater of it.
One's own admission 4. B.

If that [reasoning] is also an admission (*upagama*), then it is a treatise (*śāstra*); in that case, it would not be required, for the abandonment of the argument (*vādatyāga*) would have already occurred.
If you say that there is no abandonment of the argument at that time, then it is because it is not an admission (*anabhyupāya*).

For this is a means toward acceptance; even though it is devoid of logical proof (*anaṅga*) at that time, there is no debate without relying on a treatise, because [the opponent] does not accept [the position] then. Thus, critical examination itself is the means for acceptance.

If it were accepted without prior examination, then even though it exists at that time, it would not be a constituent part [of the proof] because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For a treatise that cannot withstand examination is not a sublater at that time.
When, then, is a treatise accepted as a constituent part of the proof?
Regarding this, the refutation is stated as follows:

Likewise, when the two domains [of perception] have been purified by both inference and direct perception, that indeed would be the time for one desiring to undertake the study of a treatise; at that time, there may be sublation by means of the treatise. (50) "Likewise" means that when the two domains—the perceptible and the imperceptible—have been established as pure through inference and direct perception, if satisfaction is not yet reached by that much alone, then it would be the time for the desire to undertake the treatise, and thus the time for its acceptance.
At that very time, there was a contradiction by means of the scripture; the broken reading has been placed below because of that.
Because reflection that contradicts that [scripture] is inappropriate regarding the objects established by it,

the adoption of a treatise is proper only upon transitioning to a third position. For when one has accepted a scripture as an object of investigation, it is not logical to reflect upon the objects well-known in that scripture in a manner that contradicts it.
For it has been examined thus: if that treatise has already been thoroughly scrutinized through a formal thesis, how can it be said that its examination must be performed again?
If there is an examination, then it was not previously examined. (112)

Therefore, having examined by means of perception and inference that which is not their object—the cause for transitioning to a third position, namely, the acceptance of a treatise—it follows that a treatise does not subvert what is the object of inference.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "For one who accepts a treatise without investigation, that treatise would be a subverter [of inference], and thus there would be a flaw in the thesis.
This is not so.
For even in that case, it is only the connected property of the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) that is sublated.
"Obstruction of what is invariably concomitant"—this is the view of the Hetuvidyā school;

however, it is not to be avoided by others, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. (52) If one must avoid obstructing the meaning of a treatise simply because that treatise has been accepted, [then there would be no way to refute any erroneous doctrine].
There would also be a fault if there were a subversion of smell, even though it is a quality of earth;
therefore, it is established that only the subversion of that which is connected to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) must be avoided, not others that are unconnected.
Now, one might object: could a caviller (vaitaṇḍika) exist in debate even without accepting a treatise (śāstra)?

Is it not the case that one who accepts what is established by valid cognition is not a nihilist, and likewise, one who does not accept what is sublated by valid cognition? For one who has no reliance on the scriptures is a nihilist.
In the third case, the nihilist who does not accept the treatise asks:
"What is the use of a treatise other than the third [case]? For indeed, by whom has this rule been established that a treatise must be accepted in all deliberations?
Now, fire cannot be apprehended by means of smoke by those who do not accept established tenets (asiddhānta).
If the operation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were dependent solely upon accepting a tenet, then even in the world, fire would not be cognized from smoke by cowherds and others.
However, it might be argued that only a matter pertaining to the next world (*paraloka*) must be preceded by the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), and no other.
That is incorrect.
If one has a definitive ascertainment of that [object] through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without having accepted a treatise (*śāstra*), then what use is a treatise as a precursor?
If it is not accepted [that the object is known without a treatise], then the suspicion of sublation by a treatise arises.
If, however, it is accepted [as a thesis], then it is known that there is a contradiction with the treatise;
therefore, that is not established at all, because even one who does not desire [the conclusion] cannot deny what is established by valid cognition.
If it is asked: "How is it that one's own treatise is abandoned when it ought not to be abandoned?"—
it is not so.
Because of the absence of a relationship,
it is thus [regarded] as possessing qualities; for that is so.

(1) The scripture is a malignant planet for a person born destitute, who does not perceive the distinction between virtue and fault; alas, by whom have these malignant planets of dogmatic tenets been bestowed upon him? 54.
If a tenet, even when contradicted by logic, cannot be abandoned, then it is not a tenet at all;
under the guise of a tenet, it is a malignant obsession from which children cannot be released.
Because of its connection and because it is innate, it cannot be abandoned. How could that connection be innate for a creature born empty [of it]? (114)
O King, how can there even be a discernment of virtues and defects for one who abandons the means of valid cognition?
Therefore, inference is not preceded by the acceptance of a treatise;

indeed, how can an inference that contradicts a treatise be determinative? Consequently, the contradiction with the treatise must be avoided by means of an illustrative example (nidarśana) that is favorable to it.
That [objection] is incorrect.
For if the proponent were to demonstrate the entire treatise within a single instance of the example, then it would constitute a valid proof; such is this extraordinary principle. (55)
Indeed, a contradiction with the scriptures is impossible to avoid,
because since the scriptures themselves contradict one another, it would follow that either all of them are authoritative or none of them are authoritative.
Firstly, if [the word] were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no resolution of all contradictions because they are mutually contradictory;
nor, if it were not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), would there be a resolution, since contradiction always exists among the words of all people—
for indeed, an unlimited number of contradictions cannot be resolved.
And since the proof is thus established, this path of conventional discourse transcends the world.

Now, if only that property of the subject (*dharmidharma*) is sublated, then even when [the reason] has been stated, what assurance is there? For it is not possible for that which sublates to be a prover;
this too is not tenable.
For in this way, there would be no proof at all;
for one who proves in such a manner must necessarily refute the opponent as well.
If a property is unrelated [to the subject], what is it that is not established when that property is unestablished? Why would the reason stated to prove it be considered flawed?
If one must avoid the sublation of an unrelated property, then the reason itself would not exist.
If one thing is sublated, why is the other not established?
For even a single instance of smoke is observed to be a prover of both the presence and absence of fire and cold touch;
if it is argued that a proof must be non-contradictory [to what is being proven], then [the opponent's position fails].
Even if [the property] were a quality of space, the contradiction would be the same;
furthermore, even if that reason were established as proving both existence and non-existence,
how could there be a comprehension of a meaning contrary to the treatise for the person being instructed?
Therefore, the conformity with the meaning of the treatise must also be demonstrated in the example;
for indeed, there can be no comprehension of the probandum from the reason if its properties are not introduced [into the example].
This is not established,
because:

Without even introducing properties [from the subject] into the example, people infer consciousness, fire, and so forth from the smoke of speech and other such signs. Let alone the case of a property well-known in scripture that lacks a [logical] connection; even when some property of that subject is introduced into the example, this world understands consciousness, fire, and so forth from the reason of "smoke in the form of speech" and the like. For it is not the case that another property [of the subject] is sublated, and thus there is no non-establishment of the fire.
There is no non-comprehension on the part of the purifier,
nor is it the case that the person to be instructed does not comprehend.

Moreover, even against the will of the person being addressed, a fact that establishes its own nature or its cause without deviation does not cease from its essential nature when it contradicts someone's argument. 58
Indeed, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, which depends upon its own causes, does not turn away from its course by the mere will of a person.

Furthermore, the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) regarding the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the essential factor; since that [non-deviation] exists, why would it not be a prover?
Now, let it be granted that he is a practitioner; however, how does that which is to be established come to be established?
To this, he says:
"the intrinsic nature."

And how could another person, who is approaching that [cause], not be made to understand it— since it is invariably connected with the desired objects to be accomplished by means of that cause? As for the indicator (*jñāpaka*), it produces cognition by the force of its necessary connection (*pratibandha*); once the three forms [of the reason] have been established, that [cognition] cannot be negated by that very same [indicator]. Indeed, one who perceives the non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*) of that [reason] could not fail to perceive it.

Because the cognition of a qualified object distinguished by its qualifiers is inseparable from the cognition of those specific qualities, everything exists; however, one might act in a manner inconsistent with the proponent's own position.

if it is argued that no collection of defects has been committed by the speaker here, such as the contradiction of a treatise (*śāstra*).

That is incorrect;

within the scope of meaningful statement, a useless statement is indeed pointless.

whereas the fault lies precisely in non-statement,
and that even here there is a fault in not stating the quality of being a property of space;
Since it is possible for even a proponent to fail to state [the reason], it is logical that failing to state it constitutes a fault when the probandum is what the disputant intends;
however, in this case, there is no possibility of a sublater of the fact that sound is a quality of space, which is the meaning of the treatise.
Therefore, it is not a fault that [the reason] is unmentioned.
But if the reason contradicts the meaning of the treatise, how could it establish even impermanence?
For by that very [contradiction], it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

To this it is replied: "If something in a certain treatise is not logical, it is refuted by one who asserts that another thing is indeed logical; such is the established practice of royal courts. (63)
Indeed, there is no contradiction with the meaning of all the scriptures,
because such [a means] exists in some scripture or another;
since a proof is a proof and a non-proof is a non-proof depending on the presence or absence of a connection, what contradiction could there be here?
"This is a royal decree: that when the unrighteous is prohibited, the righteous is also prohibited.
Furthermore, it is possible to speak by treating all matters as equal, yet there is no means [to establish the truth].
Therefore, this entire framework of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the proof (*sādhana*) must be abandoned everywhere. Without contradicting any [established] fact, it is impossible to state any proof;
rather, only the mere connection with the specific probandum under discussion is required.
If it is argued that, because otherwise it would be impossible, one must act in such a way as not to contradict the meaning of the scriptures, we say:
no.
Since there would be no distinction, it would follow that even for another [type of reason] this [fallacy] would apply; furthermore, if one were to avoid contradicting the treatises (*śāstra*),
then in that case, there would be no means of proof whatsoever, and thus the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) would collapse everywhere.
If it is asked, "Why then was the treatise accepted?"— this very point is what must be established here as intended:
that one should not first undertake the acceptance of a treatise.
Once a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has occurred, it is better to abandon [the position] even later;
for others, however, the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*) constitutes a thesis (*pratijñā*). Therefore, having accepted a treatise, one must not contradict it.
Since the operation of the rules of debate (*vādavidhāna*) proceeds on the basis of an accepted tenet (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*),

if there is no fault in the reason (*hetu*) even when the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is sublated, then how can "the non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) be a fault of the proof?
In that case as well, the fault arises from the contradiction with a fact established by another means of proof.
In this case as well, the fault is precisely the contradiction with the meaning established by the treatise;
it is not correct [to say otherwise],
because:

Since two contradictory [properties] cannot coexist in a single substratum, let there be sublation by the "contradictory-exclusive" (viruddhaikāntika); here, too, there is likewise a state of contradiction. (65)
This [reason] is well-concealed; for here, the non-deviation from mutually contradictory meanings in both [types of reasons] is indeed equal in strength.
Since both rely on scripture (*āgama*),
whereas inference (*anumāna*) functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala*) and scripture is not of such a nature,
there can be no mutual sublation between the two, as in the case of a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Nor is there a proof for both [theses], because two contradictory [propositions] cannot coexist in a single locus (*dharmin*). However, since a treatise lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in comparison to a contradictory inference, its object is indeed sublated; it is not the sublater, like the "contradictory non-deviant" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
Furthermore, the authority of a treatise that is not supported by the force of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed refuted;
therefore, the position of proposing a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason is untenable.
B.

Furthermore, since the scripture was promulgated by one who perceives objects beyond the senses, how could it be sublated by inference? Consequently, that inference which is contradicted by it is indeed not a valid means of knowledge.

If it is argued that, because the two sides possess equal strength, there is likewise a fault here just as in the case of the "contradictory non-erroneous" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) reason, that is incorrect; for:
If scripture were to invalidate a contrary inference, then all means of valid cognition would perish, and only scripture would remain.

(117) If every inference were invalidated by scripture, then the meaning of scripture could not be established for another through inference; how then could scripture serve as a formal proposition (*pratijñā*)?
Indeed, there is no inference or any other means of valid cognition that is not sublated by scripture,
because inferences such as "impermanence" or "permanence" are sublated by successive scriptures,
and even such [inferences] as "there is fire" are sublated by the scripture on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Now, if it is argued that this [scriptural cognition] is not invalid, and that it cannot be an invalidator of inference because only that which is invalidated by inference is invalid— and not everything—
then surely your own position is that that very same inference is invalid when it is contradicted by scripture.
Therefore, it is not logical for you to abandon your own position;
otherwise, there would be a sublation by that which has been examined as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa).

[Objection: Surely, in this case, investigation is nothing other than inference; therefore, how can an investigation be sublated by that scripture? [Reply: The authority of a scripture is not the cause of its being an investigation. Indeed, what is impossible therein cannot bring about the possibility of that [investigation].

Therefore, inference alone—preceded by perception—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses a firm foundation. A scripture sublated by that [inference] is not itself a valid means of knowledge; thus, it cannot serve as its counter-position. Consequently, there is no fault here comparable to the "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). Since this [reason] establishes impermanence together with the absence of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), it is indeed a valid proof and not defective. However, the "non-erroneous contradiction" is not a valid reason at all, because it is impossible for both permanence and its absence to be established by a single [reason] in one and the same locus.
However, since there is no contradiction between the absence of the quality of space and impermanence, how could there be a fault in establishing [the probandum] in a single locus? 3 B. The proof.

Even if there were no relationship of sublated and sublator between those two, if invalidation could occur despite the lack of connection due to the subversion of the meaning of the scripture, then everything would invalidate everything.
(66) "Invalidator"—thus [it is said]. He.
Even in the case of odor, because there is a subversion of its being a quality of earth,
the connection is with "by another" and "by that aforementioned reason"; for it is refuted right there, and thus if it exists, it is non-existent.
Because it is necessary to consider the merits and defects of every reason (hetu) with respect to its own specific probandum (sādhya), [one might argue]:

"Even if that quality of being a quality of space (ākāśaguṇatva) actually exists in that subject (dharmin), there is still no connection [to the desired conclusion]; furthermore, even if it were not the subject under discussion, the fact that it is not the probandum would not constitute a fault of sublation (bādhana), because one intends to consider the defect of every reason only in relation to its own specific probandum. (67)

If there were a fault characterized by the subversion of the treatise (śāstra) when that [treatise] obstructs something not to be proven by the [reason] itself—even though it does not obstruct its own [probandum]—then that same fault-causing subversion would apply equally to any other property in any other subject by means of any other reason. Demonstrating this, he says:
"The connection [of the reason] with the probandum consists in being inseparable; such [a connection] is not seen here."
"It is not seen"—thus [it is said].
Indeed, the fault here consists solely in the contradiction of the scriptures; that [contradiction] is equal even when committed by another.
For one must avoid establishing the absence of a pervading probandum (*sādhya*),
because when that which is inseparable from the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhananāntarīyaka*) is sublated, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) also ceases to exist in its absence.
Furthermore, the property of being a quality of space is not invariably concomitant with the probandum;
therefore, even in its absence, there is no contradiction of the probandum.
Moreover:

If everything seen in the treatise were to be proven because of the acceptance of the treatise, it would follow that the reason and the example are established by the very thesis [they are meant to prove]. (69) [Note:
"dṛṣṭānte" is the reading in the He version.]
The commentator of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states:

"Because of the acceptance of the treatise (*śāstra*), everything seen in that treatise is to be proven; otherwise, the acceptance of the treatise would be useless, for if its subject matter were not to be proven, the acceptance of the treatise would be of no use whatsoever."
Alternatively, nothing deserves to be accepted as an independent means of valid cognition;
therefore, having accepted a treatise, its meaning must be established.
Therefore, in opposition to that, there would indeed be a fault; [otherwise],
some [agency] would exist independently.
To this it is replied: the status of being a thesis (*pratijñā*) might belong to an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*),
because those two, too, may sometimes constitute the subject matter of a treatise (*śāstrārtha*).
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", then the entire thesis itself would be established, and consequently, faults such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) should not be mentioned.
[To this we reply: Indeed, that which is not the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*) must be stated as the reason (*hetu*); in that case, there is scope for faults such as being unestablished.
Not so,
because even that [opponent's position] is accepted by his own mouth;
furthermore, what is accepted by one's own mouth is a thesis (*pratijñā*), whereas what is accepted through the mouth of another is certainly not.

Even for others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, the statement of the probandum (sādhya) is the thesis (pratijñā); thus, even the statement of an unestablished means of proof (asiddhasādhana) would be a thesis.
For even in their case, if the meaning of the treatise were not stated, it would not be a thesis, but if it is stated, it certainly is.
For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Scriptural tradition is the proposition, but the proposition is not necessarily that which is scriptural tradition;
surely, is scriptural tradition not simply the proposition?"

Scripture is not [the thesis] because it is the instruction of the meaning of scripture; rather, the thesis is the statement of that which is to be proven. Otherwise, the thesis would be the unestablished reason and so forth, since those too are the meaning of scripture.
) 6 In the Nyāyabhāṣya 7 B, but not.
8. Having bowed, [it is said:
"All this meaning of the treatise is indeed to be established as true."

Nevertheless, that which is stated as a means of proof does not possess the status of a thesis (*pratijñā*), because it is not intended as something to be proven (*sādhya*); for in the *Nyāyamukha-prakaraṇa*, the reading is:
"In that context, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is itself desired as something to be proven, and is not contradicted by opposing meanings."

Furthermore, that which is indicated as a means (sādhana) cannot simultaneously possess the status of being the most desired (īpsitatama) and the state of being the object to be accomplished (sādhya); nor is that which is intended as a means [itself] the object (karman),
as for example, in the sentence "He eats rice with milk," the milk [is not the object].

In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, because of the restriction "not by its own nature alone," and because for the Naiyāyika the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*), due to the restriction that it is "only as a probandum"— that is, because the emphasis is on the state (*bhāva*)— the statement of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not the thesis. To this, it is replied:

9B. Regarding the means of proof (sādhana): [The two] mentioned as the primary [factors] are the means of proof; otherwise, it would not be so because of the statement of what is desired [by the proponent].
11. "It is sublated"—thus [you say]; but that which is established by logic does not cease to be a probandum merely because of a statement. || 70 ||

If this is the principle that "one accepts the treatise," then how can there be a reversal by statement of what is established by that very principle? For a statement indicates the principle; it does not contradict the principle itself.
Now, even though it is merely indicated by words, the reasoning (*nyāya*) is indeed a proof,
because it serves as the means of proving that which was designated as a "means of proof" (*sādhana*) is actually not the "probandum" (*sādhya*).
This is not so;

for if that were the case, these two would constitute a "contradictory non-deviant" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) fallacy. This is because [the opponent] accepts the treatise, and thus such statements as "this is desired" [would apply]. If, by means of logic, the fact that the probans is not the thing to be proven is established through such statements as "this is desired," [then the fault follows].
Likewise, by the statement "because of the acceptance of a treatise," there is the status of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*).
This being so, because they would establish mutually contradictory meanings in a single case, those two [reasons] would produce doubt (*saṃśaya*);
and thus...

Because of the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), it is not a prover; why? Because even that which is accepted as a probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, that which is seen in a treatise—is not intended as a prover. Furthermore, the principle [that "because of the acceptance of a treatise" it is not a prover] does not hold; for if that were the case, then what is desired by the proponent would be the probandum, rather than that which is intended as a prover.
Here [the opponent] says:
"If that which is undesired by the proponent is unprovable, then [that which is] undesired by the respondent [would also be unprovable]."
If the property (*dharma*) is not what is to be proven (*asādhya*), then how can that which subverts the unprovable be contradictory?
(71) [2] The refutation of sound’s being a quality of space (*ākāśa*): For even its being a quality of space is not intended by the proponent; therefore, it is not the probandum (*sādhya*).
For what discerning person would, by abandoning the subject at hand, pursue something irrelevant as their primary goal?
Surely, having accepted a treatise, one is inevitably tainted by fault if one contradicts its meaning through a reason stated by oneself.
Not so.
It has been established that this is not defective because it is proven by oneself and accepted by the opponent;
furthermore, even regarding contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if sound were not a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatā*), it would be heard only at the very place of its production.
If sound were a quality of space, then by its connection with that [space], it would be perceived elsewhere as well;
this is not so, because it is perceived only where that [space] is, just like color.
If it is perceived by one standing at a distance, then why does form (rūpa) not also result in being a quality of space?
Furthermore—
In that case, space would have to be either one or many;
for if it were one, its sound would be heard even from a thousand yojanas away,
whereas if it were many, it would be heard only at the location of the mouth.
Therefore, there is no cognition whatsoever of sound having the quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*). [Objection:
But surely, without having the quality of space, it could not even exist;
for an entity that persists must necessarily possess existence.

In that regard, the four great elements beginning with earth are the substratum for visible form, touch, taste, and smell; however, space is the substratum for sound because it cannot exist without being supported by something.
If that is so, then earth and the other elements must likewise be supported by space for that very same reason.
Because there is an absence of the nature of a quality (guṇatva), that very state of being non-quality is established by virtue of its dependence [upon substance].

Furthermore, if sound were a quality, it would have to be dependent [upon a substance]; yet, since earth and the other elements are themselves dependent upon qualities, they would lack the status of being substances.
That very point is not established, for if a substratum such as space exists, then form and so forth, as well as earth and the others, would necessarily be dependent upon that space.
Since earth and so forth, as well as color and so forth, do not have inherence in space,
[one might ask: what indeed is this so-called inherence that resides in earth and so forth, such as color?

If it is argued that [sound] exists through a state of complete fusion (*ekalolībhāva*), then sound cannot be a quality of space, because it is not perceived as being in a state of complete fusion with it;

and since smell is perceived in earth, it is dependent on earth, and that alone is its locus. As for sound, because it is perceived in space, it must be dependent on space, and that alone is its locus.

If it is argued that even cotton and the like, being perceived there [in space], must therefore be supported by space— since they remain there by being held by it and because they possess their own lightness (*laghutva*)— then [the same applies to] sound.
3 B. Not dependent on space; 4 B. Pervasive, etc.
If that were so, it would follow that [the property] belongs to space as well; thus, it is not a quality of space.
Furthermore, although cotton and the like have the earth as their locus, they reside in space, yet that residence is not caused by space because they are supported by the wind.
Since sound is also like this, it does not have space as its quality.

For instance, there is no hearing of sound elsewhere when it is impelled by the wind; since the wind itself is its substratum, what need is there for this assumption of something else? Just as, indeed—

Just as cotton and the like, being supported by the wind, do not possess the quality of being the wind itself, so it is with sound. For example: "Just as cotton is impelled through the sky by the wind, does anyone who knows sound ever perceive the sound moving against the wind? (120) Now, it might be argued that sound simply cannot be impelled by the wind because there is no conjunction between a quality and its substrate.
However, there is no contradiction regarding cotton because it possesses the nature of earth;
otherwise, even shadow, sunlight, and so forth would be set in motion,
for movement belongs only to a substance that serves as their substratum.
Let it be impelled.

If it is argued that [the sound] is impelled by the wind through the relation of inherence in a conjunct [substance], this hypothesis is also not tenable; for how could there be an impelling of space (*viyat*) in the case of sound?
(121) The Fourth Daily Lesson is concluded.

Furthermore, if space were thus impelled, it would no longer be inactive; moreover, for that which is all-pervading, such an impelling is extremely difficult to establish. (122) Moreover, if impulsion is desired to occur through inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), why does it not occur through mere inherence (*samavāya*)? Or rather, [why does it not occur] in the case of that which is inherent in the air (*vāyu*)? (123)
Let sound have the quality of air itself, since it travels to another location by means of that [air].
If it is argued that air has only touch as its quality, we reply:
there is no rule that a substance must possess only a single quality.
If it is argued that, according to the established tenets of others, earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch,

and it is observed that even a quality such as smell is impelled by the wind, and that in that case too the impulsion occurs precisely through the inherence [of the smell] in the earth which is conjoined [with the wind];
Since there is no perception of earth when that [wind] is perceived,
what contradiction is there in its being produced from that [earth] alone and then impelled by the wind?
If it is argued that this is because a quality (*guṇa*) is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*),
then that very state of being devoid of action is not established in the case of solitary impelling;
and if it is argued that even the state of possessing action is unestablished in the case of combined impelling—
If it is asked how a quality can possess activity, given that the impelling of a conjoined entity is unestablished;
This is another fault of his.

If, in some treatise, qualities such as "being a quality" are denied because they are illogical, then even what is logical here would not be accepted; that would be a royal decree! Furthermore, there is no such thing as "impelling" for things that perish in their own place, nor is there any so-called "activity" for a perishing entity.
What is the use of the quality of producing a similar moment in another location? Why is sound not considered by others to move like a wave upon water?
Moreover, a possessor of qualities is not perceived as distinct from the qualities themselves; for what else is perceived apart from touch and the other [sensory objects]?

(127) And if odor is drawn along by the wind together with the earth through the relation of inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), [then it would follow that the wind possesses smell].
Sound, too, is simply a quality of earth and the other elements;
therefore, let it be drawn along with earth and the rest—what is the use of postulating space?
(3) This is the refutation of the elemental nature of space.
Furthermore, let it be granted that earth and the other elements are so designated by virtue of their functions such as supporting; but how is space [defined]?
If you say that space is also [so called] because it provides room, then what is this so-called "providing room"?
There is no obstruction to their persistence;
since earth and the other elements obstruct one another’s location,
there must therefore be some other great element, such as space (*ākāśa*), by means of which their persistence is maintained.
That is space, and that too is whatever it may be;
for instance:

If there is the existence of another great element [within it], there is no obstruction to its persistence; even in the absence of one another, there is no obstruction to their persistence. (128) In the absence of one great element, another great element persists. Let space be defined as merely the absence of other great elements. (129) But where would another great element, such as air and so forth, reside if space does not exist?
Now, if space were not another great element, where would space itself abide? This would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If you argue that space is by nature without a support while being the support for something else, then air must likewise be by nature without a support while being the support for something else; thus, the postulation of a distinct entity [for space] is not tenable.
Moreover, how could space not be the support for a clod of earth as it falls nowhere? And how can there be a movement [of space] when the air is the support of the sky?

(130) If it is argued that the air prevents the obstruction of the wind’s movement, this is no answer; for the absence of obstruction to movement is simply the state of being devoid of an obstructing agent. (131)

Now, if space—which is all-pervading and eternal—is supported by something else, how can it be without a support? Yet, for another [element], it is the supporter. (132) This same state of being all-pervading and formless applies to the self as well. Why, then, is its status as a support not postulated with respect to that [other element]? (133)
For one for whom such a self does not exist, what function could there be with space?
Since the directions are also pervasive, let their function be understood as that of space.
When there is mutual pervasion, would the all-pervasive entities not become one?
[Objection: But surely the conventional usage "space is light" does not apply to the self and so forth; how then can there be identity?
[Reply: If one follows conventional usage, then the conceptualization of entities must necessarily correspond to that usage;
for space is nothing other than an aperture.

And in the absence of one who acts as a "maker of no-holes" (acchidrakāraka), there would be no conventional usage [of the term "space"]; and when those who act as makers of no-holes exist, where has space gone?
For it is not said that space moves to the side or into a crevice; and in their absence, where has space gone—to that place or elsewhere? It has gone nowhere.
If it is argued that if [the self] were destroyed, then eternal existence would be excellent, let it remain exactly so.
And the statement that "space is without fissure" is contradicted;
for otherwise, that very entity could not even exist.
Now, what is this "existence"?
Is it the state of being maintained, or the state of not being obstructed?
If it is the state of being maintained, [then...]
That is incorrect;
for jars and other objects are not supported by space, but rather by the earth.
(Now,) as for "non-injury":
That too is untrue, because [it] is perceived.

2B Because of its non-existence; 3B Here, [the phrase] "upaghāta" (injury) [is used]; since for each [object] there is an injury, by the absence of that [object], that [injury] belongs to it. But there is no injury from space; indeed, [to claim otherwise] would be clearly like chewing the air. 135

Therefore, space is said to be the absence of the four elements; there is no valid cognition for its existence in any other great element, though it is used in conventional discourse. (136) By this, the [existence of] direction is also explained away.
Even for that [space], there can be no granting of room and so forth when it is all-pervasive;

for, by virtue of being all-pervasive, there is the cognition of "west" and so on, but not otherwise. There is no other motion for it, because that would entail the consequence of its non-existence. (137)
If space is all-pervasive, then it is that very same [space] which is "east"; how then could there be a "west" for one situated elsewhere?
If it were to possess both natures in that case, then the consequence would follow that both cognitions [of east and west] would arise simultaneously.
Now, since there is no specific manifestor [for each state], some particular state of space would be manifested, yet not every state [would be so].
For instance, even though the essential nature of a father or son possesses both the form of "father" and the form of "son," the manifestation of "fatherhood" occurs only in relation to "sonhood."

The manifestation of a person as a son and so forth with respect to his father and so forth is likewise unreal, because the manifestation of a state or a direction is restricted to what is other than itself; for it is precisely from that [other] that the states of entities arise, just like "prior" and so forth. (138)

Since it is precisely in relation to persons situated in eastern and western regions that one direction is designated as "eastern" and so forth for the other, why is it not accepted that this [distinction] belongs to the entities themselves?

Because persons and the like are situated in an eastern region, that region is "eastern" in relation to another region, and that [region] in turn is [eastern] in relation to the sun and so forth; what is the use of postulating a separate "direction"?
It is by the sun and such that direction is manifested.
And by that, the eastwardness and so forth of the sun would be established; this, however, is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Since worldly convention is well-established by that much alone, what is the point of the laborious conceptualization of depending on something else?
Now, one might argue that direction is indeed a distinct category of entity because it exists as "straight" even without depending on anything else;
however, that too is untrue, because:

Even in that case, there is the perception [of it] as straight due to a difference in perspective; through extreme habituation, there is subsequently such a cognition even without another [cognition].
For instance, the worldly convention "this is straight for you" is observed;
thus, through extreme habituation, there is subsequently a following of that [straightness] even without dependence [on another cognition].
Whence is this [known]?
Because the cognition of the relationship between cause and effect elsewhere also occurs through the conformity to the presence and absence of that [cause];
for instance:
When situated in the middle of the ocean, confusion arises for men; however, the determination of the divisions of the directions occurs through the observation of planets and constellations.

(140) The direction is not perceived as something distinct merely from its connection with the constellations and so forth. For if its own nature does not manifest, how can its cognition be described? (141)
For instance,
the notion "this is the eastern direction" resides solely in the mind as coinciding with the rising of the sun;

indeed, even when the sun is seen otherwise, for those whose minds are subject to confusion regarding the directions, that very direction previously characterized as the east appears as such, not by virtue of the sun's rising.
For even the rising of the sun appears as if it were leaning toward the western direction;

regarding this, it is said: "That very direction in which the setting [of the sun] was observed by one whose mind is unerring and free from attachment is the one well-practiced as 'west' there, characterized by villages, groves, and so forth. (142)

That very garden, village, and so forth, which was previously perceived continuously as being characterized by directions such as "north" in relation to the rising of the sun and other such markers— that very direction, though it does not conform to the subsequent rising of the sun due to the force of habituation (*abhyāsa*), is nevertheless designated in conventional usage because of the attachment to a firm latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Therefore...

2. This reading, which serves as a supplement to the deficiency, has been placed outside the main line: "Due to the abandonment of the Self, which is like the sun, for those whose minds are confronted by the attachment of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), these [notions] are merely cognitions alone, because of the absence of an object of cognition.
(143) Indeed, even one whose mind is utterly exhausted by the effort of intense concentration does not perceive the true nature of the directions and so forth.

But the world, its true nature being unascertained, acts in such a manner due to a lack of reflective discernment and because its mind is led by the principle of following what has come before; what can we do about this?
For since it is beginningless, even if [the world] were real, there is no reality in this [worldly convention] either.

Why is it that even for some, such as the conceptualization of a creator god (*īśvara*) and so forth, there is no beginning or end? Therefore, this established status of directions and so on is a mere conventional arrangement; it is nothing more than a worldly convention arrived at through the study of the treatises.
If treatises were beginningless, it would not follow that all of them are true, because they contradict one another and stand in a relationship of the sublated and the sublator.
Therefore, the elders established conventions such as "prior" and "subsequent" for the sake of linguistic usage regarding objects themselves, based on their mutual dependence;
or else, due to the beginninglessness of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the very prior usage was awakened and thus employed in such a manner.
Vyavahārayati (4)(5): Refutation of Time.
And that very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva), when designated through its distinctions, receives the names of time and so forth; for instance,
the determination of the past, present, and future times of Devadatta and others arises from such cognitions as "he was," "he is," and "he will be."
Furthermore, from the statement "there was a time" (*āsīt sakāla*) and so forth, it follows that even time must abide within another time, which leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now,
if it is argued that time is prior by its very nature and not in dependence upon another time—
and that the same applies to space as well— then [the following holds].
Just as there is such a designation based on the distinction of a dharma that constitutes its very nature— as in "the eastern direction is Indra's"— so too,
objects such as trees possess eastwardness by themselves, and not in dependence upon an eastwardness relative to another time or location.
Now, time and so forth do not possess priority and the like inherently; rather, they do so in relation to the objects with which they are connected.
For instance, those kings who have passed away long ago [are designated as such] in dependence upon their connection with those [objects].
"The determination that 'this time is long past' is established therein.
To this it is replied:
"If the pastness of time results from its connection with a past entity, then that pastness of the entity would necessarily depend upon that [past] time. (147–148)
Because they would be mutually dependent, neither could be established; if their pastness were simultaneous, there would be an infinite regress.

(149) Two things that arise simultaneously cannot be causes for one another. If it is argued that those two [arise] from something else, then for that [third thing] as well, and thus there is an infinite regress. (150) Furthermore:
If sound is a quality of space,
touch is a quality of air,
and form is a quality of fire.
It must simply be stated that taste is a quality of water, smell is a quality of earth, and "ka" is a quality of space.
Likewise,
if the magnitude and so forth belong to time, then some specific property must be stated for the self and other [categories] as well, based on that.
Now, regarding the restriction and permission of things,
these arise solely from the force of their causes through positive and negative concomitance;
and since those [causes] also arise from their own causes, there is an infinite succession of time.
Moreover,
2 B. the cause.

If the power of the eternal and pervasive [Self] to obstruct or permit were also attained by the soul, then there would be no difference between it and that which is not desired [as the Self]. For instance: [151] Thus:
Time, space, the self, and ether—these are similar in their eternity and so forth;
therefore, since they occupy the same location and time and are devoid of activity, how can one who knows the distinction between them say, "this was done by this one, and not by that one"? (152)
Therefore, the doctrine that space exists is indeed non-existent;
consequently, the quality of sound belonging to space is not supported by any means of valid cognition.
Furthermore:
Since sound originates from both space and air, why is it not said to be a quality of air?
Because its audition occurs in space alone, it is therefore established as a quality of the ether (vyoman).
[Objection: A flame and the like are not seen to reside in space; how then can that [quality of being perceived there] be stated as its [space's] quality?
It is also incorrect to say that anything else is its substratum; for then the drum and other such things would also be the substratum of sound.

If it were argued that whatever is perceived as being located in something is a quality of that thing, then why is flame and the like not a quality of space? Since those too are perceived as being located in space, they would not be qualities of space. Furthermore, since there are other substrata for them, such as walls and wood, they are not qualities of space simply because they are perceived as being located therein.
That is incorrect;
if it resides in both, let it possess the qualities of both—
then why are the drum, the conch, and so forth not also the substrata of sound?
If it is argued that [the light] is heard of in another location, this is equally true for light and so forth;
and if it is argued that it is perceived even in its substrate, such as a jewel, [we reply: the same applies here.
This is the same even regarding the sound of a substance being boiled;
therefore, sound is not a quality of space,
because it is perceived where it is located, just like light located there.
Nor does space possess the quality of being a support, because it is non-obstructive;
space is formless, invisible, and non-obstructive.
Space is known when there is light, for space is designated wherever there is light; thus, space is that which possesses the designation.
Therefore, the statement that "sound is a quality of space" is not well-said;
consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in refuting its being a quality of space.
Otherwise, the word "itself" (svayam) would be redundant.
Furthermore,
the word "itself" (*svayam*)— which falls outside the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*)— is itself meaningless;
for since the word "itself" serves only to exclude what is intended by the author of the treatise as being established through the acceptance of that treatise, it is redundant here.
If it has no other purpose, and if that [purpose] were also something to be accomplished, then it would be utterly futile.
If that were the case, since it would not conform to the definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*), why would there even be this doubt regarding the purpose of engaging with one's own desire in the treatises?
[Reply: Who can prevent him from grasping what has not been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
If he has been refuted by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), by whom can he be made to proceed [toward that conclusion]?
Previously, too, he adopted this doctrine solely by his own whim; why should he not be able to adopt another one later? (73–74)
If that practitioner, acting with foresight, perceives something else [as the cause], then investigation alone is the cause for his acceptance of the treatise.

Consequently, how can there be the possibility of instigating desire [to act] on the grounds that the scriptures themselves contain the term "svayam" (by oneself) for the sake of engaging in activity?

Furthermore, not every scripture is capable of withstanding critical examination; therefore, since [the scripture] is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), activity proceeds only from what is purified [of error]. How, then, could the instigation of desire be possible?
For this reason:
2B. Those who perform actions preceded by reflection do not proceed merely out of desire; for deliberation is the first step for wise men.
If, however, one acts without prior reflection, then his mere desire is the cause; his initial undertaking is impelled by that alone.
Then, just as it was for him, so it shall be for the second and the third;
for that purpose, this instruction is given—if he does not desire it, let him simply be instructed.
|| 157 || Let him be instructed.

If the principle that a treatise is to be accepted according to one's own desire is stated by your own words, then—just as before—this too must be accepted by you solely through desire.
