In that case, it is logical to accept [the treatise] only after investigation; mere desire is no refuge here. Such a view of logic is reasonable and stands in opposition to the operation of arbitrary desire. Therefore, if the goal is to be established on the basis of what is seen in a treatise, accepting it arbitrarily is indeed improper.

In that case, even when establishing a desired object for oneself, if no one were to proceed [with an argument] there once they have abandoned the meaning of the treatise due to sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and if one proceeds by one's own will simply because there is no sublation,
what is the purpose of including the term "oneself" (*svayam*)?

In this regard, he himself provided a rebuttal to the various misconceptions regarding perception, demonstrating that [the opponent's position] results in the loss of scripture, the impossibility of establishing what is desired, and infinite regress. (75)
For the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, the entire treatise [is devoted to this]; therefore, here too, that which is established by the treatise is the probandum (*sādhya*).
If one asks by what logic the dispelling of misconceptions occurs, it is by demonstrating the undesired loss of the intended object, the impossibility of being a probandum, and infinite regress.
For there is no impairment of what is desired when there is sublation by what is seen in the scriptures;

furthermore, the logical principle— that even if something is not an essential concomitant (*anāntarīyaka*), it cannot be the probandum, and that if it were so proven despite not being an essential concomitant, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)— is demonstrated by the inclusion of the word "itself" (*svayam*).

Therefore, this [objection] is invalid; for another [author] himself stated the word "himself" (*svayam*) in order to apprehend a subject (*dharmin*) that is well-known, by excluding any distinction imposed by convention. (76)

The term "svayaṃ" (itself) is used so that there may be the inclusion of a subject (*dharmin*) which is established by itself—excluding that subject for whom a distinction characterized as being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) has been constructed by a treatise (*śāstra*), and which has not been established by the author of the treatise.
For instance,

that which is itself established as a subject (*dharmin*)— and not established by another— is the subject, and nothing else; thus, this [conclusion] is established by implication, yet it is incorrect.
For,
by the very commencement of this inquiry, the locus (*āśraya*) is established as proven,
since there is no dispute regarding categories whose distinctions are imagined according to one's own will. (77)

For an investigation (*vicāra*), being conducted upon some subject (*dharmin*) in the form of "permanent" or "impermanent" and so forth, is performed upon that which already exists in an established form. However, regarding that whose very nature is yet to be proven, let that [nature] itself first be investigated, because a proof is impossible when the subject is unestablished.
Now, if the nature of sound is indeed established, then that alone should be taken as the subject (*dharmin*);
what is the use of taking a subject with an unestablished qualification?
Now, this [argument] of one who speaks according to his desire in such a manner is intended to prove impermanence, but it is invalid because:

Because the listener has no intention regarding that [quality], and because it is therefore not established for him, the statement of the probandum as being endowed with the quality of space is futile. (158) For those who act with foresight, the employment of words is never purposeless;
yet, the opponent does not intend "impermanence" to be qualified by its being a quality of space.
Nor can that which is not intended be established by a mere thesis alone;

for in that case, it would follow that "sound is non-eternal because it is a product" could be established as having the quality of non-space, or any other desired object whatsoever, provided only that it is so pleasing to the proponent. If this were indeed the case, then...
That being so, who could prevent such a person— who is devoid of discernment and impelled by mere desire—
from grasping the meaning? Thus says the *He*.
Therefore, this is incorrect;
for by the very statement that "the subject (dharmin) must be indicated by its own nature," the impossibility of proving [it] through a prophetic declaration is already addressed. 78
For if a statement were possible in the form of a proven fact (*siddhasādhana*),
then the rule that "it must be stated only as something yet to be proven" (*sādhyatvena*) would be fruitful. || 79 ||
Or rather, it might be explained by the proponent as follows: "space."
The subject (*dharmin*) is not to be proven in its own nature,
because of the statement that it is already established by itself;
otherwise, for what purpose would its qualification by the word "itself" produce any result?
For it is thus:
a statement is not intended merely to establish the existence of the subject (*dharmin*), since that is already established by the very context of the inquiry;
therefore, it is something already established and not something to be proven (*sādhya*).
Therefore, in order to negate its status as the probandum (*sādhya*), he himself stated that the subject (*dharmin*) is not the probandum.

That too is incorrect, because there is no such person among those possessed of discernment who would prove what is already established; for how could one, having already accepted that [fact], then lead it to the status of being a probandum? (159)
In that case, the statement "by its very nature" is redundant,
because it is precisely the unestablished subject under investigation that constitutes the probandum;
for indeed, that which is unestablished does not become a locus of dispute.
Likewise,
because the reason is stated regarding what is doubtful, that which is excluded is not a locus for the reason;
the same applies to the investigation.

Likewise, it is stated here that even the term "established" (*siddha*) is used for the purpose of grasping the essential nature (*svarūpa*); for it is not intended to exclude what is already established, since its purpose is to exclude that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) while being designated as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
For this very reason, only the restriction "by its own nature alone" has been established as fruitful;
otherwise, both [the affirmation and the restriction] would have had to be established separately.
Why, then, was it stated that [the fallacy] takes the form of proving what is already established?

It should be explained as follows: [it occurs] when the subject (*dharmin*), though unestablished, is presented in an established form, and likewise when the property (*dharma*) is presented in the form of a probans (*sādhana*).
And that indication in its established form refers either to the subject alone, as in "the self is the inherent cause," or as a qualification of the subject,
as in "sound, which is a quality of space, is impermanent";
for where there is a qualification of the subject, it is expressed by the statement, "sound, which is a quality of space, is impermanent."
How is it understood that impermanence does not constitute the quality of being a property of space?
Is it that whatever sound is impermanent is a property of space, or that whatever is a property of space is impermanent?
This too must be understood from the context.
And although sound is common [to both], it has been explained accordingly;

how then [is it said] that "sound is audible"? This shows what is to be excluded by the apprehension of its own nature (*svarūpa*); for if it were for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), that would be improper.
This is true;
nevertheless, it was stated [by the opponent] by accepting that what is intended for one purpose may also serve another purpose, thinking:
"Even if it were to accomplish [the goal], there is no fault because the mention of its own form (svarūpa) serves as a differentiator."
How can there be the attainment [of an object] for that which has been refuted? For a dispute is observed regarding that point, and we shall demonstrate this later.
Furthermore, it has been described that inference has the universal (sāmānya) as its object.
In this case, even if it were not stated thus, nothing would be contradicted regarding the thesis (pakṣa).
For it has been established by the Master that inference has the universal (sāmānya) as its object;
and neither the subject (dharmin) nor anything else distinct from it is being proven as a particular, but rather as a universal.
Therefore, even if the subject (*dharmin*) has not been excluded from being the probandum (*sādhya*) by the inclusion of the word "itself" (*svayam*), there is nevertheless no fault,
because it is excluded precisely as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
moreover—
If one were to make the subject (*dharmin*) itself the probandum (*sādhya*), what would follow from that?
Why is it not possible? Because of the absence of the logical reason’s positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Indeed, this is a fault belonging to those two [the reason and the example]. (81)

But surely this defect of those two depends upon the subsequent members [of the syllogism] and is not considered a defect of the thesis; likewise, it would follow that a defect of the reason and so forth would also be a defect of the thesis. (82)
Because [the reason] is sublated by all [members] of the side (*pakṣa*), therefore [it is a fallacy] for one who possesses that as the sole mark (*liṅga*).
*saṅginaḥ*—thus H. and B.)
Other faults are not considered [to be defects of the thesis], just like contradictions with perception and so forth.
(83) Now, [one might object]:
The definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is: "that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), and which is not refuted by contradictory facts.
In this regard, if one were to make the subject (*dharmin*) itself the probandum, what fault would there be?
However, the subject cannot be proven, because a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not something that can be proven.
For if the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) were the probandum, there would be no proof of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because the reason lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that particularity;
therefore, the reason itself would be incapable in that case, as it lacks an illustrative example (*adṛṣṭāntatvāt*).
Therefore, it is not logical to say that the fault belongs to one thing and the fault belongs to another;
for if this were so, then even this [fault] would be a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself, because it renders the thesis unestablished (*asiddhi*).
In that case, every fault of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*) would become a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*).
Because of that defect, the thesis itself would be unfit for proof;

however, in a case where another probans capable of proving it is possible—such as "sound is impermanent"—there may be a defect in the probans, as in the argument "because it is visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*). For in such a case, there is no defect consisting in the thesis being unfit for proof, since it is established by means of another probans.
However, where there is no reason whatsoever [to prove it], that is a defect of the thesis;
for one's intended meaning must be demonstrated by the statement of the thesis.

Just as it is not possible [for that] because of contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*), so too it is not possible even in the case of being a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, this is indeed a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*). This is the logical principle (*nyāya*). To this, it is replied:
Is this impossibility of the thesis (pakṣa) relative to the reason (hetu), or is it inherent in the thesis itself? Both of these [alternatives] are untenable.

(160) If this defect arises from its connection with the reason, then the fault belongs to the reason itself. However, this is not an inherent defect [of the thesis], because it is established by perception (darśana). (161)
If the state of being an Arhat were not established by its very nature, and it were argued that it is therefore not established even by perception— let alone by inference—
then that defect belongs to inference itself.
For this very reason, even if the subject (*dharmin*) is already established, if it were to be made the probandum (*sādhya*), there too it would be nothing but a fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*),
because the reason lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in that case as well.

The fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) occurs when [the object] is established by inference; that is indeed a fault of the subject (*pakṣadoṣa*). However, when [the object] is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) established by perception, it is a fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Even in that case, if it is the self (*ātman*) itself that is established by perception, then there is a fault of the subject characterized as proving what is already established for both [the proponent and the opponent].
Therefore, even from the perspective of the opponent, that which is established for oneself by inference is the "subject" (*pakṣa*) for the other;
however, that which is established by scripture is not a subject at all, just like that which is established by direct perception.
Now, if the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is not established by perception, it cannot be the subject (pakṣa) due to a fault in the reason;
but if it is established by scripture (āgama), how can the universal (sāmānya) be the object of that scripture?
Furthermore, since there is indeed a positive concomitance (anvaya) with respect to the universal, how can this be a fault of the subject?

But has this not already been stated? Why then is it not a defect of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) rather than a defect of the reason (hetudoṣa)? Because it occurs only when that [reason] is present; and in this case, such occurrence-only-when-that-is-present exists.
For instance:
"If this [object] is established by scripture, what is the purpose of a logical reason? But if it is established by scripture, how can there be establishment by scripture [through a reason]? (162)
Furthermore, it is also incorrect to say that although [the reason] is unestablished for the opponent, it is established for oneself on the basis of scripture;
for:
If the authority of scripture is established even for the opponent, then it is established for both; however, if scripture lacks authority, it is unestablished for both.
Therefore, the thesis must be established by inference for oneself alone.

Objection: Is it not the case that fire, even though established by perception, does not fail to be the subject (*pakṣa*) for another person? Response: No, because it is not a subject in that particular form [of being unestablished].
For this subject (pakṣa) is established by perception only in its general form, not in its specific form;
however, it is not established by perception in its own essential nature (svarūpa).
Therefore, it is established that there is no inference whatsoever regarding what is already established by perception.
If this is so, then this is like inserting a goitre through the eye and having it emerge elsewhere;
for if there is no inference regarding what is established by perception, then there is all the less so when it is not so established,
since inference is preceded by perception.
Likewise, since perception does not operate even regarding the object of inference, how could a thesis be sublated by perception?
Furthermore, what is called "sublation" (bādhana) is not the physical destruction of an object, but rather the communication that it does not exist;
and since every negation whatsoever is due to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), sublation by inference is itself a form of sublation by non-apprehension.
And so it has been said:
because that would contradict its having non-existence as its object.
In that regard, "perceptuality" is stated [as a definition], since it has been said that inference is preceded by perception.

In that regard, it is not the case that [inference] is preceded by perception regarding a universal object; rather, where a universal such as "fire-ness" is the probandum (*sādhya*), and perception does not have that particular instance as its object, there inference does not operate, because inference is preceded by a perception that has operated upon that particular instance. But if perception does function with respect to the universal, what is the use of inference there?
That very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when being established by means of inference, would assume the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*);
for a particular characteristic itself becomes a universal when it is not perceived as a distinct particular.

This is precisely the meaning: that which is the object of perception does not become perception itself when it is being cognized by means of inference, and that which is being cognized by means of inference is not perception itself.
Therefore, that [fire] is apprehended through perception; for fire is indeed apprehended through perception in the kitchen and so forth.
Thus, the meaning here is this: a thesis is sublated by perception when it is already established by perception.
Since perception operates toward the manifestation of that [particular] and its opposite,
where there is no manifestation, the universal is simply impossible there, because a universal is manifested by a particular.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that in the case of the [proposition] "sound is not audible," the subject (*pakṣa*) is indeed the negation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And in the case of the refutation of a negation, the refutation would be understood as pertaining to that very object which is being negated, because anything else would not be contradictory to it.
In this regard:
3. B. frequents 4. B.
Surely, how can perception be refuted by inference? For it is not the object of inference, nor is it the object of verbal testimony.
For this very reason, the view that [the subject] is devoid of form and expresses a relation is refuted;
or rather, there is no fault because of the identification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object as one.
Therefore, there is no defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) consisting in the fact that an already established subject (*dharmin*) is being treated as something to be proven (*sādhya*).

In that case, because the fault belongs solely to the reason (*hetu*), that which is a fault due to a defect in the reason is not a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*); for such a fault is already excluded by the very definition of the reason itself.
Furthermore, what has been excluded by the definition of the reason need not also be excluded by the definition of the thesis.
Because it is purposeless and because it lacks an object,
[it is] connected.

Setting aside that which is sublated by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated for the purpose of avoiding [the faults of] non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and exclusion (*vyatireka*).
Having set aside the fault already excluded by the definitions of the reason and the example, the definition of the thesis is stated in order to avoid other faults.
Since the entire definition is intended solely to avoid the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*vyatireka*),
and because the presence of under-extension or over-extension would still occur in a definition even if a fault not already excluded by another definition were not excluded,
let the definition be just this much; what is the use of anything else?
If that which was performed for a certain purpose is rendered useless because it has been accomplished by another means, then for what reason is the term "by oneself" (svayaṃ) included?
[Objection: Why then is there a refutation of non-pervasion (avyāpti) and exclusion (vyatireka) here?
To this we reply:
The mention of "itself" (*svayam*) and "verbal expression" (*rupākhyā*) serves to exclude the case of deviation (*vyatireka*).
Furthermore, the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*), when not excluded by [the word] "together with" (*saha*), prevents the fault of over-extension (*avyāpti*).
By this much alone, the definition is complete; what need is there for anything else?
If the word "itself" (*svayam*) were not employed, there would be the undesirable consequence that even what is intended by the author of the treatise would become the probandum (*sādhya*).
If the particle [“itself”] were not used, then for that which is indicated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) yet remains unestablished,
and for the subject (*dharmin*) which is already established, there would be the risk of it being taken as the probandum in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*) if [the word “itself”] were not used.
But there is no other fault [in that case]; therefore, the inclusion of the term "self" (svayam) is useless, since it serves to exclude a non-fault.
For what purpose, then, is the inclusion of the term "not rejected" (anirākṛta)?

If it is argued that even if something has been refuted, were someone to nevertheless establish it as the probandum (*sādhya*), there would still be a fault in the reason (*hetu*) because it would be refuted by that very same [refutation], we say:
no.
The meaning is that [the absence of the reason in the dissimilar instance] is sublated by the fact that it is not excluded from the similar instance (*sahānirākṛta*).

For it might be argued: "Without the term 'not excluded' (*anirākṛta*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be sublated, because that very defect is already sublated by the definition of a valid reason itself."
Because it occurs only in the [subject] side, that reason is not faulty.

If even that which is desired is excluded from being a thesis, for what purpose then is the term "desired" (iṣṭa) included? To this he says: "The mention of 'desired' excludes over-extension; for it is not intended that only that which is [explicitly] rejected is [automatically] excluded."
Because it is possible for the object of pervasion to exist even when it has not been excluded;
or else,

because of the statement that "the mention of what is intended [as the subject] excludes non-pervasion," it follows that the term has the sense of pervasion, and thus even that which is excluded would be pervaded.
Regarding this, he says:

"If the term 'contradicted' (*nirākṛta*) were not employed [along with 'simultaneous' (*saha*)], then that [contradiction] too would be subject to pervasion because of the inclusion of the word 'intended' (*iṣṭa*). Why, then, is there no possibility [of such a contradiction] in the terms 'simultaneous' and 'contradicted'?"

Therefore, if even an object perceived in the treatises (*śāstra*) is to be proven, then it is already established by this very definition alone— which is itself devoid of the word "self" (*svayam*)— so what is the use of anything else in that regard?

The definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of what is to be proven (*sādhya*). Among those [cases], there is non-thesis-status (*apakṣatā*) in the case of the sublated, due to contradiction; and in the remaining cases, due to the non-application of the definition.
This is the true nature of the matter here.
The meaning is that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of what is to be proven (*sādhya*).

If the acceptance were [defined merely as] the acceptance of even those things that have been refuted and so forth, then they too would possess the status of a thesis; therefore, [the definition specifies] "not refuted," because [those things] are sublated (*bādhana*).
And because the definition itself does not apply to the remainder—namely, to those that are unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth—the definition operates only where it is intended and nowhere else.
This [objection] is incorrect.
What is established by this? If you say it is the establishment of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), then what is it that is to be enjoined here?
Therefore,
since that which is to be enjoined has already been established,
the claim that the conclusion refers back to the proponent’s own admission— which was stated for the purpose of proving what was unestablished— is not well-founded.
For where this meaning has already been established in the statement "this is its meaning," what is the use of a conclusion?
(This is the definition of a *vārttika*.
Others, however, say:
This is indeed the Vārttikakāra’s own composition defining the thesis (*pakṣa*); for such is the definition of a *vārttika*:
"the pointing out of an inconsistency in the sūtras, the refutation thereof, and the statement of a specific [qualification]."
This specific qualification is also untenable;

for if it means "that which is accepted as the probandum," then the undesirable consequence remains unavoidable that even what is intended by the author of the treatise as a means of proof would be included.

Now, as for the claim that it is known "by way of being the probandum" (sādhyatvena), and that there is no desire [to prove] it as a probandum because it is desired as a means of proof (sādhanatvena)—
that too is incorrect.
It is indeed accepted as being the probandum (*sādhya*);
however, if it is determined that it is accepted *only* as the probandum,
then this [specification] is for the purpose of excluding that which has been accepted as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
Even that which is not explicitly stated would become the probandum (sādhya) if it were merely pervaded by the [proponent's] desire;
furthermore, if the "subject" (pakṣa) were defined as that which is accepted as being the probandum,
then even that which is accepted as a means of proof (sādhana) would possess the status of a subject if it were accepted as being the probandum.

For at that time, there is no impossibility of both [occurring]; nor is this the governing rule of a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), since it would apply even to what is desired by the authors of the treatises, as that too is accepted therein.
Alternatively, by virtue of proximity, it is the proponent alone who accepts [the application].
That too is incorrect,

because even what is intended by the authors of the treatises is accepted by the proponent; furthermore, why is it not accepted that [the probans is established] by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and logical necessity (*nyāya*)?
Since a proximity established by the intellect (*buddhi*) also occurs in the case of those desired by the authors of treatises,
there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding proximity; furthermore, [the reason] would apply even to that which is rejected, because the thesis (*sādhya*) is accepted [by the proponent].

[Objection: "But surely, since there is no acceptance of a probandum (*sādhya*) when it has been refuted by sublation (*bādhana*), one ought not to employ a means of proof (*sādhana*) for such a probandum. [Reply: This too is incorrect;
for in this way, even the definition "the statement of the probandum is the thesis (*pratijñā*)" would be faultless.
And how could one who follows mere definitions be a knower of the distinction between what is worthy and what is unworthy?
Therefore, this is incorrect;
rather, this is the definition of the position [presented] in the *Nyāyamukha*.
Regarding the statement, "The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) and is not refuted by a contradictory meaning," it is said here:
if there were a sublater (*bādhikā*) of the distinction [of the thesis] from its own form, the particles, and the verbal expression.
He asks: "How can there be a sublation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by means of the *Nyāyamukha* statement 'this exists'?
He replies with the words "admission of the probandum" (*sādhyābhyupagama*), etc.
Even in that case, since [the probandum] has been refuted by way of sublation, there is no fault because the definition does not apply to the remainder.
The term *īpsita* (desired) expresses the past tense through the suffix *niṣṭhā*; it does not apply to that which is desired precisely as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Therefore, its exclusion [from the definition of the object] is already established, and thus there is no fault.

If this is so, then since the word *iṣṭa* (desired) is used here as well, the exclusion [of the means] occurs by way of presenting it as a means (*sādhana*); consequently, the statement regarding the particle (*nipāta*) would be purposeless.
2B. Why is this said? This is true;
for even when the meaning is already understood through the statement itself, the restriction is explicitly expressed by its own name.
Because of the connection with the end of the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*), it is stated [in the verse] that there is a "cutting off" of another time:

"If it were not connected with the primary element at the end of the gerundive suffix, then the phrase 'desired by oneself' would serve to exclude what is desired at another time; but since such a connection does exist, [the restriction applies]. (87)
If it were the case that even that which has been made the object of a desire at a later time would possess the status of a *pakṣa* (the subject of inquiry),
then the mention of the particle *eva* in the *Nyāyamukha* must be made for the purpose of excluding that;
to this, it is replied:
In this context, because the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used with the verb *iṣ* preceded by the prefix *an-aṅgam*, that which is intended as the object (*īpsita*) is again [specified];
thus, by that [suffix], it is the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) and so forth that are excluded as being the very "limb" (*aṅga*).
Here, in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is to be indicated as that which ends in a *kṛtya* suffix and possesses primacy.
Of what nature is it?
It is desired;
therefore, there is conformity with a subsequent time.

For example, in the expression "Devadatta, having arrived, is to be seen," the restriction [implied by the gerundive] is for the purpose of excluding other times; however, in this case, the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not a factor for the verb *iṣ*, whereas in the word expressing what is desired (*īpsita*), it is indeed a factor.

The relationship [of the word] being separated [from its primary object] means that while in the case of the desired term (*īpsita-pada*) it is not a subordinate factor (*anaṅga*), here, however, it must be explained as being indeed a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).
Alternatively, here in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, [the word "desired"] is not an essential factor for expressing the past tense; however, in the *Nyāyamukha*, it is indeed an essential factor,
since by that very determination, fallacious reasons (*asiddhahetu*) and the like are excluded.

Therefore, since the non-mentioning of "fallacy" (nipāta) there [in the definition] implies that the subject (*dharmin*) is not the probandum (*sādhya*), the inclusion of the word "itself" (*svayam*) is not for the purpose of excluding the subject from being the probandum.
Nor is it a limb [of the path] for the sake of engaging with the scriptures through desire, according to the reasoning previously stated.
Furthermore, because it lacks expressive power, it is illogical for that [object] to be desired by itself through its own nature.
Without depending on any treatise whatsoever, that which is desired by him [the proponent] is what is to be proven. (89) 1 M.
*tadvādīṣṭasya*

Since the term "himself" (*svayam*) is redundant—given that wherever something is to be praised in a treatise, the subject (*dharmin*) is already established by itself—it is improper [to use it] as a synonym for "by himself" (i.e., by the author). Therefore, "by himself" means "by himself [the proponent], not by another commentator. Consequently, without depending on the entire treatise, that which is desired by him [the proponent] is the probandum (*sādhya*).

Therefore, even when there is a sublation of a desired [property] that is conjoined with what is undesired, the thesis and the reason are not defective because the [intended] probandum remains unsublated. Thus, even if there is a sublation of what is conjoined with what is desired by the author of the treatise, there is no fault in the thesis or the reason, because the sublation exceeds the mere probandum itself.
Even if there were another fault, the mere pointing out of what is not a fault [would still be a problem];
indeed, if one subverts what is desired by the authors of the treatises, what is the use of that which has been established, since it results in the loss of one's confidence?
This has been stated here.

Even if one thinks "something [is better]," furthermore, when the destruction of everything has occurred, it is better to have obtained something; for when a jar falls into a well, it does not deserve to lose the rope as well. 164
Therefore,
it has been explained that [the phrase] "together with what is not excluded" serves as a refutation of the claim that there is no distinction from the forms of particles and verbs themselves.

3. The result of including [the term] "not refuted" (sahānirākṛta). Therein, he explains the remaining word "not refuted" (anirākṛta): "And that acceptance is held to be unrefuted by the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)."
What is the logic here?
2. The fifth daily lesson (is completed).
Because the statement of the reason occurs when there is doubt;
for when a contrary [case] has been established by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that reason lacks a basis in the absence of that [property to be proved]. Thus he says:
The reason [in that case] would be excluded, as it would lack a locus.

(91) Now, if there is a proving reason, why is the thesis not [established]? If there is not, then that fault will belong to the reason itself; what is the point of stating [the requirement of being] "unrefuted"?
This is true;

nevertheless, since [the object] is refuted at the very outset by the defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), it should be so even without regard for defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*). Therefore, this is indeed a defect of the thesis, because it exists solely as such.
For when something has been refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), no one requires a means of proof (*sādhana*).
That being the case, there is indeed no confidence; thus, what confidence can there be even in that which is supposed to be the proof?
Therefore, the object of the reason is doubtful, and here "mere absence of proving or subverting evidence" is indicated by this doubt.
It is not only when doubt is present that one understands fire through a single inference; even when doubt is not present, one indeed understands fire from a single inference.
Alternatively, the status of being the object of a logical reason (*hetu*) applies only to those cases where it is possible for doubt to arise.
It is not [ascertained] through the establishment or refutation consisting of its own nature and its opposite,
because it occurs solely in dependence upon that.
If the status of being the object of a statement of a reason belongs to that which is not sublated by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then there would be only two kinds of sublation (*bādhā*).
How does the Teacher demonstrate the fourfold nature? To this it is replied:
that sublation is said to be fourfold by way of the divisions of inference.

The demonstration of fourfold sublation— wherein three types of sublation have been shown as inferential and the fourth as perceptual— does not contradict the [prior] demonstration of two types of sublation.

In that case, even the sublation by what is well-known from scripture (*āgamaprasiddhi*) occurs through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) alone; otherwise, there would be no distinction between types of inference, because [all] would lack the nature of inference. Thus, sublation by scripture (*śāstrabādhā*) is irrelevant.
It is thus, because therein the means (abhyupāya) is a member of the effect (kāryāṅga), while the nature of things (svabhāvāṅga) is the stability of the world (jagatsthiti). || 92 ||
Regarding the statement that authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*)— which resembles an effect, resembles an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or is a conventional consensus—
is not a primary logical mark (*liṅga*), he says: [It is so] because it is speech endowed with the determination of facts as intended by one who is free from self-contradiction.
The authoritative person (āpta) has thus spoken his own words and the scripture on all sides:
"sama" means "sāmā— " as well as "sāmānyāt," and externally in the line [it is] "samatvataḥ"— thus says He (the Lord).
M.
B:

Indeed, no authoritative person (*āpta*) established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can exist for another [person], because it is impossible for one who is not all-seeing to know someone who is entirely free from mental defects.

And because it is impossible to determine [the truth] due to the confusion of worldly conventions, one has no choice but to accept [an authority] as trustworthy based on inference; however, since such a person is not trustworthy in the ultimate sense,
this statement is made alongside his own words to demonstrate their equality.
For just as speech does not proceed when the self lacks authority, so too there can be no inquiry into an object perceived through scripture if that [scripture] is not relied upon. 94

Regarding "established by scripture" (śāstrasiddha): O venerable one, if one were not to accept the validity of the self (*ātman*), it would follow that no speech whatsoever could be uttered, just as in the case of saying, "Everything I say is false."
If it is your position that everything must be spoken as false,

then this meaning of what has been said is not to be understood from my words, nor is anything at all to be done because of my words; for in that case, why have we troubled ourselves, since this matter is established even without speaking?
Even that which has been studied by those whose intellects have been shaken by poor discernment is likewise indeed discarded;
and thus, just as when one says "I speak everything falsely," this very statement is not itself negated.
For if one speaks falsely regarding that [subject], the matter under discussion is not established.
(65) Since this statement is not consistent even when negating the three times, for if the word lacks authority, there would be a loss of renown. (165)

5. If one were to proceed in this way, then everything stated would be false; for by one who utters a statement that functions as illogical due to self-contradiction and the like, the very speech itself becomes the object to be washed away.
6B Since liberation itself has attained the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and is thus accepted,
how can its lack of validity be established?
If it is argued that this is due to regret, even so there is still a contradiction; it would have been better simply not to speak at all—why the exertion?
If it is argued that it was done without prior reflection, [the same fault remains].
Is this not itself the very fault?
Reasoning consists precisely in thorough investigation;
if you are thus denying the present and the future, I say this: that too would be false. Even so, what is the point of saying this?
If it is argued that there is no fault because the word [denoting] the future does not exist at all— just like the words used in the songs of wandering bards— we say:
no.
For, given the context of debate, the purpose of debate is indeed the determination of the matter.
Nevertheless,

because that [position] is thus established by the treatise, if one does not accept it regarding the object [in question], the investigation remains the same; therefore, there is indeed parity between the treatise and one's own words.

For, in order to show that when a treatise serves as the basis for the discussion [of a subject], it is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), this author states the following point alongside his own words so that one may see their equivalence:
"If there is no acceptance of a treatise, how can there be an investigation of its meaning? (95)

If investigation does not proceed without the scripture because the very subject (*dharmin*) would be non-existent, then the scripture is a sublater; otherwise it is not. To demonstrate this, [the author] uses the expression "together with" (*saha*); for otherwise, opponents would maintain that the scripture possesses a capacity exceeding that of one's own words, and it would remain so.
An example similar to that has also been shown by him here.
B.
For it has been stated that in the absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the words of the treatise would be untenable.
Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating their equality, he provides a similar example.

If one rejects the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then because both scripture and verbal testimony would be absent, scripture itself could not be a means of valid cognition for you; thus, what would be the point of your acceptance? This would result in nothing but mutual contradiction.
A clear example of this contradiction with one's own words is found in the following scriptural passage:
In that regard, the mere indication of the direction [of the truth] is the dharma that bestows happiness after death.
Now, one might object: "Since there are indeed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can this be a contradiction with the scriptures?
For a subject (*dharmin*) does not arise from the scripture alone."
If there were no means of valid cognition whatsoever, how could the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth be established? This would constitute a contradiction with one's own words.
Alternatively, if some [established entity] is admitted, then that very thing from which its establishment arises must itself be the means of valid cognition for it.
Since the objects of knowledge are established only through the means of valid cognition,
and nothing at all can be known without the means of valid cognition, it must be said that there is no contradiction with the treatise.
If one were to speak after having accepted a treatise, saying "it must indeed be so," there would be no fault, for the treatise has been accepted. How is it to be known that this is true?
It is indeed so.
For this very reason, this is not a clear example of contradiction with the treatise; rather, the author of the Vārttika clearly states that it is merely a demonstration of the general direction.
"Since the dharma bestows unhappiness after death,
one must necessarily accept the scripture regarding such a matter";
this is a clear example of contradiction with the scripture.

Therefore, in this case, there is indeed a mutual contradiction, just as with one's own words. Consequently, where the subject (*dharmin*) is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a treatise (*śāstra*) accepted [as authoritative] therein would be a sublater precisely because it is a means of valid cognition; however, when the subject is established by what is renowned in the treatise, that which is accepted [from the treatise] would be a sublater of it solely due to its own internal contradiction.

To this, the teacher says: "Even in the case of those who rely on scripture, when there is a contradictory statement regarding a real entity, there can be neither sublation nor obstruction, because the two [scriptures] are of equal status. (98)
3. By virtue of equal power—he.
4. B. By virtue of being on an equal footing between those two;
for there is no distinction whatsoever, even for one of them, other than the authority brought about by their own acceptance, [between] the scripture and one's own word.
Therefore, because the two possess equal power, there is only a mutual obstruction and not a relationship of the sublated and the sublator;
just as in the case of one's own words. And at that time, that which possesses the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of those [words] would be the sublator of the other. (99)
1B. How else could validity refute either the thesis or the inference—whether the thesis be devoid of reasoning, or be of equal status [to the inference], or be contrary to reality? 100.
Furthermore, the equal status and the validity of the scriptures have already been refuted previously.
Therefore, this fault is admitted in the case of investigations based on what has been accepted [as a premise].
abhyupāya°
—these are the intermediate verses.

Therefore, although it is not outside of inference, this means [of knowledge] has been treated separately in order to demonstrate the distinction of its objects, because it serves as a sublation. 102.

Precisely because sublation is admitted [in this case], scripture (āgama), although not external to inference, is treated separately from inference for the purpose of demonstrating a difference in their objects; for while inference is indeed a sublater, scripture is a preventer (pratibandhaka).
And that which obstructs it is accepted [as such], and not otherwise;
for otherwise, there would be either a sublation by inference or an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), or the separate treatment [of the two] would be rendered purposeless.

Or rather, if there were a distinction [between one's own words and those of a treatise] merely in terms of verbal expression, there would be a contradiction even regarding one's own words. (103) For if, even in the absence of a specific purpose, one were to separate one's own words from the statements of a treatise on the grounds that they are distinct from inference,
it would result in nothing but the speaker’s own lack of skill, as such a distinction would be useless.

In that case, how is there a distinction between contradiction with one's own words and contradiction with what is accepted [by oneself], if both are mutually sublated by one's own words when those who speak contradictory things are refuted by their own speech,
as in the case of "everything spoken is false"?
Or, by virtue of a prior admission,

as for example when one seeking to prove that "sound is impermanent" according to the [Mīmāṃsaka] school, a separate illustration is useless even in the absence of a difference in the subject matter, because it has already been stated.

It is true that there is indeed no difference [between these two]; nevertheless, because the latter subverts what was established by the former, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet (*abhyupagama-virodha*). Furthermore, because that very same statement subverts its own meaning, there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana-virodha*). [And] based on one's tenet, the treatise is an authority (*pramāṇa*)— (ka) *Abhyupagama-virodha* refers to a case where a later statement contradicts a prior statement within the same argumentative context. *Svavacana-virodha* refers to a case where a statement contradicts itself, such as when one asserts "all statements are false. In the present context, the contradiction arises because the subsequent statement negates the validity of the preceding one, which was intended to establish a specific point. This is distinct from the contradiction with a treatise (*śāstra-virodha*), which occurs when a position contradicts the doctrines of an accepted school of thought. The text here suggests that even if one accepts a treatise as authoritative based on one's tenets, if one's own statements contradict those tenets, both types of contradiction apply.

If it is argued that, because of his acceptance [of the system], the treatise is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding all things and thus serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*); (then we reply:)
If one does not accept [the opponent's objection], what further sublation could there be?
There would be a contradiction with one's own words; for contradiction with one's own words and contradiction with a treatise are identical.
For if he were not to desire it, what could that constitute a sublation?
Or even if he does desire it, there would still be no sublation;
for the desire of one who lacks valid cognition does not produce validity.
What that was previously accepted should not be stated otherwise later; for what contradiction could there be in such an act?
7B. If it is not so, how can there be no contradiction regarding the means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? 8B. [There is no contradiction.]
In that case, there is indeed a contradiction with one's own words;

for if a contradiction with one's own speech is admitted, it follows that there is no difference between a contradiction with one's own words and a contradiction with a treatise (*śāstra*), rather than a distinct invalidation by a treatise. Furthermore, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is established by human intention, would become entirely contingent. (105)
If the authority of a treatise is established by human intention,
then that same [intention] is fully present in one's own statement as well;
therefore, there is no distinction between one's own statement and the treatise.

Now, [the opponent argues: "Since a treatise (*śāstra*) is accepted for the sake of establishing its own subject matter, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, one's own word (*svavacana*), being for the sake of others, is not so.
Therefore, there is no great effort required for what is for the sake of others. This is incorrect.

For if that which has been examined were to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then there would be a sublation (*bādhaka*) therein; if the examination has not proceeded, it does not differ from one's own word. If that which has been examined is accepted, then since its object is established by the very means of knowledge, there is indeed a sublation by the means of knowledge.
Now, if it is not examined, then that [object] is merely a word; thus, there is no distinction between one's own statement and scripture (*āgama*).
Furthermore, for two objects established through indirect perception (*parokṣa*), scripture is useless.
Therefore, regarding objects already well-known, there is no harm even if one abandons scripture.
When the subject matter is beyond the senses and one does not accept scripture as authoritative, no inquiry whatsoever proceeds.
Since there is no obstruction to investigation when the locus (*dharmin*) is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no harm whatsoever even for one who abandons the treatise;
there is only a contradiction with one's own prior commitment (*abhyupagama*).
Because it would involve a contradiction with what has been accepted, this is not a clear case of contradiction with a treatise (*śāstravirodha*);
rather, when the subject (*dharmin*) is well-known according to the treatise, since it is impossible to abandon that treatise,
that alone is the clear object of contradiction with a treatise.
For if there were no acceptance of scripture (*āgama*), no consideration would even arise regarding it.
If that is so, then by establishing that treatise (*śāstra*), one establishes the subject (*dharmin*).
Consequently, how can that treatise—which is sublated [by other means of knowledge]—establish the subject if it lacks authority? [The answer is: because it is accepted as being authoritative.
In that case, it is within one's own admission (*svopagama*) alone that the establishment of the locus (*dharmin*) constitutes validity;

yet that very same admission opposes another property (*dharmāntara*). Therefore, contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) does not differ from contradiction with a treatise (*śāstravirodha*), because both result in a contradiction with what has been admitted.
In this context, even the investigation consists primarily of pointing out contradictions, as follows:
"Lust and the like are the root of unrighteousness, yet bathing is the purification of unrighteousness. (107) 2 M.

B. Regarding the destruction [of the mind]: Thus it has been said in the *Hevajra-tantra*: "A corrupt mind dwelling within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords; even if washed a hundred times, it remains impure like a vessel that once held liquor. (167)
Furthermore, it is said:
"Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vilvaka, Nīlaparvata, and the sacred site of Kaṇakhala, one shall not be born again. (168)
At its own gate, 4 B.
in the *vilvaka* tree.

(ga) The objection regarding the contradiction with what is commonly accepted is untenable—if nothing at all is being contradicted, and there is merely a contradiction [with one's own position], for what purpose is there said to be a "contradiction with the acceptance of that"? To this he says:
"That which is not contradicted by the reasoning established by the treatise, nor by its own words..."
Whether [the object] is seen or unseen, the thought "that is to be grasped" arises.

A treatise that is not contradicted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or by one’s own words must be accepted regarding both the seen and the unseen; otherwise, if it were accepted otherwise, one would be acting without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakārin*).
Furthermore, even that which is refuted by common consensus (*prasiddhi*) is not a [valid] thesis (*pakṣa*);
in this context, "consensus" refers to a natural mark (*svabhāvaliṅga*), but not to the word of a trustworthy person (*āptavacana*).
O Lord, how could it proceed otherwise than through an essential nature (*bhāva*), since it is accepted as being so?

For in that case, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established by mere acceptance and not by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it is not a primary effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
Even if there were a real connection established therein, it would then be a primary essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) indeed.
In that case, what is produced by one's own admission is merely a contradiction of that admission—just like the word of a trusted person—so how can this be a separate form of sublation?
Or rather, this is indeed a sublation by a trusted person, since it will be stated later: "In this context, a 'trusted person' is one whose speech is unimpaired."

And because the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*) is connected with each [term]— namely, perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), authority (*āpta*), and what is well-known (*prasiddha*)— it follows that sublation (*bādhā*) is only threefold;
therefore, that [objection] is incorrect.

Because of the statement, "That sublation is said to be fourfold through the division of inference," and because the Master [Dignāga] also demonstrated the fourfold nature by providing separate examples in the passage beginning with "yatrāpi... (even where...), it would not be established [otherwise].
To this, it is replied:
This [argument] is contrary to the entire world; furthermore, it was previously made by oneself. Is this a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) formulated in the form of an inherent nature or an effect?
Sublation by what is established for the entire world is "sublation by consensus" (*prasiddhibādha*); sublation by what is established solely for oneself is the other [type of sublation].
Alternatively, this is intended to demonstrate two types of *prasaṅga*-proofs: one in the form of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) and one in the form of an effect (*kārya*).
For indeed, only two things must be performed by a proponent: the primary proof (*mukhyasādhana*) and the *prasaṅga* proof (*prasaṅgasādhana*).
This is for the purpose of showing that there is no other way [of classifying] the statements of disputants;
or rather,
it is because the meanings of words must always be understood by those engaged in worldly discourse.

But it is not so from the perspective of the treatise (*śāstra*), because there is no difference between this [treatise] and that [word]. (170) Even though [the treatise] is not primary, the contradiction with common consensus must necessarily be accepted on the basis of the treatise; therefore, it is treated separately.
Now, since there is no difference whatsoever between the treatise and one's own word (*svavacana*), the sublation by the treatise is indeed nothing other than sublation by one's own word.

Furthermore, by one who seeks to establish something else while raising a dispute regarding a subject (*dharmin*) well-known in the treatises, the validity of both one's own words and the words of the treatise must necessarily be accepted;
how then can it be that such acceptance is not mandatory? That too is incorrect.
Because it is stated by way of the opponent's own admission;

for among other disputants, an admission must necessarily be accepted when formulating an argument, even in a dispute concerning the properties of a different subject. Therefore, this is said in order to establish the following:

Therefore, one must necessarily accept the treatise (*śāstra*). Alternatively, there is the non-establishment of the intended subject; the separate mention of "treatise" refers to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), for in that case, there is no sublation of the intended meaning, even if it were said that "the mother is also barren."
Therefore, the distinction of the object is intended by way of its being external or internal.
The distinction [of the object] is the classification of the sublation well-known in the treatises.
The incidental discussion having been concluded, the subject at hand is now commenced.
What is this so-called "renown"? If it is first of all worldly renown—
If [the world] were grasped in its entirety or even in part for the sake of pervading the self,

then since eternity and other such qualities are well-known to all the world, there would be a subversion of worldly consensus by that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which subverts them, as well as [the subversion] of other things that contradict valid cognition.
Nor is there any other meaning denoted by the word "commonly known" (*prasiddhi*),
such as in the case of "a human skull is impure" and so forth;
for it would be improper to subvert what is established in the scriptures.
If that were the case, there would be the same fault in subverting [the existence of] the eternal self and so forth.
[This is because of] pervasion (vyāpti).
To this it is replied:

"Familiarity" (prasiddhi) is that unshakeable state of being denotable by a desired word; for familiarity is indeed linguistic usage (vyavahāra), and it is so called because [the word] is produced from that. (172)
The "accomplished" (*kalpita*) is the preeminent accomplishment (*prakṛṣṭā siddhiḥ*), which is "established" (*prasiddhi*);

that which arises from it is the state of being denotable by the desired term, because it is unshakable. However, qualities such as eternality (*nityatva*) and so forth, which consist of the nature of preeminent accomplishment, are indeed subject to change.
However, it is impossible to render that [notion] stable by means of a treatise;
for what is established by a means of valid cognition cannot be removed by a treatise, because its validity has been revoked by that very means of valid cognition due to being sublated. (173) 3 B.
It would not fall [into error],
for there is no sublation of inference by that which is denoted by the term "desired";
this will be demonstrated accordingly.

For, since the status of being denotable by a desired word follows human intention regarding objects, there is no occasion for inference—which would be a sublater—to intervene. (gha) The definition of an authoritative person (āpta):
for this very reason, he says:
Since it is not prohibited with respect to objects and follows the will of the person,
the person whose speech is unimpeded is here the authoritative source (āpta) regarding the status of being denotable by a desired word.
For the status of being denotable by a desired word is a universal form, such as "cowness" (gotva), which is conceptually constructed.
It is not possible to prevent that which is merely imagined through desire; for satisfaction with an object of conceptualization cannot be prevented,
nor indeed can that which is well-known to oneself be denied.
And likewise, this [point] also:
the relationship between word and object is conventional;
surely, only an entity established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can serve as a sublater.
Now, it is argued here:

self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because by that [means], the state of being expressible (*vācyatva*)—characterized by the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) with respect to the word—is established.
If this is so, then inexpressibility (*avācyatva*) is indeed established by perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is contradicted by perception itself.
If it is argued that only the relationship of cause and effect is established by perception and not any other relationship such as that of the signified and the signifier, we reply:
no, the relationship of the signified and the signifier is not merely that much.
How then can there be acceptance of it otherwise? To this it is replied:

here, "expressibility" exists as a universal (sāmānya) by virtue of being both future and past; therefore, since it pervades the individuals, how could there be a cognition of it through perception? (172)
(Refutation of the Universal) —
It is solely because of such conventional usage that, due to the presence of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it is perceived as existing;
and as will be stated later, even that [universal] is accepted as participating in conventional usage.
For the universal (*sāmānya*) intended as the referent of a word is defined as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*);
and that [exclusion] cannot be negated, because a corresponding cognition arises due to the specific restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*).
And that mental impression, awakened by the restriction of convention established by mere desire, necessarily establishes the universal.

For instance, the state of being a Brahmin and so forth is unmanifest; it is made determinate by a particular individual through intention, by means of a word functioning as a convention, via the exclusion of others. (174)
Indeed, castes such as the "twice-born" (*dvija*) and others cannot be manifested by means of individuals, because they do not possess a fixed color or configuration;
therefore, they become manifest solely through the power of conventions restricted to specific individuals, which are themselves characterized by practices restricted to those individuals.
Now, it might be argued that no convention has been established here at present by anyone, because the relationship between signifier and signified is established by beginningless intrinsic nature;
[we reply: no, for instruction itself constitutes the convention.
Furthermore, the reason why a Brahmin is not [merely] a Brahmin is this:
that his status is caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is what must be proven here; otherwise, what would be the mutual distinction between the castes of Caṇḍālas and so forth, and these [other groups]?
By this, the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is also refuted;
for even these do not possess any distinction from universals such as "donkey-ness" (*gardabhatva*),
if their application is based merely on being perceived.

In this context, the purpose [of the universal] is merely its capacity for functions such as carrying or milking; therefore, being characterized by that [capacity] is not at all inconsistent here. Likewise, for universals such as "cow" and so forth, the very fact of being the object of that single word is their defining characteristic.

Consequently, the universal is precisely the object of conceptual construction (vikalpa); thus, because its existence is attained through mere conventional usage, that property is born of linguistic practice.
It is expressed by the word "well-known" (prasiddhi).
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has been mentioned by the term "established" (*prasiddhi*); the property (*dharma*) arises from its conventional usage.

It is not only this [conceptual construction] that is called a property; it is also the means of establishment, which is denoted by the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) characterized as "established."
Rather,
[these] are indicated by the superimposition of the term "means of valid cognition" upon those things measured by perception and so forth.
Even objects measured by means of valid cognition such as perception can serve as subverters (*bādhaka*) of another object known as a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
Therefore, since it is impossible to deny that "cowness" and so forth are denotable by words intended [for them], the negation is sublated by that very fact;
for no sane person would negate a well-known object of designation such as "physician" and so on, which has been established by applying a word for the sake of conventional usage.
He says this very thing:

Because those things which arise based on that [mind] proceed according to one's will, the entire universe— whether already produced or yet to be produced— is by its very nature capable of being perceived by those who do not deny it.
Or "of those produced"—thus [it means]:

by its very nature, it is fit for the collection of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) that arise based upon it; it is fit for universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), and indeed fit for the entire universe of both produced and unproduced things that will themselves be explained later, because it is non-opposed to everything everywhere.
Fitness is simply the absence of opposition;
therefore,
it [the word] conforms to the mere object, whether it is yet to come or already past.
One who seeks to obstruct [the Veda] is contradicted by that very fitness of words.

Indeed, neither future nor past fitness of a word— such as "one desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice"— can be set aside by negation, because it conforms solely to its meaning, even in cases such as the eating of dog-meat.
In that regard as well, "suitability" (yogyatā) is non-contrariety toward the object;
for no object whatsoever is seen to be contrary to the act of smelling, whether it be perceived or established by instruction.
The word "mere" (mātra) is intended to include everything without distinction.
For example, when one says, "Feed the Brahmins," one desires merely the act of feeding and does not specify a particular recipient.
And as for that capacity which conforms to the mere object, there is no logical principle whatsoever that can negate it.
The conventional designation "bank" is sublated by that very same fitness which serves as its negator.
For the negation of capacity is not established by perception;
at most, inference might intervene, but it will be demonstrated that such inference is impossible due to the absence of an illustrative example.
Surely the Teacher says "not by linguistic convention";
[we reply] that there is no sublation by way of fitness,
for fitness is not the state of being denotable by the intended word.
And it is not the case that being well-known constitutes fitness; for fitness is the cause of being well-known, not being well-known itself.
To this, it is replied:

Precisely by the power of that fitness (*yogyatā*), in reality, every sound (*dhvani*) is established within this [fitness], even if it is not perceived; therefore, its establishment follows from that.

This is also the intention of the Teacher (*ācārya*): by the expression "linguistically established" (*śābdaprasiddha*), it is only fitness (*yogyatā*) that is being conveyed, not an already accomplished denotability (*vācyatā*).
If fitness were to depend solely upon the speaker's intention, that would mean it is merely the absence of opposition;
for the application of a word to any object whatsoever occurs by mere intention. How then could a word that functions solely according to that [intention] ever fail to apply to anything? (176)

A real entity does not, by its own nature, cause a word to function [toward it]. Fitness for convention is said to be non-contrariety [to that convention]. (177) The very production [of a word] by will is what constitutes conformity to the mere object. How could there be a desire for convention if there were no expectation even regarding the mere object? (178) When the status of being denotable by the word "wheel" is negated in the case of a jar, it is intended that in that instance, the proof is based on common usage; this is the direction [of the argument]. (179)
—these are the intermediate verses.
Now, it may be asked: how can that fitness (yogyatā), which consists in non-contrariety, be either future or past?
To this it is replied:

Since the object is something that is yet to come into being, its fitness (*yogyatā*) is likewise of that same nature; for no so-called "fitness" is observed to be distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object] itself.

In this regard, whatever object is intended to be expressed by a particular word is fit to be expressed by that word—for example, by the word "tree"—for indeed, no contradiction is ever observed anywhere.
[Objection: But surely the very example is not established, because even there, the possibility of rejection exists.
This is not so;
for when the linguistic convention of the relationship between the signifier and the signified is already in operation, whose [existence] could be denied,
since people are seen engaging in it through the comprehension of its meaning?
This indeed is the relationship between the signifier and the signified;
and so it has been said:
"When a word is uttered, that object which is understood [is the signified]."
They say that this is the meaning of the word, and not the definition of one who holds another view.
If that is the case, then the meaning of the proposition is already contradicted by direct perception; what is the use of contradicting it by means of common consensus?
To this it is replied: it is not merely this much that is to be established here, but rather—
All words are considered denotative in some place or at some time; by this logic, perception does not apply here [to negate such usage].
This has already been stated:
even when the fact that the word "moon" is a denotation is negated in the case of a jar, it still constitutes a contradiction of what is well-established (*prasiddhi-bādha*).
If it is argued that this [object] does not now appear to me as being denotable by the word "this," that is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore,
if it is argued that it does not appear to another person, nor does it appear to me now, nor is it capable [of appearing], [then the following applies].

In that case, since this [functioning] occurs by mere intention (*icchāmātra*), why is it not possible? For we observe that the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) among words and their objects varies according to place, time, and person; how then could there be any fixed rule?
According to this principle, everything is accepted as being expressible by every word, so there is no fault.

1. "He will speak" or "he will eat dog-meat"—it is by means of such [words] that an object is negated. Because it is sublated by common cognition (*pratīti*), it is sublated by way of incompatibility (*yogyatva*). || 183 ||
If now this object, such as flesh and so forth, appears to you in that manner;
If this were said, there would be sublation by perception; otherwise, how could it be?
For here there is no sublation by perception;
here there is only sublation by cognition.
That [cognition] as well, by virtue of convention alone— whether through fitness or the appearance of fitness— even in the case of dog-meat and so forth,
is contradicted by the Veda.

Now, is it not the case that this lack of restriction applies only to those worldly words which are dependent upon convention? But as for those Vedic words whose connection with their meanings is innate (*svābhāvika*), how could there be such a lack of restriction?

Furthermore, convention is established for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*) only within the realm of perceptible objects; since there is no cognition of supersensible (*atīndriya*) matters, how could one be capable of establishing a convention regarding them?

Since practice takes scripture as its sole refuge, there would follow the fault of mutual dependence; moreover, for one who follows that scripture, it is not logical to establish a convention otherwise. To this, it is replied:

Now, one might object: by whom was this Veda established as possessing its inherent meaning? In that regard, an ignorant person might establish a convention there out of malice or compassion, and a knowledgeable person might do so for other reasons. Just as a convention regarding burning and so forth for words like "fire" is made by one person according to his own will, so too could it be for dogs and the like;
thus, it is not established that this meaning is inherent, because the determination of its meaning follows worldly usage.

And in the world, there is the perception of various objects due to differences in place, time, and so forth; nor is there any certainty regarding an object that pervades [all] places, times, and so on. (186)
In that regard, sometimes an ignorant person alone might establish a convention or give an instruction concerning place, time, and so forth;
and if it were merely a succession of instructions, it would be like a lineage of blind men.
Therefore, the convention is otherwise [than that], for the purpose of casting aside those who are attached to such [ignorant] views.
Alternatively, there is no contradiction because it is precisely one who perceives beyond the senses who has provided the remedy for the discrepancy regarding the apprehension of the previous object;
or else, 2 B.
To avoid the [objection] of "contradiction by perception," it is said: here too, at the time of the investigation,
there is no cognition from the word "moon" without an inference [of the moon's existence], nor [is there cognition] of the asterism [Kṛttikā].
1.87 It is not logical that the cognition of an object from a word should be perceptual.
As the proponent of the Veda says:
"For the cognition of an object arises from the words of the Veda through direct perception," if it is stated thus.

The cognition is direct because it consists of self-awareness; however, its conventional status as direct perception is sublated by the established position that cognition is not perceived when it takes another cognition as its object.
Or, if you accept [the existence of such a cognition], let it be stated that the cognition of fire from smoke is also perceptual;
for even one who cognizes fire from a single instance of smoke would have that [cognition] be so, since there is an absence of the form of inference there.
Or, if you say that in that case there was a prior recollection, then here too [it occurred] at the time of the convention.
Otherwise, even for one who follows an interpretation, that very interpretation would be the convention;
and if the interpretation were not of the nature of a convention established by one's own will, then this fault would not exist—
but this is not the case.
It has been demonstrated that the composition of an explanation may otherwise proceed from hatred and so forth;

furthermore, if it is argued that an explanation is justified by Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) through the elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*), etymological derivation (*nirukta*), and so on, or by the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*), then [it is replied]: so be it.

If [the truth] were arrived at through a succession of commentaries, it would result in a "succession of the blind. Therefore, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that [truth], nor is there inference (*anumāna*), because it lacks faultlessness.
Consequently, even in the case of the statement "The moon is the hare-marked one" (*candraḥ śaśī*), there is no direct perception here either.

And thus it was established: "For the word and the logical mark (*liṅga*) convey their own objects by depending upon the perception and non-perception, as well as the recollection, of the presence and absence of that [object].
In that regard, that which is the moon is the hare-marked one (*śaśin*), because of its existence, and so forth.
To this he replied: "He does not say that there is no cognition at all."
For if this were the case, there would be a contradiction with common experience (*pratītibādha*);

and even if experience is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*), nevertheless, this [proposition] is false— just like the experience of two moons— and thus its contradiction with experience is demonstrated.

Because it is understood through the recollection of each preceding [instance], it possesses the nature of inference; therefore, this sublation by inference is accepted by the authors of the treatises. (189) 1B.

Since the relationship is understood at the time of convention through [the cognition of] similarity, it follows that inference is established as a limb of essential nature (svabhāva); thus, the stability of the world is proven.
2B. [Objection: Surely this is established as inference; however, how can it be a reason based on essential identity (svabhāvahetu)?
Furthermore, the cognition produced from a word, which is assisted by prior perception, is of the nature of inference and thus serves as a sublater;
moreover, the word is not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the object.
If the relationship between the cause and the effect indeed exists between the signified and the signifier, then cognition would arise from the word; such being the case, it would be inference.
Since cognition arises from inference, it depends upon the assistance of a [logical] connection.

And that relationship between the object and the word consists in their being material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*); furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the word is produced solely by the activity of the palate and other vocal organs, not by the object to be expressed.
Therefore, in this case, the relationship of cause and effect exists through intentional design, like a hand gesture (*hastamudrā*), and not otherwise.
For a causal relationship imagined through mere desire is not real, like the connection between a rope and a stake;
nor is such a cognition necessarily present.
Therefore, this is not primary inference.
How, then, is there a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)?

Whatever object, being of the nature of a material cause (*upādāna*), is manifested by convention and produced according to intention— that which has become such is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), a causal factor.
Because it occurs even in the absence of the intention to express that [specific] object;
and because when there is an intention to express something else, or when there is no intention at all, that without which something exists cannot be its cause.
Therefore,
