its status as the denotable [meaning] follows merely from its being intended as the material cause.
When a nature has reached the state of being constituted solely by that [object], it becomes expressible (*vācyatā*).

Expressibility is merely the establishment [of a thing] through its status as a material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) based on that status as a material cause is what constitutes established knowledge (*prasiddhi*).

Since the status of being a material cause (*upādānatva*) is well-established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is likewise established; therefore, its ineffability is not contradicted when it appears as a material cause. For that which does not appear as the effect of something's material cause is, at best, ineffable, because it does not appear from that word.
If that object were not manifest as the causal basis for the cognition even when there is desire, it would be inexpressible;
yet, indeed, it is not so manifested, for it has already been stated that the externality of an object does not possess the status of a causal basis, since [the cognition] occurs even in its absence.
It is not because [the object] appears when there is a desire [to speak];
for when, upon seeing an object, its verbal expression occurs through the intention to speak it due to extreme habituation, why then does its status as the material cause (upādānabhāva) not appear?

Now, if it is argued that because the external object does not appear [in cognition], it is said that for the cognizer there is no such thing; then, in that case, inference also would not have an external object as its domain, precisely because the object does not appear therein. Or, if it is argued that even from that conceptual construction, by means of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the thing, it is said that the external object exists;
then, in that case, the same would apply to its being expressible (*vācyatva*) as well.
The attainment of external objects, however, occurs at all times because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*);
nor is there an absence of the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) even if it were a valid means of knowledge,
since the relationship between signifier and signified is established precisely through such a mode of being.
Therefore, even without [it], 4 B. [it is established].
5b. That object which exists as the material cause (*upādāna*) itself must necessarily be denotable; and that status as a material cause cannot be obstructed by mere whim (*icchā*). 192.

Every object that falls within such established convention (*prasiddhi*) is said to be denotable. Therefore, because its operation is dependent upon whim, there is no fixed restriction for *dhvani*. 193.
—Such is the summary.
Therefore, it is precisely fitness (*yogyatā*) that is intended by the word "renowned" (*prasiddha*).
If one asks why this is so:
To this it is replied:
by that [statement], the uniqueness of the word has not been established; for that uniqueness would not exist if it were not accepted that everything is denotable due to its fitness.
This very point he states:
Otherwise, the reason for sublation would not be "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) here;

for if the Teacher’s intention were not directed toward "capacity," how could the subverting inference be an uncommon reason? This is because [the property of being] existent is well-established in things such as jars, which are not denotable by the word "moon.
However, when [the intention is] directed toward capacity, all of that [existence] would indeed be its denotation.
In some cases, [the reason] is unestablished because the moon does not exist;

thus the Teacher said: "Even where, due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatva*), there is an absence of inference, that which is set aside by a contradictory meaning established through verbal convention is not a [valid] subject (*pakṣa*)."

In whatever object there is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) nature for the inference that serves as its counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), from that very fact there is an absence [of that counter-inference]; and in the case of such absence, an inference based on what is established by verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*) is not a sublater (*bādhaka*). By showing that this [object] cannot be negated, he speaks thus, either to indicate certainty through a counter-means of valid cognition (*pratipramāṇa*).
For there can be no negation without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor can there be a lack of certainty when that which produces certainty exists;
and in this case...
Then,

the subsequent [term] conjoined with the preceding, and the preceding conjoined with the subsequent— when the existence of the object of the preceding [term] is established for another, these two are thus occupied. (195)
When the primary status belongs to the first member as established by verbal testimony and it functions as a qualifier, then there is certainty provided there is an absence of counter-evidence;
however, when the subsequent member is the qualifier and the first member holds the primary status, then its negation is impossible.
Now, even if inference were indeed "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa), how could its negation still be impossible?
"Inference alone is not the means of valid cognition, because perception also exists.
To this, the rebuttal is:
"The negation of that [perception] would have to come from inference, since the word-referent does not function within the range of the senses. (114)

But surely, that form which is well-known through verbal testimony is [already] established by perception; therefore, it is not an inference. Is the statement regarding "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatva) not then rendered useless? 196
Because the senses do not operate upon the meaning of a word;
for the meaning of a word cannot be directly perceived.

For even if a capacity (*yogyatā*)—determined as the meaning of a word—is indeed manifested in the practical efficacy of an object well-known through verbal testimony, one must nevertheless not act upon it; thus, there is a negation of that capacity, or else the capacity consists in its connection with the word. And a connection of that which is being manifested is not within the scope of perception.
The appearance of the sound occurs in auditory consciousness, whereas the appearance of its object occurs in conceptual cognition or visual consciousness;
and there is no mutual confusion of the objects of these two.
But surely, since fire and smoke also appear within the cognition of their own objects, how can this be so?
Let it be thus for smell and the possessor of smell and so forth; even there, this same fault applies.
Nevertheless, this is not thereby established;
for their apprehension occurs through sensory cognition (*indriyavijñāna*), and thus there is no fault here.
However, in this case, it is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone that constitutes the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cognition, and not its denotative capacity.
Furthermore, a pervasive relation is not manifested in perception,
nor is verbal usage corroborated by it;
therefore, it is not within the scope of perception.
Since perception has a real entity as its object, this [subject] is therefore within the domain of inference alone; however,
will there not be another inference, arising from a different reason, that acts as a sublater?

If it is argued that existence (*sattva*) is indeed an uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), and there might be another [type of] reason, he says: "In that case, where existence does not follow [the subject], the reasons are uncommon; how then can the citation of a reason be considered valid in this way? (115)
For where existence (*sattva*), which pervades all things without exception, is rendered unique, what need is there to speak of anything else that is non-pervasive and wretched?
For one who seeks a goal that can be accomplished by refuting a powerful counter-argument will not tolerate anything else;
for this very reason, he taught the thesis with its logical reason:
"The moon is non-moon, because it exists."
Otherwise, in the context of introducing fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*), what occasion would there be for introducing a reason (*hetu*)?
Otherwise, one might as well introduce a reason for such claims as "sound is inaudible" or "a jar is eternal.

Furthermore, if you argue that a reason is impossible here because the thesis is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that would apply equally to those cases as well; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

[Objection: But was it not already stated that he [the author] showed this [reason] to be impossible to refute? Since this same [objection] would apply even to the case of "non-audible," [we reply: It is said in response: This is indeed established by verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*), and is not called a primary means of valid cognition (*mukhyam pramāṇam*). Therefore, there is no fault in the statement, "Because of the invariable concomitance with the opposite. (197)
In this case, a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is possible for [the opponent's position], but not for perception or inference;
therefore, it will be explained that by refuting [the opponent] here, the absence of a counter-argument (*niḥpratipakṣatā*) for the inference has been stated.
How, then, is there the impossibility of a counter-argument?
For not everything is denotable;
thus he said:
The sixth daily lesson is completed.

Words depend upon convention, and that [convention] depends solely upon will; thus, there is no lack of proof for those things established by words—this is the statement regarding what is established by verbal testimony. 116.
3B. Regarding well-known [form]: every verbal form is indeed well-known, because it exists merely as a word whose convention is established by mere intention;
for there is no place where a word cannot be made to function.
It is for this very purpose that the statement beginning with "by what is well-known through verbal testimony" was made;

otherwise, it would have been impossible to demonstrate the [reason's] unique status (*asādhāraṇatā*). This has already been stated. Now, an objection is raised: if there is an absence of inference, then what is well-known through verbal testimony is uncontradicted; and if there is the state of being uncontradicted, then there is an absence of inference. Thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

The fact that [the existence of a thing] proceeds from mere desire is not established by itself; the validity of an existence established through verbal testimony is not [established] by itself. For that which is established by verbal testimony, which follows mere desire, does not depend on the consideration of the absence of a counter-argument or on anything else, because it possesses strength by itself.
Furthermore, since an existent negator is itself unimpeded, it cannot function as a means of proof.
Now, one might argue: "Existence is indeed perceived as being inexpressible; therefore, because it is pervaded by inexpressibility, why should it not be a negator?"
It has been stated that [existence] cannot be negated because it proceeds from mere desire;
however, if existence is inexpressible, how can it be expressed by the very word "existence"?

Therefore, because it is unique (asādhāraṇa), the fact that [the object] is established by verbal testimony which is not sublated is indeed a sublater of inference. If, however, there were a suspicion of sublativeness even toward that which is itself sublated, then the relationship of sublated and sublater would never exist anywhere, and the world would become one of non-comprehension.
Therefore, it is precisely what is established by verbal testimony that is the sublater, not its counter-position.
And therefore, for one who has [thus] proceeded,
regarding those things to be established by inference, there are the non-erroneous contradictories (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
5. [The author] shows the non-existence [of the probans] in those cases where [the probandum] is not established; thus, inference arises from such cognition. || 117 ||
By the expression "well-known through verbal testimony," he shows that it is not [necessarily] countered;
for just as this inference is uncountered, so too is any other, since even that would not be a sublater if there were the possibility of a counter-argument, owing to its lack of authoritative status.
Just like that which is well-known through verbal testimony,
because that [reason] is also uncommon (asādhāraṇa) for it, there is no proof of the counter-position,
as in: "There is fire here, because of smoke."
"There is no fire here because it lacks the nature of fire, like a place devoid of fire.
[Objection: "But since the designation is applied by mere whim, even a jar could be 'the moon'; thus, there is no supporting example."
But here, a place devoid of fire certainly exists;
this is not the case [in the other instance]. 1 B. A place devoid of fire.

In the case of a contradiction with what is well-known through verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*), there would be the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatā*). Why is it that here too, the probans "existence" (*sattva*) is not [considered] a sublation by means of the effect?
For when fire is established in a location by inference as something possessing a sublater (*bādhaka*), why is it not accepted as the establisher of the negation of fire? (200)

The suspicion of sublation by a contrary [reason] has already been refuted; therefore, in every case of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), no counter-evidence exists. Consequently, there is no possibility of "non-erroneous contradictories" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) in inference.
Otherwise, if sublation were possible for a means of valid cognition, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases.
If it is argued that there is confidence in a place where something is not seen, we say no;
for mere non-perception lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Even if [the probans] were possible, since it is impossible to imagine a sublater and because it has reached the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*),
this [argument] refutes the intention to express the number one;
for that too indicates either non-perception itself or a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

If it were to indicate non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), then that would be invalid (*apramāṇa*) and nothing [would be established]; if, however, it indicates a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then there is no possibility of a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*),
for no other [reason] possessing a necessary connection can exist therein, since a single thing cannot simultaneously possess both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta-anumāna*), there is no such thing as a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Now, if it is suggested that the non-existence of the non-erroneous contradiction is indicated by the statement "there is an absence of inference due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatva*"), then why is this not stated explicitly within the context of inference itself? [The answer is: Even in a case where there is an absence of inference due to being over-exclusive, that subject (*pakṣa*) is one which is set aside by a contradictory object established through either an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) or an essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
The same should be said regarding direct perception as well; for this [objection] is of no consequence.
By this very [argument], perception and inference are explained;
for one might say that no real entity exists as an object of perception.
Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia regarding the appearance of hair, gnats, and so forth;
to this, the following reply is given:
the negation of non-existence is established by means of an entity whose necessary connection is proven. For when there is a necessary connection, the entity exists everywhere. (202)
If it is said that, when the conditions are free from obstruction, the object is either doubted or otherwise,
then what has already been established would be merely restated;
if, however, the opposite were the case, then since the object exists everywhere, the counter-position would be non-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatā*).
Now, surely neither inference nor anything else can sublate perception,
because it is directly perceived;
and how can that which is directly seen be established as non-existent?
For it is not possible for both the perception and non-perception of that very same thing to occur at that very same time;
surely, then, the proof of non-existence is by means of another reason, not by non-apprehension.
Because it is not seen;
that is not so.
This is not so, because there is no sublation of any cognition whatsoever by means of a direct perception.
5B. That being the case, everything would be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in perception without distinction. || 203 ||
For even in the case of a mistaken cognition that directly perceives such things as hairs and so forth, there is no sublater;
therefore, validity does not follow from mere direct perception alone,
and by this [argument], the claim of being "unsublated" is also refuted.

If it is argued that non-contradiction (*abādhitatva*), like direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), is not over-extensive (*ativyāpin*) in its own nature, and that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is non-contradictory while being non-sublated,
then this follows the maxim: "Having obtained the *harītakī* fruit, the deity causes purging."
If non-contradiction exists, what is the use of non-sublation? There is no fault by means of non-contradiction alone;
moreover, that non-contradiction does not [consist in] the cognition of an object that is not appearing, because the appearing form [is known] through a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

And since that nature of being an obstacle is common even to inference, it is the same in both cases: if a counter-argument is possible, then neither [of the two] holds anywhere. Thus, they are equal.
Therefore, even perception is not a means of valid cognition by way of direct realization.
[they] proceed.
Therefore, he says:

"Because it would not exist if the object were absent, even perception possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When that which has a nature connected [to the object] is its cause, both [perception and inference] are equal.
For the connection (*pratibandha*) alone is the basis for being a means of valid cognition. (204)

But surely, why was it not stated right there in the discussion on perception that the absence of inference is for the purpose of demonstrating that [perception] has no counter-position? If this were the intended purpose,
then since there is no reason for deviating from the established order,
this [explanation] is not correct.

Since the validity of a word that has not been established [by other means] is devoid of contradiction, it is for this reason that the refutation of counter-measures (*pratimāna*) is stated here. (205) 2B.
If "obstruction" (*pratighāta*) refers there to the removal of a means of knowledge that acts as a hindrance to perception or inference,
then the capacity of inference based on what is established by verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*) would remain unimpeded and unestablished.
Therefore, for this reason, even the [objection regarding] the violation of what was first obtained,
as well as that which applies even to an unestablished inference— where there is no counter-inference— is refuted from afar in the case of a matured inference. || 206 ||

For where even a verbal inference (*śābdānumāna*), though not yet fully established (*aprauḍha*), is unopposed and serves as the cause for precluding [the opponent's] unique [reason], then how much more so an inference that is highly established (*prauḍhatara*) and effortlessly proven; indeed, all such [inferences] are fit to be designated by the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*).
"According to the principle that 'fitness is simply non-contrariety,' here inference functions solely by the force of the object itself,
because it is perceived in such a manner by direct perception."
Nor [is it established] by way of conformity, because conformity is likewise absent;
for just as its contrariety is not perceived, so too is its conformity, whether through direct perception or otherwise.

Therefore, how can this inference based on what is established by verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*)— which proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*)— be such that, if a property arrived at through mere wishful thinking is not sublated there as something real,
it will necessarily be arrived at through the force of a logical connection (*pratibandha*)? This alone is the purpose to be demonstrated here.
Surely,
one who is dependent solely upon his own will is certainly not sublated, because that [will] is always present and thus always apprehended. (207)
But that [inference] which arises from the power of real entities (*vastubala*) might not exist anywhere; for there is no fixed necessity (*niyatatva*) among causes regarding their effects.

Therefore, a suspicion of sublation (*bādhaka-śaṅkā*) may arise regarding a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is based on real entities. Consequently, it is only in that case that this refutation of a sublater is appropriate.

The method of rebuttal that was stated regarding the "staff-and-pillar" (*daṇḍāyūpa*) logic does not apply here, because its sequence of transgression has already been bypassed by the first [point]. (208–210)
To this it is replied:

Since inference is established through a relationship well-known from mere conventional usage based on the operation of non-entities, how can there be any doubt as to where the opponent's sublation will occur? (211)
This very meaning, being understood in this way, is not devoid of conformity with logic and dharma; it is the path.
Moreover, the abandonment of that which is subject to the dictates of desire is seen to be merely an appearance brought about by its relinquishment.
Even the renunciation of a desired object when it is easily obtained is simply a form of its prescription;
however, in reality, this is not the case, for the Mountain-King cannot be shaken.
Thus, if this entire collection of practices following wrong paths were entirely free from doubt, then this conduct of the supreme sages would not be contradicted by the Vedic injunctions.
How could there be a perception of evils here for those nihilists whose eyes are impaired by their lack of vision regarding the clearly manifest state?
Therefore, it is logical that this very [section] establishes the absence of sublation; thus follows the investigation into the relationship between the name and the named.
Alternatively, if it is argued that there is an absence of inference for one who speaks, what of it? For the cognition derived from verbal testimony has a different object than that of inference.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "yatrāpi... (even where...).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Even where there is no probative inference because of its being uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
For an inference based on the fact of being denotable by the word "moon" does not function through the power of the thing itself (*vastubalapravṛtta*).
If, then, there is no probative inference, how can there be a proof for the non-existence of the opposite?

By the statement that "what is established through verbal convention is not set aside by a contradictory [inference] when [the object] is non-existent," it is demonstrated through this negation of inference that this is not an inference based on the power of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*);
for if even this were an inference, then the negation of inference would be precluded by its contradictory.
However, its status as inference is not at all denied,
because of the statement that "the stability of the world has intrinsic nature as its constituent factor.

For in this case, it is merely what is established by verbal convention (*śabdaprasiddha*) that serves as the signifier, rather than an inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*).
For here, the state of being denotable cannot be apprehended through perception, because in that [perception] only the mere object appears.

Nevertheless, it might be argued: "If, due to its non-conceptual nature, only the mere object appears and not the relationship between the denoted and the denoter, then the relationship of cause and effect likewise does not appear at all."
In that regard, just as there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), so too is there a signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*);
this is true.
Nevertheless, while the causal relationship pertains to all objects, the signifier-signified relationship does not.
For this relationship between the signified and the signifier varies across different places, times, and persons; therefore, it certainly does not possess the nature of cause and effect.

Although the relationship of cause and effect is established by the means of valid cognition of direct perception from the perspective of ultimate reality, nevertheless, due to its universal recognition throughout the world, it appears as if it were directly perceived.
For it has been observed by me previously that smoke is the cause of fire; how could the cognition "this is that very same [smoke]" be subject to error otherwise?
Even if it were not conceptualized by me previously, it was nonetheless perceived by me before.

If it is argued that conceptual perception (savikalpaka-pratyakṣa) would thus result [as the only kind of perception], we say no; for prior to conceptualization, there is the recognition: "I saw that at that time by means of non-conceptualization itself."

Furthermore, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring at a later time cannot be the basis for the determinate nature (*savikalpatā*) of a preceding perception, because there is no connection between them; however,
if a subsequent conceptual construction lacks an object, how can non-conceptuality (*avikalpakatā*) be established by it?
Nor is perception directed toward a past object; therefore, how could its status as non-conceptual not be established?
For there is no contradiction in [the fact] that non-apprehension has a past object.
For it is thus:

the non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of the cognizer’s direct perception serves as the means for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence regarding both the past and the present.
In this very way, the entire worldly transaction [of the world] would not exist otherwise; it follows that no one would remain, nor could anyone be established.
Therefore:

When the cognizer possesses an unerring impression of memory (*amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskāra*) regarding the exclusion of what was previously perceived and what is currently being perceived, then by him the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence is set in motion. This is established for the entire world without dispute.
However, no one has such a cognition as: "The relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) has been grasped by me through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
For indeed, the word and its object are grasped as signifier and signified through mere observation; it is not [grasped] without instruction, yet that instruction is not observed to exist for them.
Indeed, no one has the cognition "this is the signified and this is the signifier" arising from the mere perception of the word and its object in the absence of instruction.
Even regarding instruction, if someone were to state it otherwise, one should simply abandon it; otherwise, there would be no certainty in the interpretation.
For the causal relationship cannot be led elsewhere.
But surely the Vaiśeṣikas declare that naming is a matter of direct perception?
For instance, when one perceives the object "this is Yajñadatta" at the time of making a convention, one understands it precisely through direct perception;
for at the time of establishing a convention, living beings see before them the object that has been made the focus of their desire to assign a name such as Devadatta.

Furthermore, when a form consisting of sound—such as "Yajñadatta" and so forth—enters the range of hearing, there arises a determinative cognition that effects worldly transaction, thinking, "This is its name.
Nor is this [name] not apprehended by a perceptual cognition belonging to a different class [from the object], provided that the necessary connection is certain;
for instance:
Recollection and experience would not be definitively established otherwise; they are mutually connected, yet they exist as distinct classes [of cognition].
The relationship between the name and the named is not perceived through direct perception.
This is incorrect,
because if the connection between the name and the named object were established through direct perception, there could be no change in its nature when another time is reached. (219)

If the relationship between a name and the object named were established by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be otherwise in another place, time, or person? For what is grasped by direct perception— such as blue or any other objective relation— does not become otherwise.

Thus, this cognition of the relationship between a name and the named is indeed seen to follow from instruction; for instance, a person clearly says, "This is its name," yet it is not entirely clear that they think, "This is the name itself. (220)
"At one time this manifestation will do one thing, and at another time it will surely do something else. By whom indeed can its ever-shifting desires be restrained? (221)
This very same situation applies to me as well; the warding off of desire is not possible for anyone by anyone at any time, even by Brahmā himself.

[Objection: But surely, according to the maxim that "one may give a name established among men that is internal, residing within, unincreased, and handed down through three generations," how can there not be a warding off of desire?
If those possessing that characteristic were many, how could [the objection] be avoided?
Moreover, this too is merely an instruction.
Furthermore, this instruction, even when being transgressed, is not unobserved;
therefore, the act of naming is not a matter of direct perception.

Consequently, the relationship between signifier and signified is not like the relationship between cause and effect; thus, inference based on what is established by verbal convention does not proceed by the force of real entities (*vastubala*).
3B. Therefore, because of that inference which conforms to the existence or non-existence of things...
It has been indicated that the occurrence of a divided [entity] is due to its dependence on that [other], which is called "its desire" (tadicchā).

Under its influence, this inference—which is well-known in verbal discourse—is set in motion by mere wish; it does not arise from the power of the real thing (*vastubala*), and therefore it does not lead to the real thing.
This is just as the meaning of words such as "agnihotra" has been conventionally constructed.

In the same way, another thing such as dog-meat could also be postulated according to one's desire. What restriction is there regarding the intrinsic natures of things that would prevent them from being objects of such arbitrary postulation?

If it is argued that no such postulation occurs because it contradicts the unseen (adṛṣṭa), this is not so; for when one postulates something for a different purpose, there is no obstruction by the unseen.
The rule regarding existence is that the attainment of the desired fruit does not occur through mere conceptualization; otherwise, everyone would accomplish everything simply by naming it so. (224)
This is true; we too have made such a vow. However, you alone are the one of great power who has set in motion this departure upon the path of misfortune;
for it is thus:

If that very succession [of teachers] were examined for the sake of certainty regarding the meaning of that which is supposedly meaningful, it would simply be a blind succession of meaningless instructions. (225) If there were those who perceive beyond the senses and are knowers of this meaning, then there would be an appearance of those who contradict one another. (226)
For no other person who perceives supersensible objects has been found by you to be so harsh;
therefore, this [objection] too is merely imagined for some purpose.
If you argue that conviction does not arise from that alone and another [means] must be postulated, and that one who knows for himself cannot possibly conceive of his own lack of knowledge—[we reply:
he himself will know it; what is the use of your worrying?
If you think, "He might deceive me by not investigating me," then let go of any hope for instruction from one who is inwardly deceitful.
He thought thus.
If it is argued that conceptual construction occurs through the following of base and suffix, [we reply:
surely even that meaning of the base and suffix is established only through instruction; therefore, that too must be supported by the observation of usage.
If it is further argued that usage itself would not exist as a dharma due to a circularity based on a succession of relations between the meanings of bases, suffixes, and so forth—[we reply: no.
Furthermore, as for what was said here— that "the Dharma becomes thus"— this too is merely an instruction; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

But is it not the case that "the moon is the hare-marked one (śaśin) because it exists, like a well-known denotatum"? Therefore, how can this inference be said to proceed by the force of real entities? To this, it was said: The word "moon" (*candra*) is established as denoting the hare-marked one (*śaśin*) through worldly convention, not through the power of real entities. Since the word "hare-marked one" (*śaśin*) is applied to the moon based on the presence of a rabbit-like mark, which is a mere conceptual construction, the inference in question does not rely on the force of real entities. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Moreover,
if one does not accept the moon's possession of "moon-ness," what cognition would that person desire?
Thus, with respect to such a person, that [reason] is considered to be "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because it lacks any corroborating instance.
Since there is no example for one who rejects all cognition,
it was stated that "there is an absence of inference due to its being over-exclusive" (*asādhāraṇatvāt*).

For it is well known that he, while refusing to accept the reality of the moon— which has attained universal renown throughout the world as the referent of the word "candra"— also refuses to accept any other cognition whatsoever.
Therefore, regarding that inference which lacks a corroborative instance (*pratyadṛṣṭānta*), such as "because it exists" (*sattvāt*) and so forth—

it has already been stated that all such reasons are inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*)— what, then, is the meaning of the argument: "The hare-marked one (*śaśin*) is not the moon (*acandra*), because it exists"?
The moon is not the hare-marked one (śaśin) because it lacks a living being (sattva); by this reason, its status as the moon cannot be established.

By what, then, is it established? And how is that [reason] a subverter? The intention is that it is a subverter by way of what is conventionally established through verbal usage (*śābdaprasiddhi*), and not by the force of objective reality (*vastubalabhāvin*).

But surely, because the moon is a single entity, it is uncommon; how then can this be obtained? [This objection is directed] against one who denies all cognition. This inference is intended to be uncommon [for that opponent].
This is not at all the case, because:
This is not stated with reference to a non-example alone;
for it is characterized as such, and because [the definition] would be contradicted if one were to say that a *dhātrī* tree is "not a tree. (121)
In the case [of the argument] "The *adhātrī* is not a tree; the *śiṃśapā* is a tree because it is an entity," there is no refutation [of the fallacy], because the tree is a single [entity].
Furthermore, a definition does not function with reference to a single illustrative example.
3. B. It is argued: "But what is this logic? A definition does not function by aiming at a single example."
Indeed, that example is not something that must be proven;

rather, another example should also be included so that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) may be formulated, for in this way the effort of the author of the definition toward the treatise is accomplished and there is no hardship for the learner.
But where there is no other example, is it observed that the definition does not apply? And yet [it is observed].
"Of one who is crooked," and so forth;
likewise ( ).
Mountains such as Meru, Mandara, Maināka, Kailāśa, and Uśīra each exist as single entities; therefore, there is no example of multiplicity [to support your claim].
To this it is replied:

a definition must be formulated so that it is free from under-extension (*avyāpti*). Since [your definition] suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*), it would fail to apply to this case according to the opponent's own statement. (231–232)
Because that does not pervade it;
for instance:

In the case of the argument "The chestnut tree is not a *śiṃśapā* because it is a living being," one must also state that there is sublation by common experience (*pratītibādhā*). How could that [sublation] follow from the logic propounded by the opponent?
For a "tree" is not a single [exclusive] category, since *plakṣa* trees and others also exist [as trees].
If it is argued that there is indeed an inference based on commonality, and therefore sublation will occur [by that inference], [we reply:]...
To this, he says:
"In this case as well, since it is observed in the world that [words] function through convention (samaya) regarding camphor, silver, and so forth, what is the meaning of calling it 'uncommon'? (122)
The designation by the word "candra" is indeed observed even in the case of camphor and other such things;
therefore, how can there be oneness of the moon?
Furthermore, words that function solely by convention do not fail to apply anywhere at all.
Consequently, even there, it follows that this so-called "contradiction by cognition" is nothing other than a contradiction by inference;

for the status of being denotable by the word "moon" in the case of silver and such things is not established through common usage at all, but is merely imagined in some arbitrary way by proponents of the Gandhayukti and other systems, and does not accord with the actual state of things.
That is incorrect;

for if that [property] were established in some instance, it would be established by the force of the thing itself, since there is no way to prevent its admission even in the case of the non-horned moon if one accepts what is established by cognition. (123)
This meaning is not [correctly] explained.

If [the quality] is not established in reality (*paramārthataḥ*) in camphor and so forth, but is merely imagined by those proponents of the art of perfumery (*gandhayukti*) and the like, then how can it serve as an example of the sublation of what is commonly recognized (*prasiddhibādha*), given that it is established as a real entity (*vastusiddha*) in the moon?
If you argue that it is established only through cognition (*pratīti*), and therefore it is a case of the sublation of cognition (*pratītibādha*); then...

If one accepts what is established by common cognition (*pratīti*), then it cannot be denied even in the case of the moon; for in the case of camphor and the like, there is indeed such a cognition. Therefore, this is a refutation by inference (*anumāna-bādhana*) rather than a refutation by cognition (*pratīti-bādhana*).
If it is argued that [the term] applies to camphor and the like because of causes such as refreshing coolness (*hlāda*), and thus that is not a valid example, then it is a common [property].
6. Regarding the admission of sublation (*bādha*), it is said here:
"Since that [sublation] is established with respect to the object, it cannot be averted even in the case of the moon."
In the absence of that object, there is no fault even in prohibiting [the term] "moon" [from being applied to other things].

(124) If the application of the word "moon" to camphor and the like is prompted by a specific cause, then because that same cause exists in the moon as well, its application there cannot be prohibited.
On the other hand, if the prohibition were based on the inherent nature [of the moon], then there would be no fault even in prohibiting it from being applied to the moon.

That a thing dependent on a real entity comes into being through the absence of that entity is not unestablished; therefore, this applies to those [cognitions] produced by words whose conventions are restricted to non-entities.
Objects such as strength and so forth are suitable for [the production of] properties, because there is no obstruction to the desire for those properties.

Since properties arise merely through conventions fixed upon non-existent things, all objects are suitable for them; therefore, to obstruct that suitability is a fault characterized by the contradiction of cognition.

Is it not the case that every word is indeed applied to a cause (*nimitta*), such that even for words like *ḍavittha* and so forth, there must be some cause in the form of a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), and not merely based on conventional usage alone? This is what is being asserted.
This is incorrect;

there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "a word, having taken up a basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), applies to that which possesses such a basis," because if one were to require yet another basis even for the basis itself, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
For in this way,
because there would be an infinite regress of dependencies,
if that [cognition] were established anywhere, it would be established by the force of the thing itself.
The phrase "possessing a cause" (*nimittavatī*) is the ellipsis [of the sentence].
If one accepts [the existence of a thing] based on what is not established by cognition, there would be no restriction even in the case of a rabbit [as a moon].
If one accepts the meaning of a word based on mere cognition, there would be no restriction even in the case of what is not a rabbit.
For the relationship between the signified and the signifier, when occurring anywhere at all, cannot possess a fixed restriction,
because there is no means of valid cognition for such a restriction;
in that case, just as it occurs with respect to the cause even without a cause, so too does it occur with respect to that which possesses the cause.
For there is no occurrence otherwise than through desire even for a cause;
this is my fixed rule, like the moon.

If it functions there by its very nature, then by what could that same nature be prevented from functioning elsewhere as well? If you say that it functions only toward the universal (*jāti*) and so forth because it has a real connection with them in the ultimate sense, how is this to be known? For a word is observed to function according to mere intention.
How could it function otherwise than by its own measure?
Since it is observed while functioning, it is designated as "functioning," and not otherwise.
Since it is possible for [non-perception] to occur through the mere operation of desire,
we do not perceive any distinction between that which operates by mere desire and anything else.
If it is argued that non-perception occurs by means of desire—
This very perception occurs even when there is a desire regarding the past; for non-perception is not a sublater of every desire,
but rather it is a sublater only of that which is present and proximate, not of everything.
Therefore, if someone had the desire for this [teaching] regarding the Buddha who passed away long ago, what is contradictory in the present-day practice based on his instructions?

Thus, since the application [of the teaching] occurs both with respect to the cause (*nimitta*) and that which possesses the cause (*nimittavat*), what is the point of postulating a useless cause? This is what is said.
7B. Another, however, says:

[the cognition] does not first arise with respect to the sign (nimitta) and subsequently with respect to that which possesses the sign (nimittavat), because such a sequential occurrence is not observed.
Now, if "cowness" is perceived as the property of being an object (*padārthatva*) upon seeing some particular sign (*nimitta*),
that is not due to its being a different word;
for a word is expressive only when it is employed with respect to that which it signifies.

The establishment of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator for everything arises through the power of practical application (*prayoga-bala*). For when one conceives of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), a word ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refers only to a substance (*dravyavṛtti*), because it refers to a substance once the abstract suffix has been removed.
Now, if there is an abstract suffix for that which refers to a substance, how can there be a state of denoting merely the cause?
But when [the word] functions as a mere indicator (nimitta), then it is logical that the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) reveals that very same meaning;
for without the abstract suffix, the distinction between the two *go* words— one denoting substance and the other denoting the state— is not perceived.
From that, there is discernment through the abstract suffix;
this is not so,
for not every suffix is merely taddhita (svārthika).
In that case, when the cognition is produced by the word-form itself as a substance (*dravyavṛtti*), the understanding of the cause—that is, its qualifier—occurs; thus, nothing is contradicted.

Furthermore, the division between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*). It is the wholes (*samudāya*) alone that are understood from usage as the expressive units.

The division into base, suffix, and so forth, is merely constructed in some way or another for the sake of the instruction of beginners; otherwise, it would be impossible to instruct a beginner through the medium of speech.

Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the claim that [a word] applies to the possessor of a characteristic (*nimittavat*) by taking the characteristic (*nimitta*) as its basis;
this is the meaning of the suffix.
Another says:

"A word functions only with respect to a cause (nimitta), but that cause, while not being denoted itself, serves as a delimiter; for it is impossible [for it to be denoted] because it is the cause of that [denotation].
This is incorrect."

For if it were established for him in some respect, that would be established by the force of the thing itself; because if one accepts what is established by cognition, there is no way to prevent it even in the case of the moon. || 233 ||

If that [exclusion] were established for him with respect to some particular cause (nimitta), then it would be established by the force of the real entity (vastubala). But how can there be an engagement [of the listener] with that which is excluded by a word that does not itself indicate that cause? If there is an understanding of that exclusion, then since that too has ascended into the intellect, how could it be denotable? Even in the case of a cause, the status of being denotable is the same.
Excluded from [the other categories] 3 B.

Now, if it is argued that the substance alone is primarily conveyed while the quality—such as sweetness—is not expressed even though it is perceived, because its perception is inseparable [from the substance], we reply: the principle of primary and subordinate status does not depend on mere intention; rather, that toward which an activity is directed is what possesses the status of being primary. (234)
In this regard, sometimes sweetness alone is primary, while at other times it is the substance; such is the worldly convention (*lokavyavasthā*).
And on the basis of this worldly convention, there exists the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). To explain further:

If sweetness is for the sake of those who desire it, then always eat molasses; if the purpose is the absence of disease, then eat honey for that purpose. (235) When a certain eater is of a greedy nature, the instruction regarding molasses establishes its sweetness;

but when, due to a particular efficacy, one prescribes honey and so forth for the cessation of phlegm, then the primary function is to indicate the substance itself. Therefore, both [sweetness and the substance] are understood.
The distinction is that the status of being primary or secondary belongs to something, in a certain way, at a certain time;
in that regard, since there is no other cause for the non-perception of the two, only what is conventionally established remains.
Even so, it might be argued that the cause is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and not something that is directly denotable (*vācyatā*).
Just as in the expression "Which is Devadatta’s house?

That where the crow is," the crow itself is not denoted by the word "house," so too, even in its absence, it is simply Devadatta’s house; therefore, the crow is not something to be accepted [as the referent].

Likewise, even in the case of words such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth, when there is an inquiry regarding their status as "humanity" and the like, an improper [word] is not indicated by means of a crow, because that [crow] is impermanent.
For one who acts with foresight takes as the cause something else—such as a temple—which is indicated by the crow;
otherwise, there would be an absence of linguistic convention.
How, then, is the crow—which is itself inexpressible—an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)?
Because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is for this very reason designated by the word "crow" itself.
However, the names based on universals (*jāti*) and so forth are not established as designators of other things in such a manner.
Therefore,
even that which is inexpressible becomes a delimiter when it is presented separately;
however, that which is understood from that very word is indeed expressible.
If it is argued that because something presented to the intellect by a word is designated as "denotable," there is merely a cognition of it from the word and not actual denotability— then,
if one accepts what is established by cognition, denotability cannot be denied in the case of the moon.

The meaning is: since non-existence would also apply to that which possesses the cause (nimittavat), just as it does to the cause itself, therefore, if the denotability [of the universal] is established solely on the basis of cognition, the same [conclusion] applies to the cause as well.

2. [Objection: "But surely, when it is said 'let oil be given,' the vessel, though being perceived, should not be mentioned; for the word 'oil' does not always bring about the cognition of that [vessel]."
Since there is no possibility of a request for the offering of oil even when the vessel is brought by oneself,
it follows that what is not explicitly mentioned— that which is not conveyed by another word— cannot function as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*);
for only by means of something already indicated can anything else be indicated.

If it were not perceived as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in its application. Now, because it is first perceived as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and subsequently, through extreme repetition (*atyantābhyāsa*), that word functions exclusively to exclude that [other thing], even without the cognition of a [new] cause at that time.
If that is the case, then why does the word *agnihotra* and so forth not also apply to dog-meat? For its cause [the act of offering] occurs there just as it does in the case of a crow;
otherwise, why would the word *go* (cow) not apply to actual objects, since it is well-known to denote them? If this is argued:
How can it be said that there is no recognition [of the word] even for dog-meat in another time or place?

Therefore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is indeed indefinite, because it depends on the power of convention established by mere whim; thus, there is no harm to the Veda even if it were not of human origin, since the capacity for corruption is unavoidable everywhere.
Even regarding meat,

the inferential cognition known as "perception" (pratīti), which arises from the negation of convention, strikes down that [opponent's] capacity [to establish the meaning], thereby obstructing it. 126

Inference regarding its fitness is what opposes [the claim],
because there is no restriction on the denotata of words that function solely through convention; for what is this restriction that there must be only one denotatum?

In this regard, he who says that the hypothesis of not eating dog-meat is sublated by common experience (*pratīti*) is questioned: "If the Veda is of human origin, then this [hypothesis] is likewise sublated by common experience."
For it is well known from the statement,
"They made the *ṛc*s out of the *ṛk*-speech and the *sāmans* out of the *sāman*-speech," that the root *kṛ* here functions in the sense of remembering, not merely in the sense of producing.
For it is observed even in the case of conditioned phenomena that one says, "Make the back," or "Make the feet.
It is not [the case that these are permanent].
In this case, cognition occurs precisely because it cannot be otherwise;
furthermore, the conceptualization that "validity would not exist otherwise" would entail the consequence that all scriptures are likewise non-human (apauruṣeya).
Because the cause for that conceptual construction exists,
for this very reason the Buddhist [does not accept] the ultimate reality of the meaning or the referent of a derivative scripture (*naimittikī śruti*).
One who denies words should not be addressed by a proponent of the Veda;

if he were to say that there is no scriptural injunction based on a causal occasion (*naimittikī śrutiḥ*), he would have no fault from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Even if he should reply "no" on the strength of the relationship [between word and meaning], he still ought not to be addressed at all.

But as for one such as the Mīmāṃsaka who says "no" even to that which is conventional, it is precisely him that [the author] addresses; therefore, the objection regarding the sublation of common consensus is inappropriate.

Therefore, because there is a difference in their objects, even that cognition which is not outside the scope of inference has been treated separately for the sake of showing this distinction, just as before. || 129 ||
Just as a treatise and one's own words, when accepted as the basis for the context of discussion, constitute a sublation [of the thesis],
but not otherwise,
because they sublate the meaning of the proposition.
It is not the case that there is a sublation of error in every respect,
because the two [error and its sublation] are of equal status;
likewise, such cognition does not sublate the ultimate reality, but rather sublates the negation established merely by conventional cognition— this is the ultimate point.

A thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended by [the proponent] himself as his own position, stated in its own form, and not contradicted;
provided it is not contradicted by what is established through perception, inference, or scripture,
as for example:

"Sound is inaudible," "the pot is eternal," and "there are no means of valid cognition that have objects of cognition as their referents"— these are not [valid] positions, because even where there is an absence of inference due to uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*), they are sublated by a contradictory meaning well-known through verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*). Such cases do not constitute a [valid] thesis (*pakṣa*).

Having stated that sublation by inference and perception occurs with a reason, he says that sublation by what is established through scripture occurs by means of the mere thesis, [namely] "by what is established through verbal testimony."
Otherwise, if the Teacher had not intended to demonstrate the difference between the two objects, he would not have stated that these two possess a cause;
therefore, this is indeed the intention of the Lord of Logic (*nyāyaparameśvara*), the preeminent among all proponents of logic.
For surely, eloquent speakers whose minds are intent on discerning the purpose and whose words are rich with other relevant purposes do not speak otherwise.
For thus [it was]:
he whose intellect was firm in destroying the dense, spreading darkness raised up by those dwelling within the Vindhyas.
The mass of rays from the sun, constantly swaying upon the exceedingly high mountain of sunrise,
is like a swing for his speech.

The teacher is not subject to division; he is not obstructed by others; he is not like the sun, which has never been seen before [in this world], nor is he like the sun whose rays have set, nor is he one whose undertakings are rendered fruitless.
Therefore, it is appropriate here that there is indeed a difference in their respective domains.
The remainder has already been stated previously.
5. Regarding contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), there too, this contradiction by perception consists in the fact that sound possesses a manifold nature.
Whatever form of that which is well-known appears in scripture is non-dual, because no birth of a cognition characterized by a variegated appearance is observed;
this must certainly be stated even when there is sublation by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Even if it was not stated by the Teacher because it is already understood, one should still not say "sound is inaudible," for that would not constitute a negation of the relationship [between sound and audibility].
Rather,
that form which appears in scripture as non-dual [is so] because it is not experienced by a variegated cognition.
For there is no appearance of universals (*jāti*), relations (*sambandha*), and so forth, that is accompanied by the appearance of the word;
and how could that which does not appear [in perception] be perceptible? Furthermore, if it is excluded from perception, how can there be sublation by perception?
This will be demonstrated.

Therefore, the fault characterized by sublation by perception occurs only when one rejects the form that appears; thus, the statement of its object is for that very purpose, so that there may be sublation by perception upon the rejection of that [form] itself. (132) For this reason, it was stated by the Teacher...
The phrase "refuted by what is established through perception, inference, and authoritative testimony" includes the apprehension of the object itself, because that very form is the object; thus,
its genus and so forth are also the object.
Because there is no capacity for manifestation in direct perception [of a universal], [there is no universal].
Section 4: An Investigation of the Universal (sāmānya-cintā).
However, where there is no appearance [of an object], that is not perception; therefore, its rejection is not sublated by perception.
This very point he states: "1. A universal has the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)."

That very form is the object there; the remainder, characterized by exclusion (vyāvṛtti), is a non-substantial entity (avastu-rūpa) and thus a universal (sāmānya); therefore, it is not within the range of the senses. || 133 || 2 M.

Because it is a non-entity, there is no contradiction even when [universals] are rejected, since it is established that universal properties are not perceptible; this is what is revealed by the mention of "audibility. || 134 ||
Only that object which appears as a shimmering form present before one is the real thing;
whereas universals, relations, and so forth are merely conceptual constructs based on the exclusion of such forms, and do not possess the nature of the object itself,
since what is actually perceived is simply the distinctness from the forms of heterogeneous things.
And since no other universal appears as possessing a second form, [is this not so]? 3B.

The distinctness of that which is indeed distinct does not belong to members of the same class among themselves; how then can there be a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding those of different classes and those of the same class?
Just as, for example, cows alone are seen to be excluded from what is non-cow.
[This is] likewise [the case] with cows and horses, and from other things distinct from cow and horse.

(239) Therefore, by mere exclusion [from others], their causal efficiency is not established. Rather, it is the universal (*sāmānya*) in its positive form that, being established through differentiation, brings about the non-confusion of practical activity for those who seek it. (240–241) For there is no possibility of confusion regarding that which is cognized in its own essential nature.
Seventh Daily Lesson (concluded): (1) The Refutation of Universals.
This is incorrect because:

"If [an entity] were ever perceived by way of its own nature as a universal and so forth, then for that which is perceived by way of its own nature, a confusion of natures would not be possible. (242)

If non-confusion were possible even when the specific form (*svarūpa*) does not appear, then let the non-confusion of those things perceived as having efficacious forms be admitted. (243) For a universal (*sāmānya*) manifested by an individual (*vyakti*) cannot be manifested if the form of the individual is unperceived;
how, then, could there be linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on a distinction [between them]? (244)

As long as there is no non-confusion of individuals—whether of the same or different classes—the universal is not cognized through that non-confusion; and as long as the universal is not cognized through non-confusion, there is no cognition of the non-confusion of individuals. Thus, because of this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), there would be no cognition of the universal at all. If, on the other hand, it is argued that the universal itself is cognized first—on the grounds that there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without the prior apprehension of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—then [the objection remains].
That [reason] does not exist in the subject (viśeṣya).

Even a universal may sometimes be the very object qualified, due to their mutual relationship as qualifier and qualified; for if the universal were always the qualifier, why would there be no cognition [of it] even when the individual is doubted? That which is a qualifier is that which performs exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), and that which performs exclusion is that which is capable of removing doubt.
For thus, an object that exists by its own nature does not cease at all; however, that which lacks an existing form is simply removed by fate.
Even with a thousand qualifications, there is no removal of the former.
Therefore, the determination of the universal occurs through the exclusion of individuals.
The ascertainment that "this is that cow" proceeds solely from the exclusion of its specific form;
for the similarity between the individual and the universal is simply their similarity. Thus, due to the distinction in configuration and causal capacity, the [separate] genus is purposeless.

If the configuration of the hump and so forth, as well as the capacity for carrying loads and so forth, is the cause for the determination of a universal, then that very thing is the universal; and it is indeed non-different from those [individuals].
If there is internal difference [among them], how can that be a universal?
And for the proponent of the universal, how can there be an individual?
If it is argued that [the effect arises] only from things that are dissimilar, why does it not arise from white salt and so forth?
If it is because those [white salt and the like] lack the capacity,
then how can there be capacity among these [rice seeds and the like] which are mutually dissimilar?
If it is argued that the answer must be stated in terms of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, this is not a valid defense;
it is merely a case of stretching one's legs.

Otherwise, since the mere conventional usage of non-confusion is established simply by color and shape even without a universal (*sāmānya*), it should not be asked how this could be so without a universal; for the rebuttal that "the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things" would be like a crow failing to eat [its own food].
There is no confusion regarding the specific physical configuration, such as the hump [of a bull], because it is not observed elsewhere; however,

where there is a confusion of configuration and so forth— as in the case of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes— there the only refuge is the convention of the Vaiśyas, which consists merely of the conduct of the virtuous, even for those who drink liquor and the like.
Therefore, even going as far as possible, the cause is simply the exclusion of others; thus, [the claim that] it is "another" through a division of universals is useless.
Furthermore, 1B.
From them,
[it arises] merely through such things as drinking intoxicants and so forth.
"The determination of sin and merit, such as the killing of a Brahmin or the giving of gifts, arises from the scripture alone; therefore, the investigation of authority (māna) is useless.
This has been stated [in the previous verse].
However, there is no contradiction here even if one rejects the general properties of producing sin and merit and so forth, for that rejection does not affect the [specific] subject at hand.

If it is argued that this [universal] is revealed by the word "auditory" because it does not appear in sensory perception and thus there is no sublation by inference, and that it would be a fault to sublate its form therein— then why has it not been stated simply that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound does not exist?

Since this is stated by means of a word ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) which has relation as its cause, it is precisely the negation of relation that is intended here by such a statement; and that [negation] is to be understood solely through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, how can this be cited as an example of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣa-bādha*)?
Even by this word, the intended meaning is indeed expressed through the power of the speaker's intention; thus, there is no fault.
If it is asked, "Why is it not expressed by a denotative [word]? the answer is: no.
Because of the statement [of the Blessed One] (yataḥ ... nokti).

The rows situated in the quadrangular binding have been mostly omitted in the other version; therein (T) there is only this: if "universal" (*sāmānya*) alone is said to be the removal of the contradiction of non-perception when the qualifier and the qualified are not grasped, then because it is in every way of an inexpressible nature, it is established by relying upon that [universal].
Because it is sublated, that which is produced by its power is said to be within the range of the senses by means of the word "audible" (śrāvaṇa).
For even the word "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is not expressive of a specific characteristic,
because all words have universals (sāmānya) as their objects.

Now, if it is argued that the word "specifically characterized" (*svalakṣaṇa*), although functioning as a general term, nevertheless indicates the specifically characterized object itself through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),

then in that case, the word "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*) would also denote the specifically characterized object itself— the form indicated by its being graspable by the auditory faculty— because that is the very definition of a specifically characterized object.

For there is no other well-established universal (*sāmānya*) beyond that which is perceptible by the senses; furthermore, there is indeed a purpose, namely, the expansion of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Demonstration that [the object] is well-known through its measure.
Because its status as a sublater is based upon— indeed, relies upon— the established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because it sublates by its very force;
for an object established by a *pramāṇa* is indeed the sublater of another object not established by a *pramāṇa*.
For that [contradictory cognition], being perceived as contradictory, brings about the awareness of the non-existence of the other;
its very demonstration of that non-existence constitutes its status as a sublater (*bādhaka*), not a relation of sublated and sublater (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).
Therefore, this is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by which the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound is established through this [other] means of knowledge.
For a presentation that includes its supporting arguments (*saparikara-pratipādana*) leads to a clear understanding; this is the purpose [of the discussion].

Even though there is a contradiction with inference, the Sāṃkhya—who perceives the manifestation of existing things alone and has not discerned the true nature of reality—accepts the eternality [of things], such as in the claim: "A pot is eternal."
In that case, the capacity of causes would be sublated by inference; therefore, an investigation [into causes] without the existence of a cause would be in vain. (249)
For the constant search for what is considered a cause would be in vain without actual causality,
since there would be nothing at all for it to produce.
If it is argued that "manifestation (*vyakti*) is produced," [we reply:
surely manifestation is also of the very nature of the object; since the object is eternal, manifestation too must be eternal, and thus it would always already exist, so nothing remains to be done.

Furthermore, if manifestation is produced and is not distinct from the object, then it [the object] would be distinct from itself due to the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).
If there were no difference [between cause and effect], it would follow that even the substance itself is the effect;
nor is there any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the existence of a jar or the like within the lump of clay.
If it exists there because it is an effect, then what function could the causal operation have? (250)

If it is your view that manifestation cannot exist without *sattva* (being), and that manifestation must arise from everything—just as the manifestation of lamps and such [arises from their causes]—then why is it not accepted that production occurs from everything, just as it does from a potter and so forth? Furthermore, even an atom is seen elsewhere when a lump of clay is brought [to the potter]. (251–252)
If it is argued that it exists there even though it was not seen, then it would also exist in a donkey’s horn;
if it is not seen later, then it must have been seen later.
If the jar is perceived later, let it come into existence only later, just like its manifestation.

If it is asked, "How can there be existence prior [to manifestation], since manifestation would otherwise be illogical? let this be another fault; however, it cannot be said that [existence] is unperceivable.
Now, non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension; therefore, since apprehension itself does not exist, how can there be the absence of an entity?

If this were so, the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn would not be established, and consequently, the logical reason "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced" would be invalid.
Consequently, even for one seeking a hare’s horn, there would be the acquisition of its material cause (*upādāna*),
because [of the following verse from] the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: 2.

That [cause] exists there; therefore, it is apprehended as its cause because of its arising from that. If it were not produced from that, it would be considered non-existent. It is understood to possess the power to produce that [effect] simply by virtue of its existence; otherwise, if it were perceived in any other way, its existence would not be understood. Now, if it is argued that whatever has arisen from something is understood to exist therein—

How can that [existence] be understood prior to its arising, since it was not known before? For an arising is established through existence in such a way that the effect arises from the cause; likewise, it would have to arise from that very existence. (256–257)

For when it is established that whatever effect is preceded by something belongs to that [cause], how could an effect preceded by its existence belong to that very same thing? (258) If it is argued that this is like [the case of] another [cause], since all effects arise from power (*śakti*), then power would indeed have power as its cause; and if there is no difference [between them], how could this be so?
(259) Furthermore, if the universal (*jāti*) arises from the power of the individual (*vyakti*), is the individual distinct from that power?
If the universal (*parā*) does not exist, it would be unproduced; if it exists, how can it be produced?
Furthermore, that manifestation (*vyakti*) is a cognition (*buddhi*), and since that too exists [prior to the act of manifestation], it cannot be something produced.
Now, if manifestation is the act of being perceived (*samvedana*), what kind of production could there be for that which is already unproduced?

Therefore, the view that the causal factors produce the individual manifestation is not supported by valid cognition. However, regarding a jar situated in deep darkness, the knower of inference possesses a means of valid cognition [for its existence].
But for one who knows the means of valid cognition, there is no such proof for jars and the like within a lump of clay and so forth.
Consequently, everything is impermanent because it is produced, just like the individual manifestation.
Therefore, how can this position of permanence be sublated by inference,
given that it concerns its own subject (*svadharmin*) which is established through perception, inference, authoritative testimony, and common consensus? (264)
If that is so, then for what purpose is there this separate statement regarding the subject itself (*svadharmin*)?
For it is as follows:

It is a reasonable view that a thesis which is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not [to be accepted]; however, whether [that contradiction occurs] in another [context] or in that very same subject (*dharmin*), what utility does this have here?
Where then...
For that which is sublated in respect to another subject cannot be considered unsublated;
since it is entirely impossible to establish what has been sublated, it lacks the status of being a logical reason's object and thus is not a valid *pakṣa*—this is the established principle.
To this, it is replied:

In all cases, the property (*dharma*) which the proponent intends as his own probandum (*sādhya*), if there were sublation (*bādhā*) regarding that which possesses such a property, it would not [constitute a fault] regarding a different property in the subject (*dharmin*). This is because, although that property may exist in the subject according to both one's own and others' views, [the fault applies only to the intended property]. (136)

Nevertheless, if there is a sublation when the subject (*dharmin*)—which possesses the property (*dharma*) that the proponent himself intends to prove—is sublated, then that constitutes a fault; it is not a fault, however, when a subject qualified by some other property is sublated. Thus, the mention of "one's own subject" (*svadharmī*) serves to prevent this [undesired] consequence. For what would be the harm if another subject were sublated?
This is the underlying principle here.

When the subject (*dharmin*) possessing that specific property is sublated, there is sublation; there is no harm when another property is [sublated]. Since this meaning is already established by the definition, the mention of "its own" (*sva*) regarding the subject is not repeated here, so that it may be well-known that in the case of sublation, there would be sublation of the subject as well.
Because the contradiction of that which is supported follows from the contradiction of its support.

Since it is established by the very definition [of a thesis] that it must be stated in its own form as "itself," the proponent intends the subject (dharmin) itself as endowed with its own properties (svadharma).
If that were the case, then when that very [subject] is sublated by something inconsistent with it, no fault would follow for the [reason], nor would there be any possibility for another [fault];

this is not so, because even when the subject (*dharmin*) is sublated, there would be the consequence of the absence of its property (*dharma*) as well, by way of contradicting its locus (*āśrayavirodha*).

Otherwise, by stating that "such a property is to be proven," one would consider that very [property] to be the sublation of the subject itself; therefore, the statement [of the reason] must refer to its own subject.

The mention of "M" (the subject) is for this reason: a fault occurs only when there is a sublation of that very property as qualified by the subject under discussion— namely, that "dharma is of such a kind"— and not when there is a sublation of the subject itself, which is considered to be without fault.
Now, this too is established by implication; it is true that some have arrived at the view that even the sublation of a mere substratum (dharmin) constitutes a fault.
Whether that sublation of its property occurs through the medium of the substratum or directly, it remains a fault. (140)
In every respect, the sublation of the property to be proven is a fault;
this [objection] that "space and so forth are non-existent" is true.
Nevertheless, this is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions;
for some indeed assert that there is a fault even when the mere locus (*dharmin*) is sublated.

Just as when it is stated by others that "space and so forth do not possess a prior form that is not produced by other [causes], because they are not the cause of sound and so forth all at once," the opponent replies:
"In the same way, the subject (dharmin), such as space, is also non-existent in its own nature."
In this way, there is no sublation whatsoever of the desired probandum.
The proponent says:
