space and so forth do not exist as something previously non-existent that becomes produced by means of auxiliary causes, because effects such as sound are not produced all at once.

If form were unproduced, it would produce its own effects, such as sound and so forth, all at once. To this, the opponent replies: "In that case, this very state of being unproduced establishes the absence of prior form for space and the like; likewise, it also establishes the absence of substantiality for the subjects (dharmin) such as space."
The refutation of the substratum (*dharmin*) alone is not the only fault;
for there is no such fault for the proponent, since it is precisely this that he intends to prove: that space and so forth do not exist as real entities (*vastubhūta*).

Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that space and so forth—which are non-arisen and lack a previously unestablished form—do not exist as properties of a subject (*dharmin*) that is a non-entity (*avastubhūta*), because they would not arise all at once due to the absence of a cause.
However, since the proof and the probandum (*sādhyasādhana*) reside in a subject established by conceptual construction (*vikalpapariniṣṭhita*), the subject is not a real entity (*vastubhūta*).
Thus, even if that purely [conceptual] subject were sublated, there is no fault; this is the meaning of the expression "one's own subject" (*svadharmin*).
For when that which possesses the property of another [subject] is being sublated, it does not follow that the property itself is not established;
therefore, since there is no contradiction in the establishment of the subject possessing the property to be proven, there is no fault.
Alternatively, in the case of the substratum (dharmin), there can be no previously non-existent form that is newly produced, because it would not be a cause [for its own production] even once;
this is the meaning.
Space is impermanent;
in that case, the opponent's position that space is permanent is sublated by the sublation of the locus (dharmibādhitam).
Even so, let space be the subject (*dharmin*) which is sublated by impermanence;

for the reason must necessarily sublate the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyaviparyaya*). Since a permanent subject does not possess the form of the property currently under discussion, what fault could there possibly be in its being sublated?
If that property were established by subverting that [substratum], there would indeed be a fault regarding the substratum of the property.
It might be argued that space is thus impermanent, because a change in the voice occurs; for when the throat is obstructed by phlegm and the like,
a change in the voice arises, since the space within the throat-cavity is indeed impaired.
For instance, the contraction, expansion, and so forth of cavities are observed; this instability [of space] constitutes its impermanence.
Now, if it is argued that there is simply the existence of another object [in those places], and that space itself is what constitutes the expansion and so forth, why is it not perceived as before?
If you say it is because it is obstructed—
As for the claim that there must be a support for that which is eternal, this is trivial;
moreover,
a composite whole such as a cloth has not even arisen, being nothing more than the mere movement of one thread into another thread.
If it is asked why there is no separation [of the body] when [the head] is pulled, [we reply:
why is there no separation of the body when the throat-pit (*galavila*) is also pulled? This is trivial.
Therefore, space is either impermanent or a non-entity; such is the Buddhist position, and this is their definitive conclusion.
Alternatively, the established position is that space is simply light and so forth conjoined with resistant objects, while space as something else—unconjoined with other objects—is impermanent;

thus, it is the state of being qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that is established for such a subject (*dharmin*). Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in subverting other subjects.
For,
when both members of the pair are indeed the probandum, that which obstructs the property to be proven—

"The sublation of the locus (*dharmin*) therein is what is described by the term 'sublation' (*bādhā*). (143) Even though the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is indeed established as part of the composite [subject] to be proven, nevertheless, when that locus is sublated in such a way that the very property under discussion is thereby obstructed, it constitutes a fault; this is what is stated by the expression "its own locus" (*svadharmin*), and not in the case of the sublation of some other locus imagined by others which is unrelated to it.
Because of which:
1. Dharma.
In the same way, since the subject (*dharmin*) here is also what is to be proven (*sādhya*), it is not the subject alone;

for the subject is already established in its own nature (*svarūpa*). Since there would be no utility in establishing a property (*dharma*) for a subject that is itself unestablished, its proof is intended as being qualified [by the property], not by way of its own nature.
Therefore, there is indeed no fault in the sublation of the mere [locus].

For, when a locus is intended as such by virtue of a specific form, there is no fault in the restriction of sublation to that form; this is because space, whether in its nature as a real entity or in its eternal nature, was not what was intended as the locus.
Moreover,

if the subject (*dharmin*) were to possess a nature other than its similarity to the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), or if there were a nature other than that of the reason (*hetu*), who are we— mere investigators of reality— to negate it? Indeed,
nothing that has come into being through the power of reality (*vastubala*) can be negated by anyone, even by one intent on investigating reality, as it proceeds in its own course.
Since the one who relies on valid cognition follows an object established by valid cognition,
if there were such a sublation here [of that object], then pleasure and so forth would not have the capacity to produce anything else,
because they do not cause the production of sound and so forth simultaneously, as in the previous case.
For the *pradhāna*—which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion—is held to be the cause of manifest entities such as sound and so forth;
therefore, because it would lack a cause at all times, pleasure and the rest would be non-entities (*avastu*).
Indeed, if the permanence of the nature of the *pradhāna* is sublated, they must necessarily be non-entities.
That is incorrect,
because in this case, there would have to be an absolute (aikāntika) reason for the contradiction.

Because there is no contradiction between successive action and impermanence, and because there is doubt regarding its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), the "residual" (śeṣavat) variety [of inference] is accepted here;
for the reason of successive action functions by means of the negation of non-successive action.
Since there is no contradiction with the impermanence of sequential action,
it does not imply the absence of impermanence; how, then, could there be a sublation of the locus (*dharmin*), and through that sublation, a sublation of the property (*dharma*)?
Therefore, the mention of one's own subject (svadharmivacana) is necessary;
since the property to be proven (sādhya) is intended by [the proponent] himself as a property of the subject, its locus [the subject] must be stated.
It has been indicated that neither the mere locus (*dharmin*) alone, nor one that relies on something else, is what is to be sublated (by a counter-argument).
For, if the mere locus were sublated, there would be no sublation of the probandum (*sādhya*) intended by the proponent;
nor [would there be sublation] if the locus were sublated as having a substratum other than that [intended one].
Therefore, there is a fault in subverting a property that is useful for the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Consequently,
it is stated that by the explicit mention of "itself" (*svayam*), the subversion or non-subversion of other properties is indicated.
Thus, it is stated that [the property] belongs not only to its own subject (dharmin) but also to another subject.
For this very reason, he says:

"For when a subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma) is not sublated therein by something established through perception, inference, or scripture that is contradictory to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), that is a valid thesis (pakṣa); otherwise, it is a fallacy of the thesis (tadābhāsa). This is precisely the meaning previously stated.
5. Faults of the Thesis (*pakṣadoṣāḥ*) 1.
Faults of the thesis independent of the reason (*hetu*):

Is it not the case that there are other fallacious theses as well, such as those with an unestablished subject (*aprasiddhaviśeṣya*), those with both [subject and predicate] unestablished (*aprasiddhobhaya*), and those with an unestablished predicate (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*)?
An example of one where the subject is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣya*) is "the self is omnipresent.
An example of one where the predicate is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) is "sound is perishable" when addressed to a Sāṃkhya.
An example of one where both are unestablished (*aprasiddhobhaya*) is as follows.
The self is the inherent cause; why, then, is it not mentioned among these?

This is not correct, because this [allegation] is not a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), since it is established as belonging to a subsequent member [of the syllogism]; for its status as a fault of the thesis is determined by the mere presentation of the thesis itself. (268)
If someone were to make "the omnipresent self" the probandum (*sādhya*), such that the self is endowed with omnipresence, what fault would there be in the thesis (*pakṣa*)?
If it is argued that there is a fault because the reason (*hetu*) lacks a locus due to the non-existence of the subject (*dharmin*), [we reply: no.

In that case, the fault lies with the reason (*hetu*), not with the probandum (*sādhya*), because [the probandum] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [reason].
Thus, in the argument "sound is perishable," where is the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) unestablished?
If it is in sound, then this is not a fault.
For it is precisely from this [reason] that the probandum is established; otherwise, what would be the meaning of "probandum"?
Now, if it is argued that the reason is unestablished because its opposite is established, even if such an opposite were established for a fool, that alone does not constitute a fault in the thesis.

If the contrary is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the thesis is indeed sublated by that very *pramāṇa*; thus, the fault characterized as being "contrary to authority" (*āgamaviruddha*) is not a separate fault [from the sublation].

If, on the other hand, it is established by an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); thus, the fault belongs to that [example] alone, not to the thesis.
However, in the case where both [the reason and the example] are unestablished (*aprasiddha*), there is a fault in both ways; therefore, all these are indeed faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*).

Now, if it is argued that the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) arises solely from the fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), because in every respect the thesis itself is not established, then all faults such as those of the reason would become faults of the thesis;
there would be no fault of the reason whatsoever that does not obstruct the thesis.

Since the entire defect of the means of proof (sādhana) results in the obstruction of the thesis (pakṣa) itself, nevertheless, the status of being a "defect of the thesis" belongs to that which is designated merely as the proposition (pratijñā). 149
1. [A fault] does not arise merely from the existence of that alone; for if it were so, then a fault of the proof (sādhana-doṣa) would also result in being a fault of the thesis (pakṣa-doṣa).

Now, if it is argued that a defect of the proof (*sādhana-doṣa*), even though it subverts that [thesis], is not a defect of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*) because there is no such rule here; and if it is further argued that since this occurs by transgressing both the nature and the time of the thesis and falling instead upon the nature and time of the proof— which is distinct from the thesis— it is not a defect of the thesis but rather a defect of the reason (*hetu*) itself, such as lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), etc.— that too is incorrect.
Because it is equal [to the subject], there is no non-concomitance; for non-concomitance is indeed a lack of connection, and that [lack of connection] belongs to both because it resides in both.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the fault of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) consists in the unestablished nature of the locus (āśrayāsiddhatā), which depends upon the probandum (sādhya), not upon the means of proof (sādhana).
However, the dependence upon a means of proof is indeed a defect of the means of proof;
it has been stated in this regard that if both [the thesis and the means] were to establish each other through mutual dependence, how could that be a defect of the thesis?

Nor is there this restriction— that when the locus (*dharmin*) is established, only the connection with the property to be proven (*sādhya*) needs to be established and it must be indicated by its essential nature alone—
because of the statement [in the *Nyāyamukha*]: "it should be stated by its very own form."

How, then, was it stated that because a proof is impossible when the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished, the reason itself is impossible there due to the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)? The intended meaning is this: therefore, even a collection consisting of an unestablished property and a locus is indeed the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Therefore, since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is a fault independent of the reason (*hetu*),
that fault which depends on subsequent members [of the syllogism] is what remains attached to it.
Therefore, it has been stated that defects such as the unestablished locus (*asiddhāśraya*) and so forth are not defects of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
This has already been explained:

"A defect is not accepted as a defect of the thesis if it depends upon a subsequent member [of the syllogism]. Likewise, it would follow that even a defect of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) and so forth would be a defect of the thesis. (150, 269)

Because they are sublated by every [instance] of the thesis, therefore only those defects which adhere to the mere [thesis] itself are considered defects of the thesis, and no others, just as in the case of contradiction with perception and so forth. (270)

Therefore, it is the logical principle that there is no fault of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) such as an unestablished locus (asiddhāśraya). Now, one might object: "The inference 'sound is non-audible' or 'a jar is eternal' is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), because they are presented by way of affirmation, like the [invalid] statement 'the moon is not the moon,' which contradicts the essential nature of the property (dharmasvarūpa)."
There is no sublation of the subject, its property, or the specific form of the subject,
nor is the example unshown; we do not know what the reason for this [objection] could be.
To this it is replied:
[the relationship between] the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin).

By this very [example], the sublation of the subject (dharmin), its properties (dharma), their specific qualities (viśeṣa), and the essential nature (svarūpa) of the subject— all of which constitute parts of the probandum (sādhya)—

has been demonstrated. Indeed, by this very example, which is intended to demonstrate the refutation of the essential nature of the property, the sublation of all essential natures and specific qualities has been shown.
If it is asked how there can be the perception of one thing by means of another,
[we reply that] because the nature of being a probandum (*sādhya*) is no different [in all cases],
it is impossible to point out an illustrative example for every individual instance, nor is there any purpose in pointing such an example out.
Since the property of that subject is easily understood by the mere presentation of a single example, an example is indeed merely illustrative. 2. Refutation of the Whole (avayavin).
But how can there be a distinction between the property and the substratum?
Its status as a distinction is not stated in relation to those [previously mentioned] properties.
Otherwise, the means of proof would be futile; therefore,
it is a property of that [subject].

In this regard, a mere direction for illustration is stated: for the perception of an object, there exists another object characterized by substance and conjoined [with it] which possesses perceptibility.
A thesis concerning that which is imperceptible and undifferentiated is purposeless. (152)
These are the examples: the whole is not other than its parts, because no difference in weight is perceived;
nor are the parts other than the whole, because it would follow that [the parts] would be imperceptible;
nor does substance exist, because it would follow that qualities and substances would themselves be both substance and non-substance.

One [type of fallacy] occurs by the negation of the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*), and another by the negation of the specific qualities of the subject and its properties; these two examples follow their respective order. First:
"Whatever is distinct from that form is perceived as being exactly so; and if that form is not perceived, then the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established. (271)
For that which is not perceived as distinct cannot be directly perceived as distinct;
yet it is perceived as non-distinct while being accepted as distinct—hence this contradiction.
Because it is said to be "gone," there is a contradiction for that very reason.

3. Refutation of Substance, Quality, and Universal: If the parts are not distinct [from the whole], then perceptibility is unimpeded; wherever the whole is perceived, its parts must likewise be of such a nature. (272)
3. For that which is invisible and distinct, if the whole were not perceived even when its parts are perceived, it would not be anything other [than those parts].
Alternatively, the parts are not other than the whole, because that would entail the consequence of [the whole] being imperceptible;
for if they were other, then when those [parts] are imperceptible, it would follow that the whole is also imperceptible,
since it is not logical for a whole to be perceptible while its parts are imperceptible, just as in the case of the first [postulated] whole.
Now, if it is held that only the gross composite (*sthūlavayavin*) is perceptible and nothing else,
it has been demonstrated that "grossness" in a single entity is contradictory;
therefore, it is established that the composite is merely a collection of parts and there is no other [entity] distinct from them, nor are the parts anything other than that.

Likewise, the connection is that "there is no substance" means "it is not distinct from qualities," because it would follow that qualities and substances would either both be substances or both be non-substances;
the meaning is that either the quality would possess substantiality or the substance would possess the nature of a quality.

For instance, if there were a distinction [between substance and quality], then by virtue of their mutual exclusion, the principle would be that form (*rūpa*) is apprehended as a quality (*guṇa*) of a substance (*dravya*) when it is established by existence (*sattā*), and the same applies to other qualities.
Consequently, since the two exist through mutual exclusion, how could there be a discernment such that "one is a quality" and "the other is a substance"?
Even if they do not exclude one another, how could there be any discernment?
Now, if it is thought that the distinction consists in "the quality-ness of a quality" and "the substance-ness of a substance," that too is incorrect;

for apart from its own intrinsic nature, "quality-ness" and so forth do not exist. Furthermore, even if there were a distinctness of "quality-ness," existence (sattā) would still be present therein. (273)

Consequently, that previous consequence regarding the non-distinction of substance remains unrefuted; for if [substance] were existence (*sattva*), then everything would be substance, whether it be distinct from or not distinct from [existence].
(274) Since substance-ness and otherness exist through mutual exclusion, there is no differentiation between them; this point is indeed established.

However, in the case of distinction, there might be the suspicion of a differentiation: "it is a substance because of its connection with substance-ness," and "it is a quality because of its connection with quality-ness."
That too is not correct;
for how could there be the state of being substance and non-substance between two things that exist through mutual exclusion, such as form and taste?
If it is argued that this is because of their connection with qualities such as *guṇatva* (the nature of being a quality), etc., [we reply: no.
The nature of a quality (*guṇatva*) is not manifested by the manifestation of a specific quality, nor otherwise; rather,
both the nature of a quality and the nature of a substance (*dravyatva*) consist merely in having a common form.

Its specific distinction is called "being manifested by an individual of a different class," and "being an individual of a different class" consists in being superposed by a different class; thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). [This applies] to both substance and non-substance.
Now, if it is argued that the distinctness of classes (*jāti*) is intrinsic and mutual,
even in that case, the cause of their differentiation is precisely the fact of being superposed by different classes.
If individual entities are excluded by their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then the same applies to them as well; thus, a further universal (*jāti*) would be useless.
If it is argued that "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) belongs to [the category] "quality" (*guṇa*) because it is the basis for the cognition of a uniform form, [we reply: no.
What is the use now of this useless "universal" (sāmānya), since the status of being the basis for a cognition of a universal form is established by specific [particulars] alone?
Thus, there is no difference whatsoever between substance and non-substance in terms of their own nature.
Therefore, if [substance] exists as a real entity (*dravya*), there would be no distinction at all between substance and non-substance;
however, since it does not exist, a distinction arises.
Thus, it is logical that substance is conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), whereas the qualities (*guṇa*) other than it are not.
An example by way of refuting the specific nature of both [the subject and the predicate] is as follows:
"Every sentence has a false meaning."
"All speech has an unreal object"—in this statement, when the specific nature of both the speech and its unreality is intended to be negated, the fault lies in that [negation]. (275)

When it is intended to refute "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and "falsity" (*anṛtatva*) in their general forms, then there is a refutation of both natures. However, when the subject (*dharmin*) is the sentence and the properties to be refuted are its permanence and its having a false denotation, then there is a refutation of both specific instances; for by refuting every particular sentence and every instance of having a false denotation, its validity is established through the force of the statement itself. Therefore, there is a refutation of the absence of being a sentence and of having a false denotation.
And here, some specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣa*), such as impermanence and so forth, is to be understood.
For if impermanence were not established, the acceptance of the speaker’s authority would be entirely in vain.

If there were permanence, nothing would be produced by the speaker, and thus the speaker would be entirely useless; therefore, this contradicts one's own words: if the sentence were eternal, the speaker’s role would become redundant, and it would follow that [the sentence] exists as an already established entity even without the assistance of the form of speech. || 276 ||

For the speaker cannot be considered an auxiliary to the sentence if he does not contribute to the nature of the sentence itself; since no benefit accrues to the sentence from a contribution not made by it, one who provides no assistance is not required by the sentence, yet the speaker is indeed required.
Therefore, its impermanence must be established; consequently, by way of refuting that specific qualification, this is stated to be a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* provides merely an indication by way of an example.
Following this direction, for the purpose of understanding the explanation of the remaining examples, it is not merely the distinctness of the whole (*avayavin*) from its parts that is being proved;

rather, by virtue of possessing the definition of a substance—namely, "substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause"—the whole is established as such. Furthermore, if its distinctness were to be proved merely through its state of being perceived, [that would be insufficient].

In that case, since it is already established that the parts exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*) while the whole exists ultimately (*paramārthasat*), proving merely their difference would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore,
there would be an absence of gravity and downward motion [in the whole].
For the whole (avayavin) is accepted as the effect, since it is impossible for it to exist in its unperceived parts;
thus it is observed.
And if another [entity] that is non-distinct [from the object of cognition] were being proven, it would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
For the form of an erroneous cognition is already well-known as being merely the exclusion of parts, atoms, and so forth;
therefore, if that very [form] is what is being proven, there is necessarily the status of proving what is already established.
Moreover, in the very act of perception, there arises for those situated in close proximity to one another at no great distance a cognition of a single, dense form regarding their intermingled hair;
therefore, the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from the forms of consciousness cannot be established by that alone.
Consequently, it is the possession of the defining characteristics of a substance (*dravya*) that must be proven in that case.
In that case, since the definition is satisfied by its possession of heaviness as a quality (*guṇa*), downward motion as an action (*kriyā*),
and being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of both, the distinctness of its form from consciousness (*vijñāna*) is established;
and thus:
Furthermore, there would be both lightness and downward motion if this [weight] were merely a depression of the scale. || 154 ||
3. "If this [were so]..."—thus [it is said].
For if there were necessarily a downward movement caused by weight, then the end of the scale being pulled down by it would also bend;
yet that does not occur.
Therefore, he says that because it exceeds its constituent parts, it does not possess the characteristics of a substance:
"Because of its movement, it is devoid of qualities and action; therefore, it is not an inherent cause."
The conclusion is that since it is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of those two qualities and actions, it does not exist as such in their absence;
for that very reason, it is not perceptible, because it is not seen in the form of its effects.
(155) It possesses no perceptibility whatsoever.
For its movement is twofold— figurative and primary; it is not, first of all,
figurative, because its effects, such as heaviness and so forth, are not observed.

Nor should one metaphorically designate [the object] as "form," because apart from its constituent parts, nothing is perceived; for what is apprehended is the aspect of consciousness itself appearing as grossness,
and since no additional entity is seen,
there is no sublation of that [consciousness], as the specific difference [of an external object] necessarily follows from it.

The fact that another particular is the probandum (*sādhya*) is due to its connection with the definition of a substance (*dravya*), based on the mere fact of its being "other" than what has been stated; this follows as an invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatvena*), because otherwise, mere otherness would not constitute a probandum.
For instance:
When the downward movement of gravity is abandoned, there remains only its appearance; and this appearance is not difficult to establish even if it is non-different from consciousness.

(277) Even for those whose visual power of perception has been distorted by ophthalmia (*timira*), hairs, gnats, mosquitoes, flies, and the like—though categorized under the side of non-existence—appear as if perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
yet they do not cease to be non-existent merely because of that appearance.

Regarding this, another said: "Because a series of substances, down to the most subtle, is capable of being weighed—just like a mass of rays—it follows that there is no movement of the gravity belonging to a different substance. (156)

Because the series of substances beginning with subtle dyads and so forth do not produce a change in the measurement of weight upon being placed on a scale, it is impossible to perceive a distinct heaviness belonging to another substance situated in the midst of many substances; thus, there is no perception of a specific deviation in the scale’s inclination.

For even when two lumps of gold are joined and a further composite whole (*avayavin*) arises—possessing its own qualities and actions—the internal series of substances beginning with dyads still persists therein.

Consequently, that [gravity] which falls between the preceding and succeeding states of gravity is not perceived, just as the weight of a hundred iron needles falling into the midst of a bale of cotton is not perceived;
yet, even though it is unperceived, there is neither its gravity nor its downward motion. Therefore, because it is devoid of both quality and action, this [argument] is unproven (*asiddha*).
That is incorrect, because if gravity is not perceived, how could it have an increased motion? For this alone is the hope for its cognition; how then can it be its effect? (278)
Apart from the specific downward movement caused by gravity, only a mere appearance is established;
and even if that were established, it would not constitute a violation of the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Furthermore:
When that [powder] is joined gradually, and then joined all at once, there would be a difference in weight; therefore, when weighed separately and together,
for when the powder heap is joined gradually, because of the presence of many individual weights, the weight is great.
If they were joined only once, there would be only a single composite whole; thus, there would be no great burden [of complexity], nor would there be the consequence of distinctness.
Nor is there perception of such distinctness [in that case];
however, it is perceived when a collection of many threads falls together.
Therefore, that is not a valid example.
Furthermore, when the entirety of the previous composite whole has perished, there remains only a single composite whole existing at the limit;
thus, in the absence of multiple composite wholes, the case is exactly the same as in a heap of dust that is joined either simultaneously or otherwise. Hence, there is no fault.

That being the case, it would not be logical to say that "the substance is weighed by the garland," nor would it be logical for the final [element] to have the characteristic of being inferred through heaviness (*gaurava*).
1. Non-perception of gravity:
Alternatively, as long as the gravity of the two constituent parts remains the same even when they have become separate, the gravity of the whole composed of them is likewise exactly that;
therefore, there is no difference in the depression of the scale.

In that case, since the whole (avayavin) arises upon the destruction of all its parts, there would be the destruction of even the atoms (paramāṇu); thus, the claim that "atoms are eternal" contradicts your own tenet.
If it is argued that destruction occurs through disjunction (vibhāga), but there is no disjunction of atoms because they lack parts (anavayavatvāt).
Because it is impossible for there to be partlessness [in such a case],
for corporeal things must necessarily possess spatial divisions of east and west.
Therefore, it is logical that there is no destruction of the composite whole.
Furthermore, even if it were the case that atoms are destroyed, we would suffer no loss whatsoever; for if that were so—

It is not logical for there to be numerical equality between the *māṣaka* and the other units in sequence. [Verse 158] A composite consisting of five *māṣakas*, such as a *suvarṇa-māṣaka* and so forth, would not exist, because the individual *māṣaka*-parts and their composite wholes would have already perished due to [the reduction of the whole to] oneness.

The phrase "only one golden [thing]" and so forth would be possible because, while there may be the existence of multiple heavinesses, there is the possibility of numbers such as five; however, in the case of oneness,
there is only the number one, since the whole is one.
Now, even if weight (*gaurava*) is a single entity, such a designation [of degrees] occurs; however, in that case, number (*saṃkhyā*) is not ultimately real.

Therefore, as long as the constituent parts (*avayava*) have not perished, the number residing in them is logically possible. That [designation of degrees] is based on the similarity of units such as *māṣaka* and so forth; thus, when multiple substances are present, because composite wholes (*avayavin*) arise sequentially, there is a specific determination of weight by necessity.

Now, [if it were argued that] even a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) would not be perceived as a whole, successively increasing [in size], just like the single [atom] because there is no distinction among all [atoms], this is not so; for even when one atom is unperceived, the atom itself is not unperceivable. Therefore, the same does not apply to the collection of those atoms. Thus, this [objection] is not tenable. (279)
For it is not the case that when this [single part] is perceived, the heaviness of its aggregate is also perceived;
for even when the heaviness of a single part is not perceived, the heaviness of the load is perceived,
and a collection of parts constitutes what is designated as a "load of cotton."
Furthermore,
it is not the case that there is no perception when [the object] is not being characterized.
From a great heap of mustard seeds, there is a superior mode of progression; [this is] the view of the wise— so say Hevajra and Tathāgata.
If the gravity of the entire series of effects is not perceived at all,
[then] there is no weightiness.
The weight [of an object] down to a mustard seed is not negligible; it possesses color, smell, and minute imperfections.
That [weight] is difficult to perceive when being weighed because the heaviness of the effect is not observed in its cause. (160)
A mustard seed is one-fourth of a *raktikā*;
from that mustard seed onwards, up to a great mass, no increasing heaviness is perceived in the continuous series of successive effects.
However, as for heaviness prior to the mustard seed, it is found to diminish, such that each preceding stage is even less perceptible than the one before it—this is the conclusion reached.

Therefore, because the weight of the effect is not perceived, the logical principle—that by the method of exhaustion (pāriśeṣya), the cause itself must be weighed—is indeed perfectly clear. For it is only that which is perceived as being useful for the specific weight [of the effect] that is to be weighed, and nothing else; for when the weight of each subsequent effect is not perceived, that weight belongs to the cause as well.
If weight were [the cause], then its cause would be that, and its cause would be that as well; thus,
following this sequence until the causes are atoms, since those atoms lack any other constituent part (*avayava*) that could serve as their cause.
For it is thus: the fourth part,

When the final constituent part of the balance is destroyed, the heaviness of those two [the pans] remains; we observe that very same [heaviness] again even when those two are further destroyed. Therefore, by means of inference, we know that heaviness resides in atoms. Consequently, no substance exists that possesses the defining characteristics of a substance.
Furthermore,
even if the weight of the parts is not perceived individually, it is the weight itself that is observed in them; the whole,
however, is not visible.
Its existence is established solely on the basis of the observation of its effects;
and yet, that entire thing is non-existent.
For that object is not seen like a part [of it], nor is its effect observed. 8. But is it not seen? M. No.
Just as with the non-perception of gravity, because all weights are perceived by the scale;
that [perception] is the indicator for the lack of increase or decrease in the qualities of the *māṣaka* and so forth.

Just as when a form or other object is not seen by one's own sense-faculty, how could it be understood to exist through perception and inference if it is not cognized? [Objection: But even in the case of gravity, since movement is possible through other means, why should it be considered non-existent?

Nor [is it the case] for another [entity], such as form and so forth, because it is not perceived; thus, the whole (*avayavin*), such as a *māṣaka* coin and so on, is not something additional to its parts.
How then was a specific restriction stated by the Master [Vasubandhu] as "because the difference in the bending of the scale is not perceived"?
It is because that bending is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*).
Even when merely being spoken of, how could it not indicate even that which is devoid of essence?
Thus, one must understand: "Why is everything not perceived? What is to be known here?
It is that, according to their respective capacities, there is no cognition of form and so forth by the eye and other faculties beyond their specific limits.

For there is no perception of specific qualities such as color or taste apart from the parts, even if a whole were to exist; therefore, just like qualities or actions, the whole is simply non-existent as a perceptible entity. Thus, this is a defect of the thesis by way of sublation through a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*).
And this is the thesis.
[The thesis] is sublated by what is accepted, by one's own words, by inference, and by common cognition.
The eighth daily lesson is finished.

2B. The acceptance [of a thesis] through one's own words is possible because of the contradiction by one's own speech and so forth; however, other examples are also to be understood by the same method as previously stated. (163)

Just as in the case of the refutation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, one should understand that other examples demonstrating the logic of the refutation of the whole (*avayavin*) shown by the Teacher are also intended;
and these have already been demonstrated above.

5. The defect in the Naiyāyika definition of the thesis (pakṣa). (1) The inclusion of the term "probandum" (sādhya) is redundant. Now, is it not the case that the definition of the thesis according to the Naiyāyikas is: "The statement of the probandum is the thesis (pratijñā)"? What is the defect in this?
There would also be the undesirable consequence that even unestablished reasons (*asiddha-hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) would possess reality.
[Objection: But surely, for the Naiyāyikas and others, that which is being proved is called "the probandum" (*sādhya*).
However, since the unestablished reason and example will be established later,
how could there be the consequence that they constitute a thesis?
This is true.

If it were possible to specify the probandum as being present, then because verbal suffixes (*kṛtya*) have reference to all three times, that which is not of such a nature [i.e., not presently established] but is presented to another as such would still be intended as the probandum. // 164 //
For all verbal suffixes denoting action (*kṛtyapratyaya*) have the three times as their domain;

therefore, even the state of being a future goal (*bhāvisādhyatva*) would constitute a thesis (*pratijñā*). How so? Because at that time, the goal is designated as not having that nature [of being already established].
Even that which is the probandum is at that time indicated as the means of proof; therefore, at that time it is not a non-probandum,
nor is an unestablished [reason] a means of proof with respect to the probandum.
Therefore, its status as a means follows after that; its designation as a thesis (*pratijñā*) is precisely by virtue of its being a subsequent end to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
[The former] is a means toward another, while [the latter] is the state of being that which is to be accomplished.

Now, one might object: just as the word "sādhya" (the thing to be proven) does not convey the sense of being "proven" when used in relation to a grammatical factor—as in the expression "a jar is being made"—so too, even that which is designated as a "means of proof" (sādhana) will not cause it to be understood as such. Therefore, how can there be the undesirable consequence that an unestablished means of proof constitutes a thesis? This is true, provided that the context of conveying meaning were not the governing factor here.
But in the context of making [the meaning] understood, since it excludes everything that is unestablished, the term "probandum" (sādhya) does not rely upon a specific [unwanted] qualification.
By virtue of its function in making [the meaning] understood, the term "probandum" includes all other things to be proven, as opposed to the factors (kāraka) that are to be excluded.
Therefore, [the word "existent"] is not capable of excluding other things to be proven;

however, the exclusion of that which is to be proven by an agent follows from the context of the "indicative reason" (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Furthermore, since nothing exists with a cause, it must also exist without a cause.
Because it would follow that everything exists everywhere,
and because there is no basis for the claim that the probandum (*sādhya*) indicated as being unestablished is the "subject" (*pakṣa*),
the term "probandum" is not capable of implying the intended qualification.
However, since the exclusion of what is to be accomplished by a causal factor (*kāraka*) pertains to the context of communication (*pratyāyana*), there is no parity with that [logical reason];
therefore, the examples of unestablished and doubtful reasons have been provided.
M [states] the well-known example:

"Thus, O He, otherwise, even though [things] such as a hare's horn are unestablished for all [parties], they would be subject to proof (sādhyatā). And in that case, the fallacy of a reason with an unestablished example would follow. 166. Thus, the doctrine of a reason with an unestablished example would result.
If, for instance, one were to argue against a Sāṃkhya that "sound is impermanent because it is produced,

like a jar," or "because it is visible, like space," without regard for the context, then anyone who establishes a contrary definition would likewise face the absurd consequence that even things such as a hare's horn could be treated as a probandum.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even here, the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) is "the statement of what is to be proven" (*sādhyānirdeśa*). However, this does not mean that everything within the context of making something understood is a thesis; rather, only that which is "to be proven" (*sādhya*) is so called. This is because the gerundive suffix (*kṛtyapratyaya*) is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*), and according to Pāṇini’s rule (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), the object is specifically that which is most desired by the agent—wherein excellence (*prakarṣa*) resides.
Nor is that which is indicated as a means (*sādhana*)—such as the instrument (*karaṇa*)—the most desired;

otherwise, in the expression "he eats rice with milk" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), the milk, though intended as the instrument, would [absurdly] have the status of an object (*karman*), even though it is merely being brought about by the act of eating. Thus, it is not [merely] desired in that way.

Furthermore, even though the action of "defining" (*nepsiṣyamāṇa*) applies to all five members [of a syllogism], the definition of the *pratijñā* (proposition) is established by excluding the objects of the definitions of the other members, as they are under discussion as the things to be defined; thus, it is understood that "the *pratijñā* is the statement of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), which is not itself a means of proof (*asādhana*)."

Likewise, although the fourfold types of tenets— *sarvatantra*, *pratitantra*, *adhikaraṇa*, and *abhyupagama*— are introduced at the outset of the *Nyāyasūtra* through their definitions, there is no fault [in our position] because the definition of the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is understood from the rule that "the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*)," which avoids over-extension.
All of this, however, is incorrect, because:
And since everything is unestablished in some respect, [the reasons] are not tenable because of that lack of establishment.
In the investigation of the presentation and refutation of the distinctions such as action (*karman*) and so forth,
[the opponent's claim] that "it is a member of the probandum because its own nature was previously unestablished" is incorrect. 167.3.
Because it is their very nature,
they possess an identical tenet, for that [tenet] is characterized by their own formal commitment.
Indeed, a tenet (*siddhānta*) does not consist in the exclusion of unestablished reasons and examples, because everything that is unestablished is accepted;
for that which is accepted as seen in a treatise (*śāstra*) is precisely what constitutes an "accepted tenet" (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*).

Even if that [unestablished reason] is accepted as a cause, its status as something yet to be proven (*sādhyatā*) necessarily follows, for that which is unestablished cannot function as a reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that verbal suffixes denoting action (*kṛtyapratyaya*) have all three times as their object; the word "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) is likewise a suffix whose object pertains to all three times, since the mention of "action" is intended as an illustration.
Consequently, the status of being a tenet (*siddhānta*) is equal for everything.
Then follows the rebuttal beginning with the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Now, since the definitions of the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*) are the subject at hand, the rebuttal regarding the definition of the means of proof is as follows: "The statement of the object to be proven is the thesis (*pratijñā*). Thus, the thesis is the object to be proven itself, not the statement of the means of proof. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.33)
...that too is incorrect,
because all the characteristics of the members [of a syllogism] are unestablished, since their meaning is not established prior to the statement of those characteristics.

Consequently, if "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (pratijñā) were taken to mean the statement of everything that is to be proven, then everything other than that would be a means of proof; or alternatively,
if it meant the statement of the probandum as distinct from the means of proof, who would be capable of making such a distinction?
If it is argued that there is still doubt, we say no,
because the answer to this will be stated hereafter.

2. "In that case, the suffix -tavya (kṛtya) in the word *uttara* does not have 'the goal' (*sādhya*) as its object; for the kṛtya suffix occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), and the object is that which is most desired by the agent. Furthermore, that which is intended merely as a means or an instrument (*upāya*) cannot possess the status of being 'most desired' (*īpsitatama*)."
How then can that [means] be the object to be accomplished?
It is not so,
because it is precisely the means of accomplishment that is intended as the most desired object by virtue of being the thing to be accomplished.
Furthermore, no suffix denoting excellence (*atiśaya*) is accepted there,

because while some admit the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), others have rejected the superlative suffixes (*ātiśāyika*). Nor will the past-participle suffix (*bhūtapratyaya*) or the singular number (*ekavacana*) govern that case, since the desired forms are *kaṭau* and *kaṭān*.
And since it indeed possesses the status of an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (an accepted tenet), the claim that "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*)" is incorrect;
for in this context, the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), or the aggregate (*samudāya*) might be the probandum.

3. For one who maintains that the property (*dharma*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) which possesses similarity with the probandum in respect to that property would be meaningless with regard to the locus (*dharmin*).
If the property were the probandum, then its statement would constitute the thesis (*pratijñā*); thus, there would be the fault of [the reason] being redundant with the thesis.

Likewise, the definition of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*)— stated in the *Nyāyasūtra* as "an example is that which, through similarity with the probandum (*sādhya*), possesses the property of that [probandum]"— is contradicted;

for the properties of being produced (*autpattimatva*) and so forth do not exist in the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely impermanence (*anityatva*), such that it could possess the state of having those properties, as is the case with a jar and the like.

Since the subject (*dharmin*) is already established, the statement that "the reason (*hetu*) is the proof of that which is to be proven" (*tad-dharma-sādhana*) [as found in the *Nyāyasūtra*] is not tenable;
for if both [the subject and its property] were to be proven, the fault would apply to both sides. [Objection: But surely it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) that is to be proven?
The collection is not established, nor does the property of having an origin belong to it; to this it is replied:
even if the collection is the probandum, there is mutual qualification.
In that case, both the definition of the reason (*hetu*) and the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished.
For the definition of the reason is: "The reason is the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the example," while the definition of the example is:
"An example is that which possesses the property of the subject due to its similarity with the probandum. (Verse 169)
This [reason] would be contradicted if the probandum were a composite whole;
for since a composite does not exist apart from its constituents, those two [constituents] alone would be the probandum.
And there is no similarity between the example and the property of the subject as qualified by the property to be proven, such as having an origin and so forth.

In such a case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished for the opponent; thus, there is no definition of a reason. Furthermore, since there is no similarity between the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by impermanence and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as a pot, there is no definition of an example. Consequently, the definitions of the reason and the example are not established because they are impossible. [Objection: The word "probandum" (*sādhya*) will refer to the subject (*dharmin*), according to the principle that words applied to a whole (*samudāya*) also apply to its parts.
In the Nyāya Sūtras 5...
that too is incorrect.

Since [the term *sādhya*] cannot [logically] apply [to the subject], if it is maintained that the word *sādhya* refers to the locus (*dharmin*), then there is no need for a treatise; let it proceed according to usage in the world itself. (170) [Note:
Having previously written "itself" (*svayam eva*), this reading was later corrected.
For what is the use of stating definitions at that time?

Just as one might explain a poorly formulated definition otherwise because the intended meaning is impossible, so too will one falsely imagine the nature of the reason (*hetu*) and other factors; and just as that [reason] would then fail to be a prover, the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the treatise itself would likewise be rendered useless.

But surely, when you say that "the reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) pervaded by a part of it," you yourself accept that the word *pakṣa* refers to the locus (dharmin) through metaphorical usage; for in that case,
the subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus (*dharmin*), since the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part.
For here too, that same fault [applies], since this is not the case.

The subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property is sought to be known constitutes the "thesis" (*pakṣa*). When its property (*dharma*) serves as the reason (*hetu*), how can there be any question of metaphorical usage here?
For it is precisely that subject—the locus characterized by the specific property to be proven which is the object of inquiry—that is the thesis;
and since the reason is the property of that very primary thesis, there is no fault.

[Objection: "But if the composite whole (*samudāya*) is unestablished, how can it be established that 'this is its property' (*tasya dharma*)? This too is not tenable, because if the establishment of the composite whole is required, how could that [whole] be the subject (*pakṣa*)? For it is only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is in doubt that the mere locus (*dharmimātra*) possesses the status of being the subject. (283)
For when the aggregate is well-established, it cannot be the subject of the inquiry because its specific nature has already been ascertained;
thus he said:

In that case, however, since the thesis (pakṣa) is defined as "that which is intended by the proponent himself as something to be proven," if it were already established, how could it be "intended as something to be proven"?
Therefore, what is the meaning of the term "property of the subject" (pakṣadharma)?
If it is argued that [the reason] is a property of the subject whose property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is doubtful,
then how is it that its being a property of that [subject] is not established when the composite (samudāya) is unestablished?
How, then, was it stated that [it is so] "by metaphorically applying the name of the composite to its part"?
To this it is replied:

the employment of metaphorical usage is for the sake of resolving the objection. For when it is stated that "it is a property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*), there is the fault of over-extension regarding the definition. In that regard, they indeed object: "The statement 'property of the subject' (*pakṣadharma*) is not correct."
For at the time of determining the essential nature of the reason (*hetu*), the subject (*pakṣa*) does not yet exist;

rather, having perceived the reason in a mere locus such as a specific location, one subsequently recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Only after that does the cognition of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), such as permanence, arise.
Since that cognition is absent prior [to the recollection], only the mere locus remains known. If it is argued that the property to be proven is merely suspected [at that stage]:
Not so, because there is no fixed rule;
for surely a logical reason operates when there is doubt— how then can there be no fixed rule?

[The reason] does not [apply] to that which is merely rejected by what is established, because it is not intended to be refuted; rather, a reason operates only with respect to what is certain and what has been [previously] set aside, due to the absence of purpose and the lack of capacity [otherwise].

Therefore, one should simply say "a property of the subject" (dharmidharma). To this it is replied: if one says "a property of the subject," then since even a property of the subject of the example would be a logical reason (hetu), visibility (cākṣuṣatva) would also be a logical reason.

Therefore, since the subject (*dharmin*) would be included as part of the "thesis" (*pakṣa*), he states the inclusion of the "thesis" [in the definition] so that it may be understood how the subject alone can constitute the thesis;
this is because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part.
Even though at the time of grasping the reason (*hetu*) the collection (*samudāya*) does not exist within the intellect, it will nevertheless come into being later.
But surely, how can that which will exist later be present in the first [moment]?
For this very reason, it is a figurative usage (*upacāra*); otherwise, it would be literal (*mukhyatā*).
If it is asked how there can be a figurative application (*upacāra*) through cognition regarding that which is not present, [we reply:
is there poverty even in a daydream?
For it is not seen that one weaves a cloth from this thread;
for in that case, if it is not to be woven, it is not a cloth, and if it is to be woven, it is no longer the thread.
Regarding the statement, "The cloth must be woven," the speaker's intention therein is this:
that which will become a cloth is what must be woven.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose here?
there is indeed a purpose: when the word "sūtra" is mentioned, there would be the unwanted extension [of the term] to things such as cloth (*śāṭaka*) or garments (*paṭaka*);
therefore, this statement is made precisely for the sake of excluding other things.

Thus, here too, that which will be the subject (*pakṣa*) wherein the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) is to occur is its property (*dharma*); therefore, there is no consequence of [the reason] being a property of the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). Consequently, the meaning is this:
it is the property of a subject whose property to be proven is doubtful (*sandigdhasādhyadharmin*).
How then is it that a part of that [subject] is its property by virtue of the speaker’s intention,
yet it is not a "portion of that" [subject] because the word *pakṣa* does not denote a composite whole? This is the statement.
That is incorrect;
for how can the fault of another indeed be attributed to someone else?
This is indeed the fault of the wicked-minded commentator;
surely one person does not eat a karkaṭikā fruit while another suffers the cutting off of his nose.
A "pakṣa" (the subject) is the aggregate of the property to be proven and the locus of that property.

In that regard, if it is stated in general that [the reason] is pervaded by a portion of that [subject], then the subject (*dharmin*) itself would also be merely a portion of that [subject] and thus pervaded by it; consequently, the definition characterized by being pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) would not hold.
Therefore, he says:
"A part of that" means "its property";
although the word *aṃśa* (part) can denote a general category, here it is understood specifically as a "property" (*dharma*) due to the intention of the speaker.
Because the pervasion of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) by another property-possessor (*dharmin*) is not established,
the meaning of the phrase "not a part thereof" is that it is not merely a single part, since the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) does not denote a composite whole.
For by the word "pakṣa" (the subject), that which possesses the property-bearer (dharmin) as qualified by the doubtful property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is expressed;
therefore, the word "pakṣa" does not denote the aggregate (samudāya),
yet the cognition of the aggregate-meaning occurs through the force of implication (sāmarthyāt).
The "part" (aṃśa) of that subject (dharmin) is, by implication, the property (dharma) itself; for it is not the case that the [subject] itself is its own property,
provided that the term "pakṣa" refers to the aggregate.
If the parts possess an equal degree of primacy,
then [the subject] would be pervaded by that part; thus, it might also follow that it is pervaded by the part characterized as the locus (*dharmī*),
and this is undesirable.
Therefore, it is explained as follows:
for that reason, we have not anywhere imagined another word [to apply] elsewhere on account of impossibility;
moreover—

This point of defeat is called "admission of the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*). It consists in failing to remove a fault from one's own position while pointing out a fault in the opponent's position;
or alternatively, it is the acceptance of a subject (*dharmin*) that is suitable for conventional usage as being [identical to] our own purpose.
Let it be; however, the metaphorical usage [of "proposition"] is not tenable here.
Furthermore, when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to assume a metaphorical one.
Moreover, regarding the statement "the proposition is the indication of the probandum" (*sādhyānirdeśaḥ pratijñā*), there must be either an emphasis on the former term or an emphasis on the latter.
The statement of the probandum alone is the thesis, not the statement of the proof;
or rather, the statement of the probandum is the thesis and nothing else in that regard.
2B. [The opponent argues: "In the *Nyāyasūtra*, the prior restriction is useless and undesirable; however, in the other case, it is not so."

If the initial restriction were [intended] as a mere exclusion, it would be redundant; for the status of the statement of the proof as a "proposition" (pratijñā)—which is what that restriction would exclude—is already sublated by the specific rules defining the "reason" (hetu) and the "example" (dṛṣṭānta).
This is because a general rule (utsarga) operates only after its scope has been determined by the exceptions (apavāda) that have been formulated.
If, however, the restriction is applied to the latter [the thesis], then the statement of the probandum, the reason, and the example would also constitute the thesis; this is undesirable.

[Objection: But what is the fault in restricting it so that the thesis is only the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) and not of what is already established? For the probandum is not implied by the means of proof and the other members.
On this point, it is said:
"By the force of the statement of the means of proof, the status of being the probandum is understood to reside in that object.
For every means of proof (sādhana) is employed for the sake of proving what is not yet established;
once something is established, what is the use of a means of proof?

By the very power of explaining the definition of a means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no possibility that it would apply to a thing already established as being a probandum; therefore, the restriction is not for the purpose of excluding that [already established thing], nor is there any need to suspect that the means of proof is over-extended by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth. (171)
