The restriction "only as that which is to be proven" in the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) is intended to exclude that which is presented as a means of proof (*sādhana*), even though it is not yet established, by taking into account the function of the words themselves. For it is not the case that there is no capacity for proof in such instances. To this, he says:

Because it is pervaded by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, there is no room for doubt; for just as that which is indicated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) while being unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the exclusion of sound is rejected because it is indicated precisely as the thing to be proven (*sādhya*),

so too, by the definition of the reason and so forth— namely, "the reason is that which proves the probandum through similarity with the example"— the very thing that is the reason is [rejected] by way of its being a means of proving the probandum.

Thus, it can be explained that [the fault] lies in the example itself; therefore, there is no defect in the definition of the thesis (*pratijñā*) regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, as stated in the *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.32–39.

If the restriction is placed on the former [the thesis], then the statement defining the thesis would be useless; therefore, that statement results in pervasion (*vyāpti*), as it is understood by implication. (172) Since the restriction on the former is useless, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), there is a restriction on the latter, and its result is pervasion.
For instance,

since "the statement of the probandum is the thesis (*pratijñā*) alone," even if there were pervasion by another definition, the sentence would still have the result of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), meaning that it is the thesis alone and not a non-thesis. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that the statement of the probandum, even when stated as a means of proof (*sādhana*), is indeed the thesis.
Otherwise, would it not be admitted that [the reason] is itself stated to be futile?

And thus, the charge of an unestablished example or reason would follow. Therefore, when the opponent offers a rebuttal by means of the definition of the reason and so forth, the rebuttal of the [opponent's] own previously unestablished nature and other such defects is [already accomplished].
Likewise, this objection beginning with "because everything is unestablished" and so forth is not a fault either.
The demonstration of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) through mutual contradiction has already been accomplished by this very [method], but it does not establish one's own desired [thesis].

This is merely a demonstration of mutual contradiction; the intended goal is simply the refutation of the opponent’s position, for the objective of this reason is not the establishment of the probandum.

Therefore, this is indeed a restrictive determination of the subsequent term; and thus, through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), whatever lack of being a proposition (*apratijñātva*) there may be is entirely refuted,
[establishing that] it is only a proposition (*pratijñaiva*) and not a non-proposition (*nāpratijñā*).
That which was [previously] unacknowledged as being a means of proof is now also set aside; having thus refuted the definition of a proposition (*pratijñā*),
he now speaks in order to refute the definition of a fallacious proposition (*pratijñābhāsa*).

The claim that there is a fault in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) when there is a contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis is incorrect; for that [example] was stated by the unlearned as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
As the opponent has said: "A fault in the thesis called 'contradiction between the thesis and the reason' [is asserted]. (286)
For example: "Sound is eternal" [is a contradiction]; contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) is, for instance, [saying] "because everything is impermanent."
The proposition is "Sound is eternal," and the reason is "because everything is non-eternal.
If everything is non-eternal, how can sound be eternal?
For without sound, the state of being "everything" would not exist.
Now, as for the question of how sound can be eternal when it is [in fact] impermanent, he says in response:
"This is not a flaw in the thesis."
For, [in the case of] contradiction, non-connection with what is desired, lack of assistance, and simultaneous existence—
thus all defects of the members [of a syllogism] would constitute defects of the proposition (pratijñā). || 173 ||
When there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), it is called the fallacy of the proposition known as "contradiction" (*virodha*).
This contradiction consists in the non-connection with what is intended (*iṣṭāsambandha*); and that non-connection with what is intended is non-beneficial (*anupakāraka*).

If coexistence (*sahāsthiti*) is the reason (*hetu*), then it does not assist that [probandum] because it is defective; thus, it would contradict the probandum (*sādhyavirodhin*). In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all defects of the members [of the syllogism] would indeed be defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*).
For no defect of a member, such as the reason and so forth, is contradictory by way of the contradiction characterized by non-assistance to the probandum.
Consequently, it would follow that every defect of the logical mark (*liṅgadoṣa*) is a defect of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*),
yet this is not the case;
for...
It has been established that a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) does not depend on another [member of the proof].
However, if a fault of the thesis were to depend even on another [member], then there would be no such thing as a fault of the means of proof (*sādhanadoṣa*) at all;

for, since it would be included within the fault of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) by virtue of contradicting the meaning of the proposition, there would be no separate mention of faults of the means of proof.
For what person of unconfused intellect would speak of that which is included within one [category] as being separate?
Therefore, such a fault of the thesis is simply non-existent.
Alternatively, contradiction may be defined as the nature of coexistence.
In that case,
it would be an "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reason because it is impossible in the intended subject;

for if a reason is impossible in the intended subject (*pakṣa*), it is unestablished, and thus it would be refuted by its very status as unestablished, rather than by contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).

Now, if there is a refutation of that which has been proposed as a thesis (*pratijñā*), then the fault of the thesis is that it is sublated by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it is established; thus, this is not what is called "contradiction" (*virodha*). Furthermore...
That very object of the thesis would be refuted;
thus one should proclaim that sound possesses impermanence and causality.
If one were to proclaim that sound possesses a cause by virtue of its impermanence, then what further observation of the meaning remains here beyond the mere presentation of the example? (175)
This narrative is not for the sake of a reason (hetu), but rather for the sake of a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta):
"Sound is eternal."
Since everything is impermanent,
it should be stated here as well that because everything is impermanent.
However, such a statement was made because of a lack of training;
as it has been said:
"For that was stated by the untrained merely as an example by way of dissimilarity."
Indeed, we perceive no purpose here other than the narration of an illustration;
if it is asked why this is so, it is because:
For this would indeed be a valid reason if sound itself were to establish impermanence; however, this is not tenable,
because:
7. Investigation of the Universal:

Having designated [an object] as distinct in its particularity, if one then follows it through its universal, there is neither pervasion by that [universal] nor any result in following the universal. What, then, is the purpose of following the universal? || 176 ||
Regarding the general application:
indeed, all applications are understood by following the principles of verbal logic.
And verbal reasoning consists of injunction, prohibition, and restriction;
and even an injunction is both subverting and subverted.

Likewise, there is also a restrictive rule (niyama) regarding the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in the case of a general injunction and a specific injunction; in that regard, sometimes the former is the sublated and sometimes it is the sublator.
In every respect, the rule is that the particular (viśeṣa) sublates (bādhaka) the general injunction (sāmānyavidhāna), which is the object to be sublated (bādhyam);
for it is precisely thus that linguistic usage is observed.
And in this case, regarding the particular sound (śabda) in the statement "sound is eternal" (nityaḥ śabdaḥ), there is the prescription of the distinct particular property of eternality (nityatva).
Furthermore, since the affirmation of impermanence applies to the subject in its general sense, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is logical.

This is just as in the case where it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"; although the giving of curd was established as a general rule, it is sublated by the giving of buttermilk which is specifically prescribed, because the general rule (the *utsarga*) takes effect only after setting aside the domain of the exception (*apavāda*).
Therefore, its pervasion of the particular occurs through the following of the universal;
and this is not the result of following the universal [itself], because of the force of the statement and because the statement allows for such an interpretation.
By way of description: if this is the intended meaning, then one should say, "Sound is eternal because it is impermanent."

If it is argued that there might be a coincidence of two distinct qualifications upon a single object when they have not yet fulfilled their respective purposes—and that in such a case, a contradiction would arise due to confusion—[we reply:
no such possibility exists;
for it is not possible for one who has just prescribed permanence regarding that very same thing to become confused at that very moment by prescribing impermanence.
Furthermore, one who lacks even an understanding of the meaning of sentences has no entitlement to engage in debate.

Now, as for an example of the contradiction between a proposition (*pratijñā*) and a reason (*hetu*), if someone were to say something such that it could somehow be conceived as an instance of this, then [one might argue] that because there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason, "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*) is a fault.
Therefore, this very application [of the reason] is desired: "Sound is eternal because it is non-eternal";
for in this way, by necessity, non-eternality would belong to sound alone.
Therefore, there is a contradiction in the refutation of eternality;
for this very reason, it is said in the Nyāyasūtra: 3.2.14.
The word [for negation] must exist as something already established; therefore, he says:
"In the word."
The Teacher said:
There might be a refutation of the meaning of the proposition here by means of a reason, if the word were [itself] established.
The refutation occurs precisely by means of the word's own established status,
because two contradictory things cannot coexist; furthermore, since this is merely a demonstration elsewhere, it is not a refutation itself—
this is simply the presentation of a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
If it is argued that there is no cause now, he says: "Therefore... (5B).

Where the deviation of the counter-example of the probandum is described by means of the fifth [case-ending], there the example is [stated]; however, the reason is considered to be [stated] through the application (upanaya).

If it is asked, "How is it understood that 'whatever is impermanent is all [non-eternal], and sound is non-all'?", he says: By stating [the reason] in another object that is contradictory [to the conclusion], one expresses the difference of the audible [sound]. (177)
And that [existence] is not tenable for universals because they do not reject difference.
It exists— [he says].
By demonstrating that impermanence—which is the opposite of permanence—resides in an object other than sound, he thereby asserts the distinctness (*anyatā*) of sound.

[The opponent argues: "Everything is pervaded by impermanence, and since sound is impermanent, it must be other than that [everything]; thus, sound lacks the property of being 'all' (*asarvatva*). In this way, because this reason (*hetu*) establishes distinctness, and because sound itself is included within "all," that distinctness is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus he says.
And that [reason] is not tenable for universals because they do not reject particularity;
for a universal does not acquire its own nature by rejecting particularity, since it is restricted to the domain of the rejection of internal subdivisions among the particulars themselves.
Furthermore, it might be argued that by the word "all" (*sarva*), a collection (*samudāya*) is expressed,
and a single sound-part is not a collection.
That is incorrect;
for if each [part] were thus excluded individually, nothing would be "all," and it would be observed that the tree is not the *śiṃśapā* alone— thus, the distinction [between them] would be rejected.
That is incorrect;

for just as in certain contexts one might say, "A tree is not a *śiṃśapā* alone," the negation applies to the occurrence of all that is heard, yet it does not follow from that [negation] alone [that the tree is non-existent].
1. That [universal] is not all [of those particulars], because it is impossible for it to exist in that which is not the reality of all the various particulars. || 179 ||
Now, if it were argued that "all" is merely the word itself due to the speaker’s intention,

then, in that case, the term "non-all" would be a synonym for "word," and there would be the fallacy of the unestablished nature of a portion of the thesis (pratijñārthekadeśāsiddhatā), just as in the argument: "Sound is non-eternal because it is a sound."
Now, how is it that the sound-ness of sound is unestablished?
For nothing is possible in the absence of its own nature;
yet, it is not called "unestablished" because of being unestablished as a subject by way of its own nature, but rather because it is unestablished as a reason (hetu).
For causality exists only when there is difference, and not otherwise;
why?
Because a distinction between the signified and the signifier is necessarily present.
A word is not made known by another word, because that which is to be made known is unestablished;
nor is an unestablished thing proved by what is unestablished.
Even if the word were established, it would still not prove [the object].
For that which is already established is not proven by that which is [itself] established.
Nor is it [proven] by way of its own nature, because it is unestablished as a subject (*dharmin*).
Now, it may be argued that the identity of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is not admitted.
If there is no difference between the subject (*dharmin*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*), what contradiction could there be?
There is indeed a contradiction;
for if one says, "It is impermanent because of its being sound-ness," the composite whole (*samudāya*) would not be the probandum (*sādhya*).
But surely, by implication, it is sound alone that is impermanent; thus there is no contradiction with its being a composite entity.
For when one says "it is impermanent because of its being sound," impermanence is not understood to belong elsewhere, nor is it understood as something isolated.
For smoke is not "not possessed of fire" simply because it is smoke;
rather, in that case, there is no distinction due to the relationship between the universal and the particular.
Here too, if one were to argue in this way—"This [sound] is eternal because it is sound, like the word 'cow'"—then it would indeed be a valid reason.

In this case, however, in the argument "all sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound" (*śabdatvāt*), there is no relationship of genus and species (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) due to their difference.
Now, is it not the case that if "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is the subject (*dharmin*), its status as the probans (*sādhana*) is contradictory?
If there is an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), why is it not a means of proof (*sādhana*)?
On the other hand, if there is no such connection, then there is simply the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
Therefore, the fault known as "unestablished" (asiddhatā) does not apply,
because [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to its being over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa).
Consequently, for a reason that exists in the subject (dharmin), the fault is precisely its inconclusiveness.
It is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, if it is argued that the connection with being restated is not established and is therefore called "unestablished," [we reply:
there is nothing distinct whatsoever that remains to be further explained.
In that regard, one must state either "sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of sound" or "it is non-eternal";
however, neither of these two [positions] exists.

When it is stated that "sound is impermanent," another reason is required; to exclude that [other reason], the phrase "because of being sound" (śabdatvāt) is stated again. (288) In the case of the statement "it is perishable because of being sound," when other subjects (dharmin) are excluded, the application of the word "sound" possesses its functional efficacy once more. (289) If it were said, "it is impermanent because of being sound," there would be a dependence upon another property (dharma).

And regarding the statement "sound is impermanent," because there is a dependence on another reason (*hetvantara*), the inclusion [of both reasons] in both cases is for the purpose of refuting that; thus, there is no fault.
To this, it is replied:
If the capacity of "sound-ness" (śabdatva) [to prove the point] exists, then another reason (hetvantara) is redundant; if it lacks that capacity, then what is the use of that repetition?
Therefore, since that which was intended to be expressed in the restatement is not present here, the fault is simply "unestablished" (asiddha).
Why is the fault of "lack of concomitance" (ananvaya) not mentioned here instead?
Let it be; this fault also applies in the case of a cumulative argument (*samuccaya*).

However, in the case of a restricted argument (*niyata-kathā*), it is not tenable because there is no defeat of one who has already been defeated, and because of the requirement to point out the grounds for censure (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the subject (*dharmin*) itself is indeed untenable as a means of proving its own properties (*svadharma*).
If it were not capable [of being proven], there would be the consequence of no dispute; and thus the reason would be rendered futile. Therefore...

Because there is a distinction between the object to be known and the means of knowledge, the probans—which is to become the property of the subject—is unestablished; thus, the subject is unestablished for its own proof.
(180) For a distinction between the object to be known and the means of knowledge is observed; in the absence of that [distinction], the state of being a probans is unestablished.
For a lamp, while illuminating by means of its luminosity, is not capable of accomplishing its own causal function if that [luminous] nature is not perceived;
and a signifier brings about the cognition of the signified only when there is a difference,
yet here there is no difference from the nature of the substratum.

If it is argued that [the reason] is unestablished because its status as a prover is unestablished, and that the status as a prover is likewise unestablished because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unestablished, we say:
no.

If there were difference, there could be an investigation into the underlying continuity (*anvaya*); however, since in this case there is no difference at all, what role would an investigation into continuity have when the subject itself is already flawed?
Therefore, the subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in its own proof.
[Objection: But lamps and the like are indeed established in their own proof.
"It is true that [the means of knowledge] are established, but it is an unequal comparison to say that they establish what is not perceptible by being themselves non-perceptible;
for there is no dispute regarding the nature of a lamp when it is seen."
But here, even when sound is perceived, there is indeed a dispute regarding its impermanence;
for if there were no dispute,
its status as being established by direct perception would be just like that of "sound-ness" itself.

If it is argued that the fault is equal everywhere because the distinction between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmiviveka*) is unestablished in all entities, we reply: no, for there is a distinction by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Is it not the case that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "being sound" (*śabdatva*) are also established through perception, just like a lamp?

Now, if it is argued that because of the distinction [between them] based on the conceptualization of different properties (*dharmabheda*), there is no relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*),
this is equally applicable even to the case of a lamp; for in that case as well, there certainly exists a distinction in conceptualization, namely that "this is the nature (*svarūpa*) of the lamp."
Nor is it [the case] conventionally, because the nature of a lamp is distinct; for just as there is a conceptualization of difference in that regard, so too is there no proof.
In the state of being devoid of activity or non-activity, the designation "lamp" refers to its own nature;
however, that which is merely its own nature is indeed its own nature,
because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) therein.
Causal efficiency follows from intrinsic nature;
however, in the case of a lamp, which is a subject possessing properties, there is no such thing as an intrinsic nature for that which is devoid of activity.
It is not tenable to claim that there is no activity because the intended object (or action) does not exist,
for that would lead to an over-extension;
nor, by speaking in such a manner, is any purpose whatsoever accomplished.
If it is argued that there is a conceptualization of difference, [we reply] no, because that [difference] is established even through the relation of universal and particular.
Therefore, the subject (dharmin) is not the means of proving its own nature,
because there is no difference [between them]; however,
among "producedness," "impermanence," and "sound," there is indeed a distinction created by their exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
For it is thus:
the state of being a means of proof.

Since the nature of an object is a single entity that is directly perceived by itself, what other part of it could there be that has not been seen and must therefore be examined by means of valid cognitions?
For the self-nature of the object is one; since it has been directly realized through perception, what else remains of it to be examined?

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that only the substratum (*dharmin*) is established by perception, while impermanence and so forth are not? What then is the property (*dharma*)," we say: no, because [the substratum] is one with impermanence.
For there is no such thing as "impermanence" that is distinct from that [sound];
for if it were something other than impermanence, how could the substratum—the sound—be apprehended? Otherwise, both would be non-existent, since they would not persist through time;
if it does persist through time, then it must be accepted as being permanent.

Even by a thousand other means of knowledge, there can be no apprehension of impermanence [in that which is already grasped]; for how could there be a sublation by another means of knowledge of what has been directly perceived?
Every other means of knowledge is rooted in perception.
For princes who devour their own progenitors are like crabs;
they are not authoritative cognitions,
whereas direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the primary authority among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Is it then that Mahākāla alone is devoured by the ḍākinīs?
Or rather, is it that neither permanence nor impermanence is perceived through direct perception,
but rather the mere intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of all things is cognized by it?
Whether it be permanence or impermanence, [the cognition] depends upon a subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

But surely, how could impermanence—which is its very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—not be apprehended? For permanence is the state of pervading extended moments of time, whereas impermanence is the opposite.

In that context, the apprehension of permanence occurs when there is an apprehension of the entity’s pervasiveness over time; if that [pervasiveness] is not apprehended, then the cognition of impermanence is necessarily attained.
For at the very moment that the pervasiveness of entities across different times is not perceived, the cognition of impermanence becomes perfectly clear.
If it is argued that pervasion alone is not perceived, and not impermanence,
then what indeed is this so-called "impermanence"?
If it is argued that at that very time there exists another name which serves as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), or that it exists later at that same time;
Why is it not perceived by direct perception?

How could that which is not being perceived be identical with it? For only that which is perceived as identical can be its very self; for that which is perceived as related must necessarily be [distinct from] it.
If it is argued that although it is not perceived as being identical to that [object], it is nevertheless subsequently perceived as being related to it—
that very [perception] is [the basis for its existence].
Another dharma 3 B.

However, it is not logical [to claim] that something which meets the conditions for perception is related to that [non-perception] if it is not cognized by direct perception; how then can it be said "that exists"? For there is no other way of understanding its non-existence. (295) 4B.
In the absence [of an object],
where there is no perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, it is precisely that which is established as non-existent;
there is no other way to prove non-existence.
And so it has been said:
"For those who state that [the object] is established by means of valid cognitions, the opposite follows by implication.
Now, if this [non-perception] were an error, then there would be no fault even in the absence of perception.

If, in every apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*), error were to prevail, then in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the subject, how could inference be a means of valid cognition? (296) How could a reason (*hetu*) whose connection with the subject is unestablished attain validity? When neither perception nor inference would be a means of valid cognition, (297) then the establishment of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) would occur; thus, [the world] is mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*).
When there is no apprehension of future or past form through direct perception, then,

provided that the connection with the subject (*dharmin*) is established through direct perception, the proof of a future or past entity is achieved through the inference of the logical reason (*hetu*).
In that case, the establishment of an object other than the one perceived would have a valid basis;
however, if the identity of the future and past forms is asserted,
then inference becomes redundant because the object is already established by the means of perception.
If error were real, there would be a total annihilation [of all things], and thus nothing at all would exist;
therefore, impermanence (or permanence) is indeed established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Alternatively, if it is not established by direct perception, it is because it is a property (*dharma*).
For it is the mere substratum (dharmin) alone that is established by perception; otherwise, there would be no inference,
because all properties (dharmas) would be established through perception itself.

That [objection] is useless and false, because when a property (*dharma*) is established through perception, the locus (*dharmin*) is thereby established; however, even perception is not a means of proof for a mere locus devoid of properties. (300)
Indeed, a substratum (dharmin) devoid of its properties (dharmas) is never established, because it must necessarily be apprehended as "soundness" (śabdatva) and as a "category" (padārtha).
Therefore, just as there is the apprehension of soundness and so forth, there is likewise the apprehension of eternality and so forth; in this regard, there is no distinction whatsoever.
Now, if some deviating property is not perceived by direct perception, what fault is there in this?

For example, it is possible to perceive the mere verticality of a post and a person without perceiving either the state of being a post or the state of being a person; yet, because [verticality] pervades both, there is no cognition of the object [as one or the other] without [the specific property]. (301)
For it is not possible to grasp that very form while abandoning its pervasive nature; if that [nature] is not grasped, then it is simply not grasped at all.
[Objection: But is it not the case that even a long object is indeed seen, even when it is not apprehended as "long"?
It is not so, because only the part is perceived there;
nor is that length [of the whole] [perceived],
for that length belongs to the whole.
And that is to be understood through inference; for it is thus:
And that is to be understood through inference.
When one part moves, it is understood that the whole moves; therefore, by means of this [observation], the oneness of this [whole] is established through inference.
When one constituent part is being pulled, the entire collection of all parts is perceived as being pulled along with it; thus, it is not an inference that "this is one with that other."
In that case, it is only a mutual relationship that is inferred, not identity;
nor is that [identity] the object of inference, for if perception does not operate, it could not become the object of another means of valid cognition.
Indeed, it is not logically possible for that very same thing to be both seen and unseen;
therefore, whether it pervades time or does not pervade it, it is apprehended by perception itself and is not an object of inference.

In this regard, if a thing does not possess that form as an object of direct perception, it does not have that form; for indeed, yellow and so forth, when apprehended by direct perception as blue, cannot be considered to be "exactly thus" [blue] by virtue of being grasped as non-pervasive throughout other times.

Otherwise, if all the collection of temporal parts (*kālakalā*) were combined [simultaneously], then everything would be completed at that very moment, and consequently, there would be the absurdity (*prasaṅga*) of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be performed throughout the entirety of time occurring at once.
If it is argued that this is not so because future and past temporal parts are not apprehended [at that time], then we reply:
if they are not apprehended, their pervasion [by the present] is likewise not apprehended; thus, it follows that only its connection with that specific [present] time is apprehended.
And thus, like lightning and so forth, it is indeed impermanent, as shown by its exclusion from direct perception.
By that very [means] 4 T.
The ninth daily lesson is completed.
Now, if destruction occurs for things such as lightning, it is impermanence; it is not merely by virtue of their connection with that [moment of] time.
Indeed, since there is no destroyer whatsoever, how can there be destruction?
If it is argued that destruction occurs solely due to the impact of clouds,
then why is it not accepted here as well that there is an impact from things of both similar and dissimilar kinds?
Therefore, even in the case of lightning, destruction is simply the non-perception of it at a subsequent time.
And since it pertains to all objects, its eternality cannot be apprehended;
[thus] memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: But even when jars and other things are perceived at a later time, how can it be said that they are not being apprehended?
No, because that very [time] is not apprehended;
indeed, even the preceding time is not apprehended.
Furthermore, what is this existence or non-existence of time?
Indeed, there is no such thing as a moment, day, month, or the like—time distinct from entities such as form—that is established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There is no cognition of a "month" on the first day, nor is there a cognition of a "day" during the first watch of the night.
If it is argued that, since at the second moment neither the preceding nor the succeeding [moment] is perceived, time such as a day and so forth is nevertheless cognized through memory, we say:
no.
Because recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), for recollection does not establish a previously unknown object;

being preceded by perception, that which is based on memory does not have as its domain an object not [previously] perceived. And by perception, time such as a month and so forth is not grasped. (303)
If it is asserted that time consists in the nature of a collection [of moments], it has been established that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending such a collection.
(304) If it is thought that this is not unestablished because it is proven by multiple perceptions, [we ask: can the proof of multiple perceptions ever be accomplished by anyone?
(305) 1 B reads *nāsiddham*.
The invalidity of recollection has already been established previously. That which arises from recollection is conventional, but it is not ultimate.
(306) Since time itself is conventional, its pervasion is clearly conventional as well. Therefore, let it be understood that impermanence is the very nature of existence.
(307) If this distinction were indeed the intrinsic nature [of things], how could it be conventional? A conventionality without a basis would be neither the probandum nor the proof. (308)

The establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) occurs precisely because a relationship is possible; for in the absence of the existence of a relationship, there can be no probandum or probans. To this it is replied: "Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from one [thing] as manifold [is] conceptualized as a single form; it takes this as its object, and thereby the determination of the property-possessor (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) is established. (310)

The exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of all entities from things of their own class and from others is apprehended by perceptual cognition; concomitance (*anvaya*), however, exists only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). (311) If perception (*adhyakṣa*) were conceptual because it follows the operation of the sense organs, then there would be no concomitance even when [entities] exist together, since perception occurs in terms of "prior" and "subsequent.
(312) For one by whom only a single [entity] was first seen, its concomitance does not appear, because that would entail the appearance of all individual instances (*vyakti*) simultaneously. (313)

2. Since it is established that the manifestation [of the universal] does not appear due to distance and other factors, if the individual (vyakti) is not perceived, there can be no perception of the universal (sāmānya) which pervades it.
If it is argued that there is a similar perception of the [new] individual in another instance due to the mental impression (saṃskāra) from the perception of the previous individual;

This is not so, because the cause for the recollection of a mental impression (saṃskāra) is that which was deposited by the apprehension of that very object; how then could there be cognition of a different object from an impression produced by the apprehension of an individual [particular]? [315] 3B. In the case of its manifestation...

For the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of an individual is the cause of memory and cognition only with respect to that very same [individual], not for the perception of a previously unperceived object,
nor for the perception of a previously perceived object, nor for the recollection of something never seen. Furthermore,
since the universal (*sāmānya*) is a different entity from the individuals, how could there even be a recollection of it when it has never been seen?
Nor do we perceive anything other than the manifestation of clear and non-clear forms, based on the observation of the recollection of prior and subsequent objects;
for in perception, apart from the distinct forms of two [objects], there is no cognition of another form,
since it is simply two manifestations that appear therein.
If it is argued that [the object] appears because a cognition with a corresponding form arises, that is untrue;
for it has been stated that appearance is to be established by means of inference. Is the appearance of a wall or the like established by means of inference? (316)

If the prior appearance has been forgotten, then inference might be stated for the sake of remembering it, or some other effort might be made; however, [this is not the case] at the very time of the appearance itself.
For a wall or such things appearing [in consciousness] is not to be established by inference, nor are walls and so forth [established in that way].
Indeed, there is no worldly consensus that "because there is an appearance in the form of a wall, therefore the wall exists" or "the wall appears."
Rather, it appears because one perceives it by its own nature as distinct from the form of others;
nor does the universal manifest through a nature that is distinct from the form of the individual.
If it is argued that we do not indeed perceive the universal (*sāmānya*) as having a different color or shape,
and that the nature of the universal is simply external to color and shape—
then in that case, the universal does not exist at all, because there is no external entity that is external to color and shape.
If it is argued that its nature is indeed all-pervasive, then that which is dissimilar in color and shape is simply dissimilar;
for all-pervasiveness does not possess color and shape.

If it is argued that the pervasiveness belongs only to color and shape, [we reply: if that pervasiveness were perceived as pervasiveness itself, then it would indeed be perceived at another time. If this is the argument, [we respond: no.
This is not so,
because there is no difference between the existence and non-existence of the individual;
for even when the previous particularity has perished, it is perceived in that very same way.
And there is no destruction of the preceding [moment] through non-discrimination.
If it is asked how there can be destruction of that which has been perceived there, [the response is:
if it has perished, why is it not perceived by another in the previous location?
Or, if it is argued that this is because of the absence of pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*), [we reply: no.
That form is indeed perceived, though its mere spatial pervasion is not apprehended due to concealment;
what is this concealment?
It is the state of being invisible.

If it is argued that how can that which is visible possess the nature of being invisible, since in another location it possesses the very nature of being visible, and that therefore the object does not exist [there]—
to this we reply: it has been established that the object does not exist apart from its nature as something visible.
Furthermore, if the property of being perceived in another location were to perish upon the destruction [of the individual], then pervasion itself would be destroyed;
and thus,
the universal (sāmānya) would not be eternal.

And thus it follows that the universal is nothing other than the individual itself, because anything distinct from the individual— such as a common form— is a mere conceptual construct and therefore lacks objective reality;
if that is so, then how can there be a cognition such as "these are similar"?

There is no fault in this because of their similarity— due to the similarity in color, shape, and action— and precisely because of that similarity, it is "thus," just like the similarity [of the term] *rāṣṭrakūṭa* and so forth;
moreover, ...
Regarding one who says that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the basis for a cognition of a common form:
a common cognition will arise either because of the performance of a single purposeful action, or because it is produced by a single cause.
It is not produced by a common form, like the commonality [perceived] among Brahmins and others.
1 B. Universal (sāmānya)
(2) Regarding the determination of merit and demerit even in the absence of commonality of caste such as Brahmin and so forth:
[Objection] But how can there be a determination of merit and demerit without the existence of castes such as Brahmin?
And even if castes do exist, how [can there be such a determination]?
For caste is not destroyed,
nor does one drink liquor,
and there is no determination of merit and demerit other than through scripture as a means of valid cognition.
How could that very scripture establish [its meaning]?

For it is not possible to establish the injunction "a Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" without reference to a genus (*jāti*), because it is impossible to establish it with respect to every individual instance.
There is no fault, however, [in our position] because [the injunction] proceeds from an instruction based on the apprehension of a common form.
Furthermore, the uniformity of reflective judgment arises solely from beginningless latent impressions and instruction;
apart from these, no other means of valid cognition is established here.
Moreover—

The cognition of similarity possesses a form distinct from the individual [particulars], just like a body [is distinct from its parts]. Otherwise, it should be understood that it would be the behavior of the blind. (317) The perception of a self distinct from the particular does not attain established validity; for if there were consciousness otherwise than that, the existence of the object of knowledge would not be real.
(318) If the cognition of similarity is associated with a form distinct from the individual [particulars]...
Since it is not established in that manner, how could there be an establishment of the universal from it? If it were merely a cognition, then the universal is not established;
for the establishment of a specific object does not follow from mere cognition alone.
Whatever the form of a cognition, that alone is established from it; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is both different and non-different [from its particulars], we say no.
Because they are mutually contradictory:
for if that which is different from the distinct were non-different, how could it have distinctness? And if there is the appearance of distinction, how could it be non-distinct? (319)

If some difference is admitted, then that very thing would be a universal; yet its non-difference [from the particular] would not exist, because of the extreme difference. (320) If non-difference from another is admitted, then that entity would be neither different nor non-different; however, if it were non-different from that very [particular], it would again become a thousandfold. (321) Therefore, being extracted from that, it would simply not exist, having reached destruction. If it were both different and non-different, it would follow that it is both visible and invisible. (322)

It would follow that the seen and the unseen are one; thus a great marvel has arisen, since an object is established as both existent and non-existent by virtue of its being visible and invisible. (For instance:
For in this way, even that which is dead attains the nature of the immortal through oneness; therefore, let it be understood that the universal has a merely imagined form.

Consequently, the distinction between property and property-bearer arises from the difference in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*); where that [distinction] does not exist, there is indeed the fallacy of the thesis being a part of its own meaning (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
(324–325) The universal is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*).
In investigations of the ultimate truth, identity and difference are denied of things that exist only conventionally, because such [distinctions] are not established as they truly are.
(182) The conventional universal, being real, is indeed distinct from the individual, as is discerned through positive and negative concomitance.
And that [universal] is indeed of the nature of the phoneme and so forth;
for if it were not established as the phoneme and so forth apart from the individual instance, it would not exist in another individual, and thus there would be no establishment of difference. (326)

It is logical that what is excluded and what is inclusive are not non-different; therefore, the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished through conceptual construction.

However, there is no apprehension of difference by the senses; thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), it is because that which is established by perception possesses ultimate validity.
Since inference operates where it is preceded by perception, the nature of the means of proof is a cultivation based on conventional existence.

In reality, however, for that [universal], neither identity nor difference is supported by valid cognition; since their distinction exists merely through conceptual construction, in truth it has the nature of the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, let it be understood that only the individual is established through perception;
furthermore, the proof of the individual through inference is preceded by perception.
Therefore, however, if the universal were established, it would not be a cognizer of difference;
consequently, its occurrence in difference would not be possible, because differences are never-ending.
For instance:
If the universal is perceived, then, in the absence of the mention of particulars, its occurrence would necessarily be through differentiation;
for no one acts toward that which has not been determined.
Alternatively, if the perception of the universal is preceded by the observation of the individual, then there is the apprehension of their relation.

Since it must be the case that wherever there is a universal, there must also be an individual, the operation [of the word] occurs with respect to a particular; for one who perceives that very particular, how could there be a cognition of the universal?
Consequently, it follows that the cognition of the universal would result in the apprehension of the individual through inference.
And thus, since the cognition of an individual occurs through inference based on an inference, there must again be a cognition of a universal in that case as well;
from that universal, too, there would be a further cognition of another universal of individuals, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If, however, one eventually cognizes the individual, then since there is no difference [in the nature of the object], one should have cognized it at the very beginning; what is the use of this exhausting succession?
Furthermore, since the accomplishment of all purposeful action depends upon the cognition of the individual, [the universal] would not even function;
therefore, it is logical that the universal is merely constructed by the intellect and is not external.
Surely, for one who does not perceive a difference,
even when there is the apprehension of the form of the cognition, how can there be an external operation?
It is exactly so, because the relationship of cause and effect is observed in this very way.
In that case, for us as well, there will be the occurrence [of the word] in the individual based on the cognition of the universal, since the relation of cause and effect is the same here too;
thus it follows that "having reached the myrobalan, the deity purges"—
if indeed the relation of cause and effect alone suffices, what is the use of an internal, redundant universal?

Therefore, let it be understood that everything is a universal in the sense of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*). For if there were no real entity as a universal, there would be neither engagement nor desistance [from action]. One who accepts a universal must necessarily accept the cognition of the individual, because otherwise there would be an absence of purposeful activity.
Let the cognition of the individual arise from that very same mark, such as smoke; what is the use of a universal?
Furthermore, even if it were from a universal serving as a mark, the cognition of that [individual] would still arise from that very mark.
Moreover, there is no connection between the mark-individual and another individual.
But as for the universal, because it is all-pervasive, one accepts its existence [thinking] "it exists";

this is incorrect, for even if the universal were all-pervasive, if it were perceived in that very same way [as it is in one individual], how could it truly be accepted as making another individual known? (334)
Even though the universal is all-pervasive, if that pervaded [property] existing at the time of inference is not apprehended, how could its pervader be apprehended? Furthermore,
if there were cognition [of the pervader] despite the relation [between the two] being unapprehended, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
because there would follow the cognition of even another instance of a different universal.
If it were replied that there is no such connection [between the word and its object], then comprehension would occur even for one who has not grasped the connection;
moreover—
How this is to be understood was explained previously;
furthermore,
if the cognition of an individual arises from the universal, then the universal must also be cognized from the word.
If it is argued that the individual is not thereby obtained because this cognition is unreal,
then all cognitions of universals would likewise be unreal; what then is the use of a universal?
Is it not the case that a universal exists everywhere? However, because the individual instances are not perceived, there is no correspondence [with reality].
Since only the individuals possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), and since it is impossible to perceive them without a universal, the universal is therefore accepted.
The non-perception of the individual, however, is due to the absence of a mark (liṅga) that is connected to it.
[Objection: But surely even from a mark, only the universal is to be cognized; if the individual is perceived therein, why is it not perceived everywhere?
If it is argued that only the universal is denoted by the word, then it follows that the individual is also cognized through the inferential mark (liṅga);
and in that case, the aforementioned defect remains.
Furthermore, it might be argued that a separate universal is faulty,
whereas there is no fault if it possesses both natures;
but that too is incorrect.
Even in this case, does the fault of [the cognition being] manifest not occur?
For even from that, there is no comprehension of the individual through the universal, because it does not touch upon the individual.

(335) Indeed, if the universal is held to be either distinct or non-distinct from the individual, then cognizers do not transcend two possible courses: namely, whether the cognition of the individual occurs or otherwise.
If it is argued that there is cognition because all experience is possible, why does one not act?
If there is no cognition, how can there be action?

If it is argued that even what is already cognized is treated as uncognized for the sake of setting [the person] in motion, then it is contradictory to say that the very same thing is both apprehended and unapprehended in that same form;
for affirmation and negation cannot simultaneously obtain their own nature within a single locus.
If it is argued that there is therefore a distinction between the synonyms, [we reply:
by what means is it established that a thing is perceived as distinct through one synonym but not through another?
For how could one act for the sake of that which has not been so perceived?

If it is argued that [the word] is merely a synonym for that very thing, then how can there be the cognition "of that very thing" if it is not already cognized? Even if it were cognized, the [synonym] would not function; thus, that same fault remains.
Therefore, if the characteristics of the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) exist only as conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), then in that case,
[the argument] "sound is impermanent because it possesses soundness" would also be [valid].

For one for whom the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct [from the particular], why does it not follow that [the reason] is a part of the thesis (*apratijñārthaikadeśatva*), since the connection with that universal is already expressed by the word "subject" (*dharmin*) itself?
[Objection: In this case as well, it will not be so, because it is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) that is being expressed.
The connection with a universal, the exclusion from others, or the cognition of that [exclusion]—the connection with a universal does not occur at all without the cognition of it.
It is perceived.
The cognition of that form [of the universal] has already been refuted. Therefore, it is only exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) that is cognized here through the word.
(337) If it is accepted that the connection with a universal is cognized through the word for particulars, then how can that be cognized when the individuals themselves are not cognized?
For whomsoever there is food, for that very person there is the breaking of the vessel;
however, it has already been determined previously that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of particulars is not fit to be expressed.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) alone is the meaning of a word.
Now, how can even exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) be cognized without the cognition of the excluded object?
If it is indeed cognized, what is the use of exclusion?
If you argue that the postulation of exclusion is due to its being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*), then why not simply accept a universal (*sāmānya*) instead?
Acceptance [of a universal] occurs by following after [the perception of] exclusion; for is it not the case that the cognition of worldly people is "Am I apprehending an exclusion?",
since there is a cognition of distinctness?
There is no fault, for it is simply a matter of common cognition; to explain:

If it were not cognized through the word by way of its distinction from what is undesired, then there would be no engagement with that object through such a differentiation. For one must necessarily have a cognition of it in a form distinct from what is of a different class; otherwise, one would not engage [with it] while avoiding what is unintended.
If it is argued that its distinction from the unintended follows simply from the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) itself—
If it is argued that even when there is a connection with another property, how could there be such a state [of being as it appears] when the thing itself is not actually such;
and that its cognition as such occurs because of that connection—[we reply:
for that which is not of that nature, and which is not perceived in its own form when connected with another, cognition [of it in that way] is simply not tenable.
If the cognition of difference is understood through their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*),
then the connection with a universal (*sāmānya*) is useless;
for that very difference would not be perceived if there were no universal.

In that case, from what source would there be the discernment of difference among universals if they were connected with other universals? If their state were discerned by their very own nature, then the same consequence would apply to individuals as well; thus, the universal is useless.
And when there is a cognition of difference between two things, then how [could there be a universal]? For a universal does not subsist in only one thing;
therefore, this person must necessarily cognize the difference between the individuals, and since that difference from heterogeneous things belongs to all of them, that very thing is the universal.

But surely, in the absence of a universal (jāti), how could that very distinction between similar and dissimilar [individuals] exist? For instance, when individuals are mutually distinct, the universal is not [itself] mutually distinct. There would indeed be a distinction among the individuals, yet that [universal] lacks any perceived reality. (339)

If difference were based on individual instances, then just as there is a difference between a *śāvaleya* (a spotted cow) and a *bāhuleya* (a black cow) from a *karka* (a white horse), so too would there be a difference between a *karka* and a *śāvaleya* from a *bāhuleya*; consequently, it would follow that these two [the *karka* and the *śāvaleya*] belong to the same class.
It is not possible for one who perceives everything to establish a distinction through a means of cognition (*karana*) when making a convention (*saṃketa*).
This [objection] is neither logical nor illogical, because:
Even if the universal exists, the fault that has been refuted does not apply;
for it is held that the universal is manifested by the individual, not by its own inherent nature.
Because its manifestation is not observed in places devoid of individuals and the like, manifestation itself must be disregarded; and yet, that [manifestation] is not observed in all cases.
Therefore, even in that regard, the pervasion of the performance of convention is not established.
Even a universal must be perceived before a convention can be established or linguistic usage can occur;
moreover, a universal is not perceived apart from an individual instance.
For if the convention were established through the perception of a restricted universal upon seeing all individuals, it would be free from confusion;
yet even then, since it is only the individuals that are seen, the universal is indeed useless.
For instance, when this convention "this is a cow" is made by seeing a single individual, how could there be a cognition of a restricted universal?

If it is argued that among universals such as "animality" (paśutva) and so forth, there is no discernment of any one universal by way of exclusion [from others]—that "cowness" (gotva) is the object of convention here—then we reply: how can that "cowness" be distinguished? How can such a discrimination be made?

If it is argued that "that which is manifested by such individual instances" implies that the individual instances themselves possess this nature, then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*):
the characterization of the universal depends upon the unity of the individual instances,
and the unity of the individual instances depends upon the characterization of the determined universal.
If it is argued that the discrimination [of the universal] occurs spontaneously as "cow, cow," we say no;
for the universal "cow" is characterized precisely by its non-occurrence in white horses (*karka*) and other such animals.
If it is argued that the very cognition "this is a cow" is the apprehension of "cowness" itself,
then surely how can a cognition whose object-form has not been manifested indicate the object?
If it is argued that we do not perceive any object of cognition in this [conceptual cognition] apart from color and shape,
and that this very [color and shape] is the universal because it is recurring, we say: no.
Because such a following (anugama) is impossible;
for a form of a phoneme that follows other individual instances would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its being perceived as following [them] even when a single instance is observed.
And if it were so, there would be the cognition of every individual; for if [the universal] is manifested by the individuals, it is not cognized as such [independently].
If this is argued, then there would be no cognition of it whatsoever.
If it is argued that [the universal] is cognized as far as the perception of the individual extends, we say no,
because the universal does not consist of merely that much.
If that were so, then since the universals would be nothing other than the individuals themselves, there would be no further universal; thus,
in response to the claim that "the universal is simply the production of such a cognition," it would follow that the universal is merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
For many things, the universal (*sāmānya*) is simply the exclusion of what is other;

indeed, it is impossible to demonstrate a universal other than this mere exclusion of heterogeneous entities. Furthermore, heterogeneity itself is precisely the exclusion of what is different from that [universal], for just as one thing is distinct from another, so too are subsequent and further instances; there is no illustration otherwise.

Furthermore, it is impossible to point out a universal by saying "this is that," because, being non-distinct, there can be no such demonstration; yet this cannot serve as a valid response, as it would entail the non-existence [of the universal].
For it is not possible to establish a universal while excluding the individuals, as that would entail the impossibility of linguistic and practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
It is not correct to say that "the same applies even to the negation of a universal," because linguistic convention is possible even when it is based on the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).
Just as with non-action and non-substance,
for universals as well, mutual exclusion alone is the cause for their conventional usage.
Because of non-attachment;
2. B. in that state; 3. B. and likewise, the knowledge thereof.
Now, the connection with individuals (*vyaktiyoga*) is the cause for the conventional usage of difference between universals; nevertheless, this remains a fault,
because if [a universal] is not different by its own nature, how could it be differentiated from another?
From the connection with "white," the distinction "the white one" is perceived;
indeed, the distinction of one thing does not inhere in another.
If it is argued that the universal indeed inheres [in the individual] because of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*),
then since the non-difference of the universal inheres in the individual, the individuals themselves would consequently be non-different;
thus, due to the connection with all universals, even a cow would be a horse and so forth.
Furthermore,

the universal of cowness (*gotva*) and the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of individual cows do not differ from one another among their own and other classes; therefore, how could individuals be the differentiators of the universal?

Now, if individuals are distinct from their own very nature [as well as] from those of a different class, then let that very distinction itself be the universal; what is the use of postulating another?
Even if another universal is accepted, it is still that same distinction among individuals which serves to differentiate one universal from other universals.
In that case, is this particularity (viśeṣa) a universal (sāmānya) that exists as an established entity?
Or is it a universal in its own right, distinct from other universals,
such that the differentiation of the possessors of the universal arises from their connection with it?
Just as white color exists by itself, while the cloth exists through its connection with that [color]—
that too is not tenable, because:
5B. A jar’s color-form, such as white, is never perceived alone anywhere. Therefore, how can its own whiteness be perceived?

(343) Since whiteness and so forth always reside in a substance and are never seen apart from it, how could anyone perceive that [whiteness] itself is the form [of the jar]? By what means could it be known?
Why is it not accepted that its purity arises from the substance itself,
just as whiteness does?
(4) Refutation of Substance:
Now, if whiteness is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that substance, then what is the nature of that substance itself? That same fault remains.
If it is argued that [the substance] is perceived as "substance" (*dravya*) alone, [we reply that] even the cognition "substance" is not untouched by color and shape.
Since cognition consists of color and shape, which are merely qualities,
how can that other substance be the object of cognition?
Nor does shape admit of being something distinct from color and the like;
it is simply color that appears in such forms as roundness and so forth.
[Objection: But surely substance also appears?
For indeed,

even by means of tactile cognition, there is an appearance of identity in the form "this is that same jar"; moreover, recognition does not pertain to a mere quality, otherwise one would have [the cognition] "color is touch."
Furthermore, it is not logical for form (*rūpa*) to be perceivable by the sense of touch; therefore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is logically possible only with respect to a substance (*dravya*).
Thus, whatever is apprehended by a cognition whose object is distinct [from that of another] is distinct from it, just as a cloth is distinct from a jar;
and since a substance is apprehended by a cognition whose object is distinct [from that of form], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To this it is replied:
there is no observation of recognition with respect to an object distinct from form and so forth; for one who does not remember [the past] has no [access to] the object of a prior cognition.
(344) First of all, in the act of seeing, there is no appearance of a jar or the like.
Nor does it appear in the cognition of touch; for at first, only a single part appears, and that appears in the same way even in the absence of other parts,
yet that [single part] is not the jar.
It is not the whole that pervades all parts of every direction, because it is the whole of which the pot is a part; nor is the pot mere color,
since the term is applied to the inherent cause of color.
Furthermore, since recognition does not exist at that time,
the notion that the apprehension of the whole occurs through the appearance of various successive parts, qualities, and so forth,
is also untenable.
Since, at that time, it is possible to perceive only another part [of the object], there is no possibility of perceiving the configuration (saṃsthāna) as a whole;

likewise, even when [the quality] has perished, the arising of memory regarding another quality occurs. Let the comprehension [of this] proceed from inference, for it is not preceded by direct perception.
When there is perception of other qualities and parts in a jar and so forth, yet there is no perception of further qualities and parts, how could the jar not be merely that much?
[How could it be] other qualities?
(5) Refutation of Recognition:

Now, if the cognition of a composite whole such as a jar arises from recognition aided by memory, then when the qualities of that composite are analytically separated, one might even ask, "What is the jar there?
However, their inseparability [from one another] exists because they depend upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends non-separation, because [the two] are perceived as mutually exclusive; rather, non-separation is to be apprehended by the cognitions of recollection and recognition. Nor can a collection attain validity if both recollection and recognition individually lack validity.
[Objection: Regarding the parts, is it not observed that those who are individually incapable of carrying a palanquin become capable when acting otherwise [in combination]?
In that case, because they produce their effects therein, "power" (śakti) is simply the nature produced by such previously existing causes and is not something distinct;
but here, in the case of memory and recognition, what is the effect?
If it is argued that there is a cognition of the whole,
we say no,
because there is no cognition of anything else apart from those [parts].
Now, if another cognition arises in the form of a certainty,
that [first cognition] is non-existent;
for a certainty that lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is indeed no certainty at all.
Indeed, certainty cannot arise from a non-means of valid cognition (apramāṇa), for that would result in the means of valid cognition being rendered useless.
Now, if at that time there is certainty regarding other parts by means of inference, then the cognition of the whole arises from the recognition of identity;
for there is no identity between one part and another part, nor between one quality and another.
That too is incorrect, because inference is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa-puraḥsaratvāt*).
Whatever has been apprehended by perception exactly as it is, that very thing must be cognized by inference in precisely that same way.
Therefore, since the thing is apprehended by perception as being inseparable from its [intrinsic] nature, it is likewise apprehended through inference as possessing that very same nature.
And therefore,
[the term] "of the solitary" means of that which is separate.
Unity [of the object] follows from recognition; otherwise, how could that which was perceived by direct perception regarding a previously seen thing proceed directly into the path of cognition?
For it is not possible to apprehend something in one way through direct perception and then apprehend it in another way even by means of a thousand recognitions.

1. The Definition of the Reason (Hetulakṣaṇa).
The characteristic of the cause is stated therein:
