just as the state of existing in the middle of a cloth [requires a substratum]; and the state of existing in the middle of an absence is likewise a state of existence.
4B cloth; 5B a jar and so forth as a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The state of remaining in non-existence occurs by itself alone, because non-existence has that very nature;
for it is not the case that the lacquer’s connection with the wood requires another connector when the lacquer itself is joined with the wood, since it becomes so by itself.
This [position] is incorrect.
For just as lac, by its very nature, attains union with fire through contact with wood;
yet...

Non-existence, by its own nature, is incapable of performing the functions of pervading or occupying a middle space. (358) If that entity were non-pervasive, then non-existence would be rendered meaningless.
Furthermore, if non-existence were also pervasive, how could anything else exist within it? (359)
By its mere nature, it is not pervasive; for if there were an absence of a middle state, it would follow that it is non-pervasive.
If you say, "It is accepted as being only non-pervasive," then what is the use of an absence [of a middle state] now?

For non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed postulated so that there may be no confusion; yet, since that [non-existence] is established by its very nature as being non-pervasive (*avyāpin*) among categories of things (*padārtha*), its uselessness is unavoidable.
How could it be pervasive through non-existence, or even through its own cause accompanied by non-existence? What contradiction is there in this?
That too is incorrect;
for if non-existence were to make a pervasive entity non-pervasive,
it would have had to be mixed with it previously— otherwise, how could there be such a change?
Indeed, it is not possible to establish that which is pervaded as being the pervader.
For if it were all-pervasive from the outset, there would be a confusion of categories;
if, on the other hand, its own nature did not exist previously, then it is not seen to be otherwise [later] than that.
Now, in its own nature, it is neither all-pervasive nor non-pervasive;
it is pervasive due to its connection with pervasion,
and non-pervasive due to its connection with the absence thereof.
And so it has been said:
"Whether as 'diverse' due to external adjuncts, or again as 'non-different,' this proliferation (prapañca) regarding the natures of entities is observed only when they are conjoined.
That too is incorrect, because: [verse 362]
Otherwise, if there were for it a cognition that excludes duality, then, through its connection with another, it would be understood as partaking in two entities.
Otherwise, however, this would be the case:
that entity, the others distinct from it, and yet another beyond those two, would all be cognized in their own intrinsic nature, independent of any limiting adjuncts.
If there were a cognition of that mixture, it would be nothing but an error; thus, the non-existence of the object would follow, and this would establish the reality of ignorance (avidyā). (364)
Then,
since that [self] which possesses attributes is itself distinct from its attributes merely by virtue of their existence, the postulation of further attributes is futile.

There is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is divided by itself, from within the possessor of the adjunct (upādhimat), or by means of another adjunct; and if it were divided by its very own nature, then that same state of being divided would remain even when there is a dependence upon another possessor of the adjunct.
If it is argued that difference [is established] by depending on something else, we say no; for there is no utility in those differences to that extent.
4 B, being... man.
5–6. Since there is a distinction from all [other things] by virtue of their own distinct natures, what is the point of postulating another distinction here? (365)

Now, if one were to argue that "difference" arises from the cognition "it is different from this" and "different from that," then such a conceptualization of difference cannot be dismissed as purposeless when it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If that is so, then because of the perception that even a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is different, another level of difference must be admitted; and since there would likewise have to be a difference from that [adjunct], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of differences.
By its very nature, the absence of difference alone follows;
let this fault be welcome,
for this indeed is our accepted position.
This is not so;

for even if difference does not exist by way of its own nature, it might [be thought to exist] through the form of another. But how could there be "otherness" for that [entity] if difference itself is absent? (366)
For how could that which is not differentiated by its own nature be differentiated by the nature of another?
In the absence of differentiation, the other-nature itself would simply not exist.
For if there is no difference [of the other] from its own nature, then the "other" does not exist at all;
since that is absent, how could there be a difference from it?
On the other hand, if the differentiator is distinct by its own nature, then even the substratum (dharmin), though non-different [from it], will be differentiated by it.
That too is incorrect, because:
"If its difference from another were by way of its own nature, then for one who is moving far away, it would be impossible to draw near. (367)

When another differentiator is itself differentiated by its own nature from that [first], then for anything other than that, how could there be ear-ornaments of *kiṃśuka* flower-clusters dyed by fate?
It is impossible for something to be both different and non-different.
Indeed, difference does not become a difference by merely splitting another;

therefore, when there is a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a single thing, that same [difference] belongs to the difference as well as to that which possesses the difference. Thus, difference is not [derived] from another;

rather, the essential nature itself is the difference by virtue of its own nature of non-connection with others. Consequently, identity alone is the essence of the meaning of "difference," and thus difference itself is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
That alone must be expressed through the intended purport (*tātparya*); otherwise, even the expression of word-meanings would not occur,
because that which is confused cannot constitute a word-meaning,
for a real entity (*vastu*) is that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).
Furthermore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not possible in a universal conjunction;

and that exclusion from other entities is cognizable through perception by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). When a convention is established regarding that [exclusion], it alone is what is cognized by the word. Thus, exclusion alone is the denotation of the word, for it is impossible to denote that which is excluded by means of that which is not excluded.
(2) Refutation of the Universal:

Now, if that exclusion resides within the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object], then if the intrinsic nature itself is not denoted, how can there be a denotation of an exclusion that is non-different from it?

On the other hand, if the exclusion were distinct [from the object], then it would simply be the universal (*jāti*) itself being presented by another means, since it would follow after its own individual instances.
Thus, it is only the positive form (*anugata-rūpa*) that is to be established, not the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); so how can a statement have exclusion as its result?

This is not the case, because it is that very [object] which, being excluded from others, is called a "jar. It is not by connection with a universal (*sāmānya*) that there is difference for that which is already excluded. (368)
This has been established:
that which is not itself excluded cannot be excluded through its connection with another;
for if it were connected with a universal, it would simply be a universal itself.

Or rather, there could be no similarity for that which is dissimilar; even through connection with another, it is not logical. If it were similar by itself, the postulation of a universal would be redundant.
Even in the absence of a universal, the dissimilar thing does not possess the nature of that universal. (369)
Even if it were to possess a universal, it would not be identical [to that universal],
because it appears in its own distinct form.
For it is logical that when there is an appearance of difference, it is like a universal; however,
when there is an appearance of non-difference, it is simply a universal—
if there were no apprehension of difference, it would be called either "universal" or "particular."
Now, its appearing both as distinct and as non-distinct is unreal,
because:
If it appears as distinct, then it would be like a particular; if it appears as non-distinct, then it would be a universal.
For it is not logical for a single entity to have two natures—both distinct and non-distinct.

It is not the case that the universal is distinct from the individual in one respect and non-distinct in another; rather, it is established that it is distinct in some respect and non-distinct in another.

That [entity] is real and the other is not, because a universal cannot possess two forms due to their mutual distinction; in that case, there would have to be two separate entities, and the other would be a further universal. (371)
Because of the difference between the two forms of the universal, it follows that it is merely an individual; furthermore, its status as a universal is not tenable due to the difference in its forms.
(372) If the universal has two forms—one distinct from something and the other non-distinct from another—then, because those two are mutually distinct, they would possess the nature of individuals.
If it is argued that an individual is not something other than its distinct nature because it is called an "individual" due to its connection with "individuality" (*vyaktitva*),
then surely individuality is a universal (*sāmānya*); therefore, through connection with that, there would be sameness.
If its manifestation were non-different [from the universal], pervasiveness would not follow.
Furthermore, if one imagines two forms [of the universal], the same undesirable consequence as before would arise.
Therefore, the very nature of manifestations is indeed difference.
Therefore, that universal [is a universal] by virtue of its individuality;

or else, it is a universal through connection with a universal; in that case, there would be yet another universal, and thus those two together [would not be a universal] because they possess a universal.
For a universal is not like a particular; therefore, the cognition that "it is the same" regarding the two universal forms does not apply to the individual (vyakti),
because the individual is not conjoined with universals, as it is established by way of distinct universal forms.
It might not be in the individual;
2. B. [End of section].
If it is argued that, despite the difference between particularity (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*), they are distinct in one respect while non-distinct in another,
then another higher generality would arise for those two as well due to their difference.
That being the case, there would be individuality for both the universal and the form of the universal;
consequently, there would be no identity with the previous universal, because of the lack of connection with that universal due to the intervention of another universal.
Therefore, since there is not even a single [part] common to all, there is no connection with a universal; hence, this cognition of a uniform form is devoid of a real object.
Since there would be no end to the generalities of generalities for those who maintain such a position,
the entire unmanifested [reality] alone would be the object of cognition.
Even at the conclusion [of the process], it is clearly evident;

for those who do not accept a universal (*sāmānya*), the existence of a universal is impossible there. Furthermore, since the final [moment] is identical [to its predecessor], the preceding universal would also exist due to that non-difference; thus, the cognition of a universal would have a real objective basis (*sālambana*). But this is not the case, so this argument is trivial.

If, even among such differences, a difference exists that is distinct and pervades all differences, then—even though non-distinct things are joined with mutual difference—their being joined with that [difference] does not subvert their non-difference; thus, everything would indeed be non-distinct.
If it is argued that there is a difference between the universal and its instances:
If there were no difference between the individual and the universal, then the universal would not exist; rather, it would simply be the individual itself.
And since that [exclusion] is not different from itself, it follows that non-duality (advaita) results.
Therefore, exclusion alone is the universal;
for is it not the case that exclusion from what is of a different class is no different from exclusion from what is considered to be of the same class?
How then can it be understood as being excluded from that which is of a different class?
This is indeed true; it must be so apprehended.
If every cognition were to grasp the intrinsic nature [of its object] in its entirety, then that which is non-different could not be divided by distinction in any way whatsoever.
However, when it occurs again through division...
Even from mere delusion, there is attainment; such is the course of worldly convention.
Then that which is to be attained is consumed as non-different, though it arises from a mixture of differences. (377)
For indeed, by one situated at a very great distance from a post, even though a distinction exists, it cannot be apprehended,
because only the general configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is perceived there; yet a mere configuration devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) is not possible.

However, because it does not appear due to its distance, a mere appearance arises identically everywhere; thus, that very thing which is distinct from the individual instances is the universal (*sāmānya*).

Through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object, that [universal] itself appears as non-different; this is "difference" conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), but not in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
Why is there not non-difference in the ultimate sense?
Because, in the conceptualization of unification, neither of the two appears.
Well then, let difference be ultimate.
Since it is the universal alone that appears,
whatever appears as distinct must necessarily be something distinct.

That too is incorrect, because that [universal] would exist through the appearance of a form that is not connected with the individual; for a universal is not a mere universal like the form of an individual. (378)
Now, even that which is "mere" [the universal] is non-existent because it would have to be connected with another universal;
for the commonality of universals exists only through their connection with a distinct [higher] universal. Beyond that, however, the individual itself is clearly the universal. (379)

In that case, the universal would be nothing but an erroneous cognition, because it is identical to those individual instances. If that were so, there could be neither cognition nor activity directed toward the individual;

for it is not logical that the cognition and engagement with an individual should occur when one is cognizing the nature of an erroneous cognition, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that activity proceeds from error, we say no,
because there is no other state of non-error.
In that case as well, there would be only the apprehension of the essential nature (svarūpa) and not the apprehension of the individual (vyakti);
consequently, if one were to admit a succession of errors regarding the higher and lower levels, it would lead to an infinite regress, resulting in non-apprehension altogether.
This is of no consequence;

for if that is so, then there is no connection with a universal—neither as something distinct nor as something non-distinct; nor is it of the nature of an illusion; nor is there even the cognition of an individual.
What, then, is the means for the comprehension of an object through word and inferential mark?
[It is] precisely the object itself.

Since it results in the exclusion [of other meanings] due to the erroneous nature of cognition, it is by process of elimination an instrument (upāya). What other principle could there be for the comprehension of meaning from a word? (380)

[Objection: Surely, the determination of a real entity must proceed by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), yet no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found that apprehends the cognition of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). To this, it is replied:
Since activity is observed to proceed by way of exclusion from what is other than that [object], why is it not determined that a sentence has exclusion as its result?
(381) For it is observed that those engaged in worldly practice act through the exclusion of what is other than that [object],
and there is no acting based on non-cognition.
From that, the cognition of exclusion is drawn forth;
for that [object] is cognized through perception and conceptual thought as being devoid of connection with others.
In that regard, in perception, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) residing solely within the intrinsic nature of the thing is the object of cognition;
however, conceptual constructions do not have real entities as their objects.
Therefore, mere exclusion alone is the object of words and conceptual construction.
Now, one might ask: "In the cognition of a real entity, how can there be a cognition of its exclusion (*vyatireka*) in parts?
To this it is said:
There exists a real entity which is the object of the application of exclusion and which falls within the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
But what person rich in wisdom would postulate another distinction based on whether [the universal] is real or unreal?

Let there be for you only that much which is reached through the connection with non-exclusion (*avyatireka*); if the application of a purpose is achieved by means of the universal alone, what benefit is there in its particularity? (382–383)

To the extent that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) cannot be cognized without an object, only that much is sufficient for the practical purposes of those engaged in worldly discourse. Furthermore, it is not possible to cognize exclusion as being necessarily connected with a real entity (*sattya-vastu*), since its cognition is observed even through connection with what is unreal;
therefore, a sentence has exclusion alone as its object, because the [corresponding] entity is unreal therein.
Now, if the entity exists, then its absence [vyatireka] also exists; if it does not exist, how can that which is merged within it be real?
This is because the entity itself is unreal.
To this, it is said:

Even though this [distinction] is being perceived, why is it considered unreal? If it is unreal because of contradiction (*visaṃvāda*), then why is difference (*bheda*) not considered real? (384) First, the proponent of non-exclusion (*avyavacchedavādin*) must be questioned:
what is this so-called unreality of that which is the object of perception?
If that [object] exists precisely in the form in which it is perceived, how can it be unreal? If, on the other hand, it exists in a form not perceived, then everything would be unreal;
thus, for the opponent's position, there is nothing whatsoever that is real, and the unreal alone is real—this is like the milk of a donkey.
Now, if there is no nature as that which is to be attained (*prāpyarūpatā*), then it is untrue because of its non-correspondence (*visamvāda*), and not because of its own-nature (*svarūpa*).

Even if it possesses truth by way of its own-nature, for one who seeks the nature of what is to be attained, it is indeed untrue in the absence of that [attainment]; thus, the perception of the opposite is untruth.
Since that which has an unattainable nature is apprehended as having an attainable nature due to a mistaken cognition,
this exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is therefore established as being real.
A thing is attained by those engaged in worldly activity as something excluded from others; in that case, any further distinction regarding the exclusion of real or unreal entities is futile.
(385) If that which is attained is real, then the reality of the exclusion follows from its attainment.
But surely, the exclusion of an unreal entity was what was understood by him, yet that was not attained, since it was the exclusion of a real entity that was attained.

Nor is there non-contradiction when one thing is cognized and another is attained; therefore, how can there be truth in exclusion? What kind of misplaced inquiry is this from one who is dogmatically attached to what is not the case?
For distinction is indeed attained, and by that much alone is the satisfaction of worldly convention fulfilled.

Furthermore, those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*) are not capable of ascertaining the distinction between the higher and the lower once they have attained satisfaction; for it is by means of determining such distinctions through exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) that one encounters the experience of contradiction.

Therefore, this "non-contradiction" is spoken of out of regard for the pleasure of worldly people, and not as non-contradiction in the sense of reality when investigating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This has been stated:

"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is exclusion (*vyatireka*) is merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*); its validity is established through worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.214)
7) Because of this statement: if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is cognized by means of another means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);

if it were cognized without a means of valid cognition, then the same would apply to the object of cognition (*prameya*). Consequently, the apprehension of the object of cognition would not be dependent upon the means of valid cognition.
Therefore, it has been said:

"Validity is apprehended through conventional usage, but not in reality. Through a means of valid cognition, the mind [apprehends] reality; otherwise, an infinite regress would result. (386) Thus it was stated.

For even in that case, if the investigation is a conventional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an infinite regress has been pointed out; if it is not a means of valid cognition, then that same [inconsistency] will apply to the object of cognition (*prameya*) as well. Thus it has been stated.

"The definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) becomes useless because everything is already established; [to say] 'without a means of valid cognition' is not tenable. Therefore, non-contradiction (avisaṃvāda) everywhere is based merely on conventional practice (vyavahāra), relying on the unexamined nature of subtle reality, and not from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha).
For instance:

"On this side is the riverbank; on that side is a tiger. By what means can there be a way for a living being? For non-contradiction is not tenable in either case, whether [the object] is different or non-different [from the cognition].

If the object to be reached were different from the perceived [object], how could there be an absence of contradiction—that is, non-contradiction—when one has reached something else? On the other hand, if it were non-different in its entirety..."
That being the case, since that [object] has already been apprehended at that very moment, for what purpose would one act, or what would one obtain from it? Thus, there would be no correspondence;
this is the maxim of "a tiger on this bank and a river on that."
Therefore,
it is exactly so.
A sentence has exclusion as its result and never has a real entity as its object; for even when the particle *eva* is not employed, that which is understood from such [words] is [exclusion].
॰pi
Let this matter rest for now;
is such a thing seen anywhere?
It is indeed seen.

In the usage of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and the verb (*kriyā*)— as in "Pārtha is the archer," "Caitra is the archer," and "the blue lotus"— [the respective case endings apply].
The distinction is as follows: when the qualifier is emphasized, there is the exclusion of non-connection;
when the qualificand is emphasized, there is the exclusion of connection with another; and when the action is emphasized, there is the exclusion of that which is absolutely incapable.
How is it that, even in the absence of an explicit restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), there is a determination of a specific restriction through the context, the speaker’s intention, and so forth?
Is it not just as in the case of "Pārtha alone is the archer," where the restriction is understood through the proximity of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)?
Just as [the term] excludes other qualificands,
so too, when a qualifier is present, it excludes other qualifiers;
consequently, in the statement "Caitra is indeed an archer," there would follow the exclusion of all other qualities.
And this is not logically tenable; nor is there any distinction between the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*).
This is true.

In that case as well, the exclusion of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*) is understood regarding the objects, due to established convention, functional capacity, and the following of the speaker's intention through the expressive power of the word. For instance,
when a context of doubt arises as to whether "this man is an archer or not," and the statement "Caitra is an archer" is employed, [it serves to exclude others].
At that time, it effects the exclusion of doubt regarding that very [object]; thus, only the two alternatives are excluded.
Otherwise, one who speaks without effecting a refinement in the listener would not be a speaker;
therefore, only the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is understood, and nothing else.

Likewise, in that case as well, regarding a statement that excludes connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), if a specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is under discussion— such as "Between Pārtha and Rādheya, who is the wielder of the bow?"— then it is only Karṇa who is excluded [by the answer],
"Pārtha alone is the archer," and there is no exclusion of Rāma and others.

Likewise, even in the case of *yogavyavaccheda* (exclusion of connection), if it is formulated as "Caitra is a bowman," does another quality of his exist? If so, then there would be an exclusion of all other qualities— excluding only those that are invariable concomitants— such that Caitra is a bowman but not a scholar and so forth.

Even in the case of an inquiry regarding Pārtha, if there is a context of doubt such as "Is there anyone else in the world who is an archer?", then it is precisely the exclusion of all other possible qualificands; for at that time, everything [else] is introduced as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, [the meaning is] "archery" (dhānuṣkya).
He applies himself;
5 [he attains] the state of being a wielder of the great bow.

Because it excludes non-connection with that [property], the qualification of the property-bearer (dharmin) or the property (dharma) does not incur the fault of lack of continuity (niranvaya-doṣa) when [the property] is qualified by it.
For when the connection of that property with something else is well-established, it is precisely its non-connection [with the subject] that is suspected.
Therefore, because it establishes that [property] through its application to that [subject], there is exclusion of others; thus, there is no fault of non-concomitance (anvaya),
since this very [exclusion] is established by the well-known fact that "this is indeed a property of the subject," and not something unreal.
Because non-connection is the counter-correlative and because the opposite of connection is its contrary,
this meaning is understood by implication.
Indeed,
when a connection with something else has already been established, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) falls upon that very thing [as the subject], because of contradiction;
for it is that which is doubtful which is either excluded or affirmed.
Neither established nor prohibited,
the counter-correlate conforms to the speaker's intention; the word is likewise, and comprehension occurs in this very manner.
For it is not the case that the capacity of words to convey meaning differs from what is intended;
indeed, it has been established that sounds which convey meaning do not function by their own inherent nature like a lamp.
2. The varieties of reasons (*hetu*).

[Objection: "But surely, even with the qualifier 'of Pārtha alone,' the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) excludes only connection with another (*anyayoga*), not non-connection (*ayoga*); thus there is a contradiction with the context. [Response:
There is no contradiction, because the doubling of the negative particle (*na*) was corrected later in the manuscript.

Although Pārtha’s status as a qualifier is presented by the word, it does not exist for him in an ultimate sense. Here, the qualifier is said to be dependent due to its subordinate nature and thus functions as a property (*dharma*);
however, Pārtha, being the substratum of the quality of being an archer, is indeed the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
For the real principle (*vastava-nyāya*) is one thing and the verbal principle (*śabda-naya*) is another;
and since, in this context, the property of the object (*vastu-dharma*) is understood by virtue of the subject matter, there is no fault at all.

Here, the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*), which consists in exclusion (*vyavaccheda-rūpa*), is perceived through both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) by way of distinction; thus, there is no fault of non-comprehension (*apratīti-doṣa*).

For when a qualifier functions by excluding connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), the existence of that [quality] in one thing would entail the non-existence of it in another; furthermore, there would be no distinction in the particle [eva] as it connects both the qualifier and the qualified. If "producedness" were a property of the subject alone, then everything else would be unproduced, and no other location would possess smoke.
This [position] contradicts both perception and inference;
for smoke is perceived directly elsewhere,
and [the diversity of objects] is established through inference by such reasons as the diversity of cognitions.

Or, [the property of being produced] may be apprehended through perception; and through worldly convention, by means of inference characterized by qualifiers and so forth, there is the cognition of a particle used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), or of its meaning—such as the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—or of the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*) or something else. What, then, could be "otherwise" in that case?
This very point is explained in the analysis of the meaning of the compound *pakṣadharma*:
because it is understood through a distinction that the meaning of a compound sentence is either a difference (*bheda*), a connection (*saṃsarga*), or both difference and connection.
"Let it be that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is ninefold; why was it specified by the Teacher (*ācārya*) in that way?

[To this, he replies: "Indeed, only that many [reasons] need to be specified for the purpose of demonstrating the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the valid reason (*samyaghetu*); there is no need for nine.

The verbal method (śābdanaya) employs two pairs of reasons and their contraries for the sake of establishing essential nature and effect; the remainder establishes exclusion regarding the particular and the universal based on dispute. (195)
Since all nine [types of evidence] are applicable, there is a mention of nine;

however, because the status of being a reason belongs only to two—namely, essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*)—due to their respective necessary connections of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*), and not to the others, there is a mention of two;
furthermore, because these two alone are contradictory when used to prove the opposite, there is another pair [of reasons].

Since others have established the definitiveness (*aikāntikatva*) even of that which is non-definitive based merely on its presence and absence, the other two [characteristics] are stated for the purpose of excluding that.

As for the description of the remaining three, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the predominance of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); the meaning demonstrated is that the reason (*hetu*) is a means of cognition by way of exclusion, and therefore, by means of inference, exclusion alone is the probandum (*sādhya*).

(1) There are nine properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); therein, those nine properties of the subject are: the cognizable (*prameya*), the produced (*kṛtaka*), the impermanent (*anitya*), the produced (*kṛta*), the audible (*śrāvaṇa*), the effort-born (*yatnajā*), the non-effort-born (*ayatajā*), the tangible (*sparśa*), and the impermanence (*anityatva*). These nine [are applied] to [the respective subjects] such as the impermanent and so forth. 392

Now, since "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "following immediately upon effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) are one and the same, how can there be multiplicity even when [the property] recurs? How can there be the status of a reason (*hetutā*) and how can there be contradiction (*viruddhatā*)?
Furthermore, how is it not a case of novelty (*navatva*)? For that very same thing recurring cannot be the locus of a difference in number.
To this it is replied:

Because the three middle [categories] are eternal, non-eternal, and produced by effort; and [the remaining] are effortless, non-eternal, and eternal, as established by the means of proof such as "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva) and so forth. (393)
Therefore, everything is logically consistent;

for indeed, that which is called a "means of proof" (sādhana) is nothing in itself by its own nature, since it acquires the status of being a means of proof only in relation to the probandum (sādhya).
Furthermore, when the probandum (sādhya) involves contact with difference, that very same [reason] would be both a valid reason and a contradictory one; thus, nothing at all is established by that.
Therefore, there are two reasons:
"impermanent, because of being produced" is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).

And as for the statement "because it follows immediately upon effort," how was it understood that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), while "following immediately upon effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*)?
Why does the reverse not occur?
Because it possesses those characteristics and because there is an absence of any other characteristic, there is no reversal.
This is untenable;

for there is no pervasion [of the probandum] by anything other than the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because deviation is possible when [the reason] resides in the cause. Therefore, the result is that [pervasion] occurs in two ways. || 196 ||
Because producedness possesses an equal pervasion [with the probandum],
and because an effect does not possess an equal pervasion with respect to its cause due to the deviation of the effect [from the cause].
Since causes do not necessarily possess those [properties], the entire effect has a twofold occurrence; and because effort-necessity is twofold,
it is therefore an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

For it is not the case that everything impermanent initiates the effect of cognition immediately following effort; therefore, the reason [impermanence] exists in two ways among its similar instances (sapakṣa). However, for those who initiate the effect of cognition through other causes, all things are indeed impermanent.
Because it pervades it, the effect— cognition— is in reality nothing other than a svabhāvahetu;
thus, existence is said to be nothing but perception,
and not an existence characterized by cognition that follows immediately upon effort.
Otherwise, it would follow that all other things are non-existent;
therefore, knowledge—its distinctions being fashioned by the presence and absence of positive and negative concomitance—ascends to the pinnacle of the category of effects.
Consequently, that knowledge is the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*), designated by the term "that which follows immediately upon effort."
But how is it known that knowledge produced by a subsequent effort is a non-eternal effect?
To this he says:
"Because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort, [this is] the 'balancing the effect' (kāryasama) sophistry."
Manifestation is also not necessarily the result of effort;

for instance, while the effort of bringing a lamp near does not establish the production of a jar, the effort of rotating the wheel and other tools does so. Since both cases are observed, how can there be a single-sided conclusion?
And so the author of the Bhāṣya has said: "If we were to establish that sound is eternal, then [one would have to say] 'sound is manifested'; otherwise, it would be produced.
However, because of the common usage of the term 'making' in the expression 'he makes a sound,' we understand that sound is indeed produced."
Because the root *kṛ* has the sense of "application" (or "effort"), as in the expression "make my feet" or "make my back";
furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a reason for the eternity of sound.

Therefore, for that which exists eternally, there is only manifestation, just as a jar [is manifested]; so too for the word, [manifestation occurs] by means of a lamp or [by means of] the palate and so forth.
Vātsyāyana.
3. B. pṛṣṭham. Or: "the back."
That which has a proof established through valid cognition for both its own time and other times—its apprehension is indeed its manifestation; there is no definition of manifestation other than this.
Likewise, the apprehension from some cause of that which already exists previously is not "being an effect," for it was not an effect at that prior time when it was known [to exist].
The Eleventh Daily Lesson is completed.

To this it is replied: Knowledge following immediately after an effort [must belong] to that which already exists, because there is no rule for its arising otherwise; furthermore, the sense-organ and the word are in no way useful [for its production]. (197)
Just as a jar, which comes into existence immediately after an effort, is the product of that effort and not something manifested by the potter’s effort—

since otherwise it would follow that the entire collection of causal factors is rendered useless— for if everything already existed in everything, nothing would need to be sought by anyone, and the world would be devoid of all activity.
A restriction (niyama) is established by causal factors; otherwise, there would be a state of disorder. What, then, is this so-called "restriction" by virtue of which [this order exists]?

For that which is devoid of [any other], there exists no such thing as a restriction consisting in the exclusion of others; therefore, there can be no exclusion of causes even by means of hundreds of reasons.

Furthermore, how could there be a transition for that which is non-existent, and if it were to transition, its arising would be that very same [non-existent] state? Moreover, for every proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*), restriction certainly does exist.
Therefore, for that which is non-existent, its production is not logical anywhere.
Furthermore, if it is argued that manifestation is produced for an existent thing through its differentiation—[then we reply: it is already existent.

If that [non-existence] were also to be produced, there would be a twofold conceptualization: if it is non-existent, action is impossible; even if it were non-existent, how could it be a cause? Furthermore, existence and non-existence do not both belong to a single thing in accordance with valid cognition. (400) 2 B [The term *karaṇa* refers to the act of producing.]

Even if it exists, that [effect] always exists; what then has been done there by the causal factors (*kāraka*)? If it is argued that the causal factorhood consists in the power of action through non-existence, then such causal factorhood is futile.
Therefore, a jar produced by a potter and other agents, which comes into being immediately after their effort, is not something manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
Just as that very same object, which is manifested by a lamp, is perceived at a later time, so too will sound be manifested by effort;
it is not [non-existent] because of the prior existence of a means of valid cognition for the jar.

If it is argued that there is no means of valid cognition for the existence of sound prior to its production through effort, whereas its existence [is established] here by recognition, and therefore it must have existed previously—
this is not so.
4B. The Refutation of Recognition (Pratyabhijñā-nirāsa) 5B. When [Recognition is] Refuted.
Since the cognition of recognition has been refuted hundreds of times,
that which has been discarded does not return,
nor does the dead come back to life.
Furthermore, what does recognition establish? Does it establish the existence of something already known, or something that exists between two known things?
If it establishes something already known, then since that has already been established by the previous cognition and dealt with by memory, what is the utility of recognition in that regard?
Recognition establishes that "it exists even now," whereas memory establishes [the object] only as it existed at that [past] time,
just like what was previously seen.
That is incorrect because of [the nature of] recollection;
for if recognition were to proceed from the existence of recollection, then that recognition regarding an object of memory would necessarily be non-sensory. (402)

And no cognition other than one born of the senses and memory is accepted [as a means of valid knowledge]. Therefore, due to the absence of being sense-born, memory lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

For the senses do not function toward an object that is being remembered; otherwise, even places such as Kānyakubja would become objects of direct perception (pratyakṣa), and it would follow that even deceased persons would be objects of direct perception.

Now, if it is argued that the function of the sense organ operates upon what is being perceived, and even when [the object] is being perceived, the purpose of recognition is the cognition of identity with what is being remembered—
that is incorrect.

Since recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be identity of its object? For if the property (*dharma*) is unreal, the unreality of the substratum (*dharmin*) is evident. (404) The connection with a previous time is not established by recollection; rather, it is merely the appearance of form that occurs even without recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). (405) Indeed, there is only the appearance of white or yellow, but there is no appearance of an eternal form.
Since that [nature] exists even at the very first manifestation,
if it is argued that permanence— characterized by persistence over time— is indeed manifested there as well,
for there is no perception that negates it.
They say that the perception of the creator [the Lord] is not for the purpose of negating an entity; rather,
it is for the purpose of negation.

If the apprehension of an object pervading temporal divisions were unimpaired by perception (*akṣata*), then there would be an apprehension supported by all temporal divisions up until the limit of death (verse 406).
Therefore, the support of a previous time is not through perception, but through memory;
since memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), the unity of the object as perceived by it is unreal.
If the substratum is unreal, then the property is also unreal;
or, if the present [property] is real while the prior one remains unreal, then their identity would certainly be characterized by both reality and unreality. (407)

If two things possess both reality and unreality, then their identity must also be characterized by both reality and unreality; it is not logical for it to be unreal alone, for that would be arbitrary.
If its status as true or false were determined by the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), such that it is true by virtue of being present and false by virtue of not being present;

then, since the present form is true, the unity residing therein must also be true because it conforms to the nature of the substratum. However, the unity remembered [in the past] would consequently be false for that very reason. Thus, the unity of the object is not established. If this oneness is indeed true, why is there no corresponding cognition?
Presentness— this is the explanation,
What is the reply regarding the two actions?
[The answer is: "Why is there a contradiction for the self within itself even in its own statement?
Even in the statement, "Perception is not a means of valid cognition regarding that which is perceived by oneself," the object of cognition (prameya) is [as follows]— the commentary.

Now, this recognition is observed to occur when [an object] is seen as distinct from what was previously seen; therefore, it is determined that when it occurs regarding what is being seen as non-distinct, [the object] is indeed non-distinct.
Thus, this cognition of recognition, by excluding the distinct, remains fixed upon the non-distinct.
Such is the extent of reality: namely, the distinct and the non-distinct.
Therefore, by excluding what is different from it, it establishes non-difference;
otherwise, it would not exist at all,
for it is certainly not possible to exclude [an entity] from everything.

This is incorrect, because even when there is difference, there exists another specific property (*viśeṣa*) by which [the cognition] is excluded; it is better to assume that very specific property rather than postulating a separate entity. (411)

It is better to postulate that this [recognition] is merely a specific kind of difference arising simply from the emergence of a recognition-cognition, rather than to postulate non-difference, which is of a different genus from difference; for this emergence of recognition is not observed among things such as blades of darbha grass or young shoots that have been cut and grown again, even though they produce a reflective awareness of an identical form.
Therefore, it is logical to postulate the same [namely, a specific difference] in other cases as well.
In that case, a clump [of hair] is perceived as being situated in the middle; therefore, even though there is a distinction there, one does not conceive of non-distinction,
whereas it is not so here— thus, the comparison with the mass of hair is indeed unequal.
This very thing has become a most substantial grasping at the *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass by one who is falling;
for it is thus:

Therefore, in that case, what is called "cutting" is a severance, a non-joining with the subsequent [moment]; and since that occurs through the abandonment of the preceding [moment], how could there be a cognition that joins [them]?
Furthermore, the view of non-joining is the same in both the example and the case to be illustrated.
Furthermore, even when there is disintegration, one who maintains the recognition of the deceased—that evil-minded person strikes himself with his own self;
for once the previous form has perished, there can be no identity with that which has perished. Thus, it has been demonstrated that if there is plurality, unity cannot exist.
Moreover, that which has perished is never within the range of the senses; therefore, it must reside within the range of memory alone.
Since the validity of memory has already been refuted previously, eternity is thus established only through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). 414
Therefore, memory, having already been established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does not now establish the object as a real entity when it brings that object to mind.
However, the object existing at that time is what is apprehended by that [cognition]; therefore, it is indeed the prior state that is understood through the means of valid cognition. || 415 ||
How could the firm ascertainment of identity with that [object] be anything other than a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For it would be a contradiction in itself if a conviction, even one firmly arisen, were to be rejected by the wise once it has occurred.
(416) Even one whose mind is being encouraged by a conviction consisting of an unshakable certainty would, if he were to reject that very certainty, be acting inconsistently.
Then there would be one thing in his speech and another in his mind;
this is the entire essence of the realization of those who advocate *pratyabhijñā* (recognition). Those who have ascended too high fall down even instantaneously.
For one who has climbed very far to an exceedingly precarious place, a fall is imminent.
For a lamp, though it burns brightly for a great distance, goes out when it inclines toward extinction.
Likewise, if memory has as its object an experienced thing, how can it be said to have perished?
If it has as its object an experienced thing, how can it be memory?
(419) If memory had as its object an experienced thing by its very nature, there would be no recollection of the past,
because the past was not apprehended through direct perception.
If that which was previously unapprehended were instead apprehended by memory, then it would not be memory; for memory does not have an object that has never been known before.
Even if that were the case, it still would not be recognition.
For recognition is held to have as its object a thing perceived by direct perception;
otherwise, it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that "that very same [thing], having passed away, is called 'prior,'" [we reply:]...
That too is mutually contradictory:

when it is past, it is not graspable; when it is graspable, it is not thus [past]. In its remembered form, that which is past is not a real entity. Furthermore, because the certainty [of recognition] is firm, its validity is established; likewise for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the connection with the senses is useless.
If that which possesses certainty even without a connection to the senses were indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
then this would be merely the whim of a wicked person incapable of investigation;
for it is thus:

Cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of the existence of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*). Non-contradiction pertains to the present [cognition], but not to that which has already perished in the past.
(422) If that unity [of the two cognitions] did not exist, then that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would not occur; for even by another fire, that purposeful action is indeed accomplished.

However, its oneness—consisting in the performance of that purposeful action—is accepted as merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), characterized by the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what does not perform it. For designations and conceptual constructions such as "one" are of a consistent nature based solely on the capacity for that object;
indeed, discerning people do not heed designations and certainties whose objects lack causal efficacy.
Therefore, oneness, as the performance of that purposeful action, is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Therefore, inference does not have that [perceived] form as its logical mark (*liṅga*),
because form is manifold due to its connection with other imagined properties; thus,
recognition is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for unity in reality.
In that case, why is there no recognition (pratyabhijñā) regarding jars and the like— which are capable of performing their respective telic functions—
such as the cognition "this is that very same jar" or "it is similar to that"? Indeed, recognition is simply the cognition [of such similarity].
Moreover,
it is this very same jar that has been brought here, and this is that very same cold water;
for it is so.
When it is said, "Bring another," and one brings that other individual instance, there arises the certain conviction: "That very same [thing] has been brought again.

(423) When a jar or something else, such as a small pot (*piṭharikā*), is intended to be brought as "another" than a jar, then upon the utterance of "Bring another," if a different instance from that jar is brought, there is observed the conventional usage: "This very same jar has been brought.
1 B *piṭharakādirā*
However, because linguistic usage is so deeply rooted and because of attachment to beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there arises the conceit that the word has a figurative existence;
therefore, the certainty of a word’s identity is not established through recognition. Rather, such an illusion occurs because the capacity for signification is identical [in different instances].
(424) If it were indeed another [word], how could trust be instilled in another?

For indeed, no one places trust in anything unless it has been fully understood. Even when there is identity [of cause], there is no trust because deviation is observed. Yet, someone may place trust in another thing that is similar to that [known object], by relying on the non-deviating possibility of a common causal formation (*saṃskāra*), as is the case with [the recognition of] "that person's son" and so forth.
Likewise, [this] refutation of the permanence of the self applies even to the son and so forth, who belong to the continuum of that appropriation.

Now, how can there be a desire for restitution if there is momentariness? Furthermore, it is utterly impossible if there is identity [between the giver and the receiver]. For, the returning of what was given is joined with fear and shame; but for one in whom fear and shame are predominant, by what could that fear and shame be produced? (427)

Now, due to its proximity, there is the appearance of that which is swallowed by it as being the self; even when it is not swallowed by it, there is the swallowing of it, and this delusion occurs even with respect to the self.
(428) Even in the continuum of moments, that very same delusion persists; why then is this not the cause for conventional linguistic usage?
Even in the case of permanence, because of the arising of causes, there is no further cause for the conceit of another;
[this is] due to the mutual relationship of cause and effect.

Even for one who accepts the self as eternal, there is no logical justification for the conceit based on the relationship of cause and effect; for the self does not deviate from its unitary nature across time. Consequently, since modifications such as fear and shame would be impossible for it, how could there be fear arising from fear?
Then fear arises for him;
being afraid due to that [connection], he experiences some affliction, but not by his own nature, because he is not inherently afraid.
The mere relationship of cause and effect alone is the basis for such conventional usage; yet,
suffering does not become actual suffering merely by virtue of conventional usage.
If it is argued that one is indeed afflicted because of the connection [to the son], even though the affliction is distinct from the son's own suffering,
we say no;
he is not afflicted by a separate affliction residing within himself, but rather [is considered afflicted] by virtue of that [connection].
Otherwise, one would also be afflicted by the suffering caused by an enemy; therefore, this relationship characterized as the afflicted and the afflictor certainly exists for it.
5. Liberation (mukti).
No.

Even if one's own son were an enemy, there would be no harm caused by the suffering inflicted upon him; therefore, suffering exists in the form of being afflicted oneself, not from the act of afflicting another. (430)
Therefore, since it is merely momentariness, it does not differ from the continuum; thus,
the entire conventional usage regarding a "self" is of that same nature.
For it is merely by way of a continuous series (*santāna*) that the conventional usage "this is that very same thing" occurs;
therefore, sound is not eternal. Consequently, how could its manifestation occur immediately after an effort?
Rather, its production alone is the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it possesses the defining characteristics of such production.

Because it varies according to the variation of its cognition, the status of being an effect does not truly belong to sound; jars and other objects do not vary according to the variation of lamps and the like.
(432) [The status of being an effect belongs to this.]
Indeed, the manifested object is not differentiated by the smallness or greatness of the manifestor; for instance, a blue lotus manifested by a lamp is seen as red,
while one manifested by moonlight is seen as yellow or white.
A face revealed by a sword, though fair, appears dark, and so forth; [this refers to] the manifestation of light and so on.
That too is incorrect, because:
"If entities possess a nature other than that of their manifestor, then, by virtue of producing that other nature, the manifestor would become a creator. (433)
For if the manifestor were to cause that form to disappear, it would have to reveal a nature contrary to its own;
but how could that non-existent form of his be revealed?
Otherwise, even things such as a rabbit’s horn would be revealed.
If it is argued that even that [error] is indeed manifested through what is called misapprehension (*viparītākhyāti*), the answer to this has already been given.
That which has such a form;
its own nature.
From the perspective of erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*):
If it is argued that this is an error, and therefore there is no fault in this [position].
That is incorrect,
because:
if that which is the manifester is the producer of error, how can it be a manifester?
For only that which illuminates something can clearly be a manifestor;
otherwise, even things such as cataracts would possess the nature of a manifestor.
Indeed, for those [cataracts] as well, there is no further fault than their causing error.

Now, even in the case of an error, another form of that [sound] is apprehended; therefore, for the wise, the manifestor of this [sound] is considered to be the effort [of articulation] and so forth, not the *dhvani*.
(436) [Refutation of *Sphoṭa*:

Even if there is indeed a distinction of the word-sound (*śabda*) due to its contact with *dhvani*, such as smallness, greatness, and so on, nevertheless, this is produced solely by error and does not exist in reality.]

Even in the case of an error, another reality of the word does indeed appear in the form of the *sphoṭa*; to that also it is replied: if there were a reality of the word distinct from its erroneous form, it would have to appear as something separate; otherwise, it would not be understood as an error. (437)
For that which appears as non-different from what is different cannot be understood as "different"; otherwise, it would simply be non-different.
(438) Even if there is error within an error, the error itself is dissolved; when there is the cognition of non-error within an error, it is recognized as "error. (439)

For it is not logically tenable that there is no manifestation of the real nature of the word as distinct from the form appearing in error, provided that such a real nature exists. If it is argued that "the distinction does not appear because of error," then since the distinction would also be another real form of the word apart from the form of error, the consequence follows that it too must manifest distinctly; thus, one would have to postulate further error, and further distinctions of form, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and consequently the non-apprehension of the real nature of the word.
Even in the case of error, it would not be an error; for the true form of the word alone would remain, and since that alone would appear, there would be no such thing as error at all. 6B.

Therefore, when the word "real" (sattya-rūpa) appears as the actual reality, there is no such thing as error; it is established that when all objects of cognition are abandoned, [only] error remains as error. || 440 ||
But surely, there exists a purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the comprehension of an object produced by the mere word;
however, there is no difference in the cognition of the object caused by [qualities] such as "greatness.
Therefore, by virtue of performing purposeful activity, the *sphoṭa* alone is real, while the other is unreal.
By the reverse,
that too is unreal.

For it is not intended that a word’s causal efficacy consists in the communication of an object; rather, the emergence of the appearance of that object arises from the cultivation of the conventional sign (*saṃketa*). (441) 1 B.

The knower of words considers the cause of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) to be the [perceived] object; it is regarded as a producer through a traditional succession, yet it is not held to be a differentiator. (442) There is no differentiation [of the effect] by means of the differentiation of the material cause (*upādāna*), nor by that of the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*). Even in that case, because it is merely an auxiliary, sound (*dhvani*) is not considered a differentiator. (443)
Furthermore,
from the very convergence of similar latencies (vāsanā), there arises a cognition of an object in the form of a conceptualization (vikalpa) having the aspect of that object.

In that case, however, sound is an auxiliary cause that produces [the cognition] indirectly by way of awakening latent impressions (*vāsanā*); therefore, it does not possess the capacity to differentiate [the object].

On the other hand, the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of sound consists in the direct production of the cognition of that [object], and this very [efficacy] is indeed differentiated according to whether [the sound] is distant or near, by way of being clear or indistinct, and by its co-occurrence with agitation or lack of agitation.
Therefore, how could difference not be that which performs a causal function for its own sake?
Thus, difference is indeed a real entity and not merely an illusion.
Furthermore, if sound were eternal, cognition [of it] would not necessarily occur immediately following an effort.
If it is argued that [the word] does not convey the meaning even previously because of the capacity for conveying belonging to what has been heard, and otherwise there would be no conveying—
then surely that very [capacity] which existed at the time of the convention persists even now.

If it is argued that there would then be cognition itself, and not a prior non-cognition due to a subsequent effort, because [that effort] is absent at the time [of the initial non-cognition]; and if it is further argued that this is not so because of the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*); then [the response follows].
For a manifestor is that which produces a manifestation at the same time [as the object];
this, however, is incorrect, because:
Just as that which manifests a thing existing at the same time would be a manifester, so too would the manifester of the manifested be a manifester by its entire self.
(444) Likewise, if it were to be manifested by that [manifester] while persisting through another period of time, [the same fault would apply].
In that case, how could there be a dependence on a manifestor for it at another time?
(445) For a manifestor does not become a manifestor unless it manifests a form that is not contrary [to its own nature],
nor is anything produced by a manifestor at another time for the manifestation of a form that persists through that interval.

The unmanifest requires a manifestor; otherwise, there would be another manifestor for that, and yet another for that, so that manifestation itself would never occur, and an infinite regress (anavasthā) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, the claim that it is not perceived prior to subsequent cognition is also untenable, because it is impossible for there to be a necessary restriction regarding the cognition of a form that already exists before the effort, only to be known immediately after that effort.
For it is not logical that the very same form which existed previously should be unperceived while that [object] itself is being perceived;
moreover, because that previous effort was in every way useless for it,
since it has been manifested by another [effort] in its entirety.
If it is argued that form manifests itself only as conjoined with its own time, then what is this?
Is it the exclusion of one thing by another?
Even a difference in effort does not cause a division when there is oneness of the preceding and succeeding cognitions.
If there were multiplicity, the object of knowledge would also be distinct from the time of the cognition; [otherwise,
it would have to be] all-pervasive in nature.
4. The task (kṛtya).
5. [The task].
If [the object] has arisen from its location,
then there is an absence of obstruction; however, when there is perception [of it], that is not due to the existence [of the object], because it is obscured by an obstruction.

A mat, even though present, is not seen when it is concealed by a wall; yet, when that [obstruction] is removed by another means, it becomes an object of perception once again. This is established through direct perception and determined by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding sound as well, the absence of an obstruction is brought about through effort.

Since there is no perception of things even when they exist if an obstruction is present, whereas there is perception when that [obstruction] is absent, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the failure of perception is caused by the absence of an obstruction.
Having bowed, [he says]: "In the case of an obscuration, there can be neither change nor something else, because it is perceived by direct perception as being in that very state.
This is the statement of another who has not reflected upon the higher and the lower [truths].

If its proof were [established] even in the interim through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), then that recognition would be an inference and not preceded by perception.

If it is argued that there is no perception of the unmodified entity at the very time when it is not perceived due to being obstructed by a veil, but rather that its perception occurs later once it is free from obstruction—then [we reply]:

either its existence or its lack of modification would have to exist at that [earlier] time; however, its intermediate state is cognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) despite being beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*).
And likewise, there is inference because [the mind] is unmodified now; therefore, it was so even previously—since this conforms to the definition of inference.
Yet, in that case, in the absence of perception, how can that inference be preceded by perception?
If it is argued that in all cases the relation of priority and posteriority is established solely by the means of valid cognition that is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),

and that since inference is preceded by [another] inference, and that inference too must be preceded by another inference, this would lead to an infinite regress (*aparyavasāna*) resulting in a "blind tradition" (*andhaparaṃparā*);
therefore, it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and thus [the relation] is preceded by direct perception.
Even in that case, there is no direct perception;
for another person does not have the cognition that "this has been apprehended by another through direct perception," unless that other person should say so.
Nor is another capable of perceiving even one's own truthfulness, because of the absence of validity in speech.
"That which has been practiced by him is precisely what has been practiced by me"—
for it is not possible for that which is perceived as mixed with another's practice to be recognized in such a way [as one's own] that "this is that very same thing."
Consequently, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*),

because the identity [of the two] is understood through their reciprocal description; or else, if it is understood through inference, then [the inference proceeds] from the observation of a change in the eyebrows (*bhūvikāra*).
Since he too has apprehended that very same [object],
it is therefore established that there is only suchness (*tathābhūtatā*), and not oneness; thus, this is not logical,
for inference does not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
For fire is not established as being that very same [fire] simply because smoke arises;
likewise, why is there not oneness between pleasure and the like and the self through their identical conventional treatment, such as the occurrence of horripilation?
Or, if it is argued that there is no oneness because pleasure and the like are perceived as mutually distinct, [then the same applies to the self].
That being the case, even for two things that are being perceived, since they are perceived as unmixed by either self or other, their difference alone is logical;
even their co-location is perceived precisely through the absence of such [mixed] perception,
for there is no location other than the very nature of the entity itself.
Therefore, it is not established that there is perception [of things] even when they exist, due to the presence of an obscuration; this is the conclusion.

Now, there is indeed a cognition [in the form], "That very thing which has been understood by another has been understood by me," and there is no sublation [of this].

One might imagine [this], for nothing that is being scrutinized by subtle analysis deserves to be established as real.
That is incorrect;

And thus, the undertaking of the treatise would be futile;

(455) Indeed, the worldly practice consisting of the relation between cause and effect continues uninterrupted for those engaged in worldly affairs, precisely through a blind tradition.

For since saṃsāra is seen as nothing other than mere convention,

It abides; there is no distinction between reality and unreality—this is the ultimate truth. One should consider that which is "unreal" to be simply reality itself when left unexamined. (457)

For when reality (*tattva*) is investigated, everything becomes non-dual; however, through the investigation of what is not that [reality], that very same thing takes on the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is unreality (*atattva*)—namely, *saṃsāra*.

Therefore, since the desired eradication of *saṃsāra* necessarily follows from such an investigation, how could renunciation (*apavrajyā*) be anything other than the vision of the reality of one's conduct? To that extent, worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*) is certainly not sublated. Thus, this very practice is indeed the established conduct of learned people.

In this regard, for the sake of gradually removing ignorance, impermanence is first established concerning that which the world misconceives; therefore, whatever is perceived at any time must be understood as being exactly as it is perceived, because it is grasped through the exclusion of preceding and succeeding moments. for even through refinement (*saṃskāra*), there is the perception of that very same [object] in such a manner. Even when there is refinement, that which does not exist [in the object] is not perceived therein. (463)
1B. That which does not exist—of which permanence cannot be perceived because it is non-existent—is nothing other than the perception of existence itself;

Now, even if it is indeed not perceived, how can there be an absence of impermanence?
For non-perception is precisely the characteristic of non-existence for that which possesses the conditions for perception; nor is its nature such that it lacks the conditions for perception.
How is there an absence of permanence?
For this very reason, apprehension itself is existence; in its absence, how could there be existence? Thus, permanence is impossible.
But in the view that sound is assisted [by the effort], that very [effort] is what is impermanent;

Such knowledge, which has an occasional result, is established as its mark.
If this sound or another [object] were to persist through a different time, it would be perceived in that very same way; thus, an occasional perception would not be the effect [of such persistence].

For its form is never occasional, nor is there a perception of it otherwise than as that very form; yet if this [perception] were an error, then indeed one who perceives only what is near is not capable of perceiving an all-pervasive form. And when one lacks such capacity, the object of apprehension does not become something else, even if it is an error.
Because it is non-contradictory, it is indeed a valid means of cognition;
for an error is sublated by a non-erroneous perception,
and at that time, it can be determined to be an error.
This is incorrect, because it is refuted by the cognition of recognition, which establishes a form that pervades both time and space.
The capacity of recognition has already been rejected here; it has been established that its sublation occurs by means of perception itself.

Furthermore, it has already been established that recognition is sublated by perception itself;
moreover,
if the apprehension of an object were fragmentary, this would apply even in the case of pervasion (vyāpti).
All things would be one and the same, and their apprehension would occur part by part.

then every single thing would be one and the same, because of the recognition that "this is a thing" and "that is a thing" regarding everything.

Therefore, there is no valid means of knowledge anywhere that can apprehend a non-different thing as having a different form. It is real [only as difference].
But when a thing is distinct, the establishment of its non-distinction arises solely from conceptual construction; it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For if distinction were real, that non-distinction would be merely fashioned by the artifice of imagination, established only by the means of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*);

And linguistic usage does not occur based on non-difference alone;
therefore, there must be a distinct substratum (dharmin) of which non-difference is the property (dharma). For if the substratum were non-existent, its non-difference could not likewise exist.
