Perception does not cognize that "it will be grasped by me," yet it is indeed grasped; however, memory does cognize this. This is truly most wonderful! For while perception, which has the nature of grasping, has no activity regarding that [future object], it is memory following upon it that possesses such activity. This is a great skill in discerning the true nature of things, for it is impossible to grasp a future form due to doubt.
Perhaps it might not even exist;
yet if it should come to be, I shall certainly take hold of it.
Subsequently, through recollection, one will objectify it as "it was grasped," because of the cognition [in the form] "that too was grasped"; thus,
there is indeed the operation of grasping.
The twelfth daily lesson is completed.
For even if an object has been apprehended, how could one act toward it here [in this world] if it remains doubtful? To be both apprehended and doubtful are mutually contradictory.
If that [doubt] were to persist, then it would have to be considered as already apprehended; thus, the operation of apprehension would be immense.

For existing cognition must have either the nature of apprehension or otherwise; there is no other possibility, because these two are mutually contradictory and consist in the exclusion of one another.

Even in the case of perception, there is doubt: "If it is perception, how [can there be doubt]? For there is no doubt regarding what is apprehended, whereas doubt arises regarding what is not perceived. (475)
If there were apprehension [of the future] just as there is of the present, there would be no doubt because of its non-difference [from the present];
nor, at that time, would it be something being apprehended as merely present, since it is not different from the nature of the future and the present.
Or, if it were considered "future" due to its connection with a future time...
In that case, then, things do not possess their status as present and so forth by way of their own intrinsic nature; rather, it is merely the coexistence with future, present, and past entities,
since there is no other time.
Or, if it exists, that too is simply a functional entity (*padārtha*) acting as a cooperative cause;

in that case, when its future form is apprehended, the state of being future would already have been apprehended, and thus no doubt could arise. If it is argued that "being future" consists in being concomitant with impermanent entities, [the response follows].
Nor is it the case that [the self] is not perceived,
because it is impossible to grasp something that has not come into being; furthermore, the claim that there is a recollection such as "this very thing was grasped by me"—
whereby the nature [of the object] is indeed grasped even if the concomitance is not— this too is not correct.
For it is your own view that the intrinsic nature [of an object] is neither past nor future;
therefore, since you accept the apprehension of present cognition, let only the present be apprehended.

Just as there is a cognition of blueness through a cognition that appears as blue because they coexist, so too there is a cognition of presentness even when there is an appearance of the present. (476) But if [the object] is not apprehended, how can there be recollection?
But surely this same objection applies even to the theory that [the object] is apprehended;
for when it is being apprehended, there is no memory, since memory occurs only after the apprehension.
If its form did not exist at the time of the past perception, that memory would not exist.
How then could a memory arising now know [the object] as being "prior"? Since it is non-existent and formless, how can the memory possess that form?

It is an extreme audacity to claim that a memory knows an object that does not have that form. Furthermore, if the self were ignorant [at that time], then even so, it would indeed know the prior state.

For its capacity for apprehension is also applicable to recollection; however, if apprehension and recollection were distinct from the self at the outset, then those two—apprehension and recollection—could not belong to it, because it would lack that nature. (480)

If there is no distinction between recollection and perception when there is an appearance as being present, then that [self], which lacks the nature of those [states], cannot be the perceiver or the rememberer, because it would follow that the body would also be so;
if you argue that this is not the case because [the self] is impermanent.
If it is thought that this [distinction] might also apply to space and so forth because these two [causes] do not have inherence therein,
that too is equivalent to being non-existent.
Because its connection with grasping and recollection arises from synthesis (*anusandhāna*), this same [synthesis] would apply equally even to space and so forth;
for otherwise, memory would not be possible. (481)
The intelligent [agent] is not postulated, for this [notion of agency] is not logical without some entity existing at both prior and subsequent times;
thus, let this belong to space and so forth themselves— what is the point of the effort of postulating a separate entity?
In the same way, inherence (samavāya) must also be questioned;
or else, one must accept the eternity of memory and the other [mental states] if they reside in that very self.
Having recalled that very [object] which has arrived, how was it known where there is non-apprehension or doubt? Where there is apprehension...
Since recollection is absent at that time, how can there be an understanding of prior existence? (482)
Therefore, the claim that [sound is perceived] by means of perception is trivial;
consequently, it is impossible for there to be a grasping of sound immediately following effort through the recollection of what preceded,
because sound is impermanent due to the perception of forms that are neither prior nor subsequent— this is established.
Therefore, neither by perception nor by recollection is the state of having prior and posterior forms grasped.
Thus [ends the discussion of] that state.
As for what was said— that knowledge which is of a different nature [from sound] does not follow immediately after effort— that can be refuted otherwise:
even if it is indeed of a different nature, it is still possible for it to follow immediately after effort.
For in this case, an excessively subtle analysis is not necessary;
therefore, by this very example, both types of evidence— the effect and the essential nature— are demonstrated here as well.
Now, why have only the examples of the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāva-hetu*) been shown separately, and not other types as well? To this, the resolution is:
"Existence is that which follows immediately upon effort, or that which is one's own self and indivisible."
"That [reason] would be non-deviant because of that" means that its differentiation is for this purpose:
whatever exists immediately after an effort is the very reason [for inferring that effort], because of its non-deviance;
for nothing other than an effect can be non-deviant when it lacks the nature of being an effect.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a logical reason (*hetu*) functions solely through non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and not by virtue of being an effect (*kāryatā*)? For even ash is an effect of fire, yet it does not possess non-deviation [from fire];
likewise, water, though a conjoined entity, makes known its container even without being an effect. [Reply:
This is incorrect, because we do not say that only that which is an effect is a signifier.
Rather, the indicator is distinct [from the object] precisely by virtue of being an effect; without being an effect, it does not indicate.
Just as the effect of ash indicates fire exactly as it is—even if that fire is past or located in another place—so too does it indicate such a thing.
For this very reason, the capacity to indicate is necessitated by the state of being an effect, by which it is distinguished through its specific nature.
Indeed, even here the relationship between the sign (nimitta) and the signified (nimittin) is exactly of this nature;

however, if it were understood through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then the substratum (*ādhāra*) would become the indicator (*gamaka*) of the superstratum (*ādheya*). But since the substratum exists even without the superstratum, it cannot be the indicator.
Furthermore, things such as water do not exist without a substratum; therefore, that [substratum] is the indicator (*gamaka*).

If that is so, it follows that the effect alone is the indicator, for whatever does not occur in the absence of something else is the effect of that thing. And since the persistence of the contained (*ādheya*) does not occur without a substratum (*ādhāra*), it is therefore an effect.
But it is not the case that stability alone is the effect, nor that water alone is the effect;
rather, in that case, it is stability itself that indicates [the presence of water], not the water. Thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Or, it is water as qualified by stability that indicates [its presence].
Why should it not be the case that it is precisely the state qualified by water that causes [the cognition], and why is this alone logical?
Because it is that very state which, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), serves as the means of comprehension; and there is no "water" other than the state itself.
Now, is it not the case that even this falling water is indeed water? That water is not merely that [specific instance], but other water is also water.
Furthermore, it has been established that there is no universal (sāmānya) called "water-ness" (jalatva); or, even if such a universal existed, it would not be a means of cognition (gamaka).
The individual instance alone is the indicator, and since that is an effect, nothing other than an effect can possess the status of an indicator;
if it is held that this individual instance is one and the same [in all cases], that too is incorrect.

If it is argued that there is no fault even when [the entity] exists in such a manner through successive stages— due to the consequence that "it is the same as it remained" and "it is the same yet otherwise"—
then, in that case, since there is no perception of identity between the prior and subsequent states, how can there be a single individual?
Indeed, that which is not being perceived cannot be established as one with another by means of perception;
for perception and non-perception are not [equivalent], since it is impossible to establish the existence of a thing through non-perception.
Furthermore, recognition has already been refuted.
Therefore, when examined in every case, it is the very fact of being an effect (*kāryatā*) that is the basis for being a means of cognition (*gamaka*).

Since water, ashes, and other such things possess "being produced" (*janyatva*) by way of that very form [of being an effect], they remain as means of cognition precisely through that; thus, there is no understanding [of the probandum] from anything else.
This is because the nature of the self (*ātman*) is such that it possesses its own distinct divisions.
Whatever constitutes the essence of a thing is its indicator; thus, the *śiṃśapā*, being the essence of a tree, is the indicator of treeness.
For is it not the case that just as the *śiṃśapā* is the essence of a tree, so too the tree is the very essence of the *śiṃśapā*, since identity cannot exist without residing in both members?
No,
because there is an absence of non-divisibility;
for a tree exists even apart from the *śiṃśapā*, such as in the case of the *palāśa* and other species.
But the *śiṃśapā* tree is not so; therefore, it is that very [tree], possessing non-differentiation, which is the means of cognition.
Is this not so?

If it is argued that even when identity (*tādātmya*) is equal [between the two], the lack of distinction (*avibhāga*) serves as the indicator, then identity would be the sole basis for being an indicator. (484) However, even in the absence of identity, such non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is likewise observed; therefore, identity is not the basis for smoke being an indicator. (485) For its status as a causeless [indicator] cannot be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
This is incorrect;

for it has been stated that this [inferential] capacity never exists anywhere without identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, those two are the basis for the non-deviation of the indicator. Even though there is a distinction between these two, the nature of being an indicator differs: that which indicates what is identical with itself is indeed identical to it, but not that which indicates what is different.
Because that effect is produced by distinct [causes], the cause is distinct from it;
for this very reason, he says:
It has been stated that those [reasons] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which lack such a necessary connection are not valid reasons, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
If [fire] were a prover by virtue of conjunction, why would fire— not being conjoined with smoke— also not be a prover of smoke?
If it is argued that this is because there is an absence of non-deviation,
then that very non-deviation is simply the relation of cause and effect for the negative inference (*vyatirekin*); thus says the opponent here.
If being a signifier were due to the relation of cause and effect, then since that relation resides in both [terms], fire would also be a signifier;
this is because it is stated that "existence is not inseparable from effort."

And there is no other relation of cause and effect apart from the entities that are the cause and the effect; therefore, it is not by virtue of being a "relation of cause and effect" that the cause is an indicator [of the effect]. In that case, the cause would likewise not be an indicator by virtue of being an effect.
2B Why does the cause not serve as a means of cognition?
It certainly does; it is not otherwise.

But that [object] cannot be known in the manner in which it is known; for while it is indeed non-indicative in that very form [in which it is thus known], it is nevertheless indicative in its actual nature.
For instance:

1B. Fire does not acquire the status of being a cause by merely producing smoke if it is not [previously] known as such. If it were to become known as a producer, then it might indeed be a signifier (*gamaka*).
As for the objection that "it is impossible to know it in that way," that is not a fault; for in that case, smoke would simply be its effect, since [fire] is absent when smoke is absent. (488–489)
For indeed, in the case of a pervader, every cause must be distinct; this same principle should also be stated regarding the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

In that case as well, since even a tree would be an indicator by virtue of having the nature of a *śiṃśapā*, and since identity (*tādātmya*) is not easily understood [in such a case], the status of being an indicator does not exist.
Otherwise, if there were indication through speech, there would be comprehension due to the lack of distinction.
Therefore, every instance of a state of being [the indicator] must be based on the non-differentiation of the entity from its effect.

Just as the identity and causality between a tree and fire are not restricted—such that a *śiṃśapā* tree is not necessarily fire, nor is smoke necessarily caused by fire—so too, the capacity to indicate (*gamakatva*) is likewise non-restricted.
If there is no restriction, how can something be an indicator?
Because the basis for being a signifier exists without restriction;
for such a basis is possible only if there is conformity to that [basis].
If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the whole] being real even otherwise,
and that this is exactly the same in the case of conjunction (saṃyoga), we say no, because:
Those things such as conjunctions for which there is no such restriction [as being invariably concomitant] are not reasons, because they are subject to deviation; this has already been stated. (492)

The substratum related by conjunction (*saṃyogin*) [does not indicate the superstratum] because conjunction is symmetrical with the superstratum; however, the substratum related by inherence (*samavāyin*)— namely, the categories of universal, quality, and action— does indicate the superstratum.
Because an invariable concomitance known as the relation of cause and effect is impossible,
likewise, even when a universal is perceived alone while its individual instance has perished, it does not lead to the cognition of that which possesses the universal,
precisely because the relation of cause and effect is impossible.
If it is thought that the thing to be established (the probandum) makes known the substratum because the relation of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is possible therein,
then, in that case, it is simply the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) that serves as the indicator.
If it is argued that "it is indeed inseparable concomitance," that too is incorrect;
for inseparable concomitance itself is the relation of cause and effect.
Therefore, he says:
"Or, if there were an obstruction, that [obstruction] itself would be the means of comprehension;
for necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is the restriction, and what is non-restricted is not a means of proof. (204)

And that restriction—that the capacity to indicate [the probandum] exists only when there is a causal relationship between one thing and another, and not otherwise—has been established. It has been explained that two reasons (*hetu*) and two contrapositives (*viparyaya*) are specified for the sake of establishing identity (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*). Now, he explains that "particularity and generality" [arise] from dispute:
particularity is the common [element], being exclusively negative (ekāntavyatirekin),
while generality is exclusively positive (ekāntānvayin).

The opponent asserts that even those two [reasons] which are inconclusive (anaikāntika) possess the capacity to prove [the point]; to this, the Teacher demonstrates their lack of proving power with the words beginning "that which exists" (yas san), etc.
Now, one might object: "Is it not logical that the lack of proving power belongs only to reasons other than the inconclusive ones?
To this he replies: "True."
If exclusion were established from a single instance alone, it would not be established, because there remains the suspicion of deviation within the subject itself;
for instance:
The necessity of exclusion is called inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*);

and that [necessity] does not exist in things that lack a causal bond. For that very reason, the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs. How, then, can vital breath and so forth be established as being excluded from that which is soulless?
If there were an invariable concomitance by way of identity (*sātmakatva*),
that would not be possible in the case of things that are unconnected,
because it is impossible to establish [the reason] through its own presence as being excluded from every dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Indeed, it is not possible to perceive all opposing factors such that one could ascertain "it is not here" or "it is not there"; however,
this is possible by way of positive concomitance (anvaya),
because:

The apprehension of that [invariable concomitance] as being restricted is the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and this is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is perception; therefore, from the apprehension of such restriction, the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is implied, for otherwise there would be no apprehension of a restricted form. To explain:

Even when another thing exists, that [effect] does not exist; and when that [cause] exists, it necessarily exists. Even in the absence of another thing, its non-existence does not follow; therefore, there is no understanding of its being an effect.
For when the fragrance of sandalwood does not exist even when other things exist, yet it does exist when that [sandalwood] exists—
Then it is established that the fragrance of sandalwood is its effect, and not otherwise; this is the determination.
And since that determination does not exist without negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), negative concomitance also is established as being of the same nature as that [determination].
[Objection: But surely positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established as being pervasive [in the sense that] "from this, its arising occurs everywhere. [Reply:
This is not so;
for its comprehension is achieved by that much alone—namely, that "its arising is from this very thing"—and at that very moment, it is understood that it does not arise from anything else. // 494 //

At that time, it is not the case that [the effect] exists elsewhere than from this; while this is indeed the basis for its being indicative, it is nevertheless from this alone and not from anything else.
And thus, there is indeed such a cognition; for those who immediately perceive its non-existence in the absence of that [cause], having seen its non-arising prior to anything other than it—
surely, even if it were not produced from us, it might arise from some other particular cause.

For it is not the case that everything which is "not other" is necessarily identical; therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, even if [the effect] is absent when [the cause] is present, the absence of deviation (*avyatireka*) is not certain, because that which is unobservable might still be possible.
(2B) If [the effect arises] from something other...

This is incorrect because this reason would belong to you alone, and this favor [of yours] would be for you alone. If there is no desire even for your own favor, then alas, you are indeed [the one who acts] in every respect.
This reason is a prover of you alone, because it is otherwise impossible.
If this which has been set forth is not accepted, then let another way be sought; but since none exists, you are like a woodcutter sharpening his axe for his own destruction.
Moreover,
how could this absence [of the effect] occur instantaneously due to the absence of that [cause], unless there were another cause immediately following? (496)
Even though it is impermanent, that [effect] certainly arises when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present without deficiency,
whereas in its absence it does not arise immediately; thus, it is possible for it to have Śāka and other such things as its cause.

If it is accepted that even that [result] arrives and departs in an instant, then that [result] is like a demon subdued by fire; thus, fire alone is the cause. If it were to arise from something else as well, then—due to the absence of positive and negative concomitance—it would be a mere accidental coincidence, and the search for means by those who act with foresight would not bear its fruit with necessity.
For us non-dualists (*advaitavādins*), however, there is no such thing as a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*);

therefore, if one were to accept a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), the status of a perfectly clear positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be established,
because—
Furthermore,
if it were established that [the probans] exists either in the subject itself or in the state of being a reason, then there would indeed be negative concomitance (vyatirekitā).
Therefore, with respect to a specific [property], neither negative concomitance (vyatireka) nor positive concomitance (anvaya) is established.
For that which does not possess the nature of another cannot, by necessity, be absent when that other is absent.

For that which is not itself obstructed cannot be the cause of another's cessation, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); likewise, the reason [in the argument]— "this living body is not soulless, because it would otherwise follow that it lacks the capacity for perception and so forth"— is [invalid].
For when that which possesses no connection ceases, there is no cessation of another thing that is connected to it;
nor is that which possesses a connection non-pervasive;
and without the connection of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*), there can be no relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*).
If it is asked why it does not occur by another mode as well, we say no, because no other mode is possible; for even that [other] mode, once established, would be a proof of what is intended.

And thus, because there is neither negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) nor positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for that which is intended to be distinct from this [subject], there is an absence of both; therefore, "the living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth" is indeed non-probative.
How then did the Teacher call this a "negative-only" (*vyatirekin*) inference, given the absence of both?
For him as well, this very thing would be intended to be said; it is fit to be said.

This is not a fault, because it was stated that the negative-only (vyatirekin) [reason] is based solely upon non-perception; therefore, otherwise, it would be inconclusive (anaikāntika) as a means of proof. || 207 ||

The Teacher has demonstrated that this is a "negative-only" (vyatirekin) argument by relying on a negative concomitance (vyatireka) established merely through the non-perception [of the reason] in the opponent's view; however, it is not one where the negative concomitance is certain. Otherwise, if a certain negative concomitance were possible, it would be a true indicator (gamaka), and thus the Teacher would not have included it among the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reasons.

Therefore, the teacher’s intention here is not to establish a definitive negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). [Objection: The absence of breath and so forth pervades the absence of a self (*nairātmya*), and since that [absence] does not exist in a living body, the pervader being excluded necessarily entails the exclusion of the pervaded—the absence of a self—from the living body; thus, how is the self not established?

Since there is no proof that the absence of breath and so forth pervades all instances of selflessness, if breath and so forth were to cease upon the cessation of the self, then [the former] would indeed [follow]; but that is not the case. (208)

If the pervasion between the two counter-examples were established, then the cessation of "non-breathing" and so forth in a living body would entail the cessation of "selflessness," whereby the self would be established even without positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
However, that very pervasion between the two counter-examples cannot be established without reaching the subject (*pakṣa*);
for as long as there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the self, its status as a negating factor (*nivarttaka*) is not established at all.
Furthermore, the cessation of that which is not itself subject to cessation is not established as being pervaded by the cessation of the object to be ceased;

therefore, since there is no cessation of the non-pervaded even in the absence of the cessation of the pervader, there is no cessation of the non-pervader— thus, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not establish the existence of the self (*ātman*).

5B. There is pervasion of the self [of the reason] by the exclusion of one thing through the exclusion of another, because it is impossible for there to be the exclusion of one thing without the exclusion of the other.

If it were the case that [the cognition] has that as its nature or is produced from that, then even in the perception of that [object], there would be cessation [of the cognition] even without an obstacle; if that were so, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
If it were the case that it has that as its nature or is produced from that...
Now, if it is argued that the self is this entire world— beginning with the vital breaths—
and that everything has proceeded from the self because the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*),
this is not a valid refutation, for:
This [self] is established in its apprehension, its perception, its comprehension, and its attainment;
for if the self is apprehended, it is established that another entity also possesses that same nature, because it shares the defining characteristics of that [self].

But that very [inherence] is not perceived; how then can the reason "because it has that as its characteristic" be established? Furthermore, in this case, inherence is based on cognition, since the self is not perceived;
however, the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception, and is not itself imperceptible.
How could there be "in the self," since its nature and its production [from that] do not exist?
Furthermore, for that which is absolutely imperceptible, seeing and non-seeing are not established.
Nor is there a lack of self (nairātmya) in things such as jars, because... [the reason follows].

If [the self] were entirely beyond perception, its non-existence would follow from the fact that it is not perceived. Since there is no proof for the non-existence of the self, how can its pervasion [by breath, etc. be established?

(497) For, in the case of something that meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) establish its status as a cause or a pervader. However, there is no perception of the self; therefore, how could it possess the nature of being a cause or a pervader?
And in the absence of that, it is not established that breath and so forth have the self as their essence or are produced from it.
Moreover, how can there be the negation "not" in a jar or the like for that whose form has not been seen elsewhere?
And how can there be the pervasion of exclusion for one whose negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unknown? (211)
For when something is perceived in one place or at one time, it is understood that it does not exist here or now; such is the cognition of the entire world.
But as for that which has never been an object of cognition, how can there be any mention of it as "not existing here"?
Indeed, no conceptual constructions regarding anything ever arise with respect to what has not been seen.
If, however, the negation of identity depends entirely upon something else, [then consider this:

for a conceptual construction (*vitarka*) indeed proceeds only when something has been perceived elsewhere; but as for whether it exists or does not exist when that thing is not being seen, how can there be any certainty?
If it is merely the negation of identity— that this supreme Self does not exist [in the body]—
and not the certain conclusion that the Self does not exist in jars and other things,
then its omnipresence is all the more established.

If, by perceiving it as distinct [from the self], there is the certainty that "the self is not [present] here," then let this same [certainty] apply to a living person as well: "the self is not present here. Just as a jar or other object, being perceived as distinct [from the self], is understood to be "without a self," so too should the living body be;
for even that is not perceived as distinct from that [self]. (499)
Therefore, because of the absence of perceptibility, there is no understanding of the self's non-existence in things such as a jar;
thus, for the self whose distinctness is not known, how can there be a pervasion by exclusion? For the self is not pervaded by the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth.
Indeed, when the exclusion of one thing is pervaded by the exclusion of another, then that [latter] exclusion is pervaded by it.

Furthermore, it is not known that the exclusion of the self (*ātma-vyāvṛtti*) is pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth (*prāṇādy-abhāva*); therefore, how can the pervasion of the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth by the self be established, such that the establishment of the self would follow from the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth? Consequently, there is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) here.

1. [Objection: Since the self is distinct [from the body], why is it that there is no cognition that "the self does not exist," just as one cognizes that "vital breaths and so forth do not exist in a jar"? [Response: This is an unequal comparison.
For the existence or non-existence of the vital breaths and so forth is perceived in some cases through direct observation,
not from mere non-perception alone.
Likewise, if the self were visible, its existence or non-existence would be perceived.
Since the conditions for perception are met, there is indeed a perception of the absence of breath and so forth in a lifeless body;
however, the claim that "the self is thus" is a misconception.

Furthermore, even if jars and the like were indeed devoid of a self, nevertheless, the self is not thereby established; for [the existence of the self] is not negated by the absence of breath and so forth.
Indeed, if the self did not exist in a living body, breath and the other [vital functions] would also be impossible.
Because the absence of self is observed in things such as a jar to be the negator of breath and so forth,
[the reason] does not [prove the point],
since it is the absence of something other [than the self] that acts as the negator.
For indeed, by the absence of that cause for which breath is not observed in a jar, if that [cause] were also absent in the body, its occurrence within the body would be illogical. (213)
Intellect, effort, and so forth are likewise entirely absent in a jar;

therefore, is it because of their absence that there is a cessation of breath and the like, or is it because of the absence of the self? What indeed is your reason for dispelling this doubt? In this regard, if that very cause—such as intellect—by whose absence breath and the like are not observed in a jar were also absent from the body, then the consequence would follow that breath and the like would be missing [from the body].

Furthermore, it is not the case that cognition and the other [mental factors] do not exist; so how could there be the consequence of the cessation of breath and so forth? Now, if there is a similarity between living bodies and jars in terms of being devoid of a self (*nairātmya*), even though there is indeed a dissimilarity caused by the presence or absence of cognition and the rest, nevertheless, due to the lack of a self, the living body—like a jar and so forth—would also be devoid of breath and the like.
Alternatively, it is said here that [the subject] possesses a self by virtue of having a nature devoid of breath and so forth;
for if reality were perceived through some similarity even when things are different, [then this would follow].
In that case, since jars and other such things possess the property of being objects of cognition (*prameyatva*), why is their possession of a self (*sātmatva*) not likewise cognized?
For even so, there is no lack of some degree of commonality [between them]. (214)
If invalidity were indeed the basis for all desired [cognitions],
then who would be capable of establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence without it?
For validity does not arise from mere desire.

Rather, wherever there is the possibility of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the desire of a discerning person does not contradict even what is undesirable when brought forth by that valid cognition; for it is logical that valid cognition should function independently, without dependence on desire.
Otherwise, without the independence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there would be no determination of existence and non-existence;

for [existence] would consist in the presentation of the probandum as the object by the proponent's desire, while [non-existence] would consist in its abandonment by the opponent's desire—thus, there would be no non-confusion in the determination of existence and non-existence.
We shall therefore demonstrate that even those things such as cognition (buddhi) and so forth would [consequently] exist as the absence of a self (ātman).
Therefore, as for what was said— that there is no cessation of the vital breaths and so forth when the intellect and other faculties exist— that is incorrect;
it is not incorrect,
because it is precisely other [factors] that are the activators in that case.
If the self were determined to be the initiator of cognition and so forth, it would be logical that when [the self] ceases,
they cease; but this is not the case, because memory, desire, effort, vital breath, the closing of the eyes, and so forth, arise from those [preceding causes].
Memory, desire, and effort give rise to breathing, the winking of eyes, and so forth;

these arise from that [consciousness]. Objects, senses, and cognitions arise from their own respective classes, depending upon mutual causal conditions and participating in positive and negative concomitance.
This self-nature extends only this far; there is no further persistence in the postulation of another [self].
When some undesirable [state] occurs, or elsewhere, from that [self] arise memory, desire, and effort, and from those proceed the vital breaths, the blinking of eyes, and so forth.

If it is asked, "From what do memory and the other [mental states] arise? [the answer is: they arise from cognitions dependent upon objects and sense organs, originating from their own respective classes;
for the object is preceded by an object, and likewise, the cognition of the sense organ depends upon a mutual causal relationship with its object.

Since this personal existence is bound to such a collection of causes and conditions, what is the use of anything else that is superfluous? But surely memory—which consists in the synthesis of the preceding and the succeeding—cannot exist without a self; for instance:
He alone by whom something was seen is the rememberer; for what was seen by one cannot be the object of remembrance for another.
[Objection: But even this is merely a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); how can there be any positive establishment [of the self] from it?
For remembrance is not observed to occur when there is identity, because the identity between the earlier and later moments is not apprehended through perception.
And since recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*),
although what was perceived by another is not recollected [by oneself], it will nevertheless be recollected with its specific distinctions;
for it is not the case that everyone who is "another" is identical.

It has arisen as such from its own cause, by virtue of which it alone—and nothing else—is the cause of recollection, due to the necessity of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). For recollection does not arise merely because of a self; rather, it arises from the state of a continuum (*saṃtāna*) produced through proficiency and repeated practice. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of recollection occurring at that very time [for everyone].
Now, it is not said that memory exists only when a self exists,
because memory is absent in another self;
yet even this is not correct.

For, because memory changes according to the changes in that [prior experience]—as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—this is the relationship of cause and effect; otherwise, it could not be established.
Since memory follows the positive and negative concomitance of the practice of prior experience and changes according to its changes, the self is not the cause.
If [recollection] does not occur without an eternally pervasive [self],

then it would follow that time and so forth are also causes, since there is no distinction [between them and the self]. Alternatively, if [recollection] does not occur without one who is an experiencer and a rememberer, [then such a self must exist].
This is indeed non-existent;
for by means of memory and experience, the rememberer and the experiencer are postulated. How can it not be understood that their existence is like [a city] in the sky?
501.1 B saḥ
For it is by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for memory and experience that some rememberer and experiencer is postulated;
however, this is not something distinct from space and so forth. Thus, let it be postulated that there is some single [entity].

And that [self] is not distinct from space and the like, because there is no difference [between them] in terms of being all-pervasive, eternal, formless (*amūrta*), and so forth. Now, if it is argued that the self perceived as the agent in the notion "I" is not merely formlessness—[we reply:
indeed, in the cognition "I," it is the body alone that appears, as in "I am Devadatta, a descendant of Garga, dark-complexioned."
If it is argued that the body is impermanent, [we reply] no; rather,
it is the states of the body that are impermanent.
However, since the abiding subject is not distinct [from the body] in the next world and so forth,
this very conception is preferable;
for remembrance and the like are perceived as having the body as their substrate, and not as being presided over by something formless.
Now, first of all, the cognizer is established as being eternal; since his body is different [from him], what is the use of further investigation?
B.
...only one; 2 B.
...beginning with [the letter] ṇa.
That too is incorrect, because a collection of states is not perceived as something distinct [from them]. For this very reason, the establishment of our position regarding the body remains unrefuted.
(502) Furthermore:

In that which is eternal and unchanging, how can there be recollection and experience? If the knower is that very same [eternal] nature, why would it be a knower of objects? (503) If it undergoes modification through pleasure and so forth, its eternity is not tenable; if it does not undergo modification through pleasure and so forth, its state of being happy and so forth is not tenable.
(504) Since recollection is the fruit of experience, why is it not [the self]? Or, because of the cognition "I am," it is not merely cause and effect. (505)
For in this way, every person understands their own agency, thinking: "I am perceiving through memory that object which was previously seen and ascertained. (506) [Note:
3B reads *an-anya-niścitam*]
That is incorrect,
because:

"I remember what was seen before"—this [cognition] is not [valid] merely by the arising of a self. If every cognition were valid simply because it has the self as its cause, then everything would be valid; consequently, everything would be established for everyone, which is a great inconsistency.
Therefore, only that which arises from an unimpaired basis is valid.

And this being the case, since the cognition produced by the eye and other senses does not apprehend what is synthesized, how could the unity of the preceding and succeeding [moments] be established as real? For, without a cognition that functions as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the self cannot perceive itself or anything else as synthesized; thus, the statement that "it possesses the capacity through memory and also exists in synthesis" would lose its truth. The self does not, without such a valid cognition, cognize itself or another as something synthesized.
Therefore, when I say "I remember," this is merely conventional;
thus, everything is entirely consistent precisely through its conventional self.
Moreover:
That [reason] is equivalent to that [invalid reason] because of its deviation with respect to breath and so forth;

for it is not [non-deviant] because of its deviation. And if you ask how there can be a separation from the non-probandum even in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), we reply: indeed, it is stated thus.
"By virtue of its occurrence in the probandum, the meaning [of the term] follows; this is the same for other cases as well.
(219) "By virtue of its occurrence in the probandum"—[this means that] there is no difference between audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) and [the breaths] such as *prāṇa*.
Since the pure negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is identical in both cases, what logic dictates that one of them possesses deviation (*vyabhicāra*) while the other does not?
[The opponent replies: But surely the negative concomitance is not identical, because their objects (*viṣaya*) differ.

For audibility indeed deviates from both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), not merely because it is excluded from that which lacks the probandum, such as vital breath and so forth;
[one might object: "But since audibility is excluded even from the similar instances, its non-concomitance with the similar instances is being established."

That [reason] is equally applicable even to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth; for even in that case, the presentation of its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absence from them is of no use,
since it is simply stated that there is exclusion from what is not the probandum (*asādhya*) and thus existence in the probandum (*sādhya*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that by means of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), there is the observation of two [properties] through one. Restriction (*niyama*) is the determination of what is being determined; otherwise, if exclusion from the non-provable (*asādhya*) were to occur even from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), then that restriction would be purposeless.

For this very reason, you yourselves have also established—through presumptive implication—that there is the observation of two [properties] through one, and thus, from this statement, there is exclusion from the non-provable alone.
Such non-deviation is not established in cases where there is no positive concomitance (anvaya);
for how could that non-deviation— which is characterized by a restriction and pervaded by positive concomitance— exist in the absence of the pervader's positive concomitance?
Alternatively, the notion that "the interruption [of the practice] occurs precisely because it is incurable" cannot be understood without the cognition of a positive concomitance (anvaya),
for it is impossible to observe every instance of the counter-example (vipakṣa).
But by way of positive concomitance (anvaya),
[the cognition] occurs because it is bound to the self; since it is excluded from what is other, how could that which has not been excluded from what is other be bound to it?

Now, if the existence of the probandum does not exist, then its non-existence must follow; how then can there be non-deviation [of the reason] from that which is unprovable? For what other kind of negation of a negation could there be than through affirmation? (221)

The restriction that "the non-provable does not exist at all" negates non-existence in the provable, meaning "it does not exist in the non-provable alone, but it is not non-existent in the provable. This negation of a negation would indeed establish an affirmation.
Now, (if one were to argue...)
The cessation of what is non-existent cannot be established; therefore, it does not occur in the case of things that cannot be accomplished.
If one says "no," is that very [negation] considered the cessation of the non-existent? (222)
Now, because there is no similar instance (sapakṣa) for the reason "breath and so forth," there can be no exclusion from it;
for it is impossible to exclude something that does not exist, since it lacks the status of being an ablative (apādāna).
And there is no such thing as "non-existence" from which a cessation could be perceived;
if there is no cessation [from that],
how can there be a cessation of cessation?

If you say that [the negation] is also not [established], then surely, when there is a negation of the negation of cessation, how can there be a negation of the negation of the negation of cessation in the case of what is non-existent? Thus, because of infinite regress, there is no comprehension;
for "negation" and "cessation" are one and the same thing.
That which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to cessation is indeed the point of departure (*apādāna*) with respect to that same cessation;
for surely, that with which there exists a conjunction is the point of departure upon the separation from it,
and there is no conjunction with a non-entity (*abhāva*).

How much more so, then, is that which does not occur [there] not an *apādāna*? For an *apādāna* is merely the point of separation, not the presence of conjunction. Otherwise, how could it be said that "he has always abstained from evil"? (508) If you argue that there is no conceptual possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) of such a thing in that case, then why is it not accepted here as well? Therefore, let it be understood that its status as an *apādāna* is all the more certain. (509)

Where that object never occurs at any time, that [object] is all the more its *apādāna* (point of departure), because the absence of cessation is a positive affirmation (*vidhi*), which is the existence of a thing even though it is non-existent.
1. "The non-existence of a thing, yet the non-existence of that non-existence does not exist"—behold this, O kinsman, which is a mere boast! 223
Look, O friend:
the non-existence of "not" is not a mere negation; rather, it is an affirmation characterized by the existence of a real entity.
Thus, non-existence exists even for that which is non-existent;
yet, even if it possesses a logical form, it does not exist within non-existence, nor does the other exist within its opposite. What is this other than the behavior of the blind?
For:
Affirmation and negation exist through mutual exclusion; since there is no third possibility, it is illogical to say that "it is neither.
When an entity is absent, its non-existence is necessarily present; thus, that very absence is designated as "cessation," for that which is not present therein has not ceased from that state.

If it is argued that even though [the locus] is not present there, non-existence is not simply the absence of existence because being a locus is impossible, and that [non-existence] too does not exist there;
It is not [the case that they are identical], because existence and non-existence consist in mutual exclusion; how then could there be a negation of both?
For existence necessarily acquires its status through the exclusion of non-existence.

For since there can be no existence in the absence [of non-existence], and since existence is excluded from non-existence, it necessarily follows that upon the cessation of that [non-existence], existence must occur;
otherwise, if it were not to occur even when non-existence has ceased, it would never exist at all.
For instance:
If an entity is not perceived when there is non-existence, and if non-existence itself does not exist, then the entity is perceived.
That [perception] is also not a negation, because non-apprehension is non-existent. Even if both [entity and non-entity] are non-existent, the existence of non-existence is not thereby precluded.
Although both entity and non-entity are non-existent, nevertheless the non-existence of the entity is certainly not precluded.
For in this way, if an entity does not exist,
then non-existence also would not exist;
because when an entity is not apprehended, it is precisely that which is cognized as non-existence.

Therefore, the negation, while actually occurring as characterized by the perception of that which is distinct from the object [negated], is established by perception through its exclusion from positive affirmation (*vidhi*). Consequently, by the very operation of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the establishment of the state of being otherwise occurs when there is a change; no other mode is possible.
Whatever is excluded there by perception is entirely other than that which is grasped by a perception apprehending a positive entity;
and that which is not determined as having that [positive] nature by such a perception is simply its non-existence in that form, not a third category.
Even when non-existence (*abhāva*) is being delimited, how could there be another category [of existence] such that "that which is not delimited in that way is indeed existence"?

Since there is no other category, that [non-existence] must be either existence or non-existence; however, in the case of non-existence, its having a locus (*sādhikaraṇatā*)—namely, "it is not in this"—cannot be delimited, because that very [locus] itself is not delimited.
For that which is non-existent cannot be delimited, because it is non-existent.
If there is a cessation [of the reason] with respect to that [subject], why is its occurrence not desired?
Even that [occurrence] is not a negation; what is it about this cessation that is being denied?
(224) Let us first direct our inquiry toward you yourself.
If there is no exclusion from that non-existent similar class (sapakṣa), what kind of occurrence could there be? Since there is no other alternative,
it follows that such an exclusion would not be of the nature of non-existence.
If it were argued that existence consists in the form of occurrence (*vṛtti*), and that even this does not exist, [we reply:
no; for if occurrence has not ceased, then non-occurrence (*nivṛtti*) is thereby established, since this very [non-occurrence] would be what is demonstrated.
Negation is cessation; therefore, what is it that is negated? For that very thing which has been established cannot logically be the object of negation.
Consequently, cessation is simply the negation of activity; thus, there is no negation of that [cessation itself].
If it is argued that there is no cognition of it as either the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or the point of departure (*apādāna*), and therefore there is no cessation from it,
to this it is replied:
apart from affirmation and negation, there is nothing else that is verbal (*śābda*).
That linguistic convention does not apply to non-existent things; thus, in this matter, one has reached a state of silence.
If someone were to challenge you: "Surely the vital breath and so forth are not observed in the similar class (sapakṣa);
therefore, having been excluded from it, why is that which is 'uncommon' (asādhāraṇa) not a means of proof?"
If that were the case, then "invisibility to hearing" (*aśrāvaṇatva*) would also be a probans;
therefore, it must be stated that there is no exclusion [of the probans] from the absence of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) as a rule, otherwise one would fall into silence here.
Even if it were a pillar made of stone,
let it be so;
for it is not possible for it to determine itself in any way whatsoever.
Speech can be restrained, but not the intellect;
one must necessarily understand it in some way or another.
Moreover:

If non-existence cannot be cognized either as a locus or as an ablative, then, because it would always exist in its entirety [as a mere absence], there would be a total cessation of all worldly discourse;
for this reason:

There is no negation of that which exists, nor does it apply to that which is non-existent; by this logic, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has reached its dissolution in the world. Since the meaning of *nañ* is simply absence (*abhāva*), how can there be the employment of it when that absence itself cannot be delimited?
Since the intellect employs the expressive word for the sake of that which is to be expressed, this pair of non-existences cannot possibly exist for the purpose of cognizing it. (513) 2 T.
The thirteenth daily lesson is concluded.
If only non-existence were made the object [of cognition],
the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be entirely purposeless.
Since the negative particle (*nañ*) is not employed unless its object has been determined,
or if it were employed, it would serve no purpose;
therefore, that whose absence [is asserted] must be made the object [of cognition].
If that were so, how could there be the non-existence of that very thing which is being perceived? Or, if it is perceived in one way while its non-existence is in another way,
then it is as follows:

It is argued that it is precisely the existent that is negated through connection with certain places and so forth; to this it is replied: if there is a negation of place and time, then [the thing] exists and is not negated.
It is not as it is, nor is it negated in the manner that it exists.
(227) Furthermore, even the negation "it does not exist here now in this form" is simply impossible; for instance:
If that form, that time, and that place exist, how can they be denied?
If, however, they do not exist, it is impossible for them to be made objects of cognition, because non-existence cannot be determined [by the mind].
If, on the other hand, they are made objects of cognition, then they must likewise exist as having a substratum and so forth.
Otherwise, it would be impossible to make [the absence] an object of cognition;
for determination by way of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) is necessary, as it cannot otherwise occur.
In this regard, if the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa-bhāva*)—namely, "it does not exist in this place"—is made an object of cognition, [then the absence is established].

How can non-existence be an object of cognition? Furthermore, even if that which is being negated is not itself negated, if that were the case, then by the very attribution of it to the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there would indeed be a turning away from the similar class; so how could there be no exclusion from the similar class?
Therefore, the conventional practice of affirmation and negation cannot possibly have an external basis;
consequently, there would be the cessation of all conventional practice.
[Objection: But surely the conventional practice of affirmation is possible?
Therefore, there is no annihilation of conventional discourse,
because there is no prescription of that which has been made an object [of cognition].

If the apprehension "the jar exists" is by way of its being existent, then that itself is the affirmation; what further purpose would there be in affirming it with the word "exists"? On the other hand, if it were by way of its being non-existent, then because of the contradiction, it would not be possible to affirm that "the non-existent exists. If it is determined to be existent, affirmation therein is redundant; if it is determined to be non-existent, affirmation therein is redundant. (514)
There is no establishment of affirmation and negation—
Since it is determined by way of non-existence, no further positive injunction is possible;
therefore, all affirmation and negation is accepted here as being based on the meaning of words—which relies upon existence and non-existence—and not upon any external substratum. (228)
For the object of valid cognition is one thing, and the object of a word is another;
the object of a word rests upon both existence and non-existence,
whereas the object of valid cognition does not rest upon existence and non-existence in that way.
For the object of valid cognition cannot exist otherwise [than as it is perceived], because it is apprehended in a determinate form;

however, the cognition produced by a word is the same whether the object has perished or not. Therefore, since the referent of a word depends upon both existence and non-existence, it is not a valid means of cognition (*pramā*). || 515 ||
Therefore, when an object is examined by a conceptualizing intellect, it serves as the basis for affirmation and negation;
yet because conceptualizations lack any necessary connection to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*),
not everything that is non-conceptual is necessarily a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it has occurred in an affirmative form (*vidhirūpa*), then it is invalid; therefore, a negation (*pratiṣedha*) is required to establish its invalidity.
If, however, it occurs in a negative form (*pratiṣedharūpa*), then the affirmation (*vidhi*) follows; indeed, in that case, this cognition would simply be erroneous (*bhrānta*).
Then, because self-awareness is non-erroneous, it manifests itself precisely as suchness.
For it is not possible to show the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) otherwise, because that would entail the loss of its own nature;
for if it were to appear under another form, that very [other] form would be its intrinsic nature there as well, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, when its own nature exists, its being the material cause of another entity is negated;
and since that subject is apprehended in its own form, how could it be common to both affirmation and negation, such that it might be connected with both?

To this it is replied: that substratum (dharmin) is perceived as connected with those two [the property and the absence] even when [the absence] is not present; because verbal usage occurs in such a manner, it too is accepted as participating in conventional discourse. (229)
Indeed, this linguistic convention does not depend upon an external or internal intrinsic nature, but rather depends upon words;
nor is there a cognition of an external or internal intrinsic nature from a word. 1. B. [This is] comprehension.

[Objection: But since there is nothing else apart from that [particular], upon what basis does the conventional usage of affirmation and negation rest? [Reply: We say it rests upon the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). What, then, is this so-called "exclusion of others"?
If it is argued that what is cognized from a word is indeed this very [object], then one must ask: what is it that is cognized?
Although not even the slightest [reality] exists,
nevertheless, this conventional usage persists because it carries along a beginningless delusion.
The subject, characterized by word and meaning, appears as connected with affirmation and negation;
for even though such an external or internal [object] does not exist when investigated,
it has been stated thus:
Is it not the case that for him there is no form whatsoever? Indeed, a form consisting of superimposed external objects does exist for him.
If it is argued that there is no other form [of cognition] apart from the knowledge and the object of knowledge, and therefore it is illusory;
If that [object] is also cognized in its own form, how can it be erroneous?
On the other hand, if it is not an object of cognition, how can it be determined that it exists when it is not being cognized?
If it is argued that its erroneous nature is known later on...
First of all, it is not perceived by way of its own nature;
how then could it be the object of the determination "it exists"?
If it were perceived by way of another's nature, that other perception would be erroneous.
If one says "it is not," there would be an infinite regress; furthermore, even if that [object] exists, if its reality is not ascertained, it is called an error—
what, then, is its reality?
Is not its very nature indeed the non-contact with objects? How can it be unreal?
For remaining in one's own nature is not unreality.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is untrue because it produces a determination in a manner other than [how things actually are], then the determination itself must be untrue, since it is produced by that [cognition]. If it is further argued that the determination is also indeed untrue, [we reply:]...
Nor is it the case that the certainty [of the cognition] is otherwise, because it is produced by a latent impression (*vāsanā*); thus,
the claim that "the certainty is therefore erroneous" is also not tenable.
Since that [conceptual cognition] also abides in its own form,
the referent of a word is therefore indeed formless;
how then does the linguistic usage "it exists" occur?

It is conventionally expressed as "it exists" because it is understood as "existing" through the linguistic usage characterized by the application of words; it is communicated under the name "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as the exclusion of the apprehension of universals and so forth. However, if one were to say "nothing at all," there would be terror among opponents.
For this very reason, he says:
"That too is accepted as participating in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); otherwise, there would be a total cessation of conventional usage," lest another objector should reject [the position].
For indeed,
the exclusion of others by means of a word occurs solely through the relation of cause and effect among things that are otherwise mutually unperceived.
When it is said, "Bring fire," one proceeds by avoiding what is not fire.
Even when cognizing fire through sound, conceptual construction arises as a self-awareness that does not touch the actual object;
from that arises the conceptualization of purposeful activity,
and from that follows the experience of the nature of movement.
Therefore, the conventional usage of "attainment" or "otherwise" does not imply that there is any such thing as a relationship between signifier and signified.
Nor is it the case that it is not un-undertaken.
Otherwise, in the affirmation and negation of things, there would be the affirmation and negation of the entire nature of a single property;
for if there were no difference due to the lack of manifold natures, it would be like the simultaneous affirmation and negation of many [properties]. (230)
Because of the non-selfhood of the self, there is no coexistence of affirmation and negation within a single substratum. || 231 ||

If there were no difference between the subject (dharmin) and its properties (dharmas), then upon the affirmation or negation of a single property, there would follow the affirmation or negation of all properties; for when that [property] is affirmed, it cannot be said that its own nature is not affirmed, as that would entail the non-affirmation of the [subject] itself.
Likewise, regarding negation: indeed,
when there is no difference between the prescription of a cow and its negation, there can be no fragmentation [of the object],
because it is not logical that while something has been communicated by a word, its very nature should remain uncommunicated.
If it is argued that although this [object] has indeed been established, it is not apprehended due to error, then everything would be unapprehended; thus, there would be a collapse of cognition.
Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain that "some things are apprehended while others are not."
Because division does not exist;
for it is only when division exists that this occurs, and not otherwise,
since existence is defined as nothing other than perception.
Since existence itself is divided by that division,
how can it be said that one part alone is determined and not the other?
This is quite trivial.
Now, even if momentariness is not ascertained, blue is nonetheless ascertained; and indeed, there is no such thing as what is perceived being logically untenable.
In that case as well, there is a contradiction;
for if, by means of certainty, there is an apprehension of blueness, it would be devoid of the establishment of momentary duration.
The proof of the momentariness of existence established by one [means of valid cognition] is not subverted by others.

(517) If that which is established by a means of valid cognition were subverted by another means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress, as that too would be subverted by yet another; thus, there would be a total lack of certainty.

Now, even if the ascertainment of blue does not operate with respect to momentariness, nevertheless, momentariness is not sublated by that [ascertainment], nor is the ascertainment of blue sublated by its own proof, because both proceed together;
for there are three types of logical connection—conjunction (*samuccaya*), alternative (*vikalpa*), and sublation (*bādhana*).
Conjunction is as in "this is blue and it is a lotus," due to the conjunction of the two properties.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is [like] "Is it a post or a person? because the two cannot exist in one place; sublation (*bādhana*) is [like] "It is a rope, not a snake," because the state of being a snake is impossible. What fault is there here in the conjunction of blue and momentariness?

To this it is replied: How can there be a synthesis here through the application of the characteristic of sublation? Nowhere is it possible for that which is to be sublated to be synthesized with its very sublator. For if the determination of blueness were to occur to the exclusion of momentariness, then momentariness would indeed be sublated.
Indeed, the apprehension of a form distinct from that [object] is itself the sublation (*bādhana*) of the presentation of that [object's] form;
for is this not the sublation "it is not here" by means of the pramāṇa of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)?
And it is not the case that perception is a sublater for anyone;
this is not tenable because:

This ascertainment (*niścaya*) is indeed not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it is its result (*phala*). Rather, the apprehension of that [object] as distinct from others is the means of valid cognition, and from that [apprehension], ascertainment arises.
Indeed, this ascertainment is not an independent means of valid cognition;
rather, it follows upon the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There is no change in its nature;
even if, for some reason, it does not actually arise despite the emergence of a cognition of isolation,
its negation still occurs by virtue of its very capacity for such [arising].
We shall establish this further below; in that regard, if blue were ascertained apart from its momentariness, [it would follow that it is permanent].
If momentariness has already been refuted by that very [reason], how can it be established by another?
Or, if it has indeed been established by that [first reason], it is nevertheless clarified by the other.
To this, it is replied:

In that case, if it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be a lack of clarity regarding its prior movement? Furthermore, it is a contradiction to claim that the object has not been made clear and yet has been established. || 520 ||
How indeed could this lack of clarity exist even when there is certainty?
Here, clarity exists; elsewhere, certainty is illogical.
Therefore, it should be understood that either the former [cognition] was erroneous or the latter. For two cognitions that are mutually contradictory cannot coexist regarding a single object.
Therefore, when one [attribute] is enjoined, there is the injunction of everything that is not distinct from it; thus, the introduction of other words and other conceptual constructions is redundant.
Now, if it is argued that diverse limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are the objects of diverse words and conceptual constructions, then this objection does not apply.
That is incorrect, because there is a distinction.

If there is no subsumption within a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) of that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited— meaning, if the two prohibitions are mutually distinct from one another and from their substratum— then those objects are established as entirely separate, and the substratum is nothing other than them; how then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?

For instance, in the expression "blue lotus," when a quality and a substance are being presented, there is no other substratum for those two; thus, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
nor is there a cognition of the relation between qualifier and qualified, because they present distinct meanings.
Like a jar and a cloth; otherwise, blue would not exist as a distinct entity.
The cognition of the substance occurs precisely through the apprehension of the blue color, because there is no cognition of it in discrete parts;

even if [the substance were] the universal and the quality, nevertheless, there would still be no cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the absence of another word denoting the substratum.
Now, if it is the blue substance itself that is perceived, and not the mere quality of blueness,

then since two things would be denoted by a single word, and likewise by another as well, how could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) when four or three [entities] are being denoted? For entities of distinct forms, even when presented by one or many words, do not participate in coreferentiality.
Now, if it were impossible to cognize blue and so forth in isolation, then there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of distinct cognitions;

however, since those qualities such as blue can occur without a fixed genus, and genera and so forth can occur without fixed qualities, the employment of another word is for the purpose of establishing their necessity.

If that [distinction] were non-existent, then the fact that blue and so forth are distinct from perception would not be understood; otherwise, how could that very same object be cognized by means of a word as well? (523)
If an abstracted quality such as "blue" does not appear in perception, then it should likewise not appear from a word either,
since the apprehension of the relationship [between word and object] occurs only with respect to that [perceptual appearance].
If, on the other hand, there is no such cognition because [the object] is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), [then the objection remains].
If it is argued that what is being perceived cannot be imperceptible because it is not present [elsewhere],
we say no.
If it is argued that [the cognition] occurs even when the object is not present because the operation of the sense organs is absent,
we say no.

If the sense organ itself is the cause of cognition insofar as it brings about the manifestation of its own nature, what difference is there between the functioning and non-functioning of the sense organ?
Furthermore, where there is proximity [of the object], how could there be a cognition otherwise?
If it is argued that the absence of the operation of the sense-organ does not destroy anything, yet it destroys clarity—
if indeed there is an absence of clarity; [then...]
Nevertheless, blueness must be conveyed precisely through its inherence in a specific substance;
otherwise, how could it be conveyed? And thus, there would be no need for the employment of another word.
Now, if blue and so forth were to reside in indeterminate substances,
then in that case, even "blue" would be understood as indeterminate from the word "blue," and the "lotus" would also be [understood as such] because it is denoted by that same expressive term.
Furthermore, there can again be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between two terms whose denotations are not fixed, because it is impossible for them to convey a single referent.
The claim that such cognition arises precisely from mutual exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is also not tenable;

for how could there be an exclusion of what has already been apprehended by another? Indeed, it is in the act of exclusion itself that the status of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as the denotable object is established.
(524) If blue and other such things were presented by words in an indefinite manner, they could not subsequently be restricted by another [term].
For that which is apprehended by perception is not sublated by another means of knowledge, as that would entail the consequence of [the first] being erroneous.
If it is argued that doubt is then removed by another word, we reply that what has been established through a conjunction (samuccaya) cannot be sublated.
But when there is a conceptual construction such as "Is it a blue lotus or something else?", then the cessation of that conceptual construction is established by means of another word.
That too is incorrect, because:
"If even a conceptual construction were a real object understood from that word, then upon the encounter with another word, from what could its cessation arise? (525)
If that very object is unreal and a mere domain of conceptual construction, how can it be made otherwise by another [means of knowledge],
since both possess the status of valid cognition?
Or, if it has been established by that [cognition] as being merely of a doubtful nature;

And the state of being doubtful consists precisely in being removable by a firm conviction; therefore, removal by something other than that [doubt] is logical, for it is not the case that what is already established as such could be "not such."
That too is incorrect, for the state of being negatable has already been established by that very same word; what, then, will remain to be enjoined by a subsequent word? (526) [Objection:

But surely, the state of being negatable is established by the first cognition through a general rule (*niyama*), whereas it is established by the subsequent one through a specific rule (*niyama*); thus, there is a purposeful application.
That too is incorrect;

for it is established that how could a non-restriction, which has been arrived at by the force of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), be made otherwise even by another means of valid cognition? (527)
Therefore, there is indeed a lack of authoritative status for either the former or the latter, because the former does not establish [the object],
and the latter is likewise of such a nature.
If it expresses only the universal, then [the specific term] is redundant; furthermore,
an inference based on a conceptualized universal would be a sublation [of the claim].
Nor can it be established by inference, because even that [inference] is sublated by perception; thus, there is no apprehension of qualifiers such as "intense flames" and so forth.
If it is argued that there is doubt even in that case because it is a doubt in a general sense, we say no.
Because the apprehension of a universal consists in doubt,
the apprehension of a universal is indeed the apprehension of an indefinite particular;
for a universal cannot possibly possess a fixed form.
For indeed, wherever there is a cognition of a universal, there is no such thing as an individual [corresponding to it]; therefore, all cognition of a universal is an illusion. 528
In that case, what is the use of non-interference elsewhere?
For even if a universal is being perceived, it does not bring about a perception restricted to a specific individual;
therefore, the perception of the universal is indeed subject to interference.
If it is argued that the universal does not exist because it is merged within the individual, that is incorrect;
for if it is merged within the individual, what use would the universal have? A universal has no utility anywhere, such as in tasks like carrying loads or milking, as an individual does. (529)
