If that which was the intended object of this undertaking is corrupted, then surely it is not logical for that very corruption of conceptual construction—which has the individual as its object—to occur without the apprehension of a universal.
[Objection: Even when there is certainty regarding a universal, that very universal must be the one certain; how then could there be doubt regarding another?
When one thing has been ascertained, it is not logical to have doubt regarding another,
because if there were certainty in every case, it would follow that there would be doubt in all cases.
Nevertheless, it might be argued:
Only a possible object can be the subject of doubt, and not anything else;
for indeed, when something is observed to be possible in a certain place, yet is seen to deviate there, it is precisely upon seeing that [deviation] that doubt arises regarding that very place. (530)
For doubt is not possible regarding that which is both possible and deviant;
rather, when a general property (*sāmānya*) is perceived, doubt arises concerning that [specific instance] in which it is possible.

Thus, when "cowness" (*gotva*) is ascertained in a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and so forth, and "horseness" (*aśvatva*) in a white horse (*karka*) and so forth, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
) 1 B [is] endowed with;
that, therefore, is incorrect.
Since there is no cognition of anything else here other than the mere cognition of a doubtful form such as "Śābaleya," how can there be a conceptualization of a universal?
Is this a Śābaleya, or a Bāhuleya? Only a mere clamor is heard.

However, since we do not ascertain specific particulars such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), people merely perceive conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the form of the brindled cow and so forth; in this same way, other conceptualizations of universals (*sāmānya*) are also to be understood.
Or alternatively:

Because cognition of a universal form arises from attachment to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is thus comparable to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no postulation of a real entity that serves as the basis for similarity.

Therefore, linguistic usage consisting of affirmation and negation does not have an external object as its support, because [otherwise] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth would be impossible;
rather, it is only the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves that are apprehended by words and conceptual constructions.

But through the definition by implication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*), there is the cognition of that which possesses those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). If, then, the various adjuncts constitute the probans (*liṅga*), once the substance has been ascertained by that probans, there can be no doubt; so what is the use of communicating further adjuncts?
It is not that the substance is not known, but rather that it is not known *of what kind* it is; for that purpose, further adjuncts are set forth.
That is incorrect:

if that object is perceived in its own essential nature by means of one limiting adjunct (upādhi), what further effect will the cognition of another limiting adjunct produce? (533) On the other hand, if it is perceived otherwise when in conjunction with one limiting adjunct, the association with another limiting adjunct is incapable of producing anything further. (534)
Furthermore, if it were the case that only the mere conjunction with another [object] is what is conveyed by another word, and not its specific distinction,
then how could there be the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) when it is conveyed in isolation?
Indeed, it cannot be established by the mere adjunct of purposeful action alone.
Now, if it is argued that there is cognition of the substrate through that [quality],
it is not so,
because it has already been established by means of the previous quality itself.
Now, as for the demonstration that [the self] is devoid of any other limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) than its previously mentioned one, it has been stated by [the author] himself:
"It cannot be [established] by anyone else.
But surely, if it were made otherwise by another limiting adjunct, it would be established by a cognition that functions as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
How could it be established otherwise even by thousands of other conditions (*upādhi*)?
For that which has been established by one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be established otherwise by another means of valid cognition.
Since [the entity] exists as inseparable from all its conditions due to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), how could it be cognized otherwise?
Or, if it were established [as such], that very nature of it would be [its own]; how could it be otherwise defined by another?

Furthermore, there is no definition as something else by another; rather, it is merely a superimposition from elsewhere. However, the exclusion of that other is impossible by necessity, for it cannot be both endowed with those properties and endowed with properties other than them.

That [non-existence] is false, because if the attainment of other animals has been established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it cannot be overturned even by a thousand superimpositions (adhyāropa). On the other hand, if there is no attainment of others, since the meaning of that [word] itself is established by valid cognition, what is there to be removed here by another qualification (upādhi)? Indeed, nothing at all.
Therefore, by means of non-erroneous cognition, everything that is to be cognized is [established] just like the object of the means of valid perception; hence,
the presentation of it as having external adjuncts is useless.

If, however, the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are distinct and the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*) is likewise distinct, then by the mere indication of the adjuncts— through indirect indication (*alakṣitalakṣaṇā*)— there would be no synthesis within a single substratum (*dharmin*).
On the other hand, if even when the adjuncts are indicated, the possessors of the adjuncts are [indicated] in that same way,
then since there is a cognition through a single adjunct, there would be a grasping of all adjuncts.
For it is not the case that there is no such apprehension by means of perception.
Now, even by perception, sometimes only the configuration is grasped from a distance, whereas when in close proximity, the color is directly perceived in the object nearby.
2B. Furthermore, that [position] is also untenable:
if there were a perception of color and shape alone without a substance, then a substance would never be perceived; thus, it would follow that it is not a real entity at all. (537)
Now, it is not possible to apprehend a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is not a substance; nor is color (*varṇa*) non-substantial. Therefore, how could there be anything further that is a substance?
If you ask, "In that case, how is there co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even for you [the Buddhists]? [we reply:]...
Thus it is said:

"With reference to a single subject (dharmin) which is the locus of various properties, when one [property] is affirmed, the others appear as if they possess that [affirmed property], yet remain indifferent [to its negation]. (232)
Just as the intellect, when performing a negation, constructs a conventional usage that is devoid of reality— being distinct from that [negated object] and dependent upon other things—
even so do those who have reached [the truth], having abandoned conceptualization, rely upon the distinction between objects.
They do not invalidate the worldly object arising from beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā).

Indeed, for us, this conventional usage— which concerns grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like— does not refer to ultimate reality, because it proceeds by relying on the meaning of words that are established as non-entities.
For instance,
the establishment of the referent of the word "sound" as a subject (*dharmin*) occurs in dependence upon the exclusion of non-sound (*aśabdavyāvṛtti*);
and that sound is accepted as being eternally stable on the strength of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
And since it is not excluded from the state of being produced,

even though impermanence appears [in the cognition], it is— as if unperceived— established as if non-existent because it removes erroneous conventional usage. Therefore, when another conventional usage is set in motion by the means of valid cognition that establishes impermanence, it is understood that it has been established and ordained as existent at that time, because it removes the object of erroneous conventional usage.
Consequently, that subject (*dharmin*) which consists of both word and its object is apprehended as having a nature that possesses those [properties];
and when [the property] is negated, it is removed from there. Then, through the cognition of it as being distinct from that, it is perceived in relation to properties contrary to it;
thus, cognitions themselves possess both affirmation and negation, yet it is not the case that an entity moves away from its established form in such a manner.
For it is thus:
"In this very way I practiced in the past"—it is that very practice which, being directly perceived as such, has been brought within the scope of conventional discourse;
however, therein nothing whatsoever has been established or negated by successive conceptual constructions.
3B. By way of indifference [to other objects], the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Indeed, conceptual constructions do not touch upon the form of a past cognition, because that [past cognition] does not exist at that time.

For this very reason, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the object of words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), because it merely excludes error. When, however, there is no occurrence of error—

as when a conceptual construction such as "this is a jar" arises immediately after perception, or when the cognition of fire arises from smoke without any intervening cause— [how can apoha be the object]?
In that regard, how is it that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? This [position] is not at all sound; for instance:
Fire, which was previously an object of non-activity, has been made an object of activity; thus, even in that case, the state of being an object of non-activity is removed. (539)
There is no turning back,
for it is thus.
The ascertainment of fire says: "This fire is the object of my activity; why this indifference on your part?
Thus, the function of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists merely in the removal of the state of indifference regarding that object;
for in that case, the fire is not perceived in its own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*), nor is there any perception of it otherwise than as an object of cognition.

There is no apprehension [of the object] by means of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the thing that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because blue is not the referent of a word; for there is no presence of prior and posterior forms [in such a construction].
Indeed, the thought "this is that" is not a conceptual construction at all, because it is mental direct perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) is not apprehended by it, then it is not direct perception.
It has been explained, and will be further explained, that the apprehension of presentness itself is not the apprehension of momentariness;

therefore, linguistic conventions such as the relation of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are based upon the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

For when there is a distinction in meaning within the domain of linguistic usage, everything is logically consistent, because that [meaning] itself is excluded from everything else. Indeed, exclusion is not something other than that; otherwise, the synthesis of a single object would be impossible.
How then is it that the word is impermanent? The case-ending is based on this distinction.
Regarding the expression "the body of a stone statue," since exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are indeed non-different, how can there be a distinction?
For it is not the case that the exclusions of a real entity are themselves distinct.

This is not a fault, for their differentiation exists conventionally; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not exist. Therefore, the basis for the forms of difference and non-difference regarding the meaning of words is [conventional];
with respect to the ultimate, there is never any differentiation.
Conventionally, however, they possess both natures; for thus,
from this or that [cause], an object that is both its own effect and not its own effect is distinguished as one.
As if their accumulations and depletions had been carried away by various disturbances,
even one who does not possess those [qualities] is brought [into view] through some connection by those who rely on different perspectives; therefore, they too have not recognized the deception.
Now, if this worldly convention exists only conventionally and is based solely upon latent predispositions (*vāsanā*),
why is it not considered non-contradictory by worldly people and not abandoned through conceptualization?
Indeed, no one abandons a convention that is non-contradictory.
This has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "that very thing, without conceptualizing it as such," but how is this so?
Indeed, even one who is utterly deluded does not remain without considering the sublation by valid cognition;
to this it is replied:
[there is] non-conceptualization because of non-contradiction.
For when non-contradiction is established, it is not appropriate for a person engaged in practical activity to scrutinize subtle internal distinctions;
indeed, one who seeks non-contradiction is capable of conceptualizing only for the sake of attaining it.

Where, then, would his concern with the contradiction regarding difference or non-difference be of use? Functional efficacy does not arise from sweetness that is distinct [from the substance]; [otherwise] it would not come from molasses. (541)
The accomplishment of purposeful action (arthakriyā) occurs merely through the exclusion of what is not that [the thing itself].

However, the differentiation of properties (dharmabheda), which is constructed by the forms of cognition based on the limits of its own effects and their opposites, arises from beginningless latent predispositions (vāsanā);
it is non-erroneous because it is connected to a real entity.

In that regard, when examining the distinction between appearances, a person who has attained satisfaction born from obtaining a desired result does not concern himself with the investigation of the reality of the thing;
even one intent on investigating the true nature of things, seeking its causal efficiency, follows only worldly convention. That is the thing (*vastu*).
5 B. One intent on trade;
and thus it has been said:

Abandoning [the distinction between] form and linguistic convention while remaining on the worldly path, both the ignorant and the wise are alike regarding cognition and verbal expression. Therefore, that subject (*dharmin*)— through the disturbances characterized by conceptual construction, which are based on the differentiation of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)— is led toward perception from some connection with linguistic usage, as if by accumulations and aggregations.
The "path of perception" is characterized by attainment, [defined] by the marks of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*);
therefore, those conventional practitioners have fully understood the nature of error.
Consequently, the exclusion [of the reason] from non-existent counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), or its presence in similar examples (*sapakṣa*), is not contradictory.
1B. Refutation of the permanence of the self through the lack of full comprehension— furthermore:
When the selflessness of jars and so forth is established, the pervasion [of breath and other functions] by their absence is proven, but not otherwise.
Nor is it established that the self does not exist in jars and so forth;
because the application of a proof for existence would be doubtful, it cannot be non-existent.
Furthermore, non-existence [of the self] is not tenable because it has been accepted [as a premise] without valid means of cognition (apramāṇa).
For how can the self, which is doubtful in the living body, be free from doubt in a jar or similar object?
Indeed, that which is doubtful cannot be made an object of proof by means of breath and so forth, or by any other [reason].

And therefore, even if there is no exclusion from the non-existent, the exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa) is doubtful; because of that doubt, the exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is also doubtful. || 238 ||
If there is doubt regarding the self, then only jars and the like could be the similar instances (sapakṣas);
consequently, the exclusion from those similar instances would be doubtful. Therefore, how can this be a negative-only (vyatirekin) inference?
[Objection: But surely, according to the Buddhist admission, jars and other things are indeed devoid of self.

If that is so, then since all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self, there would be no self even in the living body. [Response: If you say that the Buddhist admission is simply without proof, [we reply: it is not so.
In that case, then, since jars and other things are also accepted as having that [nature], they would not be soulless; thus, the same fault remains,
because of that very acceptance.
When one restriction is established, the exclusion is indeed established; [the other] is established— [so says] He.
Even when two categories have been observed, there may still be doubt regarding those that have not been observed.
(239) Even though there is non-observation, there is indeed doubt concerning those things that have not been observed and which do not meet the conditions for perceptibility;
for no one is capable of establishing non-existence based on mere non-perception alone.
Moreover,
although the absence of a self in jars and the like is established, even so, breath and the other [reasons] are not capable of proving a self;
for it is not established that they are excluded from the heterologue (vipakṣa), since their presence there is also possible.
But surely, how can that which is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa) reside in that very same place?
For it is not logical that one thing could be both selfless and possess vital breaths (prāṇa), etc., and otherwise;
for this "half-old-woman" approach (ardhajaratiya) is not permissible, as a restriction to a single state is alone logical.
This is not so,
because there are objects that, though not pervading every individual instance, belong to that same class.
In some cases, no certainty is observed through perception, as with iron being scratched by a stone;
when there is no observation of a contradiction in existence, who could dispel doubt?
One should not [object] that "selflessness" (*nairātmya*) is entirely the same [in both cases], such that by virtue of being selfless, the living body would be devoid of breath and so forth; rather,
some things are indeed selfless while others possess breath and so forth, otherwise.
Just as one piece of earth is scratched by another piece of iron,
so too,
when no contradiction is observed between two entities, who could dispel doubt?

1. One might object: "Indeed, if the contradiction between selflessness (*nairātmya*) and [the presence of] vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is not established, then there can be no exclusion of selflessness by means of the absence of vital breath and so forth.
For selflessness is not contradicted by the non-coexistence with vital breath and so forth, nor by any other characteristic of contradiction, such that one could exclude it."
Now, [it might be argued that] even if there is no direct contradiction, there is a contradiction through a mediated succession; thus, sounds and so forth are the subverters of selflessness.
That is incorrect, because [the negation occurs] due to a restriction in some cases, and what else could that be? It is the nature of being the effect of that [self]. (241)
If breath and the other [vital functions] were restricted to the self,
there would be an indirect contradiction with the absence of self (nairātmya), because a pervaded [property] is contradicted by the contradiction of its pervader; however,
there is no such restriction of breath and the others to the self, since restriction is impossible without either identity (tādātmya) or origination from it (tadutpatti).
Otherwise, a restrictive rule would be impossible;
furthermore, it is not established by means of valid cognition that breath and so forth are effects of the self or have the nature of the self.
Therefore, even from the standpoint of selflessness (*nairātmya*), the exclusion of this [breath] remains doubtful.
Therefore, even from the absence of self,
because there is no necessary connection with the self, its exclusion remains doubtful.
For that which is not connected [to the property] does not exclude its opposite;
even if that were granted, the self is nonetheless not established through selflessness.
For this reason, one does not accept the non-existence of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) as being a positive entity.
Just as, even in the absence of non-difference, the vital functions such as breathing do not [belong] to the similar instance (sapakṣa).
243.2 B. *prāṇanādikaḥ*; *prāṇādir na sapakṣataḥ*—He.

If a reason lacks exclusion from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), then it is a reason that possesses positive concomitance (*anvayin*); if it lacks positive concomitance, then [the thesis] "that which is not selfless is not possessed of a self" [cannot be established]. (244)
It is not subject to positive concomitance (anvayin): just as there is no presence [of the probans] in the similar instance (sapakṣa) even when the absence of the similar instance does not exist,
so too, even in the absence of selflessness (nairātmya), there is no self in the living body.
Is this not an improper objection?
For even in the case of a similar instance (sapakṣa), there is no presence [of the reason] despite the absence of its exclusion, because that [reason] does not exist there.
For there is no occurrence of existence when [the cause] is absent; however,
since that [breath] exists in a living body, and because there is no absence [of the cause], existence is necessarily [restricted] to the other category due to the absence of anything else.
This is true;
the desired conclusion is not established merely by the presentation of an incongruous example,
provided that there is no absence [of the reason] in the similar class (sapakṣa).
If it is argued: "In that case, the entity itself has not ceased;
rather, when non-existence has ceased, the entity necessarily exists as the very exclusion of non-existence, and thus there is no such fault because there is no similar instance (sapakṣa)."
It is not [the case that it is] due to the impossibility of its being a non-entity;
for if there is the existence of breath and so forth, how could there be the absence of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)?

For just as there is no reversal [of the reason] even when there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) despite the absence of breath and so forth, so too in the case of a living body, there would be no reversal even in the absence of selflessness. Now, if it is argued that there is a reversal because the living body exists, [we reply: no, because it is not present in the similar instance;
for the occurrence of an entity is impossible where it does not exist.
In that case, it follows that non-existence itself has not ceased;
for there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence, so while that [existence] has been excluded, there is no contradiction with non-existence,
and thus that [non-existence] remains unexcluded.
Just as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is non-existent, so too in that case there is no contradiction in its non-existence;
for even that non-existence does not exist therein.

If that were the case, one might argue: "Even though the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is present in a living body, there is no actual exclusion of selflessness [from the subject], just as in a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), even if there is both presence and absence, there is no non-existence because that [subject] exists."
This is not so, because how indeed could one who is errant with respect to another being be restrained? Otherwise, how could he be errant due to his own fault rather than that of another? (544)
For how could that which is itself inconstant be otherwise inconstant or constant with respect to another entity?
Furthermore,
if something does not exist when [the cause] exists, it is neither existent nor non-existent as something existing.
Why is it not accepted that even what is non-existent is "non-existent" by virtue of being associated with what is existent?
Just as the non-existent lacks the status of a substratum, so too does it lack the status of a superstratum; this is a trivial point, and it has already been refuted previously.
Moreover,
selflessness (nairātmya) is not merely non-existence, but rather the absence of a self possessing a specific, determinate form;
and the absence of such a self cannot be established simply by the non-perception of a determinate form.
Indeed, absences do not differ from one another, because when there is a difference between entities, there is a corresponding difference between their absences;
and if there were no specific determination of entities, how could there be a difference between their absences?
Furthermore, the self is not perceived as having a determinate nature such that its existence could be established by the absence of its opposite;
therefore, in the absence of selflessness, there would merely be the cessation of non-existence, but no establishment of a self. Thus:

If a reason is non-deviant from the similar class (sapakṣa), then that reason is positive (anvayin); if it is not positive, then it is non-deviant [only] if it is like "that which lacks self is not possessed of a self" (545).
Furthermore,
that whose own nature is established as being invariably concomitant with its own activity is also included.
Therefore, that very [nature] is the cause of cessation; and it is the same which, in the case of positive occurrences, is the cause of their engagement.
That smoke whose nature is invariably concomitant with fire is established as the cause for engaging in positive activities;
that same [smoke], when it itself ceases, is the cause for the cessation of the fire.
Furthermore, it is the established view of those who follow valid means of knowledge that fire alone is the cause of the occurrence of smoke and the like, and not anything else;
and that invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) depends upon a proof.

1B. Perception and non-perception require a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes invariable concomitance (*vyākhyānāntarīyakatva*), for these two constitute the nature of cause and effect.

Indeed, perception and non-perception, which establish invariable concomitance, do not become established as the means of proving positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) without [the aforementioned] means of valid cognition.
But surely, the proof of the necessary concomitance of the causal relation between two distinct things is not [established by] seeing and non-seeing;
for it is those very acts of seeing and non-seeing that constitute the causal relation.
For there is no causal relationship other than through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),
nor are there any positive and negative concomitances other than through perception and non-perception;
however, for one who [holds otherwise]...
The non-occurrence of another entity when that [other] exists is not necessarily understood;
it is not a means of proving another entity because there is no necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*).

Even if that [entity] exists, there is no rule that another must be absent; thus, the absence of the latter when the former is absent is not understood, because the former lacks the status of being a pervader (*vyāpakatā*).
Furthermore, that which is non-pervasive cannot, when it ceases, cause another to cease;
nor is the self established as pervasive. Therefore, how could it be the cause of the cessation of breath and so forth?
For this reason:
2B. There is a rule regarding the existence [of these], because their non-existence is impossible; for if they were absent, those things which exist eternally would not exist.
Indeed, the self does not itself cease from its presence in space and time, because of the actual existence of its pervasion by eternity.
Therefore, because of the absence of that [Self], the non-existence of breath and so forth is unestablished.
(5) Due to the diversity of the power of the causal complex (*hetu-sāmagrī*), there is a manifold nature;
for the Self is the cause of breath and so forth by mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, as it does not depend upon negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
That all causal relations everywhere [are identical] is also untenable,
because effects arise from causes with distinct natures.
How could that which arises from them have the nature of being produced by them if it were to arise from something else in their absence?
(249) If the causal relationship were established by mere positive concomitance alone, then it would follow that it exists even in their absence;
consequently, how could that which arises from something else while they are absent possess the nature of being produced by them?
If it is argued that it may arise from something else, we say no;
for there is no such form in anything else.
If it were not of that nature, it would simply not exist;
for it is through the diversity of the potencies of their causal complexes that things possess their manifold forms.
1b. If that [difference] is not the differentiator, then this world would have attained a single uniform nature. 248.
But surely, difference arises from a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*); how can this be so?
That a distinction is indeed perceived,
whether it arises from a difference in causes or otherwise, is merely another point of inquiry; that [objection] is untenable.

Since the self is postulated as being unperceived due to the obstruction of the vital breaths and so forth, how could there not be such an obstruction for it even in the absence of a restrictive rule?
Just as the self is all-pervading, eternal, and a cause by mere presence, so too are space and the other elements.

Therefore, since the movement of space and so forth is like that of the self, the [intended] object is not established. Now, if the vital breaths and so forth do not exist without a self as their impeller, then the self is inferred to be like one who inflates a bellows,
or like one who moves the eyeball by means of the sense organs, or like a spectator looking through a window by means of vision.
That too is incorrect,
because it is not supported by any means of valid cognition that an omnipresent being devoid of action can be a motivator.
Since perception does not occur without the instruments [of cognition], the Self is not established [as a separate entity].
|| 547 || The Fourteenth Daily Lesson is completed.
For the one who inflates a bellows is an agent and an impeller; likewise, [the self] would not be so because it is non-pervasive. But how could such a self be an impeller?
Indeed, for that which is of a pervasive form, the status of being an impeller is not logically tenable.
Now, if there is an impeller for that [body], there would be another impeller for him as well, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, a person who is situated behind a window and endowed with the instruments such as the eyes is not of this nature [i.e., not self-luminous]; how then could he be a spectator?
Or, if one were to say that he too possesses instruments...
In that case as well, there would be the "logic of being separated by a window," resulting in an infinite regress.
Furthermore, the causal relationship between fire and so forth is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); how could that be otherwise?
Now, if it were the case that [fire] arises there too from mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, it would follow that it could arise from something else even without those [causes].
Otherwise, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would also be possible;
and if that were so, how could that which arises from something else—such as the head of Indra—even in the absence of those [causes], be considered produced by fire?
If it were produced by both, then since it does not arise from anything other than those two, neither of them would be the cause.
Therefore, even if it were to arise from something else, it would neither be its effect nor the effect of anything else; thus, there would be no causal relationship at all.

This being the case, since the difference or non-difference of effects depends upon the difference or non-difference of causes, those two [difference and non-difference] would not exist due to the absence of that [causal relationship].
If it is asked, "How can this [position] be rejected when it is observed [to be so]?"
Nor is it impossible for perception itself, even though the relation of cause and effect is impossible [in that case].
It is certainly not impossible.

For blue would indeed be seen [as distinct] from the cognition of blue only when there is a restriction of its apprehension; otherwise, it is not apprehended at all, and there can be no distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous. (548)

If there were a fixed rule that such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces only erroneous or non-erroneous cognitions, then there would be a definite restriction regarding the objects of cognition (*prameya*).

Otherwise, if it were merely a random appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), it would follow that all worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed. Alternatively, if the appearance itself is inherently distinct from others and is the object of cognition for a reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyaya*), [then the restriction holds].
That too is untrue;
for the worldly convention of people is not established by mere appearance alone.
When there is a manifestation, what more remains to be done than the appearance of that very [manifestation] itself?
For the practice of discerning people is such that an entity capable of performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*) is to be accepted, while any other is not.
That which appears as mere manifestation becomes, at that very moment, neither to be abandoned nor to be accepted;

thus it is mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*) and non-dual. Therefore, there is neither difference nor non-difference, and that relationship of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Since the self is not the cause of anything, there can be no inference of it from anything whatsoever. 4 B.

For the manifold nature of entities arises from the diversity in the power of causal complexes directed toward action; if that [power] were non-differentiating, this world would necessarily be of a single form—
just as "non-duality" is understood as being of a single form, wherein nothing is to be rejected or accepted and which is mere appearance.
Now, it may be argued that since the fire-nature of Indra’s head exists as well as something distinct from it,
the effect (smoke) will arise from that [distinct thing] as well.
To this, he says:
If there were both differentiation and non-differentiation, the state of having an undivided nature would be contradicted.
It would be...
If a single entity were to possess multiple forms, there would be two distinct forms: fire and that which is other than it;
for the distinction between entities is characterized by a difference in their form.
Therefore, fire alone is the producer of smoke, and thus there is no deviation in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
For there is no other "Indra's head" apart from its nature as fire;
rather, that form by which it would be distinct is precisely its non-producer. How, then, can there be any suspicion of deviation?
If that non-producing nature of one thing were indeed the very same as that of the other, then it would be identical.
Its non-arising is not its nature; how then could that [non-arising] be possible for it?
Therefore, the natures of cause and effect are mutually determined.
Consequently, just as when one sees the cause itself, the effect is also understood when it is seen.
Now, how can one [effect] arise from many, as in the case of the moisture resulting from milk and water?
For the power of liquidity, from which that moisture arises, is indeed one and the same in both. (253)
Is its nature both different and non-different? And if it were different, how could there be fluidity?
Or if it were different—[the variant reading is] "how could the deity [be] not different?"
For it is said that there is no distinction [in the cognition] because that form of the cognition is undifferentiated.

Indeed, milk and water do not possess an identical nature due to their exclusion from other hard forms; thus, their unity arises from oneness through such exclusion. Likewise, it is the same for the effect, namely, the state of being moistened.
For even moisture is not ultimately distinct [from fire];

rather, it is designated as such through the exclusion of other things (tadanyavyāvṛtti), so there is no deviation. Likewise, even though there is difference, fire is the basis for the cognition "fire."
In whatever part it possesses smoke, by that very part there is such a movement.
(255) By that part— O friend— from its arising as a constituent of the cognition of fire, while depending on something else.
Smoke is non-deviant from that; likewise, the other [effect] is established as such.
255.3 T. siddhaṃ—he॰, ca.

In the same way, just as in the case of milk and water, although there is a distinction due to their exclusion from other things, they serve as the basis for the cognition of "substance"; so too, although there is a distinction, it serves as the basis for the cognition of "fire" precisely through its exclusion from other things.
By that very aspect—namely, by being the cause of the cognition of fire—it is apprehended.
Except in cases of a material deviation, smoke does not arise without being a constituent part of the cognition of fire; therefore, there is no deviation from that [rule].
For it is thus:
Because fire exists in a state that is a modification of smoke and fuel,
it has its locus therein.
If there is smoke without fire, it is not true smoke; if there is smoke, it must possess fire.
Smoke is a transformation of fuel, and fire is merely a constituent part of those two; there is no fire other than that.
Therefore, if that [object] characterized by heat and so forth were the head of Indra or the like, then it would not be smoke, but rather mere chaff and such.
Why is this so? For that which is unobserved cannot be subject to a restrictive rule such that "it does not occur otherwise.
In that case, why is it that even a blue object does not occur otherwise at another time?
Why is this so?
If it is argued that, such being the case, it would not be blue at all,
this is the same as saying it would not be smoke at all.
"Why is this so?"—this [objection] is the same in other cases as well.

[One might argue: "Is it not the case that blue and so forth are defined by their own nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), and that smoke and so forth are defined by their being produced (*janya-lakṣaṇa*)? Since even in those cases their own nature is indeed the definition, these two are not the same."
It is so; regarding this, it is said:
The status of a thing as a real entity does not arise merely from the appearance of its own nature;
for the manifestation of a nature is the same for those with erroneous cognition and those with non-erroneous cognition.
(551) Indeed, the mere manifestation of blue, yellow, and so forth, as a simple nature, is identical for both erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions; thus, a real entity is not established.
The distinction [between these types of reasons], however, is produced by the relationship of cause and effect; but enough of this digression.
If it is asked, "How is there an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) for the essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)?", it is said in response:

The state of being inseparable (nāntarīyakatā) should be understood according to its respective cause, as was previously stated regarding destruction and the quality of being produced (kṛtakatva). Since it has already been established that destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere fact of being an entity (vastumātra), there is no need to repeat what has already been chewed over.

Therefore, the causal relationship is characterized solely by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); it does not exist between the self (*ātman*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and thus [the latter] are not indicators [of the former].
This entire intention is also that of the Teacher (*ācārya*). If one asks, "How is this known?"...
This entire method regarding the nature of being causeless is to be inferred for all negative-only (vyatirekin) reasons, so that the statement of "audibility" may be seen as analogous.

For the purpose of explaining the similarity of all examples of negative-only reasons, the Teacher demonstrated that audibility is inconclusive; thus, it should be understood that this entire method was intended by the Teacher as well.

Thus, it has been established that the purely negative (vyatirekin) is not a valid reason, because every purely negative reason is dissimilar to the property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), and because that [property] is inconclusive due to its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). To explain:

Exclusion from both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not real; it is called "exclusion" merely on the basis of the possibility of its non-perception. (552) Apart from the two groups—those that are eternal and those that are non-eternal, and those that are selfless and those that possess a self—there is no other category, because the contradiction consisting in mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence is real; otherwise, the world would be devoid of conventional discourse and would become incoherent.
And if there were nothing that could not belong to either category,
such that audibility were excluded from both the eternal and the non-eternal, then it would indeed not exist at all because it would lack a locus (*anadhikaraṇatvāt*).
If it is argued that sound itself is the locus:
The same fault does not apply to "sound-ness" (śabdatva) either;
for that too would certainly not exist, since it is excluded from everything else.
For instance:

"If there is doubt regarding whether sound—which is itself inexpressible—is eternal or non-eternal, then how can there be a justification for a reason when that [sound] is devoid of both [properties], given that this doubt concerns those two? (553)
For it is not the case that doubt regarding those two [permanence and impermanence] can arise for one who has ascertained [the object] as being excluded from them;
therefore, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is not a cause of doubt, since the doubt arises solely on account of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*).
But [one might ask]: if there is doubt because of "sound-ness," why should another factor also not possess the status of being a cause of doubt?
Now, it is argued that whatever has been observed in one place, when observed elsewhere, may give rise to suspicion;
and this very capacity is said to be the cause of doubt.
Why, then, is audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) not a cause of doubt?

This is not so, because when a positive injunction is observed, there is doubt regarding what is prohibited; yet, when there is doubt between existence and non-existence, who would embrace their own position? (554)

For where there is doubt regarding a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, that [doubt] occurs by way of perception through a positive formulation; but in the case of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), it occurs by way of negation. What, then, is the difference between these two? [Objection: But surely, since audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is not observed in either the eternal or the non-eternal, it is only logical that it is a cause for non-comprehension of those two.
This is not correct, because only the face of non-apprehension has been perceived. Thus:

When the exclusion of one [property] occurs by necessity from its counter-positive, then indeed there is no exclusion of both, because their coexistence is impossible due to mutual contradiction. (555) Since it is not possible for two mutually contradictory properties to be excluded [from a single locus] in an absolute sense, neutrality cannot be attained here.
But surely, doubt arises precisely because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both being in one place; it is not caused by the reason of "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*).

If, at best, that [non-hearing] is merely the non-apprehension of the reason, then in the case of the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) as well, doubt arises solely from the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) and is not produced by a specific cause;

for even that [inconclusive reason] is a cause of doubt by way of its being observed, while "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) is likewise a cause of doubt by way of its not being observed— this is the same for both.
Furthermore, if doubt exists, it cannot be removed by that very [reason]; therefore, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is likewise stated as a cause of doubt—this is trivial. Moreover:

The state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is observed in both [the existent and the non-existent]; why does it not produce certainty regarding both? For if there were a positive injunction (*vidhāna*) upon the conjunction of seeing both, then it would apply to both as well.
Indeed, that which is observed in a certain place should effect only its own affirmation; how could there be a reliance on a second part, namely "it does not exist"?
Now, it is not logical for two mutually contradictory things to exist in one and the same place;
therefore, the doubt resides in the subject itself and is not mediated by the observation [of the reason].

Even when there is an observation, the doubt is mediated solely by the doubt regarding the subject; that [doubt] remains the same even when [the reason] is not observed in either of the two [similar or dissimilar instances].
But surely, doubt is produced by exclusion from one alternative; for since there is certainty through the exclusion from both [alternatives],
that which is excluded from two groups— between which no third possibility exists— is the cause of non-comprehension in that very form.
And likewise, this very [reason] was stated by the Teacher as a negative-only (vyatirekin) one;
for he said:

"That uncommon probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) which encompasses all [instances] through whatever distinction [is necessary] is a cause of doubt, because it is associated with that [property] and because it is excluded from those [instances] exclusively. How then can this be a cause of doubt solely due to its exclusion?
This is not so. It has been done.

This has already been stated: since the ascertainment of a thing arises from its exclusion from two [categories], there would be an ascertainment of its non-existence elsewhere in both cases as well. Furthermore, how could that which effects the exclusion be a cause of doubt regarding that very same thing? For the exclusion of those two is not established by anything other than that [exclusion].
For how could that which is excluded from something else not be a means of establishing its exclusion?
If it is argued that it is not a cause for cognition precisely because it establishes the exclusion of both,
this is not the case.

Since the causality of every reason lies in the establishment of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), it is established that exclusion is what is proven by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*). (559) It is true that a reason is indeed a prover of the exclusion of others; however, it does so by way of implying the affirmation of something other than that [exclusion].
But here, nothing else is implied, because both [terms] are excluded; however,
it is true that through the exclusion of permanence by means of being produced, impermanence is implied.

No impermanence other than the constant exclusion [of permanence] is established; for the purpose of inference is fulfilled by that very exclusion of the other. Therefore, inference has its purpose accomplished merely by the exclusion of the superimposition of permanence upon the impermanent.

If it is argued that because the exclusion of one between the two alternatives— permanence and impermanence— necessarily establishes the other by its own nature, that [object] will therefore never fail to exist, we say: no.
If it is asked: "Since that [non-existence] is established through direct perception, how can it be [an example of] the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)?"

Let this matter rest for now; however, if both [the object and its cognition] are excluded by the fact of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*), then the establishment of their otherwise-ness would be proven by perception (*pratyakṣa*), and thus it would be the very reason (*hetu*).
If you argue that it is not the reason because it is established by another reason that proves only one of those two, [we reply:]...
When something is established by direct perception, how could one thing [be established] by another?
Is perception a negator of the reason or an affirmer?
If perception does not perform negation,
then the affirmation or negation of another [property] by means of another cannot occur through the property of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*).
If two [alternatives] are excluded, how can there be an affirmation by another?

Otherwise, if there were an affirmation by yet another in that case as well, how could even that other have the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Thus, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases; moreover, perception is not non-excluding.
For if that were the case, even an injunction would not exist;
an injunction is the presentation of a thing, and a thing is not presented without the negation of what is other than it.
This is because:

That object would either be unmixed with anything else, or it would be mixed with another; for if it were mixed with another, it would not be that [specific] object from the perspective of conventional usage. Or else, even through another [means], there would be no possibility of negation. Herein, this is investigated: *anyāsaṃsargi tadvastu bhavedvānyena miśritaṃ | anyena miśraṇe vastu na syādavyavahārataḥ || 561 tathā vā na niṣedhasya parasmādapi sambhavaḥ || 562* In this regard, it is examined: That object would either be unmixed with anything else, or it would be mixed with another; for if it were mixed with another, it would not be that [specific] object from the perspective of conventional usage. Whether an entity is by its own nature excluded from others or not excluded,
and whether it is so apprehended by perception or not—
if it is apprehended, how can there be a negation of another?
For that very thing is the negation of another in that context: namely, its appearing as having a different form through the exclusion [of the other];
otherwise, because cognition would be confused, there would be no practical activity, and thus valid cognition would be fruitless.
Now, the practical activity of negating one thing by means of another valid cognition [is established].
That too is incorrect, because:

"If there were a sublation by another [means of knowledge] of that which is perceived through direct perception, then, given the invalidity of direct perception, the other [means of knowledge] would also be invalid. (563)
If perception were not a valid means of knowledge, what confidence could there be in anything else?
Moreover, if the mixing with another object is indeed caused by the other [cognition], then it cannot be negated even by a hundred other means of valid cognition.
For it is not possible to alter the intrinsic nature [of a thing];
if the negation is that "it is unmixed with some form," then by whatever form there is mixing, it must have been apprehended by perception in that very form as well.
If there is apprehension in various ways [of what is not that], how can there be the exclusion of the object?

[If it is argued: "When another person perceives it, the exclusion is understood," [we reply: it has been established that if another person perceives it [in a different way], there would be a lack of confidence in all cases.
When one has just entered from a camel into another [place], such as a womb-chamber, there arises another direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); by that, the former [perception] is sublated.
For indeed, at the first entry into the womb-chamber, the initial sight is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, that [subsequent cognition] is sublated by it, but not the means of valid cognition itself.

Consequently, if the perception were to apprehend the word as excluded from both [classes], then there would be no doubt regarding the other [class], nor otherwise; likewise, there would be no doubt regarding its audibility.
Therefore, because audibility is not excluded [from either class], doubt arises.
Thus, every negative inference (*vyatirekin*) has been established by the Teacher as being based merely on non-perception;
how then is there the statement, "because of absolute exclusion" (*ekāntavyāvṛtteḥ*)?
The meaning of "because of the exclusion of certainty" (*naikāntena niścaye vyāvṛtteḥ*) is not "because of the exclusion of absolute certainty" (*ekāntasya niścayasya vyāvṛtteḥ*);
for there is no certainty regarding this [object] as being either eternal or non-eternal, whether through its presence or its absence.
Therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is indeed no exclusion; hence, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
Thus, it has been explained that there is a distinction based on dispute;
now, the universal (sāmānya) is being explained:
just as that which is exclusively excluded (vyāvṛtta) is a probans through negative concomitance (vyatirekī), so too is that which is exclusively concomitant (anvayī).

For instance, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), sound is impermanent, just like a jar and so forth; since that [impermanence] is excluded from non-existent space (*ākāśa*), the reason is positive (*anvayin*). Indeed, space possesses neither existence nor non-existence, because it is non-existent.
"Therefore, a reason that possesses an invariable positive concomitance (*avyabhicāritānvaya*) is indeed a prover;
this is not so,
for even if such [a reason] is impossible in the case of the non-existence of space (*ākāśa*),"
Nevertheless, its status as an object of cognition does not cease in any way whatsoever.

Even for non-existent things, there is indeed some manner of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*); otherwise, there could be no linguistic or practical activity (*vyavahāra*) through affirmation and negation,
for existence alone cannot be the basis for such activity.
For the natures of entities are established as mutually exclusive within the domain of conventional discourse; otherwise, they would lack causal efficiency and thus become non-entities.

Furthermore, if there were no distinction between self and other for those seeking causal efficiency, who would engage in activity, where, or for what purpose? Consequently, everything would be utterly non-existent.
Indeed, one who perceives the non-existence of the opponent's position is unable to establish his own position;
furthermore, that [space] must necessarily be cognized as the mere absence of obstructive objects, otherwise it would follow that one could not even move from one place to another.
Therefore, by one who establishes existent objects according to their specific determinations, non-existence itself is established as an object of cognition (*prameya*).
That which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*);
for a means of valid cognition does not have the real entity (*vastu*) alone as its object, since the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition is the act of determination (*pariccheda*).

If it is argued that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is only that which performs the function of delimitation, provided it is not sublated by another [cognition] regarding its own object, then— because non-existence is delimited by a cognition that establishes non-contradiction with worldly practice (*vyavahārāvisaṃvāda*)— non-existence is indeed an object of cognition (*prameya*). Thus, [the reason] "because it is an object of cognition" does not lack an invariable concomitance (*avyabhicaritānvaya*).
Therefore, because it is common to both [the real and the unreal], it is not conclusive. Now,
if "knowability" (*prameyatā*) is said to mean simply being determined by perception,
then, in that case, knowability would consist solely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) arising from a perceptible entity.
Consequently, it follows that only the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the indicator [of existence].
And since that [capacity] is possible even for a non-entity (*avastu*) through the occurrence of exclusion (*vyatireka*), how can it be a positive reason (*anvayī hetu*)?
Furthermore, it has already been established that exclusion occurs even for what is non-existent.

By this, properties such as "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) and so forth are also explained.

Therefore, the logical reason (*hetu*) characterized by effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*) is exclusively that which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*).
[Objection: But has it not been established that non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is also a third type of logical reason?
However, [the author] establishes that negation is everywhere proven through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and so forth;
this is now a demonstration of the specific types of reasons (*hetu*) whose objects are real entities (*vastu*).

If that were the case, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of non-apprehension would have to be established; yet it has already been demonstrated that there is no mode of connection other than identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).

To this it is replied: through the absence of the cause and the pervader, the absence of the pervaded and the effect is understood; there is no other means whatsoever for establishing non-existence. (567)
For non-existence (abhāva) is indeed not some independent object of conventional discourse; rather, it is simply the absence of a specific intended entity.

And that entity, while being doubted due to its being beyond the senses, cannot be established as "non-existent" merely by the fact of its non-perception, because its non-perception does not necessarily lead to the cognition of non-existence, since it may have reached a state where it is inherently unperceivable.
In this way, however, its absence is established if its cause does not exist;
and since that very [non-perception] has been shown to be of two kinds through the relation of invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), non-perception is indeed based on an established relation.
3 B. [The probandum] is established.
Removed marker: sect; 5. Consideration of Non-apprehension (Anupalabdhicintā) 1. Non-apprehension is a distinct logical reason (hetu).
Why is an example not cited? Because it has indeed already been cited,
since the exclusion of the object is described precisely through the exclusion of the cause's own-nature.
The non-apprehension mentioned as "the example of what is established" is not separate;
indeed, the example for non-apprehension is already included [within the previous categories].
What is the reason?
By stating the exclusion of the nature of the object (the effect) and the nature [of the probandum] solely through the exclusion of the nature of the cause,
this has been made known:
for when its status as the self or as the cause is established, there is indeed negative concomitance (*vyatirekitā*).
1B. The non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), beginning with "it is established as being its own self," has also been pointed out,
because it is precisely through the non-apprehension of the cause and the intrinsic nature that an entity is negated.
And as it has been said by those who state that [the probandum] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth:
how is it established that "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) is the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)?

To this it is replied: even there, because the vital breaths and so forth do not cease from the imperceptible Puruṣa, it has been indicated that this [non-apprehension] is a cause of doubt when applied to a perceptible object. || 261 ||

An opponent has stated: "If the absence of breath and so forth in a jar and the like were due to the absence of the self, then the self would also be excluded from a living body, and consequently, breath and the other [vital signs] would also be excluded from it.
To this, the Teacher has replied:

"In a jar and the like, the existence of the self is indeed not perceived; because the self is invisible, its presence there is not established by mere non-perception, just as [the self is absent] from the body."
Therefore, it has indeed been indicated that non-apprehension is the means of cognition regarding an object that is perceptible.
Now, if exclusion is the means of proof, then every reason is merely a case of non-apprehension; how then can there be a triad of reasons?
This is not a fault.
For this reason,
negation, which does not admit any portion of a real entity, is what is established by this method (naya).

A real entity (*vastudharma*) [is established] even with respect to a real thing (*vastu*), for there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by way of affirmation through the two preceding [reasons]. Even with respect to a real thing, such as a location (*pradeśa*), an exclusion is not what is being proven; rather, a negation (*niṣedha*) is proven regarding that which does not admit the existence of a real entity.
However, by means of the two previously mentioned reasons— the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*)— through the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*),

there is indeed a distinction because of the difference in their objects; thus, even though the nature of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is the same, there is a difference in the actual entity (*vastubhāva*).

Now, one might ask: what is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature? He replies that it is identity (*tādātmya*). In this regard, existence consists in being perceived; there is nothing other than perception [for existence], for non-existence is not something different from non-perception, but rather non-perception itself.

Now, is it not the case that the non-apprehension of cognition is the absence of cognition, and the non-apprehension of existence is the absence of existence? Since the absence of existence is non-existence (*abhāva*), how can there be identity between these two?
And just as there is a difference between cognition and the object of cognition, so too must there be a difference between their respective absences.
Indeed, it is not the case that an object exists only through its cognition, for it can exist even in the absence of such cognition;
for instance, the existence of objects is apprehended through inference even when they are beyond the senses. Is the existence of fire not inferred by the sight of smoke? (568)
Furthermore, even in that case, existence is not merely the apprehension by inference,
because there is deviation from the rule regarding existence even in the absence of inference; thus,
the cessation of inference does not necessarily imply non-existence.
This is not correct, because inference also operates with respect to the past and the future;
for non-existence is not established merely by the non-perception [of something] among other things that are themselves unperceivable.

For the conventional designation of non-existence is established through the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility; moreover, their existence is not something other than their perception,
because it is a contradiction to say that something is capable of being perceived yet is not perceived.
Therefore, the perception of the existence of an object that has reached the conditions for perceptibility is itself [the proof];
for if perception is the state of being perceived, it is simply the very nature of the object.
Now, if apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is defined as the act of perceiving residing in the agent,
even then, existence characterized by such apprehension is already attained by that [agent];
and since it is non-different from that, there can be no cognition of difference, because difference is cognizable only through distinction.
Because it is non-deviant from that [object], apprehension is called "existence";
and the apprehension of entities does not arise from an apprehension at a time simultaneous with and distinct from them,
but rather solely from an apprehension characterized by being perceived as having entered into that [very object].
Therefore, he will state that existence is indeed perception, and consequently, non-existence is simply the non-perception of that;
for in the ultimate sense, there is no distinction whatsoever between various absences.
But when there is a distinction based on a difference in the qualifiers of an entity, there is a distinction such as "the absence of a cloth" or "the absence of a cart";
moreover, an entity does not attain its true nature without a qualifier.
Now, since the qualifying attribute that constitutes existence is one and the same for both existence and non-existence,
therefore even their absences are likewise one; and this remains so from the perspective of ultimate reality, even though there is a difference in the objects to be negated.
1 B ॰sthakriyo 2 B vyāptaiva 3 B ॰sya bhedaḥ
Now, if non-apprehension is indeed non-existence, then there is no disagreement at all;
this is true, because:
Thus, this single example of the "inexplicable" (anupākhya) is intended to inform those who are ignorant;

for it is meant for one who lacks thorough understanding and does not realize the non-difference between the absence of cognition and the absence of the object of cognition— this being the single [type of] non-apprehension characterized by intrinsic nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).

Or rather, for the sake of convincing that ignorant Sāṃkhya who is utterly deluded and obstinately holds the view that "everything exists everywhere," the non-perception of a single intrinsic nature is presented;
what, then, is established therein?

Because the object is absent, the subject is negated therein, just as [the term] "non-fire" is used regarding something that does not burn, even though there is doubt concerning the application of the name "knowledge.
For the existence of both knowledge and its designation depends upon the existence of the object.
And that doubt concerning those two ceases— both the cognition and the verbal expression of that doubt regarding its object necessarily cease—
because of the existence of the opposite of that object.
Just as there is no doubt regarding fire when its burning nature is absent—

since in another alternative (pakṣāntara) where burning exists, there might be doubt about fire— but when that [burning] is absent, because the opposite is present, how could such a doubt possibly arise?
Just as there is no state of non-fire other than the absence of burning, and just as there is no state of non-fire other than the absence of burning,
so too, among things that are perceptible, there is no other form of non-existence than non-perception.
The terms for that meditative absorption (dhyāna) are established because they are based upon it and exist through its presence.
Indeed, non-existence is not something other than the very nature of non-perception regarding those things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility;
therefore, when that [non-existence] is established, its identity with that [nature of non-perception] is necessarily established.
Non-existence as its very nature: Now, is it not the case that non-existence is established by non-apprehension?
How then can there be identity between the probandum and the probans?
That too is incorrect;

for it is not established here, nor does that which is unestablished attain establishment through being unestablished. There is no necessary connection (pratibandha) here, and therefore that [identity] does not exist.
As for what is said— that there must be a distinction between the probandum and the probans—
precisely that relationship of probandum and probans is not established here;
so how can such a distinction be established?

Indeed, that which is unestablished cannot be established by means of what is unestablished; as long as the relationship of probans and probandum is not established for the opponent, there is no establishment of difference.
And as long as there is no establishment of difference, there is no relationship of probans and probandum.

For the relationship of probans and probandum exists only when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); and for one who rejects identity (*tādātmya*), there is no other necessary connection between non-apprehension and absence.
Indeed, there is no causal relationship between those two;
for it is by means of absence that non-perception is produced,
since it is only when someone removes a jar or the like that non-perception occurs.

This is true: if non-existence were known by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through non-apprehension, then its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that [non-apprehension] would not be established merely through their co-occurrence; otherwise, how could the proliferation of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) be averted? Once the connection is established by a means of valid cognition, the non-apprehension functions as a means of valid cognition; once the non-apprehension is established as a means of valid cognition, the connection is established. (570)
Because they are mutually dependent, not even one of them is established; for this very reason, the effect produced by each other is not proven.
Therefore, non-existence is not established through non-perception, due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
But when there is a necessary connection based on identity (*tādātmya*), that very non-perception is the absence; thus, it is merely the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) that is being established.
For this convention—"what is not seen among the perceptible is non-existent"—is already established;
once that [convention] is established, the cognition and the verbal expression regarding its being an effect are also established without doubt. (266)
But surely, even in establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), there is no example at all;

for the entirety of conventional usage must be established by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone, and in that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the need to establish further examples.
And since conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is itself an effect of non-perception,
it is improper to establish an effect from that cause;
for causes do not necessarily possess their effects.
That is incorrect, because this conventional usage based on the perception and non-perception of what is visible is already established.

Since the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence is based solely on that [perception], it is of the very nature of non-apprehension; for this fitness is not distinct from the object itself.

Furthermore, a conscious person, necessarily prompted by the sight of that [fitness], must engage in the conventional usage of non-existence—which is based solely on that—by remembering it; thus, that conscious person necessarily becomes possessed of awareness.
Even if one does not engage in physical or verbal activity, let it be so;

for the validity of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in its being the means for establishing the cognition of that validity, and not in its being the means for establishing physical or other such activities.
Therefore,
while the object is indeed present, one who fails to recite it here due to delusion—
"Only on the basis of similarity with the established [case] is the other person reminded of the convention"—this is the summary.
Just as the relation of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception, [so too is the convention established]. || 267 ||
For words such as "effect" and so forth are indeed postulated for the sake of conventional usage regarding those two [cause and effect].
Indeed, there is no other nature of cause and effect apart from the distinction between perception and non-perception;
the meaning of "this is its effect" is simply that it does not exist without this [cause].

If, however, it were distinct from this [inherence], then it would certainly exist even in the absence of that [inherence]; such being the case, a further connection would be useless. On the other hand, if it did not exist in the absence of that, then that [inherence] itself is the connection, and thus a further one is useless.
Is it not the case that when a relation exists, [the effect] does not exist in its absence and exists when it is present?

If it is maintained that "when the relation exists, it exists when that [cause] is present," then one must consider that the relation of the preceding [cause] would also exist even in the absence of that [effect]. (572)

For a relation necessarily resides in two things; how could it exist if only one were present? If fitness (*yogyatā*) were the relation for the arising of an effect from a cause, then it would be logical that the existence of the effect comes solely from the cause. For the cause is of such a nature as to be produced by its own causes.
Furthermore, no relation of cause and effect other than positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) appears even to those who perceive beyond the senses.

Therefore, since the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), how is it that the term "effect" and so forth is applied for the sake of linguistic convenience? It is because, even without a difference in the words themselves or a difference in the objects, these very terms "seen" and "not seen" are designated by the word "effect" and so on to facilitate practical usage; thus, [the convention is established] with brevity.

The successful accomplishment of an effect from its cause occurs because it is included within the nature [of that cause]; thus, this illustration has been shown separately by means of explaining the different types of reasons.
For, in reality, a capable cause is nothing other than the very nature of the effect.
Therefore, non-apprehension is nothing other than a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
consequently, it is not presented as a separate category.
From here onwards, up until the 270th verse (*°samudbhavaḥ*), no translation is found. [Objection:

But how can the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) be included within the reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) without a relation of identity (*tādātmyapratibandha*), given that there is no mutual difference between two entities, just as there is no non-difference?
Indeed, for that which is devoid of self, the possibility of identity is not tenable;
for a rabbit's horn is certainly not identical in nature to a donkey's horn—
this is what is being refuted here.
Non-apprehension has as its very nature a character opposite to that which is to be negated;
for it is through the experience of the apprehension of one thing that one thinks, "I do not apprehend this."
The arising of conceptual cognition occurs in the form "I perceive" or "I do not perceive.
Indeed, an empty non-existence is not more capable of entering the domain of the investigation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) than anything else;
nor does that [non-existence], even when established, possess any established nature by virtue of its own essence alone.
That [non-existence] is accepted as such only by those whose eyes are the discernment of the intermixture of entities;
for in that case, if [the entity] is excluded from other objects, places, times, and states by its very nature, what is the use of postulating another non-existence?
And if it is not excluded by its very nature, then likewise, another non-existence is useless.
It was already established previously that [absence] is useless in one case and impossible in another;

therefore, it is designated as the "absence" of a jar or the like through such a distinction of properties (*dharma*) which constitute its very nature (*svabhāva*), precisely because it is devoid of the existence of anything else.

The perception of one object as having a nature distinct from the intended object, and the experience of that perception by way of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), gives rise to a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consisting of a mental state revolving around the memory "I do not perceive this.
In that case, the very experience of the location is itself the non-perception of the other;
for the meaning here is precisely this: "I do not perceive this by means of another's own-nature."
Non-apprehension of this [object] by way of its own nature means: "This does not exist in that form.
Regarding the non-perception of a location:
surely, since there is nothing here that could destroy it, its absence is established in this manner; how then can there be a statement of the contrapositive?
This is true, provided that no other meaning is included here.
But that is indeed included within it;
for thus [it is said]:
But surely, when one says "that jar is not here," what is being established is that its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is absent; how then can this be called a statement of the opposite?
Is it that the location is devoid of that form, or that the jar is devoid of this [location]? To the wise, no distinction whatsoever appears here in any way.
