If that [location] were not devoid of this form, then this [jar] would also not be devoid of that; since the meaning is perfectly clear, why should there be any delusion for another?
Therefore, its non-existence here is simply its being distinct from that;
and since the cognition "I do not perceive it" arises precisely from seeing a place devoid of it,

and the cognition "I perceive it" arises through its being perceived in the form of something else, then because perception and non-perception are identical in nature, perception itself is non-perception.
Now, one might object: "Let this non-perception [of another cognition] be granted; however, how can there be non-difference between the cognition and the cognized object?
This is not a fault, because it is established that cognition and the cognized object are non-different;
or else, the word *vā* is used in the sense of *iva* (as if).

If it is argued that, because "I perceive" is an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), perception is determined as such; likewise, through the determination "I do not perceive," non-perception [is also established],
but [this applies] to another [type of non-perception].
There is no capacity for the cognition of non-existence regarding that which is not distinct [from existence],
because it is impossible to alter what has been apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And this has already been established, so it is not stated here;
for indeed, without memory, there is no possibility of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Since the recollection of a counter-positive does not occur without a specific experience [of that object], [one might argue]:
"But surely, the establishment of the distinction between entities arises precisely from the possibility of their non-existence; how then can there be non-confusion without non-existence?
This is not so.
For this reason,
there are 270 verses here in the Tibetan translation (T).
The distinction between objects is understood only from a specific cognition; likewise, self-awareness of that [cognition] as it truly is is the cause for the awareness of its difference.
(271) For if the cognition were not specifically cognized as distinct from other cognitions, [it could not be so distinguished].
If there is no apprehension of the specific qualities of the object of cognition,
and if that form is not experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then its particularity is likewise not apprehended;
it could only be apprehended through the awareness of its absence.
For the emergence of the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) does not occur without the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
nor is there recollection of the counter-correlate in the absence of a cognition of the qualified [object];
therefore, there must have been a prior experience of that qualified object.
In that case, non-existence would likewise be for the existent as well, and thus non-existence itself would be purposeless;
furthermore, if that very conventional usage of "non-existence" is established by means of non-existence,
what is the point of establishing what is already established by something else?
In the establishment of conventional usage, that very non-apprehension has the nature of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*);
therefore, the conceptualization of difference arises precisely from the state of self-cognition as distinct from anything else,
and that very difference is the absence of what is other than it.
Therefore, the distinction between two cognitions is established through themselves; from those [cognitions], the distinction between their respective objects [is established].
Otherwise, due to infinite regress, the distinction of nothing whatsoever would be established.
The exclusion of others is established for a cognition solely through its self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Furthermore, the conventional usage of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is thus concluded by the phrase "of that object as well.
However, if the distinction [between objects] were not derived from perception itself, but rather from the means of valid cognition consisting in non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*),
then, due to infinite regress, there would be no comprehension.

For if the conceptualization of difference were [effected] by the means of cognition known as non-existence (abhāva), that non-existence too would not be established by another through the non-existence of something else. That [other] would require yet another, and that another yet another, leading to an infinite regress; thus, there would be no practical discourse (vyavahāra).

If difference, not apprehended by means of non-existence (*abhāva*), is perceived by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the operation of that non-existence occurs only when there is recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); and such recollection as a counter-correlate occurs only when difference has already been grasped through perception. Thus, non-existence is useless, for even now, as before, the grasping of difference occurs through perception alone.
3. The fifteenth daily lesson (is completed).
Now, even so, since differentiation does not exist without non-existence, non-existence is not purposeless.
That being the case, even there, another recollection of the counter-positive would have to be responsible for the manifestation of the absence.

Even that [perception] would require recollection, leading to an infinite regress; and this is stated even while granting such a possibility, for it is not actually possible at present for there to be a recollection of the object currently being perceived as its counter-positive (pratiyogin), by means of which, upon the emergence of non-existence at that time, there could be a grasping of its difference from this [present object]. Therefore, in the view of others, there is simply no apprehension of difference.
1B. Through the experience of a specific form, there is no exclusion of anything other than that;
therefore, the non-perception of that [other] is simply the perception of what is qualified by it. (273)
The very experience of a specific form is the proof for the non-existence of anything other than it;
however, without the experience of that specific form, the non-existence of another thing therein cannot be established.
[Objection: But surely, from the experience of a specific form, only its being of such a nature is established.
How can there be an absence of that [difference] therein?
For it is not the case that what exists in another place or time is absent therein, because such a thing has reached the conditions for non-perception;
therefore, it is not non-existent.

In the experience of a specific form, how can there be the exclusion of others? For if there were no exclusion of others, that very specific form would not be established. Indeed, if the specific form of a jar or other object is apprehended, what is the use of the cognition of the absence of anything else? (578)

Nor can there be an experience of a specific form even through the apprehension of a thousand non-entities; for the apprehension of the essential nature must necessarily be sought without the apprehension of each particularity of that nature,
and it has been demonstrated that no other entity can be apprehended as having an essential nature of its own.
Therefore, the experience of a specific form itself is the proof of the non-existence of another;
even non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is simply the apprehension of that [specific form] as something else.
Consequently, this non-apprehension is established by itself through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it functions solely with respect to its own [object], it indicates the establishment of the absence of that [other object].

It is thus established that non-existence is simply the perception of a specific, restricted form; therefore, the identity between non-existence and non-perception, as well as their establishment through direct perception, is proven. Consequently, there is no fault regarding the lack of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) due to being unestablished (*asiddha*), and that non-perception is indeed a capable logical reason (*hetu*).
It is only the occurrence within its own locus that prompts the conventional usage of "absence";
otherwise, if non-apprehension were the absence of experience and absence itself were the absence of an entity, then, due to infinite regress, it would be unestablished— thus he says.

2B. If the non-existence of an object is understood through non-apprehension as being distinct from the apprehension itself, then the non-existence of that apprehension must be understood by another [non-apprehension], leading to an infinite regress. || 275 ||
Just as the non-existence of an entity is [established] through non-apprehension, so too non-apprehension is of the nature of the non-apprehension of apprehension;

and since the non-existence of that [latter] would likewise require another non-apprehension, there is no liberation from infinite regress. Alternatively, if the non-existence of the object is established by the absence of apprehension because apprehension is the means for establishing it—
But since the existence of apprehension does not require another means of proof, its non-existence likewise does not require another means of proof;

this is incorrect, for it is logical that apprehension is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), whereas to claim that the cognition of its absence occurs through itself is an extreme audacity. (579)
For if there were self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this [object] would indeed exist; yet, if its non-existence is established by perception, it must be through the cognition of something else.
(580) Now, if the non-existence of the cognition is established by the perception of another, then it follows that the object is also [established as non-existent] by the perception of another.
But surely, because the object has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāptatvāt*), it is not established through the perception of another.
Since that which is other than its cognition is "form," and because of the very nature of cognition as cognition, there is an absence of any other form; thus,
that absence is established by the perception of that [other].
And thus,
by saying "I do not perceive this," he rejects only the perception with reference to the Supreme Person, not that this thing does not exist.
Therefore, this non-apprehension, understood through one's own direct perception as "it is not there," is characterized solely by the absence of cognition; thus,
that [object] is non-existent.
How can the non-existence of one thing be understood through the apprehension of another?
If it were [understood] by virtue of being distinct from that [other], then why would it not be a case of non-apprehension?
Indeed, the proof of the absence of one cognition cannot occur through the awareness of another cognition without [the latter] being distinct from that [former].
And since the non-apprehension of that [object] consists precisely in the apprehension of what is distinct from it,
how can the absence of cognition of anything other than that be established by perception?
Furthermore, the qualification "having reached the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is not necessary, because there is no deviation [from the rule].
That being the case, there would be no qualification [for non-apprehension], yet its status as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhitā*) does not depart;

therefore, whatever negation there may be, it is all due to non-apprehension. Thus, absence characterized by exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), and that very same [absence] is non-apprehension in relation to something else.

Furthermore, as for this use of the first-person pronoun (*uttamapuruṣa*) in the form "I do not perceive this," it is characterized by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) defined as the exclusion of cognition; it is not, however, for the purpose of negating the non-existence of the object itself.
Since that [non-apprehension] is not distinct from it, the non-existence of the thing is simply that very [non-apprehension].
For when existence and apprehension are one and the same, then the exclusion of the thing is also established by perception itself; its occurrence cannot be [established] piecemeal.

But surely non-existence is established through the non-perception of the pervader; for thus, the existence of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility is pervaded by perception, and from the absence of that [perception], there is the establishment of the non-existence of the object possessing its form.
Therefore, this is true [even though it arises] from that which is essentially void.

This non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) does not establish non-existence. For if the non-existence of something characterized by perceptibility—established through perception via the non-perception of its pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*)—were [the case], then that non-existence would be established by perception everywhere; thus, there would be no such thing as "non-perception of intrinsic nature. (582)

If that very non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) establishes absence for one who is not confused, then let it be made an object of cognition by means of memory even for one who is confused; what is the use of postulating another non-perception?

Or, if that same [non-perception] which serves as a non-perception of essence (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) for the confused person will likewise serve for the non-confused person—as in the case of the cognition of smoke—surely the threefold nature [of the reason] does not thereby disappear.

Furthermore, there is no difference between the pervaded and the pervader here from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it was previously established that existence is nothing other than perception.
For the proponent of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) maintains this position: that the existence of a perceptible object is necessarily pervaded by its perception.

And this [point] is exactly the same even in the theory of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*); for when there is identity (*tādātmya*), there is necessarily a relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*),
and thus it has been established that apprehension itself is existence.

Since it is not distinct from its own nature because there is no deviation from the pervasion of the cause of that effect, the non-perception of that [effect] is said to be nothing other than the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). Therefore, how could one who, being utterly deluded, explains the non-perception of an effect as being included within the non-perception of its own nature, fail to explain the non-perception of cognition as the non-perception of its own nature?
Consequently, the existence of one thing is itself the non-existence of another, and the perception of one thing is itself the non-perception of another;
and that is precisely the non-perception of its own nature.
2. Non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the sublater of existence.
[Objection: Even so, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) would be impossible.
[Response: True; it is indeed accepted that all [types of non-perception] are included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone. Thus, nothing is lost for us.
How, then, is there a distinction?
There is a difference due to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader, due to the occurrence of increase and decrease,
and due to the difference in distance between the tree and the *śiṃśapā*.
Tree-ness is inclusive, whereas *śiṃśapā*-ness is exclusive;
thus, the non-perception of the pervader at a distance [is established] in relation to the pervaded.

However, the distinction between these two is that one is "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) while the other is "non-perception [of something] that has reached the conditions for perceptibility.

Yet, because there is a relationship of mutual pervasion (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between "existence" and "perception characterized by the conditions for perceptibility," it is impossible to conceive of a difference between them;

therefore, it is established that non-perception is indeed nothing other than the non-perception of the essential nature, and thus non-perception is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
For this very reason, because certainty is impossible regarding that which is unperceivable, its existence elsewhere is precluded;
just as, for example, conceptual construction and the like cannot be established in other sentient beings who lack the [necessary] signs. || 276 ||
Therefore,
since this [inference] has non-determination as its result, it is not capable of establishing exclusion.
The first [type] is employed for the sake of establishing a reason through certainty alone.

This non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) does not bring about the certainty of the absence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because certainty is impossible in cases such as distant locations.
For this is not a non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) with respect to something invisible;

rather, it is the first type [of non-perception]— namely, the non-perception of the cause and the pervader— which functions to ascertain the exclusion of the reason from the entire dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), as described in such passages as "by the very exclusion of the nature of the reason."

Even in that case, having accepted it as a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), does not the probans "there is no cold touch here because of fire" indeed constitute a distinct type of logical mark known as the "contradictory" (*virodhi*)?
How is it described by way of its specific divisions?
Because even that [non-existence] is included within non-apprehension itself; for this reason:

In its own applications, that [non-apprehension] is employed either in its own form or in the form of a sublation of the object; for it exists when [the object] is present and does not exist when it is absent.
Indeed, a contradictory reason is merely a variety of that very non-apprehension, just like its other varieties.

Otherwise, the opponent would also have to provide separate definitions for the contradictory, the effect of the contradictory, the pervader of the contradictory, and so forth; but since this is merely a manifold division of that very same [non-apprehension], there is no such fault. To explain:
Either its own form is employed—
namely, the non-perception of essence, cause, pervader, or effect—
or else the nature of the sublation of a non-prohibition is employed.
"There is no cold touch here because of fire"—
just as non-perception establishes absence, so too does the perception of something contradictory, whether directly or indirectly.
Why is this?
Since contradiction is that which causes cessation,
how is contradiction established? The cognition of contradiction arises because, when fire is present, coldness and the like— which possess their complete causes— are absent.
For contradiction is characterized by perception and non-perception;

therefore, from the perception of the contradictory [factor], the non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility is established. In this case, the non-perception of fire located at a distance—which has met the conditions for perceptibility—is established through inference, and it proves its absence. Thus, the perception of contradiction is not distinct from the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Indeed, that very sensation of heat is the absence of the sensation of cold, and because it is devoid of that [cold], there is also the sensation of neither-hot-nor-cold.
Therefore, the non-perception of one thing is simply the perception of the other;
likewise, the perception of a contradictory effect is also a non-perception of essential nature established through inference based on the "effect-as-reason" (*kāryahetu*).
In the former case, the perception of the contradictory, there is an inference by virtue of dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*).
1B [The non-refutation] of the pervasion and so forth;
2B of the meaning, which is the non-refutation;
3B ... the increase.

4B. The non-apprehension of that [is the means of proof], because mutual exclusion is established; or else, there is a contradiction characterized by the state of mutual exclusion, like the permanence and destruction of an entity.
For the negation of identity between two things— such as the eternal and its opposite— is established by way of their opposition characterized by mutual exclusion,
just as, for example: "This place is not possessed of a jar, because it is perceived in the absence of that jar."
In all cases, the perception of the opposite (viparyayopalabdhi) is the very means of proving non-existence directly,
because it subverts other means of valid cognition, as in the case of "dependence" and "necessity.

Just as there is contradiction when two things mutually subvert each other, so too is there contradiction when they are subverted by a means of valid cognition, as in the case of "dependence" and "necessity."
For instance, "dependent" and "independent" are mutually contradictory;

furthermore, "necessity" and its opposite are also contradictory in the sense that they are characterized by the sublation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to their mutual exclusion. This constitutes another form of contradiction, as follows:
A contradictory state arises from that which is dependent; this applies even to the permanent and the impermanent. In the ultimate sense, contradiction consists in mutual exclusion.
(585) If, in this way, a valid cognition establishes a contradictory [state] based on dependence, yet there is no other such thing as a "contradiction of valid cognition" itself.
This is true;
nevertheless, because it is in fact contradictory by virtue of being pervaded by a contrary property, this has been stated.
What, then, is the purpose of this?
The perception of what is pervaded by a contradictory [property] is also a means of establishing a negation; this is shown for the sake of clarity, as follows:
"The destruction of even an existing entity that has come into being is not necessarily certain, because it depends upon other causes"—such is the formulation observed in practice.
Another, however, says:

"When the perception of that which is pervaded by a contradictory effect is employed, since the nature of the effect is included within the reason (*hetu*), the reason is not distinct from non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) because they are entirely one. Therefore, even though the reason is threefold, it is merely a subdivision of that [non-perception] itself. (586–587)
Non-apprehension alone is the single logical reason for [proving] both effect and essential nature,
because they are subdivisions thereof.
Indeed, its particular instance does not differ from it;
for there is no difference between a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and the universal "cowness" (*gotva*).
In that case, this is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), specifically the perception of an effect that is contradictory [to the negation of the probandum].

The essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is also the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because it establishes the absence of non-eternality in the case of fire,
[and] the absence of eternality.

Thus, if this non-existent [object] is postulated as a logical reason (*hetu*) in accordance with its necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then it must be either an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or an effect (*kārya*)—by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*).

When there is a necessary connection with impermanence or with fire, the reason is contradicted by that which is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*); therefore, the conceptualization of the existence of that [non-existent object] is based on its non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

In that case, having abandoned the conception of a direct cause and resorted to a mediated one, it is impossible for smoke to have a direct operation toward the cessation of cold—which is contrary to fire—within the process of reaching the fire; rather, its operation is directed toward the cessation of cold itself. Therefore, the conception of causality through a mediated sequence is what constitutes inference based on an inferred [middle term] (*anumitānumāna*).

Nor is it the case that when two or three [meanings] are conveyed by a single word, this reason [for their distinction] is not different; for the object does not exist according to the power of the word, otherwise some distinction would have to be imagined as being merely a matter of usage. This being so, [the distinction remains real]. (589)
"There is no sensation of cold here because of smoke"—
this inference of fire from smoke is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*);
the proof of the absence of the sensation of cold by means of fire is the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*).

The establishment of the conventional usage of the absence of cold through the non-perception of cold is "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Therefore, this is merely another form of inference based on an inferred [middle term] (*anumitānumāna*) among the indirect causes;
nor does the presentation of these three by a single term imply their identity or their status as distinct reasons.
The principle is that this is a compound of application (*prayoga-samāsa*), not a compound of form (*rūpa-samāsa*);
therefore, it is incorrect to say that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the reason in every case.
Now, [if you argue] that in the proof of exclusion (*vyavaccheda-sādhana*), all non-apprehension [is the reason].
It is not merely due to the difference in objects, but rather due to the difference in causes;
and thus it has been said:
By this [negation], a portion of the object that has not been admitted is negated;
however, by the previous two [means of knowledge], there is an exclusion (paryudāsa) from the object through affirmation.
Thus [ends] the section on the investigation of the intrinsic nature of entities (bhāvasvabhāva).
Now, it may be thought that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone is the means of proof for exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
If that were the case, why not simply say that perception is self-cognition?
Therefore, this [position] is incorrect;
rather, the distinction [between them] arises solely from the difference in their formal application (*prayoga*), due to the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory.
Since destruction is dependent [on other causes], it does not have an inevitable occurrence;
for how could there be a necessity for that which arises from another cause to be present?
Since that other cause also depends upon its own cause, there would again be a lack of necessity for yet another; thus, there would be no certainty regarding the occurrence of the effect.
Alternatively, if it is argued that the very cause of an entity, such as a potter, is also the cause of its destruction, then there is certainty.
To this it is replied:
if existence arises from a cause that is itself existent, what is the use of these laborious indirect sequences? For instance:
If that cause, having produced another destruction, were the destroyer of that [entity],
what would happen if it were to produce that very same perishable entity? (281) If, by producing destruction, its own cause itself were the destroyer of that [entity]...

If it is argued, "Let it produce only that which is perishable; what is the use of this succession? In this matter, the answer must be stated in terms of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things," [we reply]:
otherwise, because it is the intrinsic nature of things, this is not so; for instance:
Who could be a benefactor to that [entity] which exists as a perfected self?
And who could be one who is not a benefactor to it, such that it would depend upon him?
If a cause of destruction is impossible for that which exists with a perfected nature, then it must exist with a nature other than that perfected one; it must exist with a nature that is yet to be.
And thus, that [cause] is not the cause of its destruction.
The text is broken here.
Now, if he were the maker even of a particularity that is already established,
then that particularity would have to be either established or other than that [established thing].
If it were established, the same undesirable consequence as before would follow.

Now, if that [nature] is already established, it is impossible to make it have that nature; therefore, since it would be distinct from that nature, even if it were enjoined, it would not be of any benefit to it—what, then, would it be for it?
The meaning is: it would be nothing at all.
Or, if there were a second alternative, it would simply be something already enjoined, and thus it could not be enjoined again.
Furthermore, does that entity persist through a subsequent period of time due to its own cause, or otherwise?
If it is the former position:

If [the Self] has already pervaded all time and moments and accomplished all that is to be done, then what will the Destroyer do? For when the water has already flowed away, what indeed is the use of building a dam? A dam is for the purpose of obstructing the flow of water; it is not a dam if it does not obstruct the water. Indeed, such a dam would be nothing more than a mere exertion. (591–592)
Now, if there is no such apprehension of it, then how could a cause of destruction function when its own object has not been determined?
If you argue that it functions by determining a future entity,
we say no.
If the nature of the established entity is not determined, what possible use could there be for a cause of destruction?
If it is argued that its use lies in the potsherd, which possesses a contrary nature, [we reply:
surely even that contrary thing is simply a remover.
In that case as well, the same previous logical difficulty remains;
for [a cause] could not be a destroyer merely by way of mutual exclusion.
Rather, the cause of destruction, characterized by emptiness, would produce the non-existence of an already established entity through its persistence over time.

If it is argued that emptiness (*śūnyatā*), when applied to something that persists over time, does not contradict it and thus cannot be its subverter— just as water [does not subvert] its container, whereas a full jar [of water] is indeed a subverter of that [container]—
we say no.
In that regard, since subsistence over a period of time is not established, one might argue that it is precisely such a period established by inference that is being negated; however,
that is incorrect.

That which is not established by inference cannot be negated as such; nor can another thing be negated on the grounds that it simply does not exist. (593) Just like perception, inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, what is established by it is truly existent. How could there be non-existence?
For if it were non-existent, the cognition of it would be false, and thus neither perception nor inference would exist.

If it is argued that since those [opposites] are absent, there is no establishment of an entity, and thus for what could there be a division—since a division can only belong to something that is possible—[we reply: this is merely a repetition of the same point through a different formulation;
it does not constitute a definitive determination of the reality of things, so this is trivial.

Now, [the opponent claims that] the cause of destruction brings about a change in that very thing, characterized by its transformation into shards and so forth. To this it is replied: Is this change in the jar and such desired to reside in the jar itself, or rather in the substance of clay? Since the change is established in the jar and such, why is it not considered an existent entity? (594)
If that alteration exists in the form of the jar, then the jar itself is the substratum of that alteration; in that case, since the jar was perceived in its own form, how could it be otherwise?
Or, if the jar is not perceived, of what would this alteration be?

The transformation of the jar is designated as being preceded by that [destruction]. Now, if destruction must exist for there to be a state preceded by it, then that destruction would itself be a transformation, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if the transformation belongs to the substance of clay, then since that [clay] has not perished at all, how can there be a destruction characterized as its transformation?
Even in that case, the prior substance of clay has not perished, because it is absent [as such] while the subsequent state exists.
[Objection: "But surely this same fault applies to your position as well; for at the time of the effect, the cause no longer exists, so how can that be its effect? [Reply:
This is not so, because:

A cause must necessarily exist prior [to its effect]; that which is simultaneous is not a cause. To claim that destruction is simultaneous with the entity is an incorrect response. For it is not logically tenable that the entity exists at one time and its destruction at another; rather, at the very moment the entity exists, it is destroyed—thus it is right to say it has perished.
However, it is not logical for non-existence to exist within non-existence, because there is no further death for one who is already dead.
It is indeed appropriate that [the state] exists at the end of the effect even when [the cause] has died, since it is a different state of being;
yet non-existence is simply its emptiness.

Because there is a cognition of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the form "that does not exist," whereas the non-co-referential designation "the destruction of the object" occurs through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were its own designation), just as in the case of "the body of a stone statue.
However, such co-referentiality is not found in the expression "fire is smoke."
But is it not the case that here too there is no ultimate co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
since the preceding form, which is being remembered, is perceived as having perished;
and there can be no such co-referentiality with the destruction occurring at a subsequent time?
That too is incorrect;
for if that were the case, there would be a great contradiction,
as follows:

In reality, there is no destruction of the form that is being remembered; therefore, to say that the visible form is destroyed at that time is a rash assertion. For "destruction" is said to mean non-existence, and non-existence does not apply to a state that is currently present.
But in the state where [an entity] is non-existent, that very thing does not exist; how then can there be "non-existence"?
Therefore, for one who maintains that non-existence is distinct [from existence], there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "it does not exist.
Consequently, non-existence is not other than existence.
Therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for that very non-existence which occurs at a later time is the existence of the preceding [entity] characterized by its exclusion,
and the non-apprehension of that [existence] consists in the apprehension of another form.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that if there were the apprehension of [an entity] conjoined with a subsequent perception whose nature is to grasp a present form as both the object and the subject, it would follow that there must be an apprehension of the cause of that [conjunction].
Therefore, since cognition occurs through mere arising as something not conjoined with another, destruction is independent of anything else.
Now, [one might object]:...
For such is its very nature that it perishes in dependence [on something else]; how then could it be independent? To this, it is replied:
"If an entity were all-pervasive, what would it depend upon? Or if the entity were not all-pervasive, its dependence [on another] would be in vain.
Since this has been stated, he says for that very reason:
And being independent, what entity could ever be other than it is,
such that it would not be desired as subject to destruction?
For that very thing which is perceived by direct perception as perishing at the very outset— how could it ever be otherwise?
Just as for the proponent of eternalism, if an entity were independent even for a moment during its state of perishing, it would not be an entity of another entity;
for if an entity were independent regarding its destruction and did not depend on anything else for even a single moment, that entity would not exist as an entity for even a moment.
For it is thus:
that which is causeless is either eternally existent or eternally non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else.
Thus it has been said;
likewise, how could destruction, which occurs after the moment of existence, be of the same nature as that [existence]?
Furthermore, if there is no identity between them, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
This [objection] is merely clutching at straws;
for how could an entity that exists in such a way [as a positive thing] be an entity within a non-entity? (284)
Existence itself, when not conjoined with a subsequent existence, is destruction. How could that [destruction] occur in the absence of existence?
For it is not logical that something should be identical to its own absence and yet exist when that [existence] is absent.
If this is so, then since destruction exists, how can something be "destroyed" while destruction itself exists?
Even if destruction exists as something distinct [from the entity], since its own nature (svarūpa) has not fallen away,
how can there be destruction? If it is argued that this very falling away [of the nature] is what constitutes the presence of a distinct destruction;
Let it be so; nevertheless, the point remains that this [entity] must be the object of cognition precisely as something distinct. Let its state of being perceived remain as it is.
This is indeed what constitutes the distinctness of a distinct thing: namely, its non-obstruction by the form of another.
Any contradiction resulting in its impairment has already been refuted.
Since contradiction is not established without destruction,
therefore those things which exist independently of anything else are necessarily existent as such.
And because there is no possibility of an obstacle to the causal complex in its own operation:

just as the final causal complex, being free from the suspicion of any obstruction, requires nothing else for the production of its own effect and is thus determined by that [result], so too is the entity [determined] in its destruction. Therefore, since it is independent regarding destruction, the entity is momentary; whereas if it were dependent—
If it is argued that because destruction possesses the quality of having an origin, its occurrence is necessarily certain, we say:
no.
Because there is no necessary connection;
for without a necessary connection, a reason cannot establish what is to be proven.
Even if destruction were causeless, it could not serve as a proof of the probandum through identity.
But causality for that which is to be proven is not logical because it occurs subsequently.

For it is not reasonable for destruction, being something that occurs later, to be the cause; moreover, the effect of that which possesses origination occurring earlier is not necessarily present from the cause. (598)
Therefore, it is not a cause by virtue of being that [destruction's] cause. But how is it known that identity (tādātmya) occurs in the absence of a cause?
Or rather, how is destruction caused, given its conformity with positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the mallet and so forth?
For it is precisely that property of the effect which is stated here:

if non-existence were destruction consisting in the failure to produce a subsequent [entity], then since that [non-existence] was already observed previously, how could it be caused by a cause of destruction? (599)
For how can that which is observed even in the absence of something else have that as its cause?
It has already been established that a cause is not determined by mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone;
and just as there is the cognition of a jar—unconnected with anything else—in the presence of shards and so forth when the destroyer is near, so too is it immediately after its arising.

For it has been established that even previously, no conjunction with another form is perceived, because that would entail the consequence of being perceived until the point of death; and if it is argued that here too, non-conjunction itself is the destruction,
and that non-conjunction is produced by destruction alone—

That is incorrect because, due to incapacity and lack of purpose, that action is not performed by destruction alone. For destruction is not capable [of acting] upon what has not been assembled, nor indeed upon what has already been assembled.

If it were the case that this [entity] had arisen already assembled from its causes and was thus grasped by perception exactly as such, then what would be the utility of destruction? For in that case, destruction would be ineffective.
Alternatively, if it were not composite from its own causes,
then destruction would be purposeless,
because there is no further production of what has already been produced.

Therefore, by its very nature, it is momentary alone as understood through direct perception, because otherwise its cognition would be impossible. And that which cannot be cognized otherwise does not become otherwise, since its being otherwise is sublated by direct perception. Therefore, it is determined solely by that [momentariness] independently, and not by anything else.

Just as the final causal complex [is necessary], surely even the setting and rising of the sun are inevitable despite their dependence; for if there were independence, rising and setting would occur immediately after one another.
Furthermore, while the causal complex is fixed without distinction, it nonetheless pertains to other entities such as sprouts and the like.
If that were so, then by that very example, there would be only a contrary conclusion, and not the establishment of the probandum under discussion.
To this it is replied:
"The pervasion of sunrise and sunset does not apply to the rising and setting of the sun; for sometimes it may be otherwise, and there is no proof for the contrary. (601)

Even if there were indeed further observations, still, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between rising and setting on the one hand, and the states of setting and rising on the other.
For instance, the story of the devoted wife (*pativratā*) is heard;
and it is possible that in winter, after a long time, there may be a state of rising, yet because of the possibility of setting suddenly, such an extreme occurrence is likewise possible. (602)
Nor is there any concealment of the setting sun by mountains or the like; and while that concealment exists from our perspective, other beings—namely, the yogis—indeed perceive it.
Furthermore:

Regarding the point that for those things which are dependent, [the result] is necessarily present: even if it were granted that for some this necessity exists while for others it does not, there would still be doubt;
as for what was also said—
"The final causal complex is restricted to an entity distinct [from itself],
whereas destruction is not distinct [from the entity];
that too is incorrect, because:"
Since it is determined by its own cause to have a nature other than that [of the entity], why is this not likewise postulated for destruction, which consists of its own nature?

For so-called "destruction" is not some distinct non-entity; rather, it is simply the reality of the entity itself as perceived when no longer conjoined with other things, according to the maxim of "the body of a stone-son. (603)

Likewise, regarding the destruction of an entity as the object of such a demonstration: just as the final causal complex is necessarily restricted to the nature of producing that sprout, so too an entity is necessarily restricted to the conventional usage of a subsequent nature that is not yet assembled. What, then, is undesirable about this? Furthermore, its necessity is established in a general sense by virtue of its independence;

the conceptualization of distinctions between the states of a thing and a non-thing is merely a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), like the conceptualization of the pot-term as being either material or immaterial.
Therefore, the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) is indeed a specific variety of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
And that [non-perception] functions as a reason only within the context of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), provided that the existence and its opposite are established.
Consequently, that which exists in two ways among those of the same class is a valid reason.
In the case of the opposite, it is contradictory;
other than that, the uncertain is of five kinds.
Among these, the dispute regarding the capacity of particulars and universals to serve as probans has been refuted.
The remaining three types are intended to demonstrate the capacity for logical proof (*gamakatva*) by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*);
for it is said in that very same [text]: "the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) and the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*)."

A reason is not established as a means of comprehension by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because even when there is an excess of mere existence (*bhāvamātra*), it is in all three ways a non-comprehender.

(604) If positive concomitance were the determinant for being a means of comprehension, then [the reason] "because of impermanence" would also be a means of comprehension for [the probandum] "not immediately following effort," since there exists a positive concomitance with non-existence (*abhāva*).

Now, if it is argued that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is a means of proof merely by its non-existence [in the dissimilar instance] because it is a means of proof in dependence upon association with negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then the following would also be a means of proof:

"This is eternal because it is tangible. But this too is not a means of proof, because the positive concomitance is equally absent. Then, let this be the means of proof: "It is non-eternal because it follows immediately after an effort."
For here, positive concomitance (anvaya) is strong while negative concomitance (vyatireka) is weak;
for instance, the primary cause does not require a distinction from anything else. In cases such as eating and so forth, it is never observed that the motivating factor depends on something external.

If positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were the determinant factor for establishing proof, it would not require completeness; disregarding it entirely, it would establish proof just like the act of eating [which is the cause of satiety].

However, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the determinant factor; it requires only the existence of positive concomitance, and not its equality or other such qualities, as in the case of the argument: "It is impermanent because it follows immediately upon an effort."
That which follows immediately upon effort is necessarily non-eternal; it serves as a means of cognition precisely by excluding eternality.
Other reasons (hetus) are likewise [to be understood] in this manner. To explain:

That by which [a property] is excluded from the eternal would establish its absence; however, that which exists in the non-eternal is not a prover of its absence. (606) Even if it is observed in the non-eternal, it does not thereby prove the absence of the eternal. But when the absence of eternality is observed, there is necessarily a transition to another category in establishing that absence.
However, what is observed does not necessarily exist elsewhere;

if it were otherwise, then if [the reason] were a means of cognition by way of observation, it would only lead to the cognition of the fire that was observed, and not to the cognition of all other instances.
Consequently, there would be a lack of validity regarding the attainment of those other instances.
Now, that [object] too is indeed already embraced [by cognition],
because it is impossible to embrace it through a subsequent observation.
In that very same context—it is impermanence;
in that very same context—it occurs in the case of permanence.

Is it not true, however, that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is also ascertained precisely through the medium of its positive concomitance (*anvaya*); so why is there not a predominance of positive concomitance?
For perception has no authority in determining the exclusion [of other objects],
since perception determines only the state of being perceived, and nothing else.
If it is argued that the perception of one thing is not the cause for the ascertainment of another,
because ascertainment occurs even with respect to something other than the mental formation (*saṃskāra*), that is incorrect.

Indeed, when mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are manifested by the appearance of the form of a given object, they serve as the basis for its determination; however, there is no certainty regarding anything other than that.

But when that very same necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is apprehended primarily through the aspect of exclusion (*vyatireka*), then by means of that, the reason becomes the indicator of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). [Objection:
If the necessary connection is understood through the medium of positive observation (*darśana*), how can the necessary connection be understood through exclusion?
This statement is also not appropriate;

for it has already been explained that even when the connection exists through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it cannot be considered possible if one disregards the primacy of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Indeed, if the apprehension of the connection were achieved through positive concomitance alone, it would occur through that specific instance itself, and not by means of a verbal statement.
For indeed, there can be no comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) from another statement at that time;
and if it were later understood through that [other statement], then because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the prior [statement] would not have any connection at all, owing to such deviation.
If it is argued that the relation [resides] in the generality of individuals (*vyaktisāmānya*), what indeed is this so-called "generality of individuals"?
For surely, without its own nature being discerned, it cannot be cognized as being related or otherwise.
If it is argued that [the universal] is the basis for the cognition of similarity among individuals, we reply:

although there is the cognition "it is similar," it is impossible to demonstrate what the basis for that cognition is, even if it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); perhaps it may be known through inference (*anumāna*) from the observation of its effects.

Let it be understood that the cause is a generality, but not that generality [of the effect] itself, because it cannot be defined as "this" (in its specific identity); or rather, the basis is the production of a single effect—what need is there for anything else?
For instance:

"In this matter of what is to be done, no difference whatsoever exists among us"—thus the entire world stands in a state of single-minded agreement. Therefore, this smoke does not exist without any one of these various fires; thus, because it is excluded from their absence, the apprehension of the relationship [between smoke and fire] occurs solely through the connection of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), and not by any other means. Consequently, it is exclusion itself that is established by the reason (*hetu*) or by the word.
From this, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) alone is understood primarily;
however, by implication, it is cognized as being inseparable from the existence of the individual (*vyakti*). In the absence of non-fire, a specific instance of fire is necessarily entailed.

Otherwise, there would be no exclusion of the naked (nagna) at all. Now, it might be argued that five types of inconclusive (anaikāntika) reasons have been stated, beginning with "the other" (anya) as being uncertain; however, this is not correct, because another type—the non-erroneous contradictory (viruddhāvyabhicārin)—is also inconclusive.
It is not because of a failure to fully understand the intention;
for this meaning is determined to be of five distinct types.
Furthermore, that which is ascertained to exist in similar instances and to be absent in two ways from their absence is a valid reason (*hetu*);
that which is ascertained in the opposite manner is contradictory (*viruddha*).
And all such [reasons] are necessarily constrained by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
But another [reason] is not certain at all;
that very same [reason] is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) because it is restricted [to one side]. This is the meaning of the sentence.
Since this very definition applies to the *śeṣavat* and the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) as well, their status as inconclusive cannot be avoided.
Therefore, everything is entirely faultless;
for,
when the scope of a non-erroneous contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) has been taken away by another [reason], its scope is not connected to the probandum (*sādhya*).
How then can it be that "non-deviant" and "unobstructed" are themselves non-deviant? This is indeed a contradiction;
likewise, to say that "the non-deviant is a cause of doubt" is also a contradiction.
In our position, however, it is a cause of doubt precisely because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*).
If it is asked how it can be non-deviant (*avyabhicāritva*), we reply that there is no fault, as this is by way of [our] own admission (*abhyupagama*).
And so it has been said:
"In that case, when one accepts that 'sound-ness' (*śabdatva*) is eternal, then this would indeed be a valid reason (*hetu*), because— "
Nowhere is there the possibility of perceiving audibility as being perishable;
for it is only because it is perceived as eternal that its capacity to indicate [the nature of sound] is possible.
It is a "indicator" precisely because one accepts the definition of being an indicator.
Since the Vaiśeṣika maintains that a reason is indicative merely by its being seen or not seen,
and since that [condition] exists here, it follows that [the reason] would indeed be indicative;
to this, the Teacher says:
It might be a prover if no one were to state "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as a reason for impermanence;
however, for one who perceives both to be provers, doubt arises precisely from his own admission.
Therefore, for the Vaiśeṣika who accepts this, there is an entry into extreme difficulty.

For if the impermanence of sound is intended, then the permanence of "sound-ness" (śabdatva) should be applied; for by means of that, even another [property] would become a prover of permanence. Indeed, it is not the case that what is subject to the same logical principle does not behave accordingly.
That would not be logical; and if that were so,
there would be the total abolition of all worldly transaction.

The logical principle regarding the probans *kṛtakatva* (being produced) is the same for *śrāvaṇatva* (audibility) as well; thus, this too is non-deviant from the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyaviparyaya*) by *kṛtakatva*, and is therefore not a means of valid cognition (*gamaka*). Consequently, one must understand the Master’s intention to be that a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) exists only through the acceptance of another [party], and not otherwise. B. *kṛtakatva*.

If, however, one accepts that "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is eternal because of that statement, then the cause of doubt remains entirely unobstructed; thus, the definition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the reason (*hetu*), namely that "the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)," [is undermined].
By implication, that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a reason;

conversely, that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is non-contradictory (*aviruddha*). Thus, that which is not a property of the subject is not contradictory. Furthermore, while the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is a property of the subject, that which is not a property of the subject is not inconclusive.
Therefore, it must be designated by its own name; thus,
even if the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished, it remains simply "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Even if one or the other is unestablished,
it is likewise "unestablished," as the Teacher [Dignāga] stated.

Because a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) occurs through a property established for both parties, it is not accepted [as a valid reason] when there is doubt regarding one of the two, nor when there is non-establishment of the property-bearer (*dharmī*). (612) If, then, the reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*),
how is it that [in the argument] "sound is impermanent because the uncreated is permanent," [the reason is not established]?
Because that which is impermanent is produced;
likewise,
because there is no production of what does not exist, because of the appropriation of material causes, and because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything.
"Because that which is possible is made possible, and because of the existence of the cause, the effect pre-exists [in the cause].
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 9) To this, it is said:

Where the presence [of the reason] in the probandum and its absence in the absence [of the probandum] are stated using the ablative case, there the example is [stated]; the reason, however, is considered to be [stated] through the application (*upanaya*).
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is produced, and sound is produced. (614)
Likewise, [the inference] "Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced,
and sound is produced"— this is by means of a word ending in the fifth case (the ablative).
The example here is shown by means of the fifth [case-ending];
for indeed, the reality of the meaning is that an example is established through both similarity and dissimilarity,
and thus the [reasons] such as "the non-production of the non-existent" and so forth should also be understood in the same way.
And how these are not reasons has already been demonstrated;
moreover, a reason that lacks an established connection (pratibandha) possesses no capacity here for proving the probandum (sādhya), and for this very reason they are not reasons. (615)
Regarding the reason "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced": how is this a valid reason?
It is because the production of non-existent things, such as a rabbit's horn, is never observed;
yet, by this much alone, one cannot establish the opposite through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
If the activity of some non-existent thing is not observed,
how can there be this pervasion (*vyāpti*) that it is so for all [non-existent things]?
For the establishment of negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) does not occur without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of the contrary.

How can the pervasion of the absence of fire by the absence of smoke be established, unless smoke is established by means of valid cognition as being pervaded by fire? Indeed, even for one wandering throughout the entire world, it is impossible to realize the pervasive negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— that "this is not present here or there"— in every single place.
Since a wandering [inference] that pervades both time and space is impossible,

when the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) is grasped through positive concomitance (anvaya), the establishment of the pervasive negative concomitance (vyatireka) follows by the very force of that [positive concomitance];
and this has already been demonstrated previously.

Therefore, these are not [independent] reasons; rather, only that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is a reason, and it may be either contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, by means of this process of demonstrating existence and non-existence, inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) alone has been elucidated.
The remaining elaboration for the purpose of defining the residual form is to be understood from the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* itself; thus was the mind of this author of the *Vārttika* directed.

O debater, the mind that is indifferent to the threefold nature of forms—neither harboring constant partiality nor aversion, and not creating darkness through attachment to one's own side or hostility toward another's—is indeed what brings about the awakening to reality; this is the conduct of the wise, known as the state of impartiality. Therefore, you should apply your intellect to that. (617)
Exposition: This stainless doctrine of the venerable Dharmakīrti is accessible only to those who are like him.
"How could one like me be capable of explaining this? Let the reason for this be reflected upon for a long time.
(618) "But if another [person] comes to understand it through mere practice, then partiality toward this [work] is justified for the sake of establishing the true meaning.
This distinction between self and other regarding what is logical and illogical has achieved its purpose. (619)
This has been composed in brief for the sake of awakening others; however, it would be possible here to speak much more effectively.
Indeed, no one has yet composed a commentary on this mass of jewels obtained from the ocean, for there is no recipient of such magnitude.
Vulgar people desire ornaments merely for the sake of passion, seeking only the physical beauty of the body.

"I have composed this ornament for the Vārttika not out of pride. (622) Thus, those whose minds are intent on accomplishing the welfare of others should always cultivate a disposition that is beneficial and skilled in the principles of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. (623)
Has anyone ever seen another ocean besides the Ocean of Milk from which Lakṣmī and the Moon— the bestowers of joy upon all the worlds— were produced by the Creator? (524)
Having composed this irreproachable work, which is skillful in meaning and stainless, I have obtained [this merit].
By that [merit], may there be a radiant accomplishment that accomplishes the welfare of the entire world, and may it always exist for this world. 625.4 B.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the section on inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) titled the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*.
And thus concludes this *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkārabhāṣya*.
This is the third chapter in the great commentary (*mahābhāṣya*) on the *Vārttikālaṅkārapramāṇa*.

And this *Pramāṇamahābhāṣyavārttikālaṃkāra* is completed; it is the work of the teacher Prajñākaragupta, who, like the thousand-rayed sun, is skilled at dispersing the mass of darkness of the false teachers.
5. *Pramāṇamahābhāṣya-vārttikālaṃkāra*, composed by the great scholar Prajñākaragupta; containing more than sixty chapters (*āhnika*).

(1) It was translated [into Tibetan] by the Kashmiri paṇḍita Bhavyarāja, the eye of the world, the wise Prajñā (Blo-ldan-śes-rab). (2) Furthermore, it was finalized as a revised reading by the Kashmiri paṇḍita (mkhan-po) Kumāraśrī, the eye of the world, the monk Āryaprajñā (’Phags-pa’i Śes-rab), a resident of Shu-chen.
6A. It was written by the monk Bhūticandra, who desires knowledge.
Whatever is unclear or impure in this, may the people forgive it;
the ornamentation was written in the north.
